The latest Chromebook scheme comes alongside efforts to expand local technology production. In November 2025, Google began manufacturing Chromebooks in collaboration with the Ministry of Defence Production and the National Radio and Telecommunication Corporation (NRTC) in Haripur, with plans to produce around 600,000 devices annually. Pakistan also signed an agreement with Google in August 2026 to provide students with one year of free access to advanced AI tools, including Gemini, and offer 150,000 Google Career Certificates to young people in 2026.

title: FM Dar, Chinese envoy discuss CPEC, trade and regional stability
description: Dar underscores importance of high-level engagements to advance Pakistan-China Community
content: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met Chinese Ambassador Jiang Zaidong in Islamabad on Sunday, discussing bilateral cooperation, including the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), trade and investment, and regional developments, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) said. According to the statement released by MoFA on X, FM Dar “appreciated the continued progress” in the Pakistan-China “all-weather strategic cooperative partnership”, which encompasses cooperation under CPEC, connectivity, trade and investment, agricultural modernisation and people-to-people exchanges. Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China, H.E. Jiang Zaidong, called on Deputy Prime Minister/Foreign Minister Senator Mohammad Ishaq Dar @MIshaqDar50. DPM/FM appreciated the continued progress in the Pakistan-China all-weather strategic cooperative partnership, including… pic.twitter.com/eWuIafkKdQ — Ministry of Foreign Affairs - Pakistan (@ForeignOfficePk) October 25, 2026 FM Dar “underscored the importance of sustained high-level exchanges” to further advance the “Pakistan-China Community of Shared Future in the New Era”, according to the statement. The meeting also provided an opportunity for the two sides to “exchange views on regional developments”, the ministry said, adding that they had reaffirmed “the importance of dialogue and diplomacy for sustainable peace and stability in the region”. Read: Pakistan, China agree to align development plans, launch CPEC 2.0 Pakistan and China marked the 75th anniversary of their diplomatic relations this year, with both sides seeking to expand cooperation beyond traditional infrastructure projects. The next phase of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, known as CPEC 2.0, is expected to focus on industrialisation, agriculture, mining, information technology and artificial intelligence. At the seventh round of the Pakistan-China Foreign Ministers’ Strategic Dialogue in Beijing in January, the two countries agreed to align their development priorities and deepen cooperation in trade, investment, science and technology, cybersecurity and people-to-people exchanges.

title: Security forces kill terrorist commander in Qila Saifullah operation: state media
description: Sources say he has been involved in attacks on security forces, kidnappings for ransom since 2022
content: Security forces killed a terrorist commander of Fitna Al-Khawarij, Adil Shah, alias Darvesh, during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Qila Saifullah, Balochistan, under Operation Radd-ul-Fitna 3, Radio Pakistan reported, citing security sources. The federal government last year officially designated all terrorist groups operating in Balochistan as Fitna al-Hindustan, accusing India of sponsoring a proxy war through the outfits. Fitna al-Khawarij is the state designation term for the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan. The high-tempo intelligence-driven operations are being conducted as part of the ongoing "Radd-ul-Fitna-3" campaign, which the military's media wing has described as a counterterrorism operation aimed at eliminating Indian proxies. According to the sources, the commander had been associated with Fitna al-Khawarij since December 2020 and had been managing the terrorist group's financial affairs since 2024. He had also been involved in facilitating permanent residences for foreign terrorists in Zhob, Sherani and Shaban, the source added. Security forces are actively carrying out operations against terrorists in Balochistan under Operation Radd-ul-Fitna Three#News #RadioPakistan https://t.co/r4AriojEr2 pic.twitter.com/T4vIdU2I3S — Radio Pakistan (@RadioPakistan) October 25, 2026 Shah had been involved in attacks on security forces and kidnappings for ransom since 2022, and 19 first information reports (FIRs) had been registered against him, and a bounty of Rs2.5 million had been placed on his head, the source added. Read: 3 terrorists killed as security forces foil attack on construction camp in Gwadar: state media Security sources reiterated that operations against terrorists in Balochistan would continue until the last terrorist was eliminated, Radio Pakistan reported. Terrorism is a growing problem for Pakistan, with the number of attacks rising every year since 2022, according to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a global monitoring organisation. Data from ACLED shows attacks in Pakistan rose nearly fourfold to 2,425 in 2025 from 658 in 2022, and over the same period, TTP attacks increased more than sevenfold to 838 from 118. Although K-P has borne the brunt of terrorism, Balochistan has also remained a major target of Indian proxies, which often target civilians and military installations in the province. Over the past few years, Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist attacks, with militants frequently targeting convoys, abducting security personnel and civilians, and attacking security and civilian installations. In a similar incident last week, 20 trainee police personnel were abducted by unidentified armed men while travelling between Kalat and Mastung in Balochistan. The abducted personnel belonged to the districts of Kharan, Nushki, Chagai and Washuk in Rakhshan Division. They included eight personnel from Kharan, five from Nushki, four from Chagai and three from Washuk. Read more: Two terrorists killed in Balochistan IBO: state media The forces continued operations across the provinces against what the state describes as Indian-sponsored terrorists and their proxies. Still, despite these efforts, the groups have continued to target civilian and defence installations. In one such attack in July this year, at least 30 people, including 27 police personnel, were martyred when terrorists identified by the state as the Indian proxy Fitna al-Hindustan ambushed police personnel deployed in the Kach Mangi Phase III area of Ziarat, triggering hours-long gun battles. The attackers also abducted several civilians and police personnel after the assault. In the aftermath of the attack, the Pakistan Army, Frontier Corps and Balochistan Police launched a joint operation, which remains underway, with forces intensifying action against terrorists across the province.

title: Naqvi assures no trees will be cut at Islamabad’s F-9 Park
description: Says F-9 Park upgrades to include better lighting, a lake, coffee shops, improved walkways, and thousands of new trees
content: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Sunday assured that no trees will be cut and no new concrete structures will be built at Islamabad’s F-9 Park, following concerns raised by environmental activist and schoolteacher Usman about plans to upgrade the capital’s largest green spaces. The clarification came after Naqvi on October 21 announced plans to revamp F-9 Park along the lines of London’s Hyde Park and to establish additional parks in Islamabad. He said the government planned to renovate F-9 Park and develop four new parks in the capital. “Let me make it absolutely clear that not a single tree will be cut, 100% guaranteed. No new concrete structures,” Naqvi said in a post on X, responding to a video shared by Usman on Instagram. F-9 Park holds a special place in the hearts of everyone living in Islamabad. Let me make it absolutely clear that Not a single tree will be cut 100% guaranteed. No new concrete structures. Instead, we are planning better lighting, a beautiful lake, coffee shops, improved… — Mohsin Naqvi (@MohsinnaqviC42) October 25, 2026 Naqvi said the proposed improvements to Fatima Jinnah Park, commonly known as F-9 Park, would include better lighting, a lake, coffee shops and improved walkways, along with the plantation of thousands of additional trees. “Our only goal is to make F-9 Park greener, safer, more beautiful, and more enjoyable for families and visitors,” he said, adding that the park held a special place in the hearts of Islamabad’s residents. In his video, Usman said F-9 Park, which spans around 400 acres, was important for the city’s environment and the future of coming generations. “Because this park is part of our hearts and souls,” he said, adding that around 2.45 billion litres of rainwater fell on the park’s area annually before being absorbed into the ground and contributing to groundwater reserves. “Please do not develop it for the sake of development,” he said, urging the authorities to plant more trees and introduce a wider variety of species to increase greenery and improve air quality. “Instead of building huge structures here or turning it into a high-rise park, plant more trees,” Usman said. The exchange comes after months of controversy over the cutting of trees across Islamabad, where the CDA removed more than 29,000 paper mulberry trees as part of a drive to address pollen allergies. The operation affected several areas, including F-9 Park, Shakarparian and parts of the city’s residential sectors. The authority said the trees were removed on scientific and legal grounds and would be replaced with indigenous, environmentally suitable species. The large-scale felling drew criticism from environmental advocates and residents, who questioned the removal of mature trees and the impact of infrastructure projects on Islamabad’s green cover. In a February response to the Islamabad High Court, the Ministry of Climate Change said prior approval was mandatory for tree cutting and raised concerns that the operation had been carried out without the required consultation with environmental authorities. F-9 Park, officially known as Fatima Jinnah Park, has itself been at the centre of the controversy. The CDA previously told the Supreme Court that about 7,000 paper mulberry trees had been removed from designated areas of the park in 2024, with the authority saying the operation was intended to reduce pollen allergies and would be followed by replantation.

title: China's automation and job creation
description: Why China's high-tech drive still banks on the human worker
content: The most striking paradox of the contemporary world may be unfolding in China. For much of modern political and economic thought, economic prosperity, technological innovation and political liberalisation have been seen as developments that reinforce one another. The assumption is that an open society, freer exchange of ideas and political pluralism create the conditions in which innovation flourishes. China complicates that assumption. From the political perspective, China remains a highly centralised one-party state, with a political system fundamentally different from Western democracies. Yet economically and technologically, it has emerged as one of the world's most formidable competitors, from electric vehicles and solar panels to artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and robotics. The contrast has become increasingly visible in the country's extraordinary push into humanoid robots. At the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, more than 2,000 robots from 666 teams competed in 51 events. Chinese robots have also been setting remarkable performance benchmarks. One Chinese humanoid, Tiangong Ultra, recently ran 100 metres in 8.86 seconds– faster than the human men's world record of 9.58 seconds. The spectacle is fascinating, but the more important question lies beyond the robot races. If machines are becoming increasingly capable of doing human work, how does a country with hundreds of millions of workers continue to create employment? That is where China's experience becomes particularly relevant for big population countries such as Pakistan. China is not simply trying to stop automation. Nor is it treating technological unemployment as an unavoidable consequence that society must simply absorb. Instead, its emerging approach is to push automation and artificial intelligence while simultaneously trying to create new industries, expand services, retrain workers and generate employment elsewhere. Khalid Mansoor, former Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on CPEC Affairs and Minister of State, argues that the interesting Chinese lesson is not that technology has somehow failed to destroy jobs. Rather, it is that China is attempting to create new sources of employment faster than technology eliminates old ones. "There is an important irony: China is one of the world’s most aggressive adopters of robots and AI. Yet it is simultaneously pursuing an explicit ‘employment-first’ strategy," he said in a comment to the ET. That distinction could become one of the most important economic questions of the AI age. The robot and the worker China's employment challenge is enormous. According to the figures cited by Mansoor, China had around 725 million employed people at the end of 2025, including about 475 million urban workers. The country created 12.67 million new urban jobs during the year, while its migrant-worker population reached roughly 301 million. At the same time, China's demographic structure is changing rapidly. Its population declined by 3.39 million in 2025, while people aged 60 and above already represented around 23% of the population. This creates a contradiction. China needs automation because its workforce is ageing and shrinking. But it also needs employment because hundreds of millions of people continue to depend on work and income. "The Chinese policy concept increasingly emphasises human-machine collaboration," Mansoor said. The objective is not necessarily to ask how many workers can be eliminated by a robot. It is to ask how much more productive an individual worker can become when equipped with AI, robotics and advanced machinery, he highlighted. That distinction matters enormously. A textile worker assisted by automation is not necessarily the same economic proposition as a textile worker replaced by automation. If technology raises the productivity of the first worker, the economy can potentially use the additional productive capacity to expand output, exports and new businesses. Mansoor points to China's employment-first approach as an example of this thinking. Rather than treating automation as an argument for abandoning labour-intensive sectors, China is simultaneously seeking to sustain employment in areas such as manufacturing, construction, trade, tourism, catering, elderly care, childcare, logistics and community services. The logic is straightforward: if one category of work becomes more automated, employment has to expand somewhere else. From factory jobs to employment ecosystems China's most interesting achievement may therefore not be the robot itself but the industrial ecosystem built around technology. Consider an electric vehicle. The employment question is not simply how many workers assemble an EV on a factory floor. The wider ecosystem includes batteries, charging infrastructure, power electronics, software, dealerships, logistics, maintenance, financing and recycling. The same logic applies to solar energy. There are manufacturing jobs in polysilicon, wafers, cells and modules, followed by installation, grid integration, storage and maintenance. Artificial intelligence produces another chain: chips, data centres, cloud computing, software applications, robotics, maintenance and AI-enabled businesses. In other words, the factory may become increasingly automated while the economy around the factory becomes more complex. This is one reason China's industrial strategy deserves attention. Mansoor argues that China is deliberately creating entire employment ecosystems around emerging industries instead of focusing only on the number of workers employed directly by a particular factory. There is, however, a necessary qualification. China has not solved technological displacement. Research cited in the supplied analysis suggests, said Mansoor, that robot adoption can reduce employment and wages for some categories of workers while increasing demand for higher-skilled workers. China's rapidly developing gig economy also provides work but raises questions about job security, benefits and human-capital development. Even China's humanoid-robot boom illustrates the gap between technological achievement and commercial reality. Reuters reported in August that Chinese humanoid manufacturers had produced world-leading hardware, but many machines remained too slow, unreliable or insufficiently adaptable for broad factory deployment. The lesson, therefore, is not that China has defeated the job-loss problem. It is that China is experimenting with how to manage it. Local govt system secret for booming economy Dr Muhammad Farooq Afzal, founder of the Economic Diplomacy Forum China-Pakistan, identifies China's local-government system as a major factor behind its development and public-service delivery. According to his assessment, around 75 per cent of China's budget is spent locally, with roughly 25 per cent going to the central or federal level. Whether every element of this model can be transferred to Pakistan is a separate question. But the contrast raises an important issue about devolution. China's economic story also becomes more complicated when viewed through its provinces and regions. A visitor arriving in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang, encounters a very different China from the high-tech image projected by Beijing, Shenzhen or Shanghai. In Xinjiang, Muslim communities include Uyghurs, Hui, Kazakhs and Kyrgyz. Rural areas contain orchards and farms, while urban Urumqi combines Chinese Hanzi with Uyghur script and bustling commercial areas such as the Grand Bazaar. China’s development has been equitable across all segments of its society, including its Muslim-majority provinces. However, many Muslims there appear less connected to their faith, with some holding traditional Muslim names while expressing indifference to religion. This may stem from China’s focus on material development over abstract or theological pursuits, a pragmatic approach that carries significant weight when viewed from the perspective of someone living in Pakistan. A visit to the Wu Yi Tongxiangdong Mosque in the 12th Division of the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps offers another picture of China: agricultural land, orchards, local communities and a mosque serving the surrounding population. In Urumqi's urban commercial areas, meanwhile, the Erdaoqiao Mosque sits alongside the Grand Bazaar, where traders and shopkeepers interact with visitors from different countries. This provincial diversity is important because China's development has not been built only from Beijing. It has involved an extraordinary degree of experimentation at local and regional levels. And perhaps the clearest example is Shenzhen. From a small economy to global hub Shakeel Ahmad Ramay cites, in an article, the Shenzhen experience as a case study that Pakistan should examine carefully. Shenzhen's transformation began after it was designated as a special economic zone and received extensive infrastructure and administrative support. The city was subsequently given greater authority over financing, investment and trade decisions. The result was an economic transformation that turned what was once a relatively small economy into one of China's most important economic centres. The lesson, however, is not simply to copy Shenzhen's label and establish another special economic zone. It is to understand the institutional architecture behind it. Shenzhen introduced faster government approvals, a one-roof model for public services and mechanisms designed to reduce the administrative burden on investors. Authorities facilitated electricity, water, taxation, trade and other business requirements. The local government also invested in roads, sewerage, telecommunications and other infrastructure. More importantly, government services expanded beyond conventional administration. Investors could receive assistance related to accounting, legal services, business planning, marketing, import-export procedures, skills training and management consulting. The state, therefore, did not simply announce an investment zone and wait for investors to arrive. It attempted to make the zone function. That distinction is highly relevant to Pakistan. The China-Pakistan institutional gap Pakistan's 18th Amendment transferred substantial political and financial responsibilities to the provinces. Yet, as Afzal argues, provincial governments have not always passed comparable authority and resources down to local governments. The issue is particularly important for economic development because businesses do not operate at the federal level alone. They need roads, water, electricity, municipal services, permits, local infrastructure, skills and functioning markets. A federal government can announce an industrial policy. A provincial government can establish an economic zone. But the investor ultimately encounters a local administration. That is where policy becomes either reality or paperwork. The Chinese experience suggests that the central question for Pakistan should not be whether it wants technology or employment. It needs both. The first requirement is to make employment a macroeconomic objective. Every major industrial, trade, investment and technology policy should be examined through a basic question: how many productive jobs can this policy create, and what kind of skills will those jobs require? The second is to avoid protecting obsolete employment indefinitely. A more sustainable model is to move workers from declining activities into new ones through retraining, productivity improvements and industrial expansion. The third is to build labour-intensive export industries while using technology to raise productivity. Pakistan has potential in textiles and apparel, food processing, agriculture, engineering, surgical instruments, sports goods, construction, IT and business-process outsourcing, among other sectors. The objective should not be to choose between workers and AI. It should be to create AI-enabled labour-intensive exports. The fourth requirement is vocational training. China's employment approach increasingly links skills development with labour-market demand. For Pakistan, that means producing technicians, electricians, mechanics, machine operators, software specialists, healthcare workers and other vocational professionals alongside university graduates. The fifth is to think about ecosystems. An EV plant is not merely an assembly line. It can become the centre of an ecosystem involving suppliers, batteries, charging, software, finance, logistics, dealerships and repair services. That is the difference between attracting a factory and building an industry. The road from Karachi There is also a more basic lesson in infrastructure. Afzal points to Pakistan's transport network as an example of misplaced priorities, arguing that stronger north-south connectivity could reduce logistics costs and integrate markets more effectively. For an economy seeking exports, the question is not simply how many kilometres of motorway are constructed. The question is whether the road network connects factories to ports, farms to markets and cities to each other at competitive cost. This is where the experience of China's provinces becomes relevant. Economic transformation did not happen because China discovered one magic policy. It happened through the accumulation of infrastructure, local experimentation, industrial policy, administrative reform, investment facilitation, skills development and export-oriented production. The larger question The political structure of China remains fundamentally different from that of Western democracies. Its approach to political freedoms, expression and governance cannot simply be separated from any assessment of its development model. But economic systems should also be examined on their own terms. China presents a particularly difficult case for simplistic assumptions because a country that is politically centralised and restrictive in ways that differ sharply from Western liberal democracies has simultaneously become a major centre of technological innovation and industrial competition. Its robotics drive is an especially vivid illustration. But the deeper story is not a robot running 100 m in less than nine seconds. It is what happens after the race. Can technology move from demonstrations into factories? Can it raise productivity? Can new industries absorb workers displaced by old technologies? Can ageing societies use automation to compensate for shrinking workforces? And can developing countries adopt technology without abandoning the millions who still need productive employment? China is still working through these questions itself. That may be precisely why its experience matters. The real contest of the AI age may not be between machines and workers. It may be between economies that can successfully reorganise work around technology and those that allow technological change to outrun their ability to create new productive opportunities. For Pakistan, the lesson is less about copying China's political system or replicating Shenzhen. It is about understanding the machinery underneath China's economic transformation: technology plus industry, industry plus infrastructure, infrastructure plus local implementation, and all of it tied to employment and productivity. The robot may be the most visible symbol of China's technological rise. The less visible story is how the country is trying to ensure that there is still an economy around the robot, and work for the people living in it.

title: India’s vanishing voters
description: With millions of names removed from the electoral rolls, the world’s largest democracy faces a credibility crisis
content: More than 130 million names have disappeared from India’s voter rolls since last year, according to reporting by The New York Times, a revision of the world’s largest electoral register that the Bharatiya Janata Party-led government describes as routine housekeeping and that critics say will lead to depriving eligible voters of their democratic right. The Election Commission says the exercise is meant to eliminate duplicate entries, deceased voters and other ineligible names from a register of roughly a billion people. However, the poll body has not published a breakdown of the changes made to the lists by district or reason, and it has not said how many voters who appealed have been restored. Independent researchers say they cannot yet verify either the government’s account or the opposition’s charge that the removal of names was aimed at voters less likely to support Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government. By early October the argument had moved from paperwork to the streets. Demonstrations demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, met mass detentions, restrictions on movement and the suspension of mobile services in parts of India’s capital. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), at least 43 journalists were temporarily detained while covering the protests on October 10 and 11. Several said they were beaten, had equipment seized or were forced to delete footage. Amnesty International and three other human rights groups called for the release of those held arbitrarily and an investigation into alleged abuses by security forces. But much of this has fallen on deaf ears in New Delhi. Those who have been observing the situation have two questions that they believe sit at the center of the debate, and neither has an easy answer. What happens when citizens cannot be confident their names will stay on the register? And what happens when journalists trying to establish whether the process is fair are stopped from reporting what they see? That said, declaring India’s democracy dead, as some critics would like, settles nothing, and nor does accepting that everything is routine. The politics of a missing name With roughly a billion registered voters in the country, removing 130 million names amounts to a substantial change to the record through which people exercise their rights. The Times reported on October 7 that about 20 million people had been marked dead while still alive, and described allegations that the revision fell disproportionately on Muslims, a minority often disliked by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Two senior party officials, speaking anonymously, said the exercise had been designed to strengthen the party’s electoral advantage. For its part, the Indian Election Commission says the revision improves accuracy by removing dead, duplicate and otherwise ineligible entries. Updating registers is legitimate work, lists cannot stay accurate indefinitely, and piles of outdated records can themselves undermine democratic confidence. So the question is not whether lists should be revised, but whether the process is transparent and fair, and whether the people affected have a realistic chance to challenge a wrong deletion. What the revision has changed, according to The Times’s account, is where the burden of proof now sits. Instead of officials checking records and confirming a name before removing it, the process has removed first and left people to appeal afterward. From disputed records to street protests The protests that gathered force in October were driven by demands for accountability from the Election Commission, including calls for the chief election commissioner to step down. The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party, student groups and opposition parties helped mobilize them. The response to the protests has become a concern in its own right. Ahead of the October 10 march, authorities restricted gatherings, suspended transport and limited movement into parts of New Delhi. Amnesty reported more than 10,000 people detained across the country before the rally, many while traveling to the capital, thousands more were reportedly held during the protests, though the figures do not show how many stayed in custody. Police were deployed in large numbers and mobile services were cut in parts of central Delhi, while demonstrators were intercepted before reaching Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site, and taken to temporary detention facilities. Some restrictions may have been justified by specific security concerns, but a blanket approach raises a serious question: whether the Modi government was answering a genuine threat to order or using public-order powers to stop people assembling at all. Amnesty and its partners argued that the right to peaceful assembly should not depend on police permission, and called for the release of those held solely for exercising their rights, along with investigations into allegations of excessive force, ill-treatment and sexual harassment. According to the Indian Constitution, expression and peaceful assembly are protected, subject to lawful restriction. But lawful restriction is not unlimited discretion, and a demonstration declared unlawful does not make everyone detained at it a criminal. How restrictions are imposed, why, and whether courts can be reached all matter. A democracy’s commitment to order, experts say, is tested not by whether it can stop a crowd gathering, but by whether it can do so without suppressing lawful dissent it finds inconvenient. Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, which allows temporary restrictions in the interest of public order, drew attention during this period. Amnesty argues such powers are being used against peaceful demonstrations. The orders issued, the circumstances the police cited and the way the restrictions were enforced are all matters of record. What makes the Indian case worth watching is that it is not unusual. Governments elsewhere reach for public order when protests challenge their decisions, and the temptation grows when the decision being protested is one the government would rather not debate or take. Experts who study protest policing say the pattern is common across democracies, with restrictions justified on grounds of order that would be hard to defend if applied to other kinds of assembly. According to them, the legal authority to restrict is not, by itself evidence that the restriction was necessary or proportionate. When reporters become the story For journalists covering the October demonstrations, the experience was not only witnessing police action, in many cases they were the target of it. The CPJ’s investigation, updated on October 15, documented the temporary detention of dozens of journalists in New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Pune and Mumbai over two days, drawing on news reports, interviews and verified posts by reporters, editors and newsrooms. Several stated they were held despite showing press credentials. Others described being dragged into police vehicles, assaulted, threatened or obstructed while filming. At least five were struck by police, according to accounts the New York-based press freedom organization reviewed. Phones and equipment were seized, and at least one journalist said he was forced to delete footage. Rana Ayyub, a columnist for The Washington Post, told the CPJ that police beat her with a baton after she questioned their conduct, and that the injuries still hurt. Ryan Thomas, an assistant multimedia producer at The Caravan, was filming a detention when officers dragged him onto a bus despite his visible press card, he said they hit him repeatedly on the head, slapped him and prodded his stomach with a gun butt before releasing him. Mohammed Aslam Hussain and Sheikh Abdul Mukarram of Siasat Daily said police took their phones, broke their microphone and returned the handsets with the data wiped. All of this needs independent investigation, and individual accounts should be checked against footage, medical records, witnesses and complaints. But the numbers, the similarities and the circumstances make the episode hard to wave away as a series of unrelated misunderstandings. On October 11 the Supreme Court secured assurances from the solicitor general, Tushar Mehta, that lawyers, journalists and other professionals would not be restricted, and directed that nobody be detained except by procedure established by law. The CPJ reported that detentions continued regardless. Delhi Police, for its part, offered a different account, as reported by the media. A senior officer told The Hindu that some journalists may have been held because they were working close to protesters and did not move away, and that some protesters had posed as reporters. That claim deserves examination and police have a real interest in telling reporters from participants, but a press card cannot become something officers may disregard at will. Where an officer believes someone is obstructing police or breaking the law, the grounds should be specific, lawful and open to challenge, press freedom experts noted. Matters, they say, look worse where journalists are allegedly beaten, their equipment taken or their footage deleted, because then police are not simply managing a crowd, they are deciding which evidence survives and what the public gets to see. Jahnavi Sen, managing editor of The Wire, told The Associated Press that the number of detentions was unusual, and suggested police seemed determined to stop images of their response from circulating. The cost of controlling the record Journalists were not the only people whose ability to communicate was restricted. Mobile internet was suspended and reportedly blocked in stadiums used as detention centres, which Amnesty and its partners said cut detainees off from lawyers and families. Shutdowns also stop people sharing news of arrests, finding missing relatives or documenting what security forces do. Narendra Modi’s government, like any administration facing protests, has defended such actions on security grounds, and to be fair, a narrow, time-limited restriction may sometimes be justified to protect lives and public safety. The justification, though, has to be specific and the scope proportionate, since a broad shutdown around a demonstration reaches far beyond the people taking part. Amnesty also reported that Instagram accounts belonging to the outlets Molitics and Journo Mirror were blocked in India during their coverage, under the country’s information technology rules. In this case, limits on accounts and access, they said, raise the question of whether authorities were restricting information well beyond the physical sites of the protests. Modi’s mandate and its limits Modi has been in power since 2014, building what many observers believe is a formidable political machine and a powerful national presence. His supporters point to his election wins and his development agenda as evidence of a durable mandate. Those achievements are part of the picture, so are the concerns critics raise about pressure on dissent, on independent media and on religious minorities, and the ongoing debate over the rolls has pulled several of them together around the institutions that decide how citizens take part. All that said, it would be premature to conclude that the revision was designed to help the BJP. The Times’s reporting raises serious questions, though they still need corroboration from records, testimony and independent examination, and both the government and the Election Commission deny political manipulation. What a government cannot do is treat its majority as an answer to questions about accountability, and Modi’s majority, experts argue, is no defence against conduct that human rights groups have documented as a breach of international norms. What remains to be established The first task, and the hardest, is to find out what happened to the people whose names went missing, and whether they had a fair chance to object. According to experts, the 130 million figure needs breaking down by category, place and reason: how many were dead or duplicated, how many had moved, how many were eligible and wrongly removed. If Muslims, women, migrants or poorer citizens were hit disproportionately, the evidence should show how far, and whether that came from the design of the exercise, its implementation or something else. Unequal impact, experts believe, would warrant investigation even without proof of intent. Rights groups have called for an inquiry into the treatment journalists have received during this recent episode. “Police should account for each detention, give the legal grounds, return equipment still held, and submit allegations of assault, intimidation and forced deletion to independent investigation with published findings, while the authorities should say what they have done to give effect to the Supreme Court’s directions.” Amnesty and its partners want those held solely for exercising their rights released, and allegations of abuse by security forces and of violence by non-state actors, investigated. All that puts the onus on the BJP authorities to show they take such complaints seriously rather than treating criticism as an attack on public order, but whether Modi’s administration will do so is another question. On the evidence of recent weeks documented by international media and rights groups, those in power in New Delhi appear to feel no obligation to answer the questions being raised about the treatment of protesters, about citizens barred from exercising their right to vote, and about journalists trying to document what is happening in India.

title: When the term ‘Heatwave’ is no longer enough
description: A groundbreaking investigation explains that massive “heat storms” now “swarm the planet”
content: In a landmark piece of climate journalism, Reuters has just published a groundbreaking investigation arguing that the term “heat waves” no longer adequately captures what is happening on the planet. A better term is “heat storms,” wrote Maurice Tamman, a veteran investigative journalist who was the lead reporter on “The Age of Heat Storms” project. “Supersized heatwaves used to be rare,” Tamman wrote. “No longer. Now they swarm the planet.” In a video accompanying the report, he explained that, “whereas heatwaves were once small and relatively self-contained, now we live in a world where these heatwaves are massive.” Drawing on interviews with dozens of scientists and researchers, Reuters defined a “heat storm” as an episode of “abnormally high temperatures” that lasts for at least five consecutive days and covers more than 1% of Earth’s surface, an area roughly the size of half of Canada. Whereas the planet averaged about five heat storms in the 1960s, the largest of which covered 6% of the planet and lasted for 46 days, the average today is 102 heat storms per year, the largest of which affected 85% of Earth’s surface “and virtually every single human being living in 2023 and 2024.” Heat storms, Tamman added in the video, are not only larger and stronger than heatwaves, they “are also different in another way: They are cascading, where there is an endless series of storms, one after the other.” Indeed, for the last 18 years straight, “at least one heat storm has been roiling the planet, and often more than one,” according to a fresh analysis of global temperature data that Reuters conducted with the scientists. Tamman, who won a Pulitzer Prize in 2025 for an exposé of the global fentanyl trade and has covered climate change for years, was drawn to this project after having long been “frustrated by a disconnect between scientists and the public,” he wrote. It can be useful for scientists and policymakers to talk about the need to limit global warming to 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, he acknowledged, but “what is an ordinary person to make of that? Not much.” Extreme heat, on the other hand, is something that ordinary people viscerally understand — and that nearly everyone on Earth has now experienced. In recent months, global warming and the heat that follows has become even more visceral, bringing ever more extreme events like last summer’s Nepal glacier collapse and the deaths of more than 35,000 people across Europe. Like the best climate reporting, the Reuters investigation both humanized and localized the story. One installment told the story of Justice Trumpler, a 17-year-old high school football captain in Texas who invites college recruiters to watch him play, only to succumb to non-stop vomiting in the 100 degrees Fahrenheit heat and end up in the hospital. Another installment described how hundreds of the iconic pink dolphins that inhabit the Amazon river were literally cooked to death by extreme heat. In the Philippines, a math teacher saw a student face-down on his desk, crying; when the teacher coaxed him to sit up, the boy’s face and chest were covered in blood from a spontaneous nosebleed, a common malady in extreme heat. All this and more is happening, bear in mind, after average global temperatures have risen by “only” 1.4 degrees C. And because emissions continue to increase, temperatures are projected to rise to at least 1.7 C by roughly 2050, the UN Environment Programme said in its annual “Emissions Gap” report, released this week. A key reason emissions keep increasing, The New York Times reported, is that the US under President Donald Trump has reversed the country’s previous efforts to limit fossil fuel production. To limit the amount of “overshoot” of the Paris Agreement goal of 1.5 degrees C of temperature rise, UNEP said, “a massive global scale-up” in emissions reductions will be needed, a goal certain to be discussed at the COP31 UN climate summit taking place in Turkey from November 9 to 20. To help both the public and policymakers grasp how harshly even today’s 1.4 degrees C of global warming is transforming life on Earth, the Reuters project suggested that heat storms be given names, just as hurricanes routinely are. “Naming events,” the report said, “is ‘a powerful way for people to understand that something is happening,’ Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, told Reuters. Yet ‘we don't currently do that with heatwaves,’ he said, even though heat has been estimated to kill almost half a million people a year.” In online discussions, some meteorologists have bristled at the term “heat storm.” David Dickson, Covering Climate Now’s resident meteorologist, noted that “storm” is a term “with a very distinct meteorological definition that is the opposite of what happens during extreme heat (storms occur with low pressure, heat with high pressure).” However, Dickson added, “I can't think of a better name, and think it does the job in communicating impacts quite well — and we already have other things described as storms that aren't, i.e. solar storms.” For nearly a decade, thousands of climate scientists have been deliberately using the term “emergency” to describe how fast and dangerously global warming is intensifying. Activists picked up the “emergency” framing as well, but the Reuters findings underscore that that framing has always been fundamentally a matter of science, not politics. This article is published as part of the global journalism collaboration Covering Climate Now

title: The AI tutor in pocket
description: As Pakistani students turn to AI for homework, teachers question if it helps learning or just offers easy answers
content: The third equation of motion had Zohan Ali confused. He knew the formula, but the derivation was another story. Somewhere between the speed-time graph, the area of a trapezium and the algebra that followed, he was losing track of how the equation came together. Ali, a Class 9 science student, was studying kinematics. He could have memorised the derivation from his physics textbook, but he wanted to understand it. So, he turned to Artificial intelligence (AI). His question was fairly specific. He told the chatbot he was a ninth-grade student following Pakistan's board syllabus and asked it to explain the derivation as a private tutor would. It started with the graph. The area beneath it represented the distance travelled. From there, it explained the trapezium formula, substituted the variables and worked through the remaining algebra. “Seeing each line of algebra laid out clearly helped me grasp the logic instead of just memorising the proof,” he says. This wasn't Ali's first attempt at studying with AI. He had heard classmates discussing it back in class 8, when he was struggling with physics numericals. Private tuition wasn't always answering his questions, and he wanted to see whether a chatbot could explain things differently. He now uses the chatbot regularly when he gets stuck. Sometimes he asks it to explain a concept. Sometimes he uses it to prepare for tests. And sometimes, with homework piling up, he admits that getting an answer without working through the question himself can be tempting. “Honestly, yes,” he says when asked whether he ever uses AI for quick answers. “When I have multiple homework assignments due the next morning alongside heavy board exam prep, it's tempting to use AI to find quick answers.” There is a difference between asking a chatbot to explain a physics equation and asking it to finish the homework. For Ali, both possibilities are only a prompt away. A tutor that never closes Fardeen Saleem has two sets of deadlines to worry about. There are campaigns and other responsibilities at the private company where she works as a brand manager, and then there is the coursework for her MBA in marketing. Keeping up with both leaves her with limited time to sit down and work through difficult topics. She remembers spending considerable time going through different resources whenever something in her coursework wasn't clear. These days, she often starts by asking ChatGPT. If the first explanation doesn't help, she asks it to simplify the answer or explain the same concept through an example. “Earlier, I would spend considerable time searching through different resources just to understand a concept,” she says. “It has made my learning process more interactive.” Much of her coursework involves applying marketing theories to business situations. She uses AI to understand concepts such as consumer behaviour, market segmentation and SWOT analysis, and to see how these frameworks might work in practice. It also helps her organise material before she begins an assignment. Fardeen uses several platforms, depending on what she needs. ChatGPT is her regular choice, while Claude helps with longer documents and Perplexity with finding information that includes references. She also searches Google Scholar for academic papers. She is aware that AI can get things wrong, particularly when it comes to references, and says she checks information against original sources. The ability to ask questions repeatedly is something Ali has also found useful, although his concerns are rather different from Fardeen's. Before a Biology test, the class 9 student was having trouble with topics including cellular respiration and photosynthesis. He asked AI for simpler explanations and then for a ten-question practice test, including explanations of the answers he got wrong. Ali says he scored above 85 per cent in the unit test, having previously struggled to score between 65 and 70 per cent. He credits the preparation with helping him understand the material, though there were other factors that may have contributed to his result. For Fardeen, who has to fit university work around her job, the biggest advantage is not having to spend as long searching for an explanation that makes sense. She can ask another question, compare two concepts or request a different example before returning to her coursework. AI enters the classroom When Tahir began teaching problem-solving to his Class 8 students at Daanish School, two concepts were proving particularly difficult: pseudocode and algorithm optimisation. Explaining them through the textbook wasn't getting him very far, so he decided to show the students how different AI models approached the same problem. “I tried different AI models for the same problem in front of them and the results were clear,” he says. He asked the models to optimise a path between two points, allowing the students to see how the problem could be approached. “Students were amazed to see the results.” Tahir teaches computer science and robotics to classes 6 and 8. A software engineering graduate, he is also pursuing a master's degree in Artificial Intelligence. He recently joined teaching and has been experimenting with ways to make difficult concepts easier for his pupils to understand. Being a boarding school, Daanish does not allow students to keep mobile phones with them all the time. But classrooms have smart screens, and tablets are available for accessing Google Classroom and searching for information. “I have installed ChatGPT in their screens on their request,” Tahir says. Students either look up information themselves or ask their house masters for help. Language is another difficulty he encounters. Some pupils are comfortable reading English textbooks, while others struggle with the wording. Tahir says he has noticed that students understand topics more quickly when they are given examples from everyday life. “I have noticed that they pick up very quickly if they are given real life examples,” he says. Students who struggle with English also use AI to find Urdu meanings and translations of textbook passages. Alongside general-purpose chatbots, teachers are also exploring AI applications designed specifically for education. One such platform is Gauth, which allows students to photograph or type in academic questions and receive step-by-step explanations. Beyond solving problems, its Quizify and Flashcard features help turn study materials into revision exercises, while TLDR produces shorter summaries of lengthy content. The platform also includes an AI Tutor for interactive explanations and Gauth Atlas, which uses illustrations to explain topics such as biological structures and scientific processes. These features give students different ways to revisit difficult lessons, although understanding the explanation remains more important than simply obtaining the answer. The use of AI in education is also gaining institutional attention. Under an agreement with the government, Gauth is set to provide more than 4,000 free subscriptions to teachers across Pakistan, including those associated with the government-backed Daanish Schools. Tahir says teachers at Daanish School Islamabad have begun exploring the platform and how it might be used in their classrooms. AI is also being used beyond regular lessons. Students have begun preparing speeches for school functions and assemblies with its help, working alongside their teachers. Tahir says their curiosity sometimes leads them to look up unusual questions and then put those same questions to their teachers. For him, AI has become another resource in the classroom, but he is wary of teachers depending on it for everything. Preparing quizzes and assignments entirely through AI, he argues, can overlook the different abilities of students sitting in the same class. “Teachers can understand that not every class has all bright students,” he says. “AI should be there just for supporting and not for doing everything.” When the answer comes too easily Maroof Ahmed was going through his class 10 students' physics essays when he came across a sentence that made him stop reading. “Electromagnetic induction serves as the quintessential linchpin of modern power distribution, seamlessly facilitating the transition from mechanical kinetics to electrical potential.” The assignment was about electromagnetic induction, how it powers household devices and one limitation of the technology. Ahmed had expected the students to explain the topic in their own words. The boy who submitted this essay usually wrote in fairly simple English. Suddenly, his work was full of elaborate vocabulary. Ahmed, who has been teaching physics and chemistry for more than eight years, decided to ask him about it after class. What did he mean by “quintessential linchpin”? Could he explain “flux linkage”? The boy couldn't. He looked down, embarrassed, before admitting that he had copied the answer from chatbot into a Google Doc. He hadn't even read the whole thing. There were three other assignments due that night. Rather than give him a zero, Ahmed took him to the staff room and asked him to spend 20 minutes reading what he had submitted. He had to look up the unfamiliar words and then write a summary himself. Ahmed says he has become accustomed to seeing students turn to AI whenever they encounter a difficult question. He remembers a time when pupils would bring him notebooks filled with attempts at solving a numerical, even if most of those attempts were wrong. These days, he says, some students reach for a chatbot before trying to solve the question themselves. “The willingness to sit with a problem, try three wrong approaches, and figure it out independently has diminished because they are accustomed to instant step-by-step solutions,” he says. He finds the problem particularly noticeable when he changes a familiar physics question slightly. Students who have learnt a particular solution can struggle to work out what to do when the numbers or conditions are different. Kashaf, at university, has faced a similar problem from the other side. She is in the final semester of her software engineering degree and regularly uses chatbots while working with Python and machine learning. On one assignment, she received AI-generated code that ran without errors. That should have been good news, except she couldn't understand everything the programme was doing. “AI-generated code can work without me immediately understanding every part of it,” she says. Kashaf went back to chatbot, this time asking it to explain the code line by line. She ran the programme herself, checked its output and made small changes to see how they affected the results. She has also used AI to understand Decision Tree and Random Forest models, particularly how they are trained and used to make predictions. “This shows that getting a working solution is not the same as actually learning how to develop one,” she says. For Ahmed, the challenge is deciding how much a student's submitted work tells him about what the student knows.l “Traditional take-home written assignments and generic essay topics are no longer reliable indicators of student competence,” he says. The class 10 student had submitted an essay containing terms he couldn't explain. Ahmed only found that out because he asked him to talk through what he had written. The students on the other side of the screen For students at Daanish School, using AI during a lesson is relatively straightforward. There are smart screens in classrooms and tablets available for academic work. But Tahir knows that not every student in Pakistan has access to the same facilities. He worries about those who have no personal device or reliable internet connection, particularly as AI becomes a more common part of studying. A student with access to a chatbot can ask for another explanation after school, practise questions or revisit a topic as often as needed. Someone without that access must rely on whatever help is available elsewhere. The difference is not necessarily in the students' abilities, Tahir believes, but in the resources available to them. The issue becomes more complicated when language is involved. At his school, Tahir has seen pupils turn to AI to translate difficult English passages into Urdu. Some understand the subject but struggle to follow the language used in their textbooks. For a child who cannot afford regular private tuition, having access to explanations outside school hours could be useful. But that possibility comes with an obvious limitation: the student first needs a suitable device, an internet connection and enough familiarity with the technology to ask useful questions. Ahmed, who teaches physics and chemistry in Karachi, has also seen students use AI to translate material into Urdu and other languages they understand more comfortably. He considers this one of its practical uses, especially when difficult terminology gets in the way of understanding a lesson. Yet he is reluctant to treat access to AI as an answer to every learning difficulty. Students still need someone to recognise when they have misunderstood a concept, he argues, and teachers must be able to judge whether the explanation a student has received is correct. There is also the question of what happens when students begin depending on the technology for work they could have attempted themselves. Ahmed has seen pupils turn to AI almost immediately when faced with unfamiliar questions, rather than first trying to work through them. The same tool that helps one student understand a difficult English passage may allow another to complete an assignment without understanding it. For teachers such as Tahir and Ahmed, making AI available is only part of the challenge. How students are taught to use it matters just as much. The real test is what remains For Ahmed, the way forward involves changing what teachers ask students to do. He wants more oral questioning, classroom exercises and assignments that require pupils to explain how they reached an answer. While Tahir is equally cautious about allowing AI to take over the teacher's role, Ali has his own way of finding out whether chatbot has actually helped him learn something. After using it to understand a difficult topic, he closes the screen and tries to explain the answer aloud, in Urdu or English, without looking at his notes. He calls it his “re-explain test”. If he gets stuck, he knows he needs to study the topic again. Fardeen, who uses AI while studying for her MBA, puts it simply: “There is a difference between using AI to learn and using it to avoid learning.” For Ali, that difference will matter when he sits his board examinations. He will have to work through the physics questions himself, without a chatbot to take him through the steps.

title: Saif Ali Khan attack trial begins as nurse tells court intruder demanded INR10m
description: First witness identifies the accused and recounts how the intruder attacked her and the actor at his Bandra home
content: The trial in the knife attack on Bollywood actor Saif Ali Khan began in Mumbai, with the first witness telling the court that the intruder had demanded INR10 million during a break-in at the actor’s Bandra residence in January 2025. The nurse, who cared for Khan and Kareena Kapoor Khan’s younger son, Jeh, identified the accused, 31-year-old Mohammad Shariful Islam, during her testimony on Friday, according to Gulf News. The nurse, who is the complainant in the case, has worked with the family for more than five years and was the first witness called to testify, the report said. According to the The Indian Express, the nurse told the court a noise had woken her at around 2am on January 16, 2025. She initially noticed that the bathroom light was on and assumed Kareena was inside. After waking again, she saw a man wearing a cap moving towards Jeh’s bed. The child was four years old at the time. The nurse said she rushed towards the bed and attempted to pick up the child when the intruder attacked her with a hacksaw blade and told her to remain silent. When she asked what he wanted, the man allegedly demanded INR10 million. The commotion alerted another nanny, who raised the alarm. Khan and Kapoor Khan then emerged from their rooms, and the actor confronted the intruder, asking who he was and what he wanted. According to the witness, the man subsequently attacked Khan and another member of the household staff. Khan managed to overpower the intruder, while others took refuge in a room and locked themselves inside. The accused had fled by the time additional staff members arrived, according to Gulf News. The nurse sustained cuts to two fingers during the incident. Khan was taken to Mumbai’s Lilavati Hospital following the attack, where he underwent emergency surgery for multiple injuries. Doctors reported six wounds, including two deep injuries to his left hand and neck. A fragment of a knife was lodged near his spine, and surgeons removed a piece of the blade measuring approximately 2.5 inches. The actor was discharged from hospital several days later. Mumbai Police arrested the accused near Hiranandani Estate in Thane on January 19, 2025, three days after the incident. Police said he had used several aliases, including Vijay Das and Bijoy Das, according to Gulf News. Described in the report as a Bangladeshi national, the accused remains in judicial custody. He faces charges under India’s Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including robbery with a deadly weapon, causing grievous hurt and house trespass. He has also been charged under the Foreigners Act and the Passport (Entry into India) Rules. The trial followed two unsuccessful attempts by the accused to plead guilty. According to Gulf News, his lawyer, Vipul Dushing, submitted an application in late August stating that his client was willing to plead guilty and seeking leniency. The court rejected the request on September 11 and ordered the trial to proceed. The accused again indicated on October 8 that he intended to plead guilty to all charges. Hindustan Times reported that the court rejected this second attempt as well, paving the way for witness testimony to begin. Khan has previously spoken about the ordeal in an interview with journalist Barkha Dutt on Mojo Story, recalling that he feared he might die as he lay injured on the floor. The actor also said he had considered forgiving the intruder, although he struggled to move past the possibility that the man had tried to kill him. As proceedings continue, the defence is expected to cross-examine the nurse. Other members of the household staff are also expected to testify, while Khan himself could be called as a witness. The report did not specify a date for the next hearing.

title: Mohatta Palace to host ninth Sindh Literature Festival
description: The 9th edition of the festival will be held on November 21 and 22
content: The ninth edition of the Sindh Literature Festival (SLF) will take place at the historic Mohatta Palace in Karachi on November 21 and 22, 2026, bringing together literature, culture, history and the stories that connect communities across Sindh. The dates and venue were announced on the festival’s official Instagram account, which invited audiences to join the two-day gathering celebrating the province’s literary and cultural heritage. The announcement marks the return of the festival for its ninth edition, continuing an initiative that has provided a platform for writers, poets, scholars, artists and readers to engage with Sindh’s diverse cultural traditions. View this post on Instagram Established in 2016, the Sindh Literature Festival has become a recurring cultural gathering focused on promoting Sindhi literature, indigenous languages, music, history, and the arts. According to the festival’s official website, it aims to create opportunities for established and emerging writers to interact with readers while encouraging conversations about the region’s social, cultural, and intellectual life. Previous editions have featured panel discussions, book launches, poetry recitals, theatre, musical performances and conversations on subjects ranging from language and education to history, politics, heritage and environmental concerns. The festival has also provided space for discussions about the Indus River, the preservation of cultural identity and the role of literature in responding to contemporary challenges. The event has been organised by the Sindh Literary Foundation, with journalist Naseer Gopang identified on the festival’s official website as its founder and producer. The festival’s earlier editions have addressed a range of themes reflecting Sindh’s history and contemporary concerns. The fifth edition, held at the Arts Council of Pakistan in Karachi in March 2022, marked the centenary of the discovery of Mohenjo-daro, bringing archaeological heritage and the Indus Valley Civilisation into focus. The sixth edition, held in March 2023, highlighted climate change and global warming under the theme “Aalam Sabh Abaad Kareen”. Its programme included literary and cultural activities intended to encourage public engagement with environmental issues. In December 2024, the seventh edition took place at Liaquat Memorial Library in Karachi under the theme “Save Indus, Save Life” and the eighth edition was held at the Beach Luxury Hotel in Karachi on November 15 and 16, 2025, under the theme “Celebrate the Power of the World”. These editions demonstrated the festival’s continuing interest in connecting literary expression with the wider social, historical and cultural experiences of Sindh. The choice of Mohatta Palace as the venue adds a historical dimension to the upcoming festival. Located in Karachi’s Clifton area, the palace was built in the late 1920s for businessman Rai Bahadur Seth Shivratan Mohatta. It is now a recognised historic monument under the Government of Sindh and operates as a museum. The palace’s architectural heritage and role as a cultural venue provide a fitting setting for an event centred on literature, history and artistic expression. Hosting the festival at the site also brings together two aspects of the city’s cultural landscape: its historic built heritage and the continuing traditions of storytelling, writing and debate. As the festival prepares for its ninth edition, it continues to underline the importance of preserving literary traditions while making space for new ideas, voices and cultural conversations. Its return offers readers and culture enthusiasts another opportunity to engage with the stories, histories and creative expressions that shape Sindh’s identity.

title: Mona Lisa off limits as Paris shuts museums over protest fears
description: Tourists caught off guard by wave of closures, Paris Opera, Art Basel Paris fair cancel programmes
content: Disappointed tourists poked their heads through ​the Louvre's locked gates on Saturday, shut off from the Mona Lisa as galleries ‌and museums across Paris closed as a precaution ahead of fresh demonstrations. "When we came, we thought there could be a problem but not that the museum would be closed," Italian social educator Selena Bertoni, 31, said in ​front of the Musée d'Orsay. On a four-day trip to Paris she had paid €50 ($56) for ​two tickets to see its Impressionist paintings and other masterpieces. "Bad timing," she said, ⁠with a shrug. The closures came one week after nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living and ​deteriorating public services descended into some of the worst street violence that France has seen in years. The ​violence and damage prompted the government to impose localised curfews and close many public venues ahead of demonstrations planned on Saturday. Top Tourist Destination The shutdown extended across much of the capital's cultural sector, including the Orangerie, Jeu de Paume ​and Picasso museums, while the entire Tuileries Gardens complex that leads out of the Louvre was ​sealed off. "This is the third museum we have come to that is closed. They should've warned us," French ‌visitor Heidi ⁠Rosar, 21, said. At the Louvre, the locked black iron gates blocked access to the entire site and the garden. "We wanted to at least see the pyramid," 67-year-old Canadian Don Nowschuk said, referring to the museum's landmark glass entrance. On a two-night stay in the City of Light, Nowschuk suggested the ​local authorities might be ​overreacting. "There is so much ⁠security that you would think it would be enough to secure the museum," he said. "It's a bit weird to see so many cops with ​guns around Paris. We are used to guns but not like this." The ​disruption extended ⁠to the performing arts sector. The Paris Opera shuttered both the Palais Garnier and the Opéra Bastille, citing safety concerns for staff and audiences. Organisers of the prestigious Art Basel Paris fair also cancelled its weekend ⁠programme. The ​cultural centres posted warnings about the closures on Friday, but ​some people never thought to check. "How could we have known? We didn't think a museum could be closed. We are ​a bit naive," 59-year-old French woman Catherine Sebbagh said.

title: Claude Monet's 'Iris' becomes most expensive artwork sold at auction in France, Sotheby's says
description: Painting was one of several works up for auction ​from ​Schlumberger ⁠Collection, expected to sell ​between €22m-€30m
content: Claude Monet's "Iris" was sold late on Thursday ​for €50 million ($56.05 million), becoming the ‌most expensive work of art sold at auction in France, Sotheby's ​said. The painting, completed toward ​the end of Monet's life, ⁠attracted frantic bidding with ​six people battling it out ​for 45 minutes for the piece, before the final two continued to ​scrabble for a further ​20 minutes. "Iris" finally went to an Asian ‌collector ⁠who bid over the phone. The painting was one of several works up for auction ​from the ​Schlumberger ⁠Collection and had been expected to sell ​between €22 million and €30 million. The ​previous ⁠French auction record was set in 2010, by Amedeo Modigliani's "Head ⁠of ​a Caryatid," which ​sold for €43.2 million. This comes after news in September that two paintings by the Impressionist master Claude Monet that have never been shown in public are to be sold in Paris next month by the billionaire Schlumberger family of France. "Iris" was described as a large painting Monet completed toward the end of his life, has been valued at 22 million to 30 million euros ($25-34 million), which represents "the highest estimate ever given for a painting offered at auction in France", Sotheby's said as it unveiled the sale at its Paris headquarters. Alongside "Iris", three other canvases by Monet were also included in the sale on October 22, among them "Saule Pleureur" (Weeping Willow), valued at 9-12 million euros. The sale comes in the year marking the centenary of Monet's death on December 5, 1926, which is being commemorated by two Paris exhibitions opening in late September: "Monet, Painting Time" and "Stories of Landscapes, from Monet to Hockney."

title: As actors get more physical, Bollywood embraces intimacy coordinators
description: Indian film industry hires intimacy coordinators to choreograph scenes, ensure consent and protect boundaries
content: India's film industry, where scenes featuring nudity or sex often rely on improvisation and mutual trust, is gradually welcoming professionals tasked with choreographing intimacy to protect actors and ensure consent. Once unheard-of in Bollywood, intimacy coordinators are becoming an increasingly familiar presence on sets as filmmakers embrace stricter standards after the #MeToo movement put a spotlight on sexual exploitation in entertainment industries around the world. The shift comes as streaming platforms have pushed storytelling into a more nuanced territory, creating greater demand for realistic portrayals of sexuality. "Just like a stunt director handles a fight scene... for scenes of intimacy, we map out exactly where the hand goes and where the hair goes so nothing is left to awkward improvisation," said Aastha Khanna, one of a small but growing group of intimacy coordinators in Bollywood. Most arrive on set armed with "modesty tools" that allow performers to simulate intimacy while minimising unnecessary physical contact. A typical kit includes crotch guards, nipple pasties and doughnut cushions, which ensure a safe distance between performers during sex scenes. The emergence of such coordinators reflects a broader transformation in an industry where intimate scenes traditionally relied on trust between actors and directors, often with few formal safeguards. Khanna said coordinators are usually hired before casting begins. "The idea is that actors know there are intimate scenes in the script and can decide whether they are comfortable with them before signing on," she told AFP. PHOTO: AFP Bollywood, one of the most prolific movie-making machines in the world, largely sidestepped physical intimacy on screen for decades because of strict government guidelines and powerful censors. Kissing and sex were implied symbolically, with flowers brushing against each other, crashing waves or a crackling fire standing in for overt desire and consummation. Even when filmmakers pushed the boundaries, the mechanics of filming intimate scenes remained largely unstructured. Among the first mainstream Hindi productions to formalise the practice of intimacy direction was Gehraiyaan, backed by filmmaker Karan Johar and released on Amazon Prime Video in 2022. Intimacy coordinator Khanna worked to establish personal boundaries and choreograph scenes, while intimacy coach Neha Vyaso conducted workshops focused on physical dynamics and consent. This model has gradually spread across productions meant for streaming services, which industry experts say have been the primary drivers of change. "There's much less censorship and more openness to stories that explore taboo subjects," Vyaso said. Crime drama franchise Mirzapur, known for its graphic content, started off without intimacy coordinators in its early seasons. But lead actor Rasika Dugal said such specialists fill a critical gap. "In the initial seasons, we had to navigate boundaries individually based on personal comfort," she said. "It is very important to have intimacy coordinators so nobody is violated in any way and everyone's concerns are properly taken care of." Bollywood's glamorous exterior long concealed a chaotic backstage culture where personal boundaries were routinely crossed. "There have been instances where the actor ended up kissing his co-star without her consent. We ensure that none of this happens in the flow," Khanna said. But professionals like her remain far from universal, numbering just over a dozen across India's film and television industries. In many commercial blockbusters, there is not much scope for their expertise because major actors often avoid explicit physical intimacy or even kissing on screen. Certain films feature intimate scenes without a dedicated coordinator, while some experienced directors continue to manage scenes themselves. With no formal guidelines or any requirement to hire an intimacy coordinator, some in the industry hope film associations will eventually introduce industry-wide standards. To Khanna, the role of a coordinator extends well beyond simulated sex. "A scene of intimacy is not necessarily just a spicy or a romance scene, it is a much larger umbrella" that can encompass violence, dominance, harassment and nudity, she said. "The work that I do mitigates a situation where a person may go through several years of therapy and the scar may not heal."

title: Govt rejects $490m loan over cost
description: Debt office balked at 8% all-in cost vs 6% target; financing needs hit 20% of GDP
content: Pakistan has turned down a $490 million commercial loan proposal by the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) Group due to higher interest rates, amid elevated gross financing needs (GFN) that the finance ministry has estimated at around 20% of the size of the nation's economy. The facility was refused a couple of months after Pakistan took a $300 million loan from United Bank Limited, which originated the amount from Bahrain and Dubai in August this year, according to the sources. The government obtained these loans by waiving income tax on the profits the bank would earn by extending them. The decision to turn down the offer from the IsDB's arm, the International Islamic Trade Finance Corporation (ITFC), was taken last week, according to government officials. The facility had been offered for a period of one year. The finance ministry spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment about the government's decision. The officials said the Debt Management Office (DMO) of the finance ministry took the decision to turn down the loan due to higher cost. The debt office has been working without a permanent director general since January this year. The finance ministry has now asked the Economic Affairs Division to look for a new loan facility, either from the ITFC or any other source at competitive rates, the sources added. Pakistan's GFN, including external requirements, remain high as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has now projected a current account deficit that is higher than the official estimates. The IMF's latest report projected the current account deficit at 1% of gross domestic product (GDP), or nearly $4.5 billion. This is at least $1.5 billion higher than the $2.5 billion to $3 billion figure pitched by the Pakistani authorities during recently concluded talks.
