In the same report released this week, the IMF showed Pakistan's GFN around 22% of GDP for the last fiscal year, which finance ministry officials found on the higher side. However, according to the finance ministry's annual borrowing plan for fiscal year 2026-27, "total gross financing needs are projected at Rs28.647 trillion, approximately 20% of GDP". This is inclusive of the total federal fiscal deficit of Rs7 trillion and, after adding domestic and external maturities, of over Rs21 trillion, according to the finance ministry's own report based on original budget estimates. The same report noted that net external financing is projected at Rs813 billion, equivalent to $2.8 billion. The net amount is after repaying maturing debts, which suggests the actual borrowings will be higher than this amount. The finance ministry is betting on inflows from multilateral lenders that are expected to be the primary external funding source for $1.6 billion net lending to meet these requirements. Regarding the ITFC's $490 million facility, the debt office was of the view that the interest rate offered by the lender was considerably high, as it had hoped for an interest cost of around 6%. The sources said the ITFC's offered all-in cost of about 8% was higher than the December 2027 maturing bond, which was trading at 6.1%. In September this year, the government raised $3 billion through Eurobonds at interest rates higher than those Pakistan paid in 2021 against five- and 10-year Eurobonds, showing a comparison of both transactions. The key reason behind relatively low interest rates on the debt raised in 2021 was that US Treasury rates were very low, ranging from 1% on five-year bonds to 1.64% on 10-year bonds. Current US Treasury rates were over 5% due to prevailing global geopolitical and consequent economic uncertainties. The finance ministry stated that it raised $1.75 billion through a five-and-a-half-year Eurobond at a coupon rate of 7.5%. The face value interest rate on the five-year Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) Eurobond was also 3% higher than the comparative US Treasury bond. During the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's (PTI) time, it was 5% higher than the comparative US rates. The actual interest rate on the PML-N five-year transaction was 7.75%. The finance ministry also raised $1.25 billion through a 10-year Eurobond at a 7.9% face value interest rate. The sources said the government has also processed the income tax exemption for a foreign-origin commercial loan of $300 million. A finance ministry official said foreign commercial loan facilities have been offered on the condition that taxes applicable in Pakistan will not be borne by the lenders, and that the tax was either to be borne by the government or a tax exemption granted. They said the law empowers the federal cabinet to waive these taxes, which eventually have to be paid from the budget, as it was direct borrowing by the finance ministry.

title: Power supply chains face a new test
description: For grid expansion at required pace, availability of key components is critical
content: The world's power sector is entering a period in which the availability of electricity will depend not only on generation capacity but also on the ability to secure the equipment, materials and services needed to build and maintain the electricity network. Transformers, cables, switchgear, turbines, solar modules and batteries are increasingly becoming strategic inputs rather than routine procurement items. Electricity demand is rising rapidly as industries electrify, data centres expand and countries add renewable-energy capacity. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that annual grid investment must increase by around 50%, from about $400 billion today to roughly $600 billion by 2030, to keep pace with electrification and climate goals. Yet factories producing critical equipment are already under pressure. Long lead times for large power transformers, high-voltage cables and other grid equipment can delay projects even when financing and generation capacity are available. According to the IEA's Building the Future Transmission Grid report, lead times for large power transformers have almost doubled since 2021, reaching up to four years for the largest units. High-voltage cables now take two to three years, while direct-current cables for long-distance transmission can exceed five years. The Utilities for Net Zero Alliance (UNEZA) estimates its members alone will need close to 90,000 kilometres of transmission cable by 2030 – more than twice the Earth's circumference – and over 270 high-voltage transformers, with waiting times now exceeding three years. A country may therefore have sufficient investment capital, plans for new generation and growing electricity demand, yet still find that its grid cannot expand at the required pace because critical components are unavailable. Manufacturing and mineral processing are heavily concentrated. China accounts for around 60% of global mined production of magnet rare earths, more than 90% of refining and nearly 95% of permanent magnet production, according to IEA data. In solar manufacturing, China produces roughly 80% of global PV modules and over 90% of polysilicon and wafers. Lithium, copper, cobalt, nickel, graphite and rare-earth elements are increasingly viewed not simply as commodities but as strategic inputs into the energy transition. Over half of strategic energy minerals are now subject to some form of export control, making diversification a security imperative rather than a procurement preference. Renewable energy adds another layer of complexity. Solar and wind generation are variable, requiring stronger transmission networks, storage, flexible generation and more sophisticated grid-management systems. The supply chain must therefore support not just additional generation but an increasingly complex electricity system. The rapid growth of data centres and AI applications is adding to this pressure. The IEA projects that data-centre electricity consumption could rise from about 415 TWh in 2024 to roughly 945 TWh by 2030, with the US and China accounting for almost 80% of the increase. Large computing facilities require reliable and continuous electricity supplies, often in locations where existing grids have limited spare capacity. A modern power supply chain is also an information system. Utilities need visibility across several tiers of suppliers to know where critical components are manufactured, what raw materials they depend upon and how quickly alternative sources can be activated. Digital technologies can help. Internet-connected sensors, AI, advanced forecasting and digital twins can improve inventory management, predict equipment failures and provide earlier warnings of potential disruptions. Better data-sharing between utilities and manufacturers can also help suppliers plan production instead of responding only when orders arrive. But technology alone cannot solve a supply shortage. If several utilities place orders for the same specialised equipment at the same time, better software cannot manufacture transformers or high-voltage cables faster. Procurement strategy therefore matters. Utilities need to move beyond the lowest-bid approach and consider quality, delivery reliability, technical capability, supplier concentration, cybersecurity and geopolitical exposure when selecting suppliers. Long-term contracts can give manufacturers greater confidence to invest in production capacity, while utilities obtain greater assurance of future supplies. Collaborative procurement could become particularly important. Utilities and governments can provide manufacturers with clearer multi-year demand forecasts while standardising equipment specifications where technically possible. This can reduce unnecessary customisation, shorten procurement cycles and allow manufacturers to benefit from larger production runs. Diversification is equally important. A resilient supply chain does not mean abandoning global trade or producing everything domestically. It means avoiding excessive dependence on a single supplier, country or transport route for a critical component. Strategic inventories can also have a role. Maintaining stocks of every item would be prohibitively expensive, but selected critical components, particularly those with long manufacturing lead times, can be held to reduce the consequences of unexpected failures or supply disruptions. The same principle applies upstream to critical minerals. Greater investment in mining, processing, recycling and alternative materials can reduce dependence on concentrated sources. International partnerships and regional supply arrangements can complement domestic production. The circular economy offers another opportunity. Power-sector companies do not always need to respond to rising demand by buying entirely new equipment. Transformers and other assets can sometimes be refurbished and kept in service longer. Copper, aluminium and steel can be recovered from retired equipment, while batteries and solar technologies offer increasing opportunities for recycling and second-life applications. Cybersecurity is becoming another essential element of supply-chain management. Power systems increasingly depend on digital technologies and connected equipment, making suppliers themselves part of the security perimeter. IBM's 2024 Cost of a Data Breach report put the global average cost of a data breach at $4.88 million, a 10% rise in a year. Procurement decisions therefore have to consider not only technical specifications but also the security of associated software, communications systems and vendors. The shortage of skilled labour and manufacturing capacity adds to the challenge. Expanding production of specialised grid equipment requires engineers, technicians, factory workers and testing facilities. Building such capacity can take years. Governments and utilities therefore need to provide manufacturers with enough visibility of future demand to justify long-term investment. For developing economies such as Pakistan, these global changes carry special significance. Pakistan's power sector remains heavily exposed to imported fuel, equipment, technology and capital goods. Cumulative solar imports have exceeded $3 billion in recent years, with the overwhelming majority sourced from China, according to trade data. A weakening currency can raise the local cost of imported equipment, while procurement delays can postpone projects and increase financing costs. Dependence on external suppliers also means that international disruptions can quickly become domestic problems. This makes supply-chain resilience relevant not only to new generation capacity but also to the reliability of the existing transmission and distribution system. Maintaining adequate stocks of critical components, developing reliable local suppliers where economically viable, improving demand forecasting and establishing longer-term relationships with strategic manufacturers could reduce some of these vulnerabilities. Localisation, however, should not become an excuse for inefficient production. Domestic manufacturing makes economic sense where Pakistan has the skills, market size and cost advantages to compete. In other areas, diversified international sourcing may remain more efficient. The objective should be supply security at a competitive cost, rather than self-sufficiency for its own sake. The writer is a mechanical engineer

title: Karachi's waste is a Rs1.2b economy it ignores
description: Informal recyclers already turning waste into economic value yet remain excluded from formal waste-management planning
content: Karachi floods during the monsoon and chokes under summer pollution. Both crises have multiple causes, but waste management connects them in ways the city can no longer afford to ignore. Cleaner air could add an estimated 2.7 years to the average Karachi resident's life. Industry and transport are the largest contributors, but waste is part of the same crisis. Uncollected garbage accumulates in drains, on vacant plots and at open dumpsites, and when burned adds black carbon and other pollutants to air that met the World Health Organisation's (WHO) daily guideline on only three days in 2024, according to PAQI's 2025 national report. An official of the Sindh Solid Waste Management Board (SSWMB) said Karachi generates more than 14,800 tonnes of waste daily, including over 3,000 tonnes in District Central alone. Around 42% is organic. Karachi is also reported to account for 25% of Pakistan's recyclable plastic waste. PAQI's 2025 source inventory attributes 7% of Karachi's PM2.5 emissions to open waste burning. Waste as economic value A 2014 World Economic Forum report estimated the circular economy at over $1 trillion per year in material savings globally, with recycling in Europe alone already supporting 500,000 jobs. Pakistan imported virgin plastic resin worth $3 billion in 2022, compared with $707 million in tea imports. Better collection and sorting could reduce dependence on some virgin resin imports. Pakistani businesses are already showing what recovery can look like. Concept Loop converts difficult-to-recycle multilayer plastic packaging into construction products such as pavers, blocks and tiles, turning material that would otherwise clog a drain or burn on a roadside into a product with a market price. The company has received support through Karandaaz's GreenFin Innovations programme and reports that its pavers were used in a Mari Petroleum project at Daharki in Sindh, diverting over 7,000 kg of low-value plastic waste. The Sindh Enterprise Incubation Centre reports that Concept Loop has recycled over 1,300 tonnes of plastic and produced more than 100,000 square feet of building materials. However, Karachi needs a system to recover recycled waste. Regulation can shift behaviour when it is enforced consistently. Rwanda banned plastic bags in 2008, one of the first countries in the world to do so, and later expanded the ban to cover single-use plastics. According to the Global Green Growth Institute, enforcement included border inspections to prevent smuggling, strict penalties for violations and government support to help businesses transition to alternatives. Karachi does not need to replicate the ban. It needs what made it work: enforcement, alternatives and businesses brought in from the start. Organic waste should become a product Lahore's Mehmood Booti composting project shows that waste recovery and carbon finance are not theoretical possibilities in Pakistan. Lahore Compost Limited began operating there in 2006 under an arrangement with the City District Government, processing municipal waste into compost while pursuing carbon revenue from methane reductions. The proposed carbon finance project also received $5.524 million in World Bank funding. The original operation ran until 2016. It is a historical example, but the lesson applies: composting requires clean organic inputs, a reliable market and sustained management. The potential of carbon finance is demonstrated by the World Bank's account of the Monterrey Waste Management and Carbon Offset Project in Mexico, which generated and sold more than one million metric tonnes of certified emissions reductions between 2005 and 2017. Carbon revenue should supplement, not replace, reliable funding for basic waste collection and disposal services. Karachi's Bagh Ibne Qasim biogas plant shows what this looks like in practice. The facility converts organic and livestock waste into biogas, with reported processing of around two tonnes of organic waste daily and production capacity of 150 cubic metres of gas. The project was designed to supply subsidised cooking fuel to 70 to 80 households in Clifton at Rs2,000 per month. Fixing the system: accountability, financing It was reported in July 2026 that the World Bank had downgraded Karachi's $100 million Solid Waste Emergency and Efficiency Project to "Moderately Unsatisfactory". Delays to four transfer stations, contract management problems and no measurable waste disposed through a sanitary landfill were among the concerns. Investment without functioning management and public accountability does not deliver. Karachi's informal recyclers are already turning waste into economic value, yet remain excluded from formal waste-management planning. A 2023 study estimated that they recover 4,100 tonnes of waste daily, valuing Karachi's informal recycling economy at Rs1.2 billion annually. Yet workers remain vulnerable, with the Fair Circularity Initiative estimating monthly earnings at around Rs42,500 to Rs43,300, below the Rs60,434 monthly living-wage benchmark calculated using the Anker methodology. Pune in India offers a practical model through its SWaCH cooperative, which integrates over 3,900 waste pickers, diverts approximately 80,000 tonnes annually and has been associated with estimated municipal transport savings of Rs16 million a year. Karachi can build on its existing recycling economy by giving registered kabariwalas access to sorting facilities, protective equipment, working capital and fair municipal contracts. Financing waste services through user charges has a record. Worcester in Massachusetts introduced a Pay As You Throw programme in which households pay per bag of waste they discard, reducing volumes and increasing recycling rates. Closer to home, Punjab under the Suthra Punjab programme introduced a sanitation fee ranging from Rs300 per month for smaller urban households to Rs5,000 for the largest properties, collected alongside property tax. A fee without reliable service is a tax with no corresponding benefit. Any comparable charge in Karachi must be tied to published service standards and transparent expenditure. From waste crisis to circular economy Karachi's waste is an economic opportunity sitting in plain sight. The city already has businesses converting plastic into products, informal workers recovering materials at scale, and local projects demonstrating the potential of biogas and composting. What is missing is enforcement, accountability and money tied to results. Progress should be measured not by projects inaugurated but by waste recovered, pollution reduced and a formal, transparent system that works. THE WRITER IS AN ASSISTANT PROFESSOR AT THE SCHOOL OF ECONOMICS AND SOCIAL SCIENCES, IBA. SHE HOLDS A PHD IN ECONOMICS FROM CLARK UNIVERSITY

title: Macroeconomic effects of financialisation
description: Shareholder value orientation increases debt, reduces real investment and aggregate demand
content: In the era of financial globalisation, most of the business firms follow a shareholder orientation strategy. Shareholder orientation means that business firms intend to show high profitability. They usually show this profitability by downsizing the workforce and then distributing higher profits among shareholders to satisfy them. This shareholder orientation strategy at the micro level disappoints in terms of profit rate at the macro level. In other words, the financial gains enjoyed by business firms at the micro level cannot be realised at the macro level. A shareholder-oriented business firm focuses on higher profitability. Their Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) are incentivised through stock options, which means that higher dividend payouts will increase their salary/compensation packages. These CEOs outsource certain functions to minimise their labour force. They also hire contractual workforce in order to lessen their wage bills. Since these managers have short-term contracts, they intend to increase profitability in order to raise their compensation. Business firms, which focus on shareholder value orientation, also resort to share buybacks. As these firms do not retain profits, they have to either borrow from banks or issue bonds. Such borrowings increase their corporate debt-to-equity ratio. Hence, these firms become highly leveraged in the course of time and their dependence on debt increases. A leveraged firm intends to have easy access to credit. Credit access is easier when circumstances are normal. As the circumstances are far from normal, credit access becomes difficult. Under these circumstances, these business firms become financially constrained. Such situations may be a prelude to a firm-creditor conflict. Business firms are meant to invest in real capital ie, investment in machines, men and materials. The realisation of real investment is uncertain. Shareholder value orientation does not allow business firms to invest in risky ventures. These firms become selective in their investment projects as they tend to choose less risky projects. This selection of investment projects does not increase aggregate demand, as and when required. Specially, selection and continuation of risky investments are necessary during the phase of recession. Many business firms listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) have adopted a shareholder orientation strategy. Firms from cement, banking, insurance, textile and pharmaceutical sub-sectors have bought back their shares in the last four years as they held excessive cash in their balance sheets. Few of them have bought their shares twice in the last couple of years. Similarly, financialised households are involved in debt-financed consumption. These households buy and consume durable and luxury products and services through borrowings. Such borrowings increase the debt-to-income ratio of consumers. If access to credit is easy, consumers will increase their consumption. In an economy, a small percentage of high-net-worth consumers are bondholders while a large percentage of low-income individuals are consumers. High-net-worth individuals have a low propensity to consume while low-income individuals have a high propensity to consume. Debt-financed consumption transfers income from low-income consumers to high-income ones which, in turn, reduces aggregate demand. Access to credit entices consumers to increase consumption in the short run. Debt-financed consumption increases the debt burden on consumers. Owing to debt servicing and repayment obligations, consumption decreases in the long run. In short, shareholder value orientation increases the level of debt in the economy. Moreover, it decreases the level of real investment which, in turn, reduces aggregate demand. The decline in the level of aggregate demand has contractive effects on the macroeconomy. This situation does not bode well for the aspiring millions. The writer is an independent economist who authored a book: Pakistan's Structural Economic Problems in the era of Financial Globalization

title: Draft auto policy balances hopes and realities
description: Equilibrium is a must between protection, competition; tariff cuts put parts industry on notice
content: Pakistan's automobile industry stands at a critical crossroads as the government prepares to introduce the Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-31. The proposed framework aims to transform a largely assembly-based sector into a competitive, export-oriented manufacturing industry. For years, manufacturers have sought policy consistency, lower production costs, protection for local vendors and incentives for technological development. Consumers, meanwhile, expect affordable vehicles, better quality, improved safety and greater market competition. The challenge for policymakers is to balance these competing expectations without repeating the weaknesses of earlier automotive policies. The draft policy has set an ambitious direction, including an export target of $6 billion over five years, gradual tariff reductions and greater adoption of electric vehicles. According to details reported after the prime minister approved the draft on October 20, 2026, the document is expected to move to the federal cabinet for in-principle approval before further legislative consideration. It proposes reducing tariffs on completely built-up vehicles and completely knocked-down kits to as low as 15% by 2030-31. This represents a significant shift from the protection-oriented approach that has historically shaped Pakistan's automobile market. The industry's expectations, however, are more complicated than the policy's headline targets suggest. Local assemblers and parts manufacturers want a predictable tariff structure that allows them to plan investment and compete with imported vehicles. Parts manufacturers are particularly concerned that rapid tariff reductions could expose domestic vendors to cheaper imported components before they have achieved economies of scale or technological competitiveness. The Pakistan Association of Automotive Parts and Accessories Manufacturers has warned that tariff cuts on imported parts to 15% without addressing domestic cost disadvantages could weaken local manufacturing and turn Pakistan into an import-dependent market. The concern is rooted in the structure of the industry. Pakistan has attracted several new automobile brands over the past decade, increasing competition and expanding consumer choice. However, additional assembly capacity has not automatically translated into higher production, deeper localisation or significant exports. The Pakistan Institute of Development Economics notes that the number of automobile manufacturing and assembling firms has increased to more than 15, while production capacity has more than doubled over the last decade. Yet sales have remained relatively stagnant and the industry continues to depend heavily on imported CKD kits and high-value components. This indicates that increasing the number of assemblers is not the same as building a strong manufacturing base. Official production figures also highlight the gap between capacity and actual market demand. The Pakistan Economic Survey 2024-25 reported car production of 76,339 units during July-March FY2025, compared with 55,678 in the corresponding period of FY2024, an increase of 37.1%. Production of jeeps, SUVs, pickups and light commercial vehicles rose by 79.8% to 26,147 units. Although the recovery was encouraging, it followed a period of weak demand, high financing costs, inflation and exchange rate instability. The figures demonstrate that the sector remains sensitive to macroeconomic conditions and cannot achieve sustained expansion through policy incentives alone. The proposed export target is another major test. The draft envisages combined vehicle and parts exports of $6.01 billion over five years, with annual targets rising from $256.6 million in 2026-27 to $2.19 billion in 2030-31. It also proposes export-linked incentives and penalties for manufacturers that repeatedly fail to meet their obligations. The direction is positive because Pakistan cannot continue treating the domestic market as the industry's principal destination. However, exports require internationally competitive prices, consistent quality, economies of scale, reliable supply chains and compliance with global safety and environmental standards. These capabilities cannot be created simply by setting targets. Localisation must therefore become a practical industrial strategy rather than a numerical requirement. Pakistan has spent decades encouraging local production, yet many technologically advanced components are imported. Domestic vendors need access to modern machinery, technical training, research facilities and partnerships with international manufacturers. Small suppliers also require affordable financing and predictable orders to justify investment. If tariff reductions are introduced before local firms become competitive, the result could be industrial contraction rather than modernisation. Conversely, indefinite protection would weaken incentives to improve productivity and quality. A gradual, evidence-based transition is essential. EVs provide another opportunity, but affordability and infrastructure remain major constraints. The draft proposes a 1% sales tax on battery electric vehicles, with different rates for range-extended and plug-in hybrid vehicles. It also proposes increasing the financing limit for EV purchases from Rs3 million to Rs10 million and extending repayment from three to five years. These measures could encourage adoption, but consumers also need accessible charging facilities, reliable electricity, battery warranties, maintenance networks and clarity about battery replacement costs. EV incentives should support mass-market mobility rather than primarily benefiting buyers of expensive vehicles. The proposed establishment of the Pakistan Automotive Testing Institute is an important step towards improving vehicle safety, certification and export readiness. Pakistan needs enforceable standards for crash protection, emissions, durability and manufacturing quality. Consumers should also benefit from transparent pricing, realistic delivery commitments and effective after-sales services. The new policy's success should ultimately be measured not only by investment announcements or the number of assembly plants, but by whether vehicles become safer, more affordable and technologically advanced. The government has also stated its intention to use an Automotive Development Levy to support export incentives and industrial development. The draft estimates collections exceeding Rs232 billion over five years. Such funds must be managed transparently, with measurable outcomes and independent oversight. Support should reach productive investment, technology upgrading, vendor development and research rather than becoming another permanent subsidy for established players. Pakistan's draft auto policy offers an opportunity to move beyond an assembly-led model towards genuine industrial competitiveness. But the gap between industry hopes and policy realities will remain unless tariff reform is matched by lower production costs, stronger local suppliers, consistent regulation and export capability. The government must protect neither inefficient manufacturers nor consumers from competition; instead, it must create conditions in which efficient producers can compete and buyers receive better value. The real achievement will be a sustainable automobile industry that earns foreign exchange, creates skilled employment and delivers affordable, safe and reliable vehicles to the Pakistani market. THE WRITER IS A MEMBER OF PEC AND HOLDS A MASTER'S DEGREE IN ENGINEERING

title: The model that fuels Europe's protests
description: 21% of EU population at risk of poverty or social exclusion, with Spain highest at 25.7%
content: Europe is once again experiencing a series of protests. Several countries are already seeing them, including France, Portugal, Italy and Spain. France is experiencing the worst of the current wave. Protesters are burning property and looting shops, malls and anything in their path. They are confronting police and law enforcement agencies. France has had to deploy the army in major cities to control the unrest. Italian protesters are following suit and have started looting shops and malls. The circle is expanding, with Belgium now also affected, and there is fear other countries could follow. The question is why countries are falling into protests one after another, and what drives them. A common reason is the rising, unbearable cost of living and the weakening of public welfare and service institutions. In France, protests began with students unhappy with the education system. They complained about school facilities, teacher availability and university fee structures. Other groups joined them, citing the rising cost of living. People in Spain are agitating over rising housing prices and other essentials. Italians are protesting over similar issues. The causes are the same across Europe. Cost-of-living issues and the delivery of services such as education are rooted in Europe's economic and social system. It is unfortunate that poverty and social exclusion have worsened over the years. Let us try to understand this using European Union (EU) data. Figures for 2025 show that almost 21% of the EU population is at risk of poverty or social exclusion. This means 92.7 million people are at risk. The worst part is that 19.3 million children are at risk, which puts the EU's future at stake. It is shocking that major economies also have high poverty risk, including Spain at 25.7%, Germany at 21.2%, Italy at 22.6% and France at 20.8%. Some experts believe the data is manipulated and the actual numbers may be higher. Ongoing violent protests and rising numbers point to this dimension. Inequality is another problem that haunts the EU over time. These indicators are disturbing, especially when the EU claims the best governance, political and economic system in the world. It claims that the economic model, capitalism, has helped the West achieve high economic growth and development. A thorough look at the history of rapid growth highlights two disturbing facts. First, the system presented and advocated as the best in human history is responsible for the current mess. A deep dive into the liberal economic model indicates certain flaws. One, it recognises that it will create losers and winners. Losers would be compensated and winners would pay to compensate them. Thus the state, with experts, devised tools such as taxes and built institutions to implement them. This would not be possible without a strong state role. Unfortunately, the role of the state was weakened over time in the name of the free market. Powerful business groups acquired more space in decision-making and in setting the rules. They also exploited liberal democracy to occupy the driving seat by funding candidates and parties. As a result, the state continued to lower taxes for corporations and raise them on ordinary citizens. Two, Riba is the main reason for the failure of the liberal economic model. It favours the winners and undermines the losers. It discourages investment in productive sectors and encourages wealth accumulation. The capitalist financial system offers lucrative opportunities to accumulate money, and seems attractive because wealth can be created with little effort. This creates many problems. For example, less investment in productive sectors leads to fewer jobs, which increases unemployment, poverty and suffering. Three, there is no system for redistributing wealth and resources. Tax or corporate social responsibility systems contribute little to compensating the losers. This creates the illusion of competition without building mechanisms to protect the losers. Second, the current situation dispels the myth that the liberal economic system ensures rapid growth and development. It has revived debate about colonisation's role in Europe's growth, including how European countries exploited weak but resource-rich countries. Europe did not hesitate to commit crimes against humanity and genocide to fulfil its economic agenda. After the old colonial system collapsed, Europe, with the United States, invented the Bretton Woods institutions to continue exploitation. However, the new system is also in decay. Therefore, Europe cannot solve its problems. In this context, Europe needs a new economic system if it wants to solve its problems and end agitation. Europe can explore two options. First, the Islamic economic system offers answers to all of Europe's questions and problems. It has a sophisticated system to ensure wealth redistribution through Zakat. It encourages investment in productive means by forbidding Riba. The whole system revolves around people's welfare and the betterment of society. It prohibits exploitative profits and keeps people's needs first. However, Europe does not believe in Islam. Moreover, the Islamic model is unfortunately not in practice anywhere in the world. So Europe can pursue a second option. The second option is the Chinese economic model. It centres on people's welfare. It has all the ingredients of modern economies, including a free market, openness and competition. However, the state does not leave the economy to the invisible hand. Rather, the state plays a prominent role in protecting common people's interests without compromising growth goals. As a result, China has grown exponentially, eliminated poverty and ensured the welfare of its people. Unfortunately, instead of learning from the Chinese model, the EU declared China an ideological rival and is doing everything it can to undermine it. However, it is encouraging that many European experts and ordinary citizens are discussing the Chinese model and want to learn from it to tackle European problems. Therefore, many people think now may be the time for the Red Star to shine over Europe. However, we have to wait for the final conclusion, as the liberal order's actors and beneficiaries will fight back to sustain this order and keep extracting benefits. They need to understand that no system can sustain itself without meeting people's basic needs. Thus, if they want to sustain it and revive its glory, they must listen to and care for people's needs. Otherwise, nothing can help them, and the system will continue to decay, leading to its collapse. THE WRITER IS A POLITICAL ECONOMIST AND A VISITING RESEARCH FELLOW AT HEBEI UNIVERSITY, CHINA

title: Netanyahu rebuked for plan to use crypto to bypass economic sanctions
description: More than 100 ‌economists express alarm, say proposal will lead to higher unemployment, fall in foreign investment
content: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces re-election this week, is drawing criticism from economists and political rivals ​after suggesting Israel could use cryptocurrency to help shield its economy from potential international sanctions. In an interview ‌with Israel's Channel 10 on Friday, Netanyahu said he was preparing for a scenario in which broader sanctions were imposed on Israel. Last month, Britain, France and Canada said they would block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in what was the latest in a series of actions ​targeting Israel's settlement policy, underscoring its growing diplomatic isolation among some of its traditional allies. Read: UK, France and Canada sanction Israeli West Bank settlements, in support for two-state solution "There could be sanctions, ​and sanctions on banks, so you need to set up a bypass economy," Netanyahu said. "You know, ⁠there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that." Netanyahu: They have been trying to impose sanctions on us for three years, and we have blocked every single attempt. We have done so through countermeasures, for example against Britain, when we closed its consulate in Jerusalem, and by bringing back countries that had left… pic.twitter.com/xFsVDnr7b3 — Clash Report (@clashreport) October 24, 2026 Asked whether he was referring to cryptocurrency, Netanyahu replied: "Very ​true, very true," adding that blockchain technology was another possibility. The comments drew a rare rebuke by the Bank of Israel, which said ​cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions and that political leaders should focus on policy that would render such measures unnecessary. "The right course for Israel's economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners, and to focus on preventing sanctions and ​their negative impact on the economy," it said. Netanyahu on Sunday continued to defend his record, urging voters to back him and ​saying he and US President Donald Trump had two years left to work together to topple Iran's rulers. Plan draws criticism On Sunday, more than 100 ‌economists, including ⁠former Bank of Israel officials, ex-central bank governor Jacob Frenkel and several Nobel laureates, signed a letter expressing alarm over Netanyahu's proposal. They said it would lead to higher unemployment, a fall in foreign investment and the collapse of Israel's economic standing in the world. Israel central bank rejects Netanyahu’s plan to use crypto to evade sanctions https://t.co/n21BLVfiOE — Financial Times (@FT) October 24, 2026 "As we have seen in countries that have suffered similar sanctions, such as South Africa, Iran, and Russia, the ​living standards of Israeli citizens ​would plummet dramatically, and ⁠the state's ability to finance its security and defend itself against its enemies would be severely damaged," the letter read. "Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic ​isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one ​accepted in criminal ⁠organisations, that will not help in the slightest." Netanyahu's main rival in Tuesday's election, Gadi Eisenkot, called the crypto plan "madness" and said he feared that the "BibiCoin policy" would drive companies abroad and undermine national security. Read More: Opposition leader says Netanyahu ‘no longer fit’ to lead Israel Opposition leader Yair Lapid said: "Netanyahu has gone off the rails ... He promised the citizens of Israel before these elections that they'll be standing in line for ​an hour and a half for bread, like in Russia and Iran." Opinion polls point to a potential stalemate in the election, with neither Netanyahu's ruling coalition ​nor an opposition alliance securing a governing majority in parliament.

title: Putin says accusations of Russia provoking European protests are ‘clear overkill’
description: Says allegation points to 'weakness and inability' of some leaders in European countries to take responsibility
content: Russian President Vladimir Putin called accusations that Russia was provoking mass protests in major European cities a “clear overkill.” Speaking in an interview with the VGTRK broadcasting company published on Sunday, Putin said he was surprised that the initial reaction in Europe was not anti-Russian but anti-American. “Claims immediately began to be thrown out that the events taking place in Europe are the result of the activities of the current American administration and its support for right-wing parties and movements,” he said. Read: Kremlin dismisses allegations of Russia's involvement in Europe unrest Putin said that was “strange and completely unexpected” to him, as he did not expect European leaders to attack “their main ally and protector, so to speak, in the military sense of the word, across the ocean.” “But they quickly came to their senses and switched to their traditional accusations against the Russian Federation,” he said. Blaming Russia for all mortal sins as is happening now, amidst the mass unrest in European countries, has become a standard practice for the West, Vladimir Putin told Vesti reporter Pavel Zarubin:https://t.co/zJnAK3SlsY pic.twitter.com/BkPionkaiz — TASS (@tassagency_en) October 25, 2026 The president added: “There is nothing unexpected here. As is known, Russia has always been accused of all mortal sins. But now I am ready to respond.” Putin said claims that Moscow was provoking mass demonstrations in major European cities are an obvious exaggeration even to ordinary citizens of European countries. “My first reaction when I saw this was surprise, because to say that we are provoking mass protests in major European cities is a clear overkill, which, in my opinion, is obvious to ordinary citizens of European countries,” he noted. “Nevertheless, they have now taken this well-trodden and worn-out path, and we see some accusations against Russia,” he added. Putin said this points to “the weakness and inability of some leaders in European countries to take responsibility for what is happening.” “This is bad. Why? Because it means they do not analyse the events, do not look for the causes of what is happening, but simply shift the blame onto someone, first the US, now Russia,” he said. Nationwide student protests have been underway in France for several weeks. Read More: France deploys 70,000 police to try to contain nationwide protests French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, speaking at an OECD-hosted conference on October 21, accused protesters of using “hostile narratives” from Russia, China, Iran and the MAGA community. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on October 19 that nobody takes such “absurd accusations” seriously. US President Donald Trump had blamed the unrest on mass migration.

title: Apple's iPhone Duo faces early durability concerns as users report cracked screens
description: Owners report inner-display cracks near hinge within hours of purchase, raising questions about phone's reliability
content: Apple’s first foldable iPhone is facing early durability concerns after owners reported cracks in the inner display near the hinge, in some cases within hours of purchase. Photographs shared on Reddit and technology forums show cracks along the screen’s central fold, with some damaged displays developing bright lines of pixels. However, the cause remains unclear, and the reports do not establish how widespread the problem is. One Australian customer said their iPhone Duo’s display cracked after approximately six hours of ownership and fewer than 20 openings. According to MacRumors, the owner felt something beneath the screen near the hinge while opening the phone to show a friend, followed by an audible crack. The customer reported no visible external damage. Apple initially offered an express replacement, but the owner instead visited an Apple Store and received a replacement device on the spot. Similar images have circulated online, with Tom’s Guide and Digital Trends reporting complaints involving devices in several markets. However, social media posts alone cannot establish a failure rate or confirm that all reported cases share the same cause. The complaints have also drawn attention to the phone’s hinge mechanism and dust resistance. Tom’s Guide covered a durability test by YouTuber JerryRigEverything, which reportedly found dust entering the hinge area. During a subsequent bend test, a green line appeared on the inner display before it stopped responding. The test involved deliberate physical stress and does not establish that the same damage occurs during normal use. The location of the reported cracks has prompted speculation about possible pressure from internal hinge components, manufacturing tolerances or trapped debris. None of these explanations has been confirmed. Users have also taken to X to share their concerns about the device’s durability. In a post on Saturday, Sam Kohl warned against taking the iPhone Duo to the beach, highlighting concerns about the device’s potential vulnerability to environmental elements. The post can be viewed here. Another user, fenibook, reported on Friday that two cases of inner-display failure had already emerged on the phone’s launch day, adding that further reports over the following days would help establish whether the problem was more widespread. The post is available here. Apple had not publicly identified a cause for the reported failures in the coverage reviewed. The complaints have emerged as the iPhone Duo attracts strong interest following its launch. A separate report highlighted strong demand during the phone’s initial sales period, while another noted limited store availability at launch. Supply constraints could complicate replacement arrangements for affected buyers, although there is no evidence linking limited availability to the reported screen damage. For now, the reported failures remain a developing story rather than proof of a widespread defect. More verified cases, technical inspections and an official response from Apple will be needed to determine whether the incidents point to a broader reliability problem.

title: Wall St week ahead earnings flood, Fed meeting will test rickety AI market rally
description: Capital spending from hyperscalers is boosting the bottom lines for a wide swath of companies involved in AI buildout
content: US stock investors face a pivotal week, with corporate earnings reports led by major AI players and a ​Federal Reserve meeting posing critical tests for a suddenly shaky market rally. Weakness in technology shares left investors on edge about the state of the AI trade that ‌has driven the US equity bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary. The Nasdaq Composite posted a slim loss on Friday, a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest daily drop since June. Investors were disappointed by quarterly reports from Meta and Lam Research. Meta is one of the hyperscalers spending massively to build out data centres, while Lam is a high-flying semiconductor company, one of a group that has been among the biggest ​AI stock winners. Read: Among AI crowd, some investors position for slower hyperscaler spending growth Three other hyperscalers, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, headline a packed week of quarterly results, including about one-third of S&P 500 companies. The Fed's interest rate policy meeting ​on Wednesday also could rattle markets. "There are a lot of balls in the air," said Nick Giorgi, chief equity strategist at Alpine Macro. "Next week, ⁠you have a lot more tech earnings, and right now the market is taking a discerning eye as it relates to all the spending that goes along with artificial intelligence," Giorgi ​said. "The market's just not giving the benefit of the doubt to companies that are spending a ton of money on building this all out, which to us is actually very healthy, but still ​does augur for some short-term pain." Investors also have their focus trained on the US midterm elections on November 3, with growing bets that the Democrats will wrest control of the US Congress away from President Donald Trump's Republican party. The series of market catalysts could ratchet up volatility over the next couple of weeks and challenge optimism that has helped lift the benchmark S&P 500 index up 11% in 2026. Hyperscalers on the hot seat Robust US ​profit growth has underpinned the stock market's gains this year in the face of headwinds including spiking Treasury yields and rising energy costs stemming from the Middle East conflict. With more than ​100 companies having posted results so far, third-quarter S&P 500 earnings are on pace to have climbed more than 32% from a year ago, according to LSEG IBES data. Next week is the busiest of the ‌reporting season. "I ⁠think earnings will determine whether this ... tech pullback is a buying opportunity, or is there a deeper correction ahead," said King Lip, chief strategist at BakerAvenue Wealth Management. "What we need is just another round of really strong earnings." Alphabet and Microsoft report on Wednesday. Amazon's results are due on Thursday. Focus will be on the guidance the companies give on capital spending plans and whether they are seeing returns on the massive outlays. Capital spending from hyperscalers, expected to be around $800 billion this year, is boosting the bottom lines for a wide swath of companies involved in the AI buildout. But ​investors are wary of the sustainability of such ​spending amid mounting financing costs. "Earnings are critical ⁠to the overall confidence level of the AI trade and how much longer the spend will continue," said Kevin Mahn, president and chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh Asset Management. Fed expected to pause on rates, for now Quarterly reports next week from chip companies Intel and Sandisk also could influence ​the AI trade. Elsewhere, other high-profile companies set to report next week include drugmaker Eli Lilly, oil majors Exxon and Chevron and industrial equipment ​giant Caterpillar. The prospect for ⁠more interest rate hikes also comes into focus with the Fed meeting. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, in an effort to control above-target inflation, but Fed funds futures late on Friday suggested a less-than-10 % chance the Fed will hike again when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, according to LSEG data. One factor: Investors are dubious that the Fed will want to ⁠increase rates ​just a week before the midterm elections. However, markets are leaning toward a hike at the next meeting in December, ​with futures suggesting a roughly 80% probability of such a move then. Walter Todd, chief investment officer at Greenwood Capital, said he will be watching for any hints about the rate path at Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference following the decision. "Does he ​say something to give an idea about December, because right now the expectation is there is going to be a hike," Todd said.

title: Japan to simulate cyberattacks as PHP flaws roil global internet
description: Cybersecurity experts say AI is helping to make cybercrime faster, ⁠cheaper, harder to detect through task automation
content: Japan said on Friday ​it would set up a team to simulate cyberattacks using AI to identify weaknesses in technology systems as ‌organisations scramble to curtail risks from flaws in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the internet. Government and company websites across the world went offline this week after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the widely used programming language prompted millions of hacking attempts, forcing website operators to rush to protect ​or temporarily shut down their systems. Highlighting the extent of the disruption, Japan's third-largest mobile carrier, SoftBank, said on Friday ​it was suspending its emergency alert system for mobile users. Read: Data of over 10M customers exposed in cyberattacks on Japanese firms Japan is setting up a team to simulate cyberattacks as it scrambles to identify security weaknesses in systems that rely on PHP. https://t.co/9fkwdtPbH3 — The Japan Times (@japantimes) October 24, 2026 That means customers would not receive early warnings ⁠for earthquakes, tsunami alerts or disaster and evacuation information as the system undergoes maintenance to address a PHP vulnerability, SoftBank said. Japan ​is regularly affected by natural disasters and is one of the world's most earthquake-prone countries, with typhoon Champi currently approaching the southernmost prefecture ​of Okinawa. SoftBank, which has more than 30 million smartphone customers, said users could still receive earthquake warnings through services such as an app from its Yahoo business. "An attack can succeed by getting through just one hole ... for that reason it's important we shift our mindset and think from the perspective of ​the attacker," Japanese industry minister Ryosei Akazawa said on Friday. "Defenders also need to make use of AI and respond proactively, staying ​one step ahead." Nobuo Miwa, president of Tokyo-based cybersecurity firm S&J Corp, said the government response was too slow. "This is like trying to take on a ‌bomber ⁠with a bamboo spear," he said. Emergency shutdowns this week from Tokyo to Helsinki of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services marked one of the most dramatic tests of the decades-old programming tools that keep the web running. Companies including brokerage Nomura, lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, airline ANA and East Japan Railway (JR East) temporarily suspended some internet services as part of emergency measures. Japan's Ministry of Finance, National Tax ​Agency and Meteorological Agency also ​suspended some online services. On Friday, ⁠JR East said some group services had resumed while others would be restored once confirmed safe. Nippon Paint said it had applied a security patch as a precaution and its website is back ​online. Attackers are likely targeting Japanese businesses for their thorough records, which are no longer protected by ​a language barrier ⁠because of AI, said Eva Chen, CEO of Trend Micro. Read More: Japan passes 'Active cyber defense' taking effect from 2027 Japan has been too comfortable with its existing infrastructure, which it felt was safe enough, she said. Cybersecurity experts have said AI is helping attackers automate tasks from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, ⁠cheaper, and ​harder to detect. The developers of PHP released fixes on Wednesday for vulnerabilities that had ​lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using AI. They urged users to "update immediately".

title: PHP foundation 'under-funded' with one full-time staff member, director says
description: Recent events show how heavily companies, governments rely on PHP, which underpins up to 70% of sites globally
content: The discovery of two ​serious flaws in PHP this week set off a global scramble to ‌keep websites safe from hackers, showing just how critical the three-decade-old open-source programming language is to the internet. Yet the nonprofit foundation that supports PHP, which may underpin up to 70% of sites globally, operates on ​a shoestring budget. “We have one full-time staff member (that's me) and 14 mostly ​part-time contractors,” Executive Director Elizabeth Barron of the PHP Foundation said via ⁠email in an interview on Friday. Board members are unpaid volunteers, and funding ​comes from donations and grants. Read: Millions of hacking attempts as companies, governments rush to patch PHP flaws The foundation works with outside researchers and companies, including OpenAI ​and cybersecurity firms Wiz and Calif, to investigate security flaws and coordinate fixes, including Wednesday's patches. While Web security company Cloudflare has reported millions of hacking attempts, Barron said the foundation had no ​evidence hackers were able to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were disclosed, or ​on sites that have been patched. "We received no further indication from OpenAI, Wiz or Calif, with ‌whom ⁠we're working closely on this issue, regarding any issues on patched systems,” she said. Artificial intelligence has proved both a help and a burden to the foundation. It helped researchers find the flaws, which had been present for a decade, and Barron ​said it made programmers ​more efficient. However, it ⁠is also increasing maintainers' workloads. The PHP project is receiving nearly twice as many proposed code changes as a year ago, “yet ​the number of contributors hasn't doubled,” she said. Reviewing contributions ​and bug ⁠reports requires “a massive amount of human input and experience.” Read More: Government websites in Europe, elsewhere go dark as software flaw sparks security scramble Recent events have shown how heavily companies and governments rely on PHP, Barron said. “Given that reliance, it is clear that PHP ⁠is incredibly underfunded.”

title: Bill Gates warns of 20 years of turmoil from artificial intelligence
description: Microsoft co-founder says AI could disrupt jobs, reshape society even under best-case scenario
content: Bill Gates warned that artificial intelligence could trigger two decades of economic and social upheaval, disrupting jobs and life even if the technology is managed successfully. In an interview with the Decoder podcast posted Thursday, the Microsoft co-founder said the transition to an AI-driven economy would create winners and losers, potentially reshaping employment and raising questions about people's roles in society. "My big concern is this 20-year transition period, where they'll have winners and losers and a lot of disruption," said Gates, 70, adding that society would have to navigate the upheaval before potentially entering an era of abundance. Read: 3 in 5 AI models fail terrorism safety tests: Study He described the timeframe as an estimate rather than a firm prediction, acknowledging that the transition could be shorter or longer depending on technological advances and decisions about slowing development. Gates said advances in AI and humanoid robotics could eventually allow machines to perform much of the physical labour carried out by humans, including building homes, growing food, and even performing surgery. While the advances could reduce shortages of goods and services, he suggested societies might deliberately reserve certain activities for humans, including childcare, food preparation, arts, and sports. Read More: Global financial watchdog calls for more human oversight of agentic AI The billionaire philanthropist also highlighted AI's potential benefits in healthcare and agriculture but warned that governments and society are not adequately prepared for its rapid development. He urged stronger government oversight and technical safeguards against cyberattacks and biological threats, arguing that AI companies alone cannot be responsible for managing the risks. Gates also warned that even under the most favourable circumstances, AI's development could bring one of the most tumultuous periods in human history. "I hate being the bearer of concerning news on this, but it's even worse not to tell people that this is coming. We have choices as humans to make about how we shape it," he said.

title: Shadab puts Pakistan in tri-series final
description: Seasoned all-rounder hits maiden century to inspire hosts to one-wicket victory over England
content: Shadab Khan eventually lived up to the expectations as he hit his maiden century to put Pakistan in the final when they conquered England by one wicket in a crucial ODI tri-series clash at the Gaddafi Stadium Lahore on Sunday. Set to chase 242, Pakistan were reeling at 154-9 in the 34th over and there was no hope of a resurrection. However, Shadab engineered a stunning knock, hitting unbeaten 113 off 96 balls to steer the hosts to unbelievable victory with 17 balls to spare. Shadab hammered five sixes and 13 fours in his first century of his career. He dominated an 89-run tenth wicket unbroken stand with Haris Rauf, who remained not out on seven which came off 19 balls. The 89-run unbeaten tenth wicket partnership between Shadab and Haris is the highest in a successful ODI chase, surpassing Deryck Murray and Andy Roberts' previous record of an unbeaten 64 for West Indies against Pakistan in the 1975 World Cup. Jamie Overton was the pick of the bowlers with 3-43 while Gus Atkinson and Liam Dawson claimed two wickets each. Set to chase 242, Pakistan suffered a lengthy collapse. The hosts kept losing wickets at regular intervals Green-shirts got off to a shaky start as Gus Atkinson and debutant Henry Crocombe struck early to put them under immediate pressure. Fakhar Zaman departed for ten off 18 balls, caught by Jamie Overton off Atkinson, before Crocombe dismissed Saim Ayub for six, also caught by Overton. Atkinson then removed Babar Azam for ten, bowled, leaving Pakistan struggling at 31-3 inside seven overs. Stumper Saad Baig briefly revived hopes of a recovery with an aggressive innings of 32 off just 22 balls, striking seven fours. His attacking approach helped Pakistan move forward, but Jamie Overton ended the counterattack by having him caught by Will Jacks to leave Pakistan reeling at 74-4. Salman Agha and Hasan Nawaz attempted to rebuild the innings through a more cautious partnership. Salman made 26 from 49 deliveries while Hasan scored 15 off 33 balls. Liam Dawson broke through by dismissing Hasan, caught by Harry Brook, before Overton removed Arafat Minhas for one, caught by Joe Root. Pakistan slipped to 103-6, with pressure mounting. Salman became Dawson’s second victim when he was caught by Sam Curran for 26, reducing Pakistan to 122-7. Overton then claimed his third wicket by dismissing Shaheen Afridi as Pakistan fell to 131-8. Will Jacks then removed Razaullah (8) and now there was no such hope left. But Shadab had thought otherwise to gift a sensational win to the hosts. Earlier, Ben Duckett struck his fifth one-day international century to take England to a seemingly good total. Duckett scored 105 off 111 balls, including ten fours and two sixes, anchoring England's innings after they lost three wickets for 19 runs inside the first five overs. Tom Banton fell for four, Joe Root scored five and captain Harry Brook was run out for one as Pakistan made an early breakthrough with the new ball. Duckett rebuilt the innings alongside Sam Curran, who contributed 42 off 52 deliveries. The pair added 126 runs for the fifth wicket before Curran was dismissed by Shaheen Shah Afridi for 42. Duckett reached his century off 104 balls, but Pakistan struck regularly in the latter stages to prevent England from building a commanding total. Shaheen finished with 4-46 from 8.4 overs, also reaching the milestone of 150 ODI wickets. Left-arm spinner Arafat Minhas claimed 2-26, while debutant Razaullah also took two wickets, conceding 38 runs in eight overs. Razaullah marked his ODI debut with the dismissals of Will Jacks, who scored 13, and Liam Dawson, who made five. Gus Atkinson provided a late contribution with an unbeaten 36 off 28 balls, including three sixes, but England were dismissed with 20 balls remaining. The third straight loss put England on the brink of elimination. Earlier Pakistan opted to field first after they won toss. Pakistan made two changes, bringing in Shadab Khan in place of Faheem Ashraf. Fast bowler Razaullah will make his ODI debut as he has replaced Naseem Shah whose left hand finger has dislocated. But skipper Shaheen Afridi said that he would be fit for the next game against Sri Lanka. England made one change, bringing in Henry Crocombe in place of Josh Tongue. Henry will make his international debut as a fast bowler. Pakistan have won their previous two matches and they need just one win to qualify for the final.

title: Agha returns as Pakistan unveil Test squad
description: A host of youngsters earn maiden call-ups as several senior players face the axe for SL series
content: Pakistan on Saturday unveiled an initial 14-member squad for their two-match home Test series against Sri Lanka with three players earning maiden call-ups and several players from the recent England tour were left out. Babar Azam will continue as captain for the ICC World Test Championship series, which will be played in Rawalpindi and Lahore from November 9 to 21. Left-handed batsman Mohammad Taha and Mohammad Suleman, along with promising batsman Sameer Minhas have received their maiden call-ups following impressive performances in domestic cricket. Taha, 26, is the leading run-scorer in the ongoing President’s Trophy Grade-I first-class tournament, having amassed 730 runs in seven matches, including three centuries with 225 being his highest score. Suleman has scored 652 runs in the same competition, also hitting three centuries, while Sameer has made 405 runs in seven matches during his maiden first-class season after impressing with Pakistan’s Under-19 side. Ten players from Pakistan’s England tour have been omitted from the initial squad: They include Aamir Jamal, Imam-ul-Haq, Khurram Shahzad, Mohammad Ali, Mohammad Rizwan, Muhammad Awais Zafar, Sajid Khan, Shan Masood, Abdullah Shafique and Ubaid Shah. However, Ubaid has been included in the 13-member PCB Patron’s XI squad for a three-day side match against Sri Lanka from November 4 to 6 at the Islamabad Club. The selectors will add two fast bowlers from the warm-up squad to the Test team after the match, with the final pace combination to be decided following the practice fixture. Saad Baig will captain the Patron’s XI. Six members of the initial Test squad will also get an opportunity to face Sri Lanka in the warm-up match. Test squad: Babar Azam (captain), Abdullah Fazal, Ali Usman, Arafat Minhas, Azan Awais, Mohammad Abbas, Mohammad Ghazi Ghori (wk), Mohammad Suleman, Mohammad Taha, Razaullah, Saad Baig (wk), Salman Ali Agha, Sameer Minhas, Saud Shakeel Patron’s XI: Saad Baig (captain, wk), Abdullah Fazal, Ali Shabbir, Ali Usman, Azan Awais, Mohammad Salman, Mohammad Suleman, Mohammad Tayyab Arif, Mohammad Taha, Saqib Khan, Sameer Minhas, Shoaib Akhtar Junior, Ubaid Shah

title: Spurs seal rare win at Chelsea as Palmer sees red
description: The Blues fall to their first home defeat against Tottenham since 2018
content: Tottenham clinched a Premier League win at Chelsea for just the second time in 36 years as a woeful own goal from Blues keeper Mike Penders was followed by Cole Palmer's red card in Saturday's 2-0 victory. Roberto De Zerbi's side clinched their second successive league win thanks to Penders's howler in the second half at a rain-lashed Stamford Bridge. Chelsea forward Palmer was sent off for a second booking moments later before Mathys Tel produced a superb solo effort to condemn the Blues to their first home defeat against Tottenham since 2018. Since 1990, Tottenham had won just once in 41 previous away matches against London rivals Chelsea in all competitions. Ending that miserable run gave Tottenham only their second win in their last 16 league games against Chelsea, both home and away, and their first since 2023. After a dismal start to the season, Tottenham have climbed to 12th place after building on Monday's win against Coventry, which ended their wait for a first league win this season. It was a bitter blow for fourth-placed Chelsea, who had beaten Bournemouth and Everton in their previous two league games. They were booed off at full-time and remain very much a work in progress under Xabi Alonso in the Spaniard's first season in charge. With Joao Pedro sidelined by a late injury, Morgan Rogers was Chelsea's central striker, but their revamped attack was short of bite. Teed up by Rogers after Pedro Neto stole possession from Mateus Fernandes, Palmer went close to an early opener with a curler that Antonin Kinsky tipped over at full stretch. Tottenham responded with a spell of probing pressure as Omar Marmoush met Andy Robertson's cross with a shot that was repelled by Penders. Alonso's men pieced together the best move of the half with a flurry of one-touch passes to reach Jordan Henderson on the edge of the area, but the midfielder's low drive was palmed away by Kinsky. Spurs spring a surprise Neto tested Kinsky with a fierce blast but the Tottenham keeper was up to the task with a save at his near post. Tottenham suffered a blow when often-injured midfielder James Maddison limped off in a premature end to only his second start since May 2025. Maddison had already missed training sessions since his long-awaited start against Coventry and his latest fitness setback suggested it was a failed gamble to start him at the Bridge. In keeping with the sloppy fare, Neto fired straight at Kinsky from a dangerous position after Palmer pounced on Sandro Tonali's wayward pass. When Palmer's run was halted by Fernandes's handball, the Chelsea star escaped with a yellow card after barging into his rival with such aggression that the Tottenham midfielder was sent crashing to the sodden turf. Tottenham exacted swift revenge in the 77th minute. Fernandes's in-swinging corner should have been caught by Penders, but he opted for a punch that was completely mistimed as he diverted the ball into his net for a comical own goal. It was a horrible moment for the 21-year-old Penders, who was making his first league start in the absence of Emiliano Martinez following jaw surgery. Rubbing salt into Chelsea's wounds, Palmer was dismissed three minutes later for an ugly stamp on Conor Gallagher. Tel wrapped up Tottenham's memorable triumph in fitting style in the 87th minute, skipping away from Chelsea's flat-footed defence to drill a fine finish into the bottom corner from the edge of the area.

title: Australian MotoGP cancelled due to bad weather
description: Marquez remains 10 points clear of injured rival Jorge Martin
content: Marc Marquez was denied the chance Sunday to stretch his world championship lead over injured Jorge Martin with the last Australian MotoGP at Phillip Island cancelled due to treacherous conditions. Organisers pulled the plug despite a sell-out crowd with persistent rain and poor visibility making racing unsafe. The Moto3 and Moto2 races were also called off. "Limited visibility has resulted in the cancellation of the Australian MotoGP," organisers said. It was an inglorious end to nearly three decades of the sport at the waterfront circuit two hours from Melbourne, with the Australian race moving to a city-centre street circuit at Adelaide next year. While a blow for Ducati's Marquez, it was an escape for Aprilia's Martin, who had been ruled out of the race with a fractured forearm sustained when he crashed during the sprint on Saturday, won by his fellow Spaniard. He risked sliding further behind seven-time world champion Marquez with only four legs of the season to go, starting next week in Malaysia. Instead he will leave Australia just 10 points adrift. Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi is third in the standings, 50 points behind Marquez. Whether Martin can ride at Sepang remains to be seen. His team said in a statement the break was not as bad as initially thought and he would not need to return home to Spain for surgery. "The only confirmed injury is a non-displaced fracture of the distal radius," Aprilia said, meaning the bone remains aligned. "Consequently the rider will not be returning to Spain and will undergo the necessary treatment over the coming days." The picturesque and often windswept Phillip Island track has been a staple on the calendar since 1997. But its contract expires this year. Promoter MotoGP Sports Entertainment wanted to broaden its appeal and shift it to Melbourne's Albert Park, which hosts the Australian Formula One. The Victoria state government was adamant it should remain at Phillip Island. With negotiations breaking down, South Australia stepped in and secured the race for six years from 2027 in Adelaide -- the first MotoGP to be held in a city‑centre location.

title: Fritz to face Musetti in Lyon title match
description: The American defeats Tommy Paul 6-3, 7-5
content: Second-seeded Taylor Fritz drilled 15 aces while overwhelming fellow American Tommy Paul 6-3, 7-5 on Saturday to reach the final at the Grand Prix Auvergne-Rhone-Alpes in Lyon, France. Fritz also saved all nine break points he faced during the strong semifinal performance against the fourth-seeded Paul. Fritz had a ‌32-26 edge in winners and both players committed 21 unforced errors. Fritz will next face sixth-seeded Lorenzo Musetti, who defeated fellow Italian and top seed Flavio Cobolli 4-6, 6-2, 7-5 in the other semifinal. Musetti saved four match points in the final set to hold off Cobolli. He committed just 22 unforced errors compared to 36 for Cobolli. Musetti will be chasing his third ATP title. He is 4-3 all-time ⁠against Fritz and has won four of the past five meetings. Fritz will be aiming for his 12th career ATP crown. BNP Paribas Fortis European Open Germany's Jan-Lennard Struff recorded 15 aces and outlasted top-seeded Arthur Fils of France 6-4, 6-7 (7), 7-6 (5) to reach the final in Brussels. Fils carded 17 aces and saved 7 of 10 break points but could not stop Struff, who won the final two points of the tiebreaker to win the match. Struff had a 43-42 edge in winners and won 18 of 27 points at the net. Struff next faces Dutchman Tallon Griekspoor, who rallied for a 2-6, 6-3, 7-6 (4) victory over No. 3 Francisco Cerundolo of Argentina. Griekspoor ‌had a ⁠9-3 edge in aces and committed 24 unforced errors, nine fewer than Cerundolo. Griekspoor has won all three previous meetings against Struff. He is looking for his fourth ATP title, while Struff is vying to win his second. Almaty Open Top-seeded Russian Daniil Medvedev advanced to his second straight Almaty Open final Saturday when third-seeded Alexander Bublik of Kazakhstan retired with a knee injury ⁠after losing the opening set 6-3. Defending champion Medvedev had a 9-3 edge in aces in the first set as Bublik struggled to move on the court. After the match, Bublik said he injured his knee in his quarterfinal win over Russian ⁠Karen Khachanov on Friday and was advised by doctors not to play shortly before the start of Saturday's match. Medvedev will now face Georgian qualifier Nikoloz Basilashvili, who defeated No. 7 Greek Stefanos Tsitsipas 6-4, 6-7 (5), 6-3 ⁠in his semifinal. Basilashvili had a 35-19 edge in winners while Tsitsipas had an 11-7 advantage in aces. Medvedev won the lone meeting against Basilashvili, winning in the round of 32 in 2022 at Vienna. Medvedev is gunning for his 25th career ATP title while Basilashvili is looking for his sixth.

title: Cheaper house loans a growth driver
description: Gap matters as only 18% of approved subsidised financing reaches borrowers
content: Ask Pakistan's business community about the economy and relief often outweighs confidence. Memories of punishing inflation and currency instability remain fresh, while global wars, energy shocks and domestic political uncertainty cloud investment decisions. Against this backdrop, the push for affordable housing offers a welcome bright spot: an opportunity to generate employment, revive industry and help families acquire their first meaningful asset. Housing combines economic opportunity with a basic human need. The State Bank cites an estimated shortage of 10 million homes, concentrated among lower- and middle-income households. At an October planning review, annual demand was estimated at 700,000 units against supply of approximately 250,000. These estimates are imperfect, but the direction is unmistakable: Pakistan continues to add to an already substantial housing deficit. For a working family, home ownership can offer protection from rising rents, greater financial security and an asset to pass to the next generation. Its social value extends to children's stability, privacy and dignity. Affordable housing policy therefore deserves to be judged by how widely it distributes these benefits. The federal government's Apna Ghar programme provides financing of up to Rs10 million at a fixed customer rate of 5% for the first 10 years with Rs66,000 monthly installment only. The advertised repayment period extends to 30 years, with market-linked pricing after 10 years. Eligible properties include houses up to 10 marla (2,700 square feet) and flats up to 1,500 square feet. This represents meaningful support for households otherwise priced out of mortgage finance. Demand is encouraging. The programme's dashboard reported approximately 191,900 applications and 75,200 approvals as of October 9. An earlier October review reported Rs426 billion in approvals and Rs76 billion in disbursements, alongside a Rs700 billion financing target covering 125,000 homes. The gap matters: only about 18% of the approved amount had reached borrowers. Converting approvals into completed transactions is now the critical delivery challenge. Punjab offers a complementary approach through Apni Chhat Apna Ghar. Its construction loan component provides up to Rs1.5 million interest-free, with the provincial government requiring repayment over nine years at approximately Rs14,000 monthly. It serves eligible owners of small plots – up to five marla in urban areas and 10 marla in rural areas – who need financing to build. This can reach households requiring a modest construction loan, although families without land still need a separate solution. The economic benefits extend well beyond property transactions. The Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26 estimated construction's direct contribution at 2.35% of GDP, with growth of 5.73%. Large-scale manufacturing, separately accounting for 8.17% of GDP, grew 6.11%. Construction creates demand across several manufacturing industries; their contribution should not be confused with, or mechanically added to, construction's direct share. Some cite 19% YoY growth in construction sector in Q1 of FY27.
