Demand travels through the economy in stages: cement, steel and aggregates first; cables, pipes, glass and tiles next; paints, furniture and appliances as homes approach completion. Alongside factories, masons, electricians, plumbers, transporters and small retailers benefit. The finance ministry reported that domestic cement dispatches increased 7-8% during 1QFY27. This indicates improving construction demand, although the increase cannot be attributed entirely to subsidised mortgages. The fiscal connection is also substantial. FBR recorded approximately Rs108.7 billion in domestic sales tax collection from cement alone in FY2025, excluding its other tax contributions. Higher formal production can expand sales, excise and income tax receipts across the supply chain. However, additional revenues must be weighed against subsidy costs; housing finance should not be assumed to pay for itself automatically. International experience provides useful lessons. India's PMAY-U 2.0 combines construction assistance, affordable rental housing and interest subsidies; eligible borrowers receive a 4% subsidy on the first INR800,000 of their loan, subject to programme limits. Indonesia's FLPP offers subsidised mortgages at 5%, with down payments starting at 1%, and explicitly includes informal-income workers. The lesson is to combine affordable credit with housing supply and inclusive eligibility. Pakistan's central challenge is access. A salaried employee can produce payslips; a tailor, driver or electrician with comparable earnings may struggle to prove repayment capacity. SBP's August regulations already require banks to use applicable informal-income assessment models and recognise evidence such as rent payments and utility bills. They also permit general mortgage tenors of up to 30 years and a debt burden ceiling of 65%. These broader limits should not be mistaken for automatic scheme eligibility, or comfortable household affordability. The next phase should therefore prioritise implementation and fairness. Banks should assess verified cash flows, rent payment histories and digital receipts, allow suitable co-borrowers and offer repayment schedules matching irregular earnings. Carefully capped guarantees can support deserving borrowers, while grants, incremental construction and affordable rentals are needed for families unable to sustain a mortgage. Supply must expand alongside credit. Faster approvals, reliable land titles, serviced plots and affordable apartments near employment centres would help prevent subsidies from being absorbed into higher selling prices. Financing an existing home changes ownership; financing additional construction creates new housing supply and a stronger industrial stimulus. Borrowers also need transparent legal, valuation and insurance charges, enforceable processing deadlines and effective complaint channels. Affordability assessments should preserve money for food, education and healthcare and explain potential instalment increases after the subsidy expires. Recovery must follow lawful procedures, with restructuring options for genuine hardship. Finally, publish outcomes by income, gender, district and employment type, alongside disbursements, completed homes, defaults and subsidy costs. Any increase in loan limits should follow evidence that lower-income applicants are being served adequately. Perhaps it is time for assisting with the down payments also at a slightly higher mark-up as "Help to Buy" scheme in the UK. Amid global conflict and economic uncertainty, housing finance is a promising policy success taking shape. Its lasting achievement should be measured in secure homes, productive jobs and broader ownership of wealth. The strongest endorsement will come when workers building Pakistan's homes can afford homes of their own. The writer is an independent economic analyst

title: Hina Javed’s family seeks judicial commission in open letter to Punjab CM
description: Acknowledges domestic employee’s alleged involvement but says evidence concerning Faisal was being ignored
content: The family of Hina Javed, who was found murdered at her home in Rawalpindi's Lalkurti on August 20, on Sunday, demanded an immediate judicial commission to investigate the case, rejecting the findings of a police investigation committee and alleging that evidence relating to the main accused has been overlooked. In an open letter to Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, the family called for an impartial investigation, saying it no longer expected justice through the existing inquiry process. “We do not accept the findings of the investigation committee in the Hina murder case,” the family said, urging the chief minister to take notice of the disregard of evidence concerning accused Faisal Asghar. The family said it had made several unsuccessful attempts to contact CM Maryam directly and had raised its concerns about the police investigation committee through various forums and government representatives. It also called on the chief minister to review the case file in detail and ensure that no accused person was protected. The family raised questions about the handling of forensic evidence, alleging that DNA had been found on Hina’s neck belonging to Faisal and his father. It also said Hina’s father-in-law had initially reported a burglary at the house. Forensic reports concerning the mobile phones of Hina and the accused were still pending, the family said, adding that important messages had been deleted from her phone. It alleged that investigators had shifted their focus towards the domestic employee before the forensic reports and fingerprint results had been received. While acknowledging the domestic employee’s alleged involvement in the murder, the family said evidence concerning Faisal was being ignored. “The intensity of the violence inflicted on Hina and the mutilation of her body reflect the extent of the hatred,” the letter said. The family also questioned the police investigation committee's authority to determine guilt or innocence before the case reached court. “Whether a person is guilty or innocent is for the court to decide,” it said, adding that conducting an investigation and delivering a verdict through the same process created a conflict of interest. The family urged the Punjab CM to intervene in her capacity as chief minister and as a woman, recalling her previous position that violence and abuse against women were a red line. It called for all those responsible to be held accountable under the law and for no accused person to receive protection. In a separate statement on social media on Sunday, CM Maryam said the investigation into Hina’s murder had not been completed and pledged to ensure justice for the family. “We will leave no stone unturned to ensure justice in the Hina murder case,” she said, adding that she would meet the family personally. Read: Hina Javed’s autopsy reveals brutal torture Earlier, Police arrested her husband, Faisal, and domestic worker Zeeshan Arshad in connection with the murder. Investigators conducted DNA and polygraph examinations of both suspects at the Punjab Forensic Science Agency as part of efforts to establish their possible roles in the crime. On September 30, the Punjab government constituted a three-member high-powered committee, headed by Additional Inspector General of the Crime Control Department Sohail Zafar Chattha, to review the investigation after receiving forensic reports. The committee subsequently launched a fresh investigation, examining forensic evidence, visiting the crime scene and reviewing possible shortcomings in the earlier police probe. Meanwhile, the victim's family has repeatedly expressed dissatisfaction with the investigation and demanded the formation of a judicial commission to ensure an independent and transparent inquiry. In the latest development, an autopsy report revealed extensive injuries on Hina's body, including a broken neck, a deep wound to the back of her head, and multiple signs of violence. The case has also reached the National Assembly Standing Committee on Interior, which has summoned senior Punjab police officials for a briefing scheduled for October 29. The investigation remains ongoing, and the allegations against the suspects are subject to judicial determination.

title: Kundi says K-P cannot function without Centre's cooperation
description: Calls for joint anti-terror efforts, rule of law, and revolution in education, health
content: Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Governor Faisal Karim Kundi on Sunday said improved relations with the federal government were a welcome development for the province, stressing that K-P could not function without the centre’s cooperation. Speaking to the media after attending a gathering in Swabi, the governor said the province’s problems could only be resolved through joint efforts with the federal government. Promoting cordial and brotherly relations with the federation and other provinces was among his top priorities, he added. Kundi said six months was a long period and stressed that all stakeholders must work together through coordinated action to combat terrorism. Read: K-P to get Rs160b package from Centre He also called for action against encroachments without discrimination and strictly in accordance with the law, pledging to apply the law to himself first. The governor said the media had every right to offer constructive criticism, adding that positive criticism helped improve institutional performance. He underscored the need for a revolution in education and health, as well as far-reaching measures to improve institutions and provide better facilities to the public.

title: Seven killed as passenger jeep plunges into ravine near Muzaffarabad
description: Driver lost control while navigating difficult stretch of road
content: Seven people, including two children, were killed when a passenger jeep fell into a deep ravine in Shakar Patiyan, on the outskirts of Muzaffarabad, Radio Pakistan reported. According to rescue officials, the jeep, which was carrying grass, was travelling from Shakar Patiyan to Siri Dara when the driver lost control while navigating a difficult stretch of road, causing the vehicle to plunge into the ravine. Rescue teams faced severe difficulties in reaching the accident site because of the difficult terrain. The authorities later confirmed the deaths of all seven occupants, including the driver, Abdul Waheed. The incident came a day after four children from the same family were killed and four others injured when a van carrying them to a religious school plunged into a deep ravine in Azad Jammu and Kashmir's Neelum Valley. The van plunged nearly 500 metres into the ravine, killing three children on the spot and injuring four others. One of the injured children later died at the District Headquarters Hospital in Athmuqam, police confirmed.

title: ECP proposes 12 amendments to regulate AI, curb misuse in elections
description: Draft rules seek to regulate AI use by political parties, media and election observers, prohibit deceptive deepfakes
content: The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) proposed 12 amendments to the 2023 codes of conduct for political parties, media organisations and election observers to curb the misuse of artificial intelligence (AI) during elections. According to sources in the ECP, the draft amendments proposed five changes to the code of conduct for media organisations, five for political parties and candidates, and three for election observers. The commission has sought public and stakeholder feedback on the proposed amendments by Nov 20, with the measures aimed at regulating AI-generated content, prohibiting deceptive deepfakes and ensuring transparency in election-related communication. Read: AI able to manipulate elections worldwide, expert says Under the proposed rules for media, outlets would be required to clearly disclose when content generated or modified through AI is broadcast, published or released. The draft strictly prohibits the use of deepfake technology to create fabricated images, voices or statements of political party leaders, candidates, election officials, members of the judiciary, armed forces personnel and other state officials if the content is false, defamatory or intended to ridicule them. Media organisations would be permitted to use AI tools for preparing, translating, presenting or analysing election-related content, provided they disclose such use to their audiences and remain responsible for the authenticity and accuracy of the material. The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA), the Social Media Protection and Regulatory Authority, and the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency would monitor undisclosed or unlabeled AI-generated media content and report violations to the ECP, with appropriate action to be taken in cases of non-compliance. The proposed amendments also require media houses to promptly remove misleading or undisclosed AI-generated content from their platforms, or correctly relabel it, when directed by a regulatory body or the ECP. For election observers, three amendments have been proposed, requiring them to remain vigilant for AI-related manipulation during the observation process and immediately report any such instances to the ECP. The draft also bars observers from using AI to generate, alter or enhance their observations, factual findings, photographs, videos or reports submitted to the commission. Five amendments have been proposed for political parties and candidates to regulate their use of AI-generated material during election campaigns. Under the proposed provisions, political parties and candidates would not be allowed to create, publish, broadcast or distribute AI-generated or manipulated content, including deepfake images, videos and audio clips, without clearly labelling it as AI-generated. The draft prohibits the use of AI-generated material intended to deceive voters by falsely portraying a person’s image, words or actions. It also bars the creation of fabricated, ridiculing or defamatory images, voices or statements of political leaders, candidates, election officials, members of the judiciary, armed forces personnel and other state officials through deepfake technology. Political parties and candidates would be required to preserve all AI-generated content produced during the election process. The proposed rules further prohibit the use of AI-powered bots, automated accounts and similar tools to manipulate online engagement or create fake trends. The use of AI for voter outreach through robocalls or voice-cloned messages would also be regulated, with a clear disclosure at the beginning of each call or message that the content has been generated through AI. The proposed amendments aim to strengthen transparency and accountability in election campaigning and media coverage while addressing the risks posed by fabricated digital content and AI-driven voter manipulation.

title: FinMin seeks to allay fuel shortage fears
description: Aurangzeb says country's energy supplies stable, admits shortcomings in meeting gas, LNG demand
content: Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Saturday said Pakistan's crude oil and other energy supplies remained satisfactory despite escalating regional conflicts, seeking to allay concerns over a possible fuel crisis after lawmakers raised questions in the Senate about petroleum availability through December and the country's preparedness for further disruptions. However, he acknowledged that additional measures would be needed to meet domestic gas and liquefied natural gas (LNG) requirements. Addressing a ceremony at a private university in Lahore, Aurangzeb said Pakistan had so far avoided energy shortages, queues at petrol pumps and law-and-order problems arising from an energy crisis. He said arrangements were in place to meet energy requirements until November, while preparations for the winter were continuing amid uncertainty over regional supplies. His remarks followed Friday's Senate debate, during which Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) Senator Sherry Rehman questioned whether petrol would remain available through December as the conflict in the Middle East intensified. She called on the petroleum and energy ministers to brief parliament on contingency plans, including the possibility of rationing, and warned that disruptions to energy supply routes could have serious implications for Pakistan's energy security and economic stability. Rehman also highlighted the country's dependence on imported liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), saying around 70 per cent of its requirements were met through imports and 30 per cent through domestic production. Pakistan had received five LPG cargoes last year, while only two were expected this year, she told the Senate, demanding that the government present a clear supply plan. Opposition leader Raja Nasir Abbas also warned that the widening regional conflict, stretching from Iran to Yemen, threatened key maritime chokepoints and could aggravate Pakistan's energy difficulties. He pointed to an existing LPG shortage and flour shortages in Punjab, criticising political leaders for focusing on power struggles instead of public concerns. He also called on Pakistan to mediate between Yemen and Saudi Arabia. Responding to concerns over fuel affordability in the Senate, Minister of State for Finance and Revenue Bilal Azhar Kayani had maintained that there was no fuel supply problem and said more than 10 million people were benefiting from targeted fuel subsidies. He said motorcyclists were receiving Rs500 worth of free petrol per week, while owners of vehicles with engine capacities of up to 800cc were receiving Rs1,000 in relief on 10 litres of petrol. Assistance was also being provided to rickshaw and loader operators and users of small cars. Aurangzeb said the government had taken effective measures to secure energy purchases and supplies despite regional conflicts. While the arrangements currently in place were sufficient to meet requirements until November, he acknowledged that further steps were necessary to address gas and LNG needs, with planning for the winter still under way. Targeted relief reaches millions The finance minister said the government had opted for targeted subsidies instead of general subsidies to ensure that relief reached those who needed it most. Under the scheme, assistance had been extended to motorcyclists, users of three-wheelers and owners of vehicles with engine capacities below 800cc. Aurangzeb said 12 million unique individuals had benefited from the scheme so far, while the total number of people benefiting from the relief was estimated at 40 million to 50 million. Aurangzeb also highlighted improvements in Pakistan's economic indicators, saying information technology (IT) export services had grown from $1 billion to $4.6 billion. IT exports were expected to reach $5.5 billion during the current fiscal year, he added. He said Pakistan's foreign exchange reserves had reached a record high and were sufficient to cover more than three months of imports. In contrast, he recalled, reserves in the past had fallen to a level sufficient to finance just two weeks of imports. Aurangzeb said Pakistan's credit rating had improved three times since April last year, while significant steps had been taken to restore access to international financial markets. The minister said Pakistan had undertaken a private placement in April this year, accessed international markets through the issuance of a Panda bond and issued bonds worth three billion euros in the first week of September. He said orders received from investors for Pakistan's Eurobonds were twice the amount issued, reflecting interest from investors in Asia, the Middle East, Europe and the United States. Aurangzeb said international investors were increasingly assessing Pakistan's economic outlook beyond its current programme with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which is scheduled to conclude in October next year. He maintained that Pakistan's economic stabilisation was being accompanied by structural reforms and that the process had moved beyond planning into implementation.

title: High fuel prices add to households' woes
description: Poultry retailers in Lahore charge above official rates
content: Rising fuel prices, food costs and transport fares are adding to the financial strain on households in the country, with petrol prices increasing 26.11% and high-speed diesel 26.39% in the first nearly four months of FY2026-27. Petrol prices rose to Rs377.71 per litre on October 24 from Rs299.50 on July 1, an increase of Rs78.21 per litre, according to available price records. High-speed diesel climbed to Rs393.66 per litre from Rs311.47 over the same period, an increase of Rs82.19. Higher fuel costs are also increasing expenses for passenger transport, freight operators and the movement of agricultural produce, adding to pressure on household budgets and supply chains. The price index for 51 essential commodities rose about 5.81% between July 2 and October 22, according to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics' weekly Sensitive Price Indicator (SPI), adding to the pressure on salaried workers, daily-wage earners, pensioners and low-income families. The fresh surge in food and fuel prices squeezed household budgets across major cities as chicken is being sold for as much as Rs700 per kilogram, beef for Rs1,500 per kilogram in Karachi and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) has become Rs150 per kilogram more expensive. The rising costs have also pushed up transport fares and raised the prospect of a Rs5 to Rs10 increase in the price of roti from next week, while consumers complain that authorities have failed to curb profiteering and provide relief. In Karachi, soaring food prices have made it increasingly difficult for low- and middle-income households to afford even two meals a day. Chicken prices have risen by as much as Rs200 per kilogram during the current month, taking the price of chicken meat to Rs700 per kilogram. Consumers say beef and mutton were already beyond their purchasing power, and chicken has now become increasingly unaffordable as well. Beef is being sold in the open market for Rs1,200 per kilogram with bones and between Rs1,400 and Rs1,500 without bones. Heifer meat is available for Rs1,400 per kilogram with bones and between Rs1,600 and Rs1,700 without bones. Consumers say meat is not available anywhere at the government-notified rates, while shopkeepers openly violate official price limits with little fear of action. Flour prices have also added to the pressure on household budgets. 2.5-number flour is selling for Rs150 per kilogram, while flour milled at traditional stone mills, commonly known as 'chakki atta', costs Rs180 per kilogram. Cooking oil has reached Rs600 per litre, following an increase of Rs40 per litre in the prices of edible oil and ghee over the past month. Meanwhile, an increase of up to Rs150 per kilogram in LPG prices over the past week has further aggravated the cost-of-living crisis. The higher fuel costs have also led to increases in fares charged by rickshaws, taxis and Qingqi three-wheeled motorcycles. Tandoor operators have warned that they may raise the price of roti by Rs5 to Rs10 from next week if LPG prices do not come down. Bakery owners are also preparing to increase prices, citing higher gas costs and rising prices of flour and refined flour. Buns, rusks, sliced bread, biscuits and other bakery products are among the items whose prices are being raised. Vegetable prices remain high in Karachi. Onions are selling for between Rs160 and Rs180 per kilogram, tomatoes for Rs100, carrots for Rs150, cucumbers for Rs100, peas for Rs400, okra for Rs250, round gourds for Rs300, bottle gourd and ridge gourd for Rs160, and spinach for Rs100 per kilogram. Consumers complain that there is no effective check on rampant inflation, that official price lists are absent from markets and that profiteers are operating freely. They say the government has failed to provide relief from rising prices. Similarly, in Lahore, the government-notified price of broiler chicken meat has reached Rs577 per kilogram, but retailers are selling it for Rs600 per kilogram, in violation of the official rate. The district administration has been unable to prevent the overcharging. Meanwhile, consumers in Rawalpindi and Islamabad are facing further increases in chicken and egg prices following earlier rises in the cost of vegetables, fruit, pulses, flour and gram flour. In the open market, live chicken is selling for Rs450 per kilogram, chicken meat for Rs700 per kilogram and boneless chicken for Rs1,000 per kilogram. Broiler eggs are priced at Rs265 per dozen, while local desi eggs are selling for Rs600 per dozen, adding to the difficulties faced by consumers.

title: Give diplomacy a chance
description: Only a sustained dialogue process can lead to a new consensus
content: Diplomats are huddling for a cause. They want to save the region, especially the Middle East, from once again becoming a theater of warfare. The absence of a firm word from the United States that it will not embark on a misadventure, coupled with its dubious signals that it wants to settle scores with Iran, has kept global peace on tenterhooks. Thus, the huddle in Istanbul of foreign ministers from Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia (the R4), along with their counterparts from France, Germany, Italy and the UK, was a serious and highly appreciated attempt toward de-escalating the situation. The Makkah Agreement and the Badr Pact are acting as necessary defensive shields to ward off crises and provide a source of strength. Keeping an eye on jingoism from the Houthis, as well as Israel, is a sine qua non for preserving the prevailing, uneasy peace. These two actors are unpredictable and possess the disruptive capacity to derail the CBMs that are being worked out in all sincerity. At the same time, it is necessary for Washington and Tehran to return to the table and proceed unconditionally with implementing the Islamabad MoU. Bickering over long-term issues, such as the future regional order and the nuclear riddle, will surely act as a distraction. The need of the hour is to ensure that there is no return to war, and that the two cardinal geo-economic maritime routes - the Bab-El-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz - remain open. Development bodies fear a recession, and the IMF foresees a 1.7% contraction in global growth. This can only be warded off by working together toward a broad-based peace agenda, and the meeting in Türkiye was a step in the right direction. It's time to give diplomacy a chance. Only a sustained dialogue process can lead to a new consensus, paving the way to address regional conflicts that have long acted as a spanner in the wheels of peace. Resolving the Palestinian dispute must remain on the agenda if a perpetual peace accord is to be attained in the region.

title: A prescription for shortages
description: Domestic pharmaceutical industry is having its own problems
content: A commonly used insulin product is in short supply across Pakistan, after its German manufacturer halted supplies for a year-long factory upgrade. The supply disruption has wreaked havoc for people with chronic illnesses that require imported medicines. Supplies of the rapid-acting insulin have fallen from 3,500 kits to just 1,000, and the health ministry concedes that the disruption - which is also affecting Asia, Australia and Europe - may worsen. The government has reassured that alternative insulin products made by other big-name foreign companies are available, but while this statement is true, the competing brands also cost at least 20% more, and could also face supply headaches, since there is a global shortage. Also important is that even switching medicine brands for a while could negatively affect patients. It is also worth noting that last year, the Pakistan Medical Association warned that at least 80 essential medicines had become unavailable, including drugs for cancer, diabetes and cardiovascular disease. The main factors for the delay appear to be financial policy, supply disruptions and domestic policy paralysis. Around 40 newly registered life-saving medicines remain in regulatory limbo because the federal government has delayed approving their retail prices, while 105 hardship-category medicines have had their price cases frozen for over two and a half years, forcing manufacturers to halt production. At the same time, the domestic pharmaceutical industry is having its own problems, as drug makers continue to push back on price controls. The government must get ahead of the curve by expediting price approvals for essential medicines, improving stock monitoring and communicating transparently with suppliers and the public. In the long term, Pakistan cannot remain wholly dependent on imported insulin analogues. Local production and diversified supply chains deserve serious investment. A medicine's availability on official registers means little when a patient cannot find it - or afford it - at the neighbourhood pharmacy.

title: Untreated wastewater
description: Unchecked discharge of hazardous effluents carries serious consequences for the environment
content: Sindh's failure to treat wastewater has become a glaring example of administrative neglect. Untreated waste is being discharged from multiple locations across the province. Particularly alarming is the state of Karachi's wastewater treatment infrastructure. According to former Supreme Court judge Amir Hani Muslim, only one of the city's four treatment plants is partially functional. This is an unacceptable situation for a metropolis that generates hundreds of millions of gallons of sewage daily. Unchecked discharge of hazardous effluents carries serious consequences for the environment. Industrial chemicals and toxic substances can contaminate soil, damage fragile ecosystems and threaten biodiversity. Decomposing sewage creates unhygienic conditions and exposes nearby communities to disease. Equally concerning is the improper disposal of medical waste, which often ends up mixed with ordinary municipal refuse because hospitals lack adequate disposal facilities. A major concern is the limited capacity of existing treatment plants, many of which remain dysfunctional or operate well below their intended capacity. Rapid urbanisation and industrial expansion have considerably increased the volume of wastewater generated, yet corresponding investments in treatment infrastructure have failed to keep pace. The result is an overburdened system in which untreated sewage and industrial effluents are routinely disposed of without adequate safeguards. Weak monitoring and inconsistent enforcement have allowed these practices to persist. The problem has persisted for years, largely because wastewater management has received neither the investment nor the administrative attention it requires. The provincial government must undertake a comprehensive assessment of existing treatment plants and prioritise their rehabilitation alongside the development of additional facilities. Hospitals, meanwhile, must be held accountable for the segregation and safe disposal of hazardous medical waste. Authorities must also ensure that industries operate functional treatment facilities and comply with prescribed standards.

title: The reverse renaissance?
description: People and groups possess a righteousness of their own shade
content: For millennia, the human quest and consciousness have centred on evolving ways, tenets and actions that refine the state of nature. These efforts impose necessary restraints - rooted in dignity, honesty, courage, non-harm, truthfulness and rationality - that transform the individual's inherently absolute freedom into a form of collective freedom. The restraints that have survived the tests of time have given humankind a heritage which, when acted upon, yields both individual and collective dividends. Those who follow these virtues, often refrain from wronging others and from being wronged, and ultimately attain greatness. Then there are those who, against the order of this human heritage, openly engage in wrongdoing and ultimately meet their downfall. Nevertheless, they remain clear about their means and ends. They owe all they are to the vices. And there are others who seek self-defined righteous rewards and outcomes by travelling a righteously paved path of evil. That is, for all their vicious ends, they pursue them through means that righteous societies would otherwise engage in. These people and groups possess a righteousness of their own shade; they portray their evil acts as justified and paint them in the language of virtue. They tend to seek the wages of virtue without necessarily practising the lofty principles of human heritage. They do not outright reject virtuous values; instead, they turn those values into a mask for their designs. They are righteously wrong, wrongfully right, and, in a few instances, righteously wronged. Today, we as a society have all three types of people. The first group, the fewest in number, rarely holds a say or sway in the country. Yet they bear the sins of the other two. The second, though also in the minority, holds a high say in the country. Both as groups and as individuals owe their stakes and sway in the country to evil acts. They, for all their supports to and from the rulers, enjoy absolute impunity and include feudal and tribal warlords, parasitic pirs and electables. Then there is the third, largest and dominant group, which engages in all evils yet wants to remain in the good books. Members of this group wish to democratically autocratise. They trade fallacy truthfully. They enslave people to serve them. They practise injustice in just ways and vices in pious ways. How does this group dominate and sustain itself? In two phases: first, through pretensions and misinterpretations. This group initially tends to present its acts as justifiable in the light of virtue - through misquoting, selective representation and framing themselves in sync with ideologies they overtly advocate. But as everything has a limit, they eventually fail the test of time and sanity, and risk culpability in the people's eyes. It is after this that this group enters the second phase and justifies its vices by pointing to those of others. That is, their evil acts are blamed on the evil of those around them. "They do this, this, and this; what if we have done anything wrong? Isn't it merely a fraction of what others do?" They console themselves - and, of course, others - with this reasoning. In this way, every wrong is justified with a greater evil. Thus, evil acts are becoming sources of prestige, and prominence is being redefined as committing wrongdoings. Power is becoming the new truth. Meanwhile, democrats turn on democracy, journalists on truth, protectors on security, clergy on piety, judges on justice and civil society on the oppressed. Religion becomes a source of worldly riches and impunity. Yet all they are doing is right, just and legitimate in their own right. Who, in the midst of all these wrongdoings and the wronged, is actually doing wrong? Perhaps the virtuous and the public. Today, our society is undergoing a reverse renaissance that distorts the exalted values evolved over millennia and turns them into masks for wrongdoing. For most of us, real wrongs are not the ones the majority commits, but the ones left undone. And no wrong is currently left undone in society. Are there any?

title: The perils of sacred politics
description: Pakistan is no exception
content: Religion has always been a useful political tool. Unlike ordinary political slogans, faith speaks to people's deepest convictions. It gives leaders something that political manifestos rarely can: moral authority. History is full of examples. Kings in medieval Europe claimed they ruled by divine right. Across the Muslim world, rulers often sought religious endorsement to strengthen their legitimacy. Politics gains power when it borrows the language of faith. Pakistan is no exception. In fact, it may be one of the clearest examples of this pattern. Almost every major political leader has, at one point or another, wrapped political objectives in religious symbolism. Zulfikar Ali Bhutto introduced religious measures during a period of political unrest. Nawaz Sharif sought greater authority through the language of Shariah. Imran Khan frequently invoked the idea of Riyasat-e-Madina. Yet no contemporary politician illustrates the relationship between religion and politics more clearly than Maulana Fazlur Rehman. For nearly half a century, the Maulana has remained a significant figure in Pakistani politics. Governments have changed, military rulers have come and gone, but he has managed to remain relevant. Despite rarely commanding overwhelming electoral strength, he has often exercised influence far beyond the number of seats his party holds. Few politicians have mastered political survival quite like him. He has worked with governments he once criticised and criticised governments he once worked with. There is nothing unusual about political compromise. Politics is, after all, the art of negotiation. What makes the Maulana's case interesting is that he speaks not merely as a politician but also as a religious leader. This dual role raises questions that go beyond ordinary politics. Even more striking is the contrast between the Maulana's commitment to democracy and the internal structure of his own party. For decades, he has been one of Pakistan's most vocal advocates of constitutional rule, parliamentary supremacy and representative government. Yet the JUI-F has remained under his leadership for almost half a century. This raises a legitimate question. If democracy is the best principle for governing a country of 240 million people, should it not also be robust enough to function within a political party? The clearest example came during the controversy over madrassa registration. Maulana Fazlur Rehman made the passage of the Madrassa Registration Bill one of the conditions for JUI-F's support for the 26th Constitutional Amendment. He argued that seminaries should remain independent and resisted arrangements which, in his view, would place them under excessive government control. There is nothing illegitimate about political bargaining. Every politician negotiates. The question is why madrassas repeatedly appear at the centre of those negotiations. If the objective is educational reform, then debates should revolve around curriculum, standards, transparency and opportunities for students. Instead, madrassas often emerge as political leverage in larger power struggles. That is where an educational issue begins to resemble a political instrument. One question is worth considering here: when a religious leader enters politics, who holds him accountable? For decades, the Maulana has criticised corruption, elite privilege and failures of governance. Yet after nearly half a century in politics, the public is entitled to ask what tangible improvements his influence has produced for the causes he claims to champion. Religious seminaries remain underfunded, graduates continue to face limited opportunities and many of the social problems that religious parties have long promised to address remain unresolved. Pakistan has wrestled with that question for decades. The career of Maulana Fazlur Rehman offers a useful lens through which to examine it. His political journey reminds us that faith can be a source of moral guidance, but it can also become a source of political leverage. The challenge for any society is ensuring that the first does not become subordinate to the second.

title: Russia: pragmatism not appeasement
description: Trump's willingness to engage Moscow can contribute to such an outcome
content: With barely a couple of weeks remaining before the US midterm elections, one debate attracting particular attention is President Donald Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports and its potential implications for the war in Ukraine. The prevailing interpretation is that Trump is motivated by two immediate objectives: lowering fuel prices to improve his electoral prospects and pressuring President Volodymyr Zelensky to accept his proposed terms for ending the war. To me, however, this is a simplistic reading of Trump's intentions. I see a broader strategic purpose behind the move, one that extends beyond the immediate electoral cycle and the question of how to end the war in Ukraine. My argument rests on the premise that, given his low approval ratings, Trump may already be anticipating a difficult outcome for the Republicans in the midterms. Rather than focusing exclusively on the election itself, he may be positioning himself for the political landscape that follows it. His longer-term strategy, it seems, is driven by two interrelated ambitions: shaping the legacy he leaves behind as president and improving the Republican Party's prospects in the next presidential election. The greatest challenge confronting the world today is how to sustain global economic stability and endurance in an increasingly fractured international system. For far too long, the West has portrayed President Vladimir Putin as a dictator leading a dangerous adversary and an autocratic ruler waging a brutal war against a democratic republic. This narrative was consistent with the post-WWII international order constructed by the US and its allies - an order founded on liberal values, a rules-based system and respect for international law. Yet, unnecessary American wars, the retreat of liberal democracy, technological disruption, deglobalisation, mass immigration, deepening political polarisation and the proliferation of grey-zone conflicts have all contributed to the erosion of that order. The actions of Russia and China, therefore, must be understood not merely as challenges to the existing system but also in the wider context of the struggle over what kind of international order will replace it. President Trump appears determined to secure the distinction of being the American president who brings the war in Ukraine to an end. This ambition, however, may reflect a broader recognition that the international system is changing and that the old order cannot be restored. As illiberal and autocratic tendencies gain ground across the world, the challenge is to develop a new framework of global governance that acknowledges and accommodates the ideological, cultural and civilisational diversity of the international community. Such an arrangement would require the US to make room for both Russia and China within the emerging order, allowing the great powers to compete for influence without being drawn into direct military confrontation. The objective must extend beyond ending the wars in Ukraine and Iran to preventing future conflicts in emerging geopolitical flashpoints, including the Caucasus, the Horn of Africa and the Balkans. Trump's apparent strategy is to compel Zelensky to the negotiating table by signaling that Washington's willingness to underwrite Ukraine's defence is no longer unconditional. The reported energy ceasefire arrangements, delays in the delivery of American interceptor missiles, restrictions on intelligence-sharing and disruptions affecting Ukrainian drone operations attributed to blocking access to Starlink – all point towards a possible recalibration of American policy. Taken together, these measures could be interpreted as instruments of pressure designed to alter Kyiv's calculations and make a negotiated settlement more likely. Two historical analogies offer useful insights into what might happen if President Trump succeeds in placing economic pragmatism above the continuation of what I regard as reckless wars in Ukraine and Iran. The first takes us back to the Yalta Conference of February 1945, when Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin discussed the post-war reorganisation of Europe, the future of Germany and the establishment of the UN. Their meeting reflected a recognition that the post-war world could not be organised without an understanding among the great powers. Today, a similar question confronts the international community. Considering that all three are likely to meet first at the sidelines of the Pacific Rim Countries Conference in Hawaii and a month later at the G20 Summit Meeting at President Trump's Doral Resort in Florida, can they find common ground on the principles that should govern an emerging world order? If their anticipated meetings provide an opportunity for meaningful dialogue, the three leaders should use it to develop a workable framework for global governance - one that acknowledges their respective spheres of influence, limits external interference in areas of vital strategic interest and replaces the pursuit of absolute global leadership with an acceptance of great-power coexistence. The second analogy lies in President Richard Nixon's historic opening to China in the early 1970s. At the time, Washington's rapprochement with Beijing unsettled many American allies, much as Trump's apparent willingness to engage Moscow has generated unease among Western capitals today. Nixon's initiative demonstrated that strategic engagement with an adversary need not amount to surrender; it can instead transform the geopolitical environment and create opportunities that confrontation alone cannot deliver. The US and China had spent years on opposing sides of ideological and geopolitical struggles, yet both eventually recognised the strategic advantages of opening diplomatic channels. The subsequent normalisation of relations culminated in the establishment of formal diplomatic ties in 1979, alongside the US commitment to maintain unofficial relations with Taiwan under the Taiwan Relations Act. If President Trump can persuade Kyiv to participate in a credible peace settlement, the question of guaranteeing Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity must be central to the negotiations. The US, Russia and China need to recognise that the pursuit of unconstrained global leadership by any one power can deepen insecurity for all. Their task is to move beyond an endless struggle for primacy. The objective should be a global economy that is vibrant and sustainable and which is capable of enduring geopolitical shocks. If Trump's willingness to engage Moscow can contribute to such an outcome, his legacy may ultimately be measured not by the concessions he made to an adversary, but by whether he helped establish a world in which great powers could compete without continually resorting to war.

title: Turkish court seeks investigation into nationals allegedly involved in abuse of Gaza flotilla activists in Israel
description: Court maintains arrest warrants for Netanyahu, 34 other defendants
content: An Istanbul court ordered prosecutors to investigate Turkish nationals allegedly involved in the mistreatment of participants in the Gaza-bound Global Sumud Flotilla while they were held in Israel, during the first hearing of a case against 35 defendants, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Istanbul 11th High Criminal Court ruled that individuals identified by complainants as Turkish citizens who participated in alleged abuses against them in Israeli custody should be identified and referred to prosecutors for necessary legal action. The court also ordered that existing arrest warrants and Interpol Red Notice requests against all 35 defendants remain in effect. The case concerns Israel's armed interception of the Global Sumud Flotilla, which was carrying humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip. Flotilla participants describe alleged mistreatment During the hearing, complainant Osman Cetinkaya said he had joined the flotilla as a doctor to deliver medical supplies to Palestinians in Gaza. He said Israeli soldiers confiscated five or six boxes of medical supplies from their vessel and that participants were subjected to mistreatment at Israel's Ashdod port. Cetinkaya said he wished to pursue his complaint against the defendants. Another complainant, Zeynep Tekocak, said she had been subjected to two strip searches and had an altercation with Israeli soldiers after refusing to remove her headscarf. "They recorded me wearing the clothes they gave me instead of my headscarf and mocked me," she told the court. Read: Three years of genocide: Israel’s traditional Asian allies shift stance on Gaza Tekocak said one of the soldiers who detained her had told her he was from Turkiye's central province of Yozgat. "They took our personal belongings, and I have not been able to recover any of them. Our privacy was seriously violated. I am filing a complaint," she said. Turkish lawmaker Sema Silkin Un also testified, saying she and approximately 80 other participants were held in a poorly ventilated room after being detained. She said that an Israeli soldier insulted Islam while they were reading the Quran. Un said detainees were not allowed to sleep and were subjected to verbal abuse and psychological mistreatment. "We were not even allowed to close our eyes where we were held. Sleeping was forbidden," she said. She added that police officers who arrived the following day insulted Turkiye and the detainees in Hebrew. Lawyers call for broader investigation into Gaza Riza Saka, president of the Istanbul No 2 Bar Association, described the proceedings as historic and called for further international evidence to be included in the case. He referred to provisional measures ordered by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in proceedings concerning allegations of genocide in Gaza. Saka requested copies of relevant ICJ documents and a UN report concerning allegations of genocide in Gaza. He also referred to the arrest warrants and Red Notice requests issued against Netanyahu and the other defendants. Lawyer Yasin Samli argued that the case involved allegations of genocide, crimes against humanity and attacks against civilians. Samli said lawyers had submitted eight volumes of evidence, including five concerning alleged crimes against women and children in Gaza. Court seeks separate indictment over alleged crimes against Gaza civilians In its interim ruling, the court noted that the existing indictment primarily described actions taken against the Global Sumud Flotilla, while allegations concerning crimes committed against civilians in Gaza were presented only indirectly and in general terms. The panel said investigations into genocide and crimes against humanity could be conducted upon a request from Turkiye's justice minister. Read More: Israel committed 'brutal violations' against aid flotilla activists: ICBSG Taking into account the principle that courts are bound by the factual allegations set out in an indictment, the panel ordered a formal request to prosecutors concerning a possible new indictment. The request calls for alleged crimes against civilians in Gaza, separate from the actions involving the flotilla, to be described in concrete terms and linked to supporting evidence. The court said evidence submitted by the Istanbul No 2 Bar Association and the International Jurists Union should be considered in that process. Court orders asset inquiries, requests ICC documents The panel also ordered inquiries into whether any of the 35 defendants hold movable or immovable assets in Turkiye. It directed that a request be sent through the Justice Ministry for documents from proceedings involving the defendants before the International Criminal Court (ICC). The court additionally ordered that a UN report submitted concerning allegations of genocide in Gaza be requested through the Justice Ministry. The panel accepted applications to participate in the proceedings from complainants and several organisations, including the Istanbul No 2 Bar Association, MAZLUMDER, the International Jurists Union and the Association of Lawyers of the Earth. The hearing was adjourned until March 30, 2027.

title: Protesters clash with police over India dam project bordering China
description: Around 40 police personnel injured as protesters throw stones, vandalise hydropower company's offices
content: Indian protesters angry over a proposed Himalayan mega-dam, intended to counter an upstream Chinese hydropower project, have clashed with police and torched buildings, officials said. The violence in northeastern Arunachal Pradesh state erupted late on Friday during protests against the proposed 11,200-megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project of state-run hydropower company NHPC, Chief Minister Pema Khandu told reporters on Saturday. “The mob destroyed a lot of properties, police station, the NHPC office was vandalised, several elected representatives’ homes were ransacked,” Khandu told reporters. Around 40 police personnel were injured by stones thrown by protesters, who also vandalised the NHPC’s offices. Police fired tear gas canisters to disperse the crowd. Read: UN experts urge Indian authorities to cease 'use of excessive force' to curb protests Khandu urged opponents of the project to engage with the government. “Question us, have dialogue with us, instead of violence,” Khandu said. India says the proposed dam is needed to counter China’s $167-billion Yaxia project, a likely record-breaking hydropower scheme upstream in Tibet. New Delhi fears the Chinese project could affect water flows downstream, and says the proposed Indian dam would create a vast reservoir to store water and help maintain flows into the Brahmaputra river. Beijing has said its project will have no “negative impact” downstream. China claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of southern Tibet. India says the state is an integral part of its territory. India’s proposed dam, which would be by far its largest hydropower project, has drawn fierce opposition from local communities who fear the loss of their homes and land. Read More: Injuries in China's Tibet rise to 76 after earthquake, death toll remains at 16 The project underscores tensions between the two most populous countries, which share a disputed Himalayan border patrolled by tens of thousands of troops. India’s foreign ministry said on Friday the two sides remained in regular contact to manage border tensions, after a top Indian border police official Shatrujeet Kapur reported “face offs” between Indian and Chinese forces. “The situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns,” foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told reporters in New Delhi. “Both sides continue to use existing diplomatic and military mechanisms to resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation.”

title: Rain and hail offer Lahore residents reprieve, city’s global AQI ranking slips to 13
description: PMD says provincial capital to witness temperature dip up to 18.5°C tonight
content: Rain and hail were reported in several parts of Lahore on Saturday, improving air quality as the city ranked 13th among the world’s most air-polluted cities, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 133. Precipitation was reported in Gajjumata, Nishtar, Chungi, Walton, Township and Harbanspura, as well as Gulberg, DHA, Model Town and Raiwind Road areas. According to the met department, the temperature of the provincial capital also dipped after precipitation. At 7pm, Lahore’s minimum temperature stood at 18.5°C. Read: Lahore tops polluted cities' list again In the global ranking recorded around 8pm on Saturday, Lahore stood 13th, with an AQI of 133 considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups". Dakar, Senegal, topped the list with an AQI of 297, followed by Kuching, Malaysia, at 208 and Mumbai, India, at 186. A different local air-quality update placed Lahore sixth among the most air-polluted Pakistani cities, with an average AQI of 172. Monitoring stations recorded readings of 222 on GT Road, 211 on Ravi Road and 204 in Model Town. شمال مشرقی پنجاب کے لیے موسم کی صورتحال pic.twitter.com/qdNtwaxVT4 — Pak Met Department محکمہ موسمیات (@pmdgov) October 24, 2026 Separately, the Pakistan Meteorological Department issued a weather alert today, reporting an active weather system over Gujranwala and adjoining areas. It forecast strong winds, thunderstorms and rain in Lahore, Sialkot, Narowal, Gujranwala, Sheikhupura, Kasur and surrounding areas. A subsequent daily forecast predicted mainly dry weather across most districts of Punjab tonight and tomorrow (Sunday). It said Murree, Galiyat and adjoining areas were expected to experience cold and partial cloud cover.

title: NA apprised of Rs24b irregularities in BISP
description: Documents show over 140,000 govt employees, pensioners received funds
content: Financial irregularities amounting to Rs24 billion have been uncovered in the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP), with more than 140,000 government employees and pensioners found to have received funds intended for deserving families, while recoveries have amounted to just Rs710 million. According to documents presented by the Poverty Alleviation Ministry in the National Assembly, 140,488 government employees received payments from the programme despite being ineligible. The irregularities were identified in 2019, but payments continued for six years. During the fiscal year 2019-20, government employees and pensioners received Rs23.13 billion, while a further Rs900 million was paid out even after government employees had been identified. Official records show that more than 12,000 employees received Rs146.7 million in 2020-21. The documents further reveal that 2,447 government employees received funds in 2021-22, followed by 2,235 in 2022-23 and 12,078 in 2024-25. The findings also revealed that 236 BISP employees were among those who received funds earmarked for poor beneficiaries. Against the total irregularities of Rs24 billion, recoveries have reached only Rs710 million. The FIA recovered Rs540 million, while other government departments recovered Rs145 million. BISP recovered a further Rs21.5 million from its own employees. The records of employees allegedly involved in the irregularities have been forwarded to the relevant departments for further action. Authorities have also decided to scrutinise the records of more than 600,000 government employees and pensioners. The disclosures have brought renewed attention to the programme's oversight mechanisms, particularly its failure to prevent payments from continuing after the irregularities were identified and the limited amount recovered against the reported sum.

title: German firm blamed for insulin shortage
description: Aseefa raises concerns over slow internet speeds nationwide
content: The issue of insulin shortage was raised in the National Assembly on Friday, with parliamentary secretary informing the house that an insulin product used by patients with Type 1 diabetes was in short supply in Pakistan after its German manufacturer halted supplies while upgrading its products. Responding to a matter raised by MNA Syeda Amna Batool, the secretary said there had been no shortage until June, with stocks available until September. However, supplies from Germany were disrupted in October, leading to the current shortage. He said supply disruptions were also reported in Europe. "The impact of the shortage is being felt not just here, but across Asia, as well as in Australia and Europe." The secretary further said alternative insulin products with the same dosage and mode of action were readily available in Pakistan and that patients could switch to them on their doctors' recommendation. "The product is manufactured in Germany. It is an issue that we are trying to resolve. The lawmakers also raised the issue of slow internet speeds across the country. During Question hour, the Ministry of Information Technology told the House that Pakistan had 210 million mobile subscribers, including 161.7 million mobile broadband users. Lawmakers were also briefed on the Cabinet Division's spending plans to digitise government officials' performance reports, an insulin shortage and the national cricket team's performance. PPP MNA Aseefa Bhutto Zardari complained that connectivity was poor across the country and that even 4G was not working in Nawabshah. She said internet speeds needed to improve for all citizens, including businesses. Abdul Qadir Patel, a member of the panel of chairpersons, sarcastically asked whether 4G had died and that was why 5G was being introduced. He said internet speeds had deteriorated further since the current government took office. When Parliamentary Secretary Sabeen Ghauri was unable to explain what 5G meant, Aseefa offered to explain it to her. The Ministry of IT said Pakistan had 210 million mobile subscribers, of whom 161.7 million used mobile broadband. In the first phase, 5G services would be stabilised in 24 cities before being extended to other urban centres. Proposals to reduce mobile taxes, promote local manufacturing and allow duty-free imports of 5G equipment were also under consideration. Officials said 3G and 2G services were affected in some areas by unrest and militant activity. The ministry also outlined its Spark and Elevate programmes to promote research and innovation.

title: PM&DC retains 60% marks for admissions
description: Council says the eligibility requirement has not been relaxed
content: The Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PM&DC) has clarified that the requirement of at least 60 per cent marks in FSc (Pre-Medical) or an equivalent qualification remains mandatory for admission to MBBS and BDS programmes. In a clarification issued in response to reports circulating on digital media, the council said the eligibility requirement had not been relaxed. According to PM&DC admission regulations, candidates must secure a minimum of 60 per cent marks at the intermediate level or in an equivalent examination to qualify for admission.

title: NCCIA rescues 13-year-old Karachi girl in probe into suspected dark web network
description: Officials say the wider case involves 42 suspects, including 12 juveniles, as investigators probe child exploitation
content: What began as an online interaction allegedly drew a 13-year-old girl into the orbit of a suspected dark web network, where children were reportedly assigned tasks and paid to produce pornographic animated content. A timely intervention by the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) has now brought the case to light, raising concerns about the online exploitation of minors. The agency rescued the girl during a crackdown in Karachi's Rabia City, uncovering what investigators suspect is a wider network involving child exploitation and the production of pornographic cartoons. The probe has also revealed suspected links to individuals in Germany and the United Kingdom, according to NCCIA officials. Investigators are examining whether children were deliberately targeted, manipulated and paid to carry out tasks as part of the alleged operation. Officials have also launched a probe into the possible use of so-called “red rooms” on the dark web to assign tasks to minors. Read: NCCIA arrests 4 suspects over child sexual abuse material trafficking in Islamabad Speaking at a press conference, NCCIA Deputy Director Shehzad Akbar said the agency had acted on credible information about the suspected network. The girl’s father was informed, and the two devices used by the child were seized with his cooperation. Akbar rejected suggestions that the initial task assigned to the girl involved killing a cat. He said, however, that the child was allegedly being subjected to psychological manipulation similar to tactics attributed to dark web groups operating internationally. Had the network not been exposed, the situation could have become more serious, he added. The investigation is continuing to establish the role of suspected local handlers and identify other children who may have been targeted. According to information shared by the officials, the wider case involves 42 suspects, including 12 juveniles. Investigators are examining evidence that children were allegedly paid to produce pornographic animated content, with some reportedly receiving around $100, described in the information provided as approximately Rs6,000. The agency has seized 19 mobile phones from Pixel Craft, a company reportedly operating for around two years, five phones from Art Office and 17 from Art Design, which reportedly employed 17 people. Officials are investigating the companies’ possible links to the suspected network. Akbar said a man identified as Fudan was allegedly operating the network. Preliminary findings also indicate that the companies provided logos, banners and other digital design services to foreign clients. Investigators are examining whether these businesses were connected to the alleged exploitation activities. Also Read: NCCIA arrests accused in $126m US postal fraud The deputy director said the agency had previously detained a boy in Karachi who was allegedly searching online for ways to take revenge on another person. In a separate case, the NCCIA arrested a suspect identified as Hamza on Thursday over alleged anti-state propaganda. Officials said the allegations were being investigated further. The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) Karachi Zone has arrested an absconding accused nominated in a case involving alleged unlawful social media activity. The arrest was made in Gulistan-e-Johar, Karachi, on the directions of DG NCCIA Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi. The… pic.twitter.com/jG3zXygBRt — NCCIA (@NCCIAOFFICIAL) October 23, 2026 Cybercrime crackdown Akbar said the agency had recovered 39 accounts on WhatsApp, Instagram and other social media platforms over the past 15 days. It had also blocked 95 accounts allegedly linked to financial fraud and taken action against 38 accounts suspected of harassing women through fake identities. The agency is pursuing cases involving the hacking of social media accounts, online financial fraud and harassment through fabricated identities. It has also received numerous complaints about the hacking of WhatsApp Business accounts. Investigators are separately examining allegations that individuals have been operating social media accounts under women’s names and using fabricated identities to harass others. The NCCIA said investigations into the suspected child exploitation network and other cybercrime cases were underway.

title: PHC bars arrest of inactive K-P deputy speaker, suspends eviction notice
description: Allows Suraiya Bibi to stay in official residence, bars her arrest
content: The Peshawar High Court (PHC) on Thursday suspended a government notice ordering the inactive Deputy Speaker of the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Assembly Suraiya Bibi to vacate her official residence, allowed her to continue living there and directed law-enforcement agencies not to arrest her. A two-member bench comprising Justice Ijaz Anwar and Justice Faheem Wali issued the written order arising from the previous hearing. Advocate Yasir Khattak appeared on behalf of the petitioner, the inactive Deputy Speaker. In its detailed order, the court noted that the relevant presidential ordinance makes no mention of the offices of Speaker or Deputy Speaker. Similarly, the administrative directive requiring vacation of official residences contains no reference to these constitutional posts. The judges therefore found sufficient ground to stay the eviction process pending further examination of the legal position. Read: PHC stays arrest of K-P Assembly deputy speaker, orders de-sealing of official residence During arguments, counsel for the petitioner contended that the K-P Assembly Speaker and Deputy Speaker Act 2026 confers a clear legal right on the Deputy Speaker to occupy the official residence for the duration of her term. He further argued that law-enforcement agencies are barred from conducting any raid or taking coercive action against the residence while the office-holder remains in position. Opposing the petition, the Advocate General submitted that an emergency empowers the provincial government to reclaim official residences allotted to ministers, advisers and the Deputy Speaker. He also apprised the court that a criminal case under Section 406 of the Pakistan Penal Code has already been registered against the Deputy Speaker on the complaint of the Deputy Commissioner of Chitral. After hearing both sides, the bench suspended the notice to vacate the residence, expressly authorised the petitioner to remain in occupation and ordered that she should not be arrested. The matter will be taken up again on the next date of hearing. The ruling provides immediate relief to the inactive Deputy Speaker and places the burden on the provincial authorities to justify the eviction drive in light of the statutory protections available to the holder of the office.

title: Police clash with protesters in Rome as demonstrators march toward prime minister’s office
description: Authorities report 28 preventive detentions as 500 soldiers deployed to city centre
content: Demonstrators in Rome clashed with security forces on Saturday after attempting to march toward the prime minister's office, amid heightened security in Italy following violent protests last weekend. Authorities stepped up security measures in cities ahead of the demonstrations. Despite the precautions, tensions escalated, and clashes broke out between police and protesters in some areas. Various groups held demonstrations in the capital throughout the day. In the morning, far-right groups protested last weekend's demonstrations in Milan, which were marked by unrest. In the afternoon, left-wing groups and students took part in a march against "war and imperialism." Read: Italy probes Israeli minister, others The march ended peacefully, but young people who left the procession later confronted security forces near the Colosseum. Tensions did not escalate after the students changed their route. The unauthorised march continued for some time at various locations around the Colosseum. A group of demonstrators also entered the ancient amphitheater and chanted slogans. After hours of protesting in the city centre, the demonstrators tried to march to the prime minister's office in the evening but hit a police barricade near Santa Susanna Square. While negotiations continued between police and protesters seeking to proceed, some demonstrators threw bottles, explosive devices and fireworks at security forces. Police responded with water cannons and, in some places, batons. Read More: France deploys 70,000 police to try to contain nationwide protests The situation appeared to calm briefly, but police used water cannons again after demonstrators resumed throwing explosive devices. One protester was seen injured, with blood covering his head after being struck by an object. The demonstrators eventually changed their route and left the area after realising police would not allow them to pass. Italian media reported that security forces detained 28 people early Saturday as a preventive measure ahead of the demonstrations in Rome. Clashes reported in several cities Protests about the rising cost of living and against the government were also held in Naples, Bologna and Turin, in addition to Rome and Milan. Media reports said scuffles between protesters and police broke out at times in Bologna and Turin. Following last weekend's unrest in Milan, 500 soldiers were deployed to the city centre, and shop windows were covered with wooden boards. Although tensions flared between demonstrators and security forces at times Saturday, the unrest did not escalate. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni thanked law enforcement officers in a post on the US social media platform X. Voglio ringraziare le donne e gli uomini delle Forze dell’Ordine che anche oggi, nelle piazze italiane, hanno lavorato per garantire la sicurezza dei cittadini e il diritto di manifestare pacificamente, nonostante i tentativi di alcuni violenti di provocare scontri e disordini.… — Giorgia Meloni (@GiorgiaMeloni) October 24, 2026 "I would like to thank the law enforcement officers who are working to ensure the safety of citizens and the right to peaceful protest, despite some violent groups trying to provoke clashes and disorder in Italy's squares today as well," she said.

title: Obama backs El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race, Trump dismisses rally turnout
description: Former US president defends El-Sayed against attacks over Muslim identity, alleged ties to Muslim Brotherhood
content: Former United States president Barack Obama endorsed Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan on Saturday, defending him against attacks over his Muslim identity as President Donald Trump dismissed the rally's turnout. Speaking before more than 4,300 supporters at Cass Technical High School in Detroit, Obama backed El-Sayed, who faces Republican Mike Rogers in a closely contested Senate race ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. "Abdul is fighting for change, real change, change that will bring an end to this war," Obama said, referring to the US war against Iran. Read: From tech giants to anonymous nonprofits, the biggest donors in US midterms Obama also praised El-Sayed's proposals to reduce the influence of money in politics and expand access to affordable healthcare. He said the candidate would "finish the job we started" with the 2010 Affordable Care Act. The former president defended El-Sayed against Republican attacks questioning his religious background and alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. He drew parallels with false claims about his own identity and religion during his presidential campaigns in 2007 and 2011. "We have seen this movie before. I starred in it," Obama said. "This stuff didn't work on me. Not in Michigan, it's not going to work for Abdul," he added. Read More: Trump's approval falls to record low of 31% as midterms near, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds Trump, speaking later Saturday at a Republican campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, mocked Obama's appearance and claimed the Detroit event had attracted almost no supporters. "You know, I saw Barack Hussein Obama was in Michigan, and the place was empty," Trump said, despite reports documenting thousands of attendees. Trump and other Republicans have repeatedly accused El-Sayed of extremist affiliations, including links to the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed has denied the allegations, and no credible evidence has emerged establishing such ties. In a later post on his Truth Social platform, Trump criticised Obama's record of supporting unsuccessful Democratic presidential candidates, citing Hillary Clinton's defeat in 2016 and Kamala Harris' loss in 2024. https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/117499714815544938 "He said that Crooked Hillary Clinton was going to WIN, he campaigned hard for her, and she lost in all directions and ways. He then campaigned full out for Kamala, and likewise, she lost," Trump wrote. Obama also campaigned for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson, who faces Republican Representative John James. During the rally, Obama described the midterm elections as an opportunity to impose greater accountability on the Trump administration. "We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government," he said. Trump is scheduled to campaign in Michigan on Sunday in support of Republican candidates.

title: Israeli defence minister admits having forced 2,000 Palestinians from homes in West Bank city of Hebron
description: Troops turn Palestinian homes into barracks, observation posts after forcing residents to leave
content: Israel’s defence minister acknowledged Saturday that Israeli forces had forcibly displaced around 2,000 Palestinians from their homes in Hebron in the southern occupied West Bank. Defence chief Israel Katz told public broadcaster KAN that displaced residents would not be allowed to return until what he called “Hamas infrastructure” in the city was dismantled. His remarks came as an Israeli military operation in the city of Hebron entered its second day, disrupting education and municipal services. Hebron’s education directorate suspended school Sunday and Monday, while Hebron University and Al-Quds Open University moved Sunday’s classes online. The municipality said rubbish was accumulating as the closure of the city’s entrances prevented access to disposal sites outside it. Read: 'Apartheid automation': How Israel uses AI to monitor Palestinian land, movement and lives Israeli forces sealed off Hebron and nearby Halhul on Friday after two Palestinians attacked an Israeli checkpoint. Two Israeli soldiers were killed and three others were also wounded, while Israeli forces killed both attackers, according to Israeli figures. The army announced late Friday that it had launched an operation expected to last several days, involving Shin Bet and Border Police forces. Israeli army says it raided 400 sites in West Bank, detained dozens of Palestinians Israeli forces turned Palestinian homes into barracks and observation posts after forcing residents to leave Hebron on Saturday, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported. Troops took over homes in the Khallat Manna and Dahiyat al-Zaytoun areas of southern Hebron to be used as barracks, official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported, citing sources. They also forced residents from homes in other neighbourhoods and used the properties as observation posts, said sources. The evictions follow the forced displacement of hundreds of families since Friday, amid extensive raids, road closures, and tight restrictions on movement. Read More: Opposition leader says Netanyahu ‘no longer fit’ to lead Israel Near Bethlehem, Israeli forces blocked dirt roads leading to the town of Tuqu and fired tear gas and stun grenades toward Palestinian vehicles traveling along rough alternative routes, Wafa reported, citing Palestinian security sources. The agency said ongoing closures across Bethlehem and surrounding towns and villages left Palestinians depending on unpaved roads to travel between communities. The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, has seen escalating Israeli military attacks and occupier violence since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023. The attacks have included killing and detaining Palestinians, demolishing homes and other structures, burning mosques and vehicles, bulldozing farmland, preventing farmers from accessing their fields, and displacing Palestinian communities, alongside illegal settlement expansion.

title: Republican ‘Muslim Brotherhood’ attacks on El-Sayed seek to exploit Democratic divisions
description: El-Sayed and Rogers vie for a Senate seat that could determine whether Democrats regain control of the chamber
content: Republican US Senate candidate Mike Rogers and allies, including President Donald Trump, are escalating efforts to link Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, with Trump falsely branding him a “jihadist”. Pollsters and political strategists say the approach aims to dissuade Jewish and Black voters in the Detroit area who backed El-Sayed’s primary opponent, Haley Stevens, from supporting the Democratic nominee. “It gives them even more reason to pause and not vote for El-Sayed,” said Dennis Darnoi, a Republican political consultant.
