title: A warrant is not a proof of political neutrality
description: A warrant is not a proof of political neutrality
content:
Federal agents arrived at Ilhan Omar's Washington home before dawn on October 12. They executed a search warrant and carried away boxes. The search came 22 days before Election Day, with the Minnesota congresswoman on the ballot.
The Justice Department says the search was part of an ongoing criminal investigation. Reports indicate that investigators are examining decades-old immigration paperwork. Omar denies wrongdoing.
A judge authorised the search. That matters. But a warrant answers whether the government has a legal basis to search a particular place for evidence. It does not answer why officials chose this target, whether comparable cases receive comparable scrutiny, or why they acted when they did.
Those questions deserve answers, especially when senior administration officials have targeted the person under investigation for years.
No public official should be immune from criminal investigation. If credible evidence of wrongdoing exists, the government should pursue it regardless of the subject's politics.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly attacked Omar and demanded that she leave the United States. Vice President JD Vance has accused her of immigration fraud and publicly discussed with senior White House official Stephen Miller how to investigate her. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has also raised the prospect of action involving her family's immigration history.
These statements do not prove that the search was politically directed. Nor do they establish that the allegations are false. But they raise a legitimate question: has the investigation been insulated from political pressure?
When senior officials publicly discuss how to pursue a named political opponent, pointing to a warrant is not a complete answer. The government must show that investigative decisions rested on evidence and impartial standards, not political hostility.
The search took place less than a month before an election. The Justice Department has long maintained that investigative steps should not be timed to influence an election or advantage or disadvantage a candidate. The frequently cited 60-day rule is an informal norm, not a statute that automatically invalidates every action taken during that period. Its purpose, however, is important: law enforcement must not become a tool for shaping electoral outcomes.
Reporting indicates the investigation had been underway for some time and that administration officials discussed it months before the search. If investigators needed to act when they did, the government should explain why.
An investigation can be legitimate while its timing remains questionable. Similarly, proximity to an election does not, by itself, prove political motivation. The point is to examine the chronology, not assume the answer.
The 2022 search of Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago property does not settle the matter. Trump was not a candidate on the ballot in that year's midterm elections. The circumstances differed. Each case should be judged on its own facts and the same standards of impartiality.
Omar's lawyers have also alleged that the Justice Department failed to follow judicially ordered procedures meant to protect her constitutional rights as a member of Congress. They have sought the return of seized property and the preservation of search recordings.
These are allegations, not established findings. The courts should resolve them. But the underlying issue matters: constitutional protections governing congressional independence do not disappear when the executive branch investigates one of its sharpest critics.
Those protections do not place lawmakers above the law. They help prevent the executive branch from improperly interfering with the legislature's functioning.
The investigation reportedly concerns immigration paperwork from the period when Omar arrived in the United States as a child. She later became a naturalised citizen. Authorities can investigate genuine evidence of fraud, but a decades-old file should not become a reservoir of suspicion that can be drawn upon whenever a citizen becomes politically inconvenient.
Naturalised citizens have the same constitutional protections as citizens born in the United States. Citizenship is not a lesser status, and it should not be treated as conditional on political loyalty.
The implications reach well beyond Omar. A search, a public allegation, or the threat of renewed scrutiny can damage reputations and discourage others from speaking out. People without a congresswoman's platform or legal resources may be even less able to challenge official suspicion.
That is why impartiality matters even before a case reaches trial. The government can chill political participation without ever securing a conviction.
Congress should seek a clear chronology of the decision to search Omar's home, including the reasons for its timing, the relevant approvals, and whether the Justice Department's Public Integrity Section was consulted. Congress should preserve relevant communications and properly review allegations of noncompliance with judicial orders.
Such oversight need not obstruct a legitimate investigation. Sensitive evidence can be handled through protected briefings. But confidentiality should not become a permanent shield against scrutiny of how public power is used.
Republicans should support this effort on principle. Would they accept the same conduct if a Democratic president spent years attacking a conservative lawmaker, senior officials discussed how to pursue that person, and federal agents searched the lawmaker's home weeks before an election? If not, they should explain why this case is different.
Defending Omar's rights does not require endorsing her politics or prejudging the investigation. It requires insisting that the same rules apply to everyone.
Americans can criticise Omar and vote against her. None of that diminishes her right to due process.
The agents searched Ilhan Omar's home. The question now is whether the institutions meant to restrain executive power can show that the law remains a safeguard against political retaliation, not a means of carrying it out.

title: The world is losing patience
description: The world is losing patience
content:
What connects a young protester in Nepal, an Indian student who calls himself a 'cockroach', a family priced out of housing in Spain and a civilian seeking shelter in Gaza? Their circumstances differ, but each case raises an uncomfortable question about the institutions meant to protect their future. From the streets of major cities to the battlefields of West Asia and Europe, established systems of power are being challenged, sometimes by citizens, sometimes by rival states, and increasingly by their own contradictions.
Across Brazil, Argentina, Albania, Belgium, Italy and Spain, protests over corruption, austerity, political accountability and declining living standards reveal a widening gap between government promises and public expectations. South Asia offers even starker examples. Sri Lanka's economic collapse drove protesters into the presidential palace in 2022. Bangladesh's student uprising ended Sheikh Hasina's rule in 2024, and Nepal's youth-led demonstrations brought down a government in 2025.
India's 'Cockroach Movement' is a striking variation. It began in May as online satire after the Chief Justice of India likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches, a remark he later clarified. It then grew into street protests over jobs, leaked entrance examinations and political accountability. Its rise shows how institutional arrogance can turn economic frustration into organised political resistance.
Are these Gen Z revolutions, or failures of governance?
Young people did not create the problems they are protesting against. They inherited them. What sets this generation apart is its ability to compare opportunities, expose privilege and mobilise across digital platforms. But social media explains the speed of mobilisation, not the origins of discontent.
The economic explanation is more revealing. The traditional social contract promised that education, hard work and following the rules would lead to upward mobility. That promise is increasingly unreliable. GDP can grow while wages stagnate, housing becomes unaffordable and opportunity stays concentrated among a privileged few. When economic progress fails to translate into personal security, even functioning political institutions struggle to command public confidence.
In The Captive Mind (1953), the Polish poet Czes?aw Mi?osz described Ketman: professing loyalty in public while privately withholding belief. Systems can survive on such outward conformity for a long time, but not indefinitely. When institutions' claims to legitimacy no longer match people's lived experience, private doubt eventually becomes public. Economic hardship may ignite anger, but the perception of hypocrisy gives it political force.
Yet overthrowing a government is easier than rebuilding one. Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal remind us that political change does not automatically produce competent institutions, fiscal stability or jobs. The real challenge begins when the protesters leave the streets.
A similar crisis of credibility confronts the international order. Russia's war in Ukraine, the devastation in Gaza, military confrontation involving Iran, Israel and the US, and recurring hostilities involving the Houthis expose the limits of diplomatic restraint. International law remains the declared foundation of global order, yet its inconsistent enforcement raises the question of whether rules constrain power or merely reflect it.
The economic consequences are just as serious. Wars disrupt trade, inflate energy costs, displace populations and divert scarce resources towards military spending. A confrontation in West Asia can raise transport costs in Karachi and food prices across South Asia. An economy need not take part in a war to pay for it.
Technology adds another contradiction. AI and advanced military systems are expanding what states can do without necessarily improving how they govern. A government may possess sophisticated surveillance, predictive algorithms and precision weapons while remaining unable to deliver basic public services or respond meaningfully to its citizens. States can become more powerful technologically even as their societies become more vulnerable economically and politically.
These developments demand something more serious than another debate over whether the world is becoming multipolar. The pressing question is how power should be exercised, constrained and held accountable, both within states and between them.
For Pakistan, the answer is particularly consequential. We should read our neighbours' upheavals as a lesson in economics, not a prediction about politics. According to the Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26, about 66% of our population is under the age of 30. The Labour Force Survey 2024-25 puts unemployment at 7.1% overall and close to 13% among those aged 15 to 24. Even degree holders face an unemployment rate of nearly 11%. Meanwhile, 762,499 Pakistanis registered for overseas employment in 2025. This is the broken social contract in Pakistani numbers: education no longer guarantees work, and for many, work means leaving. The question is not whether young Pakistanis are patient. It is how long the economy will keep testing that patience. Regional instability, energy dependence, low productivity, fiscal constraints and climate vulnerability already limit our room for manoeuvre. Strategic autonomy cannot rest on diplomatic positioning or military preparedness alone. It requires economic strength, effective institutions and a population with a real stake in the country's future.
Some of these questions will be on the table at Margalla Dialogue 2026, convened by the Islamabad Policy Research Institute on 10-11 November under the theme 'Global Order in Transition: Navigating Strategic Uncertainty'. Its agenda is useful precisely because it refuses to treat geopolitical realignment, West AsiaSouth Asia connectivity, technological change, national resilience, economic security and international law as separate conversations. Two questions deserve particular attention. Can technology strengthen governance rather than merely increase control? And can economic resilience become the foundation of national security rather than its neglected component?
These are not abstract questions for conference halls. Their answers will decide whether countries respond to uncertainty through confrontation and coercion, or through institutional reform, cooperation and economic opportunity.
The emerging world order will not be judged only by which powers rise or fall. Its more consequential test will be whether it restores credibility to the institutions that govern people's lives and the relations between nations.
The world is not running out of power. It is running out of patience.

title: A weak mind  the absence of truth
description: A weak mind  the absence of truth
content:
Marcus Aurelius writes in his Meditations five signs of a weak mind: "Surrendering control to external circumstances; complaining and playing the victim; seeking external validation and obsessing over others' opinions; letting uncontrolled emotions dictate actions; and resisting the present moment and avoiding duty."
For me, the intriguing question is how to develop a strong mind.
The other day, I had a seasonal flu attack. To offset its malaise, I decided to watch a movie and selected Reporting Live. The movie relates the turbulent journey the two journalists venture on to unravel the truth. The two characters, after facing ineluctable trials and tribulations – though they stagger for a while – succeed in unearthing the truth. But very few moments later, they are murdered in a plotted road accident.
To evade facing or speaking the truth is the cause of all mental and physical ills. To bury the truth nine feet deep under the weight of compromises is tantamount to burying one's own existence. It stifles the soul; it clips the wings of imagination; it deprives man of a dignified life.
The antonym of truth is not falsehood; it is compromise or expediency. Apprehensions of bad consequences we might reap for treading the path of truth might force us to make existential compromises. Some might be thinking, "It's easier said than done." Yes, the path of truth never runs smooth.
Suffocating censorship rampant at various levels and in fluid forms discourages truth seeking and speaking. Government employees are barred from pointing out loopholes in government policies. The proverbial Vigo Dala, the threat of being shown the door, and social stigmatisation stalk us away from pursuing the truth. Truth is now deemed to exist in textbooks only. Slowly and steadily, we are becoming a nation of weak minds, showing little resistance to injustice. A nation mired in existential worries cannot afford to pursue the truth.
Yes, a weak mind surrenders control to external circumstances as he lacks grit to lock horns with circumstances. He terms it a foolhardy attitude to fight for truth and gives in to expediency. He adopts a pleasant demeanour and finds solace in agreeing with all. It is advised to keep everything in moderation, even moderation itself, as its cloyed excess reeks of hypocrisy.
In this age of social media, where everyone's worth is calibrated on the number of views, likes, comments and shares, the epidemic of external validation finds the most suitable clime for its growth. Social media facilitates us to cash in on our patina and hide our inner truth of failure to face the truth. It will widen the chasm between our inner real and outer assumed, resulting in utter chaos of mind and heart.
Seeking external validation often leads to playing victim all the time. The 'sinned against more than sinning' attitude shears us off all the responsibility and accountability of contributing our part in turning the circumstances untoward. Excuses and subterfuge abound in the repertoire of a truth-evader.
Truth is an objective serving as a lodestar to direct our wayward thoughts and actions towards our destination. Having an illusory pivot of our cognition leads us to lose control of our actions to emotions.
A weak mind always demurs at facing the truth. It procrastinates at the right moment and behaves emotionally at the spur of the moment. Yes, the Prince Hamlet, the epitome of intellectual fickleness. A languid or livid activation originates in intolerance of truth. A mind that transforms knowledge into actions is always a strong mind.
No need, at the very least, is there to fear the false because they are inherently weak. Montaigne says that a liar is "brave towards God and a coward towards men". The loudest one in the room is the weakest one in the room. The urge to confront them springs from the truth you are going to stand by.
Francis Bacon, in his essay, Of Truth, compares the utter bliss of standing on the truth with the pleasures of viewing natural beauty: "... but no pleasure is comparable to the standing upon the vantage ground of truth (a hill not to be commanded, and where the air is always clear and serene), and to see the errors and wanderings and mists and tempests in the vale below."

This young sporting brigade has successfully replaced the departing seniors and brought a new energy to the field. Their sharp fielding, aggressive attitude, and hunger to win have impressed all. title: Public act of violence
description: Public act of violence
content:
Scenes of a young woman being assaulted in broad daylight on Lahore's Mozang Link Road is a disturbing incident of lack of tolerance against women and an equally troubling indifference to violence in public spaces. Footage of the incident shows a motorcyclist blocking the woman's path before repeatedly slapping her and pulling her hair. Reportedly suffering a fractured nasal bone, the victim was subjected to an assault that no disagreement or provocation could possibly justify. Equally distressing was the apparent inaction of several onlookers who stood watching as the violence unfolded.
The suspect's subsequent arrest, followed by his release on bail against a surety of Rs100,000, has understandably provoked outrage. However, public anger, no matter how justified, cannot replace due process. The footage provides compelling visual evidence of the assault, but criminal responsibility and punishment must ultimately be determined by a court of law. Bail does not constitute an acquittal, nor should it be mistaken for the conclusion of legal proceedings. It is imperative that investigators build a strong case and ensure that the victim receives the protection and legal support necessary to pursue justice without intimidation. Calls for retaliatory violence, even when driven by sympathy for the victim, offer no lasting solution. Instead, the courts must ensure that the matter proceeds without unnecessary delay and, should the charges be proved, impose a sufficiently stringent punishment within the law. An exemplary judicial outcome would send a far stronger message than public humiliation or revenge.
Lasting deterrence depends not on the intensity of public outrage but on the certainty that violence carries meaningful legal consequences. Justice delivered through due process would vindicate the victim's rights while reinforcing a principle that society urgently needs to uphold.

title: Kabul s denial
description: Kabul s denial
content:
The Afghan Taliban appear increasingly unwilling to acknowledge ground realities. Their intransigent attitude towards Pakistan is pushing them to make unrealistic claims. One such claim from Taliban 2.0 was that they lacked the "capabilities to fuel insecurity in other countries". Nothing could be more astonishing than this statement as it stands in contradiction to the modus operandi of the reclusive regime in Afghanistan. It is a proven fact that Kabul is patronising a horde of non-state actors, including the outlawed Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, responsible for a spike in terrorism inside Pakistan. Likewise, IS-K and Al-Qaeda are fomenting terrorism in neighbouring countries by using Afghan soil with impunity.
Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid has simply hoodwinked the public about these ground realities by saying that Pakistan's finger-pointing over terrorist incidents is meant for "domestic distraction". It is also a flawed assessment from the Taliban spokesperson that "it is not in his country's interest to create insecurity in Pakistan or to support any acts of instability there". The facts speak for themselves, and he would be better advised to refer to a host of reports from UN and other bodies, squarely blaming the Taliban for being behind the export of terrorism.
Islamabad has rightly rebutted such absurd claims from the Taliban leadership by citing the cross-border terrorism index of the UN Security Council's Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team as well as a report from the US Congress. Likewise, the US Lead Inspector General's report on Operation Enduring Sentinel for JanuaryMarch 2026 stated that the Afghan Taliban continued to allow the banned TTP to operate from Afghan territory. That is why Pakistan was compelled to fly sorties over terrorist hideouts inside Afghanistan, after a complete lack of cooperation from Kabul to exterminate the terror nexus.
Kabul must get real and understand that its stunt is leading it into a quagmire. Millions of Afghans are malnourished and lack avenues of social mobility, as Kabul nurses a feel-good factor with the militants. The gun-toting militants are an existential threat to the regime as well as the peace and stability of the entire region. No point in living with ostrich syndrome.

title: Teachers and the learning crisis
description: Teachers and the learning crisis
content:
World Teachers' Day, on 5 October, called on governments to stand with teachers. In Pakistan, that commitment must survive beyond the speeches. It must reach the classroom, where teachers are expected to deliver learning despite unequal pay, uneven deployment and inadequate professional support.
The Pakistan Economic Survey 202526 reports education expenditure at 0.8% of GDP in 202425. The Education 2030 financing benchmark is 46%. This distance matters because improving teaching requires sustained funding for preparation, classroom materials and the work conditions. Provincial governments need credible spending plans, with published allocations and actual expenditure, so commitments can be assessed against delivery.
The consequences are visible in children's learning. ASER 2025 finds that only about half of Class 5 children can read a Class 2-level story. The finding exposes a serious failure: children can spend years in school without mastering foundational skills. Enrolment and learning must be pursued together.
Teacher shortages also require a more precise diagnosis. Tabadlab's Dec 2025 report, The Missing Ustaani, using 202223 school census data, identifies 195,550 vacant sanctioned teaching posts. Vacancies, however, are not interchangeable with the additional teachers needed to meet a particular classroom staffing benchmark. National totals can conceal schools with surplus staff alongside schools struggling to function.
A quarter of public primary schools for girls operate with one teacher, rising to 52% in Balochistan and 51% in Sindh. Expecting one teacher to provide individual attention without additional support is a failure of system design.
Provincial departments should publish school-level staffing needs and use transparent rules for recruitment and transfers. Redeployment must be combined with targeted hiring where shortages remain. Remote postings need incentives, safe transport and suitable accommodation. Staffing decisions should protect girls' access to education and their progression beyond primary school.
Pay deserves equal scrutiny. A study of 436 science and math teachers, published by UKFIET in 2026, found that private-school teachers accounted for 85% of those earning below Rs20,000 monthly; women constituted 82% of that lowest-paid group. These are findings from one sample, not national estimates. They nevertheless raise serious questions about how the profession values qualified women and sustains teaching in low-fee schools.
Fair salaries and secure employment should accompany meaningful professional standards. Promotion should recognise demonstrated teaching practice and professional growth. Raw examination scores alone cannot fairly measure a teacher's contribution when children enter classrooms with vastly different opportunities and levels of preparation.
Professional development must become part of everyday teaching. The Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel identifies structured support for teachers and instruction matched to children's learning levels as cost-effective approaches. Pakistan should translate that evidence into usable lesson guides, regular classroom coaching and simple assessments that help teachers identify gaps and adapt instruction. Pre-service preparation should include supervised classroom practice.
Teachers also need preparation for multilingual and multigrade classrooms, and for including children with disabilities. Books in languages children understand, accessible materials, safe drinking water and functioning toilets belong in the same reform agenda. Digital resources should support teaching.
Curriculum and exams must reinforce this work.
Implementation needs clear responsibility. Provincial departments should publish annual progress on staffing, teacher support and foundational learning, with additional resources directed towards the schools facing the greatest disadvantage. Teachers must help shape these reforms, and headteachers must have the support to sustain them. Pakistan will honour its teachers when it makes effective teaching possible in every classroom.

title: Nancy Guthrie case  Retired FBI agent points to potential breakthrough
description: A retired FBI agent says jail informants and inmate calls could help investigators solve Nancy Guthrie s disappearance
content:
A retired FBI agent says jail informants and inmate calls could help investigators solve Nancy Guthrie's disappearance
A retired FBI agent has suggested that jail informants and inmate communications could provide crucial leads in the ongoing investigation into the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie, the 84-year-old mother of Today co-anchor Savannah Guthrie.
Speaking to NewsNation correspondent Brian Entin on the October 21 episode of Brian Entin Investigates , former FBI special agent Maureen O’Connell discussed how information gathered from inmates could help investigators identify those responsible.
Asked whether jail calls could play a role in the case, O’Connell said they could be significant. She explained that law enforcement officers in Pima County, Arizona, would likely be working with existing jail informants and seeking information from people arrested in connection with other cases.
However, O’Connell cautioned that individuals aware of the investigation’s public profile might attempt to exploit the situation by offering misleading information in exchange for potential benefits.
The former agent also stressed the importance of keeping certain investigative details confidential. She said genuine leads could be distinguished from false claims when a person provides information that has not already been disclosed publicly.
Her comments come as the search for Nancy continues without a publicly identified suspect. Her family reported her missing on February 1, after she was last seen on the evening of January 31 in Tucson, Arizona.
Investigators have released photographs showing a masked individual on Nancy’s front porch and made alleged ransom notes public as part of the investigation. Savannah Guthrie has also offered a $1 million reward for information that helps locate her mother.
Despite these efforts and continued public attention, authorities have yet to name a suspect. O’Connell’s remarks highlight the potential value of confidential information and inmate communications as investigators continue pursuing leads in the Nancy Guthrie disappearance case.

title: Elden Ring film reportedly has  200m budget  A24   s most expensive production yet
description: Alex Garland   s Elden Ring adaptation reportedly has  200m budget  making it A24   s costliest film to date
content:
Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation reportedly has $200m budget, making it A24’s costliest film to date
A24’s upcoming Elden Ring film, directed by Alex Garland, reportedly has a budget of nearly $200 million, potentially making it the studio’s most expensive production to date.
According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, the studio is spending close to $200 million to adapt FromSoftware’s acclaimed dark fantasy role-playing game, excluding marketing costs. Earlier reports had put the production budget at approximately $100 million.
The revised figure would place Elden Ring well ahead of A24’s previous high-budget productions.
The studio reportedly spent around $70 million on Marty Supreme , starring Timothée Chalamet, while Garland’s Civil War had a reported budget of $50 million.
The investment reflects the scale of A24’s plans for the video game adaptation. Although the studio is known for independent films, the reported budget puts the project in a different financial category from many of its previous releases.
The original Elden Ring has sold more than 36 million copies, according to analyst Rhys Elliott, generating over $2 billion in revenue.
Its commercial performance could help attract audiences to the film, although the game’s success does not guarantee that the adaptation will achieve similar results at the box office.
The film stars Kit Connor, known for Heartstopper , and Cailee Spaeny, whose credits include Alien: Romulus . Production reportedly wrapped earlier in the summer, with the film scheduled to arrive in cinemas on March 3 2028.
George R.R. Martin is also involved as a producer. Martin previously helped FromSoftware develop the lore behind the original game, which follows a Tarnished protagonist exploring the Lands Between in a quest to become Elden Lord.

Priyanka Chopra Jonas has shared how her four-year-old daughter, Malti, is developing her own fashion sense, revealing that the youngster already chooses her own clothes.
Speaking exclusively to PEOPLE at InStyle’s Imagemaker Awards in Los Angeles on October 15, the actress discussed the lessons she hopes to teach her daughter, whom she shares with husband Nick Jonas.
"I already feel she has inherent style — she picks her own clothes," Chopra Jonas said. "We've always given her agency, and she always is well turned out."
The actress also explained her approach to teaching Malti about beauty and self-confidence.
"When it comes to beauty, you just have to know who you are and have a sense of self, and that always ends up being confident and beautiful … she's, you know, doing it well at a young age," she added.
Chopra Jonas, 44, and Jonas, 34, welcomed Malti via surrogate in January 2022, just over three years after their wedding.
The couple generally keeps their daughter's upbringing private but occasionally shares family moments on social media.
In a May cover story for Vogue Arabia, Chopra Jonas spoke about balancing her professional commitments with motherhood and praised Jonas for his involvement in raising their daughter.
"My whole existence revolves around her, what time she has to go to school," she said. "She is the best thing I've accomplished in my life and represents the best of Nick and me."

"My husband is very hands-on and even today — because I had to jump on this interview — he was the one preparing her for silly hair day at school. He did the cutest lopsided pigtails on her," she said.
At the Imagemaker Awards, Chopra Jonas received the Woman of Impact Award for her work amplifying women's voices and challenging stereotypes on screen.
Reflecting on the recognition, she said her younger self would have been surprised by her achievements and her determination to overcome challenges.

"Taylor thinks she can have it all," the source said. "And she plans to. At 36 she knows she still has time to start a family. She's in no rush."
For now, the couple reportedly remains focused on their respective commitments. Swift has been attending Chiefs home games to support Kelce as he continues his NFL season.

title: Shadab deserves fair treatment
description: Pakistan   s dramatic win offers hope  but consistent performances and responsible selection remain essential
content:
Pakistan’s dramatic win offers hope, but consistent performances and responsible selection remain essential
KARACHI: Social media was flooded with criticism of Shadab Khan preceding Pakistan’s dramatic victory over England. Questions were raised about Sufyan Muqeem’s exclusion, Arafat Minhas not being given a bowl, and whether Shadab was being selected because of his father-in-law, Saqlain Mushtaq, and former Islamabad United coach Mike Hesson.
After Pakistan’s top order collapsed, I had barely five per cent hope of victory. I went out for dinner, keeping an eye on the score. When Shadab and Haris Rauf put together a partnership, I began watching on my mobile before returning home to see the thrilling finish. It was undoubtedly one of Pakistan cricket’s finest victories.
I have known Shadab since before his international debut. While I was in England, an acquaintance told me about an exceptionally talented young all-rounder who could represent Pakistan. That prediction came true, and Shadab played a key role in Pakistan’s Champions Trophy triumph.
No cricketer can perform consistently in every match. Like others, Shadab has experienced ups and downs, with fitness issues affecting his form and forcing him out of the team. Unlike players backed by aggressive public relations campaigns, he has no constant social media cheerleading to portray him as a hero regardless of his performances.
Expectations among Pakistani fans are high, yet Faheem Ashraf rarely faces the same level of scrutiny despite producing few outstanding performances. Shadab, meanwhile, remains a frequent target. The criticism intensified after his marriage to Saqlain Mushtaq’s daughter, with people using insulting nicknames such as “Damad Khan”.
Having known both men, I am confident Saqlain would never have asked anyone to select Shadab, nor would Shadab have sought his father-in-law’s influence. Online abuse has placed the all-rounder under immense pressure, forcing him repeatedly to defend himself.
Social media has eroded restraint. People who might hesitate to confront someone face-to-face readily post insults from behind their phones. Players deserve criticism for poor performances, but personal attacks are unacceptable. Artificial intelligence, meanwhile, is transforming healthcare and other fields worldwide, yet some people use it to target and ridicule others.
Shaheen Afridi faces similar treatment over his relationship with his father-in-law, Shahid Afridi. Despite Pakistan’s encouraging ODI performances under his leadership and his own wicket-taking form, the taunts continue.
Pakistan’s latest victory offers hope ahead of next year’s World Cup in South Africa. The team’s ability to fight back after losing nine wickets against England has revived optimism. Shadab’s reprieve on review, when replays showed the ball had hit his bat before his pads, proved decisive.
However, one remarkable win cannot hide persistent top-order failures. Shadab cannot rescue Pakistan with a century every time; every player must contribute. The team must also improve its balance, with Saim Ayub struggling to justify his place. Selectors should give deserving young players a genuine opportunity.
Poor results have also damaged public interest in ODI cricket, with several stands remaining empty during matches in Rawalpindi and Lahore. Consistent performances are essential to win back disappointed fans.
The PCB should confirm Shaheen as captain until the World Cup, ending uncertainty and allowing the team to focus. If senior and junior players maintain their form, Pakistan could break its cycle of early exits from ICC tournaments.
Let us hope the team builds on this victory, restores supporters’ confidence and gives the country more reasons to celebrate.

title: When blood ties break  Money  property disputes strain Pakistani families
description: Economic pressures and property disputes are driving relatives apart  weakening traditional family bonds
content:
Economic pressures and property disputes are driving relatives apart, weakening traditional family bonds
Once bound by blood and tradition, Pakistani families are increasingly being torn apart by money, property disputes and changing lifestyles. From fathers disowning sons to brothers becoming bitter rivals, relationships that once offered lifelong support are giving way to silence, resentment and estrangement.
A recent incident in Karachi, involving the alleged suicide of Dr Umar and his family, highlighted the extent to which family ties can deteriorate. Dr Umar’s brother, Muhammad Abu Bakr, told police that the two had not been in contact for the past 10 years. Their estrangement was so severe that Abu Bakr did not even know how many children his brother had. He learnt only after the incident, when he arrived in Karachi, that Dr Umar had three daughters.
The father of Dr Umar’s wife, Mahwish, also told police and the media that he had been out of contact with his daughter for a considerable period. As a result, he was unaware of the family’s deteriorating financial circumstances. He said he had visited his daughter’s flat for the first time after the incident.
Read : Domestic disputes overwhelm family courts
Announcements and public notices declaring estrangement between close relatives regularly appear in newspapers and on social media. Fathers disown sons, while brothers publicly sever ties with one another, often following prolonged family disputes.
Abdul Jabbar, a Larkana resident, told The Express Tribune he had considered disowning his drug-addicted son but dropped the idea after friends intervened. However, the two have long remained out of contact.
Last April, Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) MNA Mir Aijaz Jakhrani publicly severed ties with his half-brother, Azad Jakhrani, days after their father’s death. Their relationship had deteriorated following the death of Ejaz’s son, Zaid, and later soured further over their father’s property.
Social scientists say several factors are contributing to the breakdown of family relationships, including urbanisation, changing lifestyles, financial pressures and inheritance disputes.
Also Read : Divorce, khula cases swamp family courts
Dr Riaz Ahmed Shaikh, a professor in the Department of Social Sciences at Shaheed Zulfikar Ali Bhutto Institute of Science and Technology (SZABIST), Karachi, told The Express Tribune that rapid urbanisation had largely dismantled the traditional joint-family system.
In rural communities, extended families traditionally lived together and supported one another in times of need. In cities, however, larger families often cannot live under one roof, weakening everyday interaction and mutual support.
Dr Shaikh also pointed to changing marriage patterns. In the past, marriages between cousins often kept extended families closely connected. As marriages increasingly take place outside the immediate family network, he said, relationships with blood relatives may become less close.
Advocate Muhammad Ismail Rajput said rising needs and growing aspirations were also creating friction within families. Financial difficulties can trigger disagreements when relatives are unable to meet one another’s needs, while competing ambitions and expectations can widen existing rifts.
Property and other family disputes frequently end up in court, where relatives become opposing parties in lengthy legal battles. Rajput said thousands of cases involving family members were pending before different courts. As disputes drag on, relatives who once shared close bonds can begin to treat one another more like adversaries than family.
Sindh Law Minister Zia-ul-Hassan Lanjar told the provincial assembly that around 200,000 cases were pending in the province, including 72,000 civil cases and over 25,000 family cases. Karachi’s District East recorded the highest number of civil and family disputes, highlighting how financial pressures, changing lifestyles and property conflicts are straining family ties.

Game of Thrones star Peter Claffey reportedly joins Marvel's 'X-Men' reboot as Beast, though Marvel has yet to confirm
Peter Claffey, known for starring in HBO’s A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms , has reportedly landed a key role in Marvel Studios’ upcoming X-Men reboot.
According to a report by Knight Edge Media, the Irish actor has been cast as Hank McCoy, better known as Beast, in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) project. The casting has not been officially confirmed by Marvel, and ScreenRant reported that it had contacted Disney for comment.
Claffey has gained attention for playing Ser Duncan the Tall in A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms , a Game of Thrones spin-off based on George R. R. Martin’s fantasy stories. His reported casting follows rumours linking him to the role of Beast, with actor Charles Melton also mentioned in speculation surrounding the character.
Peter Claffey has reportedly been cast as Beast in the ‘X-MEN’ reboot film. (via https://t.co/ka1QwUNys1 ) pic.twitter.com/SiE9GTqxqE
Beast, whose real name is Dr Henry Philip McCoy, is a prominent member of the X-Men. The character is known for his scientific intelligence, strategic thinking and distinctive blue, furry appearance. Although Hank initially resembles a human, he undergoes physical changes that give him his recognisable appearance.
The character has previously been portrayed in live-action films by Kelsey Grammer and Nicholas Hoult. Grammer played an older version of Beast in X-Men: The Last Stand and later appeared in The Marvels . Hoult portrayed a younger version of the character in X-Men: First Class , X-Men: Days of Future Past and X-Men: Apocalypse .
Marvel Studios is developing a reboot of the X-Men franchise as the characters are set to become part of the MCU. The original comic series, created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby, debuted in 1963 and introduced a team of mutant superheroes led by Professor Charles Xavier.
Further details about the upcoming X-Men reboot, including its cast and storyline, have yet to be officially announced.

title: Egyptians claim squash titles
description: Al Hammamy  Rowan Elaraby triumph in Karachi finals
content:
Al Hammamy, Rowan Elaraby triumph in Karachi finals
KARACHI: Egyptian players Karim El Hammamy and Rowan Elaraby claimed the men’s and women’s titles, respectively, at the Venice ABC Open 2026 international squash tournament which concluded here at the DHA Creek Club on Sunday.
Second seed El Hammamy defeated top seed Curtis Malik of England 3-0 in the men’s final with the set score being 11-6, 12-10, 11-3 in 48 minutes.
El Hammamy, ranked World No 49, overcame an injury to beat Malik, World No 25, to lift the title at the $82,000 tournament.
In the women’s final, fourth seed Rowan Elaraby of Egypt defeated second seed Amina El Rihany of Egypt 3-0 to win the crown.
Rowan, World No 47, did not allow her opponent to settle down and sealed an emphatic 11-6, 11-8, 11-5 victory.
Sindh’s Labour Minister Saeed Ghani also witnessed the finals while DHA Bahria Administrator Brig (retd) Ameer Nawaz Khan was the guest of honour. Squash legend Jahangir Khan was also present.
In the semi-finals on Saturday Curtis overcame Yassin Shohdy of Egypt 3-2 in a closely contested battle. Karim on the other hand conquered Yee Xian Siow of Malaysia 3-0 in the pre-final.
Egypt's Raneem Elaraby and Amina El Rihany on Saturday advanced to the final of the women’s section.
Fourth seed Elaraby, on Saturday whacked compatriot Haya Rizk 3-1 in the semi-final.
El Rihany also produced a strong performance, overcoming third seed Nour Shahin by the same score-line in the other semi-final.
It was a PSA copper event in which 24 men’s and 23 women took part.
Pakistan’s experienced players Asim Khan and Nasir Iqbal were also part of the event but they failed to deliver.
Nasir exited at the first hurdle while Asim fell in the quarter-finals.
The event missed rising star Noor Zaman and Mohammad Ashab Irfan due to their engagement in the Silicon Valley Open in the United States when Noor exited at the quarter-finals stage after upsetting world No4 Karim Gawad of Egypt in the pre-quarter-final.

title: Children   s laureates pledge book royalties to Sally Rooney after UK saleshalt
description: Haughton  Ireland   s children   s literature laureate  and Davies  the laureate for Wales  are ones who announced support
content:
Haughton, Ireland’s children’s literature laureate, and Davies, the laureate for Wales, are ones who announced support
Children’s authors Chris Haughton and Nicola Davies have pledged to donate royalties from their books to Irish novelist Sally Rooney in a show of solidarity after her publisher stopped supplying her work in the UK over concerns surrounding her support for Palestine Action.
Haughton, Ireland’s children’s literature laureate, and Davies, the children’s laureate for Wales, announced their decisions following the controversy surrounding Rooney’s bestselling novels, including Normal People, Conversations with Friends and Intermezzo. Her publisher, Faber, announced on October 14 that it would no longer supply her books in the UK because current legislation prevented it from passing her British sales earnings on to her.
Haughton said he wanted to highlight what he described as the absurdity of the situation, arguing that authors should be able to express their political beliefs without facing restrictions on their work.
“I really want to express my full support for Sally Rooney,” Haughton told The Guardian. “As authors, we need to be focused on freedom of expression, this is everything we’re about, and this is just showing solidarity with an author who has bravely spoken out.”
He added that sending Rooney his royalties would expose what he sees as the contradiction at the heart of the situation. Haughton, whose books have sold millions of copies worldwide, said he would donate royalties from his UK book sales to the novelist.
Haughton has previously been arrested twice for holding placards allegedly supporting Palestine Action, a direct-action group that was proscribed under UK terrorism legislation in July 2025. He said the organisation had been effective in attempting to stop arms supplies to Israel and expressed confidence that his position would be vindicated by history.
Davies also pledged her support, saying she would donate her next half-year royalty payment from The Day War Came, her children's book about a child refugee fleeing conflict. She pointed to the humanitarian crisis in Gaza as a reason for speaking out, arguing that she could not advocate for children in Wales while remaining silent about the suffering of children in Palestine.
Rooney's situation stems from her public commitment to direct proceeds from her work towards Palestine Action. Under UK law, providing money to an organisation proscribed under terrorism legislation can constitute a criminal offence when a person knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that the funds may be used for terrorism. The offence carries a maximum prison sentence of 14 years.
Following discussions with Rooney, Faber said it could no longer supply her work in the UK in any format, while confirming that it would continue publishing and selling her books in other territories. Existing copies already held by British retailers were not being recalled, although the publisher would no longer replenish their stock.
The decision has prompted wider debate about freedom of expression, artistic independence and the consequences of the UK government's proscription of Palestine Action. More than 3,700 people were reported to have been arrested in Britain for alleged support of the group since the ban was introduced, with many cases involving people holding protest placards.
A legal challenge to the proscription is due to be heard by the UK Supreme Court on November 4 and 5. The case is expected to examine whether the ban disproportionately interferes with rights to freedom of expression and peaceful protest.
The pledges from Haughton and Davies add to growing support for Rooney among writers and other public figures, as the debate over the relationship between counterterrorism legislation and artistic freedom continues.

title: WAPDA win National Athletics Championships
description: Maria Bibi breaks national 5 000m record in Karachi
content:
Maria Bibi breaks national 5,000m record in Karachi
WAPDA emerged as overall champions of both men’s and women’s sections of the 54th National Athletics Championship, winning 27 gold medals.
Maria Bibi set a national record in the women’s 5,000 metres on the final day at the NED University.
WAPDA finished atop the overall standings with 17 gold medals in the men’s events and ten in the women’s competition. Navy finished second overall with nine golds, while Higher Education Commission (HEC) took third place with eight golds.
Maria clocked 19 minutes and two seconds to win the women’s 5,000m, breaking the previous national record of 19:04.05 set by Olympian Rabia Ashiq in 2012. WAPDA’s Nazia Ehsan took silver in 19:49.50, while HEC’s Goonish Batool finished third in 20:10.80.
WAPDA’s sprinter Shajar Abbas won the men’s 200m in 20.75 seconds, ahead of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Attaullah, who clocked 20.90. HEC’s Haseeb Ahmed took bronze in 21.40.
HEC’s Khaula Umar Khan claimed the women’s 200m title in 24.80 seconds, with Sindh’s Iqra Riaz second and WAPDA’s Malaika Shehzadi third.
Navy’s Usman Ghani won the men’s high jump with 1.96 metres, while WAPDA’s Sohail Amir took the men’s 5,000m title in 15:16.20.
Navy secured gold in the men’s 4x100m relay in 42.00 seconds, while WAPDA won the women’s event in 48.63.
WAPDA also claimed victories in the men’s triple jump and hammer throw, alongside several field events. Navy’s Amtil Rehman was among the standout performers, winning four gold medals, while Shajar collected three.
The championship was held under the supervision of the Athletics Federation of Pakistan and organised by the Sindh Athletics Association, with support from Lok Sahaita.

title: Alex Winter explains why he wanted to humanise a controversial figure in Primetime
description: Alex Winter discusses playing Bill Conradt in  Primetime  and why the film explores the human side of difficult cases
content:
Alex Winter discusses playing Bill Conradt in 'Primetime' and why the film explores the human side of difficult cases
Actor Alex Winter has explained why he wanted to portray Texas district attorney Bill Conradt with empathy in Primetime , the upcoming film directed by Lance Oppenheim.
Winter, best known for playing Bill S. Preston in the Bill & Ted trilogy, was selected to play Conradt, whose story became connected to the controversial television programme To Catch a Predator .
Speaking to Rolling Stone on October 25, Winter said he was drawn to the film’s examination of media, internet culture and society’s treatment of people accused of wrongdoing.
The actor explained that he wanted to present Conradt as a human being without excusing his actions. To prepare for the role, he researched Conradt’s background, working environment and life, speaking with district attorneys and other people familiar with the region where he worked.
Winter described the case as tragic and criticised the way television coverage can prioritise ratings over a nuanced understanding of the people involved.
He also discussed the film’s wider message, arguing that presenting people as human beings does not mean overlooking harmful behaviour. He believes that understanding the people involved is important when considering both those accused of wrongdoing and those who have experienced abuse.
Primetime features Robert Pattinson portraying To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen. The cast also includes Creed Bratton, Jonathan Lipnicki, Phoebe Bridgers and former NBC executive Jeff Zucker.
Beyond the film, Winter reflected on his Broadway experience in Waiting for Godot , where he performed alongside longtime friend Keanu Reeves. He described the production as one of the greatest experiences of his life and said it renewed his interest in theatre.
Winter is also preparing for another stage production, Incident at Vichy , planned for New York in May, while continuing to develop future film projects.

title: The Terminator  sees streaming demand rise amid growing AI concerns
description: The Terminator  franchise generated nearly  300m in global streaming revenue as interest in AI themed films grows
content:
'The Terminator' franchise generated nearly $300m in global streaming revenue as interest in AI-themed films grows
James Cameron’s The Terminator franchise has experienced a rise in streaming viewership and revenue amid growing public concern about artificial intelligence, according to data from Parrot Analytics.
The franchise has generated nearly $300 million in global streaming subscriber revenue since 2020, making it the leading performer among several science-fiction properties exploring the risks of advanced technology.
The Matrix has generated $132 million over the same period, while Blade Runner has earned $56 million.
Parrot Analytics’ Streaming Economics model estimates that four science-fiction franchises have collectively generated more than $500 million in global subscriber revenue during this period.
The report links renewed interest in these films to real-world discussions about AI, artificial general intelligence and deepfakes.
In the United States, The Terminator franchise had accumulated $169 million in streaming revenue by the first quarter of 2026.
The data shows a sharp acceleration in revenue growth beginning in early 2023, around the time ChatGPT brought generative AI into mainstream public discussion.
Audience demand for the films has also increased. In 2023, the original The Terminator ranked 20th among the most in-demand films released before 2000 in the United States. By 2026, it had risen to sixth place in the same category.
The change has been even more pronounced globally for Terminator 2: Judgment Day. The 1991 film moved from 40th place among the world’s most in-demand classic films in 2023 to second place in 2026, according to the report.
The figures suggest that attention towards artificial intelligence may be contributing to the commercial performance of older science-fiction films.

Prince William reveals he tried to move Travis Kelce out of photo with Taylor Swift and his children
Prince William has revealed that he tried to move Travis Kelce out of a photograph featuring Taylor Swift and his children, unaware of the picture’s significance to the singer’s relationship with the NFL star.
The Prince of Wales shared the story during a surprise appearance on The Graham Norton Show. According to the BBC , the audience gasped when William walked onto the stage.
The photograph was taken in 2024, when Swift performed at Wembley Stadium in London. It was also the first picture Swift posted of herself with Kelce in the frame.
"I wasn't until recently," William told Norton when asked whether he understood the photograph’s importance.
He continued, "I hadn't appreciated the picture. And actually, I was trying to move him [Travis Kelce] out of the photo. Travis kept coming back in and I couldn't work out why he kept coming back in. I was trying to move him out, so it was just me and Taylor and the children."
Kelce, meanwhile, previously spoke positively about meeting the British royals on the New Heights podcast, which he hosts with his brother, Jason Kelce.
"He [Prince William] was the coolest m—erf—er," Kelce said. He also recalled being unsure whether royal protocol required him to bow or curtsy, or whether he could simply shake William’s hand.
William had met Swift before, at a 2013 Kensington Palace gala for the Centrepoint charity. The pair joined Bon Jovi to perform "Livin' On A Prayer", an experience William later described with embarrassment.
"To this day, I still do not know what came over me. Honestly, even now I'm cringing at what happened next, and I don't understand why I gave in," he said, explaining that Swift had encouraged him to join her.

JoJo Siwa reveals she and Chris Hughes independently picked the same dream engagement ring design by coincidence
JoJo Siwa has revealed a surprising coincidence with boyfriend Chris Hughes, sharing that the couple independently chose the exact same engagement ring design while discussing their hopes for the future.
The singer and dancer, 23, disclosed the story during an exclusive interview with PEOPLE at the Industry Dance Awards in Los Angeles on October 21. Siwa explained that although she wanted Hughes, 33, to design a future engagement ring himself, she had already imagined what her dream ring would look like.
“I told my mom, I said, ‘Whenever he asks you, [tell him] I want him to design it completely. I want it to be completely his design,’” Siwa said, referring to her mother, Jessalyn Siwa.
However, during a dinner together, the couple decided to reveal their ideas for her dream ring simultaneously. Siwa recalled searching online for a design she liked before asking Hughes to show her his choice on the count of three.
“One, two, three. And we flipped it. And we were holding the same photo from Google!” she said, describing the ring as having a blue emerald shape. Siwa added that the chances of them selecting the same design were “so slim”.
The couple's relationship appears to be going strong, with Siwa describing things between them as “lovely”. They were approaching their 18-month anniversary at the time of the interview.
Siwa and Hughes met in April 2025 while competing on Celebrity Big Brother UK . Their friendship developed into a romance, which they confirmed in June that year.
The pair have also spoken openly about their hopes for marriage and children. In July 2025, Hughes told Us Weekly that they had discussed their future together, describing these conversations as exciting when two people are deeply in love.
Siwa has previously credited Hughes as the inspiration behind her March 2026 single, “Serendipity”, explaining that their unexpected meeting influenced the song.

“Please donate to help cover my legal fees, so that I do not have to think about Ethan ever again,” she said
Twitch streamer Morgan “Frogan” has appealed for donations to help cover $73,000 in outstanding legal fees following the dismissal of a lawsuit brought against her by Ethan Klein’s company.
Frogan shared the update on X, revealing that her legal expenses had exceeded $100,000. “I still owe $73K after it costing well over $100K,” she wrote, asking supporters to contribute towards the remaining amount.
“Please donate to help cover my legal fees, so that I do not have to think about Ethan ever again,” she added.
Her fundraising campaign on GoFundMe had set a target of $200,000 and had raised $45,491 at the time of reporting. The appeal comes after the copyright dispute was voluntarily dismissed, leaving Frogan with substantial legal costs despite the case ending.
Ted Entertainment Inc., the company behind Klein’s online content, voluntarily dismissed the lawsuit without prejudice on September 8, 2026. A dismissal without prejudice means the case has ended but may be filed again, subject to applicable legal requirements.
The lawsuit was filed in June 2025 and accused Frogan, fellow streamer Denims and Kacey “Kaceytron” of copyright infringement. The dispute centred on their reaction content involving Klein’s video, Content Nuke - Hasan Piker . Frogan has maintained that her use of the material constituted fair use.
The legal battle unfolded amid wider tensions between online creators and streamers over reaction videos and the use of copyrighted material. Frogan’s latest appeal highlights the financial burden that legal disputes can leave behind, even when a case is no longer proceeding.
The lawsuit is separate from recent allegations involving Klein’s personal life. His wife, Hila Klein, has recently made public allegations of infidelity against him, but those claims are unrelated to the copyright case involving Frogan.

Makoto Yukimura says 'Vinland Saga' anime’s third season is not currently in production, leaving its future uncertain
The future of Vinland Saga season three remains uncertain after manga creator Makoto Yukimura confirmed that work on the next instalment is not currently underway.
Yukimura shared the update in response to a fan asking about the anime’s continuation on X.
Sorry my friend, I have no good news about that. The project is not currently in progress.
Neither Kodansha, which publishes the Vinland Saga manga, nor MAPPA, the studio behind the second anime season, has issued an official announcement about a third season.
Based on Yukimura’s manga, Vinland Saga follows Thorfinn, a young Icelandic warrior whose life changes after the death of his father, Thors.
Seeking revenge against the Viking leader Askeladd, Thorfinn becomes a ruthless fighter, only to lose his purpose when Askeladd dies.
The story takes a different direction in its second season, which aired in 2023 and was produced by MAPPA after Wit Studio animated the first season in 2019.
Thorfinn becomes a slave on a Danish farm, where friendships and painful reflection lead him to reconsider his violent past and embrace his father’s pacifist beliefs.
The second season concludes with Thorfinn determined to find Vinland, a land where he hopes to build a community free from war and violence. A third season would continue his journey, although its production status remains unclear.
One factor that can complicate anime production is the production committee model, in which several companies share the costs and responsibilities of developing a series.
Vinland Saga ’s production committee includes Twin Engine, Kodansha, Production I.G. and MAPPA.
Despite the series’ established audience, no release date or production timeline has been announced for Vinland Saga season three.

Molly Ringwald shares how communication and respect have sustained her marriage to Panio Gianopoulos for over 20 years
Molly Ringwald has shared the relationship advice that has helped her maintain a lasting marriage with husband Panio Gianopoulos for more than two decades, highlighting communication, mutual respect and avoiding hurtful language during disagreements.
The Sixteen Candles actress, 58, discussed the secret to their long-lasting relationship in an exclusive interview with PEOPLE, explaining that couples should focus on how they handle arguments rather than trying to avoid conflict altogether.
“I think the secret is to make sure that you take care of your relationship, to communicate,” Ringwald said.
The actress, who shares three children with Gianopoulos, also emphasised the importance of treating each other with respect, even during difficult conversations. The couple are parents to daughter Mathilda, 23, and twins Adele and Roman, 17.
Ringwald said she encourages her children to understand that disagreements are a normal part of relationships, but the way partners communicate can make a difference. She advised against name-calling, contempt and using absolute statements such as “you always do this” during arguments.
Instead, the actress suggested addressing a partner’s behaviour without turning criticism into a personal attack. She acknowledged that maintaining a healthy relationship requires consistent effort, comparing it to caring for a garden that needs regular attention to flourish.
Ringwald and Gianopoulos began dating in the early 2000s after meeting through an online literary salon, where they initially connected over books with mutual friends. Their conversations later moved to email before they met in person.
The couple married in a private ceremony in July 2007. Ringwald had previously been married to Valéry Lameignère from 1999 to 2002.
The actress has also praised Gianopoulos for his parenting, describing him as an amazing father in a previous interview with Good Housekeeping . She admitted that he seemed to have a natural instinct for parenting, challenging her initial assumption that she would automatically know what to do as a mother.

title: Green eyes decider return
description: Fit again all rounder targets South Africa showdown after swift recovery from abdominal tear
content:
Fit-again all-rounder targets South Africa showdown after swift recovery from abdominal tear
Cameron Green says he is ready to return to action after making a surprisingly swift recovery from an abdominal muscle tear ahead of Australia’s final Test against South Africa.
Green suffered the injury during the one-day international series between the teams but has made encouraging progress in the weeks since, raising hopes of featuring in the series decider.
“Pretty surprised with how quickly it’s actually healed, or how functional I feel only a few weeks after,” Green said of the injury.
“It was really bizarre. I think there’s definitely a pretty clear link between getting hit and then doing the injury. I think it’s too much of a coincidence for them not to be related.
“Basically I got hit where you don’t want to get hit and then two balls later, I went to play a shot just behind the wicket – obviously had to lengthen my muscle, and I think my muscle was pretty keen to not move at that stage after I got hit.
“It’s quite a unique injury. There are not many people that have done the injury and then tried to play a few weeks later. The (medical staff) didn’t have much to go off … (but) it’s all good to go for the last game.”
Green participated in a net session ahead of the third Test in Cape Town as Australia and South Africa prepared for the series decider.
Australia claimed victory in the opening match before the hosts responded in the second Test to level the contest.
Green, who played in last year’s World Test Championship final against South Africa, said the encounter had offered important lessons about the demands of facing the Proteas’ formidable bowling attack.
“(Batting at three in the WTC final) was a tough experience for sure. Pretty unique that you’re playing South Africa with the Dukes ball in England. I think there’s a lot of good learnings, a lot of tough learnings,” Green said.
“Obviously they’re such a quality bowling line-up that you’ve got to be on your game at all times to succeed against them, regardless of where you bat.
“But certainly up the top of the order is incredibly difficult – their opening bowlers are so great with the new ball, you’ve got to work really hard, especially at the start.”
The all-rounder, who made his Test debut in 2020, has batted at positions ranging from number three to eight but believes the middle order best suits his game.
“I’ve had a lot of experience up and down the order. I think I’m well suited at four and five,” he said.
Green demonstrated his ability at number five in Australia’s home series against Bangladesh, finishing as the leading run-scorer across the two matches with a century and a half-century.
Despite his preference, he said he was prepared to adjust his role according to the team’s needs.

title: Rybakina crushes Fernandez to win fourth title of season
description: World number one cruises to a 6 2  6 2 win in 73 minutes
content:
World number one cruises to a 6-2, 6-2 win in 73 minutes
World number one Elena Rybakina won her fourth title of an outstanding season with a ruthless straight-sets victory over Leylah Fernandez in the Ningbo Open final on Sunday.
The top seed and defending champion cruised to a 6-2, 6-2 win in 73 minutes over the world number 30 from Canada.
Rybakina, the Australian and US Open champion, collected her 15th WTA crown in all and went a long way towards securing the year-end number-one ranking.
"Thank you all you guys for an amazing atmosphere," the Moscow-born Kazakh said in her victory speech to the crowd.
"Every day it's amazing to play in front of you. It gives a lot of motivation and energy to keep on going.
"A second win here, it's such a special place for me."
Rybakina broke and then held her own serve with a delicious two-handed crosscourt backhand for a 4-2 lead in the opening set.
She immediately put Fernandez under pressure again on the Canadian's serve and it was soon 5-2 to the reigning champion when her opponent fired into the net.
The 27-year-old Rybakina, who missed this month's Wuhan Open with a foot injury, began to turn the screw and sealed the set to love in under 40 minutes.
Fernandez, who was looking to win her second title in as many months, was broken once more as a clinical Rybakina grabbed a 2-1 second-set lead.
Rybakina saw off two break points in the fourth game to hold, and with that, Fernandez's resistance was broken.
Rybakina was within sight of retaining her trophy after breaking once more for 5-2, then sealed the deal on her first championship point with a searing forehand.

Emily Osment has explained why she requested an intimacy coordinator while filming romantic scenes with Montana Jordan for the CBS sitcom Young Sheldon, citing their 11-year age gap and the importance of making both actors comfortable.
The revelation appears in Jessica Radloff’s new book, Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw’s Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy , as reported by Variety .
Osment joined the series in its fifth season, when she was 30, while Jordan was 18.

“It made everything easier having one there. I think it’s something that’s really important,” she added.
Osment also said she wanted Jordan to have the opportunity to express any discomfort during their scenes. “I don’t know if Montana even knew if he could ask for that. Like, let’s give him the option, too. Make him comfortable,” she said.
Alex Reid, who directed 36 episodes of the sitcom, acknowledged that the production had overlooked the challenges involved in filming kissing scenes because the show did not feature sex scenes.
“We totally dropped the ball,” Reid admitted, recalling how uncomfortable the actors had felt while filming an early scene together.
Series co-creator Steve Molaro supported Osment’s decision, saying she had “every right to ask” for an intimacy coordinator.
Osment and Jordan later reprised their roles in the spin-off Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage , continuing their on-screen partnership beyond Young Sheldon .

Meghan wrote to her father that she was aware of the allegations and wouldn't allow him to meet her children
Meghan Markle reportedly sent her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., a final letter in December 2025, informing him that she knew about allegations against him involving child sexual abuse material and that he would never meet his grandchildren, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.
According to a report by The Sun , cited by PEOPLE, the Duchess of Sussex sent the letter while her father was recovering in a hospital in the Philippines after undergoing a leg amputation. The letter reportedly marked the final time she intended to contact him, bringing another development to their long-running family estrangement.
Sources cited in the report said Meghan wanted to ensure that her father received and read the letter. Hospital staff reportedly delivered it to him, and he read it several times.
The letter allegedly addressed the accusations that had recently emerged publicly, with Meghan telling her father that she was aware of the allegations and would not allow him to meet her children. The reported communication also stated that she would not contact him again.
The development follows reports that Thomas Markle Jr., Meghan’s half-brother, allegedly discovered hundreds or thousands of images depicting child sexual abuse among belongings at his father’s former home in Cebu, the Philippines. He reportedly alerted authorities in the Philippines and contacted the FBI.
Thomas Markle Sr., 82, has denied the allegations, describing them as lies. The claims have not been established as fact, and authorities are examining the allegations.
Meghan addressed the situation publicly on October 23, saying she was deeply distressed by the reports and that her decision to keep her father away from her children had been made to protect them.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” she said in a statement to PEOPLE.
The Duchess also revealed that she had been made aware of troubling allegations against her father after a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. She said she had been assured that the claims were being investigated.
The Metropolitan Police subsequently confirmed receiving a letter containing allegations of alleged offending outside the United Kingdom in January 2019. content:
Reiner has pleaded not guilty to two counts of first-degree murder following his parents’ deaths on December 14, 2025
Nick Reiner has been granted court approval to access money from his approximately $1.6 million family trust fund to cover jail expenses while awaiting trial over the alleged murders of his parents, filmmaker Rob Reiner and photographer Michele Singer Reiner.
A judge ruled on Friday, that successor trustee Jodi Pais Montgomery could deposit up to $300 at a time directly into Reiner’s jail commissary account.
The decision comes as the court considers whether California’s Slayer Statute applies to the trust.
The 33-year-old remains detained at the Twin Towers Correctional Facility in Los Angeles. His lawyers previously argued that he had been unable to access funds to purchase basic necessities.
In court filings last month, his attorneys, Anita P. Wu and Geoffrey A. Neri, stated, "Nick still has not been able to access even $5 from his trust to buy basic subsistence items from the jail commissary."
The Nick Reiner Children’s Trust was established by his parents in 1993, naming him as its sole beneficiary.
His legal team argues that at least $558,000 should have been released when he turned 30 in September 2023.
They also maintain that more than $325,000 originated from his grandfather, comedian Carl Reiner, who died in 2020.
Those opposing the distribution cite California’s Slayer Statute, which can prevent individuals from benefiting financially from the unlawful deaths of those they killed.
Reiner has pleaded not guilty to two counts of first-degree murder following his parents’ deaths on December 14, 2025.
Prosecutors allege that the couple were fatally stabbed at their Brentwood home. The allegations have yet to be proven in court.

title: Infantino laughs off resignation talk
description: The FIFA chief seeks to move past the failed investment proposal with support growing ahead of the 2027 election
content:
The FIFA chief seeks to move past the failed investment proposal with support growing ahead of the 2027 election
FIFA president Gianni Infantino laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning in the wake of the failed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, pointing to overwhelming support from member associations around the globe.
Three months after facing calls to resign after he abandoned the proposal that sought ‌private investment in a new entity controlling commercial rights linked to major FIFA competitions, Infantino now finds himself in a position of strength.
His prospects for reelection strengthened on Friday after the head of Asian football endorsed him for a fourth term, with Asian Football confederation (AFC) President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa saying Asia was united behind Infantino.
"I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the ⁠world. I think what is important is that in an organisation like FIFA, there can be different views, different points of view," Infantino told the BBC as he laughed off a question about whether he had considered stepping down.
"But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone ... then we need to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority.
"I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all African countries have ‌endorsed ⁠me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world."
The AFC had previously joined European body UEFA and CONCACAF, which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean, in criticising the FFE proposal.
But a divided CONCACAF and the AFC's U-turn have left Europe increasingly isolated while exposing the lack of a viable alternative candidate for the FIFA presidency.
Infantino is seeking a fourth ⁠term until 2031 and potential candidates must submit their nominations by November 18.
He apologised at a FIFA Council meeting in Zurich last week over the way the FFE proposal was handled but that did not sway European football associations such as ⁠Germany and England.
However, the 56-year-old Swiss-Italian administrator added: "It's OK to disagree ... but then we need to be able to move on.
"There are different points of view. It's not always easy to bring them all under one ⁠roof, but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views," Infantino added.
"Then it will be up to the FIFA member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want FIFA to be run."
