title: What writers have taught us about war
description: From Tolstoy to Hemingway  the lessons of history and literature remain painfully relevant
content:
From Tolstoy to Hemingway, the lessons of history and literature remain painfully relevant
Leo Tolstoy, a Russian writer, produced War and Peace in 1867, a voluminous fictional narrative of the Napoleonic Wars. Tolstoy weaves history and philosophy into his imagination, with the predominant thought built around the premise that human history is carved by millions of unknown and unrecognised ordinary people. It is not shaped by kings, queens, monarchs, generals or politicians. Leadership, in Tolstoy's vein of thought, has to be representative and in full consonance with the collective spirit of the people.
In his book, Tolstoy gives a deep meaning to the need for human enrichment. He says, "We can know only that we know nothing. And that is the highest degree of human wisdom." Wisdom, it follows, is humble: to recognise that what is known to man is but a drop in the ocean of knowledge. At one point, attention is drawn towards the virtues of patience and greatness. He says, "The strongest of all warriors are these two... time and patience." About greatness, he says, "There is no greatness, where there is no simplicity, goodness, and truth."
Tolstoy was essentially anti-war. In a life organised by destruction, it is inevitable that reason and empathy will get totally refuted. Mankind's obsession with war has repeatedly produced the very opposite of what its leaders claim to seek: security, stability and a better future.
In 1950, John Foster Dulles wrote a differently titled book, War or Peace. Unlike Tolstoy's War and Peace, Dulles's book was meant as a blueprint and a way forward for setting the direction of US foreign policy during the intense Cold War. The difference in the titles is significant. Tolstoy's title suggests that war and peace can coexist within the sweep of history; Dulles's suggests choosing between the two.
Dulles evaluated how catastrophic a conflict with the Soviet Union could be. He argued that societies must be mobilised for achieving peace rather than saving all their moral and spiritual resources for engaging in war. He also emphasised tolerance and peaceful coexistence, and the importance of what the then nascent United Nations could do to avoid wars and conflicts.
The question remains: why does humanity repeatedly choose war when it knows what war costs?
War does not determine who is right — only who is left. Neither does it give victory in the face of human loss. H.G. Wells wrote, "If we don't end war, war will end us." Emerson's idea was that "Peace cannot be achieved through violence, it can only be attained through understanding."
Great empires have upon them a heap of sand of time. In their heyday they defeated all enemies, real and perceived. They killed ruthlessly for a transitory glory. They rejoiced at the spill of blood of the innocent, the weak and the oppressed. Yet time, in its natural and regular fury, obliterates the high and mighty alike. No unjust or cruel state has survived the vicissitudes of furious time.
History recalls that all empires were built upon the shifting sands of fleeting time. The funeral of nations and civilisations fails to teach the current powerful states that this too shall pass. The majestic jubilations of victory over the underprivileged will meet no different fate than what history tells us about arrogant warring nations. The sickle of time shall mow down the powers of today. It is inevitable.
War at one time in history was essentially a profession. People had to go to war to keep the coffers going and brimming. War is an expensive game. It leads to heavy and higher taxation, and its negative economic outcomes take a long time to be corrected. Europe, ravaged by the First and Second World Wars, took four decades to regain its economic foothold.
But the cost of war is not measured only in damaged economies or ruined cities. People forget that the cost of war is always the young.
King Baudouin of Belgium, in a speech to the US Congress in 1959, made an apt observation: "Youth is the first victim of war; the first fruit of peace. It takes twenty years or more of peace to make a man; it takes twenty seconds of war to destroy him."
One man killed is a murder, while killings by hundreds and thousands create war heroes. A human malady. Unfortunately, war loves to seek only the young as its victims. Warfare can never remain within the realm of civilised behaviour. Civility remains silent when war drums are beating at their highest decibel levels.
Abraham Lincoln is not remembered because he waged a battle or started a war. Instead, history recognises him for bringing harmony between Blacks and Whites. He abolished slavery. His going to war wasn't motivated by his ego to seek personal glory, but by the solidly noble purpose of equality of men.
The distinction matters. War may be presented as an instrument of history, national pride or political necessity, but those who pay its price are rarely the people who make the decision to begin it.
The famous American writer Ernest Hemingway stated: "They wrote in the old days that it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country. But in modern warfare there is nothing sweet nor fitting in your dying. You will die like a dog for no good reason."
The killing fields of Gaza are a perfect picture of what the writer said. The innocent and the young are being butchered on the streets while the leadership resides in lofty mansions, oblivious or, more appropriately, callous to the plight of displaced men, women and children. The horrors of war stare at us. We continue to twiddle our thumbs.
Currently, the world is witnessing with pain three active theatres of war: the ongoing war in the Middle East, which threatens not only global peace but also has serious economic repercussions as the movement of oil is seriously impaired; the continuing conflict in Gaza; and the war in Ukraine, which threatens peace in Europe.
The war has been brought to Iran, the Persian Gulf, Saudi Arabia and adjoining countries. The consequences of conflict are no longer confined to the battlefield. They travel through economies, energy supplies, borders and ordinary lives.
Russia was provoked by Ukraine. Parking NATO forces at its doorstep wasn't a fair and good decision. The US reaction wouldn't have been different if Russia were to park its missiles in the Atlantic. It was hence inevitable that Russia wouldn't sit and twiddle its thumbs at the prospect of NATO forces staring at them. They had to react and they did.
In today's warfare, there is hardly any military victory. The surrender at Dhaka happened fifty years back. The end to a war is through negotiated settlement. "Better a lean peace than a fat victory," Thomas Fuller wrote.
And yet war continues to be manufactured, supplied and sold.
"Once the weapons were manufactured to fight wars. Now wars are manufactured to sell weapons," writes Arundhati Roy. Almost two score years ago, when I read Anthony Sampson's The Arms Bazaar, I thought I was reading fiction. But, on hindsight, I realise I was reading what was to come. The toys of warfare are manufactured by those who are not at direct war, but these are tested for their killing and destructive accuracy in different parts of the world.
John Foster Dulles had written in War or Peace: "The world will never have lasting peace so long as men reserve for war the finest human qualities. Peace, no less than war, requires idealism and self-sacrifice and a righteous and dynamic faith."
The words are worth remembering because peace does not simply happen when war stops. It requires effort, patience, negotiation and, above all, the willingness to see the enemy as human.
Nelson Mandela wrote: "If you want to make peace with your enemy, you have to work with your enemy. Then he becomes your partner."
War and peace cannot coexist as permanent alternatives. War or peace is not merely a matter of selecting one option over another. Peace, and only peace, has to be the solution to conflicts.
An old woman, a mother to her only son, lamented that if, after giving martyrdom to someone who was her flesh and blood, the warring parties were ultimately going to sit at a table to negotiate peace, why couldn't they do the same before firing the first bullet, dropping the first bomb or launching the first missile?
Her plea is the plea of all mothers, all siblings, all spouses and all citizens of the world.
Perhaps that is where the argument finally comes back to Tolstoy. History is not made only by those who order armies into battle. It is also made by the millions of ordinary people who endure the consequences.
The world leadership must move beyond War and Peace and War or Peace. It must submit to just peace.

title: Inside the long climate fight
description: Peter Betts chronicles the long  messy road from Rio to Paris and the climate battles that followed
content:
Peter Betts chronicles the long, messy road from Rio to Paris and the climate battles that followed
For almost two decades, whenever governments sat down to argue over how to stop cooking the planet, he was usually near the front of the room. Peter Betts (1959-2023), a British civil servant, ran Britain's climate negotiating team for thirteen years.
Six of those years, he was also the EU's lead negotiator. Betts wrote this book The Climate Diplomat – A Personal History of the COP Conferences in the last eighteen months of his life, dying of a brain tumor, and you can feel that fact on almost every page without the book ever quite becoming sentimental about it. It is an insider account of what he saw and did at the various Conference of the Parties (COP) – annual United Nations climate change conferences – but his real achievement is that he refused to let his diagnosis soften his judgement.
Betts starts his narrative from Rio in 1992 – the "Earth Summit" that produced the UN climate convention which has served as the foundational cornerstone for modern international climate change agreements and environmental diplomacy. Then Kyoto in 1997, where a much younger Betts helped the United Kingdom (UK) broker binding targets for more than thirty rich countries while everyone else signed up to nothing, a lopsidedness that would cause trouble for the next twenty years.
There is a good but bitter chapter on George W. Bush pulling America out of Kyoto in 2001, and on the UK government's decision -- against the instincts of nearly half of Whitehall bureaucracy -- not to leave along with the Americans. COPs at Bali (2007) and Poznan (2008) are discussed briefly, partly because Betts had moved out of climate-related departments for seven years by then and only came back in 2008, just in time for what everyone was calling "the big one."
Copenhagen in 2009 is where the narrative really gets going and the best chapter in the book is about it. The negotiating text ran to hundreds of pages because China, India and Saudi Arabia kept blocking any attempt to trim it. The Danish hosts underestimated how many people would turn up, so delegates from tropical countries stood in the sleet for hours.
A leaked document embarrassed the Danish hosts during the talks. Betts strongly suspects the Chinese delegation leaked it themselves, even though they denied it to his face. He is also honest about his own side's failures – the EU went in stubborn and came out with almost nothing, something that still visibly annoys him years later.
After the chaos of Copenhagen, the 2010 talks in Cancun were calmer, more of a rebuilding year. Betts takes real pride in one thing that came out of it: he helped start an informal group called the Cartagena Dialogue, where rich countries and poor, vulnerable countries talked to each other directly, instead of only through the usual rigid camps of "developed" versus "developing" nations. It sounds like a small, unglamorous thing. However, Betts argues this quiet relationship-building eventually grew into a much bigger alliance of about a hundred countries, and that alliance was a key reason the Paris Agreement came together five years later.
Durban in 2011 brought the famous late-night ministerial "huddle.” Doha in 2012 planted the seed of the loss-and-damage fund; Warsaw (2013) and Lima (2014) are mostly plumbing. Paris in 2015 is the payoff Betts had spent his career chasing. Marrakech in 2016 turns cold fast, with Brexit and Trump's first win landing almost together. Glasgow in 2021, the last COP he lived to see, ended on a mixed note – more adaptation money, and the first COP text ever to name coal, though softened from "phase out" to "phase down" after India objected.
The book does recount events in a chronological order but it can also be grouped by themes: first, the rules and structure of the UN climate process; then the personalities who shaped or wrecked individual summits; then the political troubles of Brexit and Trump; and finally, Betts's suggestions for what should happen next. He admits climate progress has been far too slow for the scale of the crisis.
Still, real gains have been made renewables and EVs are now cheap, and technologies like offshore wind are fully proven. He also argues that global talks like the COPs, though messy, remain essential: they still push – the world further than it would go alone, driving emissions targets, finance pledges, and fossil fuel commitments, even with the constant risk of being watered down or hijacked. His final point is simple: patient, long-term diplomacy pays off.
The writing itself is clear and engaging, but this is not really a book for someone who does not already know the basics of how COPs and the Paris Agreement work. It is at its best when it moves past the technical details and focuses on people like Betts himself, a fireman's son from South London who ended up brokering deals between the US and China, or the doomed but capable Danish team running the 2009 summit. His widow's account of his late-night phone calls home from these conferences, and the notes describing his illness and how the book got finished after he could no longer speak clearly, are hard to read but add a lot to the book.
The final section lays out his suggestions, worth checking against the four COPs since he died. Some of his suggestions were adopted during the subsequent COPs: Sharm el-Sheikh in 2022 set up the loss-and-damage fund, Dubai in 2023 got it running, and Baku in 2024 tripled the old $100 billion finance target to $300 billion, with a longer-term goal of $1.3 trillion. There was also stronger language in 2023 about moving away from fossil fuels than any previous summit had managed. But his other ideas fared worse. His call for regular check-ins on countries' climate pledges, instead of waiting five years, never happened. Neither did he hope that China and the Gulf states would start contributing more, like rich countries do. The fossil fuel language actually got weaker afterward – dropped completely in 2024, and still missing in 2025- blocked by the same oil-producing countries that appear throughout the book.
His deeper worry was not a line of text but that climate would get swallowed by culture-war politics on both sides of the ideological spectrum in the developed countries like the United Kingdom, leaving the worst-behaved countries to fill any gap left by retreating major powers. That fear has aged badly in the sense that it proved right: Trump pulled the US out of the Paris Agreement again within days of taking office in January 2025. Betts did not live to see it, but reading his final chapters now, his final plea about pursuing " the art of the possible" versus turning climate into a culture war does not read like a pep talk anymore but like a prediction that came true.
The book's sympathies stay with the negotiators managing the developing world's demands, not with those making them. The $100 billion finance pledge, admitted "shamefully never...met in full," gets a single buried sentence. India's equity argument – that the rich world got rich by burning the carbon budget first is met mostly with Betts calling it "an alibi" for growth, rather than highlighting the injustice behind it. He flags the imbalance himself, but this remains a memoir of the room, and that room was rarely African, South Asian, or Pacific. The perspective of developing countries or the Global South is missing from the book. Despite all its flaws, The Climate Diplomat is an exceptional and unrepeatable document: a dying man's determination to leave behind not comfort, but usable knowledge.
The reviewer is an Islamabad-based international development professional.

title: An anthology of missed opportunities
description: Pakistani filmmakers have repeatedly experimented with anthology films  but weak storytelling has kept the format from finding a lasting audience
content:
Pakistani filmmakers tried anthology films, but weak storytelling kept the format from finding an audience
From Chand Suraj to Teri Meri Kahaniyaan and Sheroes, Pakistan's anthology films have promised variety but struggled to leave a lasting impression. Is the format to blame, or have our filmmakers simply failed to get the stories right?
The name Sheroes may sound appealing, but the film released in theatres didn’t do the film industry any favours. It was a hastily made project, stitched together from three short films that could have aired on TV as a telefilm or as episodes of an anthology series. Most theatres pulled it by the end of its first week.
Was this decision justified? Maybe, maybe not. But one thing is clear: asking the audience to support Pakistani cinema is no longer feasible. They can spot a poorly made attempt from a mile away, thanks to Netflix, Amazon Prime, HBO Max, and Apple TV being part of their lives. That’s why they didn’t show up for the latest anthology released in theaters.
For those unfamiliar, an anthology film combines two or more relatively independent narratives into a single feature film, linking them through a shared theme, setting, or idea. Its popularity is straightforward: viewers get multiple stories for the price of one, and filmmakers can explore various characters, genres, and points of view without stretching a single plot into a full-length film.
Worldwide, anthology films are considered box-office gold. Love Actually weaves together stories about love and relationships, while New York, I Love You explores the many facets of its namesake city through short films directed by different directors. These films show how diverse narratives can come together to create an enjoyable cinematic experience.
Bollywood produced quality anthology films before the advent of Netflix, and now Lust Stories is bringing the format to OTT platforms. However, the format doesn't guarantee success; a single weak segment can ruin the entire project, and inconsistent storytelling can make an anthology feel like a series of separate films. Although the format offers flexibility, the stories provide the essential content.
How many anthology films has Pakistan produced so far, and how have they fared at the box office? Two were released more than 50 years apart, and both bombed at the box office. The first brought together Waheed Murad and Nadeem for the first time, and the second featured Mehwish Hayat, Shehryar Munawwar, Wahaj Ali, Hira Mani, Ramsha Khan, among others.
Let’s discuss these attempts and try to determine why they failed before deciding whether anthology filmmaking is a poor fit for Pakistani cinema or whether the films themselves failed to make a strong case for it.
Before Chand Suraj, Waheed Murad and Nadeem hadn’t worked together in a film; one was the West Pakistan heartthrob, and the other was a star emerging from the East Wing. Directed by Shore Lakhnawi, this film promised to bring them together but instead did something unusual for Pakistani cinema.
Released on December 25, 1970, the film consisted of two separate stories: Waheed Murad and Rozina in the first part, and Nadeem and Shabana in the second. By uniting two leading actors and two romantic plots under a single title, it offered viewers a different approach from the usual star-based films.
The idea worked because, instead of focusing on a single hero, it presented two distinct stories, which may have increased its popularity. Moreover, it fit the state of cinema at the time by combining actors from both West and East Pakistan.
Instead of seeing their favourite actors on screen together, the audience saw Waheed Murad in one half and Nadeem in the other, which was one of the main reasons the film bombed at the box office. Audiences weren’t ready for such an experiment, which might have worked with better execution.
It therefore deserves consideration as a film ahead of its time, even if that doesn’t replace assessing it on its own merits; its importance lies in its willingness to adopt a format Pakistani cinema would revisit decades later. The industry moved on, and anthology filmmaking remained an exception rather than a widespread trend. However, more than five decades later, the idea returned, this time with well-known television stars, several directors, and a modern audience to win over.
Teri Meri Kahaniyaan, released on Eid-ul-Azha in 2023, featured Nabeel Qureshi, Marina Khan, and Nadeem Baig, who told three distinct stories: Jinn Mahal, Pasoori, and Ek Sau Taeeswaan. The selection aimed to provide variety, moving from a horror-comedy to a romance and then to a relationship drama.
Ali Abbas Naqvi and Basit Naqvi authored Jinn Mahal, a story about a family facing financial hardship who seek refuge in a house said to be haunted. The situation offers opportunities for supernatural thrills, humour, and social commentary. Long before horror-comedy became a thing, this one-hour short film gave audiences a glimpse of what would later become a genre in itself in Bollywood.
Vasay Chaudhry's Pasoori examines romance and the pressures of social expectations within the context of a wedding; it also marks Marina Khan's first feature-film direction. The story offers an opportunity to examine the choices available to women and the sacrifices conventional standards demand.
However, a relevant theme is only the beginning; the characters must feel real, the emotional stakes must be believable, and the endings must be justified. The now-retired Ramsha Khan was the weakest link in the story because she didn’t seem believable enough to miss her own wedding to appear in a singing competition, the invitation to which she received on the day of the event.
The film Ek Sau Taeeswaan, written by Khalil-ur-Rehman Qamar and starring Mehwish Hayat, Wahaj Ali, Amna Ilyas, and Zahid Ahmed, examined marriage, fidelity, and commitment. The relationship-focused narrative demonstrated the format's potential: a short story can have an emotional impact without the length of a traditional feature film.
The three sections didn't need to provide the same level of engagement, since that was exactly the point. Although an anthology can include various genres, it is still necessary to deliver a consistently satisfying experience. The appeal of three stories cannot make up for one that is poorly developed or a transition that disrupts the film's momentum.
Teri Meri Kahaniyaan was a worthwhile experiment, but a variety of stories alone wasn't enough to make the format a complete success. The issue was never whether Pakistani filmmakers could put together three stories; the question was whether the three stories together were good enough to warrant a cinema visit.
Sheroes: When the message overtakes the movie
Released earlier this month, the film Sheroes combined three stories about women: Gear Up, Artist, and Punch. Sindh Films, the provincial government's film initiative, produced it, and it featured Zara Noor Abbas as a police officer, Kinza Hashmi in the art-forgery segment, and Ushna Shah as a boxer.
The idea had real promise: by including a police officer, a painter, and a boxer, the film offered three distinct lenses through which to examine women's ambitions and the challenges they face. This approach gave each main character a separate story, eliminating the need to develop a single theme throughout the film. At the same time, it allowed the film to move beyond the usual assumption that women in Pakistani cinema should mainly have romantic or supporting roles.
Capable protagonists and important themes do not guarantee that films will be good. A police officer needs a compelling conflict, a painter needs more than an interesting idea, and a boxer needs a fight with emotional weight. Their decisions must carry consequences, their journeys must be believable, and their endings must feel well earned.
None of the three short films offered anything substantial; the conflict in Gear Up was hilarious, the idea in Artist was bland, and Punch wasn’t anything you hadn’t seen before. The first two were directed by Saqib Khan, and the last by Badar Mehmood. Each film seemed to have been made in haste, which was evident in the final product.
It may be a mistake to treat anthology filmmaking as the issue, since it is a format rather than a genre and guarantees neither success nor failure. When Chand Suraj was made, it tried something uncommon; Teri Meri Kahaniyaan explored what could be achieved by using various genres; and Sheroes presented three stories, all focused on women. Each had a premise that could work. The real test was always how it was executed.
Although Chand Suraj may have been ahead of its time in adopting a format, the industry never made a lasting tradition; later films show that revisiting an idea decades later does not necessarily lead to success. Even with well-known stars, several directors, and social-issue themes, attention can still be drawn, but that alone is not enough to replace engaging storytelling.
Pakistani audiences don’t always reject anthology films; they reject films that don’t meet their expectations. They expect believable characters, engaging plots, strong direction, and stories that leave an impression. Whether a film centers on one protagonist or three, it has to capture the audience's attention.
Pakistan doesn't need to give up the anthology; it just needs to use it more effectively. The format will work if each section is justified and the entire collection offers something greater than the sum of its parts. Whether or not it's part of an anthology, good films are worthwhile. All the rest is just packaging.

title: The shopping trap
description: From social media temptations and boredom fuelled browsing to the guilt of unopened parcels  here is how to break up with needless spending
content:
From social media temptations to guilt of unopened parcels, how to break up with needless spending
Lying in bed, scrolling through Instagram, you think you are minding your own business, when a woman with flawless, clear skin appears on your screen, holding a bottle that promises to change your life- and face. Three reels later, you are watching a stranger organise her kitchen with pastel-coloured containers, and suddenly your own kitchen seems like a personal failure. By the time you stumble upon a pair of trousers that would look fabulous on someone with a completely different lifestyle, you have five windows open to check the prices of everything that will complete your home and your wardrobe.
You were not dreaming of buying storage boxes for your perfectly functional kitchen. You know full well skin creams are not magic. And those trousers? You have nowhere to wear them. Yet, somehow, your shopping cart is filling up faster than your weekend plans.
Welcome to the age of recreational shopping, where a few minutes on social media can turn into a full-blown lust to acquire things you never knew existed, let alone needed. The temptation is everywhere, social media is the seductress, and the checkout process is ridiculously easy. Sadly, it is the ease of online shopping that makes the line between wanting something and convincing yourself it is imperative to your being has become alarmingly thin.
The problem is not that we shop. Shopping is a perfectly ordinary part of life, and buying something lovely can be a genuine pleasure. The trouble begins when purchasing things becomes a reflex rather than a decision. It becomes an activity we turn to whenever life gets dull, stressful or just a little too quiet.
Your phone is a very persuasive salesperson
Once upon a time, window shopping required leaving the house. Today, the entire shopping mall lives inside your phone. It is there when you wake up, when you take a break at work, when you are waiting for your food, and when you should be sleeping.
You find those in-store shopping assistants annoying? The ones who hover and push you to try things? Well why don't you find the influencers irritating? The ones who for no reason recommend their favourite products on your reel every day? Then there are the incessant ads of brands presenting ordinary objects as solutions to your life problems. Can’t be bothered to go to the gym but maybe if you buy a matching gym set, you just might.
Had a difficult week? Treat yourself. Feeling uninspired? Start a new hobby with this needlessly expensive starter kit.
Social media also creates the uncomfortable impression that everyone else is living beautifully. Their immaculate homes, their on point wardrobes, their 12-step skincare routine make their lives appear to be a carefully curated collection of aesthetically pleasing moments. Naturally, you vie for the same life upgrades.
The longer you scroll, the longer your wishlist gets
When you open an app to check one item, 40 minutes later you will emerge with a wishlist containing a linen bedsheet set, a portable blender, three lip tints, a handbag organiser and a gadget designed to slice avocados into perfectly symmetrical pieces (somehow, breakfast feels incomplete without it).
This is the magic of endless scrolling. Every swipe introduces another possibility, and every possibility creates another want. Algorithms learn from what you watch, click on and linger over, feeding you more of the same. Pause over a video about home organisation, and soon your feed is full of storage solutions. Watch a few outfit videos, and you may find yourself drowning in recommendations for clothes.
The result is a wishlist that seems to grow of its own accord. And wishes are remarkably good at multiplying.
The danger is that repeated exposure can make unfamiliar products feel familiar, and familiar products begin to seem necessary. When you see the same shoes in several videos, they start to look like a wardrobe essential. When every second person recommends a particular serum, you begin to suspect your skincare routine is somehow incomplete without it.
There is also the fear of missing out. Limited-time discounts, countdown clocks and declarations that an item is almost sold out create a sense of urgency. Suddenly, you are not simply deciding whether you want something. You are racing against an imaginary deadline.
But wait. Why are you stressing out about shopping for pleasure? Try this experiment: the next time you find yourself eyeing something online, save it to a list and leave it there for a week. Do not revisit it obsessively. Do not let a discount convince you that the clock is ticking on your happiness. Then, at the end of the week, check whether you still want it. You may discover that what felt indispensable on Monday has become completely forgettable by Sunday.
Sometimes, we shop because we want something. Sometimes, we shop because we want to feel something.
A dull afternoon or a stressful day, or an evening spent with nothing to do can send us straight into the arms of an online shopping app. Browsing provides instant entertainment. There are new products to discover, reviews to read, prices to compare and imaginary future selves to dress.
For a little while, the world feels full of possibilities. Perhaps that new moleskin planner will make you more productive. Maybe the scented candle will transform your bedroom into a sanctuary. Surely, a new pair of trainers will inspire you to wake up at six every morning and head out for a run.
No! Things are not motivation. Your mindset is. Buying something can offer a brief burst of excitement, especially when we are bored or feeling low. Anticipating a purchase may be as appealing as owning the item itself. The difficulty is that the pleasure can be short-lived, while the expense remains.
This is how boredom shopping becomes a habit. You feel restless, you browse, you buy, and you feel better for a moment. The next time restlessness arrives, your brain remembers the easy route to a little excitement.
Unfortunately, the underlying problem has not gone anywhere. You are still bored, lonely, stressed or tired and lazy. You simply have another parcel on the way.
Next time you are itching to dive into the world wide shopping ocean, call a friend, instead. Take a walk or cook something new. Rearrange a bookshelf or revisit a hobby to pass a quiet evening. Most importantly, learn to recognise what you are actually looking for. When you open a shopping app, pause and ask: am I looking for a particular item, or am I simply looking for a distraction?
There are few experiences quite as emotionally complicated as receiving a parcel you were desperately excited about three days ago.
At first, there is the thrill of the notification: your order is out for delivery. You track the rider, anticipate the knock at the door and picture the glorious moment of unpackaging. Then the package arrives, and you tear it open with the enthusiasm of a child on a birthday morning.
And then, sometimes, you want to cry at your birthday party.
The dress does not fit as expected. The organiser is way smaller than it looked online. The gadget that promised to revolutionise your kitchen is tossed in a drawer that holds other gadgets you believed would revolutionise your kitchen.
Worse still, you remember how much you spent. The excitement gives way to guilt, especially when you consider what you could have used that money for instead. There is also the uncomfortable realisation that you have contributed to a growing pile of possessions that require storage, maintenance and, occasionally, a desperate attempt to find someone who might want them.
Sometimes, the guilt is followed by a familiar promise: never again. But only until the next sale.
But instead of berating yourself for an unnecessary purchase, look at it as information. What prompted the order? Were you bored? Were you trying to cheer yourself up? Did you buy something because everyone online seemed to have it? Identifying the trigger helps you recognise it the next time it appears.
And if an item is unused, returnable and genuinely unnecessary, check the return policy and send it back if you can. There is no virtue in keeping something merely because you feel bad about buying it.
The good news is that resisting the urge to shop does not require extraordinary willpower or a vow to live with three shirts and a single saucepan. It requires making unnecessary purchases a little less automatic.
Make your social media feed work for you
Unfollow or mute accounts that constantly tempt you to buy things you do not need. You do not owe an influencer your attention. Reduce exposure to shopping content, unsubscribe from promotional emails and turn off notifications from retail apps. Your feed should entertain you, not function as an endless catalogue of things to purchase.
Put a little distance between wanting and buying
Introduce a cooling-off period for non-essential purchases. Wait 24 hours for smaller items and perhaps a week or longer for expensive ones. Remove saved card details if necessary, so checking out takes more effort than a single thumb movement.
A 50 per cent discount is not a financial victory if you would never have bought the item at full price. You don’t save money by spending it on something unnecessary. Before checking out, ask whether you would still want the product if it were not on sale. If the discount is the only reason it appeals to you, close the tab.
Keep a note on your phone for things you would like to buy, but do not purchase them immediately. Include the price. Review the list once a week or once a month. You may find that your enthusiasm disappears, or that only one item remains genuinely useful. A wishlist should help you make thoughtful decisions.
A spending plan does not have to mean eliminating every little pleasure from your life. Decide how much you can comfortably spend on clothes, books, beauty products or other treats each month. Once that amount is used, wait until next month. This makes spending a conscious choice rather than an activity without boundaries.
Find out what your shopping habit is trying to fix
Notice what you feel immediately before you start browsing. Are you anxious after a difficult day? Lonely on a weekend? Avoiding a task you do not want to complete? If shopping has become your default response to uncomfortable feelings, experiment with another response. Take a walk when restless, call someone when lonely or break an overwhelming task into smaller steps. You simply need alternatives to buying something.
Before purchasing another black shirt, storage basket or notebook, check what you already own. Rediscover forgotten clothes, reorganise your bookshelves or put together new combinations from your existing wardrobe. Sometimes the novelty we seek is already sitting in our cupboard, waiting to be noticed. A little creativity can be more satisfying than another delivery.
Give your money a more exciting destination
Saving is often less appealing when it means simply not buying things. Give the money a purpose. It could fund a holiday, or a course you genuinely value. Transfer the amount you would have spent on an impulse purchase into a separate savings pot. Watching that balance grow can provide its own little thrill.
You can admire a beautiful handbag without owning it. You can enjoy watching a kitchen makeover without buying matching jars. You can appreciate an outfit on someone else without recreating it in your wardrobe. Not every attractive object needs to become part of your life. Sometimes, looking is enough.
A little less shopping, a little more living
Wanting is human, and there is nothing wrong with buying something that brings joy or serves a useful purpose. The goal is to make sure that your purchases reflect your priorities rather than submission to clever advertising, and a particularly persuasive algorithm.
A good place to start is with one simple rule: before buying anything non-essential, ask yourself whether you want the item, the feeling you imagine it will give you, or the version of yourself you believe it will create.
You may discover that you do want the shoes, that they fit your budget and that you will wear them for years. Wonderful. Buy them and enjoy them. But you may also discover that what you really wanted was a break from a stressful day, a little fulfillment on a dull afternoon or reassurance that you are doing enough.
Know that a parcel cannot reliably deliver those things.
So the next time your thumb hovers over the checkout button, give yourself a moment. Close the app. Step outside. Look at your bank balance, your wardrobe or the pile of parcels still waiting to be unpacked. Then remember that you do not have to buy your way into a better life. Sometimes, the most satisfying purchase is the one you decide not to make.

title: Pakistan for equitable civil nuclear cooperation
description: Pakistan for equitable civil nuclear cooperation
content:
Pakistan has underscored the fundamental importance of equitable, non-discriminatory civil nuclear cooperation to help secure its national energy future.
"Efforts to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction must not impede international cooperation in the peaceful uses of dual-use technologies, which is vital for the economic development of the Global South," Pakistani delegate Syed Atif Raza told the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday during a debate on the annual report of the IAEA, the Vienna-based UN organization.
At the same time, Raza, a counsellor at the Pakistan Mission to the UN, highlighted that Pakistan is a party to the principal international instruments of nuclear safety and security.
"All countries must retain their inalienable right to utilize nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, consistent with their respective non-proliferation and international legal obligations," the Pakistani delegate said.
Pakistan, he said, maintained that compliance or safety issues should be resolved through technical bodies like the IAEA without political bias.

title: Imran to be moved to Islamabad jail
description: Imran to be moved to Islamabad jail
content:
Prison likely to be inaugurated next month
The first phase of new state-of-the-art Model Jail in Islamabad's Sector H-16 has been completed, with preparations for its inauguration scheduled from November 1 to 10.
Fifteen hundred prisoners, including former prime minister Imran Khan, are expected to be shifted from Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail to the facility in the initial phase.
According to jail sources, the initial plan envisaged transferring 2,000 inmates, but the number has now been reduced to 1,500. The first phase includes three completed barracks, a 35-bed mini-hospital, a mosque and a kitchen.
Sources said the second phase of the project will continue and is expected to be completed during the first quarter of 2027, between January 1 and March 31.
The new jail has been constructed on 90 acres in Sector H-16 of Islamabad.
The National Highway Authority has also been directed to upgrade roads and access routes connecting the facility with the motorway and Kashmir Highway. Preparations for a PC-I and the design of a major interchange near the jail have also begun.
The project, initially estimated to cost Rs3.5 billion, has exceeded Rs20 billion over four years, largely due to rising construction material costs, according to the report.
Under the first phase of relocation, only undertrial prisoners whose cases are pending before courts will be transferred from Adiala Jail.
Convicted prisoners will not be included in this initial movement, allowing undertrial inmates to be produced before courts directly from the Islamabad facility under enhanced security arrangements.
The transfer of convicted prisoners is expected to begin in 2027, with February mentioned as a possible starting point, sources said.
Jail sources further indicated that former prime minister Imran Khan could be shifted from Adiala Jail to the new facility between November 20 and 30. A special ward for him has reportedly been completed, while installation of its closed-circuit television surveillance system is in its final stages.
Adiala Jail sources also confirmed that lists of Islamabad-based prisoners and undertrial detainees had been finalised and preparations were under way for their transfer in November.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has already inspected the new facility and directed the authorities to meet the October 31 completion target, according to the report.
The Model Jail is being designed with a range of facilities, including a sports ground, library, mosque, imambargah and church. Separate wards have also been established for women and children.
The project is intended to provide a modern correctional facility for Islamabad, while easing the burden on Adiala Jail and enabling undertrial prisoners from the federal capital to be housed closer to the courts where their cases are being heard.

title: Centre eyes financial control of 12 K P districts
description: Centre eyes financial control of 12 K P districts
content:
Finance, planning departments asked to prepare budget details
The federal government is considering separating the financial affairs and development planning of 12 districts of K-P from the provincial government's jurisdiction, with the provincial finance and planning departments directed to complete the necessary paperwork.
According to official sources, the move follows the imposition of emergency and governor's rule in K-P, after which administrative control of the 12 districts was transferred to the federal government.
Under the proposed arrangement, authority over the preparation, consultation, approval and implementation of development projects in these districts would shift from the provincial government to the federal government.
Financial and administrative arrangements are being reviewed to determine how the proposed changes would be implemented. The sources said federal and provincial officials were in contact over the financial implications of the proposed arrangement.
The provincial finance and planning departments have reportedly been directed to compile figures relating to the development and non-development budgets of the 12 districts to facilitate a review of their financial requirements and allocation of resources.
The issue has also raised questions about the provincial government's financial share following the transfer of administrative control of four additional districtsDera Ismail Khan, Bannu, Tank and Lakki Marwatto the federal government.
Sources said uncertainty persisted over how the financial allocations for these districts would be handled under the proposed arrangement.
Under the NFC framework, changes to the distribution of financial resources among the provinces fall within the commission's constitutional mandate.
The federal government cannot unilaterally reduce K-P's share in the NFC Award merely because administrative control of certain districts has changed, the sources said.

title: FCC rules on high court powers
description: FCC rules on high court powers
content:
Sets aside SHC order on transfers, disciplinary action
The FCC has ruled that high courts can examine the legality of administrative actions but cannot ordinarily assume the executive's role by dictating decisions on postings, duties and disciplinary proceedings against government employees.
Setting aside a Sindh High Court (SHC) order concerning police officer Munir Samo, the FCC held that judicial review under Article 199 of the Constitution was meant to correct unlawful actions and ensure compliance with the law, not to take over administrative decision-making powers.
The court converted Samo's petition into an appeal and allowed it, declaring unlawful the SHC's June 30, 2026 order issued at its Larkana circuit.
Justice Rozi Khan Barrech authored the 10-page judgment. A two-member bench comprising Justice Barrech and Justice Syed Arshad Hussain Shah heard the matter.
The high court had directed that Samo be immediately removed from the Special Branch, kept in Karachi for one year and barred from operational or field duties. It had also ordered disciplinary proceedings against him and directed the authorities to report back to the court.
The FCC observed that an inquiry conducted on the SHC's directions had not established Samo's alleged involvement in a raid. His role as a group officer was found to be limited to issuing intelligence reports, and the inquiry officer had not recommended action against him at that stage.
The high court, however, expressed dissatisfaction with the initial inquiry and directed the Larkana senior superintendent of police to conduct another investigation. The purpose of the second inquiry was to ensure a fair, impartial and comprehensive assessment of the allegations.
According to the FCC, the high court did not adequately consider the significant findings of the subsequent inquiry while issuing directions against the officer. The judgment described the disregard of findings from an inquiry ordered by the court itself as an important legal issue.
The court held that adverse administrative or disciplinary action against a public servant must be supported by the record and inquiry findings. Constitutional jurisdiction, it added, could not be exercised on the basis of speculation, assumptions or grounds unrelated to the available evidence.
The FCC noted that the high court's directions went beyond requiring the authorities to act in accordance with the law. Instead, the court had itself determined Samo's posting, restricted his duties and prescribed the nature of disciplinary action against him.
In the circumstances, the judgment concluded, the SHC had exceeded the permissible limits of judicial review. The FCC underscored that the Constitution rests on a division of powers among the legislature, executive and judiciary.
The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them, and the judiciary interprets the law. No state institution, it said, could encroach upon the constitutionally assigned domain of another.
Policy formulation, rules of procedure and routine administrative matters fall within the executive's domain, the judgment stated.
Judicial review allows courts to examine administrative decisions for legality but does not ordinarily authorise them to substitute their own decisions for those of the competent authorities.

title: LPG dealers  strike leaves consumers scrambling for cooking fuel
description: LPG dealers  strike leaves consumers scrambling for cooking fuel
content:
Around 5,5006,000 shops shut in Lahore, other cities
Consumers already struggling with exorbitant liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices are now facing a worsening shortage after dealers abruptly shut their shops in protest against "harassment by enforcement agencies" and inaction against LPG companies and alleged profiteers.
The strike has forced people to search for alternative cooking fuels, with coal and firewood sellers also raising their prices.
Around 5,500 to 6,000 LPG shops have been closed in Lahore and several other cities, leaving consumers carrying empty cylinders from one shop to another in search of gas.
The shutdown comes after consumers had been forced to buy LPG at exceptionally high prices for the past week and a half, while dealers say they can no longer bear the losses and penalties imposed on them.
Speaking to The Express News, shopkeeper Kashif Bilal Asghar said personnel from the PERA Force and Civil Defence visited shops and confiscated LPG filling pumps. He said each pump cost between Rs50,000 and Rs60,000, while dealers were also being fined between Rs5,000 and Rs10,000.
Asghar maintained that shopkeepers were not responsible for the high prices, arguing that LPG companies and the alleged profiteering network were supplying gas at inflated rates while retailers bore the consequences.
He alleged that the OGRA had not taken action against a single LPG company or plant, despite profiteering worth billions of rupees. Instead, he said, enforcement agencies were targeting shopkeepers.
The dealers have now shut their businesses in protest, saying they would no longer submit to pressure from the LPG mafia.
The shutdown has compounded consumers' difficulties, particularly those already struggling to afford cooking fuel. Residents questioned what they were expected to do when LPG was unavailable at the price fixed by OGRA and could no longer be obtained even at higher market rates.
With LPG unavailable, many people have turned to shops selling coal and dry firewood.
However, the increased demand has also pushed up the price of coal by Rs10 to Rs20 per kilogram. Coal that was previously sold for Rs40 per kilogram is now being offered at between Rs50 and Rs60 per kilogram.
Small food businesses have been among those worst affected by the shortage, as many tandoors and eateries depend entirely on LPG to operate. The disruption has left vendors struggling to keep their businesses running while the cost of alternative fuels continues to rise.

title: From 786 to the muslim villain
description: How Bollywood   s Muslim characters went from poets  patriots and loyal friends to increasingly politicised figures of suspicion  extremism and antagonism
content:
How Bollywood's Muslim characters went from poets and patriots to figures of suspicion, extremism and antagonism
Do you remember Yash Chopra’s Deewaar that made it to screen some five decades ago? Vijay, played by Amitabh Bachchan, works as a coolie at a Bombay dock and pinned to his blue uniform is an employee badge marked 786. When his senior colleague Rahim Chacha explains that the number carries the numerical value of Bismillah — “In the Name of God” — it becomes more than an identification badge. It becomes a symbol of faith, blessing and protection.
Later, during a confrontation, a bullet strikes the badge and Vijay survives. Several times in the film’s most memorable moments, he kisses the badge and touches it to his eyes — a small gesture that says as much about faith and cultural belonging as any dialogue could.
For millions who grew up watching Bollywood, 786 was not a threat, a political marker or a shorthand for extremism. It was simply a familiar Muslim symbol — one that could sit comfortably on the chest of the film’s hero.
Deewaar helped cement 786 as a recognisable Muslim cultural symbol in popular cinema, reflecting a period when Muslim characters and symbols could be woven into mainstream Bollywood storytelling without necessarily being reduced to political stereotypes.
For decades, Bollywood gave its Muslim characters something that now feels increasingly rare: the freedom to simply be human. They could be princes and poets, lovers and loyal friends, policemen and porters, mothers and ordinary citizens. They could be flawed, funny, tragic, patriotic or rebellious. Their religion was part of who they were, but it did not always define what kind of person they were. Today that has changed and what we see is a striking shift towards, hate, bigotry, politicisation and (cheap) antagonism.
Across the decades from the 1960s to the early 2000s, Hindi cinema offered us rich Muslim characterisation so that deeply empathetic and memorable Muslim characters repeatedly appeared across three broad archetypes: royal and poetic Muslim figures, the fiercely loyal and self-sacrificing friend, and ordinary citizens navigating social hardship. These characters led lives that extended far beyond their religion.
Interestingly, the ‘billa number 786’ resurfaced again in episode 20 of Kaun Banega Crorepati season 18), in a question asked to Saif Ali Khan. “Which ones of these numbers should be on the badge?” An image of a dockyard badge was shown and 786 was one of the options. As Khan replied correctly, he raised his right arm, and host Mr Bachan explained the symbolism of the number in a cautious, and secular and befitting manner.
In the 1960s, when the “Muslim Social” genre flourished, Muslim characters were defined by tehzeeb, Urdu poetry, etiquette and tragic romance. In Mughal-e-Azam, Prince Salim and Anarkali became icons of pure, revolutionary love defying royal constraints. In Chaudhvin Ka Chand, Aslam (Guru Dutt) is a selfless friend willing to sacrifice his own happiness and marriage after discovering that his best friend loves the same woman. Later, in Mere Mehboob, Anwar (Rajendra Kumar) is a respectful, highly educated and poetic university student.
Through the 1970s, the blockbuster Sholay’s AK Hangal as Rahim Chacha, the village's blind imam, delivers one of Indian cinema's most poignant moments, looking up to the heavens and selflessly lamenting that he does not have more sons to sacrifice for the village's safety, after his only son is murdered by Gabbar Singh. In Garm Hava, Salim Mirza (Balraj Sahni), is a deeply honourable and resilient Muslim shoe manufacturer who refuses to leave India for Pakistan after Partition. He chooses to remain and fight for his rights as a proud Indian citizen. In Amar Akbar Anthony, Akbar Ilhabadi (Rishi Kapoor) is a young qawwali singer who represents religious harmony and fights alongside his brothers to protect his family. The important cinematic idea was that being Muslim and being Indian were not presented as competing identities. In Muqaddar Ka Sikandar, Sher Khan begins as a rival before becoming a fiercely loyal brother-figure to the protagonist, standing by him until his final breath.
The 1980s brought action, underworld stories and parallel cinema, but Muslim characters continued to occupy morally powerful spaces. In Umrao Jaan, the titular character (played by Rekha) is portrayed with dignity, intelligence and emotional depth as a poetess and courtesan surviving personal tragedy. In Coolie, Iqbal Khan (Amitabh Bachchan) is a fiercely righteous railway porter who fights exploitation, protects the poor and remains deeply devoted to his faith. Even when the character was morally compromised, cinema could allow for transformation. In Salim Langde Pe Mat Ro, Salim (Pavan Malhotra) is a small-time thief in Mumbai who undergoes a moral awakening, seeking an honest life despite institutional hardships. The Muslim character could be a criminal, but he could also change, a distinction that matters.
The 1990s brought political tension, but Bollywood continued to produce Muslim characters who embodied belonging rather than suspicion. In Mammo, Mehmooda (Farida Jalal), is a warm and deeply empathetic matriarch whose story explores the human pain created by bureaucratic citizenship laws between India and Pakistan. In Zakhm, Pooja Bhatt plays a Muslim woman who lives under a Hindu identity to protect her children while holding onto her faith with profound, silent dignity. Sarfarosh had Inspector Salim (Mukesh Rishi), an unyielding and patriotic police officer whose loyalty to India is questioned because of his religion. He delivers a powerful affirmation of his allegiance and risks his life to bust a cross-border weapons ring. The message was clear: a Muslim could be questioned about his patriotism, but the film could ultimately reaffirm his place within the nation.
The early 2000s continued that tradition. Veer-Zaara gave audiences Zaara Haayat Khan, a progressive and independent Pakistani woman who honours her family's word while dedicating her life to running a girls' school in an Indian village. The film also featured Saamiya Siddiqui, played by Rani Mukerji, an idealistic human rights lawyer fighting systemic prejudice to secure justice for an innocent Indian prisoner. Maqbool, meanwhile, gave Irrfan Khan a darker but richly layered Muslim character: an underworld lieutenant caught in a Shakespearean tragedy, consumed by guilt and psychological conflict. This was an emerging shade, the Muslim character did not have to be virtuous to be human.
As Narendra Modi’s political dominance grew, so too did a new vocabulary of Muslim representation in mainstream Hindi cinema. Gone, or increasingly pushed to the margins, were the Muslim characters who embodied tehzeeb, loyalty, sacrifice and ordinary belonging. In their place emerged a narrower set of figures: the radical militant, the terrorist, the historical Muslim antagonist, the abusive patriarch and the manipulative character associated with radicalisation or forced conversion.
The change is not simply about whether a Muslim character is “good” or “bad.” It is about what Muslimness itself has come to signify on screen. This shift has unfolded alongside a profound change in India's political climate.
At some point in the early 2000’s when Modi executive power began taking shape, the Muslim character in Bollywood morphed into the radical militant or terrorist, such as Rehan Khan in Fanaa, and cross-border antagonists in films such as Kurbaan. Here, questionably, religious identity was linked with extremist violence.
In Darlings, Vijay Varma as Hamza is a domestic abuser. Strict and unyielding Muslim fathers in films such as Secret Superstar and Gully Boy contribute to a recurring pattern identified by critics as the Muslim male figure as an oppressive husband or father. The radicalised or manipulative figure appeared in The Kerala Story, with its narrative of forced conversion and radicalisation. This became one of the most controversial examples, drawing accusations of communal divisiveness and generating intense public debate.
Last year, in periodic war drama Chhaava, where the portrayal of Mughal emperor Aurangzeb (Akshay Khanna) was thrashed by critics of being revisionist or sectarian, framing historical Muslim rulers as brutal and fanatical, historical antagonists. The abusive Muslim patriarch is also a great Bollywood favourite. While these films are not identical, and their characters, genres and political purposes differ, yet they point towards a narrower cinematic vocabulary.
Bollywood has always had Muslim villains, along with criminals, extremists and morally compromised characters from every community, but the range of Muslim characters has changed. Where are the ordinary Muslim citizens, the loyal friend, the patriotic policeman, the poet, the neighbor, the family man, the person whose Muslim identity is simply one part of a larger human story? While earlier cinema repeatedly made room for them, increasingly, the Muslim character arrives carrying a political meaning – he is the terrorist or radical or the criminal, the abusive patriarch, the historical enemy, just someone whose loyalties must be questioned. The transformation has occurred during a period in which nationalism, terrorism, religious identity and Hindu-Muslim relations have become increasingly central to India's political discourse.
Perhaps the easiest way to understand what has been lost is to look back at what once seemed entirely natural. In a 1970 BBC interview, veteran actor Dilip Kumar was asked by host Mahendranath Kaul to end their conversation with a song. Dilip demurred, explaining that singing was not his craft. But when Kaul reminded him that his fans in both India and Pakistan would be disappointed if he refused, he relented. That small exchange belongs to a very different Bollywood — one that could accommodate Indian and Pakistani audiences within the same cultural imagination, long before the politics of the Modi era began narrowing that space.
Since cinema does not operate in a vacuum, it reflects the anxieties, conflicts and politics of the society around it. And when the political imagination changes, popular culture changes with it. Not that the political establishment directly instructed filmmakers to portray Muslims negatively. Nor does it mean every post-2014 film follows the same template, but the shift in characterisation is difficult to ignore.
For decades, Bollywood gave Muslim characters the full range of human experience. The worrying change is not that some Muslims became villains, but that being Muslim itself increasingly became a cinematic clue about who the villain might be. That is a much bigger story than any single film. And it may be the clearest indication of how India's political transformation has seeped into its popular imagination.
Interestingly, the ‘billa number 786’ resurfaced again in season 18 episode 20 of Kaun Banega Crorepati, as a question asked to Saif Ali Khan. As he replied, he raised his right arm, and host Mr Bachan explained the symbolism of the number in a cautious and secular manner.

title: Nintendo eShop game disappears after reported Switch 2 jailbreak exploit
description: SmileBASIC 4 reportedly disappeared from some eShop regions after researcher used it to jailbreak Switch 2
content:
SmileBASIC 4 reportedly disappeared from some eShop regions after researcher used it to jailbreak Switch 2
A game on the Nintendo eShop has reportedly disappeared from several regions after a researcher used it to demonstrate a software-based jailbreak for the Nintendo Switch 2, including modifications to Mario Kart World featuring Hatsune Miku.
Sammy Hajhamid, known online as pepsipu , announced the exploit, called ns2jb, on X and published a technical explanation on his blog.
The tethered jailbreak reportedly targets Switch 2 firmware version 23.0.1 and allows arbitrary native code to run on the console.
According to Hajhamid, the exploit began with SmileBASIC 4, a coding game originally released for the first Nintendo Switch that also runs on its successor.
A flaw identified by OpenAI's Codex provided the starting point for developing the exploit, which eventually reached the console's system file service.
Hajhamid described it as, to his knowledge, the "first such exploit for the Switch 2".
For the demonstration, the researcher modified Mario Kart World to feature characters including Hatsune Miku, Cinnamoroll and Peter Griffin.
He said the modifications took one day of what he called vibecoding, while developing the jailbreak itself took approximately two weeks.
Nintendo Life reported that SmileBASIC 4 appeared to disappear from the eShop shortly after the exploit became public. TechSpot reported that the game was unavailable in the United States and Europe but remained listed in Japan.
However, it was unclear whether Nintendo or SmileBoom, the game's developer, was responsible for its removal.
Nintendo has not publicly acknowledged the reported jailbreak.

title: My Chemical Romance sued over Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders inspired costumes
description: My Chemical Romance faces legal action over dancers wearing Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders inspired uniforms
content:
My Chemical Romance faces legal action over dancers wearing Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders-inspired uniforms
My Chemical Romance is facing a lawsuit from the owner of the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders brand over dancers wearing costumes resembling the team's signature uniforms during a recent concert at the Hollywood Bowl.
According to TheWrap , Pro Silver Star Ltd., which owns the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders brand, is seeking a temporary restraining order and injunction over the band's alleged unauthorised use of the uniforms. The company is also requesting monetary damages, although it has not specified an amount.
The legal action concerns the band's first of five sold-out The Black Parade shows at the Hollywood Bowl on October 21.
During the song "Teenagers", dancers wearing cheerleader-inspired outfits performed a routine before picking up rifles and appearing to defend the band from soldiers.
In its filing, the company described the performance as part of a theatrical production set in a fictional dictatorship.
"On Oct. 21, 2026, Defendants staged 'The Black Parade,' a theatrical concert production set in a fictional dictatorship and featuring pyrotechnics and armed conflict," the filing stated.
It continued, "As part of that production, female performers took to the stage in the DCC Uniform — and then armed themselves with rifles in a staged firefight, only to be depicted being shot."
Pro Silver Star argued that the costumes could mislead audiences about the performers' identities. "Audience members and online commentators understandably believed that the performers were the real Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders and said so in social media posts that continue to circulate," the filing added.
The company claims it asked My Chemical Romance to stop using the uniforms, but the band refused.
Pro Silver Star stressed that it did not object to the band's music or artistic expression, but took issue with the use of its recognisable costumes during the staged violence.
"Silver Star is not litigious, and it takes no issue with MCR's music, its artistic ambitions, or any message Defendants seek to convey," the filing stated.
The company said it was asking only for the performers not to wear the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders uniform, arguing that alternative costume designs were widely available.

title: Biosafety panel defers GM corn  cotton cases
description: Biosafety panel defers GM corn  cotton cases
content:
NBC sends applications back, says recommendations lack clarity
The National Biosafety Committee (NBC) deferred consideration of pending Food, Feed and Processing applications for soybean meal imports, renewal of genetically modified (GM) corn biosafety licences and several cotton-related applications at its 38th meeting, holding that the recommendations forwarded by its technical arm did not provide sufficiently clear conclusions for decision-making.
The committee, which met at the Ministry of Climate Change and Environmental Coordination, directed that the cases be re-examined by the Technical Advisory Committee (TAC), with clear recommendations and conclusions submitted to the NBC for final consideration.
Members also sought clarification on the holding of GM corn commercialisation activities. A representative of the Ministry of National Food Security and Research explained that in 2019 the government had decided to place commercialisation of biotech food crops on hold until a comprehensive policy framework was developed.
That gap has now been addressed through the approval and notification of the National Agricultural Biotechnology Policy (NABP) 2025, which provides a regulatory framework for the evaluation and commercialisation of agricultural biotechnology products, he said.
The reservations that led to the 2019 decision have therefore been resolved, and relevant authorities have been informed to proceed under the approved framework, according to the explanation given to the committee.

title: Martha Stewart says work life balance does not exist  criticising concept
description: Martha Stewart dismissed work life balance as unrealistic  explaining why she prefers to maintain demanding schedule
content:
Martha Stewart dismissed work-life balance as unrealistic, explaining why she prefers to maintain demanding schedule
Martha Stewart has rejected the idea of work-life balance, arguing that professional and personal responsibilities cannot always be evenly divided.
Speaking on the Richer Lives by SoFi podcast with financial expert Vivian Tu, the 85-year-old entrepreneur shared her views on managing a career alongside personal commitments.
When Tu asked how she balances her personal life with her business and media ventures, Stewart dismissed the premise.
"Just get that through your thick skulls. You can't balance it, it doesn't balance," Stewart said.
She added that she was sceptical of the concept, explaining, "This thing about balance, I don't know who thought about that, but it just doesn't work." Stewart said she sometimes envied people who appeared to achieve it, but described them as "boring".
Her demanding routine reflects her approach to work. According to Business Insider, Stewart typically starts working at 7 a.m. and reportedly wakes at around 4 a.m. to read, complete puzzles and exercise.
She spends five days a week at her New York City office overseeing her lifestyle brand, media business and other ventures.
Stewart has also criticised remote working. Previously speaking to WWD , she said, "You can't possibly get everything done working three days a week in the office and two days remotely." She has also questioned France's traditional August holiday period, asking, "Should America go down the drain because people don't want to go back to work?"
Stewart began her career as a model before working as an institutional stockbroker on Wall Street.
She later established a catering business from her Connecticut farmhouse, which helped lead to her bestselling 1982 book, Entertaining. Her business subsequently expanded into publishing, television and home products.
Despite professional setbacks, including a five-month prison sentence from October 2004 to March 2005 following convictions related to the sale of ImClone Systems stock, Stewart continued her career.

RJ Mitte’s sister Lacianne Carriere has shared memories of actor and grief following his death at 34
RJ Mitte’s sister, Lacianne Carriere, has shared an emotional tribute to the Breaking Bad actor, describing the moment she learnt of his death and reflecting on their close relationship. Mitte died by suicide on October 12 at the age of 34, according to E! Online.
In an Instagram post published on October 23, Carriere shared previously unseen photographs and videos of her brother, recalling an ordinary detail that became a painful reminder of her loss.
“There are just no words. You were just here,” she wrote. “Your strawberry Fanta was still sitting on my coffee table when I got the call. Life hasn't felt real since then.”
Carriere said she had spent many evenings since receiving the news with Mitte’s closest friends, sharing stories and remembering his personality.
“Since the phone call I've been sitting around with your closest people almost every night sharing the craziest stories that could never be said anywhere else and god that was just you..,” she wrote. “You were the life of the party, coolest guy that we all tried to keep up with but never could.”
She also described how deeply her brother had influenced her interests and identity, from music and films to video games and collecting keepsakes.
“I just lost my other half. I lost my brother but I also lost my father…,” she wrote, adding that his influence had shaped “every single aspect” of her personality.
Although she admitted she did not know how she would recover from the loss, Carriere promised to keep his memory alive.
“I loved you completely,” she concluded. “And you loved me the same. That's all. The rest is confetti.”

title: Karachi s autumn heat was a warning nobody read
description: Karachi s autumn heat was a warning nobody read
content:
When a city's answer to extreme heat is a private purchase
Karachi is not supposed to sweat in September, and it is certainly not supposed to do so in November. These are the months when the city exhales, evenings turn bearable, and families plan weddings and long walks by the sea. This year the calendar and the thermometer refused to agree. Days stayed hot, nights stayed heavy, and the relief that autumn traditionally promises arrived late or not at all.
What happened next is the real story, and it is not a story about weather. It is about attention. Above-normal heat in the shoulder months was widely noticed and quietly forgotten. A forecast was shared, a few officials remarked that the season was unusual, and the conversation moved on to the next headline. Nobody treated the warm spell as what it actually was: a rehearsal, an eye-opener, a free warning delivered before the next summer arrives.
Consider how most of us responded. Those who could afford it called the technician, serviced the air conditioner, and went back to sleep in comfortable rooms. That is understandable, and nobody should be blamed for protecting their family. But it is also revealing. When a city's answer to extreme heat is a private purchase, the heat becomes a question of income. The comfortable adapt. The rest simply endure.
And who are the rest? The labourer on a construction site, the street vendor with no shade, the woman cooking in a one-room home with a tin roof, the elderly resident whose power goes out just when the afternoon is at its worst. They do not service anything. They drink water when they can, rest when they are allowed, and hope the day passes without incident. Their preparation is not a plan; it is stamina.
Karachi does have a Heatwave Management Plan, and it is a serious document written by serious people. It appears in newspapers. It features in progress reports and review meetings. Yet if you walk through the neighbourhoods it is meant to protect, you will struggle to find it. On the ground, the plan is visible at a handful of spots, where a water sprinkling ceremony takes place, a few officials or stakeholders gather, cameras click, and a nearby business entity usually bears the cost. The cool water is welcome. But a photograph is not a system, and a sprinkled body dries in minutes.
None of this is said to blame any single institution. Government agencies are stretched, private companies do contribute, often generously, community organisations know their streets better than anyone, and the media does report heat when it turns dramatic. The trouble is not that any of these actors is absent. The trouble is that each of them stands with its back to the others.
The government prepares a plan and expects compliance. The private sector funds a gesture and expects visibility. Communities wait for instructions that rarely reach them. The media looks for a spike or a dramatic image, and loses interest when the mercury dips a degree or two. Four capable players, four separate rooms, and no one holding the door open.
The cost of this arrangement is counted in human lives, though never fully. A few hundred deaths are officially recorded in heat emergencies, and even that figure carries an uncomfortable asterisk. Heat rarely announces itself on a death certificate. A person with a weak heart collapses in a stifling room. An elderly man is found lifeless after a night without electricity. The recorded cause reads cardiac arrest, kidney failure or simply old age. Heat stroke is written only when it is unmistakable, and in a crowded hospital unmistakable is a high bar. So, the real toll hides inside other categories, and what is not counted is rarely prevented.
This is why the unusual warmth of September and October matters more than it appears. These were not peak-summer days, when everyone is alert and emergency desks are open. They were quiet days, and showed how unprepared we are when the alarm is silent. A city that reacts only to headlines will always be late, because heat does its damage in the gaps between headlines.
What, then, should change? Not another grand document or a bigger launch ceremony, but a different geography of responsibility. The Heatwave Management Plan must travel down from the city level to the town level. Every town should have its own version, shaped by its own streets, households and shaded places. Town administrations are closest to the people, and local leaders, teachers, shopkeepers, mosque committees and neighbours already know who lives alone, who works outdoors and who has no fan.
Decentralisation would give the private sector something better than a photo opportunity: a clear, local need to support. The media would have a nearby, accountable story to follow. And communities, who are so often treated as recipients of welfare and safety projects rather than partners in them, would finally have a seat at the table. Most safety schemes falter at precisely this point: they are designed for people, not with them.
Heat will not wait for our coordination. The warm autumn was a message, polite enough to be ignored. The next one may not be. If we want a city where protection from heat does not depend on the size of an air-conditioning bill, we must stop working with our backs to each other, and start facing the same direction, town by town, street by street.
