title: Iran s Pezeshkian blames US for interim deal failure  urges new try
description: Iran intensifies plots against US officials in the Middle East  report
content:
Iran intensifies plots against US officials in the Middle East: report
Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian, in ​remarks broadcast ​on state TV ⁠on Saturday, ​blamed the United ​States for the failure of an interim ​deal ​with Iran, but said ‌there ⁠should be a new attempt at concluding ​it.
"We ​were ⁠having negotiations; the ​cowards [Americans] messed ​everything ⁠up...I still think we should ⁠go ​and ​conclude it," Pezeshkian said.
Iran intensifies plots against US officials in the Middle East: report
US intelligence found that Iran has sharply stepped up efforts to target American officials in the Middle East and other countries, with lethal plots reaching advanced stages, Axios reported on Friday.
The report cited a memo dated October 23 from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, which said the information is relevant to more personnel than are currently cleared to see it.
The one-page unclassified memo does not name targets, countries outside the Middle East, or the nature of the plots.
The report said the underlying intelligence has been shared with senior State Department staff, and Clayton offered to downgrade it as much as possible so Rubio can share it more widely.
A US official told the outlet that the intelligence is one reason the agency is reducing embassy personnel in the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon, Qatar, and Jordan, as first reported by CNN.
Trump says US may do another military operation against Iran
President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran just as the Iran war nears its eight-month mark and rising fuel prices weigh on the US midterm elections.
"We may do another little Epic Fury," Trump told a rally in Florida, using the US military's term for its war on Iran. He did not elaborate.
Trump said the US could end the war quickly but questioned whether Washington should seek a swift conclusion or allow the conflict to gradually wind down.
Trump, who has offered shifting goals and timelines for the war, has said in recent campaign remarks that the war will end soon, "one way or the other."
He said this month the US would not launch an attack on Iran before the November 3 elections that will determine control of Congress, where Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers.
Trump vows to deal with Cuba after Iran settled
US President Donald Trump on Friday used a campaign rally in Florida, where Cuban Americans are a potent voting bloc, to vow to address his concerns about Cuba once the Iran war is settled.
In a 90-minute speech in Fort Myers, Florida, Trump repeated that more military action against Iran may lie ahead as he tries to address the causes of a spike in oil prices that has put Republicans on the defensive ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
With an eye toward the senior Americans who live in Florida, Trump said he planned to spend $250 million to hire at least 5,000 new nurses in elder care facilities all across America.
While the Iran war has no end in sight, Trump talked tough about Cuba, part of a pattern of putting pressure on the communist government there after ousting the leader of Venezuela early this year.
Trump, who won 68% of the Cuban American vote in Florida in the 2024 election, said American naval forces from Iran will stop at Cuba on the way home.
"We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands, and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," he said.
Secretary of State Rubio, a former US senator from Florida, has been handling much of the Cuba portfolio for Trump.
Iran Revolutionary Guards say two tankers hit mines south of Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Friday that two tankers struck naval mines while attempting to use what they described as "an unauthorised route" south of the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported.
Iran has detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes, officials say
Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials ​told Reuters.
Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington ‌collapses.
The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections.
"If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one ​of the officials said.
The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah ​Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for IRGC, said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath ⁠the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency. But the ​global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications ​research firm TeleGeography.
The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea.
The US Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters ' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.
The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's leadership that a renewed US military ​campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.
Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centres and ​AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.
Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian ‌security official ⁠said.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and US companies fear for their investments in the region.
"Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (US President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.
Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and ​the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.
Restoring ​connections during wartime could be difficult, ⁠experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.
The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran ​has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.
The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and ​Asia, with capacity routed ⁠through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.
Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with US technology firms.
Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its ⁠facilities in Bahrain. ​The IRGC named US tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the ​height of the war in March.
Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and US technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.
Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea ​and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

Stephanie March will reprise her role as Alexandra Cabot in season 28 of 'Law & Order: SVU', returning in episode nine
Stephanie March is set to return as assistant district attorney Alexandra Cabot in the upcoming ninth episode of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit season 28, bringing the familiar character back to the long-running crime drama.
March has portrayed Cabot in more than 100 episodes of the NBC series. She first joined the main cast in season 2 in 2000 and remained a regular until season 5 in 2003. Her character eventually had to fake her own death and enter witness protection, marking a major turning point in her storyline.
Following her departure from the main cast, March returned as a guest star several times over the years. Her appearances included seasons 6, 10, 11, 13 and 19, with her most recent appearance in 2018. Her return in season 28 will mark another appearance for the character, who has remained a recognisable part of the show's history.
Beyond Law & Order: SVU , March also starred as Alexandra Cabot in Conviction , a legal drama that served as a short-lived spin-off of the crime series in 2006.
The actress's other credits include Ricky Gervais' 2009 comedy film The Invention of Lying , the 2017 independent film Who We Are Now and the 2019 mockumentary The Social Ones . She also appeared in Ava DuVernay's 2023 film Origin and collaborated with the filmmaker on the 2022 television series Naomi . In 2023, March appeared in the Amazon Prime Video series Harlan Coben's Shelter .
Created by Dick Wolf, Law & Order: Special Victims Unit holds the record as the longest-running primetime drama in American television history. The series airs on NBC on Thursdays at 9pm.
The current cast includes Mariska Hargitay, Ice-T, Peter Scanavino, Kelli Giddish, Kevin Kane, Aimé Donna Kelly and Corey Cott. Wolf executive produces the series alongside Hargitay and several other producers. Universal Television produces the show in association with Wolf Entertainment.

title: Regional powers back Islamabad MoU
description: Regional powers back Islamabad MoU
content:
Muslim, European powers meet in Istanbul
Pakistan, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Egypt on Friday threw their collective weight behind the Islamabad-brokered understanding between Iran and the United States, as regional and European powers stepped up diplomatic efforts to prevent another round of hostilities in the Gulf.
The endorsement came at a crucial R4 foreign ministers' meeting in Istanbul against the backdrop of renewed concerns that the United States and Israel could again strike Iran, potentially unravelling the fragile pause in hostilities and further disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The meeting brought together Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty.
In a joint statement issued after the talks, the four countries underlined the "urgent need" to address the US-Israel conflict with Iran only through dialogue and diplomacy and to prevent attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, including vessels.
Significantly for Islamabad, the ministers "expressed support for the Islamabad MoU and welcomed continued diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation," while reaffirming their commitment to a lasting negotiated settlement.
The reference was seen as recognition of Pakistan's continuing diplomatic role in efforts to prevent the resumption of the Iran conflict. Dar briefed his counterparts on Islamabad's mediation efforts during the subsequent expanded meeting with European foreign ministers.
The Istanbul gathering assumed greater significance because the R4 also sat with the major European powers for the first time. France, Germany and the United Kingdom - traditionally known as the E3 - were joined by Italy, effectively turning Friday's gathering into an eight-country consultation between four regional and four European states.
The discussions covered Iran, the Strait of Hormuz, Yemen, Palestine and wider threats to maritime security.
The urgency surrounding the meeting was underscored by Turkish Foreign Minister Fidan, who warned after the talks that renewed military action against Iran would only deepen instability.
"Military intervention in Iran is by no means a solution. No one supports this at the moment," Fidan told reporters.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani similarly warned ahead of the meeting that there were signs hostilities in the Gulf could resume after the US elections, arguing that preventing another war should be the immediate priority.
The R4 statement also reflected growing concern over disruption to one of the world's most important maritime arteries.
The ministers stressed the importance of freedom of navigation and called for the "swift and full resumption of safe, secure and unimpeded passage" through the Strait of Hormuz. They rejected restrictions affecting lawful navigation, warning that disruption of sea lanes threatened energy, food and fertiliser supplies as well as global supply chains.
On Yemen, the four countries adopted an equally firm position, strongly condemning Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.
They expressed full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government and urged the Houthis to halt military operations and return to the political process.
The statement is significant for Pakistan since Islamabad, Ankara and Riyadh are also partners in the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed in August. Dar and Fidan, during their bilateral meeting in Istanbul, condemned the attacks on Saudi Arabia and agreed to maintain close coordination under the defence arrangement.
Palestine remained another major focus. The R4 described Israeli occupation as a fundamental source of regional instability, called for an end to violence and settlement activity and reiterated support for an independent Palestinian state based on the June 4, 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
The ministers also demanded uninterrupted humanitarian assistance and reconstruction in Gaza.
Following the ministerial consultations, the participating foreign ministers called on Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Dar conveyed greetings from President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir.
According to the Foreign Office, the meeting with Erdogan involved "candid exchanges" on regional and global developments and emphasised continued dialogue and diplomatic engagement.
Earlier in Islamabad, Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said the R4 had emerged as a mechanism to deal with regional instability and was now being broadened through engagement with European powers.
"The discussions will cover issues affecting the entire region, including the safe passage of maritime sea lanes, the situation in Yemen, the Houthis, and the Strait of Hormuz," Khan told his weekly briefing.
He said the primary objective was to explore ways of promoting peace and stability and de-escalating the overall situation.
The spokesperson also confirmed that Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had completed their ratification procedures for the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, while Türkiye was undertaking the required domestic legal process.
He stressed that the agreement was defensive in nature and consistent with the UN Charter, adding that any decision to invoke its collective-defence provisions in response to attacks would have to be taken by the three partner countries in accordance with the agreement.

title: Fuel fears dominate Senate as winter looms
description: Fuel fears dominate Senate as winter looms
content:
Minister of State for Finance and Revenue Bilal Azhar Kiani said there were no fuel supply problems
Concerns over Pakistan's petroleum supplies amid escalating tensions in the Middle East dominated the Senate proceedings on Friday, with lawmakers demanding clarity on the government's contingency plans even as the finance minister maintained that there was no fuel shortage.
The house, met here with acting Chairman Syedal Khan Nasir in the chair, also debated the use of the carbon levy, relief in the super tax and compensation for civilians affected by operations in South Waziristan, while complaints against Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) officials were referred to the relevant standing committee.
Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) Senator Sherry Rehman questioned whether the country would have sufficient petroleum supplies in December and urged the government to brief parliament on its contingency and possible rationing plans.
She said renewed attacks on Iran and the escalating conflict in West Asia had heightened uncertainty over energy supplies, with implications for economic stability and ordinary citizens. "What is the government's plan for the availability of petroleum products? Will there be rationing? Members of Parliament have concerns whether petrol will be available till December," she said, insisting that the government must address these concerns.
Rehman said Pakistan relied on imports for nearly 70% of its liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) requirements, while domestic production accounted for the remaining 30%. She said the country had received five LPG cargoes last year, compared with only two expected this year, and called for a clear supply plan to be presented before parliament.
However, Minister of State for Finance and Revenue Bilal Azhar Kiani said there were no fuel supply problems. He told the house that more than 10 million people were benefiting from the government's targeted fuel subsidy scheme, while Rs1,676 billion had been budgeted under the petroleum levy for the current fiscal year.
He said the government was providing targeted relief to motorcyclists, rickshaw and loader operators, and users of small cars to mitigate the impact of regional tensions on petroleum prices.
Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas also warned that conflict threatening key energy routes could aggravate Pakistan's energy difficulties. Linking the external crisis to domestic shortages, he said Punjab was already facing a flour shortage while the country was experiencing an LPG shortage. He also called on Pakistan to mediate between Yemen's Houthi movement and Saudi Arabia.
Rehman also questioned the utilisation of the carbon levy imposed on petroleum products, alleging that the proceeds were being absorbed into general federal revenues rather than spent on environmental protection and climate resilience projects.
Citing a meeting of the Senate Standing Committee on Climate Change, which she chairs, she said the finance ministry had acknowledged that the levy was not being spent on environmental projects. She argued that the money was transferred to the Federal Consolidated Fund without being earmarked for climate action.
Referring to water shortages in Balochistan and the absence of resilience schools in Sindh, Rehman questioned how the levy's proceeds were being distributed among the provinces. She said the levy should not continue in its existing form unless it was restructured to ensure that the money was ring-fenced for climate mitigation and resilience measures.
Separately, Minister of State Kiani informed the Senate that the super tax had been abolished for businesses with annual incomes ranging from Rs150 million to Rs500 million, while the rate for those earning Rs500 million or more had been reduced from 10% to 8%.
The house also took up a calling-attention notice regarding compensation for civilians affected by security operations in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas in 2008 and 2009.
Responding to the notice, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry said Rs117 billion had been distributed among affectees in South Waziristan. The release of another Rs65 billion in outstanding payments was awaiting completion of an audit and proceedings before the relevant committee, he added.
During the Question Hour, lawmakers expressed dissatisfaction with the government's response to complaints against FBR and Pakistan Customs personnel. The matter was referred to the relevant standing committee for further consideration.
The proceedings ended after Senator Falak Naz Chitrali pointed out a lack of quorum. A headcount confirmed that the required number of members was not present, prompting the chair to adjourn the session until 4pm on Monday.

title: PM sets wheat support price at Rs4 500
description: PM sets wheat support price at Rs4 500
content:
Orders time-bound plan to eradicate foot-and-mouth disease
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday approved an indicative wheat price of Rs4,500 per maund for 2027, up Rs1,000 from last year's Rs3,500.
However, the proposed price of Rs4,500 is still Rs500 less than the price demanded by farmers.
The prime minister said the increase was meant to provide relief to growers facing higher production costs, rising petrol prices and inflationary pressure.
He said giving farmers an effective incentive to sow wheat was among the main objectives of the decision, a Prime Minister's Office news release said.
The prime minister said the decision would be an important step towards strengthening national food security, encouraging local production and bringing stability to the agriculture sector.
The new price is expected to help farmers recover their input costs and earn a reasonable profit, he said.
The prime minister acknowledged the guidance of President Asif Ali Zardari and Mian Muhammad Nawaz Sharif in the matter, as well as the consultation and cooperation of the chief ministers of Punjab and Sindh.
He expressed special thanks to Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz for her cooperation and valuable suggestions during the consultative process, and appreciated her role in it.
He also thanked Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah for his cooperation.
Separately, National Food Security Minister Rana Tanveer Hussain has promised a better support price for wheat farmers this season, saying Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will coordinate with the provinces to establish a uniform rate as the government seeks to stabilise the market.
Speaking to the media on Friday after inaugurating the upgraded Central Plant Quarantine Laboratory (CPQL), the minister said farmers had received low prices for their wheat. He expressed hope that market prices would decline within a few days, adding that bringing wheat to the market was the responsibility of provincial governments.
"Ensuring food supplies for a population of 260 million is a challenge," he said. "The federal government has reserved one million metric tonnes of wheat and issued directives to preserve the stocks. Pakistan has a surplus of rice and tomatoes," he added.
Turning to the sugar sector, the minister said farmers often struggled to secure an appropriate price for sugarcane in the following season when sugar production exceeded domestic demand. He attributed some of the difficulties to inaccurate data and said the prime minister had directed the development of a mechanism to ensure 100% accuracy.
"The country currently has a surplus of sugar that could be exported to benefit farmers," he said, adding that the ex-mill price was below production cost. He told reporters that sugarcane crushing was scheduled to begin on November 15.
Tanveer also acknowledged that farmers lacked adequate information and awareness. "The government has undertaken awareness initiatives in coordination with provincial administrations," he said, adding that efforts were under way to reduce palm oil imports by developing alternatives.
Speaking about the CPQL, he said the laboratory had been upgraded at a cost of Rs400 million. The facility had previously been in disrepair, its machinery was non-functional and the grant allocated for it had been wasted, he added.
"Importers and exporters had lodged numerous complaints about testing standards, and bribery had become widespread. I cannot say that angels have been working here, but we have broken the mafia. Today, all the mafias have been eliminated," the minister said.
He said the Ministry of National Food Security had partnered with the International Centre for Chemical and Biological Sciences, operating under the University of Karachi's HEJ Research Institute of Chemistry, to upgrade the laboratory. Trained and experienced HEJ staff had been deployed at the facility, he added.
The upgraded laboratory will enhance testing capacity, strengthen export capabilities and enable commercial testing of pesticide residues, he said. The number of interceptions in the plant quarantine sector had already fallen from 376 to 23, and the new facility was expected to bring further improvement.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif approved the restructuring of the Livestock and Dairy Development Board and directed that the selection of its chairman and members be carried out transparently and strictly on merit.
The prime minister chairing a review meeting on reforms in the livestock sector, said the board should be made an effective and active institution by inducting capable and experienced professionals from the private sector, a Prime Minister's Office news release said.
The prime minister directed the authorities concerned to present a comprehensive action plan for the complete eradication of foot-and-mouth disease, with clear targets, measurable results and a fixed timeframe.
He announced that the federal government was establishing a plant in Islamabad for the production of modern and effective livestock vaccines, using its own resources.

title: Twelve killed in Lasbela road accident

content:
At least twelve people were killed and around two dozen sustained injuries when a passenger van smashed into a passenger bus on Friday in Lasbela district of Balochistan.

Talking to the media, Lasbela's Edhi Centre In-charge Dr Abdul Hakeem Lasi said seven people died on the spot as a result of the crash while five succumbed to their injuries in the hospital.
"A total of 22 people suffered injuries, seven of which were in a critical condition," he added. Dr Lasi said the critically injured had been transferred to a trauma centre in Karachi.
He said relatives of some of the victims had taken their bodies to their native areas after completion of formalities. He said the passengers of the van bore the brunt of the accident.
Police are probing the causes of the accident which caused disruption of traffic on the busy route.

"Field Marshal commended the high morale and professionalism of officers and troops, directing them to continue vigilance and highest standards of operational readiness to effectively counter threats," the statement said.
ISPR said, "He underscored that we would continue the campaign against Indian-sponsored terrorist outfits to the fullest and hit them hard wherever they are."
"While paying tributes to the sacrifices of the people of Pakistan, including Shuhada and Ghazis of the security forces, CDF Munir affirmed that with the support of the people, Pakistan would surely inflict total defeat to the terrorists and their perverted ideology," the statement concluded.
Separately, in a statement, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said the attacks took place on Thursday, leaving one civilian dead and several vehicles damaged. The operations concluded without any casualties among security personnel, and order had been restored, it added.
"Security forces foiled the terrorists' designs and their bid to undermine the writ of the state and spread their misconstrued agenda," the statement said.

"The coercion of a Baloch woman into this attack is a crime not only against the state but also against the hurmat of Baloch women," the statement said, condemning the involvement of a woman in the attack.

"Security forces and law enforcement agencies remain resolute in eliminating foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country," it added.

title: DISCOs warned over detection bills
description: DISCOs warned over detection bills
content:
Complete ban has been enforced on the issuance of manual and discretionary detection bills by field staff or SDOs
Federal Minister for Energy (Power Division) Sardar Awais Ahmad Khan Leghari has taken strict notice of electricity distribution companies (DISCOs) imposing excessive and unjustified detection bills on consumers, warning DISCOs that no incorrect or arbitrary detection bill will be charged to any consumer in the future.
Addressing an important meeting with the Boards of Directors of DISCOs, the minister issued formal directives to implement a stringent and comprehensive reform framework, said a press release.
He underlined that while curbing electricity theft remains an unquestionable national priority, arbitrarily burdening innocent citizens will not be tolerated under any circumstances. Under this framework, the discretionary authority of field staff is being strictly regulated to protect consumers while ensuring that no hurdle is created for honest officers performing their duties against power theft.
In light of the Federal Minister's directives, the Power Division is mandating that all DISCOs issue detection bills exclusively through the centralized online portal developed by PITC. A complete ban has been enforced on the issuance of manual and discretionary detection bills by field staff or SDOs. Issuing manual bills will be officially treated as severe misconduct, liable to strict disciplinary proceedings and major penalties against the responsible officials and staff.
Under this framework, comprehensive proposed amendments to the Consumer Service Manual (CSM) will be submitted in the coming days to bind every process within clearly defined timelines.
Under the new framework, replacing defective or burnt meters immediately or within a maximum of two billing cycles has been made mandatory, while average billing during this period will be restricted strictly to a maximum of two months. In cases where a meter is established to be running slow or fast, recovery or credit adjustments will be confined strictly to the preceding two billing cycles.
Similarly, bringing the duration of detection billing under strict regulation, the chargeable period for illegal abstraction by general consumers is proposed to be fixed at three billing cycles. The maximum chargeable period of detection will be capped at six months for registered consumers and twelve months for unregistered consumers.
Under this reformed mechanism, the Boards of Directors of DISCOs and their Customer Services Committees have been directed to conduct monthly, in-depth reviews to scrutinize the accuracy, transparency, and legitimate recovery of all detection bills.

title: LHC sets limits for conviction in desecration cases
description: LHC sets limits for conviction in desecration cases
content:
Sets aside conviction and life sentence of mentally unstable person
The Lahore High Court (LHC) has ruled that the recovery of a burnt copy of the Holy Quran cannot, by itself, establish an accused's guilt under Section 295-B of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), stressing that the prosecution must prove the act was wilful and deliberate.
Acquitting a man sentenced to life imprisonment, the court held that evidence of long-standing mental illness could not be brushed aside merely because no formal application had been filed under Section 464 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, while reiterating that even a single reasonable doubt entitles an accused to acquittal as a matter of right.
Justice Tariq Mehmood Bajwa of the Rawalpindi bench passed these observations while allowing the criminal appeal of Shahid-ur-Rehman, whose conviction and life sentence in a case registered at Sarai Alamgir police station in Gujrat district were set aside.
The court observed that the prosecution had failed to establish conclusively that the appellant had set fire to the copy of the Holy Quran. The complainant and another key prosecution witness admitted during cross-examination that they had not seen him lighting the fire.

The ECP has revised the descriptions of several National and provincial assembly constituencies in K-P following administrative changes across the province.
The changes, which include the division of newly established Paharpur district among three National Assembly constituencies, were made through a notification.
The notification revises the composition of National Assembly constituencies covering Dera Ismail Khan and the newly established Paharpur district, which was created in 2025.
NA-43, Tank-cum-Dera Ismail Khan-cum-Paharpur, now comprises Tank district, Kulachi and Daraband tehsils, and Darazinda subdivision, excluding Koh-i-Bahara in Dera Ismail Khan district. It also includes Panyala tehsil and part of Paharpur tehsil in the newly created district.

The constituency further includes Band Kurai Qanungo Halqa of Paharpur tehsil in the new district.
NA-45 Dera Ismail Khan comprises Census Charge No. 5 of Dera Ismail Khan Municipal Committee, Census Charge No. 1 of Dera Ismail Khan Cantonment and Dera Ismail Khan Qanungo Halqa, subject to specified exclusions.
These include Ratta Kulachi, Muryali Patwar Circle, Parowa tehsil, Fatah Patwar Circle of Muryali, Koh-e-Bahara in Darazinda subdivision, Hassani and Shero Khona in Chahkan Qanungo Halqa, and Shero Nau, Mapal and Kotla Habib in Muryali Qanungo Halqa.

Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah on Friday said that a letter had been sent to Opposition Leader in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai, urging him to respond and meet Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to discuss constitutional issues.
The statement came after Achakzai said the prime minister could visit his office for tea or invite him for talks at a venue of his choice. "Or I can go to him at the prime minister's house and give him an invitation."
Speaking to reporters, Sanaullah said there was "no issue of ego or stubbornness" over a meeting between Shehbaz and Achakzai.
"This type of talk - come here or come there - does not change anything. What is the rationale for this?" he said.
Sanaullah said the two leaders could discuss constitutional matters when they met.
Separately, the adviser warned that civilians could suffer collateral damage during planned intelligence-based operations in designated districts of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa if residents failed to remove militants from their communities or move away to allow security forces to operate.
Speaking on the private television programme Naya Pakistan, Sanaullah said militants had entered Pakistan from Afghanistan and carried out attacks. He alleged that training camps across the border were funded and operated with Indian support, while reports had also suggested Israeli involvement in the attacks.
"That is why Pakistan's armed forces have closed the border with Afghanistan. You must also be aware that no trade is taking place through that route," he said.
Sanaullah said militant groups typically comprised three to 15 members and that around 70% of them were present in areas designated for the operations. A separate development committee had also been established for the affected areas, he added.
He said militants were hiding among local residents and living alongside ordinary citizens rather than operating openly. Law enforcement agencies were conducting intelligence-based operations in the areas, he added.
Sanaullah warned that civilians risked being caught in the crossfire if residents did not expel militants from populated areas or move away to allow security forces to proceed.
"People have been told either to drive these elements out of their populated areas or, if they do not want to do so, to move aside themselves so that the operation can proceed. If neither of these options is possible, there is a risk of collateral damage," he said.
Asked how the planned operations would differ from previous intelligence-based operations, given that 7,177 such operations had been conducted over the past six months, Sanaullah said the provincial government and civil administration would be responsible for maintaining control of areas after they had been cleared of militants.
The authorities would ensure that militants could not return to the cleared areas or re-establish a presence there, he said.
"Things were different earlier. Many areas were cleared three or four times, but the problem persisted because the responsibilities that should have been fulfilled by the provincial government and civil administration were not carried out. Their attitude was, in fact, the opposite," he said.

title: US First Lady secures truce for Ukraine city
description: US First Lady secures truce for Ukraine city
content:
Ceasefire to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations
Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the Russian-controlled southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations, following mediation by US First Lady Melania Trump, the White House said on Friday.
The ceasefire will enable humanitarian teams to enter the city, where residents have reported a worsening food crisis. Russian military chief of staff Valery Gerasimov said Russian troops would halt fire from 4am local time on Tuesday to facilitate the operation, while the White House said the ceasefire would begin next Thursday.
"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," the White House said in a statement.
Ukraine's chief negotiator, David Arakhamia, said the humanitarian operation would begin once the ceasefire was in place. He said the agreement followed an extended process involving Melania Trump and Pope Leo and would establish a humanitarian corridor for residents seeking to leave the city.
The Kremlin welcomed the agreement, praising Melania Trump's role and saying Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump had discussed its details. Earlier this week, Moscow said efforts were under way to ease conditions in Oleshky after Putin told the pope he was ready to cooperate.
Melania Trump said the situation in the city was critical, with its remaining population consisting largely of elderly residents requiring urgent medical care, medicines, food and clean water. She said non-military teams from both countries would visit residents and coordinate transport for those wishing to evacuate to Russia or Ukraine.
An unnamed American media organisation will accompany the teams to document the operation. Right-leaning news outlet Newsmax said its cameras would have exclusive access to the effort.
Oleshky, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, lies across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson. Its population has fallen from about 24,000 before the war to between 1,700 and 2,000, including around 50 children.

An eyewitness told Al-Mamlaka that a vehicle arrived carrying the gunmen, who fired continuously for five minutes before fleeing the scene. Between 150 and 200 people were inside and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding that most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70.
King Abdullah visited Karak hours after the shooting and vowed the perpetrators would face the "harshest retaliation", warning that attempts to divide Jordanians would fail. Jordan's prime minister said the attack was the result of "terrorist extremist blind thinking". Karak is home to a significant Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.

title: DOJ seeks court intervention if Alaska Republican loses
description: DOJ seeks court intervention if Alaska Republican loses
content:
Lawsuit cites voter confusion over two candidates named Dan Sullivan
The US Justice Department is seeking to invalidate Alaska's Senate election results if the Republican incumbent loses next month, in a rare legal move that raises questions about the President Donald Trump administration's willingness to accept defeat in the midterms.
In a lawsuit, the Justice Department alleged that Republican Dan J Sullivan Jr, who is running for the Senate, could confuse voters intending to support the incumbent senator, who is also Republican and is also named Dan Sullivan.
Republican officials have claimed that Sullivan Jr is a Democratic ruse to try and tilt the race in which Democrats hope to flip the seat – and help their outside bid to win control of the Senate. Democrats and Sullivan Jr himself have denied this.
The Justice Department asked a judge to halt certification if the incumbent's losing margin is smaller than the votes won by his namesake. US Attorney General Todd Blanche suggested the Justice Department was not trying to interfere in the election, but at the same time would not completely rule out such a scenario.
"It is not DOJ's intention toand it's never our intention toimproperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process," Blanche said. "But you know, to say that there's no circumstances that we would ever do that.
Trump said on Friday that he ordered for filing the lawsuit. "I'm the one who said do it," he said, adding that he told the Justice ?Department to pre-emptively block Alaska from certifying ?the results of its US Senate ?race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses by a narrow margin.
Democrats have accused the Trump administration of seeking to
influence the November vote by expanding
federal control over state-run elections and by repeatedly questioning the integrity of election results.
Mary Peltola, a former tribal judge and Alaska Native, has a strong chance of winning the Senate seat.

title: Auto policy puts 1 5m jobs at risk
description: Auto policy puts 1 5m jobs at risk
content:
Parts makers challenge tariff cuts on imports, citing $1.8b import substitution
The Pakistan Association of Automotive Parts and Accessories Manufacturers (PAAPAM) has urged Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to review the draft Auto Policy 2026-31, warning that proposed tariff reductions on completely built-up vehicles, concessions for new-energy vehicles and lower duties on auto parts could undermine domestic manufacturing and employment.
In a letter dated October 23, PAAPAM Chairman Abdul Rehman Aizaz cited more than 1,200 companies, 1.5 million jobs, $1.8 billion in annual import substitution and Rs700 billion worth of locally manufactured components supplied to assemblers. The association has requested a meeting with the prime minister to present alternatives before the policy is finalised.
The objection highlights a fundamental conflict. Importers and businesses seeking greater access to foreign vehicles favour lower trade barriers, while local assemblers and parts manufacturers fear that cheaper imports could undermine domestic production and investments made over decades. For parts suppliers, the concern extends beyond competition between car brands to whether locally manufactured components will remain commercially viable as assemblers gain easier access to imported parts and complete vehicles.
The automotive industry is struggling to agree on its future as competing manufacturers, importers and parts suppliers push for policies that protect their commercial interests. The draft policy has exposed divisions in a sector once dominated by Japanese carmakers but now facing competition from Chinese brands, electric-vehicle manufacturers and businesses pursuing multiple technologies.
The government's challenge is no longer simply to balance the interests of a few established assemblers. Conventional petrol engines, hybrids, plug-in hybrids, battery-electric vehicles and range-extended electric vehicles now compete for market share, investment and tax incentives. Each technology has different manufacturing requirements, import dependencies and implications for the existing auto-parts supply chain, making a common industry position increasingly difficult to achieve.
The stakes have risen as Chinese manufacturers introduce new models and technologies into a market long shaped by Suzuki, Toyota and Honda. These Japanese companies helped develop the country's automotive manufacturing base and supplier networks, but their established position is now being challenged by changing consumer preferences and new competitors. Their long-term standing will depend on how effectively they respond to this changing market.
The transition has also complicated lobbying. Some companies operate across several vehicle technologies, while others specialise in particular powertrains or components. A concession benefiting one category may disadvantage another, even when their commercial interests overlap. The result is a contest in which manufacturers, importers and suppliers are not necessarily aligned even within their own segments.
A senior official of a Japanese auto manufacturer said: "The industry is no longer speaking with one voice because the business itself has changed." Traditional assemblers, parts manufacturers, importers and companies investing in electric and hybrid technologies have different priorities. "Everyone wants a policy that supports their own investment, but the government must consider the entire industrial ecosystem."
He added that opening the market too quickly could hurt local suppliers and employment, while excessive protection can discourage competition and keep prices high. "The real requirement is a predictable policy that encourages exports, genuine localisation and technology transfer. Companies should compete on efficiency and quality, but the transition must not destroy productive capacity built over decades."
The draft policy attempts to reconcile competing demands through a combination of tariff liberalisation, export obligations and incentives for cleaner vehicles. It targets $6 billion in cumulative vehicle and auto-parts exports by 2030-31, with incentives for companies meeting export targets and penalties for those falling short. Proposals also include phased tariff reductions and preferential sales tax rates of 1% for battery-electric vehicles, 6% for range-extended electric vehicles and 9% for plug-in hybrids, subject to the remaining approval process.
These measures could increase competition and widen consumer choice, but they also raise questions about the pace of liberalisation and the future of local suppliers. Stakeholders believe import competition may put pressure on prices, yet lower duties alone cannot guarantee that consumers receive the full benefit or that domestic manufacturers remain competitive. Conversely, prolonged protection without stronger productivity, exports and localisation could leave the industry dependent on a relatively sheltered domestic market.
The policy's success will ultimately depend on whether its incentives produce measurable gains in domestic value addition, exports, technology transfer and affordability. The government must also establish clear, predictable rules so that businesses can make long-term investment decisions rather than repeatedly lobbying for changes to taxes and tariffs, stakeholders added.

Envoy seeks easier visas and direct flights as LCCI proposes dedicated trade cell
Bilateral trade between Pakistan and Bangladesh stands at around $1 billion against a potential worth several billion dollars, Bangladesh High Commissioner Md Iqbal Hussain Khan said, calling for stronger cooperation, improved connectivity, the removal of trade barriers and closer engagement between the business communities to unlock it.
Speaking at the Lahore Chamber of Commerce and Industry, he identified agriculture, textiles, pharmaceuticals, engineering, food processing, chemicals, minerals, education, healthcare and tourism as promising areas of collaboration, according to a statement on Friday. Honorary Consul of Bangladesh Qazi Humayun Fareed also attended.
He said Bangladeshi imports could expand in maize, rice and basmati rice, textile raw materials, chemicals, minerals and manufactured goods, along with sugar, wheat, cereals and spices. Bangladeshi pineapples had begun reaching Pakistan after clearances, and seasonal fruits, agricultural products and jaggery could further expand trade.
He called for easier business visas, improved e-visa procedures and stronger direct air connectivity, noting Pakistan could serve as a gateway to Central Asia while Bangladesh offered access to Southeast Asia. More than 100 Bangladeshi students study at private universities in Pakistan, and he identified opportunities in scholarships, medical tourism and tourism.
LCCI President Ali Hussam Asghar proposed a dedicated Bangladesh trade cell under the senior vice president to coordinate bilateral business activities, suggesting the identification of five priority export sectors, a link with a leading chamber in Dhaka or Chittagong and two to three virtual business-to-business meetings, followed by sector-specific meetings, trade delegations and reciprocal business visits.
He invited Bangladeshi entrepreneurs to explore partnerships in Lahore and said both countries must move beyond discussions and adopt a result-oriented strategy with measurable results.
Senior Vice President Sardar Usman Ghani called for reversing the downward trend in bilateral trade and raising it to at least $2 billion, citing pharmaceuticals, textiles, textile machinery, rice, cement, agriculture, food processing, information technology, engineering, light manufacturing and services.
He urged joint ventures and investment partnerships alongside improvements in shipping, customs procedures, documentation and the exchange of market intelligence.

title: Public transport carries less than 1  of commuters
description: Public transport carries less than 1  of commuters
content:
Private vehicles dominate mobility index; experts call for public buses-led transport policy
Pakistan's transport policy needs to shift its focus from private cars to public buses to make urban mobility more affordable, reduce carbon emissions and support local manufacturing, experts say, as a new mobility index shows that public transport accounts for less than 0.5%.
The BusCaro and Pakistan & Counting Mobility Index, launched on Thursday, showed that the cost of travelling a kilometre across eight modes of transport fell 7.9% between May and September, declining from Rs10.48 to Rs9.65. However, the index's vehicle-based weight is heavily dominated by privately owned motorcycles, cars and rickshaws, which account for 98.7% of the total weight.
The findings have renewed attention on the structure of Pakistan's transport system, where private cars and electric vehicles (EVs) frequently dominate automotive discussions despite limited car affordability and inadequate public transport options in major cities.
One industry argument is that buses make greater economic sense for a country where only around 22 people out of every 1,000 can afford a car. Expanding bus services could help transport a larger share of the population at a lower cost while reducing dependence on private vehicles. Developing local bus manufacturing could also reduce reliance on imported vehicles and components.
Mashood Ali Khan, an auto expert, said public transport played a crucial role in urban centres and megacities, and cited examples from Europe, China and India, where transport networks had been developed to serve residents and businesses more efficiently. "Routes and directions of public transport are very important so that they are convenient for the industry and residents coming within those routes," he said.
Khan said developed transport systems had invested in infrastructure, including underground networks and flyovers, to make public transport convenient and clean. Pakistan had also begun developing public transport systems, particularly in Punjab, followed by the federal capital and Sindh, but the pace of expansion needed to be accelerated.
He called on the government to introduce policies and incentives to develop public transport rapidly and transition towards electric bus fleets. He said the country needed to make public transport cleaner and more user-friendly to encourage commuters to shift away from private vehicles. He also proposed a coordinated national strategy under which all four provinces would identify their bus transport requirements, allowing the federal government to develop a long-term roadmap that could bring those needs together.
Rather than relying on imported buses, Pakistan should negotiate with established original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to set up an electric bus manufacturing plant locally or develop domestic manufacturing capacity, he said. Such an approach could combine public transport expansion with industrial investment, local production and employment generation. However, it would require a clear assessment of provincial demand, financing arrangements and the infrastructure needed to operate electric buses.
Khan said infrastructure remained a major constraint, particularly in Karachi, Pakistan's economic hub, where deteriorating roads and inadequate transport facilities undermined the commuting experience. "Due to the lack of infrastructure, it looks like we are travelling on a desert safari," he said, describing the condition of transport infrastructure in Karachi.
He added that communication gaps between federal and provincial governments often delayed projects, increasing development costs. Public transport, he said, should be treated as a basic necessity and developed under a time-bound, long-term national policy rather than through disconnected provincial initiatives.
Khan argued that the scale of Pakistan's potential bus market could justify investment in domestic manufacturing. He estimated that the country's existing bus fleet was around 2,000, while annual demand could reach 18,000 to 20,000 buses.
The mobility index also highlighted the contrast between private and public transport costs. While fuel-only running costs for privately owned motorcycles, cars and rickshaws fell 7.5% between May and September, the public transport component rose 77%, from Rs1.22 to Rs2.16 per seat-kilometre.
The increase largely reflected the restoration of fares after Punjab's Metro Bus, Bus Rapid Transit and Orange Line services had been free for a period. The index's public transport component therefore reflects a change in fares rather than simply an increase in operating costs.
The index counts 36.7 million vehicles, including 30.3 million motorcycles and 5.1 million cars, based on the Pakistan Economic Survey 2024-25.

title: Small factories choose to stay small
description: Small factories choose to stay small
content:
Rising scrap, freight and power costs leave Karachi's micro-manufacturers with margins too thin to expand
Small-scale manufacturers are increasingly squeezed by rising raw material, scrap, transport and energy costs, leaving them with slimmer profits per unit. For small businesses, expanding production can mean higher operating expenses and greater financial risk.
Some owners may therefore prefer to keep operations small to maintain control over costs, manage cash flow and protect their limited margins. For businesses with narrow profit margins, these requirements can make expansion financially difficult, encouraging owners to remain small, scale back operations or return to informal status.
Across the industrial areas of Sher Shah, SITE, Korangi, Landhi, Federal B Area and SITE Super Highway, small manufacturers producing essential packaging and high-demand domestic plastic goods are making a deliberate choice to remain small.
Despite massive nationwide consumer demand for affordable daily-use items, ranging from kitchenware such as bowls, jugs and serving plates to essential retail packaging, micro-manufacturers report that escalating raw material scrap costs, local trucking charges and fixed space overheads have squeezed profit margins to razor-thin levels.
For many, expanding operations or adding workforce capacity brings disproportionate operational friction, prompting owners to maintain lean, low-profile workshop operations.
The packaging industry, comprising producers of corrugated boxes that supply master packaging for local wholesale trade, food delivery and retail goods, is feeling the pinch of fluctuating paper scrap prices and rising local transport rates. This ecosystem relies on a vast network of big, small and micro-manufacturers, spanning suppliers of raw paper rolls and fluting sheets to small box-making units across the city.
"Our biggest challenge is the rising cost of doing business," says Sadaqat Shah, a corrugated box unit operator in the Shershah Industrial Area. "When production cost rises, our profit on a standard master carton shrinks to just a few rupees. Moving raw paper bales from warehouses to our unit adds heavy load and transport cost. If we try to scale up or install larger machinery, our electricity and rental overheads double immediately. We deliberately keep our output modest with four workers to stay steady rather than taking on unsustainable debt."
A similar dynamic is playing out across the heavy recycling and plastic processing units in the SITE industrial area as well as Korangi. Here, small workshops melt down reprocessed plastic scrap and granules to manufacture essential kitchenware and storage items, products with a huge and resilient consumer base across low- and middle-income households throughout Pakistan.
By feeding discarded plastic back into the production loop, these recycling facilities drive a vital localised circular economy that reduces landfill waste while supplying low-cost daily necessities to millions of households.
"The consumer market for basic plastic items such as plates, bowls, jugs and storage containers is huge," explains Mohammad Nadeem, a small-scale plastic moulding and recycling operator. "Every household buys them because they are affordable. But even with steady sales, electricity tariffs and machine maintenance hit small moulding units very hard. We rely on recycled granules to keep costs down, but when utility rates spike, our profit per piece drops to pennies. Keeping our operation small lets us manage daily production without taking on heavy overheads."
A parallel network of micro-manufacturers produces polypropylene bags for bulk grain, flour and industrial packaging, struggling under the same volatile material costs and high power tariffs that squeeze local moulders.
Producers of polythene retail packaging also operate under tight constraints, as micro-producers find it difficult to pass cost increases down to wholesale traders in Jodia Bazaar and local neighbourhood retail markets.
"The demand for ultra-thin shoppers for retail is huge, but we operate on very thin margins," notes Saqib Ali. "When polymer prices jump, we cannot easily raise our wholesale rates for small shopkeepers overnight. Operating a compact unit allows us to manage inventory tightly and avoid long credit lines in the market."

title: SPI inflation sticky at 11 85  YoY
description: SPI inflation sticky at 11 85  YoY
content:
Lowest quintile gets relief; weekly index up 0.65% over oil, war fears
Pakistan's weekly Sensitive Price Indicator (SPI) rose 0.65% in the week ended October 22, 2026, keeping year-on-year inflation firmly in double digits at 11.85%, according to Pakistan Bureau of Statistics' data. The index, covering 51 essential items across 50 markets in 17 cities, stood at 374.84, up from 372.43 in the previous week and 335.14 a year ago.
While the overall figure underscores persistent price pressures, the lowest consumption quintile (households spending up to Rs17,732 a month) faced a milder 8.45% year-on-year increase and a 0.51% weekly rise, noticeably below the 12.69% annual and 0.74% weekly gains for the highest quintile. This divergence offers a modest breathing space for the most vulnerable, even as broader inflation remains sticky.
Weekly increases were led by liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), which surged 22.44%, broiler farm chicken (12.20%), onions (4.19%), shirting (1.86%), plain bread (1.66%) and wheat flour (1%). On the other side, tomatoes plunged 21.99%, petrol fell 3.63%, bananas dropped 2.42% and diesel declined 1.68%, providing some comfort. Of the 51 items, 19 rose, 12 fell and 20 remained unchanged.
On a yearly basis, the pain was more concentrated. LPG was up 107%, onions 73%, electricity charges for Q1 59%, petrol 44%, diesel 42%, chicken 39% and wheat flour 36%. These gains were amplified by global energy shocks. Escalating Houthi attacks linked to the Yemen-Saudi conflict, combined with the US-Iran war, now in its eighth month, drove Brent crude to multi-month highs near or above $112-117 a barrel this week on fears of further disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz and strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure. Local fuel prices eased modestly week-on-week, but the year-on-year surge in petrol, diesel and especially LPG continued to feed into transport, cooking and broader household costs.
Furthermore, the monthly headline inflation is projected to rise around 0.9% month-on-month (9.4% year-on-year) despite a food buffer. The energy index is anticipated to play a major role as geopolitical uncertainty continues to grow. Core inflation is projected to rise 0.8% MoM, said Optimus Research.
Energy index may go up 2.6% MoM. Prices of motor fuel and liquefied hydrocarbons are expected to rise around 9.3% and 11.3% MoM, respectively, as global oil nears five-month highs. Resultantly, the housing and transportation baskets are likely to rise 0.7% and 6.7% MoM, respectively.

title: Mohmand Dam cost jumps 115
description: Mohmand Dam cost jumps 115
content:
CDWP defers decision as Wapda blames rupee devaluation for 51% of increase
Pakistan has reassessed the cost of the under-construction Mohmand Dam at a staggering Rs666 billion, an increase of 115% in the past eight years, which authorities largely attributed to rupee devaluation after 2018.
Mohmand is one of the three largest reservoirs Islamabad is building to deal with Indian water aggression.
The revised project cost was presented before the Central Development Working Party (CDWP) meeting this week, which did not take up the matter for a decision due to paucity of time, according to federal government officials. The CDWP is the first stage for approval of mega projects, which are then sent for final endorsement of the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council.
The Water and Power Development Authority (Wapda), the agency responsible for execution of the mega scheme, has assessed the cost at Rs666 billion, according to officials who have seen the documents.
In 2018, the then government had approved the project at a cost of Rs310 billion with a deadline to finish work by September 2025. Since then, the cost has been estimated to escalate by Rs356 billion or 115%, according to the authorities.
The project was planned for completion by 2025, but due to various reasons, mainly dollar exchange parity, cost escalation, design changes that translated into a price hike, the 2022 floods and security issues added to the delay, according to an explanation given by the project management to the Planning Commission during the cost review assessment.
A joint venture of China Gezhouba Group Company Limited (CGGC) and Pakistan's Descon Engineering Limited is constructing the dam.
Planning Commission officials said Wapda had informed that 51% of the overall cost increase was due to dollar parity. They said a detailed discussion was held regarding the impact of foreign exchange fluctuations on the project cost. It was explained that the project contains both local and foreign currency components and that fluctuations in the dollar exchange rate have resulted in a significant increase in the rupee equivalent of the foreign component.
The rupee devaluation impacts everything from a household kitchen to mega projects due to the country's heavy dependence on foreign resources and imports. The rupee-dollar parity has again come under the spotlight after the World Bank said this week that Pakistan's currency was not freely responding to market developments.
It has assessed the difference between the market price and the daily price as of June this year at 10%, slightly higher than the 8% difference being worked out by the central bank under its Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER).
The Planning Commission had asked Wapda to provide details of dollar-denominated contractual payments and the extent to which exchange-rate variation could be passed on to the project cost.
It was observed that the foreign component of a contract cannot simply be converted at the latest exchange rate without establishing the contractual basis and the actual payment obligations. It was pointed out that, for contracts containing foreign currency payments, the actual contractual arrangements and the applicable exchange-rate provisions need to be examined.
According to project documents, as of last month, about 57% physical work had been completed, with Rs275 billion spent on the project.
The project was approved by ECNEC in its meeting held in April 2018 at a cost of Rs310 billion, with rupee cover of Rs71.5 billion.
Out of the total proposed upward revision, the dam cost will be Rs267 billion, an increase of Rs153 billion or 134% over the old estimates. Likewise, the power generation cost went up to Rs399 billion, a surge of Rs204 billion or 105%.
On completion, the project will increase Pakistan's overall water storage capacity by 1.29 million acres and add 2.9 billion units of generation to the national grid. It will also provide 300 million gallons of drinking water annually to Peshawar.
The Mohmand Dam Hydropower Project is of strategic national importance to Pakistan as it directly addresses the country's chronic water storage deficit, energy insecurity and vulnerability to climate-induced floods.
The project faced huge setbacks in the 2022 floods, when heavy flooding in the Swat river damaged diversion tunnels. As a result, work was halted for a significant period, according to the project management's explanation to the Planning Commission.
But the Planning Commission was of the view that the project was a classic example of delays and other issues among various flagship projects being implemented under Wapda.
The Planning Commission is of the view that the project should be recommended for third-party validation for financial and physical resource utilisation, scope of works, variation orders, escalation cost, gestation period, financial closure and other matters.
It has also recommended that the revised financial plan needed updating, including the federal government's share through the Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP) for dam funding, any provincial share and loans from foreign lenders.

title: Mother  daughter found murdered
description: Mother  daughter found murdered
content:
Police say bodies were recovered from house
In a suspected blind murder case, the bodies of a mother and her daughter were found under mysterious circumstances at a house in the Qureshi Abad Garja area within the limits of Dhamial Police Station in Rawalpindi.
Both appeared to have been strangled, while one of the victims also bore marks of violence inflicted with an instrument. Police have registered a case.
According to police, the case was registered on the complaint of the deceased woman's son, Suleman Ejaz. In his statement, he said he was a resident of Gujranwala and had three brothers and two sisters.
His two sisters, identified as Roshni and Noman Ejaz, lived with their mother, Naweza Bibi, in a rented house in Mohalla Qureshi Abad, Rawalpindi.
He said Roshni had a four-year-old son, Isa, and a six-year-old daughter, Abrish, while his other sister, Noman, had no children and was divorced.
He said he received a telephone call on October 22 informing him that his mother and sister had been murdered in Qureshi Abad. He contacted his sister Roshni, who confirmed the news. He then travelled to Rawalpindi with his maternal aunt, Najma, also known as Ghulam Fatima.
According to the complainant, Roshni told him that on the night of October 22, both sisters had gone to Quaid-i-Azam Colony for some work. Noman had returned home about an hour before her. Their mother, Roshni's daughter and son, and Noman were present in the house.
When Roshni returned late at night after finishing her work, the main gate of the house was locked from inside. She knocked for quite some time, and after approximately 10 minutes, her six-year-old daughter Abrish opened the latch.
Upon entering the house, she saw Noman Ejaz lying in a room covered in blood, with blood coming from her head. She immediately went into another room, where she found her mother's body as well.
She raised an alarm, drawing a large number of neighbourhood residents to the scene. They informed the police through emergency helpline 15.
The complainant stated that his mother, Naweza Bibi, and sister, Noman Ejaz, had been unlawfully murdered by unidentified suspect or suspects for unknown reasons.

title: Shahkaar Fankaar  art showcase opens
description: Shahkaar Fankaar  art showcase opens
content:
Highlights cultural impact of United States EFP exchange programmes
The US Embassy in Islamabad, the United States Educational Foundation in Pakistan (USEFP) and the Pakistan-US Alumni Network on October 22 opened the first 'Shahkaar Fankaar Alumni Artist Showcase' in a new gallery space in the USEFP building in Islamabad.
This gallery space will feature the achievements of US government-sponsored exchange programme alumni in the arts.
The first exhibition is a solo show by Lahore-based artist Minaa Haroon, an alumna of a US Department of State exchange programme on cultural preservation. Haroon showcased her artwork which utilises inherited jewellery and accessories as carriers of memory, identity and lineage.
Minaa Haroon is a visual artist and Assistant Director (Fine Arts) at the Lahore Arts Council. In April 2024, she travelled to the United States as a visiting scholar in the Cultural Preservation Professional Exchange Program run by the US Government. "My participation as a visiting scholar in the US deepened my reflection on cultural inheritance. Through visits to museums and galleries, I encountered different ways in which histories and traditions are preserved, interpreted, and carried forward," said Haroon.
The opening included a 3D projection of Haroon's works on the exterior wall of the USEFP building by Hoola Digital Pvt Ltd, the Islamabad-based company that created the projections on the Pakistan Monument and Lahore Fort to commemorate the 250th birthday of the United States on July 4, 2026.
The opening of the showcase marks decades of US education and exchange programmes and spotlights an alumna whose achievements reflect the mutual partnership between the United States and Pakistan. Three additional alumni artists will have their work featured in solo exhibitions in the USEFP gallery in 2027.
Satrang Gallery Director and programme advisor for the showcase, Asma Rashid-Khan, and the exhibition's curator, Sarah Rajper, along with representatives from the US Department of State with other guests from Pakistan's art world, exchange alumni and members of the diplomatic corps attended the event.
Speaking at the opening, US Embassy Pakistan Director of Public Engagement Heidi Smith said that "for decades, educational and cultural exchanges have brought Americans and Pakistanis together as partners in learning, innovation and creativity.

title: Dengue cases rise to 109 in twin cities
description: Dengue cases rise to 109 in twin cities
content:
Pindi reports 67 infections, Islamabad 42 as officials pin hopes on heavy rains
Dengue mosquitoes are continuing to spread rapidly in the twin cities of Rawalpindi and Islamabad, with the number of patients in the two cities reaching 109 and new cases being reported daily.
Health officials in both cities have started praying for heavy rainfall in the hope that it will help reduce the number of dengue patients.
The number of dengue patients has risen to 67 in Rawalpindi and 42 in Islamabad. Meanwhile, the number of dengue patients reported at private hospitals and clinics in the two cities has also exceeded 100.
Dengue patients have been admitted to dedicated wards at hospitals in Rawalpindi and Islamabad.
Compared with Rawalpindi, Islamabad's health department has exercised greater efforts and launched its anti-dengue campaign earlier, helping it maintain control over the situation. As a result, the number of dengue patients reported in Islamabad this year has reached a record low.
According to the Rawalpindi Health Department, millions of dengue larvae were recovered from a total of 235,982 locations inspected in the city this year.
Of these, larvae were found at 208,768 houses and 27,160 hotspots, including open areas, tyre shops and junkyards.
A total of 1,400 dengue teams are working in the city. Following the detection of dengue larvae, 2,800 FIRs were registered, 686 properties were sealed and 2,331 challans were issued, resulting in fines amounting to Rs3,156,000. Eleven dengue workers were also suspended during the campaign for negligence in performing their duties.
Meanwhile, Islamabad has conducted more than 382,000 indoor and outdoor surveillance activities as part of its anti-dengue campaign. More than 1.29 million anti-larval operations have been carried out.
Surveillance teams have so far identified more than 7,669 locations where mosquito breeding posed a risk and destroyed the larvae found there.

title: Hina s autopsy reveals brutal torture
description: Hina s autopsy reveals brutal torture
content:
Report exposes severe injuries, including broken neck and 27-centimetre head wound
Investigators probing the high-profile murder of Hina Javed gathered additional photographs allegedly showing brutal torture before her death. The initial post-mortem report also revealed serious injuries to the victim's body.
According to the autopsy report, Hina's neck was broken and a deep, 27-centimetre-long wound was found on the back of her head. Multiple marks of violence and bruising were also found on her face, neck, arms and hands. The report further stated that her lips were torn and both arms bore visible signs of violence. Her elbows were allegedly pierced with a screwdriver.
The report also recorded blood in her lungs and an accumulation of blood in the pericardium, the membrane surrounding the heart. The broken neck and unusually long wound on the back of her head have raised further questions about the severity of the alleged torture before her death.
Hina was allegedly murdered on August 20 in Rawalpindi after being subjected to violence at her in-laws' home. It was also alleged that her body was subsequently hung in a bathroom from a shower fitting.
Her husband, Faisal Asghar, and domestic worker Zeeshan Arshad, both nominated in the murder case registered at the Civil Lines Police Station, remain in Adiala Jail on judicial remand.
Meanwhile, the victim's family has expressed a lack of confidence in the police investigation and demanded the formation of a judicial commission to ensure an impartial inquiry into the murder.
The case has also reached Parliament's Standing Committee on Interior, which has included it in the formal agenda of its October 29 meeting and sought a briefing from senior Punjab police officials on the investigation and progress made so far.
The committee has summoned the Inspector General of Punjab Police and Additional Inspector General of the Crime Control Department (CCD) Sohail Zafar Chattha. Rawalpindi Regional Police Officer Babar Sarfraz Alpa and Senior Superintendent of Police (Operations) Malik Tariq Mehboob have also been asked to brief the committee on the case.
The parliamentary committee has invited Hina's family to attend the October 29 meeting, where they will be able to present their concerns and position regarding the investigation.
In view of the latest medical findings, the family's reservations about the investigation and the case's referral to the parliamentary committee, the October 29 meeting has assumed considerable significance, sources said.

Jamaat-e-Islami (JI) has launched the third phase of its nationwide protest movement against increases in petroleum product prices and what it termed an unjust petroleum levy, holding sit-ins, rallies and public gatherings across several districts of central Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Friday.

Demonstrations were held in Peshawar, Mardan, Nowshera, Swabi, Charsadda and Khyber, where party leaders warned that the movement would continue until the government abolished the petroleum levy and provided meaningful relief to the public.

In Khyber, a rally was led by provincial deputy amir Mian Sohaibuddin Kakakhel and district emir Shah Faisal Afridi, while a public gathering was held at Farooq Azam Chowk in Charsadda under the leadership of district emir Shah Hussain Advocate.
Addressing the gatherings, the JI leaders said repeated increases in petroleum prices had fuelled inflation, while the deteriorating law and order situation and prolonged electricity and gas load-shedding had made life increasingly difficult for ordinary citizens.
They alleged that, following the imposition of governor's rule in the province, the government had launched anti-encroachment operations to divert public attention from pressing issues.
