title: PSX falls below 164 000 on oil fears
description: PSX falls below 164 000 on oil fears
content:
KSE-100 index sheds over 2,000 points amid geopolitical jitters
The Pakistan Stock Exchange's (PSX) benchmark KSE-100 index fell below the 164,000-point level on Thursday, shedding over 2,000 points as escalating geopolitical tensions and rising international oil prices heightened investor concerns over the economic outlook.
At the close of trading, the KSE-100 posted a loss of 2,006.67 points, or 1.21%, and settled at 163,924.32.
Arif Habib Limited (AHL) noted that the week's downside draw at 164,000 was delivered as the KSE-100 fell 1.21% to close at 163,924. Only 11 shares rose while 89 declined. Unilever Pakistan Foods (+3.99%), Thatta Cement (+2.9%) and Standard Chartered Bank (+1.19%) provided the largest positive contribution to the index, whereas Engro Holdings (-2.29%), UBL (-1.39%) and HBL (-2.32%) were the heaviest drags.
Key banks reported results for nine months of calendar year 2026 that were broadly in line with expectations. HBL posted earnings per share (EPS) of Rs36.84 (up 5% year-on-year) and a dividend per share of Rs18; Meezan Bank reported EPS of Rs41.02 (up 6% year-on-year) and dividend of Rs23.5 and MCB recorded EPS of Rs37.26 (flat year-on-year) with dividend of Rs27.
In a key geopolitical development, Turkiye, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia signed an agreement in Doha to boost defence cooperation and strengthen defence capabilities. The "Badr MoU" is viewed as a signal of mutual interest in deepening partnerships. "Market bias remains to the downside below the 167,000-168,000 zone. Year-to-date, the index is down 5.82%, with week-to-date and month-to-date declines of 1.50% and 3.56%, respectively," AHL said.
Total market capitalisation stood at Rs18.17 trillion ($65.6 billion). Regular-market turnover was 367 million shares valuing at Rs18 billion. Leading gainers in terms of index contribution included Unilever Pakistan Foods, Thatta Cement and Airlink Communication, while the largest losers were PTCL, Nishat Chunian Power and Power Cement, AHL added.
Topline's market review noted that the KSE-100 index witnessed a sharp sell-off, shedding 2,007 points (-1.21%), as escalating geopolitical tensions and rising international oil prices weighed on investor sentiment. The benchmark initially touched the intra-day high of 249 points before plunging to the low of 2,148 points, reflecting heightened volatility and mounting selling pressure.
Persistent geopolitical uncertainty, coupled with concerns over rising oil prices and their potential implications for Pakistan's economic outlook, kept investors on the defensive. ENGROH, UBL, HUBC, HBL and PTC emerged as the major laggards, collectively dragging the index down by 752 points and amplifying the market's downward momentum, Topline said.
Overall trading volumes were recorded at 367.09 million shares compared with the previous session's tally of 379.91 million. The value of shares traded during the day was Rs18 billion.
Shares of 494 companies were traded. Of these, 101 stocks closed higher, 355 fell and 38 remained unchanged.
Pakistan Refinery was the volume leader with trading in 25.88 million shares, losing Rs4.76 to close at Rs95.12. It was followed by Cnergyico Pk with 23.19 million shares, losing Rs0.17 to close at Rs12.35 and WorldCall Telecom with 22.16 million shares, losing Rs0.03 to close at Rs0.90. Foreign investors sold shares worth Rs376.5 million, the National Clearing Company reported.

title: NBC to take up GM corn cases on Friday
description: NBC to take up GM corn cases on Friday
content:
Committee to consider long-pending biosafety cases; none GMO still sells at premium
The National Biosafety Committee (NBC) meets on Friday to consider a range of biosafety applications, including long-pending cases related to genetically modified (GM) corn technologies, according to a statement issued on Thursday.
The agenda follows the government's approval earlier this year of the National Agricultural Biotechnology Policy, which the government says will strengthen the regulatory framework for agricultural innovations. No decision on the pending applications has been announced.
CropLife Pakistan, an industry body representing seed and crop-protection companies, said approval of the pending GM corn biosafety licences would mark a milestone for agricultural biotechnology. CropLife Pakistan Executive Director Rasheed Ahmed said such a move could accelerate the adoption of advanced seed technologies, which he said would improve farm productivity, food security and the competitiveness of the sector.
GM corn has been cultivated commercially for more than two decades and is widely grown in major agricultural economies and across the Asia-Pacific region.
The committee's deliberations come against a separate constraint on the sector. Louis Dreyfus Company (LDC) Country Head and Head of Grains and Oilseeds Muhammad Daniyal told The Express Tribune last month that Pakistan produces excellent non-GMO corn, which commands a higher price globally, but that inadequate systems for drying, storing and transporting the crop mean Pakistani corn is often not purchased in international markets at all. Where a buyer is willing, he said, agreements are struck at prices 10% to 15% below prevailing market rates. Daniyal said the issue was directly linked to the absence of basic infrastructure, and that aligning harvesting, drying, storage and marketing with required standards could earn the country millions of dollars.

title: Growth to remain moderate at 4 2
description: Growth to remain moderate at 4 2
content:
World Bank says Pakistan's growth rate not enough to create jobs for 3.6m people
The World Bank projected on Thursday a moderate 4.2% economic growth for Pakistan in the year before general elections in 2029 but urged the government to implement a plan to stay on course of macroeconomic stability in the election year.
In its Pakistan Development Outlook, the Washington-based lender said rupee-dollar parity was not "freely" responding to market conditions and a fully flexible exchange rate would better serve Pakistan's interests. The report discussed in depth Pakistan's current exchange rate policy, implying that such stability led to three macroeconomic crises in the recent past and adjustment was needed to arrest appreciation of the real effective exchange rate.
The report projected 4.2% economic growth in fiscal year 2027-28, which would be the second last year of the government, and 4.4% during the election year. It underlined that Pakistan's current-to-medium-term growth rate was not enough to create jobs for 3.6 million people entering the market every year.
"With the current International Monetary Fund programme ending in September 2027 and national elections scheduled for early 2029, developing, publishing and effectively implementing a medium-term fiscal plan that preserves macroeconomic stability is critical to maintaining confidence," said the World Bank.
The lender emphasised the need for preserving macroeconomic stability due to past episodes of loosening fiscal purse during the election year. For the current fiscal year, the World Bank projected 3.8% growth, slightly lower than the government target of 4%.
"The growth rate in the medium term does not seem going beyond 4.5%, which is too low to create enough jobs," said Sebastian Essl, Lead Author of the report. The report underlined growth-enabling reforms that were urgently required to reverse recent increases in poverty from 22% in 2019 to 29% in 2025 and create sufficient jobs for 3.6 million Pakistanis reaching working age every year.
The World Bank said that under a baseline scenario with continued sound macroeconomic management and limited structural reform progress, growth was projected to remain broadly stable at 3.8% this fiscal year. Elevated commodity and energy prices were expected to weigh on services and industry, it added. "The macroeconomic outlook assumes that Pakistan's economy will continue to be affected by the conflict in the Middle East through end-2026, with a gradual de-escalation over the course of 2027," said the lender.
"Pakistan has made real progress in restoring stability and markets have taken notice," said Bolormaa Amgaabazar, World Bank Country Director for Pakistan. But real per capita growth – the rate at which the income of an average Pakistani increases – remains stuck at around 1.6% and reforms to drive faster growth are now urgently needed, according to Bolormaa.
The report showed that a more prolonged and intense conflict in the Middle East remained the most significant risk to Pakistan's near-term macroeconomic outlook. A longer or deeper conflict would sustain elevated energy prices and increase Pakistan's import bill while weighing on export demand and disrupting trade routes.
These effects could widen the current account deficit and add pressure to reserves. Intensified domestic demand-management measures to contain energy shortages could deepen the drag on domestic activity, while sustained higher input costs would renew pressure on inflation and household purchasing power.
The report found that such growth was possible if Pakistan followed the path taken by other successful countries in pursuing ambitious economic reforms. Reforms that upgrade policies and institutions to the quality seen in the average middle-income country could drive sustained growth of up to 6.2-6.9% per annum, sufficient for Pakistan to reach Vietnam's current level of income by 2050.
The World Bank commented extensively on Pakistan's exchange rate policy, suggesting that it had issues with the current policy. "The central bank exchange rate intervention creates temporary stability but leads to disruptive adjustments, deterring investment and undermining confidence," it stated.
"Stability in the face of these shocks suggests that the exchange rate is not responding freely to market conditions. A fully flexible, market-determined exchange rate would better serve Pakistan's economic development needs: it would buffer external shocks, support private sector confidence and prevent a gradual erosion of competitiveness."
The World Bank said that the rupee remained stable against the dollar, but the real exchange rate appreciated due to higher inflation, weighing on competitiveness. The average exchange rate in FY26 was Rs280.4 per dollar, compared to Rs279.4 the previous year. With higher inflation, deteriorating terms of trade and exchange rate stability, the real effective exchange rate (REER) appreciated 10% between end-June 2025 and July 2026, it added.
The World Bank said that over the past two fiscal years, its standard deviation was below Rs2, about 0.6% of its longer-term average. This stability was held through a series of terms-of-trade shocks from FY25, including lower rice export prices and sharp increases in import prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It said that cross-country evidence demonstrated that exchange rate rigidity had increased macroeconomic risks. Among 50 emerging markets over 1980-2011, less flexible regimes were associated with greater vulnerabilities and more frequent crises. Rigid regimes also absorb shocks less well: in developing countries, negative terms-of-trade shocks cause larger output losses under fixed regimes than under flexible ones.
The World Bank said that the current account deficit was projected to widen in the current fiscal year as recovering demand kept import growth faster than exports, but remittances would remain a key offset. It said that external financing needs were estimated to average around 5% of GDP over the near term, reflecting continued reliance on external debt rollovers and remittance-financed current account deficits. Tighter global financial conditions could raise borrowing costs and reduce capital flows to emerging markets, complicating the rollover of financing at a critical juncture.

title: Adviser calls for private control of energy sector
description: Adviser calls for private control of energy sector
content:
TRUST framework targets agriculture, textiles and IT, with energy, taxation and SOEs named reform priorities
The government should transfer energy-sector management and decision-making to the private sector to promote competition, improve efficiency, attract investment and reduce costs, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Privatisation Muhammad Ali said, identifying energy, taxation and state-owned enterprises (SOEs) as the three areas most in need of reform.
Addressing the CEO Summit Islamabad 2026, organised by CEO Club Pakistan, he said high power costs undermined the competitiveness of domestic industries and stressed the need for affordable, reliable and sustainable energy supplies.
He presented a framework called TRUST, focused on targeting sectors where Pakistan has competitive strengths, implementing sustainable reforms, unlocking private capital, scaling up exports and developing talent. Sectoral priorities should be determined through five considerations: proven strength, the ability to deliver with existing institutions and infrastructure, global demand, employment generation at scale and foreign-exchange earnings. Applying these criteria, he identified agriculture, textiles and information technology (IT) and digital services as offering opportunities for employment creation, higher economic output and export growth.
Pakistan's agricultural sector, he said, needed a new wave of development focused on improving crop yields, storage facilities, processing and value-added exports, building on the gains of the Green Revolution of the 1960s. In textiles and apparel, the country needed to move beyond yarn and fabric production towards finished garments, brands and technical fabrics to increase value addition and competitiveness in international markets. Pakistani youth were already serving international clients through freelance work, and better organisation of the sector and stronger digital skills could help capture growing global demand.
On taxation, he emphasised documenting the economy to broaden the tax base and distribute the burden more fairly, saying too few taxpayers were carrying a disproportionate share.
He said Pakistan had faced severe economic challenges during 2022 and 2023, including fiscal constraints, low productivity, production curtailments, high inflation and elevated interest rates. "We cannot go through that sort of test again," he said. "So we need to do something to avoid it in the future."
Citing international examples, he said China had built on its agricultural strengths after launching reforms in 1978, South Korea had developed textiles and plywood in the 1960s, Vietnam had transformed from a rice importer into a major exporter, and Bangladesh had developed its garment industry by capitalising on existing strengths.
"These countries did not try to do everything at once," he said. "They started from what they could already do well and built upon it." Sustained effort and policy continuity had enabled long-term progress. Federal Minister for Board of Investment Qaiser Ahmed Sheikh told the summit that investment was essential for generating employment, introducing modern technologies, enhancing productivity, expanding industrial capacity and increasing exports, and that Pakistan needed both domestic and foreign investment to build a more resilient and competitive economy.
He identified IT, agriculture and agro-processing, mining and minerals, energy, manufacturing, infrastructure and tourism as sectors offering substantial investment opportunities, and said the Board of Investment was committed to facilitating investors, removing unnecessary hurdles and improving coordination among government departments. Investors required policy consistency, clear regulations, timely decisions and a predictable business environment for long-term commitments, he said.
Referring to China's three decades of double-digit growth, the minister said Pakistan could draw lessons on promoting investment, expanding productive capacity and maintaining a long-term focus on economic transformation. He said the private sector was a central partner in the country's economic transformation and that regular engagement between policymakers and business was essential for effective policy.
Sheikh said Pakistan's strengths included a young population, a large domestic market, natural resources and a strategic location, and that realising them required encouraging entrepreneurship, promoting innovation and strengthening competitiveness. Overseas Pakistanis, he said, could contribute beyond remittances through direct investment, business partnerships, technology transfer and access to international markets.
Muhammad Ali also thanked CEO Club Pakistan President and Founder Ijaz Nisar for convening the summit, saying such forums allowed meaningful discussion of economic challenges and growth prospects. WITH ADDITIONAL INPUT FROM APP

title: Banks urged to remove SME credit hurdles
description: Banks urged to remove SME credit hurdles
content:
PM aide underlines need for 100% increase in financing for small businesses
Adviser to Prime Minister for Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar Khan has called on banks and the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) to give due consideration to the financing challenges faced by SME clusters and take effective measures to address them as limited access to credit remains a major constraint on growth of many viable businesses.
The adviser held a consultative session with representatives of small and medium enterprises (SMEs), business clusters, banks, the State Bank and relevant government departments to address the challenges faced by businesses in accessing affordable and timely financing.
The representatives of various SME clusters highlighted the funding constraints and procedural hurdles affecting their businesses, including difficulties in obtaining credit and gaining access to suitable financing facilities to expand operations, meet working capital requirements and capitalise on emerging opportunities.
Khan stated that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had directed that financing for SMEs be doubled, underscoring the government's commitment to expanding access to credit and strengthening the role of SMEs in the national economy.
He stressed that banks must make concerted efforts to simplify lending procedures, improve coordination with business clusters and facilitate eligible enterprises in getting required funds. "The benefits of financial support must reach businesses at the grassroots level and translate into tangible improvements in production, investment and employment."
The adviser highlighted that SMEs were a vital pillar of Pakistan's economy, contributing significantly to the GDP, exports and non-agricultural employment. He observed that limited access to credit was a major constraint on the growth potential of many businesses.
Khan mentioned that the objective of consultations was to bridge the gap between financial institutions and businesses by identifying practical obstacles and developing workable solutions. He called for stronger coordination among banks, the State Bank, government departments and SME representatives to ensure that financing facilities meet the actual needs of business clusters.

Total stands at $26.8b; gold falls as global prices hit 2-month low
The foreign exchange reserves held by the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) increased by $19 million to $21.49 billion during the week ended October 16, 2026, according to data released by the central bank on Thursday.
The country's total liquid foreign exchange reserves amounted to $26.83 billion during the week under review, including $5.34 billion held by commercial banks. Meanwhile, the Pakistani rupee gained Rs0.01 against the US dollar to close at 276.85, compared with Wednesday's close at 276.86.
Gold prices in the domestic market fell sharply, tracking a decline in the international market, where the precious metal dropped to its lowest level in more than two months as rising oil prices heightened inflation concerns and reinforced expectations of higher rates for longer.
In the local market, the price of gold declined by Rs3,000 per tola to Rs431,536, according to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association. Similarly, the price of 10-gram gold fell by Rs2,572 to Rs369,972. On Wednesday, gold had shed Rs900 per tola.

title: IMF sees weak external position
description: IMF sees weak external position
content:
Estimates financing needs at 22-25% of GDP, CAD at $4.5b against official $2.5b
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Thursday that Pakistan's external financial position may weaken due to rising imports and moderating remittances, urging exchange rate flexibility to preserve foreign exchange reserves and tighter monetary policy to deal with rising inflation.
The global lender made these observations in its Middle East and Central Asia region report, released on Thursday, a week after the World Bank-IMF annual meetings.
"Over the medium term, external positions should strengthen in Egypt, Jordan and Morocco, supported by lower commodity prices and export diversification, but weaken in Pakistan as imports rise and remittances moderate," according to the IMF.
The fund's remarks came days after it reached a staff-level agreement for disbursement of the $1 billion fifth loan tranche, subject to the government fulfilling prior actions.
The government has projected imports reaching $70 billion this fiscal year and remittances growing to $45.5 billion. The country is struggling to enhance exports, which have not grown despite years of incentives to handpicked exporters.
The IMF has projected Pakistan's current account deficit at 1% of gross domestic product (GDP), or around $4.5 billion, which is also far higher than official estimates of around $2.5 billion. The lender sees Pakistan's gross financing needs at around 22% to 25% of GDP, well above peer countries and carrying risks.
The report points to a very deep nexus between the government and commercial banks, estimating banks' 63% exposure to public debt, also well above typical emerging market levels.
Concerns about rising government debt could lead to higher borrowing costs than in the baseline, heightening fiscal sustainability concerns in countries with large gross financing needs, such as Egypt and Pakistan, the IMF said.
"Exchange rate flexibility can help preserve reserves and facilitate external adjustment (Egypt, Pakistan) but may also increase inflationary pressures through higher import prices," the lender said.
The government remains sensitive to any advice to allow the rupee to depreciate, citing inflationary impacts and no real positive impact on exports. The rupee appreciated by one paisa to Rs276.85 to the dollar on Thursday.
Inflationary pressures have risen most sharply in Egypt, to 14.5%, and in Pakistan to 11.1% year on year in August, reflecting higher food and energy-related prices and, in Egypt, also exchange rate depreciation, the IMF said.
The IMF has projected inflation to rise to 9.9% in Pakistan, 1.5% higher than its previous forecast.
"Countries should stand ready to tighten monetary policy, particularly where inflation is already above target and the policy stance appears accommodative, with ex-ante policy rates below estimated neutral levels, a combination most evident in the Kyrgyz Republic and Pakistan."
The IMF's report comes days before the Monetary Policy Committee meeting, which may review the possibility of raising interest rates from the current level of 11.5%.
During recent review talks, the central bank had termed the monetary policy appropriately tight.
Policy-rate responses since the start of the conflict have differed across exchange-rate regimes, and among countries with flexible exchange rates, Pakistan was the only one to raise interest rates after the conflict began, it added.
Financial supervisors should continue to monitor bank liquidity and funding conditions, asset quality in the sectors most exposed to the conflict – tourism, transport and trade-related activities – and sovereign-bank linkages where public debt is elevated and banks hold large stocks of government securities, such as in Egypt, Pakistan and Tunisia, the lender advised.
The IMF has kept its economic growth forecast for Pakistan unchanged at 3.5%, lower than the official target of 4% and also less than the World Bank's projection.
During the review talks, Pakistani authorities had tried to convince the IMF that the annual growth target of 4% would be achieved.
Countries insulated from the conflict, such as Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia and Pakistan, have recorded stable or even higher hotel occupancy rates in 2026 compared with last year, the IMF said.
On the fiscal front, fiscal policy stances are expected to turn accommodative in 2026 in many regional economies, with consolidation resuming from 2027. The stance in 2026 is projected to be restrictive in countries with limited fiscal space such as Bahrain, Iraq and Pakistan, but also in Qatar and Saudi Arabia, it added.

title: Ambassador Sheikh calls for shift from    counterterrorism to IT    in Pakistan US ties
description: Urges stronger tech ties to deepen economic cooperation between two countries
content:
Urges stronger tech ties to deepen economic cooperation between two countries
Pakistan’s ambassador to the United States, Rizwan Saeed Sheikh, has called for a shift in bilateral engagement from counterterrorism to information technology, describing tech cooperation as a promising avenue for strengthening economic ties between the two countries.
Addressing the Pakistan-US Tech Connect 2026 forum in Washington, Ambassador Sheikh said technological collaboration could open new avenues for mutually beneficial partnerships between Islamabad and Washington.
In his remarks, Sheikh said the forum sought to present leading Pakistani technology companies to stakeholders in Washington and demonstrate their ability to meet international standards in emerging fields, including artificial intelligence.
The Embassy of Pakistan in Washington, D.C., hosted the third event of the ongoing Pakistan–U.S. Tech Connect 2026 series, bringing together leading Pakistani technology companies and U.S. industry leaders to explore partnerships in artificial intelligence, cloud computing,… pic.twitter.com/hbJR2kRw3t
Emphasising the longstanding relationship between Pakistan and the United States, he said cooperation between the two countries had produced results beyond their bilateral relationship.
“Each time Pakistan and the United States have come together, we have produced results, and results not only for ourselves in the bilateral domain, but results for the whole world,” he said.
Sheikh called for a shift in bilateral priorities from traditional security concerns to technological cooperation, saying closer ties in information technology could pave the way for a mutually beneficial partnership.
Read : Ambassador Sheikh calls for stronger Pakistan-US tech collaboration
“A key goal is to make a transition in the bilateral relationship from ‘CT to IT’, moving from counterterrorism to information technology,” he said, adding that this would yield a mutually rewarding partnership in the future.
Describing the current period as the “Pakistan moment”, the ambassador said the country’s potential was particularly evident in the digital domain.
The ambassador also highlighted Pakistan’s role in regional and global stability.
“Over the past 16, 17 months, we have seen the best of Pakistan's defense and diplomacy. We have emerged as a factor of stability as well as a stabilizing agent, a stabilizing force, a stabilizing nation,” he noted.
Sindh Governor Syed Nehal Hashmi, who attended the forum, said US enterprises were looking for reliable partners capable of delivering long-term value.
He urged Pakistani technology companies to translate their digital capabilities into concrete business opportunities, pilot projects and high-value contracts.
PSEB Chief Executive Officer Faisal Jeddy, Ignite CEO Bilal Abbasi and OPEN Global DC Chapter President Hassan Khalid also highlighted the expansion of Pakistan’s technology sector.
They said Pakistan had substantial technical talent, while the US market offered opportunities for companies seeking to expand their businesses and develop scalable solutions.
Discussions at the forum focused on the need for Pakistani technology firms to move beyond routine IT services and labour arbitrage towards developing proprietary intellectual property and scalable products.
Also Read : Ambassador Sheikh urges Pakistani-Americans to drive 'mutually rewarding' economic engagement
The shift, participants noted, could help position Pakistani companies as higher-value partners in the global technology industry.
Concluding the event, Sheikh reiterated that Pakistan had arrived on the global technology stage and praised the participating companies as representatives of the country’s capabilities.
Inviting international partners to “come and profit from the promise of Pakistan”, he said competitive costs could attract businesses initially, while the performance of Pakistani technology professionals could help sustain long-term partnerships.
He urged participants to use the platform to help redefine and promote Pakistan’s image internationally.
The event was organised by the Embassy of Pakistan in collaboration with the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication, OPEN Global and the Pakistan Software Export Board (PSEB) to facilitate direct engagement between Pakistani technology firms and their American counterparts.
The forum brought together representatives of 16 Pakistani technology companies working in areas such as artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data analytics, financial technology and healthcare technology. Representatives of US technology and financial firms, multilateral institutions, government agencies and the Pakistani-American business community also attended the event.
The initiative aimed to develop commercial partnerships in enterprise solutions, digital transformation, product development and strategic IT collaboration through executive discussions and business-to-business meetings.

title: Alien  and  Picket Fences  star Tom Skerritt dies at 93
description: Tom Skerritt  known for  Alien   and  Picket Fences   has died at 93  leaving behind a celebrated screen legacy
content:
Tom Skerritt, known for 'Alien', and 'Picket Fences', has died at 93, leaving behind a celebrated screen legacy
Tom Skerritt, the veteran actor known for his roles in Alien , Top Gun and the television series Picket Fences , has died aged 93. His death was confirmed by his publicist to Variety . He died of natural causes on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.
Skerritt earned widespread recognition for playing Sheriff Jimmy Brock in the CBS drama Picket Fences , which ran from 1992 to 1996. His performance earned him a Primetime Emmy Award in 1993, along with another nomination the following year. He also received Screen Actors Guild Award nominations for his work on the series.
The actor appeared in several acclaimed films throughout his career, including Robert Altman’s MASH (1970), in which he played surgeon Duke Forrest. In Ridley Scott’s science fiction horror film Alien (1979), Skerritt portrayed Captain Dallas aboard the spaceship Nostromo, appearing alongside Sigourney Weaver.
He later played Commander Mike “Viper” Metcalf in the 1986 action film Top Gun , starring Tom Cruise. Other notable credits included A River Runs Through It , The Turning Point , Steel Magnolias , The Dead Zone , Contact and Ted .
Skerritt also built an extensive television career, appearing in shows such as The West Wing , Law & Order: SVU , Brothers & Sisters , The Good Wife and Madam Secretary .
Born Thomas Roy Skerritt in Detroit, Michigan, the actor attended Wayne State University and the University of California, Los Angeles. He also served in the US Air Force before beginning his acting career. His feature film debut came in the 1962 Korean War drama War Hunt .
Skerritt is survived by his wife, Julie Tokashiki, whom he married in 1998, and his four children: Andy, Matt, Erin and Colin.
His decades-long career spanned film and television, establishing him as a familiar presence across several generations of audiences.

title: Boiling Europe and the far right narrative
description: Boiling Europe and the far right narrative
content:
France's government points to the scale of the violence - with more than 150 officers injured
The images from last Saturday tell a story that France's political class would rather not read. City halls in flames in Limoges; anarchist graffiti scrawled across the mayor's office in Marseille. Luxury boutiques looted, banks smashed, police vans battered with clubs and bricks. Half a million people took to the streets, and while the vast majority marched peacefully, a violent fringe turned the day into one of the worst eruptions of disorder France has seen in decades.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called it the work of the "ultra-left" and criminals, and President Macron promised to prosecute and punish "the sowers of chaos".
On the same Saturday, Brussels saw young people clash with police over education costs. Lisbon filled with thousands protesting a housing market where prices have doubled since 2017. Milan's cathedral square was cleared with tear gas; Bologna's police used water cannons. In Albania, students demanded the prime minister's resignation. The common thread runs from the Mediterranean to the North Sea: a generation and a working class that have concluded the institutions of liberal democracy are not delivering.
France's government points to the scale of the violence - with more than 150 officers injured - as proof that its response is justified, resulting in 1,200 arrests. A teenager lost his hand after picking up a stun grenade; the police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of excessive force. The UNSA police union warned that officers are being treated as "punching bags" and that "the rope is stretched to its maximum". When both the protesters and the police feel abandoned by the state, the state has a credibility problem, not a security problem.
The timing is toxic. Macron, in the final stretch of his presidency, is facing a fragmented political landscape and economic mess. The Yellow Vests, whose numbers Saturday's protests surpassed, were a warning shot. The presidential election is months away, and the prime minister has already accused the demonstrators of using violence as a "warm-up".
There is a temptation in European capitals to treat this as a policing problem: more arrests, tougher tactics, a firmer line. The rage on display is not an argument against French democracy; it is an argument that the prosperity of the past be made available in the present.
Into this vacuum steps a right-wing political class with a narrative already prepared. Across Europe, leaders of populist parties have spent the past two years constructing a framework that requires no specific riot to activate it; it is produced continuously in everyday politics, waiting for events to confirm it.
In France, Marine Le Pen, the founder of National Rally, has regularly talked about Islamic communitarianism, insisting that secularism is "non-negotiable". Her party President Jordan Bardella, during a speech in Israel, condemned antisemitism and anti-Zionism. He also emphasised the key messages of his party: combating Islamism and restricting immigration to France. He stated that "Since Oct. 7 in particular, in France and in Europe, we have been witnessing the deadly honeymoon between Islamism and the extreme left. One provides the fanatics, the other institutionalizes evil, provides the excuse of victimization and the appearance of a good conscience."
In Germany, Alice Weidel of the AfD has claimed that Jews in her country are "exposed to Muslim criminality", citing Palestinian demonstrations in Berlin and asserting that "Jews can no longer walk on the streets"; forget about Gaza genocide.
In Britain, Nigel Farage described a Muslim demonstration in Tower Hamlets as "like a foreign invading army marching through our streets", warning that "the deluded left" has been "in league with very strange bedfellows". In the Netherlands, Geert Wilders's PVV manifesto opens: "This is your country! The Netherlands is full, overflowing, packed to the brim."
The Budapest conservative conference held in June 2025 and chaired by ex-PM Victor Orbán, brought together controversial figures including Dutch politician Geert Wilders, Slovak PM Robert Fico and German AfD leader Alice Weidel. Orbán declared: "What is happening in Europe is not migration, but an organized population replacement aimed at changing the cultural foundation of Europe."
The narrative logic is consistent across all five countries. First, frame "Islamism and the left" as an alliance, Bardella's "honeymoon", Farage's "strange bedfellows". Second, Orban's linking immigration to "population replacement" and electoral engineering, Wilders stating that the Netherlands is "packed to the brim". Third, use "no-go zones" and "streets where Jews cannot walk" as concrete evidence that the state has lost control. Fourth, present oneself as the only protector, Bardella claims the National Rally is "the best shield for French Jews"; Wilders presents himself as the only one daring to "say it as it is".
This framework does not require the French riots as a trigger. But once such events occur, it can be activated instantly: the violence becomes evidence of "Islamist totalitarianism" and "left connivance", legitimising the far-right's agenda without any need for evidence.
What this narrative omits is the diagnosis. The protesters in Paris were not marching for Islamism or against secularism; they were demanding teachers, facilities and affordable fuel. The unrest in Brussels was about education costs; in Lisbon, housing; in Milan, the cost of living. These are class grievances, not civilisational ones.
Earlier, Eric Kaufmann's book, Whiteshift , often invoked in these debates, actually argues the opposite of what the right's narrative implies. Kaufmann contends that Western societies can avoid conflict by allowing whites to adapt to demographic change through assimilation and the broadening of racial boundaries. His preferred pathway is "join", not "fight". He calls for a "multi-vocal nationalism" that legitimises both ethnic identities and cosmopolitan visions.
The right's narrative has a hole at its centre; it can describe the fire, but it cannot explain the drought; it can name the arsonists, but it cannot address the conditions that made the ground dry. Until someone in power does, Europe should expect more Saturdays like this one and the right should expect its narrative to keep working, because it never has to solve anything.

title: The critical minerals war
description: The critical minerals war
content:
All this trade war has negatively affected Western and US industries
The China-US Trade War began in the Trump's first term. Since then, weaponisation of critical minerals and rare earth elements has been a central economic battlefield. China used export restrictions and technology bans to leverage its dominant supply chain position, while the US focused on stockpiling, domestic production incentives and restrictions on Chinese components.
In 2023, China banned the export of rare earth mining, separation, refining and magnet-making technologies to all foreign countries, explicitly targeting Japan, Australia and Vietnam, so they are unable to use Chinese intellectual property to build alternative supply chains for the US. Late 2023, US manufacturers moved manufacturing to Mexico, Vietnam and Malaysia. But China introduced strict end-user certificates for raw graphite, gallium and germanium, defeating USA's 'friendshoring' plan. In 2024, China used its Dual-Use Export Control Regulations to warn tech suppliers in South Korea and Japan that re-exporting components containing Chinese-origin gallium, germanium or antimony to US defence contractors would trigger retaliatory blacklisting. Late 2025, China implemented Extraterritorial Jurisdiction, asserting that any company in a third country, like Germany, Japan or South Korea, exporting components to the US that contain 0.1% or more of key Chinese heavy rare earths like dysprosium or terbium required direct export licences from Beijing.
In return, between 2019 and 2023, US DoD partnered with Australia to process heavy rare earths domestically and in Texas, explicitly cutting out Chinese refining loops. Next, the US restricted tax credits for electric vehicles that sourced battery minerals, lithium, cobalt and graphite from China. Since 2022, the US has pressured Indonesia to restrict Chinese ownership shares in nickel refineries and asked them to impose strict forced labour bans and transparency rules on China. In Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, the US has aggressively bid against Chinese state-owned enterprises for critical mineral concessions in cobalt and copper. In 2024, the US signed bilateral critical mineral agreements with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan for Western mining investments, offering security guarantees and capital to counter Chinese market dominance in titanium, tungsten and rare earths.
In the case of Indonesia, to protect proprietary chemical configurations and decades of catalyst tech from leaking to Western supply chains, leading Chinese firms took the drastic step of completely dismantling multi-billion-dollar production lines in Indonesia and shipping the machinery back to China. This forced a sharp contraction in global battery-grade nickel supply, flipping a massive market surplus into a calculated shortage. Agreements with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are also in limbo, as China is the single largest trading partner for all five Central Asian states. Beijing routinely pairs infrastructure investments with security guarantees to ensure that Central Asian states remain tightly bound to Chinese processing networks. Getting bulk minerals out of Central Asia to Western markets without crossing Russian or Chinese aligned territory or infrastructure is also a bottleneck.
The most difficult part of processing rare earths is separating virtually identical elements from one another using complex, multi-stage liquid-liquid solvent extraction. China has spent decades perfecting these chemical recipes at an industrial scale. The US, Europe, Japan and Australia do produce world class extraction and mining equipment; however, China holds a near-monopoly on specific metallurgical refining technologies and specialised chemical separation intellectual property - particularly for heavy rare earths.
All this trade war has negatively affected Western and US industries. The US cannot produce precision weapons, munitions, jet engines, airframes, sensors and night-visions without them. Wind turbines, solar panels, EVs and battery manufacturing are facing a standstill. Shortages in semiconductors, chips and circuit components has effectively turned a booming AI industry into a bubble. This is a war between the Global North and the Global South, a war between the G7 and BRICS. And China is winning it without firing a bullet.
When Pakistan talks with the US about a potential $1 trillion to $6 trillion worth of minerals, how does that sit within the context of the bigger picture? Antimony, neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium are used in the defence industry, high-strength permanent magnets and EV motors; cobalt and graphite in lithium-ion batteries; titanium and tungsten in defence manufacturing; and copper concentrate in power grids, data centres, EVs and AI hardware – all of which are present in K-P and Balochistan. So, which side of the decoupling equation do they sit on?
Pakistan is deeply entrenched in China's security architecture. Pakistan's success over India in Operation Sindoor last year and its growing strategic role in the region based on the strength it gains from its alliance with China only mean that Pakistan is increasingly becoming an integral part of the Global South, not the Global North. Pakistan's membership request in BRICS, and CPEC being a flagship projects of China's BRI, mean that the country is part of the Global South, not the Global North. Being on this side of the equation is not just a matter of luxury for Pakistan but a question of its survival in the violent global environment of today.
It is understandable for China to be happy about the US gaining a major inroad into rare earths and critical minerals on allied soil. Minerals worth $6 trillion have the potential to shift the balance for China, which has dominated the supply chain until now.
One wonders why China might not deploy asymmetric, highly targeted pressure points to slow down, render unviable, or structurally block the flow of Pakistani minerals to the US, and why it would not demand enhanced protection for Chinese-led projects in Balochistan and K-P making it operationally and financially burdensome for Pakistan to secure parallel US mining ventures in the same regions. It is logical for Beijing to seek explicit guarantees from Islamabad that US geological survey teams and mining entities operate far away from sensitive assets under construction, dual-use ports, and strategic CPEC transit corridors. It may even leverage debt restructuring timelines or future CPEC Phase-II investments to exert diplomatic pressure on Islamabad.
Pakistan would need to rethink this rebalance, which virtually means making the country a new battleground for the two global powers. Or perhaps our strategists know that it's all talk and no walk!

title: Give FBR more than a new name
description: Pakistan increasingly confuses tax policy with revenue collection
content:
Pakistan increasingly confuses tax policy with revenue collection
The federal government is again considering whether Pakistan needs a new tax collection agency. According to a report in The Express Tribune of Oct 16, 2026, the FBR has been asked to present proposals for human-resource reform, revamping and restructuring to the PM by October 19, 2026, while the creation of an altogether new organisation is also under discussion. The urgency is understandable: against this year's Rs15.263 trillion target, officials, as per the report, already fear a shortfall exceeding Rs650 billion.
The danger is equally familiar. Pakistan may abolish FBR in name and recreate it in substance. The late Dr Pervez Tahir saw the problem clearly. In 2019, first in "FBR: the end is nigh" [The Express Tribune, March 15, 2019] and later in his memorable "Giving FBR a decent burial" [The Express Tribune, November 8, 2019], he argued that repeated restructuring had failed.
Dr Pervez (called 'PT' affectionately by his friends) explained that the organisation itself embodied what he called "Revenuecracy": a system geared towards extracting readily collectible revenue rather than building an equitable tax system. He proposed one professional tax-collection agency for federal, provincial and local taxes, separated from tax-policy formulation, institutionally autonomous and placed within a federal framework involving the provinces.
This scribe has been arguing along similar lines for decades. The idea of a federal National Tax Agency or Pakistan Revenue Authority - replacing the fragmented collection through the FBR and multiple provincial bodies - has been repeatedly proposed in books and articles. The objective is one taxpayer interface, one return where practicable, integrated databases, harmonised administration and professionally managed collection removing multiple costs, while elected governments and legislatures determine tax policy. That distinction is crucial.
Pakistan increasingly confuses tax policy with revenue collection. A rational policy asks who should pay, according to ability, and what tax structure best promotes investment, employment and fairness. Revenuecracy asks from whom money can be collected fastest.
The salaried class, incorporated businesses, importers, exporters, bank depositors, electricity consumers and telecom users are easy to reach. Politically influential and undertaxed sectors remain harder to confront. Mere changing FBR's letterhead will not cure this. Nor will throwing more borrowed money at "transformation" (sic).
Another $200 million foreign-funded programme was approved only last month, purportedly taking external financing for tax-system modernisation over the years to nearly $5 billion. Meanwhile, FBR's tax-to-GDP ratio remains around 10.3%, the previous annual target was missed by more than Rs1.1 trillion, and the latest traders' scheme has produced derisory results.
Technology is necessary. Faceless assessment, digital invoicing, production monitoring and intelligent risk selection can reduce discretion. They cannot substitute for institutional design.
A genuinely new agency should satisfy at least four tests. Tax policy must be separated from tax collection and placed under a representative, professionally staffed policy institution accountable to Parliament, not an administrative unit in the Ministry of Finance, as is the case today.
Collection should progressively become a single-window operation covering federal and provincial taxes through constitutional agreement. The new body must recruit and promote professionals on competence rather than reproduce existing service hierarchies. It must be judged not simply by gross collection, but by voluntary compliance, refund performance, quality of assessments, cost of collection and reduction in litigation.
Existing officers should be free to compete for positions on merit. The old cadres should not automatically migrate en bloc into the new institution, otherwise institutional culture will migrate with them.
Dr Pervez called for giving FBR a decent burial seven years ago. The government now appears closer than ever to accepting his diagnosis. It should also heed his warning. Pakistan does not need FBR-II. It needs a new relationship between taxpayer and State. Renaming Revenuecracy would merely postpone the funeral.

title: Smog warning
description: Punjab has announced a series of preventive measures  including inspections of smoke emitting vehicles
content:
Punjab has announced a series of preventive measures, including inspections of smoke-emitting vehicles
A spell of rain may temporarily clear Lahore's skies, but it cannot wash away the fact that smog has become an annual public health crisis. Within days of last week's brief respite, air quality deteriorated once again, with official readings reaching highly unhealthy levels this past Wednesday. As winter approaches, the city faces the prospect of another punishing smog season, raising serious questions about whether the authorities are sufficiently prepared to protect millions of residents.
Years of exposure to hazardous air should have made prevention a permanent government priority rather than an emergency exercise undertaken when pollution reaches intolerable levels. Punjab has announced a series of preventive measures, including inspections of smoke-emitting vehicles. These initiatives are necessary, but their effectiveness must be judged by improvements in air quality. Seasonal crackdowns have repeatedly failed to produce lasting relief because the underlying sources of pollution remain largely unchecked. Of particular concern is the danger to children. Unicef has warned that polluted environments increase children's susceptibility to acute respiratory infections and can impair lung development. In November 2024, the agency estimated that more than 11 million children under five were exposed to severe smog across Punjab's worst-affected districts. Such warnings demand preparations that extend beyond advising families to remain indoors.
Much also depends on the government's ability to anticipate dangerous pollution episodes. At the same time, authorities must ensure strict compliance with industrial emission standards and improve public transport and provide farmers with practical alternatives to crop burning. Lahore cannot continue surrendering several months of every year to poisonous air. Clean air is not a seasonal privilege to be restored by favourable weather. It is a basic public health necessity.

title: Judge  jury and executioner
description: Such encounters violate Pakistani law  international guidelines  which permissible only when necessary  proportionate
content:
Such encounters violate Pakistani law, international guidelines, which permissible only when necessary, proportionate
The entire country appears doubtful of the police claims regarding the circumstances under which the suspect in the killing of a teenager in Multan was himself killed. Tauqir Nazir, a contractor, allegedly killed teenager Waseem Abbas over a work dispute earlier this week by running him over in a car. Nazir was arrested, produced before a magistrate and remanded into police custody. Within hours, police claimed Nazir had tried to flee custody and was killed in a shootout near Bahawalpur. Police claim that his accomplices killed him, though supporting evidence is currently limited. Similarly, the alleged fraudster who drove student Laiba Ijaz to suicide was also killed by his accomplices during an escape attempt.
While it is true that both killings could have gone down exactly as described by the police, it would not surprise anyone to learn that certain details were curiously inaccurate. The HRCP has already demanded an independent inquiry, warning that extrajudicial killings violate due process and deprive victims' families of the truth. But while the higher-profile cases always seem to get authorities' attention, rights groups have noticed and are demanding a transparent inquiry. After all, the last nine months of 2025 generated dozens of problematic fights. An HRCP fact-finding report documented at least 670 CCD-led encounters in Punjab between April and December 2025, leaving 924 suspects dead. Only two police officers were killed in the same period. That casualty imbalance - more than two fatal encounters a day - cannot be explained by professionalism. It points to an institutionalised practice of staged killings. The Punjab government has rejected allegations of staged encounters, but denial is not evidence.
The official script is also suspiciously uniform: suspects always fire first, police always respond in self-defence, and the dead are always "hardened criminals". Civilian witnesses are absent, magisterial inquiries are skipped, and families are intimidated into silence. Such encounters violate Pakistani law and international guidelines, which is permissible only when necessary and proportionate.

World Bank's 2026 report noted that Pakistan recorded a GDP growth of 3.7%
The IMF has painted a dismal picture of the regional economy, forecasting a 1.3% contraction in 2026 as a result of the war in the Middle East. Pakistan, which is in the eye of the storm due to severe supply chain disruptions and soaring oil prices, is likely to see a sharp decline in production. The Fund's latest outlook is a point of concern that demands immediate corrective measures. The global lender, however, predicts a rebound of up to 6.6% growth in 2027, a projection that remains contingent upon the trajectory of energy supplies. The region has already suffered a slump in energy production alongside a severe slowdown in tourism and investment. Furthermore, the IMF warns that external financial conditions could tighten globally if investors reassess AI-driven productivity gains while interest rates rise.
Pakistan, however, has walked a tightrope as far as its commitments to the IMF programme are concerned, earning a pat on the back for clinching macroeconomic stability. Reflecting this progress, the World Bank's 2026 report noted that Pakistan recorded a GDP growth of 3.7%. This turnaround has subsequently driven an improvement in the country's credit rating, backed by the fact that total liquid foreign exchange reserves have surged past $21 billion. Similarly, global lenders have exhibited renewed confidence in the economy; when bonds worth $750 million were floated, the market response was a definitive success. Last but not least, the central bank has been astute in managing the policy rate as average headline inflation is officially estimated at 7.1%, while the state has successfully engineered a substantial financial cushion.
The country, nonetheless, faces an arduous road ahead as unemployment, political instability and external shocks cast a long shadow over a fragile economy. Likewise, climate degradation, a drawdown in agrarian production and thinning exports are daunting challenges that can only be overcome through strategic structural reforms. A surgical overhaul of the taxation machinery is inevitable to stay afloat.

title: Pakistan s hunger crisis
description: Pakistan s hunger crisis
content:
Reducing hunger is possible if required political will exists to prioritize food security
Pakistan's food insecurity crisis is a stark warning about the consequences of extreme weather, economic hardship and inadequate protection for vulnerable households. Although climate change is intensifying these pressures, persistent hunger cannot be explained by weather alone. Poverty, inflation, displacement, insecurity and weaknesses in agricultural and food-distribution systems all shape who can afford food and who goes hungry.
The latest analysis by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), an international initiative that monitors food insecurity, covered 45 vulnerable rural districts across Balochistan, Sindh and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, with a combined population of approximately 35.6 million. Drawing on household survey findings and other data, the IPC estimated that 7.5 million people in these areas faced acute food insecurity between December 2025 and March 2026, including approximately 1.25 million experiencing emergency conditions. The assessment identified the lingering effects of the 2025 monsoon floods, prolonged drought and dry spells, and localised insecurity as key contributing factors.
Food insecurity is particularly concerning in areas already affected by insecurity and political grievances. In parts of Balochistan and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, the IPC identifies localised conflict alongside climate-related shocks as a factor undermining livelihoods and access to food. Although hunger does not automatically lead to unrest, the combination of economic deprivation, disrupted livelihoods and insecurity can exacerbate existing grievances and deepen communities' distrust of the state.
Pakistan's experience also demonstrates the devastating effects of climate-related disasters. The devastating 2010 and 2025 floods caused massive damage and economic losses, undermining livelihoods and disrupting food supplies. The unprecedent scale of these losses highlighted how extreme weather can threaten not only immediate food availability but also the longer-term ability of families to earn an income and recover from shocks. Pakistan is now experiencing the effects of El Niño, with significantly below-average monsoon rainfall across much of Sindh and southern Punjab. Combined with irrigational water shortages, these conditions are expected to reduce crop production and agricultural incomes, further worsening food insecurity among poorer rural households
Yet, climate disasters need not inevitably produce hunger. Their effects depend on public preparedness, social protection and households' ability to recover. Pakistan's persistent nutritional challenges underscore the importance of addressing structural deprivation. The World Food Programme estimates that 40% of Pakistani children under five experience stunting, reflecting chronic undernutrition and public-health problems that extend beyond immediate food emergencies.
Reducing hunger is possible if the required political will exists to prioritise food security. Brazil's previous socialist government, for example, drastically reduced hunger through a combination of cash transfers, expanded school meals and public food-purchasing programmes which supported smallholder farmers, while strengthening local food supplies. Such policies contributed to Brazil's exit from the FAO's Hunger Map in 2025.
Pakistan itself needs to set aside subsidies and price incentives that encourage water-intensive cultivation of crops such as rice and sugar. It needs to support smaller farmers to diversify into crops better suited to local conditions. Our policymakers also need to pay more attention to providing better social protection and food assistance, which can reach marginalised communities more effectively, particularly in remote and conflict-affected districts.
Without stronger political commitment, more equitable social protection, effective institutions and resilient agricultural systems, extreme weather and economic hardship will continue to push Pakistan's most vulnerable households into hunger.

title: DSP among 4 CTD  police personnel martyred in Karak attack
description: Two suspected terrorists killed in Karak encounter  two civilians injured in Bannu motorcycle bomb blast
content:
Two suspected terrorists killed in Karak encounter; two civilians injured in Bannu motorcycle bomb blast
Four police personnel, including a deputy superintendent of police (DSP) of the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD), were martyred on Thursday in an exchange of fire with armed men in the Khurram Muhammad Zai area of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa's Karak district.
According to police, a search and strike operation was launched within the limits of Latamber police station following a tip-off. An exchange of fire ensued between police and unidentified armed men, resulting in the martyrdom of CTD DSP Imranuddin, Station House Officer Afzal Awan and two constables, Amjad and Kazim.
Reports also suggested that two suspected terrorists were killed in the encounter, though further details were awaited.
Read : 12 killed, 35 injured as TTP strikes anti-smuggling checkpoint in K-P's DI Khan
A heavy contingent of police was dispatched to the scene, while reports indicated that an intense exchange of fire was continuing in the area.
Later, the funeral prayers for the police personnel were held with full state honours, which were attended by senior civil and military officials, police officers, family members of the martyrs and people from various walks of life.
A police contingent presented a salute to the martyrs, while senior officials laid floral wreaths on their coffins to pay tribute to their sacrifices. Participants also offered prayers for the martyrs and their bereaved families.
The provincial police chief paid tribute to the courage, sense of duty and professional commitment of the personnel, saying the brave members of the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Police had confronted terrorists valiantly and laid down their lives without backing away from their duties.
He said their courage, unwavering dedication to duty and sacrifices for the protection of the public would serve as a guiding light for the entire police force.
Following the funeral prayers, the bodies of the martyrs were taken to their respective native villages.
Separately, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi paid tribute to the four police personnel, commending their bravery in confronting terrorists in Karak.
Also Read : Three commanders among eight terrorists killed in DI Khan operation: security sources
While expressing his heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families, he said the sacrifices of the martyred personnel would always be remembered.
The minister said K-P Police officers and personnel had made immense sacrifices in the fight against terrorism, adding that the nation remained indebted to the martyrs for their unparalleled sacrifices.
He said the debt owed to the martyrs would be repaid by eliminating terrorism from the country.
Two civilians injured in Bannu motorcycle bomb blast
In a separate incident in Bannu, terrorists opened fire on a police party during routine patrolling within the jurisdiction of Merian police station.
Police retaliated, after which a remote-controlled bomb planted in a motorcycle parked along the roadside exploded, injuring two civilians.
The police party remained unharmed, while the injured were shifted to the District Headquarters Hospital for treatment.
Police have launched an investigation into the incident.

title: Brian Selznick   s  Run Away With Me  to become a feature film with Gianni Nunnari
description: Brian Selznick   s queer YA romance  Run Away With Me  is getting a film adaptation  with Gianni Nunnari set to produce
content:
Brian Selznick’s queer YA romance 'Run Away With Me' is getting a film adaptation, with Gianni Nunnari set to produce
Brian Selznick’s young adult novel Run Away With Me is being adapted into a feature film, with Hollywood producer Gianni Nunnari attached to produce the project through his company, Hollywood Gang Productions.
Selznick, the award-winning author and illustrator known for The Invention of Hugo Cabret , will write the screenplay based on his 2025 novel. Deborah Belford de Furia will serve as an executive producer, alongside James Canellos and Michael Ritter.
Published by Scholastic, Run Away With Me is Selznick’s first novel written specifically for young adult readers. Set in Rome during the 1980s, the queer coming-of-age romance follows Danny, a 16-year-old American spending the summer in Italy, who meets Angelo, a mysterious Italian boy.
Their encounter develops into an intense first love as they explore Rome together. The story also weaves in queer love stories from the 17th century, 19th century and 1940s, examining relationships that have been hidden or erased from historical records. The novel combines prose with more than 100 pages of Selznick’s illustrations.
Nunnari, who was born in Rome, has produced films including 300 and Immortals and served as an executive producer on The Departed and Se7en . He is expected to draw on his Hollywood and European industry connections to develop the film, with plans to shoot on location in Rome.
“I’m thrilled my book is being brought to life by such an extraordinary team,” Selznick said, adding that the filmmakers were eager to tell a story highlighting the importance of love.
Nunnari described the project as personal, citing his connection to Rome and the experience of falling in love. He called the film a universal story of love set in the Italian capital.
Selznick’s other works include Wonderstruck , which was adapted into a film directed by Todd Haynes, and The Marvels . His novel The Invention of Hugo Cabret inspired Martin Scorsese’s film Hugo , which received five Academy Awards.
Further casting and release details for the Run Away With Me film adaptation have not yet been announced.

title: Govt cuts petrol by Rs1 60  increases diesel by 1 64 paisas for Oct 23
description: Petrol price decreases to Rs377 71 per litre  while HSD will cost Rs391 75
content:
Petrol price decreases to Rs377.71 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs391.75
The federal government on Thursday decreased the price of petrol by Rs1.60 per litre while increasing the price of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs1.64 per litre for October 23.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs377.71 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs391.75 per litre for Friday.
The latest revision comes a day after the government decreased the price of petrol by Rs2.71 per litre while increasing the price of diesel by 31 paisas per litre, for October 22.
Read : Oil jumps on escalating Middle East conflict
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
On September 13, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.
Also Read : Govt mulls $2b LNG import decision
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.
Oil prices climbed about ​3% to a five-month high on Thursday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy ‌supplies from the key exporting region.
Brent futures rose $3.51, or 3.2%, to $112.33 a barrel at 1:05 p.m. EDT (1705 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude rose $2.14, or 2.2%, to $99.29.
"Reports ​of Middle East crude oil exports exceeding pre-conflict levels are more than countered by attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and the ​Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and on its oil infrastructure," PVM Oil analyst Tamas Varga said.
Morgan Stanley analysts estimated that Middle East crude oil exports were around 17 million barrels per day last week. Crude exports from the region averaged about 18 million bpd in the 12 months before the start of the Iran ​war, according to Kpler.

Allison Holker shares how she and her children honour late husband Stephen ‘tWitch’ Boss through family memories
Allison Holker has shared how she and her three children keep the memory of her late husband, Stephen ‘tWitch’ Boss, alive through family traditions, meaningful keepsakes and conversations about their time together.
Speaking exclusively to PEOPLE at the Dancers Against Cancer’s Industry Dance Awards in Los Angeles on October 21, the professional dancer, 38, explained how the family remembers Boss, who died aged 40 in December 2022.
Holker said they honour him through everyday activities, including eating his favourite foods and sharing memories. She also described how she helps their son, Maddox, 10, feel connected to his father by giving him Boss’ gold chain to wear when he feels discouraged.
The necklace has become particularly meaningful during family photographs, when Holker makes sure Maddox wears it so his father remains symbolically part of the moment. She added that her daughters, Weslie, 18, and Zaia, 5, also wear their father’s clothes as a way of feeling close to him.
Holker and Boss met in 2010 while appearing on So You Think You Can Dance and married in 2013. Boss adopted Weslie, Holker’s daughter from a previous relationship, and the couple later welcomed Maddox and Zaia.
In a May 2023 interview with PEOPLE, Holker discussed how the family supported one another following Boss’ death. She said her children had also become a source of strength for her during the difficult period.
Holker has continued to honour her husband publicly on significant dates, including the anniversary of his death and his birthday. In a September 2025 Instagram tribute marking what would have been his 43rd birthday, she recalled celebrating with some of his favourite activities, including Korean barbecue, visiting a comic book store and eating cookies and cream.
Through these traditions, Holker continues to celebrate Boss’ life and preserve his memory for their children.

Operation against terrorists in nearby hotel underway; Naqvi lauds forces for foiling attack
Security forces have killed three terrorists belonging to Fitna al-Hindustan while foiling an attempt to attack an unoccupied camp of a construction company in Balochistan's Gwadar, state-owned Radio Pakistan reported on Thursday, citing security sources.
According to the report, security forces acted promptly to thwart the attack on the vacant camp.
The sources said security forces had also surrounded three more terrorists.
Read : Armed men abduct 20 trainee police personnel travelling from Kalat to Nushki: officials
In a separate attempted attack, an operation was under way against terrorists hiding in a local hotel near the Gwadar Highway, the report said.
Citing security sources, Radio Pakistan reported that four terrorists had been surrounded by the forces.
The Gwadar general officer commanding was personally leading the operation on the ground, the report added.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi praised security forces for foiling the attempted attack and lauded the forces’ professional capabilities for killing three terrorists during the operation
“We are proud of the brave sons of the soil who are fighting against terrorists,” Naqvi said, expressing pride in the personnel engaged in counterterrorism efforts.
He said the entire nation stood united against terrorism and supported the security forces.
Naqvi added that operations would continue until terrorists and their facilitators were completely eliminated.
Also Read : Two terrorists killed in Balochistan IBO: state media
Terrorism is a growing problem for Pakistan, with the number of attacks rising every year since 2022, according to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a global monitoring organisation. Data from ACLED shows attacks in Pakistan rose nearly fourfold to 2,425 in 2025 from 658 in 2022, and over the same period, TTP attacks increased more than sevenfold to 838 from 118.
Although K-P has borne the brunt of terrorism, Balochistan has also remained a major target of Indian proxies, which often target civilians and military installations in the province.
Over the past few years, Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist attacks, with militants frequently targeting convoys, abducting security personnel and civilians, and attacking security and civilian installations.
In a similar incident last week, 20 trainee police personnel were abducted by unidentified armed men while travelling between Kalat and Mastung in Balochistan.
The abducted personnel belonged to the districts of Kharan, Nushki, Chagai and Washuk in Rakhshan Division. They included eight personnel from Kharan, five from Nushki, four from Chagai and three from Washuk.
The forces continued operations across the provinces against what the state describes as Indian-sponsored terrorists and their proxies. Still, despite these efforts, the groups have continued to target civilian and defence installations.
In one such attack in July this year, at least 30 people, including 27 police personnel, were martyred when terrorists identified by the state as the Indian proxy Fitna al-Hindustan ambushed police personnel deployed in the Kach Mangi Phase III area of Ziarat, triggering hours-long gun battles. The attackers also abducted several civilians and police personnel after the assault.
In the aftermath of the attack, the Pakistan Army, Frontier Corps and Balochistan Police launched a joint operation , which remains underway, with forces intensifying action against terrorists across the province.

description: Middle of Nowhere Vol  2  Tex Mex Tapes  will be released through Lost Highway Records on January 15  2027
content:
'Middle of Nowhere Vol. 2: Tex Mex Tapes' will be released through Lost Highway Records on January 15, 2027
Kacey Musgraves is extending the era of her latest album with a new companion project, Middle of Nowhere Vol. 2: Tex Mex Tapes , scheduled for release on January 15, 2027.
The Grammy-winning country singer announced the 16-track album on Thursday, October 22. The release will feature 11 original songs and five covers, expanding on the country, Tex-Mex and regional Mexican influences explored on her sixth studio album, Middle of Nowhere , released in May.
Musgraves will give fans an early taste of the project with two tracks, “Weekend in Texas” and “Mi Tesoro”, arriving on Friday, October 23. The latter is her interpretation of the norteño classic, while the new collection also includes a Spanish-language version of “Uncertain, TX”, featuring Mexican music group Intocable.
The album’s tracklist includes “Pretty Horses”, “Hard Conversations”, “Denim on Denim”, “Figure Out My Life”, “Caballero”, “The Vacation Song”, “(Hey Baby) Qué Pasó?”, “Rodeo”, “Desert Eyes” and “Pity Party”. It also features a live version of “Tú Solo Tú”, recorded with Mariachi Oro de América, alongside “All My Exes (Kacey’s Version)” and a cover of “Before the Next Teardrop Falls”.
The companion album builds on the musical direction of Middle of Nowhere , which drew inspiration from Musgraves’ Texas upbringing and incorporated traditional country sounds alongside influences from Norteño, Zydeco and bluegrass. The original record featured collaborations with Willie Nelson, Miranda Lambert, Billy Strings and Gregory Alan Isakov.
Musgraves previously explained that the album’s title came from a sign in her hometown of Golden, Texas, describing the area as “Somewhere in the Middle of Nowhere”. The phrase became a starting point for a project exploring solitude, personal growth and the idea of finding a sense of home beyond a physical location.
The singer has continued to revisit the album’s Mexican musical influences since its release. Earlier in October, she released a Spanish-language version of “Uncertain, TX” with Intocable, reworking the original track through a collaboration rooted in the cultural sounds of Texas.
With Tex Mex Tapes , Musgraves is expanding that exploration through new material, reinterpretations and live recordings. The release arrives as she wraps up her Middle of Nowhere Tour , with two final performances scheduled in Seattle on October 26 and 27.
Middle of Nowhere Vol. 2: Tex Mex Tapes will be released through Lost Highway Records on January 15, 2027.
