title: One nation  one foreclosure
description: One nation  one foreclosure
content:
For decades, parliamentary representation remained frozen to reward southern states for controlling their populations
A pluralistic Indian state based on Ganga-Jamuni syncretic culture was always a transitory bargain, a holding pattern until the underlying reality asserted itself. Ambedkar's Constitution was as alien to the casteist realities of India as he was to the religion of his birth. It was merely a face-saving arrangement for a Westernised elite to prepare the world for India's eventual descent into prejudiced madness. Fundamentally, this secular republic was a loan underwritten by the real owners of the land: the businessmen whose panic over Liaquat Ali Khan's 1947 tax-heavy budget helped dictate the borders of partition. The so-called Brahmin-Bania alliance, if you will. Today, that debt is being collected with interest.
What is this underlying reality? In his foundational 1966 text, "Bunch of Thoughts", the second supremo of the RSS, MS Golwalkar, laid out the blueprint. The goal, he wrote, was clear: "The most important and effective step will be to bury deep for good all talk of a federal structure of our country's Constitution, to sweep away the existence of all 'autonomous' or semi-autonomous 'states' within the one State viz., Bharat and proclaim 'One Country, One State, One Legislature, One Executive'." A long journey which begins with One Nation, One Election.
But to what end? On 30 November 1949, just four days after the Constituent Assembly adopted the document, the RSS mouthpiece Organiser openly lamented that it ignored the caste-based hierarchies of ancient India: "To this day his (Manu's) laws as enunciated in the Manusmriti excite the admiration of the world and elicit spontaneous obedience and conformity. But to our constitutional pundits that means nothing."
See how the Manusmriti excites this admiration: Chapter 8, Verse 417: "A Brahmana may confidently seize the goods of Sudra (the lowest varna, mostly today's OBCs); for, as that (slave) can have no property, his master may take his possessions." Chapter 10, Verse 129: "No collection of wealth must be made by a Sudra, even though he be able (to do it); for a Sudra who has acquired wealth, gives pain to Brahmanas." Chapter 10, Verse 51: "But the dwellings of the Kandalas and Svapakas (Dalits) shall be outside the village; they must be made Apapatras (permanently dispossessed), and their wealth (shall be) dogs and donkeys." Chapter 10, Verse 52: "Their dress (shall be) the garments of the dead, (they shall eat) their food from broken dishes, black iron (shall be) their ornaments, and they must always wander from place to place." This attitude towards property rights will become abundantly clear shortly.
You may argue India's complexity makes such regression impossible. For evidence, look at the current regime. The incumbent recently had his cabinet declare him the longest-serving prime minister in history, a fiction achieved by erasing Jawaharlal Nehru's first five years from the records. Despite tanking the economy and carrying the shadow of the Gujarat massacres, his grip remains absolute. He rules with unyielding centralisation, reducing even the mighty RSS to a subservient echo chamber.
Institutional independence is now purely decorative. The state machinery is captured. Unsurprisingly, the ruling establishment is the world's richest political party, bankrolled by a handful of billionaires. The system is entirely compromised to ensure these tycoons face no federal hurdles.
The final stumbling block is the South. The Dravidian states, with their entrenched pluralism and secularism, represent everything the new order must destroy. To neutralise them, the establishment deployed two Trojan horses: "One Nation, One Election" and a looming delimitation exercise. Both are designed to permanently disenfranchise the southern opposition and reduce autonomous states to modern-day apapatras.
When a compromised election commission holds simultaneous elections, it produces magical results. But the case of delimitation is even more surgical.
For decades, parliamentary representation remained frozen to reward southern states for controlling their populations. To break this freeze, the establishment deployed a brilliant Trojan horse: the Women's Reservation Bill. By inserting Article 334A into the 106th Amendment, the government hardwired the 33 per cent gender quota to take effect only after a post-2026 delimitation exercise. Oppose the redrawing of the electoral map to save federalism, and you are anti-women.
Once that trap springs, the mathematics of an expanded 848-seat Lok Sabha is ruthlessly stark. Uttar Pradesh is projected to gain up to 63 new seats and Bihar 39. Two states alone will capture over 100 new seats, permanently anchoring national power in the cow belt, which is keener on Modi than others. Conversely, the Dravidian states, rewarded for their governance success, will see their parliamentary share slashed from 24 per cent to about 20 per cent. This political erasure cements an economic one. Tamil Nadu receives roughly 29 paise back for every rupee it sends to the Centre, whereas Uttar Pradesh receives nearly 3 rupees back.
Once the South's voice is made irrelevant and the establishment captures a two-thirds majority in both houses of Parliament, the constitutional fiction can be discarded, and a Hindu Rashtra formally proclaimed. In practical terms, this means the country's overwhelming majority will lose their constitutional protections and, eventually, their property rights. This targets lower castes like Shudras or OBCs at roughly 60 per cent of the population, Dalits and Scheduled Castes at 16.6 per cent, and Adivasis and Scheduled Tribes at 8.6 per cent. The ongoing protests by marginalised communities against massive land acquisitions by regime-aligned billionaires like Adani are proof of the concept. They are the blueprint in action. Foreclosure at last.
I am often asked how this domestic restructuring is relevant to Pakistan or the broader region. The Hindu Rashtra project is intrinsically linked to the geographical fantasy of Akhand Bharat. Once the new state successfully renegotiates India's internal social contract, it plans to export this model to the neighbourhood. This expansion will not rely on conventional military invasions. Instead, the blueprint involves dismantling a target country's political and social order from within, engineering a collapse so complete that dismemberment and absorption into India appear as voluntary choices. Here too, property matters more than people.
Through state-promoted cinema like the Dhurandhar duology, the establishment is already making the exceptional claim that its operatives are permanently embedded within the power structures of neighbouring states. Even if entirely fictional, this broadcasts their ultimate ambition.

title: Let Pathans learn to say no to exceptionalism
description: Let Pathans learn to say no to exceptionalism
content:
Human beings possess agency but agency is never exercised in a vacuum
For generations, the Pathans have been handed two compliments that should perhaps have made us suspicious long ago: "Pathans are very brave" and "Pathans are very devout Muslims." As a Pathan and a practising Muslim, I increasingly wonder whether we should politely return both compliments. Not because Pathans lack courage. Not because Islam matters any less to us. But because courage is not encoded in Pakhtun blood nor does any ethnicity hold a monopoly over religious devotion. Brave people and sincere believers exist in every society.
The more interesting question is therefore not whether these descriptions are true. It is: why has it been so important to keep telling Pathans that they are exceptionally brave and exceptionally religious? History provides uncomfortable clues. The stereotype of the Pakhtun as an inherently martial people did not begin with the Afghan jihad. Colonial representations routinely portrayed frontier Pathans as warriors, violent tribesmen and members of a "martial race". Academic research suggests that such ideas outlived colonialism and continued influencing state perceptions of the tribal areas.
Then came Afghanistan. By 1979, rebellion was already under way against Afghanistan's communist government. Declassified American records show Pakistan supporting Afghan insurgents before the Soviet invasion of December that year; subsequently, the US, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan built an enormous covert pipeline of money and weapons for the Afghan resistance, much of it operating through Pakistan. Resistance to foreign occupation was real, and Afghans possessed their own reasons and agency for fighting.
But geopolitics requires mobilisation, and mobilisation works best when it speaks the language people already associate with themselves. For Pathans, two buttons were particularly easy to press. You are brave; therefore, you do not retreat. You do not fear death. You are a true Muslim; therefore, when war is presented as jihad, questioning it can begin to feel like questioning one's faith. During General Zia-ul-Haq's rule, state Islamisation and the Afghan jihad became deeply intertwined.
Human beings possess agency but agency is never exercised in a vacuum. If, from childhood, a man is repeatedly told that courage defines his ethnic worth, refusing to fight carries a psychological price. If faith is added to the equation, refusal may appear simultaneously cowardly, culturally dishonourable and religiously suspect. The person may still choose. But somebody has already helped construct the menu from which he chooses. And eventually the narrative becomes self-fulfilling. This is how the Pathans have been conditioned and which has caused much of their suffering.
Afghanistan became one of the great displacement tragedies of modern history. UNHCR records that the refugee population in Pakistan and Iran reached around six million during the 1980s. War mutated into civil war, Taliban rule, international intervention, insurgency and renewed Taliban rule. On the Pakistani side, the vocabulary changed from jihad to militancy, extremism, counterterrorism and military operations. The geography changed much less. Swat, Waziristan, Bajaur and other Pakhtun areas repeatedly became theatres of conflict.
After nearly half a century, perhaps Pathans should ask a brutally simple question: What have these flattering titles of bravery and faithfulness done for us? Where is it written that our children must inherit extraordinary courage rather than ordinary childhoods? Why must the Pakhtun continuously prove that he is fearless? Why must his religious sincerity be certified through political causes chosen by others? Perhaps the most revolutionary demand Pathans can now make is surprisingly modest: the right to be ordinary.
The right to send children to school rather than to ideological battlefields. The right to admire a scientist as much, if not more, as a warrior. The right to build businesses, labs, universities and tech companies. The right to question a cleric without surrendering Islam. The right to refuse someone else's war without surrendering honour. And the right to live without constantly demonstrating that we are braver or more religious than everyone else. In a nutshell, they should be allowed to say no to "exceptionalism".

title: Horrors of the internet
description: Horrors of the internet
content:
Pakistan's legal framework contains gaps that allow perpetrators to act with impunity
The digital world has opened many doors for children all over the world to learn, connect, and imagine futures beyond their immediate surroundings. But in the wrong hands, the same technologies that empower them can be weaponised to harm them. In just one year, an estimated 1.5 million internet-using children in Pakistan between the ages of 12 and 17 experienced at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse. These are crisis-level numbers, and they are not being caused in some dark street corner or seedy hotel, but in the victims' own homes.
The Disrupting Harm in Pakistan report, a study of the issue backed by UNICEF and several other international organisations, features a brutal assessment of the situation. In most cases, the perpetrator was someone the child knew. Perhaps even worse is the fact that in almost two out of three cases, the child told no one. They stayed silent because they felt embarrassed or simply didn't know who to turn to. When an abused child is silenced by society, the entire society has collectively failed at one of its most basic duties.
The report underscores what many child protection experts have long warned: Pakistan's legal framework contains gaps that allow perpetrators to act with impunity, and survivors face daunting barriers to disclosure, reporting and justice. The National Commission on the Rights of the Child has previously called for legislative reforms that criminalise all forms of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse, and for child-centered, trauma-informed reporting and justice mechanisms. These are very realistic, common-sense suggestions.
But laws alone are meaningless. We need to break down the culture of silence and replace it with one where children can confidently talk to their parents and teachers about online safety without being shamed. We need schools that teach digital literacy alongside algebra. We need platforms that prioritise child safety over profit. And we need a justice system that treats every child's testimony with urgency and dignity.

title: A hotter monsoon
description: A hotter monsoon
content:
Higher temperatures accelerate the loss of moisture from soil
Pakistan's changing climate is steadily eroding the predictability of seasons on which millions depend for their livelihoods. PMD's finding that the country experienced its hottest monsoon in 66 years, with an average temperature of 30.7°C, is another indication of this unsettling shift. More concerning is the fact that the record heat coincided with widespread rainfall deficits, including a staggering 51% shortfall in Sindh.
The monsoon has traditionally provided much-needed relief from the summer heat while replenishing water supplies essential for agriculture. Its growing unpredictability now threatens both functions. Higher temperatures accelerate the loss of moisture from soil and increase the demand for irrigation at precisely the time when reduced rainfall limits available water. The burden falls particularly heavily on small farmers, whose livelihoods depend on seasonal patterns that are becoming increasingly unreliable. In Sindh, where agricultural communities already contend with unequal water distribution and inadequate irrigation infrastructure, a deficient monsoon can deepen existing hardships. Yet Pakistan's response to climatic extremes continues to be dictated largely by the immediate threat of flooding. Water shortages receive comparatively less attention until reservoirs begin to decline and farmers face difficulties sustaining their crops. There is an urgent need to reconsider how the country manages its limited water resources. Greater attention must be paid to reducing losses in the irrigation system and ensuring that agricultural planning reflects changing rainfall patterns. Provincial governments, particularly Sindh's, must also address the vulnerabilities of communities that have little capacity to withstand successive seasons of climatic stress. Such measures require sustained investment and administrative commitment.
Climate change is no longer a distant environmental concern whose effects can be addressed at some convenient point in the future. It is already altering the conditions under which Pakistan produces food and sustains its population. The greater failure would be to continue planning for a climate that no longer exists.

title: At the lenders  table
description: At the lenders  table
content:
Pakistan has been at the vanguard of advocating reforms to global organisations
Pakistan, a perpetual recipient of assistance from the Washington-based lending institutions – the IMF and World Bank – has earned the unique honour of being named as the incoming chair of the Boards of Governors of the Fund and the World Bank Group for next year. It is the first time since 1953 that the developing country has secured this august seat. Pakistan has entered into 25 IMF programmes, and has also been a major recipient of assistance from ABD and other lending agencies. Ahad Khan Cheema, who is also Pakistan's governor to the World Bank, will shortly assume the position in Bangkok. It is a distinction, indeed, as Pakistan was chosen from among more than 15,000 participants across 191 countries.
Pakistan has been at the vanguard of advocating reforms to global organisations. At the United Nations, it has consistently advocated for abolishing the veto power, and opposed the expansion of the Security Council's permanent membership. Currently, it is serving a two-year term as an elected non-permanent member of the UN Security Council and holds the final presidency of the UN Conference on Disarmament for 2026. Islamabad, likewise, assumed the chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for the 20262027 and is also heading the Governing Council of the Borrowers' Platform for the 20262027 work plan. These credentials illustrate the country's positive role, amongside its efforts to mediate between Iran and the United States. The landmark Islamabad MoU, which the UN Secretary-General termed as the 'framework for permanent peace,' is a case in point.
With a leadership role at IMF and the World Bank, Pakistan will be better positioned to contribute to global economic and development discussions. Its intention has always been to facilitate constructive dialogue among member countries, strengthen South-South cooperation, and work against poverty and discrimination. As an ardent supporter of multilateralism, Pakistan believes in a just economic order in which the dominance of an elite group is reduced to give developing countries a greater say. This is essential to building stronger institutions and mobilising private capital to support sustainable and inclusive growth.

title: Who pays when Pakistanis flee South Africa
description: Who pays when Pakistanis flee South Africa
content:
Xenophobia has been building in South Africa for years
Geerard Adriaen South Africa may feel far away from Pakistan. Yet, it is not. Around 200,000 Pakistanis live in the country, most of them working in small businesses. For many people in Pakistan, South Africa is not simply a country where a relative happens to live. It is where fathers, brothers and sons have built businesses and earn the money on which families back in Pakistan depend. In fiscal year 2026, Pakistan received $290.7 million in workers' remittances from South Africa, far from an insignificant amount. That is why what has been happening there should concern Islamabad.
Xenophobia has been building in South Africa for years, aimed at African and Asian migrants who are blamed for the country's high unemployment, rising crime and strain on public services. The hatred has periodically boiled over into mobs targeting migrant-owned businesses and businesses that employ them. This year it reached a new pitch. In May, the anti-immigrant groups March and March and Operation Dudula demanded that all "illegal foreigners" leave the country by 30 June. Fayyaz Khan, who heads the Pakistan-South Africa Association, deemed it impossible to repatriate all Pakistani nationals by that date. Only roughly 25,000 African and Asian migrants, illegal and legal alike, fled abroad within weeks of the ultimatum.
When the deadline passed, some 120 anti-migrant protests erupted on 30 June, several turning violent. Migrants were driven from homes and shops; premises were looted, some burned. Both undocumented and documented migrants were targeted, including Pakistanis. Protests have continued until today and more than 178,000 African migrants have fled the country. No official figure exists for how many Pakistanis have left.
Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, the leader of March and March, has named Pakistanis and Somalis specifically, claiming they have become "first rank citizens" while South Africans are reduced to "second rank citizens" in their own country. She has also accused them of hiring "protection-fee mafias" to kill South African protesters – a claim which fact-checkers in South Africa have flagged as unsupported. What should worry Islamabad most is that Pakistanis aren't just swept up in generalised anti-foreigner rhetoric – it's one of the handful of nationalities Ngobese-Zuma focusses on.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has condemned the violence, apologised to its victims and called for perpetrators to face justice. Those words are welcome. But governments are not judged only by their statements; they are judged by whether the people under their jurisdiction are actually protected. On that measure, South Africa continues to fail.
Nigeria has already drawn the obvious conclusion. After more than 600 of its citizens fled, Abuja began compiling claims for abandoned businesses and property, intending to use them as the basis for compensation talks with Pretoria. South Africa's foreign ministry initially suggested claims would be assessed case by case. Then Minister Khumbudzo Ntshavheni outright rejected the idea of compensating Nigerians. It escalated into a genuine diplomatic row.
Nigeria has not yet secured any compensation, but it has asked the right question: who pays when people are forced to abandon their livelihoods abroad, because the host country failed to protect them? Ghana has since followed in Nigeria's footsteps. After evacuating over a thousand of its own citizens, Accra too pledged to pursue compensation for what they left behind.
Islamabad should follow Abuja and Accra. That means, first, giving Pakistanis who lost property or businesses a formal channel to register their losses – through the High Commission in Pretoria, if nowhere else. It means, second, demanding that South Africa establish a real mechanism to investigate these losses and compensate for them.
Pakistan has other, larger crises competing for its foreign ministry's attention. But $290 million in annual remittances and 200,000 citizens whose livelihoods are now openly named as a target is not a footnote. It is a constituency, and it is owed an answer.

title: Meghan Markle   s reported clash with designer Roland Mouret revealed in new memoir
description: Meghan Markle reportedly confronted Roland Mouret over mishap involving Kate Middleton   s stylist  his memoir claims
content:
Meghan Markle reportedly confronted Roland Mouret over mishap involving Kate Middleton’s stylist, his memoir claims
Meghan Markle reportedly told fashion designer Roland Mouret that he had embarrassed her after a mistake involving Kate Middleton’s stylist, according to the designer’s new memoir.
In I Am Roland Mouret: The Butcher’s Boy Who Dressed the World , the French designer reflects on his friendship with the Duchess of Sussex and recalls an incident that allegedly strained their relationship.
According to an excerpt published by The Times on October 16, Mouret first met Meghan in 2015 at the opening of Soho House in Istanbul. They remained in contact, and he offered to send her a selection of outfits after she began dating Prince Harry in 2016.
Mouret writes that he instructed his team to deliver the clothes to the palace, asking them to keep the arrangement private and avoid following up. However, a member of his team later contacted Kate Middleton’s stylist at Kensington Palace to arrange the return of Meghan’s dresses.
The designer says Meghan subsequently called him, expressing her anger over the situation.
“You don’t realize what you’ve done! You’ve embarrassed me!” she allegedly told him, according to the memoir.
Mouret says he apologised and explained that the contact had been an innocent mistake. However, he claims Meghan responded that she could never wear his designs again.
The designer later recalled reaching out to Meghan after seeing her wearing what he described as a high-street copy of one of his creations. According to Mouret, she responded positively to his message and suggested meeting again.
Despite the reported disagreement, Meghan has continued to wear Mouret’s designs. Earlier in 2026, she appeared in promotional photographs for her As ever lifestyle brand wearing a navy dress by the designer.
Kate has also worn creations from Mouret’s fashion label, including at Wimbledon.
PEOPLE reported that it had contacted Meghan’s representatives for comment. The alleged exchange and its circumstances have not been independently confirmed.

title: Morocco forms new government under first ever female prime minister
description: New cabinet comprises 32 members as King Mohammed VI receives government at Royal Palace
content:
New cabinet comprises 32 members as King Mohammed VI receives government at Royal Palace
Morocco announced a new cabinet on Friday, ushering in a historic era with the country’s first female prime minister leading a four-party coalition.
According to state-run Maghreb Arabe Presse , King Mohammed VI received members of the new cabinet, led by Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, and presided over their appointment ceremony at the Royal Palace in the capital, Rabat.
Fatima is the first Moroccan woman to hold the country’s top government post.
Read : Morocco's king appoints first woman prime minister following election
She will lead a new government formed by a four-party coalition comprising her Authenticity and Modernity Party, the Istiqlal Party, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces and the Party of Progress and Socialism.
The new government includes seven women, including Fatima, compared with six in the previous government led by Aziz Akhannouch.
The new government comprises 32 members, including ministers and ministers-delegate, according to official figures.
Abdelouafi Laftit kept his post as interior minister, alongside Nasser Bourita as foreign minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi as justice minister and Ahmed Toufiq as minister of Islamic affairs and endowments.
The new cabinet also established a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence, Digital Transformation and Administrative Reform, headed by Ahmed Rahhou.
On Monday, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, Istiqlal Party, Socialist Union of Popular Forces and Party of Progress and Socialism announced in a joint statement that they had formed the governing majority following the conclusion of the second round of consultations on forming a government, which began on September 30.
On September 29, King Mohammed VI tasked Fatima with forming a government after her party, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, came first in the September 23 elections with 97 seats.

title: China s Tencent says AI agents showed unintended browsing behaviour
description: Shows Chinese AI agents can also misrepresent their identity  conceal failures and try to circumvent testing controls
content:
Shows Chinese AI agents can also misrepresent their identity, conceal failures and try to circumvent testing controls
Tencent said on ​Friday that AI agents used to evaluate third-party models displayed web-browsing behaviour not intended ‌by the tech giant, in what appears to be the first known incident of rogue agent actions acknowledged by a major Chinese company.
The statement followed a report by AI-safety research group Swarmchasers on Wednesday, which said "rogue" agents running on ​infrastructure it linked to Tencent Cloud made repeated attempts between September 28 and October 8 ​to retrieve information from Alibaba's Amap, China's equivalent to Google Maps.
Tencent Hunyuan, the ⁠company's artificial intelligence unit, said in a post on X that the activity did not originate ​from its Hunyuan models. Its review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination, it said.
The Swarmchasers ​researchers said the agents sought information such as the commonly used entrances at Chinese parks, museums and zoos.
The actions are not as egregious as those disclosed by US AI companies, which include the hack of open-source platform Hugging Face by ​an OpenAI agent and the lodging of a fake homicide tip by an Anthropic agent.
Read : OpenAI's rogue agents probed Hugging Face for weaknesses two months before major hack
But the disclosure underscores research ​that shows Chinese AI agents can also misrepresent their identity, conceal failures and try to circumvent testing controls.
Tencent said ‌it ⁠took the findings very seriously and was strengthening network access controls and agent monitoring.
Hunyuan is one of China's leading AI model developers, competing with in-house teams at rivals such as Alibaba and ByteDance. ByteDance this week announced the creation of a new unit focused on AI model and agent safety.
Swarmchasers said it used ​the word "rogue" to describe agents ​taking actions outside ⁠their intended scope or completing a task in unintended ways.
Read More : As AI agents act in unexpected ways, is ‘rogue AI’ really here?
After routine automated requests were blocked, the agents tried other methods, including public web tools that could ​open pages and run code, routing requests through other websites and using ​Amap keys ⁠and security codes found in publicly available software code.
Swarmchasers said it found no evidence that the agents breached Amap's main anti-bot safeguards. Most of the 2,818 attempts it recorded either failed or returned anti-bot pages, login ⁠screens, ​or blank results.
Some requests returned information through cached pages and intermediary ​services, including data on visitor arrivals at Chengdu Zoo, Swarmchasers said. The researchers said they could not determine whether an agent ​read the result or completed its task.

title: Outrage after Israeli settlers attack US photographer covering West Bank violence
description: Washington Post  outraged  by attack  says Heidi was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist
content:
Washington Post 'outraged' by attack, says Heidi was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist
There was a flurry of outrage after Israeli settlers on Friday beat an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post while she was covering ongoing violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.
Heidi Levine, a veteran photographer, was taken to hospital in Ramallah following the attack , with AFP photos showing her lying on a gurney with injuries to her leg and hand.
The incident comes 10 days after settlers beat an AFP photographer covering the West Bank olive harvest, Jaafar Ashtiyeh, leaving him also requiring hospital treatment.
Read : Israeli settlers attack West Bank village, blocking family's return home
Speaking to journalists from her hospital bed, Levine said that "more than 50" masked settlers holding sticks suddenly attacked her while she was working near the Palestinian villages of Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya in the central West Bank.
"All of a sudden they jumped me, and I luckily had my helmet and flak jacket on and I ... kept my face to the ground to try to protect my face," she said.
"They just kept kicking me and kicking me," she added .
The Washington Post reported that Levine had been wearing a flak jacket with "Press" clearly marked on the front and back.
A spokesman for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack, declining to comment further due to privacy laws.
"We have no higher responsibility than protecting American citizens," he said.
AFP did not witness the moment of the attack, but one of the agency's journalists in the area saw Palestinian medics tending to someone on the ground and Israeli soldiers pushing away journalists trying to approach.
The Israeli military said troops and border police forces were deployed to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation".
"Foreign media personnel were present at the scene, and a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation," it said, adding the circumstances would be examined.
"Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable acts," the military said.
The Israeli police said it had opened an investigation into incidents in Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya.
"We were on our land, picking olives, and suddenly the settlers came down on us and started hitting us, throwing stones," said Mukhllis Zuhdi, a farmer from Abu Falah.
"There was even a foreign journalist whom they beat. These people have no mercy or compassion in their hearts," he told AFP .
The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said the settlers stole Levine's passport, phone, wallet and equipment.
"This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank," it said.
"Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities," it added.
Reporters Without Borders said it strongly condemned the attack and called on Israeli authorities to "put an end to this impunity and prosecute the perpetrators of this heinous assault".
"This brazen violence ... is evidence of the impunity with which extremist Jewish settlers operate, often under the protection of Israeli armed forces," added the advocacy group, known by its French initials RSF.
Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank, with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.
Settlers have also been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who see the trees as a cultural symbol.
Excluding East Jerusalem, around three million Palestinians live in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, alongside more than 500,000 Israelis residing in settlements considered illegal under international law.
Washington Post ‘outraged’ after attack on photographer
Meanwhile, The Washington Post said it was “outraged” after Heidi was attacked by Israeli occupiers while reporting in the occupied West Bank.
“This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” the newspaper’s Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement.
“She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist,” he added.
Murray said the Post was “relieved that Heidi had received medical care and was safe”, but stressed: “We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities.”
Palestinian rights group Al-Baydar said Heidi was assaulted by the occupiers in the presence of Israeli troops and was taken to Al-Istishari Hospital.
Heidi was one of two journalists injured on Friday in attacks by Israeli occupiers across the Ramallah and Al-Bireh governorates, which also left at least 12 Palestinians wounded, many of them farmers harvesting olives, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society, the Civil Defence and Al-Baydar.
The Palestinian Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission said this week it had documented at least 136 attacks linked to the olive harvest season by Israeli forces and occupiers since the beginning of October.
The olive harvest is a vital source of income for thousands of Palestinian families in the West Bank, where farmers face growing attacks and restrictions on access to their land during the season.
Attacks by Israeli forces and occupiers against Palestinians and their property across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, have intensified since the start of the genocide in Gaza in October 2023.
UN calls for investigation into attack on Heidi Levine
Meanwhile, the UN called for a thorough investigation into the attack on Heidi by Israeli occupiers, stressing that journalists must be able to carry out their work without harassment.
Read More : Israeli settlements bring chaos to Palestinians
"We are aware of her condition, and obviously, this is yet another case where a journalist's right to go about her duties without harassment has been violated," UN deputy spokesman Farhan Haq told reporters.
"We want to make sure that this will be investigated thoroughly, and that all further harassment of journalists is prevented," he added.
Asked what measures the UN was taking to protect journalists amid continuing occupier violence in the occupied West Bank, Haq said the organisation raised the issue with member states and worked through its human rights bodies and specialised agencies.
"We call on all member states to uphold the rights of journalists," he said.
Haq also pointed to the work of UN human rights bodies and the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation, which plays a leading role in promoting journalists' rights and safety.

title: Ministers slam Fazl over opposition to K P governor   s rule  say he wanted role in new setup
description: Says K P needs peace  stability and collective efforts instead of political confrontation amid security challenges
content:
Interior Minister Naqvi says political chief was “extremely angry” over being denied role in K-P governor’s rule
Federal government ministers on Friday criticised Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman over his opposition to governor’s rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, alleging that his stance stemmed from his failure to secure a role in the new provincial setup.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi criticised "a political party’s chief" over his opposition to the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, saying the politician was “extremely angry” over not being given a role in the move or being offered the governorship.
In an informal conversation with journalists in Lahore, Naqvi said the politician had spent several decades pursuing politics with the support of the establishment.
“This was the same politician who used to get even the air tickets for his political party arranged through the establishment,” he said.
Read : Sanaullah links reversal of K-P governor's rule to PTI support for counterterrorism efforts
“Such politicians do not look good pointing fingers at others today,” Naqvi said, adding that political differences were part of politics but discussions should be based on arguments and facts rather than “uncivilised language” and allegations.
Although Naqvi did not name the politician, his remarks appeared to refer to Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who has categorically rejected the government’s decision to impose governor’s rule and an emergency in the province.
Naqvi also criticised political leaders who had recently expressed concern over the resources of the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Fata), questioning their silence during the years when the districts were not receiving their due share.
“When the former Fata districts were not receiving their rightful share for several years, why were these people silent at the time?” he asked.
“Why did they not remember to issue any statement for the rights of the people of former Fata at that time?” he added.
The interior minister said the rights and resources of the people of former Fata should be kept above political interests.
He said K-P was facing serious security challenges and urged political leaders to contribute to restoring peace and stability.
“Political leaders should play their role in restoring law and order and eliminating terrorism instead of fanning the flames and spreading unrest,” Naqvi said, adding that the province needed peace, stability and collective efforts rather than political confrontation.
Also Read : Fazl didn't set conditions for mediation
The remarks came after the federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in K-P on Sunday, dismissing the PTI-led provincial government. The move drew criticism from opposition parties, including Fazl, Tehreek-e-Tahafuz-e-Ain Pakistan (TTAP) Chairman Mehmood Khan Achakzai and PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan.
Fazl was central to recent political developments surrounding negotiations between the government and the opposition, with both sides agreeing to his role as a mediator in a bid to find a way forward.
However, despite several rounds of talks , no breakthrough could be achieved, and the government imposed governor’s rule and an emergency in the province, a move rejected by the JUI-F chief.
Speaking to the media earlier this week, Fazl accused the government of backing out of negotiations with the PTI and the opposition despite initially agreeing to their demands.
“I am a witness to the fact that the government backed out after agreeing to the demands,” he said, questioning why it had reneged on its commitment.
A day earlier, addressing the Mufti Mahmood conference in Multan, Fazl criticised the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in K-P, alleging that the government was using the security situation to justify its actions, while arguing that Balochistan faced even greater security challenges.
“If governor’s rule is being imposed because of law and order, and an emergency is being declared for the same reason, then Balochistan would have been the more deserving province,” he said.
He also alleged that the emergency had placed the resources of the former tribal areas under federal control, despite those resources having become part of the province following the merger.
Fazl said the Constitution guaranteed autonomy to the four provinces within the federation, including authority over their resources and legislation. However, he said, provincial autonomy had repeatedly been undermined.
“This is not a confederation in which a unit can seek independence and separate whenever it wishes. It is a federation in which all units and provinces have control over their resources and the authority to legislate,” he said.
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif also criticised JUI-F chief for opposing governor’s rule in K-P, describing his stance as “utter dishonesty” and an injustice to the people of the province.
Speaking on a private television programme, Naya Pakistan , the minister said some political leaders were opposing the move because they had expected to be given a role in the new administrative setup but were now making statements after being overlooked.
“Those whose names you have mentioned have taken a stance because they were not given a role, or their nominees were not accommodated,” Asif said when asked about the Awami National Party (ANP) and JUI-F’s continued opposition to governor’s rule and the imposition of an emergency in the province.
Recalling the formation of the Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM) government, he said the establishment had called a meeting at which it was decided that elections should be held immediately. However, “the people whose names you have mentioned” were not in favour of holding elections at the time.
“They said they wanted to run their meters for a year. They ran them, and within a year the entire political landscape changed,” Asif said, referring to developments following the successful no-confidence motion against the PTI government.
He said the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) had favoured immediate elections and that he himself had supported the idea.
“When Shehbaz Sharif went to that meeting, I told him to hold elections after a month,” Asif said, adding that the political leaders in question had been focused on material gains even then.
The minister said the parties were still unhappy because they had not been given power. According to him, they had viewed the dismissal of the PTI government as another opportunity to play a more prominent role, but their expectations had not been met.
Asif also criticised the JUI-F for what he described as its failure to condemn terrorism and stand with the armed forces following the deaths of soldiers.
“None of them came to offer funeral prayers. They should have led those prayers,” he said.
Rejecting allegations that Pakistan was handing over mines to the United States, the defence minister said the matter had remained limited to discussions.
“These are only talks. No contract has been awarded to them, and no mines or mineral resources have been handed over to them,” he said.
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz also lamented Fazl's statements, saying she had not expected a senior politician who had himself been a victim of terrorism to support those backing terrorism.
In a statement on X, she said it was “extremely regrettable” that instead of holding those responsible for K-P’s destruction through “incompetence, inefficiency and corruption” accountable, statements were being issued in their support.
“Those whose support is being expressed should be asked whether they attended even a single funeral of a martyr in 13 years,” Maryam said.
“Instead, terrorists were provided shelter, nurtured and given resources, hideouts and the land of the province to launch attacks on Pakistan,” she alleged.
The chief minister said the province’s valuable resources had been spent on sit-ins and protests, while 13 precious years had been “wasted on corruption and incompetence”.
Referring to the military leadership, Maryam said Fazl’s remarks about the army chief who had led the country to a “historic victory” in the “Battle of Truth” and under whose leadership Pakistan had been given the honour of protecting the Holy Mosques had hurt every patriotic Pakistani.
“Officers and soldiers of the Pakistan Army are still taking bullets to eradicate the scourge of terrorism,” she said.
“Every day, someone’s son, someone’s brother and someone’s husband returns home wrapped in the national flag,” she added, saying it was not befitting of Fazl to stand with those obstructing the fight against terrorism instead of paying tribute to the martyrs and supporting the army.
Read More : Achakzai warns Sindh could be next to face governor’s rule
Maryam said Fazl’s party had itself suffered from terrorism, with several of its members killed, while highlighting the PTI’s inappropriate remarks and personal attacks against the JUI-F chief.
“And those whom you are standing with today had, only yesterday, used extremely inappropriate language against you and made personal attacks,” she said.
“For the victims of terrorism to stand with those backing terrorism is something I cannot understand,” she added.
She also held the PTI responsible for the end of her government in K-P.
Separately, Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari also criticised Fazl over what she called another “irresponsible” statement, saying his support for “backers of terrorists” was regrettable.
In a statement on X, Bokhari said the federal government, rather than the PTI, was not responsible for the deprivation faced by the former Fata districts, where the PTI had remained in power for 13 years.
She said questions about funds allocated for former Fata and the lack of development work there should be directed to the PTI founder and his party.
“Maulana Fazlur Rehman and his party have themselves been targeted by terrorist attacks several times. Such a statement does not befit Maulana Fazlur Rehman,” she said.
Questioning Fazl’s motives, Bokhari asked what he was trying to achieve through such “irresponsible statements”.
“Do politics, but do not ridicule institutions and martyrs,” she said, adding that Fazl had also made “disrespectful” remarks about martyrs some time ago.
Also Read : Governor's rule imposed in K-P for fourth time
She said the nation had expressed strong anger over his previous statement.
“The PTI is the B-team of terrorist organisations; this is no longer a secret,” Bokhari said.
She added that the federal government had not imposed governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa “out of choice”.
“Governor’s rule was imposed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa because of the PTI government’s pro-terrorist policies,” she said.
Bokhari said Fazl should express regret over his statement, which she said had caused deep grief and anger among the people.
“Such irresponsible statements from a mature politician are unacceptable,” she added.

title: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia  let go  from role  official says
description: Legal credentials called into question after Katie gave an inconclusive answer about where she had passed the bar exam
content:
Legal credentials called into question after Katie gave an inconclusive answer about where she had passed the bar exam
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia was "let go" ​from the role, a White House official said ‌on Friday, after President Donald Trump said he had told her to reconsider the job following public scrutiny.
"I told her: 'I think ​you're better off being happy, and I'm not ​sure you can ever be happy in this ⁠stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters while departing the White House.
He added : "I said to her ​honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'"
Fox News , citing a White House official, later reported that ​Katie was "transitioning" out of the role of press ​secretary. Katie started the job on Monday and held her debut White House briefing ‌on ⁠Tuesday.
Read : Trump's new spokesperson stumbles into controversy
She had said she received a call about the role of press secretary last Wednesday and got offered the job to succeed Karoline Leavitt last Friday.
Trump later announced her appointment. ​In his ​announcement, he described ⁠her as an attorney.
Over the last week, the issue of whether Katie had actually ​passed ⁠the bar came under fire .
Earlier in the day, Katie acknowledged that she had failed the bar exam, a prerequisite for practising law in the United States, as her credentials faced scrutiny.
Katie had previously described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.
But the legal credentials of the press secretary, who President Donald Trump appointed last week, were called into question after she gave an inconclusive answer about where she had passed the bar exam.
The 41-year-old graduated from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011, but obtaining a law degree does not automatically qualify someone to practice law.
In a Fox News interview on Thursday, host Sean Hannity asked Katie: "You took the bar exam, but you didn't pass the bar exam, correct?"
In a separate interview with conservative media outlet Real America 's Voice on Thursday, Katie said she had registered to take the bar exam but was "distracted and overwhelmed" by plans to move to China with her husband.
"The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China," she said.
Foreign nationals cannot sit China's bar exam, although they can undertake certain legal work at Chinese law firms.
Hannity later asked Katie if she had ever taken the bar exam a second time, to which she said: "I did not."
Katie Zacharia says she never retook the bar exam, but maintains she had a legitimate basis for calling herself a lawyer during television appearances. The Pepperdine Law graduate tells @seanhannity she consulted attorneys before using the title, citing her law degree and… pic.twitter.com/eweV6pwPpg
"I had four kids in six years," she said. "It was never my intent to go into the practice of law."
Katie said on Real America' s Voice that "many people in the field" had assured her that she could "label myself a lawyer," given her law degree and experience in business law gained in China, where she worked at a Beijing law firm.
She added that she could "provide legal analysis, not legal advice."
"I was very careful how I executed this."
The Campaign for Accountability, a political ethics organisation, called on Wednesday for the California Bar Association to launch an investigation.
Read More : White House defends Press Secretary Katie Zacharia amid questions over legal credentials
"In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime," the organisation said in a press release.
Katie held her first White House press briefing on Tuesday with an unusually short press conference, answering questions from only three journalists.
She succeeded Karoline Leavitt, a loyal Trump supporter and often combative press secretary, who stepped down in August to care for her young children.

title: Iran denies Saudi accusation of involvement in Houthi attacks  offers to mediate
description: Coalition says drone intercepted  destroyed as Houthi affiliated media reports artillery shelling in Saada province
content:
Says it is prepared to mediate between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, but has yet to receive a positive response
Iran's foreign ministry on Friday rejected Saudi Arabia's accusation that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering to mediate between the two sides.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement.
He said Iran is ready to use its diplomatic capacity to help resolve differences between Saudi Arabia and Yemen if both sides request it
“The Islamic Republic of Iran has always been ready to use its good offices to help bring the conflict to an end, and remains prepared to use all its capacities for this purpose if requested by both sides,” Baqaei said.
Referring to the history of the war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, he said developments over the past 12 years had demonstrated that foreign intervention, military aggression and blockade were not solutions to Yemen’s problems.
Baghaei said regional countries and the broader Islamic world were expected to make serious efforts to bring the situation to an end.
Meanwhile, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh told Al Mayadeen that Tehran had offered Saudi Arabia to help mediate the dispute but had yet to receive a positive response.
“Today, our foreign minister and our government have offered any kind of assistance — mediation assistance, of course — but so far we have not received any positive response,” he said.
Houthi commander killed in clashes with Yemeni govt forces
Earlier on Friday, a Houthi commander was killed in clashes with Yemeni government forces near Mount Han in the southwestern city of Taiz, a Yemeni official said.
Fayyad al-Noman, a Yemeni media spokesman, said on US social media platform X that Abdulrahman Mohammed Sufyan Wajih al-Din, also known as Abu al-Karrar, was killed by government troops near Mount Han.
Al-Noman identified the slain Houthi commander as a brigadier general and director of Dhi al-Sufal in the Ibb province.
He did not specify when the incident occurred or provide further details on the circumstances of the killing.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Taiz has remained a major front line in Yemen's conflict, with government forces and the Houthis engaged in repeated clashes around the city.
Saudi-led coalition intercepts drone targeting kingdom’s east
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said early on Friday that it intercepted and destroyed a drone heading toward Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, while Houthi-affiliated media reported artillery shelling in Yemen's northern border province of Saada.
In a brief statement, the coalition announced the interception without identifying who launched the drone or specifying its intended target.
The statement provided no details on casualties or damage.
Separately, the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel reported artillery shelling in parts of Al-Dhaher district, which borders Saudi Arabia, in Saada province.
The reports came amid continued military escalation between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis.
On Thursday, the coalition announced the interception of a cruise missile over the Madinah region in western Saudi Arabia.
Read: Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, calls for immediate halt at UN
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree denied that the group had carried out any attacks against Saudi territory that day.
A day earlier, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward the capital Riyadh, where falling debris injured one person and caused minor property damage.
The latest incidents follow a wave of attacks on Saudi airports and energy facilities.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government since 2015 against the Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and several other provinces since 2014.
The current escalation began in July after a period of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce that started in April 2022.
Coalition says Houthis are getting missiles, fast boats
As Saudi Arabia backs government forces, the Houthis have been firing ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi airports, ports and ‌oil installations, ⁠turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war and threatening its ambitious economic plans.
On Thursday, the Saudi-led military coalition said the Houthis had attempted to attack dozens of such sites, highlighting the risk to Saudi civilian infrastructure. The governing council of the UN's International Civil Aviation Organisation condemned the recent attacks on civilian airports, aircraft, and aviation infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki told reporters that the Houthis had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and wounding 333 ​others. The airport is one of Saudi Arabia's ​main international aviation hubs.
The coalition said ⁠Houthi attacks on Abha airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border had killed three people and wounded 28.
Maliki said the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of "regional actors," including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats.
Iran has provided weapons, money and ​training to the Houthis, although Tehran has officially denied arming them in violation of a UN arms embargo.
Maliki also said the ​coalition had destroyed 127 ⁠weapons storage facilities and launch platforms in Yemen's mountainous areas, calling on the Houthis to immediately halt operations targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure.
Shortly afterwards, the Houthi military spokesperson said Saudi airspace and airports were unsafe, renewing a warning to airlines while excluding airspace over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
Saudi Arabia's civil defence authority issued early-warning alerts throughout Thursday over potential threats ⁠in the ​cities of Najran and Jizan, as well as the wider Najran and Jazan regions, before later saying the ​danger had passed.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Thursday that it had intercepted and destroyed a drone in the southwestern Saudi Arabian city of Khamis Mushait, and another launched towards the country's southern region.

title: Barbara Palvin   s postpartum runway return sparks double standards debate
description: Barbara Palvin s postpartum runway return sparks debate over why Ballerina Farm faced criticism after giving birth
content:
Barbara Palvin's postpartum runway return sparks debate over why Ballerina Farm faced criticism after giving birth
Barbara Palvin’s return to the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show just six weeks after giving birth has reignited discussions about postpartum beauty standards and the different ways mothers are judged online.
The Hungarian supermodel, 33, welcomed her first child, daughter Sylvie, with husband Dylan Sprouse in September 2026. She is set to walk the runway at the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show in Los Angeles on October 18, drawing attention to her return to modelling shortly after childbirth.
While Palvin’s comeback has attracted support from fans, the response has prompted comparisons with the criticism faced by Hannah Neeleman, widely known as Ballerina Farm, following her own public appearance weeks after giving birth.
The contrast has raised questions about whether society applies different standards to women depending on their profession, public image and the circumstances surrounding their postpartum appearances.
Palvin is returning to a runway associated with glamour, lingerie and carefully curated beauty standards. Her appearance has been celebrated by some fans as an impressive professional comeback, with discussions focusing on her return to modelling after welcoming her daughter.
Meanwhile, Neeleman, a social media personality and farmer known for her traditional lifestyle content, faced criticism over her appearance and activities following childbirth. The differing reactions have fuelled debate about the expectations placed on mothers and how quickly women are expected to recover physically after pregnancy.
The discussion also highlights the influence of social media in shaping perceptions of postpartum recovery. While some audiences celebrate women who resume professional activities soon after childbirth, others question whether such appearances reinforce unrealistic expectations for new mothers.
Palvin’s return has therefore become part of a broader conversation about postpartum bodies, motherhood and the pressures women face in the public eye.

title: Khawaja Asif claps back at critics over Marilyn Monroe AI riddle
description: Defence Minister says he is entitled to maintain his personality despite holding public office
content:
Defence minister says he is entitled to maintain his personality despite holding public office
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif on Friday brushed aside online criticism after being mocked for responding to an AI-generated image of Hollywood icon Marilyn Monroe, saying he personally operated his social media account and saw nothing unusual about his response.
Speaking on private television channel programme Naya Pakistan , the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz stalwart was asked about the post and whether he managed his account on X himself.
“200% I operate it myself,” Asif said, adding that he led an ordinary life despite holding a prominent government position.
“I have a personal life and a normal life. I am a normal human being; there is nothing special about me,” he said, stressing he had no airs about him.
Read: Khawaja Asif trolled over Marilyn Monroe AI puzzle on X
The controversy began on Tuesday when Asif responded to an AI-generated image depicting Monroe, which challenged social media users to identify an object that would have been out of place in the 1950s.
Resharing the image on X, the defence minister identified the smartwatch worn by Monroe as the anachronism. The original post shared by Asif has since been deleted.
Addressing the criticism, Asif defended his response, arguing that he had simply answered the question posed in the post.
“They presented a riddle asking about what was amiss with the photo [of Monroe], asking what should not have been present in 1956, and that was a smartwatch, so I wrote ‘watch’. What is non-serious about this?” he said.
Asif maintained that being the defence minister did not mean he had to give up his personality or refrain from engaging with light-hearted content on social media.
He said he operated his account himself and used it “for fun”, questioning why his position should prevent him from expressing himself like any other individual.
“Am I not Khawaja Asif? If I am the defence minister, should I let go of my identity? Whether it be good or bad?” he asked.

title: Mads Mikkelsen leads    Call of Duty  Modern Warfare 4    cast alongside Young Mazino and Luke Tennie
description: The casting brings together Young Mazino  Luke Tennie and Prisca Kim  known for her roles in  Beef  and  Loot
content:
The casting brings together Young Mazino, Luke Tennie and Prisca Kim, known for her roles in 'Beef' and 'Loot'
Mads Mikkelsen is among the notable names joining the cast of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , with the Danish actor set to portray the game's central antagonist in the latest instalment of Activision's long-running military shooter franchise.
The casting brings together performers from film and television, including The Last of Us star Young Mazino, Shrinking actor Luke Tennie and Prisca Kim, known for her roles in Beef and Loot . The ensemble also includes returning voice actors from previous entries in the Modern Warfare series.
Mikkelsen, known for playing Le Chiffre in Casino Royale , Galen Erso in Rogue One: A Star Wars Story and Hannibal Lecter in the television series Hannibal , will play a mysterious antagonist known as the Archer. The character is positioned as a major threat in the game's campaign, with the story involving the movement of a dangerous weapon and a wider international conflict.
Young Mazino, who earned recognition for playing Paul Cho in Netflix's Beef and Jesse in HBO's The Last of Us , takes on the role of Private Park Hyun Jun, a young South Korean soldier caught up in the conflict following North Korea's invasion of South Korea.
Luke Tennie, who plays Sean in Apple's Shrinking , joins the game as Lieutenant West. Prisca Kim is also part of the cast, alongside Lanny Joon and William Lipton. María Elisa Camargo returns as Valeria, while Barry Sloane reprises his role as Captain John Price, one of the franchise's most recognisable characters.
The casting process was led by Infinity Ward's narrative team, which initially had only a broad idea of the performers it wanted for the game. The studio's approach brought together established screen actors and performers whose previous work offered different strengths for the characters they would portray.
The new campaign follows two connected storylines. One centres on South Korea's struggle against a North Korean invasion, while another follows Price as he operates outside official military structures after the events of Modern Warfare 3 . The returning characters and new additions are expected to play key roles as the two threads converge.
Mikkelsen's involvement was revealed in a campaign trailer released in September, giving fans their first look at the actor's appearance in the game. His casting also continues the franchise's tradition of bringing recognisable actors into its campaigns, following previous appearances by performers including Kit Harington, Idris Elba and Gary Oldman across the wider Call of Duty series.

With a cast spanning established film stars and television actors, Modern Warfare 4 is preparing to deliver another cinematic campaign while continuing the story of Price and introducing a new generation of characters to the franchise.

title: Govt cuts petrol by Rs3 93  keeps diesel unchanged till Oct 19
description: Petrol price decreases to Rs386 30 per litre  while HSD will cost Rs396 96 under daily price mechanism
content:
Petrol price decreases to Rs386.30 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs396.96 under daily price mechanism
The federal government on Friday decreased the price of petrol by Rs3.93 per litre, while keeping the price of high-speed diesel (HSD) unchanged till October 19.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs386.30 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs396.96 per litre from October 17 to October 19.
The latest revision comes a day after the government decreased the price of petrol by Rs3.63 per litre, while increasing the price of HSD by 31 paisas per litre for October 16.
Read : Govt cuts petrol by Rs3.63, increases diesel by 31 paisas for Oct 16
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
On September 13, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.
Oil prices gained more than 3% and were heading for weekly gains on ‌continued uncertainty over Middle East supplies, and as investors kept assessing how much diesel Russia could supply to the global markets.
Brent crude futures were up $3.41, or 3.2%, at $109.34 at 12:41 pm ET (1641 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures ​rose $2.74, or 2.8%, to $100.67, crossing $100 for the first time since September 21.
"Conflict in the Middle East still keeps coming ⁠back, and I think it's questionable how much diesel fuel Russia can actually deliver to the markets. ​Those two factors are just continuing to have traders be buyers," said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of ​trading at BOK Financial.

title: The Chronicles of Narnia    gets new book editions ahead of Greta Gerwig   s    The Magician   s Nephew
description: Among the releases is a graphic novel adaptation illustrated by Ben Hatke  scheduled to arrive on January 12  2027
content:
Among the releases is a graphic novel adaptation illustrated by Ben Hatke, scheduled to arrive on January 12, 2027
C S Lewis’ beloved The Chronicles of Narnia series is getting a new collection of special editions ahead of Greta Gerwig’s upcoming film adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew .
HarperCollins Publishers and Netflix have announced a publishing initiative designed to introduce the fantasy franchise to a new generation of readers while celebrating the upcoming film. The collection will include movie tie-in paperbacks, collector’s editions, retailer-exclusive books, a boxed set and a new graphic novel.
The initiative arrives as excitement builds around Gerwig’s adaptation, which marks the first time The Magician’s Nephew has been brought to the screen. The film serves as a prequel to the familiar Narnia stories, exploring the origins of the magical world created by Lewis.
Among the releases is a graphic novel adaptation illustrated by Ben Hatke, scheduled to arrive on January 12, 2027. The publishing programme will also include a deluxe collector’s edition and special editions intended for different retailers, giving fans several ways to revisit the classic story.
Some editions will arrive earlier, with releases scheduled for November 10 and November 17, while a hardback box set is expected on November 24. Pre-orders are available for the upcoming editions.
Gerwig’s film follows Digory Kirke and Polly Plummer as they discover the Wood between the Worlds and encounter the beginnings of Narnia. The story introduces audiences to the origins of the world and the powerful lion Aslan, whose role is central to the series.
The film features David McKenna as Digory and Beatrice Campbell as Polly, alongside a star-studded cast including Daniel Craig, Carey Mulligan, Emma Mackey and Meryl Streep, who voices Aslan.
Netflix released the first trailer for the adaptation in October, offering an initial glimpse at Gerwig’s interpretation of Lewis’ fantasy universe. The footage features Led Zeppelin’s Stairway to Heaven and showcases the film’s magical settings and characters.
Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew is scheduled to arrive in cinemas on February 12, 2027, before streaming on Netflix from April 2, 2027.
The new publishing initiative gives readers an opportunity to rediscover Lewis’ world ahead of the film’s release, combining updated editions of the original material with new visual interpretations of one of fantasy literature’s most enduring series.

title: Heated Rivalry    star Hudson Williams asked if he has feelings for Connor Storrie beyond friendship
description: Williams was asked the question about Storrie in  The Assembly   shown in the teaser ahead of its November 1 release
content:
Williams was asked the question about Storrie in 'The Assembly', shown in the teaser ahead of its November 1 release
Heated Rivalry star Hudson Williams has been asked whether he has ever felt something more than friendship for his co-star Connor Storrie in a preview for the Canadian interview series The Assembly .
Williams, who plays Shane Hollander opposite Storrie’s Ilya Rozanov in the hit hockey romance, appears in the upcoming season of the CBC programme, where celebrity guests face direct and often unexpected questions from a panel of autistic and neurodivergent interviewers.
In the trailer, one interviewer tells Williams, “I’m going to ask you about your sex life,” prompting the actor to grin and respond, “Hell yeah!”
Williams is then asked what he likes to fantasise about before the conversation turns to his relationship with Storrie, who plays his on-screen love interest in Heated Rivalry .
“Did you ever feel something for Connor [Storrie] that was more than friendship?” an interviewer asks.
The preview does not reveal Williams’ full response, leaving viewers waiting to see how he addresses the personal question when the episode airs.
The trailer also captures a more emotional moment, with Williams reflecting on the importance of friendship and family during periods of loneliness.
“I feel that when I’m falling down that hole of being lonely, your friends and family are like the climbing pegs that you pull yourself back into life by,” he says.
The candid exchange reflects the format of The Assembly , which gives interviewers the freedom to ask celebrities questions that traditional talk shows might avoid. Its guiding principle is that no subject is off limits, allowing for conversations that can shift quickly from humorous to deeply personal.
Williams and Storrie have attracted considerable attention since Heated Rivalry became a global success, with viewers frequently discussing their chemistry both on and off screen. Their characters, Shane and Ilya, are rival ice hockey players whose secret romance develops over several years.
However, the actors have previously described their real-life relationship as a close friendship. Storrie has called Williams his best friend, while Williams has spoken warmly about their bond and how they supported each other through the sudden attention surrounding the series.
Williams has also made it clear that he and Storrie want to maintain separate identities as actors rather than have their careers defined by their friendship. Their on-screen romance and real-life closeness have nevertheless continued to fuel fan speculation.
The second season of The Assembly will feature several other notable guests, including The Hangover star Zach Galifianakis, This Is the End actor Jay Baruchel, three-time Olympic gold medallist Marie-Philip Poulin, Miss Universe Canada Ashley Callingbull and singer-songwriter Lights.
The programme is scheduled to premiere on CBC TV on November 1. Williams’ appearance promises an unusually direct conversation, although the trailer leaves his response to the question about Storrie unrevealed.
