title: E passport replaces old system as costs double
description: E passport replaces old system as costs double
content:
Old machine-readable travel document discontinued
The cost of obtaining a new passport has nearly doubled as the authorities have discontinued machine-readable passports and shifted exclusively to e-passports for new applications nationwide.
The normal fee for a five-year, 36-page passport has risen from Rs4,500 to Rs9,000, while the urgent fee has increased from Rs7,500 to Rs15,000.
The change applies to Lahore and the rest of the country, although machine-readable passports already issued to citizens will remain valid until their expiry dates.
Under the new fee structure, a five-year, 36-page e-passport costs Rs9,000 under normal processing and Rs15,000 under urgent processing.
The supplied report puts the former fast-track fee for a machine-readable passport at Rs12,500 and gives the corresponding e-passport fee as Rs22,000. It says fees for 72-page passports will also increase in the same proportion.
Passport and Immigration Department sources said 5,572,130 passports were issued nationwide in 2025. Of these, 3,275,263 were issued under the normal machine-readable category, 1,839,487 under the urgent category and 276,789 through fast-track service. Close to 180,000 e-passports were also issued during the year.
The figures cited for previous years show that 6,596,520 passports were issued in 2024 and 6,717,938 in 2023.
A combined total of 13,314,458 passports were issued during those two years, averaging approximately 6.7 million annually. The report describes the 2025 total as the highest in the country's history for a single year, although the figures it provides for both 2023 and 2024 are higher.
The shift to e-passports is part of a wider move towards modern travel-document technology, with many countries adopting electronic passports. The Directorate General of Immigration and Passports has introduced the system in Pakistan using modern technology and additional equipment.
For the project, the department has installed 10 additional modern printing machines and six laminators. It has also established round-the-clock services at 232 offices, alongside 93 window counters at Pakistani missions abroad that operate day and night.
According to the figures cited in the report, passport fees generated Rs47,645,523,500 for the national exchequer in 2024, while collections in 2023 were approximately Rs50 billion.
The report further says that an average of Rs40 billion a year was deposited into the government treasury during the 2023-24 and 2024-25 fiscal years, roughly twice the amount collected in earlier years.
Based on an average fee of Rs7,000 to Rs15,000 per passport, the report estimates that passport issuance generates between Rs40 billion and Rs50 billion in annual net revenue for the government, separate from the federal excise duty (FED) collected by the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR).
Passport authorities maintain that e-passports cost more to produce than machine-readable passports because they incorporate modern technology. The department says the new fees have been fixed in line with those higher production costs. Existing machine-readable passports will remain usable until their validity expires.

title: Hottest monsoon in 66 years recorded
description: Hottest monsoon in 66 years recorded
content:
Temperatures hit 30.7°C as Sindh records a 51% rainfall deficit
Pakistan's 2026 monsoon season has recorded the highest average temperature in 66 years, with the national average reaching 30.7 degrees Celsius and surpassing the previous record of 30.6°C set in 2019, according to a report issued by the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD).
The record comes seven years after the previous peak, while most parts of the country received below-normal rainfall, with Sindh recording the largest shortfall.
According to the report, Turbat in Balochistan recorded a temperature of 48.5°C during the monsoon season. The season's hottest days in the area fell on July 7, 12, 30 and 31, spanning the beginning, middle and end of the month.
In contrast, Skardu in Gilgit-Baltistan recorded a temperature of 6°C on September 23 and 26, reflecting the colder weather conditions towards the end of the monsoon season.
The report highlighted significant regional differences in rainfall, with most parts of the country receiving less rain than normal. Gilgit-Baltistan was the exception, recording above-normal rainfall.
According to the PMD data, monsoon rainfall in Sindh remained 51% below normal, while Balochistan recorded a shortfall of 34%. Rainfall in Azad Jammu and Kashmir was 18% below normal, followed by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa at 16% and Punjab at 4%.
In contrast, Gilgit-Baltistan received 5% more rainfall than normal, making it the only region mentioned in the report to record above-normal monsoon precipitation.
Despite the overall rainfall shortfall across most regions, some areas experienced heavy downpours.
Lahore airport recorded 252 millimetres of rainfall in a single day on July 23, 2026, while Gujranwala received a cumulative total of 607mm during July.

title: K P orders safety checks at schools
description: K P orders safety checks at schools
content:
Technical teams to submit district-wise reports by Oct 26
The Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government on Thursday directed the Communication and Works (C&W) Department to constitute technical teams to inspect all government school buildings across the province following the deadly collapse of a classroom roof at a private school in Peshawar.
Earlier in the day, a roof collapse at Al-Khair Education System in Dir Colony claimed precious lives and left students and teachers injured, prompting concerns over the structural safety of educational institutions.
In a letter issued on October 15, the Elementary and Secondary Education Department asked the C&W Department to nominate qualified technical teams for every district to conduct a comprehensive assessment of school buildings in coordination with the respective district education authorities.
The teams will examine roofs, ceilings, walls, beams, foundations, staircases and other structural components to identify defects, maintenance issues and potential safety hazards.
Under the terms of reference, the inspected buildings will be classified into three categories: safe, requiring repairs or improvement, and potentially unsafe buildings requiring urgent technical assessment.
The teams will also recommend repairs, structural strengthening and rehabilitation measures, along with implementation priorities and timelines for corrective action.
Buildings found to pose an imminent threat to students and staff must be reported immediately to the relevant district authorities, with recommendations for precautionary measures, including restricting access or suspending their use where necessary.
The department has directed the technical teams to coordinate with male and female district education officers to ensure that all government schools, including separate boys' and girls' institutions, are covered by the exercise.
The C&W Department has been asked to submit comprehensive district-wise inspection reports, detailing structural deficiencies, safety classifications and recommended remedial measures, by October 26 at noon.
The teams will also be required to issue a building safety clearance certificate or no-objection certificate (NOC) for each inspected school, indicating its structural safety status, suitability for continued use and any conditions or repairs required.
The education department has stressed that the exercise be treated as a top priority, given the need to safeguard students, teachers and other staff in government educational institutions across the province.
The directive also makes clear that authorities must not wait for the province-wide survey to conclude before acting on buildings identified as posing an immediate safety risk.

Alliance seeks independent support base as PTI steps back
With the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) now ready to take a back seat, Tehreek-e-Tahafuz-e-Aain-e-Pakistan (TTAP) will establish its own political arm and develop a formal organisational structure at the provincial level, a TTAP leader has revealed.

TTAP, which drew much of its strength from PTI, was now in dire need of its own dedicated support base, the leader said. Given the government's strong-arm tactics, PTI could no longer flex its muscles as it had in the past.
With PTI's support virtually unavailable for the time being, TTAP leadership felt the multiparty opposition alliance needed to build its own support base to organise events and get its message across.
The leader said the alliance had asked its provincial chapters to develop organisational structures and establish working groups and research groups.
Asked why TTAP was pursuing the initiative again despite having announced it several times in the past, the leader said the biggest hurdle had been PTI itself, despite TTAP's desire to establish its own organisational structure.
He said PTI had initially viewed the move as an attempt to establish a parallel power centre, leading to heated discussions between the two sides. However, recent developments had made PTI realise the benefits of such an arrangement.
He said regional parties could offer only limited street power because of their relatively small support bases, adding that PTI had therefore remained TTAP's main source of strength.
Now that PTI chairman had agreed to and fully endorsed the initiative, TTAP had once again embarked on the mission, he said.
The move would allow TTAP to generate political pressure independently of PTI and enable it to challenge what it considers government injustices against the party, the leader added.

title: Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks on KSA
description: Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks on KSA
content:
Calls for halting settler violence in West Bank
Pakistan on Thursday strongly condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's civilian and economic infrastructure, reaffirming its support for the kingdom's security and right to self-defence amid escalating regional tensions.
Speaking at a United Nations Security Council (UNSC) debate on the Middle East, Pakistan's acting Permanent Representative, Ambassador Usman Jadoon, said, "These attacks must cease immediately."
He reiterated Islamabad's support for efforts to secure a peaceful settlement in Yemen.
Pakistan also backed the UN special envoy's efforts to resume dialogue aimed at achieving a comprehensive and lasting peace in Yemen.
Pakistan also joined the call for halting settler violence in the West Bank and abandoning attempts to annex occupied Palestinian territory.
"In the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, settlement expansion, particularly the E1 project, threatens to sever Palestinian territorial contiguity. Settler violence, demolitions, land seizures and forced displacement are entrenching annexation and dismantling the foundations of peace," Jadoon said.
"All settlement activities must cease; settler violence must be halted; and accountability ensured."
The E1 plan was greenlit by Israel last year and would further separate east Jerusalem, occupied and annexed by Israel and predominantly inhabited by Palestinians, from the West Bank.
Jadoon added that the international support for a two-state solution to the Palestinian issue must be accompanied by concrete measures to preserve Palestine's territorial integrity and viability.
"The two-state solution remains the internationally agreed framework and the indispensable foundation for just and lasting peace," he said, adding that Resolution 2803, the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, and the New York Declaration provided mutually reinforcing frameworks for advancing that objective.
"Pakistan supports their full and good-faith implementation," he added. He also condemned Israeli incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque and demanded respect for the historical and legal status quo of the holy sites.
Regarding Gaza, Pakistan expressed concern over continued ceasefire violations, Palestinian deaths and restrictions on humanitarian access.
Jadoon warned that the approaching winter threatened to worsen the suffering of families living amid destruction without adequate shelter or essential services.
He called for the Gaza ceasefire to be fully upheld, humanitarian assistance to be delivered unhindered and at scale, and recovery and reconstruction to proceed without delay.
Pakistan also stressed the need to support the work of the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees, and demanded the release of withheld Palestinian revenues to enable the Palestinian Authority to fulfil its responsibilities.
Jadoon rejected forced displacement and any attempt to fragment Gaza and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, which he said constituted a single territorial unit.
He called for a "credible, time-bound and irreversible" political process to end the Israeli occupation and establish an independent, sovereign, contiguous and viable Palestinian state on pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital.

title: September FPA capped at Rs2 56 unit
description: September FPA capped at Rs2 56 unit
content:
Rs32.7b impact on November bills; RLNG at domestic rates eases burden by 83 paisa
The Ministry of Energy (Power Division) has averted a potential Rs5-6 per unit hike in the September 2026 Fuel Price Adjustment (FPA), limiting the projected adjustment to Rs2.56 per unit despite rising international fuel prices and constraints on liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies.
The division said targeted load management for approximately two to two-and-a-half hours during September helped reduce reliance on costly alternative fuels, including furnace oil and high-speed diesel, saving consumers from an additional burden of up to Rs3.44 per unit. It added that the provision of imported re-gasified liquefied natural gas (RLNG) for power generation at domestic gas prices eased the burden by a further 83 paisa per unit.
Consequently, the September FPA is expected to be Rs1.45 per unit higher than August, with an estimated financial impact of Rs32.7 billion on consumers' electricity bills in November 2026.
The Power Division said international fuel prices rose sharply amid regional conflict and disruptions following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude prices surged beyond $120 per barrel against the benchmark of around $70 assumed during determination of the base tariff.
Despite Qatar's force majeure declaration, Pakistan met its RLNG requirements through contracted supplies and additional spot cargoes.
The statement said the combined impact of fuel price and quarterly tariff adjustments during January-August 2026 was limited to 65 paisa per unit, an increase of only 1.9% over the base tariff. It attributed this partly to tariff rationalisation measures and an additional consumption package for industrial and agricultural consumers.

title: Forum backs shift to gigabit universal service

The Asia-Pacific Telecommunity (APT) Symposium on Digital Transformation and the Universal Service Fund (USF) concluded in Islamabad with member states aligning on a collective roadmap to move universal service funds from traditional voice and basic coverage models towards agile, outcome-oriented frameworks supporting high-speed fibre, gigabit broadband and resilient digital ecosystems, according to a statement issued by the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication (MoITT) on Thursday.
The three-day forum was co-hosted by the ministry and USF Pakistan, bringing together policymakers, regulators and telecom industry leaders from across the region. APT Secretary-General Masanori Kondo announced the conclusion, describing the symposium as a platform for practical exchanges, partnerships and advancing the Tokyo Statement 2025 commitments.
Speakers and experts engaged across 10 sessions on future-proofing universal service funds, shifting from simple infrastructure access to quality, capability and AI readiness. Discussions covered low-cost fibre backhaul, mobile broadband, satellite connectivity and green telecom infrastructure to scale deployment in underserved and rugged terrains.
The forum examined regulatory incentives, device subsidy programmes and financial mechanisms to improve affordability and sustainable financing, making connectivity accessible to low-income households, small enterprises and marginalised communities. Sessions covered targeted policy interventions, digital literacy programmes for women and girls and digital entrepreneurship support to close the gender digital divide.
Stakeholders also stressed empowering local content and ecosystems through culturally appropriate, language-specific digital services and e-government platforms to stimulate local economies and drive digital adoption.
Delegates also deliberated on harnessing emerging technologies, bridging persistent digital divides and driving equitable digital transformation across member states, reviewing regional digital progress under the Tokyo Statement 2025 and aligning regional strategies.
In his closing remarks, USF Pakistan Chief Executive Officer Chaudhary Mudassar Naveed thanked APT for partnering with Pakistan and recognised the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA), session chairs, panellists and international delegates. Special recognition went to operators and technology partners including Jazz, PTML, Zong, Huawei and GSMA.

content:
Value addition, improved standards will help sector expand global footprint
Adviser to Prime Minister for Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar Khan has emphasised that Pakistan's marble industry has significant potential to contribute to industrial growth, employment generation and foreign exchange earnings, provided the sector moves beyond conventional extraction practices towards modern processing, quality finishing and higher value-added products.
He chaired a meeting of the Steering Committee on the National Marble and Natural Stone Policy to review the challenges facing the marble industry and discuss measures to enhance value addition, improve finishing standards, modernise production processes and increase exports.
Khan pointed out that the steering committee had been constituted to address the longstanding challenges facing the marble and natural stone sector, unlock its export potential and modernise the industry in line with international standards.
The adviser informed the meeting that four technical groups had been formed under the steering committee to develop focused recommendations on marble finishing, technology up-gradation, value addition and export promotion. These groups will work towards identifying practical solutions to industry-specific challenges and developing a roadmap for strengthening the sector's competitiveness in international markets.
Khan underscored the government's commitment to working closely with the private sector to address operational bottlenecks, improve the industry's business environment and facilitate sustainable growth. He said the committee would provide a platform for identifying challenges and formulating actionable solutions in consultation with industry stakeholders.
Private sector representatives, who were present in the meeting, highlighted several structural constraints affecting the industry's performance, particularly outdated extraction techniques, inadequate access to modern technology, logistical challenges, limited value addition and insufficient outreach to international markets.
They observed that conventional blasting methods used in quarrying often resulted in substantial wastage of valuable marble, reducing the quantity of usable stone and undermining the industry's overall productivity. They stressed the need for adopting modern extraction technologies and improving processing techniques to minimise wastage and maximise the commercial value of natural stone resources.
The participants emphasised that improving finishing standards, product quality and processing capabilities was essential to making Pakistani marble more competitive in international markets. They called for paying greater attention to logistics, market development and export facilitation to enable local producers gain access to new buyers and expand their international footprint.

content:
Total deposits stand at $26.9b; gold steady despite global rally
The foreign exchange reserves held by the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) increased by $16 million to $21.47 billion during the week ended October 9, 2026, according to data released by the central bank on Thursday.
The SBP's foreign exchange reserves stood at $21.469 billion compared with the previous week's level of $21.454 billion, reflecting a modest increase in the central bank-held reserves. Pakistan's total liquid foreign currency reserves, including those held by commercial banks, reached $26.863 billion during the week under review.
The net reserves held by commercial banks stood at $5.394 billion as of October 9. Furthermore, the Pakistani rupee extended its marginal gains against the US dollar in the inter-bank market on Thursday, appreciating 0.01% to close at 276.92, up Rs0.03 from Wednesday's closing rate of 276.95 per dollar.
Meanwhile, gold prices in Pakistan remained unchanged at Rs437,836 per tola, even as international bullion prices rose more than 1% because of a weaker US dollar and declining Treasury yields.
According to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association (APGJSA), the price of 10-gram gold also remained unchanged at Rs375,373. The local market held steady after gold prices had settled at Rs437,836 per tola on Wednesday, following an intra-day decline of Rs3,000.
In the international market, spot gold rose 1.1% to $4,149 per ounce by 12:36 am EDT (1636 GMT), recovering after falling to a one-week low in the previous session, as per Reuters. US gold futures for December delivery gained 1.5% to $4,170.10 per ounce, reflecting the recovery in bullion demand.
The US dollar index declined 0.4%, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield fell to a three-week low. A weaker dollar makes gold, priced in dollars, less expensive for holders of other currencies, while lower yields reduce the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion.
However, stronger-than-expected US Producer Price Index (PPI) data continued to complicate the outlook for monetary policy. Investors were also monitoring remarks by Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh for signals about the central bank's future rate decisions. Despite the hotter inflation reading, expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike this month remained subdued, providing some support to gold.
Adnan Agar, Director of Interactive Commodities, said international gold was trading in the $4,140-$4,150-per-ounce range, after reaching the intra-day high of $4,170 and low of around $4,110. He said the market had declined in the previous session but subsequently recovered, although uncertainty continued to cloud its direction.
Agar said market participants were discussing the possibility of gold falling towards $4,000 per ounce. A further decline below that level could potentially push prices towards $3,700. However, he noted that strong international demand could support a recovery, with prices potentially rebounding quickly after a decline. The outlook therefore remains sensitive to movements in the dollar, Treasury yields, inflation data and expectations about Federal Reserve's policy.
Meanwhile, domestic silver prices fell by Rs212 to Rs6,148 per tola, according to APGJSA. While international gold staged a recovery, the unchanged local gold rate and declining silver price highlighted differing movements in Pakistan's precious metals market.

title: Duty levied to shield parts makers
description: Duty levied to shield parts makers
content:
Revenue Division proposes imposition of additional duty to discourage imports
The government has levied 11% customs duty on 13 additional items in the automobile sector to protect local auto parts manufacturers.
These goods include radial and other tyres for heavy commercial vehicles, licence plate, bracket-side reflector, side reflector, right/left side plate, front decorative component (partially legible), foot rest and plate thereof, wheel assembly and parts thereof, windscreen and parts thereof, seat base and tail box and parts thereof, centre covers and parts, and plate and parts.
The Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) of the cabinet has granted its approval in a recent meeting. The Revenue Division/Federal Board of Revenue (Customs Wing) briefed the ECC that SRO 693(I)/2006 dated July 1, 2006 contained the list of auto parts and components which had been localised (manufactured locally) and additional customs duty under sub-section (5) of Section 18 of the Customs Act, 1969 (IV of 1969), as determined by the Engineering Development Board (EDB)/Ministry of Industries & Production, was required to be levied to discourage the import of such parts, which were now being manufactured locally.
At present, more than 1,200 Pakistan Customs Tariff (PCT) codes related to auto parts, components, etc are covered under this SRO on which additional customs duty is levied at different rates, as determined by the EDB. The SRO is updated on recommendations of the Ministry of Industries from time to time. Encouraging the localisation of auto parts and components is expected to conserve foreign exchange, generate employment opportunities and create export avenues in the long run.
The Revenue Division told the ECC that the Ministry of Industries vide a letter dated September 7, 2026 had shared further recommendations for updating the list of localised parts and components in SRO 693(I)/2006 so that a higher rate of additional customs duty could be collected on these parts and components.
Accordingly, in light of recommendations of the Ministry of Industries, the Revenue Division proposed that SRO 693(I)/2006 may be updated, as per draft amended SRO, for the imposition of additional customs duty under sub-section (5) of Section 18 of the Customs Act, 1969.
It revealed that a draft summary, prepared for the ECC, was circulated to the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Commerce. The Revenue Division solicited approval of the ECC for the proposal. The ECC reviewed the summary titled "Amendment in SRO 693 for Levy of Additional Customs Duty on Additional Items" and approved the proposal.

title: New tax agency under consideration
description: New tax agency under consideration
content:
FBR to present overhaul plan on Oct 19; current target being missed by Rs650b
The government is considering establishing a new tax collection agency, or further restructuring the existing machinery, after finding the Federal Board of Revenue's (FBR) performance unsatisfactory despite repeated reform attempts.
The FBR will present "comprehensive proposals on HR reforms, revamping and restructuring" to the prime minister on October 19, according to directives issued by the Prime Minister's Office on Thursday.
Government officials said the idea of an altogether new organisation was floated at a meeting at the highest level last Saturday. Internal discussions have since begun, with FBR Chairman Rashid Langrial tasking officers to prepare a plan for Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
When asked whether a new agency was under consideration, the FBR spokesperson said: "The FBR's reform is a robust and ongoing process, and dozens of ideas and proposals come under discussion." He added that "until any of them becomes a formally approved policy, no comment can be made".
In a second reply on the same issue, the FBR confirmed the prime minister had directed it to bring forward comprehensive proposals for human resource reform and restructuring, adding that work was under way.
"The government's aim is a stronger, more efficient and more taxpayer-friendly FBR, and the prime minister is personally overseeing an ongoing reform process to that end," it said.
The FBR further said substantial reforms had been put in place across people, technology and processes, and that to build on these and fill the remaining gaps, the prime minister had directed the FBR to bring forward comprehensive proposals. Work was under way, it said.
The FBR said the focus was on reforming the board itself and denied "talk of outsourcing revenue collection function to a private company", calling it "totally baseless".
Sources said discussions were at an initial stage, with no concrete proposal finalised on the future shape of the FBR or a revenue agency. Setting up a national tax agency was among the discussion points.
Any decision to transfer the FBR's powers to a new agency would require amendments to a host of laws, including the FBR Act 2007 and at least four tax laws.
Reform attempts since 2000 include restructuring the Central Board of Revenue into the FBR, merging service cadres, redefining the entity on functional lines and, in 2024, an over Rs55 billion transformation plan. During the caretaker setup, an attempt was also made to split the FBR into Customs and Inland Revenues.
According to an official involved in the deliberations, the thinking so far is that the FBR would not be dissolved, and officers who do not opt for a new body would remain until retirement.
Sources said a narrow tax base, a stagnant tax-to-GDP ratio and below-par tax collection were among the reasons behind forming a new organisation.
The FBR's tax-to-GDP ratio remained at 10.3% last fiscal year, and the FBR missed its original annual target by over Rs1.1 trillion.
This year's target of Rs15.263 trillion requires over 17% growth. The FBR surpassed its first-quarter target but grew at hardly 7%. Sources expect growth of around 12%, a shortfall of over Rs650 billion that would affect planning for over Rs1 trillion in spending under the National Economic Initiative through provincial cash grants.
On the transformation plan's outcomes, the spokesperson said collection rose from Rs9.2 trillion to Rs13 trillion in two years.However, the reply does not fully reflect ground realities, as the spokesperson has counted the impact of additional taxes and nominal economic growth towards the contribution of the transformation plan. The government imposed one of the highest taxes under the International Monetary Fund (IMF) plan, which in the first year also contributed to an increase in the tax-to-GDP ratio.
Secondly, the Economic Coordination Committee of the Cabinet had approved the first spending package of Rs32.5 billion for six months in November 2024. Out of the Rs32.5 billion, an amount of Rs5.6 billion was approved for buying 1,087 new cars of 1,300cc engine capacity. About Rs19.7 billion were for spending on anti-smuggling initiatives.
For giving up to four extra salaries, the ECC accorded approval for Rs2.5 billion for six months while another Rs3.4 billion had been given for enhancing the FBR's operational capacity. An annual Rs4 billion is also given for transformation of the Pakistan Automation Revenue Limited (PRAL), with the latest tranche approved this month.
The FBR is also struggling to broaden the tax base. Of the 19 million people who have national tax numbers, only 6.9 million submitted returns by Thursday evening. The 8.5 million returns had been filed in the last tax year.
The government had also launched the fixed tax traders' scheme in the hope of bringing 3.7 million retailers into the net, including one million this year.
However, the FBR spokesperson said that as of Tuesday 137 new traders had filed their returns and paid Rs5 million in taxes, on average Rs36,465 per new trader.
The FBR said many reforms were under implementation. It said on the human resource side, to name just a few, third-party auditors have been engaged from chartered accountancy firms to add capacity, officers are being trained through programmes with institutions such as LUMS, and a new performance management regime now assesses officers on actual results rather than routine ratings.
On the technology and process side, Customs has moved to faceless assessment and Inland Revenue is moving the same way, which reduces discretion and direct contact between officers and taxpayers. Digital invoicing and POS integration now track business transactions in real time, an AI-based risk management system guides selection for audit and clearance, and third-party data is being integrated. These are only some of the many interventions under way.

description: Esther McGregor and Emilio Sakraya to star as Violet and Xaden in Prime Video   s upcoming    Fourth Wing    series
content:
Esther McGregor and Emilio Sakraya to star as Violet and Xaden in Prime Video’s upcoming ‘Fourth Wing’ series
Prime Video has cast Esther McGregor and Emilio Sakraya as Violet Sorrengail and Xaden Riorson in its upcoming Fourth Wing television adaptation, based on Rebecca Yarros’ bestselling fantasy novel.
McGregor, known for We Were Liars and Babygirl , will play Violet, while Sakraya, whose credits include Those About to Die and Warrior Nun , will portray Xaden. The characters share an enemies-to-lovers relationship in Yarros’ novel.
Amazon declined to comment on the casting, according to Deadline.
The Fourth Wing series follows Violet as she enters Basgiath War College after her mother, General Lilith Sorrengail, forces her to abandon her plans to become a Scribe. Instead, Violet must train to become a dragon rider in Navarre, where candidates face dangerous trials and the risk of death.
At the college, she encounters Xaden, a mysterious cadet from a rebellious family who possesses shadow-wielding powers. The story explores the dangerous bond between dragon riders and their dragons, with survival depending on their ability to endure the brutal training.
Amazon MGM Studios acquired the television rights to Yarros’ Empyrean book series in 2023. Prime Video officially greenlit the adaptation in May 2026, with Meredith Averill serving as showrunner and executive producer. Lisa Joy is set to direct the series premiere and executive produce alongside Jonathan Nolan and other members of the production team.
The Empyrean series currently includes Fourth Wing , Iron Flame and Onyx Storm . Yarros is working on a fourth novel, with a fifth book also planned. The television adaptation could span multiple seasons if successful.
The series is produced by Michael B. Jordan’s Outlier Society, Kilter Films and Premeditated Productions.
McGregor is also filming Prime Video’s Life Is Strange , while Sakraya recently completed work on the third season of Netflix’s One Piece , in which he plays Koza.

title: Chuck Lorre says  The Big Bang Theory  stars were outraged over proposed pay cut
description: Chuck Lorre says  Big Bang Theory  stars resisted pay cuts to fund salary raises for Mayim Bialik and Melissa Rauch
content:
Chuck Lorre says 'Big Bang Theory' stars resisted pay cuts to fund salary raises for Mayim Bialik and Melissa Rauch
Chuck Lorre has revealed behind-the-scenes tensions involving The Big Bang Theory cast, claiming its leading stars were outraged when asked to accept a pay cut to accommodate salary increases for co-stars Mayim Bialik and Melissa Rauch.
In his new memoir, Sitcom , the television producer recalled how Bialik and Rauch joined the series towards the end of its third season before becoming regular cast members in season four. Lorre credited their additions with helping sustain the sitcom, suggesting it might otherwise have run out of steam after seven or eight seasons.
According to Lorre, executives Les Moonves and Bruce Rosenblum later approached the main cast, who were earning $1 million per episode plus profit participation, and asked them to take a 10% pay cut to fund raises for the two actresses.
Lorre said he expected the actors to agree but was surprised by their reaction. He recalled that they were outraged by the request, leaving the executives to withdraw from the discussion without securing the expected cooperation.
The memoir also revisits Lorre’s turbulent working relationship with Charlie Sheen on Two and a Half Men . Lorre described the early years as enjoyable but said the production became increasingly difficult during season eight, when Sheen frequently missed work.
He recalled a particularly troubling incident in which Sheen struggled to remember his lines and needed furniture to remain upright during filming. Lorre said the situation raised serious concerns about the actor’s wellbeing and ultimately led him to shut down production.
Elsewhere in Sitcom , Lorre discusses casting challenges, including CBS executives’ initial opposition to Melissa McCarthy for Mike & Molly . He also reflects on his brief involvement with Scientology and his marriage to Arielle Mandelson.
Lorre’s memoir offers a candid account of the disputes and decisions behind several successful television comedies.

title: Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia  calls for immediate halt at UN
description: Reaffirms support for Kingdom   s security and sovereignty  urges full compliance with the Gaza ceasefire
content:
Reaffirms support for kingdom’s security and sovereignty; urges full compliance with the Gaza ceasefire
Pakistan on Thursday strongly condemned continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including its civilian and economic infrastructure, and called for an immediate halt to the strikes while reaffirming its unwavering support for the kingdom’s security, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Speaking at a United Nations Security Council (UNSC) debate on the Middle East, Pakistan’s Acting Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Usman Jadoon, expressed deep concern over the rapidly deteriorating situation in Yemen.
He said Pakistan backed the UN special envoy’s efforts to revive dialogue aimed at securing a comprehensive and lasting peace in Yemen.
Statement by Ambassador Usman Jadoon, Acting Permanent Representative of Pakistan to the UN, At the UN Security Council Open Debate on the Situation in the Middle East (15 October 2026) *********** Madam President, I thank Acting Special Coordinator – Mr. Ramiz Alakbarov for… pic.twitter.com/UJyj2sVlYY
The ambassador strongly condemned continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including its civilian and economic infrastructure, and called for an immediate halt to the strikes.
“We reiterate our unwavering support for the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the brotherly Kingdom, and reaffirm its right to self-defence under international law against any external attacks,” he said.
The condemnation comes amid an escalation in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and injuring 333 others. Abha airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia was also targeted amid renewed hostilities.
Yemen’s civil war reignited in July after a UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have since claimed hundreds of strikes on Houthi-held territory. The Houthis say the attacks have killed civilians, including women and children. Reuters could not independently verify those claims.
The Saudis entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of ‌the Yemeni capital ⁠Sanaa. The war became a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine.
A 2022 ceasefire reached by the Saudis and the Houthis unravelled this summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.
Jadoon said that Pakistan remains committed to advancing dialogue and diplomacy in the region to help de-escalate tensions, resolve differences and promote lasting peace and stability in the region.
Turning to the Palestinian issue, the ambassador said the two-state solution remained the internationally agreed framework and an indispensable foundation for a just and lasting peace.
“This international commitment to the two-State solution must be accompanied by concrete measures to preserve the territorial integrity and viability of the State of Palestine,” he said, while expressing support for the full and good-faith implementation of relevant UN resolutions and the New York Declaration.

Expressing concern over Israeli actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, he said settlement expansion, particularly the E1 project, threatened to sever Palestinian territorial contiguity.
“Settler violence, demolitions, land seizures and forced displacement are entrenching annexation and dismantling the foundations of peace,” he said.
He called for an end to all settlement activities in accordance with relevant UN resolutions, a halt to settler violence and accountability for those responsible.
E1, which stands for “East 1”, is an area east of Jerusalem between East Jerusalem and the large Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim. Experts have warned that the project could divide land the Palestinians hope will form part of an independent state, threatening the possibility of a two-state solution.
Jadoon also strongly condemned what he described as provocative and illegal incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque/Al-Haram Al-Sharif and called for respect for the historical and legal status quo of the holy sites.
He said continued ceasefire violations, the killing of Palestinians and restrictions on humanitarian access in Gaza remained a matter of grave concern.
The approaching winter threatened to worsen the suffering of families living amid widespread destruction without adequate shelter or essential services, he added.

“The ceasefire must be fully upheld, humanitarian assistance delivered unhindered and at scale, and recovery and reconstruction advanced without delay,” he said, stressing that the indispensable work of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) must be supported.
Pakistan rejected forced displacement and any attempt to fragment Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, which, he said, constituted a single territorial unit.
The ambassador also called for the release of withheld Palestinian revenues to enable the Palestinian Authority to fulfil its responsibilities.
He said collective efforts must focus on a credible, time-bound and irreversible political process to end the Israeli occupation and establish an independent, sovereign, contiguous and viable State of Palestine on pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital.
“This remains the only credible foundation for a just and lasting resolution of the Palestinian question,” he said.
“So long as the occupation continues and the Palestinian people’s legitimate yearning for self-determination goes unfulfilled, lasting peace in the Middle East will remain out of reach,” he said, reaffirming Pakistan’s unwavering support for the Palestinian people.
On Lebanon, Jadoon said full implementation of UN Security Council Resolution, respect for the cessation of hostilities and Israel’s withdrawal from occupied territory remained essential.
He said the Lebanese government’s call for the continuation of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) and a sustained UN presence in the country merited serious and favourable consideration by the Security Council.
On Syria, Pakistan welcomed the government’s efforts to foster internal stability and put the country on a positive trajectory.
“We reaffirm support for Syria’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity,” he said, adding that the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and Security Council resolutions 338 and 497 must be fully respected.

title: The space economy comes down to Earth
description: For Pakistan  bigger opportunity is therefore to build businesses  public services  research around satellite data
content:
For Pakistan, bigger opportunity is therefore to build businesses, public services, research around satellite data
Space policy in Pakistan is still discussed through launches, satellites and national prestige. That is understandable, but increasingly outdated. The global space economy is shifting from what goes into orbit to what comes back from it, for instance, data, connectivity, navigation, weather intelligence and services that improve decisions on Earth.
The numbers are striking. The OECD estimates global space-related revenues at $550-600 billion in 2025, already approaching the scale of the semiconductor industry. The World Economic Forum and McKinsey project the broader space economy to reach $1.8 trillion by 2035, up from $630 billion in 2023. Crucially, the fastest growth is expected not in rockets and spacecraft, but in "reach" sectors enabled by communications, positioning, navigation, timing and Earth observation.
For Pakistan, the bigger opportunity is therefore to build businesses, public services and research around satellite data.
That opportunity is becoming tangible. Pakistan launched PRSC-EO1 in January 2025, followed by PRSC-EO2 and PRSC-EO3 in 2026. SUPARCO lists applications ranging from precision agriculture and irrigation management to crop-yield prediction, urban planning, glacier and water monitoring, and disaster response. These uses sit directly inside some of Pakistan's most persistent economic vulnerabilities.
Agriculture is an obvious starting point. Satellite imagery combined with AI can identify crop stress, estimate acreage, monitor irrigation, predict yields and improve agricultural insurance. For a country repeatedly hit by floods, droughts and heat stress, Earth observation can also make disaster management less reactive. The OECD notes that more than 90% of observations assimilated into modern weather-forecasting systems come from satellites. This is not "space science" in the narrow sense, it is economic planning.
The same logic extends to cities, transport and finance. Satellite positioning underpins logistics, fleet management and digital mapping. Earth-observation data can identify unplanned urban expansion, monitor infrastructure, map flood exposure and help insurers price risk. WEF estimates that supply chains and transportation, food and beverages, defence, consumer industries and digital communications will generate more than 60% of the increase in the space economy through 2035.
Pakistan should stop treating a satellite launch as the end of a mission. Economically, it is only the beginning.
The missing layer is a domestic market that turns raw space data into usable products. The OECD reports that about 70% of data from active Earth-observation missions is now openly available globally. A Pakistani start-up does not need to own a satellite to build a crop-monitoring platform, flood-risk model, logistics product or climate-intelligence service. It needs access to data, computing capacity, skilled people, government demand and room to test and sell.
AI makes this more important. The OECD identifies AI-enabled data processing as a major frontier of space innovation. Competitive advantage will not belong only to countries that collect the most imagery, but to those that extract the best decisions from it. A satellite image of a field has limited economic value until an algorithm can tell a farmer, lender or insurer what has changed and what to do next.
Pakistan's National Space Policy already recognises commercial exploitation and private-sector participation. The challenge is to turn that language into an ecosystem.
First, Pakistan needs a national geospatial data common. Non-sensitive data from publicly funded missions should be available in standardised, machine-readable formats, with clear licensing and APIs for universities, start-ups and businesses.
Second, government should become an early customer. Ministries and provinces could issue competitive challenges around crop forecasting, illegal construction, flood mapping, water stress and road monitoring.
Third, SUPARCO should increasingly become a market-maker as well as an operator of space assets. A space-data accelerator linked with universities, agriculture departments, insurers, banks and telecom companies could help turn research into commercial services. Small validation grants and shared cloud-compute credits may generate faster returns than another demonstration project.
Fourth, Pakistan should measure the space economy properly. OECD work shows why conventional statistics miss much of its value: satellite-enabled activity appears inside agriculture, transport, telecoms, finance and software rather than under a neat "space" category. Without measurement, policymakers will celebrate inputs without knowing the output in exports, productivity or jobs.
There is also a strategic reason to act. Nearly 15,000 operational satellites were in orbit by mid-2026, while private operators accounted for 88% of satellites launched in 2025. Growth also carries costs. The OECD counts 45,860 tracked debris objects and more than 140 million smaller potentially damaging objects. Countries that fail to build domestic analytical capacity risk becoming permanent buyers of intelligence produced elsewhere.
The next phase should therefore be judged differently. How many farmers use satellite-derived advice? How much disaster loss is avoided? How many insurers price risk using local geospatial models? How many start-ups export space-enabled services? How many public decisions improve because data arrived earlier and was interpreted better?
A satellite becomes economically valuable not when it reaches orbit, but when its data reaches a farmer, insurer, logistics company, city planner or entrepreneur who can turn it into a better decision.

title: What next
description: Political inadequacies  in this case of the PTI  of which the instances are too many to quote
content:
Political inadequacies, in this case of the PTI, of which the instances are too many to quote
The test of any policy initiative, even if it involves showing an elected government out, is to ask the question: What next? In the case of K-P, where the PTI was shown the door, this question has assumed even greater relevance. In a way, the dissonance between the K-P/PTI and the Centre had been pervasive, and what ensued was the culmination of a long feud, misplaced or not. Whether it could have been avoided with better political management and honest and sincere coordination between the federation and a federating unit remains moot. PTI could have done a better job of its role and function – unless the aim was to only show the federal government down.
A standing threat to its political existence as a party and its government in K-P could have been avoided with a better sense of the dilemma that rode its prospects. From better governance to avoiding the pitfalls of keeping a feud going, there were off-ramps it could have taken. Instead, we have a situation of a drastic breakdown in which no side wins.
One thing is clear, though, that the responsibility to bring the change in K-P now rests with a single authority: the governor, his advisory council, his party, or the Centre that he represents with a single purpose to bring peace to a militarised province where cumulative failures of the past have only wrought strife and turmoil. Terror events in the province have increased manifold – there is a list being circulated from reliable quarters in support of why the intervention was inescapable.
That gives birth to two separate issues emanating from the Governor's rule and Emergency being simultaneously imposed on K-P: one, the PTI, its status, its relevance to national politics and its prospects in the future political architecture – especially given that the system is as pervasive as it is. This raises issues of fidelity and domains, but they are better left aside in the current environment. Second is the urgency to bring peace back to a troubled province with a consistent policy and strategy to eliminate terrorism and any signs of insurgency.
Political inadequacies, in this case of the PTI, of which the instances are too many to quote – beginning with its own governance record at the Centre and how it had permitted outside influence to mar democratic culture, to the dismissal of the two provincial assemblies that it still held the power over after it lost its government in April 2022, to now – when lack of conception in what might still help in its most trying times gave way to knocking heads against walls for want of creative choices. The party ran out of ideas and political choices as soon as it set itself on the path to what would be an ideological struggle. It was a case of visionless leadership and visionless politics.
In Pakistan, it is easy to place the Establishment in the dock over any or the slightest pretext, but if that be the only purpose of politics, there better be other things to do for those who indulge in it. In the end, this, and the only political impulse PTI exhibited, led to its demise. It can apply generically to the brand of politics in Pakistan across the board, but the others have negotiated their existence around those inadequacies. If it mars the credibility of democracy, it is for the unfortunate people of Pakistan who have no choice and no better hope.
The Centre now better get its act together. Failure can only be debilitating. Not only because terror will rule the roost in K-P, and further inland if we are that unfortunate, but it will engender outside control in a region of Pakistan with a record of ethnic affiliations that have tended to diffuse national boundaries. It is possible to regain control of all our regions, whether that be of the twelve districts where terrorism has found permanence under foreign elements, or of the entire province. We have done it before, and we can do it again. The duration, and the efficacy with which these operations are conducted, will decide if local hearts and minds will stand with the effort. If not, God forbid, the results can be entirely counterproductive; nay, dangerous to the foundations of the federation and its integrity. The failure of politics to coexist and to find a workable via media has rendered the nation to such risks. Failure in the new construct is not an option.
PTI too has its task cut out. If it seeks to find relevance in politics through its adversarial stand-off with the Establishment alone, it can only be self-defeating. While we may go on and on to seek some rationale in how the military has gained such eminence in our national make-up, we may never be able to resolve the conundrum to its desired end; it shall have to be the redefinition of politics and its characteristics away from what it has become in Pakistan – self-serving and rapacious – to being more purposeful in the interest of the people and the state. Rent-seeking and extraction must give way to a more grounded, realistic approach to policy choices in the interest of the common man. Currently, it is only the elites and those in power who benefit from the policies that have pushed the country to the brink. The politics being practised is not only irrelevant, it has also rendered it unsustainable for the needs of the country and its people.
Similarly, PTI will need to reinvent itself if it must sustain. Its purpose, its defining characteristics and its ethos will need a different thought process and a separate set of leaders who still wish to challenge the duopoly of the two other main political contenders. That is a great purpose. But then to be distracted by taking on fights which do not fall into your pale not only changes the character but the structure or the lack of it, and the means to that ill-defined aim. A party turns into a mob. If it must still be relevant, it must quickly revert to being a political party. Personalised enmities cannot be permitted to translate into institutional stand-offs. Such events are only episodic in nature, while political parties have a long-term aim and purpose which they cannot sacrifice at the altar of misplaced short-termism and in getting even with individuals.
Pakistan is once again at the crossroads. This one is self-created and self-imposed. Now that we have created a situation of our own making, we must navigate through it too with shared responsibility and equanimity. Showing dust to an adversary may be gladiatorial, but it isn't the stuff of nation-building. Its absence in our recent politics has brought us to this point; it is incumbent now upon all to help rebuild what we have broken.

title: Water is a right  not a weapon
description: Water is becoming increasingly entangled with geopolitics and conflict
content:
Water is becoming increasingly entangled with geopolitics and conflict
In January, United Nations researchers issued a stark warning: the world has moved beyond a water crisis and into a state of "global water bankruptcy". This warning was issued via a new flagship report from the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health, which also pointed out how decades of overuse and environmental degradation have pushed many rivers, aquifers, lakes, wetlands and glaciers into a post-crisis condition from which their historical 'normal' may no longer be recoverable.
Such a warning could hardly be timelier. Water is becoming increasingly entangled with geopolitics and conflict. In the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on critical infrastructure have highlighted the vulnerability of desalination facilities that supply drinking water to millions across the Gulf. When water infrastructure becomes part of a military confrontation, the consequences extend far beyond the battlefield.
But direct military conflict is not the only danger. Even the mismanagement of water can deepen existing political and social tensions. The Nile has become a source of prolonged tension between Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Environmental degradation around Lake Chad has intensified competition over scarce resources between pastoral and agricultural communities, and enabled Boko Haram to exploit weak governance and socioeconomic marginalisation to increase its influence.
The UN has thus aptly emphasised that water can be a driver of conflict, a weapon of conflict or a casualty of conflict. Conversely, however, water sharing can also serve as a basis for cooperation. It is in this latter context that the militarisation of the Indus river system needs to be understood. India's decision in 2025 to place the Indus Waters Treaty in "abeyance" disrupted a framework that survived several wars and decades of political hostility. While this treaty has several flaws which need to be addressed, suspending a treaty which enables institutional cooperation at a time of accelerating climate stress is especially dangerous.
Climate change is transforming the Himalayan rivers, and the Indus basin is already under immense pressure from rising temperatures, changing precipitation patterns and shifts in snow and glacial melt. The Indus is not simply a river divided between two hostile states. It is part of a rapidly changing cryosphere. Understanding these changes requires continuous scientific observation, hydrological data and cooperation across borders. Yet the deterioration of Indo-Pak relations threatens precisely the mechanisms that could make such knowledge possible.
Whatever disagreements India and Pakistan have over dams, allocations or security, they share a basic interest in knowing what is happening to the rivers and aquifers on which hundreds of millions depend. That means restoring regular hydrological data exchange and creating mechanisms for joint or independently verified monitoring of shared natural resources to better contend with climate impacts.
Moreover, for lower riparian countries such as Pakistan, the problem is not simply that there is too little water. Much of the water available is used inefficiently and distributed inequitably, while investment in drinking water, sewerage and sanitation remains far too weak. A country can therefore have a water-security crisis even while enormous volumes of water continue to flow through its rivers and irrigation systems.
Achieving water security cannot mean only building more dams or trying to control rivers. It must also mean using water efficiently, allocating it fairly, protecting aquifers and watersheds and ensuring that ordinary citizens have reliable access to safe water. Pakistan need not wait for India to restore the Indus Waters Treaty before undertaking these domestic measures.

title: Tax evasion warning
description: Tax evasion warning
content:
The Prime Minister's recent warning to tax evaders was effectively an admission that the government is incapable of meeting its revenue targets without taking coercive measures. At the same time, by declaring that there will be no concessions for those who dodge their fiscal responsibilities, the administration has explicitly identified a major challenge as being the culture of impunity, where the wealthy and influential treat tax laws as mere suggestions. Unfortunately for the government, the public already knew the problem, so there will be no brownie points until action is taken.
Despite years of incremental reforms, an unfair and unmanageable portion of revenue is still being squeezed out of the salaried class, just because the government still can't offer the rich enough carrots or threaten them with a suitable stick. While the common citizen sees their take-home pay eroded by inflation and rigid tax brackets, vast sectors of the economy - particularly in real estate and large-scale retail - operate in the shadows, shielded by political patronage. Their mere existence at this time points towards failure to craft and implement an equitable tax policy.
The government must move beyond rhetoric. True enforcement requires the courage to target the "untouchable elite" - powerful landlords and industrial titans who have historically negotiated their way out of arrears. Continuing to offer preferential treatment through "amnesty schemes" or "tax whitening" options, under the guise of broadening the tax base, will admit that the Prime Minister's fears were justified.
At the end of the day. the success of these reforms will be measured against the number of big tax evaders who face serious penalties, rather than the millions of salaried people who have already been squeezed past their limits.

title: Beyond the impasse
description: Both the opposition and the government are back to square
content:
Both the opposition and the government are back to square
With political instability at its peak, the TTAP has formulated a narrative to make headway. The six-party alliance has made it a condition that no talks will be held with the government unless the opposition leadership is granted an audience with the incarcerated PTI leader, Imran Khan. It also demanded an end to Chief Minister Sohail Afridi's detention, alongside the release of all legislators and workers, including Khan's three sisters. The debut meeting of the opposition since the imposition of emergency and Governor's Rule in K-P took stock of the prevailing political situation. It vehemently condemned the federal intervention in the province and decided to knock on the doors of the Peshawar High Court to challenge what it called an assault on the people's mandate.
Both the opposition and the government are back to square one, as talks failed – driven by the uncompromising rigidity on both sides. Had the ruling coalition ceded due political space to the PTI, and had the party shown greater flexibility instead of choosing absolute confrontation, this untoward situation could have been avoided. The question, nonetheless, is: what's next? By resorting to a major constitutional measure, the federal government has left little room for immediate political reconciliation. Consequently, the Center finds itself in a delicate position, as sustaining this impasse over the long term presents significant challenges. Furthermore, managing the security situation entirely on its own places a heavy administrative burden on the state.
In a highly competitive political environment, the administration continues to shoulder the complex responsibilities of ensuring efficient public service delivery, managing economic stability and maintaining law and order. Initiating a constructive dialogue offers a sustainable way to ease these governance pressures. In this context, facilitating requested communication, such as a meeting with Khan, and easing political tensions could help foster the long-term stability needed to move past the current impasse.

title: Classrooms of neglect
description: Compensation may provide some financial relief to grieving families  but it is no substitute for accountability
content:
Compensation may provide some financial relief to grieving families, but it is no substitute for accountability
A school should be the last place where parents fear for their children's lives. Yet the deaths of 31 students and a teacher in Peshawar's Al-Khair School roof collapse is an incident that should spring authorities into action. In a country where educational institutions are expected to shape the future, even the most basic guarantee of physical safety remains uncertain.
The tragedy reflects a wider culture of negligence in which structural safety is overlooked until a building collapses and innocent lives are lost. That an apparently weakened structure could be burdened with additional construction - even as children continued to attend classes - raises questions that cannot be answered through expressions of grief alone. More troubling is the frequency with which such disasters occur. The deaths of 14 children in a Lahore tuition centre collapse earlier this year should have prompted a comprehensive reassessment of school building safety. Instead, another tragedy has followed, suggesting that lessons are neither being learnt nor translated into preventive measures. The problem lies as much with regulatory indifference as with those who compromise construction standards to save costs. Private educational institutions cannot be allowed to operate in buildings whose structural integrity has never been properly established. Equally, the authorities responsible for granting permissions and monitoring compliance cannot escape scrutiny when their oversight proves ineffective. A school licence must represent an assurance of safety rather than merely permission to conduct business.
Compensation may provide some financial relief to grieving families, but it is no substitute for accountability. Nor can official promises restore the trust shattered by such an entirely preventable disaster. The government must abandon its reactive approach to public safety and establish a system in which dangerous buildings are identified before they become death traps. Until that happens, the state's repeated assurances about protecting children will ring hollow. Education is a fundamental right, but that right becomes meaningless if children must risk their lives merely to exercise it.

title: Rule by word of mouth
description: Rule by word of mouth
content:
In Pakistan, public officials may do only what the law allows
On October 3, the government launched a "Plastic-Free Islamabad" drive. Within days, a campaign against litter had become a campaign against lawful trade. Retailers and consumer goods companies were told to stop selling products packed in polyethylene terephthalate (PET), the clear plastic used for bottled water, soft drinks, juices and cooking oil. The instructions were verbal, attributed to the offices of the Chief Commissioner and the Chairman of the Capital Development Authority (CDA). From October 12, teams began sealing shops. No one has produced a written order, gazette notification or provision of law.
In Pakistan, public officials may do only what the law allows. The CDA Ordinance, 1960 limits the Chairman to duties "assigned to them by or under this Ordinance". It deals with master plans, development schemes, land acquisition, buildings and, where notified, municipal functions. Its commodity-specific control concerns natural resources used as building material. Nothing in it lets the CDA decide which lawful goods may sit on a shop shelf. Even where it permits sealing, it requires a written order and a chance to be heard.
The Islamabad Capital Territory (Administration) Order, 1980, and the notification under it, let the capital's administrator exercise powers that existing laws give a "Provincial Government", subject to federal instructions. That is a power to apply existing laws, not to create new bans. The Ministry of Interior cannot supply authority that Parliament has not given. Ministerial pledges to rid the city of plastic bottles by December 31 are policy announcements, not law.
Islamabad does have a plastics law. The Single-use Plastics (Prohibition) Regulations, 2023 were made by the Pakistan Environmental Protection Agency (Pak-EPA) under the Pakistan Environmental Protection Act, 1997. They name PET in their definition of plastic, then ban six items: polythene bags, straws, plastic crockery, cutlery, food-service ware and stirrers. PET bottles are not on the list. Instead, from July 2028, beverage bottles must contain at least 50 per cent recycled plastic. The choice was deliberate: PET is to be recycled, not banned.
On October 15, a Pak-EPA official told media that the agency is Islamabad's only environmental regulator and that there is no legal basis for removing PET bottles from sale. When the designated regulator says a product is lawful, other offices cannot quietly decide otherwise.
The costs are real. Sealed shops lose daily takings, and their owners have no formal order to challenge. Supply chains are disrupted. In the recycling sector, which depends on the value of used PET, jobs in collection and sorting are at risk.
Business groups have objected. The Overseas Investors Chamber of Commerce and Industry wrote to the Interior Minister seeking withdrawal of the ban. The Collect and Recycle (CoRe) Alliance approached the BOI and the SIFC. The American Business Forum appealed to the Interior Minister. Their message was the same: enforce the 2023 Regulations; do not replace them with an informal ban.
The Constitution is on their side. Article 4 says no action detrimental to a person's life, liberty, body, reputation or property shall be taken except in accordance with law. Article 18 protects lawful trade, subject only to qualifications "prescribed by law", and a verbal instruction prescribes nothing. Article 10A guarantees due process, which at a minimum means notice and a hearing before a livelihood is shut down. Section 24A of the General Clauses Act, 1897 requires officials to act fairly and give reasons for their orders. Sealing a shop without an order denies its owner every one of these protections.
This is not the first time verbal directives have stood in for gazetted rules. Each episode teaches businesses the same lesson: in Pakistan, the rule that matters may not be the one written down. That lesson raises the cost of capital, deters reinvestment and undermines the predictability that investment facilitation bodies exist to promise.
The administration should withdraw the instructions and de-seal affected shops. If PET needs tighter control, Pak-EPA can consult stakeholders and amend the 2023 Regulations through the procedure the law prescribes. Islamabad deserves to be clean. It also deserves to be governed by law.
