title: IHC orders blanket closure of shisha caf  s
description: IHC orders blanket closure of shisha caf  s
content:
Court directs withdrawal of existing NOCs until new rules are framed
The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Wednesday ordered the closure of all shisha cafés in the federal capital, directing the authorities to withdraw the no-objection certificates (NOCs) previously issued to them. The court ruled that all such establishments must remain closed until new rules are framed.
IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar issued the directions while hearing a petition seeking action against illegally operated shisha centres in Islamabad. The court's detailed written order will be issued later.
During the hearing a day earlier, the chief justice had summoned the Islamabad chief commissioner and deputy commissioner to explain how illegal shisha cafés were operating in the capital. The court had also directed them to submit affidavits assuring that no illegal shisha café would be allowed to operate.
The chief justice observed that no shisha café should operate in Islamabad until the relevant rules and regulations were framed. He questioned whether the authorities would permit illegal activities simply because the rules had not yet been introduced.
The court had previously directed that establishments operating in accordance with the law could continue their business, but the direction had been misinterpreted, the chief justice observed.
CJ Dogar also asked whether the government had framed rules to regulate shisha cafés. In response, the government's counsel informed the court that the proposed rules had been prepared and forwarded to the government for approval, which was expected shortly.
On the other hand, the Islamabad district administration launched action against sheesha cafes following the IHC order to close such establishments across the federal capital.
As a first step, the Shalimar Assistant Commissioner sealed four sheesha cafes in E-11, while Islamabad Deputy Commissioner directed all assistant commissioners to take immediate action in their respective areas.
The district administration has decided to launch a crackdown to ensure the implementation of the court's directions. All assistant commissioners have been instructed to take action against sheesha cafes without delay and ensure that the court order is implemented without discrimination.
According to the district administration, the no-objection certificates (NOCs) issued to cafe owners have been cancelled in compliance with the court's order.
The administration has directed assistant commissioners to take action against all types of cafes operating both indoors and outdoors. The instructions apply to establishments covered by the court's directions, and officials have been asked to ensure compliance in their respective jurisdictions.
The district administration stated that the court's orders would be implemented in full and without any discrimination.

title: Wanted suspect killed in 'CCD encounter' | The Express Tribune
description:
Wanted suspect killed
in 'CCD encounter'
content:
Police say accused was wanted in murder, robbery and child sexual abuse cases
A proclaimed offender wanted in several serious criminal cases, including murder, robbery, attempted murder and the sexual abuse of children, was killed in an alleged exchange of fire with a Crime Control Department (CCD) team in the Jatli police precinct late at night, while his accomplices "managed" to escape.
According to sources, the incident happened on Devi Data Main Road, where the CCD team was conducting routine snap-checking when motorcycle-borne suspects allegedly opened fire on the personnel.
The CCD team returned fire, killing one suspect identified as Hamad alias Maadu. He reportedly belonged to Khadiyot, an area of Kahuta.
Sources said the deceased was a PO wanted by law enforcement agencies in several serious cases, including murder during a robbery, attempted murder and the alleged sexual abuse of underage children at gunpoint.
The suspect was reportedly regarded as a source of fear in the area and allegedly posted videos of celebratory gunfire on social media to intimidate local residents. A pistol was reportedly recovered from the deceased following the exchange of fire, while his accomplices escaped under the cover of darkness.
The CCD team has launched a search operation in the area to arrest the fleeing suspects, with searches under way at various locations.
The body was shifted to the Tehsil Headquarters Hospital for an autopsy and other legal formalities.

title: PNCA hosts immersive exhibit
description: PNCA hosts immersive exhibit
content:
The Pakistan National Council of the Arts (PNCA) inaugurated a landmark solo exhibition titled "What Remains to Be Seen" which features the works of distinguished impressionist painter NusratJi at the National Art Gallery, Islamabad.
NusratJi is one of Pakistan's most distinguished impressionist painters with over 25 solo exhibitions and extensive international exhibitions across the UK, Canada, USA, UAE, Bahrain, and beyond. She has made a significant contribution to Pakistan's visual arts landscape.
The "What Remains to Be Seen" exhibition is divided into two galleries: Gallery 1, which presents the 'immersive experience' featuring projected imagery, light and sound, and Gallery 2, which comprises 'drawing & painting' exhibits featuring original paintings and 50 drawing studies. The exhibition is an immersive visual experience exploring memory, perception and the shifting space between what is seen and what remains unseen.
Addressing the audience at the inauguration ceremony, NusratJi talked about her artistic journey spanning over four decades.
In her statement, she said, "If colour has its charm, line has its own ecstasy." She explained that the exhibition features 100 studies alongside original paintings, drawn from life around her and it features the Thar Series, folklore, horses, architecture, calligraphy and nature, all of which carry energy, action and an inner rhythm of its own.
Other speakers at the ceremony included Dr Arjumand Faisel, Dr Mamoona Khan and Mr. Sajjad Haider. They spoke about Nusrat's paintings, drawings and the concept of the immersive exhibition.

title: Twin cities choke on toxic air
description: Twin cities choke on toxic air
content:
Air pollution reaches alarming levels in Islamabad, Rawalpindi ahead of smog season
Air pollution has reached alarming levels across Rawalpindi, Islamabad, Murree and other districts of the Rawalpindi division even before the onset of the smog season, raising concerns about the spread of respiratory and other pollution-related illnesses. Efforts by the Environment Protection and Climate Change Department to improve air quality have so far failed to produce the desired results.
Lahore's Air Quality Index (AQI) has reached a hazardous 228, while Rawalpindi has recorded an AQI of 147, rising to 163 in areas around industrial units and brick kilns. The AQI in Murree, popularly known as the Queen of the Hills, has crossed 100 to reach 115. Among other districts in the Rawalpindi division, the AQI stands at 150 in Attock, 137 in Jhelum and 143 in Talagang, while Islamabad has recorded an index of 100.
Air quality has deteriorated across the region, with Lahore emerging as one of the most polluted cities. Last year, the environment department had imported modern vehicles and equipment to control pollution and improve environmental conditions across Punjab. However, air quality readings continue to indicate worsening pollution despite these measures.
The deteriorating air quality has reportedly led to an increase in cases of irritation of the eyes, nose and throat, as well as colds and other respiratory complaints, even before the peak smog season. Government hospitals and neighbourhood clinics are receiving increasing numbers of patients suffering from these ailments.
Environmental inspectors have identified vehicle emissions, growing traffic congestion, smoke from ageing vehicles and heavy trucks, industrial emissions and brick kilns as major sources of pollution. The use of low-quality coal and biomass in industrial units and brick kilns further contributes to the problem. Open burning of garbage, tyres and other waste is another significant source of harmful emissions.
Weather conditions also play a role. From October to February, falling temperatures and atmospheric conditions can trap smoke and pollutants close to the ground, intensifying air pollution.
Medical experts have advised residents to take precautions as air quality deteriorates. Motorcyclists, pedestrians and others spending time outdoors have been advised to wear masks, preferably N95 respirators, when pollution levels are high. People should avoid strenuous outdoor exercise, particularly during periods of poor air quality, and keep doors and windows closed when outdoor pollution is severe. Children, older people and those suffering from asthma or heart conditions have been urged to take extra care.
Taking serious notice of the rising AQI, Deputy Commissioner Nadeem Nasir has ordered immediate and stringent measures to curb pollution.

title: PEMRA bans live coverage of terror attacks
description: PEMRA bans live coverage of terror attacks
content:
Orders channels to air only verified information
The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) on Wednesday directed satellite television channels to refrain from broadcasting or providing live coverage of explosions, blasts, firing and terrorist attacks, warning that violations would invite legal action.
In a notification issued on October 13, the regulator reiterated its prohibition order dated February 20, 2023, directing news, current affairs and regional-language channels to refrain from broadcasting, rebroadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.
"All satellite TV channel licensees are once again hereby directed to refrain from broadcast, re-broadcast and live coverage of any unfortunate/unpleasant incident such as explosion, blast, firing, terrorist attack etc," the notification read.
"Satellite TV channels must broadcast only such verified information, warranted by the concerned department/law enforcement agency," it added.
The notification also directed channels to "effectively use time delay mechanism" and ensure the constitution of an independent editorial board in accordance with PEMRA laws, a Supreme Court judgment in suo motu case No 28 of 2018, and an Islamabad High Court order issued on September 5, 2022.
The regulator warned that violations would invite legal action under Sections 29A, 30 and 33 of the PEMRA Ordinance, 2002, as amended.

title: FCC rejects Bushra Bibi s petition
description: FCC rejects Bushra Bibi s petition
content:
Rules Al-Qadir Trust appeal should be decided expeditiously
The PTI has suffered a major setback in the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), which has dismissed a petition filed by former prime minister Imran Khan's wife, Bushra Bibi, seeking suspension of her sentence in the Al-Qadir Trust case.
The court observed that the main appeal should be decided expeditiously rather than undertaking a parallel examination of the matter.
"The principal grievance urged by learned counsel for the appellant pertains to the repeated adjournments allegedly sought by the National Accountability Bureau (NAB), resulting in prolongation of the proceedings on the application for suspension of sentence. Be that as it may, the main appeal having already been fixed for hearing, the appropriate course would be to secure its expeditious adjudication rather than undertake a parallel examination of the merits of suspension of sentence at this stage," a three-page order issued by a division bench of FCC led by Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan said
Imran and Bushra remain incarcerated in Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail. They were sentenced on December 20, 2025, to 17 years in prison in the Toshakhana-II case, while in January last year, an Islamabad accountability court sentenced Imran to 14 years and Bushra to seven years in prison in the Al- Qadir Trust case.
Salman Safdar appeared on behalf of Bushra Bibi before the FCC.
The order said that the appellant's assertion that the appeal involves a voluminous record necessitating elaborate arguments does not, by itself, furnish sufficient justification for interference with the order.
"It is, therefore, incumbent upon the counsel for appellant to extend full assistance to the High Court in the hearing of the main appeal, whereafter NAB shall be equally obligated to advance its arguments without seeking unwarranted adjournments."
The FCC observed that they found no sufficient ground warranting interference with the order at this stage.
"We, however, expect that the High Court shall endeavour to decide the main appeal, affording both sides adequate opportunity of hearing while discouraging unnecessary adjournments. Consequently, the instant appeal is dismissed, with the aforesaid observations," the order read.
Since its establishment, the PTI had been showing reluctance to approach the FCC whose judges are appointed by present government.
Our apprehensions have come true after rejection of Bushra Bibi's petition without issuance of notice to other side, a PTI lawyer said.
It is worth noting that the present government amended the National Accountability Ordinance (NAO), 1999, to empower the FCC to hear appeals against high court decisions in NAB cases.

title: PTI leadership goes into hiding

content:
'Afridi was alone when taken into protective custody'
Most members of the former Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) cabinet have reportedly gone into hiding amid fears of arrest following the imposition of governor's rule and emergency in the province. Details have also emerged regarding the protective custody of former chief minister Sohail Afridi and other senior PTI leaders.
According to sources, 16 ministers, six advisers, eight special assistants and 23 parliamentary secretaries have remained out of public view for five days. Their mobile phones are reportedly switched off, making it difficult to contact them.
The sources said the provincial cabinet and PTI's provincial leadership began distancing themselves from Afridi on the night of October 10-11, as reports emerged that the federal government had decided to impose emergency rule. The move was formally announced on October 11.
Afridi had reached the Chief Minister's House from Mardan on October 10 when, according to sources, he was informed during a core committee meeting that the federal government had decided to impose emergency rule.
Several of his close associates reportedly left the Chief Minister's House one by one. When Afridi was taken into protective custody the following day, members of his inner circle were also absent, the sources said.
Two cabinet members, Fazal Shakoor and Dr Amjad Ali, had allegedly been abducted even before the imposition of governor's rule. The PTI has separately claimed that eight members of the provincial assembly and three members of the National Assembly are missing.
In a separate account of the October 11 operation, sources said the process to take Afridi into protective custody began at noon at the Chief Minister's House. He was found alone in his room after his close associates had left.
A team that included a senior police officer met the former chief minister and remained with him for around 45 minutes, according to the sources. Afridi appeared upset and disappointed with the conduct of the PTI leadership, they added.
During the meeting, officials asked him about his plans for the long march. Afridi reportedly said he had not intended to take the march to Islamabad and that talks with the government, involving JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, had taken place the previous night.
According to the sources, Afridi told the officials that the federal government had agreed to the demands for a meeting with PTI founder Imran Khan and his transfer to a hospital.
He said discussions had also taken place with party leaders and that he had been waiting for instructions to announce the end of the march.
Asked about proposed amendments to the Police Act, Afridi reportedly said he had not intended to amend the law but had raised the issue to exert pressure.
Official sources said Afridi was neither handcuffed nor placed in a prison van. Instead, he was moved in a vehicle to a secure location, they added.
Provincial Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati was also taken into protective custody from the Speaker's House. PTI leader Junaid Akbar, a provincial lawmaker, a party social media official and former Gilgit-Baltistan chief minister Khalid Khurshid were also present there and taken into custody.
The sources said the operation to take Afridi, Swati, Akbar and the other individuals into protective custody was completed in around two hours. They were subsequently moved to a secure location.

title: SC rules cancelled mutations cannot establish ownership
description: SC rules cancelled mutations cannot establish ownership
content:
Says disputed property claims require declaration of title alongside possession
The Supreme Court on Wednesday has ruled that cancelled mutation entries cannot, by themselves, establish legal ownership of property, observing that where title is disputed, a suit seeking possession alone is insufficient and must also seek a declaration of ownership.
The court dismissed an appeal concerning possession of one kanal of land in Kamalia, upholding the Lahore High Court's judgment.
In a judgment authored by Justice Shahid Waheed, the court held that the legal heirs of deceased appellant Abdul Rahim had failed to establish their lawful title to the disputed land. The relevant mutations had been cancelled by the District Officer Revenue on November 23, 2004, while the original sale deeds were not produced before either the trial court or the appellate court.
A three-member bench comprising Justice Jamal Khan Mandokhail, Justice Shahid Waheed and Justice Irfan Saadat Khan heard the case on October 13, 2026.
According to the judgment, the appellant claimed to have purchased the land from Ilahi Bakhsh and others through Mutation No. 8106 dated September 30, 1985, and filed a suit for possession on July 21, 1993.
The government educational institution concerned, however, maintained that the land had been in the possession of Government Normal School Kamalia since 1926. The institution is now known as Government College Elementary Teachers Kamalia.
The Supreme Court observed that revenue entries do not, by themselves, constitute documents of title, and their cancellation does not automatically invalidate the underlying sale deeds. However, the appellant failed to establish ownership through the required legal evidence because the original sale deeds had not been produced.

title: PSX rebounds  gains 641 points
description: PSX rebounds  gains 641 points
content:
Index-heavy stocks support late recovery following profit-taking
Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) staged a sound recovery on Wednesday as renewed buying towards the close lifted the benchmark index firmly into the positive territory, reversing the previous session's trend after volatile trading amid domestic political uncertainty and rising international oil prices.
The KSE-100 index gained 641.07 points, or 0.39%, and settled at 165,417.51. It touched the intra-day high of 165,629.35 and low of 164,060.34. Earlier, the market opened on a cautious note, with the index rising to 165,032.13, gaining 255.69 points, or 0.16%, by 9:33 am. However, continuous fluctuations pushed it into negative territory and the bourse hit 164,770.12 at 12:38 pm, down 6.32 points.
Sentiment remained subdued amid political uncertainty following the imposition of governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. Selling pressure was evident across key sectors; however, fresh buying of index-heavy stocks of banking, oil and gas, and power sectors supported the recovery and helped the market close in the black. Internationally, oil prices climbed after two vessels were struck in the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian officials announced new tactics to target ships as Tehran sought to keep oil prices high ahead of US midterm elections.
KTrade Securities wrote in its market wrap that the KSE-100 index gained 641 points (+0.4%) as oil prices remained stable near $106/barrel and the absence of fresh negative news improved investor sentiment. Despite early gains and subsequent profit-taking, renewed buying towards the close helped the market recover and finish firmly in the green, reversing the previous day's trend.
Support came from commercial banks, investment banks, cement, fertiliser and refinery stocks, with Engro Holdings, Lucky Cement, Fauji Fertiliser, Bank AL Habib and NBP among the key contributors. Meanwhile, Cnergyico Pk, K-Electric, The Bank of Punjab and TRG Pakistan led individual stock volumes, with total turnover remaining subdued around 150 million shares.
KTrade said low volumes reflected caution due to high oil prices, geopolitical uncertainty and currency concerns, while sustained buying and higher turnover were needed to maintain momentum. "Limited positive activity was observed at the PSX, driven primarily by buying interest in the refinery sector, although overall market participation remained subdued. Investors maintained a cautious stance amid a lack of fresh triggers and persistent geopolitical uncertainty," commented JS Global analyst Nawaz Ali.
Arif Habib Limited Deputy Head of Trading Ali Najib said value buying and institutional participation in select stocks drove the recovery, lifting the KSE-100 above 165,000. Oman and Iran concluded discussions on a proposed Hormuz deal, but final arrangements depended on US-Iran talks and other outstanding issues, Oman's foreign minister said. Engro Holdings, Lucky Cement, Fauji Fertiliser, Bank AL Habib and NBP collectively contributed 382 points to the index's gains, while MCB, Hub Power, Pakistan Oilfields, PTCL and National Foods eroded 134 points.
Najib said the KSE-100's recovery above 165,000, alongside improved volumes, may offer near-term support, though US-Iran tensions, high oil prices and domestic political uncertainty could fuel volatility and restrict gains.
Overall trading volumes jumped to 585.9 million shares against Tuesday's total of 383.7 million. The value of traded shares stood at Rs20 billion.

title: Iqbal sets  100b export target for 2035

Planning minister says export success requires policy continuity beyond political transitions
Federal Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has said Pakistan must raise exports to $100 billion by 2035 to reduce dependence on external borrowing, urging policymakers to prioritise competitiveness, investment and long-term policy continuity.
Inaugurating the 39th International Conference and Annual General Meeting of the Pakistan Society of Development Economists (PSDE) at the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE), he called for a globally competitive, export-driven economy to overcome recurring balance-of-payments crises and strengthen economic sovereignty. The conference is being held under the theme "Mission $100 Billion: The National Race for Sustainable Export-led Prosperity."
"A nation's economic sovereignty rests on its ability to pay its way in the world," the minister said, highlighting Pakistan's widening export gap with successful Asian economies.
Under URAAN Pakistan, he emphasised competitive clusters, complete value chains and integration into global supply networks. He urged PIDE and the research community to develop actionable export roadmaps identifying products, markets, missing capabilities, institutional responsibilities and delivery timelines. He stressed that export success requires policy continuity beyond political transitions and welcomed research that challenges government assumptions.
Delivering his presidential address, "Why Pakistan Does Not Export More: Rewiring Pakistan's Economy for Global Competitiveness," PIDE Vice Chancellor and PSDE President Dr Nadeem Javaid argued that Pakistan's export weakness reflects an economic incentive structure that has made competing internationally less attractive than serving protected domestic markets.
He described a self-reinforcing export trap: a narrow export base intensifies foreign-exchange pressures, which constrain the investment and productive imports needed to build competitiveness.
"One hundred billion dollars is the scoreboard, not the strategy," Dr Javaid said, stressing that pathways must build firms' capabilities, with support disciplined by measurable performance and success judged by better jobs, higher real wages and improved living standards.

title: FBR receives only 130 returns under traders  tax scheme
description: FBR receives only 130 returns under traders  tax scheme
content:
Scheme offers one-page return, minimum Rs25,000 annual tax and protection from routine inspections; official says 500,
The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has received only 130 income tax returns under its special tax scheme for small traders and shopkeepers, far below the 500,000 to 600,000 filings it had expected, a senior official said.
Speaking on The Express Tribune podcast, Sayyeda Maimuna, Second Secretary at the FBR headquarters' Transformation Delivery Unit, said the scheme had been introduced in consultation with traders to simplify tax compliance, expand the tax base and reduce the burden of complicated filing procedures.
Under the scheme, eligible traders can pay a minimum annual tax of Rs25,000 or 1% of their annual turnover, depending on the applicable calculation. They can file a simplified, one-page return through the Tax Asaan app or the FBR's online system. Maimuna said the initiative addressed traders' concerns about complicated tax returns, professional fees and the time required to visit government offices. Small shopkeepers without access to digital facilities can seek assistance at Regional Tax Offices' taxpayer facilitation centres.
"We have brought this scheme to fill the gap. We want our tax base to expand," she said, expressing disappointment over the low number of returns filed despite consultations with trade bodies. She said traders could either opt for the special scheme or file their regular income tax returns. Those choosing the normal filing route would remain subject to the applicable tax laws and requirements.
Maimuna clarified that individuals earning below the annual taxable income threshold of Rs600,000 were not required to pay income tax, although they could still have to fulfil applicable return-filing obligations. She said the scheme offered participating traders protection from routine FBR inspections, raids and shop sealing, with a green identification display outside their premises indicating their participation. However, she cautioned that the simplified system did not mean the FBR would ignore significant discrepancies between declared earnings and information obtained from third parties. Where substantial contradictions emerged, the board could bring the matter to the attention of relevant trade associations.
The official said small traders had also been exempted from certain technical requirements associated with point-of-sale (POS) systems and digital invoicing, while the scheme provided relief from withholding tax under Section 153, subject to applicable conditions.
Addressing concerns about sharing financial information with the tax authorities, Maimuna said the law required the FBR to protect taxpayers' data. She added that the board was investing in digital systems to improve its ability to identify economic activity and promote a cashless, paperless economy.
She urged traders facing difficulties in registering or filing returns to approach their Regional Tax Offices for assistance. Maimuna also outlined the penalties applicable to non-compliance, saying these could include fines for failing to file income tax returns or wealth statements, as well as measures such as blocking SIM cards, disconnecting electricity connections or sealing business premises where legally authorised.
She advised taxpayers to consult the FBR's official website for authentic notifications regarding filing deadlines, warning against relying on fake announcements circulating online. Traders who believe their rights under the scheme have been violated can approach the relevant Regional Tax Office, lodge a complaint with the Federal Tax Ombudsman or contact the FBR through its helpline and official email channels.
Maimuna said broadening the tax base would distribute the tax burden more fairly across traders, professionals, property owners and salaried individuals. However, she added, the benefits of wider compliance would emerge gradually rather than immediately.

title: MNCs oppose recyclable bottles ban
description: MNCs oppose recyclable bottles ban
content:
Islamabad's restriction on reusable plastic sparks fear among foreign investors
Panic has gripped the American Business Forum (ABF), the Overseas Investors Chamber of Commerce and Industry (OICCI) and the Collect and Recycle (CoRe) Alliance after the federal authorities suddenly decided to ban the use of recyclable bottles by the beverages sector in breach of international and local regulations.
The move to suddenly ban the use of 100% recyclable polyethene terephthalate (PET) in the Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) has sent shockwaves, mostly among multinational companies, which were already complying with the international and local environmental standards. ABF requested the withdrawal of the proposed ban on PET bottles and the effective enforcement of the ICT Single-Use Plastics Regulations, 2023, in an appeal to the minister for interior.
Separately, the OICCI and the CoRe Alliance approached the minister for finance, minister for investment and minister for climate change to review the proposed ban, which was also threatening foreign investment and the circular economy.
"The CoRe Alliance seeks your office's intervention to withdraw the proposed ban on PET bottles, ensure effective enforcement of the ICT Single-Use Plastics Regulations, 2023, and support the government's broader efforts to promote ease of doing business, attract and retain foreign investment, and maintain a predictable, investment-friendly regulatory environment," read a letter sent to the investment minister.
The alliance ensured its commitment to advancing circular economy solutions in Pakistan. The multinational companies and their advocacy groups in Pakistan stated that the leading international regulatory frameworks, including the European Union's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR), prioritise packaging recyclability, effective collection and recycling systems, and Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), rather than imposing blanket bans on recyclable PET beverage packaging.
They panicked after the Islamabad Capital Administration started raiding shops for using PET bottles without realising that these bottles were already in compliance with the regulations. The alliance said that there was also no notification issued by the CDA or the Ministry of Interior for banning PET and its removal from trade. They said that the PET bottles were fully compliant with the Pak EPA Single-Use Plastics Regulations of 2023. PET is on the positive list of plastic packaging.
The alliance, the OICCI and the American Business Forum said that reportedly, on the instructions of the Office of the Chief Commissioner, and chairman Capital Development Authority (CDA), retailers and Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) companies in ICT were advised to discontinue the sale of products packaged in polyethene terephthalate bottles across various categories.
The CoRe Alliance believes that such a ban would be scientifically unjustified, environmentally counterproductive, inconsistent with international circular economy best practices, and detrimental to businesses operating in the country, it added. Furthermore, the proposed ban contradicts the spirit of the ICT Single-Use Plastics (Prohibition) Regulations, 2023.
PET is a lightweight, food-grade, 100% recyclable polymer with an established collection and recycling value chain. Unlike some plastics, post-consumer PET bottles are commercially valuable and sought after for recycling into fibres, packaging and new bottles, supporting economic activity and livelihoods across collection, sorting and recycling.
A ban could undermine this circular economy value chain. Scientific life-cycle assessments evaluate packaging impacts from raw material extraction and manufacturing to transportation, collection and end-of-life management, according to CoRe. Replacing PET with glass, aluminium or other single-use alternatives may not improve environmental outcomes, as heavier materials can increase transportation emissions while others require more energy and resources for production, it added.
The priority should therefore be to strengthen existing PET waste collection, segregation and recycling systems to prevent environmental leakage, rather than banning a valuable and recyclable material, according to these representative bodies.
Similarly, the ICT Single-Use Plastics (Prohibition) Regulations, 2023, notified under the Pakistan Environmental Protection Act, 1997, already provides a regulatory foundation for addressing plastic pollution. Rather than pursuing a blanket PET ban, the government should strengthen implementation through mandatory producer-funded collection and recycling systems, measurable recovery targets, waste segregation and investment in recycling infrastructure, it added.
Various reports indicated that local administrative authorities commenced enforcement actions, which included the sealing of several retail outlets across the city. Industry experts and business leaders have warned against such coercive measures.

Adviser to the Prime Minister on Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar Khan, who attended as chief guest, said Pakistan and China enjoyed a longstanding friendship founded on mutual trust and respect, and that the next phase of cooperation must translate the relationship into industrial investment, technology transfer, manufacturing and export growth. The proposed venture aims to promote technology transfer, develop local manufacturing capabilities and explore production of export-ready vehicles under the Made in Pakistan banner.
The adviser said electric mobility offered Pakistan opportunities to expand its manufacturing base and develop local supply chains, adding that cooperation with Chinese companies could move the country towards higher-value production.
The event was attended by about 150 dignitaries and a 14-member Chinese business delegation.

title: Restructuring of regulatory bodies soon
description: Restructuring of regulatory bodies soon
content:
Govt believes some regulators do not work independently, operate under influence of ministries
The government has decided to conduct a study to restructure regulatory bodies as some organisations exercise regulatory powers from within ministries, raising questions about their independence.
The government has described some as "blurred ministry and regulator roles". It feels that they are under the influence of some ministries and the regulatory bodies are exercising regulatory powers from within the ministries, which raise questions about the independence of regulators. The proposed focus of the study will be on making the federal regulators effective and accountable without eroding the independence credible regulation depends on.
Owing to this, the government is of the view that the situation requires a review. The role of regulators is to safeguard the interests of consumers but they are working under complete control of the ministries while ignoring the welfare of consumers.
Moreover, rapid expansion has taken place since 2024 and new authorities for virtual assets, seeds and food safety have come on stream. This also underscores the need for a review of the regulators to ensure their independence.
The government is working on autonomy versus accountability of the regulators. Recurring tariff, licensing and enforcement questions have been raised. In the energy sector, two regulators are functioning, whose decisions have a direct impact on consumers. These include the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) and the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra).
These regulatory bodies come under the administrative control of the cabinet but are following directives from the Ministry of Energy. Hardly, they are said to have taken decisions that shield the interests of consumers.
In the power sector, Nepra has allowed companies to set up power plants by giving the incentive of capacity charges, which put a burden of over Rs2 trillion on consumers every year. In a recent case, the regulator increased the multi-year tariff of K-Electric but reversed the decision following a motion filed by the Power Division. Such decisions are alleged to have caused controversies.
Earlier, in the rental power case, the Supreme Court ruled that Nepra should not follow the "manipulated" decisions of the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC).
Similarly, Ogra has been locked in controversies as in the past it granted licences to oil marketing companies despite not meeting the requirement of building storages. It also issued licences to LPG marketing companies in bulk, though only a few had LPG supplies.
Sources were of the view that the federal bodies with regulatory powers had been developed over seven decades, which now require a review under the present circumstances. The study will address three questions – how they were designed, how well they functioned and whether statutory aims were met.
It will also examine the purpose of the law and the failures each law fixes, whether it still holds and whether regulation is still the right tool. The study will propose key recommendations relating to legal, institutional, financial, capacity and system gaps.
The federal bodies have been divided into three groups. First is related to sector and independent regulators, which include Nepra, Ogra, the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority, State Bank of Pakistan, Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan, Competition Commission of Pakistan, Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan and Pakistan Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority.
The other category comprises technical, safety and professional services, which include Pak-Environmental Protection Agency, Pakistan Standards and Quality Control Authority, Pakistan Engineering Council, PNDC and quarantine departments. The third category has hybrid and borderline bodies including the Higher Education Commission, HRSA, Public Procurement Regulatory Authority, Alternative Energy Development Board, PDA and Special Technology Zones Authority.

title: Gold falls on US inflation fears
description: Gold falls on US inflation fears
content:
Prices drop Rs3,000/tola locally; rupee edges up to 276.95/$
Gold prices in Pakistan fell sharply on Wednesday, shedding Rs3,000 per tola, as bullion extended its decline in international markets amid rising expectations of a US Federal Reserve rate hike following stronger-than-expected inflation data.
In the local market, gold prices settled at Rs437,836 per tola, according to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association. Similarly, the price of 10-gram gold decreased by Rs2,572 to Rs375,373. The latest decline followed an increase of Rs900 per tola on Tuesday, reversing the previous session's gains as international prices came under pressure from a stronger US dollar and rising Treasury yields.
In the international market, spot gold fell 1.7% to $4,086.06 per ounce by 9:03 am EDT (1303 GMT), touching its lowest level since October 7. US gold futures for December delivery dropped 1.6% to $4,108.60 per ounce, as per Reuters. Gold extended its losses for a third consecutive session after US consumer prices accelerated in September, strengthening expectations that the Fed could raise rates this month.
The US dollar index gained 0.4%, making dollar-denominated gold more expensive for holders of other currencies. Meanwhile, rising yields on 10-year US Treasury bonds added further pressure on the non-yielding precious metal.
Adnan Agar, Director of Interactive Commodities, said international gold prices had touched the low of $4,080 per ounce during the day, after reaching the high of $4,190. The market was trading around $4,090 at the time of his assessment. He attributed the downward pressure to rising US inflation, which increased expectations of tighter monetary policy, while elevated oil prices could add to inflationary pressures.
Agar said some international analysts were anticipating the possibility of gold declining towards $3,700-$3,800 per ounce in the coming days. He added that a sustained recovery in gold could depend partly on a decline in oil prices. Conversely, oil moving towards $100-$108 per barrel could weigh further on bullion by reinforcing inflation concerns and expectations of higher interest rates.
However, the outlook will depend on subsequent economic data, central bank signals and movements in the dollar and bond yields. Meanwhile, the Pakistani rupee gained Rs0.01 against the US dollar, closing at 276.95 in the inter-bank market.

title: Pakistan eyes double B rating  FinMin
description: Pakistan eyes double B rating  FinMin
content:
Aurangzeb cites 22-year-low fiscal deficit, three years of primary surpluses
Pakistan is aiming to enter the double-B sovereign rating category through sustained economic improvements, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb has said, citing a fiscal deficit at a 22-year low, three consecutive years of primary surpluses and foreign exchange reserves at a historic high covering three months of imports, according to an official statement issued by the Ministry of Finance on Wednesday.
The minister held a series of engagements with international investors, credit rating agencies, multilateral financial institutions and US officials on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
At the Citi Macro Forum and Standard Chartered Bank's Sovereign Investor Roundtable, he outlined a capital market strategy including further Panda bond issuances, Sukuk and a proposed rupee-denominated, dollar-settled international bond, emphasising lower borrowing costs, longer debt maturities and reduced rollover risks. He said economic growth could reach or exceed 4% this fiscal year.
In a meeting with S&P Global Ratings, the minister highlighted the September bond issuance, strong investor participation and progress under the IMF programme, along with improved tax collections, reserve accumulation and reduced swap and forward liabilities. He noted S&P's emphasis on policy continuity, reform implementation, a lower interest burden and stronger external buffers.
Addressing the MENAP meeting with the IMF managing director, he cited economic growth of 3.7% and the October 7 staff-level agreement. He reaffirmed commitment to targeted, budget-neutral and time-bound subsidies to protect low-income groups, and called for diversified energy sources, deeper regional integration and investment in logistics and food systems.
In a meeting with Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) President Zou Jiayi, the minister identified power transmission and railway modernisation as priorities, with AIIB targeting approval of a transmission project before the end of the year. Discussions covered the Karachi-Rohri section of the ML-1 railway project, possible co-financing with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and emergency budget support for energy and food security pressures.
With MIGA Managing Director Tsutomu Yamamoto, he said financing terms should reflect Pakistan's improved ratings and renewed market access, expressing satisfaction that MIGA had revised its pricing. The meeting reviewed a hydropower-related case before the UK Supreme Court.
Meeting IMF Deputy Managing Director Nigel Clarke, the minister emphasised political ownership and sustained reform implementation, noting stronger reserves and a declining debt-to-GDP ratio. He also met US State Department Ambassador Yon to review a trade framework agreement, energy diversification, Reko Diq, critical minerals, Boeing aircraft acquisition, digital asset regulation and DFC and EXIM Bank financing.

title: NTP built on inflated figures
description: NTP built on inflated figures
content:
Manufacturer says tariff was 10.3%, not 18.54%; ministry cites ACD and RD
Manufacturer Aamir Allawala told a government-sponsored seminar on Thursday that authorities used a wrong figure of 18.5% for the National Tariff Policy (NTP) to make a case for a 52% cut by claiming Pakistan had the highest tariffs in South Asia.
Allawala disclosed that the government included customs duty, additional customs duty (ACD) and regulatory duty (RD) to show Pakistan's tariff in 2023 was 18.54%, but said comparative tariffs of India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and other regional economies were based only on customs duty. He used World Trade Organisation (WTO) data to prove his point and shared the link to the source.
He said that against the claimed tariff figure of 18.54%, Pakistan's tariff was 10.3%, which was not only lower than the regional average but also far lower than India and Bangladesh.
Interestingly, the commerce ministry had last year shared similar figures on its website as part of the tariff policy but subsequently removed those slides.
When contacted, the commerce ministry spokesperson said the WTO "has not clarified about the inclusion or exclusion of para-tariffs of any country including the countries located in South Asia, however, WTO does not include para tariffs in the calculation of simple average in their tariff profile report," according to the commerce ministry.
It was responding to a question about the tariff rates given in the NTP for regional countries that were inclusive of para-tariffs, as was in the case of Pakistan.
The World Bank, which provided technical support for the preparation of the tariff policy, did not respond to a set of questions about using any wrong numbers for making a case for tariff cuts.
The commerce ministry said para-tariff, as per the WTO, means border charges, fees or levies imposed on foreign trade transactions that function like a tariff but are not included in a country's official customs tariff schedule. It added that the WTO calculates countries' tariffs based on the information provided by the respective countries.
Allawala shared these startling details at the 39th International Conference and Annual General Meeting of the Pakistan Society of Development Economists (PSDE). The conference was organised by the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics under the banner of the Ministry of Planning.
The drafters of the policy, currently in its second year of implementation, challenged the statement, which if proven correct can open a Pandora's Box for the World Bank, the Prime Minister's Office, the commerce ministry and the National Tariff Commission.
According to Allawala, the NTP inflated Pakistan's tariff to make it look like the highest. It added Pakistan's extra import duties to Pakistan's number only, turning the WTO's 10.3% into 18.5%, and compared that with every other country's customs duty alone. It did the same in its trade-weighted chart: 10.36% shown in the NTP, against the WTO's 7.6%, according to Allawala.
The basic premise used for the NTP that Pakistan's tariffs were the highest in South Asia is not correct and an apple had been compared with an orange to prove that, he said. The NTP should be reopened and the error rectified, he added.
To a question whether the Prime Minister's Office, the World Bank and the commerce ministry misled the nation, Allawala said he would not judge intentions, as it was a complex matter and there was a possibility that the Prime Minister's Office might not have been properly briefed.
To a question whether the prime minister should order an investigation to ascertain the facts, Dr Rubina Athar, a strong proponent of trade liberalisation, said the figures were misleading, as those used for the NTP were also often quoted by the World Bank in different studies.
The session was moderated by senior customs official Mukaram Jah Ansari.
It is correct that Bangladesh's and India's tariffs comprise customs duty but Pakistan's tariff by definition is inclusive of customs duty, ACD and RD, said former National Tariff Commission chairperson Dr Rubina Athar, a core member of the NTP team.
She said the para-tariffs are other taxes at import stage like sales tax and withholding taxes, which have not been included in Pakistan's 18.5% tariff in the base year. Tariff Policy Board member Dr Manzoor Ahmed, also part of the NTP core team, said the figures quoted by Allawala and Dr Rubina were correct in their own rights.
The commerce ministry spokesperson said the figure of 18.54% represents Pakistan's overall average tariffs, including 10.3% customs duty, 3.65% ACD and 4.57% RD.
Under the policy, Pakistan has decided to cut import duties from 20.1% to 9.7% by 2030 - a reduction of 52% in protection that has panicked many industries.
To a question whether it was correct that based on 2023 data, after excluding para-tariffs, Pakistan's simple weighted average most-favoured-nation (MFN) applied tariffs was 10.3% compared to India's 17% and Bangladesh's 14.1%, the commerce ministry spokesperson said the definition used by the WTO for para-tariffs is different from what is being assumed in the question.
According to the WTO Tariff Profiles 2024, Pakistan's simple average MFN applied tariff rate of 10.3% combined with 3.65% ACD and 4.57% RD makes it the highest in South Asia. India's was 17%, Bangladesh's 14.1%, and Nepal's 12.7%.
Allawala said Bangladesh has regulatory duty and supplementary duty. Sri Lanka charges Ports and Airports Development Levy, CESS and Social Security Contribution Levy. Türkiye has additional customs duties and additional financial liabilities, all of which are para-tariffs. However, the NTP added para-tariffs only for Pakistan and not for any other country.
The government and proponents of the NTP, aimed at demolishing half of the protection wall, argued that due to high import tariffs Pakistan's exports were not increasing.
But Allawala argued that Pakistan's low exports are not because of high tariffs. They are because of the geopolitical security situation, Pakistan's lack of intelligent strategic FTAs that practically close off African, Central Asian and South American markets for Pakistani exports, and a systemic cost disadvantage with the highest electricity tariffs, interest rates and taxation in the region.

title: Kelly Clarkson’s dispute over a $15,000 bird takes another twist as owner responds | The Express Tribune
description: Kelly Clarkson is welcome back to Brooklyn's Art of Play store, despite a dispute over a $15,000 automaton bird
content:
Kelly Clarkson is welcome back to Brooklyn's Art of Play store, despite a dispute over a $15,000 automaton bird
Kelly Clarkson is welcome to return to Art of Play, the Brooklyn curiosity shop at the centre of a public dispute over an expensive mechanical bird, co-owner Adam Rubin has said.
In an interview with PEOPLE , Rubin said the singer was “welcome anytime” despite their disagreement over her visit to the store. Clarkson, 44, previously claimed that a shop employee treated her condescendingly when she asked about buying an automaton bird named Molly, which was displayed with a $15,000 price tag.
The American Idol winner compared the experience to Julia Roberts’ character in Pretty Woman , alleging that the employee assumed she could not afford the item and offered to find her something comparable.
Art of Play disputed Clarkson’s account, explaining that Molly was a one-of-a-kind piece that was not available for purchase. However, the shop later clarified that a nearly identical automaton could be ordered through its creator in Seattle for $15,000. Staff also claimed they offered Clarkson a similar item for $2,000, but she left before viewing it.
Clarkson subsequently challenged the store’s explanation, sharing a photograph of Molly’s price tag and accusing the shop of being rude and dishonest.
The controversy escalated after Rubin told New York magazine that the bird’s price had been raised to $15 million because of increased public interest. He described the disagreement as an “insane misunderstanding” and criticised Clarkson for publicly discussing the encounter.
Security footage shared by journalist Pablo Torre on YouTube on October 13 showed Clarkson inside the store for several minutes. The footage captured her speaking with an employee, looking at items and eventually leaving the premises.
Despite the public disagreement, Rubin said he was willing to move on, noting that everyone has a bad day. He added that the situation changed when Clarkson used her platform to criticise the business.

title: Ben Affleck reveals what he learned from Jennifer Lopez during their marriage
description: Ben Affleck praises ex wife Jennifer Lopez s work ethic  calling her the hardest working person he has ever known
content:
Ben Affleck praises ex-wife Jennifer Lopez's work ethic, calling her the hardest-working person he has ever known
Ben Affleck has praised Jennifer Lopez's work ethic and career achievements, saying he learned a great deal from the singer and actress during their relationship and marriage.
The 54-year-old actor shared his thoughts during an appearance on The Moment with Jorge and Paola Ramos , released on Wednesday, October 14. Asked about what he learned from Lopez and her experiences navigating Hollywood, Affleck said it was difficult to summarise everything he gained from knowing her.
Affleck described Lopez, 57, as a pioneer who continued pursuing opportunities despite being told that certain achievements were impossible. He also highlighted how she used social media to demonstrate that audiences were interested in her work.
The Animals actor said Lopez faced significant criticism throughout her career, suggesting that a double standard influenced how her professional achievements were perceived. He praised her willingness to take risks, invest her own money and build a successful career through determination.
“I stand in enormous respect for what she’s been able to achieve,” Affleck said, adding that she had consistently believed in herself even when others did not.
He also offered a personal assessment of her work ethic, describing Lopez as “probably the hardest working person that I’ve ever known”.
Affleck and Lopez first became romantically involved in the early 2000s and ended their engagement in 2004. They rekindled their relationship nearly two decades later, married in July 2022 and separated in 2024. Their divorce was finalised in January 2025.
Despite their separation, the former couple maintained a professional connection through Kiss of the Spider Woman , the 2025 film produced by Affleck and Matt Damon's company, Artists Equity. Affleck also attended the film's New York premiere to support Lopez.
During the podcast, Affleck said he had learned not only from Lopez but also from her family and the people he met through them. He added that he wished her continued success, saying she deserved it.

title: After the K P emergency  rethinking confrontation
description: After the K P emergency  rethinking confrontation
content:
PTI has lost the government through which it could still translate its public support into administrative decisions
With the imposition of emergency and governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, PTI has lost the one provincial government through which it could still translate its public support into administrative decisions. For its supporters, this is another painful setback. For the party's leadership, it should also be an occasion to reflect on where its political strategy is taking it.
Before the intervention, there was at least an opportunity for dialogue. An important disagreement concerned counterterrorism policy. PTI wanted the K-P government to have a meaningful role in shaping the approach to militancy in the province. The federal authorities wanted assurances about cooperation in combating terrorism. Access to Imran Khan was another unresolved issue. The discussions ended without an agreement.
It is understandable that a party should hold firmly to a position it considers important. But political leadership also involves deciding how to advance that position when agreement proves difficult. Could some progress have been secured while keeping the remaining questions open? Was there room for an arrangement that preserved the provincial government's ability to function and allowed discussion on security policy to continue?
We cannot know that a different approach would have prevented the intervention. We can, however, ask whether permanent confrontation has helped PTI preserve its political strength or gradually deprived it of the means to use that strength.
This question deserves a thoughtful answer because the attachment of millions of Pakistanis to Imran Khan is real. His popularity has survived imprisonment, restrictions and repeated setbacks. Yet the party's responsibility extends beyond demonstrating that its leader remains popular. People also place their trust in a political party because they hope it will make their lives easier.
For a family struggling to pay for medicine, the value of a provincial government lies partly in whether the public hospital works. For parents, it lies in the school their children attend. For a young person, it may lie in the possibility of finding employment. These expectations give political power its purpose. Losing the ability to meet them is a substantial loss, even when public sympathy for the party remains intact.
PTI's experience since 2022 needs to be considered in this light. After losing federal office, it had the option of becoming an organised parliamentary opposition. Its withdrawal from the National Assembly, followed by the dissolution of the Punjab and K-P assemblies in January 2023, reflected the belief that pressure would bring early national elections. That expectation was not fulfilled.
Those decisions may have been taken in the sincere conviction that they would restore the party's mandate. Looking back, however, it is difficult to overlook how much institutional space was surrendered. PTI retained a substantial following while losing opportunities to govern, scrutinise decisions and remain involved in the everyday business of the state.
There is a human difficulty here too. Once supporters have endured hardship for a cause, leaders can find it harder to recommend a compromise. They worry that an incomplete settlement will disappoint those who have sacrificed so much. But this is precisely when leadership matters. Someone has to explain why a limited gain may be worth securing, why a pause can be useful and why continuing within an imperfect system may offer more possibilities than withdrawing from it.
Pakistan's economic condition makes that judgment especially urgent. The World Bank estimates that Pakistan accounts for about 48% of those living below the $3-a-day extreme-poverty line in its Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping. Nearly every second extremely poor person in this region lives in Pakistan.
Meanwhile, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has described economic stabilisation as "stunted and borrowed". His warning concerns the country's capacity to grow and provide opportunities in the years ahead.
Given these circumstances, one would hope that political energies would increasingly turn towards finding a workable way forward. The years spent in confrontation are also years in which children leave school, young people remain unemployed and households fall further into debt.
Other societies have faced the difficult task of moving beyond entrenched hostility. In South Africa, the ANC entered negotiations with the apartheid government despite a history of profound injustice. Agreements concerning prisoners, returning exiles and political participation helped make further progress possible. The Pretoria Minute also recorded the suspension of ANC armed action. Cooperation developed through practical commitments while deep disagreements remained.
The circumstances were very different, but the lesson is relevant: opponents must eventually allow each other room to negotiate. Some willingness to put aside hatred is necessary before a shared political future can be built.
PTI's repeated reliance on confrontation also raises a question about political training within the party. Are its workers being prepared to remain disciplined under provocation, and are they encouraged to see negotiation as a legitimate part of political struggle? Without that preparation, anger can become difficult to contain, and compromise difficult to explain. Martin Luther King Jr understood this challenge. In his Letter from Birmingham Jail, written in April 1963, to eight white Alabama clergymen who had criticised the civil rights demonstrations, King explained how participants were trained for nonviolent action and asked to consider whether they could endure abuse without retaliating. For Pakistani parties, the lesson is that leadership must cultivate restraint and prepare supporters for the negotiations through which political progress becomes possible.
None of this requires PTI to abandon its principles or follow the accommodations through which other parties have compromised civilian independence. It requires a strategy that keeps its supporters represented and its capacity for public service alive.
The loss of the K-P government makes this discussion painful, but necessary. PTI has shown that it can sustain loyalty through adversity. It now needs to show how that loyalty can be turned into lasting political influence and practical relief. Its supporters deserve a future they can help build, alongside a cause they are asked to defend.

title: The Afghan chessboard   competition and challenges
description: The Afghan chessboard   competition and challenges
content:
Last week we mentioned that in Afghanistan the 'Great Game' continues with changed players
Last week we mentioned that in Afghanistan the 'Great Game' continues with changed players. The US would like to keep its engagement with the ruling clique – willingly or unwillingly – due to Washington's geostrategic interests in the region including counterterrorism, its ongoing competition with China and Russia, and, most of all, Afghanistan's proximity to Iran, China, Russia, Central Asia and a nuclear Pakistan. Pashtun IEA, reportedly, has been trying to be in the US good books again, irrespective of its propaganda.
Washington, on the other hand, has a history with the non-Pashtun Northern Alliance (NA) and other groups, and remained supportive of Afghanistan's pro-Western First Republic (2001-2021) during decades of Afghan nation-building. These avidly anti-Taliban Afghans may be down but are not out. Resistance by Afghan opposition to the IEA's obscurantist rule is intensifying in the non-Pashtun north, as mentioned previously.
IEA's recalcitrance on issues like human rights, women right to education and work, inclusivity in the government, and, more significantly, terrorism is not easily ignorable by the West Plus, even if ideological divergence is put aside. Deep-seated nexus among Al Qaeda, TTP and IEA and their overt jihadism keep the chances of another 9/11-type catalyst alive. In that event, the US re-focus on Afghanistan, with or without European Allies, cannot be ruled, to nudge or participate in regime change.
Short of that catalyst, the US would ensure a pliant IEA using leverages like NGO-level engagement, cash subsidies, diplomatic isolation, non-recognition, etc, but would otherwise leave Taliban alone. In West Plus's assessment (correctly), there is no viable alternative to the IEA at present. Afghan opposition gaining enough strength to challenge IEA militarily would be long drawn. Hence, the West Plus would keep nudging IEA towards self-reform and in-house change.
Russia has been sending mixed signals on Afghanistan using its regional framework like the Moscow Format. Russian motivation for engagement ostensibly stems from keeping Afghanistan-generated terrorism and narcotics trade in check; regaining lost geostrategic foothold in Afghanistan; denying space to the US/West; protecting its soft underbelly in Central Asia; exploiting Afghanistan's mineral riches; and presumably avenging the loss of Soviet Union, consequent to the Pakistan/West-supported Taliban jihad (1979-89).
Moscow has significantly ramped up its diplomatic and military engagement with Kabul. It is the first and only country to recognise the Afghan regime in July 2025. Militarily, both sides have signed a military-technical cooperation agreement to repair and restore Afghanistan's Soviet-era military hardware. Russia sees IEA indispensable in suppressing the IS-K, which is responsible for a deadly attack in Crocus city hall, Krasnogorsk (2024). Foreign Minister Lavrov, during Moscow Format consultations, committed to provide technical and intelligence support to enhance IEA's CT capabilities. Russia has repeatedly commended IEA for controlling narcotics trade from Afghanistan, and its ability to reduce opiate production by 90% since 2022. Most importantly, Moscow has issued strict warnings against Western military return to the region. Lavrov, on October 5, during Moscow Format, called 'categorically unacceptable' any US/NATO military deployment in Afghanistan, or in Central Asian countries. This ostensibly blocks any US move to reclaim or return to Bagram Air Base.
Diplomatically, Moscow has proposed reintegrating Afghanistan into SCO via a specialised contact group. Russian presidential envoy Zamir Kabulov offered to mediate between Islamabad and Kabul as an 'independent mediator' to de-escalate tensions. Other projects between Russia and Afghanistan include establishment of a dedicated trade working group to prioritise infrastructure development and jointly explore transport and energy connectivity to link Afghanistan with Central and South Asia.
Moscow's strategic motivation seems multi-layered. In CT, a softer approach secures Russia's soft Central Asian underbelly and southern flank against terrorism. Diplomatic and economic engagement enables Moscow to prevent Taliban regime from eventually tilting towards Washington, which Taliban deeply desire, the US willing. In an ostensible break with the US under Trump, India too rides the Russian bandwagon in its own competition with Pakistan. Indian manoeuvre to reduce Pakistan's space in Afghanistan may also be Russia's 'peripheral' interest, under its broader alignment with New Delhi and Modi. However, the Russia-India-Afghanistan Combine works under different geostrategic compulsions. Russia leverages these trilateral ties against Washington; India plays to contain a resurgent China and keep Pakistan under pressure, besides protecting its Chabahar investment and its logistics for its base in Tajikistan; whereas Afghanistan wants diplomatic and economic space, both from India and Russia, and invite the US Plus's engagement in the process. Although, New Delhi and Moscow see Taliban with weary eyes.
Regionally, the Sunni Gulf and Saudi Arabia compete for influence on the Afghan real estate, also under different motivations. Gulf and KSA want to limit Iranian influence; some in the oil-rich Gulf want to put Pakistan under pressure through insurgency-like situation in Balochistan; Iran vies for influence under its Shia credentials in Hazarajat, for example; whereas Turkey supports Turkic speaking Northern Afghanistan, especially the Uzbek enclave. Neighbouring Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan stand for respective ethnic minorities in the Northern Afghanistan.
China sees engagement with a recalcitrant Kabul, worthy of strategic payoff by: a) keeping the Uighur militancy by ETIM under check through IEA and pacifying its Muslim Turkestan (Xinjiang); b) helping stability along Pakistan's Western border to allow Islamabad greater attention towards the Indian border; c) protecting CPEC, its ambitious BRI's pilot project; and d) positioning itself to exploit Afghanistan's mineral riches beyond Aynak cooper mines.
In all this jockeying for power, IEA, even if under pressure, remains an attractive partner. Countries are induced to ignore Kabul's human rights record and political repression, for given reasons. IEA presently seems militarily and politically entrenched; however, its future consolidation and sustainment would largely depend upon situation in Northern Afghanistan and Kabul's relations with Islamabad. The Afghan North is in turmoil; and in the mid to long-term, the Pashtun South may join it, driven by economic desperation. The mute noise of discontent is already there, as reports after reports validate the increasing poverty under IEA rule across Afghanistan. That noise can become a crescendo. One will not put a timeline on it, as the trigger may be one terrorist attack, not even as spectacular as 9/11.
So, IEA makes the next move on the chessboard. Meanwhile, Islamabad needs to be aware of the Indian money, Israeli technology and Afghan manpower arrayed against it. (Concluded)

description: Six ways to remember a martyr
content:
Somewhere, a soldier is sitting in a bunker, eating cold food, thinking about his mother's phone call he couldn't take
I have never had to wake up at 4am in the freezing cold, carry a heavy pack up a mountain, and stand guard for hours while everyone I love is far away. Most of us haven't. We complain when the internet is slow, or the traffic is bad, and somewhere, a soldier is sitting in a bunker, eating cold food and thinking about his mother's phone call he couldn't take yesterday.
Some never cross their own doorstep again. The soldier who died is gone, but what he leaves behind is a family still setting a plate at the table, a school bag still hanging on a hook, and a young wife who suddenly has to be both parents. The medal is placed in her hands, she is thanked at a ceremony, and poof! The cameras leave. That is where we confuse the closing of a ceremony with the closing of a wound. Medals matter, but a medal is a moment. A family's grief lasts a lifetime, so our remembrance should too.
Therefore, we can turn our gratitude into action, starting with these ideas.
Put their names where life happens: Name a road, a bridge, a roundabout, or a park after a martyr. Every time someone says, "Meet me at Shaheed Hassan Chowk", a name is spoken aloud again. Name school classrooms, libraries, hospital wards and sports grounds after them too. A child who studies in the "Captain Ali Library" will wonder who he was, and that curiosity is how a memory survives. Name ambulances and rescue vehicles after them, so their names arrive wherever help is needed.
Tell their real story: A plaque shouldn't just say a name and a date. It should say he loved cricket, he was the youngest of five, and he used to send half his salary home to pay for his sister's school. Ranks are forgotten. People are not. Add a QR code to every plaque and every tree, so anyone can scan it and read the full story in seconds.
Plant a tree for each of them: A martyr's tree in a public park, with a small tag, grows taller every year. It is a living memorial, and it gives shade to strangers, which is exactly what he did for us. Plant a rose bush beside it too, because roses bloom again every year, just as memory should.
Look after the family properly: Free education for martyrs' children, reserved seats in colleges, priority in healthcare, and help with jobs for widows and parents. We can also make sure the family's own street gets a proper road, clean water or a school because the martyr's home village deserves better than being forgotten. Set up a Martyrs' Family Fund for weddings, funerals and emergencies, and pair each family with a local volunteer who checks in every month, not once a year.
Bring their stories into our schools: Invite families to the national day assembly and let them speak, if they wish. Students hearing from a martyr's mother will learn more than from any textbook. Create an "Adopt a Martyr's Story" programme where each class researches one martyr and presents it at assembly. Print martyrs' names on the bottom of school notebooks and exam papers, small reminders in ordinary places.
Make their memory part of our culture: Hold an annual "Martyrs' Film Festival" where young filmmakers submit short documentaries about fallen soldiers. Commission murals in every district, painted by local artists, showing the martyrs of that area. Ask poets and writers to compose a "Book of Names", with one poem or paragraph for every martyr, published each year.
None of this is difficult or very expensive.
It only needs us to care enough to do it.

title: The right to refuse
description: The right to refuse
content:
Supreme Court refuses to commute death sentence of man convicted of murdering a woman
The Supreme Court's refusal to commute the death sentence of a man convicted of murdering a woman for rejecting his marriage proposal is a welcome affirmation of a fundamental principle that remains dangerously misunderstood in Pakistani society. A woman's right to choose whom she marries is absolute, and her refusal cannot be construed as an insult warranting retaliation. By rejecting the convict's plea for leniency, the apex court has rightly made clear that wounded male pride cannot serve as a mitigating circumstance for murder.
A rejected marriage proposal is perceived by some men as an affront to their authority, with the consequences ranging from persistent harassment to deadly violence. Such attitudes are frequently sustained by social customs that place a man's honour above a woman's autonomy. The court's observation that marriage requires the free consent of both parties is therefore particularly significant. Neither religion nor tradition can be invoked to justify the denial of this basic right. Pakistan continues to witness cases of violence against women whose only perceived offence is exercising their independence. More troubling is the tendency to dismiss threats and harassment as personal disputes until they culminate in violence. The authorities must recognise that intimidation following a rejected proposal is not a private matter but a potential warning of a serious crime.
While the Supreme Court has delivered a firm message, judicial pronouncements alone cannot dismantle generations of discriminatory thinking. Law enforcement agencies must respond promptly to complaints of stalking and threats, while families must abandon the belief that a woman's choices are subordinate to male approval. Justice must not be confined to punishing perpetrators after lives have been lost. No woman should have to pay with her life for saying no.

title: Fiscal fault lines
description: Fiscal fault lines
content:
Pakistan's economy entered FY27 with a veneer of stability that masked deep structural vulnerabilities
Pakistan's economy entered FY27 with a veneer of stability that masked deep structural vulnerabilities. Unfortunately, no amount of reforms will change the fact that the GDP growth prediction remains extremely low for a developing country, and inflation is forecast to be relatively high. The inflation outlook is particularly concerning. Having decelerated from a peak above 38% in May 2023 to single digits, consumer prices are now projected to rise by nearly 10% in FY27.
Surging oil prices and disrupted trade routes amid the Middle East conflict are primary drivers, as oil and gas constitute a large share of Pakistan's imports. Meanwhile, the government's relief scheme for motorcyclists and small-car owners has drawn IMF criticism for being "broad-based" and "costly", underscoring the tension between populist measures and fiscal prudence.
On the external front, the current account is expected to shift from balance in FY26 to a deficit of 1% of GDP in FY27. The SBP has rebuilt reserves to $21.45 billion, providing roughly three months of import cover - which is useful, but not enough to address broader concerns. Meanwhile, the rupee has appreciated to around Rs277 per dollar, but the real effective exchange rate stands at 107, raising concerns about currency valuation and export competitiveness. Public debt also remains unsustainable.
While the debt-to-GDP ratio declined to 68.3% in FY26 from 70.6% a year earlier, the nominal stock rose 7.7% to Rs86.72 trillion. Debt servicing consumes more than half of federal revenue, leaving little fiscal space for development or social spending. Unemployment is forecast to ease to 6.5% from 7.1%, but with a labour force expanding by roughly 2 million annually, growth of 3.5% is insufficient to absorb new entrants.
The IMF's downward revision of Pakistan's FY27 growth forecast in its World Economic Outlook - downgraded by 0.6 percentage points mainly due to the Mideast conflict's economic drag - highlights the fragility of the recovery. Policymakers will thus have their hands full as they chart a way to achieve reform goals such as macroeconomic stability.

That word oligarch is always used when the western journalism talks about some rich Russian businessman who may have connections to the Russian government. I actually looked up the meaning of that word. An oligarch is someone who uses his or her enormous wealth to influence government decisions, politics and society. When you plug in that definition, you'd realise that Elon Musk and Miriam Adelson are the biggest American oligarchs.
American culture has this weird tendency where the people are made to believe that corruption and bad things are what other nations and other governments do and that we have a watchdog system that keeps a check on every government branch. Some months ago, Elon Musk was asked if he hated Muslims. He didn't say no. Instead he gave an answer that people give when they want to hide their hatred but also cannot make it public.
