title: Pakistan s universities should form character by design
description: Pakistan s universities should form character by design
content:
On a university campus, it must begin with those who lead, teach and serve
Previously, I wrote in these columns that character is stamped on us, like the mark on a coin, by what we do again and again. Universities do much of that stamping, although they do it more by default than by design. They receive young Pakistanis at around eighteen, when habits are still soft and the brain is still maturing, and send them out as doctors, teachers, engineers, civil servants and business executives. So how should such character formation begin?
It begins with clarity about who we want to be. On a university campus, it must begin with those who lead, teach and serve, because students learn who to be by watching exemplars among their teachers. The habits students pick up from their teachers last a lifetime.
A decade of research at the Oxford Character Project frames character formation in three words, BE, KNOW and DO: who to be, what to know and what to do. Our universities usually start with DO: rules, codes and disciplinary committees. Yet experiments show "don't be a cheater" reduces cheating; "don't cheat" does not. The Oxford research points to BE as the starting point. Our own tradition has long done the same, joining taleem, instruction, with tarbiyat, the character formation of the person. The lesson is that a university that informs minds without forming persons has done only half its work.
Pakistan's 280+ universities and Degree Awarding Institutions, with nearly two million students, have given the country remarkable people, yet they form character more by default than by design. The 2017 tragedy at Abdul Wali Khan University in Mardan remains a painful reminder that a campus can provide education and still fail at character formation. Those who teach need it too: a 2023 Nature analysis placed Pakistan among large research-producing nations with the highest rates of retracted papers. Most are withdrawn because of misconduct, such as plagiarism or fabricated data: failings of character, not of intellect.
The Higher Education Commission has answered with courses, most recently Understanding of Holy Quran (Fehm-e-Quran) I and II, one credit hour each, compulsory for Muslim students since Fall 2025. These are welcome, but character is not delivered like content, one credit hour at a time. We can learn from Oxford's research, which names seven strategies that form character: habituation, practising virtue in small acts until it becomes second nature; reflection, looking back honestly on our experiences; exemplars, learning from people whose lives we admire; a shared language of virtue; moral reminders at the moment of decision; systems that make good conduct the easier path; and friendships in which we help each other grow. All seven begin with one decision: who we mean to be.
Abroad, America's Wake Forest University has used these seven strategies since 2017, helping more than 75 faculty build character into their courses. At home, Lahore's Superior University has made "Leading with Character" its guiding philosophy, from top management to students. The lesson: a university becomes what its people decide to become.
Who we mean to be deserves to be written down as a personal mission statement. Once written, a mission statement works as a personal constitution. Like a nation's constitution, it sets the principles against which every decision is tested and serves as a compass when the road is unclear. Research on moral reminders shows how it helps: because we want to think well of ourselves, being reminded of our commitments makes wrongdoing much harder to justify, even in our own minds. But any constitution is only as good as the way it is honoured.
A good personal mission statement must cover every role we play. A student is also a son or daughter; and a rector, a vice chancellor or professor is also a parent, a colleague and a mentor. The accounts officer who releases a scholarship on time teaches fairness as surely as any lecture. Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) taught that each of us is a shepherd, responsible for our flock. Each of us, then, leads someone, and none of us is exempt from the character that leadership demands.
Because our roles compete for the same hours, a personal constitution must also set priorities: which role leads when two collide, and what we will not sacrifice for success. Hazrat Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) recalled that Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), leader of a whole community, served his family at home and went out to pray when the time came.
BE is only the first step. KNOW asks us to understand ourselves under pressure, the people we serve, and where a judgement matters more than rules. DO turns both into small daily acts: one act of courage, a commitment kept when it is inconvenient, a friend with permission to tell us the truth. The Quran puts the test plainly: "Why do you say what you do not do?" (Surah al Saff 61:2).
Toxicity, deceit, exploitation and egoism are all around us, and it is tempting to withdraw and leave change to others. Yet "Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is within themselves" (Surah al Ra'd 13:11). Imagine campuses designed for character, where vice-chancellors, professors, staff and students have each written down who they mean to be and what guides them, and then live it every day. Such universities would send Pakistan not only graduates with degrees, but citizens with a decision-making framework. Our campuses will form character either way. Let us form it by design, one personal constitution at a time: written, understood and lived.

title: Wealth management in AI age  will machines replace human adviser
description: Wealth management in AI age  will machines replace human adviser
content:
Artificial intelligence is no longer confined to technology laboratories.
Artificial intelligence is no longer confined to technology laboratories. It has entered our banks, investment platforms and financial institutions and, increasingly, our personal financial decisions. From analysing markets and preparing financial plans to detecting fraud, AI is rapidly changing how wealth is managed. This raises an obvious question: will it eventually replace the human wealth manager?
Traditionally, wealth management has rested on the relationship between a client and an adviser. The adviser does far more than recommend investments. He or she tries to understand the client's finances, family responsibilities, ambitions, tolerance for risk and long-term priorities. A portfolio that looks optimal on a spreadsheet may be wholly unsuitable for someone who cannot emotionally bear large swings in its value.
AI is exceptionally good at the mathematical side of this equation. Modern systems can process vast quantities of financial and economic data in a fraction of the time a human analyst would need, compare investment alternatives and monitor portfolios. They can also automate routine administrative work, freeing professionals to spend more time with clients. Recent industry research from LSEG describes this as a shift from gathering information to interpreting and coordinating insights.
For ordinary investors, this could be valuable. Personalised advice has long been expensive, and therefore associated with the wealthy. AI-powered tools could reduce costs and extend financial guidance to people who could never afford it.
But accessibility should not be confused with reliability.
One of the biggest dangers of AI-based advice is that an answer can sound convincing without being correct. Financial decisions involve uncertainty, incomplete information and changing circumstances. A system may produce a sophisticated-looking recommendation while missing the individual's complete financial picture. Research from MIT Sloan found that AI can offer useful guidance on saving, spending and investing, but that its recommendations vary with the quality of information supplied by the user. The researchers also identified weaknesses in responding to income shocks, rebalancing portfolios and managing retirement drawdown. Investors should think twice before treating a chatbot as a personal financial adviser.
Then there is the question of accountability. If a human adviser's recommendation causes a client serious harm, regulatory and professional responsibilities apply. An AI system has no professional responsibility or fiduciary judgment. Responsibility ultimately rests with the institution, adviser or individual who deploys it. That is why human oversight will remain critical.
The UK's Financial Conduct Authority, in its 2026 wealth-management research, acknowledges both sides. AI can reduce friction, improve efficiency and help close the advice gap, but the regulator also warns of risks involving fraud, cybersecurity and consumer harm. These concerns are far from theoretical. The more financial institutions rely on interconnected digital systems and third-party technology providers, the graver the consequences of a major technological failure. The Financial Stability Board has recently placed AI-related cyber risk among its principal concerns for financial stability, according to Reuters.
Privacy is equally important. Wealth management requires highly sensitive information: income, assets, debts, tax circumstances and often family details. Institutions must ensure that convenience does not come at the cost of confidentiality.
Algorithmic bias is another worry. AI learns from historical data, which may carry existing inequalities. If an algorithm reproduces them, automated decisions could disadvantage particular groups of customers. The US Government Accountability Office has likewise flagged data quality, privacy, bias and cybersecurity as key risks of AI in financial services.
Interestingly, investors themselves do not appear to be asking for a fully machine-driven future. A 2026 HSBC survey of around 10,000 affluent and high-net-worth investors across ten markets found that 73 per cent use AI for finance and investment. Yet only 12 per cent said it was the most influential factor in their latest investment decision, while 62 per cent named financial professionals and institutions as their main source of ideas.
This points to a more realistic outcome: AI will not necessarily replace the adviser, but it will change what the adviser does. Less time will go on collecting information, preparing routine reports and repetitive calculations. More will go on interpreting AI-generated insights, managing risk and, above all, acting as a trusted human partner in decision-making.
That matters because money is deeply tied to human behaviour. Consider an investor whose portfolio has fallen 20 per cent in a market crisis. An algorithm can explain historical probabilities and estimate recovery periods. A human adviser can sit with that investor, understand the anxiety driving the urge to sell and prevent a damaging emotional reaction. That dimension cannot easily be reduced to code.
For developing economies such as Pakistan, the AI revolution offers both opportunity and risk. Digital financial services and AI tools could bring investment education and basic financial guidance to a far larger population. But low financial literacy, limited understanding of investment risk and inadequate consumer protection could leave inexperienced investors especially vulnerable to misleading AI-generated recommendations.
Pakistan must therefore think beyond simply adopting financial technology. Regulators, financial institutions, universities and technology companies should work together on responsible AI adoption, stronger data protection, transparent algorithms, effective consumer safeguards and better financial literacy.
The goal should not be to choose between humans and machines, but to combine their strengths. AI can process more information than any individual adviser, spot patterns and speed up analysis. Humans bring context, empathy, accountability, ethical judgment and an understanding of circumstances that may never appear in a dataset. The future will not belong to the institution with the most sophisticated algorithm alone, but to those who can pair technological intelligence with human wisdom.
The real question is not whether AI can manage money. It is whether we are prepared to ensure that, as AI takes on ever more important parts of our financial lives, a responsible human being remains willing to explain the decision, challenge the machine and stand behind the advice. That is where the future of trustworthy wealth management will be decided.

title: Four Nobels  one human quest
description: Four Nobels  one human quest
content:
Every October, Stockholm becomes the capital of curiosity
Every October, Stockholm becomes the capital of curiosity. Nobel week is more than a parade of famous names; it reminds us that civilisation advances because someone spends years asking a question others have overlooked. Of the six prizes associated with Nobel season, five were created under Alfred Nobel's will. Peace, however, is awarded separately in Oslo by the Norwegian Nobel Committee, while Economic Sciences was established in 1968 by Sweden's central bank in Nobel's memory. That leaves four prizes - Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, and Literature - that form intellectual quartet.
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel "for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics". Their work transformed a light-sensitive protein from algae into a tool that can switch selected cells, neurons, on or off with remarkable precision. It gave neuroscience a way to move beyond observing the brain and begin interrogating specific circuits. Light, once something the eye detected, became an instrument for asking the brain how it works.
Physics then took us from the brain to the universe. Francis Halzen received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. Neutrinos are elusive, passing through matter with barely a trace. IceCube turned a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice into a detector capable of catching the faint signatures of these cosmic messengers. There is something poetic in using the coldest ice on Earth to learn about the most violent events in the cosmos.
Chemistry brought the journey back to the molecular scale. Henri B Kagan and Kenso Soai were honoured for discoveries involving non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Their work showed how tiny initial differences between left- and right-handed molecular forms can be dramatically amplified. Molecular handedness matters profoundly in biology and pharmaceuticals, and it also touches one of life's enduring puzzles: why living systems overwhelmingly favour molecular orientations.
Then came Literature, and with it Anne Carson. The Canadian poet, classicist, essayist and translator received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature for a "bold and inventive oeuvre" that, through playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature. Carson is an apt companion to this year's scientists because she too works at boundaries. Poetry becomes criticism, translation becomes reinvention, ancient Greece enters modern life, and fragments become new wholes. Her work reminds us that discovery is not confined to laboratories; language, too, can reveal worlds that were present but unseen.
Taken together, these four Nobel Prizes tell a unified story. Medicine used light to probe the brain. Physics used Antarctic ice to detect ghostly particles from the cosmos. Chemistry showed how a barely perceptible molecular imbalance can become decisive. Literature honoured a writer who makes ancient voices audible again. In every case, the achievement lies in perceiving what was difficult to perceive.
That may be the deeper lesson of Nobel week. Universities divide knowledge into departments because administration demands names on doors, timetables and budgets. Nature is less obedient. A photon may belong to physics and medicine at once; chirality connects chemistry with life; a classical text can belong simultaneously to scholarship and poetry. Great intellectual advances often occur where such boundaries become porous.
For those of us who have spent a lifetime in universities, this is worth remembering. Education should not produce specialists who know more and more about less and less. It should cultivate curiosity able to cross disciplinary walls. The 2026 laureates remind us that knowledge begins when someone notices a faint signal, a flash of light, an elusive particle, a tiny molecular preference, or an old line of poetry, and refuses to dismiss it as insignificant.

title: Unstoppable rabies
description: Unstoppable rabies
content:
A disease that is entirely preventable continues to claim lives in Sindh
A disease that is entirely preventable continues to claim lives in Sindh, exposing the provincial government's persistent failure to address a public health crisis that has been allowed to worsen for years. At least 38 rabies cases have been reported this year at just two major hospitals in Karachi, while more than 26,000 dog-bite cases have been recorded at these two facilities alone.
The provincial government's response has largely consisted of announcing programmes and making assurances that have yielded little tangible improvement. The Sindh Rabies Control Programme was launched in 2022, yet its implementation has been hampered by inadequate funding and limited operational coverage. As recently as December last year, officials acknowledged that only about Rs66 million of the Rs265 million allocated for vaccination and sterilisation during the financial year had been released. In May, the chief minister launched another province-wide campaign, while a fresh strategy for managing Karachi's stray dog population was announced last month. Meanwhile, the number of people suffering dog bites remains alarming. Such repeated announcements mean little unless accompanied by sustained implementation and measurable results. The government must explain why, despite years of programmes and considerable expenditure, it has failed to bring the situation under control. Although the government claims to have upgraded 278 anti-rabies units across Sindh, their effectiveness needs to be assessed independently.
The way forward requires a coordinated and sustained response. Mass dog vaccination and sterilisation must be expanded across the province, supported by reliable funding and regular monitoring. Health facilities must follow standardised treatment protocols, while public awareness campaigns should reach communities where misconceptions and reliance on traditional remedies continue to endanger lives. The provincial government must also establish clear accountability for failures in both animal population management and emergency medical care.

title: K P s terror surge
description: K P s terror surge
content:
Terrorist incidents in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa surged by almost 200% between March 2024 and September 2026
Terrorist incidents in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa surged by almost 200% between March 2024 and September 2026, with police and security personnel targeted in 73% of attacks recorded this year. One of the most concerning findings in the government security reports recently shared with the federal cabinet was that terrorist drone attacks more than doubled in the past year, reaching 170 in 2026.
The federal government and security forces responded to the security situation with increased intelligence-based operations, eliminating hundreds of terrorists and disrupting militant networks across K-P. If only all parts of the government were working together, the results might have been even better. Unfortunately, the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government, especially its top leadership, has been preoccupied with political activity and rallies in other parts of the country, rather than governing.
Even late in the game, when the federal cabinet was considering emergency measures, the provincial government seemed more focused on planning rallies. Even the security reports explicitly blamed the K-P government's "flawed policies and its soft approach towards militants" for enabling terrorist elements to establish a foothold. More than 9,000 police posts remain vacant, the Safe City project is confined to Peshawar, and the CTD faces severe shortages of weapons and trained personnel. The chief minister also insisted on negotiating with terrorists, which directly undermined the federal government and security establishment.
The situation now is remarkably different, as the federal government has taken K-P's elected leadership off the board. Going forward, Islamabad will bear full responsibility for improving security in K-P, as it will have direct control of the provincial security apparatus. We can only hope that the unfortunate series of events that has led us here can be reversed, and K-P sees some semblance of security again.

title: Flawed poverty paradigm
description: Flawed poverty paradigm
content:
Pakistan's societal strata are sinking deeper into destitution
Pakistan's societal strata are sinking deeper into destitution. The UNDP's Multidimensional Poverty Index report has unmasked the grim reality of the country's stagnant social mobility. Poverty is on the rise, leaving more than one-third of the population facing severe deprivations in healthcare, education and basic living standards. Alarmingly, 38.3% of Pakistanis are "multidimensionally poor," compared to just 16.4% people in India and 14.9% in Bangladesh. These sobering statistics follow closely on the heels of a World Bank assessment, which revealed that Pakistan accounts for approximately 48% of the region's "extreme poor" living on less than $3 a day.
These statistics paint a grim picture for an economy where the lion's share of revenue is consumed by debt servicing and defence, leaving less than Rs1.5 trillion for national development out of a massive Rs17 trillion budget outlay. Unsurprisingly, the human cost is devastating: over 40% of children under five suffer from stunting, approximately 26 million children remain out of school, 70 million people lack access to basic sanitation, and the population of unemployed stands at a staggering 5.9 million.
The fact that these UNDP estimates rely on household surveys from different years is more than enough to highlight the urgency of this widespread deprivation. Furthermore, the world body warns that an additional 12.9% of the population remains highly vulnerable to falling into acute poverty. Critical sectors - including nutrition, child mortality, school attendance, sanitation, drinking water, electricity and household assets - are in desperate need of a comprehensive Marshall Plan. They can no longer be resuscitated through the piecemeal measures.
Sustained economic progress requires a strategic shift toward human resource development, a goal that remains unattainable without meaningful grassroots empowerment. The existing lopsided paradigm of funding from the federal to the provincial domains is infected with lethargy and corruption, further compounded by a lack of accountability. Structural poverty can only be mitigated by mobilising the masses for self-development and placing local communities directly at the vanguard of decision-making.

title: Protest movements in South Asia face their own test
description: Protest movements in South Asia face their own test
content:
CJP shows that people treated as politically disposable can turn humiliation into solidarity
India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) offers South Asia an uncomfortable lesson: people treated as politically disposable can turn humiliation into solidarity. What began as online satire has become a movement demanding answers about examinations, employment and the credibility of elections.
The name followed Chief Justice Surya Kant's reported comparison of some unemployed young people to cockroaches in May. He subsequently said his criticism concerned people using bogus degrees, not India's youth. That clarification belongs in any honest account. The wider question is why an image of contempt found such a receptive audience.
On October 10, 2026, Reuters reported the detention of founder Abhijeet Dipke ahead of a Delhi demonstration seeking election chief Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. Authorities restricted transport and mobile internet, citing public order. The movement had already helped force the education minister's resignation over examination paper leaks in July.
The current dispute concerns revisions to voter rolls. Critics allege partisan exclusion; the Election Commission rejects wrongdoing and says entries were flagged during a draft exercise, with opportunities for reinstatement. These competing claims require transparent scrutiny.
An examination scandal becomes politically explosive when a qualification is a family's only plausible route out of insecurity. An electoral dispute becomes more dangerous when citizens already doubt that peaceful participation can change their lives. Economic frustration and institutional distrust reinforce each other.
South Asia has seen this interaction before. Sri Lanka's 2022 uprising grew from economic collapse. Bangladesh's 2024 protests began over public employment quotas before becoming a revolt against Sheikh Hasina's rule. In Nepal in 2025, anger over corruption combined with opposition to a social media ban.
These histories do not establish an inevitable regional domino effect. Each country has its own institutions, divisions and political choices. They do suggest that a grievance can widen rapidly when those responsible refuse accountability and treat dissent itself as the problem.
Pakistan should examine this warning without the satisfaction that a neighbour's difficulties so often provoke. Our question is whether a young citizen can obtain decent education, compete fairly for work, challenge an injustice and influence public decisions without money or patronage.
For governments, the answer must appear in budgets and everyday administration. Tax policy should ask more of privileged wealth and ease the burden on ordinary consumption. Public spending should improve schools and services, while recruitment and examinations must be open to credible independent scrutiny.
Young people also need meaningful participation between elections: functioning local governments, representative student bodies and political parties that allow newcomers to rise. Repeatedly inviting them to celebrate the nation while denying them a voice in its affairs cannot build lasting loyalty.
Protest movements face their own test. Mobilising anger does not confer immunity from scrutiny or provide a programme for governing. Violence against opponents and minorities destroys democratic claims. Removing a minister or government achieves little if arbitrary power survives under new management.
The likely regional development is further mobilisation around concrete failures of opportunity and representation. Whether it produces reform, repression or another cycle of disappointment will depend on choices made by governments and movements alike. No honest analysis can name the next capital or predict the timetable.
South Asia's rulers still have room to respond through fair opportunities, credible elections and accountable institutions. That room narrows whenever peaceful criticism is answered with humiliation or coercion. A generation asking for a future should not have to bring a capital to a halt before anyone listens.

Albusaidi, visiting at the invitation of Deputy Prime Minister and FM Ishaq Dar, was received by the Economic Affairs Division secretary and the FO additional secretary (Middle East).
His Excellency Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi @badralbusaidi , Foreign Minister of the Sultanate of Oman, arrived in Islamabad today on an official visit to Pakistan during 13-14 October 2026. He was received at the airport by Additional Secretary Economic Affairs… pic.twitter.com/ALpb65f9HN

The 8th Session of the Pakistan-Oman JMC will also be held in Islamabad during the visit and would be co-chaired by the two foreign ministers.
Albusaidi is also expected to pay a courtesy call to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
In an earlier statement , the FO had said the meeting would provide an "important platform" to review the "full spectrum of bilateral relations" and strengthen cooperation across various fields.
The FO had said the visit reflected the longstanding fraternal relations between Pakistan and Oman and was expected to further deepen mutually beneficial cooperation across multiple sectors.
Albusaidi's visit coincides with regional diplomacy to contain escalating hostilities in the Middle East.
The two countries have participated in mediation efforts to bring a negotiated settlement to the US-Iran war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Oman has engaged in talks with Iran to establish temporary or safe commercial shipping routes through the near-closed waterway.

title: Govt was left with  no option  but emergency  governor rule  PM Shehbaz
description: Says  Pakistan comes first   nothing is more important than the country   s progress and survival
content:
Says 'Pakistan comes first', nothing is more important than the country’s progress and survival
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday said the government had been left with "no option" but to impose an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa amid the deteriorating security situation in the province, saying “Pakistan comes first” and nothing was more important than the country’s progress and survival.
The federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in K-P on Sunday under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution. The government cited the deteriorating law and order situation and what it called a lack of support from the provincial administration in the fight against terrorism.
Addressing the PML-N’s parliamentary party meeting , the prime minister praised the “brave people” of K-P for their sacrifices in the fight against terrorism, saying the menace had been eradicated from the province by 2017 but resurfaced after the PTI came to power.
“After that, terrorists had started returning to Swat. They were given a free hand and brought back,” he said.
" میں آپ سب کا دل کی اتھاہ گہرائیوں سے شکر گزار ہوں کہ آپ میری درخواست پر یہاں تشریف لائے۔ یہ ایک ایسا موقع ہے جب پاکستان کے صوبہ خیبر پختونخوا میں گزشتہ چند ماہ سے صورتِ حال انتہائی خراب، بلکہ دل خراش رہی ہے۔ یہ وہ صوبہ ہے جو پاکستان کے خوبصورت ترین صوبوں میں سے ایک ہے۔ وہاں کے… pic.twitter.com/ofQt3RAjqG
The prime minister stated that after the PTI formed the government in K-P in 2024, the federal government had made every effort over the past two and a half years to resolve issues through engagement.
The premier said meetings had been held with former chief minister Ali Amin Gandapur, who was assured of the federal government's full support in the fight against terrorism, further adding that meetings had also been held with non-functional chief minister Sohail Afridi.
"2024 میں پی ٹی آئی کی حکومت بنی تو ان اڑھائی سالوں میں ہم نے حتی المقدور کوشش کی۔ ان کے سابق وزیراعلیٰ علی امین گنڈاپور سے ہماری کئی ملاقاتیں ہوئیں اور ہم نے ہر طریقے سے انہیں یہ باور کرانے کی کوشش کی کہ ہم آپ کے ساتھ چلنے کے لیے تیار ہیں۔ ملک کی ترقی اور خوشحالی کا یہ سفر ہمارا… pic.twitter.com/Ro8wUChZVq
“Every day, our people, our armed forces and police personnel are being killed. There are daily sacrifices in Balochistan and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. If this brutality is not completely eliminated, the progress we have made over the past two and a half years will come to a halt,” he said.
PM Shehbaz said the government had made progress over the past two and a half years through a “unique partnership”. However, he added, if a provincial government was bent on dismantling that partnership, a political party was intent on destruction and stood in the way of the country's journey towards development, action would have to be taken.
Referring to his meeting with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director in New York, the premier said the lender's chief had praised Pakistan's recent reforms, describing the country as “a new Pakistan”.
وزیراعظم محمد شہباز شریف نے مسلم لیگ (ن) کے پارلیمانی پارٹی کے اجلاس سے خطاب کرتے ہوئے کہا کہ نیویارک میں آئی ایم ایف کی مینیجنگ ڈائریکٹر اور لندن میں سٹی بینک، جے پی مورگن سمیت عالمی مالیاتی اداروں کے نمائندوں سے ملاقاتوں میں پاکستان میں گزشتہ ڈھائی سال کے دوران ہونے والی… pic.twitter.com/od7hpNFK8U
He said delegations from six leading banks had also appreciated the country's recent progress, although they had expressed reservations over incidents of terrorism in Pakistan.
The prime minister said that while terrorism was spreading and instability was being created, the PTI was devoting all its resources and time to political agitation, including long marches and sit-ins, instead of focusing on development and prosperity.
"یہ دھرنے اور لانگ مارچ، کون نہیں جانتا کہ گزشتہ سال اسلام آباد میں کیا ہوا؟ 2014 میں کئی مہینوں تک ڈی چوک خالی نہیں کیا گیا، وہاں گندے کپڑے دھوئے گئے اور قبریں کھودی گئیں۔ اسی دوران چینی صدر کا دورۂ پاکستان بھی مؤخر ہو گیا۔ جب کوئی ملک کی ترقی روکنے پر تُلا ہو اور دہشت گردی کے… pic.twitter.com/3GSad2inec
He added that the people of K-P had been waiting for development projects for 13 years, but the provincial government's time and resources had been consumed by long marches and sit-ins, further asking how any civilised society could tolerate this.
“What option did we have in these circumstances? Should we have sat back as silent spectators and, after everything had been destroyed, said that this was our fate? No, this is not our fate. God willing, we have to build Pakistan,” the PM said.
Read : Emergency, governor's rule imposed in K-P after president signs summary on PM Shehbaz's advice
The prime minister said that after the dialogue process collapsed, the government decided, following deliberations and consultations, to impose an emergency in the province.
Referring to the negotiations, PM Shehbaz said the final draft had been almost ready for signing after all the demands had been met. However, at the last moment, the other side said it wanted to consult the K-P chief minister, he added, adding that “the rest is history”.
وزیراعظم محمد شہباز شریف نے مسلم لیگ (ن) کے پارلیمانی پارٹی کے اجلاس سے خطاب کرتے ہوئے کہا کہ پیپلز پارٹی اور مسلم لیگ (ن) کے نمائندوں کی شرکت سے دن رات مذاکرات جاری رہے اور معاہدے کا متفقہ مسودہ بھی تیار ہو گیا، تاہم آخری مرحلے میں مذاکرات ناکام ہو گئے۔ بعد ازاں مولانا فضل… pic.twitter.com/slo3ivqyoS
The prime minister said that after a two-and-a-half-hour cabinet meeting attended by representatives of all coalition partners, the government decided to impose an emergency and governor's rule in K-P.
“We decided that this is the moment when we must stop waiting any longer to save Pakistan, otherwise, everything will burn, and we will be left wringing our hands,” he said.
Read More : ' Govt can't keep sleeping when it comes to citizens' security': DPM Dar on K-P emergency, governor's rule
The premier said the government had been compelled to decide to impose an emergency because “Pakistan comes first”, adding that nothing was more important than the country's progress and survival.
The prime minister further stated that an emergency and governor's rule had now been imposed in K-P and an advisory council comprising experts and professionals had been formed. The council included doctors, educationists and financial experts, he added.
وزیراعظم محمد شہباز شریف نے مسلم لیگ (ن) کے پارلیمانی پارٹی کے اجلاس سے خطاب کرتے ہوئے کہا کہ خیبرپختونخوا میں ایک ایڈوائزری کونسل قائم کی گئی ہے جس میں ماہرین، پیشہ ور افراد، ڈاکٹرز، ماہرین تعلیم اور مالیاتی امور کے ماہرین شامل ہیں۔ حکومت کی کوشش ہے کہ صوبے میں بنیادی سہولیات کی… pic.twitter.com/TmMMoOIydn
He noted that the people of K-P were proud and hospitable and the decision had been taken solely to restore their happiness, development and dignity.
PM's meeting with parliamentary delegations
Earlier, the prime minister took delegations of Pakistan Muslim League (Q), Balochistan Awami Party (BAP), Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party (IPP) and Pakistan Muslim League (PML-Zia) into confidence over the government’s decision to impose emergency and governors' rule in K-P during a meeting at the prime minister’s office.
وزیراعظم شہباز شریف سے پاکستان مسلم لیگ (ق)، بلوچستان عوامی پارٹی، استحکام پاکستان پارٹی اور مسلم لیگ (ضیاء) کے پارلیمانی وفد سے ملاقات وزیراعظم کا کہنا تھا کہ گزشتہ کئی سالوں سے خیبر پختونخوا میں پاک افواج، سیکیورٹی فورسز اور پولیس کے کئی اہلکاروں نے جامِ شہادت نوش کیا اور… pic.twitter.com/ipMoqe1DYX
PM Shehbaz explained the reasons behind the federal government’s decisions, stating that the conduct of the PTI government in the province and its failure to adopt an unequivocal stance against terrorism had posed risks to Pakistan’s growing economy.
The premier noted that the provincial government had neither clearly condemned terrorism nor taken effective action against terrorist groups. Referring to the sacrifices of security personnel, he said numerous members of the Pakistan armed forces, security forces and police had laid down their lives over the past several years while defending the country.
PM Shehbaz said the federal government had provided more than Rs800 billion to K-P under the National Finance Commission (NFC) arrangements to support efforts against terrorism.
However, he said the provincial government had failed to take effective measures to strengthen the capacity of its Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) and establish Safe City projects to improve its counterterrorism capabilities.
During the meeting with a parliamentary delegation, the premier said an impartial technocratic advisory council had been established to assist the governor in improving law and order, strengthening the economy and eliminating terrorism in the province.
The parliamentary delegation expressed its support for the federal government amid the prevailing situation and appreciated the prime minister’s leadership during what it described as difficult circumstances.
The delegation also said the people of K-P had remained deprived of adequate development in health, education and infrastructure during the PTI’s tenure in the province.
It expressed confidence that, with the federal government’s cooperation, development and prosperity in K-P would advance in line with other parts of the country.
Separately, the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) assured Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of its full cooperation with the government’s decisions regarding K-P.
The assurance was given during a meeting between the prime minister and an MQM-P delegation led by party convener and Federal Education Minister Dr Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui.
The delegation included Federal Health Minister Syed Mustafa Kamal, Senator Aamir Waliuddin Chishti, Senator Khalida Ateeb and several members of the National Assembly.
وزیراعظم محمد شہباز شریف سے کنوینر متحدہ قومی موومنٹ ، وفاقی وزیر تعلیم ڈاکٹر خالد مقبول صدیقی کی زیر قیادت متحدہ قومی موومنٹ کے وفد کی ملاقات ہوئی. وفد میں وفاقی وزیر قومی صحت سید مصطفیٰ کمال، سینیٹر عامر ولی الدین چشتی، سینیٹر خالدہ اتیب، اراکین قومی اسمبلی ڈاکٹر محمد فاروق… pic.twitter.com/EIfMXYF9lI
During the meeting, the two sides exchanged views on the country’s overall political situation, while the prime minister took the delegation into confidence regarding the situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
PM Shehbaz described the decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule in the province as a difficult one, taken in the best interest of its people. He said the government had made every effort to avoid the step and had engaged in negotiations in good faith, but had not received a positive response from the other side.
He said terrorist attacks in K-P were increasing, targeting civilians and security personnel, while the provincial government had failed to openly raise its voice against terrorist groups.

title: Police claim situation in Khyber under control after reported clashes | The Express Tribune
description: Deny cops abduction reports; urge people to not pay heed to ‘rumours’
content:
Deny cops abduction reports; urge people to not pay heed to ‘rumours’
The Capital City Police Peshawar on Tuesday urged the public not to pay heed to what it described as "baseless rumours", saying the situation in Bara had been "brought under control" amid reports of clashes between protesters and security personnel.
The police also denied reports that any personnel had been abducted and said around 50 people had been arrested for allegedly "attempting to create unrest".
The statement said cases would be registered against those involved in damaging public property and disrupting law and order under relevant provisions relating to terrorism and sabotage, with strict legal action to follow.
Read : Govt was left with 'no option' but emergency, governor rule: PM Shehbaz
The statement came after clashes reportedly erupted in Bara Bazaar on Tuesday during a protest by Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) workers against the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. Protesters set fire to a National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) office and allegedly took 15 police personnel hostage, according to police.
A protest by the PTI turned violent in Bara Bazaar in Khyber district, with protesters setting fire to a NADRA office, damaging government property and pelting stones at a Rescue 1122 office.
Several people, including two children, were reportedly injured in firing during the protest.
PTI lawmaker Iqbal Afridi said 11 party workers had been injured and one killed. The casualties could not be independently verified.
ضلع خیبر، جمرود میں گورنر راج کے خلاف پُرامن احتجاج. عوامی حقوق پر کوئی سمجھوتہ نہیں، گورنر راج نامنظور pic.twitter.com/4cBa4VAwLa
Khyber District Police Officer Waqar Ahmed said hundreds of PTI workers gathered in Bara Bazaar on Tuesday afternoon to protest against governor’s rule. Police used tear gas and fired into the air to disperse the crowd, which temporarily broke up.
About 90 minutes later, hundreds of protesters led by provincial assembly member Abdul Ghani marched from Minar Chowk towards Bara Chowk, chanting slogans against the government. They set fire to traffic signals upon reaching the intersection, according to the account provided by the district police chief.
As tensions escalated, protesters allegedly detained 15 police personnel inside the tehsil municipal office and took away their weapons and uniforms. Ahmed said the personnel remained in captivity at the time of reporting.
Protesters also set fire to the NADRA office and pelted the Rescue office with stones. Police again used tear gas and fired into the air to disperse the crowd. Two PTI workers were injured by tear gas shells during the demonstrations, Ahmed said.
Separately, reports from Bara Bazaar indicated that several people, including two children, had received gunshot wounds. Further details about the casualties were not immediately available.
Protests were also held at Bab-e-Khyber in Jamrud, where demonstrators chanted slogans against the government’s measures. Further details about the demonstration were not immediately available.
Tensions remained high at several locations in Khyber district following the protests and violence. The status of the police personnel allegedly detained by protesters, the number of injured, and the extent of damage to public property remained unclear.

title: Negotiations were a sham     Raja Nasir Abbas lambasts government for pre planning governor   s rule
description: Senate deliberates on K P s governor rule and emergency
content:
Senate deliberates on K-P's governor rule and emergency
Leader of the Opposition in the Senate Allama Raja Nasir Abbas on Tuesday alleged that negotiations with the government were a sham, claiming that the decision on governor’s rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa had already been made before the talks concluded.
The federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in K-P on Sunday under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution. The government cited the deteriorating law and order situation and what it called a lack of support from the provincial administration in the fight against terrorism.
The upper house opened the floor for debate on the move.
خیبر پختونخوا میں ایمرجنسی کے نفاذ کے خلاف سینیٹ میں قرارداد پیش اسلام آباد: جمعیت وکلاء فورم پاکستان کے مرکزی صدر سینیٹر کامران مرتضیٰ سینیٹر مولانا عبدالواسع سینیٹر مولانا عطاء الحق درویش نے خیبر پختونخوا میں ایمرجنسی کے نفاذ کے خلاف سینیٹ میں قرارداد پیش کردی۔ pic.twitter.com/GKPvQxCv5Q
“The negotiations were a sham. You had already made up your mind,” Abbas said, arguing that the opposition had shown flexibility by stepping back from its demand for a meeting with Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf founder Imran Khan, while the government had refused to reconsider its position.
Speaking during a Senate session chaired by Senate Chairman Syed Yousuf Raza Gilani, Abbas said the opposition wanted to meet Imran to seek his guidance in light of the prevailing global situation, adding that denying access to a detained political leader raised questions about the government’s commitment to political dialogue.
“We are not being allowed to meet Imran Khan, who is a prisoner and the head of a political party,” he said.
Abbas maintained that the opposition had demonstrated a willingness to compromise during negotiations but alleged that the government had already decided on its course of action.
He also criticised the reported move towards imposing governor’s rule in K-P, warning that such measures could deepen political tensions and undermine efforts to restore peace in the province.
Questioning the message being conveyed to young people in K-P, the opposition leader said the authorities’ actions suggested that political struggle and recourse to the judiciary carried little weight. He warned that pushing people away from democratic and political processes could increase frustration and potentially contribute to further instability and militancy.
Referring to the governor’s reported remarks urging people to leave their homes, Abbas argued that such statements could have the opposite of their intended effect by encouraging more people to take up arms.
He cautioned that policies pursued in the name of "restoring order" could aggravate terrorism and unrest, rather than address their underlying causes.
Drawing a comparison with former military ruler Pervez Musharraf, Abbas said that even Musharraf had tolerated dissent to some extent, questioning why a government operating under a democratic system could not accommodate political disagreement. He also alleged that PTI lawmakers, including members of the National Assembly and provincial assemblies, were being abducted.
Abbas said the political crisis could still be resolved through dialogue and corrective action.
He urged the government to end governor’s rule, warning that the move would not deliver lasting peace and could instead inflict further damage on the country.
“Peace cannot be established through such measures. Pakistan will suffer the consequences,” he said.
Earlier, the Senate session began with prayers for those who lost their lives in the Multan railway incident, with Abbas leading the prayers. The house also approved a motion to defer the question hour.
The panel of presiding officers was announced, with Senators Shahadat Ahsan, Manzoor Ahmed and Abdul Qadir nominated to the panel. Then the upper house moved to the discussion on emergency and governor's rule.
Interior minister says negotiations with PTI collapsed over intra-party differences
Later in the session, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said that the government had approached the opposition for negotiations with sincerity. He claimed that the options of imposing an emergency or governor’s rule had been available as early as November 24, but insisted that the government had not wanted to take either step.
He urged opposition leaders to confirm that he had continued contacting them until the night before the possibility of an emergency was discussed.
Recounting the negotiations with the opposition, Naqvi said the initial discussions had focused primarily on terrorism, with the first seven or eight points concerning the security situation. He said PTI leader Asad Qaiser had assured the government of cooperation on the issue and indicated that he would consult the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government before proceeding further.
“After that, we discussed political issues,” Naqvi highlighted.
Naqvi said he had also approached Barrister Gohar Ali Khan and asked him to identify the changes the opposition wanted in “paragraph four” of the draft proposal.
During the negotiations, the interior minister said Asad Qaiser had subsequently indicated that the opposition was willing to support measures concerning terrorism, including an emergency.
According to the minister, six proposals were sent in the final draft.
He claimed that after the draft was finalised, it was forwarded to the K-P chief minister, who then shared it with Murad Saeed. Naqvi alleged that the process broke down following these consultations.
Naqvi also questioned whether Murad Saeed alone was responsible for the collapse of the negotiations, suggesting that other factors and people within the party may also have played a role.
“Imposing an emergency or governor’s rule was not easy. None of us wanted it,” he said.
At the same time, he said, “We did not want our security personnel to be martyred in Peshawar while no provincial assembly representative was present,” referring to the security situation in K-P.
He added that government representatives had attended the funerals of security personnel in the province, accusing the provincial government of failing to provide similar support.
The interior minister also alleged that around 80% of terrorism-related activity was emanating from Afghanistan. He said the government had never singled out any tribe in its statements on militancy.
Naqvi said the government had raised concerns about alleged contacts between certain individuals associated with the PTI-led provincial administration and the Taliban.
“We told them that several of their people were linked to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), and we have evidence,” he said, adding that the government also had information about financial transactions involving individuals connected to the matter.
The minister also recalled previous negotiations with PTI leaders over a planned protest on November 25.
“The government had offered the opposition a venue to hold its protest, but the opposition had instead demanded that a telephone conversation be arranged [with the PTI founder].”
According to Naqvi, the call was facilitated, and the conversation took place, but differences emerged within the opposition, with some party members refusing to accept the outcome. The minister said the government was subsequently asked to arrange a video message from the PTI founder, Imran Khan.
Naqvi claimed that he asked Barrister Gohar to go and record the message, but Imran Khan declined to avail the offer. The minister maintained that the government had reminded the PTI founder that his party was preparing to stage a sit-in and that the message needed to be recorded immediately, but he ignored the call.
Naqvi concluded this part of his remarks by praying for the success of security forces in the fight against terrorism and saying the federal government would work alongside the people of K-P.
Addressing Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, PTI-backed Senator Ali Zafar accused the government of violating the Constitution by arresting the chief minister, speaker and other ministers in K-P, warning that the move would weaken state institutions and undermine democracy.
Speaking during a Senate session, Zafar said the government had inflicted an “indescribable wound” on the state by taking actions that, he argued, were contrary to the Constitution.
The senator questioned, “Which constitutional provision allows the federal government to take control of a province in the guise of combating terrorism?”
“We are all united in our resolve to defeat terrorism. However, while fighting this war, we must not throw the Constitution into the dustbin,” he took the interior minister to task.
Zafar maintained that counterterrorism measures could not be used as a justification for dismissing a provincial government or imposing governor's rule and emergency provisions at the government's discretion. He said an emergency could be declared in circumstances such as a foreign attack, while internal disturbances required adherence to the constitutional process, including the relevant role of the provincial assembly.
He urged the government to bring the relevant summary for imposing governor's rule and an emergency before the Senate for consideration, as well as present the evidence before the upper house for its claims that a provincial government consists of terrorists or their facilitators.
Disputing the government's account of negotiations, Zafar said it contradicted “facts”.
Warning against attempts to suppress political dissent through administrative measures, Zafar said the government could remove an elected administration but could not eliminate a political movement or control public opinion.
“You can remove a government, but you cannot end a movement. You cannot restrict the thinking of the people,” he asserted before the upper house.
He added that the government's actions were not only harming its political opponents but were also damaging the country and weakening the state.
Concluding his address, the PTI senator appealed to the government to reverse its actions and engage the opposition in dialogue.
Dar defends emergency and governor's rule, says suspended K-P govt failed to curb terrorism
Leader of the House in the Senate Ishaq Dar also defended the government's position on the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule, saying the Constitution allows such a measure in the event of a threat of external aggression.
Towards the end of today’s session, Dar said the government was not taking any step outside the Constitution and maintained that the president could also proclaim an emergency and summon a session of parliament within 10 days.
“Whatever has happened has been done entirely in accordance with the Constitution and the law,” he reiterated the government’s stance.
He assailed the suspended K-P government over the province's security situation, claiming that terrorist attacks had tripled since Sohail Afridi assumed the charge of chief minister.
“The KP chief minister has failed to discharge his responsibilities in his own province.”
The deputy prime minister also questioned the provincial government's performance in combatting militancy, saying it had failed to establish an effective Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) despite the PTI remaining in power in the province for 13 years.
“How many times has the PTI government condemned terrorism?” Dar demanded answers, urging the party to publicly denounce terrorist attacks. The minister urged the K-P government to reconsider its leadership and take a clear stand against terrorism.
Speaking on the current ground reality of the province, Dar said the government had attempted to ensure that the advisory council established for K-P did not have a political background, adding that professionals had been appointed to the body, citing the importance of involving qualified professionals in public administration.
“We will make every effort to extend our full support to the K-P advisory council,” he stressed during the speech.
Dar also referred to the previous imprisonment of President Asif Ali Zardari, saying he had spent over a decade in prison, while reiterating his preference for reconciliation over confrontation. Adding that he hoped that PTI founder Imran Khan would eventually be released from prison, as he also stands for “political reconciliation”.
“May Allah facilitate the release of the PTI founder from prison,” he emphasised, while cautioning against placing political interests above national stability.
“The country should not be pushed towards uncertainty simply because a political leader or party failed to get its way.”
Outlining the lapses of the PTI-backed suspended K-P government, Dar said that around Rs800 billion had been transferred to the provincial government through the National Finance Commission (NFC) award and asked Zafar to seek an explanation from his party about how the money had been spent.
“One per cent of the NFC share continued to be allocated to K-P for counterterrorism efforts,” he detailed during the session of the upper house.
He lamented that the provincial government had failed to establish an effective CTD despite receiving substantial financial resources from the centre.
“The K-P chief minister has failed to discharge his responsibilities in his own province,” DPM Dar remarked.
He concluded his speech while expressing confidence that the provincial assembly would be called into session after six months.
The Senate was then adjourned till 4pm tomorrow.

title: Sri Lanka deny Pakistan whitewash
description: Kusal Mendis  87 not out  leads from the front as visitors roar back to down the hosts with an enviable ease
content:
Kusal Mendis (87 not out) leads from the front as visitors roar back to down the hosts with an enviable ease
Skipper Kusal Mendis led from the front to enable Sri Lanka deny Pakistan whitewash when they crafted an eight-wicket win over the hosts in the third and final T20I on Tuesday.
Despite the loss Green-shirts sealed the series 2-1.
At the Pindi Stadium in Rawalpindi Mendis struck an unbeaten 87 off 48 balls as Sri Lanka chased the 169-run target in 17.1 overs after losing two wickets.
Earlier, Sahibzada Farhan hit a superb 76 to propel Pakistan to 168-8 in the allotted 20 overs.
After losing Lahiru Udara (1) cheaply Mendis took the centre stage and catapulted his side to a great win following two back-to-back losses. Mendis, who brought in his fifty off 33 balls, smashed
four sixes and nine fours in his excellent unbeaten knock. He added 59 runs off 41 balls for the second wicket stand with Sineth Jayawardena who fell for 26-ball 38, striking five fours and two sixes. Mendis then shared 98 runs for the third wicket unbroken partnership with Kamindu Mendis to make his side home safely.
Kamindu hit 40 not out off 27 balls with four fours. Mohammad Imran and Arafat Minhas got one wicket each.
After being put into bat first Farhan found himself in tough situation as wickets kept falling at regular intervals at the other end. However he stood like a rock and took his team to a fighting total in the end.
He brought in his 13th fifty of his career off 34 balls and hammered seven fours and three sixes in his 47-ball knock. He added 66 runs off 37 balls for the seventh-wicket stand with Arafat Minhas who chipped in with brilliant 20-ball 34 not out, hammering two sixes and two fours.
Dasun Shanaka was the pick of the Sri Lanka’s bowlers who claimed 3-31 in his quota of four overs.
Eshan Malinga, who ripped through Pakistan’s top order, captured 2-38 in his four overs. Nuwan Thushara got 2-38 in four.
After being invited to bat first Fakhar Zaman and Sahibzada Farhan provided a brisk start to Pakistan, scoring 34 off 19 balls. Medium-pacer Eshan Malinga provided breakthrough to Sri Lanka when he removed Fakhar Zaman (12) and inform Maaz Sadaqat (0) in a single over to put his team ahead.
Fakhar, who wanted to hit it hard, but only edged it to third man fiddler Lahiru Udara.
He struck one six and one four from seven balls. Maaz, who had hit fifties in his previous two games, was held at mid-off by Chamindu Wickramasinghe.
Sri Lanak kept Pakistan under check. Leg-spinner Vijayakanth Viyaskanth then got rid of Hasan Nawaz (16), held excellently at long-on boundary to leave the hosts at 67-3 in the ninth over.
Hasan smashed two fours from 17 balls. Dasun Shanaka then sent Khawaja Nafay (3) back, who handed an easy catch to the backward point fielder when he came down the wicket but failed to middle it.
Shanaka then had Mohammad Imran Randhawa (6) and Abdul Samad (15) in quick succession to leave Pakistan gasping at 107-6 in the 15th over. Samad smacked two fours and a six from ten balls.
However Farhan and Arafat then did well to boost the total.
Farhan was also decalred as the man of the series for scoring 238 in the series. He also broke Abhishek Sharma's record of 229 runs in a single series which he has scored against Afghanistan this year.
Pakistan made four changes, bringing in Sufiyan Moqim, Abdul Samad, Razaullah and Arafat Minhas. Shadab Khan, Saim Ayub, Naseem Shah and Abrar Ahmed were rested.
On October 9 Pakistan defeated Sri Lanka by four wickets when they chased the 183-run target with seven balls to spare. In the second clash on October 9 Pakistan downed Sri Lanka by 82 runs to seal series. Now from October 18 Pakistan will host ODI tri-series, also involving England to kick-start their preparations for the next year’s World Cup which will be hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

title: At least seven killed  over 50 injured as Rehman Baba Express derails near Multan
description: Officials dispatch relief  medical van from Multan to assist passengers  traffice on both sides of track suspended
content:
Railways minister orders investigation, says compensation will be paid to deceased and injured passengers
A passenger train derailed near Multan on Tuesday morning, resulting in the death of at least seven people including a minor child and injuring over 50 others.
According to officials, Peshawar-bound Rehman Baba Express met the tragedy at Sher Shah Bridge at around 5:15am when a number of its carriages went off the tracks, with some overturning
Soon after the incident, rescue workers and the Pakistan Army teams arrived at the accident site and started shifting the dead and the injured to the hospital.
Rescue sources claimed that at least seven people, including three women, two men and a one-and-a-half-year-old girl, died as a result of the derailment. They said over fifty people were transferred to hospital for treatment and a few of these injured were in critical condition.
A spokesperson for Multan’s Nishtar Hospital said 21 patients were still receiving treatment, while one injured person was in critical condition. The hospital had called in additional staff to ensure medical care for the victims.
The cause of the derailment remained unclear. Some sources claimed that the train was travelling at a high speed when the accident occurred, but this claim could not be independently verified.
A passenger also claimed that the nuts and bolts of coach No 9 of the Rehman Baba Express had been repaired near Rohri. However, the account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the reported repair had any connection with the accident.
The accident disrupted train schedules, particularly services travelling from Karachi towards Rawalpindi. Railway officials said some trains were being diverted through an alternative route, while clearing the affected track and completing relief operations could take several more hours.
Railway authorities said train operations had been restored via the Lodhran-Jahanian route.
Rescue operations continued at the accident site as authorities worked to clear the derailed carriages and establish the cause of the tragedy.
According to the train's guard in charge, the driver felt a sudden jolt near Sher Shah, and several coaches derailed just seconds later. However, it is too early to determine whether the accident occurred due to a fault in the railway track or because a part of one of the coaches fell onto the track.
Meanwhile, some passengers alleged that the driver had been operating the train at excessive speed. According to them, they had asked the driver to reduce speed near Bahawalpur because passengers in the fourth and fifth coaches were experiencing severe jolts. They claimed that the train's speed was not reduced.
The Divisional Superintendent of Railways in Multan said it was too early to comment on the cause of the accident. An inquiry committee had been formed to investigate the incident.
Railway spokesperson for Multan Division Kaleem Akhtar said train services on railway lines passing through Multan were suspended following the accident. Railway cranes were being used to remove the derailed coaches, a process that took several hours.
Until the track was cleared, trains passing through Multan will be diverted via alternative routes through Lodhran and Khanewal, potentially causing delays for passengers.
The Nishtar Hospital administration in Multan declared an emergency following the incident, its spokesperson said.
Minister for Railways Hanif Abbasi, speaking to the media at the site, said he considered himself responsible for the train accident, as he visited the site and vowed action against anyone found involved in the incident that killed five passengers.
Abbasi said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had called him following the accident, adding that one of the injured passengers remained in critical condition. A young girl was also among those killed.
“Expressing grief alone will not solve the problem,” Abbasi said, acknowledging that Pakistan Railways faced numerous challenges that had not received adequate attention in the past. “This accident should not have happened,” he said, adding that he was surprised the train had derailed at the location despite having been attended to at Samasatta.
Abbasi said he was not holding any particular individual responsible at this stage but assured that action would be taken against all those found involved. “As the minister, I consider myself responsible,” he said.
He also praised the district administration for carrying out rescue operations promptly and said Pakistan Army personnel were also present at the site. The government would also provide financial assistance to the affected families, he added.
“Running away is not in our nature,” Abbasi said, adding that he had no personal relationships with anyone in the department beyond work. He said the incident had left him unable to smile, reflecting the gravity of the loss of life.
Acknowledging the need for improvements across the railway system, the minister stressed that mechanical issues had to be addressed and that long-distance trains would be a particular focus of upcoming efforts.
He said work on the Rohri-Karachi track would begin in January and announced plans to introduce coaches with stronger couplings designed to prevent them from breaking. Abbasi also pointed to problems in the railway procurement process, saying some projects had been put out to tender as many as eight times.
President Asif Ali Zardari expressed concern over the derailment of the Rehman Baba Express and offered condolences to the families of those killed, while wishing the injured passengers a speedy recovery. He directed the relevant authorities to ensure assistance and all possible facilities for affected passengers and called for a transparent investigation to determine the cause of the accident.
صدرِ مملکت آصف علی زرداری کا ملتان کے قریب رحمان بابا ایکسپریس کے پٹڑی سے اترنے کے واقعے پر اظہارِ تشویش۔ صدرِ مملکت کا حادثے میں جاں بحق ہونے والے مسافروں کے اہلِ خانہ سے دلی تعزیت و ہمدردی اورزخمی مسافروں کی جلد صحت یابی کے لیے نیک تمناؤں کا اظہار۔ صدرِ مملکت کی متعلقہ حکام…
Railways Minister Hanif Abbasi expressed deep grief over the incident, extended sympathies to the bereaved families and directed officials to ensure the best possible medical facilities for the injured.
He said compensation would be paid to deceased and injured passengers in accordance with the railway insurance policy and directed the Federal Government Inspector of Railways to investigate the accident.
Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) Senator Sherry Rehman also expressed grief over the deaths of the five passengers, saying she was deeply saddened by the loss of precious human lives.
ملتان میں رحمان بابا ٹرین حادثے میں پانچ مسافروں کے جاں بحق ہونے پر افسوس کا اظہار کرتی ہوں، قیمتی انسانی جانوں کے ضیاع پر دلی رنج و غم ہے ،متاثرہ خاندانوں کے دکھ میں برابر کے شریک ہیں، زخمی ہونے والے 30 افراد کی جلد صحت یابی کے لیے دعا گو ہوں، پیپلز پارٹی کے جیالوں سے اپیل ہے کی… pic.twitter.com/qPzNIWCcRH
“We share the grief of the affected families and pray for the speedy recovery of the 30 injured,” she said in a post on X. Rehman appealed to PPP workers to donate blood to help the injured passengers and urged the provincial government to accelerate relief efforts, ensure immediate medical assistance and provide the best possible treatment to those wounded in the incident.
Pakistan Railways has faced repeated accidents involving passenger and freight trains, raising concerns over the safety and maintenance of its ageing infrastructure. In April 2026, it was reported that more than 20 railway accidents had occurred since the start of the year, including derailments, collisions and mechanical failures.
These included the Tezgam Express derailment near Lodhran, the Shalimar Express collision with a stationary freight train near Rohri, and the Karakoram Express separating into two sections near Khanewal after a coupling failure.
In a report released in December 2025, Pakistan Railways said it recorded 95 accidents between January 1 and December 20, 2025, including 46 passenger-train derailments and 43 freight-train derailments. The report cited limited modernisation of tracks, signalling systems and safety infrastructure as continuing challenges.
A May 2025 report also highlighted the condition of the railway network, saying more than 6,500 kilometres of track had exceeded its natural lifespan. Railway expert Muhammad Sabir Awan cited incorrect track alignment and non-compliance with safety procedures as causes of derailments, while former chief engineer Muhammad Afzal Bajwa stressed the need for funding to upgrade ageing tracks.

title: People of Karachi feeling the pinch
description: People of Karachi feeling the pinch
content:
Subsidies are not a favour; it's about time city is given what it deserves
The Red Line Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) bridge collapsed in Karachi's Gulshan-e-Iqbal and killed a security guard on duty. This was just another story, another headline. And that is all Karachi is; a story, a headline of an unfulfilled promise that is now forgotten.
The BRT project was launched in 2022, had a 30-month deadline and was expected to be completed in June 2024. Not only has it cost time and damaged vehicles but also cost lives and livelihoods. Imagine the cost escalation during this time.
For long, Karachi and its people have suffered at the cost of policies and general ignorance that completely discount the city's influx of people. Its rapidly increasing boundaries now go so far out that you don't know where Karachi begins and where it ends. Add the deteriorating law-and-order situation, dilapidated infrastructure, projects that are left stranded, lack of basic utilities and you have a city that is undoubtedly and certifiably among the worst to live in.
On the other end of the spectrum is life in the capital city where policymakers walk along the power corridors and pay little heed to the bumps in the south. But why does everyone in Karachi feel the pinch; there is an easy answer. Pakistan's direct taxation stood at Rs5.792 trillion in 2024-25. Karachi's LTO (Large Taxpayer Office) and MTO (Medium Taxpayer Office) alone contributed Rs1.94 trillion, according to data available with the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR).
This is one-third of all direct taxes in Pakistan. Karachi's contribution to GDP, by several estimates, is over one-fourth. This is one city, which hosts around one-tenth of the population. One can imagine how economically productive this 10% of the population is that it contributes one-fourth of all productivity and one-third of all direct taxation. This is just the part that is documented.
Now add all the projects that Pakistan has all over the country. The cheapest electricity largely comes from hydro and nuclear generation, much of which is located in the north. But the fact that these projects are geographically located there does not mean they were financed by the people of that region alone. They were built through national public resources, funded by federal revenues and taxes collected from across Pakistan. Karachi, as the country's principal commercial and revenue-generating centre, could argue that it should get a bigger share. But it is not the case.
The question, therefore, is one of equitable access to the benefits of national investment. If Karachi contributes significantly to the national pool that finances the country's infrastructure, it should not be treated as though access to the resulting low-cost power is a concession or favour. Now, the capital may argue that such capital expenditure and major infrastructure projects are financed by international financial institutions over the life of the projects rather than directly through taxpayers' money.
However, these loans do not exist in isolation: principal repayments, interest payments and sovereign obligations are ultimately serviced through public revenues. What gives international lenders the confidence to extend such financing in the first place? The answer lies in the state's repayment capacity, fiscal credibility and overall solvency, all of which depend on the revenues generated by the national economy. In Pakistan's case, Karachi remains one of the most important engines of that economic and revenue base.
In other words, whether the benefits of that national investment are being shared equitably? A national system should not socialise the cost of infrastructure across the country while concentrating its benefits in particular regions and then presenting any subsequent support to Karachi as a subsidy or favour.
Not to add fuel to the fire, Karachiites also pay for the PHL surcharge, which is an extra fee made part of electricity bills across Pakistan to pay the interest and markup on government power-sector loans. In other words, the city pays for the circular debt of the power sector despite having zero contribution to it. From May 2023 till June this year, the PHL surcharge paid by Karachi has been ascertained to be around Rs124 billion.
The recent revision of KE's tariff framework has also raised significant concerns among Karachi's industrial community. In May 2025, Nepra determined K-Electric's tariff at Rs39.97/kWh against a requested rate of Rs44.69/kWh. This was subsequently revised to Rs32.37/kWh in October 2025, a rate Nepra Appellate Tribunal upheld on September 22, 2026. Now, reports suggest there has been a suspension in that order. Imagine the utility being in its third year of the Multi-Year Tariff control period FY2024-2030 and still having itself confined in a box when it comes to serving Karachi.
Such a substantial revision has created uncertainty and without the environment that enables adequate and predictable investment becomes increasingly challenging. IESCO, FESCO, GEPCO are next in line to be privatised, however, under these circumstances, the case for the privatisation agenda may have a long way to go. Shanghai Electric pulled its $1.77 billion offer to acquire KE owing to regulatory uncertainty and ambiguous economic situation of the country.
The centre argues that Karachi gets subsidy, but that is for customers to ensure the uniformity of the consumer end-tariff across the country. Karachiites do not have the liberty of dams. Put all cities and provinces in one basket, the South alone cannot be blamed for not having access to what our North possesses. Hence, subsidies are not a favour. It's about time Karachi was given what it deserved.
The writer is an economist with nearly 20 years of experience

title: Narnia    trailer introduces Aslan  Daniel Craig   s magician and the White Witch
description: Netflix unveils    Narnia  The Magician   s Nephew    trailer with Aslan  the White Witch and Greta Gerwig   s fantasy world
content:
Netflix unveils ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’ trailer with Aslan, the White Witch and Greta Gerwig’s fantasy world
Netflix has released the first trailer for Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew , Greta Gerwig’s upcoming fantasy film based on C.S. Lewis’s beloved book series The Chronicles of Narnia .
The trailer introduces audiences to the magical world of Narnia, featuring Aslan, the White Witch and an array of mythical creatures.
Set to Led Zeppelin’s “Stairway to Heaven”, the footage follows Digory and Polly, played by David McKenna and Beatrice Campbell, as they discover the Wood between the Worlds. Their adventure begins when Andrew Ketterley, the magician played by Daniel Craig, gives them a magical ring that transports them to fantastical lands.
The trailer also features Emma Mackey as Jadis, who becomes the White Witch, and introduces Aslan, the mythical lion voiced by Meryl Streep. Other cast members include Carey Mulligan and Ciarán Hinds.
Gerwig, who directed the 2023 hit Barbie , said she grew up with the Narnia books and considers them an important part of her life. She approached Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos about adapting The Magician’s Nephew after the streaming company acquired the rights to the franchise.
The director described her vision for the film as a rock opera, with music playing a central role in bringing the fantasy world to life. She contacted Led Zeppelin members Robert Plant and Jimmy Page to secure permission to use “Stairway to Heaven” after showing them an early version of the film.
The movie also marks Gerwig’s first feature film since Barbie and a major theatrical release for Netflix. Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew is scheduled to arrive in cinemas on February 12, 2027, before streaming on Netflix from April 2, 2027.
Gerwig hopes the film will leave audiences feeling inspired by its adventure and encourage them to embrace their own creativity.
