title: A city adrift  the broken altar of gold and dust
description: A city adrift  the broken altar of gold and dust
content:
Karachi once stood as an ocean-kissed mirage of sovereign ambition
Before the iron tracks rusted and the avenues dissolved into salt and stone, Karachi stood as an ocean-kissed mirage of sovereign ambition - a gleaming beacon among the legendary jewels of Asia. It was a city born not of ancient feudal decrees, but of the fierce, unyielding pulse of the sea. Its white-stone facades reflected the golden brilliance of a coastal sun, its broad boulevards breathed with the rhythm of world trade, and its air carried the intoxicating scent of endless promise. Built by the relentless tide of hardworking migrants, merchants and visionaries, this once-modest fishing village arose from the sand to become the undisputed titan of the region, carrying the financial destiny of a young nation upon its broad, iron shoulders.
In the early decades of its modern life, Karachi was an oasis of order and elegance. It was a haven where cosmopolitan night life thrived, where clean electric trams glided smoothly through pristine avenues, and where grand municipal gardens offered shade to dreamers from across the globe. Travelers returning from distant shores spoke of it in the same breath as Tokyo, Singapore and Beirut - a rising star of the Orient whose harbour harboured the future.
Yet, what time could not erode and foreign empires could not crush, decades of predatory governance, unchecked corruption and systemic neglect have torn asunder. Karachi today presents a tragic spectacle: an Asian colossus purposefully reduced to an urban wasteland, its magnificent crown replaced by a wreath of dust, its vast revenues siphoned into administrative abysses while its bones fracture beneath the weight of relentless decay.
The tragedy of Karachi is not found in a natural decline, but in an artificial starvation. The city exists as a boundless river of wealth flowing outward, met by a parched desert of return. It is an economic furnace that consumes its own vitality to warm distant hearths, leaving its own home in darkness. From the roaring docks of Port Qasim to the bustling commercial arteries of its financial heart, Karachi single-handedly generates approximately fifty-five per cent of the total direct federal tax collections managed by the state, while handling over ninety per cent of the nation's international maritime trade to act as the solitary lungs through which an entire country breathes.
Within the provincial boundary, this tragic disparity becomes a stark and terrifying chasm. The city produces an astonishing ninety to ninety-five per cent of all provincial tax revenues collected across the length and breadth of Sindh. Motor vehicle taxes, commercial tolls, business licences and property levies flow incessantly into distant coffers, yet the very roads that yield these trillions are left as broken, dust-choked trenches. Generating between twelve and fifteen per cent of the nation's entire Gross Domestic Product, the metropolis functions as an engine of unprecedented scale. Yet, under the rigid mechanics of national wealth distribution, barely twelve to fifteen per cent of these federal revenues ever trickle back through formulaic awards, while provincial development allocations hover at a meager fifteen to twenty per cent. Stripped of the very fuel required to maintain its gears, the engine grinds itself to dust.
The grand boulevards that once rivaled the finest avenues of the continent have weathered into fractured ruins. University Road, once a proud spine of learning, transit and youth, lies as a hollowed monument to administrative indifference - a cratered track where commuters swallow dust instead of hope. Where electric trams once glided and sparkling streetlamps illuminated vibrant nights, basic infrastructure has vanished into the vast abysses of dishonesty. Clean water has become a prized luxury hoarded by predatory cartels, public transit remains a ghost of a forgotten golden age, and basic civic dignity has been sacrificed upon the altar of unbridled avarice. Rulers treat its vast income not as a sacred trust to be nurtured, but as a perpetual harvest to be stripped bare.
The bond that binds a human soul to a metropolis is forged in the quiet, sacred intimacy of life, labour and death. A city belongs to those who sow their sweat into its burning pavement, who build its bridges with their bare hands, who celebrate their sacred festivals under its coastal lights.
To treat such a sanctuary as a mere colony - a cash cow to be milked without nourishment - is a betrayal of the sacred covenant between a people and their home.
History is an unyielding witness to the truth that no administrative boundary is carved in eternal granite. Great empires, ancient realms and sprawling administrative unions have all yielded to the relentless, correcting tides of time, and everyone who loves the land has a grin seeing prosperity and happiness return to their mother earth. The metropolis belongs to everyone who lives and owns it. When the structural weight of exploitation becomes too heavy for the foundation to bear, the dynamic of history shift. Karachi as of now remains an unfinished poem written in salt, sweat and stone - a suppressed titan yearning to return to its golden times. It holds within its battered frame the immortal spirit of its golden years. Stripped of prevalent paralysis, freed from the grasp of unchecked corruption and allowed to govern its own wealth, this great metropolis possesses the strength to rise overnight. It requires only the return of its own chest of gold to heal its wounds, rebuild its grand avenues and reclaim its rightful throne as the undisputed, sparkling jewel of the Asian coast.

title: Dalit dilemma  politically needed  yet politically ignored
description: Dalit dilemma  politically needed  yet politically ignored
content:
Dalits in Pakistan have lived with a painful contradiction for years
For generations, Dalits in Pakistan have lived with a painful contradiction. They are citizens, voters and contributors to the economy, yet their distinctive historical and social condition remains largely invisible in mainstream political discourse. Political parties speak about minorities, poverty and marginalisation. But how often do they speak about Dalits as Dalits?
It is estimated that almost 85% of the people counted among Pakistan's Hindus and Scheduled Castes belong to historically Dalit communities. Despite their substantial demographic presence, their specific political, social and economic grievances remain largely unrecognised. They are large enough to matter electorally, but rarely recognised as a distinct political constituency with their own voice, demands and aspirations.
At the same time, a striking imbalance persists in political representation. While historically privileged and relatively affluent Hindu groups, estimated to constitute around 15% of Pakistan's Hindu population, regularly secure a disproportionately large share of parliamentary representation, Dalit communities - estimated at around 85% - remain significantly underrepresented. A community representing the overwhelming majority of Pakistan's Hindu population often receives only a fraction of the political representation enjoyed by the much smaller, more privileged segment. This raises a fundamental question of democratic equality: if Dalits constitute the majority within the Hindu population, why does their presence in Parliament remain so disproportionately small?
The Dalit experience also challenges the assumption that marginalised communities suffer because of a lack of ability or ambition. Whenever Dalit students have been given a genuine opportunity to compete on merit, many have demonstrated exceptional ability. They have secured top positions in competitive examinations, including the CSS, won international scholarships, gained admission to professional degree programmes and succeeded in highly competitive academic environments.
These achievements demonstrate a reservoir of talent within communities too often described only through poverty and deprivation. The problem is not simply whether Dalit students can compete. It is what happens after they succeed.
For many Dalit young people, the transition from education to public employment and professional advancement remains difficult. Merit in examinations and scholarships can open doors to education, but fair access to employment is equally important. Concerns about unequal opportunities in recruitment, including through the SPSC and other public-sector institutions, deserve serious examination.
Equality of opportunity cannot mean merely allowing someone to sit for an examination. Merit must have a fair chance to translate into employment and advancement. If Dalit students can win scholarships abroad, secure top positions in competitive examinations and gain admission to professional programmes, there is no justification for assuming they cannot compete for government and professional positions.
In this context, PPP, the party ruling Sindh province, has taken an important step by creating political space for Dalit leadership within mainstream parliamentary politics. This deserves recognition - not because the Dalit struggle is over, but because it has only begun.
The greatest political disadvantage of a marginalised community is not merely poverty; it is invisibility. When specific problems are not recognised, they disappear into broader categories. Dalit poverty becomes ordinary poverty. Caste discrimination becomes a generic minority issue. Landlessness becomes an agricultural problem. Bonded labour becomes merely a labour issue. Educational exclusion becomes simply an education issue.
This is why Dalits need recognition as a distinct political constituency.
The PPP's tradition of democracy, social justice and empowerment of disadvantaged communities provides an opportunity to take this agenda further. Dalit representation demonstrates that a Dalit citizen need not remain merely a voter or welfare beneficiary. A Dalit can be a legislator, policymaker, organiser and leader.
Yet representation alone cannot transform the lives of a historically disadvantaged population. Representation must translate into policy, resources and measurable improvements.
The next step should be a comprehensive Dalit Empowerment Agenda for Sindh.
First, land and housing. Dalit families need meaningful access to land, secure residential rights, housing opportunities and sustainable livelihoods rather than indefinite dependence on welfare.
Second, education and employment. Increasing enrolment is not enough. Dalit students who demonstrate excellence need a pathway from school to university, professional qualifications and employment. Scholarships, hostels and mentoring are important, but transparent recruitment is equally essential.
Third, bonded and forced labour. No community can achieve genuine empowerment while vulnerable families remain trapped in exploitative labour relationships. Existing laws must be enforced, with effective protection for those seeking to escape exploitation.
Fourth, political participation. Representation must move beyond reserved seats. Dalits should increasingly participate in local governments, provincial institutions, public administration and mainstream electoral politics. The goal should be a new generation of leaders able to compete on merit, public service and popular support.
Fifth, dignity and equality. Development is not only about roads, buildings and budgets. It is also about whether citizens are treated equally regardless of birth. Pakistan's constitutional promise of equality must become a lived reality for Dalits.
With its substantial Dalit population and progressive political traditions, Sindh can become a model for Dalit empowerment in Pakistan. The PPP can lead this transformation because it has already opened an important political door. But that opening must become a comprehensive programme of representation, economic opportunity, education, transparent recruitment, social protection and equality.
This issue should ultimately transcend party politics. If the PPP has opened the door, other political parties should walk through it - not by ignoring Dalits, but by offering them better policies. That would strengthen democracy.
The objective should not be to create a permanent Dalit vote bank for any political party. It should be to create Dalit political power. There is a profound difference: a vote bank serves a political party; political empowerment serves a people.
The Dalit question is therefore much bigger than electoral arithmetic. It concerns the unfinished promise of democracy itself. Citizens cannot remain economically and socially disadvantaged while being told that their political rights have been fulfilled simply because they can vote.
For Dalits, the demand is not charity. It is equality. Not token representation, but participation. Not political patronage, but political agency. Not merely inclusion in someone else's agenda, but the ability to help define their own.
That is the beginning of genuine political empowerment.

title: Elite suction machine
description: Elite suction machine
content:
Arduous task ploughing through unending and questionable list of names selected for the national awards this year
It was an arduous task ploughing through the unending and at places questionable list of names selected for the national awards this year. Absent from this list was the name of the person who deserved this award the most – Espen Barth Eide, the Norwegian Foreign Minister. He taught us how to disembark from a commercial flight (and not a Gulfstream), walk down the passenger boarding bridge, carry our own luggage and not have an entourage of a dozen friends and family members. This event happened at about the same time when two government officials were being royally chauffeured in a four-horse-drawn buggy, escorted by seven minions – four mounted on horseback, two holding an umbrella and one serving as a hanger-on. Perhaps history will remember this as one of the most decadent and disgusting visuals of coloniality.
Whether it is a victory in war, a diplomatic triumph, a pact with another country, a national day or simply receiving a foreign dignitary, restraint quickly gives way to vicious extravagance, wastefulness and frenzy. Ceremonies and medals proliferate, banners and hoardings multiply and billboards and buntings mushroom. Simplicity, modesty, austerity, dignity and humility are tossed overboard. The gates of the dwindling state treasury are flung wide open, and the taxpayers' money is brutally squandered – for media campaigns, immodest personal publicity and unabashed self-projection.
The ruling elite of Pakistan has invented a rare and rapacious machinery that relentlessly pulverises the poor and sucks out every morsel from their meagre existence. Called the 'Elite Suction Machine' (ESM), it must not be mistaken for the real suction machines that remain idly parked as show pieces in our sewerage departments: machines whose dormancy sends 100 sanitation workers to their deaths in raw sewage gutters every year. On the contrary, the ESM is at work 24/7, constantly inventing fresh opportunities to plunder resources from the poor and diverting them to the already privileged.
Operating at the two ends of the food chain, the ESM sucks from the poorest and feeds to the richest. In 2025, the salaries of the Chairman Senate and the Speaker National Assembly were quietly raised from Rs205,000 to Rs1,950,000 per month – an increase of 850%. In the same unfortunate year, workers' minimum wage was raised by a miserable 8.1% (from Rs37,000 to Rs40,000) in the provinces while the Federal Government ruthlessly kept the minimum wage frozen at Rs37,000.
Yet another infamous achievement of ESM is the creation of one of the world's most skewed ratios between the minimum wage of workers and the salaries received by the chief executives of public sector organisations. Based on the 2025 minimum wage of Rs40,000, the ratio between the salary of a worker and that of the SBP Governor is 1:100. Likewise, this ratio is 1:70 for the Chief Justice and 1:50 for the Chairman Senate. This of course does not include the numerous unspoken benefits bestowed upon this self-entitled class – not to mention the Rs90 million luxury vehicle purchased to massage the Chairman Senate's ego.
ESM's additional features include built-in processes to hide the corruption and misappropriations routinely practised by its members. To prevent disclosure of information relating to these shady activities, the National Asse¬mbly paid an astonishing amount of Rs35 million to private lawyers to suppress information requested under the Right to Information laws. Ironically, even the suppression expenses were extracted from the taxpayers.
For how long can a society endure such a grotesque disparity between a ruling elite gliding majestically in luxury vehicles and exclusive Gulfstreams, while the poor sink deeper into filthy, disease-ridden sewage gutters? Would such a ship, sooner rather than later, not sink under the burden of its own sinful stewards? The ESM ought to be completely dismantled by withdrawing all perks, facilities, hefty salaries and luxury vehicles of the ruling elite and redirecting the resources towards better wages and pensions for the poor.

title: Preying on ambition
description: The suicide of Laiba Aijaz is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating human toll of unchecked fraudulent schemes
content:
The suicide of Laiba Aijaz is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating human toll of unchecked fraudulent schemes
The suicide of Laiba Aijaz, a BS gold medalist from the International Islamic University Islamabad, is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating human toll of unchecked fraudulent schemes. Driven by the dream of pursuing higher education in the US, Laiba's family entrusted their life savings of Rs7.1 million to a predatory education consultant. For Laiba, the realisation that the admission documents were fake proved too heavy a burden. Unable to face her father - a hardworking milkman who earned their livelihood on a motorcycle - she tragically chose to end her life by hanging herself.
This loss highlights a systemic crisis. Across the country, fraudsters operate with absolute impunity. They mask their criminal operations behind plush career consultancies, fake admission agencies and illicit call centres, exploiting the desperate aspirations of students and job seekers alike. While public vigilance is necessary, the ultimate responsibility lies with the state. Government systems exist precisely to protect ordinary citizens and simpletons from such sophisticated predators.
As an urgent counter-measure, the FIA must immediately track, arrest and prosecute the consultant involved under anti-fraud and abetment of suicide laws. The consultant, who is reportedly taken into custody, must have his bank accounts frozen forthwith so that the defrauded amount can be recovered and returned to Laiba's family as early as possible, though it serves as no compensation to the grieving parents.
As part of steps in general to check such felonies, there is a need for the government to: 1) establish a centralised regulatory body under the Ministry of Education to license all education and career consultants; 2) launch an easily accessible government website where students and parents can verify the credentials of any consultant and check a blacklist of banned operators; 3) deploy law enforcement and digital forensics teams to raid deceptive plush offices and illegal call centres operating without verified credentials; and 4) take steps for public awareness.
The state must act now to ensure that no more Laibas fall prey to the cruel traps of fraudulent consultants.

title: Priced out of survival
description: Priced out of survival
content:
For thousands of cancer patients in Pakistan, struggle to survive is increasingly a struggle to afford treatment
For thousands of cancer patients in Pakistan, the struggle to survive is increasingly becoming a struggle to afford treatment. It has recently been revealed that nearly 25% of cancer patients at Karachi's Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre are unable to complete their treatment. Even where surgery and radiotherapy are provided free of charge, the prohibitive cost of medicines leaves patients with little choice but to abandon treatment.
With the cost of complete cancer care estimated at Rs3m to Rs4m, treatment remains beyond the reach of most Pakistani households. Years of back-breaking inflation have already eroded purchasing power, leaving families struggling to meet their everyday needs. For those confronted with a cancer diagnosis, the burden can be devastating. Savings accumulated over a lifetime may disappear within months, while borrowing or selling possessions offers little assurance that treatment can continue. Some patients are consequently forced to return home, only to seek medical attention again when their condition has deteriorated. That the chances of survival should depend so heavily on financial circumstances is a damning reflection of the country's healthcare priorities. Pakistan's charitable organisations and philanthropists have helped countless patients access medical care, but their contributions cannot substitute for a dependable public healthcare system. Cancer treatment requires continuity, something that uncertain donations and intermittent medicine supplies cannot guarantee. The government must therefore move beyond piecemeal financial assistance and establish a permanent mechanism to ensure that patients, particularly those from low-income households, can complete their prescribed treatment.
The state must recognise that access to cancer care is not a privilege reserved for those with sufficient means. No patient should have to choose between the possibility of survival and the financial security of their family. Allowing poverty to determine who receives treatment and who does not is a failure that no responsible healthcare system should accept.

title: Simmering K P
description: Simmering K P
content:
An uneasy calm prevailed in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa a day after the imposition of Emergency and Governor's Rule
An uneasy calm prevailed in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa a day after the imposition of Emergency and Governor's Rule. While no formal street protests have been reported yet, the same cannot be ruled out in the coming days. A widespread crackdown, resulting in the arrest and detention of numerous PTI provincial leaders and supporters - including Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and his cabinet members - has forced the beleaguered party into a cautious wait-and-watch stance. Meanwhile, party stalwarts have voiced plans to galvanise an anti-government movement, calling on tribal chieftains to join them.
The province remains mired in an administrative dilemma, with several districts hard-hit by law and order issues placed under a state of Emergency, while the remaining are under Governor's rule. Educational institutions across the region were shuttered yesterday, with no official timeline for when classes will resume. Meanwhile, Peshawar has effectively been transformed into a blockaded fortress, as shipping containers seal off all entry and exit points. The heavy deployment of security personnel alongside the enforcement of Section 144 continues to paralyse daily civic life. Demonstrations have erupted in outlying districts, where PTI supporters protested the crackdown on a provincial leadership that boasts a two-thirds majority.
The political temperature continues to soar as opposition parties deliberate on how to gel into a proactive grand alliance. Once again at the center of attention, JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman has strongly condemned the federal government, accusing it of backtracking on assurances to find an amicable solution before unilaterally imposing federal rule. With trust in the judicial process wearing thin, there is a widespread belief that a protest movement is brewing just beneath the surface.
This looming unrest poses a severe challenge to the ruling coalition, which is relying heavily on administrative clampdowns to suppress dissent. As the opposition remains at a bitter standstill, it remains unclear how and when the government plans to reintegrate the embattled province back into the political mainstream.

title: Exploiting the love of learning
description: Exploiting the love of learning
content:
In any healthy society, there are plenty of people who seek higher education
In any healthy society, there are plenty of people who seek higher education. They come from a variety of social and economic backgrounds, and demonstrate both the capacity to perform, and a desire to further their education at institutions that are better than what is available locally. Our society is no different. It has plenty of students who are eager to seek better opportunities to learn and shape their ideas and use that training for a better life.
Then there is this other reality that in the same society someone, working as an individual or as part of a group, would exploit this fundamental love of learning. This person, or a group, would defraud the students and their families of their life savings, cause extreme distress to the student, and unimaginable pain to the loved ones. As we grapple with the immense loss of a young and brilliant student in Islamabad, whose life ended so tragically, we must ask questions of how can we allow this to happen?
The purity of seeking higher education, and the evil of exploiting that goal for financial reward by someone, must not be allowed to coexist. There are fundamental questions about crime, fraud and exploitation that must be answered by law enforcement agencies, but there are other questions that also merit serious reflection by all of us. Starting off, we must recognise that people want to seek higher education opportunities abroad because a large number of our own institutions are not good enough. Institutions suffer from chronic lack of funding, poor governance and lack of seriousness on the part of faculty and administration. But that is not the only reason. We know well that education abroad is also a means to leave the country where people feel devalued and know that a fair shot at progress, growth and success is unlikely. Those who have serious academic and intellectual ambitions know that politics and privilege are much stronger drivers of academic jobs than intellectual capacity and creative abilities. Combine this with the extraordinary growth of 'consultants' who offer services with an astronomical price tag, sell grand dreams and are masters at gaming the system. Corruption, bribery and underhand dealings around document attestation and visas add to this poisonous cocktail of false illusions.
So how do we start combatting this dangerous enterprise? Here we can learn from other areas of public services (e.g. information around health services) where unregulated private practices can cause serious harm. First, consulting practices must be seriously regulated by the government with proper licensing, reporting and taxation. Unlicensed services should not be allowed to operate. Second, there has to be some expectation (and tax incentives) for the private institutions in higher education consultation that a per cent of work must be done pro bono, or with reduced fee services that allow people with modest means to get advice and help in navigating the increasingly complicated network of international higher education. For the philanthropists who may have means and a desire to contribute, perhaps creating and supporting non-profits that provide quality mentorship for those who do not have deep pockets. And this takes me to my final point – those of us (including myself) who have benefitted from quality higher education abroad, and still engage with, or work in institutions of higher learning, need to be more available to guide and help those who can benefit from our experience. I, along with many of my colleagues, do try to provide some guidance to those who reach out, but that is often ad hoc and unstructured. We need to be more organised, and offer our time, to the best of our ability, to those who are not welcome at big businesses because they do not go to elite schools, live in gated communities or drive fancy cars. Pursuit of higher education cannot be the domain of only the rich, and those who come from smaller homes should not be made to sacrifice their assets or their lives just because they dream of learning more.

title: ATC orders jail authorities to facilitate lawyers  meetings with Imaan  Hadi
description: Islamabad court adjourns further proceedings until October 14
content:
Islamabad court adjourns further proceedings until October 14
An anti-terrorism court (ATC) in Islamabad on Monday directed jail authorities to facilitate meetings between lawyer Imaan Mazari, her husband Hadi Ali Chattha and their legal team, which had been unable to meet them in connection with a case involving the removal of barriers.
ATC Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra issued the directions during the hearing, which was attended by former human rights minister Shireen Mazari and lawyers Riasat Ali Azad and Aimal Khan. During the proceedings, Azad argued that the case could not proceed without allowing the legal team, comprising Azad, Zainab Janjua and Aimal Khan, to meet their clients.
The judge observed that anti-terrorism law required trials to be conducted on a daily basis and asked the prosecution how many witnesses it intended to produce. The prosecutor said there were nine witnesses. The judge subsequently directed the prosecutor to ensure that the accused were given access to their lawyers.
Also Read: Barricade removal case: ATC rejects plea to drop terrorism charges against Imaan, Hadi
Chattha questioned why he and Imaan were not being brought before the court, arguing that their continued absence undermined the requirements of a fair trial. He said they had been in jail for eight months and questioned how they could defend themselves and proceed with the case under such circumstances.
He also raised concerns about the confidentiality of meetings between lawyers and their clients, pointing out that cameras had been installed in the areas where meetings were held inside the jail. “The court has to decide our fate. Please summon us to court,” Chattha said, adding that it was for the court to determine whether he and Imaan were terrorists.
The court adjourned further proceedings until October 14.
Imaan and her husband Chattha were rearrested on September 17 , shortly after the Supreme Court granted them bail and suspended their sentences in a separate social-media posts case. They were produced before an Islamabad ATC in connection with a case registered at Kohsar Police Station.
Police sought 30-day physical remand, but ATC Judge Abul Hasnat Muhammad Zulqarnain rejected the request and sent the couple on judicial remand. The judge noted that although they had been nominated in the FIR as members of an unlawful assembly, no weapon had been attributed to either accused.

On September 27, the court issued a contempt notice to the Adiala jail superintendent after the authorities failed to facilitate the signing and transmission of the documents and also failed to produce the accused through video link. Two days later, the issue was resolved after Imaan and Chattha signed the required powers of attorney.
On September 29 , the ATC ended the contempt proceedings against the jail authorities and separately confirmed that notices had been issued on the couple’s bail applications, with arguments scheduled before Judge Abul Hasnat.
On October 7, the ATC had framed charges against Imaan and Chattha in the case related to the alleged violation of a designated route and incitement during the arrival of an international cricket team, despite defence objections that legal requirements had not been fulfilled.

title: UK premier says Iran    almost certainly    directed UK air base plot  announces sanctions
description: Iran denied involvement in the Fairford air base incident  urging Britain to provide evidence for its allegations
content:
Iran denied involvement in the Fairford air base incident, urging Britain to provide evidence for its allegations
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that last month’s alleged terror plot targeting a British air base was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), as he announced fresh sanctions against two Iranian men.
However, Iran on Monday denied any involvement in an incident at Britain's RAF Fairford airbase, which has been used by the United States in its war with the Islamic republic.
"The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any".
Addressing Parliament, Burnham said the UK assessment was that the alleged plot, which led to five arrests on suspicion of terror offenses, was highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran.
“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard,” he told MPs.
“We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams.
“And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.”
In late September, a major security incident occurred at RAF Fairford, a Gloucestershire airbase used by the US Air Force. The incident triggered a large-scale counter-terrorism investigation.
Separately, the UK government also announced that it summoned Iran’s ambassador for ongoing "malign activity."
Read More: US removes B-1 bombers from UK base amid security concerns
“Iran’s continued attempts to undermine the security of the United Kingdom and international partners through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable," Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement.
"This Government will never waiver in our commitment to tacking Iran’s unacceptable actions and protecting our national security. We have already designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) under our new state threats powers," he added.
Britain has also imposed sanctions on two Iranian men, including an asset freeze and a ban on entering the UK.
'We stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis'
Burnham also addressed the escalating situation involving Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, saying he had discussed the issue with US President Donald Trump last month on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
“In my meeting with President Trump, we discussed the situation in the Middle East. I confirmed Britain's decision to send air defense and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refueling support," he said.
"I can confirm today it has already completed 14 operational missions. This support is needed to protect civilians. I condemn the appalling attacks on the King Khalid International Airport. We will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis,” he added.
Burnham also ruled out reopening the Brexit referendum or revising his government's manifesto commitments on relations with the EU, while advocating closer cooperation with the bloc to boost economic growth and address migration.
He also said he respected the result of the 2016 referendum, in which Britain voted to leave the EU, but argued that pragmatic cooperation with European partners could serve the country's interests.
"I am not reopening the referendum. I respect the referendum result," he said.
Also Read: UK examines foreign state involvement in airbase plot
Burnham said his government would pursue opportunities to strengthen the British economy and improve cooperation to tackle migrant boat crossings in the English Channel.
"The deal that I've inherited coming into office represents an opportunity to secure progress on both of those things," he said, adding that rejecting such opportunities would be "a dereliction of duty from any member of this House," he noted.
Ahead of next month's UK-EU summit, Burnham called for discussions on the future relationship between Britain and the bloc, saying closer ties could help promote growth, control migration, and strengthen security.
"If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling migration, upholding our values and our security, it is a conversation we must have," he said.
However, Burnham ruled out rejoining the EU single market or customs union or restoring freedom of movement, citing commitments in Labour's 2024 general election manifesto.
Mentioning what he “can’t do” to improve growth in the UK, he said: “I also want to maintain trust in politics. And I'm afraid I'm not prepared to revisit the red lines in our manifesto.”
The manifesto pledged to keep Britain outside the EU while seeking to reset relations and deepen ties with European partners.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of attempting to distract the public by raising claims of Russian interference in the 2016 referendum.
She questioned whether he considered the referendum result legitimate and called on Burnham to publish evidence if he believes Russia influenced the outcome.
"This is lazy thinking from people who don't have solutions to the real problems we face," Badenoch said.
But Burnham accused the Conservatives of being "in denial about, and not open to seeing, how we can move forward to a better position for the country."
He said public opinion in Britain has shifted in favor of a different approach to relations with the EU, while insisting that his government would respect its existing commitments.

title: Fact check  Viral visuals do not show tense law and order situation in K P after imposition of governor s rule  emergency
description: Several people  majority PTI supporters  have been sharing visuals on multiple social media platforms since October 11
content:
Several people, the majority of whom were Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters, have been sharing visuals on multiple social media platforms since October 11, 2026, allegedly showing the tense law and order situation after the imposition of governor's rule and emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P). However, the visuals are old and unrelated.
The federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in K-P on October 11 following the president’s approval of the recommendations by the federal cabinet. The measures have been approved under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution.
The decision to impose the emergency provisions came during an emergency meeting of the federal cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, where he was briefed on the security situation in K-P. Cabinet members reviewed the situation and took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”, according to the Prime Minister’s Office.
A couple of hours after the imposition of emergency was announced, K-P Information Minister Shafi Jan, who had been accompanying now-dysfunctional K-P Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on the PTI’s long march, claimed the latter had been taken into custody.
Later, the PTI issued a statement , condemning the “arrest” of Afridi and others and describing it as an act of “political victimisation and an attempt to weaken the province’s elected leadership and democratic institutions”.
Communication and internet services have also been disrupted in the province.
On October 11, a person shared a video on Instagram of a large crowd and security personnel in the street with the following caption: “In Peshawar, people actually stood up to the army.”
The same account shared the same clip on X with a similar caption, gaining 302,100 views.
Another account shared the same video with a similar caption, accumulating 232,100 views.
A pro-PTI user, based on their past posts, posted the same clip with the same caption, gaining 169,000 views.
Several other users also shared the same clip on X, as seen here , here , here , here , here , collectively gaining 163,000 views.
A fact-check was initiated to determine the veracity of the claim due to its high virality and keen public interest in K-P’s situation after the changes to its governance and the information gap amid the connectivity and internet issues.
A reverse image search was conducted to trace the source of the video, which yielded the same visual shared by several social media accounts in early July 2026.
A Facebook user shared the same video on July 9, 2026, with the following caption: “FC and public go face to face at Quetta Civil Hospital.”
An Afghan media outlet, Angeza Radio , also posted the same clip, dated July 9, 2026, with the following caption: “Popular objections against the Pakistani army have increased in Balochistan. After 35 policemen were kidnapped by anti-Pakistan militants and the bodies of 21 people were found in the Mangal Ziarat area of ​​Balochistan, some residents of the area started protesting against the Pakistani army. According to reports, the protestors did not allow the participation of the Pakistani army in the funeral ceremony of the killed farmers and demanded that the army leave Balochistan.”
Therefore, the claim that a viral video shows people standing up to the army is misleading. The video is old from July 9, 2026, showing people protesting against the army in Quetta.
Another clip was shared by a fan account of YouTuber Imran Riaz Khan on X on October 12, allegedly showing a protest in Peshawar, with the following caption: “Mohsin Naqvi, look”
Several other pro-PTI users also shared the same clip on X, as seen here , here , here , here and here , collectively gaining 50,000 views
A reverse image search was conducted to trace the source of the image and yielded a TikTok video , dated August 26, 2026, featuring the same visuals as the viral ones, with the following caption: “The Thai Nguyen - Hanoi Expressway is one of the most important arterial roads, playing a key role in connecting trade and economic development between Thai Nguyen province and Hanoi.”
Further reverse image search yielded a Facebook post , dated August 26, 2026, with the following caption: “Thai Nguyen will not sleep tonight! Vietnam wins against Thailand – and the streets of Thai Nguyen are bursting with red! The red flag with a yellow star fluttered in the wind, and cheers echoed throughout the streets. People took to the streets, celebrating a victory that was truly something to be proud of! There are moments when just looking at something makes you realise how much you love Vietnam.”
A keyword search using relevant terms such as “Vietnamese national team”, “Fans in Thai Nguyen” and “win” revealed a report published by Vietnam. Vn on August 26, 2026, titled “Fans in Thai Nguyen celebrate the victory of the Vietnamese national team.”
As per the news report, after the Vietnamese national team’s victory over the Thai national team, fans took over the streets around Vo Nguyen Giap Square to show support and cheer their team
Therefore, the claim that a viral video shows people protesting in Peshawar is false. The video is old from August 26, 2026, showing sports fans celebrating in Vietnam.
Video of security personnel running in the street amid gunfire
Another video was shared on October 11, 2026, by an X user who appears to support PTI, based on his past posts, allegedly showing security personnel running in the street amid gunfire with the caption: “May Allah’s mercy be upon the KP situation, which is out of control.”
The video showed what appeared to be security personnel running in the streets amid heavy gunfire.
However, a reverse image search yielded that the footage is from Syria and was shared three days earlier, rather than showing the situation in K-P.
According to an Iranian media outlet, Kurd Press , unrest broke out in Hasakah, Syria, on October 8 and 9, 2026, following the destruction of Kurdish signs and symbols around a Syrian flag-raising ceremony in Al-Salam Square. Protests spread to other parts of the city, with security forces reportedly firing into the air to disperse crowds. Several civilians were reported injured by gunfire, although the final number of injuries remained unclear.
The same visual with a similar context was also covered by an Iraqi news outlet, Kurdistan 24 .
The claim that a viral video shows security personnel running in the street amid gunfire is false. However, the video is old from October 8, 2026, from Syria.
Video of protesters pelting military vehicles
A fourth video was shared on an Instagram account that appears to support PTI, based on its past posts, that showed people throwing stones at what appears to be a military vehicle.
A reverse image search found that the same footage had circulated in different contexts in 2026.
On June 6, 2026, an apparently pro-PTI account shared it, claiming it was from Gilgit. Earlier, in February 2026, another apparently pro-PTI account on X shared the video , claiming it showed events in Islamabad that month.
However, the footage is two years old and shows clashes in Islamabad during a PTI march in October 2024.
In October 2024, PTI held major anti-government rallies and protests demanding the release of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan and protesting against government restrictions and proposed constitutional amendments. The protest was led primarily by the then K-P CM Ali Amin Gandapur and party leaders; PTI supporters attempted to march toward Islamabad’s D-Chowk starting October 4, 2024.
Therefore, the claim that a viral video shows people throwing stones at a military vehicle is false. The footage is two years old and shows clashes in Islamabad during a PTI march in October 2024.
Video of Peshawar University students marching towards Governor House
Another clip shared by PTI supporters, based on their past posts, allegedly showed Peshawar University students marching towards the Governor’s House in protest against the governor’s rule.
PTI Europe ’s official X account shared the same video on October 11, showing students in white uniforms marching with the following caption: “Well done, young people of Peshawar University. We will not accept Governor’s Rule or Emergency under any circumstances.”
A video of the same incident from a different angle was also shared by PTI Bannu chapter on X with the following caption: “Peshawar University students have taken to the streets leading to the Governor’s House. Pakistan’s situation, especially Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s situation, is dire. O Allah, have mercy.”
The video in a similar context was further shared by several other users, as can be seen here , here , here , here , and here .
However, a reverse image search yielded the same visuals shared by an Indian media outlet, The Free Press journal , on October 5, 2025. The article was titled: “Pakistan: Teachers, Students Protest Across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Against Plans To Outsource Government Colleges”.
According to the article, which cites Pakistani media outlet Dawn , teachers and students from government colleges protested in various locations across K-P against the decision to outsource low-enrollment colleges and the proposal to require an MPhil degree and research work for teacher promotions.
A keyword search conducted yielded Dawn’s report on the same incident, sharing similar visuals and corroborating the same details.
Therefore, the claim that a viral video shows Peshawar University students marching towards the Governor's House is false. The clip is old from October 7, 2025, showing teachers and students protesting in K-P against the decision to outsource low-enrollment colleges.
The claim that viral visuals show the tense law and order situation in K-P after the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency is false.
This fact check was originally published by iVerify Pakistan — a project of CEJ-IBA and UNDP.

title: Oil prices fluctuate on Trump s Russian diesel comments  attacks on Saudi
description: Brent rose 69 cents or 0 7   to  105 41 a barrel by 2 23pm PKT  US WTI was at  92 42 a barrel  up 57 cents     or 0 6
content:
Brent rose 69 cents or 0.7%, to $105.41 a barrel by 2:23pm PKT; US WTI was at $92.42 a barrel, up 57 cents, ​or 0.6%
Oil prices oscillated on Monday ​as the market considered possible further supplies after US President Donald Trump hailed fresh Russian ‌diesel exports against supply-constricting signals after major attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Retracing earlier losses, Brent crude futures rose 69 cents or 0.7%, to $105.41 a barrel by 2:23pm PKT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $92.42 a barrel, up 57 cents, ​or 0.6%.
The Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility for a Saturday strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed ​13 people and wounded more than 300. Further attacks happened on Sunday.
In addition, more attacks ⁠on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz have been reported this month, threatening to dampen a ​recovery in Middle East crude exports seen in September.
A tanker was struck by a drone in the vicinity of ​Oman's Sohar, while another was damaged transiting Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported.
Goldman Sachs, in a note, raised its Brent price forecast for December to $90 a barrel from $85, estimating a risk premium of just over $20 a barrel.
Read: K-P emergency fuels PSX sell-off as index drops over 700 points
"We forecast WTI ​prices, which are unusually low vs Brent because of high US-Europe shipping costs, to average $81 in December ​2026 and $73 in 2027," they added.
In the Gulf of Mexico, energy majors Shell, Chevron and BP were seeking to redeploy personnel ‌and ⁠restore production at their platforms after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday.
ICE gasoil futures fell 4.3% to $1,419.5 per metric ton after President Trump said on Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets, with more to come later.
"The immediate ​impact of the deal ​is questionable, as Russia’s ⁠refining capacity has been severely reduced," PVM analyst Tamas Varga said. "However, Moscow has partially lifted its ban on diesel exports, allowing 500,000 tons (around 3.7 million barrels) ​to be released onto the international market —equivalent to roughly one day of US ​consumption and around ⁠13% of global demand."
Trump also unexpectedly announced on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire, but Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he was still waiting to see details, while Russia did not comment.
The ⁠International Energy ​Agency's Fatih Birol said all members should assess whether additional diesel ​releases are necessary and that countries which have not yet fully delivered pledged volumes should accelerate releases prioritising diesel.

title: Policies will come from Islamabad  not Kabul   Kundi vows closer coordination with Centre
description: Naqvi says  not everything will change in single day  as first time in two years Centre and province are on same page
content:
Naqvi denies claims of division, says 'not everything will change in single day', seeks more funds for affected areas
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Governor Faisal Karim Kundi on Monday vowed closer coordination between the provincial and federal governments, saying policy decisions for K-P would be made in Islamabad rather than in Afghanistan.
“The days when people fought with the federal government are now over, and you will see coordination between the provincial and the federal government. Our policies will come from Islamabad and not from Kabul, Jalalabad or Kandahar”, said Kundi in a press conference in Peshawar.
Kundi also pledged full support to the police and security forces in K-P, promising to “own them” and provide them with weapons and increased salaries as they fought on the "front lines" in the battle against terrorism.
He stated that members of the advisory council had assumed their responsibilities and were taking briefings on a “war footing”.
“I want to thank the people of K-P who rejected the circus that was staged in the name of protests. In the past two days, there was no response from the people and sweets were distributed as people marked a day of liberation. Their container is still there and remains unclaimed even now”, he added.
Kundi remarked that he was waiting for those who announced that they would surround the Governor House and climb over its walls. “I want to again thank the people of K-P for rejecting this nuisance of 13 years as we set forth on a new journey together”.
“Our first priority remains the fight against terrorism, and our government will support our police, armed forces, FC and security forces. Our focus will be on security first, and development would come second”, he added.
Kundi further pledged to provide resources to the provincial police and the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD), saying the government stood firmly behind the forces.
“I want to tell my police that we will own you and will provide you with the weapons you need to fight on the front lines in this fight against terrorism. We will not compromise on any of your needs and will make you well-equipped”, he said.
K-P governor stated that he had asked the inspector general of police and the chief secretary to increase police salaries, further adding that the compensation package for the families of security personnel who died in the line of duty would also be enhanced.
The governor said the federal government had previously offered K-P modern armoured vehicles, but the previous provincial government had not received them, further adding that the armoured vehicles provided by the interior minister had now been received.
On the directions of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, today I handed over 10 newly acquired Armoured Personnel Carriers (APCs) of Islamabad Police to KP Police to strengthen their ongoing counterterrorism operations. In view of the prevailing security situation and rising terrorist… pic.twitter.com/CUGHErTTXU
Kundi stressed that there would be no compromise on law and order and that no vandalism would be allowed in K-P, further adding the task was to “clean up” 13 years of mismanagement, and that efforts would be made on a “war footing” to try and accomplish it within three months.
He underlined that his government had taken up K-P’s case with the federal government, but the previous provincial government had failed to effectively advocate for the interests of the province.
“We know what resources are available to us, and we will present our case with facts and arguments to the federal government,” he said.
Kundi questioned the previous provincial Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) government, arguing that people had not been provided security, further accusing the PTI of supporting terrorism. “Do you want that kind of democracy in which citizens are not safe, and policies come from Afghanistan”?
Kundi added that everyone involved in corruption would be held accountable, adding that those found guilty would be arrested and punished. “Individuals facing cases will have to appear before the courts and face legal proceedings against them”.
While responding to a question, the governor informed that former K-P chief minister Sohail Afridi was in “protective custody”.
He further said the Apex Committee had decided to deport undocumented Afghan nationals.
“Anyone who does not have valid documents will be deported.”
خیبر پختونخوا کے عوام نے نفرت اور انتہا پسندی کی سیاست کو مسترد کر دیا، گورنر فیصل کریم کنڈی #FaisalKarimKundi #KhyberPakhtunkhwa #Emergency pic.twitter.com/Ef2ZC1yrZu
Earlier, Kundi and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi called for closer Centre-province coordination against terrorism as K-P held its first Apex Committee meeting after the imposition of emergency measures and governor’s rule.
A day earlier, Kundi had convened the first Apex Committee meeting after the federal government formed an 11-member advisory council to oversee administrative affairs in K-P. The K-P governor also chaired the advisory council’s inaugural meeting, where he said the state was determined to rid the province of terrorism.
Today, Kundi and Naqvi co-chaired the provincial Apex Committee meeting at Governor’s House, which was attended by members of the Advisory Council and senior officials.
“There are many other issues, but our first priority is to eliminate terrorism. We can sacrifice development, but we cannot compromise on security,” Kundi said, calling for greater coordination between the federal and provincial governments and stronger support for law enforcement agencies.
He said the police and the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) needed the resources and facilities required to confront terrorist threats. "We have to fulfil their demands because they are our frontline force,” he said.
“We should focus on result-oriented measures, not cosmetic steps to show that we are working for peace. Fewer things may be done, but the results should be visible,” he added
Kundi further stated that people in the province wanted "peace, development and prosperity," but insecurity had prevented many from living freely and travelling without fear.
"They see people elsewhere living freely, conducting business and going about their lives. We have to create the same conditions here,” he said.
The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Apex Committee meeting is underway at Governor’s House, co-chaired by Governor Faisal Karim Kundi and the interior minister. Advisory Council members and senior officials are also attending the meeting. @MohsinnaqviC42 @fkkundi #KhyberPakhtunkhwa … pic.twitter.com/1yOpELukw1
According to Kundi, lasting peace would also help attract investment and support economic activity, pointing to the province’s natural resources, agriculture, energy potential and tourism opportunities.
He called for close coordination between the federal and provincial administrations, saying the government would continue working through the relevant committees to address security gaps and ensure that institutions worked together.
“There should be no situation in which we are not on the same page,” he said.
Naqvi said the meeting marked the first time in two-and-a-half years that he could confidently say "the federal and provincial governments are on one page."
“The hardest task was faced by the people who were fighting this war. There were times when people would not even attend the funerals of those who had been martyred,” he said.
Naqvi paid tribute to security personnel who "fought terrorists even without the necessary support from the government" and said that a government had to lead the fight against terrorism rather than leave security forces to carry the burden alone.
“No matter how many resources you provide, a war cannot be won unless the government there leads it,” he said.
Naqvi added the authorities had repeatedly asked the provincial government to cooperate in counter-terrorism efforts over the past two-and-a-half years, but the necessary coordination had not materialised.
“The people have not changed. They are the same people. But when the government leads, you will see how much better the results can be,” he said.
Naqvi cautioned that "not everything will change in a single day" and that the hardest times may still come, but the governor, the police, the advisers and the federal government will face them together.
Read: 'Govt can't keep sleeping when it comes to citizens' security': DPM Dar on K-P emergency, governor's rule
“If we stand together, there is no way they can defeat us,” he added.
The interior minister also called for a return to a five-district security plan, under which police and other relevant institutions would receive additional support in phases.
“If you cannot provide protection or facilities to a police officer, and your opponent has modern weapons while the officer has only a pistol, how can you expect that officer to fight effectively?” Naqvi said.
He welcomed the work being undertaken by the relevant security authorities to strengthen the police, saying the proposed measures could prove to be a turning point for the force. Naqvi also praised the public for remaining peaceful over the preceding 24 hours, saying there had been concerns that protests might disrupt life across the province.
“The province is largely peaceful, and the people want peace. Their expectations are clear; now it is up to us to deliver,” he said.
He urged the new administration and security institutions to work together, expressing confidence that improved coordination and sustained efforts would produce results.
Later, addressing the meeting of Regional Development Secretariat members, Naqvi said a campaign had been under way since Sunday, suggesting that the government was dividing K-P.
He dismissed the claims as untrue, insisting that the province would continue to function as a single administrative and political unit.
“K-P is one province, and that’s how it will work. We will make it run together,” he said.
Explaining the arrangements, Naqvi drew a comparison with the South Punjab Secretariat, which he said had been operating for years with a separate secretariat, an additional inspector general of police and an additional chief secretary. He said the same approach would be followed in the districts concerned in K-P, adding that the arrangements should not be confused with the creation of a new province.
Naqvi said the government's immediate priority was to consult tribal communities and ensure that their representatives had a meaningful role in identifying and resolving local problems. He stressed that the council to be established and the consultations with tribes were central to the process.
“The consultations that we need to have with the tribes — that’s the most important,” he said, adding that the government needed to focus its efforts on these areas rather than diverting attention elsewhere.
Federal Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi addresses a meeting of Regional Development Secretariat members, stressing the need to formulate a development strategy in consultation with local representatives. He calls for strengthening police and other law enforcement agencies to… pic.twitter.com/hQEKiQJvvG
He said the government would bring together representatives who genuinely spoke for their communities and ask them to identify the problems they faced before working on solutions.
“We will ask them: ‘What issues are you facing?’ And then focus on fixing those,” he said.
Naqvi said the security situation was another major concern, pointing to the ongoing conflict with terrorists in the affected areas. He said the police and other law enforcement agencies had to be strengthened to respond to the threat, making security a central part of the government's efforts.
“The biggest issue, because there’s a war going on with terrorists in that area, then we have to, no matter what, make our police and our other agencies strong there,” he said.
He also called for substantially greater financial allocations for the affected areas, arguing that spending needed to reflect the security challenges and requirements of communities there.
To illustrate the disparity he believed was necessary, Naqvi said that for every rupee spent in the rest of K-P, three rupees should be spent in the affected areas.
Naqvi said the administrative arrangements and law enforcement agencies both needed to be strengthened, with the federal government providing financial assistance and other support wherever required. He added that the government would continue implementing measures in response to the needs identified by the relevant authorities.
He stressed that the measures could not be implemented by one authority alone and would require coordinated efforts. The core committee and the administrator, he said, would play important roles in ensuring that the arrangements worked effectively.
“We have to work on it together,” Naqvi said, adding that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was overseeing the process alongside the provincial government.
Federal imposes emergency, governor's rule
The federal government imposed emergency measures and governor’s rule in K-P on Sunday after the federal cabinet approved the recommendation and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif advised President Asif Ali Zardari to invoke Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution. Zardari signed the summary, transferring executive authority from the provincial government to Governor Faisal Karim Kundi.
The government cited escalating terrorist attacks, threats to lives and property, attacks on government installations and law-enforcement personnel, and what it said was the provincial government’s failure to take adequate measures against terrorism.
The two constitutional provisions serve different purposes . Article 232 provides for the proclamation of an emergency in circumstances including war, external aggression or internal disturbance beyond the control of a provincial government. Article 234, meanwhile, provides for intervention when the constitutional machinery of a province cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
The proclamation invoked Articles 232(1) and 234(1), stating that the provincial government could not function constitutionally under the prevailing circumstances. Under the new arrangement, the federal government could direct the governor to assume some or all functions of the provincial government, while the powers of the provincial assembly would be exercised by Parliament or under its authority. The chief minister, provincial ministers, advisers, special assistants and advocate general ceased to hold office with immediate effect.
The emergency was declared in 12 districts , rather than across the entire province. These comprised the eight merged tribal districts — Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Kurram, Orakzai, North Waziristan, South Waziristan Upper and South Waziristan Lower — and Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Bannu and Lakki Marwat.
Read more: K-P experiences fourth spell of governor's rule
The emergency covered the Bannu and Dera Ismail Khan divisions in full and parts of the Peshawar, Kohat and Malakand divisions, while Hazara and Mardan divisions were exempted. The federal government also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets under Article 245 to assist the civil administration and protect citizens, property and government installations.
To assist Kundi in administering the province, the federal government constituted an 11-member advisory council . Its members are Tariq Mahmood Pasha, Dr Aamir Abdullah, retired Lieutenant General Nigar Johar, Samar Bilour, Dr Sarfaraz Ali, Aamir Javed, Dr M Irshad, Kifayatullah, Tayyab Qureshi, Usman Saifullah Khan and Asif Rafiq. Sanaullah Advocate was appointed the provincial advocate general. The council is intended to support the governor in overseeing provincial administrative affairs under the new arrangement.
Alongside the province-wide transfer of executive authority, the federal government ordered the establishment of an Area Development Secretariat to oversee administration, security, law enforcement and development in the 12 designated districts. The secretariat is to operate under an Area Representative and Development Council, with the additional chief secretary for the designated districts also serving as their administrator.
Under the federal order, the administrator can direct civil administration, police and military authorities, supervise relevant departments and order the allocation or transfer of funds. The order also places provincial officers and personnel serving in those districts under the secretariat’s administrative and operational control.

title: Saudi led coalition says Houthi ballistic missile intercepted over Riyadh
description: Unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh s international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday  causing a fire
content:
Pakistani resident killed, dozen injured in new attack on Saudi airport
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Monday evening that it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh.
In a post on X, the coalition announced the “interception and destruction of a ballistic missile” fired toward the city.
The announcement followed notices from Saudi Civil Defence saying the danger had passed in Riyadh, minutes after an early warning was briefly issued over a “potential danger.”
التحالف: اعتراض وتدمير صاروخ باليستي أطلقته الميليشيا الحوثية الإرهابية باتجاه الرياض.
Riyadh has faced repeated Houthi attacks in recent days, with strikes on King Khalid International Airport over two days forcing the temporary suspension of operations.
Pakistani resident killed, dozen injured in new attack on Saudi airport
One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack ​Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Saudi-led coalition forces in ‌Yemen said an unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. A Pakistani resident was killed and eleven people were wounded, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
#Statement | Follow-up on the attack targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. #GACA pic.twitter.com/L7aaMrvj9P
Coalition forces also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. They later added that a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in the country's Eastern Province, and a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait had been intercepted. Emergency alerts were also issued in Abha, in the ​south, early on Monday but the danger had since passed, the Saudi Civil Defence said.
The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis, ​who are fighting a ground war in Yemen against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said the events of recent weeks were serious and the kingdom's response must be "equally serious", as Yemen's Houthis step up attacks on the kingdom, killing more than 15 people in two weeks.
Footage released by Saudi state television of the Saturday attack on the Riyadh airport showed scores ⁠of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam's two holiest sites. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, while parts of the roof appeared to cave in.
CCTV released by Saudi Arabia shows the moment of an attack on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 on October 10 https://t.co/WD9KLEvvhB pic.twitter.com/JmlLp3UbRq
Read: Saudi-led coalition says new attack at Riyadh airport causes fire, day after strike kills 13
The ​airport was closed after the attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Skies over Saudi capital Riyadh largely empty after deadly Houthi strikes on airport
The skies above ​the Saudi capital Riyadh were largely empty on Monday ‌after attacks by Yemen's Houthis on the city's airport, with about 60% of scheduled flights expected to be cancelled, according ​to aviation analytics firm Cirium.
King Khalid International Airport ​in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, cancelled ⁠99.7% of all scheduled flights on Sunday, Cirium data ​showed. More than a third of flights scheduled across ​the kingdom were not expected to operate on Monday, while flight tracking website FlightRadar24 estimated cancellations at Riyadh airport at about 78%.
The Saudi ​capital's airport remained closed on Sunday after an attack ​that killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others. The ‌strike ⁠followed another attack claimed by the Houthis a day earlier that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi ​civil aviation in ​years, forcing ⁠airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services. The Federal Aviation Administration told US ​airlines on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to ​or ⁠over Saudi Arabia.
Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a previous suspension ⁠of ​services to and from the Saudi ​capital until the end of the month.
Houthis claim responsibility for other attacks
In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and said ​the group had also struck the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco.
The Saudi government's media office and Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.
The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the strike on Dammam's King Fahd International Airport late on Sunday, adding that "damage assessments and safety inspections of airport facilities are under way."
An eyewitness aboard a taxiing aircraft at Dammam told Reuters that around 8:30pm (2230 PKT) on Sunday, they saw a projectile strike ​the tarmac beside several parked aircraft, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate. Passengers disembarked and were told to leave.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed several delays and cancellations on Sunday for arrivals and ​departures at Dammam airport, the kingdom's third-largest.
The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said.
The US and Britain's embassy in Saudi ‌Arabia in a ⁠post on X advised British citizens against all but essential travel to Jeddah, Dammam and all airports in the kingdom except the airport in Madinah.
Security Alert: U.S. Mission Saudi Arabia (October 11, 2026) The U.S. Mission is aware of additional attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and targeted attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on October 11. U.S. government employees working in Saudi… pic.twitter.com/vumnc8XRDn
US aviation authorities issued a notice to US airlines to use caution while flying to or over the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet ​to come, God willing," Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said ​in statements carried by Al Masirah television.
Read more: FM Dar condemns Houthi attack on Riyadh airport, says Pakistan is in touch with Saudi authorities
US President ⁠Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.
In a Telegram post, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said he told his Saudi counterpart that Tehran was ready to help facilitate ​dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
A five-day conference of the international energy organisation WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention ​centre about 10 km (6 miles) from ⁠the Riyadh airport, the Saudi energy ministry said.
A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead, according to a media advisory from the ministry. It was not clear which ministers attended.
Italy's energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link.
German officials were trying to organise a return flight for economy minister Katherina Reiche. She was supposed to return to Berlin from Riyadh on Monday but the ⁠ministry said it ​appeared likely her flight would be unable to take off.
Separately, Saudi authorities announced that schools in Riyadh would shift in-person classes to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday.
Sunday's attack brought the death toll in attacks on Riyadh's airport to 18 for the week. In Saturday's attack, the dead included four Saudis while the remainder were foreign nationals, Saudi authorities said.

title: Military conducts successful test of indigenous Fatah 4 cruise missile
description: ISPR says the weapon system is equipped with advanced avionics  state of the art navigational aids
content:
ISPR says the weapon system is equipped with advanced avionics, state-of-the-art navigational aids
Pakistan conducted a successful test launch of an indigenously developed extended version of the Fatah-4 ground-launched cruise missile, the military’s media wing said on Tuesday.
The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said the weapon system was "equipped with advanced avionics and state-of-the-art navigational aids" and could engage targets at extended ranges with "high precision and lethality".
According to the media wing, the test also validated additional "technical parameters" of various sub-systems incorporated for improved accuracy and enhanced survivability.
Read : Pakistan Army successfully test-fires Fatah-4 cruise missile
"Today's launch was witnessed by senior officers from Pakistan Army along with scientists and engineers of the developing agency," the ISPR further added.
Pakistan today conducted a successful test launch of the indigenously developed extended version of Fatah-4, a ground launched cruise missile. Equipped with advanced avionics and state of the art navigational aids, the weapon system is capable of engaging targets at extended… pic.twitter.com/8dilUuQiWA
It said the president, prime minister and services chiefs commended the successful test launch and appreciated the "technical prowess, dedication and commitment" of all those who contributed towards achieving the milestone.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi congratulated the nation on the successful test.
Naqvi stated that the successful test was a “commendable achievement of our scientists and engineers”, further adding that it was a “significant development” in the defence sector. “I congratulate our scientists and engineers, and we are proud of them”.
“Pakistan’s defence is impregnable,” he added.
On September 30, 2025, the Pakistan Army had successfully conducted a training launch of its newly developed Fatah-4 at a range of 750 kilometres.
The Fatah-4 is designed to evade enemy missile defence systems due to its terrain-hugging capabilities, ensuring high precision when engaging targets. The missile’s features enhance its lethality and survivability, boosting the effectiveness of Pakistan’s conventional missile systems.
