title: Pakistan  allies back Saudi response to attack
description: Pakistan  allies back Saudi response to attack
content:
R4 nations condemn deadly Riyadh airport strike
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Turkiye on Sunday strongly condemned a deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and backed the Kingdom's right to take "all legitimate measures" to counter the threat, as Islamabad signalled firm support for its key Gulf ally amid a sharp escalation in the Yemen conflict.
In a joint statement issued by the Foreign Office, the four countries, grouped as R4, condemned "in the strongest terms" the ongoing Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, particularly the strike on King Khalid International Airport that caused civilian deaths and injuries and damaged civilian infrastructure.
"The Group further reaffirms its solidarity with and support for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including its full support for all legitimate measures and steps it takes to counter these attacks, deter the sources of their threats, and prevent their recurrence," the statement said.
The wording appeared significant as Saudi Arabia weighs its response to the latest attacks, which have dramatically raised tensions in the region.
Saudi authorities said 12 people were killed and 309 wounded in Saturday's attack on the Riyadh airport, the deadliest Houthi strike on the Kingdom in years. Six Pakistani nationals were among those injured. Another projectile struck the airport on Sunday, according to the Saudi-led coalition.
The R4 countries described the attacks as a "flagrant violation" of Saudi sovereignty and territorial integrity and a direct threat to the Kingdom's security and stability.
They held the Houthis "fully accountable" for the attacks and their repercussions for regional and international peace and security, demanding their immediate and unconditional cessation.
The collective statement followed separate strong reactions from Pakistan's top leadership. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack as "heinous" and said Pakistan stood firmly with KSA.
Speaking separately at a federal cabinet meeting, the prime minister drew attention to Pakistan's defence commitments to the Kingdom.
"We have a bilateral agreement, a trilateral agreement with regard to defence [of Saudi Arabia]," Shehbaz said. "And Pakistan will not tolerate any kind of aggression. Our agreements demand it and so do our bonds of brotherhood."
He described threats to Saudi Arabia, particularly the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah, as a "red line" and said Pakistan would cooperate with Riyadh "in every possible way".
In a statement posted on X, he said he was deeply saddened to learn that six Pakistani nationals had got injured as a result of Houthis attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. "I pray for their speedy recovery. Our Embassy in Riyadh is in close contact with the Saudi authorities and is extending all possible assistance to the affected families," he said.
Earlier, the Foreign Office described the targeting of a civilian airport as a "heinous act of terrorism, a flagrant violation of international law and a grave threat to regional peace and security".
It said the continued targeting of civilians and critical infrastructure by the Houthi militia was "utterly unacceptable" and must be unequivocally condemned by the international community.

title: PTI may challenge emergency in court
description: PTI may challenge emergency in court
content:
Experts differ on scope of judicial review as lawyers condemn move to remove elected K-P government
The PTI may challenge the imposition of an emergency and governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) before the Peshawar High Court (PHC), with legal experts divided over the constitutional validity of the measures and the scope of judicial review.
Former law officers and lawyers believe the party can question the federal government's decision on grounds of mala fide and non-fulfilment of constitutional requirements.
However, other legal experts argue that the Constitution provides a significant safeguard against judicial challenges to presidential proclamations issued under Articles 232 and 234.
The composition of the bench hearing any potential petition could be crucial. If the PHC decides the matter, an appeal against its ruling could be filed before the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), whose judges are appointed by the executive.
The FCC can also summon records from any court under Article 175E(5) of the Constitution where a case involves a substantial question of law regarding constitutional interpretation.
A former attorney general said the PTI could challenge the measures on the ground of mala fide, arguing that the constitutional requirements for such extraordinary action had not been fulfilled.
He questioned whether the federal government had formally corresponded with the K-P government over any alleged lack of cooperation in countering terrorism before taking the decision.
"The issue was first raised at the last meeting between the PML-N, the PPP and the PTI. This was not a meeting between the federal and provincial governments," he said.
The former law officer said the court should direct the federal government to produce the record and material on which the decision was based. He noted that Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had reportedly held several meetings with K-P chief minister Sohail Afridi. He also referred to statements attributed to the prime minister and federal ministers suggesting that the measures would not be taken if the PTI called off its long march.
According to him, these circumstances raised questions about whether the action was prompted by the planned march rather than any failure by the provincial government to cooperate on counterterrorism.
The former law officer also questioned the speed with which the federal cabinet considered the matter, saying it was placed before the cabinet on a Sunday and the meeting reportedly lasted barely an hour.
"How did the cabinet consider the material in such a short span before approving this extreme action? Why were Articles 232 and 234 invoked simultaneously when the requirements of the two provisions are distinct?" he asked.
Advocate Waqas Ahmed said both proclamations could be challenged if the constitutional conditions stipulated under Articles 232 and 234 had not been met.
"Article 232 requires a constitutionally recognised emergency, while Article 234 requires a failure of constitutional machinery in the province. Mere law-and-order problems or political instability are not sufficient, by themselves, to justify these extraordinary measures," he said.
He added that their validity would have to be assessed against the constitutional conditions, the material relied upon and compliance with the prescribed procedure.
Advocate Abuzar Salman Niazi cited the Supreme Court judgment in Sardar Farooq Ahmed Khan Leghari v Federation of Pakistan, arguing that a proclamation of emergency was not necessarily immune from judicial review merely because the Constitution contained an ouster clause.
"The court may examine its validity where the exercise of power is without jurisdiction, coram non judice or mala fide. The judgment also recognised that constitutional powers must satisfy the prescribed conditions for their exercise," he said.
However, advocate Hafiz Ahsaan Ahmed Khokhar offered a contrasting interpretation, arguing that the presidential proclamations imposing an emergency under Article 232 and governor's rule under Article 234 must be examined alongside Articles 48(2), 148, 149 and 236(1) and (2).
He said the combined operation of Articles 48(2) and 236(2) provided a strong constitutional defence against proceedings seeking to invalidate the proclamations.
Article 48(2), he explained, protects the validity of presidential action taken in the exercise of discretion specifically conferred by the Constitution, while Article 236(2) expressly provides that the validity of a proclamation issued or order made under Part X of the Constitution shall not be called into question in any court.
"Since Articles 232 and 234 fall within Part X, this express constitutional prohibition provides a formidable preliminary objection to proceedings seeking to invalidate the proclamations themselves, including proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court," Khokhar said.
He added that Article 236(1) provided for the revocation or variation of a proclamation through a subsequent proclamation, while parliamentary approval and oversight had to be exercised in accordance with the applicable constitutional requirements and time limits.
Where these procedures were followed, he said, parliamentary scrutiny could reinforce the constitutional basis for the measures and support judicial restraint in matters involving executive assessments of national security and constitutional governance. "Accordingly, a challenge directed solely at the validity of the proclamations faces a substantial constitutional bar under Article 236(2), reinforced, where applicable, by Article 48(2)," he added.
Meanwhile, the response from the legal fraternity has remained divided.
The Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Bar Council has yet to issue a public statement on the development. A lawyer said the council's anti-PTI group held a majority, making a call for a strike in the province's courts unlikely.
In contrast, eight members of the Pakistan Bar Council belonging to the Professional Group have condemned the imposition of governor's rule and an emergency in K-P, as well as the removal of the elected provincial government led by chief minister Sohail Afridi.
In a joint statement, the members described the action as illegal and alleged that it had been taken by a government and parliament already facing allegations of massive rigging in the general elections.
They said the imposition of governor's rule and an emergency, along with the formation of an advisory council, was marked by mala fide and illegality.
The statement alleged that the political system had undermined the rule of law and constitutional supremacy, concentrating power in an authoritarian state while weakening elected civilian governance.
The lawyers questioned whether the prevailing security situation justified an emergency, pointing out that terrorism had affected Pakistan for four decades despite the sacrifices of civilians and armed forces personnel.
They argued that Article 234 permitted governor's rule only when a provincial government could not be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. "The provincial government and the Provincial Assembly were both discharging their functions in accordance with the Constitution," the statement said.
Questioning the argument that the provincial government had failed to cooperate in the fight against terrorism, the lawyers referred to the security situation in Balochistan, where, they said, a PPP-led government was reportedly working closely with the military despite continuing terrorist attacks. The PBC members also linked the rise in terrorism and declining public confidence in the federation to what they described as democratic deficits, economic mismanagement, violations of fundamental and human rights, restrictions on access to justice following the 26th and 27th constitutional amendments, and corruption.
While expressing support for the armed forces in their fight against internal and external aggression, they called upon the president to withdraw the proclamations, restore the elected K-P government and respect provincial autonomy.

title: Terror attacks in K P surge 195  since 2024
description: Terror attacks in K P surge 195  since 2024
content:
Terrorist incidents in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) increased by 195% between March 1, 2024, and September 23, 2026, while drone attacks rose sharply, with the provincial police and Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) facing serious shortages of modern weapons, operational equipment and trained personnel, according to two security reports presented to the federal cabinet.
The reports, prepared by the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa police and intelligence agencies, were presented by Director General Intelligence Bureau (IB) Fuad Asadullah at a high-level cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Sunday.
According to the reports, the sharp rise in terrorist attacks over the past two years had become a serious security challenge for the province.
They attributed the worsening situation to terrorist elements based in Afghanistan, local facilitators, what they described as the provincial government's flawed policies and its soft approach towards militants, as well as inadequate preparedness and counterterrorism measures at the provincial level.
The reports said 73% of terrorist attacks recorded in K-P during 2026 targeted police and security personnel, underscoring the growing pressure on law enforcement agencies.
They highlighted a dramatic change in terrorist tactics, particularly the use of drones. No drone attacks against police and security forces were reported in 2024, but the number of such attacks reached 170 by 2026. The reports also pointed to a 107% increase in terrorist drone attacks over the preceding year.
Explosive attacks remained another major concern. The number of improvised explosive device (IED) attacks rose to 181 in 2025, while 159 such incidents had been recorded by September 2026.
The reports stressed that strengthening the operational capacity of police and other law enforcement agencies had become essential to counter the evolving tactics of militant groups.
The reports also highlighted significant gaps in the province's policing infrastructure, noting that the Safe City project for the entire province remained limited to Peshawar.
More than 9,000 posts in the K-P police were vacant, while the police and CTD faced severe shortages of modern weapons and essential operational equipment.
The situation was particularly challenging in the southern districts most affected by terrorism, where a shortage of armoured and protected vehicles was hampering police mobility and operational effectiveness.
The reports said police and CTD personnel lacked adequate modern surveillance and intelligence-gathering equipment.

title: Soldier martyred  twelve terrorists killed in Kurram
description: Armed forces thwart an infiltration attempt along the Pak Afghan border in K P s Kurram district
content:
Armed forces thwart an infiltration attempt along the Pak-Afghan border in K-P's Kurram district
Security forces killed 12 terrorists and Afghan Taliban while thwarting an infiltration attempt along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa's Kurram district, with one soldier martyred during the exchange of fire, the military's media wing said on Sunday.
According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the movement of a group of khawarij trying to approach international border from Afghanistan to Pakistan was detected and effectively engaged by security forces on October 10.
The security forces, maintaining a high state of alertness and vigilance, effectively thwarted the infiltration attempt. The ISPR said that "Afghan Taliban posts also opened fire to support the infiltration attempt by khawarij".
"Skilful and precise engagement by vigilant troops resulted in the killing of twelve khawarij and Afghan Taliban," the statement added. The ISPR said that Naib Subedar Hidayat Aman, 40, a resident of Ghizer district, was martyred during the intense exchange of fire. It added that he had "fought gallantly, paid the ultimate sacrifice and embraced shahadat".
The statement further said that the incident along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border once again vindicated Pakistan's "objective and factual stance" regarding the wilful abject failure of the Afghan Taliban regime to deny the use of Afghan soil to the terrorist organisation, rather facilitate and patronise cross-border terrorism.
"The Afghan Taliban regime has consistently failed to honour its international counter-terrorism obligations," the ISPR said.
The security forces remained resolute and unwavering in their commitment to defending the country's frontiers, the statement added.
A sanitisation operation was underway to eliminate any other Indian-sponsored kharji found in the area, the ISPR said. It added that the counter-terrorism campaign under the vision of Azm-e-Istehkam, approved by the Federal Apex Committee on the National Action Plan, would continue at full pace.
The campaign, being conducted by the security forces and law enforcement agencies, aimed to eliminate the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism in the country, the statement added. "These sacrifices of our brave soldiers further reinforce our unwavering commitment to safeguarding our nation and its frontiers at all costs," the statement concluded.
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif tribute to the security forces for foiling the infiltration attempt along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border.

description: Surrender took place at Pakistan House during a public forum convened by the chief minister
content:
Surrender took place at Pakistan House during a public forum convened by the chief minister
Former militant commander Noor Khan Bugti surrendered to Balochistan Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti in Sui on Sunday, with 60 individuals, including his associates and family members, laying down their arms and pledging allegiance to Pakistan.
The surrender took place at Pakistan House during a public forum convened by the chief minister, where Noor Khan Bugti and his companions took oath of loyalty to Pakistan, pledging to abandon militancy and return to the national mainstream.
According to a press release issued by the Chief Minister's Secretariat, Noor Khan Bugti had remained in hiding in the mountains for the past two decades and was allegedly involved in several terrorist activities. Following his surrender, he and his family will settle in Sui.
Addressing the gathering, Chief Minister Bugti said that establishing stability in Balochistan and across the country was a collective responsibility, requiring recognition of the state's authority and abandonment of violence.
The chief minister said Pakistan was the shared homeland of all citizens and there could be no compromise on its security, sovereignty and stability. He added that violence could not provide lasting solutions, while peace, mutual trust and the rule of law were necessary for progress and prosperity.
He said the people of Balochistan wanted peace, development and prosperity, urging young people to use their abilities for the country's progress and play a constructive role in national development.
Bugti said the decision to return to the national mainstream would benefit not only those involved but also their families and the region's future. He added that state institutions were working to establish lasting peace, but cooperation from all sections of society remained vital.

title: Ministers accuse PTI of failing to curb terrorism
description: Ministers accuse PTI of failing to curb terrorism
content:
Naqvi says attacks surged; Tarar alleges PTI'-terror nexus
The federal government on Sunday defended its decision to impose emergency rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), accusing the PTI-led provincial government of failing to curb terrorism, refusing to cooperate with federal authorities and allegedly maintaining links with militant groups.
At a press conference alongside other officials, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar argued that the deteriorating security situation and the provincial government's alleged reluctance to take ownership of counterterrorism efforts left the federation with little choice but to invoke extraordinary constitutional measures.
Naqvi said efforts continued for about a month to bring the K-P government on board, with back-channel contacts and negotiations taking place alongside discussions over PTI's planned long march.
He said the federal government had been addressing PTI's demands, including meetings with its incarcerated founder Imran Khan and the provision of medical treatment, even before the party's planned protest. However, repeated attempts to reach an understanding failed, with the final contact taking place at 11.45pm on Saturday.
The interior minister said the government had revised a draft agreement four times, but a new draft arrived when the matter appeared close to finalization. He insisted that the government's principal concern during the negotiations had been terrorism, rather than PTI's planned sit-in.
He also claimed that provincial representatives agreed during negotiations that emergency measures should be introduced in certain districts.
The minister said terrorist incidents had increased by 195% and fatalities by 113% over the preceding year and a half. He further claimed that 518 police personnel had been killed over 18 months.
Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said the federal cabinet held a detailed meeting lasting more than two hours, during which reports from relevant institutions were presented. The K-P governor had also submitted a report to the federal government as part of his constitutional responsibilities, he added.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar went further, alleging that the PTI-led provincial government had a deep nexus with terrorist groups and was not serious about eliminating militancy.
He claimed that reports from the Intelligence Bureau and law enforcement agencies described the situation as extremely alarming. Alleging that terrorists had been given safe access to the province and financial resources, he said the relationship between terrorists and the PTI had reached a stage of power-sharing.
Attaullah questioned whether the provincial government was unable or unwilling to fulfil its constitutional responsibility to protect citizens. He also alleged that groups responsible for attacks on civilians, hospitals, mosques, police stations and security personnel had been empowered by the provincial administration.

title: Presley Gerber s ex speaks three weeks after his death
description: Presley Gerber s ex speaks three weeks after his death
content:
Isabella Jones pays tribute, shares photos
Isabella Jones has paid tribute to Presley Gerber three weeks after the 27-year-old's death, sharing a series of photographs of her former boyfriend on Instagram.
"My sweet Presley," Jones wrote in the caption. "I will miss you for the rest of my life."
Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, died late last month following an apparent overdose and cardiac arrest, according to reports. He had reportedly been struggling with addiction and mental health issues.
Following his death, a spokesperson for Crawford and Rande Gerber asked for privacy as the family grieved.
"The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time," the spokesperson said in a statement.
Jones and Gerber reportedly began dating in 2024. Her Instagram tribute comes as those who knew him continue to remember him and reflect on their relationships with him.
Lexi Wood, who dated Gerber in 2022 and later remained connected to him through their friendship, also shared a tribute following his death.
"It's hard to put into words what it means to lose someone who was such a meaningful part of my life for so many years," Wood wrote.
She added that friendship had remained central to their relationship through its different stages. Wood also described Gerber as kind, open, loving and courageous, recalling his romantic and thoughtful nature.
Jones and Wood's tributes offer personal reflections on Gerber's life and the connections he maintained with people close to him.

title: Paris Fashion Week trends create global buzz
description: Paris Fashion Week trends create global buzz
content:
Fashion writer comments on revolutionary styles unveiled at just-concluded event that fashionistas are adopting worldw
Paris Fashion Week might have just wrapped, but fashionistas are already plotting how to work some of the standout fall fashion trends into their wardrobes. A fashion writer has kept a close eye on the Spring/Summer 2027 runways and the equally stylish celebrities sitting front row, from Zendaya's effortlessly cool denim at Louis Vuitton to Emma Stone's head-turning cobalt-blue ensemble. And with a trip to Paris on her calendar next month, she's been paying extra attention to the looks I can realistically re-create for her own European getaway.
While the runways delivered plenty of dramatic, high-fashion moments, you don't need a designer budget (or an invitation to the shows) to take inspiration from them. She's narrowed down the surprisingly wearable trends that can instantly elevate your fall outfits. Better yet, she found affordable Amazon alternatives, including cozy sweater dresses, satin midi skirts, and fun coats, that capture the spirit of Paris Fashion Week without the luxury price tags. Whether you're packing for a European getaway or refreshing your everyday fall wardrobe, these finds are worth adding to your cartstarting at just $19.
Sarah Pidgeon made a convincing case for the return of peplum trench coats at Balenciaga's Paris Fashion Week show, where she paired a waist-defining leather jacket with jeans. Unlike the exaggerated peplum tops of years past, this upgraded version feels decidedly more refined, with a subtle flare that adds shape without overwhelming an outfit. The Chouyatou Peplum Jacket offers an affordable way to try the style, while the Tanming Funnel-neck Jacket combines two current outerwear trends in one.
Of all the colors spotted at Paris Fashion Week, cobalt blue might be the one that's most exciting to introduce into the fall wardrobe. Emma Stone made a striking entrance at Louis Vuitton's Spring/Summer 2027 show in an electric-blue skirt suit, proving that the bold shade deserves a spot alongside fall's usual neutrals. While I'm not quite ready to commit to a head-to-toe cobalt outfit, the Trendy Queen Cropped Cardigan and Elleven Oversized Blazer offer two easy ways to try the trend. For a pop of color in your footwear, I'd reach for the Cushionaire Miss Mary Jane Flats.
Chloé went all in on romantic lace at its latest Paris Fashion Week show, sending dramatic, occasion-worthy looks down the runway. While the designs were stunning, I'm taking a more understated approach for my fall wardrobe during my upcoming European travels. Think peekaboo lace details that add a romantic touch to cozy staples, like the Wiholl Fall Midi Dress and Saodimallsu Turtleneck Sweater Dress. The Verdusa Lace T-shirt offers another easy way to embrace the trend, whether layered beneath a cardigan for a day of sightseeing or dressed up for dinner.
Louis Vuitton gave plaid a fresh spin at its Spring/Summer 2027 Paris Fashion Week show, proving there's more to the classic print than traditional fall flannels. And while the collection won't hit stores until next year, I'm already taking inspiration from the runway's unexpected styling for my fall wardrobe. The Cider Plaid Wide-leg Trousers would look especially chic with a fitted sweater and boots, while the Idealsanxun Plaid Mini Skirt is practically begging to be paired with tights and knee-high boots for a weekend in Paris. For something more relaxed, the Chyrii Button-down Flannel is an easy, classic layer for crisp fall days.
Alexa Chung's Paris Fashion Week appearance reminded me why satin-like skirts deserve a permanent place in my closet. The fabric has an inherently dressed-up feel, but the right styling can take it well beyond dinner reservations. This fall, I'm pairing silky midi skirts with chunky sweaters, leather jackets, and boots for outfits that feel put-together without requiring much thought.
Chanel's iconic cap-toe ballet flats have been on my wishlist for ages, so naturally, Ayo Edebiri's cap-toe slingbacks at the brand's Paris Fashion Week show caught my attention. While the designer versions come with a hefty price tag, I'm eyeing more affordable two-tone styles that offer the same polished look. Classic ballet flats are especially appealing for fall trips to Europe, where I want shoes that can take me from sightseeing and shopping to dinner without needing a shoe change.

title: Brooklyn store fires back at Kelly Clarkson over    Pretty Woman    shopping complaint
description: Art of Play responds to Kelly Clarkson   s    Pretty Woman    complaint  claiming she tried to buy an item not for sale
content:
Art of Play responds to Kelly Clarkson’s ‘Pretty Woman’ complaint, claiming she tried to buy an item not for sale
A Brooklyn store has responded to Kelly Clarkson’s allegations that she received poor treatment during a shopping visit, comparing the experience to a famous scene from the 1990 film Pretty Woman .
Clarkson, 44, criticised Art of Play, a home goods boutique in Brooklyn, in a post on X on October 10. The singer and former American Idol winner claimed a staff member appeared to assume she could not afford an item she wanted to purchase and offered to find her something comparable instead.
“Wow, dude. You're an idiot and just lost a huge sale,” Clarkson wrote, adding that shoppers could visit the store if they wanted to experience treatment similar to Julia Roberts’ character in Pretty Woman .
Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me. Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a…
In the film, Roberts’ character is dismissed by sales staff who believe she cannot afford their merchandise. She later returns to the shop with several shopping bags to demonstrate what they missed out on.
Art of Play addressed the allegations in an Instagram statement on October 11, offering a different account of the encounter. The store claimed Clarkson had asked to purchase a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton that was permanently attached to the wall and not available for sale. The item also plays a role in magic shows hosted at the boutique.
The retailer acknowledged that Clarkson’s description of feeling judged in a shop was an experience many customers could relate to. However, it also expressed surprise at the online backlash, saying the small business had faced widespread criticism from millions of people who had never visited.
The store thanked supporters and said it hoped to clear things up with Clarkson in the future. It ended its statement with a reference to her hit song "Stronger", writing, “What doesn’t kill you makes you stronger.”
The incident prompted mixed reactions online, with some supporting Clarkson and others questioning her decision to publicly identify the business.
Art of Play sells distinctive home goods, puzzles, games, toys and books, and hosts close-up magic performances.

title: Artemis Fowl  animated series officially greenlit by Disney six years after movie
description: Disney  develops new animated  Artemis Fowl  series with author Eoin Colfer as executive producer six years after film
content:
Disney+ develops new animated 'Artemis Fowl' series with author Eoin Colfer as executive producer six years after film
Disney is developing a new animated Artemis Fowl television series for Disney Channel and Disney+, six years after the release of its live-action film adaptation.
The announcement was made on October 11 during the “25 Years of Artemis Fowl” panel at New York Comic Con, celebrating the bestselling book series by Irish author Eoin Colfer. Colfer will serve as an executive producer on the upcoming animated adaptation, which has received an official green light from Disney.
The action-adventure series will follow Artemis Fowl, a 13-year-old genius who discovers a secret world inhabited by powerful fairies with advanced technology. Hoping to help his seriously ill mother and save his family, Artemis devises a plan to capture one of the fairies and steal its magic.
According to Disney, Colfer's book series has sold more than 35 million copies worldwide and been translated into 48 languages.
“I am proud and delighted to be part of the formidable team that is putting the ‘Artemis Fowl’ animation on screen,” Colfer said in a statement, expressing confidence in the creative team behind the project.
Ben Juwono, known for Moon Girl and Devil Dinosaur and Big Hero 6: The Series , will executive produce alongside Colleen Evanson, whose credits include DuckTales and Monsters at Work .
The new series follows Disney's live-action Artemis Fowl movie, released in June 2020. Directed by Kenneth Branagh, the film starred Ferdia Shaw as Artemis, alongside Judi Dench, Josh Gad, Colin Farrell, Lara McDonnell and Nonso Anozie.
The film focused on Artemis attempting to rescue his kidnapped father and received largely negative reviews, earning an 8% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes.
The upcoming animated adaptation instead centres on Artemis's efforts to save his mother. Disney has not yet announced the voice cast, episode count or premiere date, and it remains unclear how closely the series will follow the original novels.

title: Rich nations must pay climate debt
description: Rich nations must pay climate debt
content:
Should play their part in just transition, principle of equity and historical global warming tax
Climate Just Transition (CJT) is a buzzword these days. It urges the world to move away from unsustainable, climate-intensive practices and towards sustainable, climate-neutral and climate-friendly practices. The need for transition has grown as climate change-related disasters and impacts become more frequent. The cost, both monetary and human, is rising sharply.
For example, the 2022 floods cost Pakistan around $30 billion, and the human tragedy cannot be calculated. Climate change has further worsened food insecurity over the years. Pakistan is not the only country facing climate disasters or impacts; the same story is unfolding everywhere. In this context, the transition is a necessity, neither a luxury nor a choice.
However, the transition must be human-centric, not business-centric. It must be designed around human needs and grounded in fairness. Fairness demands a transition that gives due focus and respect to the needs of marginalised communities and groups, as well as poor and developing countries. The transition must not compromise people's decent livelihoods and opportunities to grow. Moreover, countries should not be pushed or lured by funding into commitments or actions beyond their capacity or historical responsibility. Thus, it will be a complex and tedious task, but with wisdom and fairness, it is achievable.
For that purpose, the scope of transition must be designed according to the countries' capacity, not the wishes of developed countries or the greed of the private sector. In this context, the Just Transition must be anchored in the first principle of Article 4 of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). The principle states, "The parties should protect the climate system for the benefit of present and future generations of humankind, on the basis of equity and in accordance with their common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. Accordingly, the developed country parties should take the lead in combating climate change and the adverse effects thereof." Therefore, there is broader consensus that the UNFCCC's first principle inspires the Just Transition concept.
A deeper analysis of the principle indicates that it was devised to achieve two objectives. First, to care for the needs of present and future generations; as noted, humans exploited resources without regard for future generations' needs. Second, to act according to capabilities and to ensure the implementation of common and differentiated responsibilities, as well as historical responsibilities. Common and differentiated responsibilities indicate that climate change is a shared threat.
However, determining each nation's responsibility requires considering historical responsibility and capacity, including financial, technical, technological and human resources. Historical responsibility was considered essential to create justice among present, past and future generations.
Unfortunately, the principle was never implemented in its true spirit. Developed countries refused to fulfil their responsibilities under the historical responsibility clause or to act on their commitments at the UN. The story began with their refusal to implement the binding commitments under the Kyoto Protocol to reduce GHG emissions. They never took it seriously, repeatedly postponed action, or watered down their commitments to reduce GHG emissions.
The same policy or strategy has been applied to financial commitments or promises. Instead of fulfilling their financial obligations, developed countries are trying to exploit the situation in their own interest and create opportunities for their companies and states. For example, they promote loans or expensive debt through private institutions or multilateral bodies. Oxfam reports on climate financing and debt are eye-opening and provide us with a clear picture of what is happening in the name of climate financing.
At the same time, they have begun introducing new measures and deploying tools to pressure developing and poor countries to take actions beyond their capacity and responsibility. For instance, the European Union has introduced the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Through the CBAM, the EU imposes a levy on imported goods by comparing carbon emissions within the EU with those of the importing country for a given product.
For example, if producing one unit of a product emits 10 kg of carbon in the EU, but the same product is manufactured in another country at a lower price but with higher carbon emissions, it will be subject to a carbon levy. On the face of it, it is a policy to fight climate change and its related impacts. They also promote it as an innovative tool to fast-track the climate transition. In reality, it aims to maintain the competitiveness of EU companies and discourage them from investing outside the EU.
Developing countries too disagree with the EU. They see it as contrary to the principles of equity and historical responsibility. They argue that they have limited resources to adopt new technologies and energy sources necessary for the transition. On the other hand, developing countries view CBAM as discouraging FDI from EU companies and others. It has a detrimental impact on their dream of economic growth and development. In the long run, it also hampers the green transition agenda. If the EU wants developing nations to fast-track the transition, it must provide financial assistance without taxing them irrationally. This is a genuine concern and demand.
Despite the harsh environment and injustice, developing and poor countries remain committed to the Just Climate Transition because they are highly vulnerable to climate impacts and disasters. Against this background, developing countries have two choices. First, they can continue with their current practices and delay implementing the climate transition agenda. This will have severe implications for the global climate change agenda.
Second, build their own financial resources by introducing new import levies on goods from the EU and other countries, such as a historical responsibility tax on EU companies. A historical tax should also include private companies, which are major contributors to global GHG emissions and beneficiaries of the Industrial Revolution. Developing and poor countries should strongly pursue the concept of historical taxation at the upcoming COP in Turkey. This is rational, as developed countries promote the private sector as a leader in fighting climate change; they must also pay for their historical contribution to GHG emissions. As the host, Turkey can facilitate the process.
Before concluding the discussion, it is important to highlight one area of concern in the CJT debate. Unfortunately, planetary needs and boundaries are largely missing from the transition debate. The debate focuses more on reducing GHG emissions, promoting green and new energies, private-sector interests, and economic growth, with less attention to human needs. The planet seems to have been taken for granted, with a focus on business needs. This continued neglect of planetary needs and respect for boundaries is feared to have a detrimental impact on climate, sustainable development and the future of humanity and the planet. It also contradicts the rights of future generations. Thus, to make the transition just, we also need to balance human needs with planetary needs and boundaries.
In conclusion, we can draw four key inferences. First, securing support from all public groups, countries and society is essential. Without society's support, no transition can succeed, let alone the fundamental lifestyle changes it requires. Therefore, to ensure a just transition, we must balance the ambition to reduce GHG emissions with human needs.
Second, the West will not fulfil its commitments and will continue to divert attention and responsibility towards poor countries. The story is the same from the Kyoto Protocol to the Loss and Damage Fund. They will also continue to lure poor countries with financial incentives into commitments beyond their capacity. Third, developing and poor countries need to be innovative and develop ideas, such as historical taxation, to counter developed countries' strategies to shift responsibility or action. Fourth, this debate on a just climate transition must recognise and include planetary needs and boundaries and policies and actions must reflect those needs and boundaries.
THE WRITER IS A POLITICAL ECONOMIST AND A VISITING RESEARCH FELLOW AT HEBEI UNIVERSITY, CHINA

title: Lost in aggregate numbers
description: Lost in aggregate numbers
content:
Role of provinces is very important in export target, but it is least defined
Uraan Pakistan, the national economic plan launched at the end of 2024, aims to raise exports to $60 billion a year by 2029. It expects provinces to finance a major share of their development budget. For the last few years, the Ministry of Commerce has emphasised that exports cannot be raised by the federal government alone and provinces must play their part. This view now appears to have been adopted at the highest level.
In September, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar called again for "a coordinated, whole-of-government approach" to exports. Such an approach implies that the Ministry of Commerce, other federal ministries, the State Bank of Pakistan, the Federal Board of Revenue and the provincial governments all work towards a common export target. Of these, the role of provinces is perhaps the most important and the least defined. The convergence of views within the government on the role of provinces must be duly appreciated.
However, the fundamental question that arises is how provinces can be asked to share responsibility for a national target when nobody knows how much each of them already exports. The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) publishes exports by product and by destination. The SBP does the same for export receipts. Neither publishes export figures by province.
Customs records identify the port which cleared a shipment and the firm whose name is on the invoice. As such, any attempt to construct provincial numbers ends up tracking the port of exit or, at best, the registered address of the exporter. On this basis, a mango grown in Multan but shipped through Karachi appears as an export of Sindh. Marble quarried in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa but cut and invoiced in Karachi is treated likewise. This implies that basic questions have no answer. It is not clear how much Punjab exported last year, or what is in the export basket of Balochistan. Without a baseline, there can be no provincial target. Without a target, nobody can be held accountable for missing it.
The problem, however, goes beyond accountability. The absence of provincial figures gives rise to at least four issues. The first relates to the incidence of trade costs, which falls unevenly on particular places. Since the closure of the Pak-Afghan border in October 2025, the loss, by one estimate about $890,000 a day, has fallen on transporters and perishable exporters in K-P and, to some extent, in Punjab. Similarly, 30-40% of mangoes and other perishables are lost for want of cold storage. The lost sales, put at over $200 million a year, belong to farmers in southern Punjab and Sindh. Consequently, nobody can tell how much of a province's trade these losses eat up or where removing them would yield the highest return.
The second issue is that national figures leave export policy blind to regional differences, even though export structures differ widely across provinces. Punjab's strengths lie in textiles, surgical instruments and pink salt. Sindh has chemicals, garments, fish and the port of Karachi. K-P has marble, furniture and gypsum, plus border trade through Torkham and Ghulam Khan. This trade amounted to almost $1.4 billion in 2024-25, prior to the border closure. Balochistan has minerals, dates, livestock and fish. Federal policy, however, treats Faisalabad and Gwadar alike.
The third issue relates to competitiveness. A country that cannot see where its exports originate cannot tell which industrial clusters are gaining and which are losing ground. Nor can it see where logistics costs bite hardest. A furniture maker in Peshawar must transport goods over 1,000 km to reach Karachi; a garment maker in Korangi need not. Policy which ignores this difference will continue to favour exporters already located near the port.
The final issue relates to traceability. From the end of 2026, the deforestation regulation of the European Union will require leather and wood to be traced to the land where the cattle were raised or the trees grown. The EU forced-labour regulation, which applies from December 2027, permits the flagging of risky products and regions. Exporters to Pakistan's most important GSP+ market will, therefore, have to demonstrate exactly where their goods were made.
India, by contrast, publishes exports by the state of origin and NITI Aayog ranks states on export preparedness. In Pakistan, nobody keeps score. There are two reasonable grounds for caution. Trade policy is a federal subject and devolving it could fragment it. Also, provincial competition could degenerate into a subsidy race. However, publishing data is not the same as devolving trade policy. Following the 18th Amendment, the provinces control much of what determines export costs. Provincial accounts would simply enable them to see the results of their own choice. Competition over a public scorecard is, in fact, healthier than competition over handouts.
A whole-of-government approach needs a whole-of-government scoreboard. Until exports are counted where they are made, the target of $60 billion will remain a federal headline rather than a provincial commitment. Data alone will not, however, be sufficient. Provinces also need an incentive to act and the capacity to do so. Three steps are recommended.
First, provincial export figures must be published. Customs records of the FBR, SBP payments data and the exporters' registry should be linked to the origin of goods. Much of the required data already exists in customs declarations, sales tax registrations and factory addresses. What is missing is the effort to integrate it.
Second, each province should be given an export target for at least five priority sectors. These should combine established sectors with those that could diversify the export basket. Punjab, for example, might pair surgical goods, sports goods and rice with auto parts and pharmaceuticals. Each target must have a budget attached, financed mainly from provincial development budgets, with matching funds from the federal government. The funds should be used for testing laboratories, cold storage and certification rather than tax concessions.
Third, a trade desk should be set up in each provincial Board of Investment. It would gather market intelligence for the province's export basket and share it with Pakistan's trade missions abroad. A desk in Quetta tracking Chinese demand for dates is likely to pick up signals that a federal ministry can easily miss. The desk should also help small firms meet the standards of buyers. In addition, it must work with the Intellectual Property Organisation of Pakistan to register and defend the geographical indications of a province. Much of Khewra's pink salt, for instance, is sold abroad as generic "Himalayan" salt.
Pakistan's exporters already bear the cost of the country's blind spots, at the border, at the port and on the factory floor. A whole-of-government approach to exports must begin by counting what they make and where they make it.
The writer is Head of Policy (Trade, Investment and Industrial Cooperation) at the Centre of Excellence for CPEC, PIDE

title: Need for National Tax Court
description: Need for National Tax Court
content:
Such court should absorb appellate jurisdiction presently fragmented between Inland Revenue and Customs
Law Reform Report No 142 of the Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan proposes an International Commercial Court of Pakistan as a specialised Federal Superior Court. Crucially, Clause (3) of the draft Article 212A expressly permits parliament to confer original or appellate jurisdiction over "taxation" and other economic and commercial matters.
That opening should not be treated as drafting surplusage. Pakistan's tax jurisprudence is now too economically consequential, technically complex and internally contested to remain dispersed among departmental appellate authorities; two tax tribunals, five High Courts, the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) and Supreme Court. The recent super-tax litigation illustrates the problem. In January 2026, the FCC upheld Sections 4B and 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 ["the Ordinance"]. Its detailed judgment treated Section 4C as a standalone tax on a composite concept of "income", capable of reaching income otherwise falling under normal, final, minimum and separate-block regimes. The FCC expressly held that dividend, profit on debt and capital gains could enter the Section 4C base even where the ordinance otherwise treats them under special charging provisions. For exporters under the then final tax regime, it accepted the "imputable income" mechanism under Section 4C(2)(iii), grossing up final tax to derive an income figure for super-tax purposes.
The reasoning is consequential. Export proceeds for tax years 2022 and 2023 were taxed under Section 154 as final tax based on receipts. Dividend income is specifically charged under Section 5, while Section 8 declares the tax imposed under Section 5 to be final and keeps that amount outside the computation of taxable income under the ordinary heads.
The FCC nevertheless reasoned that Section 4C does not tax these streams twice; it counts them once for a distinct super-tax charge. In the case of exporters, it expressly held that the imputation mechanism brings a final-tax-regime exporter into comparability with a normal-regime taxpayer. That construction may be defended as giving effect to parliament's express inclusion of dividends and imputable income in Section 4C(2). It nevertheless raises a serious issue of statutory coherence: what does "final" mean if another income tax can subsequently be imposed upon the same separately treated stream without an express overriding clause? Will any foreign direct investment come after such erratic over-taxation!
The issue became sharper in July 2026 when the Supreme Court decided Commissioner Inland Revenue vs Saudi Pak Industrial & Agricultural Investment Company and connected matters. A bench comprising Chief Justice Yahya Afridi and Justice Aqeel Ahmed Abbasi rejected the tax department's attempt to tax corporate dividend income at the normal corporate rate under Section 39 of the Ordinance. Justice Abbasi, writing for the court, held that dividend constitutes a separate block of income governed by the specific charging provision in Section 5. Section 39 is residual; machinery provisions cannot dilute a substantive and specific charge.
The Saudi Pak judgment did not discuss Section 4C. However, the interpretive principle it reiterates is important: where parliament has created a specific charging regime, courts should not lightly permit other provisions to destroy its statutory character. Applying this principle, FCC may review its judgment to this extent while deciding thousands of pending review petitions. This is precisely why Pakistan needs specialised tax adjudication. Complex tax disputes are not merely arguments about rates. They require simultaneous command of charging provisions, computation rules, final-tax regimes, accounting concepts, constitutional legislative entries, retrospective taxation, international transactions and the relationship between general and special provisions.
A court deciding these matters must also understand that certainty itself is an economic asset. The proposed Article 212A provides a constitutional route. Instead of creating an International Commercial Court concerned primarily with cross-border contracts and arbitration, parliament should use Clause (3) to establish a specialised taxation division – or, preferably, a National Tax Court within the same constitutional architecture. The commission itself envisages expansion of the proposed court's jurisdiction to taxation and other economic matters. Such a court should absorb the appellate jurisdiction presently fragmented between the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue and Customs Appellate Tribunal, with judges selected for demonstrated expertise in taxation, commercial law and accounting. This is not an argument for another layer of litigation. The opposite is required. The appellate chain should be shortened. Fact-finding should terminate at the specialised forum; only substantial questions of law should travel further through a tightly defined route to the National Tax Court. Identical federal tax provisions should not acquire different meanings merely because proceedings originated in Karachi, Lahore, Peshawar, Quetta or Islamabad.
The super-tax controversy teaches another lesson. Tax law cannot become predictable merely by declaring parliament supreme in fiscal policy. Parliament unquestionably levies taxes. Courts still have to determine what parliament actually enacted, how one charging provision interacts with another, whether retrospective legislation disturbs vested or past-and-closed transactions, and whether constitutional limits on legislative competence have been crossed.
Indeed, the FCC itself subsequently struck down Section 7E after holding that, in substance, it was a tax on the capital value of immovable property falling outside federal legislative competence. That judgment demonstrates an elementary but vital principle: the label attached to a tax cannot determine its constitutional character; substance must. Pakistan does not need a National Tax Court to collect more for the state or to grant more relief to taxpayers. It needs one to produce coherent law. Proposed Article 212A offers an opportunity to create that institution before another generation of tax disputes travels from assessment to tribunal, High Court, constitutional court and/or Supreme Court. The test should be simple: one federal tax law should produce one authoritative interpretation across Pakistan. Tax certainty is not a concession to business. It is part of the rule of law.

title: From stabilisation to growth
description: From stabilisation to growth
content:
Pakistan needs to turn economic stability into jobs, incomes and exports
Pakistan may have stabilised its economy, but it has yet to make that stability work. Inflation is no longer at crisis levels, external pressures have eased and foreign exchange reserves have recovered. Yet these improvements have not translated into a corresponding sense of opportunity for businesses or households. For the young graduate, the small manufacturer or the entrepreneur trying to expand, macroeconomic stability remains a distant statistic unless it creates jobs, investment and rising incomes.
This is the central weakness of Pakistan's recovery. Stabilisation was necessary, but it was never meant to be the destination. It was supposed to create breathing space for the harder work of expanding production, attracting investment, increasing exports and creating employment. The question now is whether that breathing space is being converted into a stronger economic base. There is reason for some optimism. Foreign direct investment has improved in the opening months of FY27. Net FDI reached $494.5 million during July-August, up 24.1% from $398.6 million a year earlier, while August alone recorded $315.9 million. These are encouraging numbers. But they need to be viewed in the backdrop of the low base effect in FY26, when annual FDI remained modest. More importantly, the recent improvement remains selective, with financial and power businesses accounting for a significant share of inflows. There is still limited evidence of a broad investment wave flowing into manufacturing, exports and new productive capacity.
Foreign investors had faced delays in repatriating profits and dividends during the foreign-exchange shortages, creating an uncomfortable memory for international investors about the ease of taking legitimate returns out of Pakistan. Those restrictions have since eased as foreign-exchange availability improved, with the recent profit and dividend repatriation data showing repatriation of $557.6 million in the first two months of FY27. But while restoring repatriation is important for rebuilding confidence, the earlier experience is likely to remain part of investors' assessment of Pakistan. For new foreign investors, the question is therefore not only whether they can bring capital in, but whether they can confidently take legitimate returns out in the future.
And this is where the perception of the business environment becomes important. The recently released National Citizen Survey 2026, conducted by the Institute for Public Opinion Research (IPOR), offers a revealing domestic perspective. Based on 5,155 face-to-face interviews across all four provinces, the survey found that 91% of respondents considered it difficult to start or run a business in Pakistan. Taxes were identified as the biggest obstacle, while access to finance, corruption and bribery, high energy costs and government regulation also featured prominently. The significance of these findings goes beyond the difficulties faced by Pakistani businesses. A foreign investor considering a factory, technology operation or export platform in Pakistan is effectively asking the same questions as a local entrepreneur: how predictable is taxation, how costly is energy, how easily can capital be accessed, how much regulatory friction will be encountered and how reliably will contracts and rules be enforced? The difference is that a foreign investor can choose another country.
A factory is a long-term commitment. An investor therefore looks beyond the next year's inflation rate or the latest increase in foreign-exchange reserves. The questions are more fundamental: will the tax regime remain predictable? Can electricity be obtained at a competitive price? Can contracts be enforced? Can profits be repatriated when due? Will regulations remain broadly consistent? These are not peripheral considerations; they determine whether an investment is viable.
Pakistan therefore needs to move beyond improving financial indicators towards improving the conditions under which businesses actually operate. A tax refund delayed for months is not simply an administrative inconvenience. It is working capital trapped outside a business. Expensive energy is not merely a utility problem; it reduces international competitiveness. Regulatory uncertainty is not simply frustrating; it raises the cost of committing capital.
The investment problem is inseparable from the export problem. Pakistan cannot permanently resolve its external vulnerability by borrowing whenever foreign exchange becomes scarce. External financing can provide valuable time and borrowing is not inherently harmful when it finances productive investment. But repeated borrowing to fill a structural foreign-exchange gap merely postpones the underlying problem. The lasting solution is to increase the economy's capacity to earn. Exports are therefore not just another growth indicator. They are the foundation of external resilience. A country that earns more foreign exchange through competitive exports can import machinery and technology, service its external obligations and expand without repeatedly hitting the same balance-of-payments constraint.
This requires a change in the way investment is viewed. The objective should not simply be to attract more dollars, but to attract capital that expands productive capacity. Investment in export-oriented manufacturing, technology, logistics, agro-processing and other tradable sectors can generate a continuing stream of foreign exchange. It can also create domestic supply chains, transfer skills and raise productivity.
Pakistan's investment rate remains low for an economy seeking sustained growth, while its export base is still narrow. An economy with a modest investment base and limited export footprint will struggle to generate the productivity gains and employment required to transform living standards. This is why the debate over stabilisation should ultimately move beyond inflation, reserves and financing arrangements. Those indicators matter, but they are means rather than ends. The real test is whether businesses are investing, whether firms are becoming larger and more productive, whether exports are becoming broader and more competitive, and whether employment is expanding. The connection to ordinary households is direct. Investment expands productive capacity. Productive capacity creates jobs. Jobs generate incomes. Higher productivity raises wages and competitiveness. Greater exports generate foreign exchange.
THE WRITER IS A FINANCIAL MARKET ENTHUSIAST AND IS ASSOCIATED WITH PAKISTAN'S STOCKS, COMMODITIES AND EMERGING TECHNOLOGY

title: No straight path for markets
description: No straight path for markets
content:
Consolidation after rapid advance does not invalidate investment case
Pakistan stock market's extraordinary rally from around 40,000 to beyond 180,000 in 2.5 years from June 2023 to January 2026 reflected improving fundamentals (from low 3.5x price-to-earnings (P/E), liquidity (rate cut from 22% to 11.5%), sentiment and diplomatic goodwill. Much good news arrived – and was priced in remarkably quickly. After roughly eight frustrating months, investors are questioning equities and eyeing property or fixed income. With the index closing October 1 near 168,637, disappointment is understandable. But consolidation after an exceptional advance does not invalidate the investment case.
In my August 25, 2025 Tribune column, "KSE-100 races to 150,000 – too fast, too soon?", I highlighted the rapid re-rating from 6x to 8x earnings. On February 23, 2026, I wrote: "The KSE-100's long-term average P/E of 8x to 9x has been reached relatively quickly." The implication remains relevant: earnings must eventually catch up with expectations.
The government deserves credit for navigating a prolonged regional war. September's $3 billion Eurobond, sovereign-rating upgrades and fiscal consolidation demonstrate resilience. SBP still projects the FY27 current-account deficit within 0-1% of GDP. UAE deposits were repaid, although Saudi support helped finance the outflow. These are meaningful achievements, although borrowed reserves must ultimately give way to export earnings and investment.
Successful IMF reviews would unlock $1.2 billion later this year, subject to board approval. I would support another two or three years of reform continuity under an IMF framework, if necessary. Pakistan needs durable institutions and export competitiveness; fresh dollars, bilateral deposits and prospective swap facilities cannot substitute for them.
The export package offers a tangible bridge towards growth. Budget measures reduced collection on export proceeds from 2% to 1.25%, with super-tax exemption for qualifying exporters. Working-capital financing at 8.5% and long-term financing at 2% for two years, followed by 5% for eight, can support investment. Rebates apply to incremental exports: 1% where annual growth is up to 10% and 2% where it exceeds 10%.
Redirecting fiscal space from remittance incentives towards productive capacity is sensible; the discontinued incentives reportedly cost around Rs76 billion last year. Policymakers should also review Naya Pakistan Certificate yields against global alternatives, balancing overseas investors' expectations with sovereign borrowing costs.
Domestic demand has support too. Around Rs60 billion has been disbursed under the prime minister's Apna Ghar programme, with a substantially larger approved pipeline. Progress towards privatising Fesco, Gepco and Iesco could become a stronger catalyst than another financing announcement, provided ownership changes deliver investment, lower losses and better service.
Energy remains the principal threat. Refined-product prices, freight and insurance can magnify the crude-oil shock. Disrupted LNG supplies through Hormuz and reliance on expensive replacement fuels threaten electricity costs, industrial margins and household purchasing power. Sustained oil prices below $100 would improve the outlook. A sudden 4-5% rupee depreciation or rate increase exceeding one percentage point could postpone recovery by several quarters; these are stress scenarios, not mechanical thresholds.
Companies are adapting. Nishat Mills and DG Khan Cement recently announced solar-and-battery projects, while Lucky Cement is expanding renewables. Textile firms such as Nishat Mills, Indus Dyeing, Kohinoor Textile, Gul Ahmed, Premium Textile, Saif Textile, etc are installing large-scale solar, wind and battery projects. Such investments can improve resilience and margins. But industrial migration away from the grid leaves remaining consumers carrying more fixed costs. Competitive incremental energy pricing and removal of industrial cross-subsidies must accompany DISCO reform.
Recovery also requires discrimination. SBP reports improving activity after a weak June quarter. September results, largely available by end-October, should help distinguish sustainable volume growth, operating-margin improvement and cash generation from tax relief or exceptional gains. Investors should identify businesses capable of compounding earnings over the next two to three years.
Market participation offers another encouraging signal. PSX had 656,218 investors in September, roughly 0.25% of Pakistan's population. India's NSE reported 127 million unique investors in January, approximately 9% of its population. Although reporting dates and coverage differ, Pakistan's participation gap is enormous. Digital onboarding and simpler KYC can broaden ownership; lasting stability requires regular saving, rather than leveraged retail speculation.
Recent IPOs and the listing pipeline broaden the opportunity set across electronics, dairy, poultry, tyre exports, property, oil marketing, pharmaceuticals and credit information. Successful offerings demonstrate demand, but subscriptions are no substitute for valuation discipline. New businesses must prove cash generation, governance and returns on reinvestment. For young savers, equities also overcome practical property barriers: large deposits, title verification, transaction costs, maintenance and slow exits. Diversified shares or equity funds permit smaller, regular investments and partial withdrawals. Accumulate quality on weakness with a five- or ten-year horizon, reinvest distributions and avoid leverage. Owning businesses means participating in production, employment and capital allocation – not merely betting on the next price tick.
Expectations must normalise. A 15-20% nominal annualised return is a reasonable long-term ambition under favourable conditions, not an annual entitlement. Entry valuations, inflation, taxes and costs matter. At 15%, capital roughly doubles in five years and quadruples in ten; eight disappointing months do not destroy that arithmetic.
If war risks recede and earnings strengthen, my conditional December 2027 scenario is 225,000-250,000. A valuation near 9x forward earnings would require commensurate earnings growth and dividend yields; the multiple alone cannot establish an index target. To highlight, KSE-100 companies earned Rs2,000 billion profits in fiscal year 2026 and that is real money not speculative crypto coins. A sustained 10-12x P/E rating would demand much stronger foundations: export- and investment-led growth above 5%, better ties with eastern and western neighbours, political accommodation, widening tax-to-GDP ratio, improved security in Balochistan and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and goodwill converted into FDI.
A high index level does not automatically mean expensive businesses. The opportunity is to buy improving businesses at sensible prices while uncertainty persists. Buybacks such as of Engro Holdings support that assessment, but cannot replace it. Pakistan's next durable rally must be earned through productivity, exports and reform. Young investors who save consistently stand to benefit more.
The writer is an independent economic analyst.

title: Matthew Lawrence says Sally Field became a    mother figure    on the set of  Mrs  Doubtfire
description: Matthew Lawrence recalls how Sally Field became a mother figure while filming  Mrs  Doubtfire  with Robin Williams
content:
Matthew Lawrence recalls how Sally Field became a mother figure while filming 'Mrs. Doubtfire' with Robin Williams
Matthew Lawrence has reflected on his experience filming Mrs. Doubtfire , revealing how co-star Sally Field became a mother figure to him while they worked on the 1993 comedy.
Lawrence, who played Chris Hillard, the son of Field's Miranda Hillard and Robin Williams' Daniel Hillard, said the cast developed a close bond during production. Speaking to Entertainment Weekly , the actor recalled how the group built a family-like atmosphere on set.
“We really became a family unit on that set,” Lawrence said, adding that the cast spent time getting to know one another even before rehearsals began.
Field, who played the mother of three children in the film, was particularly caring towards Lawrence, who was just 12 years old during filming.
“She was so caring, so kind. I don't know how anybody could have anything bad to say about the lady,” he said, praising the Oscar-winning actress for her kindness throughout the experience.
Lawrence also credited Field, Williams and Pierce Brosnan, who played Miranda's boyfriend, for striking the right balance between treating him as a young actor and allowing him to feel included.
According to Lawrence, the three stars neither talked down to him because of his age nor exposed him unnecessarily to the adult world. He described their approach as a wonderful experience and one of the most memorable opportunities of his career.
Released in 1993, Mrs. Doubtfire follows Daniel Hillard, played by Williams, who disguises himself as a Scottish nanny to spend time with his children after separating from Miranda. Lawrence starred alongside Lisa Jakub and Mara Wilson as the couple's three children.
More than three decades after the film's release, Lawrence said he still occasionally encounters Field and continues to find her just as warm and welcoming.
Earlier this year, Lawrence also published The Lawrence Brothers Detective Agency , a graphic novel created with his real-life brothers that paid tribute to Field and Williams.
His latest recollections offer a glimpse into the lasting relationships formed behind the scenes of the beloved comedy.

title: Shakira breaks Amazon Music livestream record with Madrid concert
description: Shakira   s Madrid concert became Amazon Music   s most viewed livestream by female artist  featuring duet with Dua Lipa
content:
Shakira’s Madrid concert became Amazon Music’s most-viewed livestream by female artist, featuring duet with Dua Lipa
Shakira has set a new Amazon Music livestream record with her Madrid concert, which became the platform’s most-viewed livestream performance by a female artist.
The Colombian singer performed on October 3 at Shakira Stadium in Madrid as part of her 12-date residency at the temporary venue.
Amazon Music announced the record on October 4, following the concert’s broadcast across Amazon Music, Prime Video and Twitch.
The performance featured a special appearance by Dua Lipa, who joined Shakira on stage for an acoustic rendition of “Antología”, originally released on Shakira’s 1995 album, Pies Descalzos.
Dua Lipa later shared her appreciation for the performance on Instagram, writing in Spanish, "I felt that you, me, and the audience were one. Very grateful to take home such a beautiful memory!!!"
The appearance followed Dua Lipa’s own performance of “Antología” in Spanish during the Bogotá stop of her Radical Optimism Tour.
Shakira’s Madrid residency forms part of her Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour, which supports her 2024 album of the same name. The singer began the residency on September 18, with the final concert scheduled for October 11.
A temporary venue was constructed at Madrid’s Iberdrola Music complex specifically for the series of performances, giving Shakira a dedicated space for the 12-show run.
The livestream milestone adds to the reach of the residency, extending the concerts beyond audiences attending in person.

title: Rihanna hints at 170 unreleased songs as fans await her next album
description: Rihanna has hinted at having at least 170 unreleased songs as anticipation continues for her first album since 2016
content:
Rihanna has hinted at having at least 170 unreleased songs as anticipation continues for her first album since 2016
Rihanna has hinted that she has at least 170 unreleased songs in her music archive, offering an update on her long-awaited ninth studio album during a TikTok livestream.
The 38-year-old singer made the remark during an October 6 broadcast promoting Fenty Beauty’s holiday collection.
When her business partner Jennifer Rosales asked how much unreleased music she had, Rihanna used a box of beauty products to illustrate the size of her catalogue.
"If there are 10 products in a vault, then I have at least 17 vaults," she said.
Rihanna did not reveal any song titles or confirm which recordings could feature on her next album, widely referred to by fans as “R9”.
Her last studio album, ANTI, was released in January 2016, leaving fans waiting for a follow-up for more than a decade.
In an April 2024 interview with Interview, Rihanna discussed how her creative process was changing, saying, "Maybe the visual ideas are leading me to the songs that I need to make."
By February 2025, she told Harper's Bazaar that she had found a direction that felt right after years of recording and reconsidering concepts.
"There's no genre now," she said when asked about expectations of a reggae album. She also explained that she wanted to make music that reflected her artistry rather than being designed for radio, adding, "I cannot put up anything mediocre."
Her partner, A$AP Rocky, offered another update in August during an appearance on BET's The Jason Lee Show .
"But yo, she in the studio right now," he said, before adding, "Sorry babe."

Tom Welling jokes about viral NSFW hotel window photo after accidentally sharing a revealing image from New York City
Tom Welling has responded with humour after accidentally sharing a revealing photo of himself while attempting to capture the New York City skyline from his hotel room.
The Smallville star, 49, addressed the viral incident on October 10 by commenting on an Instagram Reel that joked about spotting him at his hotel window. The actor is in New York for New York Comic Con, where he is celebrating the 25th anniversary of the superhero series.
The Reel featured a tourist's perspective of the city, with on-screen text referencing the possibility of seeing Welling standing at his hotel window. Responding to the post, the actor wrote, “Came for the sights.”
The incident began on October 9, when Welling shared an Instagram Stories post featuring a photograph of the New York City skyline. He captioned the image “Hello NYCC”, but the picture also inadvertently revealed his reflection while he was taking the photograph nude. He later deleted the post.
Welling's Smallville co-star Michael Rosenbaum also joined in on the joke. Rosenbaum recreated the hotel window photo, posing in a T-shirt and boxers while holding a sign reading “perverts” over his lower body. He captioned the post, “Just looking after my boy.”
Welling reshared Rosenbaum's humorous tribute on his own Instagram Stories, appearing to take the teasing in good spirits.
During a New York Comic Con panel celebrating Smallville , Welling also recalled another embarrassing photo incident from the show's filming days. He said co-star John Glover once brought him a fan-edited image depicting him nude and asked him to sign it.
Rather than correcting Glover, Welling jokingly agreed that the image was real and signed it.
The actor's response to the viral hotel photo has added another humorous moment to his public appearances during the Smallville anniversary celebrations.
