Manolo Gonzalez Vergara shared post about narcissism after excerpts from Joe Manganiello’s upcoming memoir emerged
Manolo Gonzalez Vergara, the 35-year-old son of actress Sofía Vergara, has seemingly addressed claims made by his mother’s ex-husband, Joe Manganiello, in an upcoming memoir.
On October 8, Manolo shared an Instagram Story featuring a chart comparing a “good man” with a “narcissistic man”. The graphic listed traits including “good men set boundaries / narcissistic men gaslight”.
He added the caption, “Remember kids, when dealing with a narcissist, it doesn't matter how much you do for them, because they will resent you for it and nothing will ever be enough, and they'll always somehow try to paint you as the bad guy 🍾💃.”
The following day, Vergara, 54, reposted her son’s Story. She also shared a post from Tom Brady that read, “The ability to laugh at oneself is probably the highest form of intelligence. The inability to laugh at oneself is a sure sign you're dealing with an idiot,” adding a clapping hands emoji.
The posts came after excerpts from Manganiello’s memoir, Bloodlines, due for release on October 13, were published earlier in the week.
According to People , the 49-year-old actor wrote that his autoimmune illness had affected his marriage to Vergara, describing their relationship as having “become devoid of any emotionality whatsoever”. He also reportedly claimed that Vergara denied him affection, even when he asked for it.
Manganiello and Vergara married in 2015 and divorced in 2024. The former couple have also offered different explanations for the end of their marriage.
Vergara previously told a Spanish newspaper that their marriage “broke up because my husband was younger; he wanted to have kids, and I didn't want to be an old mom. I feel it's not fair to the baby.”
However, Manganiello reportedly disputed that account in his memoir, saying he had “gave up” the idea of having children because of his illness.

title: Wladimir Klitschko seeks police help over Hayden Panettiere   s missing jewellery
description: Wladimir Klitschko is seeking police involvement after alleging Hayden Panettiere   s jewellery may have been pawned
content:
Wladimir Klitschko is seeking police involvement after alleging Hayden Panettiere’s jewellery may have been pawned
Wladimir Klitschko is seeking permission to involve police in recovering jewellery he believes belonged to his late former partner, actress Hayden Panettiere, according to newly obtained court documents.
The retired Ukrainian boxer, who shares an 11-year-old daughter, Kaya, with Panettiere, claims that a non-family member previously connected to the actress pawned belongings that may have included her jewellery.
According to documents obtained by TMZ , the pawn shop has declined to disclose information about the items unless contacted directly by law enforcement.
Klitschko is asking a judge to authorise him, in his capacity as guardian of Kaya, to approve a police investigation into the missing jewellery. He believes the items could form part of his daughter’s inheritance.
The filing raises additional concerns about the protection of Panettiere’s estate. Klitschko alleges that emails he had been notified about were accessed and destroyed by non-family members.
According to the documents, a security company was hired to protect the actress’s home and its contents after concerns that someone had gained unauthorised access.
Following Panettiere’s death on August 16, the property’s locks were changed, while storage units containing her designer clothing were moved to prevent potential theft.
Panettiere, known for her roles in Heroes and other television and film projects, died aged 36. The report states that her death resulted from the effects of several substances, including fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine, which led to cardiac arrest.
In the days following her death, Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, alleged to The New York Times that the actress’s former boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, had pawned some of her belongings before she died. An anonymous source reportedly corroborated Vogel’s claims.

title: Houthis and the spreading conflict in the Middle East
description: Houthis and the spreading conflict in the Middle East
content:
The current conflict in the Middle East is drawing closer to Pakistan
The current conflict in the Middle East is drawing closer to Pakistan. As discussed later in this article, the crisis in Yemen, which was once part of British India, may bring hundreds of thousands of desperate people into Pakistan, escaping the war in their homeland. For Islamabad, the situation is further complicated by the involvement of two of its close allies - Saudi Arabi and Iran - operating on the opposite sides of the growing conflict. There is further complication by the involvement of non-state actors in the conflict. That is the case in particular as the Houthis, a tribal group based in Yemen, has become a target for the US. Yemen was once a part of the Bombay presidency in British India. Complicating the situation for Pakistan is its close relations with Saudi Arabia which is helping the formal government in Yemen.
The expanding war in the Middle East began on February 28, 2026 when Isreal joined the US in the intensive bombing of Iran. The stated aim was to change the regime dominated by Islamic clerics who had taken control of Iran in 1979 when Emperor Raza Shah Pehalvi fled from Tehran and Ayatollah Ali Khomeni returned from self-imposed exile and took control of the country. He brought into being a regime that followed what he and his followers claimed was the Islamic way of governance.
Since the Emperor had been supported by the US, the Islamic regime in Tehran adopted an anti-American approach to foreign affairs. The most significance manifestation of this approach was the raid on the American embassy in Tehran and the capture of more than 400 people who worked there. They remained in the custody of the Islamic regime for several years.
With this as the historical background, the American government led by President Donald Trump decided to take military action. It was encouraged to take this path by Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, who believed that Iran's nuclear programme posed an existential threat for his country. The February 28 bombing did not produce the intended results. The bombing of a presidential compound in Tehran killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei and a number of his senior colleagues They were succeeded by a group even more conservative than those who were killed in the American-Israeli attack.
Tehran reacted to the attack by having the groups it had created and trained to follow it. Among those Tehran supported were the Houthis, an Islamic group that had captured a part of their homeland, in Yemen. The group came into being as a religious movement in the early 1990s. It focused on Zaydism, an offshoot of Shiite Islam. Its leaders mounted an armed rebellion against Yemen's government, saying they were battling corruption and poor governance.
In 2014, the Houthis took over Sanaa, Yemen's capital, starting a civils war. The government in Yemen asked Saudi Arabia and the UAE for help, which led to a civil war that resulted in the deaths of hundreds of thousands people. The Houthis survived, cementing their rule over northern Yemen. After a truce in 2022, the Houthis used ensuing peace to become stronger and self-reliant, expanding their access to sophisticated miliary hardware.
While the Houthis became self-reliant, the government weakened. "The Yemeni government is basically a fiction at this point ," said Gregory Johnson, a fellow at the Arab Gulf States institute in Washington. "They spend more time fighting one another than they do the Houthis."
When Washington and Tel Aviv attacked Iran, the Houthis appeared willing at first not to get involved. They hoped to gain greater access to oil revenue. However, the US-Iran talks got stalled. With Saudi Arabia on the American side in the conflict with Iran, the official government in Yemen fought the Houthis. The Houthis survived and with the ongoing conflict, the group developed its own strategy. On September 3, they sent 80,000 of its fighters into battle advised by Iranian experts. One of the first places where the Houthis broke through the government's forces was in the mountains called Kadaha and from there they moved west to the coast. Their aim was to control access to the Red Sea which connected with the Suez Canal and was a prominent shipping route for the world.
On September 9, six days after the Houthis launched their Red Sea operation, the government forces collapsed. They withdrew all the way to Aden in the east, handing the entire Red Sea cost, including an island inside the critically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, to the Houthis. On October 4, the Yemeni government's leader declared a full-blown war agist the Houthi militia. The government's goal, he said, was to reclaim all the territory lost to the Houthis over the past 12 years. For Yemeni civilians, already facing extreme poverty and hunger, the war's return worsened the situation. More than 180,000 people have been displaced in recent weeks, often piling into pickup trucks and motorcycles as they rush to escape the fighting. They are moving to the coast which is separated by a narrow body of sea water from Pakistan. Could Pakistan be facing another refugee crisis as the escapees get into small rickety boats and head towards Pakistan's Balochistan coast. As we know from the case of southern parts of Europe, the rush towards safer ground by people who are determined to escape from their troubled homelands, narrow strips of water does not offer much resistance.
Pakistan has a long history of accommodating troubled foreigners. It started its existence as an independent state in August 1947 by receiving eight million Muslims who had left their homeland in what had become Hindu-dominated India. While exact numbers are not known, probably as many 4 million Afghan citizens have come into Pakistan. We should be ready to accommodate the displaced Yemenis. As the situation faced by 200 million Muslims worsens under Narendra Modi's programme to make what he now calls Bharat a truly Hindu entity, tens of thousands may head towards Pakistan.

title: In the company of Ghalib
description: In the company of Ghalib
content:
Two of Ghalib's verses have, at different milestones of my weary existence, drawn me deep into the ocean of imagination, gently beckoning me into an intimate, almost audacious dialogue with the master. I have never regarded these spiritual echoes as attempts at criticism of the genius of Ghalib's divine poetry. Rather, they are merely my modest, trembling responses, devotional offerings (niyaz) to verses that have remained permanently etched in the recesses of my memory, despite its dwindling reservoir.
The first catalyst was that haunting couplet:
(Ghalib says that all calamities have finally passed, except for the one sudden death that remains.)
While Ghalib's thought lingered in my mind, my own response took a slightly different turn:
Life itself, I realised, is the true unexpected event unfolding from moment to moment; it is the beautiful, unpredictable anomaly. Death, conversely, is the absolute certainty, the undeniable truth from which none of us can escape. Perhaps it is only with advancing age that this apparent paradox begins to reveal its meaning. We spend our lives treating death as a rude interruption, though it is, in truth, the only appointment that was fixed for us from the dawn of creation.
The second verse visited me in a starkly different setting:
Dhanpa kafan ne daagh-e-uyoob-e-barahnagi
Main warna har libaas mein nang-e-wujood tha
(The shroud has hidden the stains of my nakedness; otherwise, in every earthly attire, I was a disgrace to existence itself.)
The occasion was the burial of an old friend in Karachi. As we stood around the freshly dug grave, some relatives, in the timeless manner of human gatherings everywhere, whispered their mundane observations about the deceased. There was no profound solemnity in those fleeting remarks; death, even when heavy with grief, rarely silences the chatter of the living. Ghalib's couplet followed me home that evening, echoing in the quiet. I found myself wondering whether the kafan, or shroud, does something far more complex than merely cover the mortal remains. It symbolises an attempt to conceal the imperfections that were so painfully visible during life.
In the finality of death, perhaps our shortcomings are laid bare to the world we leave behind, even as we are politely said to have found rest beneath the silent earth. It was another of those moments when Ghalib's words opened a door, and my own imagination, with far less authority but equal sincerity, wandered through the threshold.
Years later, quite recently, while walking along a quiet trail in Milton, Canada, a sudden, fierce gust of wind caught me unawares. At my age, with the frailties that accompany the twilight years, I felt a fleeting, whimsical sensation that the wind might dissolve me and carry me away. The thought defied logic, but poetry has never sought permission from reason. I wrote:
We spend so much of our existence travelling, both literally across borders and metaphorically through time, that eventually the traveller becomes indistinguishable from the dust upon the highway. And when one finally halts the journey, one looks back to discover how much of life has already quietly slipped into the past.
Perhaps that is why the concept of migration has taken on a different, more poignant meaning for me in these autumn years. For decades, Canada has been a familiar, gentle second home. My wife and I have regularly spent large parts of the year here, wrapped in the warmth of our son, his wife, and our grandson, all proud Canadian citizens. Yet it was only last year, at our son's gentle urging, that we finally began the formal immigration process. What had once been a series of prolonged visits gradually took on the quiet, enduring permanence of a final home.
For someone born amid the historic upheavals of Partition, migration is a defining scar of my generation. Decades later, the journey continues in a different form, with the old traveller once again facing departure, arrival, and the elusive meaning of home.
That bittersweet sentiment distilled itself into another couplet:
Kab talak rote raho ge hijraton ka gham liye
Kya kabhi khana-badoshon ki taraf dekha nahin
Perhaps every migrant carries the ancient soul of a nomad within them. We change our countries, our houses, and our postal addresses, but the haunting question of where we truly belong remains stubbornly, beautifully alive.
And then came perhaps the strangest test of love: to encounter, after decades, the very beloved whose glimpse had once been a life's longing, and yet have to avert one's eyes:
Sarf-e-nigah kar kay guzarna parra hamay
Because space in an op-ed is always an unyielding master, I shall not burden the reader with the intricate circumstances or the heavy thoughts that gave birth to each of these humble attempts at poetic monologues. I will simply leave a selection of my mutafarriq ash'aar, these independent verses, here, like small, polished stones left along a winding path, allowing them to speak in their own quiet manner:
Ab to hujoom-e-gham mein tera gham hai is tarah
Kaisa mai-khana hai saqi, ke jahan peene ko
Tishna-kaami se bhare jaam-o-sabu rakhe hain
Is qadar mehv-e-tamasha hoon teri duniya mein
Kaun uth kar gaya mehfil se, mujhe hosh nahin
Dayar-e-ghair mein aa kar base hain aakhir-e-shab
Chiragh-e-zeest bujhe ga to phir seher hogi
Allow me to conclude with a brief confession in verse. I composed this qit'a while reflecting on the daunting audacity of taking even a minor liberty with the themes of Ghalib, whom I regard, without an iota of doubt, as the supreme architect of Urdu poetry:
Ghalib ki hai dehleez, zara soch ke jaana
Ik aalam-e-afaaq hai us khaama-gari mein
To approach Ghalib's world is to stand at a threshold where every word contains an ocean, and every thought opens into an expanding universe. Whatever my modest verses may amount to, they are never an attempt to stand alongside his light. They are merely the fragile footprints of a devoted reader who, having wandered so long through the enchanted, moonlit corridors of Ghalib's poetry, occasionally forgot his own insignificance enough to answer back.

title: Praise intolerance
description: Praise intolerance
content:
The hardest thing to swallow is another person's praise, and that too if they are commended in our presence
The hardest thing to swallow is another person's praise, and that too if they are commended in our presence. The digestion goes worse if the extoled person happens to be any of our colleagues. Some teachers don't even like students admiring other teachers. They waste no time enumerating the demerits of the eulogised teacher. It's not the success of the colleague that turns us mad; it's our morbid desire to be lionised by the ones who occupy our minds. Psychology suggests that a friend's success disturbs the insecure soul more than an enemy's does.
Some teachers suffering from praise constipation downplay their students' achievements, fearing generational defeat. The students' knowledgeability fed by modernism puts them way ahead of their teachers who keep themselves stagnant. A teacher should feel proud of his disciple's surpassing him. If the student doesn't excel or isn't allowed to, it's a failure of the education system.
Some narcissist parents, instead of appreciating their children's laurels, start comparing themselves with them. Suffering from praise indigestion, they start nitpicking in their children's likes and dislikes. They fail to understand that their children are undergoing age transition and hormone imbalance. The constant presence of friction turns familial bonding sour, destroying family peace and happiness.
The due and just praise of a person is something abstract that can't be reduced by our begrudging manoeuvring. If, for the moment, we counter anybody's praise with self-concocted demerits in his success, over time, his merits and demerits will inevitably dawn upon people. At workplaces, when what is seen is deemed truth and reality, when words eclipse actions, and when recognition is divorced from merit, praise is always misplaced. When the undeserving people are eulogised for long, the deserving ones, in their weaker moments, might resort to truth speaking to bring forth the reality buried under appearance and falsehood.
Sometimes, when one's talent or success is disproportionately admired without analysing its far-reaching consequences, it might sink hollowness in one's soul. Then, he will remain hankering after the praise, and in doing so, he will push others down and behind through belittling them and devaluing their successes. To such a person, it becomes impossible to digest anyone's praise. Such morbidity leads us to remain in the tow for others' faults. Sometimes, finding no faults, we invent faults in others and decant them in people's minds in a bid to neutralise the accolades and subsequent praise.
One thing such a person must bring home to himself is that the real comparison is not with others; it's between himself today and himself yesterday. Comparing our backstage with someone's stage never proves a healthy comparison. Comparison is 'the thief of joy', says Theodore Roosevelt. Man will have to defeat himself to continue his self-growth. It will lend him mindfulness, leaving no room for comparison with others. Also, praise must be taken as elusive. If someone is praised today, the other person might also be applauded someday because heartening assurance of being recognised is there in the ecosystem. Such a milieu is far better than the one wherein none is appreciated.
People afflicted with compliment intolerance have been praised disproportionately in their childhood. Quite strangely, the child who is overly praised and the one who isn't duly applauded both crave recognition abnormally in their later age. One must always be aware of praise inflation and overpraising, which cultivate reliance on external approval. Psychologist Jim Taylor explains that children know their achievements.
The only guardrail is to remain purpose-orientated. When our performance is contingent upon external validation, the deprivation thereof will dishearten us and force us to make comparisons. However, when we perform for a purpose, the fulfilment lies in the effort itself. Striving for recognition and vying for superiority through praise are poles apart. 'I want to be excellent' speaks of constructive ambition, while 'I want to be more excellent than him' surrenders one's peace to comparison. Maturity is not the death of our ego; it's the education of our ego.

title: A different ball game
description: A different ball game
content:
There is a clear difference in how international organisations treat Pakistan in hockey and cricket
The news that Pakistan is missing out on the Asian Hockey Champions Trophy scheduled to be held in India from October 27 to November 5 - resulting in Bangladesh taking their spot - highlights a clear double standard. When it comes to hockey, governing bodies can quickly finalise replacements and enforce scheduling. However, if this were a cricket tournament, the International Cricket Council (ICC) and the Asian Cricket Council (ACC) would bend over backwards, delaying decisions and creating hybrid models just to keep both nations in the draw.
This stark contrast between how hockey and cricket handle geopolitical tensions reveals a harsh reality in modern sports: financial clout matters more than principles. Pakistan had formally approached the Asian Hockey Federation, seeking either the relocation of the entire tournament or the staging of Pakistan's matches at a neutral venue, citing concerns over the safety of players and officials given the sensitive Indo-Pak bilateral situation. However, the proposal was turned down. Hockey failed to get the cricket-like VIP treatment.
The deciding factor is not diplomacy or safety; it is pure revenue. A Pakistan-India cricket match is one of the most lucrative fixtures in global sports, generating astronomical broadcasting rights, sold-out stadiums and unparalleled advertising revenue. The ICC simply cannot afford to lose the financial windfall of a high-voltage cricket clash. Hockey, lacking that massive commercial appeal, enjoys no such leverage, allowing administrators to make swift, uncompromising decisions when teams refuse to travel. This disparity proves that international sports governance is rarely dictated by uniform rules. Instead, financial muscle dictates the terms, leaving less commercialised sports like hockey to face rigid consequences while cricket operates under its own set of rules.

title: Marching for merit
description: Marching for merit
content:
Unsuccessful SPSC candidates smaller presence should not diminish importance of demands
The unsuccessful candidates of SPSC, who have embarked on a long march from Hyderabad to Karachi, may not command the numbers or attention enjoyed by India's youth-led 'cockroach' movement. Yet their comparatively small presence should not diminish the importance of their demands. The strength of a protest should not be judged by the number of people taking to the streets, but by the legitimacy of their grievances. For young people who have spent years preparing for competitive examinations, questions surrounding the fairness of recruitment are matters of considerable consequence.
Having spent more than 80 days protesting outside the commission's office, they have now embarked on a long march from Hyderabad to Karachi. Their persistence should be reason enough for the provincial government to listen. Competitive examinations are supposed to offer an avenue of advancement based on merit, particularly in a society where opportunities are scarce and patronage continues to influence access to employment. Any perception that this avenue is compromised threatens to deepen an already troubling sense of disillusionment among educated youth. The legal dispute surrounding CCE 2024 has further complicated matters. The Sindh High Court's order for rechecking answer scripts was subsequently suspended by the Federal Constitutional Court, allowing the recruitment process to continue. This does not absolve the commission of blame for any wrongdoing, just as the protesters' failure to qualify does not invalidate their concerns.
What is required is an impartial examination of the allegations, conducted without prejudice to those who have already qualified. A fresh examination cannot be justified solely by public pressure, but neither should demands for scrutiny be dismissed without a transparent response. The least the Sindh government should do is engage the protesting candidates in a meaningful dialogue.

title: Governor s rule in K P
description: Governor s rule in K P
content:
Hopes for a political thaw were put to rest yesterday as the Centre clamped an Emergency and imposed Governor's rule
Hopes for a political thaw were put to rest yesterday as the Centre clamped an Emergency and imposed Governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa province. The situation hit this pass as both sides rigidly stuck to their positions. The Federation could have avoided this extreme measure had it granted the opposition its due political space. Conversely, Chief Minister Sohail Afridi's unrelenting rhetoric and vows to march on the capital pushed the situation to the brink.
The government's decision to invoke Articles 232 and 234 - coming as a desperate bid to assert firm control over the province - is driven by what it says the PTI's deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism. The party, however, claims it "was being left out of security decisions concerning the province". CM Afridi sought a review of the Centre's counterterrorism policy, framing the stance as his constitutional duty to align with a K-P Assembly resolution that urged the Federation to consult the province before launching any military operations.
However, dismantling a PTI government backed by a two-thirds majority risks worsening the situation. Reports of the CM having been taken into custody may serve as a precursor to further chaos, especially with protesters already mobilised. Crucially, TTAP, the six-party opposition alliance, has also announced its intention to resist the move tooth and nail. Beyond immediate condemnation, the PTI maintains it is being victimised for "seeking a lawful recourse within the system" - a reference to its demand for implementing the August 18th Supreme Court decision concerning access to Imran Khan, their jailed leader.
This recourse to Governor's rule, while serving as an immediate administrative measure to contain terrorism, cannot substitute for a political consensus. Both K-P and Balochistan are in desperate need of a political remedy that federal interventions are unlikely to provide. Amid an unrelenting terror threat and a volatile geopolitical environment, political stability is indispensable. Thus, the immediate need for national reconciliation cannot be overemphasised. Halting the slide requires an inclusive, broad-based dialogue to restore genuine political order.
On whether the imposition of an Emergency and Governor's rule will withstand legal scrutiny, the urgent need to tackle the rising tide of terrorism likely provides sufficient justification to earn a nod from the apex court.

title: Russia s Taliban gamble
description: Russia s Taliban gamble
content:
Russia's growing embrace of Afghan Taliban regime is raising uncomfortable questions in Islamabad
Russia's growing embrace of Afghan Taliban regime is raising uncomfortable questions in Islamabad. Is Moscow simply pursuing its security interests, or is there more to its increasingly accommodating approach towards a regime that Pakistan accuses of sheltering terrorist groups responsible for attacks inside the country?
The questions gained urgency after the eighth round of the Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan ended on October 5 without a joint statement for the first time since the forum was established in 2017. The meeting brought together Pakistan, Russia, China, India, Iran, Afghanistan and several Central Asian countries. But differences between Islamabad and Kabul over cross-border terrorism prevented participants from agreeing on a common position. Pakistan's special representative for Afghanistan, Ambassador Muhammad Sadiq, reiterated Islamabad's concerns about terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory, particularly the TTP. Afghan acting Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi rejected the allegations and called for resolving outstanding issues through dialogue. What made the meeting more significant was Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov's acknowledgement of the Taliban's efforts against Daesh and drug trafficking, and his call for greater engagement with Kabul.
Russia formally recognised the Taliban government in July 2025. Lavrov's latest remarks, therefore, do not represent a sudden policy reversal. They underline a growing divergence between Moscow's approach and Islamabad's expectations. What explains Russia's approach? The obvious explanation is strategic. Moscow wants to preserve its influence in Afghanistan, prevent instability from spreading into Central Asia and contain the threat posed by Daesh. It also wants to limit the prospect of renewed Western military influence in the region. Yet some in Pakistan suspect that historical grievances may also have a role to play. Moscow has not forgotten the Soviet Union's defeat in Afghanistan during the 1980s, when Pakistan played a central role in supporting the Afghan resistance with American and Saudi assistance. Some believe that Russia's growing relationship with the Taliban could partly reflect a desire to counter Pakistan's historical influence in Afghanistan.
Another theory links Russia's approach to Pakistan's changing international alignments. Islamabad has developed closer ties with the Trump administration, while its Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye has added another dimension to its strategic relationships. Some observers speculate that Moscow may view these developments with suspicion, particularly if it believes Pakistan is moving closer to Washington or becoming part of a regional security arrangement that could affect Russian interests.
Recent military contacts have added to the questions. A Taliban military delegation participated in exercises in Russia and visited an exhibition showcasing military equipment and technology shortly before the Moscow Format meeting. These contacts indicate expanding engagement, although they do not establish that Moscow has decided to supply weapons to the Taliban.
For Pakistan, the concern is straightforward: closer regional engagement with Kabul could reduce pressure on the Taliban to act against the TTP. Islamabad argues that dialogue must produce verifiable action against groups launching attacks inside Pakistan. Russia, meanwhile, appears convinced that maintaining relations with the Taliban offers a practical way to protect its interests. Moscow has little reason to abandon its broader relationship with Pakistan simply because the two countries differ over Afghanistan. But the absence of a joint statement in Moscow exposed the limits of regional cooperation. Countries that share concerns about Afghanistan are increasingly divided over how to deal with its rulers. Ultimately, Russia's gamble rests on whether the Taliban can be relied upon to deliver what they promise. Pakistan's experience shows that the Taliban cannot be trusted and have a tendency to betray their benefactors.

title: Pakistan   s US envoy highlights Lahore   s cultural and literary legacy at New York festival
description: Rizwan Sheikh describes Lahore as a fountainhead of creativity and intellectual discourse
content:
Rizwan Sheikh describes Lahore as a fountainhead of creativity and intellectual discourse
Pakistan’s Ambassador to the United States, Rizwan Saeed Sheikh, underscored Lahore’s cultural and literary legacy at the Lahore Literary Festival held at the Asia Society in New York, highlighting the city’s contribution to Pakistan’s intellectual and artistic traditions.
The ambassador was accompanied by Aamer Ahmed Atozai, Pakistan’s consul general in the US metropolis.
In his inaugural remarks, Sheikh traced Lahore’s enduring contribution to Pakistan’s intellectual and artistic landscape, drawing on his longstanding personal association with the historic city.
He said nothing quite matched Lahore in its glory, vibrancy and cultural significance, highlighting the city’s continuing contributions to literature, drama, theatre, film and the performing arts.
Describing Lahore as a fountainhead of creativity and intellectual discourse, the ambassador also recalled the historic significance of the Lahore Resolution, adopted in 1940.
He described the resolution as a landmark work of political literature that eventually became a reality, laying the ideological foundation for the creation of Pakistan.
Drawing a parallel between Pakistan and the United States, Sheikh said Lahore held a place in Pakistan comparable to that of New York in America, embodying cultural dynamism, intellectual vitality and national identity.
The festival brought together writers, intellectuals and artists to celebrate arts and literature and promote cultural understanding between Pakistan and the international community.

title: Haley Cavinder opens up about the DM that led to her wedding with Jake Ferguson
description: Haley Cavinder reveals how a simple golf related DM from Dallas Cowboys star Jake Ferguson sparked their romance
content:
Haley Cavinder reveals how a simple golf-related DM from Dallas Cowboys star Jake Ferguson sparked their romance
Haley Cavinder has revealed the unexpected direct message from her now-husband, Dallas Cowboys tight end Jake Ferguson, that sparked their relationship in 2023.
The former college basketball star shared the story during an appearance on PEOPLE’s WAG World , hosted by Skyler Caruso. In the episode released on October 9, Cavinder, 25, recalled how Ferguson first contacted her.
“He just DMed me and asked how my golf game was,” she said.
At the time, Cavinder had recently graduated from the University of Miami and said she was not actively looking for a relationship. Ferguson, 27, also played it casually as the pair began getting to know each other.
However, their connection developed quickly. “We spent 10 days together straight, and he’s just a good, down-to-earth human being,” Cavinder recalled.
She praised Ferguson for remaining grounded despite the attention that comes with being a professional athlete. Cavinder said her first impression of him had remained consistent throughout their relationship, adding that he continued to make her a better person.
Her twin sister, Hanna Cavinder, also shared her initial reaction to the relationship. Hanna admitted she initially thought Ferguson seemed too good to be true and wanted to see whether his behaviour would remain consistent over six months.
Haley explained that her sister’s approval was important because of their close bond. She described Hanna as the most important person in her life and said she wanted the person she dated to get along with her twin.
Ferguson eventually won Hanna over, with Haley jokingly pointing to her engagement ring and wedding band as evidence of his commitment.
Ferguson proposed to Haley in April 2025 during a beachside moment. The couple married on June 20, 2026, in a beachfront ceremony at the Biltmore Hotel in Miami.
Since their wedding, Cavinder said married life has felt much the same as dating, although she now considers them a family, alongside their dog, Boozer.
The couple dated for three years before tying the knot.

title: Fazl accuses govt of backtracking on talks with PTI  rejects emergency in K P
description: Questions rationale for K P emergency  accuses govt of using terrorism as a pretext
content:
Questions rationale for K-P emergency, accuses govt of using terrorism as a pretext
Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman on Sunday accused the government of backing out of negotiations with the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) and the opposition despite initially agreeing to their demands, and categorically rejected the imposition of governor’s rule or an emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P).
Speaking to the media, Fazl said his party rejected the government’s decision to impose an emergency or governor’s rule in the province, describing it as an attack on democracy and the rights of the people.
“This is an assault on democracy and the rights of the people,” he said, adding that the JUI-F would use all democratic avenues to oppose the move, including taking the matter to the public, parliament and the courts.
Read : Emergency, governor's rule imposed in K-P after president signs summary on PM Shehbaz's advice
Explaining the sequence of events, Fazl said he had returned to Pakistan on Oct 7 after performing Umrah and met a PTI delegation the same day. The party had expressed a desire for him to play a role in resolving the crisis, he added.
He said he had conveyed to the PTI delegation his view that the government had left no room for negotiations. Despite this, he met a government delegation the following day, which also asked him to play a mediatory role.
Following his involvement, Fazl said, the PTI confined its long march to K-P and suspended its plan to move towards Islamabad, while making no major announcement. The government, meanwhile, postponed its plan to impose governor’s rule, which, according to his information, had been scheduled to be announced on that day.
“Since steps towards the long march were postponed on one side and the decision to impose an emergency was deferred on the other, we thought both sides were serious about reaching an understanding,” he said.
Fazl said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif subsequently invited him to dinner, an offer he accepted after consultations within his party. However, he added, the positions of the two sides became clear during the meeting.
“The government’s position was that the long march should first be called off, while the PTI demanded that it be allowed to meet Imran Khan and that Khan sahib be taken to a hospital for treatment in accordance with court orders,” he said.
Fazl said he asked both sides whether they agreed to these demands and suggested that they avoid arguing over which side should act first. If both agreed to the demands, he said, they could then decide whether he should assume the role of negotiator.
He said he first contacteDPM d the PTI leadership and held a conference call attended by K-P Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and party chairman Gohar Ali Khan along others. He asked the PTI whether it was willing to call off the long march, to which the party responded that it would be prepared to do so if its demands were accepted.
Fazl said he met the prime minister on Sunday, who agreed to accept the PTI’s demands. Both sides had agreed to reach a decision before a Cabinet meeting scheduled for the morning, with the possibility of postponing the meeting until the evening if necessary, he added.
According to Fazl, the prime minister called him at 9:30am and said he would present the proposals he had made before the Cabinet. Fazl said he initially took this as a positive indication that the prime minister wanted to take the Cabinet into confidence.
However, about an hour later, Deputy Prime Minister (DPM) and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called him and informed him that the Cabinet had decided to impose governor’s rule.
“At 10:30am, DPM Dar called and said the Cabinet was leaning towards imposing governor’s rule and an emergency,” Fazl said. “I asked him on what grounds an emergency or governor’s rule could be imposed in K-P and told him to explain the reasons.”
He said DPM Dar cited the provincial government’s ineffectiveness in the fight against terrorism as the reason for the proposed action.
“I asked him whether the Balochistan government had not failed in dealing with terrorism, and why an emergency was not needed there but was needed here,” Fazl said.
The JUI-F chief accused the government of reneging on its commitments despite agreeing to the proposals.
“I am a witness to the fact that the government backed out after agreeing to the demands,” he said, asking why it had broken its commitment.
Fazl rejected the use of the fight against terrorism as a justification for imposing an emergency and criticised the role of the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), a coalition partner in the federal government.
He said it was the third or fourth time that the PPP, which presented itself as a champion of democracy, had been in government when an elected provincial administration faced what he described as an assault on democracy or an emergency.
“Whenever a provincial government has been subjected to an assault, or an emergency has been imposed, it has happened when the PPP is in government and Asif Ali Zardari is president,” he said.
Discussing military operations, Fazl blamed what he called flawed policies pursued from the era of former military ruler Gen (r) Pervez Musharraf to the present for the country’s deteriorating security situation. Repeated military operations had failed to produce results, he said, describing this as a failure of policy.
He said he had been asked to support a military operation in the region and had no objection to doing so, but demanded an account of the outcomes of operations conducted between 2010 and the present.
Pointing to the deteriorating security situation in K-P, Fazl said people could no longer move freely in Dera Ismail Khan and police were unable to remain safely inside their stations.
“Police stations are emptied, and police personnel spend the night in houses in neighbourhoods rather than staying at their stations,” he said.
He questioned why the government wanted to focus only on terrorists while refusing to discuss its own failures and flawed policies.
“Will we discuss only the terrorists and not your failures? Will we not discuss your flawed strategy?” he asked.
Fazl said that if an emergency had to be imposed, it should be imposed on the federal government, which he described as illegitimate.
Reiterating his opposition to the decision, the JUI-F chief said his party would challenge the move through parliamentary and judicial forums.
“We categorically reject the decision to impose an emergency and will use parliament and the courts to oppose it,” he said.

title: Maaz  Farhan sizzle as Pakistan seal series
description: Left hander misses ton as Farhan fires again before bowlers secure 2 0 unassailable lead
content:
Left-hander misses ton as Farhan fires again before bowlers secure 2-0 unassailable lead
Pakistan on Sunday took 2-0 unassailable lead in the three-match T20I series when they whipped Sri Lanka by 82 runs in their second show at the Pindi Stadium in Rawalpindi.
Pakistan rode on superb batting display from Maaz Sadaqat (96) and skipper Sahibzada Farhan (73) to pile-up 215-3 in the stipulated 20 overs. This is also a record total at this venue, eclipsing the previous 195-5 which Pakistan had scored against Zimbabwe on November 23, 2025.
Young pacer Imran Randhawa, who made his Test debut against England recently, then took 3-11 in four overs to restrict Sri Lanka to 133-7.
This is also the heaviest win from Pakistan against Sri Lanka.
Sri Lanka were never in the run as they kept losing wickets at regular interval.
After Salman Mirza removed in-form Lahiru Udara (5) early, it was Imran Randhawa who put great pressure by picking up the wickets of Sineth Jayawardena (22), Kusal Mendis (9) and Sahan Arachchige (0) in quick succession to break the back of the visitors.
Saim Aub then had Dasun Shanaka (9) before Shadab got rid of Kamindu Mendis (23) to leave Sri Lanka gasping at 74-6.
Chamindu Wickramasinghe resisted with 24-ball 29 before falling to Salman Mirza.
Maheesh Theekshana remained top-scorer with 32 not out which featured four fours.
Imran was ably backed by his new ball partner Salman Mirza with 2-28.
Earlier Maaz Sadqat and skipper Sahibzada Farhan did a glorious job to enable Pakistan post a big total on a batting track.
Maaz and Farhan shared 88 runs off 48 balls for the second wicket stand to take the hosts to a decent total in the end.
Farhan was dropped on 12 when he skied one early in the innings. However, he capitalised on the opportunity and went on to hit his second successive fifty of the series. He brought in his fifty off 31 balls and hammered five sixes and four fours in his commanding 44-ball 73.
Earlier, he, along with Fakhar Zaman provided a rapid start to the hosts, sharing 55 off 35 balls for the opening stand.
Fakhar fell for 17-ball 22 with four fours to off-spinner Maheesh Theekshana.
Maaz, who brought in his second successive fifty off 30 balls, then went after the ball and played some superb strokes.
He also hit Theekshana for three glorious sixes in one over which yielded 22 runs.
He along with Hasan Nawaz scored a rapid 72 runs for the third wicket partnership to take Pakistan to a huge total.
Maaz hammered seven sixes and six fours in his gallant 51-ball 96.
He lost his wicket off the final ball of the innings when he went for a big hit in a bid to complete his century but was held in the deep.
Hasan Nawaz remained not out on nine-ball 19 with one six and one four.
Pakistan scored 46 in the power-play, were 90-1 in ten overs, reached 145-2 in 15 and made 70 runs in the final five overs.
Theekshana remained the most expensive bowler as he finished with 1-55 in his quota of four overs.
Eshan Malinga (1-41) and Dasun Shanaka (1-30) were the other successful bowlers.
Earlier, Sri Lanka won the toss and elected to bowl first. Pakistan made one change, bringing in Salman Mirza in place of Razaullah who had made his T20I debut in the previous game at the same venue.
The third and final game is scheduled for Tuesday at the same venue.

title: State determined to rid K P of terrorists  says Kundi at first advisory council meeting after governor s rule
description: K P governor will perform the functions of the provincial government on behalf of the federal government
content:
Governor chairs special security meeting to review province security situation, convenes first Apex Committee meeting
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Governor Faisal Karim Kundi on Sunday said the state was determined to rid the province of terrorists, as he chaired the first meeting of the provincial advisory council following the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in K-P.
“Pakhtuns are the biggest victims of terrorism. Therefore, it is the government’s resolve to rid the people of K-P of terrorism and provide them with an environment where their children can go to school, conduct business, travel and dream of a better future. My first priority will be peace and public security,” Kundi said while chairing the first meeting of the provincial advisory council.
Kundi chaired the meeting as the federal government formed an 11-member advisory council to oversee administrative affairs in K-P. The governor would perform the functions of the provincial government on behalf of the federal government. The move came as the government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in K-P after the president signed the summary on the advice of the prime minister, following the federal cabinet’s approval of the recommendation.

During the meeting, K-P governor underscored that restoring peace, strengthening security, ensuring stability and accelerating development in K-P were his foremost priorities, stressing that the extraordinary administrative measures taken in view of the prevailing situation were aimed at strengthening state institutions and eliminating terrorism, not targeting any political party, individual or section of society.
Read : Emergency, governor's rule imposed in K-P after president signs summary on PM Shehbaz's advice
He stated that he was speaking not merely as the provincial governor but as someone who understood K-P’s suffering, challenges and public aspirations, further adding that his sole objective was to take the province back towards peace, security, stability and development.
“Our fight is against terrorism, the mindset and networks that sustain it, and the environment that allows it to flourish and weakens the rule of law,” Kundi said.
Kundi further stated that the people of K-P had paid a tremendous price for terrorism, with police officers, military personnel, Levies personnel, government employees, religious scholars, teachers, traders and ordinary citizens sacrificing their lives.
"Mothers have lost their sons, children their parents, and families their loved ones. The time has come for the people to receive their right to peace after these sacrifices".
Kundi said that to break the terrorist ecosystem, the state would also have to act against facilitation networks, financial support, extremism, illegal weapons, drugs, unlawful movement and other mechanisms sustaining terrorism, further noting that the effective implementation of the National Action Plan and other relevant counterterrorism measures would remain a priority.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi chairs a meeting of the newly appointed 11-member advisory council. Advisers include Kifayat Ullah Khan for interior, Tariq Mehmood Pasha for finance, Amir Javed for law and others. @fkkundi #FaisalKarimKundi #KhyberPakhtunkhwa … pic.twitter.com/7oHDmN7Z3b
“The law will take action against anyone who commits terrorism, and it will also reach those who facilitate it,” he said, clarifying that the action would not target any nation, language, region or political affiliation, but would be directed exclusively against elements violating the law.
Kundi said his first priority would be "peace and public protection", with particular emphasis on effective counterterrorism operations, further adding that the state must stand firmly behind police personnel confronting terrorists and ensure that neither they nor their families are left unsupported. "The capacity of the police and the Counter Terrorism Department will be strengthened through improved resources, training, technology, intelligence support and modern weapons".
K-P governor outlined that his second priority would be to strengthen the "writ of the state" in conflict-affected districts, whose residents had endured terrorism, displacement, inadequate basic facilities and prolonged deprivation, while pledging greater attention to ensuring these areas received their due share of development, education, healthcare, employment, roads, electricity, water and administrative services.
“The state's duty is to give greater attention to areas where deprivation is greater,” he remarked.
Kundi identified "public service delivery" as his third priority, saying a government should be judged by the facilities it provides rather than its statements, further adding that his administration would focus on improving government hospitals, schools, roads, municipal services, healthcare, education and justice. “The state exists for the citizen, not the citizen for the state.”
Addressing young people, he said the province’s future lay in education, employment, sports, technology, business opportunities and a society in which young people could realise their ambitions. “The state's responsibility is to give young people not guns, but pens, books, skills, employment and hope.”
“We will make it a land of peace. We will make it a land of development. We will make it a land of opportunities,” he added.
Earlier, the federal government formed an 11-member advisory council to oversee administrative affairs in K-P and ordered the immediate establishment of an Area Development Secretariat (ADS) in 12 designated districts to improve law and order, public safety, strengthen governance and promote development.

The federal government has also appointed Sanaullah Advocate as the Advocate General of K-P, according to the order.
The order stated that provincial government affairs would be conducted in accordance with the relevant constitutional provisions and the K-P Government Rules of Business, 1985, in a manner consistent with the federal directive.
Govt orders establishment of Area Development Secretariat in designated districts of K-P
In a federal government order issued in a Gazette notification, the federal government notified that the ADS would operate under the supervision of the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC).
According to the order, the designated districts included Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Lakki Marwat, Bannu, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Kurram, Orakzai, North Waziristan, Upper South Waziristan, and Lower South Waziristan.
The federal order noted that the ARDC would comprise prominent figures from the designated districts and would be headed by a chairman, further adding that the appointment of the ARDC chairman, vice chairman, spokesperson, and members would be carried out in accordance with the prescribed procedure and tenure.
It added that the ADS would be headed by the additional chief secretary (Designated Districts) of K-P, who would also serve as the administrator for these districts, while stating that the provincial government officers and personnel from other agencies deployed in the designated districts would remain under the administrative and operational control of the ADS.
The federal directive said that the prime minister may, from time to time, order further postings and transfers in the designated districts based on the administrator's recommendations, further noting that the administrator would exercise all “administrative, managerial, and law enforcement powers” of the provincial government within the designated districts.
It further said that the administrator, in the designated districts, would have the authority to establish organisational structures for governance, security, and development, and to oversee the district administration, law enforcement agencies and relevant departments.
According to the federal order, the administrator would also be empowered to issue directives to the civil administration, police, and military authorities, adding that the administrator would be able to issue orders regarding the “operational, organisational, and administrative affairs of the ADS”.
The administrator would also have the authority to “issue orders for the allocation and transfer of funds”.
It added that law enforcement and security matters in the designated districts would be improved through coordination with federal agencies, the armed forces, and provincial institutions, further stating that departments might be restructured, and necessary measures taken, to ensure public safety, economic stability, relief operations, and the provision of essential services.
The federal order underlined that “orders, notifications, directives, and measures” issued by the administrator would hold the same legal status as those issued by the provincial government.
It added that under the federal order, the provisions of the Constitution—specifically Chapter III, Part IV, and Article 175, Clause (3)—as well as the K-P Government Rules of Business 1985, would not apply to the designated districts.“This Order shall come into force at once,” the notification stated.

title: Desi meets deli  Nishaan brings Pakistani flavours to NYC
description: With street food favourites and inventive sandwiches  this hotspot gives New York   s food scene a distinctly desi twist
content:
With street-food favourites and inventive sandwiches, this hotspot gives New York’s food scene a distinctly desi twist
New York City has no shortage of places to eat, but every once in a while, a restaurant makes you feel as though you have stepped into a familiar corner of home, thousands of miles away.
That was my experience at Nishaan , a Pakistani-American restaurant in Manhattan’s East Village, where the food, the crowd and even the walls seemed to tell a story about what it means to be Pakistani in America.
Located at 160 First Avenue, Nishaan has built its identity around an irresistible idea: what happens when the flavours of Pakistani street food meet the sandwiches and comfort foods that define New York? The answer is a menu that feels playful without losing sight of its roots.
Its Pakistani chopped cheese has become a signature, while the restaurant’s founder, Zeeshan Bakhrani, told Eater New York that his approach grew out of his experience of being both Pakistani and American, and his desire to bring the two food cultures together, thoughtfully.
That philosophy comes through in the menu. Rather than simply placing a traditional kebab inside a sandwich, Nishaan reimagines the familiar flavours and textures of Pakistani food through dishes that feel distinctly New York.
I tried the chapli kebab chopped cheese, the Buffalo tandoori chicken sandwich and the elotes chaat. Each offered a different take on the restaurant’s central concept: taking something recognisable and giving it a Pakistani twist.
The chapli kebab chopped cheese was especially fitting for a city where the chopped cheese has become a food institution. Pakistani spices bring depth to the minced meat, while melted American and pepper jack cheeses, peppers, onions, lime-cilantro sauce and tamarind chutney create a combination of richness, heat and tang. It is a meeting of culinary traditions that feels natural rather than forced.
The Buffalo tandoori chicken sandwich takes another familiar American favourite and gives it a desi personality, marrying the punch of Buffalo-style chicken with tandoori seasoning and cooling mint-chutney ranch.
The elotes chaat, meanwhile, brings together the spirit of Mexican street corn and South Asian chaat, layering contrasting textures and tangy flavours into a dish that feels perfectly at home on this inventive menu.
There is plenty more to explore, from the Pakistani achari cheesesteak and Pakistani-flavoured wings to the smash burger and gulab jamun. Even the drinks have personality. I also tried the Thai chai with cold foam, a fun, indulgent addition to a meal already full of bold flavours.
Yet Nishaan’s appeal goes beyond what arrives on the table. The restaurant was packed when I visited. Finding a table meant waiting, and the relatively small space only amplified the bustle. But the crowd was part of the experience.
Young people, groups of friends and members of the South Asian diaspora filled the restaurant, creating an atmosphere that reminded me of the lively food spots one might find around Bukhari Commercial in Karachi or in the busy neighbourhoods of Lahore.
There was something wonderfully familiar about it: the chatter, the youthful energy and the feeling that everyone had come not only to eat but also to be part of something.
The decor contributes to that feeling. Among the details that caught my attention were cute illustrations of people from different racial backgrounds running around New York and enjoying Nishaan’s food.
They captured an appealing idea of a city in which food becomes a shared language, bringing people together across backgrounds. The artwork felt celebratory rather than exclusive: Pakistani flavours were at the centre, but everyone was invited to the table.
That sense of community extended beyond Nishaan itself. The visual references and celebratory spirit around the restaurant also brought to mind other Pakistani food and beverage ventures, including Kamkeen and Kaafi.
These businesses belong to a wider movement of Pakistani-American entrepreneurs who are finding new ways to express their heritage through food and drink. Condé Nast Traveler’s recent feature on a new generation of Pakistani-American restaurants explores this shift, highlighting restaurateurs who are making Pakistani flavours more visible while creating their own distinctive identities.
That recognition matters because Pakistani cuisine is often introduced to international audiences through a relatively narrow selection of familiar dishes.
Restaurants such as Nishaan broaden that picture by showing how the flavours people grew up with can evolve without losing their character.
What stayed with me most was the sense that Nishaan was doing more than serving an inventive meal. It was creating a space where Pakistani identity could be expressed with confidence, humour and creativity.
Its food speaks to people who recognise the flavours of home, but it also gives diners unfamiliar with Pakistani cuisine an accessible way to discover them.
For Pakistanis living abroad, a restaurant like this can offer a little nostalgia alongside something entirely new.
For New Yorkers, it is another reminder that the city's food culture is shaped by the people who bring their histories, memories and appetites to it.
In a city defined by its endless appetite for reinvention, Nishaan makes a compelling case for Pakistani flavours to have a place at the table.
And judging by the crowd waiting for a seat, plenty of people are happy to pull up a chair.

title: Apple Music in Pakistan  Subscription prices  features and how to sign up
description: Now available in Pakistan with monthly plans starting at Rs379
content:
Now available in Pakistan with monthly plans starting at Rs379
After more than a decade of waiting, Pakistani music lovers can finally subscribe to Apple Music through local Apple accounts, bringing one of the world's biggest music-streaming services officially to the country.
Apple's expansion was confirmed when Pakistan appeared on its updated Availability of Apple Media Services page on September 30. The development places Pakistan among four new markets added to the service, alongside Albania, Brunei and Burkina Faso.
For listeners who have spent years relying on alternative regional accounts or other streaming platforms, the arrival means easier access to Apple's extensive music catalogue, locally relevant playlists and a range of features designed to personalise the listening experience.
How much does Apple Music cost in Pakistan?
Affordability is likely to be one of the biggest considerations for Pakistani subscribers. According to the announcement, the subscription plans start at Rs379 per month.
Individual plan — Rs379 per month: Designed for one listener, with access to Apple Music's full subscription catalogue and features.
Family plan — Rs649 per month: Allows multiple family members to enjoy the service under one subscription, with individual libraries and recommendations.
Free trial: New subscribers are eligible for a one-month trial, subject to Apple's terms and eligibility requirements.
After the trial period, subscriptions renew automatically unless cancelled. Users should check the subscription screen in the Apple Music app for the applicable price, trial eligibility and billing terms before signing up.
The local pricing makes the service accessible without needing to calculate a foreign-currency subscription, although whether it offers better value than competing platforms will depend on listeners' preferences and budgets.
More than 100 million songs at your fingertips
Apple Music's biggest attraction is the size of its catalogue. Apple advertises access to more than 100 million songs, spanning international pop, hip-hop, rock, electronic music, classical recordings and regional genres.
For Pakistani listeners, the catalogue includes music from artists such as Atif Aslam, Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, Junoon, Strings, Sajjad Ali, Hasan Raheem and Ali Sethi, alongside international performers and emerging acts.
Apple does not publish a single, verified total of individual artists available in Pakistan. Its catalogue also changes over time and can vary by region, so the number of songs is a more reliable measure of its overall scale than an estimated artist count.
The platform's dedicated Pakistan music storefront highlights local music through playlists and artist collections. These include All-Time Pakistani Hits and artist-focused selections such as Atif Aslam Essentials, Junoon Essentials and Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan Essentials.
The range offers an opportunity to move between contemporary Pakistani pop, Punjabi music, qawwali, Sufi recordings and older favourites without having to search for every song individually.
Personalised playlists and music discovery
Finding new music is a central part of Apple Music's experience. Rather than simply providing a search bar and a library of songs, the service recommends tracks, albums and playlists based on listening habits and musical preferences.
Subscribers can explore editor-curated collections, new releases, genre-based playlists and personalised suggestions. Playlists such as New Music Daily offer a way to discover recent releases, while collections built around Pakistani music provide a more locally relevant entry point.
Users can also create their own playlists, add songs to their libraries, save albums and organise music around particular moods, occasions or genres.
For listeners who enjoy building a soundtrack for a road trip, a workout or a late-night study session, the ability to curate and revisit personal collections is one of the service's most practical features.
One of the most useful benefits of a paid subscription is the ability to download music for offline listening.
Subscribers can save eligible songs, albums and playlists to a compatible device and play them when an internet connection is unavailable. This can be particularly useful during commutes, flights or periods of unreliable connectivity.
Apple Music also offers an ad-free listening experience for subscribers. Unlike a conventional radio broadcast, listeners can generally select the songs and albums they want to hear, skip tracks and return to particular recordings on demand.
The service supports synchronised lyrics for many songs, allowing users to follow along while listening. Its lyrics interface can make familiar tracks more engaging and help listeners discover the words behind songs they may have heard for years.
What about Dolby Atmos and lossless audio?
For listeners who care about sound quality, Apple Music offers two notable audio features: lossless audio and Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos.
Lossless audio preserves more of the original recording's audio information than standard compressed formats. Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, where available for a particular recording and compatible setup, can create a more immersive listening experience by placing elements of a track within a three-dimensional sound field.
These features may appeal to listeners who use good headphones, compatible speakers or other suitable audio equipment. However, availability depends on the recording and device, and lossless streaming can consume considerably more data and storage than standard-quality playback.
Users should also remember that the experience varies according to their headphones, connection and listening environment. A premium audio format alone does not guarantee a noticeable improvement on every device.
For further details on supported devices and listening options, Apple's official Apple Music page outlines the service's principal features.
Despite being part of Apple's ecosystem, Apple Music is not restricted to Apple devices.
The service is available on compatible iPhones, iPads, Macs and Apple Watches, as well as Android devices and Windows computers. Users can also listen through the Apple Music web player , subject to account and subscription availability.
This cross-platform support is important in Pakistan, where music listeners use a mixture of smartphones and computers rather than exclusively relying on iPhones.
The Music app is already integrated into Apple's devices, while Android users can access the service through its dedicated app. Once subscribed, users can build their libraries and access supported features across compatible devices.
What does the launch mean for Pakistani artists?
Beyond convenience for listeners, the arrival of an official local subscription option could create another route for Pakistani music to reach audiences.
Artists, record labels and music distributors use streaming platforms to make recordings available internationally. A larger pool of paying listeners may create additional opportunities for discovery and consumption, although the commercial impact will depend on audience growth, catalogue availability, distribution agreements and streaming royalties.
For established names, the platform provides another place for listeners to revisit their music. For newer performers, editorial playlists and personalised recommendations could help introduce their work to audiences who might not otherwise encounter it.
Apple Music's Pakistani playlists also place local music within a broader international streaming environment. That can be valuable for a music scene that spans contemporary pop, independent production, film soundtracks, hip-hop, folk traditions and qawwali.
However, availability should not be confused with guaranteed exposure or income. Streaming revenue varies according to multiple factors, and placement on a platform does not automatically translate into greater earnings for every artist.
The launch gives Pakistani listeners another official option in an increasingly competitive streaming market.
Those already invested in Apple's devices may appreciate the integration, while listeners who prioritise curated playlists, an ad-free experience, offline downloads or higher-quality audio may find reasons to explore the service. The Family plan could also appeal to households that want several people to have their own music libraries under one subscription.
Others may prefer to remain with their existing streaming platforms, particularly if their playlists, listening histories and recommendations are already well established.
Ultimately, Apple Music's arrival is less about replacing every other service than expanding the choices available to Pakistani music fans.
After 11 years, the opportunity to subscribe through a local account represents a long-awaited change. Whether it becomes a major player in Pakistan's streaming market will depend on how listeners respond to its pricing, catalogue, features and local music discovery experience.
For now, Pakistani subscribers can explore the catalogue, try the available subscription options and decide whether Apple's approach to music streaming suits their listening habits.
