title: Back when detectives had to think
description: Three 1970s TV detectives return in books that explore the appeal of clever mysteries  unforgettable characters and crime solving without modern technology
content:
Three 1970s TV detectives return in books about clever mysteries, iconic characters and solving crimes without tech
If you thought the trend of placing yourself in the 1980s was cool, you were completely wrong. It was even better in the 1970s, when Petrocelli, Banacek, and Columbo solved cases and stayed cool
The Matrix told us that the late 1990s were the absolute pinnacle of human civilisation. That may be debatable, but if any decade saw television peak, it was the 1970s.
It was a time when television detectives did not need smartphones, forensic labs, drones, or computer databases to solve crimes. They needed little more than a sharp mind, an unusual personality, a good memory, and, occasionally, a very suspicious-looking suspect.
Among the many detectives who emerged during that golden age were Anthony Petrocelli, Thomas Banacek, and Lieutenant Columbo. They all solved crimes, but that was largely where the similarities ended.
Petrocelli was the lawyer who investigated before presenting his case in court; Banacek was the sophisticated insurance investigator who specialised in seemingly impossible thefts; and Lt. Columbo was the apparently disheveled police lieutenant who made murderers underestimate him.
Three books—Sandra Grabman’s Petrocelli: San Remo Justice, Jonathan Etter’s There’s An Old Polish Proverb That Says, “BANACEK,” and Mark Dawidziak’s The Columbo Phile: A Casebook — take readers behind the scenes of these shows and their central characters. Together, they make a compelling case for why the decade still captivates television fans.
Barry Newman’s Anthony Petrocelli was perhaps the most unusual of the three because he wasn’t technically a detective or investigator. The character was introduced as the fictional attorney in The Lawyer in 1970, a film loosely inspired by the real-life case of Sam Sheppard, the neurosurgeon who was initially convicted of murdering his wife, Marilyn, in 1954.
The television film Night Games aired in 1974 and became the starting point for the Petrocelli series, which ran from 1974 to 1976. Petrocelli's method was to become an investigator before becoming a courtroom lawyer, as his predecessor, Perry Mason, did and his successor, Matlock, would later adopt.
Each episode centred on a crime and on his attempt to understand what actually happened, rather than simply accepting the available evidence. The writers incorporated the Rashomon effect into the plot, first showing a crime without the criminal. The accused and the police then narrated their versions, which were brought to a conclusion by Petrocelli, whose version was taken as the final one.
Newman gave Petrocelli an intensity that made the character feel less like a traditional television lawyer and more like someone personally driven to uncover the truth. Sandra Grabman's Petrocelli: San Remo Justice takes that world apart and examines how the series came together, including its development, cast, critical reception, and the post-show lives of its stars.
It also benefits from access to people directly involved in the production. Barry Newman contributes the foreword, and Petrocelli fan Max Allan Collins provides the introduction. The book includes about 50 photographs, an episode guide, trivia, and an index, making it especially useful for viewers seeking more than nostalgia.
There’s An Old Polish Proverb That Says, “BANACEK.” Long before he took over the reins of the popular 80s TV show The A-Team, George Peppard played Thomas Banacek. If Petrocelli was driven by justice, Banacek was driven by the challenge, and that’s how they stayed distinct.
The 1972-74 NBC Mystery Movie series featured Banacek (pronounced Ban A Check) as an insurance investigator specialising in seemingly impossible thefts. The cases often followed the locked-room tradition: something had disappeared, apparently without anyone able to explain how.
And then Banacek would explain it. His trademark was not only his intelligence but also his personality. He delivered supposedly Polish proverbs with complete confidence, including the memorable warning: “When a wolf is chasing your sleigh, throw him a raisin cookie, but don't stop to bake a cake.”
Jonathan Etter's There’s An Old Polish Proverb That Says, “BANACEK” uses those eccentric sayings as a doorway into the series' history.
The book examines Peppard's performance, the show's development, and the tradition of impossible mysteries that inspired it. It also explores the show's extensive roster of guest stars during its brief run, including Broderick Crawford, Margot Kidder, Stefanie Powers, Anne Baxter, Cesar Romero, and Victoria Principal.
But the most entertaining feature may be the episode guide, which is followed by over 100 challenges for readers to test their powers of observation and concentration and to feel like Banacek for the moment.
If Petrocelli wanted to know why a crime happened, Banacek often wanted to know how something seemingly impossible could have happened at all. But Columbo was a different case altogether, because he arrived on the scene after the crime had been planned and executed in front of the audience.
Peter Falk's Lieutenant Columbo looked as if he’d wandered into the wrong television programme. His rumpled coat, apparently absent-minded manner, and endless references to “my wife” made him seem harmless. But the appearance was deceptive.
Columbo's brilliance lay in catching a killer who believed he had committed the perfect crime. It was about watching Columbo figure out how the killer did it—and, more importantly, watching the killer realise, far too late, that the seemingly confused detective had been paying attention all along.
The ‘howcatchem’ format made Columbo fundamentally different from many traditional detective shows. The first episode of the continuing series, Murder by the Book, premiered in September 1971 and was directed by a young Steven Spielberg. The audience already knew the murderer's identity, and the pleasure came from watching Columbo gradually dismantle the murderer's carefully constructed alibi. That structure is one reason the character remains so distinctive.
The Columbo Phile: A Casebook, by Mark Dawidziak, goes beyond individual episodes to examine the character's creation, the writing of the mysteries, and the series' production history. Originally published in 1989 and later expanded for its 30th Anniversary Edition, the book also includes material on developments since the original edition and a remembrance of Peter Falk.
The behind-the-scenes material is particularly interesting because Columbo was not simply a perfect character in a perfect production. Dawidziak explores the tensions between Falk's perfectionism and Universal Studios' commercial concerns. That makes the book more than a fan's guide. It also recounts how one of television's most recognisable characters was created and sustained.
What makes these books work particularly well together is that they present three distinct portrayals of the television detective in what was apparently their golden age.
Petrocelli was the lawyer-investigator who had to understand the crime because he ultimately had to argue the case. Banacek was the problem-solver whose cases were puzzles, often built around the seemingly impossible. Columbo was the psychologist who did not necessarily overpower suspects with evidence. He let them talk, observed their behaviour, and waited for their stories to unravel.
Their personalities were equally distinct. Petrocelli was serious and driven; Banacek was confident, sophisticated, and amused by the intellectual challenge. Columbo deliberately downplayed his intelligence, letting criminals feel superior until it was too late. That contrast makes revisiting them in these books especially enjoyable.
There is always a risk with books about old television shows. Nostalgia can easily become an excuse for a collection of photographs, anecdotes, and “remember when?” moments. These three books largely avoid that pitfall by offering context.
Petrocelli: San Remo Justice examines the creation and legacy of the series while drawing on the memories of those who made it. There’s an old Polish proverb that says. “BANACEK” places Banacek within the history of the impossible-mystery genre while giving readers the chance to revisit the individual episodes. And The Columbo Phile examines both the character and the machinery behind one of television's most enduring detective series.
The books also remind us that television mysteries need not be complicated to be clever. They need strong characters, well-constructed puzzles, and writers who understand that audiences enjoy being challenged.
Perhaps that is why these shows still draw audiences, decades after their original broadcasts. Today, detectives can access fingerprints, DNA, surveillance footage, and databases in seconds. In the 1970s, a detective might have to recall what someone said in a conversation three years earlier. Somehow, that made the journey more entertaining.
The three books offer distinct paths back to that television era. For fans of Petrocelli, Banacek, and Columbo, they serve as detailed backstage passes. For younger viewers discovering these characters for the first time, they remind us that television's obsession with crime-solving didn’t begin with streaming platforms. The technology has changed, but the detectives haven’t. They still ask questions, notice details, and, eventually, solve the case.
The writer is a freelance contributor who writes about film, television, and popular culture

title: Why nobody drops in anymore
description: Once  you just rang the bell  Now  you need an appointment
content:
Once, you just rang the bell. Now, you need an appointment
There was a time when you could ring someone’s doorbell without knowing whether they were home, whether the house was tidy or whether there was enough food for you. You simply rang. If the door opened, you went in. If tea appeared, you drank it. If lunch was being cooked, you ate it. If it wasn’t, you wouldn’t. And if the host happened to be in the middle of doing something, well, you were there now.
Nobody needed a WhatsApp message saying Are you home? Followed by Can I come over? Followed, quite possibly, by Now?
The unannounced visit was not an intrusion. It was a form of social life.
That, increasingly, seems to belong to another era.
A couple of weeks ago, my friend Rosie and I arrived at a friend’s house at about 8.25pm for a dinner party. We were, as it turned out, the first guests. The dinner had been organised to bid farewell and bon voyage to a dear friend leaving the country for a longish trip. The menu had been discussed, seating arranged, the car pool coordinated and little gifts bought. Everything had been planned with the precision of a minor diplomatic summit.
We couldn’t hear it because a pair of excited dogs inside were barking loudly enough to drown out both the bell and the sound of our hostess, Amna, opening the smaller side entrance.
The gate swung open and Amna beamed at us.
“Kaisay ana hua? I’m thrilled to see you guys drop by,” she said, greeting us with warm hugs and air kisses.
It took about thirty seconds for all three of us to realise the absurdity of what she had said.
And yet the joke struck a nerve. Because when was the last time any of us had actually dropped by?
Amna put it rather perfectly: “Why don’t people drop in spontaneously anymore, just ring the bell and appear? I think we should have some homes among us where we can just drop by randomly, and casually.”
There was a time when that was exactly what homes were for.
Growing up, Nousheen remembers her parents’ and grandparents’ homes as places that were almost permanently buzzing.
“Relatives, family friends, someone or other. No permission, no appointment, just dropping in whenever you wanted. And long chats invariably.”
Friends did the same. School friends would turn up at each other’s homes. University friends would appear and stay for hours. You could spend an entire afternoon lying around on somebody’s bed, talking nonsense, discussing serious things, eating whatever happened to be available [or what their cook/mother kept producing as top-tier hospitality] and eventually deciding to go somewhere else.
You knew the parents. You knew the siblings. You might wander into the kitchen and talk to someone’s mother. You might find yourself having a conversation with your friend’s father. The boundaries between my house, your house and our social world were considerably blurrier.
Today, the first question is usually not “Where are you?” but “Are you free?” And there is an important distinction. Because increasingly, being at home does not necessarily mean being available. Home has become the one place where people feel entitled to shut the door on the rest of the world.
That has something to do with how exhausting modern life has become. Work stretches into evenings. Commutes eat up hours. Children have schedules of their own. There are errands, appointments, exercise, domestic chores and an endless stream of messages demanding replies. Even leisure has become something that needs to be organised.
There are gym slots to book, restaurants to reserve, films to schedule and weekends to negotiate. Free time itself has become a commodity, carefully protected because there seems to be so little of it. And then there is me-time where everything else is blocked and silenced so we scroll to our hearts' content without being judged or reprimanded.
So when the doorbell rings unexpectedly at 6pm on a Tuesday, the reaction may no longer be delight. It may be panic. “The house is a mess.” “I haven’t showered.” “There’s nothing to serve.” “I have work to finish.” “I was planning to do absolutely nothing.” And perhaps that last reason is the most important. People have become protective of their right to do nothing — privately, uninterrupted and on their own.
The home that was once a social hub is now often a refuge from social demands. After spending the day being available to colleagues, clients, children, customers and strangers, people want somewhere they can switch off. An unexpected visitor, however welcome in theory, can feel like someone has walked into the one space where you were allowed to disappear.
The rise of the mobile phone has made this shift even easier. A decade or two ago, if you wanted to see someone, you had to see them. Or at least call. Now you can maintain an astonishing illusion of intimacy without leaving your sofa. You know what your friend had for lunch because she posted it. You know where your cousin is on holiday. You have seen somebody’s new kitchen, dog, birthday cake and haircut before you have actually sat across from them. The phone has become a strange substitute for presence.
And because we can now ask permission before appearing, we have gradually turned asking into an obligation. “Can I come over?” “Are you busy?” “Is this a good time?” The answer may be “Of course!” But the very question has changed the nature of the encounter.
The spontaneous visit used to operate on a wonderfully low threshold. You didn't have to be invited. You didn't have to arrive looking presentable. The house didn't have to be immaculate. There was no requirement to produce an elaborate meal. You came as you were. That informality may be one of the things we have lost.
Planned socialising often carries an invisible burden. The house must be cleaned. The cushions arranged. The food thought through. The drinks and starters bought. The host must be mentally prepared to entertain.
A drop-in required none of this. If there was leftover biryani, you ate biryani. If there were only biscuits, you ate biscuits. Tea could be stretched. Chairs could be found. Someone could sit on the floor. Nobody was being judged for the state of the living room. Nobody expected an Instagram-worthy afternoon.
The declining culture of casual visiting is also tied to a profound change in who is actually at home during the day. For generations, many households had someone — usually a woman — whose daily life was centred round the home. That did not necessarily mean she had nothing to do; far from it. But there was a greater likelihood that somebody was physically there when a neighbour or relative appeared at the gate.
Today, in many families, both adults work. Children have their own routines. Domestic help may come and go. Houses can sit empty for much of the day. And even when somebody is home, they may be working from there. The old assumption that home means available has disappeared. There is also the city itself. In smaller communities, dropping in was easier because people lived close to one another and knew the rhythms of each other’s lives. In large cities, visiting can involve traffic, parking, security gates, lifts and journeys long enough to require a logistical strategy.
Even neighbours can become strangers. We live in the same apartment building but may not know the person behind the door next to ours. We pass one another in lifts with the polite nod of strangers. We know the cars parked downstairs better than we know the people who own them. We are living closer together and, somehow, further apart.
And then there is money. Sameena offers a different explanation for the decline in visiting, and one that is difficult to dismiss. “For my family anyway it has nothing to do with the pandemicreating social boundaries or social media. The prices of everything is so high and I cannot randomly entertain or host visitors.” There is something wonderfully blunt about this. Perhaps sometimes people don't visit because they are too busy or too digitally connected. And perhaps sometimes they simply don't have the money. Petrol costs money. Taking a family somewhere costs money. Feeding unexpected guests costs money. Even the seemingly insignificant expense of buying something to put on the table has become harder to ignore.
The casual visit was built on an economy of abundance — not necessarily financial abundance, but the assumption that there would always be something to share. That assumption is weaker now. But there is another cost to the disappearance of drop-ins, and it cannot be measured in rupees. We have lost the low-stakes encounter.
The person who comes over for twenty minutes and stays for two hours. The neighbour who happens to be passing. The cousin who arrives because they were “in the area”, even though they clearly weren't. The friend who comes over with no particular purpose and leaves having solved three problems, discussed five others and laughed about something completely irrelevant.
These encounters were inefficient. That was precisely their charm. Not everything had to have a purpose or productivity.
Perhaps we have become too good at optimising our lives. We organise our calendars, our work, our children's activities and our social engagements. We communicate constantly. We are rarely out of touch. Yet there is something curiously lonely about a life in which every human interaction has to be arranged in advance.
The irony is that technology was supposed to make connection easier. In some ways it has. But convenience has also removed the need to make an effort — and effort is sometimes what makes relationships real. A message saying “thinking of you” is lovely. Showing up with samosas is different.
There is, of course, a middle ground. Nobody is suggesting that we return to an era when people could walk into one another's houses without regard for privacy, work or personal boundaries. Some people genuinely need notice. Some homes are not equipped for visitors. Some days are simply bad days. The modern instinct to respect boundaries is not a bad thing.
But perhaps we have taken the principle of asking permission a little too far. Perhaps some relationships need spaces in which nobody has to prepare. Perhaps we need a few homes where the doorbell can still ring unexpectedly. Where the house can be untidy. Where the host can be in old clothes. Where there is no food, but somehow food appears. Where nobody asks how long you will stay. And where “What are you doing here?” is not a complaint but an expression of delight. Because Amna may have been joking when she pretended that Rosie and I had simply dropped by. But her question was serious. Why don't we just show up anymore?
Maybe the answer is that we have become too busy, too careful, too expensive, too scheduled and too accustomed to living behind closed doors. Or maybe we have simply forgotten that friendship does not always need an appointment. Sometimes you just ring the bell. And hope someone opens the door warmly.

title: Streets after sunset
description: When the working day ends  cyclists  runners  photographers and food lovers take to the streets to rediscover Karachi
content:
When the working day ends, cyclists, runners, photographers and food lovers take to the streets to rediscover Karachi
Jahangir Ahmed was already thinking about the tea stop when his bicycle tyre gave way. The group had been riding for nearly two hours and was approaching Burns Road when a piece of glass brought him to a halt.
He pulled up near a closed shop and got off to inspect the damage. It was after 11pm. Around 25 cyclists had set out that evening, and Jahangir wasn't particularly pleased about being the reason some of them now had to stop.
He hadn't even opened his saddlebag when two cyclists came over. Tariq, a retired engineer, turned the bicycle upside down while Ali, a university student, got to work on the tyre. They replaced the tube and had the bicycle ready to go within minutes.
An older man who had been sitting outside a paan shop nearby had apparently been watching them. He walked over with three cups of chai.
“You guys are working hard, here have some tea,” he said.
Jahangir remembers sitting at the curb with the others, drinking tea and talking to a man who was a stranger to them. It wasn't what he had expected from an evening that had begun as an ordinary bicycle ride.
Jahangir works as a senior financial analyst at a corporate office on I.I. Chundrigar Road which is quite busy during the day. His official working hours end at 6pm, although he says he rarely leaves before 7pm. By the time he gets home, there is usually little energy left for anything else.
Yet on some evenings, he changes into his cycling clothes and heads out again, sometimes not returning until after midnight and often revisiting the same street where his office is located. At night the road in the heart of Saddar is quiet and peaceful, with no signs of the chaotic daytime scenes.
The ride that ended with tea outside a paan shop was one of his journeys through Karachi, a city he had spent years travelling through without paying much attention to what lay beyond his usual routes.
Jahangir had not intended to become a night cyclist. He bought his first hybrid bicycle about three years ago, hoping to ride on weekend mornings. But after a working week that could stretch to 60 hours, getting out of bed at 5:30am was easier planned than done. The bicycle remained on his apartment balcony, gathering dust.
A colleague eventually told him about an evening ride organised by a Karachi-based group. Jahangir wasn't convinced. Riding a bicycle on the city's roads after dark seemed an unnecessary risk, particularly with traffic accidents and street crime to worry about. Still, he bought a rear light and joined a group of around 15 riders near Do Darya at 9:30pm.
He has been cycling at night ever since.
For Danish Shakeel, who has been involved in organising group rides since around 2009–10, the choice of timing was initially practical. A handful of friends wanted to cycle regularly, but daytime traffic and the heat made it difficult to enjoy the activity.
Their early rides attracted eight to 10 people, some arriving on old bicycles that had been sitting unused at home. Shakeel says weekend night rides can now attract between 50 and more than 150 cyclists, depending on the weather and route.
The participants are not all fitness enthusiasts. Students ride alongside doctors, lawyers, office workers and older cyclists. Some own expensive road bicycles, while others use rented bikes.
A typical ride begins with a briefing and equipment checks before the group sets off for 15 to 30 kilometres. Experienced riders lead from the front, while others remain at the back to make sure nobody falls behind. There is usually a stop for chai or something to eat.
“Fitness might be what gets people to sign up for their first ride, but the community and the experience are what keep them coming back,” says Shakeel.
For Jahangir, that means leaving home again at around 8:45pm after dinner and time with his family. He may not return until midnight, with another working day waiting the following morning. Yet he finds it easier to make time for those two hours than for an early-morning ride.
Muneeb Butt doesn't always know where he will end up when he leaves home with his camera. Sometimes he has a particular street or neighbourhood in mind. On other nights, he simply starts walking and sees what catches his attention.
Known as The Karachi Guy, Butt has spent years photographing the city's streets, buildings and everyday life. Saddar is among the places he returns to most often, not only for its old architecture but for the people and businesses that give the area its character.
“I think the best thing about street photography is that you can't plan everything,” he says. “You can plan to photograph a location, but you can't plan the moments that happen there.”
For Butt, walking makes a difference. From a car, he says, the journey is mostly about reaching a destination. On foot, there is time to notice shopkeepers closing their businesses, workers making their way home and the smaller details of streets that motorists might overlook.
But he doesn't necessarily find the city quieter at night. Some roads remain crowded well past midnight, while dangerous driving and broken infrastructure are just as much a part of what he encounters as the people and buildings he photographs.
Kabir bin Akmal has found another reason to venture into unfamiliar neighbourhoods: food.
About four years ago, he and his friends grew tired of spending their weekends at the same cafés in Clifton and DHA. A late-night suggestion to try nihari at Burns Road instead led to what has become a regular weekend outing.
Their group of five calls itself The Midnight Shift. Each week, a different member chooses the destination, subject to three rules: no chain restaurants, the place must be open after midnight and it must be at least 10 km from home.
The outings have taken them from bun kababs in Nazimabad to food stalls in Hussainabad, Ranchore Line and Guru Mandir. They also ask delivery riders, rickshaw drivers and security guards where they eat after finishing late shifts.
“Food was just the hook; the real discovery was the city's human geography,” Akmal says.
Where Butt stops to photograph an ordinary street scene, Akmal might pull up a chair at a roadside stall. Neither needs a major attraction or a planned event to make the journey worthwhile. Sometimes, the reason to go out is simply to see what is happening somewhere else.
There are parts of the city Ghazala Moin would love to run through at night. Saddar is one of them. She imagines passing Empress Market and Frere Hall when the shops have closed and the roads are less crowded. But she has never made those streets part of her late-night running routine. For her, the risks outweigh the appeal.
Moin, a digital product strategist, has been running at night for about two years. She had tried waking up at 5:30am to exercise, but it was difficult to sustain alongside her work. Running in the early evening was hardly appealing either, particularly during the hotter months.
One evening, she went out at around 9:30pm for a short run near her home. The weather was pleasant, there was a breeze and she found herself enjoying something that had begun to feel like a chore.
These days, she runs three or four nights a week, usually for 45 minutes to an hour. On her own, she stays within familiar, well-lit residential streets in DHA. The longer routes are reserved for weekends when she can run with others.
“The group acts as a key to the city,” she said. “It gives us the collective confidence to explore routes like Old Clifton, Gizri, or the broader coastal roads that I would never dream of running through alone at 10pm.”
There have been uncomfortable moments. Men on motorcycles have slowed down to stare or pass comments. She no longer wears noise-cancelling headphones while running outside, preferring to remain aware of approaching vehicles and people around her. Her brother receives her live location whenever she goes out.
Her parents were initially alarmed by the idea of their daughter going for a run at 9:30pm. They have become more supportive, although Moin still avoids running alone after 10:30pm.
Cycling groups face some of the same concerns. Shakeel says women join his rides regularly, but attracting more remains difficult. His organisers insist on helmets and lights, with experienced riders positioned at the front and back of the group. Even so, broken streetlights, potholes and unpredictable drivers remain a problem.
For Moin, running is about having some time and space of her own after work. But the streets she chooses, and those she avoids, are a reminder that enjoying the city at night is not quite the same as being free to go anywhere.
Butt doesn't always know where he is going when he leaves home with his camera. Sometimes he has a particular street in mind. On other nights, he walks until something catches his attention. He might stop to take snaps of an old building, a shopkeeper closing his day's business or something happening on a street he has photographed many times before.
Saddar is one place he keeps returning to. The architecture, signboards and shops interest him, but so do the people who occupy those streets long after others have gone home.
“Karachi doesn't really stop after sunset. It just changes,” said Butt, who documents the city through his photography page, The Karachi Guy.
He has seen shopkeepers making their last sales, workers heading home and tea stalls crowded late into the night. Not every street becomes quiet once the shops close. Some remain busy even at 2am.
And he isn't particularly interested in making everything look attractive. Walking with a camera has made him notice the broken roads, dangerous driving and difficulties people face getting around. He believes those things deserve to be photographed too.
“I can love Karachi and still be critical of it. In fact, I think documenting it honestly means doing both,” said Butt.
Akmal's weekend outings began with a rather different complaint. He and his friends were tired of spending Friday nights eating expensive burgers at the same cafés in Clifton and DHA.
One night, someone suggested going to Burns Road for nihari instead. They went, enjoyed themselves and decided to make a habit of visiting places outside their usual neighbourhoods.
Four years later, the five friends still take turns choosing where to eat. They still call their outings The Midnight Shift and they still follow the three rules they set for choosing an eatery. They have since eaten their way through Hussainabad, Nazimabad and Ranchore Line, often following recommendations from delivery riders and people working night shifts.
“Food was just the hook; the real discovery was the city's human geography,” said Akmal.
The outings have introduced him to people and neighbourhoods he previously knew mostly by name.
By the time Jahangir and the other cyclists left Burns Road, it was well past 11pm. There were still several kilometres to cover before he could call it a night. His legs were beginning to ache, but the puncture and the unexpected tea stop had given everyone something to talk about on the way back.
They rode south towards Clifton. Jahangir remembers the wind against his face and the sound of bicycle wheels as the group settled into a steady pace. There was little conversation now. Everyone seemed content to keep pedalling.
He reached his apartment at around 12:15am. His wife and daughter were asleep. He carried his bicycle upstairs, his hands still smelling faintly of chain grease and cardamom from the evening's unexpected stop.
The next morning would bring the familiar journey to I.I. Chundrigar Road, another day of reports, meetings and traffic. None of that had changed.
But for a few hours, Jahangir had been somewhere other than his office or his home, doing something that had no connection to deadlines or work.
And on another Tuesday or Thursday, once the day's responsibilities are out of the way, he would take his bicycle out again.

title: Spurs rescue draw at Manchester United
description: Solanke heads a stoppage time equaliser to earn 10 man Tottenham a 1 1 stalemate
content:
Solanke heads a stoppage-time equaliser to earn 10-man Tottenham a 1-1 stalemate
Ten-man Tottenham salvaged a 1-1 against fellow strugglers Manchester United thanks to Dominic Solanke's last-gasp leveller, while Arsenal got back on track as the champions survived a scare to beat Leeds 2-1 on Saturday.
In a clash dubbed 'El Sackicko' given the scrutiny on both managers, Bryan Mbeumo put United ahead in the 73rd minute at Old Trafford.
Mbeumo punished sloppy Tottenham marking to fire home from an acute angle after Matheus Cunha's pass picked him out in the penalty area.
Tottenham looked doomed when Uruguay midfielder Rodrigo Bentancur was sent off for headbutting United defender Luke Shaw in a brawl five minutes after United's opener.
But Solanke came to Tottenham's rescue in the final moments when he evaded United defender Lisandro Martinez to head in Sandro Tonali's cross.
It was a dramatic finale to a scrappy encounter in keeping with the problems gripping two underachieving teams.
Tottenham sit third bottom of the table and remain winless after losing three of their first six league games.
United are languishing in 12th place with only one league so far this season.
Roberto De Zerbi saved Tottenham from relegation on the final day of last term after taking charge late in the campaign.
But despite spending over £300 million ($429 million) on new signings in the close-season, Tottenham have failed to win any of their opening six games of a league season for just the fourth time in their history.
"I like the situation we were in with the red card. We need this situation. We have not accepted the defeat," De Zerbi said.
"I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character. I'm very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character."
Carrick's side were hoping to build on last season's impressive third-place finish.
However, United's total of six points is their fewest at this stage of a campaign since 1986-87.
"For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time," Carrick said after United were booed off.
"It hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment."
After a shock 3-0 defeat at Brighton before the international break, Arsenal were in danger of a second successive loss when they fell behind at the Emirates Stadium.
James Justin fired Leeds ahead in the 55th minute after Arsenal failed to clear Gabriel Gudmundsson's cross.
But Italy defender Riccardo Calafiori found the cure when he converted Ben White's header from close-range in the 62nd minute.
Arsenal showcased their strength in depth as substitute Bruno Guimaraes drilled the winner from the edge of the area just six minutes after coming on.
Guimaraes' first goal at the Emirates since his close-season move from Newcastle made it five wins from six league matches for the Gunners.
The north London club sit in second place behind crisis-hit Manchester City on goal difference.
City travel to Liverpool on Sunday for their first match since being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules.
"We weren't pleased against Brighton and today was an opportunity to put that right. We certainly reacted in the manner we expected," Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta said.
At Stamford Bridge, Chelsea's blistering start paved the way for a 5-1 rout of Bournemouth as the Blues won for the first time in four league matches.
Jordan Henderson gave Xabi Alonso's team the perfect start when the veteran midfielder curled home after just 68 seconds to claim his first goal for Chelsea.
The Blues struck again in the third minute through Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro made it three soon after half-time.
Evanilson got one back for Bournemouth in the 51st minute as Chelsea's run without a league clean-sheet extended to 22 matches.
Joao Pedro put the result beyond doubt in the 67th minute and Henderson, 36, bagged his second in the 70th minute with a fierce free-kick.
Aston Villa's troubled start continued with a disappointing 2-2 home draw against Brentford.
Ipswich beat winless Fulham 2-1, while 10-man Brighton won 2-0 at Sunderland to cement their hold on third place.

title: Arsenal hit back to beat Leeds
description: The Gunners come from behind to beat Leeds 2 1
content:
The Gunners come from behind to beat Leeds 2-1
Arsenal roared back to beat Leeds 2-1 and pull level with Manchester City at the top of the Premier League on Saturday, hitting the ground running after the three-week international break.
Mikel Arteta's champions struggled to impose themselves against well-organised opponents in the first half but found their mojo after half-time to make it five wins from six games this season.
Defender James Justin gave Leeds a deserved lead early in the second half at the Emirates, silencing the home crowd in the October sunshine.
But Arsenal were level minutes later through Riccardo Calafiori, and substitute Bruno Guimaraes scored what turned out to be the winner after a finely crafted team goal.
The focus returned to the pitch on Saturday after the bombshell announcement that City had been found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules.
But Arsenal, who had a perfect record before their 3-0 defeat by Brighton last month, struggled to break down Daniel Farke's physical team in the first half.
Noni Madueke, overlooked by Thomas Tuchel for England's most recent squad, was handed a rare start on the left of the Gunners' attack in place of the injured Christos Tzolis.
But neither he nor Bukayo Saka on the other flank had much joy against a defence that had conceded just three league goals all season.
Leeds had a couple of half-chances late in the first half.
First, Jayden Bogle and Anton Stach got in each other's way as Stach struck the ball against his teammate, and Bogle was denied from close range by Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya, who was out quickly to smother his shot.
Then Raya got down smartly to keep out a shot from Leeds defender Gabriel Gudmundsson from a tight angle.
Arsenal managed just one shot on target in the whole of the first half but the game opened up after the break, with chances at both ends.
Impressive Leeds midfielder Ao Tanaka forced Raya to tip over before Justin put his side ahead in the 55th minute, finishing sweetly from just inside the box after a Gudmundsson cross following a well-worked move down the left.
Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhaes got a touch with his head but failed to keep the ball out of the net.
But the Gunners were back level just seven minutes later when the unmarked Calafiori finished past England international goalkeeper James Trafford after being set up by Ben White.
Worse was to come for Leeds when Guimaraes finished powerfully after some neat play down the Arsenal left, with Saka, Martin Odegaard and Declan Rice all involved.
The win takes Arsenal to 15 points, behind leaders City on goal difference.
Enzo Maresca's City, with a game in hand, are braced for a hostile reception at Liverpool on Sunday following the announcement of their guilty verdict last week.

title: Childhood under pressure
description: When academic  social and parental expectations leave children little room to simply grow
content:
When academic, social and parental expectations leave children little room to simply grow
Watch a group of four-year-olds at a park. One is digging a hole with a stick. Another is arguing about the rules of a game that exists only in her head. A third is lying on his back, watching a cloud. None of them is in a hurry, and none is being measured.
Now ask their parents a few questions. Is he reading yet? Is she enrolled anywhere good? Has anyone thought about primary school interviews? The relaxed scene at the park suddenly looks like a waiting room with anxiety in the air], and the children's play starts to look like time that could be put to better use.
This is the childhood race. It has no finish line, no referee and no official start, and almost every family is running it. We don't run because we are cruel. We run because we love our children and fear that the world will not be kind to those who fall behind. But somewhere along the way, love and fear got entangled. In the process, we may be taking from children the very things that make them capable, curious and kind.
Childhood has always involved preparation for adult life. Children once learned by working beside their parents, herding animals, helping in shops, minding younger siblings. What is new is the idea that childhood itself is a competition, with rankings, milestones and a scoreboard.
Several forces produced this. Economies became more uncertain, and parents saw that a good job was no longer guaranteed, even to the educated. Families became smaller, so each child carried more of a family's hopes. Schools and universities grew more selective, and admission began to feel like a survival test.
Then technology put every other family's success on our phones. We no longer compare our children to the neighbour's child alone. We compare them to the best child in the country, the best child on the internet, the child whose parents post only their victories.
Ambition is not the problem. Parents who want good things for their children are doing what parents have always done. The problem is the belief that the earlier and harder we push, the better the outcome will be. That belief feels like common sense. The evidence for it is much weaker than we assume.
The pressure begins too early. Toddlers attend “enrichment” classes, while kindergarten is increasingly filled with worksheets, tests and homework instead of play. Children who read at five are praised, while those who read at seven are often seen as falling behind.
Yet evidence suggests that earlier is not always better. Finland, known for strong educational outcomes, starts formal schooling around age seven, while early childhood focuses on play, language and social development. Children are given time to develop before formal academics begin.
This makes sense when you think about how children develop. A young child's brain is not a smaller adult brain waiting to be filled with content. It is building the foundations: attention, self-control, language, the ability to get along with others, the ability to calm down after frustration. These skills develop through play, conversation, movement and relationships.
They cannot be drilled the way multiplication tables can. A child who has learned to wait for a turn, to lose a game without falling apart and to invent a story with a friend has learned things that no worksheet teaches, and that matter enormously in later life.
The costs of the race are easy to miss because they rarely arrive as dramatic events. They arrive as small, steady losses.
Free play is not a waste of time; it is where childhood truly begins. Children learn to make decisions, solve conflicts, take risks and discover themselves. No class, coaching or tuition can replace the freedom of play, where children lead, explore and learn on their own terms.
School-age children need roughly nine to twelve hours of sleep, and teenagers eight to ten. Many get far less because of homework, early mornings, late lessons and screens. Sleep is not a luxury for young people. It is when their brains consolidate learning, regulate emotion and grow. A tired child does not learn better. A tired child is more irritable, less attentive and more anxious.
Teachers, doctors and counsellors in many countries report that anxiety among children and adolescents is rising. There are many causes, but a childhood built around performance is surely one of them. A child who learns early that love, praise and attention follow good results will draw a dangerous conclusion: I am valuable only when I win. That belief is hard to shake, and it follows people into adulthood, where it becomes perfectionism, burnout and fear of failure.
This may be the saddest loss. Small children ask endless questions because they want to know how the world works. Under sustained pressure, the question changes from "What is this?" to "Will this be on the test?" Learning becomes a means to an end, a currency exchanged for marks, and once the marks are gone, so is the reason to learn.
Every race depends on comparison, and comparison has quietly become the main way we talk about children. Whose child got the highest marks? Who was selected for the team? Who is already in the advanced group?
Comparison is poisonous for two reasons. First, it is almost always unfair. Children develop at different speeds, and those differences in the early years often say little about where they will end up. Researchers have noticed something called the relative age effect: in a class, the children born just after the cut-off date are the oldest, and they often look more capable simply because they are a few months more mature. They get picked for teams and groups, receive more encouragement and, over time, actually become better. A small difference in birthdays turns into a large difference in confidence. The "gifted" label often says more about timing than talent.
Second, comparison teaches children to measure themselves against others rather than against their own progress. A child who improves steadily but is never the best will feel like a failure. A child who is always the best learns that avoiding risk keeps them on top, so they stop attempting hard things. Neither lesson serves them well.
Social media has intensified the race. Parents see trophies, certificates and perfect performances, but rarely the tears and struggles behind them. Children compare themselves with carefully curated images of their peers, turning childhood into a never-ending competition with no finish line.
It is worth asking honestly whether the results justify the sacrifice. What does the evidence suggest?
Early academic advantages often fade as other children catch up. What truly matters is not early test scores but self-control, persistence, emotional stability and meaningful relationships. Children thrive through loving care, play and encouragement not pressure. No amount of tuition can replace a home where children feel loved, valued and accepted without conditions.
Any honest discussion of the childhood race must admit that it is not a fair one. Some children start miles ahead. They have books at home, adults with time, quiet places to study, access to good schools and the money to pay for extra help. Others begin with hunger, overcrowded classrooms, exhausted parents or no support at all.
For millions of children, the struggle is not an exhausting race but the lack of a starting line. While some face too much pressure, others lack basic opportunities, encouragement and support. The challenge is not just to slow childhood down, but to ensure every child gets a fair chance to begin.
This is why the answer cannot be simply "let children be children" and leave it there. Play and rest are a right of every child, and so are good nutrition, decent schools, safe places to grow and adults who have the time to pay attention. A society that celebrates gentle, unhurried childhood for the wealthy while ignoring the children who lack the basics has misunderstood the problem. The goal is not less support for children but the right kind of support, available to all of them.
If the race is the wrong model, what should replace it? A good starting point is to ask what children need at each stage rather than what the world will demand of them later.
They need time. Time to play, to be bored, to daydream, to wander from one idea to another without an adult steering them. Boredom is not an emergency. It is the space where imagination starts.
They need connection. A child who feels safe and loved will take on challenges more bravely, because failure is not a threat to their place in the family. Shared meals, bedtime stories, conversations on the way to school and simple attention do more than most parents realise.
They need meaningful challenges. Children do want to grow, and they enjoy difficulty when it is theirs. The best learning happens when a child is a little stretched, supported and free to fail. The difference lies not in how hard the task is but in who chose it and who owns the result.
They need to be praised for the right things. Praise for effort, curiosity and courage builds resilience. Praise only for results teaches children to fear mistakes. "You worked so hard on that" and "I loved how you kept trying" are worth far more than "You're so smart."
They need adults who model balance. Children learn more from what we do than what we say. If we want them to slow down, we must show them how by resting, accepting failure and living beyond work. Our actions teach more than any lecture.
Knowing all this is one thing. Acting on it, in a world that keeps running, is harder. No parent wants to be the one who slows down while everyone else sprints. Still, there are practical steps that families, schools and communities can take.
Start by questioning the schedule. For each activity, ask honestly, "Who is this for?" If the child is enjoying it, keep it. If it exists mainly to fill a gap in a future application or to match the neighbour's child, consider letting it go. Protect at least some empty afternoons. Protect sleep. Ask your child about their day without asking about their marks. Celebrate small things: a good question, a kind act, a difficult problem stuck with. And watch your own reactions. Children read our faces closely, and a flicker of disappointment over a poor result can weigh more than we intend.
Keep early education play-based and pressure-free. Limit homework, value progress over rankings, and make time for art, sport, outdoor play and rest. Most importantly, take signs of stress seriously from sleeplessness and headaches to withdrawal or loss of interest.
We should ask whether our systems reward the right things. Reducing the pressure of one-shot exams and expanding ways to demonstrate learning can ease the race. Investing in early education, playgrounds, libraries and nutrition gives every child a fairer start.
We can change the way we speak. The language of the race, "ahead," "behind," "topper," "average," gives the game its power. If we stop asking children, "What position did you get?" and start asking, "What did you enjoy learning?" We quietly change what counts.
There is a hard question underneath all of this: what do we want for our children? Most of us, asked directly, do not say "a high rank" or "a famous university." We say we want them to be happy, kind, capable and secure. We want them to find work they find meaningful and people they love. We want them to be able to face difficulty without being broken by it.
These qualities cannot be won in a race. They grow through love, play, rest, curiosity and the freedom to make mistakes. A child who is given time may seem “slower” today, but grow into a more resilient, creative and confident adult.
Childhood is not a rehearsal for real life. It is real life, and the only childhood a person gets. Its purpose is not merely to prepare children for the future but to let them live fully in the present, to climb trees, to ask endless questions, to be bored, to be silly and to feel loved without earning it.
The next time you see a child digging a hole with a stick, or lying on the grass watching the clouds, resist the urge to hurry them along. They are not wasting time. They are doing exactly what they were meant to do. And perhaps the bravest thing we can do, in a world that rewards speed, is to trust them to run at their own pace, or not to run at all.

title: Ronaldo provisionally suspended by Portugal
description: The 41 year old forward faces a possible ban of up to six months after walkout
content:
The 41-year-old forward faces a possible ban of up to six months after walkout
Cristiano Ronaldo has been provisionally suspended after the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) announced on Saturday that it had opened disciplinary proceedings against the 41-year-old over his decision to walk out on the national team.
Ronaldo apologised to supporters earlier this week while criticising Portugal coach Jorge Jesus and said he would accept any punishment that was imposed.
"Disciplinary proceedings have been initiated against Cristiano Ronaldo," said the FPF in a statement, classifying the case as "urgent" and confirming Ronaldo is currently suspended pending a decision on the final punishment.
Ronaldo left Portugal's Nations League squad after first being made to warm up as a substitute against Norway on September 27 and not brought on, and then finding out he would not start against Denmark in the match on October 1.
The former Real Madrid and Manchester United attacker is the all-time top goalscorer and record appearance-maker in men's international football.
According to Portuguese media, under the federation's regulations, a player who misses a training session, a match, or a national team activity faces a suspension ranging from one to six months.
On Tuesday, Ronaldo accused Portugal coach Jesus of breaking his word about giving him game time in Nations League matches but said he was not retiring from international duty and would be available to play once any potential punishment was served.
"I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team," Ronaldo said, while accepting his actions must be "punished" by the federation.
Ronaldo said Jesus had gone back on his word about bringing him on against Norway, and then in a press conference before the Denmark match had not said a series of points they had agreed upon during a conversation beforehand.
One of Ronaldo's pre-approved talking points was that Jesus had "made a mistake in asking someone of the stature of Pele or Maradona to warm up and then not sending him on in the match."
Jesus chose not to respond to Ronaldo's statement when asked about it.
"I read the statement, and now, like I do every day, I'm going to the federation headquarters to work, to think about the Portuguese national team," said the 72-year-old coach.
Jesus said last Sunday he would select Ronaldo for international duty if the forward was playing for his club and was interested in being called up.
Portugal won all four of their Nations League matches and qualified for the quarter-finals with two games to spare.
Portugal host Denmark on November 14 and then travel to face Wales on November 17 in their final two Nations League Group A4 matches.
Ronaldo returned to club action on Friday with Saudi Arabian side Al-Nassr and scored as they won 3-0 against Diriyah in a Saudi Pro League match. It was the striker's 980th career goal.

title: Inter Milan dominate Parma to go top of Serie A
description: Goals from Sucic  Calhanoglu and Thuram seal a 3 0 win
content:
Goals from Sucic, Calhanoglu and Thuram seal a 3-0 win
Inter Milan surged to the top of Serie A on Saturday thanks to three goals in the first half an hour to outclass Parma 3-0 at the San Siro.
The three-week international break has not diminished the momentum of the reigning Italian champions.
Even without captain Lautaro Martinez, who was rested until the hour mark after his return from Argentina and Lionel Messi's international farewell match, the titleholders were never threatened.
Capitalising on a poor clearance by Parma's goalkeeper, Petar Sucic opened the scoring in the 13th minute.
Five minutes later, Hakan Calhanoglu doubled the lead from the penalty spot.
Overlooked for the France squad for the Nations League games, Marcus Thuram reminded Zinedine Zidane of his quality by making it 3-0 after 31 minutes with his third goal of the campaign.
"Of course I would have liked to have been selected, but you have to respect this decision," Thuram said.
"I worked really hard with the coaches and players who were there during the international break. The important thing was to play well in the first match back," he added.
Inter have 16 points from six games and move three points ahead of Roma and Lazio, who both play on Sunday, against Como and newly-promoted Monza respectively.
New Parma coach Alberto Gilardino got off to a losing start as his team never got into the game and they sit 17th with four points.
Napoli eased past newly promoted Frosinone 3-0 in Saturday's late game at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona as under-pressure coach Massimiliano Allegri collected just his third league win of the season.
The opener came when former Manchester United forward Rasmus Hojlund was fouled as he surged towards goal and Kevin De Bruyne converted the penalty.
Dutch forward Noa Lang slotted in the second on 29 minutes after Hojlund's effort was saved and De Bruyne added his second to complete the job in second-half stoppage time.
Allegri brought on Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay in the second period for his first appearance since undergoing heart surgery, in a welcome return for the player who has been Napoli's powerhouse in the last two seasons.
Napoli move up to eighth, a point behind AC Milan who visit Sassuolo on Sunday.
Fiorentina meanwhile returned to the relegation places after a 2–1 defeat to Genoa, who move out of the drop zone thanks to their first win of the season.

title: Spain beat USA in World Cup warm up
description: Spanish women return to action with 2 0 friendly win over USA
content:
Spanish women return to action with 2-0 friendly win over USA
Early goals from Patri Guijarro and Eva Navarro lifted women's World Cup champions Spain to a 2-0 friendly victory over the United States on Saturday with both teams looking toward next year's World Cup.
Adriana Nanclares saved a second-half penalty for Spain, who were back in action for the first time since they secured their place in next year's World Cup in Brazil with a 6-1 rout of Iceland in June.
Guijarro got things going early for the visitors, rifling a long-range blast past US goalkeeper Claudia Dickey in the third minute.
Navarro doubled the lead in the 14th minute when Salma Paralluelo's cross found her unmarked and she fired into the top right corner of the net.
The United States put together multiple quality chances in the second half, but a goal by Sophia Wilson was disallowed for offside.
A VAR ruling saw the Americans awarded a penalty after Wilson was brought down in the box in the 67th minute.
The spot kick was taken by 19-year-old midfielder Lily Yohannes, whose shot low and left was saved by a diving Adriana Nanclares.
Spain ended the match with 10 player after Real Madrid's Athenea del Castillo was sent off for pulling Michelle Cooper's hair in the 90th minute -- just a couple of minutes after she came into the game.
The United States were held without a goal for the second time in 2026 as they suffered their third defeat in 11 matches this year.
They fell to Japan at home in April and lost at Brazil in June -- winning rematches with each team just days after those setbacks.
They will have a chance to bounce back against Spain on Tuesday when they meet again at Subaru Park, home of Major League Soccer's Philadelphia Union.

title: Navi Pillay   s Nobel Peace Prize is a rebuke to Trump
description: The award sends a message at a time when the international order is approaching a dangerous breaking point
content:
The award sends a message at a time when the international order is approaching a dangerous breaking point
The Norwegian Nobel Committee has delivered one of the most welcome surprises in recent years. At a time when names such as Donald Trump and Mark Carney were circulating as possible recipients of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, the committee chose Navanethem “Navi”Pillay, the South African jurist whose life has been devoted to human rights, international justice and the rule of law. It is difficult to imagine a more appropriate choice for a world increasingly governed by military power, political intimidation and contempt for international institutions.
The decision is particularly significant because of what happened last year. The 2025 prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, whose struggle against authoritarianism was accompanied by troubling support for American intervention in her country. Her subsequent embrace of Trump, including presenting him with her Nobel medal, exposed the contradictions of celebrating democracy while welcoming coercive foreign power. This year, the committee has chosen someone representing a fundamentally different understanding of peace. For Pillay, justice cannot be delivered through the generosity of powerful leaders or the destruction of governments they dislike. It must rest on principles that apply equally to everyone.
Pillay's selection is more than recognition of an extraordinary career. It is a political and moral statement at a moment when the international order is approaching a dangerous breaking point. Wars continue across continents, civilians are killed with alarming impunity, and institutions established to prevent atrocities increasingly struggle to restrain those responsible. The United Nations Security Council remains paralyzed by geopolitical rivalries, while international courts face intimidation and political retaliation for attempting to enforce the law. The world has not abandoned international justice formally. It has simply become increasingly comfortable ignoring it.
This is precisely why Pillay matters. Born into a family of Indian-Tamil origin in apartheid South Africa, she experienced institutionalized discrimination long before becoming one of the world's most respected human rights jurists. Her legal career began in a society where racial hierarchy was protected by legislation and enforced through state violence. She defended political prisoners and challenged apartheid's discriminatory practices, demonstrating that law could become an instrument of liberation even when governments used it to institutionalize oppression.
Her subsequent international career carried that conviction beyond South Africa. As a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, later as a judge at the International Criminal Court, and subsequently as United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Pillay helped establish that sovereignty cannot provide unlimited protection to those responsible for atrocities. Her work challenged the convenient assumption that crimes committed by governments are somehow less reprehensible than crimes committed by their enemies. International justice, in her understanding, is meaningless unless it reaches those who exercise power.
That commitment was evident in her interventions concerning Sri Lanka. During the final stages of the country's civil war and its aftermath, when allegations of grave abuses against Tamil civilians were frequently dismissed in the name of defeating terrorism, Pillay demanded accountability. She challenged the Sri Lankan government's refusal to confront credible allegations of violations and insisted that military victory could never erase responsibility for civilian suffering. Her position was not about defending one ethnic community against another. It was about refusing to allow national security to become an excuse for impunity.
Her stance on Palestine has been even more consequential. As chair of the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Pillay confronted one of the most politically sensitive human rights crises of our time. In September 2025, the commission concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, a finding rejected by the Israeli government. Whatever the political pressure, Pillay refused to accept that Palestinian lives should receive less legal protection than those of other populations. She also insisted on accountability for crimes committed by Hamas. This consistency is what gives international law its legitimacy.
The contrast with Trump could hardly be sharper. Trump's worldview places national power, transactional bargaining and personal loyalty above international norms. His administration has treated multilateral institutions with hostility, undermined mechanisms of accountability and repeatedly demonstrated that international law matters only when it serves American interests. His approach to peace is essentially a bargain among powerful actors, where weaker societies are expected to accept whatever arrangements emerge. Pillay represents the opposite proposition: peace without justice is merely the temporary management of inequality and violence.
The significance of Pillay's South African identity should not be underestimated either. Trump has pursued an extraordinary confrontation with South Africa, particularly over its support for Palestinian rights and its legal challenge against Israel. His administration has simultaneously promoted claims of persecution against white Afrikaners, granting them preferential treatment under American refugee policies while restricting opportunities for many other vulnerable populations. The irony is unmistakable. A woman whose family suffered under white minority rule now receives the world's most prestigious peace award while Washington presents descendants of that historically privileged minority as deserving exceptional humanitarian concern.
Pillay's Indian Tamil heritage adds another dimension. Her life illustrates how struggles against racial discrimination, colonial domination and political exclusion can produce a universal commitment to justice. She has never confined her concern to people sharing her ancestry, religion or nationality. This distinguishes her from the increasingly aggressive nationalism that dominates politics in India, the United States and elsewhere. Her moral authority comes precisely from rejecting the proposition that human rights belong primarily to one's own community.
Nor does her commitment resemble the selective internationalism increasingly promoted by leaders such as Carney. Canada's prime minister speaks eloquently about international rules and the dangers of a world dominated by powerful states. Yet Western governments continue to demonstrate considerable flexibility when those rules threaten strategic allies. Defending sovereignty in Ukraine and Greenland while not caring about it in Venezuela and Iran and hesitating over accountability in Palestine cannot constitute a credible universal legal order. Pillay's career exposes the weakness of such distinctions. International law either protects everyone or eventually protects nobody.
The urgency of this message is supported by disturbing evidence. Violence deliberately targeting civilians has reached its highest level in more than three decades. From Gaza and Sudan to Ukraine and Myanmar, atrocities have become increasingly visible while meaningful accountability remains painfully elusive. Allegations of genocide are multiplying, even as the legal determination of such crimes remains contested.
Of course, awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize will not end these wars or restore the authority of weakened international institutions. But prizes are not entirely symbolic when they challenge the prevailing political climate. At a time when authoritarian populists celebrate strength without restraint and powerful democracies practice selective morality, recognizing a lifelong defender of universal justice carries considerable significance. The Nobel Committee has reminded the world that peace is not simply the absence of fighting, nor is it a trophy for leaders claiming diplomatic victories. It requires accountability, human dignity and limits on power.
Navi Pillay has spent her life defending those principles, frequently when doing so was unpopular or politically inconvenient. Her Nobel Prize offers a rare moment of encouragement in an otherwise bleak international landscape. More importantly, it sends a message that Trump and other powerful leaders would prefer not to hear: the future of peace cannot be entrusted to those who believe themselves above the law.
Ashok Swain is a professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University, Sweden.

title: PSG ease to Ligue 1 win before Manchester City test
description: Enrique   s side beat Le Mans 3 1 to secure a third consecutive win
content:
Enrique’s side beat Le Mans 3-1 to secure a third consecutive win
Paris Saint-Germain were comfortable 3-1 winners against Le Mans on Saturday before they look ahead to a tougher test away to Manchester City in the Champions League next week.
PSG's third win in a row after a slow start to the season came despite Luis Enrique starting several first-choice players on the bench.
PSG went ahead through a first-half spot kick from centre-back Lucas Beraldo but Louis Mafouta brought Le Mans level at the Parc des Princes nine minutes after half-time.
Khvicha Kvaratskhelia spent the first half sitting in his tracksuit but he put PSG ahead on 61 minutes, just two minutes after he was brought on, before Maghnes Akliouche wrapped up the win seven minutes later.
PSG move up to fifth before the back-to-back European champions travel to City, who are reeling after being found guilty of dozens of Premier League spending infractions, on Wednesday.
Monaco remain unbeaten but missed a chance to open up a larger lead at the top as Toulouse came from 2-0 down to force a 2-2 draw in the Principality.
Edan Diop put Monaco ahead and Matthis Abline added a second before half-time, but Flavio Nazinho fouled Toulouse's US international defender Mark McKenzie at a corner and Casper Tengstedt kept his cool to slot in the penalty.
Tengstedt turned provider for Toulouse's equaliser as his cross was steered in by Sion Oppong in the 59th minute.
Monaco lead Lille by a single point after the northern side beat Le Havre 1-0 at home thanks to a goal after five minutes from Dilane Bakwa, who is on loan from Premier League side Nottingham Forest.
Lorient inflicted a 1-0 defeat on Paris FC, coached by former Chelsea boss Liam Rosenior, but the capital's second club have the consolation of sitting above PSG in fourth.

title: Gordon on target as Barcelona beat Getafe
description: The Catalans ease past Getafe 3 0 to move five points clear at the top of La Liga
content:
The Catalans ease past Getafe 3-0 to move five points clear at the top of La Liga
Anthony Gordon scored his first goal for Barcelona as the Spanish champions extended their perfect start in La Liga with a 3-0 win over Getafe on Saturday.
England international Gordon opened the scoring in the second minute and Gabriel Jesus added another after half an hour for the league leaders, who have won every match they have played this season.
French defender Jules Kounde tucked home the third from Lamine Yamal's cross to cap Barca's solid win against Jose Bordalas's side at Camp Nou.
Barca moved five points clear of second-placed Atletico Madrid, who won 2-1 at Alaves earlier, and lead Real Madrid, fourth, by nine points before Los Blancos host Villarreal later on.
Barca were without their top scorer Raphinha, who sustained a hamstring problem during the international break with Brazil.
Flick replaced him with former Arsenal striker and Selecao compatriot Jesus and his side came roaring out of the blocks.
Gordon, who has impressed since joining this summer, grabbed his first Barca goal with a low deflected effort after bundling his way past three players.
The winger was Barca's brightest spark in the first half, continuing his fine goalscoring form for England in the recent Nations League matches.
Barca defender Eric Garcia forced a save from Getafe goalkeeper David Soria with a drive from distance as Flick's side controlled the game.
Getafe defender Zaid Romero gave the ball away in his own box for Barca's second, passing it straight to Jesus, who stroked into the bottom corner.
Soria denied Olmo before Yamal teed up Kounde for the third.
The defender, making a record 194th appearance for Barca for a French player, overtaking Eric Abidal, was on hand to turn home from close range from teenage star Yamal's cross.
Barca, who also won their Champions League opener, have nine victories from nine matches across all competitions.
