title: Taliban   s double game
description: Terrorist sanctuaries in Afghanistan and stalled diplomacy are reshaping Pakistan   s security calculus
content:
Terrorist sanctuaries in Afghanistan and stalled diplomacy are reshaping Pakistan’s security calculus
Pakistan is once again being pulled into a deadly vortex of terrorism. Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, the country’s two most volatile provinces, are bearing the brunt, with attacks striking with alarming frequency and lethality.
The violence, however, has two dimensions. In K-P, it is driven largely by religious obscurantism; in Balochistan, it is rooted in secular separatism. Different ideologies, different agendas — but increasingly converging on the same battlefield.
An increasingly unholy alliance has taken shape between the two: terrorists separated by ideology but united by a common enemy. And, according to Pakistani officials, both have found safe havens across the porous frontier, under the watch of — and in connivance with — the de facto Taliban rulers in Kabul.
Long before the Taliban recaptured power, Afghanistan had served as a staging ground for terrorist attacks inside Pakistan. Islamabad accused the then Afghan intelligence agency, NDS, of colluding with India’s RAW to facilitate TTP’s terror campaign.
The Taliban’s return was thus seen in Islamabad as a potential security reset, with hopes that the new regime would dismantle terrorist networks and address Pakistan’s long-standing concerns.
With those expectations, Islamabad invested heavily in keeping the Taliban regime afloat and engaged. It lobbied for international economic support, facilitated humanitarian assistance and kept political and diplomatic channels open — from religious scholars and tribal elders to ministers, intelligence officials and special representatives. Intelligence and evidence on terrorist camps on Afghan soil were shared with the Taliban, urging action.
The Taliban’s response, however, remained ambiguous, shifting between offers to mediate between Pakistan and TTP and outright denials that the group operated from Afghan soil.
“Their denial is a way to dodge responsibility,” says Hassan Khan, a senior commentator on Afghanistan. “Acknowledging TTP’s presence on Afghan soil would force the Taliban to act against a group deeply entrenched in their own ranks, particularly among second- and third-tier commanders,” he adds. “Fearing that such action could turn their own fighters against them, they deny TTP’s presence altogether.”
Publicly, the Taliban may deny TTP’s presence. But in private talks with Pakistan — both bilateral and multilateral, involving mediators such as Qatar, Türkiye and China — they have acknowledged the group’s presence and expressed willingness to act, only to keep delaying. The repeated delays have deepened Islamabad’s trust deficit.
The Taliban’s equivocation boils down to two possibilities: inability or unwillingness to dismantle the militant ecosystem thriving on Afghan soil. Pakistani officials, citing intelligence and evidence, argue it is the latter.
“If the Taliban supreme leader issues a single fatwa (religious decree), orders the TTP to leave or stop attacking Pakistan, and directs Afghan intelligence to cut off its support, the problem can be brought to an end,” says security analyst Maj Gen (retd) Raza Muhammad, suggesting the Taliban leadership lacks the will to act against the anti-Pakistan group.
Terrorism in Pakistan has surged since the Taliban’s return to power. Pakistan ranked ninth on the Global Terrorism Index in 2021, the year Kabul fell. It climbed to seventh in 2022, fourth in 2023, second in 2024 and first in 2025. The human toll continued to mount. A Pakistani tally attributes 1,327 deaths and 2,484 injuries so far in 2026 to terrorism emanating from Afghan soil.
“Pakistan has unequivocal, undeniable evidence, including videos, audio recordings and media reports, that Afghanistan is serving as a sanctuary for terrorists, with India helping finance groups responsible for deadly attacks inside Pakistan,” says Gen Raza.
But more troubling than the grim figures is the alleged presence of Afghan nationals in terrorist ranks involved in attacks inside Pakistan. Intelligence suggests Afghans make up around 70% of infiltrating fighters. More than 260 Afghan nationals killed in Pakistan in 2026 have reportedly been identified through names, addresses and family details.
These figures, however, are only part of the picture. They don’t include the terrorists whose identities remain unverified, bodies that could not be conclusively identified, and Afghan nationals still embedded in active terrorist formations.
Some cases cited by Pakistani officials are particularly sensitive. In January 2025, Badruddin Yousaf, son of Maulvi Ghulam Muhammad Muhammadi, deputy governor of the Afghan province of Badghis, was killed in a security operation in Dera Ismail Khan’s Kulachi area and later buried in Badghis.
In February 2026, Ahmad, alias Qari Abdullah or Abuzar, a former Afghan Taliban special forces member, carried out a suicide attack on a security checkpoint in Bajaur. In May, Baitullah and Jalaluddin, identified as former Taliban members, took part in twin suicide bombings at a security forces camp in the same district. This shows recruitment into terrorist tashkeels (formations) is not confined to ordinary Afghan citizens but can extend into families connected to the Taliban regime.
“It goes beyond turning a blind eye [to TTP]. The Taliban are actively backing TTP with funding and ammunition, while recruitment drives targeting Afghan nationals continue in several provinces. Recruits are then sent across the border, adding to the threat facing Pakistan’s security forces,” says Khurram Abbas, a strategic analyst of international security.
This raises a question: why is the Taliban regime willing to jeopardise its key relationship with Pakistan to protect a terrorist group? Analysts point to several reasons.
“The Afghan Taliban and TTP share deep ideological ties and a history of fighting alongside each other — bonds that make it difficult for the Taliban to turn against their former comrades and help explain their continued support for TTP,” says Mansoor Ali Khan, a former ambassador to Afghanistan.
Hassan, meanwhile, believes that TTP is deeply embedded within the Taliban’s ranks, particularly among second- and third-tier commanders who feel indebted to the group for its support during the 20-year war against US-led forces.
“The two share ideological roots, religious beliefs and a common view of ‘jihad’. TTP also recognises Taliban supreme leader Mullah Haibatullah Akhundzada as its Ameer,” he says.
“Beyond tribal ties, their social and religious networks are closely intertwined. Once seen as two sides of the same coin, the groups have become so intermeshed that distinguishing their fighters can be increasingly difficult.”
Beyond ideological affinity and battlefield camaraderie, some analysts argue the Taliban fear that moving against TTP could alienate their own ranks, trigger internal dissent and ultimately threaten their grip on power in Kabul.
“The Taliban face a strategic dilemma: confronting TTP could provoke a backlash from a group that has grown into a formidable force. Some within the Taliban leadership may fear that curbing TTP’s anti-Pakistan activities could trigger a blowback they would struggle to contain,” says security analyst Manzar Zaidi.
Abbas adds that the Taliban may be wary of pushing TTP too hard, fearing that the group could align itself with Islamic State Khorasan Province (IS-KP), a rival extremist group hostile to the Afghan Taliban.
However, TTP is not the only threat. Afghanistan has become a hub for transnational militant groups from across the region, including the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), IS-KP, East Turkistan Islamic Movement (ETIM), Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan (IMU) and al Qaeda, which operate in a permissive environment under Taliban rule.
Gen Raza believes the Taliban regime relies on these groups to sustain its grip on power. “Afghanistan has become a sanctuary not just for TTP, but also for BLA, BRA, Majeed Brigade and other terrorist groups. These outfits serve as the Taliban’s muscle, helping it stay in power and extend its reach,” he says.
These are not just Pakistan’s claims or disputed intelligence figures. UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team reports — the 35th, 36th, 37th and 38th — have also painted a similar concerning picture of a deepening terrorist threat from Afghanistan, with TTP gaining operational freedom and al Qaeda and IS-KP maintaining a presence.
One assessment identified more than 20 groups and up to 13,000 foreign fighters on Afghan soil, including around 6,000 TTP members, 2,000-3,000 IS-KP fighters and 400-1,500 al Qaeda members. The warning, then, is not coming from Islamabad alone.
“TTP’s presence in Afghanistan is now a universally acknowledged fact. UN, US, Chinese and regional assessments have raised similar concerns,” says Hassan.
“The latest UN monitoring report also points to coordination between TTP, al Qaeda and the Afghan Taliban, with al Qaeda providing training, logistics and funding, while the Taliban offer an umbrella of protection,” he adds. “It further reports assistance in facilitating TTP infiltration into Pakistan. The picture is clear: a terrorist network with sanctuary, support and the operational capacity to strike across the border.”
The foreign ministry of Russia, the only country that has recognised the Taliban government, also estimated in February 2026 that between 20,000 and 23,000 terrorists were operating inside Afghanistan, more than half of them foreign nationals.
The significance of these assessments for Islamabad is that they challenge the Taliban’s repeated denials that Afghan territory is being used as a base for terrorism.
UK Special Envoy for Afghanistan Richard Lindsay warned in June 2026 that TTP benefited from training camps, weapons, financing and safe havens inside Afghanistan. EU Special Envoy for Afghanistan Gilles Bertrand also referred to terrorist safe havens, training camps, weapons networks and financing structures inside Afghanistan.
Despite the Taliban’s denials, Pakistan continued to pursue diplomacy, expecting the de facto rulers in Kabul to address its concerns. From an eight-member Ulema delegation to Kabul in July 2022 to ministerial missions, tribal jirgas, clerics’ delegations and security-level talks, Islamabad repeatedly urged the regime to rein in TTP.
By the end of 2025, Pakistan says it had held multiple high-level visits and meetings, alongside 225 border flag meetings, 836 protest notes and 13 formal demarches. It also shared information on more than five dozen alleged TTP and BLA camps, staging areas and logistical facilities inside Afghanistan. The demands were simple and consistent: dismantle the TTP infrastructure, stop cross-border infiltration and provide verifiable proof of action.
“Pakistan has exhausted diplomatic avenues — from domestic engagement to bilateral, trilateral and multilateral forums. Yet, the Afghan Taliban have refused to provide verifiable ground-level cooperation against TTP, leaving diplomacy struggling to deliver results,” says Abbas.
After years of diplomacy and failed talks in Doha, Istanbul and Urumqi, Pakistan resorted to “limited surgical strikes” against terrorist infrastructure in Afghanistan, taking precautions to minimise civilian harm. Analysts say Pakistan’s response was calibrated and legitimate.
“When a country is attacked and suffers casualties, it has the right to respond. Pakistan’s surgical strikes are defensive, not offensive. We did not initiate the strikes. We want peace, which is why our strikes are limited. But our response is legitimate,” says Gen Raza.
The Afghan Taliban condemned the strikes as “violation of sovereignty and international law,” and escalated by targeting Pakistani border posts, launching drones and hurling threats.
“Recent threats by Afghan Taliban leaders to attack Pakistan reinforce the concern that TTP is being used as strategic leverage. By keeping TTP in its orbit, Kabul believes it can exert pressure on Pakistan’s security, foreign and Afghanistan policies,” says Abbas.
The Taliban’s noncommittal attitude has eroded their credibility. They reneged on their previous commitments under the 2020 Doha Agreement that they would not allow Afghan soil to be used by terrorist groups. Instead, the regime released thousands of TTP prisoners who have since returned to the battlefield.
The 2022 killing of al Qaeda chief Ayman al Zawahiri in a Kabul safe house further undermined Taliban assurances. During subsequent Qatar- and Türkiye-mediated talks, Islamabad sought written guarantees and independent verification of action against TTP. Kabul’s de facto rulers resisted, offering only verbal assurances instead.
“If they failed to honour the Doha Agreement, why should Pakistan trust their verbal assurances? TTP operates from Afghan soil, recruits locally and collects donations in villages and cities in the name of ‘jihad’ against Pakistan,” says Hassan.
What, then, is the way out if the Taliban refuse to change course? Options being debated range from renewed diplomatic pressure to backing anti-Taliban resistance or a wider political upheaval in Kabul. Hassan sees support for resistance forces as a last resort, but Ambassador Mansoor says Pakistan has no consensus for involvement in Afghanistan’s internal conflict or externally driven regime change.
Gen Raza agrees with Mansoor. “I don’t think regime change is a wise option. The US experiences in Iraq, Libya, Syria and elsewhere show how risky such interventions can be,” he says. “No matter how powerful a country may be, attempting to change another regime can have serious and unpredictable consequences.”
The question now is whether diplomacy can still deliver an enforceable security arrangement. Ambassador Mansoor remains optimistic despite waning trust between the two neighbours and their peoples. “Diplomacy has not failed. Pakistan still has considerable leverage to put relations back on track,” he says.
Analysts warn that the Afghan Taliban could use closer ties with India as leverage against Pakistan, potentially gaining access to drones and surveillance technology. They also see a possible two-front pressure strategy, with Delhi holding the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance and Afghanistan adding to Pakistan’s security and water-related concerns.
Ambassador Mansoor doubts Delhi can pull Kabul away from Islamabad. “Pakistan-Afghanistan ties are organic, while Kabul’s relationship with India is situational. India has long sought to exploit Afghan territory against Pakistan. If we deny it that space, its ability to undermine Pakistan will diminish,” he adds. “Pakistan, moreover, has far greater leverage in Afghanistan than India or any other country.”
Analysts say Pakistan’s security concerns are genuine, while the Taliban’s equivocation has deepened Islamabad’s frustration. They stress that Islamabad’s dispute is with the Taliban leadership, not the Afghan people, who have suffered from decades of war and economic hardship. Pakistan has historically offered Afghans refuge, humanitarian aid, healthcare, education and access to trade.
That said, Islamabad no longer appears willing to rely on verbal assurances alone. Its surgical strikes signal a strategic shift towards deterrence through limited force. “Pakistan is essentially pursuing a maximum-pressure campaign — what international relations theory calls deterrence by punishment. And I think it is working very well,” says Abbas.
Ambassador Mansoor, however, argues that kinetic force alone cannot resolve the conflict. “The better option, in my opinion, is dialogue and diplomacy,” he says, proposing a regional economic integration process linking Pakistan, Afghanistan and Central Asia rather than mediation focused solely on bilateral disputes.
Abbas argues that security must come before economic integration, warning that Pakistan cannot afford to keep bleeding while waiting for regional cooperation to take shape. “The starting point must be the handover of TTP leaders living in Kabul. A joint oversight committee involving the Afghan Taliban, Pakistan, China and other regional countries should then independently verify Kabul’s claims of action against TTP.”
Pakistan’s challenge is to turn kinetic action into a verifiable security arrangement without becoming entangled in Afghanistan’s internal conflicts. Surgical strikes may raise the cost of Taliban inaction, but deterrence alone cannot dismantle the terrorist ecosystem or restore trust. Nor can economic integration succeed while cross-border terrorism remains unresolved.
The way forward lies in combining sustained diplomatic engagement with clear benchmarks: dismantling terrorist safe havens, disrupting recruitment and financing, and preventing infiltration. And, according to experts, a joint regional oversight mechanism could help verify compliance.
Ultimately, they say, Kabul must act as a responsible state rather than a militia, abandon equivocation, stop treating terrorist groups as strategic assets, and demonstrate through concrete action, not verbal assurances, that it will no longer allow Afghan territory to be used to threaten Afghanistan’s neighbours. Otherwise, the regime risks prolonged international isolation, further complicating its quest for international recognition.

title: Saudi led coalition says new attack at Riyadh airport causes fire  day after strike kills 13
description: Trump said Washington was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict
content:
Saturday's strike killed 12, wounded over 300; Riyadh airport remains closed
The death toll from Saturday's Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh rose to 13 after an Indian national succumbed to his injuries on Sunday, the Indian Embassy said.
In a statement on Facebook, the embassy said an Indian citizen injured in the Oct. 10 attack "has unfortunately lost his life today."
The embassy expressed condolences to the victim's family and said it was in contact with them.
It also pledged full support to ensure the prompt repatriation of his remains to India.
Earlier, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said an "unidentified projectile" had targeted Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, causing a fire, hours after the Iran-backed Houthis warned airlines and travellers to stay away from Saudi airports.
The coalition also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. No further details were immediately available.
The airport remains closed after an attack there on Saturday killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others, the deadliest such strike on the kingdom in over a decade, amid an escalation of fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces.
Despite the airport's temporary closure, the Saudi Energy Ministry said a long-planned international energy conference was still going ahead in Riyadh on Sunday.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Sunday's projectile had targeted Terminal 4 of the airport, without elaborating.
Earlier, the Houthis had said in a statement on X:
"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina."
"We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said later on Sunday that further Saudi military action in Yemen would trigger a stronger response, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the ministry said in statements carried by Houthi-run Al Masirah television.
President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.
Earlier, Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes would be suspended and shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday for all students, teachers and administrative staff.
In Saturday's attack, the third on Riyadh's airport in a week, the 12 dead included 4 Saudis, 2 Bangladeshis and nationals of the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, Saudi authorities said.
Four people were killed in the two previous attacks on the airport earlier in the week. One of the attacks also caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks on the airport, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life".

Explosion, people on ground, ambulances rushing
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, but it has made only slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.

The US embassy ⁠in Riyadh said ​it "strongly recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas."
Earlier Houthi attacks had prompted a number of ​carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences. Organisers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned.

Saturday's attack has forced the temporary closure of King Khalid International Airport, but the Saudi energy ministry said a long-planned international energy conference was still going ahead in Riyadh on Sunday.
The five-day WPC Energy Congress is taking place at a convention centre some 10 km (6 miles) from the airport. State TV said more than 70 ministers, 300 company executives and representatives of over 25 international energy organisations have confirmed their attendance.
It was not immediately clear whether the participants would attend in person or virtually.
A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to go ahead on Sunday, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors, according to a media advisory. No further details were immediately available.
Separately, Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes would be suspended and shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday for all students, teachers and administrative staff.
Yemen's govt-aligned forces say they destroyed 5 Houthi military vehicles in Taiz
Yemen’s government-aligned forces said they destroyed five armoured military vehicles belonging to the Houthi group while repelling an attempted advance toward Dhubab Airport in Yemen's western Taiz province.
In a late Saturday statement released on US social media platform Facebook, the Giants Brigades said their forces "destroyed five Houthi armoured vehicles, killing those aboard."
The operation took place as the Houthis made a "desperate attempt” to advance toward Dhubab Airport on the western coast, the statement noted.
The brigades also released a video clip purportedly documenting the moment the vehicles were targeted, showing flames rising from them.
The Houthis did not immediately comment on the statement.
Malaysian premier denounces Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on Sunday "unequivocally denounced" the Yemeni Houthi group's attack targeting the main airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, which claimed at least 12 lives and injured more than 300 others.
"There can be no justification for attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure," he said on US social media company X.

Anwar said that putting innocent lives at risk "can only deepen the suffering already wrought by this conflict and carry it into places that should remain beyond its reach."
He also said Malaysia stands in solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its people "at this perilous hour," and that Kuala Lumpur remains "steadfast in our hope that diplomacy and reason will prevail before the conflict widens still further."
New Zealand's Foreign Minister Winston Peters also condemned the recent attacks on the airport and across Saudi Arabia, while expressing solidarity with Saudi Arabians and the Saudi Arabian government.

title: Trump  Zelensky clash diesel deal
description: Trump  Zelensky clash diesel deal
content:
US president says time for Ukraine to get new president
US President Donald Trump has said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" as he responded to Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of the US diesel deal with Russia.
The Ukrainian president warned a new deal to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against his nation, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday that Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries.
"He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".
Global fuel supplies, including diesel, have been severely limited by the war against Iran launched by the US and Israel, which led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil products usually flows.
Russia - a major producer - and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes on each other's energy infrastructure and transport facilities, further straining energy markets.
"We said, 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries', because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump continued.
"He could have made many deals and for some reason, he never does."
Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev described Trump's intervention as "iconic and historic", saying that Ukraine "needs leadership actually focused on peace".
The US president confirmed on Friday that an agreement had been reached with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April.
Zelensky reacted by saying it would allow Moscow to raise new funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.
He also accused Moscow of taking the deal "to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they keep dropping bombs on cities" following deadly new strikes on Zaporizhzhia.
Ukrainian president spoke to several allies on Saturday to discuss the latest developments, calling for "real decisions to protect lives in Ukraine" and to protect European security.
A Downing Street spokesperson said UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had spoken to Zelensky and offered his "complete solidarity".
The pair had agreed Russia should acquiesce to "an immediate energy ceasefire" and end its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea, the spokesperson said, as "this would immediately release more energy and food supplies into the global market".

Armed men abducted four travellers, including a Customs official, from a passenger coach in the Charsar area of Chagai district in broad daylight, police said on Saturday.

He was subsequently released near Gadar and managed to reach his home safely, bringing relief to his family.

The two incidents highlight the security challenges facing travellers on highways in Balochistan, particularly in remote areas where long distances between settlements can complicate emergency responses.
Authorities had launched efforts to recover the four people abducted from the passenger coach in Charsar, while the safe return of the Panjgur judge brought an end to his family's four-day ordeal.

title: PTI open to talks as long march presses on
description: PTI open to talks as long march presses on
content:
Afridi vows no retreat on tribal areas stance without Imran Khan's nod
Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) leadership has decided to keep the long march going while simultaneously keeping the door for negotiations with the federal government open, sources said after a high-level meeting at the Chief Minister's House on Saturday.
The meeting, chaired by Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Muhammad Sohail Khan Afridi, was attended by Acting Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, Secretary General Salman Akram Raja, Provincial President Junaid Akbar Khan, Parliamentary Leader Shahid Khattak and Provincial Minister Shafi Jan. Participants reviewed the national political situation, the ongoing phased long march and other pressing matters.
According to sources, the leadership examined the possibility of the federal government imposing Governor's Rule or an emergency in the province and termed any such step unconstitutional. The meeting reaffirmed the party's willingness to engage in talks with the government while continuing the long march. Sources said that if meaningful negotiations materialise, the march will pause at Swabi.
Chief Minister Afridi made it clear to the senior leadership that the party would not abandon its position on the security operation in the tribal districts without consulting incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan. He maintained that military or security operations alone are not the solution to terrorism in the tribal areas.
Speaking to the media after the meeting, Barrister Gohar Ali Khan said PTI desires negotiations but currently sees little prospect of them. "The long march will continue, yet we remain ready for talks," he stated. "The government does not appear serious about dialogue. We want the issues resolved through negotiations."
Gohar warned that the imposition of Governor's Rule or an emergency would constitute a violation of the public mandate. He said the federal government appeared not to have fully assessed the possible public reaction to such a move. "Our demands are clear and contain nothing unconstitutional or illegal," he added.
The long march has already begun. Party workers are scheduled to reach Swabi on Sunday. Chief Minister Afridi is expected to announce the next phase of the plan of action on 13 October. Gohar urged the federal government to come to the negotiating table before that date.
The dual-track strategy, pressing ahead with public mobilisation while leaving space for dialogue, reflects PTI's attempt to maintain pressure on the centre without closing off a political settlement. Party leaders insist their core demands remain focused on what they describe as constitutional and legal issues, including the situation in the tribal districts and broader political grievances.
As the march moves toward Swabi, attention will now turn to whether the federal government responds with an invitation for talks or continues its current posture. PTI has signalled that any decision to soften its stance on the tribal areas will require Imran Khan's explicit input, underscoring the former prime minister's continuing influence over party strategy despite his imprisonment.
The coming days, particularly the announcement expected on 13 October, are likely to clarify whether the long march escalates further or pauses in favour of negotiations.

title: Pakistan s egg consumption far below developed countries
description: Pakistan s egg consumption far below developed countries
content:
Annual per capita consumption stands at around 100 eggs, compared with 300 in developed countries
Experts have stressed the need to make eggs a regular part of the daily diet to address protein deficiency and improve nutritional health, noting that annual per capita egg consumption in Pakistan stands at around 100, compared with approximately 300 in developed countries.
They expressed these views at a seminar organised by the Faculty of Veterinary Sciences at the University of Agriculture Faisalabad (UAF) to mark World Egg Day under the theme, "The Mighty Egg: Packed with Natural Nutrition".
Dean of the Faculty of Veterinary Sciences Prof Dr Shahid Mehmood said eggs should be included in the daily diet because of their nutritional value and health benefits.
He said eggs contained 13 essential nutrients and supported health at every stage of life, from brain development in childhood to muscle maintenance and bone strength in old age.
He said the poultry sector was the country's second-largest industry after textiles and urged people to increase their egg consumption.
Chairman of the Department of Pathology Prof Dr Kashif Saleemi said eggs were a rich source of protein, vitamins and minerals.
He described them as an affordable, readily available and versatile food that could play an important role in a balanced diet. He stressed the need to raise public awareness about their nutritional benefits to help address dietary deficiencies.
Additional Director Livestock Faisalabad Dr Robina highlighted the role of eggs in improving household nutrition and addressing dietary deficiencies.
She also emphasised the importance of promoting healthy eating habits to improve public health.
Dr Muhammad Yousaf said World Egg Day, observed on the second Friday of October each year, provided an opportunity to highlight the contribution of eggs to nutrition and health worldwide.
He also referred to the growth of the global poultry industry, which was projected to be valued at $417 billion in 2026.
Marketing Manager of Mukhtar Feed Kaleem Qamar Gill said greater awareness of the nutritional and economic value of eggs could help increase consumption across the country.
He called for coordinated efforts by the poultry industry, livestock authorities and relevant institutions to promote egg consumption and raise awareness of its role in a balanced diet.

title: LHC orders protection of Takht Pari forest
description: LHC orders protection of Takht Pari forest
content:
Forest dept directed to ensure water supply to saplings, act against encroachments
The Lahore High Court (LHC) has directed the Forest Department to ensure an uninterrupted water supply to trees and newly planted saplings in Takht Pari forest and take prompt legal action against encroachments, illegal tree cutting and those responsible for setting the forest on fire.
In its written judgment, Justice Jawad Hassan of the court's Rawalpindi bench ordered regular patrolling and proper monitoring of saplings to protect the forest from damage.
He observed that forests were an important heritage of both the public and the state.
The judge noted that climate change was no longer a future threat but a present reality, emphasising the need to protect coming generations from its harmful effects.
He observed that the court had a role in mitigating the effects of climate change for future generations, adding that environmental protection was a fundamental right guaranteed under Articles 9 and 14 of the Constitution.
The judgment was issued on a petition filed by Muhammad Rameez, who had approached the high court seeking measures to protect Takht Pari forest in Rawalpindi.
The court appreciated the efforts made by the Forest Department and other respondents to protect trees.
It directed the department to ensure that forest land was not occupied or used for unauthorised purposes.
The department was also ordered to take prompt action in accordance with the law against illegal encroachments and ensure effective monitoring and protection of the forest.
The judgment further directed that legal proceedings be initiated against those involved in cutting trees or setting fire to the forest.
During the proceedings, the Forest Department informed the court that 46,000 trees had been planted in Takht Pari forest under the Punjab chief minister's plantation campaign.

title: LHC rules tuition fee doesn t justify property tax
description: LHC rules tuition fee doesn t justify property tax
content:
Strikes down notices issued to LUMS before amendment to Cantonments Act
The Lahore High Court (LHC) has declared demands for property tax from the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) for the period preceding a 2023 amendment to the Cantonments Act, 1924, unlawful, holding that educational buildings were automatically exempt from the levy under the earlier law and the conditions of public access and absence of income did not apply to them.
In a significant ruling on the interpretation of fiscal exemptions, a bench comprising Justice Hassan Nawaz Makhdoom and Justice Khalid Ishaq held that the mere charging of tuition fees could not, by itself, justify denying a property-tax exemption.
The court ruled that the authorities must examine the actual use of the relevant buildings, the nature and source of receipts, and the evidence concerning the institution's operations before deciding whether an exemption is available under the amended law.
The judgment allowed LUMS' constitutional petition and declared the impugned orders dated November 2, 2011, and April 26, 2017, along with any consequential demand founded upon them, to be of no legal effect.
The central question before the court was whether the conditions requiring buildings to be open to the public and generate no income applied to educational institutions under Section 99(2)(b) of the Cantonments Act before its amendment in 2023.
The judges concluded that the wording and punctuation of the earlier provision placed educational buildings and public libraries in a separate category from playgrounds and dharmsalas.
The conditions concerning public access and income, they held, applied to the latter category and could not be extended to educational buildings by interpretation.
The bench observed that the amendment had changed the statutory framework by placing educational buildings in a separate clause, expressly attaching the two conditions to them and replacing the mandatory words "shall be exempt" with "The Board may exempt".

title: Rain forecast promises smog relief
description: Rain forecast promises smog relief
content:
Air pollution levels across provincial metropolis vary drastically
A rain warning by the Pakistan Meteorological Department has raised hopes of temporary relief from pollution in Lahore and other parts of Punjab, but the city's air quality readings suggest that the seasonal smog threat persists.
The Met Office forecast rain, wind and thunderstorms with isolated hailstorms in upper and central parts of Punjab till October 15 with gaps. The weather system is expected to affect different areas on Sunday and again on October 13 and 14.
However, the impact of the expected rainfall will depend on the intensity and distribution of showers, wind conditions and whether pollution continues to enter the atmosphere from vehicles, industries, kilns and other sources.
According to the Punjab Environmental Protection Agency's real-time dashboard, Lahore recorded an overall Air Quality Index (AQI) of 131 at 10am on Saturday, placing the city in the moderate category.
The reading was lower than the 163 recorded at the same hour a day earlier, indicating an improvement although pollution remained unevenly distributed across the provincial capital.
The data revealed significant differences between localities with Safari Park recording an AQI of 157, followed by Shahdara and DHA Phase 6 at 155 each, while Multan Road registered 154. These locations were classified as unhealthy for sensitive groups.
In comparison, Wagah Border area recorded 93 and Egerton Road 87, in the satisfactory category.
The variation raised the question whether citywide averages adequately reflect the exposure faced by residents living and working in the most polluted neighbourhoods. The dashboard recorded a weekly peak AQI of 246 at midnight on October 4 and minimum 112 on October Saturday.
"Although the latest overall figure was lower than the previous day, the elevated levels at several monitoring stations show that the improvement has not been uniform," said an EPD official. Residents in different neighbourhoods may face substantially different conditions, making reliable monitoring, timely public advisories and targeted enforcement essential.
An expert, Dr Munawar Sabir, said, "Rain in Lahore and other areas can help remove suspended particles from the atmosphere as droplets bring some pollutants to the ground. Wind can also disperse accumulated pollution but the benefits may be short-lived if emissions continue and atmospheric conditions subsequently become unfavourable."
The PMD attributed the expected weather change to a westerly wave affecting upper and central parts of the country.
The forecast identifies Lahore among the areas where rain and thunderstorms are expected.
Q challenge is that smog is not produced by weather conditions alone. Punjab's recurring pollution episodes involve a combination of transport emissions, industrial activity, brick kilns, construction dust and smoke from agricultural residue burning.
As autumn progresses towards winter, weaker atmospheric mixing and temperature inversions can also trap pollutants closer to the ground.

title: Journalist arrested on  attempted rape  charges
description: Journalist arrested on  attempted rape  charges
content:
He was known for criticising Hyderabad police for their alleged lax actions against drug trafficking
A journalist, accused of attempted rape and known for consistently criticising Hyderabad police for their alleged lax actions against drug trafficking, was rounded up in a late night raid on his home in Hyderabad in the wee hours of Friday. While his family remained unknown about the reason behind the arrest, the Market police produced Abdul Ghafoor Sarohi before a court on Friday morning and obtained his two-day physical remand.
But the custody turned out to be short-lasting as he was released before midnight and the FIR against him was also reduced to c-class, which pertains to admitting mistake in initial police investigation. The family and neighbours of Abdul Ghafoor Sarohi told the media that around 20 policemen broke into their apartment in Qasimabad at around 3am by damaging their metal gate and took away Sarohi.
The family claimed to have remained in the dark about the cause of his apprehension until he was produced before a court in the morning in a case of an alleged rape attempt on a woman. "Police attacked my brother's home. Our family and neighbours kept asking the police about the reason for his arrest but they only replied that they had been ordered by the SSP," said Qayum Sarohi, younger brother. He lamented that his brother was rounded up in a manner as if he was a terrorist.
The journalist was booked in an FIR at Market police station on October 8 on the complaint of Sanam, wife of Rahib Mallah, who lives in Silawat Para locality in a rented house.
She accused Sarohi and an unknown person for attempting to rape her at her house at around 1am on October 5. The FIR was registered on October 8 and Sarohi was apprehended.
Sanam claimed that Sarohi dragged her in the street and tore her clothes. He, however, ran away with the other suspect on their motorbike moments later after she began to scream.
The complainant alleged in the FIR that Sarohi used to give her life threats while repeatedly asking her for meetings. The police kept Sarohi in the CIA centre after his arrest and he was shifted to the same place after grant of the two-day physical remand. The journalist complained before the judge for being tortured during custody after which the court ordered his physical checkup.
Sarohi's family and friends besides some media workers, lawyers and civil society activists, who held a protest outside the SSP office, alleged that the FIR was fake. Senior lawyer, advocate Sajjad Ahmed Chandio, said while talking to The Express Tribune that "mere registration of an FIR or allegation [thereof] isn't the only ground to arrest anyone".
Advocate Aslam Laghari who accompanied Sarohi in the court called for instituting a transparent inquiry which should be conducted by the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA). He described Hyderabad police as partisan for having allegedly managed a fake FIR. He deplored that Sarohi was brought in the court handcuffed as if he was a terrorist.

title: Umrah vaccine exemption ends
description: Umrah vaccine exemption ends
content:
Meningitis, polio vaccinations for Umrah, yellow fever for some destinations mandatory
The temporary exemption, allowing Umrah pilgrims to travel without vaccination, expired on Saturday, prompting the resumption of vaccination services for Umrah pilgrims and other international travellers at Karachi airport.
The International Traveller Vaccination Centre, operated by Border Health Services, has been activated at the Civil Dispensary near the airport's Star Gate at Jinnah Terminal. The centre will provide vaccination services round-the-clock for travellers requiring polio, meningitis, yellow fever and other applicable vaccines.
The deadline for enforcing mandatory meningitis and polio vaccinations for Umrah pilgrims, as well as yellow fever vaccination requirements for travellers to certain destinations in Africa and North America, had been extended twice between September 5 and October 10.
Border Health Services officials said Pakistani passport holders travelling abroad must receive the vaccines required for their destinations, transit points and travel itineraries. Travellers have been advised to fulfil all applicable vaccination requirements before departure and ensure that their vaccination certificates are verified.
Dr Ghulam Murtaza Shah, focal person for Border Health, told The Express Tribune that arrangements had been made at the airport centre to provide vaccinations and issue certificates.
In the next phase, centres in Larkana and Hyderabad will be activated to help residents of rural Sindh obtain the required vaccinations and certificates without travelling to Karachi, Dr Shah said.
He attributed overcrowding at the health centre partly to people arriving without paying the prescribed vaccination fees. Payments can be made through NADRA's Pak ID application.
The prescribed fee for meningitis vaccination at Karachi airport is Rs2,785, while the influenza vaccine costs Rs1,720. The influenza vaccine remains effective for one year and the meningitis vaccine for three years. Polio vaccination will be provided free of charge.
According to Border Health Services, the influenza vaccine is applicable to travellers aged one year and above, while the meningitis vaccine is required for those aged 12 and above, subject to the relevant travel regulations. International travellers are also required to receive a polio vaccine once a year, depending on their destination and applicable rules.
Under the current arrangements, pregnant women will be administered only the influenza vaccine, while breastfeeding mothers may receive influenza, polio and meningitis vaccines. Foreign nationals are exempted from applicable vaccination requirements.
Officials said, travellers facing difficulties with biometric verification of their vaccination certificates would be referred to authorised staff.
Payment receipts generated through NADRA, Pak ID or e-Sahulat will remain valid for 90 days. Five NADRA facilitation counters have also been established at the airport dispensary to assist travellers.
Meanwhile, the Pakistan Airports Authority (PAA) has introduced special arrangements to help passengers affected by flight delays and cancellations at airports across the country amid the prevailing regional situation.
According to a PAA spokesperson, special counters have been established at Karachi airport and other airports nationwide to guide affected passengers, address their concerns and provide necessary information.
The PAA has directed airlines to deploy their representatives at airports to ensure that passengers receive timely updates about changes to flight schedules, delays and cancellations.

title: Attock s historic school struggles to make room
description: Attock s historic school struggles to make room
content:
Serving general public since 1906, school is currently overwhelmed by over 1.4k students
Government Pilot Secondary School Attock, one of the district's oldest and most historic educational institutions, faces a serious shortage of basic facilities, affecting more than 1,400 enrolled students.
Established in 1906, the institution has played a significant role in the educational and social development of Attock for more than a century. Its alumni include numerous officers, politicians, engineers, doctors and other prominent personalities who have served in various fields.
According to sources, the school has an insufficient number of classrooms to accommodate its growing student population. Although the number of teachers is considered satisfactory, the shortage of rooms has prevented the administration from establishing additional sections, forcing it to accommodate more students than the available classrooms can reasonably hold.
The situation has affected academic activities and made it increasingly difficult to maintain a conducive teaching and learning environment. The school also has only eight washrooms, which are inadequate for its current enrolment.
Sources said around four years ago, when District Public School Attock was launched without its own building, 10 classrooms, a library and 10 washrooms belonging to Government Pilot Secondary School were temporarily allocated to it. The facilities were reportedly to be returned once the new school building was completed.
Although the District Public School's own building has been ready for the past two years, the classrooms, library and washrooms have yet to be returned, leaving the historic institution struggling to meet its students' needs.
The matter has also been brought to the attention of the relevant education department officials in Attock, but no effective progress has been reported so far.
Education circles and parents have urged the Punjab education minister, the provincial education secretary, the Rawalpindi division commissioner and the Attock deputy commissioner to take immediate notice and ensure that the facilities are returned to Government Pilot Secondary School.
They said the restoration of the classrooms, library and washrooms was essential to providing more than 1,400 students with an adequate learning environment and meeting the needs of the district's historic educational institution.

content:
Traders protest seven-day notices demanding records for properties dating back 150 years
The Rawalpindi Municipal Corporation (RMC), facing its worst financial crisis in two years and having failed to achieve its tax collection targets, has sought building plans for residential and commercial properties across all 46 union councils within its municipal limits, including buildings dating back 150 years, newly constructed houses, shops, markets and commercial plazas.
Traders have protested seven-day notices issued by the corporation and threatened a complete shutter-down strike.
The corporation's Building Branch has begun issuing red notices door-to-door in markets and old localities, warning property owners and occupants to submit the required building plans within seven days or face arrest, a fine of Rs100,000, imprisonment for three years, or both.
RMC area inspectors have served notices in Banni Chowk, Jamia Masjid Road, Kohati Bazaar, Circular Road, Saidpur Road, Shah Chan Chiragh, Pul Shah Nazar and Bagh Sardaran.
The notices have triggered strong protests from traders' organisations, including the Karyana Merchants Association, the Markazi Tanzeem-e-Tajran and the Citizens Action Committee, which have demanded their immediate withdrawal.
Traders questioned how owners of buildings constructed a century or 150 years ago could produce approved plans, pointing out that Pakistan came into existence in 1947, while the corporation was demanding records for buildings dating back to the 1880s. They also condemned what they described as threats of arrest, fines and imprisonment.
Karyana Merchants Association president Saleem Parvez Butt said plans were available for newly constructed buildings, but it was unreasonable to expect owners to produce documents for old properties.
He urged the city leadership of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz to intervene immediately and stop what he termed an injustice, warning that the party could face political repercussions otherwise.
Anjuman-e-Tajran Sabzi Mandi president Ghulam Qadir Mir also demanded an immediate end to the notices, urging the corporation to explore alternative sources of revenue. He said all traders' organisations would convene a joint meeting and launch a complete shutter-down strike if the notices were not withdrawn.
Citizens Action Committee chairman Malik Zaheer Awan maintained that the corporation could not demand building plans for properties constructed before 1947. He alleged that municipal officials and inspectors accepted gratification to allow buildings and shops to be constructed without proper documentation and subsequently harassed their owners.

title: PESCO loses court challenge in electric shock case

The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Saturday dismissed a petition filed by the Peshawar Electric Supply Company (PESCO) challenging a presidential order directing it to bear the medical and rehabilitation expenses of a nine-year-old girl who lost both hands after an electric shock.
Justice Azam Khan ruled that PESCO must arrange a comprehensive medical assessment of the affected child, Lubaba, at the Armed Forces Institute of Rehabilitation Medicine (AFIRM), Rawalpindi, and pay for modern prosthetic limbs, treatment and rehabilitation. In its ruling, the court observed that electricity distribution companies were responsible not only for ensuring an uninterrupted power supply but also for protecting human lives and meeting safety requirements.
PESCO had argued that its inquiry found no negligence on its part, claiming the incident resulted from an illegal direct connection rather than a fallen transmission line. However, the company acknowledged that numerous illegal connections existed in the affected area.
Lubaba suffered severe burns in July 2021 when an electricity line fell in Pir Qila, Charsadda, resulting in the amputation of both her hands and permanent disability.
The Federal Ombudsman directed PESCO on October 24, 2024, to pay compensation in accordance with the applicable rules and regulations. The complaint was initially upheld, but the findings requiring payment of compensation were subsequently withdrawn during review proceedings.
On October 30, 2025, the President's Office directed PESCO to arrange her treatment and prosthetic limbs. The company challenged the order, but the high court dismissed its petition, upholding the direction to provide the required assistance.

The federal government has accelerated action in the case of late International Islamic University Islamabad (IIUI) gold medallist student Laiba Ijaz, who committed suicide after her dreams of pursuing higher studies at Harvard University were squashed when a man posing as an agent defrauded her of over Rs7 million.
After Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took notice of the case, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry visited Laiba's home to offer their condolences on Saturday. Following the Prime Minister's directions, the Islamabad Police and the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) have also initiated investigations. The case of Laiba Ijaz's death came to light when her body was found hanging from a tree in Sector G-10, Islamabad on Friday.
Laiba's family stated that she had earned a BS degree with a gold medal from IIUI and aspired to enrol at Harvard University in the United States for further studies. The family stated that they had made significant financial sacrifices to secure Laiba's academic future and fulfil her dream.
They alleged that an individual, acting as an agent, took over Rs7 million from them on the pretext of securing her an admission and a scholarship at Harvard University. To help realise her dream, Laiba's father sold his plot and pitched in Rs2.1 million from the sale's proceeds, while her mother sold her gold jewellery.
According to the family, the suspect claimed to be an accounts officer at the Islamabad High Court and at other times presented himself as an employee of the superior judiciary or an officer of a sensitive institution. The family claims that despite the substantial payment, the promises regarding admission and the scholarship were never fulfilled.
According to Laiba's maternal uncle, Rana Amjad, the Harvard University admission letter, scholarship letter and other documents provided by the accused turned out to be fake upon verification. He stated that Laiba suffered severe distress and mental anguish after the alleged fraud came to light. Her family has demanded a thorough investigation into the matter, the arrest of all individuals involved in the alleged fraud, and the recovery of the money.
Meanwhile, Laiba's family has submitted an application to the FIA for the registration of a case and the initiation of legal action. FIA Islamabad Zone Director Syed Shahzad Nadeem Bukhari met with Laiba's family to gather details about the incident. According to FIA sources, the alleged fake documents have been obtained from the family, and raids are being conducted to arrest the accused.
During a press conference, Naqvi noted that the alleged accused had also collected money under the pretext of offering clients employment and assistance in other visa-related queries. Laiba's father too noted that the accused had extorted an additional Rs500,000 from them on the pretext of helping their son get a government job. The PM has directed the IG and Chief Commissioner to arrest the accused.

Links tech facility to rapid economic progress, prosperity
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday formally inaugurated the newly renamed Daanish IT Park (National Technology Park), hailing the country's first national technology facility as a crucial milestone for Pakistan's rapid economic progress and prosperity.
Addressing the inaugural ceremony, the prime minister emphasized that the state-of-the-art facility brings incubation centres, innovation hubs, small and medium enterprises (SMEs), startups, and industry leaders together under one roof.
He expressed strong optimism that the tech park would empower Pakistan's youth and play a pivotal role in steering the nation toward becoming a developed country.
He said that once the technology park becomes fully operational, similar facilities would be established across the country and in all provinces, helping industry, agriculture, mining and minerals, and other key sectors grow.
The prime minister said the facility would host AI experts and act as a catalyst to promote different skills in the IT sector.
He said the foundation of this project was laid down during 2017-18 but what happened after it was a part of history.
He also commended the hard work and tireless efforts of the Minister of IT and her team and relevant authorities, which transformed 'a sick project into a sound and healthy project'.
He further informed that he had directed the ministry to conduct transparent bidding, inviting renowned IT companies in the country and abroad to make the facility fully functional and keep it growing under internationally recognised SOPs without any interference from the government.
The prime minister said that Islamabad IT Park, would now onwards be called 'Daanish IT Park', highlighting the contributions made by Daanish schools in the education sector by providing quality education to talented students with poor backgrounds, and mentioned that due to their talents, those students had excelled in different fields.
He said moreover, Daanish University in Islamabad was also being established.
The prime minister said "it is not about brick and mortar, it is not about, a grand, wonderful building, it is about ecosystem, it is about innovation, having incubation centres, over there, skill development, vocational training, and centres where industrialists and entrepreneurs will be sitting, in front of great IT experts and AI experts, all of them, will be here, and this centre will act as a great catalyst to promote all these skills to all those who are ready to learn without wasting time."
The prime minister, in his remarks, appreciated the support of the Korean government and the ambassador, and shared that he had visited Korea for the first time back in 1985, where he visited the headquarters of Daewoo, a steel plant and had meetings with many other companies.
He said that during his tenure as chief minister Punjab, they also brought Daewoo's air-conditioned buses for the first time in Pakistan, in the city of Lahore.
The prime minister also lauded Korea's economy and said the country was counted amongst those leading industrious countries of the world.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif approved measures to eliminate difficulties faced by passengers at airports and to further facilitate their travel.
The Prime Minister was chairing a review meeting regarding the customs system. The Prime Minister directed the immediate installation of smart scanners at airports.
Baggage should be screened using smart scanners rather than by Customs officials, he said and issued orders to stop Customs officials from harassing passengers with unnecessary questioning.
He directed the immediate import of smart scanners via air and their installation at all the international airports.
Outdated procedures for screening passenger baggage at airports must be abandoned, he added.
He said, "Passenger convenience and comfort are the top priority and no one will be allowed to harass passengers."
Internationally prevalent automated systems will be introduced for screening passenger baggage, he remarked.
He said staff deployed for other airport services will also be trained according to international standards.
"Courtesy and respect for human dignity in service delivery must be made key components of the training.
The new enforcement system introduced by Customs is commendable and the credit goes to the FBR Chairman and his team," he continued.
He said every possible measure must be taken to prevent revenue evasion.
He said, "Tax paying businesses are worthy of respect and a zero tolerance policy will be adopted against tax evaders."
"We are custodians of the poor public's money and will make every possible effort to safeguard it."
During the meeting, the Prime Minister was briefed on the movement of goods and customs oversight at various locations across the country, including airports and seaports. A briefing was also given on the performance of the Customs Enforcement Force and the measures taken to curb the smuggling of petroleum products.
The meeting was informed that significant progress has been made in establishing and operationalizing digital enforcement stations under Customs Enforcement. In the first three weeks of its inception, the Indus Collectorate (Enforcement) seized goods worth approximately Rs 205 million in 80 operations; 865 personnel were deployed, and 26 key transit routes were covered.
It was further told that operations against smuggled items - such as fabric, vehicles, cigarettes, high-speed diesel, auto parts, and other goods are ongoing. Meanwhile, under customs sector reforms, the recruitment of 280 Goods Evaluators has been completed and their training is scheduled for October and November 2026.
The meeting was further informed that, as a result of reform measures taken by the FBR to curb smuggling, a unified and integrated entity has been established nationwide by consolidating the customs enforcement system.

title: Houthis mount fresh missiles attack on KSA airport
description: Houthis mount fresh missiles attack on KSA airport
content:
Pakistan warns Houthis, demands swift UNSC action
Saudi authorities suspended operations at Riyadh's international airport on Saturday after a fresh attack there left multiple people wounded.
In the United Nations, Pakistan issued a stern warning to the Houthi militia at the United Nations Security Council on Friday, demanding an immediate halt to ongoing missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabian civilian and economic infrastructure.
Highlighting the serious threat to regional stability, global energy security, and international maritime trade, Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, Permanent representative of Pakistan to the UN, called on the 15-member Council to take decisive action against the Yemen-based militia.
The warning comes amid a devastating wave of Houthi strikes that targeted major Saudi aviation hubsincluding King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airportkilling at least three Saudi nationals, including an airline pilot, and disrupting global aviation.
In this regard, the Pakistani envoy also drew attention of the Council delegates to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's recent statement reaffirming Islamabad's commitment to the Kingdom's territorial integrity that remains "resolute" under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.
"Yemen's descent into conflict is deeply alarming," Ambassador Asim Ahmad said, adding that the escalation of hostilities, continued Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, threats to commercial shipping, fighting around Taiz and Bab el-Mandeb, and deepening humanitarian crisis demand urgent attention.
Condemning the ongoing Houthi "terrorist" attacks, Ambassador Asim Ahmad called for an immediate end to such "reckless attacks" that pose a grave threat to regional peace and security. "The security and sanctity of the two Holy Mosques must be respected at all times."
Pakistan, he said, reaffirms its support for Yemen's sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity, and its internationally recognized government.
The Pakistani envoy demanded that Houthis cease attacks on commercial shipping in and around Taiz and Bab el-Mandeb to ensure maritime security.
Freedom of navigation must be upheld, he said. "These vital waterways cannot remain exposed to attacks that endanger seafarers, disrupt trade and compound global economic hardship."
Pakistan, he said, supports UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg's peace efforts, suggesting that all diplomatic channels must be used to contain escalation, maintain communication and facilitate a cessation of hostilities. "These efforts should restore a credible, inclusive, Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political process under United Nations auspices."
Civilians must be protected, the Pakistani envoy stressed. "Safe, rapid and unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilian infrastructure, and adequate funding for relief operations are indispensable - food, fuel and essential commercial supplies must reach all those in need."
He also reiterated the call for the immediate, unconditional and safe release of detained United Nations, humanitarian and diplomatic personnel.
"The Council must act with unity and purpose to halt Houthi attacks, safeguard regional security, alleviate suffering and restore a credible path towards a political settlement," Ambassador Asim Ahmad added.
Pakistan, he said, stands with the Yemeni people, supports efforts towards a peaceful, stable and united Yemen, and will continue to make every effort to advance lasting peace and stability in the region.
Ambassador Asim Ahmad, who will soon be leaving his post to take over as Foreign Secretary, took the opportunity to thank his colleagues on the Council, the Secretary-General and UN officials for their cooperation and support during his tenure in New York.
The situation prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the "serious emergency", a medical source said, while foreign embassies warned their citizens to avoid the facility.
The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed an attack had injured several people at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport, with a diplomatic source attributing it to a missile fired by Yemen's Houthis.
The Iran-backed group has repeatedly targeted the facility, claiming a series of strikes on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not announce any new attacks on Saturday.
A witness at the airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded and fleeing in panic.
"I was on gate 403" at the domestic terminal, the witness told AFP. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."
A medical source told AFP that the health ministry had ordered ER doctors to report to hospitals around the capital to treat the wounded on Saturday.
"We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh", with many in critical condition, the source said.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of strikes hitting civilian targets are relatively rare, with officials issuing few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
The aviation authority said the number of injured from Saturday's attack was still being assessed, adding airport "operations had been temporarily suspended pending the completion of an assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities".
A source at a local hospital said five people were in intensive care there after being wounded at the airport, with "dozens of people injured" in all.
A relative of one wounded person said they had been hit in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass. Three witnesses confirmed people being evacuated from the airport.
Two doctors told AFP that several pilgrims headed to Mecca had been injured while waiting to board their flight.
A diplomatic source briefed on the matter told AFP the airport was hit by "a missile around 3:00 pm" (1200 GMT).
"Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target," the source said.
The Yemen conflict flared back to life after a four-year, UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle Eastern war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
The scale and frequency of the recent strikes targeting Riyadh are unprecedented in the eight months of war in the region.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that supports Yemen's government militarily, and has found itself drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour's civil war.
Both Riyadh and the Houthis have signalled a willingness to keep fighting rather than pursue diplomacy.
The US embassy in Saudi Arabia said it was "aware of attacks" on Riyadh airport on Saturday and called on American citizens to avoid the area.
The Canadian, German and Spanish embassies also warned their citizens to avoid the facility. Spain's embassy, in a message on X, alerted nationals to a "new attack... by the Houthis".
A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies "indicated that they had decided to prohibit their staffs' travel to/from Riyadh Airport over the next week as a prudential step".
Near the airport, passengers carrying luggage could be seen standing on the pavement at a metro station.
Meanwhile, in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas they captured last month around the Bab al-Mandab strait, military sources told AFP.
The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the group seized the country's entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab areaa key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shippingbut they claimed to have repelled the assault.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

title: Embattled K P CM strikes defiant note
description: Embattled K P CM strikes defiant note
content:
Says governor's rule will elicit strong response
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi has warned that any attempt to impose governor's rule or an emergency in the province, or to undermine its government's public mandate, would prompt a strong public response, saying people would head to Peshawar instead of Swabi if such a move was made.
Addressing participants in the PTI long march before its departure from Charsadda, and later at Chamtar Adda and Manga Bazaar in Mardan, Afridi said the people of K-P had given their mandate to PTI founder Imran Khan and that the province would continue to follow his political direction.
"The policy in K-P will be Imran Khan's, and his rule will prevail," he said, adding that his government had no desire to cling to office but would defend its constitutional rights and the public mandate at all costs.
Afridi said the province was ready and people had already taken to the streets. He called on PTI supporters from across the country to reach Swabi on October 11, whether by car, motorcycle, bicycle or on foot.
Participants would travel under the leadership of their respective parliamentarians, he said, adding that the party would announce its future course of action in Swabi on October 13.
The chief minister maintained that the march was a peaceful political struggle within the bounds of the Constitution and the law. He said threats, coercive tactics and the use of force would not deter the protesters, warning that detaining or pressuring parliamentarians would not prevent people from coming out to defend their rights.
"This is no longer about a position or power," Afridi said, adding that neither a political office nor wealth could buy him off. He said the struggle was now about Imran Khan, the rights of the people of K-P and their right to determine their own future.
He urged supporters to remain steadfast, maintain discipline and ensure the protest remained peaceful, cautioning them against provocation or attempts to create disorder.
He also said the people of the province would not accept policies imposed against their interests or decisions about their future that disregarded their wishes and constitutional rights.
Referring to the province's security situation, Afridi said K-P's people, police and other personnel had made enormous sacrifices to restore peace.
He claimed that 80,000 people from K-P had lost their lives in the struggle, arguing that the peace achieved at such a heavy cost was now being put at risk by decisions taken behind closed doors.
He alleged that terrorism was being imposed on the province in pursuit of vested interests and warned that the consequences of such policies could be dangerous.
He said the province's people would resist what he described as an oppressive system and would protect the dignity, honour and rights of the Pashtuns.
Speaking at Chamtar Adda, Afridi claimed that K-P was the only province in the country with a government formed on the basis of the people's mandate, while other governments had been imposed on the public. He said the enthusiasm shown by march participants demonstrated their determination to continue the struggle.
He also rejected the notion that threats involving firearms or bullets would intimidate the protesters, saying they would continue to pursue their rights peacefully and resolutely.
At Manga Bazaar, the chief minister thanked residents of Mardan for welcoming the march and participating in it. Referring to the political symbolism surrounding Section 804, associated with Imran Khan, he remarked that the entire city appeared to be under "Section 804".
Afridi said supporters of Imran would reach Swabi regardless of the obstacles they faced and claimed that a large turnout would make it difficult for anyone to resort to force. He hinted that the party's next plan, to be announced on October 13, would surprise its opponents, without disclosing details.
Reiterating his warning to those threatening governor's rule, Afridi said the province's public mandate could not be set aside through administrative or constitutional measures without provoking a response from the people.
He said the movement was not intended to secure personal benefits or retain power but to defend constitutional rights, the public's right to choose its representatives and the province's interests. He urged workers and supporters to remain united and peaceful as the march continued towards Swabi.
