title: PTI govt faces ouster as Centre weighs K P options
description: PTI govt faces ouster as Centre weighs K P options
content:
President, PM huddle paves way for direct rule Federal cabinet meets today to take final decision
The federal cabinet is expected to consider imposing an emergency and governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) at a crucial meeting on Sunday (today), as the federal government weighs constitutional measures amid the PTI-led provincial government's ongoing protest march and worsening political and security tensions.
Sources said the cabinet, which will meet at 9:30am under Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, is expected to consider both options and approve advice to be sent to President Asif Ali Zardari. They said significant administrative changes, including appointing a new chief secretary, could accompany any decision.
The developments follow a meeting between President Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz at Aiwan-e-Sadr on Saturday, during which they reviewed the country's overall political and security situation, with particular attention to K-P, where the PTI launched its long march on October 4.
According to sources, the president and prime minister reached an understanding on the possibility of imposing governor's rule or an emergency in the province. However, the final decision rests with the federal cabinet, and no formal announcement had been made at the time of reporting.
The Presidency's media wing said the meeting discussed the overall political and security situation and that separate sessions of the National Assembly and Senate had been agreed upon for Oct 13.
The prime minister was assisted by Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, Federal Minister Ahad Cheema and Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Usman Awan. Senator Sherry Rehman, Syed Naveed Qamar, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla and Dr Asim Hussain assisted the president.
According to sources, K-P Governor Faisal Karim Kundi had sent the prime minister a written explanation of the grounds for emergency measures about a week earlier, as part of the legal requirements for the proposed intervention.
The reported advice argues that the province's law and order situation has deteriorated to the point where imposing an emergency has become necessary. Following cabinet approval, the prime minister is expected to send the advice to the president. The emergency would take effect after presidential approval, according to the sources.
The cabinet division is expected to place the relevant summary before the cabinet on Sunday, potentially through circulation. Sources said a notification detailing the imposition of governor's rule and emergency would be issued following the required approvals.
The proposals reportedly include administrative changes across the province, particularly replacing the incumbent chief secretary with a new, stronger administrator to oversee provincial affairs. Other senior officials could also be transferred.
Sources have separately indicated that the federal government is considering imposing an emergency in 12 districts, including eight merged tribal districtsKhyber, Kurram, Orakzai, Bajaur, Mohmand, North Waziristan, South Waziristan and Lower South Waziristanas well as Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Bannu and Lakki Marwat. Another proposal under consideration would transfer certain important provincial powers to the federal government.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, speaking informally to journalists, suggested that the government believed its options for resolving the standoff had narrowed considerably.
"What scope remains for not imposing an emergency?" he asked, urging journalists to consider how the situation could be resolved.
Naqvi said the government had made extensive efforts to find a solution and those involved could themselves explain the extent of those efforts. "We have no room left now," he said.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Shehbaz contacted JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman to discuss the political situation and other important matters. The PM congratulated Fazl on performing Umrah and invited him to the Prime Minister's House for a meeting, an invitation the JUI-F chief accepted.
Sources said Fazl favoured allowing more time for political negotiations and that the PTI had remained in contact with him. Consultations were expected to focus on the situation in K-P and possible ways to reduce tensions.

title: Imran case caught in jurisdictional deadlock
description: Imran case caught in jurisdictional deadlock
content:
SC yet to send records to FCC despite judicial order
The jurisdictional dispute between the country's two apex courts remains unresolved as the Supreme Court appears to be cautious in fixing a hearing in the matter in which it raised legal questions over the Federal Constitutional Court's (FCC) order seeking records of cases involving PTI founder Imran Khan and directing that they be fixed for hearing before it.
The delay has left questions surrounding the FCC's jurisdiction and the implementation of the SC's order for Imran Khan's transfer to Shifa International Hospital unresolved.
The FCC raised questions on September 14 over the SC's August 18 order directing the transfer for medical treatment. However, the matter is yet to be fixed for hearing before the FCC. Meanwhile, the SC has also not fixed the matter for hearing despite its September 16 judicial order.
A three-member bench led by Justice Shahid Waheed adjourned the hearing for three weeks on September 16 at the request of Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Awan.
There is little chance that the matter will be listed for hearing next week, as the head of the bench, Justice Shahid Waheed, will be sitting at the SC's Lahore Registry to hear cases.
It is also learnt that, despite the judicial order, the SC office has yet to send the records of Imran Khan's cases to the FCC for hearing.
A senior law officer believes that although the SC's order remains in force, if it takes up the case again, the FCC will be compelled to stay the SC's August 18 order regarding Imran Khan's transfer to Shifa International Hospital.
He said the SC had no option but to follow the FCC's order, which was binding on it under Article 189 of the Constitution.
Legal experts believe that if the SC ultimately sends the case to the FCC, it would effectively establish the subordinate status of the SC.
"Will the SC judges accept their demotion or resign?" a senior lawyer questioned.
Barrister Tariq Mahmood Khokhar said the FCC order was "a belated obituary of the Supreme Court of Pakistan". He said the SC's decline had been a "predicted and predictable outcome" of the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments.
"The Constitution was amended, not for constitutional reasons but for state reasons," Khokhar said.
The jurisdictional dispute between the two apex courts has also left uncertainty over Imran Khan's health unresolved, as neither the FCC nor the SC is taking up the matter.
A senior government official told The Express Tribune that, in view of the latest report, Imran Khan was completely physically fit. He said the report would be submitted to the appropriate court before the case was fixed for hearing.
On August 18, the SC ordered the government to shift Imran Khan to Shifa International Hospital for medical treatment. However, the order was not fully implemented.
Following this, petitioner Uzma Khan filed a contempt petition against Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and others over the non-implementation of the August 18 order. The same contempt matter was also fixed for hearing before the bench.
In its order, the court noted that it had been brought to its notice that certain cases arising from a judgment of the Islamabad High Court, delivered in a petition under Article 199 of the Constitution, had reached the FCC. The relief sought in those cases was substantially similar to that granted by the SC through its August 18 order.
The court noted that, before proceeding to adjudicate upon those matters, the FCC appeared to have considered it appropriate to examine the proceedings pending before the SC and had accordingly called for their records.
Referring to paragraph 6 of the FCC order, the bench questioned how the constitutional court could order the 'fixation' of cases whose records it was summoning from the SC.
However, the bench acknowledged that the FCC could summon records of cases under Article 175 E (5) of the Constitution.
At one point, Justice Naeem Akhtar Afghan said Article 175 E(5) of the Constitution did not specifically mention that the FCC could summon records of cases from the SC, unlike Article 189, which states that the FCC's orders are binding on all courts, including the SC.
Justice Shahid Waheed remarked that the bench could not disregard the FCC's order. However, he also questioned whether the FCC's order was binding on the SC.
The presiding judge said that the enforcement of fundamental rights was involved in every matter.
He noted that, under the Constitution, appeals against orders of the FCC were heard by the SC, whose decisions were final. He asked whether the SC's order in a Sharia matter would be binding on the FCC.

Tarar said the provincial government should have focused on establishing modern IT centres, building universities and schools, upgrading hospitals and improving public infrastructure across the province, including in Lakki Marwat, Mardan, Nowshera and Swabi.
Comparing the provincial administration's performance with that of the federal government, Tarar cited Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's inauguration of an IT park and the federal fuel subsidy scheme as examples of governance and public relief.
According to Tarar, the IT park would support start-ups, improve digital skills and contribute to economic growth. He also claimed that 10 million people had benefited from the fuel subsidy scheme through an IT-based registration system.

title: Pakistan warns UN of India s false flag op
description: Pakistan warns UN of India s false flag op
content:
Envoy says Islamabad has capability to defend itself
A senior Pakistani diplomat has warned the United Nations that India has formalised its last year's unprovoked military aggression into an official, declared policy, claiming a unilateral right to launch strikes against Pakistan on any manufactured pretext.
"South Asia remains hostage to a doctrine of force," Ambassador Tahir Andrabi, permanent representative of Pakistan to the UN offices in Geneva, told the General assembly's First Committee (Disarmament and International Security), referring to India's May 2025 assault and Islamabad's "precise and effective" response.
"India has since elevated that aggression into declared policy - the so-called 'new normal' - claiming the right to strike Pakistan at a time of its choosing, on any pretext it can manufacture," Ambassador Andrabi added.
However, he declared that Pakistan possesses both the capability and the resolve to decisively defend itself sovereignty against any misadventure.
The Pakistani envoy went on to say India was engaged in the largest military build-up in the region - intercontinental-range, sea-based and hypersonic systems - enabled by discriminatory exemptions of export controls, while it evades dialogue: the last formal talks between the two neighbours on nuclear and conventional confidence-building measures were held in 2012.
Pakistan, he said, does not seek an arms race, but has the capacity to defend itself, as evident by its response in May 2025.
"We will, therefore, maintain Full Spectrum Deterrence within the framework of Credible Minimum Deterrence," Ambassador Andrabi said.
"The notion that a limited conventional war can be fought, and contained, under a nuclear overhang is a dangerous delusion."
He said Pakistan's preference is not war but diplomacy, and remained ready for a meaningful dialogue on all outstanding issues, including the Jammu and Kashmir dispute, in accordance with UN Security Council resolutions.
"Our proposal for a Strategic Restraint Regime in the region remains on the table."
On war-shattered Gaza, Ambassador Andrabi said the ceasefire remains fragile. "It must hold and lead to a sovereign, viable State of Palestine, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital based on the pre-1967 borders."
As regard the wider Middle East conflict, he said Pakistan stood for immediate de-escalation, restoration of normal passage, and respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all States in the region.
The Pakistani envoy expressed regret that the Russia-Ukraine conflict has raged on for four years now.
"It is more than evident that there is no military solution to the conflict," he said.
Calling for dialogue and diplomacy, he recalled that Pakistan had acted as a mediator between Iran and the United States in an effort culminating in a ceasefire and Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.
"Repeated aggression against sovereign States, and the failure to prevent it are deeply disturbing trends," Ambassador Andrabi pointed out. "The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, defensive in character and consistent with the UN Charter, aims to promote collective efforts for peace, security and stability in the region and beyond.
At the global level, he said, Pakistan was concerned that arms control was being dismantled, with nuclear weapons being modernized.

description: Goods worth millions at risk as containers held for weeks
content:
Medicines, clothes damaged by welding heat
Containers deployed for the past 15 days to block the route of the PTI long march are now turning into a costly headache for traders as medicines, dry fruit, toys, clothing bales and other goods inside them are being damaged.
The traders say cargo that has remained locked for two weeks is already suffering from the intense heat generated when the containers were welded together, while other goods are deteriorating simply from being kept sealed.
Traders and other wholesale markets have demanded that they be immediately allowed to remove goods from containers carrying medicines, fruit, dry fruit and other perishable or sensitive items.
They warned that the cargo had already remained trapped for two weeks and could stay there for another 10 days, putting millions of rupees at risk.
According to traders, more than 100 containers loaded with commercial goods are believed to be among the 10,000 to 12,000 containers taken into custody.
They said containers carrying medicines, toys, clothing bales and dry fruit were particularly affected after containers were welded together, with the heat from the welding scorching the goods inside. Other cargo, they said, was also beginning to deteriorate because the containers had remained sealed.
Wholesale Dealers Association Vice President Sajid Khan said consignments of dry fruit and fruit had been brought from Quetta and their loaded containers were taken into custody and welded shut at Attock Bridge.
The heat generated by the welding had scorched the fruit, he said.
Sheikh Azmat, a dealer at the wholesale market in Narnkari Bazaar, said containers carrying spices were also among those being held.
"We only want permission to take our goods out. The administration can keep the containers in its custody," he said.
Bohr Bazaar trader Shafqat Abbasi said containers carrying surgical and medical supplies should also be opened to allow the goods to be removed.
"All this material is being damaged and rendered useless. If it remains locked in the containers for another week, wholesale dealers could suffer losses running into millions of rupees," he said.
The Deputy Commissioner's Office said the administration had taken empty containers into custody. However, it added that such requests would be examined and positive action would be taken after verification.
"Traders earn a halal livelihood and they will not be allowed to suffer financial losses," the office said.

title: Prisons operating at 161  capacity
description: Prisons operating at 161  capacity
content:
Three in four prisoners are undertrial, report finds
Pakistan's prison population has climbed to 110,513, pushing jails to 160.6% of their approved capacity, with three out of every four inmates still awaiting trial, according to a new report by the National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) and the Justice Project Pakistan (JPP).
The 2026 report found that 82,988 prisoners, or 75.09% of the country's total prison population, are undertrial - a figure that by itself exceeds Pakistan's total approved prison capacity of 68,832 by 14,156 inmates.
The findings point to a criminal justice system struggling to process people at the same pace at which they are entering prisons.
NCHR Chairperson Rabia Agha said Pakistan was confronting a broader justice system problem rather than simply an overcrowding crisis.
"Pakistan does not merely have a problem of overcrowding in prisons. We have a criminal justice system problem. People are entering prison at a rate that our justice system cannot dispose of at the same rate."
She was speaking at the launch of the report by the NCHR and JPP.
Agha noted that more than 28,000 people were currently imprisoned under drug laws, raising questions about why such a large number of people were being incarcerated and what reforms were needed to change this pattern.
JPP Executive Director Sarah Bilal said the report was intended to give policymakers, criminal justice practitioners and donors the evidence needed to make better decisions and demonstrate that different approaches were possible.
"The purpose of this report is to provide policymakers, criminal justice system practitioners and donors with the evidence they need to make better decisions, and to show that different approaches are possible. The tools we are introducing alongside this report are about taking that evidence a step further: supporting the reform efforts of civil society and those working within the system."
Jeroen Williams, head of Partnerships at the European Union Delegation to Pakistan, said significant efforts had been made over the past year to improve prison conditions in the country.
"Over the past year, significant efforts have been made in Pakistan to improve prison conditions."
Earlier this year, a Prison Management Information System was launched in Balochistan, and similar initiatives have also been undertaken in five prison centres in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. "If everything goes according to plan, an agreement will also be signed with UNODC to further improve prison management and conditions in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Pakistan can rely on the European Union's support in these efforts."
The report analyses Pakistan's prison crisis through the way the criminal justice system uses incarceration, examining who is arrested, access to bail, the pace at which cases are processed, which offences are criminalised and the availability of alternatives to imprisonment.
According to its key findings, Pakistan's prisons are operating at 160.6% of their approved capacity, housing 110,513 inmates against a sanctioned capacity of 68,832 - 41,681 more people than the system was designed to accommodate.
Drug-related imprisonment was identified as another major driver of the pressure on prisons. More than 28,000 people are incarcerated under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act (CNSA), accounting for more than a quarter of the overall prison population and representing a 43.4% increase from 2023.

title: Governor s rule or emergency
description: Governor s rule or emergency
content:
Provisions deal with distinct questions, including when an emergency may be declared
As the federal government weighs extraordinary constitutional measures in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa amid the province's worsening security situation and its confrontation with the Centre over the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's (PTI) long march, three constitutional provisions have moved to the centre of the debate, namely Articles 232, 233 and 234.
The provisions deal with distinct questions including when an emergency may be declared, how the failure of constitutional machinery in a province can be addressed and what happens to certain fundamental rights during an emergency.
Although the terms "emergency" and "governor's rule" are often used interchangeably in political debate, the Constitution prescribes different legal grounds and procedures for each measure.
Article 232: When can an emergency be declared?
Article 232 provides the constitutional framework for declaring an emergency in circumstances involving war, external aggression or internal disturbance beyond the control of a provincial government.
The provision allows extraordinary powers to be exercised in response to threats to the security of Pakistan or a part of the country, subject to the Constitution's specified conditions and approval requirements.

A festival celebrating the traditions and entrepreneurial skills of Pakistan's Dawoodi Bohra community was held at a Dolmen mall in Karachi, showcasing handmade crafts, traditional clothing, food and everyday household products.
The event provided a platform for local vendors, particularly women, to display their work, connect with customers and promote small businesses built around their creative skills.
Products on display included embroidered garments, crochet bags, handmade accessories, children's clothing, bedding and other household items. Food and homemade delicacies were also featured, reflecting the diversity of businesses operating within the community.
Handcrafted work is closely associated with Bohra culture, particularly the rida, a distinctive two-piece outer garment worn by women. Often decorated with embroidery, lace, appliqué and crochet, the garment combines traditional modesty with individual expression. Handmade craftsmanship is also reflected in men's traditional clothing and crocheted caps.
For some women, these skills have developed into long-term business ventures. Sakina Burhan uddin, who runs Nafees Apparels, said she had been working in the shawl business for several years and had recently expanded into a new product category.
A community vendor said families encouraged women to develop their talents and pursue business opportunities.
"There is no distinction between girls and boys when it comes to developing their skills. Husbands support their wives after marriage, fathers encourage their daughters, and brothers support their sisters," she said.
Idris Kotari, another member of the Bohra community, said events bringing vendors and customers together could help small businesses grow.

content:
'Film is for all of Pakistan, not just Punjab,' emphasises producer Hareem Farooq in exclusive interview
Actor and producer Hareem Farooq says her upcoming Punjabi-language film Mango Jutt is intended for audiences across Pakistan and not just Punjabi-speaking viewers, as the film prepares for its theatrical release on October 16.
Speaking to The Express Tribune at the film's music launch in Karachi, Farooq said the project had been a challenging but rewarding experience, adding that bringing it to the screen was a success in itself.
"My message is that people should watch this film with an open heart. It is for all of Pakistan. Just because it is a Punjabi film does not mean it is only for Punjab. It is a film for the entire country," she said.
The film stars Faysal Quraishi and Farooq and brings together action, comedy, romance and Punjabi cultural elements. It is scheduled to release in cinemas across Pakistan and internationally on October 16.
Farooq said audience feedback had been encouraging and expectations had risen as the film's release approached.
"The feedback is growing and expectations have become very high. Allah will make things work out, Insha'Allah. As I have said, for me, it is already a success," she said.
For Farooq, the film also represents an important milestone in her journey as a producer. She said visiting Karachi for the launch was particularly meaningful because of the affection she had received from the city.
"I had to come to Karachi. Without Karachi, my work as a producer would not have been complete. A city that has given me so much love, how could I launch my production house without coming here?" she said.
Reflecting on her experience as a producer, Farooq said the cast and crew had worked collectively despite difficult shooting conditions.
"I will be honest. Every actor who worked with me on the set gave their heart to the project. When we all came together, everyone would ask what needed to be done," she said.
"We shot some very difficult scenes, worked in the heat and cold, and everyone worked extremely hard. We worked together as a team."
Farooq acknowledged that the production had faced several challenges, with uncertainty at times over whether the film would reach audiences.
"There were so many challenges that, at one point, I thought I did not know whether the film would even happen. I left everything to Allah. The fact that we are standing here today, celebrating it and preparing to show it to audiences, is a success for me," she said.
The actor encouraged audiences to watch the film when it opens in cinemas, saying she was eager to see how viewers responded to the project.
Quraishi, who plays the lead role in Mango Jutt , described the film as a family entertainer featuring romance, music, comedy and action.
Speaking at the music launch, he said he and the team had been eagerly awaiting the release.
"We have been waiting for this like anything. My wife has asked me so many times when the film is coming out," he said.
Quraishi said the film's romantic elements were intended to be suitable for family audiences.
"It is a very entertaining film. Romance does not necessarily mean that you cannot sit and watch it with your family. It is a little nostalgic, caring kind of romance," he said.
He added that consent was an important underlying theme that audiences would recognise as the story unfolded.
"That is an underlying element of the film," he said.
"There is laughter, humour, action and everything else. We have tried our best to make it an amazing movie. Now we will see how people receive it," he said.
A romantic song close to Quraishi's heart
Asked about his favourite song from the film, Quraishi said he liked the entire soundtrack but was particularly fond of a romantic number featuring him and Farooq.
"All the songs are special, but there is a romantic song featuring Hareem and me that I really like. The song turned out beautifully, and we had a lovely time shooting it," he said.
Farooq also singled out a dialogue from the film that she had not expected to become so popular before release.
The line plays on the film's title and its central character: " Tu Murad Jutt nahi, Mango Jutt, tu mitha vi ain te sohnra vi ain ."
Mango Jutt is directed by Abu Aleeha and features a supporting cast that includes Shamoon Abbasi, Qaiser Piya, Honey Albela, Hassan Murad and Ayesha Jahanzeb.

Reynolds replied, “Surprising it's mostly girls. At least, that's what I've seen. And the really smart folks already know. Although the narrative at the moment is how insanely well the film is performing and how much audiences love it. So…”
The exchange took place months before Lively filed a complaint against Baldoni in December 2024, alleging sexual harassment during filming. Baldoni denied the allegations.

title: Microfinance must move beyond access

Conference talks about measureable outcomes for women, farmers, microenterprises
The Pakistan Microfinance Network (PMN) concluded the 10th Annual Microfinance Conference (AMC-X) in Karachi, bringing together government officials, regulators, financial institutions, development partners and experts to shape the next phase of financial inclusion.
It was organised in collaboration with the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (Unido) under the EU-funded Poverty Alleviation and Inclusive Development across Rural Sindh (PAIDAR) programme. Under the theme "Pathways for Inclusive Growth: Unlocking Synergies," discussions focused on moving beyond financial access towards client progression, resilience and measurable economic outcomes, particularly for women, farmers, microenterprises and underserved rural communities.
Addressing the conference virtually, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb placed financial inclusion within Pakistan's wider transition from macroeconomic stabilisation towards sustainable growth. He called for greater use of cash flow-based rather than collateral-based lending, digital credit tools and alternative data to bring more borrowers into formal finance, particularly in agriculture and SMEs.
"It's not just how much you lend, how many borrowers you have, but also start measuring outcomes," he said, highlighting borrower graduation, job creation and women's economic participation as important measures of success.
Opening the conference, Amir Khan, Chairman PMN and President & CEO, HBL Microfinance Bank, called for microfinance to be integrated into the wider financial system. "The principle behind everything to follow is to mainstream microfinance into the financial ecosystem, not as a parallel track," he said. Khan stressed that the sector's next decade should be judged not only by outreach but by whether clients were able to progress towards stronger businesses, assets and financial independence.

title: China s AI journey offers insights
description: China s AI journey offers insights
content:
Expert says cooperation should extend beyond individual projects and target technology, expertise
At first glance, Ulanqab in north China's Inner Mongolia and Bahawalpur in southern Pakistan may appear worlds apart. Yet the two regions share a striking landscape of dry weather, vast open spaces and sandy terrain. Their development stories, however, are taking increasingly different directions: while Bahawalpur is exploring new opportunities in technology, higher education and innovation, Ulanqab has leveraged its geographic, climatic and energy advantages to become a growing hub for computing power and artificial intelligence.
A visit to Ulanqab's computing facilities shows how a region traditionally associated with energy and natural resources is becoming part of China's rapidly expanding digital infrastructure. The city has been integrated into China's national "East Data, West Computing" strategy, which channels computing resources towards western regions where land, energy and climatic conditions can support large-scale data centres.
For Pakistan, the transformation raises an important question: could regions with similar dryland environments develop new economic opportunities by connecting energy, education, technology and digital infrastructure?
According to Zhang Xiaoliang, who is associated with the Economic Bureau of Chahar High-tech Zone, Ulanqab possesses several advantages that make it suitable for data-centre development.
"Inner Mongolia has its own power grid," Zhang explained, noting that electricity availability and comparatively favourable power costs are important advantages for data centres, which require stable and large-scale energy supplies. He also highlighted Ulanqab's proximity to Beijing, its relatively cool climate and geological conditions as factors supporting the development of computing infrastructure.
The city's strategy is increasingly linking computing power with green energy. Centrin Data's Ulanqab computing-power cluster, located in the Chahar High-tech Development Zone, is part of the Inner Mongolia national computing hub. The company has planned several large data centres and is developing a source-grid-load-storage project combining wind, solar and energy storage.
The wider Inner Mongolia model is also increasingly associated with green computing. More than 85% of electricity used by regional data centres reportedly comes from clean energy, demonstrating how renewable power can be integrated with energy-intensive AI infrastructure.
But the lesson for Pakistan may not be about building identical data centres. Professor Dr Muhammad Kamran, Vice Chancellor of The Islamia University of Bahawalpur (IUB), argues that the more important question is whether computing infrastructure can be connected with universities, research, industry, energy and human capital. "Computing capacity has to be tied to reliable energy, research institutions, universities, industry and people who actually know how to use it," Kamran said.
For Bahawalpur, this perspective is particularly relevant. IUB is expanding its focus on emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and quantum computing. The university has introduced AI-related learning across disciplines and established an Artificial Intelligence Research and Advancement Lab. It has also launched an advanced Quantum Computing programme in 2026.
Kamran said the value of cooperation with China should extend beyond equipment or individual projects. International partnerships, in his view, can provide technology, expertise and exposure, but Pakistani universities ultimately need to develop their own research capacity, skilled graduates and stronger links with industry.
He stated that the comparison between Ulanqab and Bahawalpur does not mean Pakistan can simply reproduce Inner Mongolia's development model. The two regions have different energy systems, industrial structures and economic conditions. Instead, Ulanqab offers a case study on how natural advantages can be connected with infrastructure and economic demand. For Bahawalpur, the opportunity could therefore lie in connecting its universities, young population, research institutions and emerging technology capabilities with broader national and international digital networks.

title: India unveils dollar curbs to defend rupee
description: India unveils dollar curbs to defend rupee
content:
RBI redirects state oil firms' dollar purchases, tightens currency hedging rules
India on Saturday unveiled fresh measures to shore up the rupee, redirecting oil companies' dollar purchases away from the spot market and tightening hedging rules as the currency hovers near record lows.
The steps by the Reserve Bank of India come as persistent pressure on the rupee, fuelled by surging oil prices and global bond yields, has driven the currency down more than 7% this year. The central bank will open a special window to meet the daily dollar requirements of three state-run oil marketing companies, easing pressure on the spot market.
Under such an arrangement, used during periods of currency stress, the RBI provides oil companies dollars directly from its foreign exchange reserves. Indian Oil, Hindustan Petroleum and Bharat Petroleum will be allowed to access the facility from Monday, the RBI said.
"Addressing oil companies' dollar requirements removes one of the largest sources of demand from the FX market, which should help reduce volatility but it will show up in a depletion of reserves," said Dhiraj Nim, FX strategist at ANZ Bank in Mumbai.
After the steps were announced, the rupee strengthened by about 0.6% against the dollar in the non-deliverable forward market, albeit in thin trading. Elevated demand for protection against further rupee losses has weighed on the currency in recent months, with importers' appetite for dollars far exceeding exporter supply.
The central bank has responded by tightening rules on speculative corporate activity and raising the cost of protection against further rupee weakness. The RBI is "trying to moderate potentially destabilising derivative demand, improve the integrity of underlying exposure verification and discourage circumvention through multiple transactions or repeated rebooking," a person familiar with the central bank's thinking said, commenting on condition of anonymity.
The central bank has mandated that forex dealers maintain a 20% "foreign exchange risk reserve" on derivative contracts used to buy foreign currency against the rupee, for the purposes of hedging current account transactions. The requirement applies to transactions with a notional value exceeding $2 million. The reserve requirement will lift the cost of buying protection against further rupee weakness, helping to discourage excessive hedging, two bankers said. Chinese authorities have previously used similar tools to discourage one-way bets against the yuan.
India's central bank has also slashed the limits on the size of derivative transactions users can undertake without proof of underlying exposure to $5 million from $100 million. The lower cap applies across all derivative products, including exchange-traded futures.

HSATI chief says increase in staple cost will add to inflation burden
Hyderabad SITE Association of Trade and Industry (HSATI) Chairman Zubair Ahmed Ghanghra has criticised an increase of Rs2,500 in the price of a wheat bag, saying the government has failed to control inflation and protect consumers from rising food costs.
He said the increase in wheat and flour prices had placed an additional burden on low- and middle-income households, which were already struggling to meet their basic needs amid persistent inflation. He urged the government to take immediate measures to stabilise prices and ensure that essential food items remained affordable.
Ghanghra stated the government had previously purchased wheat from farmers under provincial budget allocations, a policy that helped maintain price stability and provide relief to consumers. However, the government's decision to stop wheat procurement contributed to price increases and intensified difficulties for the public.
He also questioned the impact of International Monetary Fund (IMF) conditions on government policies, arguing that the authorities should prioritise food affordability while negotiating with the lender.
The HSATI chairman criticised what he described as inconsistent scrutiny of government spending and public relief measures. He questioned why increases in the salaries and benefits of lawmakers and ministers, along with purchases of new vehicles and government aircraft, did not attract the same level of concern that measures to reduce food prices faced. He said this disparity reflected an unfair burden on ordinary citizens, who continued to absorb higher living costs without corresponding increases in their incomes. Ghanghra urged the government to raise the issue of food affordability during negotiations with the IMF and take effective measures to shield essential commodities from inflationary pressures.
He also called on the authorities to investigate the reasons behind the increase in wheat and flour prices and take strict action against hoarding and profiteering. He said stronger market monitoring and enforcement could help prevent traders from exploiting supply conditions to charge excessive prices.
The HSATI chairman warned that persistent increases in the prices of essential goods, without a corresponding rise in household incomes, continued to erode purchasing power and deepen financial pressures on ordinary families.
He said the government must move beyond assurances and introduce practical measures to keep wheat, flour and other staple food within the reach of consumers. He stressed that people needed tangible relief rather than promises as rising food costs continued to strain household budgets.

title: PSX gives up gains despite IMF deal

content:
Benchmark KSE-100 index falls 0.6%; geopolitical risks weigh
The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) closed lower during the outgoing week, with the benchmark KSE-100 index shedding 1,066 points, or 0.6%, to settle at 167,089 on Friday, as persistent geopolitical tensions offset optimism over Pakistan's staff-level agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for disbursement of $1.2 billion in loan tranches.
On a day-on-day basis, Monday saw a negative start due to regional and domestic political conditions. The KSE-100 dived 2,288 points (-1.36%) to close at 165,867 by breaching the 166k level, a key support. Nevertheless, the market staged a strong comeback on Tuesday, with the index gaining 2,593 points (+1.56%) to 168,460, reclaiming the 168k level.
PSX witnessed consolidation on Wednesday, rising just 120 points (+0.07%) to close at 168,580. On Thursday, the IMF's successful review met geopolitical headwinds. The KSE-100 declined 1,139 points (-0.68%) to 167,442. On Friday, the index traded in both directions amid cautious investor sentiment, driven by geopolitical uncertainty and squaring of positions ahead of the weekend. The index lost 353 points (-0.21%) and settled at 167,089.
Arif Habib Limited (AHL) noted that the KSE-100 declined marginally by 0.6% week-on-week (WoW) to 167,089, shedding 1,066 points, as positive sentiment from the IMF staff-level agreement was partly offset by persistent geopolitical uncertainties. Pakistan and the IMF reached a staff-level agreement on the fourth Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and third Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF) reviews, paving the way for $1 billion and $210 million in loan disbursements, respectively, subject to the executive board approval, which would bring total disbursements under both programmes to $5.7 billion.
AHL mentioned that the central government debt decreased by 0.5% month-on-month (MoM) to Rs82.95 trillion (+7.1% year-on-year – YoY) as of Aug'26 compared with Rs77.46 trillion in Aug'25. The government raised Rs381 billion in the recent Pakistan Investment Bond (PIB) auction against the target of Rs350 billion, with Rs208.4 billion allocated to three-year bonds. Yields increased by 26-41 basis points across three, five and 10-year tenors, declined 19 basis points for two-year bonds, while bids for 15-year papers were rejected.
Total cement dispatches rose 6% YoY to 4.62 million tons in Sept'26, driven by a 7% increase in domestic sales, while exports remained flat. 1QFY27 dispatches grew 4% YoY to 13.14 million tons, supported by an 8% growth in local sales despite an 11% dip in exports.
SECMC, a public-private partnership between the government of Sindh and Engro along with its affiliates, was expanding its Thar Block-II coalmine to supply additional coal to Lucky Electric Power Company Ltd (LEPCL). The expansion was expected to enable LEPCL to fully transition to local Thar coal, improving utilisation and regulated returns while reducing reliance on imported coal, which would support foreign exchange savings and strengthen energy security.
Meanwhile, Sazgar Engineering's four-wheeler sales remained flat YoY at 2,474 units in Aug-Sept'26, bringing 1QFY27 sales down 12% to 3,137 units, primarily due to a weak July. Three-wheeler sales rose 32% YoY to 5,173 units during Aug-Sept'26, driving 1QFY27 three-wheeler sales growth of 45% and overall sales growth of 22% to 10,872 units.
Oil production declined 6.4% WoW to 63.7k barrels per day due to lower flows from northern fields, while gas production fell 1.4% WoW to 2,999 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd) amid reduced output from Mari, Sui and Sharf, AHL added in its report.
Wadee Zaman of JS Global noted that the KSE-100 index declined 0.6% WoW to close at 167,089, amid persistent US-Iran tensions and escalating clashes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi forces, prompting the Makkah Defence Alliance to agree on a rapid force deployment. Brent crude remained above $100/barrel, while domestic fuel prices saw mixed adjustments, with motor spirit rising by Rs6.20/litre to Rs398.96/litre and high-speed diesel falling by Rs3.92/litre to Rs395.72/litre.
On the domestic front, Zaman said, Pakistan reached a staff-level agreement with the IMF to unlock $1.2 billion under the fifth tranche of the EFF and third tranche of the RSF. The Fund urged the government to phase out fuel subsidies, broaden the tax base and ensure timely energy tariff adjustments, cautioning that risks remained elevated amid geopolitical tensions, volatile energy prices and trade disruptions.

title: Philips wins court battle over devices recall
description: Philips wins court battle over devices recall
content:
Shareholders allege misleading disclosures, management failures
A Dutch court on Saturday dismissed demands by shareholders of health technology company Philips for an investigation into allegations of misleading disclosures and management failures linked to the company's recall of sleep apnea devices.
A large group of shareholders had demanded a court inquiry, as they said Philips executives had responded too late to the problems that led to the massive recall and had failed to adequately inform investors.
Philips' shares lost about two-thirds of their value when the company recalled around 15 million sleep apnea devices in 2021, after discovering that the foam in the machines could release harmful substances and might pose health risks.
The Enterprise Chamber of the Amsterdam Court of Appeal in its ruling said it had found no indication that Philips had known about the problems long before it issued any warning.
It also said there was no reason to assume executives should have intervened earlier at the Respironics subsidiary that made the devices. Philips had denied the accusations made by the shareholders and said it welcomed the court's decision.

title: FinMin unaware of IMF fuel subsidy objection
description: FinMin unaware of IMF fuel subsidy objection
content:
Says targeted petroleum discounts will continue
Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb expressed ignorance about the IMF's concerns over Pakistan's fuel subsidy scheme during a brief interaction with The Express Tribune at the International Poultry Expo 2026, saying targeted subsidy was the way forward and the scheme would continue to benefit vulnerable segments of society.
The remarks came despite the IMF calling for the fuel support scheme to be phased out promptly, citing its high cost and broad targeting.
Asked about the IMF's position, Aurangzeb questioned where the media had heard about the objection. When told that the information had been officially issued by the IMF and reported by mainstream media, he suggested that the Fund might have conveyed its concerns to the subscriber but said he had not been informed by them.
Asked why the government had not announced smart lockdowns to conserve fuel stocks and reduce the rising fuel import bill, as it had done previously when domestic fuel prices exceeded Rs400, the minister said targeted subsidies had made such lockdowns unnecessary by allowing deserving segments of society to purchase fuel at subsidised rates.
In a subsequent interaction to clarify the matter, Aurangzeb reiterated that the targeted subsidy scheme had been successful and had benefited around 10.2 million people. The IMF, in its October 7 press release announcing a staff-level agreement on the fourth review of the Extended Fund Facility and the third review of the Resilience and Sustainability Facility for Pakistan, called for the fuel support scheme to be phased out promptly, citing its high cost and broad targeting.
Under the heading "Prioritising Social Spending", the IMF stated that any future fuel support, should oil prices rise unexpectedly, should be limited, time-bound and targeted, delivered through established social assistance programmes, and accommodated within the fiscal year 2026-27 budget envelope.
Speaking at the event, Aurangzeb said the prime minister had disclosed a day earlier that around 10 million people had benefited from the subsidy scheme. These included users of Qingqi rickshaws, other three-wheelers, motorcycles and cars with engines below 800cc.
Assuming an average household size of five people, the minister said, the scheme's benefits could extend to around 50 million people. He added that the programme would continue to support vulnerable and deserving segments of society.
Aurangzeb also said Pakistan could not afford long marches and sit-ins if it wanted to sustain economic growth of 4% or above, adding that such disruptions caused daily losses of around Rs120 billion.
The finance minister appreciated the organisers of Poultry Expo 2026 for bringing together a large number of local and foreign businesses. He said the livestock sector accounted for 63% of agricultural GDP and had recorded fairly impressive growth. However, despite Pakistan being the world's 11th largest poultry producer, its share in global poultry exports remained negligible.
He said the poultry sector needed to improve its export potential by addressing logistical constraints, strengthening disease management and reducing input costs.
Aurangzeb said the government had decided to establish a separate administrative vertical for livestock in view of the sector's importance. The proposed arrangement would give the private sector greater autonomy in decision-making, while oversight would remain with the Ministry of National Food Security and Research. He said the sector would enjoy greater operational freedom, drawing a comparison with the Export Development Fund, from which ministers and government functionaries had reportedly been removed to give the private sector greater control.
When asked why the government was involving exporters and importers in security-related measures by using their containers as roadblocks, and whether this was fair to businesses, Aurangzeb questioned whether it was fair to attack the country's capital when matters could be resolved through dialogue. He also questioned whether such actions were permissible in a democracy.

title: Businesses seek industrial tariff below 9 cents
description: Businesses seek industrial tariff below 9 cents
content:
FPCCI appreciates 12-cent rate, links cheaper power to export growth
Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce & Industry (FPCCI) President Atif Ikram Sheikh has acknowledged the government's reduction of the industrial electricity tariff from 16 cents to 12 cents per unit over the last two years. He said that a further reduction to below nine cents, extended to all industrial consumers, was the definitive way to raise exports and reduce imports.
He cautioned that the 12-cent rate and selective schemes were temporary fixes and that only a uniform reduction for all industries, including B3 and B4 category consumers, could lift exports and cut imports.
Sheikh thanked Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif and Federal Minister for Power Awais Ahmad Khan Leghari for the relief. He also acknowledged the minister's effort to bring forward two measures to meet industrial demand: an incremental consumption package and an optional two-part Time-of-Use (ToU) tariff. He welcomed the holding of three sessions with the industry on them.
The FPCCI chief said that the incremental consumption package offered a concessional rate on electricity consumed above a consumer's own baseline – which was its previous consumption. Existing load is billed as before and the incentive applies only to additional units. The two-part ToU tariff splits the bill into a fixed capacity charge per kW per month and a variable charge per unit that differs by time of use – with separate rates for non-solar, solar and peak hours. Its aim is to encourage industry to consume more during the day, when solar generation is abundant and so ease the duck curve.

title: Businessmen demand urgent reforms
description: Businessmen demand urgent reforms
content:
KCCI seeks liveable, secure, economically competitive Karachi
Businessmen Group (BMG) Chairman Zubair Motiwala has called for an urgent, coordinated drive to rescue Karachi from its deepening civic and economic crisis, questioning how Pakistan's economic powerhouse, contributing 67% of federal revenue and 54% of national exports, continues to suffer from crumbling roads, acute water shortages, unreliable utilities, deteriorating sewerage and rampant street crime.
Addressing a meeting of patron-in-chiefs, presidents, secretary-generals and representatives of Karachi-based trade bodies and industrial town associations, Motiwala demanded time-bound action, institutional accountability and measurable results, stressing that Karachi needed delivery, not promises.
Highlighting the economic cost of civic mismanagement, Motiwala warned that unreliable electricity and gas, inadequate infrastructure and low industrial capacity utilisation were driving up production costs and undermining competitiveness. He called for the early completion of K-IV, a fully operational Safe City system, a Karachi Bypass to potentially divert 70% of heavy traffic away from the city, mandatory road-restoration guarantees, independent engineering audits and a business-friendly tax regime. He also demanded transparent electricity billing, automatic consumer compensation for service failures, regionally competitive gas prices, digital land records and faster tax refunds.
Motiwala proposed identifying five immediate priorities, assigning responsibility to relevant institutions and establishing firm deadlines and measurable performance indicators. He also called for a unified platform of Karachi's trade and industrial associations, backed by active participation from their members, to press the authorities for corrective action. Emphasising that the objective was a liveable, secure and economically competitive Karachi, not political or administrative controversy, he urged all stakeholders to replace fragmented efforts and repeated assurances with a coordinated, results-driven strategy.
BMG Vice Chairman Anjum Nisar urged Karachi's trade and industrial bodies to move beyond highlighting problems and develop a unified, actionable agenda to address the city's worsening civic and economic challenges. To highlight the awful state of Karachi, he called for a common documentary exposing the city's ground realities, including corruption, extortion, excessive taxation and deteriorating infrastructure.
He advocated permanent solutions to water shortages, completion of the long-delayed K-IV project, and a practical fiscal model empowering local governments with adequate resources. He also proposed joint pre-budget consultations by KCCI and trade associations to formulate common recommendations. He emphasised stronger collective representation before federal and provincial authorities, consistent follow-up and, if negotiations failed, coordinated protest to secure Karachi's legitimate rights, stressing that the city's issues must be pursued as a common cause rather than individual organisational demands.
Vice Chairman BMG Jawed Bilwani urged Karachi's business community to unite behind three to four decisive priorities, warning that the city's longstanding problems would persist without sustained collective pressure and accountability. He demanded urgent implementation of the Safe City project, stronger action against street crime and land grabbing, protection of public land, and transparent documentation and allocation of Karachi's revenues to meet its civic and infrastructure needs.

title: Economic stability  borrowed   Iqbal
description: Economic stability  borrowed   Iqbal
content:
Minister worries stabilisation will carry cost for next general election
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has termed economic stabilisation "stunted and borrowed" and urged Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to alter growth trajectory before election cycle begins to present something to voters more than just saying we "inherited an economic crisis".
In his detailed memo, Iqbal recommended an eight-point new Growth Compatible Fiscal Stabilisation Framework for higher growth and development instead of merely saying in polls that we "inherited an economic crisis" and achieved stability. He wrote to the PM last month that Pakistan was increasingly achieving fiscal stabilisation by compressing development expenditure and borrowing more, rather than sufficiently expanding the revenue base and increasing exports.
"To me, it is stunted and borrowed stabilisation. It may improve fiscal numbers today, but if continued, it will weaken the productive capacity required to sustain those numbers tomorrow," he said.
His memo has surfaced at a time when a new World Bank report stated that one out of every two poor people in the region spanning Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan was living in Pakistan. Iqbal supported fiscal discipline but said that the issue was "the composition and quality of fiscal adjustment". A country cannot permanently balance its books by cutting the expenditure that creates its future productive capacity and borrowing more to plug its external-sector requirements, he added.
In 2018, the federal development expenditure was equal to 2.6% of GDP, which has been slashed to 0.8% this fiscal year. The Express Tribune waited for two days for response of the finance ministry to the criticism of stabilisation policies. But the ministry did not respond.
Ahsan Iqbal reiterated that the present approach to the IMF programme management has increasingly become numbers-driven, with overriding emphasis on quantitative fiscal targets. Fiscal targets are necessary, but merits and composition of the numbers matter as much as the headline deficit, he added.
Iqbal wrote to the PM "we must consequently ask a simple but critical question now: Where will Pakistan's economy stand in 2029 when this government goes back to the people". He went on to say that in 2029, it would be insufficient to point only to the inherited macroeconomic crisis or the stabilisation achieved thereafter.
"The electorate will judge the government on the economy it experiences in 2029: growth, employment, income, investment, exports, inflation, energy costs and economic opportunity," he wrote. According to official figures, economic growth was a mere 3.7% in the last fiscal year, unemployment was at a 21-year high of 7.1% of the labour force and exports contracted nearly 6% last fiscal year. Investment was stagnant at 14.4% last year and foreign direct investment fell 34% to only $1.6 billion.
Commenting on the overall success of economic policy, the planning minister said that the relevant test of economic policy is, therefore, no longer merely whether Pakistan can complete the IMF programme successfully. "It is what kind of economy emerges after the IMF programme and what economic record this government will present to the people in 2029."
He said that almost half of the government's five-year term has already passed and it effectively has about two and a half years remaining, and the final year will inevitably be dominated by the general election. "The window available for taking decisions that materially alter Pakistan's growth trajectory is, therefore, much shorter than the constitutional remainder of the term suggests".
He recommended that the finance and planning ministries should jointly identify what growth rate Pakistan is currently heading towards by 2029, what growth rate is required, and what policy changes must be made now to close that gap. Iqbal suggested that the government should establish a clear economic destination for 2029 and work backwards from it. "Otherwise, there is a risk that we successfully manage successive IMF reviews and annual budgets but arrive at the election with macroeconomic stability accompanied by insufficient growth, investment and employment."
The planning minister added that the government's engagement with the IMF must similarly evolve "from a narrow conversation about next year's numbers into a broader economic framework addressing how Pakistan will grow, invest, export and generate the revenues necessary to maintain stability over the next decade". He suggested that the PM establish a forum where the Ministry of Finance should be specifically directed to present its baseline projections for the economy through fiscal year 2028-29, including the expected growth trajectory and the likely state of the economy when the government completes its term.
"The Ministry of Finance should, therefore, be asked to present to the prime minister and cabinet a credible post-IMF medium-term economic scenario through FY2028-29, rather than limiting our horizon to the next programme review or annual budget."
The planning minister further wrote that between 2022 and 2026, successive rounds of fiscal adjustment have placed disproportionate pressure on the federal development programme. "Whenever the fiscal space contracts, the PSDP becomes the easiest expenditure to postpone, reduce or surrender." At these levels, he said, the federal development programme is approaching a point where it can no longer adequately perform its basic economic function with a through forward of Rs11 trillion. Cutting productive investment beyond a critical threshold is economic de-capitalisation, he added.
Iqbal said Pakistan continues to have a tax-to-GDP ratio substantially below that of many comparable economies. With a low tax base, there is a danger that inadequate taxation of under-taxed segments and leakages in tax collection are effectively being compensated for through cuts in development spending. "The economy sacrifices infrastructure, education, technology, water security and productivity because the state has been unable to mobilise sufficient revenues from the economy." It is administratively easier to cut PSDP than to undertake difficult reforms involving tax broadening, enforcement, documentation, exemptions and politically influential sectors," said the minister.
He feared that the greatest danger is that Pakistan may successfully stabilise at a structurally low rate of economic growth. The sequence is straight forward which is low revenue, fiscal pressure, PSDP cuts, lower public investment and infrastructure and human-capital deficits, weaker private investment, lower productivity, slower growth and weaker future revenues. "If development expenditure remains at rock-bottom levels, our potential growth rate will be damaged."

George Clooney has spoken about death of Presley Gerber, describing loss as devastating for his family
George Clooney has spoken publicly about the death of Presley Gerber, son of model Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, describing the loss as devastating for his family.
The actor, 65, made his first public comments about Presley’s death while attending The Albies 2026 with his wife, Amal Clooney, in London on Friday, October 9.

George and Amal have a longstanding friendship with the Gerber family. In the days following Presley’s death, the couple were photographed visiting Kaia’s home in Los Angeles.
The families’ relationship extends beyond their personal lives. George and Rande co-founded Casamigos tequila in 2013 alongside businessman Mike Meldman.
The idea developed from time spent together in Mexico, where George and Rande owned neighbouring homes.
Presley died on September 20 at a treatment facility in Santa Monica, aged 27. Authorities have been investigating his death as a suspected overdose.
According to reporting published on October 9, his official cause of death remained deferred pending further investigation.
Born in 1999, Presley pursued a modelling career and signed with IMG Models as a teenager.
He made his runway debut for Moschino in Los Angeles in 2016 before working with fashion houses including Dolce & Gabbana, Burberry and Bottega Veneta. He also appeared in campaigns for Calvin Klein.
In June, Presley joined his parents at the We Are ENOUGH x Aviator Nation launch in Malibu, where he participated in a panel discussion.

title: Wladimir Klitschko granted temporary guardianship of Hayden Panettiere   s estate
description: Wladimir Klitschko has been granted temporary guardianship of Hayden Panettiere   s estate ahead of December hearing
content:
Wladimir Klitschko has been granted temporary guardianship of Hayden Panettiere’s estate ahead of December hearing
Wladimir Klitschko, the former fiancé of actor Hayden Panettiere, has been granted temporary guardianship of her estate following her death in August. Their 11-year-old daughter, Kaya, is the sole heir to the estate.
According to People , Klitschko appeared virtually in court on Thursday, October 8, alongside Kaya.
He had filed a petition in Los Angeles County court on September 24, seeking permission to represent his daughter in matters concerning her inheritance.
The filing cited concerns over items seized from Panettiere’s home during a federal investigation, as well as reports that unauthorised individuals had gained access to her Los Angeles residence. Klitschko alleged that some of the actor’s possessions could be at risk of being removed or sold.
"Without an immediate appointment for these purposes, there is a high probability that property belonging to Hayden's Estate may be lost, damaged or dissipated before a duly appointed personal representative can be in place to protect it," the filing stated.
According to ABC News , Klitschko submitted a supplementary filing shortly before the court hearing, expressing concern that someone outside Panettiere’s family was selling some of her belongings, including jewellery, to a pawn shop.
He also asked the court for authority to request law enforcement investigations into the recovery of property believed to have been misappropriated.
Panettiere, known for her roles in Heroes and Nashville, was found unresponsive at a residence in Greenville, South Carolina, on August 16.
The Greenville County Coroner’s Office ruled her death an accidental overdose involving several drugs, including fentanyl.
Panettiere and Klitschko had an on-and-off relationship between 2009 and 2018 and became engaged in 2013. Their daughter was born in 2014.
Klitschko has had full custody of Kaya since 2018, when Panettiere relinquished custody amid struggles with postpartum depression and substance abuse.
In an Instagram post following Panettiere’s death, Klitschko wrote, "Nothing will erase the times we shared or the place she had in our lives."
The next court hearing is scheduled for December 7, when permanent guardianship of the estate will be considered. Kaya will not need to attend.

title: When states feel secure but people don t
description: When states feel secure but people don t
content:
Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, Lebanon, Iran and Yugoslavia have all become victims of this tragic cycle
Today's column is based on two premises. One, unhealthy politics leads to an unhealthy state. Two, the state is more secure when the people are secure. The problem is not simply that states pursue security, but that the pursuit of state security through dominance, militarisation and strategic competition can undermine the very human security it is supposed to protect. Be it Ukraine, the Arabian Peninsula, the wider Middle East, Ethiopia, Sudan or the many African states afflicted by civil war, it is the state rather than the people who have increasingly become the primary referent object of security. Politics around the world is based on the prevailing political assumption that people are secure when the state is secure.
Yet this logic often produces a tragic cycle. First, the state oppresses its own people, which invites a military intervention by big powers claiming a moral and international obligation to liberate the people from domestic oppression. The intervention, then, provokes resistance from the very people it claims to protect, who rise against a foreign military presence. The intervening power eventually withdraws. Generally speaking, at the end of the cycle, and after much death and destruction, there is little change in the lives of the people. In some cases, people continue to live under the same regime or one no less oppressive than the one they had originally sought to escape.
Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, Lebanon, Iran and Yugoslavia have all become victims of this tragic cycle. Now Ethiopia appears to be a potential laboratory for similar experiments. Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a devastating border war between 1998 and 2000, before eventually moving towards reconciliation. In 2018, their rapprochement culminated in a peace agreement for which Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019. Yet the promise of peace proved short-lived. In 2020, Eritrea joined Ethiopian federal forces in the war against the People's Liberation Front of Tigray. The Tigray leadership demanded greater constitutional and political autonomy, while Addis Ababa viewed the Tigray leadership as an obstacle to its broader national ambitions, including securing reliable access to the Red Sea. Eritrea's port of Assab lies only about 40 km from Ethiopia's northern frontier, although Tigray lies between the two.
The human cost of this conflict has been catastrophic. The 19982000 Ethiopia-Eritrea war is estimated to have claimed tens of thousands of lives, while the conflict that erupted in Tigray in 2020 produced an even greater humanitarian catastrophe. Estimates of deaths associated with the conflict including those resulting from fighting, famine and the collapse of medical services vary, with some reaching hundreds of thousands. At roughly 140 million, Ethiopia is Africa's second most populous country. It is a strategically located state whose internal instability has consequences that extend well beyond its borders. The recent deterioration in Ethiopia-Eritrea relations is particularly alarming because it suggests that the peace that once earned international acclaim and a Nobel Peace Prize is once again giving way to the logic of confrontation.
The geopolitical dimensions of the crisis make the situation even more complicated. Saudi Arabia has cultivated close relations with Eritrea, because of the latter's strategically important position along the Red Sea, a maritime corridor of vital significance to Saudi security and commerce. Egypt also maintains close relations with Eritrea, largely because of its deep concerns over Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile, upon which Egypt depends heavily for its water supply. Sudan shares a long border with Ethiopia and has its own historical, ethnic and territorial interests along the frontier. The communities living on either side of the border have strong social and family connections.
Ethiopia, on the other hand, has developed a close relationship with the UAE, which has become an important economic and strategic partner and investor. Turkey and Israel further complicate this emerging geopolitical picture. Analysts view the relationships among Israel, the UAE and Turkey through the broader lens of competition for influence in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea. Israel, in particular, has maintained a longstanding relationship with Ethiopia, providing military assistance, training and technology since the 1960s, when Ethiopia was confronting the Eritrean insurgency. Israel also wants to maintain strategic relevance in the Horn of Africa by securing a meaningful stake in the evolving architecture of Red Sea maritime security. The result is a domestic conflict whose strategic geography is attracting a wide circle of regional and extra-regional powers.
Ethiopia clearly demonstrates the central dilemma of modern international security. A domestic conflict rarely remains domestic once it intersects with the strategic interests of surrounding states and major powers. What begins as a struggle over constitutional authority, political autonomy, territory or access to resources can gradually become a contest over ports, trade routes, maritime security, regional influence and geopolitical alignment. The danger is that people are caught in the middle again, and their security calculations become secondary.
Both primacy, with its pursuit of global and regional dominance, and restraint, grounded in the principles of liberal internationalism, have failed to deliver lasting global peace. As competing grand strategies, neither has succeeded in preventing great-power wars or the proxy conflicts waged in the shadow of great-power rivalry. The world must therefore look beyond these competing approaches and confront a deeper source of international instability - the security dilemma. Through the security dilemma, one state's pursuit of security becomes another's source of insecurity, setting in motion a cycle of fear, militarisation and confrontation.
As states increasingly securitise their national interests in the name of protecting sovereignty and territorial integrity, the modern international system sees states become more heavily armed and more determined to defend their borders. Yet the people living within them become increasingly insecure, exposed to violence, death and destruction. Breaking this cycle requires a different way of conceptualising international order - one that moves beyond the endless pursuit of dominance and the limitations of restraint. The answer may lie in 'civilisationalism', an emerging concept that seeks to rethink how civilisations coexist and engage with one another in an increasingly contested world. Still a work in progress rather than a fully developed theory, civilisationalism offers a possible starting point for reimagining global peace. Details on it in my next article.

title: Rumble in the political jungle
description: Rumble in the political jungle
content:
PTI's long march turns into a circuitous one
As the PTI's long march turns into a circuitous one, it is increasingly becoming clear that it is heading nowhere - both literally and metaphorically. In fact, it may have triggered an outcome for the party far bigger than intended, and far less favourable than expected.
1. The status quo in Khyber-Pukhtunkhwa may have outlived its utility. Change is in the air. This change is a by-product of three factors (i) Uncoordinated decision-making by the PTI leadership; (ii) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi's compulsions to fulfil his leader's perceived expectations; and (iii) Spike in terrorism and PTI's inability to adjust its approach accordingly. Taken together, these three factors have set in motion a series of events that may be very difficult to reverse from here on.
2. The federal government has a few constitutional options on the table. Whichever one it decides to go with, the outcome - direct or indirect - may be as follows: (i) PTI government in K-P will lose its executive authority in any real sense of the word (or will be diluted to an extent that it will mean the same); (ii) K-P assembly will have little role that could obstruct the governance of the province from the Centre; and (iii) the office of the chief minister will be hollowed out and its occupant will either go home or will sit in his room and catch up on his casual reading. From the federal government's perspective this will be a legally water tight arrangement.
3. Immediately thereafter, there will take place in the province a massive reshuffle of the bureaucracy and civil administration. The lists have almost fully been prepared. This reshuffle will go down to the junior cadres at the provincial, district and even tehsil level. The most sweeping changes are expected in the districts affected deepest by terrorism.
4. Access to Imran Khan is expected to remain restricted while these changes are taking place. Access has proved to be the most effective weapon in the hands of the government against the PTI. It has led to confusion, lack of policy clarity, bickering and deepening of divides within the party. The court order to bring Khan to the hospital is unlikely to be complied with. Sohail Afridi's ill-planned long march may have triggered events that may have not taken place for many more months. Now everything appears expedited.
5. Will PTI's resistance make the new arrangement untenable? This one factor worries decision-makers. They underestimated PTI's pushback in the February 2024 elections. All calculations done prior to the elections pointed to a smooth affair and equally smooth results. Like now, back then too field reports suggested things would work out as planned. The initial results, as they poured in from far and near that election night, were a massive body blow to the system. Yet again, PTI's rank and file had reminded all that cared to listen that Khan's supporters could not be taken for granted. Two can, as they proved, play the game. Can they, still?
6. The party's leadership will be tested even more severely if and when they lose the huge advantages that their provincial government offers. PTI has, without any doubt, enormous vote bank in Punjab. Yet the party and its leadership has failed spectacularly, every single time, to translate this support into street power. Could the same happen in K-P if the party is out of power? Hard to say at this point because K-P remains a PTI stronghold for the last thirteen years. But if the provincial leadership remains divided and at daggers drawn, and many are detained, and the party organisation comes under severe strain, and access to Khan remains cut-off, and his family's movement to K-P is barred, can the leadership put up the kind of resistance that may be required for it to retain its credibility among its support base? PTI's Punjab leadership hasn't really wrapped itself in glory these past few years.
7. Expect the counter-terrorism policy to go into much higher gear if and when the situation changes in K-P. Knowledgeable officials inside Islamabad's Red Zone say the following factors are shaping possible options and actions: (i) The diplomatic route with the Taliban government in Kabul is not working. The recent meeting in Moscow and Russia's sympathetic attitude towards the TTA has reinforced this assessment. This approach is now under review; (ii) Opposition groups inside Afghanistan are organising themselves better and are expected to step up their efforts against Kabul. There will be greater instability and the TTA may have to start looking over their shoulders; (iii) in districts of K-P (including the newly merged districts of erstwhile FATA), aim is to uproot the presence of TTP and ensure that spillover from events that will transpire inside Afghanistan in the months to come is blocked. A similar plan is underway for Balochistan. The change of military high command in the two provinces earlier this month is connected to this evolving strategy.
8. What happens in K-P may not stay in K-P. Red Zone insiders also say the debate over new provinces and administrative units may have subsided within the public domain but the project is very much alive and perhaps picking up pace. If a change in the K-P structure does indeed take place, it will be the first of what may be a long line of bigger governance changes across the land.
9. There's a Grand Bargain in process and PTI may be missing the bus. Notice the change of tone between the PML-N and PPP. Notice also the muted - and in some ways flexible - politics of JUI-F and Jamaat-e-Islami. The give-and-take of this bargain may lead to a loose consensus on governance reforms, and enhanced security policy. Things are still fluid but a pattern is slowly becoming visible.
10. The rumble in the political jungle is getting louder and louder as PTI's long march gets shorter and shorter. Could anything go wrong?
