title: GDP share no measure of farm tax
description: GDP share no measure of farm tax
content:
Experts say agricultural revenue is lost across value chain
Whether agriculture contributes enough to Pakistan's tax revenues compared with its share of the economy has long been a recurring debate in the country's economic discourse. However, agricultural experts argue that the sector's tax potential cannot be judged simply by its contribution to GDP, as farmers' actual profitability is shaped by volatile crop prices, yields, input costs, weather shocks and changing market conditions.
They cautioned that treating the value of agricultural production as equivalent to taxable income could produce unrealistic revenue expectations, particularly for Pakistan's millions of small farmers who often sell crops at prices below official or expected rates.
Mahmood Nawaz Shah, President of the Sindh Abadgar Board, said the fundamental distinction in the taxation debate was between economic output and actual farm income. He cited wheat as an example, saying farmers could incur losses even though their production continued to contribute to GDP. During the 2024-25 wheat season, he said, the government announced prices around Rs4,000 per 40 kg and later Rs3,900, while farmers in major producing areas sold wheat at substantially lower rates.
"If the farmer sells below his cost or expected price, how can that production be treated as taxable income?" he asked, arguing "GDP captures the value of production while taxation should ultimately be linked to profitability." Shah said similar questions needed to be examined for cotton, maize, rice and sugarcane, where production, yields and market prices can vary considerably from year to year.
He rejected the argument that agriculture's share in GDP should automatically determine its tax contribution. Instead, he suggested that the government should calculate the sector's realistic tax potential using average profitability over five- to seven-year periods.
He also questioned the assumption that the agricultural workforce should correspond directly to the tax potential. Agriculture supports a large share of Pakistan's employment, he said, but its income is distributed among millions of people, resulting in relatively low income per worker in many parts of the sector.
Muhammad Ali Iqbal, President of Concave Agri Services, said the problem was particularly acute because more than eight million farmers were engaged in agriculture, with the overwhelming majority cultivating relatively small holdings. As farm sizes become smaller in many parts of the country, he said, applying a uniform tax structure becomes difficult. Farmers also face uncertain revenues because crop prices can change sharply between sowing and harvesting.
Iqbal said taxation should therefore take into account three critical variables: input costs, yield and output prices. Input costs have increased because of taxation and other market pressures, while yields remain constrained by seed quality, technology gaps and other production problems. At the same time, farmers have limited control over the prices they receive when crops reach the market.
He said the situation was different in commodities where government-supported prices or more predictable markets provide some basis for estimating income. "Price uncertainty, price transparency and price discovery are critical issues," Iqbal said, adding that the government could not accurately determine taxable income without reliable information on production and prices.
He said technology could help address the problem. Satellite imagery, remote sensing and improved yield-estimation algorithms could allow authorities to estimate cultivated areas and crop production at district and tehsil levels and cross-check farmers' declarations. Such technology, he said, could eventually help establish a more credible relationship between actual farm production and taxable income.
Aamer Hayat Bhandara of Agriculture Republic also called for digitisation of the agricultural value chain, arguing that the government should establish a transaction record covering the movement of produce from farms to markets and ultimately to processors and consumers.
He suggested that agricultural commodities entering mandis (markets) should be weighed through electronic systems, with quantity and quality digitally recorded along with the transaction. "Such a farm-to-fork digital trail could help determine the actual volume and value of agricultural trade while reducing the scope for under-reporting," he said.
Iqbal said the issue also extended beyond the farmer because much of the economic value generated by agriculture is captured elsewhere in the supply chain. Food companies, processors, exporters and manufacturers purchase agricultural commodities as raw materials and add value before selling finished products. Companies such as food processors purchasing tomatoes, chillies and other crops can therefore generate significant revenues from agricultural raw materials, even though that value may ultimately be recorded under manufacturing or other sectors. He said, "agriculture should consequently not be examined in isolation when assessing its contribution to tax revenue."
Iqbal also pointed to the fragmented and undocumented nature of agricultural transactions. Farmers and agricultural SMEs frequently receive payments late and may lack the financial and digital literacy needed to maintain formal records. This makes it difficult for both taxpayers and tax authorities to establish actual annual income.
He argued that the government should also examine whether the existing regulatory environment discourages formalisation among agriculture and food-sector businesses. Compliance requirements involving the Federal Board of Revenue, particularly when companies source raw materials from farmers who may be non-filers, can create additional burdens for formally incorporated businesses, he said.

content:
Ambassador acknowledged Pakistan's legislative progress and positive developments in areas relevant to the GSP Plus
Federal Minister for Commerce Jam Kamal Khan has invited German companies to explore investment opportunities in Pakistan and participate in the upcoming FoodAg exhibition in Karachi.
He extended the invitation as Pakistan and Germany discussed ways to deepen bilateral trade, investment and business-to-business cooperation. The discussion was held during a meeting with German Ambassador Ina Lepel, who called on the commerce minister.
Khan appreciated Germany's longstanding economic cooperation with Pakistan and its constructive role in relation to the European Union's GSP Plus scheme. He reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to fulfilling its international obligations and strengthening coordination among federal ministries and provincial governments.
The ambassador acknowledged Pakistan's legislative progress and positive developments in areas relevant to the GSP Plus, noting that these efforts reflected Pakistan's commitment to reforms and stronger institutional mechanisms. She emphasised the importance of translating legislative measures into effective implementation, measurable results and tangible improvements for citizens.

title: Pakistan  Qatar agree to review LNG deal
description: Pakistan  Qatar agree to review LNG deal
content:
Companies of both sides serve price review notice on each other
Pakistan and Qatar have agreed to review a multimillion-dollar liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply contract amid a gas glut in the South Asian nation. The two sides have already signed a deal for diverting 24 LNG cargoes to other destinations in the current calendar year.
Sources told The Express Tribune that Pakistan State Oil (PSO) and Qatar had served LNG contract review notices. PSO is seeking the consent of the federal government to review the contract with QatarEnergy, a firm designated by Qatar. The two countries had entered into two LNG contracts that would expire in 2031.
PSO and QatarEnergy have a sale-purchase agreement for 15 years covering 2016 to 2031 and the other contract is for 10 years effective from 2021 to 2031.
The second LNG contract proved controversial, signed during the PTI government, as the country did not need more LNG, which led to a market glut. Both sale-purchase agreements (SPAs) had been struck under a government-to-government arrangement. As per these deals, PSO receives 6.75 million tonnes of LNG (108 cargoes) each year.
The agreements are on a "take-or-pay" basis. Both contracts have minimal flexibility for diversion – all surplus cargoes, if sold abroad, lead to a profit accruing to QatarEnergy while all loss is to be borne by PSO.
Owing to a declining demand from the power sector, LNG supply in Sui's system had become surplus. To cope with that, the government in 2023 authorised PSO to negotiate with QatarEnergy a reduction of two cargoes per month. As a result, 24 cargoes were reduced in the 2026 annual delivery plan. The Attorney General Office provided contractual guidance on the matter.
As per terms of both agreements, price review negotiations have been triggered, for which both parties are required to negotiate the price for the remaining period. QatarEnergy served a price review notice on PSO dated March 7, 2026 in respect of SPA-II and PSO served a price review notice on QatarEnergy dated March 19, 2026 in respect of SPA-I.
Under Clause 15.2 of SPA-I, either party may issue a price review notice to renegotiate the contract price, but not before the 10th anniversary of the start date, ie, March 1, 2026. Once the notice is issued, the parties are required to meet in good faith to discuss and agree on any price adjustment.
If agreed, the revised contract price will apply from the review date until the end of the supply period, with neither party entitled to issue a further notice. If no agreement is reached within six months of the notice, either party may terminate the agreement, with termination taking effect at the end of the contract year in which the notice is served.
This effectively gives Pakistan three options: negotiate a revised price; accept the existing price if negotiations fail; or terminate the agreement (though termination carries supply continuity risk) while attempting to seek greater flexibility in the contractual framework.
Under Clause 15.2 of SPA-II, either party may issue a price review notice between March 7 and 31, 2026, setting out the reasons why the contract price no longer reflects market conditions. At the review date, the parties are required to review and, if necessary, adjust the pricing formula so that the contract price falls within the range of prices under comparable contracts, regardless of source of supply, with price review benchmarked against comparable LNG contracts and reputable industry publications.
Unlike to the extent that the buyer takes any action, or omits to take any action of an administrative nature (other than those actions taken or omissions made in the course of the performance of and not in violation of, this agreement, and save to the extent to which the seller contributed to such action or omission), which results in the buyer being subjected or exposed to taxes imposed, levied or assessed in Qatar or by any Qatari competent authority, 16.1 shall not apply. In such a case, the parties will cooperate with a view to eliminating or diminishing the imposition, levying or assessment of such taxes on the buyer.

title: Pakistan looks to tap advanced Russian agri technologies
description: Pakistan looks to tap advanced Russian agri technologies
content:
Discussions explore field trials of seeds and pesticides, tech transfer
Federal Minister for National Food Security and Research Rana Tanveer Hussain held a meeting with a delegation from the prominent Russian agricultural and agrochemical company, Schelkovo Agrohim. The delegation was accompanied by the second secretary and other officials of the Russian embassy.
The meeting focused on exploring practical cooperation between Pakistan and Russia in seed development, crop protection, pesticides, micronutrients, advanced fertilisers, agricultural research, technology transfer and investment.
Hussain said that Pakistan was seeking agricultural cooperation with Russia that could go beyond imports of finished products and lead to technology transfer, local production, joint research, breeding programmes and capacity building of Pakistani experts. He said Pakistan needed advanced agricultural technologies and seeds that would enhance productivity while demonstrating greater resilience to drought, diseases, pests and climatic stress. The Russian delegation briefed the minister on Schelkovo Agrohim's pesticides, advanced pesticide formulations, micronutrients, micro-fertilisers, biological products and high-quality seeds for various crops. The company also presented its research and production capabilities in seeds and hybrids of wheat, maize, sugar beet, rapeseed/canola and sorghum. According to the Russian delegation, the company's maize seeds are non-GMO.
The meeting identified effective pest and disease management in cotton, rice, sugarcane and vegetables as key areas for potential cooperation. Discussions also covered micronutrients and alternative plant nutrition solutions that could improve nutrient-use efficiency and potentially reduce dependence on conventional fertilisers. Hussain said that climate change posed a growing challenge to Pakistan's agricultural production. Therefore, climate-resilient technologies, drought-tolerant seeds and disease-resistant crop varieties are being accorded priority.
Discussing cooperation in the seed sector, Pakistani officials emphasised that future collaboration should not be limited to the import of finished seeds. Instead, practical cooperation could focus on access to suitable Russian germplasm, joint breeding programmes, technology transfer, seed traceability, local seed multiplication and the establishment of a Russian seed company or partnership in Pakistan.

title: Gold falls as global prices hit low
description: Gold falls as global prices hit low
content:
Loses Rs3,100 to Rs434,436 per tola; rupee inches up to 277.02/$
Gold prices in Pakistan fell on Wednesday, tracking a decline in the international market, where the precious metal dropped to a two-month low as a stronger US dollar and elevated Treasury yields reduced demand for the non-yielding asset.
The price of gold per tola fell Rs3,100 to Rs434,436, according to rates shared by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association. Similarly, the price of 10-gram gold declined Rs2,658 to Rs372,458. On Tuesday, gold had remained unchanged at Rs437,536 per tola.
The decline in the domestic market came as gold prices extended losses internationally, with investors turning cautious amid a stronger dollar and higher US Treasury yields. Internationally, spot gold fell 1.2% to $4,113.89 per ounce by 2:12 pm EDT (1812 GMT), after touching $4,066, its lowest level since August 5, according to Reuters. US gold futures for December delivery settled 1.1% lower at $4,140.70.
Other precious metals also came under pressure. Silver declined around 3%, while platinum dropped nearly 4%. Palladium also fell to its lowest level in more than a year. Adnan Agar, Director at Interactive Commodities, said gold had moved lower as expected, with the market recording a low of around $4,066 before recovering somewhat.
"Gold went down today (Wednesday)," Agar said, adding that the market was trading around $4,111, while the day's high was approximately $4,170. He said the market had been showing signs of slowdown and eventually followed that direction.
However, Agar said the outlook would depend on where gold closes. "If the closing comes below $4,100 again, the market will be in trouble," he said. According to him, a sustained close above the $4,100 level could keep open the possibility of a rebound towards $4,160-$4,180.
The latest decline in global gold prices reflects pressure from financial-market factors, particularly movements in the dollar and US government bond yields. Higher Treasury yields increase the opportunity cost of holding gold, while a stronger dollar makes the metal more expensive for holders of other currencies.
In Pakistan, the domestic gold market generally follows international bullion prices, with movements in the rupee-dollar exchange rate also influencing local prices.
Meanwhile, the price of silver fell Rs100 to Rs6,488 per tola in the local market. Furthermore, the Pakistani rupee extended its marginal gains, closing at Rs277.02 against the US dollar, up Rs0.03 from Tuesday's Rs277.05.

title: IMF tranche tied to SOE reforms
description: IMF tranche tied to SOE reforms
content:
Fund seeks amendments to govt companies' law for release of $1b
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has proposed a prior action to amend state-owned enterprises (SOEs) laws for qualifying for the next $1 billion tranche, as the scheduled time for review talks ended on Wednesday.
Chairman of the Senate Standing Committee on Finance, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla, said that the committee will evaluate the laws and pass them if they are in the national interest.
The federal government had missed all the deadlines in the past to amend these laws, which the global lender has been pushing to make sure that the entities are governed in line with best international practices.
The government was reluctant to move swiftly on these laws despite the Finance Ministry itself disclosing this week that the public debt of SOEs, excluding contingent liabilities, soared to a record Rs10.1 trillion by December last year. This was 242% or Rs7.1 trillion higher than what was earlier reported by the central bank.
Government officials said that the IMF staff has proposed a prior action to amend the SOEs laws. If a staff-level agreement is achieved on this condition, the IMF will convene the board meeting to approve the next $1 billion loan tranche after parliament amends these laws, they added.
A senior PPP leader, Syed Naveed Qamar, said on Wednesday that all the legislation should only go through parliament.
Pakistan and the IMF held staff-level talks from September 23 to October 7. Till the filing of the story, the IMF did not issue a press statement about the outcome of the talks.
During scrutiny of the budget, the IMF has also objected to Rs180 billion out of the Rs853 billion statistical discrepancy. Sources said that the IMF wanted to adjust the Rs180 billion amount against the claimed primary budget surplus of the last fiscal year.
During review talks, the IMF aired concern over the delay in amendments after Pakistan missed the fourth deadline to bring 9 to 10 laws of SOEs in conformity with the main SOE law. During each staff-level review, the government failed to meet the deadline, and every time it sought a fresh date, the latest one was August 2026.
As a result, the IMF asked the Pakistani authorities to align the laws with the SOE Act before mid-November. Subject to the agreement, the IMF board could meet in late November to approve the next loan tranche of $1 billion under the Extended Fund Facility.
The IMF has already disbursed $4.2 billion out of the $7 billion package mainly due to progress on fiscal and monetary matters.
Pakistan had sent amendments to six laws for parliament's approval in January 2026. The report added that the government now needed to make progress on the remaining three SOEs with dedicated laws.
Secretary Finance Imdad Ullah Bosal told the National Assembly Standing Committee on Finance that the laws of Port Qasim Authority, Gwadar Port Authority, Karachi Port Trust, State Life Insurance Corporation, the National Bank of Pakistan, National Telecommunication Corporation and Pakistan Railways would be amended.
The IMF expressed concern over the delay in amendments to the Sovereign Wealth Act. The extended deadline was March 2026.
Sources said that the IMF has not yet accepted Pakistan's request for adjusting the increase in the monthly stipend of the Benazir Income Support Programme beneficiaries. Currently, two benchmarks - inflation and food expenses - are used for determining the annual increase.
Pakistani authorities have requested the IMF that the annual increase in stipend should only be linked with inflation and its benchmarking with consumption cost should be stopped. The proposal further added that the resultant saving of Rs30 billion should then be allowed to be used for conditional cash transfers under the BISP. This would ensure better targeting of beneficiaries.
The IMF also did not respond to a proposal to allow the existing Export Processing Zones to sell 20% of the total production in the domestic market. The government had proposed that the existing EPZs should be exempted from the condition, and the 100% export condition should only be applicable to the new EPZs.
The government on Thursday appointed Mariam Kayani – a Grade 20 officer in the finance ministry as new senior adviser to the executive director of the IMF for three years. She would replace Saif Dogar, who has completed the term and is now returning to Islamabad.
The IMF programme has so far helped improve fiscal and monetary numbers, and all the hard reforms, including in SOEs and broadening the tax base to traders, real estate and agriculture sectors, have failed.
The failure to bring meaningful reforms has also dented the IMF's reputation in Pakistan, as the brunt has been sustained only by the salaried class and the corporate sector.
The government has also violated the conditions of giving tax breaks, and it could not liberalise the sugar sector by breaking the monopoly of the sugar millers.
The World Bank reported this week that 48% of the poor in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (MENAP) region were living in Pakistan, and poverty increased due to a prolonged period of adjustment under the IMF programme.

title: Sydney Sweeney and Marilyn Monroe share a surprising family connection
description: Sydney Sweeney and Marilyn Monroe are ninth cousins  once removed  according to new genealogy research from MyHeritage
content:
Sydney Sweeney and Marilyn Monroe are ninth cousins, once removed, according to new genealogy research from MyHeritage
Sydney Sweeney and Marilyn Monroe are distant relatives, with genealogy research finding that the actresses are ninth cousins, once removed.
The connection was identified by family-history platform MyHeritage, which traced the actresses’ family trees through their fathers. Sweeney’s father, Steven Sweeney, and Monroe’s biological father, Charles Stanley Gifford, both reportedly descend from Ezra Perry, a 17th-century settler in Sandwich, Massachusetts, who lived from around 1625 to 1689.
Roi Mandel, MyHeritage’s director of research, said the company decided to investigate a possible family connection after years of comparisons between Sweeney and Monroe.
Sweeney has frequently been compared with the late Hollywood icon because of her vintage-inspired appearances and styling. Earlier this year, she accepted a Virtuosos Award at the Santa Barbara International Film Festival wearing a vintage Ceil Chapman gown that closely resembled the dress Monroe wore on the cover of Life magazine in April 1952. Sweeney’s stylist, Molly Dickson, later confirmed that the look was intentionally inspired by Monroe.
The Euphoria star also channelled Monroe at the Los Angeles premiere of The Housemaid , where she wore a white Galia Lahav gown with a feathered skirt. The look echoed Monroe’s famous costume from the 1955 film The Seven Year Itch .
The genealogy discovery adds another connection between Sweeney and Monroe beyond their visual similarities and shared association with classic Hollywood style.
MyHeritage has previously uncovered celebrity family connections, including a reported distant relationship between Friends stars Matthew Perry and Courteney Cox.

title: David Harbour and John Cena set to star in  The Family Disappears
description: David Harbour and John Cena will star in  The Family Disappears   a new dark comedy from Fifth Season
content:
David Harbour and John Cena will star in 'The Family Disappears', a new dark comedy from Fifth Season
David Harbour and John Cena are set to lead The Family Disappears , a new comedy from Fifth Season that will be directed by Swedish filmmaker Jonatan Etzler.
Based on an original screenplay by Brendan O’Hare, The Family Disappears follows an overworked father who returns home from a work trip to discover that his family has vanished. He then finds that a mysterious newcomer has bought the house and moved in, setting the story up as a comedy with thriller elements.
Fifth Season is producing the film, with Nick Weidenfeld through Friends Night and Alexis Garcia through CAT5 serving as producers. The pair previously worked together on Friendship , the comedy starring Tim Robinson and Paul Rudd that was also produced by Fifth Season and A24.
The film is expected to have a darkly comic tone similar to Friendship and HBO’s DTF St. Louis , the latter of which recently earned Harbour an Emmy for his performance.
Production on The Family Disappears is scheduled to begin in Atlanta, Georgia, on November 10.
Harbour recently starred in DTF St. Louis and is preparing to conclude his five-season run as Jim Hopper in Stranger Things . His upcoming projects include Avengers: Doomsday , Violent Night 2 and John Rambo .
Cena, meanwhile, earned his first Emmy nomination this year as an executive producer of Prime Video’s Heads of State , in which he also stars alongside Idris Elba. His upcoming projects include Matchbox the Movie and Netflix comedy One Attempt Remaining , opposite Jennifer Garner.
Etzler most recently directed the dark comedy Bad Apples , starring Saoirse Ronan.

title: What do we know about plague institute lab worker s death in Russia
description: Russian media identified victim as Darya Shipilova  28  a laboratory worker at Irkutsk research centre
content:
Russian media identified victim as Darya Shipilova, 28, a laboratory worker at Irkutsk research centre
Local authorities in Russia's Siberian region of Irkutsk have imposed quarantine measures on people and several hospital departments amid reports of a possible "plague" outbreak.
Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology."
The employee died from her illness, according to numerous media reports and official statements, while authorities placed those who had contact with her under medical observation.
Read : Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
Rospotrebnadzor later said the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region was "calm."
The developments, however, have raised concerns and public health fears on social media.
Here is what is known about the reported outbreak:
On Friday, Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said that he convened an extraordinary meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission following reports of a suspected "highly dangerous infectious disease" in a resident.
Kobzev said Rospotrebnadzor organized and was implementing a comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures, adding that the watchdog and regional government were closely monitoring the situation.
"I would like to inform you that all identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, none of the contacts show any signs of illness, and laboratory test results have come back negative," Kobzev said.
Maxim Modin, mayor of Irkutsk's Shelekhovsky district, said the same day that several departments of the district hospital in Shelekhov suspended patient discharges and admissions.
Alexey Tsydenov, head of the neighboring Russian Republic of Buryatia, said the woman who died in Irkutsk "possibly from the plague" had not visited his region.
Tsydenov said there were no "plague" outbreaks in Buryatia, including in areas bordering Mongolia.
Two days later, Rospotrebnadzor said no emergencies had been reported while working with pathogenic microorganisms at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute.
It said the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region and the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov was "stable."
The watchdog added that no cases of infectious disease had been reported among employees of the institute over the previous 10 days.
Rospotrebnadzor said Monday that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was "calm."
Media attention intensified after local outlet People of Baikal on Friday reported that the institute employee, identified as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, allegedly broke a test tube containing "pneumonic plague."
The outlet reported that she became ill after allegedly breaking the test tube late last month and was hospitalized in Shelekhov, where she died Friday evening.
Several high-level officials have commented on the situation, urging people to rely on official assessments from relevant authorities.
"Rospotrebnadzor is the lead agency with competence in this area," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a news conference in Moscow on Monday.
"It is precisely Rospotrebnadzor's official statements that should be heeded, rather than listening to various rumors or speculations," Peskov said.
He added that the watchdog employs top-tier professionals in the field and again urged people to "heed their official statements."
US President Donald Trump said Monday that Washington was closely monitoring the reported case of "pneumonic plague" in Russia and pledged assistance.
"Years ago you could treat pneumonia easier, and the microbes and the germs have gotten stronger," Trump told reporters at the White House before departing for a campaign rally in Nebraska.
"But we'll help them. We'll help them," he added.
Responding to Trump's comments, Peskov said it is "always good when mutual assistance is offered."
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday that it was closely monitoring reports of a "suspected case of pneumonic plague" in Russia that resulted in one death.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russia the same day to provide full transparency and share detailed information about the incident with the international community.
The World Health Organization told Russian state news agency Tass that it was maintaining contact with local health authorities over the incident.
The WHO said that, based on "available unofficial information," it assessed the public health risk in the region as low.
While the exact cause of the reported illness remains unclear, official statements have raised questions about plague.
Plague is an infectious illness caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, which spreads through small wild mammals and their fleas, according to the WHO.
The WHO said bubonic plague is the most common form, while pneumonic and septicemic forms are invariably fatal unless treated early.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague is the most virulent form, with an incubation period potentially as short as 24 hours.
Plague was historically responsible for the "Black Death," a pandemic in Europe in the 14th century that resulted in more than 50 million deaths, according to the WHO.

title: Glen Powell opens up about parents    simultaneous cancer diagnoses
description: Glen Powell recalls feeling helpless after both parents were diagnosed with cancer  saying he lacked resources to help
content:
Glen Powell recalls feeling helpless after both parents were diagnosed with cancer, saying he lacked resources to help
Glen Powell has opened up about the emotional and financial challenges he faced after both of his parents were diagnosed with cancer at the same time.
The Chad Powers actor was 24 when his mother, Cyndy Powell, and father, Glen Powell Sr., received their diagnoses. In Esquire’s October/November 2026 cover story, Powell recalled how difficult it was to find the resources needed to support his parents while he was still trying to establish his acting career.
Powell said his mother’s illness was particularly severe and that his family did not have significant financial resources at the time. His desperation to help led him to contact people who might be able to assist with medical care.
“I was like a telemarketer, calling everyone I knew who could have donated to a hospital ever,” Powell said.
The actor also reflected on his fears about being unable to provide his parents with the best possible treatment.
Fortunately, both of his parents’ health later improved. Powell said the experience became a major motivation for him to achieve financial stability, so he could support his family if they faced serious health problems again.
Years later, when his parents experienced further health difficulties for different reasons, Powell was in a stronger financial position. He said he was able to pay for their treatment and arrange concierge doctors and detailed care plans.
Powell has remained close to his parents, who have supported him throughout his career. Cyndy and Glen Sr. have attended several major events with their son and have also appeared in some of his films and television projects, including Spy Kids 3 , Anyone But You and Chad Powers .

title: 3 killed  36 injured in attacks on Saudi Arabia s Abha  Riyadh airports
description: Saudi aviation authority says attacks caused material damage  Houthis claim targeting both airports
content:
Saudi aviation authority says attacks caused material damage; Houthis claim targeting both airports
Three people were killed, and 36 others were injured in attacks targeting two airports in Saudi Arabia, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation said Wednesday.
GACA said Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks Tuesday and Wednesday, with emergency and relevant authorities responding to both incidents.
The attack on Abha International Airport killed two residents -- one Moroccan and one Algerian and injured 28 people, the authority said.
#Statement Attacks Target Abha and King Khalid International Airports. #GACA pic.twitter.com/R4nrRlHRsA
The injured included two Saudi citizens and residents of Bangladeshi and Filipino nationalities, with injuries ranging from minor to serious, GACA added.
At King Khalid International Airport, a Sudanese national was killed and eight people were injured, including five Saudi, two Egyptian and a Pakistani national, the authority said.
All those injured were immediately taken to hospitals for medical treatment, GACA said, adding that the two attacks also caused material damage.
The authority said it continues to coordinate with relevant security agencies to assess the damage and take necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and airport employees.
Yemen's Houthis claimed Wednesday that they had carried out attacks targeting both airports.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with drones and carried out another operation against Abha International Airport using ballistic missiles and drones.
The attacks came amid an escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the Yemeni government against the Houthis since March 2015.
The Saudi-led coalition said that it destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Yemen’s Sanaa that was used in an attack on Riyadh.

US Mission warns of heightened security risks in Saudi Arabia
Meanwhile, the US Mission in Saudi Arabia issued a security alert Wednesday, urging Americans to exercise heightened vigilance amid hostilities and Houthi threats against airports and airspace in the kingdom.
“The Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including against civilian airports, and the military conflict has the potential to escalate,” it said.

title: Pakistan  India and the betrayal of South Asian identity
description: India pronounced the verdict before producing evidence acceptable to anyone outside its own official narrative
content:
India pronounced the verdict before producing evidence acceptable to anyone outside its own official narrative
Pakistan and India have spent nearly eight decades proving how different they are. Yet underneath the politics lies an older truth: both countries emerged from the same geographical and civilisational space. Partition gave that space two states, not two unrelated histories. Our languages still lean into one another. Our food carries the same aromas. Our music recognises itself across the border. Even our quarrels have the intimacy of a family argument that has gone on for too long.
The Indus belongs to this shared geography. It travels through mountains and valleys that existed long before either countries appeared on a map. It nourishes fields without asking which anthem is played nearby. That is why India's decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty "in abeyance" after the Pahalgam attack was so reckless. New Delhi tied the future of a water agreement to its allegation that Pakistan supported cross-border terrorism. In doing so, it turned a river system sustaining millions into an instrument of political pressure.
The attack at Pahalgam was horrifying. Twenty-six lives were lost. But accusation cannot become judgment merely because it is repeated loudly. Pakistan denied involvement and proposed an independent and credible international investigation. India chose military action instead.
India pronounced the verdict before producing evidence acceptable to anyone outside its own official narrative. That narrative has since faced uncomfortable questions. When Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was pressed on whether Pakistan's alleged role constituted state terrorism, he said his counry's intelligence agencies had provided no such information. Similarly, at a recent press conference, the Pakistani military presented an individual whom, it said, India had identified as connected to Pahalgam and later claimed to have killed. The contradiction is not a minor detail. It goes to the heart of India's case: who was investigated, what was established, and how could military punishment precede an independent determination of responsibility? These questions cannot be drowned out by television graphics and patriotic slogans.
Pakistan's own past is complicated. There were policies on militancy that damaged the country and gave others reason for suspicion. But history cannot be used as permanent evidence against a nation. Pakistan today is itself bleeding from terrorism. According to figures released by Pakistan's military, the country's law-enforcement and intelligence agencies conducted 75,175 intelligence-based counterterrorism operations in 2025, while over 1,200 civilians and members of law-enforcement agencies were killed.
There is an irony here that India should not be allowed to overlook. The Hindu god Indra is worshipped as the breaker of Vritra's hold - the divine force that struck down the power obstructing the waters and released the rivers for humanity. Water, in that sacred memory, was not the property of the strongest. Its release was an act of order, justice and life. What, then, should one call a politics that celebrates Indra for freeing the waters but applauds a government for threatening to withhold them? This is not an argument borrowed from Pakistan. It is a reminder drawn from India's own religious inheritance. A civilisation cannot worship the liberator of rivers and, in the same breath, glorify the politics of their obstruction.
India remembers Indra as the liberator of waters. Yet its present rulers speak of rivers as though they were possessions to be withheld when politically convenient. A civilisation cannot celebrate the freeing of water in scripture while applauding its weaponisation in state policy.
The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960 not because Pakistan and India trusted each other, but because they did not. Its genius lay in accepting hostility as a fact and still creating rules strong enough to protect ordinary life from that hostility. The treaty survived wars, broken diplomatic relations and decades of bitterness. It kept working because both countries understood that water could not be made hostage to every crisis.
India now claims the right to set that understanding aside unilaterally. But the treaty contains no provision allowing one party simply to suspend it. In June 2025, the Court of Arbitration held that India's declaration of "abeyance" did not affect the court's competence and that the treaty remains in force until both countries replace or terminate it through a duly ratified agreement. New Delhi rejected the court's authority.
This is what majoritarian power often does: it mistakes strength for entitlement. India's larger economy, military weight and upstream position may give it leverage, but they do not give it moral ownership of the Indus.
The politics is short-sighted in another way. India cannot sever Pakistan from South Asia without denying the geography to which India itself belongs. The two countries may have separate flags, but they share a climate system already under extraordinary stress. Glaciers are retreating, rainfall is becoming less predictable, floods are intensifying and populations are growing. This is precisely the moment when cooperation should deepen - not when water should be added to the arsenal of retaliation.
The Indus has flowed through empires that once imagined themselves permanent. It outlived them all. The question is not whether the river will continue towards the sea. It will. The question is what kind of people will live along its banks: neighbours who understood that survival required restraint, or rivals who discovered too late that geography cannot be defeated.

title: Afghanistan   losing the cause
description: Pakistan  in dealing with a recalcitrant Kabul regime  is left with the military option as the only residual leverage
content:
Pakistan, in dealing with a recalcitrant Kabul regime, is left with the military option as the only residual leverage
The relations between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban regime are in freefall, with no improvement likely in the near to mid-term. The IEA will not budge on the TTP, and Islamabad will not give an inch on its core demand that Kabul rein in the TTP and not permit Afghan soil to be used against Pakistan. The IEA refusal acts in open violation of the 2020 Doha Agreement, and shows complete disregard for the precepts of neighbourly obligations under gawandgiri (neighbourliness), Islamic amity and pashtunwali.
The bilateral ties have fractured following intense cross-border strikes by Pakistan Army and airstrikes by PAF inside Afghanistan on suspected TTP locations. This came after Pakistan had exhausted all peaceful options, diplomatic contacts, warnings, mediation efforts and repeated assurances. Situation is further complicated by the IEA's overtures to India, quite paradoxically. Regional powers, China, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Türkiye have repeatedly attempted mediation with mixed results.
Recently, both countries clashed at the 8th Moscow Format, a Russia-led regional mechanism launched in 2017 to build consensus on Afghanistan. Quite comically, IEA's interim FM, Amir Khan Muttaqi, emphasised resolution of all bilateral issues through dialogue, criticising Islamabad's 'military approach'. Pakistan's special representative, Ambassador Sadiq, delivered 'a blunt assessment', reiterating the centrality of Afghanistan-based terrorism directed against Pakistan. He highlighted the not-so-hidden TTP-IEA nexus, providing statistics, and accused IEA of being 'complicit' in anti-Pakistan terrorism. He defended Pakistan's military operations as acts of self-defence. Afghanistan has repeatedly dubbed TTP as Pakistan's internal problem. No joint statement was issued by Moscow Format due to a lack of consensus.
Pakistan, in dealing with a recalcitrant Kabul regime, is left with the military option as the only residual leverage, having exhausted the other pressure points at P2P and B2B levels. The latest Corps Commanders Conference, held on Oct 2, 2026, strongly supported current military strategy; and ISPR characterised IEA as 'delusional Taliban leadership'. The ISPR chief disclosed that during a meeting in Qandahar on August 26, IEA directed representatives of terrorist groups to step up anti-Pakistan attacks. September 2026 was the deadliest month in 12 years. Let's see if Islamabad's current strategy is working.
First, the timeframe under consideration is too short to evaluate if and when a strategy is working. Pakistan officially shuns G2G contact but tacitly looks the other way at selected B2B and P2P overtures, purely on humanitarian grounds. Despite overt hostility, Afghanistan still enjoys public support – whether it is repatriation of Afghan students and refugees or Afghan patients in search of affordable treatment in Pakistan. Possible distinction between Kabul under IEA and the wider Afghan citizenry is being made. Even military pressure is calibrated, proportionate and allows for course corrections. Targeting Taliban leadership, for example, if push comes to shove, should not be outside Pakistan's military capability.
Second, diplomatically, Islamabad must 'continue' to impress upon IEA that supporting TTP does not serve their bilateral, regional or global interests. Recognition of the interim regime and relative isolation are cases in point. Intelligence collaboration to discreetly target TTP on Afghan soil needs to be re-established to ease out the IEA from its predicament, as TTP remains IEA's historic baggage, that they can neither doff nor carry. Saner elements within Qandahar realise the insanity of Rahbari Shoora's obstinacy on this issue, and would like to revert to normalcy with Pakistan, their indispensable interlocutor.
Third, Islamabad should revive and strengthen its relations and contacts with the myriad Afghan resistance groups. If IEA can warm up to an erstwhile hostile New Delhi, Pakistan is well within its right to foster its ties with former Northern Alliance and other groups. They represent sizeable populations and enjoy clout in Central Asia and Türkiye. All is not well beyond the Hindu Kush. Badakhshan may have been temporarily pacified but the seed of resistance against IEA-led Kabul are resistant to force. Resistance groups (NRF, AFF) carried out 78+ operations during July-September 2026 (details were covered in earlier pieces). These attacks reportedly killed 126 Taliban personnel, including 14 senior commanders, besides material losses. Key IEA institutions, like ministries of Defence and Interior, and Intelligence HQs, were also targeted.
Fourth, at the geostrategic levels, the 'Great Game' continues with changed set of players. The US would like to keep its listening posts on Afghan soil, given its proximity to Iran, China, Russia, Central Asia and nuclear Pakistan. With the passage of time, there may be more palatable options to the rigid and frigid IEA, and the die for change might then be cast. In the mid to long-term, IEA will either have to reform or undergo an in-house change (for the better), or relinquish power, as it did in 2001. The US/West's sporadic engagement with Kabul presently should not be confused with a love lost. It is simply motivated by the fact that presently there are no viable and workable alternatives to the IEA, on the important real estate of Afghanistan.
Russian FM Lavrov's conciliatory tone during Moscow Format, praising IEA gains against ISK needs to be analysed in context. Russia courts IEA in its desperation to: a) keep Afghanistan-generated terrorism and narco trade in check; b) regain lost foothold in Afghanistan; c) deny space to the US; d) protect its soft underbelly in Central Asia, and; e) be poised to exploit Afghanistan's mineral riches. The Russia-India-Afghanistan nexus will work 'ostensibly' for regional security, and to keep the US (and China for India) out. China's interests complicate the picture. In all this jockeying for power, the IEA, by default, attracts centrality, hence the various forms and format of engagement with Kabul.
Fifth, as the relationship does not yield to the old formula of 'engagement' through diplomacy, mediation and pressure, and since Taliban leadership cannot be trusted as a partner, nudging towards a regime change may be 'seemingly' the last option. The 'doves', who believe Afghanistan should be left to its own devices, are living in oblivion of ignorance. With an ongoing hot war on terror, the terror swamp being on the Afghan soil, and K-P and Balochistan intertwined with Kabul and Qandahar; overlooking Afghanistan is simply not an option.
Walking away from military option without solving the TTP problem leaves Islamabad with an even bigger security challenge. Although terrorism does have a domestic dimension. Continuation of strikes conversely risks prolonged confrontation with IEA. No easy choices, hence, a policy reappraisal to include whole-of-nation approach, employing all elements of national power, to protect Pakistan's core regional and bilateral interests.

title: A four year road to nowhere
description: University Road serves as the city s primary educational artery
content:
University Road serves as the city's primary educational artery
"The work on University Road is nearing completion. The entire project will be completed within two months. Now we can say University Road has been built."
When Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon delivered these remarks on Sunday, September 27, 2026, he had just arrived in a sprawling official cavalcade for a red-carpet inauguration of the Mosamiyat Flyover, a key component of the Red Line BRT project. However, the optics of this pompous display stood in stark contrast to the grim reality on the ground.
Launched in 2022 and originally slated for completion in 2024, the 24km Red Line project has been derailed by repeated delays, negligence and gross mismanagement. Instead of becoming a beacon of modern urban transit, one of the largest development schemes in Karachi's history has morphed into a multi-year nightmare for commuters.
While the minister proudly declared a premature victory, frustrated citizens questioned the spectacle, especially amid widespread reports that the newly inaugurated flyover was unceremoniously shut to traffic immediately after the photo-op ended. Although Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah has issued a public apology for the agonising delays, words offer little comfort to the thousands of residents who endure the corridor's chaos daily.
After years of public frustration and contractor failures, the Sindh government recently resorted to approving off-budget emergency funding to hand over Lot 2, a 12.85km stretch from Numaish to Mosamiyat, to the FWO. Following the sealing of the previous contractor's offices, the FWO took over the site on April 29, pledging to first repair the battered alternative routes currently being used by traffic.
While this changing of the guard offers a glimmer of hope, the public remains understandably sceptical. For over four years, the residents of Karachi have been forced to navigate what resembles a war zone rather than a transit corridor. The physical and environmental toll has been devastating. Commuters are choking on hazardous levels of dust pollution, leading to a sharp spike in respiratory ailments among regular commuters and nearby residents. Open trenches and treacherous uneven tracks pose a severe daily hazard to motorcyclists, resulting in countless accidents and ruined vehicle suspensions.
Because University Road serves as the city's primary educational artery, the students have borne a disproportionate share of this suffering. Thousands of students attending the University of Karachi, NED University of Engineering and Technology spend exhausting hours trapped in endless gridlocks.
The economic fallout along the route has been equally catastrophic. The University Road strip has turned into an economic graveyard for many businesses. Local business owners and restaurant operators have watched their foot traffic vanish.
Perhaps most tragically, this chaotic gridlock severely impacts medical emergencies. With major healthcare facilities like the Aga Khan University Hospital and Liaquat National Hospital situated adjacent to this corridor, ambulances frequently find themselves trapped in the suffocating bottlenecks.
Citizens have heard high-sounding promises and arbitrary deadlines before, only to see target dates routinely blown past without a shred of accountability for these profound daily sufferings.
The crucial question now is whether the minister's two-month timeline is grounded in reality or is simply another political promise. Transferring Lot 2 to a military-run engineering organisation may accelerate the civil works, but monumental structural and logistical hurdles remain. Relying on emergency funding highlights the glaring systemic failures in urban planning and financial stewardship that plagued the project's initial execution.
The citizens of this metropolitan city do not need ceremonial inaugurations or belated apologies. They need functional, safe and efficient public transportation. If the Sindh government genuinely wishes to restore public trust, it must abandon staged ribbon-cutting events and deliver a fully operational bus service. University Road will only truly be "built" when buses are running on schedule, commuter hardship ceases and accountability is established for the years of neglect that paralysed one of the city's vital arteries.

title: Mpox threat
description: Isolation guidance also needs to reach households clearly
content:
Isolation guidance also needs to reach households clearly
Sindh's growing mpox caseload requires a more visible and organised public-health response before sporadic infections become harder to contain. The province has recorded 93 confirmed cases this year and 11 deaths, while the recent rise is particularly concerning. Twenty cases were reported in September and another six have already emerged in October. Karachi has recorded the highest number, followed by Khairpur and Sukkur.
The numbers remain relatively small compared with those of some other infectious diseases, but that is precisely why containment must begin early. Sindh's immediate priority must be stronger case detection. Doctors at public and private hospitals and emergency departments should be able to recognise suspected cases quickly and report them through the provincial surveillance system without delay. Laboratories must have sufficient capacity to return results promptly. Every confirmed infection should trigger careful contact tracing so that exposed individuals can be monitored and advised before another chain of transmission develops.
Isolation guidance also needs to reach households clearly. Pakistan's national guidelines call for infected people to remain separated from others until their rash has healed, the scabs have fallen off and a fresh layer of skin has formed. Vaccination should also form part of the preparedness strategy, but it must be targeted. WHO does not recommend indiscriminate mass vaccination. It advises prioritising people at greater risk of exposure, including close contacts of confirmed patients and healthcare personnel handling cases. Pakistan should assess available stocks and access to international supply mechanisms before a larger outbreak creates an urgent scramble for doses.
Mpox is containable. What turns a manageable outbreak into a wider public-health problem is delayed diagnosis and weak surveillance coupled with complacency between individual cases. Sindh still has the opportunity to interrupt transmission while the numbers remain limited. It should use it.

title: Rs10 trillion black hole
description: Rs10 trillion black hole
content:
Debt is also highly leveraged, and the numbers are moving in the wrong direction every second of every day
The finance ministry's latest SOE monitoring report is an economic horror story. State-owned enterprises have accumulated a staggering Rs10.1 trillion in debt as of December 2025 - a 14.3% year-on-year increase. But even this figure conflicts with the SBP data, which puts the same debt at Rs2.95 trillion. That is no minor discrepancy - the gap is Rs7.1 trillion, or 242%.
Debt is also highly leveraged, and the numbers are moving in the wrong direction every second of every day. Loss-making SOEs bleed Rs2.8 billion every day, or Rs730 billion annually. Government support through subsidies, grants, loans and equity injections reaches Rs6.6 billion per day, or Rs1.7 trillion each year. Combined, these figures represent an annual burden of Rs2.5 trillion, Rs1.5 trillion more than the entire federal development budget.
The power sector is the worst offender. Distribution companies have become synonymous with inefficiency and general inability to even recover dues from their customers. Circular debt stood at Rs1.675 trillion at the end of June 2026, as distribution companies contributed Rs112 billion in inefficiencies and Rs31 billion in under-recoveries during the first six months of the year. The 10 state-owned power distribution companies collectively lost Rs299 billion and absorbed Rs551 billion in subsidies during FY25, a total drain of Rs850 billion.
But the solution is not in the government's promise to privatise nine distribution companies by December 2027. The IMF has rightly questioned whether the proposed sale model will actually stem losses, as unfunded pension liabilities of Rs2 trillion, foreign-currency exposure of Rs2.6 trillion and sovereign guarantees exceeding Rs2.1 trillion further compound the sovereign's balance-sheet vulnerability.
Finance ministry officials have also conceded that "financial engineering and debt reprofiling measures alone remain insufficient". Without operational reforms across the board, including at generation and distribution, pricing and theft control levels, the taxpayer will be left footing the bill for the next series of ineffective half-measures.

title: Guterres in Pakistan
description: Guterres in Pakistan
content:
Guterres lauded Pakistan's unflinching support for the Palestinian right to self-determination
Pakistan's diplomatic contributions to global peace and security have been highly eulogised. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, on a farewell visit to Islamabad as he relinquishes his high office, commended the country's "pivotal role" in mediating between the US and Iran, and called on both parties to end the conflict and return to diplomacy. The tribute was unparalleled, as the world body chief went on to term the Islamabad MoU a "frame for future negotiations" while expressing hope that better sense would prevail to save the world from another impending catastrophe.
Guterres lauded Pakistan's unflinching support for the Palestinian right to self-determination and its role at the vanguard of the struggle against colonialism. He highlighted the broadened perspective the country brought to the august forum by championing multilateralism, noting that as an ardent proponent of UN reform, Pakistan has firmly opposed both the addition of permanent members to the UNSC and the retention of the veto power. Beyond these institutional stances, the country spearheaded the unanimous adoption of a landmark resolution against Islamophobia, successfully establishing an official commemorative day on the UN calendar. The top diplomat further commended Pakistan's humanitarian efforts in hosting millions of Afghan refugees while paying tribute to the deep sacrifices of Pakistani soldiers serving under the UN Blue Helmets in global conflict zones. Finally, he praised the critical diplomatic initiative that culminated in the adoption of Resolution 2788, a Pakistan-sponsored framework dedicated to strengthening multilateral mechanisms for the peaceful settlement of disputes.
Pakistan believes in collective wisdom at the world fora, and has opposed interventions and wars. By underscoring the importance of negotiation, mediation and preventive diplomacy, Islamabad has buoyed the role of the UN. As the world slips into a terrain of no-rules-based world order, it's time for the UN to assert its writ and work on the manifesto of making the planet a better place to live in by eradicating poverty, hunger and transgression of power-intoxicated states.

title: Preparing students for the AI age
description: Teacher who merely transfers information now competes with a machine that is available twenty four hours a day
content:
Teacher who merely transfers information now competes with a machine that is available twenty-four hours a day
On Teachers' Day, I came across a question on social media: What should be the greatest quality of a teacher? My response was: a teacher's greatest quality should be that he or she does not kill the student's curiosity. Students should be taught that knowledge begins with a question and, in some sense, ends with one too. In between, we find answers shaped by evidence, context, time and place - answers that must always remain open to scrutiny. In the age of AI, that reflection has acquired a new urgency. We need to train students to ask better questions more than feeding them answers.
For centuries, education was built around scarcity. Books were scarce. Experts were scarce. Information was difficult to access. The teacher therefore occupied a privileged position as the possessor and transmitter of knowledge. The good student was often the one who remembered most accurately what the teacher had said. AI is quietly dismantling that arrangement which, if not catered for with a better alternative, would make formal education completely redundant.
Today, a student can ask a chatbot to explain Keynesian economics, solve an equation, summarise a research paper, draft a business plan or compare competing philosophical arguments within seconds. The quality is uneven and errors remain real but the direction of travel is unmistakable. Answers, once scarce, are becoming abundant. And when answers become cheap, education built primarily around producing answers becomes increasingly difficult to defend. This does not make teachers irrelevant. It makes a certain type of teaching irrelevant.
The teacher who merely transfers information now competes with a machine that is available twenty-four hours a day, never becomes impatient and can explain the same idea repeatedly in ten different ways. Trying to preserve the old educational model by banning AI may therefore resemble protecting the horse-drawn carriage from the arrival of the automobile. The more meaningful question is not whether students use AI but what uniquely human intellectual capacities education should now cultivate.
The answer begins with questioning. AI can generate answers, but it does not absolve us from judging whether the question was worth asking in the first place. It can produce arguments, but students must still learn to examine assumptions, identify missing evidence, recognise bias and distinguish confidence from truth. It can summarise what humanity already knows far more quickly than any individual teacher, but education must still teach students when existing knowledge itself deserves to be challenged.
This changes the teacher's role fundamentally. The teacher of the future should be less an oracle and more an intellectual provocateur. Instead of asking, "Do you know the answer?", perhaps we should increasingly ask: "Why do you believe this answer? What evidence would make you change your mind? What has been left out? Who benefits if this interpretation is accepted? What would the opposite argument look like?" These are questions AI can help explore. But the habit of asking them must be cultivated.
The danger is that our education systems may respond to AI in exactly the wrong way. Worried about plagiarism and automated coursework, institutions may tighten surveillance, redesign assessments around control and become even more obsessed with proving that students produced work independently. If our response to AI is primarily policing, we may preserve the appearance of learning while missing the transformation of learning itself.
The teacher therefore has a double responsibility: to protect the student's right to question while simultaneously teaching the discipline required to evaluate answers. Perhaps the highest compliment a teacher can receive is not a student saying, "You taught me the right answers." It is a student saying, "You taught me not to stop asking questions." In the age of AI, that distinction may determine whether education remains transformative - or merely becomes an expensive way of delivering information that machines can efficiently provide.

title: Most US voters say Trump  Congress don t take AI risks seriously  Reuters Ipsos poll finds
description: 62  of voters say AI could get out of control  risk the future of humanity  84  see AI as a threat to American workers
content:
62% of voters say AI could get out of control, risk the future of humanity, 84% see AI as a threat to American workers
Most US voters think President Donald Trump's administration and Congress are not taking AI risks seriously enough and want the government to ​write new regulations for the technology, according to a new Reuters /Ipsos poll .
The six-day survey, which ended on Monday, showed that large swaths of the electorate see AI as a major threat to American jobs, underscoring growing scepticism of the technology across the political spectrum.
The fast-advancing technology has become a matter of keen national interest amid reports of AI agents running amok and hacking into corporate computer networks, and warnings from prominent researchers that it could one day pose an existential threat to humanity. Noisy, power-hungry data centres that power AI also increasingly pose a nuisance when they pop up near neighbourhoods while jacking up ​utility bills.
Read : OpenAI safety employee quits, says ‘time for trial and error is over’
Some 57% of registered voters in the poll — including a third of self-identified Republicans — said the Trump administration has not taken AI risks seriously enough or at all. ​Some 54% said the same about Congress.
AI has become a significant campaign issue ahead of the November 3 midterm elections when control of Congress ⁠is up for grabs. Some 62% of voters in the poll said the technology could get out of control and risk the future of humankind, roughly the same share of voters with ​that view in a Reuters /Ipsos poll from August of last year.
SITUATION EXPLAINED: 69% of Americans want stricter AI regulation, including 61% of Republicans. • 84% of voters see AI as a threat to American workers, more than see illegal immigration as one • 56% back limits on building data centers, including 43% of Republicans, despite… pic.twitter.com/RcIRV50biO
Trump has repeatedly voiced unhesitating support for AI and the construction of data centres, arguing they are vital to US competitiveness even as bipartisan ​criticism of the technology grows. He often says the US tech industry will fall behind its Chinese counterparts when asked why his government has not set limits on the technology's use and development, a point that AI safety advocates say is misguided.
"That's an important concern, but it's not top of mind for most Americans, nor should it be," said Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI staffer who quit in 2024 because he believed the company was not behaving responsibly.
The ​more pressing concern is that AI could cost people their jobs or threaten human health and safety, he said.
In a statement to Reuters about the president's handling of AI, a White House ​official pointed to Trump's new task force, which he said is in charge of ensuring that "America continues to lead the world" on the technology.
"The Trump administration’s priority is to ensure there is a booming economy so that ‌workers have ⁠many opportunities and experience limited volatility from any short-term disruptions," the official said when asked about voters' AI-related employment fears.
While high-profile leaders ranging from US Senator Bernie Sanders — a democratic socialist who caucuses with Democrats — to Steve Bannon — a hard right ally of President Donald Trump — have called for federal action, little has come so far.
Trump last week said executives from the six leading AI developers agreed to a set of voluntary safety principles, including working with "independent auditors" to assess whether AI systems are working as their designers intended.
Read More : Trump, AI CEOs sign voluntary safety pact, back data centre expansion
The safety agreement with the companies — Nvidia, SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and ​Alphabet’s Google — includes no stated consequences if a ​company chooses not to comply. Congress has ⁠so far failed to agree on legislation that would set guardrails on the technology, and lawmakers are expected to be away from Washington until after the midterms.
The new Reuters /Ipsos poll found 84% of voters saw AI as a threat to American workers. By comparison, only 60% saw illegal immigration as ​a threat to American workers, while 74% viewed competition from foreign workers that way and 73% said the same of large corporations.
A bipartisan ​majority of voters - including 80% ⁠of Democrats and 61% of Republicans - said they supported stricter government regulation on AI.
Many voters also oppose building the data centres that power AI, which has become a pressing issue in congressional and statewide races across the country as candidates from both parties urge a pause in the current construction boom.
Fifty-six per cent of voters in the Reuters /Ipsos poll back limits on building data centres, including 69% of Democrats, 55% ⁠of independents and ​43% of Republicans.
The poll also found growing unease with the ways that AI could be used in warfare. Some ​57% of voters think the US government should not use AI to determine the target of a military strike, up from 49% in a Reuters /Ipsos poll conducted in August 2025.
The Reuters /Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, gathered responses from ​4,506 US adults, including 3,526 registered voters. The survey has a margin of error of 2 percentage points.

title: OpenAI releases findings on hundreds of math problems
description: Unreleased AI model attempts approximately 4 000 research problems during testing  according to OpenAI
content:
Unreleased AI model attempts approximately 4,000 research problems during testing, according to OpenAI
US artificial intelligence company OpenAI on Wednesday published hundreds of mathematics research papers produced by an unreleased AI model, making the findings available for examination while warning that some may contain errors.
The collection, released on Tuesday on the code-sharing platform GitHub, contains 722 manuscripts grouped into 372 sets of related results. These can include a main finding, supporting arguments or alternative proofs.
The model attempted approximately 4,000 research problems during testing, according to the company.
Read : OpenAI says AI model solved one of mathematics' Millennium Prize Problems
OpenAI said the published results were at different stages of verification.
We’re releasing a broad range of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model. We’ve been consulting with the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study, and we have drawn on their advice and…
For many results, the company also released proofs written in Lean, a programming language that enables computers to check whether mathematical arguments follow logically. It plans to add more as they become available.
OpenAI published 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning and estimates of the computing power used. It said the average result required computing power equivalent to roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro “thinking.”
Completely unrelated to the rest of the ships today, but our models did solve some important math problems and the team documented it in the following blogpost. Remarkable new era of scientific progress. https://t.co/AYSuteVNiA
The company said it consulted the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study on how to present and share the research.
"This is an important event for mathematics, with consequences both for mathematics and for the mathematical community that extend far beyond the individual results," the group said, stressing its advisory role did not amount to an endorsement of the results.
“Making this work public is a first step. This release is the beginning, not the completion, of the process of human understanding and the incorporation of the work into mathematical knowledge,” it added. “The future of mathematical research cannot consist only of understanding results produced by AI labs.”
