title: Three quarters of inmates await trial
description: Three quarters of inmates await trial
content:
HRCP report highlights overcrowding in prisons, delayed justice
Nearly three out of every four people held in Pakistan's prisons have not been convicted and are awaiting the outcome of their cases, according to a policy paper by the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP).
The report, titled "Beyond the Prison Wall: Reducing Overcrowding in Pakistan's Prisons," says under-trial prisoners accounted for 73.41 per cent of the country's prison population in 2024, up from 66 per cent in 2017.
The report also points to severe overcrowding, saying prisons across Pakistan were operating at an average of 152.2 per cent of their official capacity in July-August 2024.
HRCP says the problem cannot be addressed simply by building more prisons, as overcrowding is closely linked to weaknesses in the criminal justice system, including ineffective bail mechanisms, prolonged court proceedings and excessive reliance on pre-trial detention.
The situation in Punjab is particularly serious. According to official prison data cited in the report, the province had 74,773 prisoners in 45 prisons in September 2026 against a designated capacity of 39,204.
This means the prisons were operating at 190.73 per cent of capacity. Of the total prison population, 54,932 were under-trial prisoners.
The report notes that Punjab's prison capacity has increased substantially over the years through the construction of new prisons, barracks and other facilities. However, overcrowding has continued to worsen.
In 2010, 52,803 prisoners were held against a capacity of 21,527, while the NCHR report recorded overcrowding at 173.6 per cent in Punjab in 2024.
HRCP identifies arbitrary arrests, slow investigations and prolonged prosecution as major factors behind the large number of under-trial prisoners. It says people can remain in pre-trial detention for months or even years because investigations and court proceedings take far longer than legally or reasonably acceptable.
The report recommends reforming the bail system to strengthen the presumption of innocence and make the state responsible for justifying continued detention.
It also calls for greater use of alternatives to detention, including release on personal recognisance and supervision, particularly in cases involving offences carrying shorter sentences.
It further recommends that bail should become a right where statutory delays have been exceeded, while accused persons should have access to the evidence against them at the bail stage.
It also calls for an independent accountability body to oversee prisons and correctional facilities.
According to HRCP, prison overcrowding is not merely a problem of insufficient space.
It can worsen health and sanitation conditions, increase the risk of violence and undermine rehabilitation, while prolonged detention can result in years behind bars for people who may ultimately be acquitted.

title: Govt must act as  model employer
description: Govt must act as  model employer
content:
SC says clarity in service rules essential for good governance
The Supreme Court has emphasised that the government, as the largest public employer, must conduct itself as a 'model employer'.
The SC stressed that questions relating to pay, seniority, promotion and retirement determine the security, progression and dignity of public servants throughout their working lives.
A six-page judgment authored by Justice Ayesha Malik noted that good governance required clarity not only at the policy stage but also in the rule making and its subsequent implementation.
"The government as the largest public employer must conduct itself as a model employer."
"Questions with reference to pay, seniority, promotion and retirement are not administrative inconveniences, they are matters that determine the security, progression and dignity of a public servant throughout their working life," the order noted.
A division bench of the SC, led by Justice Ayesha Malik, set aside the Punjab Service Tribunal's May 24, 2023 order that upheld the Education Department's decision to withdraw a school teacher's promotion.
The court held that the teacher was entitled to all back benefits with reference to his promotion from the date on which the promotion was withdrawn.
The petitioner joined the Education Department on November 22, 1995, as an elementary school teacher (Physical Education Trainer) (EST)(PE). He remained an EST(PE) until his promotion orders were issued in 2020, when he was promoted as Assistant Education Officer (Physical Education) BS-16, AEO(PE), on October 31, 2020.
The order was withdrawn on May 24, 2023, which then became the bone of contention between the petitioner and the Education Department.
The order said that a service structure must therefore provide a clear, predictable career path so that the employee can understand where he or she enters the service, how progression takes place and what conditions govern their advancement.
Where rules do not prescribe coherent promotional tracks or options, the resulting uncertainty leads to failure in governance.
"Its consequence is borne not only by the institution that created the ambiguity but by the employee who then must spend years seeking an entitlement that should otherwise have been provided for in the Rules, in the service structure."
The court further said that such structural gaps are often the consequence of policy developed without adequate data, institutional consultation or understanding of how the service actually functions on the ground.
"They are then aggravated at the implementation stage by an administrative approach that first asks why a benefit should not be given rather than whether it is due and how the governing framework can be fairly made to work."

title: Punjab imposes Section 144 for ten days
description: Punjab imposes Section 144 for ten days
content:
Five-person gatherings banned amid terrorism threats
The Punjab government imposed Section 144 across the province for 10 days on Tuesday, banning gatherings of five or more people amid what it called a "serious and imminent threat" to public peace and the safety of life and property.
The decision came a day after PTI long march reached Kohat. Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi is leading the convoy, which began its march towards Islamabad on Sunday to demand the release of party founder Imran Khan and press the government over what PTI describes as broader political and constitutional grievances.
According to the notification, the restrictions were imposed under Section 144(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, through an order issued by the Punjab Home Department.
The order said, "Credible reports from LEAs and IAs indicate a serious and imminent threat to public peace, tranquillity, and the safety of life & property across the province of Punjab by militant/terrorist organisations and Hostile Intelligence Agencies (HIAs)."
It said multiple threat alerts had been received about possible terrorist activities involving suicide bombers, vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices (VBIEDs) and target killings during large public gatherings across Punjab.
Such attacks could be used "to create mayhem, social unrest and disrupt public peace & tranquillity", the order said.
It said assemblies, rallies, gatherings, sit-ins, processions, demonstrations and jalsas could present "potential targets for such terrorist attacks", adding that the possibility of an act of terrorism during such activities could not be ruled out.
The order also said there was a "strong apprehension" that certain elements could organise activities, gatherings or demonstrations that might lead to assemblies of people and provide "easy targets for any hostile activity".

title: Youths missing after  Dunki  journeys
description: Youths missing after  Dunki  journeys
content:
Pakistanis travelled from Mauritania to Spain but never returned
The Islamabad High Court (IHC) has sought a response from the federal government on a petition concerning more than 50 Pakistani youths who allegedly went abroad through irregular "dunki" routes in search of employment but went missing.
Justice Arbab Muhammad Tahir heard the petition filed by citizen Afzal Hussain Shah, with Advocate Shafqat Abbas Tarar appearing on behalf of the petitioner.
The court issued notices to the federal government and directed the assistant attorney general to submit a report before the next hearing, scheduled for November 2.
During the hearing, the petitioner's counsel said more than 50 young men from Mandi Bahauddin, Gujranwala, Gujrat, Hafizabad and other areas illegally went out of the country in search of employment.
He said the youths had travelled on different boats from Mauritania, an African country, towards Spain between April 2024 and January 2025.
However, they failed to reach their intended destination and their families have not received reliable information about their whereabouts or immigration status in any country.
The lawyer said the families had been unable to ascertain whether the missing youths were stranded somewhere, detained, deported or living in another country under some other status.
He informed the court that the petitioner had already submitted written applications to the prime minister, foreign minister and interior minister seeking government assistance in tracing the missing Pakistanis.
The counsel requested the court to direct the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to conduct consular inquiries regarding the missing Pakistani citizens in different countries.
He also sought directions for Pakistani embassies and consulates abroad to make efforts to trace the missing youths and determine their whereabouts.
The petitioner further requested that immigration, travel and other available records of the missing Pakistanis be examined to establish their movements and current status.
He also asked the court to direct the authorities to take appropriate measures for the safe repatriation of those Pakistanis who might be stranded or otherwise unable to return to the country.

During the proceedings, Justice Tahir called the assistant attorney general to the rostrum and directed him to examine the matter. "Please look into the matter and submit a report at the next hearing," he said.

title: Dhoni fan by day   Spiderman  robber by night

content:
Peshawar police recover Rs9.3m in stolen cash, arrest key suspect in shop burglary case
By day, he was known among his friends as a fan of Indian cricket star MS Dhoni. By night, police say, his unusually slender frame turned him into a "Spiderman" - slipping through narrow exhaust ducts to break into shops and walk away with millions.
The unlikely combination helped a suspected burglary gang evade detection, according to Peshawar police, who claim to have busted the group and recovered Rs9.3 million in stolen cash from one of its alleged members.
The police say the gang's alleged "Spiderman", identified as Zahid, would exploit his slim physique to enter shops through exhaust openings while his accomplices waited outside. He and his mother have allegedly fled to Afghanistan following the robberies.
Police arrested another suspect, identified as Usman, and recovered Rs9.3 million from his possession, according to SP City Shahid Adnan.
The gang allegedly targeted three shops near Lady Griffith Girls School within the jurisdiction of Shah Qabool police station on September 3. Police said more than Rs100 million worth of cash and goods was stolen from the premises, including a solar panel shop and two other large stores.
SP City Shahid Adnan, accompanied by DSP Shaheen Shah and SHO Shah Qabool Shah Khalid Khan, disclosed the details at a press conference on Monday.
He said Peshawar CCPO Dr Mian Saeed Ahmed had taken serious notice of the incident and ordered special teams to trace the suspects. The teams comprised City Circle DSP Shehenshah Khan, SHO Shah Qabool Shah Khalid and investigating officer Aizaz Alam Khan.
Investigators used CCTV footage as well as modern scientific and technical methods to identify the suspects, the SP said.
During the investigation, police traced the gang and arrested Usman, son of Ghulam Hussain, a resident of Bhana Mari Timer Garhi and currently residing in Rehman Court, Qamar Din Ghari. Rs9.3 million in allegedly stolen cash was recovered from his possession.
According to police, interrogation also revealed the alleged involvement of Zahid, who was nicknamed "Spider-Man" by his accomplices because of his ability to squeeze through narrow openings.
Police said Zahid was also an admirer of former India captain MS Dhoni and was therefore known among his associates as "Dhoni".
Investigators said Zahid allegedly entered commercial premises through exhaust ducts, enabling the gang to carry out burglaries without using conventional entry points.
Police further claimed that some relatives of the suspects and a woman were also involved in the gang's activities. The woman was allegedly taken along during an operation so that, if the group was stopped by police, her presence could help create an alternative explanation for their movement.
Police said Zahid and his mother had escaped to Afghanistan and efforts were under way to arrest them.
Further interrogation of the arrested suspect is continuing, with police expecting more information about the gang's other alleged robberies, accomplices and the remaining stolen money.

title: PTI marchers change route  head to Khyber first

Afridi says the march would eventually move towards Islamabad when the PTI decided to do so
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Tuesday said the PTI had originally planned to take the long march towards Peshawar. However, he announced a change in the route, saying the march would first head towards Khyber and then proceed to Peshawar.
"We are playing a Test match; there are still many overs and players left. The change in route is part of the PTI's strategy," the CM said while addressing participants of the protest at University Chowk in Kohat on the third day of the march before departing for the next destination.
He also referred to the earlier change in the march's date from September 27 to October 4, saying the authorities had reacted strongly to the postponement and were now concerned about the duration of the protest.
Afridi said the march would eventually move towards Islamabad when the PTI decided to do so, declaring: "When we say we are going to Islamabad, no one will be able to stop us."
Afridi vowed to continue the PTI long march, saying all constitutional and legal avenues had been exhausted and the party was now compelled to take to the streets to seek justice for Imran Khan. He said the era of what he called "fake, imposed and mandate-stealing rulers" was nearing its end.
Thanking the people of Kohat for their enthusiasm and patriotism, he said PTI workers would not be intimidated by anyone. "My young people, your chief minister is not afraid of anyone, and the youth of my Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa are also not afraid of anyone," he said.
Afridi said the objective was to bring Imran Khan out of prison and make him prime minister again, claiming that the country would witness development and prosperity under his leadership.
He said Pakistan had enjoyed peace between 2018 and 2022, when, according to him, Imran Khan had not compromised the country's interests.
The chief minister said the seven-point demands of the long march had already been made public on social media and challenged anyone to identify even one demand that was unconstitutional or illegal.
Afridi said demands for Imran Khan's medical treatment, a meeting with him and his release in accordance with law were not unconstitutional. He questioned why courts were not hearing Imran's cases, claiming that if the cases were heard, the PTI founder would be released within an hour.
The chief minister alleged that Imran Khan was being kept in prison because he had refused to submit to powerful figures in Pakistan and abroad. He also alleged that restrictions had been placed on the former prime minister's name and image in the national media because of his popularity.
Afridi further expressed concern over reports about Imran Khan's health and alleged that his health was being "played with". He warned that the jail administration, prime minister and other relevant officials would be responsible if any harm came to the PTI founder.
He said courts, assemblies and state institutions operated with taxpayers' money and argued that people therefore had the right to demand justice. "If the courts do not provide justice, the people will seek justice on the streets," he said.
Afridi maintained that the PTI had exhausted available democratic, constitutional and legal channels before resorting to street protest.
He said since becoming chief minister, he had repeatedly approached the authorities and requested a meeting with Imran Khan. According to Afridi, he had also contacted the prime minister over the matter but was told that the request would be considered, after which no meeting was arranged.
He said the K-P Assembly subsequently passed a resolution seeking his meeting with Imran Khan, while he had also approached the chief justice of Pakistan without receiving a response.

title: LHC nullifies disputed oral gift mutation
description: LHC nullifies disputed oral gift mutation
content:
The Lahore High Court (LHC) has ruled that a deficiency in furnishing precise particulars of alleged fraud cannot, by itself, establish an oral gift or relieve its beneficiary of the independent burden of proving the transaction from which title is claimed, particularly where the gift excludes legal heirs from inheritance.
Justice Anwaar Hussain of the LHC's Rawalpindi Bench, in a detailed judgment, held that a mutation merely records an asserted transaction and cannot substitute for proof of the underlying gift.
A person relying on an oral gift must independently establish its three essential ingredients - declaration by the donor, acceptance by the donee and delivery of possession - through cogent and reliable evidence.
The court observed that the burden on a person challenging a transaction on grounds of fraud and the burden on a beneficiary claiming an oral gift as the source of title were two distinct burdens.
Failure by the challenger to prove one circumstance alleged in support of fraud could not affirmatively establish that the gift was declared, accepted or completed.
Similarly, requiring particulars of fraud could not absolve the beneficiary from proving the gift itself.
Justice Hussain noted that this distinction assumed particular importance where the alleged gift had the effect of excluding persons who would otherwise inherit the estate by operation of law.
The judge further held that particulars of fraud could emerge from the circumstances surrounding a disputed transaction, including the donor's advanced age or serious illness, inability to understand or participate in the transaction, absence before the revenue authority, or absence of declaration or acceptance.
Therefore, what constituted sufficient particulars could not be determined through a rigid or formulaic test and had to be examined in the factual circumstances of each case.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday directed the authorities concerned to take all necessary measures to ensure the uninterrupted import of gas in view of the prevailing regional situation, while ordering a comprehensive strategy and proactive steps for winter gas load management.

He issued the directives while chairing a review meeting on NHA affairs at the Prime Minister House. The meeting reviewed the progress of ongoing development work on national highways, motorways and expressways, a Prime Minister's Office news release said.
Addressing the participants, the prime minister said improved transport connectivity was indispensable for the development and prosperity of any country.
He said the government was working on a priority basis to connect remote areas with the rest of the country so that people there could have the best travel facilities and more opportunities for business and employment could be created.
The meeting was briefed on ongoing and proposed NHA projects. It was informed that the NHA's revenue had increased from Rs 109 billion to Rs 130 billion in the last fiscal year and was expected to reach Rs 160 billion during the current financial year.

title: Oscar winning  North by Northwest  star Eva Marie Saint dies at 102
description: Oscar winning actress Eva Marie Saint  known for  North by Northwest  and  On the Waterfront   dies at age 102
content:
Oscar-winning actress Eva Marie Saint, known for 'North by Northwest' and 'On the Waterfront', dies at age 102
Oscar-winning actress Eva Marie Saint, best known for On the Waterfront and Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest , has died at 102.
Saint died Tuesday at her home in Los Angeles, according to reports. She became one of Hollywood’s most recognisable actresses during the 1950s, earning an Academy Award for best supporting actress for her role as Edie Doyle in On the Waterfront .
The 1954 film, directed by Elia Kazan and starring Marlon Brando, received 12 Oscar nominations and won eight awards, including best picture, actor, director and supporting actress for Saint.
Saint went on to play Eve Kendall in Hitchcock’s 1959 thriller North by Northwest , opposite Cary Grant. The role became one of her most celebrated performances, with Saint portraying a sophisticated spy caught up in a dangerous international conspiracy.
Beyond her film career, Saint was an early television star who appeared in anthology programmes including Philco Playhouse , Robert Montgomery Presents and Studio One . She also worked extensively on stage and received multiple Emmy nominations before winning a supporting actress Emmy in 1990 for the NBC miniseries People Like Us .
Her later film credits included Nothing in Common , I Dreamed of Africa , Because of Winn-Dixie , Don’t Come Knocking and Superman Returns , in which she played Martha Kent. Her final big-screen appearance came in Winter’s Tale in 2014.
Saint also appeared on television in Moonlighting , playing the mother of Cybill Shepherd’s character, and earned two stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame for her contributions to film and television.
Born in Newark, New Jersey, Saint studied at Bowling Green State University before pursuing acting. She was married to television director Jeffrey Hayden until his death in 2016. She is survived by her two children, four grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.

title: FKA twigs breaks free from NDA restrictions in Shia LaBeouf legal dispute

content:
FKA twigs can now discuss alleged abuse by Shia LaBeouf after their dispute over NDA terms was resolved in court
FKA twigs is free to publicly discuss her alleged experiences with former partner Shia LaBeouf after the pair resolved a dispute over nondisclosure provisions in their previous settlement.
According to a filing in Los Angeles County Superior Court dated Oct. 5, the singer and actress asked for her latest case against LaBeouf to be dismissed after reaching an agreement. Under the resolution, disputed nondisclosure provisions were terminated and declared void.
The agreement allows twigs to discuss her alleged experiences and support charitable organisations without facing legal action over the former confidentiality provisions, according to court documents obtained by PEOPLE .
Her attorney, Mathew Rosengart, said the resolution allows twigs to speak about her experience, advocate for other women and support charitable organisations. LaBeouf’s attorney, Shawn Holley, also confirmed that the dispute had been resolved.
Twigs first sued LaBeouf in December 2020, accusing the actor of sexual battery, assault and infliction of emotional distress, among other claims. LaBeouf denied the allegations. The pair dated from around July 2018 until May 2019.
The former couple reached a settlement in 2025, but a subsequent dispute arose over whether twigs could publicly discuss her allegations. In December 2025, LaBeouf reportedly sought arbitration after twigs was asked in an interview whether she felt safe.
Twigs responded that she would not say she felt safe and discussed wanting to work with organisations supporting survivors. LaBeouf alleged that the comments breached their settlement’s confidentiality provisions and sought monetary damages, according to twigs’ amended complaint.
Twigs argued that the provisions were unlawful under California’s Stand Together Against Non-Disclosure Act, which limits confidentiality agreements involving sexual misconduct claims. The latest agreement resolves that dispute, with twigs seeking dismissal of the case.

The CAP chairman said the government must first establish an effective regulatory framework for all builders and developers, and no person or company should be permitted to launch, advertise, book or collect money from the public for a residential or commercial project without obtaining complete approval from the relevant authority.
He demanded that every real estate advertisement must prominently display the approval number, NOC number and date of approval issued by the competent authority. Where a project falls under the jurisdiction of the Sindh Building Control Authority, a development authority or any other competent institution, these details must be clearly mentioned in the advertisement so that consumers can verify the legal status of a project before investing their money.

content:
Index surges 2,593 points as call for govt-PTI dialogue lifts sentiment
Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) staged a strong recovery on Tuesday, with the benchmark KSE-100 index surging 2,592.79 points, or 1.56%, to settle at 168,460.11, as broad-based buying gathered pace amid hopes for reduced domestic political tensions.
Investor sentiment improved after Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called on the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) to abandon its politics of agitation and cancel its long march, saying protests would damage economic growth and Pakistan's international standing. The call for dialogue, conditional on ending the agitation, provided some relief to investors concerned about renewed political uncertainty.
The index traded between the intra-day high of 168,626.18 and low of 165,651.68, recovering strongly from the session's early levels as buying emerged across key sectors. Investor interest was witnessed in auto assemblers, cement, commercial banks, oil and gas exploration companies, oil marketing firms, power generation and refineries. Meanwhile, international oil prices eased as resilient Middle Eastern crude exports and a G7 emergency stockpile release reduced immediate supply concerns, although security risks in the region continued to cap further decline.
"The decline in international oil prices, along with the government's indication that it remains open to negotiations with the PTI to end the long march, helped improve investor sentiment," AKD Securities Director Research Mohammed Awais Ashraf told The Express Tribune. The easing of both external and domestic concerns encouraged fresh buying across key sectors and supported the broader market recovery, he added.
After Monday's heavy sell-off and margin-driven liquidation, the market initially remained subdued and consolidated on thin volumes, but improving domestic and global cues triggered broad-based buying and a strong recovery, commented Ahmed Sheraz of KASB KTrade.
Buying was visible across commercial banks, oil & gas, cement firms, investment banks and power, with Engro Holdings, UBL, Hub Power, HBL, OGDC and Mari Energies closing the session in the green.
Sentiment was further supported by easing oil prices, with Brent falling below $100 to around $98, amid improving Red Sea conditions, G7-backed strategic oil releases and price support from Saudi producers. Additionally, hopes for US-Iran dialogue also reduced geopolitical risks after President Trump indicated Washington was open to direct talks.
On the domestic front, the government's outreach to the opposition for negotiations added another layer of clarity, helping the market regain confidence. Ali Najib, Deputy Head of Trading at Arif Habib Limited (AHL), observed that following Monday's sharp sell-off, the market rebounded amid easing international oil prices and improved Middle East oil flows, which helped restore investor confidence. On the sectoral front, oil production declined 6.4% week-on-week to 63.7k barrels per day, primarily due to lower flows from northern fields, while gas production fell 1.4% WoW to 2,999 mmcfd, mainly due to reduced output from Mari, Sui and Sharf.
On the corporate front, Sazgar Engineering's total sales increased 22% year-on-year to 10,872 units in the first quarter of fiscal year 2026-27, driven by a 45% rise in three-wheeler sales, while four-wheeler sales declined 12%, Najib added.
Trading volumes fell to 432 million shares from 441.9 million recorded on Monday, while the value of traded shares stood at Rs20.1 billion.
Shares of 496 companies were traded in the ready market, of which 314 closed higher, 147 declined and 35 stood unchanged.

They also shared progress on affordable housing engagement to address supply-side constraints through potential developer finance models.
On agricultural finance, the discussion focused on IFC's AgriConnect initiative, particularly opportunities to mobilise private financing through improved storage infrastructure and the effective use of electronic warehouse receipts as collateral. The finance minister underlined the need for addressing supply-side constraints and creating greater certainty for lenders and farmers.

The finance minister and IFC also exchanged views on expanding local-currency financing and strengthening mechanisms for longer-term financing for private-sector projects. Aurangzeb underscored the importance of complementing domestic financial resources with international development finance to support productive investment.
He called for expanding financing opportunities for SMEs, entrepreneurs, agriculture and housing, noting that improved access to long-term and affordable capital would help unlock private investment, support business expansion and strengthen productive activity. Faces downside pressure below $4,280; rupee inches up
Gold prices in Pakistan remained unchanged on Tuesday, while the precious metal gained in the international market, as a pause in the rise in US Treasury yields and a weaker dollar supported demand.
The price of gold remained at Rs437,536 per tola in the local market, according to rates issued by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association. Similarly, the price of 10-gram gold stood unchanged at Rs375,116. On Monday, gold had risen by Rs1,200 per tola.
The price of silver also remained unchanged at Rs6,588 per tola on Tuesday. In the international market, spot gold rose 0.6% to $4,163.16 per ounce by 12:22 pm EDT (1622 GMT), while US gold futures for December delivery gained 0.8% to $4,191, according to Reuters.
The gains came as the dollar weakened and the recent rally in US Treasury yields paused, making dollar-denominated gold relatively more attractive. Investors were also awaiting the minutes of the US Federal Reserve's September meeting, due on Wednesday, for further clues about the central bank's monetary policy outlook.
However, the near-term technical outlook for gold remains under pressure, according to Adnan Agar, Director at Interactive Commodities. Agar said gold was trading around $4,165 an ounce, after touching the high of $4,175 and the low of $4,103. He said the international market had largely remained within a range of around $4,100 to $4,220 over the past week.
"There is more pressure on the lower side," Agar said, adding that gold could face further declines unless it breaks above the $4,280 level. If gold fails to cross that level, he sees the possibility of the metal falling towards $4,050-$4,000 an ounce.
A break below $4,000 could open the way towards $3,700, although Agar said the market would first need to test the $4,000 level before assessing the next move. He said a further $4-5 rise in oil prices, combined with a sustained increase in US bond yields, could add pressure on gold.
Meanwhile, TD Securities expects gold to rise above $5,000 per ounce next year, highlighting the continued bullish longer-term outlook despite short-term downside risks.
Meanwhile, the Pakistani rupee closed at 277.05 against the US dollar on Tuesday, gaining Rs0.01 in the inter-bank market. On Monday, the local currency settled at 277.06 against the greenback. Internationally, the US dollar extended its strong rally, supported by elevated US Treasury yields.

title: Handmade carpets to lift exports
description: Handmade carpets to lift exports
content:
Industry asked to move towards innovation, bridge public-private sector gap
Pakistan's handmade carpets have a distinctive identity around the world, and the industry has the potential to push exports higher, the head of the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan (TDAP) said on Tuesday.
"Pakistan's handmade carpets have a unique identity around the world because of their high quality and attractive designs," TDAP Chief Executive Faiz Ahmad Chadhar said while speaking at the inaugural ceremony of the 42nd international handmade carpet exhibition. "This industry has a lot of potential, which, if utilised, can further increase exports."
He said every kind of support was being given to the sector and would be expanded. "Every single dollar is extremely valuable for Pakistan," he said, adding that export promotion was being given special priority. He also said the industry must move towards innovation and the gap between the public and private sectors must be bridged.
The remarks come at a time when the sector needs a push. According to UN Comtrade data, Pakistan's exports of carpets and other textile floor coverings were about $57 million in 2024. That is a small amount when seen against the country's total exports of $30.1 billion in the last fiscal year, and against textile exports of $17.9 billion.
Data from the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics shows carpet and rug exports fell by more than 20% in 2025-26, even as some other export categories grew.
Yet the product has a long history behind it. Carpet weaving in this region is closely linked to the Mughal era, when rulers brought skilled weavers from Persia and Central Asia and encouraged the craft in royal workshops. Lahore became one of the main centres, and the city still has many of the factories and exporters in the trade today.
Pakistani carpets are knotted by hand, one row at a time, on looms that can take weeks or even months to finish a single large piece. Weavers use wool, silk or a mix of both. The most popular styles include Persian-inspired floral patterns, Bukhara designs with repeating rows of geometric shapes, and Afghan and tribal patterns in deep red and brown shades. Because each piece is made by hand, no two carpets are exactly alike, which is a major reason why buyers abroad pay higher prices for them than for machine-made rugs.
The industry also supports many households, particularly in the rural parts of Punjab, where weaving skills are passed from one generation to the next. Unlike many other export items, handmade carpets depend mostly on local labour and local raw material, so a large part of the money earned from them stays in the country.
Exporters say the opportunity is there, but they need support in areas such as marketing, modern designs and easier travel for foreign buyers. "We are hopeful that large-scale export deals at the exhibition will strengthen this industry," said Senior Vice Chairman of the Pakistan Carpet Manufacturers Association, Khawaja Mir Mudassir, at the event. "The interest foreign buyers have shown in Pakistani products has boosted our morale," he added.
Chadhar, however, said that the authorities were aware of the challenges facing the industry, including visa-related problems raised at the event, and that efforts were underway to resolve them as soon as possible.
The three-day exhibition has drawn a large number of buyers from the United States, Germany, Turkiye, China, Russia, Sweden and other countries. Organisers have also set up a stall of carpets made by prison inmates in Punjab, giving visitors an opportunity to take a look at the training and work.

title: Investment hinges on economic stability
description: Investment hinges on economic stability
content:
Aurangzeb calls population growth, climate change critical survival challenges
Federal Minister for Finance Muhammad Aurangzeb has said Pakistan has the investment framework and financing available and the world should provide the capacity needed to complete projects. Pakistan is ready for investment and has met its basic requirements by controlling its deficit, increasing foreign exchange reserves, securing an improved credit rating and issuing Panda and Eurobonds.
He made these remarks on Tuesday while addressing the "Investing in Pakistan's Sustainable Future Fair and Conference", organised by the UNDP and federal and provincial governments. The finance minister said the State Bank had provided a draft of the Green Taxonomy Framework. As part of the Climate Prosperity Plan, the Pakistan Stock Exchange was working on an ESG Index alongside a 14-day programme, which would help bring the performance and information of listed companies to the forefront.
He said Pakistan was using its own resources for funding in addition to support from the World Bank, Asian Development Bank and other financial institutions. He said investors in London and New York believed that Pakistan was moving in the right direction. "We need to work on promoting domestic investment because an increase in domestic investment will pave the way for greater foreign investment."
He said economic stability was fundamental to promoting investment, while the private sector could play an important role in economic growth and investment. Public-private partnerships were an effective means of promoting investment and cooperation between the government and private sector was essential for development projects.
The finance minister said four factors were important for economic growth, including the policy framework, financing capacity and bankable projects. Therefore, Pakistan needed to focus on improving its capacity.
Aurangzeb said population growth and climate change were matters of survival for Pakistan, which would have a population of 400 million people by 2045. He mentioned that the country remained focused on day-to-day issues, but it now needed to pay attention to the critical survival challenge as well. The World Bank and IMF were also supporting Pakistan, while the country required further assistance to build capacity. "The discussion has now moved beyond 'what and why' to 'how and who'." The finance minister said Pakistani business groups had started working together by forming consortia. Eleven IPOs were held during the last fiscal year, the highest in 20 years, while five IPOs had taken place at the Pakistan Stock Exchange during the past three months.
He said the government had a key role to play in promoting investment. The government was focusing on fiscal discipline and economic stability, while increasing exports alongside economic growth remained a priority. "Pakistan needs economic growth that is responsible and sustainable," he remarked, adding that economic policy would have to move forward while keeping global economic conditions in view.
Addressing the conference, Senator Sherry Rehman said population growth was the biggest threat to sustainability. She said 36 million children in the country were out of school and a lack of financing and capacity was hindering efforts to resolve those problems, but the private sector could help bridge that gap. She said climate-related concerns were increasing, while changing conditions made it difficult to develop bankable projects. Population growth and migration towards cities were major challenges, she said. A large number of people moving to cities did not have adequate representation.
Water supply and waste disposal would be among the major challenges in the coming years, she added. Local institutions would have to be strengthened to address urban problems, but there was a shortage of financial resources and institutional capacity to deal with these challenges.
Available resources were insufficient compared with the rapidly growing urban population. She said sustainable urban development required proper planning and adequate resources. Sherry Rehman emphasised that cooperation between the public and private sectors was proving to be a successful model, particularly through public-private partnerships (PPPs), under which the two sectors could combine their resources and regulatory frameworks.
She said developing bankable projects was not easy amid changing circumstances and a fragmented port landscape. She stressed that effective partnerships between the public and private sectors could play an important role in making development projects bankable.

title: Digital transactions hit 13 2b
description: Digital transactions hit 13 2b
content:
Reach 92% of retail payments; mobile-based solutions surge 79% in FY26
The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) has released its Annual Report on Payment Systems, highlighting that fiscal year 2025-26 witnessed a strong momentum in the ongoing transformation of the payment landscape, with consumers, businesses, and financial institutions increasingly embracing mobile apps, internet banking, e-money wallets, QR-based payments, and other digital channels. This growth has been supported by various policy measures, improved digital infrastructure, and industry-led initiatives.
Retail payments through formal banking channels during FY26 registered a significant growth, reaching 14.3 billion transactions valued at Rs673 trillion, representing a year-on-year growth of 58% in volume and 10% in value. Digital channels continued to gain traction as consumers increasingly adopted mobile banking apps, internet banking, and e-money wallets for everyday payments.
Out of the 14.3 billion transactions conducted through formal banking channels, 13.2 billion transactions were conducted through digital channels, representing a year-on-year growth of 65%. Furthermore, digital channels accounted for 92% of total retail payment transactions, up from 88% in FY25. Mobile phone-based solutions led digital transactions with over 11.1 billion transactions, registering a 79% growth, while internet banking portals processed 0.3 billion transactions, up 15% from the previous fiscal year.
The expansion of digital acceptance infrastructure at merchants/retailers' outlets further supported this growth. The POS network expanded to 337,791 terminals across 295,367 merchant locations, supporting nearly 1.5 million daily card payments compared to 1 million in the previous fiscal year.
E-commerce payments also continued to gain traction, with account-based online payments accounting for 96% of total e-commerce transactions conducted through banking channels. Branchless banking mobile app users increased to 99.1 million, while banks' mobile app users reached 30.4 million, highlighting the continued shift of everyday banking activities towards smartphone-based platforms.

title: Mari gets nod for survey aircraft
description: Mari gets nod for survey aircraft
content:
Temporarily imported airplane will carry out field detection surveys in K-P, Balochistan
The government has allowed Mari Energies to carry out airborne field detection survey operations in different areas in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), including Waziristan, and Balochistan.
Mari Energies has also been allowed temporary import of aircraft to conduct surveys of different sites in the two provinces.
Sources said that Mari had been granted a conditional NOC for carrying out an airborne Strike Field Detection (SFD) survey operation in the following areas, which included (Wali) West, Waziristan and Karak Block in K-P, Block-28, Hanna, Hanna South, Ziarat and Ziarat North Blocks in Balochistan.
However, different conditions and security points have been attached to this approval. The firm shall ensure that the survey remains limited to the areas mutually agreed. The firm shall arrange transportation, lodging and make other administrative arrangements for the duration of the survey and shall not ask for any charges in this regard.
The company must provide at least two weeks' notice regarding the arrival of the aircraft and the survey team. No photo and survey equipment will be loaded on the aircraft, other than those sensors/equipment required for survey and communication.
Mari will provide an undertaking that no survey data will be transmitted out of the country without clearance from the Strategic Plans Division (SPD). In addition, each survey sortie will be cleared by the SPD team, after having assessed the survey data acquired during the previous sortie.
The firm will permit pre-inspection of the aircraft by a team of SPD and two officers of SPD will be on board during each survey sortie for monitoring and coordination. Schedule of each survey sortie is to be communicated at least 48 hours in advance to the SPD team for clearance.
In case of presence of strategic minerals, SPD shall have priority rights and the firm shall provide space and passage to SPD in case SPD plans to carry out any activity in that area. Foreign experts, if any, may only be allowed to visit after necessary security clearance.
Use/carrying of maps, survey equipment, GPS and technical gadgetry on the project site other than the required equipment is prohibited.
Routing/safe transit of each mission (from take-off till landing) shall be devised in consultation with the Directorate of Air Traffic Services. Survey team should not be allowed to visit/photograph any key point of vital defence installation.
Foreigners will not be allowed to visit any other area without proper security cover. Local authorities will ensure personal security of the foreigners. Adequate arrangement will be made for the security of guests by the host district to avoid any untoward incident.
Mari has been advised to fulfil all the conditions/requirements in true letter and spirit and to furnish a certificate for the observance of all the mentioned conditions.

title: IMF taxes squeeze salaried class
description: IMF taxes squeeze salaried class
content:
They pay Rs144b in Jul-Sept; real estate gets 50% cut; retailers win fixed tax
The salaried class has paid Rs144 billion in income tax in this fiscal year, which is Rs90 billion more than the taxes paid by retail and realty sectors, highlighting a widening disparity under the International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme that has endorsed a 50% cut for real estate and a fixed tax scheme for retailers.
Official record of the past two fiscal years and provisional figures of the first quarter (July-September) of the current fiscal year suggested that at the completion of two years of the IMF programme, the tax contribution of the salaried class had multiplied.
But the influential trading and real estate sectors remained largely outside of the net, with the IMF either endorsing tax concessions for them or keeping its eyes closed. The IMF executive board had approved the three-year $7 billion loan package in September 2024, and the Fund's staff is scheduled to complete its ongoing visit to Pakistan for the fourth review of the programme on Wednesday.
According to the FBR's provisional tax collection data, income tax collection from the real estate sector dived 38% to a mere Rs35.2 billion in the first three months of the current fiscal year. It was Rs22 billion less than the comparative period of the last fiscal year after the government cut income tax for the realty sector by 50%, which the IMF also endorsed.
In fiscal year 2024, the realty sector had paid Rs200 billion in income tax, which hardly increased to Rs236 billion in the last fiscal year, but it has now been halved. In the budget, the government reduced the advance tax on sale and purchase of immovable property by 50%. On the sale of property, three slabs have been merged, and a single rate of 2.75% has been introduced against 5.5%.
On the purchase of property, the tax rate has been reduced from 2.5% to 1.25%. Because of this steep reduction, the advance income tax collection on the sale of property decreased from Rs39.5 billion to Rs23 billion in three months, a reduction of Rs16.5 billion, or 42%.
Likewise, on the purchase of properties, the income tax collection dipped from Rs17.7 billion to Rs12.2 billion, a reduction of Rs5.5 billion, or 31%, according to these statistics.
Official data showed that withholding taxes paid by wholesalers and retailers almost remained stagnant during the first three months of the current fiscal year. The combined withholding taxes paid by wholesalers and retailers amounted to Rs18.4 billion during the first three months. These were Rs244 million, or 1.3%, more than the last fiscal year.
Wholesalers paid Rs6.2 billion in three months, down by Rs701 million, or 10%. Instead of using the data of wholesalers to go after the retailers, the Federal Board of Revenue introduced a fixed tax scheme that has miserably failed. The traders, after making promises to become tax return filers, stayed outside of the net amid a lack of political will to go after them.
Retailers paid Rs11.3 billion in income tax, higher by Rs945 million, or 8.3%, than the comparative period of the last fiscal year. The combined taxes paid by retailers and the real estate sector amounted to a mere Rs54 billion. It was Rs90 billion less than the taxes paid by the salaried class.
According to tax officials, the income tax collection from the salaried class amounted to Rs144 billion during the July-September period of the current fiscal year. It was higher by Rs13.4 billion, or 10.2%, compared to the same period of last year.
In the budget, the government claimed that it had given a Rs52 billion relief to the salaried class by up to 3% reduction in the tax rate and abolishing the 9% surcharge calculated on the basis of the highest tax rate of 35%. It also increased the applicability limit of the maximum tax rate of 35% from Rs4.1 million to Rs7 million annually.
The massive reduction in collection from real estate has widened the gap between income tax payments made by the salaried class and the real estate sector. Before the start of the IMF programme, the annual contribution of the salaried class was Rs391 billion, which within two fiscal years of the IMF programme increased to Rs629 billion as of June 2026.
The salaried class, like other middle- and lower-middle-income groups, is also adversely impacted by the government's decision to fully recover international oil prices, charge a petroleum levy of Rs80 per litre and climate support levy of Rs5 per litre. The daily price fluctuation is also causing a hike in fruit and vegetable prices.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had promised to substantially reduce the tax burden of the salaried class once the tax base was broadened. However, instead of increasing tax collection from the highly undertaxed sectors, his government has further slashed their burden.

title: Gypsy Rose Blanchard breaks silence on alleged harassment faced by Ken Urker
description: Gypsy Rose Blanchard shares alleged evidence of online harassment Ken Urker faced before his death at age 34
content:
Gypsy Rose Blanchard shares alleged evidence of online harassment Ken Urker faced before his death at age 34
Gypsy Rose Blanchard has shared screenshots she says document years of online bullying and harassment directed at her late partner, Ken Urker, before his death.
Urker, 34, was found dead at his home in Raceland, Louisiana, on Oct. 1, his 34th birthday. The Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Office has said investigators have found no evidence of foul play so far, although the investigation remains ongoing.
Blanchard, 35, who shared daughter Aurora with Urker, posted what she described as examples of alleged harassment on social media. She said the screenshots represent only a small portion of an evidence log documenting what she described as cyberbullying, ridicule, allegations and targeted harassment.
According to Blanchard, many of the posts came from the same Reddit forum and included comments about Urker’s appearance, sexuality and relationship with her.
Blanchard said the alleged harassment accumulated over several years and urged people to remember that those targeted online are real people. She also shared photos of Urker and their daughter while describing him as “our world” and Aurora’s father.
The posts are part of Blanchard’s campaign for Kenan’s Law, a proposed measure intended to strengthen accountability for repeated harassment on social media platforms. She previously shared a Change.org petition supporting the proposal and said she has contacted a New Orleans lawyer to help refine the idea.
Blanchard told PEOPLE that she wants accountability from social media platforms and individuals who repeatedly target and harass others online. She said she hopes speaking publicly about Urker’s experience can help prevent similar situations involving other families.
Blanchard and Urker first became engaged in 2018 and later reconciled several times. They reconnected after Blanchard’s 2024 divorce from Ryan Anderson.

title: In search of volunteers
description: A rooted NGO has relationships  local credibility and the ability to mobilise people
content:
A rooted NGO has relationships, local credibility and the ability to mobilise people
Walk into any climate conference in Karachi and you will meet founders. Each leads an NGO with a name, a logo and a social media page. What is harder to find is the crowd behind them. Over the years I have come to suspect that many of our environmental groups are not movements but individuals, and that their apparent size has more to do with the last grant than with any lasting community support.
An NGO is known almost entirely by its founder's face. Then funding arrives, and suddenly there are coordinators, project officers, consultants and a team photograph. The workforce looks impressive, but it was assembled by a budget line. When the project closes, the team thins out, and the founder is once again the outfit. This is the difference between a body with a volunteer base and one with a payroll. Volunteers stay when there is no money. Employees, quite reasonably, do not.
Language has become part of the problem. People recruited for an event, handed a T-shirt and paid a daily wage or an incentive are often described in reports as volunteers. They are not. Someone who performs an assigned task for payment is an event worker, and there is nothing shameful in that; honest work deserves honest pay. The problem lies in the label, which borrows the moral credit of volunteerism while hiding the transaction.
Why is real volunteering so thin in Pakistan? Part of the answer is structural. Political parties offer workers something that civil society rarely can: access, networks, visibility and standing, especially for those near a governing party. A phone call from the right office can open doors that years of unpaid NGO work will not. This is an observation about incentives, not about any party.
Yet the fault is not only outside. Inside some established NGOs, the staff control the projects, the budgets and the access, and a newcomer finds little room. Volunteers are sometimes treated as subordinates and handed tasks, rather than welcomed as the NGO's most important constituency. This reverses a basic principle of civil society. Paid staff should exist to support and facilitate a wider volunteer movement, not the other way round. When volunteers become unpaid assistants to a professional bureaucracy, we should not be surprised that they leave.
The climate sector shows the consequences clearly. In my own work I have trained people over longer periods in climate education, activism and journalism. That is personal experience, and I offer it only as an illustration. Some of those participants went on to strengthen existing groups, which is genuinely wonderful. Others chose to register new ones of their own. I understand the instinct; ownership is attractive. But if every trained person founds another NGO, the sector multiplies letterheads without multiplying strength.
A quieter version exists. Some NGOs list many members yet function as one-person operations. The membership exists on paper and becomes active when a training, a trip, a certificate or some other benefit is on offer. A membership list is not a community, and a WhatsApp group that stirs only for opportunities is not a volunteer base.
Money deepens the distortion. Donors rightly want to fund credible partners, and recommendations from trusted contacts are a normal part of that process. Networking is not wrong. But when relationships and polished presentation begin to substitute for demonstrated community credibility, the system rewards those who are good at being seen. An NGO with strong donor connections can recommend others, and funding can circulate within a small professional circle. Once a large grant arrives, the NGO can start to resemble a company, hiring staff, consultants and event workers, and paying incentives to people brought into communities for project activities. The question donors should ask is uncomfortable but fair. Are they funding genuine civil-society institutions rooted in communities, or professional project-management entities that happen to carry the NGO label?
Comparisons between cities should be made carefully. Some Islamabad-based groups appear to draw more visible volunteer participation, though that does not make Karachi's peers weaker or the capital's stronger across the board. Proximity to federal institutions, government networks and influential individuals may play a part. Volunteers may also see association with a prominent NGO as a route to future project positions, paid assignments or visibility. That is human, and not necessarily cynical, but it reminds us that volunteering follows opportunity as much as idealism.
This brings us back to what an NGO is actually for. These bodies exist partly because the state cannot reach every neighborhood, or is not trusted when it does. A rooted NGO therefore has relationships, local credibility and the ability to mobilise people. Its strength is not the number of salaries a grant can cover. Capacity and legitimacy are different things, and a large payroll does not make a strong civil-society actor.
The way forward is less glamorous than launching another NGO. Small NGOs should consider mergers, alliances and shared platforms. Established ones should build real pathways for volunteers. Donors should test applicants against transparent criteria: community roots, verifiable volunteer participation, measurable outcomes, local credibility, sound governance, ability to survive beyond one grant, and evidence of mobilising communities rather than hiring people to run activities. Community roots must become the central test of legitimacy. Until we accept that hundreds of small, personality-driven NGOs weaken collective influence, we will struggle to build public pressure, shape policy or create a genuine climate movement.

title: Militancy  historical perspective
description: The writ of the state must manifest not merely through application of force  but through the delivery of justice
content:
The writ of the state must manifest not merely through application of force, but through the delivery of justice
The province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa faces persistent militancy that can only be understood through its historical context. Rather than isolated incidents, the current waves of terrorism are rooted in decades of regional conflict. They remain deeply tied to broader regional dynamics, institutional weaknesses and the evolving security environment along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border.
The roots of the crisis trace back to the Soviet-Afghan War of the 1980s, when the borderlands transformed into critical conduits for fighters, weaponry and resources. Militant networks and ideologues gravitated toward this frontier belt - and they did not dissipate following the Soviet withdrawal.
The situation took a lethal turn following the 9/11 attacks and the subsequent US-led intervention in Afghanistan. As US and NATO forces deployed on the ground, Al-Qaeda and Taliban fighters retreated into Pakistan's tribal belt. In response, the Pakistan Army deployed to the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas, particularly North and South Waziristan. What initially appeared to be a border-security challenge gradually escalated into a sustained insurgency.
To better understand its trajectory, the evolution of terrorism in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and the former FATA can be divided into three distinct phases: an initial escalation and peak from 2003 to 2014; a substantial decline from 2015 to 2019; and a renewed resurgence from 2020 onward.
The first phase proved to be the most devastating. South and North Waziristan, Swat, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Peshawar, and adjoining districts witnessed rampant suicide bombings, targeted killings, attacks on security forces, and large-scale civilian displacement. During this period, the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) emerged as an umbrella organisation unifying various militant factions, which triggered a sharp escalation in the intensity of violence.
The Swat Valley presented one of the starkest examples of the eroding writ of the state. Militants established a parallel administrative structure, openly defying government institutions. In response, a series of military operations - including Rah-e-Haq, Rah-e-Rast and Rah-e-Nijat - were launched. Furthermore, Operation Zarb-e-Azb, launched in North Waziristan in June 2014, successfully dismantled entrenched militant networks but failed to entirely shatter their leadership nucleus. The human toll was catastrophic, with the UNHCR recording more than two million internally displaced persons during the 2009 Swat crisis alone.
Statistical data compiled by the South Asia Terrorism Portal (SATP) underscores the sheer intensity of the conflict. In 2009, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa recorded 5,883 terrorism-related fatalities - the highest annual figure documented in the series. Following this peak, annual fatalities began a gradual and steady decline.
The second phase, from 2015 to 2019, yielded significant progress. Operation Zarb-e-Azb successfully dismantled major militant infrastructure, while Operation Radd-ul-Fasaad was launched in February 2017 to eliminate residual terrorist networks and consolidate earlier gains. This concerted military effort led to a drastic drop in violence: according to the SATP, annual fatalities in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa plummeted to 298 in 2015, followed by 215 in 2016, 129 in 2017, 167 in 2018 and 130 in 2019.
The merger of FATA with Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa in May 31, 2017 was a landmark development. Before the merger, FATA was directly administered by the federal government.
The third phase, which began in 2020, became significantly more pronounced following the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in August 2021. This shift altered the region's entire geopolitical dynamic, creating a conducive environment for the TTP to renew its operational activities. Although peace negotiations were attempted between Pakistani authorities and the TTP, the talks ultimately collapsed. In November 2022, the group formally terminated its ceasefire and announced a widespread resumption of attacks.
In these renewed offensives, police stations, checkpoints, security convoys and individual personnel across Bannu, Lakki Marwat, Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, North and South Waziristan, Khyber and Bajaur became primary targets. While the geography of the conflict remained volatile, the tactical methods adopted by the militants remained largely unchanged.
The SATP data explicitly illustrates this escalating trajectory. Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa recorded 216 fatalities in 2020, 301 in 2021, 527 in 2022, 941 in 2023 and 1,363 in 2024. The toll sharply escalated to 2,359 in 2025. For 2026, SATP documented 1,654 fatalities up to September 26 alone, comprising 247 civilians, 316 security-force personnel and 1,091 militants.
The current resurgence, therefore, does not represent an entirely new conflict, but rather another phase of a prolonged struggle deeply rooted in regional history. Unless its historical, institutional, political and socioeconomic dimensions are comprehensively addressed, Pakistan risks merely suppressing the symptoms of the crisis without permanently eliminating the underlying conditions in which militancy regenerates.
A chronological analysis of these figures from 2003 to 2026 demonstrates that the core leadership nucleus and organizational structure of the militants remain intact, with little variation in their attack patterns. Furthermore, because this violent trend has persisted across successive, ideologically diverse administrations, militancy cannot reasonably be attributed to a single provincial government or political party alone. While governments should be judged on their policies, preparedness, governance and response, the foundational roots of the conflict remain inherently regional, historical, institutional and socioeconomic.
The experience of the past two decades offers a clear lesson: while military operations can dismantle militant infrastructure, eliminate key commanders, and reclaim territory - as demonstrated in the years following 2014 - such actions alone cannot guarantee sustainable peace.
Achieving long-term stability requires a multi-pronged approach that includes effective policing, robust intelligence coordination, a functioning criminal justice system and stringent border management. Furthermore, it demands sustained socioeconomic development, strengthened local governance, the rigorous implementation of the National Action Plan and targeted actions against terrorist financing, facilitation networks and organised crime.
Above all, the writ of the state must manifest not merely through the application of force, but through the delivery of swift justice, lawful governance and public confidence. Ultimately, lasting security cannot be achieved by military means alone; it relies on the comprehensive execution of institutional reforms and transparent, accountable governance.

title: Good news from Balochistan
description: A province traditionally lagging behind in human development  is spearheading IA driven endeavours
content:
A province traditionally lagging behind in human development, is spearheading IA-driven endeavours
What strikes you first when you think of Balochistan? For most, it is the volatile security situation, outcries over human rights violations, and political deprivation. National and international media frequently highlight the exploitation of its natural resources, painting a bleak picture of a province in perpetual turmoil. Isn't that right? However, stepping outside this mainstream narrative, a harbinger of good news is quietly emerging from Balochistan.
Although the scale and scope of this initiative is currently confined to the Peoples' Primary Healthcare Initiative (PPHI) within the Health Department of Balochistan, it sets a marvelous benchmark for the Government of Balochistan to scale it up. The PPHI Balochistan is built on the blueprint of the PPHI Sindh. What Balochistan has successfully embarked on is an innovative and unprecedented IA-based solution to chronic complaints of human interference, bureaucratic discretion of powers in the final selection of candidates, paper leaks and nepotism.
While it may sound a bit surprising that Balochistan, a province traditionally lagging behind in human development, is spearheading IA-driven endeavours, this reality directly contradicts the general perception. Ultimately, this initiative called ProMetriX has a strong potential to inspire other provinces across Pakistan to replicate the model, helping to plug a widening trust deficit over the public recruitment process. Especially, the Sindh Public Service Commission (SPSC) may consider learning from this paradigm to develop its own modules of examination free from human biases.
How does this newly launched ProMetriX look like? It is a complete automated digital recruitment and assessment eco-system, first of its kind in Pakistan that ensures merit-based recruitment without any human interface. The reason this is called an "eco-system" is that it encompasses a comprehensive process from the initial job advertisement all the way to the final appointment of the successful candidate.
The effectiveness of this AI-based system can be gauged from a smooth, large-scale recruitment exercise carried out by PPHI. The initiative filled 652 cadre positions, including lady medical officers, gynecologists, pediatricians, infectious disease specialists, cardiologists, dermatologists, psychiatrists, and pulmonologists.
The salient features of this exercise include online application submissions through the PPHI portal, which automatically generate an admission slip featuring a secure QR code. Subsequently, the credentials of all shortlisted candidates are verified through NADRA to eliminate impersonation. Furthermore, all candidates are required to appear for computer-based testing. Moving away from traditional panel interviews, candidates qualifying the written test are given standardized questions to record video replies, which are then assessed by AI entirely free of human bias or interference.
The story doesn't end there. What truly underscores the robustness and transparency of this system is that even unsuccessful candidates walk away satisfied, with no doubts about the credibility of the process. Because results are generated automatically and instantly the moment a test concludes, the merit list is declared in real time. Furthermore, the system auto-generates meeting minutes and immediately issues appointment letters to successful candidates - completely bypassing traditional bureaucratic red tape. It can be said with certainty that no other organisation or department in Pakistan has implemented a hiring process quite as transparent as this.
Alongside these administrative reforms, PPHI Balochistan, the provincial Health Department and the Government of Balochistan must expedite their joint efforts to tackle the province's critical healthcare crises. Key health indicators paint a stark picture, with maternal mortality, infant mortality, under-five mortality and stunting rates remaining alarmingly high across the region. However, by pairing concerted provincial strategies with modern AI-driven tools, substantive progress is within reach.

title: Global varsity rankings
description: Quaid i Azam University  the country s strongest performer  sits in the 551 600 band  followed by NUST  then COMSATS
content:
Quaid-i-Azam University, the country's strongest performer, sits in the 551-600 band, followed by NUST, then COMSATS
Pakistan's presence in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2027 offers both reassurance and warning. Fifty-six Pakistani universities have secured ranked positions, up from 48 in the previous edition. Yet not one has entered the global top 400. Quaid-i-Azam University, the country's strongest performer, sits in the 551-600 band, followed by NUST in the 601-650 bracket and COMSATS in the 651-700 band.
Increasing the number of universities represented internationally is welcome, but representation should not be confused with competitiveness. The more important question is why Pakistan, with a large university system and a substantial pool of young people, remains unable to produce even one institution capable of competing near the upper reaches of global academia. The strongest among them function as research centres, technology incubators, sources of specialised talent and partners to industry. Their laboratories generate intellectual property, their academics participate in international research networks and their graduates strengthen the economies surrounding them. Weak universities therefore impose a cost far beyond the education sector. The changing geography of the rankings makes Pakistan's position particularly troubling since the rest of Asia is beginning to challenge us. China now has 17 institutions among the world's top 200. Malaysia, meanwhile, has entered this group through the University of Malaya, ranked joint 194th. These advances did not occur through cosmetic attempts to improve rankings. They reflect long-term investments.
Pakistan remains weak across much of this ecosystem. Research funding is thin and laboratories frequently struggle with outdated equipment, leaving little room for serious research. There is no shortcut into the global academic elite. Nor should policymakers obsess over moving universities a few positions up an international table. The real objective should be to build institutions whose scholarship is respected, whose graduates are competitive and whose research contributes to economic and social progress.

title: Time to retire quotas
description: A growing number of educated Sindhi professionals are joining chorus of Urdu speaking critics to scrap quota regime
content:
A growing number of educated Sindhi professionals are joining chorus of Urdu-speaking critics to scrap quota regime
The debate over Sindh's urban-rural quota system has been rekindled by the recent MDCAT results, in which rural candidates performed impressively and exceeded their urban counterparts on several measures. For four decades, the 60:40 rural-urban split in government jobs and educational institutions has been a cornerstone of affirmative action, designed to bridge the divide between Sindh's developed and underdeveloped regions. However, the policy now faces a fresh challenge from an unlikely coalition, as a growing number of educated Sindhi professionals are joining the chorus of Urdu-speaking critics to scrap the quota regime.
Though outstanding rural performers pop up from time to time, the raw number of top performers this year is being used to argue for ending quotas. Students from some of Sindh's most underdeveloped districts, including Tharparkar, outperformed candidates from Karachi, Hyderabad and Sukkur. This empirical evidence directly challenges the quota system's foundational premise - that rural deprivation requires special protections. At the same time, some experts have noted that rural students' improved performance has occurred despite the rural-urban resource gap not narrowing significantly - students are doing better despite the quota, not because of it.
A more legitimate critique, however, is that despite increasing urbanisation, only Karachi, Hyderabad and Sukkur are considered "urban". Larkana, which has the same population as Sukkur, is treated as rural, as are cities such as Mirpur Khas, Jacobabad and Tharparkar, which all have populations of over 200,000. Urdu-speaking critics of quotas have long accused PPP of using them for political gain. Some analysts have also claimed that the quotas discouraged urban youth from pursuing government jobs, creating an imbalance as fewer competent urban youth apply for posts and leaving urban people underrepresented in government.
However, while the necessity of quotas has become debatable, public discussions over the issue have provided an ugly reminder that bigoted attitudes towards Sindhis are still a major issue that is not really up for debate.

title: Makkah Pact in action
description: The impression that Pakistani  Turkish troops will be engaged in hot pursuit against Yemen is a misconception
content:
The impression that Pakistani, Turkish troops will be engaged in hot pursuit against Yemen is a misconception
The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement marked a significant milestone as member states agreed to implement its collective defence commitments in full. As an immediate measure, Pakistan and Türkiye will rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia to deter regional security threats against the Kingdom. While Islamabad already maintains a substantial, longstanding security presence in the Kingdom through a bilateral understanding, this trilateral escalation will significantly reinforce reconnaissance capabilities and aerial superiority.
The impression that Pakistani and Turkish troops will be engaged in hot pursuit against Yemen or any other neighbouring state is a misconception. That has been categorically clarified by either state. The deployment was prompted by escalating Houthi provocations, which Riyadh claims endangered the Kingdom's security through drone incursions near the holy cities of Makkah and Medina. Though the Yemeni militia had denied it, the belligerent acts from the pro-Iran non-state actor had led to truncation of supply lines, endangering Saudi navigation and global trade, alike.
It is highly promising that the Makkah Pact has transitioned into a formalised institutional mechanism by establishing a permanent secretariat in Riyadh. The recent meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee with key stakeholders served as a timely demonstration that the alliance extends beyond mere rhetoric, signaling that member states possess both the political will and the strategic resources to act as a robust bulwark against terrorism.
As Yemeni government forces launch a counter-offensive against the Houthis to reclaim lost territory, the trilateral alliance's surveillance, intelligence-gathering and reconnaissance capabilities will provide a critical strategic boost. This synergy represents the core essence of pooling regional resources: to deter any major assault on the Kingdom and to prevent hostile actors from escalating the conflict beyond the brink. The articulation of Makkah Pact is a masterstroke of inward-looking military integration and collective capacity to confront and counter threats.
