content:
Govt-PTI standoff, reversal of oil losses weigh on investor confidence
Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) came under intense selling pressure on Monday, with the benchmark KSE-100 index plunging 2,288 points, as domestic political tensions weighed heavily on investor sentiment, while falling international oil prices failed to provide relief.
The index settled at 165,867.32, down 1.36% from the previous close of 168,155.49. It hit the intra-day high of 167,918.37 and low of 165,764.21, reflecting volatility throughout the session. The domestic political anxiety deepened after talks between the government and the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) collapsed without a breakthrough, with the PTI pressing ahead with its march towards Islamabad. Differences over the counter-terrorism policy and access to jailed PTI founder Imran Khan were among the key sticking points, heightening concerns over renewed political confrontation. The market stayed under pressure amid volatile oil prices, which initially fell on expectations of higher Middle Eastern supplies and G7's planned release of emergency stocks before turning higher later following worries about disruptions to regional energy supplies.
According to Arif Habib Limited (AHL), eight shares rose while 91 fell with Pakistan Oilfields (+1.16%), Tariq Glass Industries (+0.81%) and Highnoon Laboratories (+0.23%) contributing the most to the index's gains. Alternatively, UBL (-1.57%), Engro Holdings (-1.77%) and HBL (-2.34%) were the biggest index drags. Meanwhile, AHL mentioned, the political party of former PM Imran Khan began its march towards Islamabad after talks with the government broke down over different demands including access to the jailed leader. Authorities placed shipping containers and other roadblocks around Islamabad to prevent demonstrators from entering the capital.
On the regional front, Yemen's government launched a full-scale military campaign to recapture the Houthi-held territory after weeks of escalating conflict between the Iran-backed group and Saudi Arabia. "After hitting the downside target of 166k, the potential for a near-term pullback rises; however, additional downside targets remain a possibility in the coming weeks," AHL wrote.
Ahmed Sheraz of KASB KTrade noted that the KSE-100 extended its correction on Monday, closing at 165,867, down 2,288 points, or 1.36%, amid broad-based selling and heightened risk aversion. Volumes remained subdued at 169 million shares, with Pakistan International Bulk Terminal, Cnergyico, K-Electric and The Bank of Punjab leading the activity.
Selling was witnessed across commercial banks, investment banks, cement, oil & gas and power sectors, where UBL, Engro Holdings, HBL, Hub Power, Pakistan Petroleum and OGDC were among the major laggards. Meanwhile, international oil prices remained elevated around $101-103/barrel, while renewed tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea added pressure to the sentiment.
Domestically, rising political noise, including the long march and speculation around potential constitutional measures, further weighed on investor confidence. "Going forward, we expect the KSE-100 to remain volatile and range bound until greater clarity emerges on the political front and geopolitical tensions ease," Sheraz said. Cumulatively, trading volumes fell to 441.9 million shares compared with 494 million in the previous session.
Shares of 499 companies were traded in the ready market, of which 55 closed higher, 409 fell and 35 stood unchanged.
First National Equities was the volume leader with trading in 50.3 million shares, falling Rs0.05 to close at Rs1.17. Foreign investors sold shares worth Rs45 million, the National Clearing Company reported.

title: Thar coalmine begins third expansion
description: Thar coalmine begins third expansion
content:
Capacity rises to 11.2m tonnes, targetting $220m in fuel savings
The third-phase expansion of the Thar Block-II coalmine has commenced in Sindh's Tharparkar district, further increasing the mine's annual production capacity from 7.6 million tonnes to 11.2 million tonnes and the use of indigenous resources for affordable power generation.
Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company (SECMC) began commercial operations in Thar Block-II in 2019 with an annual mining capacity of 3.8 million tons per annum. The second phase, completed in 2022, increased capacity to 7.6 million tons. With the third phase, the annual production will rise by another 3.6 million tonnes, the third expansion in seven years.
SECMC contributes 14% electricity to the national grid. The additional coal will be supplied to Lucky Electric Power Company Limited (LEPCL), which operates a 660-megawatt power plant. With its inclusion, SECMC will supply coal to power plants with a combined generation capacity of 1,980 MW, including 660MW Engro Powergen Thar Limited (EPTL), 330MW Thar Energy Limited (TEL) and 330MW ThalNova Power Thar Limited (TNPL).
After the expansion, the levelised coal tariff is projected to decline from $36.72 to $32.01 per tonne, resulting in an estimated annual reduction of around Rs15 billion in generation costs and saving an estimated $220 million in fuel imports. The expanded power generation will provide reliable electricity to around 4.5 million households.
Speaking at a ceremony to mark the occasion, SECMC Chief Executive Officer Amir Iqbal said, "Thar's story is a journey from the impossible to excellence, achieved through vision, collaboration and resilience." He said Thar is contributing not only to Pakistan's energy security but also to the country's economic growth.
PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said the scale of development witnessed in Thar was unmatched elsewhere in Pakistan, highlighting the transformation in the region's health and education systems. He felicitated SECMC on its achievement, with the Thar mine now ranked among the top 4% of mines globally.

title: SOEs  debt soars to Rs10 1 trillion
description: SOEs  debt soars to Rs10 1 trillion
content:
Finance ministry report says debt Rs7.1tr higher than State Bank figures
The debt level of state-owned companies jumped to a record Rs10.1 trillion by the end of December 2025, higher by 242% than the central bank statistics, which raises questions about governance reforms.
The finance ministry disclosed that the per-working-day loss of SOEs increased to Rs2.8 billion (Rs730 billion annually) and the per-day financial support swelled to Rs6.6 billion (Rs1.7 trillion per year). At the given per-day losses and fiscal support, the cumulative annual impact comes to Rs2.5 trillion, which is Rs1.5 trillion more than this fiscal year's federal development budget.
These figures were disclosed by the Ministry of Finance on Monday in an excellent analytical report on SOE monitoring for July-December 2025, which stated "financial engineering and debt re-profiling measures alone remain insufficient" to address the circular debt problem in the power sector. The findings negate the claims made by the federal government, the IMF and the World Bank about improvements in the SOE affairs, particularly the reduction in the circular debt stock and flow.
According to the Central Monitoring Unit (CMU) of the finance ministry, the total debt of SOEs jumped to Rs10.1 trillion as of end-December, an increase of Rs1.3 trillion, or 14.3%, over the same period of the preceding year. The total debt the CMU reported was Rs7.1 trillion, or 242%, higher than the total public debt and liabilities of SOEs reported by the State Bank of Pakistan. The SBP bulletin put the debt and liabilities of SOEs at Rs2.95 trillion till December last year.
The broader SOE balance sheet remains highly leveraged, with debt exposure exceeding Rs10 trillion, including Rs2.6 trillion in foreign currency-denominated liabilities, said the CMU. The publication of the report was delayed for a while and it came just two days before the end of IMF talks.
The CMU said the Rs2.6 trillion foreign liabilities of SOEs were "exposing the sovereign to elevated exchange rate pass-through risk, refinancing pressure, imported inflation sensitivity and external account volatility". The report showed the government gave Rs2.1 trillion in cash development loans to SOEs as of December last year, higher by Rs416 billion, or 25%, in a year. Likewise, there was a 40% hike in foreign loans, which jumped to Rs2.6 trillion.
The report stated that banks also gave Rs3.1 trillion in loans to SOEs and the cost of unfunded pension liabilities was Rs2 trillion, up 11%. "The aggregate loss profile of loss-making SOEs is estimated at Rs2.8 billion on a per-working-day basis, while fiscal support through subsidies, grants, loans and equity injections reached nearly Rs6.6 billion per day, equivalent to 11% of total federal budgetary receipts."
Concurrently, the CMU stated that Pakistan's combined circular debt escalated to Rs3.3 trillion and despite restructuring initiatives and the partial warehousing of liabilities through Central Power Purchasing Agency-linked financing arrangements, serviced via the Debt Servicing Surcharge (DSS), the stock still increased within the six-month period.
"This deterioration demonstrates that financial engineering and debt re-profiling measures alone remain insufficient in the absence of deep-rooted operational reforms across generation, transmission, distribution, tariff rationalisation, governance enforcement, theft control and recovery mechanisms," said the finance ministry.
The report stated that additional fiscal fragilities arise from sovereign guarantees exceeding Rs2.1 trillion and unfunded pension liabilities approaching Rs1.9 trillion, both of which represent latent contingent obligations capable of crystallising into direct federal liabilities under stressed macroeconomic conditions.
The CMU said the anticipated IFRS 9 Expected Credit Loss (ECL) provisioning requirements within the oil & gas sector could trigger incremental provisioning shocks approaching Rs500 billion, materially impairing profitability, retained earnings, dividend flows to the government and overall market capitalisation within one of the few currently profitable segments of the portfolio.
The report commented on performance of the power sector that was on the decline. Losses relating to DISCOs were primarily attributable to technical losses exceeding Nepra benchmarks, persistent under-recoveries and continuing circular debt accumulation arising from operational inefficiencies.
The circular-debt flow attributable to DISCO inefficiencies amounted to Rs112 billion, while under-recoveries contributed an additional Rs31 billion during the six-month period. Notably, despite broader restructuring initiatives, the underlying circular debt flow continued to rise to Rs374 billion on a gross basis over the first half of 2026 fiscal year as per Power Division's numbers.
The CMU said that overall the loss profile of the SOE sector continued to remain concentrated in structurally weak infrastructure and energy entities, particularly within the power distribution segment, where inefficiencies, technical losses and tariff distortions continued to transmit significant fiscal pressure onto the sovereign balance sheet.
The most pronounced increase was recorded in equity injections during the first half of last fiscal year, which surged by 190% to Rs225 billion. These injections were primarily one-off in nature and directed largely towards clearing power-sector circular debt obligations through payments to Independent Power Producers (IPPs). However, despite these interventions, the circular debt stock continued to accumulate, increasing by Rs143 billion during the six-month period, it added.
To improve fiscal transparency and mitigate the accumulation of unaccounted-for subsidy payables, the implementation of structured Public Service Obligation (PSO) frameworks supported by accurate and verifiable costing methodologies is recommended across applicable SOEs, according to CMU.
It said that Pakistan's SOE portfolio represented a material and increasingly systemic macro-fiscal vulnerability, characterised by excessive dependence on a narrow subset of profitable entities within the oil and financial sectors, while a substantial portion of the broader portfolio remained structurally loss-making and fiscally dependent.
Profitability within the oil sector itself remains materially exposed to international commodity price volatility and limited portfolio-level hedging mechanisms, thereby increasing earnings sensitivity and dividend instability during adverse pricing cycles. Accordingly, the portfolio exhibits elevated concentration risk, whereby a limited group of profitable SOEs effectively subsidises broader systemic inefficiencies across the federal SOE landscape.

title: NEPRA reviews incremental consumption package
description: NEPRA reviews incremental consumption package
content:
Power Division argues scheme's low tariff under significant pressure due to rising costs
The Ministry of Energy (Power Division) is seeking a review of the incremental consumption package introduced for industrial and agricultural consumers following an increase in the cost of electricity.
The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) conducted a public hearing on Monday to review the consumption package. A tariff of Rs22.98 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) had been fixed under the package for industrial and agricultural consumers. The incentive scheme covers industrial and private agricultural electricity consumers across jurisdictions of ex-Wapda power distribution companies and K-Electric. It applies to both Time-of-Use (ToU) and Non-Time-of-Use (N-ToU) consumers as well as covers peak and off-peak incremental electricity consumption.
The Power Division submitted a review motion during the public hearing. According to the presentation, Nepra had approved the package on December 9, 2025. The decision was formally notified on December 10, 2025 to remain in effect for three years. The division argued that there was a significant pressure on the scheme's tariff of Rs22.98/kWh as average marginal costs exceeded the announced rate over several months. The weighted average marginal cost reached Rs27.58/kWh from December through May. The loss-adjusted marginal cost produced an even higher weighted average of Rs31.83/kWh, according to the Power Division.
The division contended that the average marginal cost hit Rs36.71/kWh during April and remained at Rs33.98/kWh during May. The loss-adjusted cost rose to Rs42.37/kWh in April and Rs39.22/kWh in May.
Until such approval of the power-sector regulator, the difference is being borne by other consumers across the board that creates a central issue for the ongoing semi-annual review.
The package also contains a separate safeguard linked to consumption growth. A review is triggered when combined industrial and agricultural consumption exceeds 25% above the baseline. January recorded a monthly growth of 25.13%, while February registered a rise of 26.20%. April recorded the highest monthly growth of 34.81%. Other months remained below the 25% threshold.
The semi-annual review creates another basis for considering a tariff adjustment. Any decision taken requires reviews to maintain cost-revenue alignment. The Power Division said it also allowed marginal tariffs to be adjusted, when necessary. "The scheme must terminate if upward adjustments become necessary during two consecutive reviews." The division was required to submit such data after stakeholder consultations. The expected timeline was the first week of June 2026. Instead, raw data was provided to Nepra on July 29, 2026.
After Nepra requested a proposal following consultations, the division responded on September 9 and asked the regulator to kick off proceedings, according to the presentation. The six-month weighted average marginal rate stood around Rs32/kWh and four months had already passed under the second review period. It raised the question about whether the package should be suspended amid continued higher marginal prices. Average tariff comparisons also show different effective break-even prices. For B1 peak consumers, the effective break-even price was Rs31.15/kWh, for B2 Time-of-Use consumers, the break-even price was Rs29.05/kWh and for B3, B4 and B5 categories, the rates were Rs30.03, Rs29.62 and Rs32.91 per kWh, respectively.
The immediate issue is whether the tariff of Rs22.98/kWh reflects current marginal costs. The presentation indicates that actual costs have remained materially higher. Nepra's hearing will determine whether the rate should go up or suspension should follow. Its outcome will shape the future of the incremental consumption package.
Intervener Rehan Javed called for revising the rate according to the actual marginal cost, effective from June 2026. He also asked for refunding the marginal price charged to non-beneficiary consumers from June 2026. He pleaded to recover it from the beneficiaries at the revised rate and any residue from the government as sponsor of the package.
Amir Sheikh, another intervener, said the package was increasing the cross-subsidy cost for domestic/commercial users, adding that a majority of industries had to cross-subsidise a few large consumers.
"Gas levy has led to captive-grid conversion, so the package is not required," he said, arguing that resorting to load-shedding and allowing a reduced cost package to industrial and agricultural consumers were self-contradictory. "The only fair and sound decision is to suspend the package," he said.

title: Fish  seafood exports hit  125m
description: Fish  seafood exports hit  125m
content:
74% increase in Q1 reflects opening of new global markets including Russia, US
Federal Minister for Maritime Affairs Muhammad Junaid Anwar Chaudhry said on Monday that Pakistan's fish and seafood exports rose by 74.4% during the first quarter of the current fiscal year, reaching $125.4 million against $71.9 million during the last two fiscal years.
"The increase in export earnings underscores the growing economic potential of the marine fisheries sector as Pakistan seeks to expand its blue economy," he said in a statement. Chaudhry noted that export volume rose by 74.8% over the three-year period, increasing from 35,294 tonnes in the first quarter of 2024-25 to 61,679 tonnes in the same quarter of 2026-27.
Fish exports stood at $93.28 million during the first quarter of 2025-26, before rising to $125.4 million in the first quarter of the current fiscal year. In terms of volume, exports increased from 35,294 tonnes in Q1 2024-25 to 43,995 tonnes in Q1 2025-26 and reached 61,679 tonnes in Q1 2026-27. The minister noted that both the value and volume of fish exports had grown substantially over the past three years, with the rise in export earnings broadly keeping pace with the increase in volume.
He said the fisheries sector was an important component of Pakistan's coastal economy, providing livelihoods to fishing communities while generating foreign exchange through exports of fish and other marine products. Chaudhry appreciated the performance of the Marine Fisheries Department, particularly its record export earnings of $568 million during FY2025-26.
He said the opening of new international markets, particularly Russia, for Pakistani fisheries' products was another significant achievement, adding that recent initiatives to resume shrimp exports to the United States, along with the revival of fishing licensing regime in Pakistan's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), would help promote the sustainable utilisation of the country's marine fisheries' resources.
The minister stressed the need for addressing institutional, technical and capacity-related bottlenecks to enhance fish and seafood exports to lucrative international seafood markets, particularly the European Union. He also called for the revival of the Fisheries Training Centre of the Marine Fisheries Department to strengthen human-resources capacity, improve technical and professional standards, and enhance compliance with international fisheries and seafood safety requirements.

title: Gold up Rs1 200  global market flat
description: Gold up Rs1 200  global market flat
content:
Rises to Rs437,536/tola as Fed bets shift; rupee inches up
Gold prices in Pakistan increased on Monday despite little movement in the international market, as local prices reflected a lagged impact of previous global movements. The price of gold per tola rose Rs1,200 to Rs437,536, according to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association.
The price of 10-gram gold increased by Rs1,029 to Rs375,116. On Saturday, gold had fallen by Rs4,300 per tola. The local market's strength came as international gold prices remained broadly steady, with pressure from a stronger US dollar and elevated Treasury yields offset by reduced expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike this month.
Spot gold edged 0.1% lower to $4,137.79 per ounce by 11:41 am EDT (1541 GMT), while US gold futures for December delivery gained 0.1% to $4,166, as per Reuters. The US dollar index strengthened, making dollar-denominated gold more expensive for buyers holding other currencies. At the same time, the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds remained near two-decade highs, limiting the appeal of non-yielding bullion.
However, expectations of further US monetary tightening have weakened after recent economic data largely disappointed market forecasts. Traders currently see a 22% probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike in October, while the probability rises to 84% for December, according to market expectations.
Market participants are now awaiting the release of the September Federal Open Market Committee minutes on Wednesday, which could provide further clues about the central bank's rate outlook.
Forex.com market analyst Fawad Razaqzada said gold could face a near-term decline before buyers return more strongly, citing the combination of a rising dollar and elevated bond yields. He said recent US economic data had largely fallen short of expectations, resulting in a reduction in bets on higher rates.
Lower rates generally support gold by reducing the opportunity cost of holding the non-yielding asset, while higher rates and bond yields tend to weigh on bullion. Meanwhile, longer-term expectations remain bullish. Metals Focus expects gold to reach new all-time highs in 2027, suggesting that the current consolidation may precede another period of gains.
Silver also strengthened in Pakistan on Monday. The price of silver rose Rs66 per tola to Rs6,588, marking a new all-time high. The divergent moves in gold and silver came as investors continued to assess currency movements, US monetary policy expectations and the outlook for precious metals. Meanwhile, the Pakistani rupee closed at 277.06 against the US dollar, gaining Rs0.01 in the inter-bank market.

title: Health  education face IMF cut
description: Health  education face IMF cut
content:
Provincial cash commitments to federal govt threaten spending target
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) may cut health and education spending targets to around Rs3.9 trillion because of fiscal pressures that the provincial governments are facing after committing cash grants to the centre in addition to generating a huge cash surplus to meet another condition of the programme.
Government sources told The Express Tribune that after holding meetings with the provincial governments, it has become evident to the IMF that the target of cumulative spending of Rs4.2 trillion on health and education will again be missed during this fiscal year. For the last fiscal year, the combined spending remained Rs370 billion less than the IMF-given target.
Secretary Finance Imdad Ullah Bosal had told a parliamentary committee last month that the IMF condition on health and educational spending has been constantly missed during the ongoing programme.
Under a condition of the $7 billion bailout package, the five governments are required to spend over Rs4.2 trillion, but their total budget allocations are already Rs500 billion less than the IMF requirement.
Sources said that there was a possibility that the IMF could lower the target to Rs3.9 trillion, but the final round of discussions was pending. Even after adjusting the target downwards by Rs300 billion to Rs3.9 trillion, there would still be a gap of around Rs200 billion against the budget allocations and any revised target, subject to the final agreement between both sides.
The finance ministry could not ensure at the time of budgets in June to reconcile provincial health and education spending with the IMF's quarterly and annual targets, and there was no gap in allocations versus targets.
IMF talks are reaching their conclusion, and discussions are currently focused on finalising a consensus draft of the Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies (MEFP) – the policy document that would become the base for the next programme review. The talks are scheduled to end on Wednesday, and if a staff-level agreement is reached, Pakistan will get $1 billion under the $7 billion package and another over $200 million under the climate facility.
The sources said that at one point the IMF had hinted at making the condition more stringent by declaring it a quantitative performance criterion as against the current indicative target. The breach of the performance criterion requires the waiver of the IMF executive board. The IMF resident representative did not comment on the development.
Due to constantly missing the tax collection target of the Federal Board of Revenue, the IMF has now made it a quantitative performance criterion by enhancing its severity limit from the indicative target. The condition on health and educational spending has been missed in the past despite the IMF having imposed a limit to keep primary current spending at the projected inflation rate, while fiscal space is explicitly reallocated to social protection, health and education.
The sources said that during the review talks, the IMF mission inquired from the provinces whether they would be able to achieve the spending targets on health and education. Sindh and Punjab said that their budgets were already facing pressures due to the commitment to provide Rs1.7 trillion cash surplus and giving cash grants to the federal government under the National Economic Initiative.
However, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, which has not yet committed to provide cash grants to the centre, assured the meeting that it would meet its spending targets.
The finance secretary said last month that the health and education spending targets could not be met because of some provinces, and it remained a recurring concern in almost every review. Bosal said that due to missing the FBR's tax collection targets, the federal government had to request the provinces to curtail their expenses.
For fiscal year 2026-27, the Punjab government has allocated Rs1.3 trillion for education and health sectors out of its total provincial budget outlay of Rs5.9 trillion. Sindh has cumulatively allocated Rs1.1 trillion, K-P over Rs800 billion and Balochistan Rs268 billion for spending on health and education.
In the budget, the federal and provincial governments had agreed to an arrangement under which these governments would provide Rs1.036 trillion in cash grant provided the FBR achieves its annual target of Rs15.263 trillion. The FBR has exceeded the first-quarter target by a margin of Rs33 trillion, mainly because of setting a low target.
The federal government had also cut its Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP) by Rs126 billion to Rs1 trillion to create fiscal space for national economic initiatives. Punjab also reduced its development spending envelope by Rs150 billion.

title: Nyle DiMarco joins Hulu   s  All   s Fair  season 2 in recurring role
description: Nyle DiMarco joins Hulu   s  All   s Fair  season 2  with his role adapted for the deaf actor and advocate
content:
Nyle DiMarco joins Hulu’s 'All’s Fair' season 2, with his role adapted for the deaf actor and advocate
Nyle DiMarco has joined the recurring cast of Hulu’s legal drama All’s Fair for its upcoming second season.
DiMarco’s role is currently being kept under wraps, but the character was originally written as a hearing person and is being adapted specifically for the deaf actor. His casting continues his work advocating for authentic deaf representation in film and television.
DiMarco joins a cast led by Kim Kardashian, Naomi Watts, Niecy Nash-Betts, Teyana Taylor, Matthew Noszka, Sarah Paulson and Glenn Close. Brazilian actor Cauã Reymond has also joined All’s Fair as a new Season 2 series regular.
Created by Ryan Murphy, All’s Fair follows Allura Grant, played by Kardashian, who establishes a female divorce law firm with Liberty Ronson and Emerald Greene, portrayed by Watts and Nash-Betts. The series explores high-profile divorces, personal scandals, rivalries and shifting relationships within the firm.
Season 2 will see the lawyers of Grant, Ronson & Greene return as new alliances and conflicts develop. According to the series’ description, a major revelation will also threaten the future of the firm.
DiMarco joins All’s Fair after expanding his career behind the camera. His directorial debut, Deaf President Now! , premiered at the 2025 Sundance Film Festival before its release on Apple TV+ in May 2025. The documentary received a Humanitas Prize nomination and two Emmy nominations, including Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special and Outstanding Directing for a Documentary/Nonfiction Program. DiMarco became the first deaf filmmaker nominated for an Emmy in the latter category.
His previous acting credits include Queer as Folk , Station 19 , Difficult People and Switched at Birth . He also produced the Oscar-nominated documentary short Audible .
All’s Fair is produced by 20th Television in association with Ryan Murphy Television.

title: Ewan Mitchell being eyed for Bond villain role
description: Ewan Mitchell being eyed for Bond villain role
content:
'House of the Dragon' star may feature in next 007 film
Ewan Mitchell is reportedly being considered for a villain role in the upcoming James Bond film, according to a new rumour.
The House of the Dragon star, who plays Prince Aemond Targaryen in the HBO series, is said to be in contention for a part in the next 007 movie. Mitchell has not commented on the report, and Amazon has yet to announce the cast for Bond 26.
Amazon is developing a James Bond reboot following Daniel Craig's departure from the role after No Time to Die in 2021. The studio took control of the franchise in a deal reportedly worth around $1 billion.
Denis Villeneuve, known for directing Dune, has been confirmed as the director of Bond 26, while Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight is writing the screenplay. Casting details have remained closely guarded, although Amazon has confirmed that the search for the next James Bond is underway.
The rumour surrounding Mitchell comes on October 5, which is celebrated as James Bond Day and marks the 1962 release of Dr. No. Some fans have speculated that Amazon could reveal casting news as part of this year's celebrations.
Producer Amy Pascal previously said the next James Bond is expected to be cast by the end of 2026. Several actors have been linked to the role, including Tom Holland, Taron Egerton, Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Jack O'Connell, although no official decision has been announced.
Mitchell recently appeared in the third season of House of the Dragon. The fantasy series is set to conclude with its fourth season in 2028, while the wider Game of Thrones franchise continues to expand with upcoming spin-offs and films.

title: Mark Ruffalo warns Trump at voting rights rally
description: Mark Ruffalo warns Trump at voting rights rally
content:
'I'm gonna Hulk out and you won't like me when I'm angry', says actor
Mark Ruffalo delivered a fiery warning to Donald Trump during a voting rights event in New York, telling the president to keep his hands off the vote before joking that he was going to "Hulk out".
The Avengers star spoke at the Hands Off Our Vote event on Sunday night, where he urged supporters to remain engaged ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. The event also featured Robert De Niro and other speakers focused on voter participation and election protection.
Ruffalo described the election as a major moment and warned that efforts could be made to interfere with voters. He encouraged people to support Free Speech for People, an organisation involved in efforts concerning election security and voting systems.
He then turned his attention directly to Trump, calling on voters to oppose the president's policies and accusing his administration of trying to make people feel intimidated and powerless.
"We're not going to let 'em," Ruffalo told the crowd before addressing Trump directly. "Hands off our f***ing vote!"
The actor's comments drew a response from the audience, with someone shouting, "You tell 'em, Hulk!" The reference was to Ruffalo's long running role as Bruce Banner and the Hulk in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
Ruffalo laughed before embracing the comparison, saying, "I'm gonna Hulk out. You won't like me when I'm angry." He also told the crowd that he remained involved and was still playing the Hulk.
Ruffalo ended his speech by urging supporters not to be afraid or discouraged. He stressed the importance of standing together, remaining brave and voting.
The appearance comes during an increasingly active period of political campaigning ahead of the midterms. Ruffalo has frequently used his public platform to comment on political and social issues.
Mark Ruffalo began his career in the late 1980s and first gained recognition for his work in Kenneth Lonergan's play This Is Our Youth (1996) and drama film You Can Count on Me (2000). He went on to star in the romantic comedies 13 Going on 30 (2004) and Just like Heaven (2005), and the thrillers In the Cut (2003), Zodiac (2007), and Shutter Island (2010). He received a Tony Award nomination for his supporting role in the Broadway revival of Awake and Sing! in 2006. Ruffalo has gained international recognition for playing Bruce Banner / Hulk in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, beginning with the film The Avengers (2012).
Ruffalo earned a record-tying four nominations for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for playing a sperm donor in The Kids Are All Right (2010), Dave Schultz in Foxcatcher (2014), Michael Rezendes in Spotlight (2015), and a debauched lawyer in Poor Things (2023). He won a Screen Actors Guild Award for Best Actor for his role in the television drama film The Normal Heart (2015).

title: We have limited ourselves  says Bushra Ansari
description: We have limited ourselves  says Bushra Ansari
content:
Veteran actor reflects on Pakistani cinema, creative freedom
Veteran actor Bushra Ansari has called for greater creative freedom in Pakistan's film industry, saying Pakistani cinema cannot compete internationally if filmmakers remain restricted to a limited range of subjects and themes.
Speaking to Express Tribune, Ansari reflected on the state of Pakistani cinema after recently praising an Indian Punjabi film 'Main Vaapas Aaunga' based on the Partition of India. She said the comparison had also made her think about the creative freedom available to filmmakers across the border.
"We cannot compete with Indian Punjabi cinema because they have a lot more freedom. They have the freedom to talk about many things. It is not only about what they wear; they have much greater freedom," Ansari said.
She said Pakistani artists and filmmakers faced several restrictions, both in terms of what could be shown on screen and the subjects that could be discussed.
"We have to face so many restrictions, and then we ourselves make fun of them. That is why we have made ourselves very limited," she said.
According to Ansari, filmmakers across the border are able to explore a wider range of subjects, while Pakistani cinema often finds itself restricted to a few themes.
"They talk about one thing or another. They do not limit themselves in the same way. We have limited ourselves so much that we can only talk about a few things and then we end up making films like 'Jawani Phir Nahi Ani'. So there is a big difference between their freedom and our freedom," she said.
Ansari also pointed to filmmaker Sarmad Sultan Khoosat's Lali as an example of what Pakistani cinema can achieve when filmmakers take risks, but said that the film was not allowed to be screened in Pakistani cinemas.
The Punjabi-language film revolves around a young woman whose previous suitors have died before marriage, leading to rumours that she is cursed. Directed by Khoosat, the film explores marriage, superstition, fear and social expectations through the story of its central character.
Lali also received international attention after its premiere at the Berlin International Film Festival, highlighting the potential for Pakistani stories to reach audiences beyond the country.
Ansari said Pakistani cinema needed more opportunities to tell such stories and compete in the international market.
She also expressed optimism about the growing presence of OTT platforms in Pakistan.
"I am very happy that OTT platforms are also being made in Pakistan. I think others should also join in, so that we have a space where we can speak openly. There should be such a space, and we should be there," she said.

title: Robert Kelker Kelly   Days of Our Lives  star who played Bo Brady  dies at 62
description: Robert Kelker Kelly  known for playing Bo Brady on  Days of Our Lives   has died at 62 in Missouri after chest pain
content:
Robert Kelker-Kelly, known for playing Bo Brady on 'Days of Our Lives', has died at 62 in Missouri after chest pain
Robert Kelker-Kelly, best known for playing Bo Brady on the long-running soap opera Days of Our Lives , has died at 62.
Kelker-Kelly died Saturday in St. Peters, Missouri, according to the St. Peters Police Department. Officers responded to a report of an unconscious man who was not breathing. Police said Kelker-Kelly had reportedly complained of chest pain shortly before becoming unresponsive, with the circumstances appearing consistent with a medical event.
The actor began his television career in 1987 when he joined Another World as Sam Fowler. He later became known to daytime television audiences for his role as Bo Brady on Days of Our Lives , joining the NBC soap opera in 1992 and taking over the role from Peter Reckell.
During his time on the series, Kelker-Kelly appeared opposite Kristian Alfonso, who played Hope Brady, and Lisa Rinna, who portrayed Billie Reed. Reckell returned to the role of Bo in 1995.
Rinna later discussed her working relationship with Kelker-Kelly in her memoir, You Better Believe I’m Gonna Talk About It , describing tensions between the two actors despite their frequent scenes together. Kelker-Kelly and Rinna both joined Days of Our Lives in 1992 and received a Soap Opera Digest Award for Hottest Soap Couple in 1995.
Kelker-Kelly married Miriam Parrish in 1997 and subsequently left Los Angeles and acting. He became certified as an airframe and powerplant mechanic before pursuing a career as a professional pilot. He also taught acting and continued flying and teaching until his death.
His other television credits included General Hospital , where he played Stavros Cassadine in 2001 and returned for guest appearances in later years. His film and television work also included Dream for an Insomniac , Winter Heat and Mr. Write .

title: Justice beyond the conventional contours
description: Article 37 d  of the Constitution places upon the State the responsibility to ensure inexpensive  expeditious justice
content:
Article 37(d) of the Constitution places upon the State the responsibility to ensure inexpensive, expeditious justice
Behind every case is a human story: a family worried about its home, a widow protecting her rights, a worker seeking what is due, or simply someone who does not know where to turn. The courthouse doors may be open, yet justice can remain beyond reach when the cost of seeking it is more than a person can bear. For someone already struggling to make ends meet, the question is not always whether the law provides a remedy, but whether they can realistically reach it.
For such people, litigation is not merely a legal process. A court visit may mean losing a day's income. A lawyer's fee may compete with food, school fees or medicines. Even knowing where to go and how to begin can become a barrier. A right guaranteed by law has limited meaning if a person lacks the means to claim it. This is where justice must move beyond the conventional contours of courts and courtrooms.
Article 37(d) of the Constitution places upon the State the responsibility to ensure inexpensive and expeditious justice. Behind this commitment lies a basic principle of the social contract: citizens look to the State not merely to make laws, but to protect rights and provide remedies when those rights are violated. Justice cannot be truly inclusive if the ability to seek it depends upon the ability to pay.
Recent judicial initiatives seek to address this divide. The National Judicial Policy Making Committee announced an initiative under which financially distressed litigants may receive legal representation at State expense across the judicial hierarchy, from Magistrate Courts to the Supreme Court. The Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan is also working towards a broader framework for free legal aid and advice. The principle behind these efforts is simple: poverty should not determine whether a person is heard before a court.
But access to justice begins even before a lawyer enters the courtroom. Someone unfamiliar with the courts may not know what remedy is available or where to seek help. To those familiar with the system, these may seem ordinary questions. For someone poor, vulnerable or distressed, they can become walls between a right and its remedy.
The Supreme Court's Call Centre can help bridge this gap. Experienced legal professionals, including a retired judge and a legal consultant, have been engaged to provide legal advice over the telephone or through a visit to the Centre. For someone unable to afford even an initial consultation, this means having somewhere to turn, someone who will listen, understand the problem and guide them towards the appropriate legal forum.
The Bar forms another important pillar of this approach. It is being taken on board to provide free legal representation to deserving litigants who cannot afford a lawyer. For someone with a genuine grievance but without the means to pursue it, such representation can make the difference between giving up and having a real opportunity to seek justice.
Together, these measures create a more humane pathway to justice: guidance at the first point of contact and, where appropriate, free legal representation. Instead of expecting citizens to understand every door of the justice system before asking for help, the system begins helping them find the right one. That is justice beyond conventional contours.
Legal aid, public facilitation, telephone-based guidance and free representation serve a common purpose: removing barriers that can leave a person with a legal right but no practical way to claim it. This also gives practical meaning to Sustainable Development Goal 16: equal access to justice and strong, inclusive institutions, grounded in the wider promise that no one should be left behind because of poverty, distance or lack of legal knowledge.
The real test will be implementation. Free legal assistance requires transparent eligibility criteria, competent lawyers, clear referral mechanisms and measurable standards. The quality of representation matters as much as its availability. Justice for a poor person should never become poorer justice.
Ultimately, access to justice cannot be measured only by courthouses, judges or cases decided. Its truest measure lies in the experience of the person seeking help at a moment of need: Was that person heard? Was dignity preserved? Or did inability to pay stand between a citizen and a lawful remedy?
A courthouse may have its doors open, but justice becomes truly accessible only when poverty and lack of legal knowledge no longer decide who can walk through them. Perhaps that is the deeper meaning of justice beyond conventional contours: a system that listens when people feel unheard, helps them find the right door when they feel lost, and brings justice within reach when it once seemed beyond them. For someone who thought there was nowhere to turn, that journey may begin with something as simple as a call.

title: Autumn of 1971  what US archive reveals about stranded Pakistanis
description: Autumn of 1971  what US archive reveals about stranded Pakistanis
content:
US State Department's own historical account of the period is instructive because it is unsentimental
There is no mourning officially, not for the slaughter of a pro-Pakistan community.
Every December, a thin slice of English-language Pakistan performs the same liturgy about 1971, the same small drama: military failure, political mismanagement in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, India's intervention, the birth of Bangladesh. The stranded, stateless Bihari issue rarely gets a line.
How has this ritual remained so unchanged: the same debate restaged every year, on schedule, and mistaken for reckoning? Too little attention goes to how the crisis was shaped by outside powers, and how those calculations left a population's devastation largely unnoticed.
Today, I want to try the register of international relations: dispassionate, treaty-and-cable analysis, the great-power view from above. I have my reservations about that dispassion. As the old description of economists goes, they know the price of everything and the value of nothing. But feeling something about a fifty-five-year injustice is not a flaw, even in an argument built from declassified cables and treaty dates. Both can be true in the same piece.
The US State Department's own historical account of the period is instructive because it is unsentimental: 1971 appears not as moral drama but as a crisis Washington managed around its other priorities. After East Pakistanis overwhelmingly voted for the autonomy-seeking Awami League in the 1970 elections, Pakistan's government blocked it from governing and jailed its leader, Sheikh Mujib, a name the State Department's own retrospective leaves out.
From March 1971, Pro-Pakistan Biharis faced displacement and what I regard, personally and academically, as "genocide", as nationalist Bengali mobs attacked Urdu-speaking communities in Chittagong and Khulna – violence that the Pakistani government later cited to justify the military crackdown, but which the State Department's account omits. That crackdown and ensuing protests sent refugees into India, and by late autumn East Pakistani guerrillas, increasingly backed by India, fought Pakistani forces, until war opened fully on 3 December.
Washington's dilemma had little to do with East Pakistan itself. India had just signed a treaty with the Soviet Union; Pakistan had made itself indispensable to Washington by quietly enabling Nixon's opening to Beijing, and had recently resumed buying US arms after a channel shut since 1965.
Washington backed Islamabad initially, wary of another war and of a badly weakened Pakistan, even as international condemnation limited how far it would go.
What followed was calculated ambiguity, not commitment. The USS Enterprise (CVAN-65) moved from Vietnam toward the Bay of Bengal, signalling to Moscow and Beijing that American help was possible, but Washington stopped short of intervening, showing both the real limits of that commitment.
India's Soviet treaty helped prevent effective UN intervention and deterred China from opening a second front. Defeated on both fronts, Pakistan lost its eastern wing; Bangladesh joined the UN in 1974. The State Department's own retrospective says this damaged American standing while cementing India's regional dominance. That same crisis left an unresolved human question that neither Pakistan nor Bangladesh has treated with comparable seriousness since.
The Urdu-speaking population of former East Pakistan found itself on the losing side of a war it had mostly not chosen and was left without effective citizenship rights. Many were repatriated under the 1973 Delhi Agreement and later arrangements, while many more remained in camps for decades, until Bangladeshi court rulings culminating in the 2008 High Court judgment recognised citizenship rights for the Urdu-speaking community. That ruling addressed the legal question, not the economic or social one. The residents of Mohammadpur's Geneva Camp Dhaka and elsewhere continue to live in overcrowded conditions and informal work. While their citizenship remain recognised on paper for almost two decades, their circumstances have barely changed.
I have written at length elsewhere, in Urdu and English, through podcasts and study circles, on the contested data, the camps' inhumane conditions, stalled repatriations, the Foreign Office's posture, and policy paralysis; I will not relitigate that here.
In Pakistan, some Bihari-descended Karachi residents have managed to obtain national identity cards amid a nationalist hostility that has yet to be fully named.
Pakistan has hosted millions of Afghan refugees, while the problems of a patriotic people tied to its own history remain unresolved, a policy contrast, not a comparison of suffering, and no complaint against ordinary Afghans.
No single power orchestrated this outcome. In a crisis of superpower rivalry and diplomatic leverage, a specific, identifiable group was simply not the variable anyone was optimising for, what subaltern studies might call a people with no seat at its own negotiating table, then or now, explicable enough in the fog of 1971.
Is it harder to explain why, five decades on, the statelessness of the stranded Bihari population has failed to awaken national conscience, let alone secure repatriation for those who want it, or integration for those who do not?
I made this same argument once before, in this paper (31-07-26), from a gentler angle: somewhere between justice, diplomacy and ideology, humanity itself quietly slipped away; there has been no truth commission, no formal apology to our Bihari community; our dignity has not been restored, nor our own history understood. That failure is ours. It cannot be outsourced to Washington, or to anyone else.
Great-power calculations shaped the war. Our own apathy shaped what came after. Fifty-five years is a long time for a debt to sit unpaid, one we could still choose to pay. As Prof Gayatri Spivak argued, the subaltern cannot speak in ways that redress or restructure, and yet I dare to speak anyway.
Usually, I write about this paused tragedy with a "naive" attachment to the imkaan - the possibility of wapsi, return - for a community, guilty of loving Pakistan, still waiting, more than five decades on.

title: A teachers  day close to retirement
description: Retirement changes the meaning of routine
content:
Retirement changes the meaning of routine
This year, Teachers' Day feels different to me. I have seen many such days come and go during my academic life, usually marked by greetings from students, a few affectionate messages, some flowers, perhaps a small ceremony, and then a return to the familiar rhythm of lectures, meetings and departmental work. But this year there is an added emotion. Retirement is now very close, and what was once an ordinary annual observance has become a moment of reflection.
Retirement changes the meaning of routine. A classroom that once seemed part of everyday life suddenly begins to look precious. A casual conversation with a student, a question after class, even a familiar walk through the corridor acquires a different significance when one knows that these moments are becoming fewer. Teachers' Day, therefore, is not merely a celebration this year. It is also a reminder of how quickly decades pass.
When one begins teaching, the concerns are practical. Prepare the lecture, complete the course, set the examination, supervise students, conduct research and meet deadlines. One does not think much about legacy. With time, however, it becomes clear that teaching is not really about completing syllabi. It is about leaving impressions, often without even knowing that one has done so.
A teacher may forget a sentence spoken twenty years ago, but a student may remember it for life. Many of us have experienced the surprise of meeting former students who recall an explanation, a piece of advice or even a passing remark that we ourselves no longer remember. That is perhaps the most humbling aspect of the profession: teachers rarely know which words will stay with their students.
As someone who has spent much of his life teaching science, I have always believed that education must do more than transmit information. Science teaches a way of thinking. It demands evidence, encourages questioning, rewards curiosity and reminds us that even strongly held ideas must remain open to correction. In societies where unquestioning acceptance is often easier than intellectual inquiry, this habit of mind is especially valuable.
But teaching has never been a one-way process. Students also educate their teachers. Each generation brings its own language, attitudes, habits and expectations. Today's Gen Z students are very different from those I taught decades ago. They are digitally connected, more expressive, less formal and often less hesitant to challenge authority. Their attention spans may be shorter, but their access to information is extraordinary. They may prefer a meme, a reel or a short message to the long handwritten notes of earlier generations, but the need for guidance has not disappeared.
Teachers sometimes complain that the new generation has changed too much. Of course it has changed. Every generation does. The important question is not whether young people resemble us, but whether we are willing to understand the world in which they are growing up. A teacher who stops learning from students has already begun to retire, regardless of age.
The relationship between teacher and student also survives technological change. Blackboards may become smart boards, libraries may become digital databases and lectures may migrate online, but a student still needs encouragement. A student still needs someone to say, "You can do better." A student still needs a teacher who can distinguish between failure and potential.
That is why I am not entirely convinced that teachers truly retire. An official position ends. The name disappears from the timetable. Someone else occupies the chair. But the instinct to teach remains. One continues to explain, advise, question, recommend books and feel pleased when a younger person understands something difficult.
As retirement approaches, I find myself reflecting on decades of students, colleagues, classrooms, challenges and achievements. Universities endure while generations of students and teachers pass through them, each becoming part of the institution's continuing story. This Teachers' Day, I feel gratitude more than ceremony, for a profession that kept me connected with youth, learning and inquiry. I may soon leave the classroom officially, but the classroom will remain an enduring part of me.

title: Plastic free Islamabad
description: Islamabad can take the lead by replacing reactive policing with proactive economics
content:
Islamabad can take the lead by replacing reactive policing with proactive economics
That the 'plastic-free' campaigns launched from time to time over the last decade have failed across Pakistan needs no emphasis. Punjab launched a plastic ban but failed to pursue it. Sindh launched one but failed to sustain it. K-P and Balochistan were no different. Now, Islamabad – not for the first time – has embarked on a similar quest. Invoking the Single-Use Plastics Prohibition Regulations 2023, authorities have launched a crackdown across the federal capital territory, resulting in 122 arrests and the seizure of 293 kilograms of plastic bags.
While the authorities have shown administrative muscle in pursuit of the goal, history suggest that the momentum will likely fade into business-as-usual within weeks. Such a repetitive failure highlights a fundamental flaw in our environmental governance: we treat a chronic systemic issue with short-term, cosmetic crackdowns. Each time such a campaign is announced, it lacks critical elements, including substitute options, supply interception and sustained political will.
Let's elaborate. The authorities heavily penalise end-users and small shopkeepers without making available affordable alternatives like jute, paper or cloth bags. Their raids target the retail tail-end rather than the manufacturing hubs and wholesale distribution networks. Last but not least, environmental compliance is treated as a periodic publicity drive rather than a permanent regulatory function. When the media spotlight dims, enforcement measures fade out.
To break this cycle, the state must pivot from sporadic crackdowns to a structural overhaul. There is need for the authorities to 1) subsidise alternatives, by providing tax incentives to manufacturers transitioning to eco-friendly packaging; 2) choke the source, by enforcing strict bans directly at the manufacturing plants; 3) shift from high-profile "campaigns" to routine municipal monitoring; and 4) partner with major retail chains and citizen groups to normalise behavioural shifts through public awareness.
Islamabad can take the lead by replacing reactive policing with proactive economics and serve as a model for the rest of the country.

title: Poorly fed
description: More than 60  of Pakistanis cannot afford a healthy diet
content:
More than 60% of Pakistanis cannot afford a healthy diet
A country that can feed its people but cannot nourish them has a food policy problem. Pakistan has spent decades worrying, understandably, about whether there is enough wheat in the market and whether flour remains within reach of households. Yet this narrow preoccupation with calories has obscured a more damaging deficiency. A large part of the population may be eating, but it is not eating well.
The latest assessment by the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation makes that failure difficult to ignore. More than 60% of Pakistanis cannot afford a healthy diet. More revealing, however, is what lies behind this figure. Pakistan's food supply itself is poorly aligned with what constitutes a healthy diet. Staples and sugar are available in excess of dietary requirements, while vegetables, fruits, pulses, roots and tubers remain in short supply. This should force a rethink of what Pakistan means by food security. Preventing hunger cannot be the final ambition of food policy. A plate heavy in carbohydrates but deficient in protein, vitamins and minerals may fill a stomach without adequately nourishing the person eating it. As a result, Pakistan continues to carry an extraordinarily high burden of childhood stunting and wasting. Micronutrient deficiencies remain widespread. At the same time, obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease are becoming more common.
To solve this predicament, a number of steps can be taken. Agricultural support should increasingly encourage pulses, vegetables, fruits and other nutritionally important foods without jeopardising the production of essential staples. Responsibility cannot end at the farm gate. Pakistan's food environment increasingly exposes children to aggressively marketed products high in sugar, salt and fat. Clearer nutrition labels, tighter restrictions on advertising unhealthy food to children and sensible fiscal measures can help shift consumption. Social protection must also recognise that food insecurity is not simply the absence of food.

title: Of protests and parleys
description: Long march  that has commenced from K P with the intent to enter the federal capital is fraught with consequences
content:
'Long march' that has commenced from K-P with the intent to enter the federal capital is fraught with consequences
It's a tale of missed opportunities by both the government and the opposition. The two-day talks briefly sparked euphoria, fostering a belief that a consensus was at hand to pave the way for much-needed political stability. That belief, however, proved to be an illusion. The opposition blamed the treasury for moving the goalposts, while the government questioned the opposition's sincerity. This stalemate has unfortunately forced both sides back into rigid stances, pushing an already fragile politico-economic order into even more chaotic territory.
The 'long march' that has commenced from K-P with the intent to enter the federal capital is fraught with consequences. The government has signalled a zero-tolerance stance as the twin cities have remained highly barricaded over the last three weeks. The opposition, meanwhile, insists that its protest is to seek a lawful resolution to its grievances, most of which pertain to the implementation of the August 18 Supreme Court order. The breakdown in parleys, nonetheless, has now breached the divide, and only an act of statesmanship from either side can salvage the worsening situation.
The talks hit snags because the government – as alleged by the opposition – was unwilling to allow a meeting with the imprisoned PTI leader, Imran Khan. Secondly, the K-P government insisted that it "should be on board" regarding decisions on counter-terrorism operations in the province. But the government, the opposition negotiators claimed, was more inclined to pressure them to call off their long march as a pre-condition. Likewise, it was also mulling the imposition of Governor's rule in K-P. Encouragingly, pressure from saner elements, particularly within the PPP, compelled the government to stop short of enacting federal rule in the province.
This tension-ridden situation is not in anybody's interest. A thaw is desired, and the least that the government can do in its lawful authority is to implement the apex court order and engage the opposition in a broad-based dialogue on national issues. The PTI too will be well-advised to suspend its march and enter into talks as a gesture of solidarity. This bickering and muscle-flexing is highly undesirable.

title: Broadcasting ideas
description: British philosopher  author and broadcaster Bryan Magee hosted a 15 part series titled  The Great Philosophers
content:
British philosopher, author and broadcaster Bryan Magee hosted a 15-part series titled 'The Great Philosophers'
I keep returning to the Iqbal Memorial Lectures by Professor Abdus Salam, given in mid 1960s and broadcast by Radio Pakistan. I have written about those lectures in these pages in the past. As I listened to them again recently, I wondered about how much we may have lost in the last six decades. It goes without saying that if Salam was alive today, he would not be welcome on any public platform. A tragedy of equal measure is that even after his death three decades ago, many would think twice, and probably not even entertain the idea of playing his lectures publicly. Unfortunately, they have good reason to be concerned.
But my point today is not about the intolerance of society, though so much needs to be said on that. It is about what is viewed, by the media industry and the public sector, as worthy of supporting. Salam's lectures are brilliant, thought provoking, deeply researched and analytical. At the same time, they are about philosophy, history of science and physics – areas that were not topics of common discussion in households and gathering of friends in the 1960s. Most of all, they are in English – a language that is (and was) spoken and understood by a small segment of society. We may like to imagine the 1960s of Pakistan as a land of milk and honey, despite the evidence to the contrary, but even the most optimistic picture of that era would tell us that these topics were academic, complex and catering to a small group. From a purely market perspective, supporting these lectures is a non-starter. Why not have songs, dramas, or whatever form of entertainment is the most popular flavour of the day? Yet, Radio Pakistan chose to broadcast them, and sixty years later, they continue to have a life of their own.
The question to ask is if these ideas were worthy of support then, why not now? Why has our calculus become so narrow on ratings and revenue that we cannot imagine having serious lectures that are not punctuated by 'breaking news'? Why is the mode of discussion on our channels built on conspiracy theories or personal attacks? What about conversations on important ideas?
These days, few listen to the public broadcaster, and that is not just because of the quality of the product but also because the public broadcaster is not interested in having serious conversations that go beyond the party line. The private channels may point to serious competition for ratings and viewership, but I am not sure that is truly an honest argument. It is more convenient to choose the easy path, to churn out an 'efficient' product that is instantaneously catchy (though shallow), to disengage the mind from serious conversations that can create doubt, generate questions or challenge assumptions.
In 1987, British philosopher, author and broadcaster Bryan Magee hosted a 15-part series titled 'The Great Philosophers'. It was a series of one-on-one conversations with contemporary scholars on the ideas and impact of some of the greatest philosophers of the western tradition from Aristotle to Descartes to Kant to Marx and others. The conversations were serious, thoughtful and meant for a broad audience. The simple idea of a 15-part series on philosophers is probably going to put many to sleep, yet this was a huge success. These episodes are available freely online and continue to inspire a dedicated audience through their simple production and deep ideas. If someone were to dismiss the programme by saying that was a different era, and now times have changed, well – BBC aired them again in 2025 and once again they were broadly appreciated.
The question I am grappling with, in the era of AI and so-called efficiency, is about our own choices and autonomy. What do we choose for ourselves and why? And for those who have the power to shape discourse and broadcast ideas, what do we choose for others? We can choose to listen carefully, read broadly, and think deeply. We can ponder on important questions that surround us. No marketing campaign, race for rankings or ratings, or ideas about trends, should take that away from us.

title: PM Shehbaz approves duty free livestock imports for specialised farms to boost exports
description: Says efforts should be made to improve the entire value chain to further develop the meat  livestock export industry
content:
Says efforts should be made to improve the entire value chain to further develop the meat, livestock export industry
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Monday approved a comprehensive plan to restructure the country's livestock sector on corporate lines and boost exports by allowing duty-free imports of livestock for specialised rearing farms for re-export.
PM Shehbaz, chairing a high-level review meeting on ongoing reforms in the livestock sector, directed the formulation and implementation of livestock sector reforms with input from private-sector experts.
The premier instructed that specialised farms should be established for livestock exports and that high-yield, superior-breed livestock should be imported and reared in these specialised farms for export purposes.
Read : PM eyes tech-driven livestock boost
He said a modern livestock tagging system should be introduced to ensure that the livestock reared in these farms are indeed exported.
Prime Minister @CMShehbaz has approved the establishment of special farms for raising imported livestock to boost the country's livestock exports @PakPMO @GovtofPakistan @tdap_official #RadioPakistan #News #Livestock #Exports #Agriculture https://t.co/1V8lEEBvqu pic.twitter.com/9hshlJS2zK
The PM stated that the livestock sector should be reorganised on a corporate model to modernise it, and expertise from private sector specialists should be utilised for this purpose.
Livestock accounts for over 60 per cent of the country's agricultural sector, and the sector holds immense export potential, PM Shehbaz said, adding that a comprehensive plan with specific targets for eradicating Foot-and-Mouth Disease from the country should be formulated and presented within the next two weeks.
The premier said international certification of slaughterhouses across the country must be ensured, and third-party validation must be ensured to guarantee international standards at slaughterhouses. The Ministry of National Food Security should work in collaboration with provincial governments to eradicate livestock diseases, he added.
He said efforts should be made to improve the entire value chain to further develop the meat and livestock export industry.
The premier directed that targets for meat, livestock, and related exports be determined and presented.
The meeting was given a detailed briefing on the livestock sector, and proposals regarding the future roadmap for the sector's development and the enhancement of exports were presented.
Regarding the overall potential of Pakistan's livestock sector, the meeting was informed that the country possesses approximately 245 million livestock, with a total estimated value of around Rs 5.5 trillion. The livestock sector contributes 14.97% to the national economy and 63.6% to the agricultural economy, with an annual production of approximately 74.69 million tons of milk and 6.31 million tons of meat.
It was noted that while around 8 million rural families in the country are associated with livestock, the prevalence of small-scale livestock rearing and a fragmented supply chain hinder the full utilisation of export potential. The meeting was informed that there is immense potential to significantly increase Pakistan's meat exports. Meat exports stood at approximately $530 million in the 2025-26 fiscal year, with the bulk of current exports destined for Gulf countries, including the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Qatar. It was noted that Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, China, and other nations offer significant prospects as new and expanding markets.
The meeting was also briefed on government initiatives to boost livestock and meat exports. These include the national program for animal disease surveillance, protection, and animal traceability; the establishment of Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD)-free zones and compartments; digital monitoring of vaccinations and diseases; and the development of export-grade farms alongside international health and Halal certification systems. Furthermore, the meeting was apprised that the government is focusing on promoting feedlot farming, cold chain infrastructure, de-boning, value-added products, and export-related infrastructure, with a target set to further increase meat exports by 2028.
Federal Ministers Rana Tanveer Hussain, Ahsan Iqbal, Dr Musadik Malik, Ahad Khan Cheema, Muhammad Aurangzeb, and Attaullah Tarar, Prime Minister’s Advisor Haroon Akhtar, Minister of State Bilal Azhar Kayani and other relevant senior officials attended the meeting.

title: Tulsa King  renewed for season 5 as Sylvester Stallone heads back to New York
description: Tulsa King  is renewed for Season 5 as Sylvester Stallone   s Dwight Manfredi returns to New York with new cast members
content:
'Tulsa King' is renewed for Season 5 as Sylvester Stallone’s Dwight Manfredi returns to New York with new cast members
Tulsa King has been renewed for Season 5 at Paramount+, with the Sylvester Stallone-led crime drama set to move production from Georgia to New York.
The renewal comes ahead of the Tulsa King Season 4 premiere on October 16. The fifth season will follow Stallone’s character, Dwight “The General” Manfredi, as he returns to his New York roots after being sent to Tulsa by his mafia associates.
Stallone’s daughter, Scarlet Rose Stallone, who has appeared as Spencer throughout the first four seasons, has also been promoted to a series regular for Season 5.
Four new actors are joining the Tulsa King cast as series regulars: Erik Palladino, Glenn Fleshler, Anthony Skordi and Nickola Shreli. Palladino is known for I Play Rocky , Fleshler has appeared in Billions , Skordi stars in The Last Frontier , and Shreli is known for Power Book IV: Force .
Plans for a potential fifth season were previously reported in June, when a writers’ room was opened with the intention of moving production to New York. The relocation is also connected to New York’s updated film and television tax incentives, which have made the state a more cost-effective production destination.
Paramount Television Studios and 101 Studios produce the series. Terence Winter serves as head writer and executive producer, alongside series creator Taylor Sheridan, Stallone and other producers.
Season 4 will feature returning cast members including Martin Starr, Jay Will, Vincent Piazza, Annabella Sciorra, Frank Grillo, Kevin Pollak, Neal McDonough and Dana Delany. Gretchen Mol is also joining Season 4 as a series regular.
The Tulsa King Season 4 premiere is scheduled for October 16 on Paramount+.

title: Joshua Jackson breaks down remembering James Van Der Beek at emotional gala | The Express Tribune
description: Joshua Jackson gets emotional remembering James Van Der Beek at a gala honouring 'Dawson’s Creek' creator Williamson
content:
Joshua Jackson gets emotional remembering James Van Der Beek at a gala honouring 'Dawson’s Creek' creator Williamson
Joshua Jackson became emotional while remembering his late Dawson’s Creek costar James Van Der Beek at the Barbara Berlanti Heroes Gala in Santa Monica, California.
Jackson, who played Pacey Witter on the popular teen drama, spoke on October 3 while presenting series creator Kevin Williamson with the Barbara Berlanti Hero Award. The honour recognised Williamson’s efforts to organise a Dawson’s Creek table read that supported Van Der Beek and his family following his cancer diagnosis.
During his speech, Jackson, 48, recalled how Van Der Beek’s health deteriorated shortly before the table read and praised Williamson for helping the cast come together to support their longtime friend.
Jackson said the event allowed Van Der Beek’s children to be surrounded by people celebrating their father and recognising the love and admiration he had earned throughout his career.
Williamson also became emotional while accepting the award. Reflecting on Van Der Beek’s role as Dawson Leery, he described the actor as “the soul of the show” and spoke about watching him grow from a young actor into a husband, father and friend.
Van Der Beek was diagnosed with colorectal cancer in 2024 and died in February 2026 at age 48. The actor had remained connected with his Dawson’s Creek costars during his illness.
Williamson recalled that Van Der Beek had hoped to attend the September 2025 table read but was unable to travel because of his health. He said Van Der Beek nevertheless remained present in spirit and praised his “unshakable courage.”
The Barbara Berlanti Heroes Gala was established by Greg Berlanti in honour of his mother, who died of cancer. The event supports F Cancer’s work in cancer prevention, early detection and psychosocial initiatives.

title: At least 22 dead after two boats collide on Congo River  official says
description: At least 22 people died after two boats collided on Congo River  sinking a passenger vessel
content:
At least 22 people died after two boats collided on Congo River, sinking a passenger vessel
At least 22 people have died after two boats collided on the Congo River in the Democratic Republic of Congo, an official said.
The incident occurred near the town of Ngombe in Lukolela territory in western Equateur province at around 2 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) on Saturday, Crispin Mputu, the provincial interior minister, told Reuters .
The collision involved two vessels travelling on the river. One was a commercial boat operating between Kinshasa and Mbandaka, while the other was a passenger riverboat travelling from Mongala province to Kinshasa, Mputu said.
The impact caused the passenger boat to sink. A security source told Reuters it had 163 passengers on board.
Read More: Ebola cases top 8,000 in DR Congo amid contact-tracing gaps
Twenty-two bodies have been recovered and buried, while 59 people were rescued, Mputu said. He added that other victims might have been buried elsewhere.
The sunken vessel remains submerged at a depth of 12 metres and recovery efforts were continuing on Monday evening, Mputu said.
River transport is the main form of travel and trade in much of western Congo, where towns and cities are located along the Congo River, but accidents are common because vessels are often overcrowded and poorly maintained.

title: Zak Williams reveals Robin Williams was searching for relief before his death
description: Zak Williams remembers father Robin Williams    final months  saying the actor was seeking support before his 2014 death
content:
Zak Williams remembers father Robin Williams’ final months, saying the actor was seeking support before his 2014 death
Zak Williams is reflecting on his late father Robin Williams’ final months, saying the actor was seeking support and appeared close to finding something that could have brought him relief before his death in 2014.
Speaking on The Squeeze podcast, Zak, 43, said Robin was struggling during the period before his death and was actively trying to understand what might help him.
“The days, weeks, months prior to him dying by suicide, I was really feeling for him because he was having a frustrating time and was seeking support,” Zak said. He added that he believed his father was “not far off” from finding something that could have been more helpful.
Zak said his father’s kindness and generosity also shaped how he remembers him. “I loved him so much,” he said, adding that he had hoped Robin would eventually find peace.
Robin Williams died by suicide at age 63 on August 11, 2014. After his death, it was determined that he had Lewy body dementia, a progressive neurological condition that had not been diagnosed while he was alive. He had previously been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.
Zak has spoken publicly about the difficulties Robin experienced during his final years, including the frustration surrounding his Parkinson’s diagnosis. In a 2021 appearance on The Genius Life podcast, Zak said his father’s symptoms did not fully correspond with what many Parkinson’s patients experienced.
Zak, who advocates for mental health awareness, has also discussed his ongoing grief. In an Instagram tribute marking his father’s birthday, he described grief as something that “loops and echoes” while remembering Robin’s legacy of generosity and kindness.
