title: Minister urges creation of Hazara province
description: Minister urges creation of Hazara province
content:
Minister for Religious Affairs and Hazara Province Movement Chairman Sardar Muhammad Yousaf on Sunday called for the creation of Hazara province without further delay, saying the region's case had already been taken up by the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Assembly and the National Assembly.
Addressing a large Hazara province convention, Yousaf said the demand for a separate province was based on administrative grounds and that the movement was now focused on parliamentary and constitutional forums.
"The Hazara province movement is strong and its case is ready," he said, adding that resolutions in favour of the province had been passed three times by the provincial assembly.
Yousaf said the demand had received support from political leadership and claimed that the military leadership had also expressed support for the creation of new provinces.
He said bills seeking the creation of Hazara province had been introduced in the National Assembly in 2019 by both opposition and government members.
"The matter is now inside the assemblies," he said, urging lawmakers to take steps for the creation of the province.
Yousaf noted that bringing administrative services closer to the people was essential for improving access to government and public facilities. Delays in matters concerning public welfare, he added, could create frustration and disappointment among citizens.
Speaking on the occasion, Senator Talha Mahmood said Haripur would be the economic backbone of a future Hazara province and rejected concerns about the availability of resources.
He claimed that the region had sufficient resources to meet its requirements and contribute to the national economy.
He also linked unemployment and lack of opportunities with frustration among young people and called for reforms in the existing system. Former minister Murtaza Javed Abbasi said the people of Hazara would not accept the creation of new provinces without Hazara being included.
He said representatives of the region had already raised the issue in parliament.
Former chief minister Pir Sabir Shah said the people of Hazara were united in support of the demand, while Jamaat-i-Islami Hazara leader Abdul Razzaq Abbasi said his party fully supported the creation of a separate province.

content:
Hafiz Naeem calls for inclusion of Iran, other Muslim states in defence agreement
JI chief Hafiz Naeem has called for expanding the defence pact among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye to include Iran, Bangladesh and other Muslim countries, saying Palestine should be its foremost priority if the arrangement aims to protect the region.
Addressing thousands of participants at a Gaza March organised by the JI on Sunday, Naeem said the first objective of the defence arrangement should be to end Israeli aggression against Palestinians particularly those living in Gaza.
He welcomed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement but stressed that other Muslim countries should also be included. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye signed the pact, also called the Makkah Defence Allianc on August 7.
He said Israeli attacks on Gaza were continuing despite the ceasefire, while Israel had failed to honour the terms agreed under the truce and enjoyed the backing of the United States. He called for the Muslim Ummah to overcome sectarian, political and geographical divisions and unite in support of the people of Palestine and Kashmir.
"Instead of being divided along sectarian and geographical lines, the Muslim Ummah must unite to support the oppressed people of Palestine and Kashmir," he said, adding that Shia and Sunni divisions should be set aside for a common struggle.
Naeem said the first week of October would be observed in solidarity with the people of Gaza and Palestine. He also announced that the JI would unveil its future strategy after October 7 as part of its ongoing campaign against petroleum levy, taxes and inflation.
He said the Israeli bombardment of Gaza had continued despite the ceasefire, claiming that large areas of the territory had been destroyed. He said Palestinians were also being targeted in the West Bank, including children.
The JI chief said the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack challenged Israel's military strength and the subsequent Israeli offensive exposed the country's policies before the international community.
He described Hamas's struggle as legitimate resistance and said the group had played an important role in ceasefire negotiations. He also called for intensified efforts for the freedom of Al-Aqsa Mosque.
Naeem said the resistance of Palestinians demonstrated that determination and courage could challenge even technologically superior forces. He said Muslim governments and armies have a responsibility to prevent further bloodshed in Palestine.
He said the situation in Gaza also demonstrated the need for greater unity among Islamic movements, adding that Palestinians have continued to support Hamas despite three years of war.
The JI leader said the party and its charitable organisation Alkhidmat had sent relief worth Rs10 billion to Palestinians with public support.

title: Russian strikes hit Kyiv during Merz s visit
description: Russian strikes hit Kyiv during Merz s visit
content:
Ukraine and Germany have signed a $1.5-billion weapons deal to help fight an upsurge in Russian drone attacks, while fresh strikes and air raid sirens greeted Chancellor Friedrich Merz on a solidarity visit on Sunday.
The agreement includes combat drone weapons and support for Ukraine's battered energy sector, which Russia is targeting to cut off heating and power during the freezing winter months, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on X.
Merz was on a surprise visit to show European support as attacks increase -- and discovered the new reality of daily life in the Ukrainian capital.
Air raid sirens wailed repeatedly, including as Zelensky showed him the damage to the National Academy of Sciences, which was hit by a Russian attack drone on Monday, killing two.
"We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place," noted Merz.

One blast that was heard across the city damaged the road surface of the Northern Bridge -- one of several connecting the eastern and western parts of Kyiv over the Dnipro river which have been struck repeatedly in the last four days.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko has said the capital -- largely spared from the devastation wrought near the front line in more than four years of conflict -- should now be on a war footing.
Round-the-clock attacks have hit residential areas, petrol stations, schools, rail and communications infrastructure, while the near-constant air raid sirens disrupt daily life and put people on edge.

title: North Korea says Kim oversaw hypersonic missile drill
description: North Korea says Kim oversaw hypersonic missile drill
content:
North Korea said on Sunday it had tested a hypersonic missile under the supervision of ?leader Kim Jong Un, in a drill aimed at demonstrating the reliability of its nuclear deterrent.
State media KCNA said the intermediate-range strategic missile, which it described as part ?of a hypersonic strategic weapon system, was launched on Saturday from eastern North Korea and struck a target about 1,000 km (621 miles) away in waters off the country's east coast.
The drill was aimed at training missile troops and assessing the efficiency and mobility of North Korea's deterrent forces, the report said.
KCNA quoted Kim as saying North Korea must continue efforts to make ?its adversaries recognise the "reliability and fatality" of its strategic offensive weapons, calling such activities a form of deterrence.
He also reaffirmed that developing the country's nuclear war deterrent remained indispensable for national security and that there would be no change in that policy, KCNA said.
The launch was the latest in a series of North Korean weapons tests this year and came as tensions ?on the Korean peninsula escalated over a landmine blast in the Demilitarized Zone last month that wounded South Korean soldiers.
The KCNA report provided additional details about the missile launch disclosed on Saturday by Kim Yo Jong, the sister of Kim Jong Un and a senior official in the ruling Workers' Party.
Kim Yo Jong said South Korea and Japan had failed to track the weapon's flight, saying a special "wave-like trajectory mode" had exposed limitations in their tracking capabilities.
However, South Korea's Defence Ministry said on Sunday that its military had closely monitored preparations for the launch, detected and tracked the missile immediately after liftoff and accurately identified the launch site.

title: Up to 500 French schools to close today
description: Up to 500 French schools to close today
content:
Up to 500 schools across France will be totally or partly closed on Monday due to the protests by teenage pupils that have shaken the country, the education minister said.
Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400-500" high schools as the security conditions "have not been fulfilled", said Education Minister Edouard Geffray on Sunday, adding that 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the movement.
The teens at French high schools, known as lycees, say that their studies are being ruined by high teacher absences, overlong school days and dilapidated facilities, as well as other grievances.
Geffray said the number of schools affected on Monday would be comparable to the figure from Friday but vowed there would be a "partial, progressive return to lessons".
The movement began at a Paris school on September 17 but grew last week into nationwide protests marked in places by outbursts of violence involving teenagers and security forces, which sometimes used tear gas and batons to disperse the children.

title: Yemen govt vows to retake Houthi areas
description: Yemen govt vows to retake Houthi areas
content:
Group makes fresh gains, encircling a govt-held city
Yemen's leader announced on Sunday the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis, even as the group made fresh gains on the ground, effectively encircling a government-held city.
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country's Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab Strait -- a chokepoint for international shipping -- after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen's government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia, where the Houthis said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital yet again on Sunday.
"I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's presidential council, said in a statement.
Alimi called on all the armed forces "to begin carrying out their assigned missions, in accordance with the approved plans, until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government's interim capital Aden, according to four security sources. The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
"We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station," a police source in the area told AFP.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city.
The military sources added that fighting in the area was ongoing.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz has killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed -- 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj -- while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen's long-running civil war.

content:
A multi-agency Australian counterterrorism unit is investigating links to Australia of the co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073, who stabbed his captain and then attempted to hijack the plane, a police spokesperson said on Sunday.
The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - which comprises federal police, Victorian state police and the ASIO intelligence agency - were "investigating the man's links to Australia," the Australian Federal Police spokesperson said.
Two sources briefed on the investigation said the co-pilot studied at a university in Melbourne, capital of the Australian state of Victoria. A third source said he studied at RMIT University around a decade ago. RMIT declined to comment.
The co-pilot of the flydubai flight FZ1073, which was bound for Israel from Dubai on Wednesday, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, calling the incident a "terrorist attack".
Flight FZ1073 would have felt like a "vertical roller coaster", when it plunged 16,000 feet in about 30 seconds before being levelled out and landing safely, according to an aviation instructor who recreated the descent in a flight simulator for Reuters.
Two sources have said the co-pilot is an Omani national named Hamam Al-Hamami. Israeli officials have not ?named the co-pilot but said that he is from Oman.
UAE authorities and flydubai have not publicly disclosed the co-pilot's identity. Reuters could not independently reach Al-Hamami, who is in UAE custody, for comment.

content:
Indians rallied for a third day on Sunday to demand the election commission chief's resignation, alleging wrongdoing during a large-scale voter-roll revision.
Protests began on Friday demanding the Election Commission of India (ECI) chief Gyanesh Kumar step down after concerns at the revision that has removed millions of names from voter lists.

The harassment allegations were made after police detained scores of protesters around the government-designated protest site of Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on Saturday.
"Allegations of sexual harassment were made by three female journalists against police officers," Delhi police said in a statement, promising "a fair and impartial enquiry".
Dipke said that the accused officer "must be arrested immediately".

title: Competitiveness hinges on affordable  sustainable energy
description: Competitiveness hinges on affordable  sustainable energy
content:
Reforms must produce commercially viable and reliable energy system capable of supporting productive industry
Pakistan's export-oriented textile sector is facing a defining energy challenge as the country moves towards a more competitive power market while global buyers impose increasingly stringent requirements for sustainability, traceability and environmental performance. Industry faces the challenge of balancing reliable, affordable energy with pressure to improve efficiency, integrate renewables and cut emissions.
These issues came under discussion at a multi-stakeholder dialogue titled "Threads of Accountability: Traceability and Energy Policy for Textile Competitiveness", which brought together textile manufacturers, power-sector professionals, sustainability and verification specialists, business representatives and renewable-energy stakeholders.
The central question was how Pakistan's textile industry can participate in a transforming power market while maintaining reliable energy supplies and meeting increasingly demanding global sustainability standards.
Participants stressed that successful energy transition would require more than simply opening the electricity market or increasing renewable-energy capacity. Transparent pricing, reliable networks, commercially workable market mechanisms, credible environmental data, appropriate risk allocation and stronger coordination among industry, regulators, utilities, financiers and international buyers would all be necessary.
A major focus of the dialogue was Pakistan's emerging Competitive Trading Bilateral Contract Market (CTBCM) and its implications for industrial consumers. Muhammad Usman Bin Ahmed, Energy Transition Officer at Alternate Development Services (ADS), examined the practical requirements for industrial participation, including eligibility, competitive procurement, bilateral contracting and wheeling.
He also highlighted several commercial and operational issues associated with the emerging market, including the Use of System Charges (UoSC), security and performance guarantees, SMP exposure, balancing and settlement, hybrid bulk power-consumer arrangements and firm capacity requirements for renewable-energy supply. He presented a CTBCM readiness toolkit to help industrial consumers understand the requirements and practical considerations of participating in the competitive market.
The commercial viability of wheeling emerged as a key concern. Analysis presented at the dialogue noted that Nepra's September 2026 determination places effective UoSC at Rs9.46 per kWh for B-3 consumers and Rs12.32 per kWh for B-4 consumers, including Rs3.23 per kWh in distribution-of-subsidy surcharge. Participants noted that such charges would be an important consideration for industries evaluating alternative electricity procurement arrangements.
A power-market panel featuring Syed Iftikhar Ali, power-sector professional, Saham Qamar, Director of Power Matrix, and Hasnat Khan, Senior Vice Chairman of the Pakistan Solar Association, examined network capability, metering and settlement infrastructure, transmission constraints, UoSC and the predictability required by industrial consumers.
The discussion highlighted that industrial participation in a competitive market would require not only a regulatory framework allowing consumers to participate but also adequate infrastructure and commercial certainty to make such participation practical.
The wider cost structure of Pakistan's power sector was also examined. Rehan Javed, Head of the Energy Advisory Committee at FPCCI, highlighted major cost pressures within the country's generation portfolio, citing a combined Rs2.899 trillion increase in the disclosed costs of five major hydropower projects. Individual project cost overruns ranged from 21% to 285%. Dasu was cited as an example, with its approved cost of Rs486 billion compared with the current cost of Rs1.737 trillion, representing a 257% increase.
For the textile industry, the energy challenge extends beyond electricity. Asim Riaz, Energy Adviser at Aptma, linked power-market reform with the sector's wider competitiveness challenges, discussing changing national and global energy markets, gas-market liberalisation, captive generation, energy efficiency, renewable integration and the economics of industrial energy supply. His intervention highlighted that decisions involving renewable energy, captive generation, efficiency and electrification must ultimately make economic sense for manufacturers.
Energy costs and reliability are directly linked with textile production and export competitiveness. Higher electricity or gas costs can affect manufacturing margins, while unreliable supplies can disrupt production and increase the cost of maintaining alternative sources of power.
At the same time, global textile markets are increasingly demanding evidence of sustainable production, credible carbon information and traceable supply chains. ESG compliance, traceability and measurement, reporting and verification are therefore becoming important elements of export competitiveness.
Participants identified fragmented environmental data, limited verification capacity and inconsistencies in reporting as persistent challenges. They stressed the need to connect factory-level operational information with credible sustainability claims made by textile exporters.
This means that energy management is increasingly connected with access to international markets because manufacturers must be able to demonstrate the environmental benefits of efficiency measures and renewable-energy investments through credible data and documentation.
ADS Chief Executive Amjad Nazeer calls for moving beyond compliance-only relationships towards shared investment, technical assistance, long-term procurement arrangements and credible monitoring and reporting mechanisms.
Participants also stressed that decarbonisation should begin with measurement, energy efficiency and process optimisation, including waste-heat recovery, before industries move towards electrification, renewable generation and storage, where appropriate. Improving efficiency can simultaneously reduce energy costs and emissions while strengthening the economic case for future renewable-energy and storage investments.
The dialogue concluded that Pakistan's textile sector needs more than access to new electricity procurement models and renewable-energy options. Transparent pricing, reliable networks, credible data, appropriate risk allocation, storage and firm-capacity solutions, and stronger institutional coordination would all be required to make the transition commercially sustainable.
The discussion ultimately connected Pakistan's energy policy with its export strategy. Power-market reform that fails to provide reliable and competitively priced energy could undermine industrial competitiveness, while a renewable-energy transition without adequate storage, network planning, market mechanisms and credible data could create additional technical and financial challenges for manufacturers.

title: Deregulating wheat  sugar markets
description: Deregulating wheat  sugar markets
content:
Can Pakistan deliver IMF-mandated reforms without triggering food, political crisis?
Pakistan's recurring wheat and sugar crises are not simply the result of poor harvests. They stem from weak planning, flawed policies, administrative failures, market manipulation and political influence of vested interests that have shaped these sectors for decades. Successive governments have spent trillions of rupees on subsidies, procurement and market interventions, yet farmers hue and cry that they remain underpaid, and consumers continue to face price spikes.
Wheat has been heavily regulated since the 1960s and sugar since the 1970s. These policies were meant to protect growers, increase production, and benefit consumers, but in practice they have often benefited flour millers, sugar barons, middlemen and politically connected groups. Several influential political families hold significant interests in the sugar industry, while many flour mills are linked to politicians, their relatives or cronies. The result is a system that socialises losses while allowing private players to capture profits.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif assumed office first in April 2022 and again in March 2024. Throughout both tenures, the government repeatedly assured the public that wheat and sugar stocks were sufficient and that prices would remain stable. Yet market realities frequently contradicted these claims. Artificial shortages, abrupt shifts from exports to imports, weak oversight and speculative hoarding have repeatedly disrupted supply over the past four years.
Official data show that wheat production increased by 4.3% to 29.605 million tons, rice by 2.8% to 9.998 million tons, and sugarcane by 6.2% to 89.45 million tons. Despite these increases, flour prices have continued to rise, suggesting that the latest wheat shortage is driven less by production constraints and more by market manipulation and speculative behaviours of hoarders. Pakistanis are not consuming wheat only; they eat rice, nearly 4 million tons, corn, millet and sorghum too; hence per capita consumption of 124 kg is exaggerated.
Pakistan has also paid a heavy price for inefficient wheat imports in the recent past. The government spent more than $1 billion importing wheat, much of which remained in warehouses, got rotten and/or was stolen, and huge stocks were stolen over time, burdening the national exchequer. The country has repeatedly imported wheat and sugar when global prices were historically high and exported them when international prices were relatively low; an approach that reflects poor timing and inefficient policy.
The IMF has long argued that Pakistan's agricultural markets suffer from excessive protectionism, distorted pricing mechanisms, costly subsidies and inefficient state intervention. In September 2024, Pakistan agreed with the IMF to phase out government market intervention and support prices in agriculture – wheat during fiscal year 2024-25 and sugar by June 2026.
The government moved quickly on wheat by announcing the discontinuation of official procurement and support prices. It also formally committed to deregulating the sugar sector by June 2026, including the removal of minimum support prices of sugarcane and trading restrictions. On paper, these reforms promise greater efficiency, fiscal savings, private investment and more competitive markets. In reality, however, deregulating Pakistan's two most politically sensitive food commodities may prove "mission impossible" for the current coalition government's political partners.
The central question is not whether deregulation is economically desirable. It is whether Pakistan's political economy is capable of implementing it in its true spirit. For decades, the government controlled nearly every aspect of the wheat economy: support prices, procurement targets, public storage and strategic reserves. These measures were intended to ensure food security, but they also created inefficiencies, corruption and opportunities for rent-seeking.
The sugar sector has been similarly regulated since the 1970s. Governments fixed sugarcane prices, restricted the production of jaggery and raw sugar, approved imports and exports, imposed stock limits and frequently intervened through the state-owned entity Trading Corporation of Pakistan whenever shortages or public outrage emerged. These policies often favoured mill owners rather than farmers or consumers.
The IMF-backed reforms seek to end this interventionist model. The government plans to withdraw from wheat procurement, shut down Passco, maintain only emergency strategic reserves and allow prices to be determined largely by market forces. In sugar, minimum support prices, zoning restrictions, mill licensing and trading controls are expected to be liberalised. This would represent the most significant transformation of Pakistan's agricultural markets in generations.
From an economic perspective, deregulation has strong arguments in its favour. Artificial prices distort production decisions, encourage inefficiency, burden public finances and create opportunities for rent-seeking. Every year, the government spends billions managing procurement, storage, subsidies and emergency imports, yet artificial shortages and engineered price spikes persist. A competitive market could improve efficiency, attract investment, modernise storage infrastructure and allocate resources more rationally.
But markets do not become competitive simply because the government role exists. Pakistan's agricultural marketing system remains fragmented and dominated by middlemen (Arthis) hoarders, weak logistics, inadequate old-fashioned warehousing and limited access to commodity financing. Without modern market institutions, deregulation could merely transfer market power from government agencies to private cartels unless free import/export is allowed.
Ending public wheat procurement would transfer price risk directly to farmers. Large commercial producers may adapt, but small farmers often depend on guaranteed procurement to recover production costs and repay seasonal loans borrowed from Arthis.
On the consumer side, wheat is Pakistan's staple food. Even modest increases in flour prices immediately feed into inflation, poverty and political unrest. A more practical approach would be to build a mandatory strategic stockpile through private-sector participation. Licensed traders, flour mills, exporters, and importers with approved storage facilities could be required to maintain 10% of their stocks in government-designated warehouses involving zero investment of government. In an emergency, the government could purchase these reserves at verified purchase cost price and release them into the market to stabilise prices. Such a system would reduce the fiscal burden while preserving food-security safeguards.
If wheat deregulation is difficult, sugar liberalisation is politically explosive. The sugar industry has long been associated with powerful business interests, policy reversals and recurring market controversies. Nearly every year, Pakistan witnesses disputes over actual sugar stocks, exports, imports, shortages, subsidies or fixation of retail prices. Allowing prices to be determined entirely by market forces may improve efficiency, but only if genuine competition exists. This requires a liberal import-export policy for raw and refined sugar, no unnecessary restrictions on new entrants and transparent stock reporting.
Without strong competition laws and effective action against collusion, consumers could remain vulnerable to coordinated pricing by dominant market players. Removing regulations without strengthening regulators is not deregulation; it is merely replacing public control with private cartelization and concentration.
This is where economics collides with politics. The IMF expects Pakistan to reduce fiscal costs and minimise state intervention to reduce losses. Governments, however, survive on public confidence, and nothing erodes that confidence faster than rising food prices. Whenever wheat or sugar prices surge, political pressure inevitably forces governments to intervene through imports, subsidies, export bans or administrative price controls. Pakistan's history is full of such reversals. This makes complete and sustained deregulation extraordinarily difficult.
Successful deregulation requires far more than withdrawing government notifications. Pakistan must first build competitive commodity markets supported by modern storage facilities, warehouse financing, reliable market intelligence, efficient logistics, digital futures trading platforms, crop insurance and robust competition enforcement.
THE WRITER IS A FORMER VICE PRESIDENT OF KCCI, FORMER BOARD MEMBER OF REAP AND AN INTERNATIONAL TRADE EXPERT

title: Financialisation of global value chains
description: Financialisation of global value chains
content:
This process creates more challenges than opportunities for suppliers of developing countries
Global value chains (GVCs) have been the carriers of international trade since the 1990s. These chains describe the international disintegration of production, where different stages of manufacturing, marketing and distributing a product materialise across multiple countries.
These chains are dominated by lead firms which are based in advanced countries while suppliers are dispersed across developing countries. In the jargon, the lead firms are located in the Global North and the suppliers are based in the Global South.
Most of the writings on GVCs pay attention to governance, where the lead firms control the suppliers located in developing countries and mainly discuss the prospects of upgrading for the suppliers. A few writings describe the process of value creation, where the lead firms call the shots and capture the value from the suppliers in the chain. Few studies discuss the process of financialisation of GVCs.
The financialisation of GVCs starts with the objectives followed by the lead firms. Since the lead firms are listed on stock exchanges, they have been increasing dividend payouts to shareholders since early 2000. They have also increased share buybacks by using surplus cash.
US-based lead firms are more financialised than those of Europe. The US tax structure incentivises firms to distribute cash to shareholders. On the other hand, the European firms distribute less cash to shareholders. Thus, the surplus cash is used by the lead firms to meet financial objectives.
Lead firms have also financialised their operations as they tighten their grip on the suppliers from developing countries. They have increased the number of payment days for the suppliers since 2000. In addition, they have reduced the number of collection days from their customers. This is how they have boosted their cash position. Hence, the lead firms strengthen their cash position at the cost of suppliers.
Lead firms have reduced their sourcing cost as the number of suppliers from developing countries sprang up since early 2000. In addition, these suppliers have to meet tight deadlines. In this way, the lead firms have increased their profit margins.
Macro environment also provides financial options to the lead firms. Policy rates have been low since early 2000 across the world. Lead firms, tempted by these low policy rates, raised cash through bond issuance. They did not raise capital from stock markets since bonds remained attractive for them. This shows that the lead firms preferred bonds to raise capital.
Lead firms have been following financial goals since early 2000. These firms have been involved in financial activities. They set short-term goals where downsizing is a norm. Downsizing immediately raises the profitability of firms. Such profits are then distributed to shareholders. This is known as downsize and distribute.
Before financial globalisation, the firms used to set long-term goals. They spent on research and development (R&D) to discover new processes, products and technologies. In addition, these firms trained workers who were required to steer R&D. Capital outlays were done to upgrade physical assets with a lasting value. These long-term goals used to kindle industrial capitalism.
In short, the financialisation of GVCs has brought a change in the strategic orientation of the lead firms. These firms extract value from their GVCs and distribute it among shareholders. Lead firms are in pursuit of short-term financial gains while long-term goals have been set aside. Last but not the least, the financialisaton of GVCs has created more challenges than opportunities for the suppliers of developing countries.
The writer is an independent economist and authored a book: Pakistan's Structural Economic Problems in the era of Financial Globalisation

title: At a crossroads  navigating trade  industrial policy dilemma
description: At a crossroads  navigating trade  industrial policy dilemma
content:
SRO regime has done significant damage to industries and plans to dismantle it must continue
Pakistan, once again walking a high-stakes economic tightrope, staged a financial balancing act as record-breaking remittances reduced the surmounting debt pressures. As of August 2026, Pakistan had a current account deficit of $98 million, relatively low given the regional economic complexities due to oil price volatility and closure of the Strait of Hormuz. This was largely driven by an increase in remittances, which have been at record-breaking levels in recent months.
However, the trade balance remains strained as export growth fails to increase, showing its susceptibility to regional uncertainty. Debt obligations in FY26 were above $21.5 billion, with $10 billion expected to be rolled over. However, the positive news is the rising foreign exchange reserves as Pakistan has reported highest-ever levels at more than $21 billion after the receipt of Eurobond sale proceeds. This crucial cushion is providing shock absorbers at a time when uncertainty is growing globally.
This may be the right time to address long-term relevant issues regarding the balance of payments, especially as the IMF programme approaches its latter phases. True economic sovereignty will only be realised if Pakistan can structurally transform its economy into one that is productivity-driven, which generates much-needed export competitiveness and reduces its dependence on external financial support and funding from its ever-so benevolent diaspora.
Pakistan is at a crossroads with its new trade and industrial policies that propel the manufacturing sector but at the same time make its local producers globally competitive. Pakistan has one of the lowest levels of value addition in the manufacturing sector as percentage of GDP, gross fixed capital formation (an indicator of investment) as a percentage of GDP, exports and imports as a percentage of GDP in the Asian region.
The lack of capital accumulation, poor levels of industrialisation and an inward-looking industrial strategy have not only affected its ability to produce and export output effectively but has created an industrial sector that is unproductive and uncompetitive as regional competitors investing in their physical and human capital continue to propel industrial growth and diverge away in terms of economic activity and growth.
The recent draft of the Auto Policy 2026-2031 provides insights into the final document as the government has set export and localisation targets to increase domestic exportable production, while implementing the National Tariff Policy 2025-2030. A clearly laid path to tariff reforms will definitely help reduce uncertainty and allow businesses across the economy to implement long-term decisions. The less competitive businesses are likely to exit, leaving a larger playing field for the more competitive and efficient ones.
Furthermore, the new auto policy has provided significant incentives to the new electric vehicles, offering them tax incentives that would increase their penetration. This will help not only reduce the oil bill, but also lower the adverse environmental impact as Pakistan relies mostly on petrol and diesel consumption to power its transportation sector.
In order to better understand the potential of growth in the auto industry, two examples of developing countries that have undertaken a massive restructuring of their auto sectors and benefitted are Vietnam and Morocco. While Pakistan produces approximately 200,000 units, Morocco produced more than 500,000 units in 2025. While Morocco primarily manufactures and exports cars to the EU as more than 80% of its OEM production is exported, Vietnam has strong linkages in parts and accessories trade with the EU, US and Japan.
Both these countries take advantage of almost negligible tariff rates offered by their trading partners on their exports. It is also important to note that these countries have developed a vast network of deep trade agreements with their major trading partners that not only involves lower tariffs on both imports and exports but also ensures that the burdening costs associated with non-tariff measures (NTMs) are significantly reduced.
Unfortunately, Pakistan has not only failed to integrate itself with its major trading partners by creating a more extensive network of free trade agreements, especially within the Asian region, but has also made little progress to remove the costs associated with the non-tariff measures. The resistance to the National Tariff Policy 2025-2030 is a clear indication of the challenges in propelling productivity and trade growth.
Morocco did not try to reinvent the wheel by adopting an inward-looking strategy as it focused on attracting FDI, offering a predictable and low tariff regime as well as free zones to encourage investments. Vietnam ensured that its local producers meet the same requirements that are expected from foreign companies in terms of standards of production, while creating an effective ecosystem to support local production. However, Pakistani producers have focused on extracting benefits from a captive market without any desire to compete and innovate as they have been successful in locking out foreign competition.
The analysis of GVC-related data extracted from the UN ESCAP's Regional Integration and Value-Added Database paints a stark picture for the auto industry. Pakistan's gross exports, which crossed borders more than once, in the transportation equipment sector was about $100 million, of which 32.8% was foreign value added. Approximately $58 million of direct value-added exports were consumed in the export destination.
Vietnam reported a massive increase of GVC-related exports from about $3.6 billion in 2015 to $11.5 billion in 2024. A larger proportion of its exports are intermediate parts and accessories rather than final goods, which are assembled downstream in its trading partners. More than $4 billion worth of its exports in the auto sector incorporate foreign inputs. Vietnam's focus is mainly on the supply of parts and accessories, which is vastly different than other Southeast Asian countries, which focus on exports of final product. Their localisation rates remain low, with parts and accessories produced mainly for export. Unfortunately, ESCAP does not report data on Morocco.
Although some of the concerns of manufacturers, such as security-related issues, are valid and require a long-term geopolitical solution, many of the concerns regarding high costs of business must be tackled through business reforms and better industrial strategies. Policies must compel OEM to allow participation of their local vendors in regional and global value chains and contracts that limit export sales must be discouraged. This will require incubation of smaller-sized vendors with better financing, R&D facilities and easier access to quality certifications.
Pakistan must harmonise its global standards to ensure that its exporters are able to more easily access more competitive markets. The current SRO regime has done significant damage to industries across the economy and the plan to dismantle it must continue. In essence, the approach must be holistic with wide-ranging reforms that can structurally improve the industries and provide a platform to boost export sales.
THE WRITER IS AN ASSISTANT PROFESSOR OF ECONOMICS AND RESEARCH FELLOW AT CBER, IBA

title: Pakistan s last IMF bailout
description: Pakistan s last IMF bailout
content:
Credible opportunity exists to graduate from cycle of repeated IMF programmes
As Pakistan enters the final year of its $7 billion, 37-month Extended Fund Facility with the International Monetary Fund, it stands at a crossroads. The question policymakers must now answer is not simply how to complete the programme, but what comes next.
For the first time in many years, Pakistan has a credible opportunity to graduate from its cycle of repeated IMF programmes. The economy is hardly out of danger, and the vulnerabilities that have produced successive balance of payments crises have not disappeared. But the country is entering this final year from a considerably stronger position than it was in 2023.
Pakistan's foreign exchange position provides a much stronger buffer than it did during the 2023 crisis. State Bank reserves have risen to about $21.4 billion, while total liquid reserves, including those held by commercial banks, stand at about $26.8 billion. The central bank's reserves now provide roughly three months of import cover.
Pakistan has also regained access to international capital markets. In September, it raised a record $3 billion through a dual-tranche Eurobond, attracting almost $6 billion in orders. The transaction demonstrates that international investors are once again willing to lend to Pakistan, giving the country another source of external financing beyond official creditors.
A proposed $10 billion exchange stabilisation facility from the United States could provide an additional layer of insurance. The proposal, currently under discussion, is neither a loan nor a grant. If agreed, it could provide a financial backstop and strengthen market confidence.
More importantly, Pakistan's underlying external position has improved substantially since the crisis of 2023. In addition to the sharp increase in foreign exchange reserves, workers' remittances reached a record $41.6 billion in fiscal 2026, compared with $27.3 billion three years earlier. Services exports have crossed $10 billion, with information technology and digital services leading the expansion. ICT exports alone reached about $4.6 billion in fiscal 2026, growing by more than 20% annually.
Pakistan's current account, reflecting financial transactions with the world, including trade, investment, and transfers, has been in surplus or broadly balanced for the first time in 14 years. The government is also running a substantial primary surplus, meaning that revenues exceed expenditure before interest payments.
The rapid adoption of solar power is also reducing Pakistan's dependence on imported fuel. This is expected to reduce the annual energy import bill by roughly $5 to $8 billion, depending on international crude oil prices.
The one major macroeconomic area where there has been little progress is merchandise exports. They have broadly remained in the range of $25 to $32 billion for around 15 years. With imports continuing to grow, the trade deficit has also widened.
There are, however, reasons for cautious optimism. Pakistan is now in the second year of a five-year trade liberalisation programme, and its impact should become increasingly visible over the next two to three years through higher exports and a narrowing trade deficit.
Privatisation is also moving in the right direction. The sale of Pakistan International Airlines has broken a longstanding stalemate, while the privatisation process for the first three electricity distribution companies has advanced to the investor engagement and transaction stages. Other state-owned enterprises and public assets are also being prepared for divestment.
None of this guarantees that Pakistan will avoid another crisis. An oil price shock, geopolitical disruption, a sudden stop in capital inflows, or a return to fiscal slippage could once again put pressure on the balance of payments. The external financing requirement for 2027-28 alone demonstrates how exposed the country remains. A large reserve buffer is valuable, but it cannot indefinitely compensate for weak exports and large debt repayments.
That is why the coming year matters so much. Pakistan should complete the current IMF programme successfully. It should remain closely engaged with the Fund, draw on its technical expertise, and maintain the fiscal and monetary discipline that the programme has helped impose. But it should not assume that the expiry of the programme automatically requires another one. The objective should be different this time: to make the IMF a source of advice rather than emergency financing.
Graduating from IMF programmes would not mean that Pakistan has solved all its economic problems. It would mean that the country has finally developed the capacity to address them without another bailout. That is the real test of the current programme. Not whether Pakistan can complete another IMF arrangement, but whether it can make this one its last.
The writer is a Senior Fellow with the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics and has previously served as Pakistan's ambassador to the WTO

title: Syria condemns Israeli excavation work near occupied Golan Heights
description: Urges international action to halt violations  reaffirming its sovereignty and calling for respect for borders
content:
Urges international action to halt violations, reaffirming its sovereignty and calling for respect for borders
Syria strongly condemned on Sunday Israeli excavation work near a separation line with the occupied Syrian Golan Heights, calling it a “flagrant breach” of the 1974 disengagement agreement.
In a statement, the Foreign Ministry denounced work on the project known as “Sofa 53,” as Israeli forces resumed excavations west of al-Asha village in the countryside of the southern Quneitra province.
The ministry described the work as part of continuing Israeli violations in the buffer zone covered by the disengagement agreement.
“The continuation of the Israeli occupation’s aggressive approach, accompanied by attacks and incursions on the ground, poses a direct threat to regional security and stability and undermines international law,” the ministry warned.
It urged the international community to take deterrent measures to halt such practices and prevent their recurrence.
The ministry also reaffirmed Syria’s right to exercise full sovereignty over all its territory under international law and relevant UN resolutions, calling on the international community to fulfill its legal and moral responsibilities to protect state sovereignty and respect borders.
According to Syria’s Al-Ikhbariya television channel, the project involves excavation and construction of a military road along the separation line within the buffer zone.
Read More: Over 800 Palestinian teachers killed by Israel since Gaza war: education ministry
Israel began working on the project, also referred to as the “Great Storm” or “Sofa 53,” in mid-2022 near Hader in northern Quneitra, before extending it through Jabata al-Khashab, al-Hamidiyah, al-Qahtaniyah, Ruweihina, Bir Ajam and Bariqa.
Its route continues south through al-Asha toward the point where the Syrian, Jordanian and Israeli boundaries meet.
As part of the project, the Israeli army built a military road approximately 8 meters wide, flanked by earth berms reaching around 5 meters in height, according to the Syrian broadcaster.
It also established observation posts and military positions along the route adjacent to the ceasefire line in the occupied Golan Heights.
Syrian accounts indicate that Israeli forces have advanced between 300 and 1,000 meters beyond the ceasefire line, with military construction accelerating in late 2024, particularly after the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime.
Residents previously told Anadolu that the project’s expansion had rendered thousands of dunams of agricultural land in rural Quneitra unsuitable for farming and grazing, while disrupting water flows and altering the area’s natural landscape.
Since Assad’s fall on Dec. 8, 2024, Israel has expanded its military operations in Syria, moving troops into the Golan buffer zone and nearby positions.
Syria demands the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the areas they occupied and maintains its commitment to the 1974 disengagement agreement. Israel claims its movements are driven by security considerations.

title: Every moment in Somali pirates    captivity felt like years     says injured Pakistani sailor
description: Injured sailor recalls how pirates tied hostages to the deck as Somali forces closed in on the Honour 25
content:
Injured sailor recalls how pirates tied hostages to the deck as Somali forces closed in on the Honour 25
After five and a half months in the hands of Somali pirates, the return home brought relief to the surviving crew of the Honour 25 — but could not erase memories of the night when they were forced onto the deck and caught in a deadly exchange of fire.
The Palau-flagged MT Honour 25, carrying 18,500 barrels of oil and a 17-member crew, including 10 Pakistanis, was seized on April 21, around 30 nautical miles off Puntland while sailing from Oman to Somalia. Puntland’s Maritime Police Force said it rescued the tanker in an operation off Dharin-baar, but the pirates opened fire on the hostages, killing five people, including three Pakistanis, and injuring four others.
For Pakistani sailor Ameen bin Shams, the horrific night remains etched in his memory: pirates herding the hostages onto the deck in freezing temperatures, Somali naval forces closing in and, eventually, bullets tearing through the vessel.
Read : Aircraft carrying four injured crew members, remains of three MT Honour 25 sailors lands in Karachi
“Every moment we spent in the captivity of Somali pirates felt like years. We lived in constant fear of death, never knowing when the pirates might kill us,” said the injured sailor.
Shams said the nightmare they had feared eventually unfolded when Somali security forces launched an operation against another vessel anchored some distance from the Honour 25 and managed to free it.
Following the development, the pirates aboard their vessel ordered the crew to start the ship’s engines and move forward. It was nighttime, and the Somali naval vessel was approximately 10 nautical miles away.
“That night was nothing short of a nightmare. The pirates gathered all of us on the ship’s deck in freezing temperatures. We remained there throughout the night without proper clothing or footwear,” Shams said.
At daybreak, the pirates allowed the crew to go below deck. However, just as they were preparing to rest, they were ordered back onto the deck. All crew members, except Imran and Hussain Yousuf, were tied to the deck railing.
Imran later informed the Ansar Burney Trust by phone that he and Hussain Yousuf were inside the ship’s main engine room, while the remaining crew members had been taken back to the deck by the pirates.
By then, the pursuing Somali naval vessel had closed the distance to just one nautical mile. Security personnel gave the pirates 30 minutes to surrender the vessel and release the hostages, but they refused to comply.
Also Read : Bodies of Pakistanis killed in Somalia being repatriated, arrive in Addis Ababa: PMO
According to Imran, gunfire suddenly erupted, with bullets penetrating the interior of the vessel. The intense exchange of fire continued for more than two hours.
There were 41 pirates aboard the Honour 25. After spending five and a half months in captivity, the crew members had come to know most of the pirates by name, while the pirates also knew their names.
Imran said a pirate identified as Arab panicked during the Somali forces’ operation and opened fire in the section of the vessel where the hostages had been tied up.
The security forces soon gained control of the ship. Five pirates were killed in the operation, while 13 others were injured and arrested.
All four injured Pakistani sailors who arrived in Karachi were shifted to Aga Khan Hospital, where they are currently receiving treatment.
Ameen’s wife, Ayesha, said her husband had sustained four bullet wounds and had been admitted to the hospital.
Meanwhile, Muzammil, son of deceased crew member Mahmood Ansari, told the media at the airport that the families had repeatedly appealed for the safe recovery of the hostages, but the government had failed to listen.
“What is the point of offering compensation now?” he questioned.
The bodies of all three deceased crew members have been handed over to their families, who are making arrangements for their funerals.
The oil tanker Honour 25, sailing under the Somali flag from Oman to Somalia, was hijacked by pirates on April 21. There were 17 crew members aboard, 10 of them Pakistani nationals. The families of the Pakistani hostages spent months seeking the safe release of their loved ones, staging peaceful protests and repeatedly approaching government authorities.
During their captivity, the pirates initially demanded a ransom of $3 million, which was later reduced to $1.9 million and subsequently to $1 million. All the Pakistani crew members who were killed or injured were from different areas of Karachi.
The pirates came under pressure during a rescue operation and, while retreating from the vessel, opened indiscriminate fire on the abducted crew before fleeing the ship. Five sailors were killed, including three Pakistanis — Second Officer Kashif Umar, Third Engineer Mahmood Ansari and Boiler Rafiullah. The other two deceased crew members were an Indian sailor, Tanveer, and the chief engineer from Myanmar.
Four sailors were injured — Usman, Yasir, Ameen and Vicky from Indonesia — while Hussain Yousuf, Imran Ali and Yaseen remained safe. The two surviving Pakistani crew members later contacted the Ansar Burney Welfare Trust in Karachi using the ship captain’s mobile phone and provided details of the incident.
Puntland police said the Honour 25 had 18,500 barrels of oil on board when it was hijacked. The police had been pursuing three hijacked vessels off the Somali coast and had also rescued another oil tanker, Sibu 1, on Friday. However, 28 of the 41 pirates arrested during that operation later escaped while being transferred to jail, with several Puntland security officials accusing local police of complicity.

title: Star Trek  could leave its familiar characters behind for new stories
description: Star Trek  creator   s son Rod Roddenberry says the franchise is ready for new stories beyond its familiar cast
content:
'Star Trek' creator’s son Rod Roddenberry says the franchise is ready for new stories beyond its familiar cast
Rod Roddenberry believes the Star Trek franchise is ready to move beyond familiar characters and explore new stories and ideas.
Rod Roddenberry, son of Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry, believes the long-running science fiction franchise is ready to explore new stories after decades of revisiting its established characters and worlds.
Speaking to PEOPLE at the Broadcasting+Cable Hall of Fame Awards 34th Anniversary Gala in New York City, Roddenberry reflected on Star Trek’s 60-year legacy and the message he believes continues to define the franchise.
Roddenberry said Star Trek goes beyond science fiction, highlighting themes of diversity and acceptance. He explained that the franchise presents a future where people no longer fear their differences but instead recognise diversity as something that can help society grow.
“It’s a message about the future and what we can be,” he said.
Since the original Star Trek series premiered in 1966, the franchise has expanded into numerous television series and films. Roddenberry has been involved with several recent Star Trek projects, serving as an executive producer on Star Trek: Discovery, Star Trek: Picard, Star Trek: Lower Decks, Star Trek: Prodigy and Star Trek: Strange New Worlds, among others.
However, he believes the franchise should now look ahead rather than continue relying heavily on returning characters.
“I think Star Trek is ready for new stories,” Roddenberry said, adding that bringing back previous casts and characters has already been explored. He suggested that the franchise should instead begin “a new adventure”.
Roddenberry also said future Star Trek stories could explore advances in technology in a respectful, careful and optimistic way, while stressing that any new direction must ultimately be supported by a compelling story.

title: UK s Green Party votes to declare  zionism is racism
description: Motion calling for Zionism to be treated as racism passes at party conference in Brighton
content:
Motion calling for Zionism to be treated as racism passes at party conference in Brighton,
Motion reasserts party's commitment to Palestinian liberation, right of return, Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions, full arms embargo against Israel
Britain's Green Party formally adopted a policy declaring "Zionism is racism" after a majority of members voted in favor of a motion Sunday.
The motion, which calls for Zionism to be "treated as any other form of racism," passed by 1,022 votes to 813 at the party's annual conference in Brighton.
The vote makes the motion formal policy for the Green Party in England and Wales.
Following the vote on the anti-Zionist policy at Green Party Conference, the 5 Green MPs, the Leader and Co-Deputy Leaders have issued a joint statement pic.twitter.com/NcB2aljsTK
In 2024, the Green Party became the first political party in England and Wales to vote to recognize the Israeli government as an "apartheid" state.
The party cited international treaties, including the International Convention on Apartheid of 1973 and the Rome Statute of 1998.
Following the vote, a Green Party spokesperson said: "The motion sets out the Party's opposition to Zionism, defined as an ethnonationalist political project, and states that anti-Zionism should not be equated with antisemitism."
Read More: Over 800 Palestinian teachers killed by Israel since Gaza war: education ministry
"The motion reasserts the Party's commitment to Palestinian liberation, the right of return, Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS), and a full arms embargo against Israel," the spokesperson added.
The spokesperson said the Green Party is an "anti-racist party" and reiterated that it has consistently opposed what the party describes as the illegal occupation of Palestinian and Syrian land.
The primary motion, titled "Zionism is racism," was pushed by a group called Greens for Palestine, The Guardian newspaper reported.
The group encouraged non-party members to join the party to ensure the policy was debated and adopted, according to The Guardian .
The motion argues that Zionism is necessarily racist because it "privileges one ethnic group on the basis of the subjugation of others."
"This motion is aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism, as defined, and not at the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists," it said.

title: Peter Krause reveals he turned down Aaron Sorkin   s  A Few Good Men
description: Peter Krause recalls turning down Aaron Sorkin   s  A Few Good Men  reading while studying at NYU and bartending there
content:
Peter Krause recalls turning down Aaron Sorkin’s 'A Few Good Men' reading while studying at NYU and bartending there
Peter Krause has revealed that he once turned down an opportunity to participate in a reading of Aaron Sorkin’s A Few Good Men while the actor was studying drama at New York University.
The Six Feet Under star discussed the missed opportunity in an interview with Esquire, recalling that he worked as a Broadway bartender in the 1980s while attending NYU. At the time, Sorkin was his bar manager and was developing the play that would later become a major stage and film success.
Sorkin invited Krause to participate in a reading of the play, but the actor declined because of his demanding schedule. Krause was balancing scene-study classes and a Shakespeare production, leaving him with little time for another commitment.
Krause later learned that the play was A Few Good Men , a decision he now remembers with some regret. The play eventually opened on Broadway in 1989, with Krause working as a bartender at the Music Box Theatre.
The legal drama was adapted into the 1992 film starring Tom Cruise, Jack Nicholson, Demi Moore and Kevin Bacon, becoming one of Sorkin’s best-known works.
Despite missing out on the early project, Krause and Sorkin eventually worked together on Sports Night . Krause played sports broadcaster Casey McCall in the series, which ran from 1998 to 2000.
Krause said he remains good friends with Sorkin and would be interested in working with him again. He also expressed interest in revisiting Sports Night if Sorkin were open to reimagining the series for a modern audience.
Reflecting on his earlier decision, Krause advised young actors to make time for opportunities when they arise.

title: International law at the crossroads  evolution or erosion
description: International law at the crossroads  evolution or erosion
content:
The post-1945 rules-based international order is in a state of 'rupture'. The foundational principles and institutions still formally exist, but they no longer function as originally conceived and face an unprecedented crisis of credibility. To many, this signals the end of international law, a framework too weak to constrain the powerful and too discredited to command the allegiance of the rest. This insight examines whether international law is eroding or evolving into something new and what middle powers like Pakistan can do to shape that evolution.
The most visible sign of the breakdown of international law is the paralysis of the UNSC. The veto is not new; it is a founding feature of the UN Charter, designed to ensure great-power buy-in for the system. What is new is its pattern of use. Since 2011, the veto has been exercised to block resolutions addressing crimes against humanity and war crimes, shielding perpetrators from accountability rather than maintaining peace. The US vetoed three ceasefire resolutions in the first six months of the Israel-Palestine conflict in Gaza; Russia vetoed a resolution condemning its own invasion of Ukraine.
The rupture is also evident in the unprecedented attacks by major powers on the International Criminal Court (ICC). In December 2025, Russia sentenced ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan to 15 years' imprisonment and jailed eight ICC judges in absentia for issuing arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin.
In July 2026, the ICC's Assembly of States Parties voted to dismiss Khan over charges of sexual misconduct. What made the dismissal striking was its timing and context: credible reports indicated that the US and Israel had actively lobbied to exploit the allegations against Khan to neutralise his office's Gaza prosecutions.
Moreover, in January 2026, the US government decided to withdraw from dozens of international organisations it considered "wasteful, ineffective or harmful". This retreat has contributed to what French President Macron described as a "world without rules, where international law is trampled underfoot and the only law that seems to matter is that of the strongest".
The pattern extends beyond institutions. Since October 2023, Israel's military campaign against Palestinians in Gaza has killed over 70 thousand civilians, with the UN Human Rights Council concluding that Israel bears responsibility for the commission of genocide. The same pattern extended to Lebanon, where near-daily Israeli strikes since the November 2024 ceasefire resulted in civilian casualties. Moreover, Israel has conducted hundreds of strikes on Syria and seized its demilitarised buffer zone, which violates Syria's territorial integrity.
In April 2025, India unilaterally placed the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance – a move the Permanent Court of Arbitration found to have no legal basis. In June 2025, Israel struck Iranian nuclear facilities; the US joined days later, targeting three major nuclear sites. In February 2026, both launched a second, larger coordinated strike on Iran. The US subsequently imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and struck Iranian naval vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. These acts, taken together, represent a pattern of states placing power above legal obligation and acting with impunity.
In this period of disruption, it is reasonable to assume that international law is losing its importance and gradually eroding. But to mistake disruption for disappearance would be to misread what is actually occurring.
Koskenniemi, writing in International Relations in 2012, offers the most precise diagnosis. He points out that international law functions as "an argumentative practice in which political claims are defended and attacked". This suggests that international law does not function as an enforcement mechanism but rather serves as a shared grammar. Russia invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter to justify its invasion; the US framed its institutional withdrawals in the language of sovereignty. What we are witnessing is states stretching, weaponizing and selectively applying the grammar of international law rather than discarding it.
Louis Henkin observed in How Nations Behave (1979) that "almost all nations observe almost all principles of international law and almost all of their obligations almost all the time." This baseline holds invisibly across trade law, diplomatic immunity and treaty compliance, none of which make headlines precisely because they are working.
International law, therefore, is not disappearing, but the institutional framework through which it has been administered is visibly weakening. It is in this space that the question of middle power agency becomes urgent.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney captured the stakes plainly at Davos in January 2026: "Middle powers must act together because if we are not at the table, we are on the menu."
The historical record provides reason for cautious optimism that remaining at the table is not only possible but consequential. It was a coalition of small and middle powers that pushed the Rome Statute to adoption in 1998, securing 120 votes in favour amid objections from the US, China and Israel.
Pakistan's rise as the main mediator between the US and Iran in 2026 has shown that Pakistan can forge coalitions across both the centre and periphery of the international system simultaneously. That diplomatic capital must now be focused on shaping norms.
Pakistan can use its current UNSC seat to advance multilateralism and equitable development for the Global South. On the IWT, Pakistan may adopt a strategy at the council that frames transboundary water security and climate change as an international legal question rather than a bilateral dispute.
Additionally, Pakistan's National Security Policy 20222026 is due for renewal this year. The upcoming NSP presents a clear opportunity to embed international law as a permanent framework in policy planning from the outset.
However, none of this is achievable without investment at home. Concrete policies and strategies require more than ad hoc mechanisms and dependence on foreign legal experts. Pakistan needs a domestic cadre of international lawyers embedded within its foreign ministry, security establishment and treaty-negotiating teams who are not brought in only during crises, but are involved at every stage of policy planning. A state that cannot argue its own case is a state that has already lost.

title: How developed world is dealing with the AI threat
description: Responsibility for action lies with the authorities working in Washington  Beijing and Brussels
content:
Responsibility for action lies with the authorities working in Washington, Beijing and Brussels
The question posed above has geographic dimensions. There are three governments that need to act to deal with what has been recognised as a threat to mankind – to its very survival – by the rapid development of AI models. Responsibility for action lies with the authorities working in Washington, Beijing and Brussels. Brussels is the headquarter of the Europena Union and is the place from where the Europeans nations receive guidance for the design of public policy.
Those who are in the know of things say they don't have the knowledge about what is happening in the labs working on the development of AI systems. Carl Newport, who is a professor of computer science at Georgetown University and is the author of the book, Deep Work, made some suggestions in his article published by The New York Times on September 28. The article titled "Stop Panicking. Start asking these questions" insists "we don't yet know enough about what is happening in the work places where AI systems are being developed to come up with an effective response." The writer suggests that the US Congress should lead a public fact-finding mission that reveals the unvarnished details of AI development. This effort should ask questions of Dario Amodei and Sam Altman who are the leaders in the firms engaged in developing AI and who have expressed the most concern about what are called "frontier A.I. models".
The first question is: What specific types of AI models are dealing with the development of technology we should be are worried about? They have been using the nonspecific term AI when discussing their systems. This means that AI is a singular technology that moves along a fixed trajectory towards an ever more capable and dangerous functionality. However, AI covers a diverse collection of technologies – from self-driving cars to game-playing devices to medical imaging processing to chatbots to automated coding tools. Only some of these developments depend on the large language models (LLMs) produced by the advanced labs. The real concern is when the empowered agents in the AI systems are able to operate without guardrails.
The companies at the forefront of this rapidly developing technology don't as yet have mature research safety processes in place. It is useful to take into consideration that the leading firms working in this area – OpenAI and Anthropic – are relatively newly founded with not well-defined goals. They were created with the mission to align AI to human interests before it becomes so powerful that it can work without human guidance. If the belief is that winning the race to superintelligence is necessary to serve humanity, those responsible for developing it might not worry a great deal about associated dangers. In early September, the OpenAI chief scientist, Jacob Pachocki, wrote: "We focus OpenAI research towards recursive self-improvement (RSI) as we believe it is the only way to remain at the frontier of A.I research moving forward."
But RSI is not necessary for creating a thriving AI sector. As Carl Newport writes in the above quoted work, this way of moving forward with the development of AI is "an obsession that seems to be held mainly by two labs – Anthropic and OpenAI – that are most connected to the futurist philosophies that have long believed that RSI is being central to their apocalyptic visions." The Meta CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, called out this reality, saying that committing a clear majority of computing power toward "serving people rather than racing toward recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely."
Of the three centres of political development identified above – Washington Beijing and Brussels – it is the last named that is decisively moving forward. Ursula von der Leyen, the President of the European Commission, brought senior officials for a meeting held in a palace outside Brussels in September. The goal of the gathering was to develop an approach for minding the development of AI in the 27-nation bloc. "A.I. comes with a balance of possibilities and risks," she said at her State of the Union speech on September 16. "Without addressing these risks, we will never be able to unlock A.I.'s potential." The Brussels meeting over which Ursula von der Leyen presided dealt with the problems the EU nations were facing in their effort to guide the technology that was outpacing their ability to respond. Laws passed two years ago are having only a limited effect, proposed bills to regulate the technology are stalling without a vote, and international summits to discuss what to do were swiftly forgotten. Most governments were torn between wanting to harness AI and fearing its substantial risks.
European nations were waiting for the two leading AI nations – the US and China – to develop their approach which could serve the European nations to take a cue for their AI policies. However, policymaking in the leading nations is stalled. The Trump administration in the US has been divided over the dangers posed by the rapid development of AI, with the president labeling the worries as hoax. China has imposed some rules on AI, especially to censor chatbot content but at the same time it is racing towards the development of AI.
Pressure to take action has grown, especially after the leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind called for a slowdown of the development of the most advanced AI models and for strengthening government oversight. Researchers have described scenarios in which self-improving AI could escape human control and cause catastrophic damage. One example of the way humanity could be hurt is the development of new viruses for which no remedy exists. Public opinion in the US has turned against AI with a recent NYT poll finding that 61 per cent of likely voters in the November 2026 midterm elections opposed the construction of data centres that feed with energy and water the labs involved in developing AI.
Those who are watching the development of public policy and coordination between the US and China were disappointed that nothing concrete emerged from the summit on September 24 involving Presidents Doanld Trump and Xi Jinping. AI was on the agenda but the two presidents did not come to an agreement on how to handle the potential and risks involved in AI.
