title: Olivia Rodrigo slams Cornell University over handling of fraternity assault case  shows solidarity for victim
description: Rodrigo addressed the case on Instagram  criticising institutions she believes failed to protect women
content:
Rodrigo addressed the case on Instagram, criticising institutions she believes failed to protect women
Olivia Rodrigo has publicly expressed support for a Cornell University student known as Jane Doe, whose allegations of sexual assault involving seven fraternity members have drawn renewed attention.
Rodrigo addressed the case in an Instagram post on Saturday, criticising institutions she believes failed to protect women.
"Shame on Cornell and on every institution who protects rapists and abusers over women. I stand with Jane Doe. Her bravery reverberates across the country, and the crimes against her will not go unpunished," Rodrigo wrote.
"What she lived through matters, and so does the failure of those who could have intervened but chose not to," she added. "She deserves answers, consequences, and lasting change."
Jane Doe alleges that she was drugged with ketamine and sexually assaulted by seven fraternity members at the Chi Phi house on October 19, 2024.
She reported the alleged assault to Cornell police, but the local district attorney's office did not pursue charges at the time.
The case was recently reopened after New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed Letitia James as a special prosecutor.
James is expected to review evidence, interview witnesses and determine whether prosecution is appropriate.
"This is now an active criminal investigation," James said.
The former district attorney, Matt Van Houten, said, "We were not provided the full picture by the University." Cornell has backed an independent review of its handling of the allegations.
None of the seven men has been criminally charged, and some have denied the allegations. The case has also prompted support from other public figures and the #IAmJaneDoe social media campaign.

title: Funeral prayers held for two Pakistani civilians killed in Indian firing
description: Azmat Rasool and Mohsin Jatt were buried in their ancestral village of Jattan Wali Haveli  Lidhar  after the prayers
content:
Azmat Rasool and Mohsin Jatt were buried in their ancestral village of Jattan Wali Haveli, Lidhar, after the prayers
Funeral prayers for two Pakistani civilians killed in unprovoked Indian firing along the Pakistan-India border were held in Kasur on Sunday, with a large number of people attending, state-run Radio Pakistan reported.
On Friday, two Pakistani civilians were killed , and another was injured after Indian BSF personnel opened fire near the Pakistan-India international border in Kasur. The incident reportedly occurred when three residents from Ladhar village moved a few steps beyond a border pillar, upon which BSF personnel opened fire on the men without warning.
Azmat Rasool and Mohsin Jatt were buried in their ancestral village of Jattan Wali Haveli, Lidhar, after the prayers.
The families of the two civilians said they remained undaunted and called for India to face Pakistan directly rather than target unarmed people living along the border.
“If the cowardly Indian forces have the courage, they should face the resilient Pakistani nation directly,” the families said.
Read: Pakistan summons Indian envoy over killing of two Pakistanis along international border
Residents of the border areas also condemned what they described as a “heinous” act by Indian forces and termed it shameful.
In response to the incident, the Foreign Office on Saturday summoned India’s chargé d’affaires and lodged a strong protest . The FO said the BSF had used “unprovoked lethal force” against unarmed civilians and rejected any attempt to portray the deceased as “infiltrators”.
Pakistan called for an immediate and credible investigation, disciplinary and legal action against those responsible, and measures to prevent similar incidents.

title: Former  American Idol  contestant Caleb Flynn found guilty of murdering wife Ashley
description: During the trial  prosecutors presented messages in which Flynn expressed hatred towards Ashley
content:
During the trial, prosecutors presented messages in which Flynn expressed hatred towards Ashley
Former American Idol contestant Caleb Flynn has been found guilty of murdering his wife, Ashley Flynn, in their Ohio home while she was sleeping.
Flynn, a former worship pastor, was convicted on September 29 of charges including aggravated murder after prosecutors argued that he killed Ashley and staged the scene to make it appear that an intruder had broken into their Tipp City home. He is due to be sentenced on October 5 and faces up to life in prison without parole.
Ashley, 37, was found fatally shot in the early hours of February 16 after police responded to a report of a burglary and shooting. Flynn and the couple’s two daughters, who were nine and 12 at the time, were also inside the house but were not injured.
Flynn initially told police that an intruder had entered the home and killed Ashley. During a 911 call, he became emotional and repeatedly cried out as he reported the shooting. He gave investigators different accounts about where he had been when the shooting happened, including saying he was in his daughters’ room and later that he had been sleeping on the sofa.
Prosecutors ultimately argued that there had been no intruder and that Flynn had staged the home to resemble a break-in. An FBI agent testified that the damage to the door was inconsistent with a forced entry, while the firearm used to kill Ashley was never recovered. Flynn's defence maintained that prosecutors had not proved he was responsible for the shooting.
A major part of the prosecution’s case involved Flynn’s affair with Alleigha Botner. The pair had been involved in a relationship for more than two years, according to testimony, and Botner told the court about thousands of messages exchanged between them.
During the trial, prosecutors presented messages in which Flynn expressed hatred towards Ashley and discussed wanting her dead. In one message, Flynn allegedly wrote that he had been thinking about ways to kill her without going to prison. Botner also testified about messages between them in which they discussed Ashley’s death.
Flynn and Ashley had been married for 15 years and had two daughters. Ashley was described in her obituary as a devoted mother, substitute teacher, volleyball coach and volunteer. Her family said after Flynn’s conviction that no verdict could bring Ashley back or erase the pain her loved ones had endured.
Flynn previously appeared on season 12 of American Idol in 2013. He made it through the audition and early stages but did not reach the live rounds. During his appearance, he described himself as a music pastor from Tipp City and spoke warmly about Ashley.
Following the guilty verdict, Flynn’s defence attorney said he expected an appeal, maintaining that the defence was disappointed with the result. Flynn has continued to deny responsibility for Ashley’s killing.
Flynn is scheduled to return to court for sentencing on October 5, where he could receive a life sentence without the possibility of parole.

Say provincial govt’s stance on counterterrorism was against interests of province and people
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi criticised the provincial government’s attitude and role regarding counterterrorism operations during negotiations between the government and opposition, saying it had been tantamount to acting against the interests of the people and the province.
Naqvi travelled to Peshawar and met Governor Kundi at the Governor House, where the two leaders discussed several important provincial matters.
The meeting came as negotiations between the government and opposition failed to yield any result, with the possibility of the imposition of governor’s rule or an emergency looming over the province amid the deteriorating security situation.
Read : Naqvi blames K-P CM for talks ‘collapse’, warns Afridi will ‘be responsible’ if anyone dies during march
According to a statement issued after the meeting, the two leaders discussed various aspects of the worsening law and order situation in the province, the political situation and developments arising from the long march.
The two leaders also expressed concern over the possibility of terrorists being facilitated to safely pass through security checkpoints during the long march.
“The provincial government’s attitude and role regarding counterterrorism operations during the negotiations has been tantamount to acting against the interests of the people and the province,” it added.
The meeting noted that after an agreement had been reached on resolving the issues, the provincial government had once again demonstrated what it described as obstinacy and irresponsibility by reversing its position.
The meeting also described the use of helicopters and other government resources by the K-P chief minister and provincial ministers during the long march as an open violation of Islamabad High Court verdicts.
The two sides also discussed other matters of mutual interest and held consultations on several issues.
Later, in a post on X, Governor Kundi confirmed the meeting, which was also attended by K-P Inspector General of Police Zulfiqar Hameed and Chief Secretary Shahab Ali Shah.
Met with Federal Interior Minister @MohsinnaqviC42 , IG @KP_Police1 Zulfiqar Hameed, @CSKPOfficial Shahab Ali Shah at Governor House, Peshawar. We discussed the prevailing security situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The security of our people remains our foremost priority. Khyber… pic.twitter.com/KJc8dY3isO
He said they had discussed the prevailing security situation in the province.
“The security of our people remains our foremost priority,” he said, adding that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had sacrificed enough and every institution must work together to protect the people and defeat terrorism.
Naqvi, Kundi question Afridi’s ‘heli ride’
Later, both leaders also highlighted the use of the provincial government’s helicopter during the long march, calling it a serious violation of an Islamabad High Court order.
It is pertinent to mention that in its 37-page detailed judgment issued on Sept 18, the Islamabad High Court had warned against the use of state machinery during the protest.
The court held that government funds, vehicles, machinery or officials could not be used for any political march towards Islamabad.
اسلام آباد ہائی کورٹ کے واضح احکامات کے باوجود وزیراعلیٰ سہیل آفریدی کا سرکاری ہیلی کاپٹر پر لانگ مارچ کی قیادت کے لیے گنڈی چوک، لکی مروت پہنچنا توہینِ عدالت اور عدالتی احکامات کی کھلی خلاف ورزی ہے جب وزیرِاعلیٰ خود عدالت کے احکامات کی پاسداری نہیں کریں گے، سرکاری وسائل کو سیاسی… pic.twitter.com/jGDKYf58jk
In a post on X, Kundi said that despite the clear orders of the Islamabad High Court, CM Afridi’s arrival at Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat by official helicopter to lead the long march constituted contempt of court and a blatant violation of judicial directives.
“When the chief minister himself does not uphold the court’s orders and uses state resources for political activities, what expectation can there be for his workers to abide by the law?” he said.
Naqvi expressed similar sentiments in a post on X, while commenting on the chief minister’s use of the official helicopter, sarcastically suggesting that the journey may have been undertaken for official duties.
Sohail Afridi Sahib’s Heli ride today from Peshawar to Lakki Marwat must have been for official work, possibly related to the security situation and counterterrorism efforts. pic.twitter.com/Lkfnox0otg
“Sohail Afridi Sahib’s heli ride today from Peshawar to Lakki Marwat must have been for official work, possibly related to the security situation and counterterrorism efforts,” he wrote.
Kundi warns emergency may be imposed if needed to 'save province'
Earlier, Kundi warned that an emergency could be imposed if necessary to “save the province”, as the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) began its planned long march after talks with the federal government ended in deadlock.
The PTI had earlier postponed its planned long march to Islamabad from September 27 to October 4, with Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi announcing the revised date on September 25. CM Afridi had said the decision to defer the march was part of the party’s “political strategy” and that negotiations with the federal government would continue even after the mobilisation.
“If imposing emergency becomes necessary to save the province, then we will certainly impose it,” Kundi said while speaking to the media today.
He said the president, prime minister and other institutions could consider imposing an emergency if they believed the situation in the province had deteriorated.
Kundi also issued a warning to those taking part in the march, saying, “If an emergency is imposed, I alone will be enough for them.” He claimed PTI workers were currently “hiding and getting themselves arrested”.
“I do not make threats like them. When the field is set, I will deal with them,” Kundi said.
Read: CM Afridi lays out K-P long march schedule amid govt-PTI deadlock in talks
Questioning the scale of the PTI protest, he asked, “What long march? Is anything happening in Peshawar? Have you seen any banners?”
The governor said he had so far seen only “self-staged arrests and people going into hiding” during the long march.
“Let them cross Swabi first. It may take a month, but it will not happen,” Kundi said.
His remarks came after two rounds of government-opposition talks failed to resolve differences over PTI’s planned march to Islamabad. The talks, chaired by National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq, ended in the early hours of Sunday without an agreement.
The opposition had insisted on meeting PTI founder Imran Khan before calling off the march, while disagreements also remained over his access to personal doctors and the federal government’s proposed approach to counter-terrorism in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
PTI leaders subsequently said the march would proceed as planned. CM Afridi announced that its first phase would begin from Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat on Sunday, with caravans from several southern districts joining the procession.

title: Asian Games set to close after records  rancour and rain
description: China top the medal table with 169 golds  while hosts Japan finish second with 83
content:
China top the medal table with 169 golds, while hosts Japan finish second with 83
The Asian Games in Japan will close later Sunday after a fortnight of record-smashing displays from young stars, but marred by mix-ups, patchy crowds and accusations of mismanagement.
More than 17,000 athletes and officials, a bigger number than the Olympics, descended on Nagoya and Aichi prefecture for the continent's premier sporting spectacular.
Chinese swimming sensation Yu Zidi, just 13, stole the show in the pool with three gold medals, all in Games-record times.
She looks set to be a major medal threat at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.
The schoolgirl was named a Games MVP on Sunday to cap an extraordinary showing that saw her scorch to gold in the 200m butterfly and do the 200m-400m individual medley double.
But for that all that, the shy teenager said: "I don't think I am what people describe as a prodigy."
Also in the pool, Japanese swimmer Shin Ohashi, himself only 17, smashed the men's 200m breaststroke world record to delight the home crowd.
In athletics, where rain tumbled down over several days, Thai sprinter Puripol Boonson did the 100m-200m double and was named men's MVP.
"This time there were a lot of global athletes at this event, so the MVP gives me a lot of confidence that I can make the podium in LA," the 20-year-old said.
With the hours ticking down to the closing ceremony, when Japan will hand over the baton to Doha, top officials were on the defensive.
Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain Al-Musallam said "numbers are facts", pointing to 50 world records broken at the Games since they opened on September 19.
"The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation," he said.
This 20th edition of the Games, which were first contested in 1951, did not have a traditional athletes' village in a bid to save money.
Instead, participants were housed in wooden temporary units, on a cruise ship and in hotels.
Organisers said this was a template for future multi-sports events.
But it came with issues, with some teams complaining the units were too cramped and the beds too short.
More than that, the ballooning numbers of athletes and officials meant there were not enough beds for everyone.
One Thai Olympic official told AFP it was "like musical chairs".
The sport, including a blockbuster cricket final won by India against arch-rivals Pakistan, did sometimes shine through.
North Korean weightlifter Ri Song Gum, a 140cm (4ft 7in) pocket powerhouse, set three new world marks in one day for gold.
But problems kept coming too, including organisers playing North Korea's national anthem for the South Korean hockey team.
There were athletes' buses that did not turn up when they should, or did not arrive at all.
Two teams were sent to the wrong venue, delaying a volleyball match.
"If I were to give them a grade, it would be an F," Ryu Seung-min, president of the Korean Sport and Olympic Committee, said.
Games organisers were on the back foot as well over attendances, with the opening ceremony taking place in front of thousands of empty seats.
At the women's football semi-final between hosts Japan and South Korea there were 998 spectators in a 50,000 stadium.
Japanese Olympic Committee president Seiko Hashimoto admitted that "there were many problems", but said the country wants to host more international events in future.
She said bad weather had turned some spectators off, but was eager to point out that some sports were well attended.
About 30,000 saw South Korea beat Japan 1-0 to clinch men's football gold, although the occasion was tarnished somewhat when the South Korean flag failed to go up in the victory ceremony.
The hosts finished with 83 golds, a distant second in the medals table behind China with 169.
Japan's tally included gold for Yuki Kurihara, who won an eSports competition aged 11, believed to make him the youngest Games champion in history.
Several sports with ambitions of making the Olympics made their debut, including padel, MMA and virtual taekwondo.

Nissanka’s travel hinges on medical clearance as 16-member squad prepares to face Pakistan and England
Sri Lanka have named a 16-member squad led by Kusal Mendis for the one-day international tri-series in Pakistan beginning on October 18, with opening batsman Pathum Nissanka’s travel subject to medical clearance.
The tournament, which also features England, forms part of Sri Lanka’s preparations for the 2027 World Cup as they look to settle their core combination.
Nissanka was included in the squad announced by Sri Lanka Cricket’s selection committee but will travel with the team only if declared medically fit.
Sri Lanka will switch to the 50-over format after a three-match Twenty20 international series against hosts Pakistan.
The squad combines experienced internationals with emerging players, with Avishka Fernando, Kamil Mishara and Pavan Rathnayake among the top-order options alongside Mendis and Nissanka.
Sahan Arachchige, Kamindu Mendis and Janith Liyanage offer middle-order choices, while former captain Dasun Shanaka and spin-bowling all-rounder Dunith Wellalage provide additional balance.
Maheesh Theekshana and wrist-spinner Sachindu Colombage feature in the spin attack alongside Wellalage.
Dushmantha Chameera, Asitha Fernando, Dilshan Madushanka and Eshan Malinga make up the pace contingent.

title: Israeli media says attempt to assassinate senior Hamas figure likely failed in Gaza
description: Israeli broadcaster describes al Amoudi as Hamas  de facto leader in Gaza
content:
Israeli broadcaster describes al-Amoudi as Hamas' de facto leader in Gaza
Israeli assessments indicated that an attempt to assassinate senior Hamas figure Ali al-Amoudi in an airstrike on Gaza City likely failed, Israeli Army Radio said Saturday evening.
"Assessments are leaning toward the failure of the attempt to assassinate Ali al-Amoudi, a prominent leader in Hamas' political wing in Gaza, last night," according to the radio.
Israel's Channel 12 said it was too early to reach a definitive conclusion but Israel was struggling to obtain confirmation that the assassination attempt had succeeded despite the hours that had elapsed.
Earlier Saturday, Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported that the Israeli army had attempted to kill al-Amoudi in a strike overnight Friday into Saturday. It described him as Hamas' de facto leader in Gaza and a leading candidate to formally head the movement in the territory in anticipated secret internal elections.
Read: Hamas commander killed in Israeli strike
The broadcaster said reports from Gaza indicated that five people had been killed but al-Amoudi's name was absent from the list of fatalities. His fate remained unclear.
Hamas sources told Anadolu that al-Amoudi headed the movement's media department and was a member of its political bureau before the war began on October 8, 2023.
Following the killings of Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar and his deputy Rawhi Mushtaha in 2024, al-Amoudi became deputy to Khalil al-Hayya, who was then heading the movement in Gaza, the sources said.
After al-Hayya was elected head of Hamas' political bureau in July 2026, al-Amoudi assumed responsibility for running the movement in Gaza as acting leader pending the election of a successor, they added.
Five Palestinians, including four women, two of them Christians, were killed and six others injured early Saturday in an Israeli airstrike on a residential apartment in western Gaza City, according to a medical source.
The source identified those killed as Maysa Abu Daoud, 55, her daughter Maria Abu Daoud, 36, Yasmin al-Boubou, 48, Halloum al-Boubou, 23, and Bilal Ali Ouda, 20.

The strike came amid continuing Israeli violations of the ceasefire agreement in effect since October 10, 2025.
Gaza's Health Ministry said Israeli violations had killed 1,439 Palestinians and injured 5,052 others as of Thursday.
According to Palestinian figures, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 in Gaza since October 8, 2023, while around 90% of the territory's infrastructure has been destroyed.

title: Gill flags India   s flaws despite series win
description: Captain calls for clearer death bowling plans and sharper fielding as time runs short to settle World Cup combination
content:
Captain calls for clearer death-bowling plans and sharper fielding as time runs short to settle World Cup combination
India captain Shubman Gill urged his team to improve their death bowling and fielding ahead of the 2027 World Cup after a record run-chase by West Indies took the gloss off a 2-1 one-day international series victory.
Shai Hope’s unbeaten 162 powered the visitors to victory in the third ODI in Mullanpur, where Gill questioned India’s bowling plans in the closing overs and rued missed chances in the field.
“I feel sometimes we are not really clear whether we are attacking or we are defending, especially while bowling during death overs,” Gill said.
While reasonably pleased with India’s progress, Gill said dropped catches had disrupted the team’s momentum and made the bowlers’ task harder on a surface offering little assistance.
“We dropped around 3-4 catches, which breaks the momentum of the team,” he said.
“Fielding hasn’t been up to the mark, we were sloppy on the field, these are the areas we need to get better leading to the World Cup.”
India tested their squad depth throughout the batting-friendly series but were unable to field their preferred combination, with Jasprit Bumrah on Asian Games duty and all-rounder Hardik Pandya still recovering from injury.
Mohammed Siraj played only one of the three matches, leaving India heavily reliant on their reserve bowling options.
Gill said there was little time left to experiment before the World Cup and hoped to have his preferred line-up available for India’s next assignment.
“Hopefully the combination that we want to play (for the World Cup) is available for the next series,” he said.
Debutant Anshul Kamboj, Gurnoor Brar and off-spinner Naman Dhir handled the final 10 overs in Mullanpur as India assessed their options under pressure.
Gill identified Kamboj and Auqib Nabi as candidates for the number eight position, stressing the need for a bowler who could also contribute with the bat.
“We don’t know who will be fit at the World Cup, we wanted someone who can bowl and bat a bit at 8, Anshul can do the job even Auqib (Nabi) can do the job,” he said.
“We wanted to see which players can deliver under pressure and if they can get some experience.”
Ravindra Jadeja was rested to give other players opportunities, with Gill saying the choice of all-rounders would depend on how their skills suited South African conditions.
“Keeping the World Cup and its conditions in mind, whoever offers the most value with their skillsets will make the squad,” he said. India’s next ODI assignment is a five-match series against New Zealand.

title: Sabalenka swept out of China Open in third round

content:
Bartunkova stuns the second seed 6-4, 6-3 to reach the last 16
Aryna Sabalenka was swatted aside in straight sets by 34th-ranked Nikola Bartunkova in the third round of the China Open on Sunday, leaving the event without its top two seeds.
Czech player Bartunkova, 20, sent down four aces to beat the former world number one 6-4, 6-3 in one hour and 35 minutes.
"I focused on myself, to be calm," Bartunkova said.
"She's a legend... so I'm really happy that I won the match," she said of the four-time Grand Slam champion.
Bartunkova next faces Austria's Sinja Kraus in the round of 16.
Second-seeded Sabalenka squandered five chances to break serve in the sixth game of the first set, with Bartunkova strong on defence and firing deep.
The 28-year-old from Belarus threw on a cap for the eighth game of the first set as the women switched between playing in the shade and the sun, but it did not turn the tide in her favour.
A frustrated Sabalenka tossed her racquet at a break down in the fourth game of the second set, and lost on the first match point when she returned into the net.
Top seed Elena Rybakina -- who weeks earlier replaced Sabalenka as World No. 1 -- was ousted by Alina Charaeva in the second round on Saturday.
Top seed Alexander Zverev was scheduled to play Novak Djokovic later on Sunday in the quarterfinals of the men's 500-level event also taking place.
The 39-year-old Serbian great enters the match with an extraordinary unbeaten streak in Beijing, but Zverev -- last month's US Open champion -- is in the running for the top men's ranking.

title: When marriage was the only plan
description: A classic gets a radical makeover  but the lead character finds a woman whose predicament feels surprisingly familiar
content:
A classic gets a radical makeover, but the lead character finds a woman whose predicament feels surprisingly familiar
There is something disconcerting about watching a 19th-century woman dream of a career rather than a husband. Not because the idea is particularly radical today, but because The Doll keeps reminding us how radical it once was — and how little some of the underlying circumstances have changed.
Netflix’s Polish adaptation of Bolesław Prus’s classic novel has arrived with all the ingredients of a prestige period drama: magnificent costumes, sumptuous interiors, grand ballrooms, complicated romances, social hierarchies and enough money visibly spent on every frame to make 1878 Warsaw look like a place one might actually want to visit on a time-machine trip.
But The Doll, directed by Paweł Maślona, is not really interested in offering us a comfortable historical getaway. Beneath all that velvet, crystal, Victorian showpieces with figurines and roses, and beautifully restored architecture is a rather less decorative story about money, marriage, class and what happens to women who want a life that does not fit neatly into the role assigned to them. That may also explain why the series has proved so contentious in Poland.
Prus’s novel, originally published in the 1880s, is not simply another period classic there. It is required school reading and part of the country’s literary and cultural identity. Netflix’s decision to give it a distinctly contemporary treatment therefore amounted to more than an adaptation. And when that happened, it sparked a conversation across polish society about who owns a classic — the author, the teachers who have taught it, generations of readers, or the filmmakers attempting to make it speak to a new audience.
Maślona certainly does not approach the text reverentially. The characters speak contemporary language, including profanity that would have been unthinkable in a traditional screen version. Some of the liberties are even more startling. Stanisław Wokulski and Rzecki are shown snorting cocaine, among other departures from the familiar literary world. Netflix’s social-media campaign was equally determined to drag Prus into the present, describing relationships in the language of the internet, with references to such things as “daddy issues” and “toy boy!”
For admirers of the novel, this was not modernisation but sacrilege. For others, it was precisely the point: a classic survives by being reinterpreted rather than embalmed. The debate continues.
The result is a series that has clearly touched a nerve. It reportedly entered the top ten most-watched lists in 41 countries, while in Poland the arguments around it became sufficiently heated for Prime Minister Donald Tusk to appeal publicly for calm. Yet the most interesting modernisation is not the profanity, the cocaine or the marketing.
It is Izabela Łęcka, the lead character. Played by Sandra Drzymalska (a highly acclaimed Polish actress known for her prominent roles in international cinema) with an almost unnerving restraint, Izabela is beautiful, aristocratic and accustomed to privilege. But she is also considerably more purposeful than the decorative society woman one might expect from the setting. She does not particularly want a husband. She wants a life.
She dreams of travelling to Paris and writing about what she sees for a local, proto-feminist magazine. She watches women around her being dismissed and belittled and appears unwilling to accept that this should simply be their fate. She rejects suitors, sometimes quite mercilessly, and has little patience for the expectation that her future should consist of selecting the least objectionable man from a queue. There is a practical problem with all this. She is a woman. And, more importantly, she is a woman whose family finances are collapsing.
Her father, Tomasz Łęcki, has placed a considerable amount of money in a mysterious business venture while already carrying substantial debt. When the arrangement fails, the consequences are not merely financial. Izabela's carefully imagined future begins to disappear with it. And suddenly the question becomes much larger than whether a young aristocrat should marry.
What happens to a woman when the society she belongs to has given her no other viable way of surviving? This is where The Doll unexpectedly brought to mind My Brilliant Career, based on a 1901 semi-autobiographical novel heavily inspired by the real life and mindset of Miles Franklin, its teenage author. The two stories belong to very different countries, periods and social worlds, yet both give us young women who look at marriage and think: surely there has to be something else.
There is something particularly revealing about seeing the same problem emerge in such different cultures. We often imagine the enforced marriage of women as a particularly South Asian or Eastern phenomenon, something that belongs to societies where daughters are still expected to be married off rather than encouraged to become economically independent. The Doll is a reminder that this was hardly a problem confined to our part of the world.
Women in the West were being channelled into marriage too, and not so very long ago. The difference between being born a son and being born a daughter could determine whether a child grew up with the expectation of supporting a family or with the expectation that somebody else would eventually support her.
That is one of the harsher truths beneath the beautiful surfaces of The Doll. Izabela may live in a grand mansion and wear exquisite clothes, but privilege does not automatically translate into independence. A woman can have education, intelligence, opinions and ambition and still find herself without the financial machinery to turn any of those things into a life. A son could be an heir. A daughter could be an expense. A son could be expected to earn. A daughter could be expected to marry. Unfortunately, if the marriage failed to materialise — or if she refused it — the family could be left wondering what exactly she was going to do with herself.
The cruelty of that arrangement becomes particularly stark when one thinks of the phrase “support the family”. We have traditionally imagined this as something sons do for parents while daughters are married into another household. But what happens when a daughter is perfectly capable of contributing? What happens when she can write, work, run a business, teach, create or earn — but the social order has decided that these are not respectable ambitions for her? That is the real anachronism The Doll exposes.
Not that women in 19th-century Warsaw spoke like people on Netflix today. That they were expected to live as though economic independence were an inappropriate ambition. Izabela is therefore more interesting than the argument over whether she is faithful to Prus's original characterisation.
Traditionally, she has been read as cold, superficial and self-absorbed: a beautiful aristocrat who looks down upon others. The series gives her considerably more interior life. This has pleased some modern critics and irritated others who believe the adaptation has distorted Prus's intentions.
What is undeniable is that Drzymalska makes Izabela difficult to ignore or forget. She does not play her as a cheerful feminist heroine transplanted from the 21st century. There is very little sweetness about her. Izabela is calculating, proud and often severe. She can be blunt to the point of cruelty. She does not soften herself to make her ambitions palatable. Her face is frequently unreadable, and when emotion finally breaks through, the effect is all the stronger.
Drzymalska's best work is done in these silences. A suppressed reaction, a flicker of vulnerability, the moment when composure gives way — these become more eloquent than dialogue. Sometimes, her incredibly beautiful smile says it all.
Around her, the series assembles an entire society struggling with its own contradictions.
The mini-series also offers romance, obsession, revenge, business intrigue and the divide between the aristocracy and those who serve it. The servants are not simply background furniture in the magnificent houses. Some are given lives and personalities of their own, allowing the series to move beyond the drawing rooms and remind us that those who kept those drawing rooms functioning were humans too.
Much of The Doll was filmed in Poland’s Lower Silesian Voivodeship in the southwest, with the production making use of numerous historic locations across the region to recreate the look and feel of Polish society in the 1870s. . Joanna Macha's sets were painstakingly constructed period interiors. The ballrooms and noble residences have scale without feeling like empty showcases. The production design is extraordinary, capturing both the opulence of the aristocracy and the grimy poverty of the lower classes, making the contrast between their worlds impossible to miss. Because, ultimately, the story is about people trapped by the systems that surround them.
One does feel at times that The Doll tries to tell too many stories at once
Six episodes are asked to accommodate business, class, feminism, romance, revenge, betrayal and social ambition. There is enough material here for a much longer series, and the show occasionally feels as though it is racing to complete an argument just when it has persuaded us to care about the characters. This is perhaps its strangest weakness: The Doll does not overstay its welcome. It leaves rather too soon.
It takes considerable time to establish its world and its people, only to end before we have fully settled into them. Some of the intrigue consequently feels compressed, while some of the relationships could have benefited from more breathing space. Yet the series is difficult to dismiss because of what it leaves behind. The uncomfortable recognition that the distance between Isabela’s world and ours is not always as great as the costumes suggest.
We may have changed enormously in many ways. Women today have vastly greater access to education, employment, property and financial independence in many parts of the world. But the old assumption that a woman's security is fundamentally tied to marriage has hardly vanished everywhere. In different forms and to different degrees, daughters can still be treated as future wives rather than potential earners; careers can still be regarded as secondary to family expectations; and financial dependence can still become a mechanism through which choices are quietly narrowed.
That is why the modernisation of The Doll may be less outrageous than some of its Polish critics fear. Not just the profanity, the social-media slang will date even faster. But a woman asking what she might do with her life when everyone around her has already decided what she should be doing? That question travels remarkably well. Perhaps that is what a classic is supposed to do.
In the 1878 Warsaw that is beautifully reconstructed, the dresses, mansions and ballrooms belong to another world. The predicament does not, and that, more than the controversy surrounding its modern language or its provocative reinterpretations, may be the reason this Polish doll has found an audience far beyond Poland.

title: Gaza residents face another winter amid shelter shortages  dwindling aid
description: Families in southern Gaza appeal for urgent shelter supplies  say they fear repeat of previous winters
content:
Families in southern Gaza appeal for urgent shelter supplies, say they fear repeat of previous winters
Displaced Palestinians in the southern Gaza Strip appealed on Saturday for tents, blankets and basic supplies ahead of winter, warning that shelter shortages and dwindling humanitarian aid could leave thousands exposed to rain, cold and strong winds.
Dozens of displaced residents staged a protest in the Fash Farsh area in Khan Younis, urging international organisations and donors to provide shelter materials, food and essential supplies amid Israel’s blockade.
“Our tents are torn and our stomachs are empty. Do not leave us to the unknown,” read one of the signs by protesters.
Read: 2 Palestinians killed in Israeli strike, gunfire in Gaza despite ceasefire
Families said they fear a repeat of previous winters, when heavy rains flooded and damaged tents, leaving them exposed to harsh weather. Deaths, including of children, were also reported during periods of severe cold and after damaged buildings collapsed.
“We are heading into winter and we need tarpaulins, tents, food and health supplies so we can withstand the heavy rain and winds,” Iyad Zomor told Anadolu .
Iyad Al-Shaer said many tents offered little protection from cold, rain or wind, urging humanitarian organisations to provide shelter materials before weather conditions worsen.
Read More: Hamas commander killed in Israeli strike
Ahmed Hassan Al-Najjar, who oversees Fash Farsh, told Anadolu that 35 displacement camps there shelter 6,000 families, or about 40,000 people. He said residents were facing shortages of tents, tarpaulins, food parcels and medical supplies and called for urgent assistance.
Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 in Gaza since October 2023, while 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed, according to Palestinian figures.

title: World records prove Asian Games were a hit  says top official
description: Al Musallam highlights a haul of world records amid criticism over Games organisation
content:
Al-Musallam highlights a haul of world records amid criticism over Games organisation
An Asian Olympic chief said Sunday that more than 50 world records at the Games in Japan proved the event was a success, despite numerous complaints from disgruntled teams.
The Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya saw a catalogue of mishaps, from athletes bussed to the wrong venues to the North Korean national anthem played for the South Korean hockey team.
There were not enough beds for the over 17,000 athletes and officials, a bigger number than the Olympics.
Countries also complained of being stranded for up to six hours at the airport on arrival.
The Games produced some elite performances, although sometimes in front of rows of empty seats.
World records were broken in sports including swimming, shooting and weightlifting.
Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain Al-Musallam said "numbers are facts" as he launched an impassioned defence of the Games ahead of the closing ceremony.
"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said.
"The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation.
"We are here to present to you the evidence," he added.
To save money there was no athletes' village at the Games, organisers instead putting competitors in hotels, temporary wooden huts and on a cruise ship.
Some teams complained about the quality of the accommodation, including that the beds were too short in the huts.
Al-Musallam said the accommodation was "very well received by the athletes" and provided a sustainable model for future Games.
"We are happy to see that there is no financial burden for the organising committee and there is no white elephant staying in Nagoya," he said.

title: A life in resistance
description: Mahnaz Rahman   s memoir traces a journey from Partition and family upheaval to political activism  exile and a lifelong commitment to the rights of the marginalised
content:
Mahnaz Rahman’s memoir traces a journey from Partition and family upheaval to political activism
Some lives are lived alongside history, others seem to absorb it. In Love, Life and the Left, Mahnaz Rahman tells the story of a life shaped by some of the defining upheavals of the subcontinent — Partition, migration, class inequality, political repression and the struggle for women’s rights. Overarchingly it also makes the case for something increasingly difficult to sustain in an age of political disillusionment: the possibility of resistance.
The memoir begins before Rahman’s own birth, with her mother Dilafroze, who was 17 when she was displaced from Amritsar during Partition. In Karachi, she rebuilt her life with her mother and sister and met Zain, a young migrant from Delhi. Their relationship eventually led to the birth of Mahnaz in 1949. From this beginning, the personal and the political are intertwined. The traumas of displacement, the complications of family and the inequalities of the new society into which Rahman was born become part of the circumstances that shaped her worldview.
The interweaving of private history and public events are at the heart of Love, Life and the Left. The story follows the evolution of an individual consciousness as Rahman becomes increasingly uncomfortable with privilege and capitalism, eventually rejecting what she describes as a comfortable bourgeois life. She elopes with a radical journalist, joins the Communist Party of Pakistan and begins a life in which political conviction is not an abstract intellectual position but something that determines where she lives, whom she associates with and how she understands the world around her.
That trajectory gives the memoir its unusual scope. Rahman writes of resistance to the Zia dictatorship, exile in China and campaigns for the rights of women and minorities in Pakistan. Her story consequently becomes a record of several generations of political idealism and disappointment, but also of the persistence of people who continued to believe that society could be transformed.
Farhatullah Babar describes the memoir as more than a personal account, pointing to its larger journey through Pakistan’s political history and what he sees as the decline of resistance in the country’s politics, media and society. Shah Mohammad Marri, meanwhile, emphasises the idea of human resilience, describing Rahman’s life as one in which Marxist conviction and a commitment to the oppressed become central to her identity.
Sheema Kermani places the emphasis somewhere slightly different. For her, Rahman’s story belongs not only to the author but to a generation that “lived and dreamt” of a revolution that would create equality and justice. That observation is important because it suggests that the memoir’s interest lies beyond the biography of one political activist. Rahman’s experiences offer a window into the aspirations of people who came of age believing that political organisation and collective action could fundamentally alter society.
There is also something poignant in the tension between that idealism and the political landscape the memoir describes. The book travels through decades in which the Pakistani Left faced repression, fragmentation and changing political circumstances. Yet Rahman’s story, as presented here, does not appear to be structured simply as an elegy for a failed political project. Its title itself suggests three strands that are inseparable: the intimate life of the individual, the experience of living through history, and the political commitments that give that life meaning.
Ammar Ali Jan’s endorsement draws attention to another revealing dimension of the memoir: Rahman’s continuing attachment to Mao Zedong’s dictum, “It is right to rebel”. Whether one shares that political tradition or not, the quotation helps illuminate the principle running through the life described in the book. Rebellion here is not presented merely as youthful defiance. It becomes an ethical position — a refusal to accept inequality, authoritarianism or injustice simply because they have become entrenched.
This makes the memoir valuable as a historical document as much as a personal one. The conventional political history of Pakistan is often told through governments, military regimes, political parties and major events. Memoirs can complicate that version of history by showing how those events were experienced by people outside the corridors of power. Through Rahman’s family, relationships, political commitments and activism, the large events of the country’s history acquire a human scale. The story of a family remaking itself after Partition becomes part of a longer history of belonging, alienation and the making of Pakistan.
There is also a striking irony in the fact that Rahman’s life begins in the aftermath of one enormous rupture and subsequently becomes entangled with so many others. The rise of authoritarianism, exile and the continuing struggle over women’s and minority rights all become stages in a life that refuses to separate personal experience from political responsibility.
That is perhaps why the book’s strongest appeal may not be limited to readers who share Rahman’s politics. Love, Life and the Left offers an opportunity to understand why someone might reject comfort in favour of activism, why political ideals can survive periods of defeat, and what it means to carry those ideals through an entire lifetime.
The memoir also raises questions that remain relevant. What happens to political idealism when the revolution does not arrive? How does a person sustain faith in collective action after witnessing repression and political failure? And what does resistance mean when the movements that once seemed capable of transforming society have themselves become part of history? Those questions give Love, Life and the Left a resonance beyond its specific political moment.
The memoir’s achievement, judging from its framing and the breadth of its subject, lies in bringing together the intimate and the historical. It begins with a young woman displaced by Partition and follows the life of the daughter born from the new relationships and circumstances created by that displacement. From there it moves into political activism, love, marriage, ideology, repression, exile and campaigns for social justice. The result is not merely a chronicle of the Left in Pakistan, but a portrait of one person’s attempt to live according to her political beliefs.
In an age when political idealism can easily appear naïve and resistance can seem futile, there is something worth examining in a life that persisted in both. Love, Life and the Left asks its readers to look at Pakistan not only through the history of those who governed it, but through the lives of those who challenged the structures around them. And ultimately, it seems to ask a more personal question: what does it mean to remain committed to an idea of justice when history repeatedly gives you reasons to give up?

title: Fernandes hails Portugal s  greatest symbol  Ronaldo
description: The situation has cast uncertainty over Ronaldo   s future with the national team
content:
The situation has cast uncertainty over Ronaldo’s future with the national team
Portugal playmaker Bruno Fernandes said Cristiano Ronaldo remains the country's greatest footballing icon despite walking out on the squad this week after finding out he would not start a match.
The 41-year-old superstar said Wednesday he had left the team after coach Jorge Jesus said Ronaldo would not start against Denmark in the Nations League, a match Portugal won 4-2 without him.
Former Real Madrid and Manchester United attacker Ronaldo's future with the national team, for whom he is the leading goalscorer and most capped player, is in doubt after his walk out.
"Regarding Cristiano, I had a conversation with him, and what I told him, and what I repeat here, is this -- the most important thing is that, regardless of what happens, Cristiano Ronaldo will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team, of our football, and of the country, for what he has done not only in Portugal but throughout the world," Fernandes told reporters Saturday.
Manchester United midfielder Fernandes called for unity after a tumultuous few days in which Portugal fans' opinions have been split over Ronaldo's decision.
"He has a reserved place not only among the best of all time, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people, and the most important thing is that we stop dividing things," said Fernandes.
"There are no divisions in the national team, it is one and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside...
"We are outside of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country does not divide itself, does not make choices, that it respects all sides, but, at the same time, Cris is and will be the biggest icon of our national team, he deserves everyone's respect, regardless of who likes him more or (who likes him) less."
Portugal beat Norway and Denmark away from home without Ronaldo starting and face Norway again on Sunday.
Coach Jesus said Ronaldo was a "symbol of Portugal" and said there would be time to speak about him after Sunday's game in Porto.
"I'm going to focus on the team, on the opponent which is Norway, one of the five best teams in Europe. That's the problem right now," said the 72-year-old coach.

title: The Songs That Went Away
description: What happened to our bilingual music and artistic industry
content:
What happened to our bilingual music and artistic industry
A question Professor Dr Rukhsana A Siddiqui asked me, some time ago, has stayed with me. Did the loss of East Pakistan cost Pakistan something specific in its musical and artistic life, not in a vague, sentimental sense, but in documentable, traceable ways?
Let me state plainly, at the outset, it is not an argument that losing East Pakistan is the reason Pakistani music declined. That claim doesn't survive contact with the historical record. The single explanation most historians and musicians themselves point to for the institutional marginalisation of music during 1977–88, the shrinking of concert space, a wave of classical performers relocating for work. That is a distinct process, with its own causes, arriving a full six years after Dhaka fell in December 1971. Conflating the two would be intellectually dishonest.
What I can trace, carefully, is narrower and more useful, specific institutions, specific collaborations, specific people who moved between Dhaka, Karachi, and Lahore in a single, functioning cultural market before 1971, and what happened to those particular threads when the country split. That's the response Dr Siddiqui's question deserves.
Pakistan's split from what became Bangladesh followed a period of intense political crisis between the country's two wings. The human cost remains genuinely disputed to this day, and I won't adjudicate that dispute here, it isn't this essay's subject. What concerns us is narrower, the cultural and musical infrastructure that existed before that rupture, and what specifically became unreachable after it.
Before 1971, East Pakistan had its own film industry, built with state investment. The East Pakistan Film Development Corporation– established in 1957, gave Dhaka a studio and processing infrastructure that filmmakers had previously needed Kolkata or Lahore to access. Between 1956 and 1971, that infrastructure produced roughly 154 Bengali and 53 Urdu-language feature films– a genuine, functioning bilingual cinema, not a token gesture.
Its finest hour is a film most Pakistanis today have never heard of ‘Jago Hua Savera’ (1959). Shot entirely in a fishing village near Dhaka, it was scripted by Faiz Ahmed Faiz, directed by A.J. Kardar, and became Pakistan's first-ever submission for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. It won a prize at the Moscow International Film Festival, was screened at institutions from the Flaherty Foundation to the University of Southern California, and stands today, by the assessment of international film critics and archivists, among the finest works of neorealist cinema produced anywhere in South Asia. It was, in the fullest sense, a joint achievement: West Pakistani poet, West Pakistani director, East Pakistani setting, cast, and crew, East Pakistani production infrastructure. That particular kind of film, Urdu-scripted, Dhaka-produced, internationally minded, simply cannot exist again in its original form, because the single country that made it possible no longer exists.
Commercially, the same infrastructure produced films like Chakori (1967), released simultaneously in Urdu and Bengali "double versions" for audiences on both sides of the country– evidence of a real, functioning, cross-lingual audience and distribution network, not a hypothetical one.
If you want a single human thread that shows exactly what this bridge looked like in practice, follow the career of Robin Ghosh. Born in Baghdad to a Bengali Hindu father and an Arab Catholic mother, raised from age six in Dhaka's Wari neighbourhood, Ghosh started at Radio Pakistan's Dhaka station in the late 1950s, composed his first film score for the Bengali picture Rajdhanir Bookay (1960), and married the actress who would become Shabnam, the most successful leading lady in West Pakistani cinema for two decades. Ghosh followed her west, first to Karachi and then Lahore, and kept composing. His score for Aina (1977), made six years after Bangladesh's independence, became one of the biggest commercial successes in the history of Pakistani cinema, running for roughly 400 weeks in theatres. He won seven Nigar Awards, Pakistan's top film honour, across a career that spanned both countries.
Ghosh's story complicates any simple "we lost it all" narrative in an important way: talent that had already crossed over before the split largely stayed, and kept working, for years afterward. What ended wasn't Bengali musical talent's presence in Pakistani cinema overnight, it was the pipeline that had produced people like Ghosh in the first place, a shared training ground, a shared radio station network, a shared audience spanning both wings of East and West Pakistan, that no longer had a mechanism to keep feeding new talent westward after 1971.
The clearer case of direct loss is Runa Laila. Born in Sylhet in 1952, raised largely in Karachi where her father was posted as a civil servant, she trained in classical music and Kathak from early childhood. Making her film playback debut at 12, by her mid-teens Laila was, by multiple contemporary accounts, second only to Noor Jehan in the affection of Pakistani audiences, performing regularly on PTV, hosting her own show, singing for major Urdu films including Umrao Jaan Ada (1972). In 1974, her family relocated to newly independent Bangladesh. She went on to have a legendary career there and across India, but the specific thing Pakistan lost was concrete and dated; a teenage prodigy, fully formed by its own broadcasting and film institutions, whose subsequent decades of work happened somewhere else.
The premise that East Pakistan's cultural presence simply enriched a receptive, harmonious "one nation" musical fabric doesn't fully hold up. The most documented cultural flashpoint of the pre-1971 period runs in the opposite direction. In 1967, Pakistan's information and broadcasting ministry, under Ayub Khan's government, formally restricted the broadcast of Rabindranath Tagore's songs, Rabindra Sangeet– a cornerstone of Bengali musical and literary identity– on Radio Pakistan and later on the newly launched PTV, on the grounds that Tagore's work carried "Indian" and Hindu cultural associations incompatible with Pakistani ideology. This wasn't a fringe decision; it followed nearly a decade of official unease dating to opposition against Dhaka's plans to mark Tagore's birth centenary in 1961, and it became one of the specific grievances Bengali cultural organisations, including Chhayanaut, founded in 1963 specifically to keep Tagore's music alive in public life, cited in the years leading to the independence movement.
I raise this not to relitigate 1971, but because it changes what the honest answer to Dr Siddiqui's question actually is. Pakistan, as a state, did not simply enjoy unrestricted access to a rich Bengali musical inheritance and then lose it through separation. Part of what it lost, it had already been in the process of pushing away, a state apparatus in Islamabad and Karachi treating an entire musical tradition as ideologically suspect while people like Robin Ghosh and Runa Laila were simultaneously, and genuinely, thriving within the same country's film and broadcast industry. Both things were true at once. That contradiction, official suspicion of Bengali high culture running alongside real commercial and artistic collaboration in cinema and radio is a more honest, and frankly more interesting, story than a simple tale of harmony interrupted.
So, to answer the question as narrowly and defensibly as the evidence allows, Pakistan lost a functioning bilingual film and broadcast market roughly twice the size of what remained, with its own studio infrastructure in Dhaka that West Pakistani productions had begun to draw on. It lost a specific generation-defining talent pipeline, musicians, composers, and playback singers trained in East Pakistani conservatories, liturgical music, and radio stations, several of whom, like Ghosh and Laila, had already proven capable of producing work that topped the charts. It lost the possibility of further Faiz-calibre East-West artistic collaborations of the kind that produced Jago Hua Savera. And it lost, this is worth being honest about, a chance, foreclosed years before the actual war, to fully and officially embrace Bengali music as part of a shared national inheritance rather than treating it as a suspect import.
What it did not lose, in any simple sense, is its own capacity to make music. West Pakistani classical and film music had its own robust, independent lineages, the different gharanas, Roshan Ara Begum, Mehdi Hassan, Noor Jehan, that owed nothing to East Pakistan and continued, largely undisturbed, through the 1970s. The steep institutional decline of concert culture, classical patronage, and public musical life that people rightly associate with Pakistan today has a clearer, better-documented cause sitting six years later on the calendar, Zia's martial law, and the slow retreat of the state from supporting music as a legitimate public art.
The human insight here isn't nostalgia for a lost golden age, it's a lesson about what shared institutions quietly do. A single national broadcaster, a single national film certification and distribution system, a single national conservatory-adjacent training pipeline, does something that no amount of individual goodwill can replace afterward, it forces talent from different corners of a country to keep meeting each other, whether the state fully means to enable that or not. Ghosh didn't move to Lahore because Pakistan had a coherent cultural policy welcoming Bengali composers. He moved because a director in Dhaka happened to hire him, and love and ambition did the rest. The infrastructure created the conditions for the encounter; it didn't guarantee the outcome, and it didn't stop the state from simultaneously banning Tagore on the same airwaves.
The practical action for anyone thinking about Pakistan's musical future now is to stop waiting for a unifying national institution to hand talent a stage, and to build the smaller, unglamorous versions of what EPFDC and Radio Pakistan's Dhaka station once did by accident, cross-city, cross-language training pipelines and distribution networks that don't depend on ideological approval to function.
The better question to ask is: which of the cultural bridges we still have today between provinces, between languages, between forms of music the state considers respectable and the ones it doesn't? Are we currently one step away from losing the way Radio Pakistan lost Tagore, quietly, years before anyone called it a rupture?
I don't have a comfortable answer to that one either. But I leave you with an honest one.
The writer is a music enthusiast and cultural critic. He writes about the intersection of music, society, and the human condition. He can be reached at brian.bassanio@gmail.com

title: Trump names intelligence chief Clayton as AI czar  to head task force  WSJ reports
description: Clayton to lead new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on risks  opportunities of AI
content:
Clayton to lead new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on risks, opportunities of AI
United States President Donald Trump has appointed Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the administration's AI czar, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday, citing an interview with Clayton.
Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said.
"The president asked that a group be put together," which the administration refers to as the "Super Intelligence Force," to ensure the US remains a leader in advanced AI while protecting Americans' interests, Clayton told the Journal, adding that "the risk of not being first is high."
Read: Developing nations call for bigger say in shaping AI future
The safety of AI has become a major issue in recent weeks, with some researchers warning that people building the technology believe it could kill humans within a decade. Several Democratic and Republican lawmakers have responded with alarm and calls for more action .
Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China. He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology.
Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches , hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter.
Read More: Trump tells AI bosses to self-regulate
This is the second time Trump has named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the administration. Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term.
The task force's vice chairs will be Emil Michael, Scott Kupor and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, while members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, according to the report. External advisers will also include Sacks and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, the Journal said.

title: Three commanders among eight terrorists killed in DI Khan operation  security sources
description: A large quantity of weapons  ammunition  foreign currency  recovered from the terrorists
content:
According to sources large quantity of weapons, ammunition, foreign currency, recovered from the terrorists
Eight terrorists belonging to Fitna al-Khawarij , including three key commanders, were killed in an Intelligence-Based Operation (IBO) in Dera Ismail Khan, security sources said on Sunday.
The operation was conducted after security forces received intelligence about the presence of terrorists there, the sources said.
Fitna al - Khawarij is the term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
A large quantity of weapons and ammunition, as well as foreign currency, was recovered from the terrorists killed in the operation, according to the sources.
Security forces had continued effective operations against Fitna al-Khawarij in K-P under the Azm-e-Istehkam vision, the sources said.
They said security forces remained committed to completely eliminating terrorism and establishing lasting peace in the country.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif praised the security forces for their timely and effective action against the terrorists, according to a statement issued by the Prime Minister's Office.
The prime minister paid tribute to the security forces for killing eight Fitna al-Khawarij terrorists in the IBO. He also paid tribute to the bravery and resolve of the security forces personnel involved in the operation.
PM Shehbaz said the entire nation stood alongside the security forces in the war against terrorism.
Read: Security forces kill 11 terrorists in separate Balochistan, K-P operations
The prime minister reiterated his resolve to continue operations against Fitna al-Khawarij until the complete elimination of terrorism.
He said the complete elimination of terrorism was essential for peace and stability in the country.
Pakistan has witnessed a surge in terrorist activity over the past three months, with a series of attacks across the country resulting in the martyrdom of security personnel and civilians.
Last week, 12 people were killed and 35 others injured when a blast struck a joint checkpoint near Aman Mela in the Darazinda area of Dera Ismail Khan, with the TTP claiming responsibility for the attack.
On September 19, 23 people, including 15 police personnel, were martyred in a blast at a mosque in Kohat’s Police Lines during Friday prayers. Eight terrorists were also killed during a subsequent search and clearance operation. Later, the Ittihadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), led by Afghanistan-based Hafiz Gul Bahadur, claimed responsibility for the deadly bombing and rampage involving multiple attackers.
In a separate incident, a captain and a lieutenant were among six security personnel martyred in an exchange of fire in Hangu district, while eight terrorists were killed.
On September 1, six personnel, including two officers, and a customs department official were martyred as security forces thwarted an attempt to breach the Customs House in Balochistan.
Read more : Nine policemen martyred, 28 injured in terror attack on police checkpost in K-P's Hangu
In July, at least 30 people , including 27 police personnel, were martyred when terrorists identified by the state as the Indian proxy Fitna al-Hindustan ambushed police personnel deployed in the Kach Mangi Phase III area of Ziarat, triggering hours-long gun battles. The attackers also abducted several civilians and police personnel after the assault.
In the aftermath of the attack, the Pakistan Army, Frontier Corps and Balochistan Police launched a joint operation , which remains underway, with forces intensifying action against terrorists across the province.
