title: The new social game
description: Inside the rise of Pakistan   s urban mahjong clubs
content:
Inside the rise of Pakistan’s urban mahjong clubs
Before we learned to unwind by retreating into individual screens, relaxation in a Pakistani household was inherently loud, interactive, and gathered around a game board. When family or friends gathered for entertainment, social life came alive to the clatter of plastic dice in a ludo cup, or the sharp slap of playing cards on a coffee table, or the slow, collective tension of a tambola night.
These games weren't just about passing time. They served as a vital social fabric that brought generations together under one roof. They offered a rare offline sanctuary where neighbourhood news was traded, rivalries were stoked, and leisure remained genuinely communal. As urban life grew more fragmented and digital entertainment pulled everyone into isolated, hyper-personalised screens, that familiar routine quietly slipped away.
Now, an unexpected revival is taking shape across Pakistan's major metropolitan centres: a sudden surge of interest in mahjong.
Seeing a four-player traditional Chinese tile game take root in drawing rooms and cafes across Karachi, Lahore, and Islamabad might sound surprising at first. Yet board games have always been nomadic. History is full of pastimes that crossed borders, shed their original geographical boundaries, and found vibrant second lives with entirely new audiences.
Consider chess. Its earliest ancestor, chaturanga, originated in the subcontinent during the sixth century as a strategic war game. As it travelled along ancient trade routes through Persia and the Islamic world into Europe, it was refined, standardised, and eventually institutionalised into a competitive international sport. Today, while chess is celebrated worldwide as the ultimate intellectual test, its deep regional roots are often overshadowed by its modern-day global place.
Mahjong’s global trajectory follows a strikingly similar arc. Emerging in southern China during the mid-19th century as a tile game derived from ancient card traditions, it was imported to the West in the early 1920s by American traders. Promoted through exoticised marketing that falsely tied its origins to ancient royal courts, mahjong exploded into an American cultural phenomenon. Over decades, it adapted to diverse communities, proving that a complex cultural artifact could reshape itself to fit the social needs of entirely different societies.
The catalyst behind its growing traction in the local landscape often comes down to individual passion turning into a community activity. For Madiha Khawar, the founder of Madis Mahjong, her entry into the game was entirely accidental.
Having spent nearly two decades working in the corporate sector, she suddenly found herself at a career transition with an unfamiliar surplus of time. “Mahjong came at a very unexpected point in my life,” Madiha recalls. “I had spent almost 20 years working for a large multinational and then one fine day, I lost my job, and suddenly I started wondering, what am I going to do with all this time?”
A chance Instagram post by a friend seeking four people to form a learning circle led Madiha to take formal classes while living in Dubai. The initial learning curve was steep. “I still remember sitting through my first lesson thinking, am I ever going to understand this game? But very quickly, we became completely hooked. Even after our classes finished, the four of us continued meeting once or twice a week to play.”
As her grasp of the rules improved, Madiha found herself mentoring friends who were hesitant about the game's intricate scoring—particularly in Taiwanese Mahjong. Recognising her natural flair for teaching, a close friend pushed her to formalise her guidance.
Madiha put together a simple promotional flyer and sent it out—leading to a flood of inquiries and her first two study groups forming by the very next morning. What began as an informal venture in Dubai quickly crossed borders when Madiha visited her parents in Lahore. At the time, while sporadic private games existed in cities like Karachi and Islamabad, Lahore lacked a visible learning scene.
“When I started, I personally wasn't aware of an established Taiwanese Mahjong teaching community or club in Lahore, and most of the people who came to me were encountering the game for the first time,” she explains. “In that sense, it felt like I was introducing something very new to the city. I wouldn't want to claim definitively that nobody in Lahore had ever played Mahjong before, but there certainly wasn't the kind of visible Mahjong scene that we're seeing now.”
The demand just kept growing. There were days when I was teaching four or five classes. What surprised me most was the range of people interested in learning,” shared Madiha.
While global players migrate between distinct styles—from the fast-paced Cantonese rules and high-stakes Japanese Riichi to the joker-laden American version—it is Taiwanese Mahjong, with its 16-tile hands and intricate scoring combinations, that has largely captured the imagination of local circles.
To understand why Mahjong is capturing the imagination of Pakistani urbanites requires looking at what modern leisure has lost. In an era where social interactions are increasingly digitised and mediated through mobile screens, mahjong offers a tactile, screen-free engagement that forces complete mental presence.
Unlike casual card games, mahjong demands tactical foresight, memory, and pattern recognition. Yet, unlike chess, it is not an agonisingly solitary calculation. The rhythm of the game naturally builds in pauses. Between rounds, as players wash the tiles—shuffling them face down across a felt-lined table—the mechanical task creates a natural breather. In those moments, intense competition pauses, giving way to casual conversation, tea drinking, and shared laughter.
For players like Anum Kamran, who took up the game recently, the physical ceremony of mahjong is a central part of its draw. “It’s such a departure from anything I’ve ever played or tried before, and the thought of concentrating on something for a few hours that wasn’t a screen was very tempting. I also loved the social element to it.”
While digital adaptations of mahjong exist on mobile apps, players insist that a screen cannot replicate the sensory experience of a live table. There is a distinct satisfaction in feeling the weight of the heavy resin tiles, the smooth cool surface under one's fingertips, and the crisp, resonant clatter as the pieces collide during the shuffle.
Beyond the sensory appeal, learning the game involves immersing oneself in a subtle cultural language. Players pick up foundational Mandarin terminology and cultural rituals—learning to recognise suit characters (Wan, Biao, Tiao), understanding tile arrangements, and mastering traditional calls like Chow (forming a sequence), Pung (forming a triplet), and Kong (a four-of-a-kind). Rituals governing table etiquette, such as seating positions relative to wind directions and tile distribution, add an element of ancient ceremony to the afternoon.
“I love the ceremony and tactile part that come with the game,” Anum notes. “There are some rituals that pertain to Chinese culture, and things like who joined the table last affect where you sit and what tiles you get. It’s also nice to feel the tiles as opposed to playing on an app.”
When asked if the game lives up to its intimidating reputation, Anum clarified: “The objective of the game is simple. It takes a little while to learn to read the rules and know the nuances and scoring.”
In the urban centres where organic opportunities to meet new people outside of school or work are increasingly rare, the four-player table layout became the cause for an accidental social bridge. As individuals signed up solo to learn the game, Madiha acted as a matchmaker, assembling complete four-person tables from individual registrants.
“I didn't realise I was also going to bring people together who might otherwise have never met,” Madiha reflects. “They came together simply because they all wanted to learn Mahjong. Some of those groups have gone on to become genuinely good friends. It's honestly so heart-warming to see the special bond they've created with each other.”
For the love of mahjong her students showed, Madiha began organising mixers at home where they could continue playing after they had graduated from her course.
“When I started hosting the mixers at home, it was mainly for practice purposes and to help guide my students to make them better at their game. I actually loved the idea of keeping them small and giving people that warm, homely feeling.” These gatherings quickly took on a domestic warmth. “My mom would make tea and snacks for everyone and I would just be there in the background watching people play with so much excitement,” Madiha recalls. “I created a special bond with everyone who came to my mixers. The classes were where I taught Mahjong but the mixers were where I really got to watch the community come alive.”
For the women participating, these weekly games have evolved into essential therapeutic spaces. “Learning and playing mahjong has been such a healing experience,” says Anum. “I learnt with a friend of mine and got introduced to two fabulous ladies. Now we play every Sunday and rotate hosting. It’s the best way to spend an afternoon without phones. We giggle, play, lightly roast each other, share our distresses within the safe comforting corners of the mahjong table. It’s the highlight of my week.”
Anum points out a poetic detail within the scoring terminology of the game itself. “As part of the scoring in mahjong, there are ‘brother’ and ‘sister’ sets,” she notes, referring to paired sequence tiles. “It’s a nice parallel, because through this experience I really found sisterhood.”
Through mahjong what is happening across drawing rooms and emerging clubs is less about importing an exotic trend and more about reclaiming an old habit. Pakistani urban life has long suffered from a shortage of spaces outside of home and work where people can gather without the pressure of commercial dining or the distraction of entertainment venues. In clicking resin tiles together over tea, players are reconstructing that missing social gap. Mahjong has simply provided the modern blueprint: a game intricate enough to keep the mind sharp, structured enough to hold focus, and tactile enough to keep our hands off our phones—if only for a few hours on a Sunday afternoon.

title: Chaotic  Asian Games threaten Japan hopes of hosting Olympics again
description: Mishaps ranging from wrong venues to anthem mix ups have drawn criticism from participating teams
content:
Mishaps ranging from wrong venues to anthem mix-ups have drawn criticism from participating teams
Japan is traditionally seen as a reliable host for major sporting events but an Asian Games dogged by organisational woes has tarnished that image and raised questions over future bids, experts say.
The Games in Aichi-Nagoya saw a catalogue of mishaps, from athletes bussed to the wrong venues to the North Korean national anthem played for the South Korean hockey team.
There were not enough beds for the over 17,000 athletes and officials, a bigger number than the Olympics.
Countries complained of being stranded for up to six hours at the airport on arrival.
Teams were not shy in criticising the local organisers.
Ryu Seung-min, president of the Korean Sport and Olympic Committee, said: "If I were to give them a grade, it would be an F."
Japanese Olympic Committee (JOC) president Seiko Hashimoto admitted that "there were many problems", but said the country wants to host more international events.
Hirokazu Arai, a professor specialising in sports psychology, told AFP that Japan may struggle to escape the shadow of the Asian Games for some time to come.
"If Japan were to bid for the Olympics again, trust in Japan may have fallen and it might be harder to win a bid," he said.
"And within Japan, people may take the view that if these kinds of things are going to happen, we don't need the Olympics."
Many in Japan have questioned the value of hosting major sporting events as they grapple with the fallout from the graft-stained and pandemic-delayed Tokyo Olympics.
Cost overruns, corruption and Covid all tainted the public's memory of the Games, which took place largely behind closed doors in 2021, a year later than planned.
Japan was praised by some, however, for getting the Games on in unprecedented circumstances.
The country subsequently dropped the idea of hosting the Winter Olympics in the northern city of Sapporo because of a lack of public support.
Hashimoto, who also served as president of the Tokyo Olympics organising committee, has said Sapporo's bid could be revived.
She said the Asian Games had "reaffirmed my belief in the value of hosting international sporting events in our country".
"We also received harsh criticism because of the challenges we faced -- I am fully aware of that," she said.
"This is all part of the Games, but we need to analyse those issues so we can tackle them for the next future opportunity."
Asian Games organisers were presented with a headache when the number of athletes and officials that was initially expected ballooned by about 2,000.
Unlike at past Games, there was no traditional athletes' village in a bid to save money.
Participants instead stayed on a cruise ship, in hotel rooms and in temporary wooden huts.
Some teams complained about the wooden units, saying they were too cramped and the beds too short.
After a troubled build-up, organisers hoped the attention would switch to sport when the action got under way.
But still the problems continued, with transport and accommodation difficulties and further mix-ups with anthems and flags.
"It's like musical chairs," a Thai official said, adding that organisation at the Games had been "chaotic".
Nagoya's mayor apologised to athletes for "inconveniences", saying organisers would "sincerely reflect on the mishandling that occurred".
There were sparse crowds at some events, starting with thousands of empty seats at the opening ceremony.
Arai believes the Games have damaged Japan's international reputation as a safe pair of hands.
"The previous Games were in China, and I'm sure there were athletes who came here expecting Japan to put on a better event than China," he said.
"But I don't think you can say that's how it's turned out."
Arai says anger that had faded in the years since the Tokyo Olympics could flare up again.
"The people at the top of Japan's sporting world are moving towards trying to bring the Olympics here again," he said.
"From their perspective, they may have felt that criticism had started to die down, but this situation could cause that criticism to intensify again."

title: Making time to move
description: With work and commutes keeping people seated  staying active increasingly means finding deliberate ways to move daily
content:
With work and commutes keeping people seated, staying active increasingly means finding deliberate ways to move daily
Areeb Ahmed's working day begins with a walk.
After waking for Fajr prayers, and before getting ready for work, he walks for about 30 minutes. By the time he checks his smartwatch, he has usually completed around 3,000 steps. It is the first installment towards a target that will follow him for the rest of the day.
Then he gets into his car and drives to work.
For the next nine to 10 hours, Ahmed spends much of his time at a desk. Every hour or so, his watch reminds him that he has been sitting for too long. He gets up, walks around and tries to add another 200 or 250 steps. By the end of the working day, those small breaks might have added another 2,000.
That still leaves about half his target. After returning home, Ahmed tries to walk for another 30 minutes after Maghrib prayers. If there are still steps remaining after Isha, he finds another way to complete them.
“I don't get time for the gym, so walking is the only option I feel I can do anywhere,” he says.
Ahmed has deliberately built movement into different parts of his day. Yet when he recently tried to calculate how much of that same day he actually spends sitting, the number surprised him. Between his desk, commute and time at home, he estimated that he can actually spend around 13 of his 17 waking hours seated.
His routine also reflects a wider reality of urban life in Pakistan, where movement can easily disappear from the working day. Office hours are largely spent seated, many people drive or ride even relatively short distances, and everyday routines do not always require much walking. Staying active, therefore, can require a conscious effort to put movement back into the day.
It is a contradiction familiar to modern working life: even someone deliberately trying to stay active can spend most of the day sitting. Movement is no longer always something that happens naturally. For some, it has become something that has to be planned and counted.
Ahmed's routine is hardly unusual. For many people with corporate jobs, much of the working day requires little physical movement. The journey to work is often spent sitting in a car, followed by hours at a desk, before the same journey is repeated on the way home.
For fitness professional and gym owner Shehzar Muhammad, that lack of everyday movement is something he increasingly sees among working adults.
“Most corporate jobs are sitting indoors nine to five. People barely get to move,” says Muhammad. “In the Western world, people are walking everywhere. Here, everyone is either driving or riding around.”
The effects, he says, often become visible when people arrive at the gym. Those spending eight or nine hours behind a desk commonly complain of stiffness, poor posture and lower-back problems.
But sitting for much of the day and not exercising enough are not necessarily the same thing.
Waheed Qamar, an independent exercise expert, distinguishes between physical inactivity, not getting enough exercise, and sedentary behaviour, which refers to waking time spent sitting or reclining with very little energy expenditure. That means someone can exercise regularly and still spend much of the rest of the day sedentary.
It is sometimes described as the “active couch potato” problem: a morning run or an evening workout does not change the fact that the hours between them may involve very little movement.
That distinction matters for people whose jobs are difficult to perform any other way. Sitting through a meeting or spending hours working at a computer cannot always be avoided. The question becomes what happens between those stretches of inactivity.
Muhammad recommends deliberately interrupting them. “What can you do if you are sitting around working?” he says. “You should put reminders and alarms that you should walk.”
Qamar too recommends breaking up long periods of sitting with brief bouts of movement. Even getting up and walking periodically during the working day can interrupt stretches in which the body has remained largely stationary.
For office workers, then, staying active may begin long before anyone changes into gym clothes. Sometimes it starts simply by getting out of the chair.
Ahmed first started tracking his steps when he bought a smartwatch in 2018. For years, however, the number was little more than something he checked occasionally. He would try to reach 10,000 steps for a while, lose the routine and then start again.
The past six months have been different. It is the longest he has consistently chased the target, completing close to 10,000 steps almost every day.
The number came partly from his smartwatch and partly from fitness information he had looked up online and through AI tools. At 95kg, with a personal goal of reaching 80kg, Ahmed wanted something measurable that could keep him moving even when he could not make time for the gym.
The watch has since started shaping small parts of his day. He tries to walk while taking a phone call or take a slightly longer route when time allows. The step counter has made him more conscious of opportunities to move that he might otherwise have ignored.
Ten thousand, however, is not a magic number. The target originated with a Japanese pedometer marketed in the 1960s rather than a medical threshold, and research since then has found health benefits at lower step counts too. Qamar says the more useful goal is to increase overall daily movement rather than treat 10,000 as a pass-or-fail mark.
For Muhammad, walking should be more ordinary still. “Walking is not exercise, it should be part of your everyday life,” he says. “But because people are not used to even walking for so long, it becomes a thing, it becomes like something hard to do.”
Ahmed sees it more practically. Without regular time for the gym, walking is the activity he can fit around the rest of his day.
His 10,000-step target may be arbitrary, but following it has changed something more fundamental: he notices how much, or how little, he has moved.
Not everyone with a corporate job struggles to find time for exercise. For Abdun Nafay, staying active means fitting sport around work and family rather than waiting for the weekend to undo the week.
Nafay works in corporate communications at a manufacturing company. He estimates that four to five hours of his working day, including his commute, are spent sitting. But outside those hours, he deliberately makes room for movement. Thursday is usually reserved for padel, while during the rest of the week he tries to fit in two or three gym sessions and a game of football.
The routine is not fixed. A busy week at work or an evening with his family can take priority, but Nafay says he tries not to let one missed session turn into a longer break.
Weekends usually bring him back to the court. One recent weekend was spent largely with his wife and child, breakfast and lunch together, followed by a family walk. At night, however, he met his friends for two and a half hours of padel.
The games may begin as a chance to socialise, but they do not always stay that way. “The moment someone deliberately hits a hard smash, the court becomes a bit of a war room,” he says.
That competitiveness is part of what keeps Nafay coming back. He wants the social side of the game, but also wants to leave the court feeling that he has physically pushed himself. Sport also gives him a way to switch off from work.
What he does not do is treat those hours as repayment for time spent behind a desk. “I do not think of it as compensation,” he says. “Work and sport each have their own place in my life, and both give me a sense of satisfaction.”
Nafay's routine is more active than that of someone relying on a weekend game as their only exercise. But recreational sport also brings a different demand: after hours spent behind a desk, the body may suddenly be asked to sprint, jump and change direction.
Nafay has already discovered what can happen when that rhythm is interrupted.
Nafay learnt the importance of staying in rhythm when other commitments kept him away from football for a period. When he returned to play, he picked up an injury that took around three months to recover from.
“It made me more mindful of how I should return to a sport after a break,” he says.
It is a familiar pattern to Muhammad. Someone who has spent much of the week sitting may suddenly ask their body to sprint, jump and change direction during a game of football, cricket or padel.
“Something is better than nothing. If they are playing weekend cricket, at least they get active once or twice a week,” says Muhammad. But the sudden change in intensity can be a problem. “Someone who is sitting all day and then suddenly starts sprinting or jumping can get injured really quickly.”
That does not mean concentrating exercise into one or two days is worthless. The independent exercise expert says research on so-called “weekend warriors” has found that people who accumulate recommended amounts of physical activity over one or two days can still gain substantial health benefits.
The problem is that exercise and sitting are not exact opposites.
According to Qamar, regular sport can improve cardiovascular fitness and strength, but it does not make the hours spent largely motionless during the working week irrelevant. Long periods of sitting are better broken up with movement, even for someone who exercises outside working hours.
For Muhammad, this is why consistency matters more than relying on occasional bursts of intense activity. “Consistency is key because if it's just intensity for one day in a month compared to slowly chipping away consistently per day, I think consistency will matter more,” he says.
Nafay has noticed another change as he has grown older. He can still play hard, but recovery is no longer quite as quick. “After a football match, the fatigue is certainly there, and I may still feel it the next morning,” he says.
The weekend game, then, does not need to compensate for everything that happened from Monday to Friday to be worthwhile. It gets people moving, competing and, often, coming back the following week. But the rest of the week still counts.
There is no single way to make an otherwise sedentary day more active. Ahmed's answer has been walking. Nafay's involves a gym, a football pitch and a padel court.
For Nafay, maintaining that routine means accepting that it will not always look the same. Work and family can change the week, and exercise has to move with them. What matters to him is returning to it rather than allowing an interruption to become the new routine.
“I do not think being active means having a perfect routine,” he says. “For me, it means continuing to make time to move, play and look after my energy alongside work and family life.”
For Muhammad, the difficulty is often less about identifying what exercise to do than finding a place for it on a working day. “You're never going to have the time, you have to make the time,” he says.
Qamar similarly argues that movement does not have to be confined to a formal workout. Walking during phone calls, taking the stairs and getting away from the desk periodically can all add movement to a day that might otherwise involve hours of sitting.
Technology can provide a push. Muhammad sees value in watches and fitness apps because they allow people to track their activity and progress. But he also cautions against allowing those numbers to dictate how someone feels.
The routines may look different, but each requires the same conscious decision. When work, commuting and home life can all be navigated with very little physical effort, movement has to find its place somewhere.
There are evenings when Ahmed looks at his watch and the number is still short.
By then, there may be nowhere left to go. Work is finished, he is home and dinner is approaching. But after six months of following the target more consistently than he ever has before, leaving those steps unfinished bothers him.
“I feel like something is missing,” he says. “Whenever I land my eye on the step tracker in my mobile phone or watch, I feel that I have to complete 10,000.”
So he finds somewhere to walk, even if that means staying inside his own home. The destination, in that sense, matters less than the movement. The watch has made Ahmed more conscious of something his working day can otherwise make easy to overlook: how many hours can pass without much movement at all.
For someone who spends much of his day between a desk, a car and home, walking is no longer necessarily a by-product of getting somewhere.
Sometimes, it is the thing he has to make time for before the day is done.

title: Yamal on target as Spain hold off Czech Republic
description: Yamal  Rodri and Merino strike as La Roja secure a 3 1 win
content:
Yamal, Rodri and Merino strike as La Roja secure a 3-1 win
Lamine Yamal continued his superb goalscoring form as Spain secured a 3-1 win over the Czech Republic on Saturday in the Nations League.
The world champions moved three points clear of England at the top of Group A3, after Thomas Tuchel's side demolished Croatia 7-0 earlier on in Rijeka.
Spain cruised into a two-goal lead with Yamal and captain Rodri Hernandez on target but Jiri Slama gave the Czechs a chance by pulling one back with 20 minutes to go.
However Mikel Merino wrapped up Spain's win late on after Ladislav Krejci was sent off for the Czechs as Spain racked up a 41st consecutive unbeaten game, including the World Cup final win over Argentina in July.
"They are well drilled, I thought it would be one of the hardest games and that's how it was," Rodri told Spanish broadcaster TVE after Spain claimed a third win from three group games.
"It was tricky but we got some chances. There are some matches in which you can't generate that much, but the team was able to manage the match."
The former Manchester City midfielder scored for the first time for Spain in over two years.
"It's always special to score for the national team, I'd not been scoring many goals, let's see if I've found that dynamic -- it's important, we all have to chip in with the goals," he added.
Spain coach Luis de la Fuente made several changes in Oviedo from Tuesday's win over Croatia, including handing debuts to full-back Ivan Fresneda and striker Roberto Fernandez.
It was one of Spain's star names, though, who lit up the game early on, something he is beginning to make a habit of.
Yamal, who scored in the second minute of Spain's first two games against England and Croatia, waited as long as the sixth before breaking the deadlock.
The 19-year-old winger, a major candidate for the Ballon d'Or, produced an exquisite finish from the right of the box, curled into the top corner after taking a touch to earn himself room to shoot.
"We're doing well, I'm very happy. I was eager to return to the national team after the World Cup, and there's no better way than this," said Yamal.
Spain coach De la Fuente put his hands to his head in apparent shock at the quality of Yamal's superb strike, his 12th in his last nine games for club and country.
"I think he never stops surprising us -- I think all of us. He has so much talent, so much quality, that we still haven't seen the best version of Lamine by a long shot," said De la Fuente.
"He has a lot more to offer because he's so classy, so talented, with so much potential."
The winger's Barcelona team-mate Rodri doubled Spain's lead after 35 minutes, arriving in the box to drill into the top corner after the ball fell nicely for him.
De la Fuente took off Yamal at half-time to give the young Barcelona star a break before Tuesday's visit to face Croatia, and the pace of the game slowed.
The Czechs pulled one back through Slama, who produced an excellent low finish across David Raya after Adam Hlozek played him in.
Arsenal stopper Raya was fortunate a few minutes later when he conceded possession with a misplaced pass while out of his goal, but the visitors could not capitalise.
Raya also spilled the ball badly and Ryan Naderi turned home but the goal was disallowed for a foul on Robin Le Normand.
Czech Republic's determined efforts to battle back were derailed by Krejci's red card, with the defender shown a second yellow for pulling back Fernandez, before Merino rounded off Spain's win.

title: West Indies deny India clean sweep
description: West Indies chase down a target of 352 to secure a famous win in New Chandigarh
content:
West Indies chase down a target of 352 to secure a famous win in New Chandigarh
Shai Hope anchored the chase with an unbeaten 162 off 143 balls as West Indies prevented India from completing a series sweep with a five-wicket victory in the third and final one-day international in New Chandigarh on Saturday.
After the early loss of John Campbell in the fifth over, Hope combined with Amir ⁠Jangoo for a crucial 109-run stand to steady the innings, helping West Indies reach 78-1 at the end of the powerplay.
Jangoo struck his third ODI half-century before being run out for 67, while Sherfane Rutherford fell soon after for ⁠24. Hope, however, maintained the momentum, adding another vital 56-run partnership to keep the chase on track. Despite the dismissals of Keemo Paul and Matthew Forde, Hope remained in control of the chase.
Gudakesh Motie contributed a brisk 19 ⁠off 14 balls, as West Indies sealed ⁠victory with 10 balls to spare.
India were forced to rebuild after slipping to 4-2, but Rohit Sharma and Ruturaj Gaikwad steadied the innings with a 137-run partnership.
Sharma anchored the recovery with a fluent 92 off 85 balls before falling eight runs short of a century. After Rohit's dismissal, KL Rahul made the most of his ⁠lone batting opportunity of the series, bringing up his ninth ODI hundred.
Rahul accelerated ⁠sharply at the death, smashing 42 runs off the final 12 balls he faced to convert his century into a career-best ODI score. Gaikwad chipped in with a half-century before being dismissed by Jayden Seales. With Rahul unbeaten on 129, India finished strongly through late cameos from Naman Dhir (30 off 21 balls) and Anshul Kamboj (17 off ⁠nine balls).
Their contributions helped propel India to 351-7, with Rahul and Gurnoor Brar unbeaten at the crease. The Shubman Gill-led side had already secured the series by winning the opening two ODIs. In the second match, India completed a record chase of 406 with 6.3 overs to spare to seal the series.

title: Germany s Merz arrives in Kyiv to finalise drone deal  release aid
description: Chancellor travels with defence CEOs to show support for Zelenskiy as Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities escalate
content:
Chancellor travels with defence CEOs to show support for Zelenskiy as Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities escalate
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Sunday, accompanied by CEOs from German defence companies, in a show of support for President Volodymyr Zelenskiy amid escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Merz will announce a package of measures that includes the release €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for repairs in the energy sector, German government officials said. The visit is also expected to finalise a deal for joint production of various kinds of drones.
"I travelled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks," Merz said, saying that Russian forces were bombing towns, residential buildings and heating plants. "If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us."
"I will tell President Zelenskiy today: 'You can continue to count on our help,'" Merz added.
The German chancellor is accompanied by Minister for Economic Affairs Katherina Reiche and an economic delegation including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence, Quantum Systems and other firms.
Read: EU foreign policy chief claims Russia planning 'more sabotage acts' against Europe
Merz is also expected to press the Ukrainian government for progress on reforms requested by EU partners, including in the fight against corruption.
Zelenskiy said on Wednesday, after speaking to Merz by phone, that Ukraine would soon finalise the deal with Germany for the production of drones, missiles and related software.
A key focus is expected to be the rapid production of anti-jet drones, which Quantum, a German defence-technology company, has successfully tested. Since the summer, Russia has used dozens of high-speed jet attack drones daily to target civilian and military infrastructure.
In April, Quantum and Ukrainian manufacturer WIY Drones announced the creation of Quantum WIY Industries, a joint venture to produce the Strila interceptor drone and related air-defence technologies.
The deal also involves the joint development and production of weapons with a range of more than 1,000 km (600 miles) that Ukraine can use to launch attacks deep inside Russia.
Government officials said the increased cooperation would allow money and technology to flow back to the Federal Republic, where weapons are produced and defences against drones targeting critical infrastructure can be strengthened.
Read More: Russia issues nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic
On Thursday, Merz said Germany would not be intimidated by the rising number of hybrid attacks by Russia on European states.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Saturday that Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in Ukraine in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months. It warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against staying in or travelling to Ukraine.
Zelenskiy told Reuters on Saturday his country's armed forces would double down on their attacks on oil refineries in Russia in response to Moscow's "new doctrine" of escalating attacks on civilian infrastructure, which he said was aimed at forcing residents of Kyiv and other cities to flee.

title: Aircraft carrying four injured crew members  remains of three MT Honour 25 sailors lands in Karachi
description: Sindh governor Nehal Hashmi  welcomes injured Pakistanis upon their repatriation
content:
Sindh governor Nehal Hashmi welcomes injured Pakistanis upon their repatriation
An aircraft carrying four injured crew members and the remains of three MT Honour 25 sailors landed in Karachi's Jinnah International Airport on Sunday.
Sindh Governor Nehal Hashmi welcomed the injured Pakistanis upon their repatriation and attended the funeral prayers of Mahmood Ahmed Ansari and expressed condolences to his family.
Senior government officials such as Sindh Local Government Minister Nasir Hussain Shah, Sindh Labour and Human Resources Minister Saeed Ghani, and MQM-P leader Farooq Sattar also received the injured upon their return to the country.
Two of the injured people were from Karachi, while one was from Sahiwal and one from Peshawar. The two injured individuals from Peshawar and Sahiwal would depart from Karachi for their hometowns later on Sunday.
Rafi Ullah Khan's mortal remains were handed over to the family, and his funeral prayers would be held after Isha prayers.
Earlier in the day, the four injured Pakistani crew members of MT Honour 25, along with the remains of three others killed, were flown aboard Ethiopian Airlines flight ET 694 from Addis Ababa to Karachi on Sunday, the Foreign Office (FO) said.
In a post on X, the FO said, "Pakistan’s Ambassadors to Djibouti and Ethiopia saw off the four injured Pakistani crew members of MT Honour 25, Usman Ghani, Aqeel Khan, Ameen bin Shams and Yasir Khan, along with the mortal remains of Rafi Ullah Khan, Syed Kashif Umer and Mahmood Ahmad Ansari, from Addis Ababa."
"They are arriving in Karachi today aboard Ethiopian Airlines flight ET 694," the ministry added.
Pakistan’s Ambassadors to Djibouti and Ethiopia saw off the four injured Pakistani crew members of MT Honour 25, Usman Ghani, Aqeel Khan, Ameen bin Shams and Yasir Khan, along with the mortal remains of Rafi Ullah Khan, Syed Kashif Umer and Mahmood Ahmad Ansari, from Addis Ababa.… pic.twitter.com/t0x4VqNsuK
On Friday, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said four of the 10 Pakistani crew members affected by the hijacking had been safely retrieved following efforts by the FO and Pakistan’s embassy in Djibouti.
Dar had identified the four crew members as Yasir Khan, Aqeel Khan, Amin bin Shams and Usman Ghani and said they were scheduled to arrive in Karachi yesterday.
He had also said the remains of three Pakistani crew members who had died were being repatriated to Pakistan, with the necessary legal and other formalities being expedited.
Read: Four Pakistani crew members from hijacked MT Honour 25 to arrive in Karachi tomorrow: Dar
The minister had said the remaining three Pakistani crew members — Imran Ali, Yasin Muhammad and Syed Yousuf Hussain — remained aboard the vessel along with its captain. He said Pakistan was coordinating with friendly countries to facilitate their safe extraction and return.
The oil tanker Honour 25, sailing under the Somali flag from Oman to Somalia, was hijacked by pirates on April 21. There were 17 crew members aboard, 10 of them Pakistani nationals. The families of the Pakistani hostages spent months seeking the safe release of their loved ones, staging peaceful protests and repeatedly approaching government authorities.
During their captivity, the pirates initially demanded a ransom of $3 million, which was later reduced to $1.9 million and subsequently to $1 million. All the Pakistani crew members who were killed or injured were from different areas of Karachi.
The pirates came under pressure during a rescue operation and, while retreating from the vessel, opened indiscriminate fire on the abducted crew before fleeing the ship. Five sailors were killed, including three Pakistanis — Second Officer Kashif Umar, Third Engineer Mahmood Ansari and Boiler Rafiullah. The other two deceased crew members were an Indian sailor, Tanveer, and the chief engineer from Myanmar.
Four sailors were injured — Usman, Yasir, Ameen and Vicky from Indonesia — while Hussain Yousuf, Imran Ali and Yaseen remained safe. The two surviving Pakistani crew members later contacted the Ansar Burney Welfare Trust in Karachi using the ship captain’s mobile phone and provided details of the incident.
Read more: FO expresses condolences over deaths of five crew members in Somalia rescue operation
Puntland police said the Honour 25 had 18,500 barrels of oil on board when it was hijacked. The police had been pursuing three hijacked vessels off the Somali coast and had also rescued another oil tanker, Sibu 1, on Friday. However, 28 of the 41 pirates arrested during that operation later escaped while being transferred to jail, with several Puntland security officials accusing local police of complicity.
The Gulf of Aden and Somalia coasts have seen a resurgence in piracy since April, with at least 15 attacks recorded this year, the highest number since 2013, according to figures from the International Maritime Organisation.

content:

Rapper Lucki was reportedly injured Saturday following an altercation involving members of his entourage and people associated with Playboi Carti at ComplexCon in Los Angeles.
Videos circulating on social media appear to show parts of the confrontation, while separate footage appears to show Lucki with blood around the side of his face and neck as people helped him towards a vehicle.

title: Kainat Imtiaz retires from international cricket
description: Bowler ends international career after playing 19 ODIs and 21 T20Is
content:
Bowler ends international career after playing 19 ODIs and 21 T20Is
Pakistan fast bowler Kainat Imtiaz has announced her retirement from international cricket after a 13-year career in which she represented the women's team at the 2017 World Cup and won two Asian Games gold medals.
The right-arm pacer played 19 One-Day Internationals and 21 Twenty20 Internationals for Pakistan after making her T20I debut against South Africa in Potchefstroom in October 2010. She made her ODI debut against Ireland in Fatullah, Bangladesh.
Imtiaz, 34, was part of Pakistan's squads that won gold at the 2010 Asian Games in China and the 2014 edition in South Korea. She also represented Pakistan at the 2022 Commonwealth Games.
She played four matches at the 2017 Women's Cricket World Cup and made her final ODI appearance against Australia at the Gabba in January 2023. Her last T20I came against Thailand in Sylhet in October 2022.
Imtiaz began her cricket journey with the Karachi Schools Under-17 team in the PCB National Schools Under-17 Women's Championship in 2007 before making her domestic List A debut in 2008.
She has already begun the next phase of her career, serving as a match referee at the PCB National Women's Under-19 T20 Tournament in August and September.
Cricket runs in the family. Imtiaz's mother, Saleema Imtiaz, became Pakistan's first woman umpire on the International Cricket Council's International Development Panel in 2024. She has since officiated nine women's ODIs and 69 women's T20 internationals.

title: Naqvi blames K P CM for talks    collapse     warns Afridi will    be responsible    if anyone dies during march
description: K P chief minister shares 7 point draft  seeks assurances to call off march  decries  second class citizen  treatment
content:
PTI laments failed talks, urges govt to address deadlock and show willingness to engage in dialogue
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Sunday accused the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government, particularly Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, of sabotaging government-opposition negotiations, saying the two sides had reached agreement on 99 per cent of the draft before the process ran into a deadlock over terrorism-related matters.
Naqvi’s remarks came after hours of talks between the government and opposition ended without an agreement, despite reports a day earlier that both sides had reached consensus on a draft ahead of the PTI’s scheduled long march.
Addressing a press conference in Lahore, Naqvi praised members of the opposition negotiating team for what he described as their efforts to settle, but said the process was repeatedly disrupted by the K-P government.
“I would like to thank them. They negotiated in a very good manner,” he said, referring to Allama Nasir Abbas, Asad Qaiser, Barrister Gohar, Salman Akram Raja, Aamir Dogar and other members of the opposition team.
“They negotiated in a way that anyone would do to reach a resolution. They should be given this credit.”
However, he said the opposition team’s efforts were undermined by its party leadership and “especially its CM”.
“Unfortunately, their party and especially their CM tried to sabotage all the negotiations,” Naqvi said.
He said the opposition negotiators had been told that they had the mandate to take decisions on behalf of their side.
“When they took the decision and finalised the draft, all of a sudden, they popped up and said that they do not agree to this,” he said.
Naqvi said there had been differences on some issues but the two sides had agreed on 99 per cent of the draft.
“There were some issues in the wording and other things. All the issues were resolved one by one,” he said.
He said the draft was finalised and subsequently changed four times during 12 hours of negotiations.
“We used to finalise one thing and then change it,” he said, adding that the negotiating teams had made repeated efforts to resolve differences.
“If Sohail Afridi had to make a decision, he would have come to the negotiations himself,” Naqvi said.
He said he had spoken to Barrister Gohar two days earlier and requested that either Afridi or one of his representatives attend the talks because it was important for the K-P government to have a representative in the negotiations.
Naqvi said the government did not have a political dispute with the opposition during the talks and that the main issue was counterterrorism.
“Our issue is entirely terrorism-related,” he said.
He said the government wanted the K-P government to join the federal government in efforts against terrorism, while political matters could be addressed separately through dialogue.
Naqvi said he had asked the opposition to bring the K-P government on board because “the issues that we are facing are coming from the K-P government”.
He said Qaiser had agreed to speak to the provincial government and asked that the meeting be postponed until the following day.
The negotiating team subsequently held four hours of talks with the K-P chief minister, Naqvi said, adding that Afridi gave his feedback and authorised the team to proceed with whatever was finalised.
Naqvi said two agreements were under discussion — one concerning the political issues and another relating to terrorism.
The latter included matters related to the Police Act, kidnappings, the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan, former Fata and the National Action Plan, he said.
“We told them that what we are discussing with you is very important. It should be on record,” he said.
Naqvi said the government had not initially asked the opposition to postpone its planned long march.
“When the first meeting took place, I told them that we do not have a problem with a long march,” he said.
However, he said the PPP had sought postponement of the march after party Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari called for the political temperature to be lowered.
Naqvi said the PPP had told the opposition that it would settle the outstanding issues if the long march was postponed.
“So they said, okay, if we settle these things, we will do a long march,” he said, adding that the negotiations had therefore started positively.
Naqvi said the talks might not have been conducted in the same manner had the government known that there was no authorised person in the committee with the backing of the K-P government, or that the provincial government would veto the agreements reached by the negotiators.
“We did it with a very good policy,” he said.
The minister said the two sides had agreed completely on political issues and the statement was issue, while concessions offered by the government were intended to bring the K-P government on board in the fight against terrorism.
“We were telling them that in this terrorism that is happening in your province, you and I are standing together,” he said.
Naqvi said it was not appropriate for a province to be at war while ministers issued statements against the army or did not attend soldiers’ funerals while also claiming that that terrorists were receiving support at the local level.
“So in no way can there be a war like this,” he said.
He said the government’s request was for the K-P government to join the fight against terrorism, while political issues could be discussed separately.
“But at this time, the most important thing is that for the country, for the terrorism that is spreading the most in your province, to stop that, we will work together,” he said.
Naqvi rejected the notion that political negotiations could extend to decisions about military operations.
“If we have to do politics in that, and if we have to say that in the operation of the army, I will tell you which gun to use, which bullet to use and which drone to use, then that is not happening anywhere in the world,” he said.
Naqvi said long marches and such calls were harmful for the country, citing disruption to the stock exchange, difficulties for local residents and road closures.
“No government would want people to have such a problem,” he said.
He also warned that if the long march resulted in a loss of life, CM Afridi would be held responsible.
“If even one person dies, Sohail Afridi will be responsible,” Naqvi said.
PTI urges govt to address deadlock, show willingness for talks
Later, Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) expressed regret over the failure of negotiations between its joint team with Tehreek-e-Tahafuz-e-Ain Pakistan (TTAP) and government representatives, urging the government to address the reasons for the deadlock and demonstrate its willingness to engage in meaningful dialogue.
In a statement on X, the party said the negotiations concluded without substantive progress despite “serious efforts” to address political stability, restoration of democracy, supremacy of the Constitution and law, access to PTI Founder Imran Khan, his health and medical treatment, and the worsening security situation in K-P and other parts of the country.
PTI said the principal point of deadlock was its demand for immediate access to Khan so that the party leadership could consult him on matters of national and political importance.
PRESS RELEASE PTI Responds to Inconclusive Negotiations and Federal Ministers’ Press Conference Party Says Denial of Access to Chairman Imran Khan Remained Central Impediment; Calls for Consensus Based Counterterrorism Strategy and Immediate Attention to Khan’s Medical Care…
It said its negotiating team had conveyed that other demands could be set aside if the government agreed to this single request. However, according to the party, the government declined to make access to Khan part of the proposed agreement.
The party maintained that consultation with political leadership was an essential part of the democratic process, arguing that just as leaders of other political parties remained central to their parties’ policy and decision-making, PTI should also be able to consult its chairman on major political and national issues.
“Restricting such consultation, particularly during a critical period for the country, inevitably limits the scope for meaningful political engagement,” it said.
PTI said the situation in K-P was another major issue discussed during the negotiations.
According to the party, the government side sought the provincial government’s unconditional support for counterterrorism measures and operations undertaken by the federation and relevant authorities, as well as support for emergency measures within 72 hours in the merged districts and adjoining areas.
PTI reiterated its “unequivocal condemnation” of terrorism and stressed that eliminating terrorism, protecting citizens and restoring lasting peace must remain a national priority.
The party paid tribute to officers and personnel of the armed forces, police, security forces and other law-enforcement agencies who had sacrificed their lives in the fight against terrorism, while expressing solidarity with civilians and families affected by terrorist violence.
It said the people of the province had paid an “extraordinary price” over the years through loss of life, destruction of property and businesses, prolonged insecurity and displacement.
“Their concerns and experiences must therefore remain central to any future counterterrorism policy,” PTI said.
The party maintained that terrorism could not be defeated through force alone or through unilateral measures that could expose civilians to further loss of life, property damage or displacement.
“Past experience must inform future policy,” it said, adding that any effective strategy must combine firm action against terrorism with protection of civilian populations and sensitivity to local realities.
PTI proposed that authorised representatives of the federal and K-P governments meet within 72 hours to develop a “clear, comprehensive and mutually agreed strategy” for peace and counterterrorism.
It further proposed consultations with political parties represented in the K-P Assembly, elected representatives, tribal elders and other relevant stakeholders so that any policy could enjoy public confidence and be implemented effectively.
The party also rejected attempts to characterise the position of CM Afridi as political obstinacy, arguing that had access to Khan been facilitated, the chief minister could have consulted the PTI chairman directly on security and counterterrorism policy, potentially helping bridge differences and create greater consensus.
PTI said effective cooperation among the federal government, provincial government and relevant authorities was indispensable for national security. Such cooperation, however, must respect constitutional requirements, the role of the elected provincial government and the legitimate concerns of the people directly affected, it added.
The party said the health and medical treatment of Khan was also raised as a matter of “fundamental importance”.
The negotiating team sought immediate access to him, his transfer to Shifa International Hospital and the constitution of an appropriate medical board with the participation of his personal physician to ensure proper examination, diagnosis and treatment, according to the statement.
PTI said the government had agreed only to restore meetings between Khan and his family members and lawyers from Tuesday, but had not agreed to additional measures concerning his medical assessment and treatment.
The party welcomed the resumption of family and legal meetings but stressed that such access could not substitute for proper medical examination and necessary treatment.
“Khan’s health must be addressed with seriousness, transparency and humanitarian consideration,” it said, adding that all medically necessary steps should be taken without delay.
Responding to the subsequent press conference by federal ministers, PTI said the government should refrain from placing responsibility for the inconclusive negotiations entirely on the opposition and instead address the substantive issues that prevented progress.
It called on the government to explain why immediate access to Khan was considered unacceptable, why the requested measures regarding his medical care were not accommodated, and why a broader consultative approach involving the provincial government, political representatives, tribal elders and other stakeholders was not accepted for developing a sustainable security strategy for K-P.
PTI reiterated that it remained prepared to engage in political dialogue, constitutional processes, meaningful consultation and national consensus to address Khan’s health and treatment, restoration of democracy, supremacy of the Constitution and law, political stability, terrorism and other challenges confronting the country.
The party stressed, however, that meaningful negotiations could not succeed through predetermined positions or demands for unconditional endorsement.
“Serious dialogue requires flexibility, mutual confidence, consultation and a genuine willingness to translate discussions into practical progress,” it said.
Sherry accuses K-P govt of derailing talks
Senior PPP leader Sherry Rehman, who was part of the government negotiating team, accused the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government of sabotaging talks with the opposition, saying the negotiations collapsed after the provincial government refused to sign an agreed draft on counter-terrorism cooperation with the Centre.
In a post on X, Rehman said the government and opposition teams had finalised four drafts with their respective principals and had reopened them to accommodate changes proposed by the PTI.
However, she said the talks collapsed after the KP government unilaterally refused to sign the draft on counterterrorism cooperation with the Centre, which had been agreed upon earlier in the afternoon.

“Terrorism is a core issue for the PPP. We lost more workers and Pakistan’s iconic prime minister Shaheed Benazir to terrorists who are amassing in critical cohorts in a province that is at war but has other political priorities.”
She said the objective had been to bring the province “on board on all CT actions”.
Rehman said the negotiating team had repeatedly asked the K-P government to participate in the talks alongside the PTI’s senior federal leadership, but neither the chief minister nor cabinet representatives attended.
“If they had a viable draft they should have shown up themselves or communicated it to their committee over the two days, without constant reversals,” she said.
“There is no point presenting new drafts on social media after refusing to show up or sabotaging their own teams by broadcasting messages that subvert the process,” the PPP leader said, referring to Afridi’s post on X, in which he shared seven demands, claiming that these were the proposals put forward by his government in the draft.
She said timing and trust were key to confidence-building in negotiations, adding that a “mature working relationship” between the provincial and federal authorities could have helped make a “crucial beginning”.
“Nothing would have been unilateral,” she said.
Instead, Rehman said, the K-P government “began dictating terms after 8.30pm when all but final agreements had been signed”.
“That is when the arbitrary spiral into amateur hour began,” she said, adding that she had never in her 25 years in parliament seen “such a reckless squandering of an opening to begin political CBMs, and to bring stability to Pakistan after years of bitter political division”.
“Even before Sunday break of dawn, we did not walk away or close the doors. We waited until they stopped coming back,” she said.
She also thanked PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari and President Asif Ali Zardari for trying to create space for negotiations, while appreciating Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi for remaining patient.
Rehman also praised the negotiating teams for remaining focused despite what she described as “constant reversals”.
Earlier, CM Afridi made public the draft he said he had sent to the government’s negotiating committee, insisting that none of its seven demands was unconstitutional or illegal.
In a post on X, Afridi said he was placing before the public the draft he had sent to the negotiating committee, adding that the entire nation should know that none of the demands was unconstitutional or illegal.
He said the people were being treated as second-class citizens and alleged that the state was treating them like a stepmother.
“These were our demands, are our demands and will remain our demands,” he said.

Under the first point, the draft proposed regular meetings between the prime minister and the leaders of the opposition in both houses of parliament to discuss all important political, national, constitutional, legal and democratic issues facing the country, particularly pending matters.
It said the parties would be bound to ensure effective, workable progress towards resolving these issues through mutual consultation and negotiation within two months.
The second point called for the prime minister to form a joint political negotiating committee comprising representatives of the government coalition, the Pakistan Peoples Party and opposition parties.
The committee would hold continuous negotiations with the opposition on national and political matters, mutual differences and other important issues and seek workable solutions through consensus, the draft said.
It also called for complete freedom for democracy, politics, the judiciary and journalism.
The committee would ensure significant progress on negotiations and solutions within one month of its formation and present its recommendations to the relevant leadership, according to the draft.
The third point called for Imran Khan and his wife, Bushra Bibi, to be provided with all legal, human, and medical rights available to them under the jail manual, the Constitution, and prevailing laws, without discrimination.

Where legally applicable, necessary medical facilities and treatment would be provided while taking into consideration the medical opinions, instructions and advice of their personal or nominated doctors, it said.
The fourth point called for Imran and Bushra to be allowed to meet their family members, nominated lawyers and authorised or nominated associates in accordance with the jail manual and relevant laws.
The meetings would be held under the law and prison rules and regulations, while neither side would use the meeting facility for political or other purposes prohibited by law, the draft said.
The fifth point called for applications against sentences and other legal applications filed by Imran, Bushra, women, elderly and sick prisoners and all other detained persons to be considered within 10 days in accordance with the Constitution and law, where legally possible.
It said all cases would be decided by the relevant courts and legal forums in accordance with the Constitution, law, transparent judicial procedures and principles of justice, without unjustified delay.
Women serving political sentences, including elderly PTI leader Yasmin Rashid and Bushra, would be released at the earliest on humanitarian grounds, the draft said.
On the security situation in K-P, the sixth point called for effective, continuous and meaningful consultation between the federal and provincial governments to end terrorism, protect the lives and property of people and establish lasting and sustainable peace.
Existing policies and measures would be regularly reviewed and amended where necessary, it said.

Authorised representatives of the federal and provincial governments would hold a formal meeting within 72 hours and, through mutual consultation, formulate a clear, comprehensive and workable strategy for maintaining law and order.
Implementation of the strategy within the framework of the Constitution and law would be the joint responsibility of the federal and provincial governments, according to the draft.
The seventh point said PTI would announce the cancellation of the long march after the federal government provided written assurances on the effective implementation of the assurances and agreed measures outlined in the draft.
However, if the federal government violated the agreed assurances, the negotiating process or constitutional and legal requirements, or unnecessarily stalled the talks, PTI would reserve its right to peaceful, democratic and legal protest in accordance with the Constitution and law.
Responding to CM Afridi, Naqvi said the K-P government had backed out of a series of security-related commitments during the final phase of negotiations between the government and opposition over the PTI's planned long march.
In a post on X, Naqvi said the K-P government had agreed to sign a written agreement and submit an implementation plan within 72 hours covering a range of measures related to counterterrorism and security in the province.
He said the commitments included reconsidering the Police Act 2026 in light of the security situation and the need to protect security matters from political interference.
The KP Government had agreed to sign a written agreement and submit an implementation plan within 72 hours, covering • Reconsideration of the Police Act 2026 in light of the security situation and the need to protect security matters from political interference • Preventing…
The provincial government had also agreed to prevent terrorists from operating freely or finding safe havens in the province and to issue an "unequivocal condemnation" of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also referred to as the Tehreek-e-Taliban Afghanistan (TTA), and all other terrorist groups, Naqvi said.
It had further agreed to support the national policy on Afghan refugees, including their repatriation and the dismantling of Afghan camps in K-P, as well as to have no contact with the interim Afghan government, he said.
The commitments also included substantial funding for counterterrorism operations and the police, full provincial ownership of counterterrorism measures and stronger cooperation with the armed forces, Naqvi said.
The K-P government had also agreed to decisions on counterterrorism in former FATA and the merged districts, as well as implementation of the National Action Plan, according to the minister.
"Last night, during the final phase of negotiations, the K-P Government backed out of these commitments," Naqvi said.
"Security must not be politicised while the province is at War," he added.
Salman Akram Raja says talks broke down over K-P counter-terrorism
PTI leader Salman Akram Raja weighed in on X, saying disagreement over the federal government’s proposed approach to counter-terrorism operations in K-P was the main reason talks between the government and the PTI-TTAP team broke down in the early hours of the morning.
Leaving all other issues and much noise aside, the primary reason for the failure of the talks around 3am this morning between the government team and the PTI-TTAP team was the following: the PTI-TTAP team stood firm on its principled position that anti-terorrism actions in KPK…
“Leaving all other issues and much noise aside, the primary reason for the failure of the talks around 3am this morning between the government team and the PTI-TTAP team was the following,” Raja said in a post on X.
He said the PTI-TTAP team had “stood firm on its principled position” that anti-terrorism actions in K-P should be based on an agreement between the federal and provincial governments.
Such measures, Raja said, should also be “framed on the basis of consultation with, and the buy-in of, the different political parties represented in the KPK assembly”.
He said this position had not been acceptable to the government team, which had insisted that “all actions unilaterally initiated by it would have to be owned by the provincial government”.
Raja said the PTI-TTAP team had been clear that “we have zero tolerance for terrorism and are committed to rooting it out”.
He added that the team also had a clear position against “so-called collateral damage” in the form of innocent lives being lost and the internal displacement of the local population.
“Policies and actions aimed at fighting terror must have the support of the local population and be based on ground intelligence,” Raja said.
He also said the recommendations of a jirga held in the K-P Assembly should be taken into account. The jirga, he said, comprised “all the political and tribal notables of the province, including the merged districts”.
“The wisdom provided by the jirga held in the KPK assembly of all the political and tribal notables of the province, including the merged districts, must be heeded,” Raja said.
He said this position had not been acceptable to the federal government, which had led to the breakdown in negotiations.
PTI Sindh leader Haleem Adil Sheikh, who had been part of the six-member opposition negotiating committee, said the two-day negotiation sessions between the government and opposition teams had continued until around 2:30am, but ended in a deadlock over three “fundamental red lines”.
In a post on X, Sheikh said the committee had the backing of the core and political committees and had remained in consultation throughout the negotiations.

“We continued consulting during the negotiations, sought guidance from Mahmood Khan Achakzai and remained in continuous contact with Chief Minister Sohail Afridi,” Sheikh said.
He said the two sides had discussed several issues, reached agreement on some points and continued talks on others, but had ultimately reached an impasse over three key matters.
The first, he said, was a meeting with PTI founder Imran Khan.
“We made it clear that only Imran Khan has the authority to call off the long march; therefore a meeting with him was necessary,” Sheikh said.
When the government did not agree to the meeting, he said the opposition had proposed as an alternative that Raja Nasir Abbas be allowed to meet Imran Khan. “But the government did not agree to that either,” he said.
The second “red line”, according to Sheikh, concerned Imran Khan’s health and medical treatment.
“Our minimum demand was that his personal doctors be included in his treatment so that doubts regarding his health could be dispelled,” he said. “The government did not agree to this either, which further increased our concerns.”
The third point was the policy on security and terrorism in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
“Our demand was that no decision should be taken unilaterally,” Sheikh said, adding that the federal and provincial governments should take all relevant stakeholders, including parliamentary political parties, into confidence before formulating a joint and agreed course of action.
He said the two governments should “move forward under the National Action Plan against terrorism”.
Instead of broad consultation, however, the government had sought to make decisions within 72 hours, Sheikh alleged.
“On these three points, neither were we prepared to back down from our position nor did the government accept our demands,” he said. “Consequently, the negotiations reached a deadlock.”
Sheikh said Chief Minister Sohail Afridi would begin the long march at 4pm on Sunday, while protests planned in Sindh would also take place according to the previously announced programme.
He called on PTI organisations in all districts, including Karachi and Hyderabad, to ensure implementation of their programmes.
“Our peaceful movement will continue until the release of Imran Khan and other leaders, restoration of the Constitution, independence of the judiciary and an end to skyrocketing inflation,” Sheikh said.
“In Sindh too, every chowk will be D-Chowk,” he added.
The demands came as negotiations between the government and opposition failed to resolve the dispute over the October 4 march.
The two sides had held marathon talks at the National Assembly speaker's office, with the government seeking to persuade PTI to call off the protest and the opposition seeking assurances on its demands before taking such a decision.
The talks had made progress on several issues, but a disagreement over a meeting with Imran emerged during the final stages of the negotiations. Opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai had maintained that the authority to call off the march rested with Imran and Afridi.
The PTI had subsequently maintained its plan to proceed with the march, with Afridi announcing a five-day programme under which the procession was expected to reach Peshawar by October 8.

title: Real solutions Vs greenwashing tricks
description: France and The Netherlands are two more big economies that have released roadmaps to phase out fossil fuel use
content:
France and the Netherlands are two more big economies that have released roadmaps to phase out fossil fuel use
The biggest news during the Climate Week NYC came not from the US but from Germany, where the government of the world’s third-largest economy committed to phasing out fossil fuels by 2045. It was the first time Germany has explicitly made such a promise, Fiona Harvey noted in The Guardian. Germany’s previous pledges, Harvey added, “were only for ‘carbon neutrality,’” an important distinction. Carbon neutrality allows continued fossil fuel use if the emissions are offset—for example, by additional clean energy or tree planting. But only a complete phaseout of fossil fuels can halt global temperature rise.
Meanwhile, Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, the world’s fourth largest economy, hailed his state’s decarbonization efforts, saying in an interview with Covering Climate Now that California has run on 100% clean electricity nine out of every 10 days so far in 2026. And as the costs of solar, wind, and batteries continue to fall, while the Iran war makes gasoline and diesel more expensive, “the markets are moving in our direction,” said Newsom, who’s widely expected to run for president in 2028. “Globally, people are realizing [that clean energy] is the better option.”
An overwhelming majority of people around the world want their governments to take stronger climate action, the Associated Press noted in an article about the global oat milk company Oatly endorsing CCNow’s 89 Percent Project. “Companies should be taking much more responsibility, not only in reducing their own environmental footprint, but really working out how they can use their platform to drive a positive future,” Caroline Reid, senior sustainability director at Oatly, told the AP.
Mirroring this public sentiment, Germany and California are key members of a “coalition of the willing” that emerged from last year’s COP30 UN climate summit after petrostates vetoed calls from 80-plus countries to develop a global “roadmap” to phase out fossil fuels. Collectively, this coalition amounts to the biggest economic superpower on Earth. In April, many of its members met in Santa Marta, Colombia, to begin discussing, in UN Secretary-General António Guterres’s words, how “to sequence the decline of fossil fuel investment with the rapid scale-up of clean energy.”
Journalists have a critical role to play as governments work to phase out fossil fuels. That goal can only be achieved quickly — and speed is of the essence, scientists emphasize — if countries implement genuine climate solutions and shun false ones. News coverage that makes clear how well a given policy measures up to what’s needed, as Harvey did with her distinction between “carbon neutrality” and a fossil fuel phase-out, can keep the public informed and hold policymakers to account.
France and The Netherlands are two more big economies that have released roadmaps to phase out fossil fuel use. If enough other countries present credible plans for doing so, it “would send an unmistakable message that the age of oil, gas and coal is ending, and the smart money is shifting,” Mohamed Adow, director of the nonprofit Power Shift Africa, said in an interview with The Guardian.
As the costs of clean energy fall, humanity is in a “final battle” against the “evil forces” trying to keep the world dependent on fossil fuels, said Johan Rockstrom, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany, at a Climate Week event. Scientists at Rockstrom’s institute have studied which policies significantly reduce emissions, and which don’t. A paper published in Science evaluated “1,500 climate policies implemented … across 41 countries” and concluded that only 63 of them delivered significant reductions. There is no “one-size-fits-all” solution, but getting fossil fuel prices right — by slashing subsidies and otherwise challenging what US senator Sheldon Whitehouse calls Big Oil’s “pollute for free business model” — is essential. Complementary research the Drawdown Institute released during Climate Week highlighted a number of supposed solutions that are anything but. The institute’s list of “weak ideas and greenwashing tricks” includes carbon capture and storage, direct air capture of carbon dioxide, blue hydrogen, and corn ethanol.
A frequent topic of conversation at Climate Week was the US midterm elections, which could curb President Donald Trump’s acceleration of climate breakdown if Republicans lose control in Congress, though most Democrats (with important exceptions like Newsom and Whitehouse) are saying little about climate change on the campaign trail. Considering that 80 to 89% of the world’s people, and 74% of Americans, want stronger climate action, why do so many politicians practice “climate hushing”? And why do so many voters end up backing candidates who are indifferent at best to tackling climate change?
“We need to remember,” Rockstrom said, “that citizens have many other problems besides climate change, especially the cost of living. So, we need to make it easy for them to choose clean energy options, and that requires good policy.” It also requires, Newsom said, talking plainly about both the dangers and the solutions to the climate crisis. Leaders need to “connect the dots” between the heat, drought and other afflictions driven by climate change and “kitchen table” issues like the price of beef, coffee, and home insurance. “The cost of inaction,” Newsom added, “is incalculable.”
