title: Kim Yo Jong says North Korea tests missile
description: Kim Yo Jong says North Korea tests missile
content:
North Korea's Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said in a statement on Saturday that her country had tested an intermediate-range strategic missile.
The South Korean military said earlier on Saturday that North Korea fired a ballistic missile which flew more than 700 kilometers (435 miles) toward the sea off its east coast.
Kim Yo Jong, who is a director of North Korea's ruling party, said a drill of a "strategic weapon" was conducted toward the sea off its east coast using the intermediate-range missile.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un oversaw the drill which was carried out by "a firepower sub-unit undertaking an exclusive special mission," his sister said.
Citing statements by Seoul and Tokyo regarding how far the missile flew, she said that their results showed the limitations of their tracking capability.
"Whenever we applied the wave-like trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points," she said, without showing any evidence. South Korea and Japan also "should acknowledge the speed of the missile," she said without disclosing the speed.
The missile was also capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude with artificial intelligence technology applied, she added. "In other words, this means that there is no way to avoid this attack," she said. North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Pyongyang has sometimes said it was testing new types of weapons systems. Some of the tests have come after North Korea protested joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
The launch came after Kim Yo Jong issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul's demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone, a heavily fortified area between the two Koreas.

title: Tennessee prison chief resigns
description: Tennessee prison chief resigns
content:
The prison commissioner in the southern US state of Tennessee has resigned over the botched execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike, Governor Bill Lee said Saturday.
Lee said in a statement that commissioner Frank Strada would leave his post this month.
Pike's lawyers say she is in critical condition, unconscious and on a ventilator in a hospital, after her execution by lethal injection went wrong on Wednesday.
Pike, 50, survived two injections of the normally lethal substance pentobarbital as punishment for the murder of Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
It was the second failed execution in Tennessee this year. The state halted an execution in May after medical staff failed to tap a vein in the prisoner's arm.
Lee said he thanked Strada for "his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."
In the same statement, Strada said, "I continue to believe the Department (of Correction) carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol."

title: India detains several in Gen Z voter protests
description: India detains several in Gen Z voter protests
content:
Demonstrators say changes benefit PM Modi's ?governing party
Indian police detained several people in the capital New Delhi on Saturday, disrupting a second day of protests backed by the Gen Z-led Cockroach ?Janta Party and other opposition groups against changes to voter rolls.
The protesters say the changes benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ?governing party and are demanding the resignation of India's election chief.
The demonstrations mark the latest in a ?series of youth-led protests that have emerged this year, putting pressure on Modi unprecedented in his 12 years in power.
About 100 demonstrators removed security barricades on Saturday and chanted "vote thief, leave the post" and "Gyanesh Kumar, step down" before police ?forcibly detained some of them.
Independent Member of Parliament Kapil Sibal, left-wing All India Students' Association President Neha Bora and political activists Prashant Bhushan and Yogendra Yadav were among the protesters, according to a Reuters witness.
The police declined comment ?on the number and identity of those detained. "First they removed people from the voters list and now they are not letting us raise our voice against this. This is not acceptable," Bora told Reuters.
The chief of the Election Commission, Kumar, has not commented on the protests and the demands to step down.
On Friday, police stopped a group of protesters from gathering, bundling them into buses. Several nearby metro stations remained shut amid tight security. Though police released many of those detained on Friday, they charged several of them with allegedly violating orders banning mass gatherings in Delhi, according to a police source.
Critics say a nationwide voter-verification exercise launched last year has led to millions of eligible voters being removed from electoral rolls.
The commission, long regarded as one of the country's most trusted institutions, says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible voters.
On Friday the commission directed officials to register newly eligible voters and those omitted from electoral rolls.

title: Gaza health officials say Israeli strike kills 5

content:

title: Two Iranians face UK court over alleged Jewish plot
description: Two Iranians face UK court over alleged Jewish plot
content:
Two Iranian nationals appeared in a London court on Saturday charged with plotting acts of terrorism involving the use of a homemade bomb to attack the Jewish community in northern England at the behest of a figure believed to be based in Iran.
Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were arrested on September 20 at the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, when they are accused of carrying out "hostile" surveillance on potential Jewish targets in Manchester, prosecutors say.
These targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue, the scene of a deadly attack almost a year ago in which two Jewish worshippers were killed, prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court.
"Both defendants are accused of preparing acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a homemade explosive device," Luckett said.
He said the men were accused of being in contact with a third party who is alleged to have directed and coordinated the attack planning and provided instructions on how to assemble a homemade device, which prosecutors allege would have been made from chlorine and brake fluid.
"It's assessed that this individual is also an Iranian national and most likely operating from within Iran," Luckett said.
The court was told both men had come to Britain from Europe in small boats. Salehi had arrived in 2020 and had been granted asylum, while Ahmadyan came in 2023 and his asylum claim was still outstanding, Luckett said.
The men did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey court on October 23.

title: UAE says flydubai co-pilot attacked pilot with axe | The Express Tribune
description:
UAE says flydubai 
co-pilot attacked 
pilot with axe
content:
The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073, which was bound for Israel, attempted to carry out a "terrorist attack" with an axe during the flight, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday.
The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, a source with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
A second source briefed on the investigation confirmed the co-pilot's name. UAE authorities did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation of his identity.
Disaster was averted on Wednesday after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had attacked the captain in what Israeli officials said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying more than 170 passengers and crew.
While Emirati authorities and the airline have not publicly identified the co-pilot, Israeli officials have previously said he is an Omani national. Oman has not commented on the incident.
"Investigations into the incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack," Prosecutor General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said in a statement carried by the UAE's state news agency.
The co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft, the prosecutor general said. A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies such as crashes.
The investigation into flight FZ1073, including the suspect's motives, is ongoing, and the findings will be released once the "necessary procedures" have been completed, the prosecutor general said. The UAE is leading the investigation.
The airline is owned by Dubai's government.
The prosecutor general's comments were the first by Emirati investigators to describe the incident as an attempted terrorist attack.
Following the release of the prosecutor general's statement, Anwar Gargash, a senior adviser to the UAE president, said on X that the Gulf country had zero tolerance for terrorism and would show no leniency toward extremist rhetoric.
Flydubai said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation and that it was not in a position to comment further, a spokesperson said on Saturday.
Reuters could not immediately verify professional and social media pages reportedly belonging to the co-pilot, which suggested he had worked for other airlines.
Royal Air Maroc told Reuters, in response to a question about his potential employment there in the past, that he had undergone a three-month training with the airline in 2025 but his application to work there afterwards was rejected. RAM did not elaborate.

title: Houthis hit oil facility near Riyadh
description: Houthis hit oil facility near Riyadh
content:
Yemeni govt forces claim seizing fort in Taiz
Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on an oil facility near the Saudi capital on Saturday, where an AFP journalist saw flames and smoke, and accused the Gulf kingdom of striking Sanaa dozens of times.
Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that "Saudi enemy aircraft" hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, without providing details on the targets or casualties.
Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city.
In neighbouring Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh, an AFP journalist said.
While the Saudi authorities are yet to comment, late on Saturday, the Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, adding that they sparked fires at the targeted sites.
The AFP journalist reported seeing firefighters attempting to extinguish a blaze at Aramco's Riyadh refinery, located south of the capital, while ambulances and police vehicles were stationed near the facility.
The Houthis' Al-Masirah channel earlier on Saturday also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen's northwestern governorate of Saada, one of the group's strongholds.
It comes after the Houthis said that Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital itself on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July.
Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces have taken control of the Samaa fort after heavy clashes with the Houthi rebels southeast of the city of Taiz, Al Jazeera reports citing the government-run Saba news agency.
A military source tells Saba that government forces, backed by local popular resistance fighters from the Samaa district, took the fort after "violent battles" with Houthi fighters, with dozens of Houthi fighters killed or wounded and others fleeing.
Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides.
The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died.
The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to take control of Taiz city, which is Yemen's third-largest after Sanaa and Aden.
The Houthis also on Friday said Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours.
Saudi authorities meanwhile reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border.
Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump.
On Saturday US media outlet Axios reported that top cabinet members in the Trump administration met the day before to discuss Yemen as well as the Iran conflict, citing three US officials.
The meeting was not officially announced.

title: FO summons Indian envoy over civilian killings
description: FO summons Indian envoy over civilian killings
content:
Says BSF used unprovoked lethal force against unarmed civilians
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) on Saturday summoned the Indian Chargé d'Affaires and lodged a strong protest over the killing of two Pakistani civilians by personnel of the Indian Border Security Force (BSF) in the Bedian Sector along the International Border on Friday.
"The BSF personnel resorted to unprovoked lethal force against unarmed civilians. Such use of force was wholly unjustified and grossly disproportionate, resulting in the tragic loss of two precious lives. Pakistan categorically rejects any attempt to mischaracterise the deceased as 'infiltrators," said a statement issued by MoFA.
The statement came a day after two Pakistani civilians were killed, and another was injured after Indian BSF personnel opened fire near the Pakistan-India international border in Kasur. The incident reportedly occurred when three residents from Ladhar village moved a few steps beyond a border pillar, upon which BSF personnel opened fire on the men without warning.
According to MoFA, the incident amounted to a serious violation of fundamental human rights, including the right to life, and raised concerns over the protection of civilians under international law.
It noted that "the Indian side was called upon to conduct an immediate, transparent and credible investigation into the incident, take appropriate disciplinary and legal action against those found responsible, and formally communicate the findings and action taken to the Government of Pakistan."
Further, it added that "India was further urged to ensure respect for fundamental human rights and international law, strictly observe relevant bilateral arrangements and established border procedures, exercise maximum restraint in dealing with such situations, and take effective measures to prevent the recurrence of such incidents."

title: Bilawal credits PPP for averting emergency
description: Bilawal credits PPP for averting emergency
content:
He says terrorism should not be treated as a political issue but as a national one
PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said on Saturday that the federal government had decided to impose emergency or governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, but his party had urged it to first seek a political solution to enable all parties to fight terrorism together.
Speaking at an event in Karachi, Bilawal said emergency and governor's rule were constitutional and legal options that could be used when necessary, but political parties should make every effort to resolve the issue through dialogue before resorting to such measures.
"I understand that the federal government had made up its mind and was ready to immediately impose emergency in Pakhtunkhwa and implement governor's rule," he said.
He said the PPP believed that before using such "an atomic bomb" and imposing emergency, political parties should make a comprehensive effort to find a political solution that would enable them to fight terrorism "in a better way".
Bilawal said terrorism should not be treated as a political issue but as a national one, adding that the government and opposition should work together to counter the threat.
"We don't want terrorism to be seen as a political issue. We want it to be seen as a national issue," he said. "Whether you are in the opposition or in the government, we want you to fight it together."
He said the PPP, the federal government and President Asif Ali Zardari had remained in contact over the past few weeks as terrorist attacks continued in K-P and attacks from Afghanistan also increased.
He also referred to what he described as the role of India in the attacks, saying: "Whether these two attacks are of terrorism or of Afghanistan, whatever is happening, the hand of India behind it is also not a hidden thing."
Bilawal said the PPP wanted political parties to engage with the PTI and persuade it to end its planned long march on Islamabad.
He said the PTI had the right to protest and had achieved a degree of political success through its protest, but it should also recognise the worsening security situation in K-P.
"While you are focusing on your politics, you are focusing on your protest, terrorism is taking place in Pakhtunkhwa every other day," he said.
The PPP chairman said a formal written agreement should be reached between the PTI and the federal government under which both sides would work together to fight terrorism.
"If there is a political issue, you should keep it away from terrorism and national interests," he said, adding that political differences should be dealt with separately from the security situation.
His remarks came a day after the government and opposition held their first formal talks in years, with the two sides agreeing to continue negotiations on Saturday. The ruling coalition had decided to engage the opposition instead of immediately resorting to emergency or governor's rule in K-P.
Bilawal said the PPP wanted all political parties to reach an "amicable political solution" in the interest of the provinces and people of Pakistan so that the country did not have to resort to emergency measures to fight terrorism.
"Terrorism is the red line of the Pakistan People's Party," he said, adding that the party had lost workers and leaders to terrorism.
He warned that continued deterioration in Balochistan and K-P could have consequences beyond the two provinces, particularly for Karachi.
"Karachi is a mini Pakistan. We are connected to every city, every province," he said. "If Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa gets sick, Karachi gets a cough."
Bilawal said the PPP considered terrorism a major issue because any deterioration in the security situation in Balochistan and K-P would eventually affect other parts of the country.
Earlier in his address, the PPP chairman spoke at length about issues confronting Karachi, saying the city had been treated unfairly by the federal government despite its contribution to the national economy.
He said Karachi continued to face shortages of water, electricity and gas, despite Sindh being a major gas-producing province.
"Your Constitution says that the first right is theirs, where this resource is produced," he said, referring to the province's claim to its share of natural gas.
He also criticised the federal government over the K-IV water project, saying the Centre had failed to fulfil its commitment to contribute 50 per cent of the project's cost.
Bilawal said the Sindh government, Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab and the public-private partnership model had provided a way forward for the project.
He also criticised delays in the Hyderabad-Sukkur motorway, saying completion of the project would benefit Karachi and Pakistan's wider economy.
The PPP chairman praised Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, the Karachi mayor and local representatives for working on the city's water problems.
"We will continue to listen to all their complaints and criticisms. We will continue to do our work," he said.

title: No breakthrough after marathon PTI govt talks
description: No breakthrough after marathon PTI govt talks
author_name: AAMIR ILAYS RANA, Khalid Mehmood, Usama Iqbal, Naeem Asghar
content:
PTI leader Asad Qaiser confirmed that the talks ended without reaching an agreement
Marathon talks between the government and opposition on Saturday failed to find a middle ground in an effort to break the deadlock over the PTI's long march, as both sides pressed competing demands and remained at an impasse.
The talks, chaired by National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq, followed an initial round on Friday in which the two sides exchanged their positions but failed to reach an agreement.
PTI leader Asad Qaiser confirmed that the talks ended without reaching an agreement.
The two sides remained divided over who should take the first step to ease tensions surrounding the opposition party's planned march.
The government wanted the PTI to take the initiative by cancelling the march, while the opposition wanted the government to first facilitate a meeting with its jailed founder, according to sources familiar with the talks.
Members of the two negotiating teams were also seen stepping outside the National Assembly speaker's chamber to consult with one another during the discussions.
The sources said the two sides had reached agreement on all points by 9pm, but the talks ran into a fresh hurdle after Opposition Leader in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai raised a different position.
Achakzai said the authority to call off the march rested with PTI founder Imran Khan and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, according to the sources.
The sources said Achakzai's position led to a deadlock, while tensions increased after Afridi posted about the march on social media platform X.
The sources said President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif wanted the issues to be resolved through negotiations
This development followed the second round of talks between the government, the PPP and the opposition, chaired by National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq. The talks were convened as the October 4 deadline for the PTI-backed long march approached.
According to sources, the government agreed to several demands during the negotiations, including facilitating a meeting between opposition leaders and Imran Khan.
Sources also said an understanding was reached regarding the release of some leaders and workers detained under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO), including Imran's three sisters.
The government also reportedly agreed to consider implementing the Supreme Court's August order concerning Imran's treatment at a private hospital and offered to establish a committee to examine complaints regarding the shrinking political space for the opposition.
The government's reported concessions were linked to the opposition's willingness to call off the October 4 march, which remained the principal point of contention in the negotiations. Earlier, the government had sought cancellation of the protest, while the PTI side had linked any decision to the outcome of talks and access to Imran Khan.
The talks, however, encountered a fresh hurdle when Achakzai contacted PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan and former NA speaker Asad Qaiser and made it clear that no final announcement should be made before meeting Imran Khan.
According to sources, Achakzai maintained that any decision by the PTI or the opposition alliance to call off the street movement would require Imran's approval.
TTAP spokesperson Akhundzada Hussain Ahmed Yousufzai said Achakzai had instructed the opposition delegation to seek a meeting with Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi as its first priority, followed by meetings with Achakzai and Allama Nasir Abbas.
The preference for meeting Afridi first was linked to the fact that the K-P chief minister had announced the long march, which was earlier scheduled for September 27 but later postponed until today (October 4).
According to the spokesperson, Afridi could brief the former prime minister o0n the progress made during the two days of negotiations and obtain his response.
Achakzai's position effectively meant that the reported understanding between the government and opposition could not immediately be converted into a final announcement about the march.
Reports said Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who played a key role in the negotiations, left Parliament House with the draft understanding and went to the Prime Minister's House to consult the senior leadership before returning to Parliament House, after which talks resumed.
The second round followed an inconclusive first round held on Friday.
The initial meeting ended with both sides exchanging their respective positions but without a breakthrough. They agreed to resume negotiations on Saturday. The National Assembly described Friday's meeting as being held in a "cordial" and constructive atmosphere.
The opposition's demand for access to Imran Khan had emerged as a central issue from the outset. During the first round, opposition representatives maintained that major political decisions could not be taken without consulting the PTI founder.
The government delegation included Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Minister for States and Frontier Regions Amir Muqam, Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry and Prime Minister's Adviser Rana Sanaullah, along with PPP representatives Senator Sherry Rehman, Naveed Qamar and Ijaz Hussain Jakhrani.
The opposition delegation included Mahmood Khan Achakzai, Barrister Gohar Khan, Raja Nasir Abbas, Asad Qaiser, Salman Akram Raja, Amir Dogar and Haleem Adil Sheikh. Achakzai had earlier declined to attend the talks at the Speaker's chamber, seeking a neutral venue.
The negotiations are taking place against the backdrop of heightened tensions between the federal and K-P governments and the PTI's plan to bring supporters towards Islamabad.
A number of federal ministers have threatened to consider imposing Governor's Rule in K-P, where the PTI is in power, if the opposition continued with its plans to march on the capital.
On Friday, the military's top brass also underscored the importance of internal stability and resolved that any attempt to cause agitation or create a May 9-like situation, "on any pretext whatsoever, will be dealt with decisive force and rule of law, without hesitation and discrimination.
On May 9, 2023, the PTI supporters and workers staged violent protests after arrest of former prime minister Imran Khan from the premises of the Islamabad High Court and attacked dozens of military installations, followed by a grand crackdown against the former ruling party.

title: Trump shares senator s number in time feud
description: Trump shares senator s number in time feud
content:
US President Donald Trump on Saturday posted online the supposed phone number of a Republican US senator, escalating a feud over daylight saving time.
Trump's social media post urged people to call a phone number that he said belonged to Senator Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican. The dispute centers on the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent and end the twice-yearly practice of changing clocks by one hour.
Trump says most Americans want more afternoon sunlight, but Cotton has argued the change would plunge early risers into darkness during winter months. "Everybody in Arkansas, Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
When Reuters called the Arkansas number, it went directly to a voicemail box that did not identify itself as belonging to Cotton. It's the president's second posting in as many days about Cotton's opposition to the bill.
"Nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year and, having sunshine in the afternoon is better than early in the morning!" Trump wrote.

title: Hurriyat delegation meets AJK president
description: Hurriyat delegation meets AJK president
content:
A delegation of the All Parties Hurriyat Conference (APHC), led by Convener Ghulam Muhammad Safi, on Saturday called on President Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Dr Muhammad Najib Khan and discussed the latest situation in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir (IIOJK).
The meeting discussed Indian actions in IIOJK, alleged human rights violations, the situation of Hurriyat leaders and activists, and efforts to highlight the Kashmir issue at the international level.
The AJK president said the Jammu and Kashmir dispute was an internationally recognised issue and its final settlement should be in accordance with the aspirations of the Kashmiri people and relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions, a press release issued here said.
He said the Kashmiri people should be given their right to self-determination to decide their future, and appreciated Pakistan's political, diplomatic and moral support for the Kashmir cause.
Dr Najib Khan said the unilateral actions of August 5, 2019 could not change the disputed status of Jammu and Kashmir or affect the Kashmiri people's right to self-determination.
He called upon the international community to take notice of the situation in IIOJK and urged the UN human rights bodies and international observers to be given access to the territory for an impartial assessment of the situation.
The president also called for highlighting alleged human rights violations, arrests of political activists and Hurriyat leaders and restrictions on freedom of expression in IIOJK.
He said the United Nations should fulfill its commitments to the Kashmiri people and urged the international community to press India for implementation of relevant UN resolutions.
Ghulam Muhammad Safi and other Hurriyat leaders congratulated Dr Muhammad Najib Khan on his election as President of AJK and conveyed their best wishes to him.
The APHC convener briefed the AJK president on the latest situation in IIOJK and the challenges faced by Hurriyat leaders and activists.
He said the Hurriyat Conference would continue its political and diplomatic efforts to highlight the Kashmir issue at the global level and advocate the right to self-determination of the Kashmiri people.

title: Yadgar e Fatah monument opens to public
description: Yadgar e Fatah monument opens to public
content:
A large number of people thronged the Yadgar-e-Fatah Monument here on Saturday after it was opened to the general public, commemorating the country's victory over India in the Marka-e-Haq Operation 2025 and paying tribute to the martyrs who sacrificed their lives for the homeland.
The special ceremony jointly organized by Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, and Capital Development Authority held at the monument's premises gathered people from all walks of life to celebrate the moment of national pride.
The ceremony was attended by prominent figures including President Chess Federation Zeeshan Naqvi and emerging national cricketer Razaullah, as well as famous public personality from the world of sports, 'Chacha Cricket'.
Speaking on the occasion, cricketer Razaullah paid rich tribute to the bravery of Pakistan's armed forces and their invaluable sacrifices. He said that Pakistan's armed forces had defeated the enemy decisively in the past and would continue to do so in the future. He added that he felt immensely proud to be a Pakistani.

title: Pakistan s environmental ranking improves yet air quality lags
description: Pakistan s environmental ranking improves yet air quality lags
content:
Overall improvement in global ranking does not necessarily reflect progress in air pollution control
Pakistan has improved 22 places in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index (EPI), ranking 157th out of 177 countries, but its performance in air quality and environmental health remains among the weakest globally, raising questions about whether the overall improvement reflects actual progress in controlling pollution.
According to Yale University's 2026 Environmental Performance Index report, Pakistan scored 29.03 overall, with an environmental health score of 14.57 and an air quality score of just 7.54. Pakistan ranked 179th in 2024, but changes to the methodology and indicators in the 2026 index mean the two rankings should be compared with caution.
The 2026 index includes 47 indicators across 12 major environmental categories. Experts say the improvement in Pakistan's overall ranking cannot, therefore, be taken as direct evidence that air pollution has declined.
Available air-quality data indicate a different trend. During the first 23 days of September 2026, Lahore's average Air Quality Index (AQI) was approximately 96, compared with about 80 during the same period last year. On September 23, Lahore recorded an AQI of 153, compared with 97 on the same date last year.
Rawalpindi also recorded a higher average AQI during the first 23 days of September 2026, at approximately 116, compared with about 75 during the corresponding period last year. In Lahore, pollution levels also tend to rise during morning and evening hours, further affecting air quality.
Environmental expert and lawyer Rafay Alam said smog should not be viewed solely as a winter problem, as transport, power generation and industrial emissions remain important sources of pollution throughout the year. He noted that changes in temperature and air pressure during winter cause pollutants to accumulate closer to the ground.
Alam called for sustained, long-term policies, better public transport, greater use of electric vehicles and alternative energy, stronger controls on industrial emissions and improved fuel standards.
According to data from the Punjab Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), fines totalling Rs305.1 million were imposed for violations of environmental laws during 2025-26, 66 per cent more than the previous year. During the same period, 5,461 sites were sealed and 1,467 polluting units were demolished, while 101,159 inspections of brick kilns and industrial units were conducted.
During a one-week period, 577 anti-pollution operations were carried out across 40 districts of Punjab. Of 7,203 field visits, 607 violations were identified, fines of more than Rs22.8 million were imposed, 483 properties and industrial units were sealed and 30 cases were registered.
Authorities also confiscated 12,906 kilograms of banned plastic bags during the same period. In Lahore, 180 properties were sealed during 181 enforcement operations.
The owner of an industrial unit on Mahmood BootiBand Road, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the EPA had made it mandatory in 2023 for such industrial units to install emissions-control systems. According to him, steel mills and other industries that installed the systems were not shut down during the 2023 smog season, while industrial closures during smog began in 2024 and 2025.
"Repeated fines and temporary closures led some industrialists to prefer paying penalties rather than installing emissions-control systems," said the industrialist, who called on the government to focus not only on fines and closures but also on ensuring the installation and effective monitoring of emissions-control systems.
According to the industrialist, a standard emissions-control system can cost several crore rupees, although effective systems are also available at comparatively lower costs.
The available data do not establish that Punjab's recent anti-pollution enforcement efforts caused Pakistan's improvement in the global environmental ranking. Experts say their impact can only be assessed through continuous, long-term monitoring of air quality and industrial emissions using a consistent methodology.

title: Punjab boards to take paper checking online
description: Punjab boards to take paper checking online
content:
Boards to scan answer scripts for on-screen evaluation
Punjab's education boards are preparing to replace physical examination paper checking with scanning of answer scripts and on-screen evaluation.
According to sources in the education sector, the decision is aimed at reducing marking errors and improving accountability and students' confidence in examination results.
Under the proposed system, completed answer scripts will be scanned and converted into secure digital record before being assigned electronically to authorised examiners for assessment.
Instead of receiving bundles of papers at conventional marking centres, the examiners will evaluate scanned scripts through a controlled online platform. Punjab Education Minister Rana Sikandar Hayat has directed all education boards to introduce digital reforms and launch online screen marking initially on a pilot basis for supplementary examinations.
He has also ordered the boards to take action against examiners involved in incorrect marking and strengthen monitoring of the evaluation process.
Sources said the proposed framework would introduce stronger identity verification for examiners to prevent unauthorised persons from accessing answer scripts. Under the mechanism being considered, examiners would be authenticated through facial recognition or other secure verification measures before being allowed to enter the marking system.
The objective is to ensure that the examiner assigned a particular script evaluates it. The proposed safeguards would also make it difficult for an examiner to share login credentials or allow another person to perform marking on his or her behalf.
Earlier reforms also moved the examination system towards biometric and digital verification.
The Lahore board has made biometric thumb impressions mandatory for Class IX and XI candidates during registration, while authorities have been working to strengthen digital identification and monitoring at examination centres. The Lahore Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education (BISE) has already announced e-marking reforms under which theory papers are scanned and digitised, while examiners receive secure IDs to evaluate scripts remotely. The system is being introduced gradually, with officials indicating that its use will expand to additional subjects over time.
The sources said the proposed marking mechanism would also impose time limits for examiners. Each digitally assigned sheet would have to be evaluated within a prescribed period, allowing examination authorities to track pending scripts and identify unusual delays.
The time bound mechanism is expected to address another longstanding weakness of difficulty to determine when a paper was received, who handled it and how long was spent evaluating it. Under the digital system, each marking activity can generate an electronic record, creating an audit trail for the boards.
Complaints of incorrect marking, unchecked answers, calculation mistakes and inconsistencies between examiners have repeatedly caused concerns among students and parents.
The provincial government has been pushing the boards towards systems that reduce the risk of human error while retaining qualified teachers as the final decision-makers.
The proposed arrangement may also change the way examiners receive answer scripts. Instead of an examiner being handed hundreds of answer books, papers or individual questions may be allocated electronically in batches.
The Lahore BISE has disclosed plans involving smaller batches of questions to improve accuracy and efficiency.
Another benefit would be reduction in physical movement of answer scripts. Once papers are scanned, their digital copies can be distributed to authorised evaluators without transporting original scripts.

title: Women break free on two wheels
description: Women break free on two wheels
content:
Affordable bikes, family support and improved policing help women travel more freely
The morning traffic is beginning to swell when a woman pulls down her helmet, grips the handlebar of her scooty and joins the stream of vehicles. It may look like an ordinary commute, but for many women, taking control of the handlebar represents something much bigger: independence.
For years, women travelling to schools, colleges, workplaces, markets and hospitals have often depended on fathers, brothers, husbands or hired drivers. Their journeys were shaped not only by distance but by someone else's availability. A missed ride could mean a missed class, delayed work or a cancelled errand.
That is changing as more women take to scooters and motorcycles. Two-wheelers offer affordable mobility while giving women control over their time and routines.
Alia, from Sialkot, said unnecessary attention remained one of the biggest challenges. "You constantly feel watched and stared at. It honestly feels like you are being observed and judged everywhere you go," she said.
For Rehana and Nighat, beauty experts, family encouragement helped them overcome their initial hesitation. Nighat said riding had made her daily routine considerably easier as she no longer had to wait for public transport or depend entirely on her husband. She can now travel independently and take her mother along when needed.
Yet greater mobility has also exposed women to harassment on the roads. Rabia Sajid, another scooter rider, said some men followed female riders, honked unnecessarily, overtook aggressively or made inappropriate comments. On occasions when she felt followed, she changed her route and avoided the road afterwards.
Such experiences highlight a crucial contradiction: women are encouraged to study, work and participate in society, yet some continue to face intimidation simply for travelling independently.
Government initiatives offering free, subsidised or interest-free scooters and electric bikes are helping remove one major barrier - affordability. But access to vehicles alone cannot guarantee freedom of movement.
ASI Azra of the Islamabad Traffic Police said protecting women on the capital's roads was a priority. She said women police personnel, increased patrolling and Safe City cameras were helping strengthen security. Women facing harassment or insecurity can seek assistance through police helplines 15 and 1815, she said.
Laher Mirza, a Victim Support Officer at the Tahaffuz Centre, Rawalpindi, said continued police monitoring and patrolling had improved women's confidence on the roads.

title: Drug court keeps women accused in prison vans

The newly established Special Anti-Narcotics Court No 2, operating from a privately rented residence outside the Kachehri premises without permission from the Lahore High Court (LHC), has created serious difficulties for women accused of drug-related offences and raised security concerns.
The court premises have been rented for Rs300,000 a month but lack a washroom for women accused and a temporary lock-up. Consequently, both male and female accused are kept inside a prison van while awaiting their cases.
District and Sessions Judge Khalid Bashir Cheema heads the new court, while lawyers said the court was also operating with insufficient staff.
Women accused remain confined to the vehicle from 8am to 4pm, spending nearly eight hours inside it. They said even attending to basic washroom needs had become extremely difficult.
The women and their relatives said they were taken from Adiala Jail at 7am and brought to the court by 8am. In the absence of a lock-up, they remain inside the vehicle in the heat until their cases are heard.
They said police officials told them to return to the jail to use the washroom, while the only washroom at the rented premises was reserved for the judge and could not be used by accused persons.
The women demanded that, if the court was to continue functioning from the premises, a room should immediately be constructed as a temporary lock-up, along with a washroom. Alternatively, a separate room at the residence should be declared a sub-jail lock-up until completion of the hearings, or the accused should be shifted to the Kacheri lock-up.
Relatives said the particular difficulties faced by women accused were not being given due consideration.
Lawyers also expressed concern over the premises, saying the low boundary walls posed a serious security risk. They said there was no proper sitting room for lawyers, forcing them to conduct proceedings while standing.
According to the lawyers, shifting a court from the Kacheri premises to a private residence requires formal permission and notification from the LHC.
They recalled that former Chief Justice of Pakistan Iftikhar Chaudhry had declared seven special courts operating outside the Rawalpindi Kachehri illegal in 2013 and ordered their relocation to the Kacheri.

Capcom plans to integrate AI technology into its RE Engine as part of a long-term effort to streamline game development, following a presentation by studio programmer Satoshi Ishida.
The plans were discussed during Capcom’s recent technology conference, where Ishida outlined changes being developed through an improvement programme called “REX”. The initiative is intended to build on the existing RE Engine rather than replace it with a new engine.
According to the presentation, Capcom is facing challenges as games become larger and more time-consuming to develop, increasing the need for additional staff and an engine that is easier to use.
Ishida said AI technology would be integrated “into development workflows” as an “essential condition for streamlining future development”.
A key part of REX involves making some of its improvements open-source to help train AI. Capcom’s long-term goal was initially reported as turning the RE Engine into an “AI-generation game engine”.
However, a subsequent clarification suggested the wording may have been mistranslated. Twitter user HazzadorGamin said the intended description was that the RE Engine is becoming a “game engine for the AI era”.
That distinction could indicate that Capcom intends to develop the engine for an industry increasingly using AI-assisted technology rather than necessarily creating games with generative AI.
Capcom has previously said it uses AI to “free up time for creative work”, while also stating that it would not ship games containing AI-generated assets.

title: Steam could break  20b annual revenue record in 2026
description: Steam generated record  1 7b in September 2026 as analysts predict annual revenue could exceed  20b
content:
Steam generated record $1.7b in September 2026 as analysts predict annual revenue could exceed $20b
Steam could become the first gaming platform in its history to generate more than $20 billion in annual revenue, according to Alinea Analytics.
The prediction follows a record September for Valve’s PC gaming platform, which generated $1.7 billion in revenue during the month. That surpassed the $1.5 billion recorded in September 2025.
Steam also generated $5.5 billion during the third quarter of 2026, up 12% from the same period last year. Revenue for the first nine months reached $16.5 billion, compared with $14.5 billion during the corresponding period in 2025.
Alinea Analytics expects further game releases during the remainder of 2026 to help Steam pass the $20 billion mark. If reached, the figure would represent the first time the platform has exceeded $20 billion in annual revenue.
Among the 500 highest-grossing games on Steam in September, which accounted for around one-third of the platform’s total revenue, 20.5% were brand-new franchises.
Games from older series made up the remainder, while remasters and remakes accounted for 3.8%.
Games released in 2026 generated 33.6% of Steam’s revenue during September. Free-to-play games accounted for a further 25.6% of the month’s revenue.
Counter-Strike 2, Apex Legends, PUBG and Dota 2 generated a combined $168 million, accounting for around 10% of Steam’s total September revenue.
Wardogs was among September’s highest-grossing games, generating $86.9 million between September 1 and 30. The 100-player tactical first-person shooter features build-and-destroy mechanics.

Chad Lowe’s daughter Mabel has honoured her late sister Fiona in Instagram post following her death
Chad Lowe’s 17-year-old daughter, Mabel, has honoured her late sister Fiona in an Instagram post following the 13-year-old’s death.
Mabel shared photos of herself and Fiona throughout their childhood on October 3, including images of the sisters dancing together when Fiona was a toddler and a dance portrait of Fiona.
“I love you so much, Fiona,” Mabel wrote. “I wish your short time here was easier and I hope your mind is at ease now.”

The Lowe family confirmed Fiona’s death in a statement to PEOPLE on September 29.
“We are deeply heartbroken by the loss of our beloved Fiona,” the family said, describing her as “a loving young girl who was smart, creative and loved to dance.”
“She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents,” the family added. “In fact, she was the light of our lives.”
“Her passing is devastating for our entire family, and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time,” they continued.
Fiona was the second of Chad and his wife Kim Painter’s three daughters. The couple are also parents to Mabel and 10-year-old Nixie.
A source told PEOPLE on September 30 that Fiona’s school and wider community were coming together to honour her memory.
“The school and community are very inclusive, artistic, a warm place. Parents are friends and most are involved with the school. This is a devastating time for the community,” the insider said.
The source added that the Lowe family is “very involved” with the school and described Fiona as “sweet, quiet and kind”, saying dance was her “biggest passion”.
Another source said Chad’s older brother, actor Rob Lowe, and the rest of the family were supporting Chad and Kim following Fiona’s death.

title: Dog bite cases rise at alarming level
description: Dog bite cases rise at alarming level
content:
Govt yet to launch campaign to neuter, vaccinate stray dogs
The city is experiencing an alarming surge in dog bite cases, while the Sindh government remains confined to planning a campaign to neuter and vaccinate stray dogs, especially seven years after an identical drive failed to secure the desired objectives.
The city has recorded a 63 per cent increase in these cases in 2026 in comparison to the previous year, a meeting chaired by Deputy Commissioner Zainul Abedin Memon was briefed on Saturday.
District Health Officer (DHO) Hyderabad Dr Pir Ghulam Hussain shared that the nine Anti-Rabies Centres, functioning in Hyderabad, received 2,944 patients from January to September this year.
He apprised that during the same period in 2025 the combined figure of the year's first nine months was 1,805 patients.
As per the statistics shared by the DHO with The Express Tribune, not only the year-on-year comparison has shown a surge, the same hike is visible even in the month-to-month figures. As many as 322 people were bitten in January this year against 91 in 2025.
The highest number of these cases touched the 306 mark in July last year, while the current year's seventh lowest figure happens to be the same, 306, as registered in May.
Some 396 patients were recorded in July 2026, while the numbers for April, June, August, September and January were 359, 358, 357, 338 and 322, respectively.
Alarmingly, 558 or almost 20 per cent of the dog bite victims are still receiving medical treatment. Some 352 patients were given Equine Rabies Immunoglobulin (ERIG) doses because they were placed in category III of the rabies.
According to the DHO, dog bite cases usually enhanced during July to September breeding season. The deputy commissioner viewed the growing stray-dog population as a serious public health concern.
Memon noted that rabies becomes fatal once clinical symptoms develop in patients.
He directed the officials to monitor all the nine Anti Rabies Centers regularly to assess treatment procedures and availability of ARVs. It was decided that a review meeting would be held every two weeks.
Despite some efforts, including a drive by Sindh's Rabies Control Programme to sterilise over 25,500 dogs and vaccinate more than 36,900 across 20 districts, stray dog populations continue to grow.
The WHO recommends vaccinating at least 70 per cent of a dog population to break transmission cycles, and at the current pace, Sindh will likely never come close to that number.

title: Officers sacrifice promotions to retain posts
description: Officers sacrifice promotions to retain posts
content:
Revenue officers decline Grade-17 promotions to retain Sub-Registrar posts, prompting CM intervention
In Sindh's bureaucracy, some chairs are apparently harder to leave than they are to win. For dozens of Revenue Department officers, the allure of a coveted posting has been strong enough to make them hold on to their seats-even when a higher grade was on offer.
The issue of merit-based appointments in Sindh's government departments has reached a point where officers are competing for "good positions", while those already occupying such posts are unwilling to relinquish them even at the cost of promotions.
Recently, 63 officers serving as Sub-Registrars in the Revenue Department surprised officials by agreeing to forgo their promotion to the next grade in order to remain in their existing positions.
The officers were due to be promoted from Grade 15 to Grade 17. Their promotion had been approved at a meeting of the Departmental Promotion Committee chaired by Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah in May 2026.
However, the 63 officers subsequently submitted written requests to the Revenue Department stating that they did not want to be promoted. Surprisingly, the department accepted their requests.
The Revenue Department issued a notification on August 25, 2026, containing the names of all 63 officers. It stated that their requests to decline promotion had been approved.
Under the relevant rules, officers who declined promotion during the promotion exercise would not be eligible for promotion for the next four years. Despite this, all 63 officers were apparently willing to accept the consequences of foregoing their promotions.
The matter later went viral on social media, prompting Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah to take notice.
Following the chief minister's intervention, the Revenue Department issued another notification on August 27, withdrawing the earlier notification that had approved the officers' requests to decline promotion.
Despite the embarrassment caused to the government, there has so far been no information about disciplinary action against any official responsible for accepting the officers' requests.
The Express Tribune contacted the spokesperson for the Chief Minister's House regarding the matter, but no response was received.
The development has raised questions about the circumstances that led 63 officers to prefer remaining as Sub-Registrars over receiving promotion to Grade 17, as well as the department's decision to accept their requests despite the apparent implications under the promotion rules.
Sub-Registrars in the Revenue Department are responsible for registering documents relating to immovable property. Their duties include scrutinising and registering legal documents concerning the sale and purchase, mortgage, lease and transfer of land and other property.
They are also responsible for verifying the identities of the parties involved, confirming their consent and signatures on documents, maintaining registered documents and records, issuing certified copies and collecting registration fees and other government revenues.
The episode has also highlighted broader concerns surrounding appointments and postings in Sindh's government departments, where officers often seek postings to positions considered more desirable or financially attractive.

Monument to remain open daily from 5pm to 10pm, with free entry tickets available online
The Yadgar-e-Fatah Monument, commemorating Pakistan’s victory over India in the Marka-e-Haq Operation 2025 and paying tribute to the martyrs who sacrificed their lives for the country, was opened to the general public on Saturday.
A special ceremony jointly organised by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and the Capital Development Authority (CDA) was held at the monument’s premises, drawing people from different walks of life to celebrate what was described as a moment of national pride.
Speaking on the occasion, Information and Broadcasting Secretary Ashfaq Ahmad Khalil said the Yadgar-e-Fatah monument served as a landmark of the nation’s victory, anchored in courage and unwavering determination.

He termed the opening of the monument a moment of pride for the nation and future generations.
The ceremony was attended by prominent figures, including President Chess Federation Zeeshan Naqvi, emerging national cricketer Razaullah and well-known sports personality ‘Chacha Cricket’.
Razaullah paid tribute to the bravery of Pakistan’s armed forces and their sacrifices. He said the armed forces had defeated the enemy decisively in the past and would continue to do so in the future. He added that he felt immensely proud to be a Pakistani.
Chacha Cricket waves the national flag during the opening ceremony of the Yadgar-e-Fatah (Monument of Victory) in Islamabad on Saturday. Photo: APP
Chacha Cricket congratulated the nation on the “remarkable victory” in Marka-e-Haq and said the nation was ready to sacrifice its lives for the motherland. He said Pakistan had earned a prominent place in the world through its achievements.
A documentary was also screened at the ceremony, showcasing the eight-month construction journey of the monument and the concept behind its architecture and design.
The monument features five archways, symbolising the five pillars of Islam as well as the five pillars of the country — the government, military, media, people and the ideology underpinning the nation.
Its design also represents the three wings of Pakistan’s armed forces — the Army, Air Force and Navy — along with cyber defence and space warfare branches.
A projection-mapping show was presented on the monument, using lights and visuals to narrate its significance and highlight key moments associated with the country’s victory in the Marka-e-Haq Operation.

The Yadgar-e-Fatah monument will remain open to the public daily from 5pm to 10pm, except Mondays. Free entry tickets can be obtained through the website Yadgarefatah.net.

title: Rethinking education in Pakistan
description: Rethinking education in Pakistan
content:
Pakistan needs and deserves a major social transformation
If to do were as easy to know that were good to do,
Chapels had been churches, and poor man's cottages princes' palaces.
Pakistan needs and deserves a major social transformation, one built on the principle that opportunities for every individual should be maximised while aggressive and destructive tendencies are effectively discouraged. Such a transformation will not happen overnight. It will require generational effort. But its foundation must be laid today, and that foundation is education. If education is expected to transform society, then society must also transform the way it thinks about and provides education. That requires a fundamental change in the priorities of the political leadership that has governed this country and which has consistently treated education as a secondary concern. How can Pakistan aspire to become a modern, welfare-oriented democratic state when more than 30 million school-age children remain out of school?
Education should be treated as an end in itself, not merely as a means to an end. There is no dearth of behavioural scientists in our country, and if the quantity and quality of education we provide can be aligned with what these behavioural scientists tell us about human behaviour, character and social development, we may reasonably hope to see a change in the nature and performance of our governments, say twenty years from now. Education is one of the most vital institutions of any society because its influence extends far beyond the acquisition of knowledge and skills. It shapes the kind of individuals and citizens a society produces. The importance of this idea was beautifully captured in the opening line of Dr Asghar Zaidi's article, 'What a week at Oxford taught me about character foundation', published in this newspaper on September 29, 2026. He wrote: "Teaching has gone on in Oxford for nine centuries and it has never confined itself to what a person knows; it has always cared what a person becomes."
The analogy of the duel helps explain how societies change. An old system often survives until people begin to recognise and experience its harmful consequences, thus creating demand for something better. In societies where dueling was once accepted as a legitimate means of settling disputes, the practice continued for as long as its social legitimacy endured. However, changing ideas about law, justice and social order helped replace such practices with more institutionalised forms of dispute resolution. The same principle applies to education. Quality education is perhaps the most important shield a society can develop against incompetence reaching positions of power. The premise is that society must first change the nature and quality of education if education is eventually to change society. Such change requires a government capable of asking the right questions about the kind of society it wants to build, challenging outdated assumptions and developing policies that give education the priority, structure and resources necessary to produce that transformation.
There is a magnetic effect in the way functioning societies draw newly graduated students towards them. Graduates look forward to becoming responsible stakeholders in a society that offers them opportunities to use their knowledge, build their careers and contribute to something larger than themselves. In Pakistan, however, many university graduates look beyond their own society and see political turmoil, governments and opposition locked in an almost perpetual power struggle, and a political environment marked by protests, confrontation and intimidation. They are increasingly encouraged to imagine a more secure and rewarding professional future abroad, and many consequently begin to see emigration not simply as an opportunity but as an escape from an uncertain future at home.
One of the important responsibilities of university education is to develop in students a sense of citizenship, responsibility and commitment to the society in which they live. Yet that commitment becomes difficult to sustain when the society awaiting them outside the university appears to contradict what they have been taught inside it. A simple example used to explain order to students is the difference between a row of books neatly arranged on a shelf and a heap of books scattered across the floor. The former represents order, the latter, disorder. But when students look beyond the university walls, they may see a society that resembles the heap of books more than the orderly shelf.
The law appears inconsistent, and it very often and most relentlessly seems to favour the strong. The prevailing uncertainty and insecurity in the society decreases the incentive of university students to become committed stakeholders in the society outside. Having studied politics and history, university students are also aware of the repeated difficulties Pakistan has faced in securing its economic and security interests. They are taught to value order, accountability and institutional discipline, yet they encounter a political system in which these principles often appear difficult to sustain. The contradiction is difficult to ignore. We educate young people to become responsible citizens, while the society into which they graduate often gives them reasons to look elsewhere.
Pakistan does not lack the knowledge of what needs to be done. What it has lacked is the will to do what it knows to be necessary. If education is to become the instrument of social transformation, it must be treated not as an expenditure to be minimised or a means of producing degrees, but as the foundation on which the character of the nation is built. The real test of our educational system is therefore not simply how many graduates it produces, but what kind of citizens those graduates become and what kind of society is waiting for them when they leave the university. We cannot continue teaching our young people the virtues of order, merit, accountability and responsibility while exposing them to institutions that routinely contradict those very principles. The change we seek may take a generation, but every change begins with a decision. If, as Portia reminds us, doing what is good were as easy as knowing what is good, Pakistan would already have changed. The challenge before us is to finally turn what we know into what we can do.

title: Is PTI reading the military right
description: Is PTI reading the military right
content:
Long march, or the threat of it, has only forced it to double down and dig in its heels further
The talks in Islamabad between the government and opposition are important but the developments in Rawalpindi far more so. Let's do a deep dive.
1. The Corps Commanders' Conference on Friday issued an official statement that was pointedly sharp and direct. A bit surprising even. It addressed many key issues but I want to focus on the political one. The statement said: "Forum underscored the importance of internal stability and resolved that any attempt to cause agitation or create 9th May like situation, on any pretext whatsoever, will be dealt with decisive force and rule of law, without hesitation and discrimination."
2. In these few words, there are five very distinct and well-considered messages that are timed for maximum impact. Before I spell them out, consider the following for context: (i) talks between the government and opposition in the National Assembly Speaker's chamber are, at best, an attempt to avert a collision, and not meant to find a durable solution to the political problem; (ii) CM K-P Sohail Afridi remains aggressively ambivalent about the exact nature of the long march even as organisational and strategic disagreements within the party hierarchy weigh him down; (iii) Governor's Rule and emergency options for K-P by the federal government remain on the table primarily because they are not linked only to the PTI's long march. There's a bigger game afoot. A hint of this is contained in the five different messages within the statement of the Commanders' conference. Here's the breakdown:
3. "Forum underscored the importance of internal stability " These words go to the heart of the system's foremost priority. The logic underpinning this priority says that stability in policy, in direction, in politics, and on the streets is key to the governance agenda. The rising wave of terrorism is therefore the main challenge to this notion of stability. So is political agitation that triggers uncertainty, disruption and chaos. This is a reminder to the PTI and also a direct message.
4. "(R)esolved that any attempt to cause agitation or create 9th May like situation " A deliberate and clear reference to May 9th is essentially a reiteration that the military's policy remains unchanged when it comes to PTI's agitation. The statement could have remained broad in referring to street trouble but it chose to mention May 9th precisely because the military wants the message to be loud, direct and unambiguous. It communicates – not really between the lines – that the talks in Islamabad may agree on some give-and-take but a long march to Islamabad in a huge no-no.
5. "(O)n any pretext whatsoever " Notice this 'add-on' in the sentence to not only re-emphasise the point but to in fact enlarge and expand the ambit of its definition. Why was this needed? Simply because the statement wants to ensure that any or all reasons or justifications or explanations given for the march or protest or agitation that involve converging on to Islamabad will be rejected, and lumped together as a "9th May like" event. The statement is leaving nothing to chance.
6. "(W)ill be dealt with decisive force and rule of law " The military is telling anyone who cares to listen – primarily the PTI but also, to a lesser extent, the government – that force will be applied, and that it will be decisive. These are strong words. They are meant to communicate that there is no room for flexibility when it comes to a response to agitation of the kind that the long march is expected to be. This is the military saying don't say you were not warned. This is as explicit a warning as they come. Is it meant to be a deterrent? Yes. Is it only meant to be a deterrent? Clearly no.
7. "(W)ithout hesitation and discrimination " The choice of these particular words is telling. The lack of hesitation means the law enforcers will be given free hand to use force. It also suggests the scale of the force used may not be contained. The inference is the state will not think twice before using force to ensure stability. The reference to no discrimination on whom the force may be used on probably means that leaders and workers alike will face the brunt if such a situation does indeed arise.
8. Anyone who reads these five different reiterations of the message by the Corps Commanders' conference together should be under no illusions about what the military means. Perhaps even more important is the fact that the military high command has chosen to be unambiguous in its message at a time when PTI is struggling to figure out if the long march is indeed the best course of action to take. The party may have painted itself into a corner by giving dates. The military is conveying to the PTI there will be no negotiations if there is a gun to the head. It is also telling the government the same thing.
9. Expect very little that will be offered to the PTI. The military's statement has ensured that. Such a strongly worded statement may not have been issued if the PTI had not escalated the situation to where it has reached today. Climbing up such an escalatory ladder is easy and often tempting, but climbing down entails a cost. What will this cost be? Imposition of Emergency or Governor's Rule? Further disarray in PTI's leadership? Greater stiffening of the military's attitude towards the PTI? It is hard to say at this point. What is not too hard to understand is that PTI's internal confusion, and its inability or unwillingness to sustain pressure from its rank and file has forced it to make a series of decisions that were not well thought out.
10. The important promotions and postings within the military high command have formalised the culmination of a routine institutional process that was overdue. This may not be connected directly to the churn of politics but it does infuse greater continuity of policy with a relatively new team. PTI needs to start reading the institution better.
If there's a bottom line here, it is that the system is re-asserting itself and reinforcing its strategic agenda. The long march, or the threat of it, has only forced it to double down and dig in its heels further.

title: RoboKing in Pakistan
description: RoboKing in Pakistan
content:
Pakistan's Optimus Prime would become just another Decepticon
For all its existence, Pakistan has seen democrats, dictators and hybrids; liberals and theocrats; gerontocrats and stratocrats. All, however, either served the system at the cost of the people or inflicted such heavy blows on the country that humane leadership of integrity, vision and empathy could never gain a decisive voice. Democrats, liberals, centrists, rightists, leftists, socialists, feminists and civil society have all traded faith and trust and, for their fair share, betrayed their ideologies, manifestos and mandates. Thus, the system recycles the same leaders under different names and slogans, and barely cares a damn about any leader of vision, empathy and integrity. As a result, the great country with great potential finds itself running in a groove. The reason is not that there is no pragmatic way out of the imbroglio; it is that, for the ruling elite, the quagmire is itself the way out, since it sustains the system and all the perks and wrongdoings attached to it.
Who else, if anyone, and if given a chance, would likely change the fate of the people for the better? Where does the way out of the country's current poly-crisis lie? Does the system itself not coopt, neutralise and sabotage every possible way out?
A student recently asked, amid dehumanised human leadership and the sweeping scope of AI, whether giant, humanised, enthroned robots as kind as Optimus Prime and Bumblebee, two of the most iconic heroes of the Autobots, who wage an endless war against the evil Decepticons, would offer a panacea to the socio-economic, political and ethnic ills plaguing the world in general and Pakistan in particular. Since they inherently hold no interests, have no children for whom to plunder the national wealth and harbour no greed or lust for wealth, they would deliver for the people rather than the system. Wouldn't they?
For the student, a cyber-king or RoboKing, perfectly programmed with positive values, might help rid the country of greed and of the trading of faith, truth and public rights. However, whether a RoboKing programmed with positive values would remain uncorrupted when surrounded by the traditional elite is highly doubtful.
Granted, a RoboKing might pass as a leader of integrity, given all his programming. A king alone, however, would rarely change things single-handedly or undo the stakes of the hordes of existing human ministers, advisers, media persons, civil, human-rights and women's-rights activists, politicians and dynastic despots, among others, who thrive in symbiosis with each other and in parasitism on the country and its people. Such a king would ignite little, if any, hope, let alone instil positive traits in them. Because of their stakes, the traditional stakeholders, for all their perks and wrongdoings, would tend to lure the king into being humanised and then demonised like themselves.
For instance, to secure the perks they have amassed for their own children, they would brainwash the King into adopting children and into making offshore, or rather off-planet, assets on the Moon, Mars and elsewhere. To this end, the human stakeholders would gaslight the King and persuade him that he is human. Thereafter, aides, including those in the media, would persuade the King to amend the framework and declare himself human, only to see him later demonised like themselves.
Then the clergy would deify the king, and the judiciary would legitimise his humanness. The politicians would expunge his intrinsic values, while civil society, social activists and all those whose interests are tied to the decades-long system would bow before him.
This way, the RoboKing's inbuilt algorithm would be erased, leaving behind the dehumanised and demonised leaders the country has seen for decades. As a result, the King would receive the highest honour the system bestows: interstellar assets and interplanetary bank accounts, lunar plots, Martian spoils, yet another political dynasty, a multiplication of the system's beneficiaries, and a glowing biography penned by courtiers. As usual, he would blame his pure and inherent algorithm for the entire quagmire.
In this system, Pakistan's Optimus Prime would become just another Decepticon, mutating in robes, beads, candles, mandarins, hired pens and gavels.

title: Mental health commitments
description: Mental health commitments
content:
Pakistan has roughly 0.19 psychiatrists for every 100,000 people
Pakistan's Global Mental Health Summit has ended with an ambitious promise to move mental healthcare out of the margins of public policy. The Islamabad Declaration commits the country to better coordination, sustainable financing, community-based care and, importantly, accountable implementation. These are sensible commitments. Their value, however, will depend on what happens after the conference halls have emptied.
The scale of the challenge leaves little room for another policy that exists largely on paper. Around 32.4 million Pakistanis are estimated to require mental-health care, while the treatment gap is about 95%. Pakistan has roughly 0.19 psychiatrists for every 100,000 people. For a population of this size, specialist treatment alone can never provide the answer. This makes the National Mental Health Policy 2026-35, launched at the summit, potentially important. Its emphasis on integrating mental-health services into primary healthcare, schools and communities recognises that people cannot be expected to travel to major urban hospitals every time they require psychological support. Care has to become available much closer to where people reside. The federal government has also asked the provinces and federating areas to endorse the policy within 45 days and has promised a costed, time-bound implementation and monitoring plan within 12 months. This is where the declaration must begin turning into a health-system reform programme. Since healthcare delivery rests substantially with the provinces, national ambition will accomplish little without provincial budgets and measurable targets. Pakistan will need more specialists, but it must also build capacity among general physicians, nurses and community health workers.
The next 12 months must establish who will deliver services, how they will be financed and how progress will be measured. For millions currently outside the mental-health system, implementation is not the final stage of the policy. It is the part that matters most.
