title: A surging insurgency
description: A surging insurgency
content:
Epicentre of this deterioration is Balochistan, where fatalities increased over threefold from 265 to 829
A worrying new report on the security situation in the country includes the grim statistic that there was an 83% surge in violence-linked fatalities during the third quarter of 2026, with 1,415 deaths recorded across 385 incidents. This sharp escalation in violence described in the Centre for Research and Security Studies quarterly security report shows that the declining trend witnessed in the first half of the year is a distant memory. In fact, the spike in violence is also the highest quarter-on-quarter increase since 2021.
The epicentre of this deterioration is Balochistan, where fatalities increased over threefold from 265 to 829, accounting for 88% of the national increase. Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, which has its own torrid history with terrorism, was second-worst, recording 186 violent incidents, which in terms of quantity - ignoring fatalities - represents 48% of all attacks in the country. The TTP, which is behind most of the attacks in K-P, was also the primary threat, being linked with 13 attacks that killed 117 people, while the BLA and Hafiz Gul Bahadur group also caused significant casualties. While almost two-thirds of the casualties were "outlaws", the raw numbers of civilians and security forces martyred rose by 36% and 79%, respectively, or 54% overall. The year-to-date death toll for security forces has also crossed 1,000, making the first three-quarters of 2026 the deadliest such period ever.
The UNSC has condemned the surge in militant attacks, but no amount of condemnation will stop the violence. What is needed is concrete action targeting the governments of Afghanistan and India - which fund some of the terrorist groups and provide them with logistics and shelter - and material support for our security apparatus. At the same time, the government must do more to address the root causes of separatist sentiments, instead of just blaming outside forces. If young people felt their government was providing opportunities, they would not feel alienated or susceptible to the appeal of anti-Pakistan groups, which may offer them kinship and income.

title: IWT in spotlight
description: IWT in spotlight
content:
Breach of a major international covenant demands a global response
India finds itself isolated internationally over its handling of transboundary water politics. Legal experts, diplomats and environmentalists have strongly condemned New Delhi's unilateral suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT). At the ongoing UN Human Rights Council session in Geneva, officials have warned that weaponising water threatens the food security and livelihoods of millions across the region. Pakistan, the lower riparian state, bears the brunt of this policy as India attempts to assert regional dominance and bypass global accountability.
The panel at Geneva made vital observations regarding the indispensable reliance of populations dependent on the Indus Basin. By directly linking water governance to human rights, it underscored that transboundary agreements must not become optional when bilateral relations deteriorate. This is a foundational principle of international jurisprudence. Accordingly, the Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled in Pakistan's favour, holding that the IWT remains fully in force despite India's unilateral decision to hold it in abeyance. Furthermore, as a procedural guarantor to the landmark 1960 accord, the World Bank has viewed actions altering the treaty framework as ultra vires breach of international law. Thus, weaponising water to this degree amounts to environmental and water terrorism.
This breach of a major international covenant demands a global response, as it is no longer just a bilateral issue for Pakistan. India's disregard for transboundary water governance violates state-centric norms and forces a lower riparian neighbour into an existential crisis. At a time when environmental degeneration is accelerating, such volatile policies act as a catalyst for climate change, crippling agricultural production and disrupting critical energy grids. India's determination to construct massive hydroelectric dams in occupied Jammu & Kashmir and its mainland systematically steals Pakistan's lawful water share. The world must unite to issue a firm dictum against New Delhi, prioritising human life and legal accountability over regional hegemony.

title: Being a teacher
description: Being a teacher
content:
Popular story of Thomas Edison tells us that he was considered an incapable student
A teacher becomes truly noble when he enters a classroom, delivers a lesson, completes the syllabus, and fully grasps the responsibility of 'being a teacher'.
What a teacher can do? Few stories illustrate this better than that of Helen Keller. Deaf and blind from early childhood, Keller faced barriers that could easily have confined her to a life of isolation. Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, refused to see her disabilities as the limits of her potential. Through patience, discipline and an extraordinary commitment to teaching, Sullivan helped Keller communicate, read, write and understand the world around her. Keller went on to become an author, lecturer and advocate whose life challenged society's assumptions about disability.
Similarly, the popular story of Thomas Edison tells us that he was considered an incapable student and was rejected by his teachers. His mother taught him and helped him become a world-famous inventor, enabling him to realise potential that his teachers had failed to recognise.
These stories tell us what it really means to be a teacher.
Having been in the teaching profession for the last fifteen years, I have learned that the title of "teacher" carries a responsibility far greater than the subjects written on a timetable. A student sitting in front of a teacher is not barely a name on an attendance register or a number in a classroom. He is a future citizen, a future parent, a future professional, and, above all, a human being whose character is still being formed.
The responsibility begins with recognising that every child is different. One student may be academically brilliant; another may struggle with examinations but possess creativity, leadership or practical intelligence. One may speak confidently while another remains silent. One may need encouragement; another may need discipline. The teacher's responsibility is not to force every child into the same mould but to identify potential and provide the guidance through which that potential can develop.
This is where teaching becomes more than a means of earning a living.
A teacher can teach a student that education is not a means of survival or a route to a job. Education can teach a person how to understand life, respect others, think independently and distinguishes right from wrong. Marks may open a door, but character determines what a person does after entering it.
That is why a teacher's own character matters.
Students do not learn only from what teachers say. They learn from how teachers behave. They observe how a teacher speaks to others, how he treats weaker students, how honestly he performs his duties and how he responds to difficulty. A teacher who demands discipline but does not practise it sends a contradictory message. A teacher who speaks about honesty but compromises his own principles teaches another lesson altogether.
But responsibility for a child's education cannot rest entirely on the teacher.
Parents are important partners in the educational process. A student may spend several hours at school, but the majority of his time is spent at home or in the wider community. What does he do after school? Does he complete his work honestly? Does he read, practise and revise, or simply find ways to avoid responsibility? How much attention do parents give to these questions?
A teacher, therefore, is not simply a person who completes a syllabus. He is a facilitator, a guide and a bridge between knowledge and the learner. At his best, he can awaken curiosity in a child who has stopped asking questions, confidence in a child who doubts himself, and ambition in a child who cannot yet imagine a different future.
Years later, students may forget a formula, a definition or even a chapter from a textbook. But they rarely forget the teacher who believed in them when they did not believe in themselves.
And that is the responsibility of being a teacher.

title: Chris Hansen considers legal action against A24 over  Primetime  portrayal
description: Chris Hansen says  Primetime  is fictional and is considering legal action over his portrayal in A24 film
content:
Chris Hansen says 'Primetime' is fictional and is considering legal action over his portrayal in A24 film
Chris Hansen has criticised the portrayal of his life and work in Primetime, describing the A24 film as a “complete work of fiction” and saying he is considering potential legal action.
The film, directed by Lance Oppenheim and starring Robert Pattinson as Hansen, centres on the former Dateline segment To Catch a Predator, which ran from 2004 to 2007.
Hansen said the only non-fictionalised elements involving him are the use of his name and two or three catchphrases.
The film also focuses on the 2006 death of Louis William Conradt Jr., an assistant district attorney who died by suicide after police arrived at his home following an investigation involving decoys posing as teenagers.
Hansen said nobody wanted to see Conradt take his own life, but rejected the suggestion that the Predator team pressured authorities into pursuing him.
He said the investigation was conducted as part of law enforcement procedures and that the circumstances depicted in Primetime did not accurately reflect what happened.
Hansen also objected to the film's depiction of his personal and professional life. He said the filmmakers used his name, image and reputation without consulting him and claimed they “exploited me and my brand and my name image for commercial enterprise.”
The journalist said lawyers are reviewing the possibility of legal action, although he has not made a final decision.
Hansen also addressed the film's portrayal of his former colleagues, saying they were upset by how they were represented. He said one producer was particularly affected by the depiction.
Despite his criticism, Hansen acknowledged Primetime's box-office performance and said he believes the film's success was partly driven by A24 and Pattinson.

title: Deadlock persists as hours long govt  PTI talks end without breakthrough
description: NA Speaker Sadiq thanks members of the government  PPP and opposition for participating in the talks
content:
Achakzai refuses to back down on long march, says it won’t be called off without meeting PTI founder
The second round of talks between the government and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) continued past Saturday midnight after hours of negotiations but failed to achieve a breakthrough, with a deadlock persisting between the two sides.
The negotiators from both sides left the meeting room after 2am in the early hours of Sunday.
Speaking to Express News, PTI MNA Asad Qaiser confirmed that there still existed a deadlock.
"We informed the government of our differences regarding the meeting with the founding chairman, the release of the sisters and other demands. We have apprised the government of certain issues; our primary demand is a meeting with Imran Khan. There are issues concerning our elderly women and other matters," he said.
Qaiser said the PTI side stipulated that a meeting with Imran must take place first and only then would it proceed further.
"We hold a very clear stance on the issue of terrorism; we want peace in our province."
Leader of the Opposition in the Senate Raja Nasir Abbas told the media there was a deadlock on "small issues". He said the issue of the meeting with Imran could not be resolved.

However, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja said: "Look, we don't have a consensus on foundational issues," adding that he could not say that he foresaw both sides moving forward on a mutually acceptable plan of action.
PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar said the long march would go ahead and was "intact". He said the party's demands should be addressed and said governor rule or an emergency were not the answers to the long march.
PPP Senator Sherry Rehman said they had performed their constitutional and democratic role.
"We constantly talked with them on every point, whatever their concerns were were heard and debated and shared with our leadership. The agreement draft was changed four times."
She said it was the PPP's stance that, given the terrorism situation, there could be no compromise, and that it was "not a small matter".
Rehman added that agreement was achieved on many points but disagreements remained on some.
"They have refused to do an agreement," she said.
Prime Minister's aide Rana Sanaullah said the basic issue related to K-P's security situation, with the federal government demanding that the provincial government fulfil its responsibilities in this regard and play its role.
He said there was no reassurance from the other side about this. "They made changes in the drafts two to three times, but despite that, the K-P government is not ready to cooperate to play its role in the war against terrorism and this is absolutely unacceptable. That is why the agreement could not be achieved."
Sanaullah said the government had provided various reassurances to the PTI regarding its demands about Imran. He added that the long march would not be allowed to enter Islamabad.
Meanwhile, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi laid out the schedule for the long march from his province in a post on X at 12:46am.

According to a statement issued by the National Assembly on X, NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq said Friday’s session had been held in a “very cordial atmosphere” and expressed hope that all sides would continue the talks in the same spirit.
He also thanked members from the government, PPP and opposition for participating in the negotiations.
حکومت، پیپلز پارٹی اور اپوزیشن کے درمیان مذکرات کا دوسرا دور شروع۔ اسپیکر قومی اسمبلی سردار ایاز صادق اجلاس کی صدارت کر رہے ہیں۔ کل کا اجلاس بہت خوشگوار ماحول میں ہوا، اسپیکر قومی اسمبلی آج بھی امید ہے کے تمام فریقین خوشگوار ماحول میں مذکرات کو آگے بڑھائیں گے، اسپیکر سردار… pic.twitter.com/QSKz1WB2gE
Federal ministers Engineer Amir Muqam and Syed Mushtaq Raza Naqvi, Minister of State Talal Chaudhry and Prime Minister’s Adviser Rana Sanaullah are representing the government in the talks.
From the PPP, Senator Sherry Rehman and National Assembly members Naveed Qamar and Ijaz Hussain Jakhrani are participating.
The opposition delegation comprises National Assembly members Barrister Gohar Khan, Raja Nasir Abbas, Amir Dogar, Asad Qaiser and Haleem Adil Sheikh, along with Salman Akram Raja.
Achakzai refuses to back down on Oct 4 long march
Meanwhile, TTAP chief Mehmood Khan Achakzai refused to withdraw his demand, saying the long march would not be called off until a meeting with PTI founder Imran Khan took place.
Speaking to a private television channel, he demanded that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi be allowed to meet the PTI founder, while also giving an assurance that the chief minister would not speak to the media after the meeting.
He said a decision to call off the long march, scheduled for Oct 4, could be taken after consultation with the PTI founder, adding that whatever joint decision was reached after the meeting would be accepted.
Earlier in the evening, amid reports of successful government-opposition negotiations, PTI leader Shaukat Yousafzai welcomed the development as a positive step for the country.
Yousafzai said the success of the talks should not be viewed as a victory or defeat for any particular side, but rather as a victory for Pakistan. He noted that he had previously made the same position clear through a letter, emphasising that negotiations were the best way to resolve political differences.
Addressing the issue of terrorism, Yousafzai called on the federal government to support the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government in efforts to eliminate terrorism and improve security in the province.
He also said that the imposition of Governor’s Rule would have caused significant damage and expressed hope that the government would provide PTI with adequate political space.
Yousafzai further expressed the expectation that court decisions concerning PTI founder Imran Khan would be implemented in accordance with the law.
A day earlier, the first round of talks between the government and opposition concluded with the two sides deciding to meet again on Saturday (today) in the NA speaker’s chamber. The negotiations come amid continued tensions after PTI announced a long march towards Islamabad on September 27 that was rescheduled to October 4. Currently, the standoff between the federal and provincial governments remains unresolved.
The speaker, in a statement, said the previous day’s session was held in a “very cordial atmosphere” and expressed hope that all sides would continue the dialogue in the same spirit.
Sadiq also thanked members of the government, PPP and opposition for participating in the talks.
حکومت، پیپلز پارٹی اور اپوزیشن کے درمیان مذکرات کا دوسرا دور شروع۔ اسپیکر قومی اسمبلی سردار ایاز صادق اجلاس کی صدارت کر رہے ہیں۔ کل کا اجلاس بہت خوشگوار ماحول میں ہوا، اسپیکر قومی اسمبلی آج بھی امید ہے کے تمام فریقین خوشگوار ماحول میں مذکرات کو آگے بڑھائیں گے، اسپیکر سردار… pic.twitter.com/RjRpcdDhc1
As per the statement, Federal Ministers Engineer Ameer Muqam, Mohsin Naqvi and Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, Minister of State Talal Chaudhry and Prime Minister’s Adviser Rana Sanaullah are representing the government during the meeting. Furthermore, the PPP delegation comprises Senator Sherry Rehman, Naveed Qamar and Ijaz Hussain Jakhrani.
On the other hand, PTI is represented by Barrister Gohar Khan, Raja Nasir Abbas, Aamer Dogar, Asad Qaiser and Haleem Adil Sheikh, along with Salman Akram Raja, according to the NA’s statement.
The talks are being held as part of efforts by the government, PPP, and the opposition to engage in dialogue on matters of political importance.
Read: Govt, opposition conclude first round of talks ahead of PTI’s Oct 4 march
On Friday, the NA spokesperson revealed that detailed discussions were conducted on the country’s political situation, with the government, PPP, and opposition apprising each other of their respective positions. However, the first round of talks ended without a conclusive decision from either quarter. The parties also refrained from mudslinging in accordance with an agreement reached during the talks.
Defence Minister alleges PTI, KP govt supporting unrest
Earlier in the day, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif questioned whether the PTI and the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government hired terrorists to spread sedition, riots and chaos under the guise of protests on October 4.
He made these remarks in connection with a video he shared on X alleging that PTI’s social media accounts shared footage showing non-custom-paid vehicles from Waziristan.
In a statement shared on social media, he further alleged that “unemployed young men” were paid and sent around the camps of police and security forces to spread unrest, adding that some of them might not even have identity cards.
“Now, if these ignorant fools attack any government institution tomorrow, just like it happened in the past, and the police or forces disperse them in self-defence, then will the narrative against the state be built from the ready social media accounts sitting there, just like before?” The defence minister posed a question.
He also asked why the cops were not checking the convoy to determine whether the people travelling in the vehicles were terrorists with covered faces or ordinary citizens, and whether the non-custom-paid vehicles were carrying weapons or explosive materials.

Before the second round of talks with the government, PTI leader Asad Qaiser assailed the defence minister for his statement.

title: CM Afridi lays out K P long march schedule amid govt PTI deadlock in talks
description: Says party will neither allow nor let anyone repeat May 9
content:
Says party will neither allow nor let anyone repeat May 9
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi laid out the schedule for the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's (PTI) long march to Islamabad from his province after Saturday midnight, even as the federal government coalition and the party remained engaged in negotiations after hours of talks.
In a post on X, the chief minister laid out the plan for the long march, saying its first phase would begin at 1pm on Sunday from Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat.
انشأللہ آج گنڈی چوک لکی مروت سے ہم لانگ مارچ کا پہلا مرحلہ شروع کریں گے- آج بروز اتوار، 4 اکتوبر، دوپہر ایک بجے گنڈی چوک لکی مروت سے ٹانک، ڈیرہ اسماعیل خان، ساؤتھ وزیرستان، نارتھ وزیرستان، بنوں اور لکی مروت کے اضلاع سے تعلق رکھنے والے غیور پاکستانی لانگ مارچ کا حصہ بنیں گے۔ رات…
He said people from Tank, Dera Ismail Khan, South Waziristan, North Waziristan, Bannu and Lakki Marwat would join the march at Gandi Chowk. The caravan would then halt for the night near Karak.
On Oct 5, people from Karak would join the march at noon, with the caravan scheduled to depart at 12:30pm and halt for the night near Kohat, Afridi said.
On Oct 6, people from Kohat, Hangu, Kurram and Orakzai would join the march at noon. The caravan would then proceed towards Peshawar and spend the night near Matni, he added.
On Oct 7, the march would depart from Budh Bair in Peshawar at 12:30pm, with people from Khyber district joining there. The remaining constituencies of Peshawar would join the march at Kohat Road Bridge and the Motorway Toll Plaza, while the caravan would spend the night near Charsadda Interchange.
On Oct 8, the march would depart from Charsadda Interchange at 12:30pm, with people from Charsadda and Mohmand joining the caravan.
The chief minister said people from across K-P would gather at Khairabad on Oct 8 and spend the night there. “Insha’Allah, the plan for the next phase will be announced there,” he said.
He earlier said the PTI was Pakistan’s “largest and most popular political party” and that its planned October 4 march would begin from Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat and continue until the supremacy of the Constitution and law and the restoration of an independent judiciary.
In a post on X, the chief minister said Pakistan was a democratic country and its Constitution provided the right to peaceful protest.
He said all demands of the PTI were in accordance with the Constitution and law.
“On October 4, a sea of people will begin its journey from Gandi Chowk, Lakki Marwat, and will continue its struggle until the supremacy of the Constitution and law and restoration of an independent judiciary in Pakistan,” he said.
ہم پاکستان کی سب سے بڑی اور سب سے مقبول سیاسی جماعت ہیں۔ پاکستان ایک جمہوری ملک ہے، جس کا آئین ہمیں پُرامن احتجاج کا حق دیتا ہے۔ 4 اکتوبر کو گنڈی چوک، لکی مروت سے عوام کا سمندر اپنا سفر شروع کرے گا اور پاکستان میں آئین و قانون کی بالادستی اور آزاد عدلیہ کی بحالی تک اپنی جدوجہد…
The chief minister alleged that those who had been “forcibly” kept in control of Pakistan wanted the country to break apart, and accused them of “setting Pakistan on fire” to protect their power.
He also alleged that terrorism had been deliberately imposed on K-P again after the “regime change”, saying that when PTI had raised its voice in the summer of 2022, it had been called a liar.
“Terrorism is not a narrative war for the people of K-P and Pakistan; every citizen is affected by it,” he said.
The chief minister said PTI founder Imran Khan had always maintained that military operations against people in the country and displacing them were not a lasting solution to the problem.
He said drone attacks and so-called “collateral damage” increased terrorism, adding that he remained firm on this position.
CM Afridi said the stance was no longer limited to PTI in K-P, but was shared by every political and religious party and people belonging to every school of thought, with their signatures available as evidence in the provincial assembly jirga.
The chief minister said that during PTI’s federal government, Pakistan and K-P were known for “tourism, not terrorism”.
Read: PTI long march to roll out from Lakki
He said that when he claimed that peace could return to K-P within 100 days through a change in policy, the proposal was not acted upon.
“Who is facilitating terrorism?” he asked, while also questioning who was taking away ministers and workers along with “good” favourites, why weapons purchased for the province were not reaching the police and why the police had been forced to rebel.
He also questioned why peace had not returned to Balochistan when the provincial and federal governments were “on the same page”, and why Pakistan had ranked first in terrorism.
The chief minister said those who considered themselves “all-knowing” had been wrong in the past and remained wrong, adding that they would continue to be wrong until they changed their policies.
He said they would neither allow nor let anyone repeat May 9.
“Whoever stole the CCTV footage was the one who caused May 9,” he added.
In response to the chief minister’s social media post, one of the government’s delegates to the planned second round of consultations to end the political deadlock, Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said, “The government wants to make negotiations with the opposition meaningful and result-oriented, but statements being issued by K-P CM Sohail Afridi could hamper the process.”
حکومت اپوزیشن کے ساتھ مزاکرات کو بامقصد اور نتیجہ خیز بنانا چاہتی ہے لیکن مزاکرات کے دوران وزیراعلی کے پی سہیل آفریدی کے بیانات اس عمل کو متاثر کر سگتے ہیں، تحریک انصاف کی قیادت کو چاہیے کہ مزاکرات کے حتمی مرحلے تک اس قسم کی گفتگو سے اجتناب کریں جس سے اس عمل کو نقصان ہو ، سہیل… https://t.co/sEUG84GnmP
Speaking about the ongoing talks, Chaudhry said the PTI leadership should refrain from issuing statements that could undermine the negotiations until the process reaches its final stage.
He urged the PTI leadership to exercise restraint and avoid rhetoric that could damage the dialogue process.
PML-N-backed MNA Chaudhry also lambasted CM Afridi for his choice of words.
“The language Sohail Afridi is using against his opponents and our leadership is unbecoming of a chief minister. His remarks are extremely inappropriate and condemnable,” he concluded his statement on X.
Later in the day, K-P Information Minister Shafi Jan took to social media and said his party rejects the attempt to link K-P with terrorism.
In a social media post, the minister asserted, “In front of the media, an attempt was made to link Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and the K-P government to terrorism through images and allegations. We make it clear that linking political differences to allegations of terrorism is unacceptable.”
خیبرپختونخوا کو دہشت گردی سے جوڑنے کی کوششیں مسترد کرتے ہیں، آج میڈیا کے سامنے تصاویر اور الزامات کے ذریعے تحریکِ انصاف، وزیراعلیٰ @SohailAfridiISF اور خیبرپختونخوا حکومت کو دہشت گردی سے جوڑنے کی کوشش کی گئی۔ ہم واضح کرتے ہیں کہ سیاسی اختلاف کو دہشت گردی کے الزامات سے جوڑنا… pic.twitter.com/5HEhFl1bGk
Speaking further, Minister Jan emphasised that the people of K-P made “unparalleled sacrifices in the war against terrorism” and therefore calling them terrorists was an insult to the sacrifices of the millions of families who lost their loved ones in the war.
The provincial information minister further demanded that discussions should be based on facts and evidence instead of accusations.

title: Putting better health in more hands  Reckitt Pakistan unveils  Saaf Sehatmand Pakistan  in partnership with Aga Khan Foundation
description: The programme will provide safe water  improve toilets  build handwashing stations and teach hygiene to help children
content:
The programme will provide safe water, improve toilets, build handwashing stations and teach hygiene to help children
Reckitt Pakistan partners with the Aga Khan Foundation to launch its landmark social initiative, Saaf Sehatmand Pakistan , driving daily health and hygiene across the nation.
The agreement was formalised with the Aga Khan Foundation to support the implementation of the platform’s first school-based initiative. The initiative will be driven by Reckitt Pakistan’s health and hygiene expertise, with the Aga Khan Foundation contributing its on-ground WASH experience and community reach.
Following the signing, Saaf Sehatmand Pakistan was officially unveiled by H.E. Alison Blackburne, British Deputy High Commissioner Karachi, alongside Asif M. Hashimi, General Manager, Reckitt Pakistan; Sarah Ahmed, Marketing Director, Reckitt Pakistan; Amin Feerasta, Chairman of the National Committee, Aga Khan Foundation Pakistan; and Akhtar Iqbal, Chief Executive Officer, Aga Khan Foundation Pakistan.
Powered by Dettol and Harpic, brands that have been part of Pakistani households for generations, the platform brings together Reckitt Pakistan’s work across health, hygiene, sanitation and safe water under one long-term ambition: to help build a cleaner, healthier Pakistan.
Through this partnership, Saaf Sehatmand Pakistan will begin with a school-based water, sanitation and hygiene initiative designed to scale across Pakistan. The rogramme will provide access to safe drinking water, rehabilitate toilet facilities, build handwashing stations and deliver hygiene education to help children develop healthier habits from an early age.
Reckitt Pakistan reaches more than two million children annually through school-based hygiene education. Saaf Sehatmand Pakistan will deepen this impact by combining hygiene education with improved access to safe drinking water, toilets and handwashing facilities.
Speaking on the occasion, Asif M. Hashimi, General Manager, Reckitt Pakistan, commented:
Better Health in More Hands, Every Day is our reason to exist, and it is our responsibility to act. Saaf Sehatmand Pakistan turns the trust and expertise of Dettol and Harpic into action, bringing safe water, sanitation and hygiene to schools. Our ambition is to carry that impact from classrooms into homes and communities across Pakistan”
Amin Feerasta, Chairman of National Committee at Aga Khan Foundation Pakistan, quoted:
Every child deserves a safe, healthy and dignified learning environment. Building on the Aga Khan Foundation’s decades of experience in improving access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene, our partnership with Reckitt will help create healthier school environments in rural Sindh, enabling children to attend and remain in school.
We hope that today’s agreement will therefore be the first chapter of a long-term cooperation between Reckitt and the Aga Khan Foundation in Pakistan.
H.E. Alison Blackburne, British Deputy High Commissioner Karachi, said:
The UK strongly supports efforts to expand access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene, which are essential for children's health, wellbeing and education. I welcome Reckitt Pakistan’s launch of Saaf Sehatmand Pakistan, with the Aga Khan Foundation bringing valuable implementation expertise to help translate this ambition into lasting impact.
Beginning with schools, the platform will grow through a wider network of partners that share Reckitt Pakistan’s ambition to improve access to health and hygiene taking better health from classrooms into homes and communities while ensuring that no one is left behind.
Built in Pakistan, for the people of Pakistan, Saaf Sehatmand Pakistan marks the beginning of a long-term journey towards healthier schools, stronger communities and a healthier nation.

title: Children of displacement  The Rababis
description: The history of the Rababis of Pakistan is one of displacement and survival
content:
The history of the Rababis of Pakistan is one of displacement and survival
Growing up in Lahore, I lived inside a culture without always knowing what it was made of. Among my good friends was Ahmed Iqbal Sheikh from Katri Bawa, the old neighbourhood in the walled city of Lahore that I would later learn was home to one of the most remarkable musical communities in the subcontinent. They were Rababis. I did not know it then. We shared laughter, Punjabi, and the unspoken codes of growing up in a city layered with memory. There was no talk of kirtan, no mention of Bhai Mardana, no reference to a tradition stretching back five centuries to the very origins of the Sikh faith. But the lineage was there, carried quietly in their blood and their neighbourhood, waiting to be named.
Years later, when I studied for my Master's in music under Ustad Badr-uz-Zaman, who had recently migrated from Amritsar to Lahore after Partition. Ustad Badr-uz-Zaman had studied from the Rababis Bhai Nasira and Bhai Faiz Ali, so I encountered the tradition more closely under his tutelage.
The rababi tradition has its roots in one of the most celebrated partnerships in the devotional history of South Asia. In the late 15th century, Guru Nanak (1469–1539), the founder of the Sikh faith, undertook a lifetime of spiritual journeys across South and Central Asia. Accompanying him throughout was Bhai Mardana (1459–1534), a Muslim musician from the village of Merawat who played the rabab, a plucked string instrument of Persian and Afghan origin. As Guru Nanak received divine inspiration, it was Mardana who gave it sound. The Guru's own words, as recalled in Sikh oral tradition, were: "Mardaneya! Rabab chhed, bani aayee hai" [Mardana, play the rabab, the sacred composition has come to me]".
What makes this original relationship theologically and culturally significant is that Bhai Mardana was a Muslim disciple of Guru Nanak — a bhai (brother) within the earliest Sikh community. He served the Guru as a Muslim, and in doing so inaugurated a tradition that was pluralist in its essence. As the 17th-century Sikh chronicler Bhai Gurdas wrote: "Mardana, the hereditary musician, wonderfully plays the rabab, in the spiritual assembly [of the Guru]", a testimony that locates the rabab and its player at the liturgical heart of early Sikh devotion.
From this founding partnership, the rababi tradition developed through a network of five hereditary Muslim musician families who served successive Sikh Gurus across two centuries. These founding lineages were: Bhai Mardana's own descendants; Bhai Satta and Balwand, who served Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, and Guru Arjan; Bhai Babak, a warrior-musician of the court of Guru Hargobind; Bhai Natha and Abdullah, performers during the time of Guru Hargobind and Guru Har Rai; and Bhai Sadda and Madda, who served the last two Gurus, Guru Tegh Bahadur and Guru Gobind Singh. Their compositions — a var by Bhai Satta and Balwand, and couplets (shloks) attributed to Bhai Mardana— are inscribed within the Guru Granth Sahib itself, giving the Rababis an unparalleled scriptural status within Sikh tradition.
With the rise of Sikh political power in the Punjab in the late 18th century, and particularly with the consolidation of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's empire in the early 19th century, Amritsar became the undisputed cultural and spiritual capital of the Sikh world. The Golden Temple (Darbar Sahib) at its heart received patronage on an unprecedented scale, more than a crore of rupees invested in architectural development alone, and the Rababi community grew in tandem with it. Families of hereditary musicians migrated from their ancestral villages across Punjab to serve in the inner sanctum, eventually settling together in a neighbourhood that came to be known as Rababi-wali Gali, the Alley of the Rababis, near Chowk Passian (Pasianwala Chowk) in Amritsar.
These 12 families were distinguished by the names of their ancestral places of origin:
Khaḍūrīē (Khadur Sahib, Amritsar district); Raukē ( Thatha Bhai Rao, Ferozepur district); Ḍabbē (Dabbayan, Amritsar district); Manāvīē (Manavan, Amritsar district); Śikārpurīē (Shikarpur, Kapurthala district); Gailē (Amritsar); Diōkē (Patiala); Vangiāvālē; Rōrāṁvālīē (Roranwala, Amritsar district); Dilvālīē (Delhi); Ġafūrīē; and Mudrīē.
Following Partition in 1947, other families, including the Kartārpurīē, Kapūrthalīē, Bhaknīē, Sangrūrīē, and Lahōrīē khāndāns, migrated to Lahore and integrated into the community that gathered at Katri Bawa ki Haveli, the neighbourhood that became the post-Partition home of the Rababis in Pakistani Punjab. Today, the names of these ancestral places, though the villages themselves are largely inaccessible or long since transformed, continue to orient the community's internal social organisation, functioning as symbolic markers of kinship and lineage identity.
A persistent misreading of the Rababis, one that circulates even today, reduces them to mere Muslim musicians employed by Sikhs. The historical record, as detailed in Singh's ethnographic and archival research (2023), and as powerfully articulated in Kirit Singh's lecture on the tradition, reveals a far richer identity.
The Rababis were referred to as ‘singham de maulvi’-- ‘the priests of the Sikhs’. As tabla maestro Ustad Tari Khan, the grandson of a Rababi of the Darbar Sahib, recalled: "They did not simply do kirtan, they systematically explained it. They performed katha [narrative-based exegesis]. They were so knowledgeable that they educated our Sikh brothers".
This practice of kirtan as katha, of musical exegesis, distinguished the Rababis from ordinary performers. Like the qawwals of Sufi shrines who weave multiple poetic traditions into a single devotional performance, the great Rababis would build expansive narratives around a single shabad, drawing on verses from Kabir, Baba Farid, Guru Nanak, and others. Bhai Lal Muhammad of the Gailē khāndān, described as "the Moon of Amritsar" and said to have been as beloved in the city as Gandhi, reportedly knew the entire Guru Granth Sahib by heart and could sustain a single shabad performance for more than an hour.
Beyond their exegetical role, the Rababis occupied an indispensable ritual function in Sikh life, attending births, marriages, and deaths as auspicious presences, leading funeral processions singing compositions in raag Maru, and ritually "opening" the season of spring (raag Basant) at the Darbar Sahib. This was the role of spiritual custodians, whose presence was understood to transmit the spiritual grace inherited directly from the Gurus. No Sikh raagi could perform these rites in their place.
The unravelling of the Rababis' place within Sikh tradition was not a single rupture but a slow erosion across several decades. Beginning with the British colonial project in Punjab from 1849 onwards, the census-driven demand that communities identify with a single religion, Hindu, Muslim, or Sikh, began to impose boundaries on a community whose identity had always occupied precisely the space in between. The rise of the Singh Sabha movement and, crucially, the formation of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee in 1925, which assumed control of the historic Sikh shrines, marked a decisive shift.
Simultaneously, the democratisation of kirtan education through print culture and Western-style schools meant that Sikh raagis trained outside hereditary traditions could now be substituted for the Rababis. By the 1920s and 1930s, many Rababi families were already being displaced from the Darbar Sahib. When the Sikh Rahit Maryada, the Sikh Code of Conduct, was finally codified in 1950, three years after Partition, it stipulated that only an initiated Sikh could perform kirtan.
In 1947, the partition of Punjab along religious lines completed what colonial reform had begun. The violence that swept Amritsar in the summer of that year, including murders near the Rababis' own neighbourhood of Pasianwala Chowk, compelled the community to flee westward to the newly created Pakistan. They settled, many of them, in the cramped streets of Katri Bawa ki Haveli in old Lahore, a neighbourhood that became the post-Partition heart of the Rababi community.
The transition was difficult for the Rababi community. After Partition, those who had served the Sikh tradition for generations found themselves separated from the institutions and communities with which they had long been associated. Many Rababis who remained in Pakistan faced uncertainty about their livelihoods and place within the new social and political landscape, while those who moved to India encountered a transformed cultural environment. Bhai Chand (Bhai Sundar Giani), one of the last prominent Rababis to perform at the Golden Temple before Partition, is recorded in Kirit Singh’s research as having approached the Government of Pakistan after 1947 seeking assistance. His experience reflected the challenges faced by members of a community whose religious and cultural identity had historically crossed the boundaries that Partition sought to establish. In the years that followed, the Rababis struggled to find a clear place within the new religious and national frameworks of the subcontinent.
I have never heard a Rababi sing kirtan live. That admission, from a Lahori who studied music, who had Rababi friends from Katri Bawa, who writes on South Asian sacred music, is itself the most important thing this article can say. The tradition has become so marginalised, so absent from public life, that even those of us living closest to it have not heard it.
The contemporary situation of the Rababis in Pakistan is documented with uncommon clarity in Kirit Singh's 2025 short film Mardana's Children: The Rababis of Lahore. Ustad Moeen Ahmed Chand, a thirteenth-generation Rababi, laments the absence of opportunities for his community: "Nobody calls us to play anymore. Once a year, tourists come from abroad on Sri Guru Nanak Dev's birth anniversary, then they call us now and then. All we want is a consistent and reliable source of income."
Facing the closure of the kirtan tradition as a viable public and professional identity, many Rababis have turned to qawwali and Sufi devotional music as a means of survival, genres that are accepted within Pakistan's Islamic cultural framework and that draw on many of the same musical techniques and compositional traditions. Figures such as the late Hamid Ali Bela (1925–2001), Sain Akhtar, and the distinguished vocalist Ustad Ghulam Hassan Shaggan (1928–2015) achieved considerable recognition in Pakistan's Sufi and classical music scenes. The tabla maestro Ustad Abdul Sattar 'Tari' Khan, perhaps Pakistan's most celebrated classical percussionist, is himself of Rababi lineage. Similarly, the legendary film music director Rashid Attre (1919–1967) and master composers Wazir Ali and Muhammad Afzal came from Rababi families. The question worth asking is: what might Pakistan's music have been had these musicians also had a platform for their kirtan tradition alongside their film and classical work?
The dwindling number of Rababis in Pakistan continues without institutional support, public platform, or financial patronage. Unlike the Sufi dhamal at Lahore's Data Darbar, or the qawwali tradition at the shrines of Punjab, the Rababi kirtan practice has no shrine economy to sustain it, no state festival to revive it, and no gurdwara door open to receive it.
The Rababi tradition occupies a distinctive place between Sikh and Muslim cultural histories, which made its preservation especially complex after Partition. As Kirit Singh observed, the community reflected elements of both traditions, while changing political and cultural circumstances gradually altered the place of kirtan and its practitioners in Pakistan.
Yet the tradition has not disappeared. Its survival, often through quiet and private practice, remains an important part of its contemporary history.
In the homes of Katri Bawa, families continue to transmit the kirtan repertoire from parent to child. Bhai Tahir Iqbal of the Gailē khāndān, who teaches music alongside his son Aqeel at their academy in Model Town, Lahore, articulates the spirit of this quiet persistence: "We have a link to Guru ji. Guru Nanak made Bhai Mardana his brother. This will continue. It will go to our children, whether somebody invites us to perform or not." Muslim Shaggan, grandson of the great vocalist Ustad Ghulam Hassan Shaggan, carries the kirtan tradition forward alongside his career in Hindustani classical music. Young performers like Mohsin Ali Chand, a tabla player and kirtaniya in his early thirties, continue to learn and perform the tradition, even as they navigate the challenges of preserving a heritage that has become less widely recognised in contemporary Pakistan.
Lahore is a city of layers. It holds, simultaneously and without apology, the Mughal tombs and the colonial courts, the qawwali of Data Darbar and the gospel choirs of its old Christian schools, the Sufi kalam and the Hindustani classical raga. What it has not yet learned to hold, publicly, institutionally, proudly, is the kirtan of its own Rababis.
The urgency of this moment is documentary and moral. The last generation of Rababis who received direct transmission from masters formed before Partition are now elderly or gone. What they knew, the old compositions, the exegetical techniques, the seasonal rituals, the precise melodic inheritance of the raags, cannot be recovered from books. It lives only in bodies. That Bhai Moeen Ahmad, sitting in his modest home near Lahore's Shalimar Gardens, still teaches his sons and disciples the kirtan of Guru Nanak is not simply a musical fact. It is an act of extraordinary cultural fidelity, and of the deepest kind of Punjabi pluralism, the kind that does not wait for borders to be redrawn before it loves what it loves.
Music, as the Rababis have demonstrated across five centuries, does not belong to one religion. It belongs to those willing to carry it.

title: Punjab expands Sahulat-on-the-Go markets to ease food prices, regulate vending | The Express Tribune
description: The model is simple. Pushcart vendors move into regulated clusters with stalls
content:
The model is simple. Pushcart vendors move into regulated clusters with stalls
Punjab’s new Sahulat-on-the-Go (SOTG) markets are being positioned as a permanent alternative to seasonal relief bazaars, with the government seeking to address food affordability while bringing roadside vending under regulation.
The concept was developed by Naveed Rafaqat Ahmad of the Punjab Sahulat Bazaars Authority (PSBA). He pitched it to the government in April 2025 as a permanent, self-financing alternative to seasonal relief markets. Government approved a 14-site Lahore pilot: 816 uniform stalls on idle roadside government land.
The model is simple. Pushcart vendors move into regulated clusters with stalls, sanitation and security, allotted by open ballot. Households get vegetables, fruit, chicken and groceries at DC-notified rates close to home.
An official Monitoring and Evaluation survey of 167 SOTG customers and 80 vendors, reported in March, is largely positive. Ninety-five per cent rated accessibility well, 93pc felt secure and 92pc were satisfied with quality.
Among vendors, 94pc were satisfied with rent and 85pc considered their business viable. Most striking, 52.4pc of SOTG customers were women, double their 26.2pc share at conventional Sahulat Bazaars.
Affordability is the weak spot. Only 73pc of SOTG customers were satisfied with prices, against 82pc at conventional bazaars. Lahore's 15 units also remain thin coverage for 15 million people.
Scale is the next test. The province has allocated Rs19 billion for 2026-27 and released Rs4.83bn. Another 41 SOTG units are under construction, and coverage is planned for all 154 tehsils.
If price monitoring tightens, Ahmad's proposition will have proved larger than stall-building. It turns informal commerce into public infrastructure, where affordability, livelihoods and orderly streets become a single equation.

title: Tom Sandoval granted two year restraining order against ex Victoria Robinson
description: Tom Sandoval and Victoria Robinson agreed to two year restraining order following allegations of domestic violence
content:
Tom Sandoval and Victoria Robinson agreed to two-year restraining order following allegations of domestic violence
Tom Sandoval has been granted a two-year domestic violence restraining order against his ex-girlfriend Victoria Robinson, according to court documents obtained by People .
The Vanderpump Rules alum was granted the order on Thursday, October 1. It will remain in effect until October 1, 2028. Sandoval and Robinson both agreed to the order, meaning the case did not proceed to a contested evidentiary hearing.
Under the order, Robinson is required to leave Sandoval's Los Angeles home immediately. She is prohibited from contacting him directly or indirectly and must maintain a distance of at least 100 yards from him.
If the former couple attend the same event during the two-year period, Robinson is required to leave. The order also prohibits her from owning firearms or ammunition while it remains active.
Sandoval requested the restraining order after an alleged incident on June 3. According to court documents, he claimed he returned home from a bar at around 2 a.m. and found Robinson's father, Will Robinson, "visibly intoxicated."
Sandoval said he pushed Will Robinson away after feeling trapped and claimed the move caused him to fall.
"Feeling trapped and violated, I pushed Mr. Robinson away from me to protect myself and create distance, which caused him to fall. Mr. Robinson was the first person to put his hands on me," Sandoval wrote. "At no point did I pursue Mr. Robinson."
Sandoval also alleged that Robinson punched him in the face with enough force to cause blurred vision. Robinson was arrested on a charge of intimate partner battery with physical violence and was later released on bond.
The restraining order follows the former couple's relationship and the allegations outlined in Sandoval's court filing. The order sets restrictions on Robinson's contact with Sandoval through October 2028.

title: Pakistan   s environmental ranking improves yet air quality lags
description: Lahore   s average AQI in the first 23 days of September was 96  up from 80 during the same period last year
content:
Lahore’s average AQI in the first 23 days of September was 96, up from 80 during the same period last year
Pakistan has improved 22 places in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index (EPI), ranking 157th out of 177 countries, but its performance in air quality and environmental health remains among the weakest globally, raising questions about whether the overall improvement reflects actual progress in controlling pollution.
According to Yale University’s 2026 Environmental Performance Index report, Pakistan scored 29.03 overall, with an environmental health score of 14.57 and an air quality score of just 7.54. Pakistan ranked 179th in 2024, but changes to the methodology and indicators in the 2026 index mean the two rankings should be compared with caution.
The 2026 index includes 47 indicators across 12 major environmental categories. Experts say the improvement in Pakistan’s overall ranking cannot, therefore, be taken as direct evidence that air pollution has declined.
Available air-quality data indicate a different trend. During the first 23 days of September 2026, Lahore’s average Air Quality Index (AQI) was approximately 96, compared with about 80 during the same period last year. On September 23, Lahore recorded an AQI of 153, compared with 97 on the same date last year.
Rawalpindi also recorded a higher average AQI during the first 23 days of September 2026, at approximately 116, compared with about 75 during the corresponding period last year. In Lahore, pollution levels also tend to rise during morning and evening hours, further affecting air quality.
Environmental expert and lawyer Rafay Alam said smog should not be viewed solely as a winter problem, as transport, power generation and industrial emissions remain important sources of pollution throughout the year. He noted that changes in temperature and air pressure during winter cause pollutants to accumulate closer to the ground.
Alam called for sustained, long-term policies, better public transport, greater use of electric vehicles and alternative energy, stronger controls on industrial emissions and improved fuel standards.
Read More: Call to protect capital's shrinking green cover
According to data from the Punjab Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), fines totalling Rs305.1 million were imposed for violations of environmental laws during 2025-26, 66 per cent more than the previous year. During the same period, 5,461 sites were sealed and 1,467 polluting units were demolished, while 101,159 inspections of brick kilns and industrial units were conducted.
During a one-week period, 577 anti-pollution operations were carried out across 40 districts of Punjab. Of 7,203 field visits, 607 violations were identified, fines of more than Rs22.8 million were imposed, 483 properties and industrial units were sealed and 30 cases were registered.
Authorities also confiscated 12,906 kilograms of banned plastic bags during the same period. In Lahore, 180 properties were sealed during 181 enforcement operations.
The owner of an industrial unit on Mahmood Booti–Band Road, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the EPA had made it mandatory in 2023 for such industrial units to install emissions-control systems. According to him, steel mills and other industries that installed the systems were not shut down during the 2023 smog season, while industrial closures during smog began in 2024 and 2025.
"Repeated fines and temporary closures led some industrialists to prefer paying penalties rather than installing emissions-control systems," said the industrialist, who called on the government to focus not only on fines and closures but also on ensuring the installation and effective monitoring of emissions-control systems.
According to the industrialist, a standard emissions-control system can cost several crore rupees, although effective systems are also available at comparatively lower costs.
The available data do not establish that Punjab’s recent anti-pollution enforcement efforts caused Pakistan’s improvement in the global environmental ranking. Experts say their impact can only be assessed through continuous, long-term monitoring of air quality and industrial emissions using a consistent methodology.

title: Verity  dominates box office as Tom Cruise   s  Digger  struggles with  3 4m opening day
description: The psychological thriller earned an estimated  15 1m from 3 510 cinemas on Friday
content:
The psychological thriller earned an estimated $15.1m from 3,510 cinemas on Friday
Anne Hathaway’s Verity has taken the lead at the North American box office, while Tom Cruise’s Digger is struggling to attract audiences during its opening weekend.
The psychological thriller earned an estimated $15.1 million from 3,510 cinemas on Friday, putting it on course for an opening weekend of around $33 million to $34 million. The strong start puts Verity comfortably ahead of the weekend’s other major new releases.
Based on Colleen Hoover’s bestselling novel, Verity stars Hathaway as the titular author, with Dakota Johnson playing Lowen Ashleigh, a struggling writer who is hired to complete Verity’s unfinished book after the novelist is left incapacitated. Josh Hartnett also stars as Verity’s husband, Jeremy.
Meanwhile, Cruise’s Digger earned approximately $3.4 million on Friday from 3,321 North American locations, including previews. The figure has put the film on track for an opening weekend of around $7.5 million to $8 million.
The result marks a disappointing start for the Warner Bros. release, which stars Cruise as oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, the film follows the billionaire as an ecological disaster threatens the world after his company’s actions contribute to the crisis.
Digger reportedly began production with a budget of around $125 million before costs increased substantially, with Variety reporting that the final production budget climbed to between $160 million and $180 million. The studio also spent heavily on the film’s marketing campaign.
The opening also represents Cruise’s weakest domestic start in years. According to reports, the film is heading towards his lowest opening weekend since Lions for Lambs opened to $6 million in 2007.
Sony’s Resident Evil is holding the second position, earning approximately $3.62 million on Friday. The horror film is expected to bring in around $12 million over the weekend, adding to its already substantial domestic run.
Brad Pitt’s The Heart of the Beast follows, while A24’s Primetime, starring Robert Pattinson, rounds out the top five. Primetime earned around $2.49 million on Friday and is projected to take in approximately $7.5 million for the weekend.
With the weekend still underway, Verity is firmly positioned at the top of the box office, while Digger faces a much weaker opening despite Cruise’s star power, Iñárritu’s involvement and an extensive promotional campaign. Final weekend figures are expected after the weekend.

title: Barbie 2  may happen after all as Skydance targets sequel
description: Sources cited by Variety now claim that efforts are being made to ensure a follow up goes ahead
content:
Sources cited by Variety now claim that efforts are being made to ensure a follow-up goes ahead
Barbie 2 may finally happen after all, with Skydance reportedly looking to get a sequel to Greta Gerwig’s billion-dollar hit off the ground.
The development comes after Skydance took control of Warner Bros.’ catalogue and reportedly began considering Barbie 2 as one of its early priorities. The company is said to be interested in getting the follow-up moving as it looks for major crowd-pleasing films.
The future of the sequel had looked uncertain earlier this year after negotiations between Warner Bros., Gerwig and stars Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling stalled. Warner Bros. had reportedly spent months discussing deals with the filmmaker and leading actors, with the studio facing a December deadline before the rights could revert to Mattel.
However, sources cited by Variety now claim that efforts are being made to ensure a follow-up goes ahead. The situation could also benefit from Ynon Kreiz, the former Mattel CEO, serving as co-CEO of the new company.
It remains unclear whether Skydance has successfully reopened or advanced negotiations with Gerwig, Robbie or Gosling. The three, alongside writer Noah Baumbach, have been central to discussions about the potential sequel, with Gerwig and Baumbach reportedly having an idea for the next story.
Even if the sequel receives the green light, Barbie 2 is unlikely to arrive soon because its key talent already have other major projects lined up. Gosling has booked Marvel’s Ghost Rider, Gerwig is directing The Chronicles of Narnia for Netflix, and Robbie is attached to the next Ocean’s film.
The original Barbie, released in 2023, became a huge global success, earning around $1.4 billion worldwide and becoming Warner Bros.’ highest-grossing film. The possibility of a sequel has remained complicated by negotiations over compensation and the rights to continue the story with the original creative team.
For now, there is no confirmed production date for Barbie 2, but Skydance’s reported interest gives the long-awaited sequel a new possibility of moving forward.

title: Digger  ending explained  What Tom Cruise   s latest film twist really means
description: Directed by Alejandro Gonz  lez I    rritu  the climate crisis satire presents Cruise as oil baron Digger Rockwell
content:
Directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, the climate crisis satire presents Cruise as oil baron Digger Rockwell
Tom Cruise’s latest film Digger takes a dramatic turn midway through its story, revealing that the events audiences have been watching are not quite what they first appeared to be.
Directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, the climate crisis satire initially presents Cruise as oil baron Digger Rockwell, whose actions contribute to a catastrophic environmental disaster. An accident involving one of his oil rigs triggers a chain of events that leads to worldwide flooding as enormous ice shelves collide with coastlines.
However, around halfway through the film, the story is revealed to be a play within the film. The events involving Digger are actually part of an in-universe stage production called Fossil Fools, with Cruise playing actor Curtis Markson, who is portraying the real Digger Rockwell.
The revelation changes the way the earlier scenes are understood. The play is based on events that supposedly happened 25 years earlier, with the real Digger having become responsible for environmental destruction on a global scale. The production attempts to revisit those events while also examining the consequences of climate negligence.
Curtis is struggling with the role throughout the production. He has studied hundreds of hours of interviews with the real Digger but feels that the stage version has turned the oil baron into a much broader caricature. At the same time, Curtis is dealing with a personal crisis as he worries about his daughter, whose flight from Jamaica has gone missing during a Category 5 storm.
Jesse Plemons’ character, Kenny, also becomes increasingly important to the story. He is revealed to be Digger’s nephew and the billionaire financier behind the revival of Fossil Fools. Kenny had seen the original production as a teenager and remembers cheering alongside the audience when his uncle’s character died on stage.
The production eventually reaches its opening-night performance, with Digger dying by suicide in the play. The audience reacts with a huge ovation, while Curtis learns that his daughter is safe.
But the apparent happy ending does not last. A warning alarm interrupts the celebrations and tells the audience to increase their air-filtration masks to level four. The audience then leaves the theatre and enters a world that has been devastated by the environmental catastrophe depicted in the play.
The final moments show that the disaster has not been undone simply because it has been turned into art. The outside world remains flooded and dystopian, with grey skies, unrest and signs of a society struggling with the consequences of what happened.
That contrast is central to the film’s ending. Digger allows its characters to experience a moment of catharsis inside the theatre, but the alarm forces them to confront the reality waiting outside. The play can tell the story of the disaster, but it cannot reverse what has already happened.
The ending therefore turns Digger from a straightforward climate satire into a story about storytelling itself. The film asks what happens when a catastrophe becomes something people watch, discuss and turn into entertainment while its consequences continue to shape their lives.

title: Indian police detain several people in Gen Z led protests against voter roll changes
description: Police detained protesters on Friday as several nearby metro stations stayed shut amid tight security
content:
Police decline comment on the number ​and identity of those detained
Indian police detained several people in the capital New Delhi on Saturday, disrupting a second day of protests backed by the ​Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party and other opposition groups against changes ‌to voter rolls.
The protesters say the changes benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing party and are demanding the resignation of India's election chief.
About 100 demonstrators removed ⁠security barricades on Saturday and chanted "vote thief, leave the post" and "Gyanesh Kumar, step ​down" before police forcibly detained some of them.
Independent Member of Parliament Kapil Sibal, ​left-wing All India Students' Association President Neha Bora and political activists Prashant Bhushan and Yogendra Yadav were among the protesters, according to a Reuters witness.
The police declined comment on the number ​and identity of those detained.
"First they removed people from the voters list ​and now they are not letting us raise our voice against this. This is not acceptable," ‌Bora ⁠told Reuters .
The chief of the Election Commission, Kumar, has not commented on the protests and the demands to step down.
Read More: India's Cockroach Janta Party, student groups to protest, demand poll chief's resignation
On Friday, police stopped a group of protesters from gathering, bundling them into buses. Several nearby metro stations remained shut ​amid tight security.
Though police ​released many of ⁠those detained on Friday, they charged several of them with allegedly violating orders banning mass gatherings in Delhi, according ​to a police source.
Critics say a nationwide voter-verification exercise launched ​last year ⁠has led to millions of eligible voters being removed from electoral rolls.
The commission, long regarded as one of the country's most trusted institutions, says the exercise is ⁠intended to ​remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible voters.
On Friday, the ​commission directed officials to register newly eligible voters and those omitted from electoral rolls.

title: Aaron Sorkin says money was a    disincentive    for Jesse Eisenberg to return as Mark Zuckerberg
description: I knew what the studio was offering him to do it  but money does not motivate Jesse  It   s infuriating     Sorkin said
content:
“I knew what the studio was offering him to do it, but money does not motivate Jesse. It’s infuriating,” Sorkin said
Aaron Sorkin says Jesse Eisenberg was not motivated by money when he tried to convince the actor to return as Mark Zuckerberg for The Social Reckoning.
Eisenberg, who earned an Oscar nomination for playing the Facebook founder in 2010’s The Social Network, ultimately declined to reprise the role despite Sorkin making several attempts to change his mind. According to Sorkin, even a substantial payday did not persuade him.
“I knew what the studio was offering him to do it, but money does not motivate Jesse. It’s infuriating,” Sorkin told Entertainment Weekly. “If anything, money is a disincentive for him. It’s admirable. He’s very concerned about raising his kids with too much money.”
After realising that money would not be enough to convince Eisenberg, Sorkin said he made a list of things the actor could do with the money, including producing Broadway plays. However, Eisenberg still turned down the opportunity.
Sorkin revealed that he spent three days trying to persuade Eisenberg to reconsider. He even prepared an outline for their conversations, which included arguments about the opportunity to play Zuckerberg again and the scenes he could perform in the film.
The actor did come close to changing his mind, with Sorkin recalling Eisenberg telling him during one of their conversations that he had come closer to persuading him than expected. However, Eisenberg ultimately remained firm in his decision.
Sorkin explained that Eisenberg no longer wanted to be associated with Zuckerberg, particularly because of the physical resemblance between the actor and the billionaire and because the role remains one of Eisenberg’s best-known performances.
Eisenberg previously addressed his decision at the Karlovy Vary Film Festival in July, saying he did not want to be associated with Zuckerberg anymore because he did not like the comparison.
Instead, Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning, which Sorkin describes as a companion piece to The Social Network. Set 16 years after the original film, the new story explores how Facebook developed into a much larger and more influential company.
The film is based on events surrounding The Wall Street Journal’s 2021 investigation known as “The Facebook Files” and also stars Jeremy Allen White as journalist Jeff Horwitz and Mikey Madison as Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen. The Social Reckoning is set to hit cinemas on October 9.

title: Zach Bryan makes statement with    Free Palestine    shirt at Robert Kraft venue
description: Bryan is scheduled to return to Gillette Stadium for second show on October 3
content:
Bryan is scheduled to return to Gillette Stadium for second show on October 3
Zach Bryan drew attention to his appearance at Gillette Stadium on Friday, October 2, after taking the stage in a black shirt bearing the words “Free Palestine”.
Bryan was performing at the Foxborough, Massachusetts venue as part of his With Heaven On Tour. His clothing choice gained attention because the stadium is owned by the Kraft Group, led by New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who became involved in the controversy over Macklemore and Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour.
Macklemore made pro Palestinian comments during performances at MetLife Stadium in September, including a call for “Free Palestine” before performing “Hind’s Hall”. Kraft later confirmed that he had decided Macklemore should not perform at Gillette Stadium during Sheeran’s September 25 and 26 concerts.
Kraft said the decision followed Macklemore’s recent actions, material shared from the stage and what he described as a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that he said was offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community. Kraft also said the decision was not intended to deny anyone the right to advocate for Palestinians and said Palestinian suffering was real.
Sheeran’s Gillette Stadium shows were cancelled because of severe weather linked to a nor’easter, while Macklemore was removed from the remaining US dates of the tour. Sheeran said the decision to remove the rapper was made by the promoter after venues indicated they would not host shows with Macklemore on the bill.
Macklemore later announced the Free Palestine Tour, with dates in Dublin, Paris and London selling out.
Bryan’s shirt was notable because his concert took place shortly after the Macklemore and Kraft dispute. Bryan is scheduled to perform a second night at Gillette Stadium on Saturday, October 3.
Neither Bryan nor Kraft announced a connection between the shirt and the dispute. Its meaning remains open to interpretation.

title: Bodies of Pakistanis killed in Somalia being repatriated  arrive in Addis Ababa  PMO
description: Says arrangements are under way to bring back the bodies of three Pakistanis killed in Somalia
content:
Says arrangements are under way to bring back the bodies of three Pakistanis killed in Somalia
The bodies of three Pakistanis killed in an operation to recover a hijacked oil tanker off the Somali coast have reached Addis Ababa, with arrangements under way for their repatriation, the PMO said on Saturday
The Palau-flagged MT Honour 25, carrying 18,500 barrels of oil and a 17-member crew, including 10 Pakistanis, was seized on April 21, around 30 nautical miles off Puntland while sailing from Oman to Somalia. Puntland’s Maritime Police Force said it rescued the tanker in an operation off Dharin-baar, but the pirates opened fire on the hostages, killing five, including three Pakistanis and injuring four others.
According to the PMO statement, the bodies of Syed Kafeel Omar, Ahmad Ansari and Rafiullah had arrived in Ethiopia’s capital Addis Ababa, where Ethiopian Airlines staff were reviewing arrangements for their transfer to Pakistan.
Read : Three Pakistani sailors killed in Somali ship rescue operation
وزیراعظم محمد شہباز شریف کی ہدایت پر صومالیہ میں جاں بحق پاکستانیوں شہریوں کی میتوں کی پاکستان منتقلی کے انتظامات جاری ہیں. اس سلسلے میں جاں بحق پاکستانی شہریوں کی میتیں ایک گھنٹہ قبل ایتھوپیا کے دارالحکومت ادیس ابابا پہنچ گئی ہیں۔ ایتھوپین ایئرلائنز کا عملہ میتوں کی پاکستان…
The PMO said final approval would be granted for the bodies to be dispatched to Karachi once the necessary preparations had been completed.
In accordance with the prime minister’s directives, relevant officials were in constant contact to expedite the repatriation process, the statement said.
The prime minister had assured every possible assistance in bringing back the bodies of the three Pakistani citizens, according to the PMO.
It said PM Shehbaz had spoken by telephone on Friday with Izaan Kafeel, the son of deceased Syed Kafeel Omar, and expressed his condolences over the death of his father and assured him that the government would take all necessary measures to swiftly repatriate his body along with those of the other deceased Pakistanis.
Also Read : Four Pakistani crew members from hijacked MT Honour 25 to arrive in Karachi tomorrow: Dar
A day earlier, the prime minister announced financial assistance of Rs12.5 million for the families of each of the three Pakistanis killed during a Somali operation to rescue the crew from pirates.
He also announced free education and healthcare for the deceased’s children, while each bereaved family would be provided with a house.
The oil tanker Honour 25, sailing under the Somali flag from Oman to Somalia, was hijacked by pirates on April 21. There were 17 crew members aboard, 10 of them Pakistani nationals. The families of the Pakistani hostages spent months seeking the safe release of their loved ones, staging peaceful protests and repeatedly approaching government authorities.
During their captivity, the pirates initially demanded a ransom of $3 million, which was later reduced to $1.9 million and subsequently to $1 million. All the Pakistani crew members who were killed or injured were from different areas of Karachi.
The pirates came under pressure during a rescue operation and, while retreating from the vessel, opened indiscriminate fire on the abducted crew before fleeing the ship. Five sailors were killed, including three Pakistanis — Second Officer Kashif Umar, Third Engineer Mahmood Ansari and Boiler Rafiullah. The other two deceased crew members were an Indian sailor, Tanveer, and the chief engineer from Myanmar.
Four sailors were injured — Usman, Yasir, Ameen and Vicky from Indonesia — while Hussain Yousuf, Imran Ali and Yaseen remained safe. The two surviving Pakistani crew members later contacted the Ansar Burney Welfare Trust in Karachi using the ship captain’s mobile phone and provided details of the incident.
Puntland police said the Honour 25 had 18,500 barrels of oil on board when it was hijacked. The police had been pursuing three hijacked vessels off the Somali coast and had also rescued another oil tanker, Sibu 1, on Friday. However, 28 of the 41 pirates arrested during that operation later escaped while being transferred to jail, with several Puntland security officials accusing local police of complicity.

title: Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson reveal how they filmed  Verity  infamous bite mark scene

content:
Josh Hartnett also recalled how he left the while Hathaway and Johnson worked on getting the marks right
Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson have revealed the surprisingly technical process behind one of the most memorable scenes in Verity, involving the bite marks left on a wooden bed frame.
The actresses discussed the scene with Entertainment Weekly as they promoted the film, with Josh Hartnett also recalling how he was able to leave set while Hathaway and Johnson worked on getting the marks right.
In Colleen Hoover’s novel and its film adaptation, Verity Crawford, played by Hathaway, leaves bite marks on the headboard during an intimate encounter with her husband Jeremy, portrayed by Hartnett. Later, Lowen Ashleigh, played by Johnson, makes her own marks on the same headboard as she becomes involved with Jeremy.
Hathaway said the detail required considerably more preparation than audiences might expect. She and director Michael Showalter had multiple discussions about how the biting would work, with Showalter even demonstrating different ways to create the marks.
The production also had to find the right type of wood. Hathaway explained that the material needed to look like a genuine bed while still being soft enough for the actors to bite.
Johnson, meanwhile, said her main concern was making the scene convincing without damaging her teeth. The production ultimately used soft wood to make the sequence possible.
Hartnett recalled seeing different versions of the headboard with various bite marks after Hathaway and Johnson had worked on them. He joked that while the actresses were busy “gnawing” on wood, he was able to go home.
Director Michael Showalter described the finished detail as “kinky”, while Hathaway said the production had to introduce a sense of sensuality to the scene despite the unusual practical challenge of biting a wooden headboard.
Hoover also reflected on the unexpected importance of the detail. She said that when she originally wrote the bite marks into the book, she had no idea the moment would become such a memorable part of the story or eventually make its way into the film’s promotional merchandise.
Verity, starring Hathaway, Johnson and Hartnett, is now playing in cinemas. The film is directed by Showalter and adapts Hoover’s bestselling psychological thriller for the big screen.

title: Pakistan Champions pull out of World Championship of Legends
description: PCB NOC issue forces Bangladesh match postponement  owner Kamil Khan remains hopeful of a change in decision
content:
PCB NOC issue forces Bangladesh match postponement; owner Kamil Khan remains hopeful of a change in decision
KARACHI: Pakistan Champions have been officially ruled out of the World Championship of Legends after their scheduled match against Bangladesh in Sharjah was postponed due to players not receiving No-Objection Certificates (NOCs) from the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB).
The tournament began in the UAE on Friday, with Pakistan Champions due to face Bangladesh in Sharjah. However, the match was postponed after the PCB did not issue NOCs to the players.
Captain Shahid Afridi and Sarfaraz Ahmed opted not to travel to Dubai, although several other players had already reached the UAE.
Sources said the team owners had proposed changing the team's name to enable participation in the event, but the proposal was also rejected.
Last year, the Indian team twice refused to play against Pakistan Champions, with former India opener Shikhar Dhawan playing a leading role in the decision.
According to the current schedule, Pakistan and India were due to face each other in Dubai on October 10. Former India players Irfan Pathan, Yusuf Pathan and Harbhajan Singh are part of the Indian squad.
Officials were concerned that if Pakistani former internationals received NOCs and prepared to play India, the Indian side could withdraw from the fixture again, creating an avoidable controversy. The decision was therefore taken not to grant the players permission.
Sources added that some influential figures had also urged the PCB to reconsider its decision, but their efforts proved unsuccessful.
Meanwhile, Pakistan Champions owner Kamil Khan remains hopeful that the PCB will reverse its decision.
"We could not play the match against Bangladesh, but we still hope that the PCB will reconsider its decision. The players submitted their applications according to the prescribed procedure, and we are still waiting for a positive decision," Khan said.
He added that the PCB was their own cricket board and that they would not go against its decision.
This correspondent had reported several days ago that the team was unlikely to receive NOC.

description: The couple have travelled  worked together and shared numerous adventures during their marriage
