title: Trans community urges govt to act on rights commitments
description: Trans community urges govt to act on rights commitments
content:
The representatives of transgender community have urged the Sindh government to implement existing policies and improve access to education, employment, healthcare, housing and social protection.
The demands were presented at the Sindh Transgender Summit, organised by the Legal Aid Society (LAS) in partnership with Gender Interactive Alliance (GIA) under the Aawaz II programme. The summit brought together community representatives, government officials, civil society organisations and development partners to discuss gaps between legal protections and their implementation.
Aradhiya Khan presented the community's five-point charter, which calls for emergency safe houses managed by transgender-led organisations; full implementation of Sindh's Transgender Education Policy; enforcement of the 0.5 per cent government employment quota without discriminatory medical certification requirements; dedicated wards in public hospitals; and the inclusion of registered Khawaja Sira individuals in the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP). The charter also calls for scholarships and protection against discrimination in educational institutions, gender-affirming and sensitive healthcare, and immediate financial assistance.
During a panel discussion on lived experiences, participants highlighted the need for police sensitisation, transgender focal persons in every district, vocational training and government funding for community-led initiatives.
Sindh Social Welfare Secretary Munawar Ali Mithani acknowledged the gap between legal commitments and the community's experiences and said the government was committed to addressing the issues raised.
"Things can be done when we put our heads together. The government, NGOs, civil society and the transgender community must work collectively to turn rights into real opportunities through safe spaces, skills development, education and employment," he said. NADRA Director General Amir Ali Khan said the authority would work with the Social Welfare Department and relevant stakeholders to identify gaps in registration and access to services and review policies to make services more accessible.
The summit also featured a discussion on field realities, a community address and a theatre performance highlighting the experiences of transgender people. Legal Aid Society CEO Haya Emaan Zahid said the organisation would continue monitoring government commitments and providing legal aid and advocacy support.
The summit concluded with calls for continued monitoring and concrete measures to address barriers faced by the Khawaja Sira community across Sindh.

title: Four return to hugs  three to coffins
description: Four return to hugs  three to coffins
content:
Families of Somali pirates' captives to receive survivors on Sunday after 6 months
For five-and-a-half months, the sound of a ringing phone was enough to freeze a household - hope and dread arriving in the same few seconds. Wives waited for husbands swallowed by captivity, children grew up listening for fathers' voices that never came, and parents learned the cruel arithmetic of waiting: every passing day brought their loved ones no closer, yet made the fear of never seeing them again harder to bear. In those homes, silence was no longer silence; it was the space between one phone call and the next, between the prayer that they would come home and the fear that they would not.
Now, after almost half a year that felt like an eternity to their agonised families, four of the Pakistani sailors of MV Honour 25 are finally coming home. But their return carries the cruel weight of those who will not walk through the door. While four injured sailors are expected to reach Karachi on Sunday, the families of three others are preparing to receive their bodies - a homecoming marked by both relief and grief. The four survivors, Yasir Khan, Aqeel Khan, Amin bin Shams and Usman Ghani, are returning after receiving initial medical treatment in Addis Ababa.
For Ayesha, the wait was made even harder by a child born after his father had already left. Her son, Rahim, was just two weeks old when sailor Amin departed aboard the ship. The boy spent his earliest months without knowing his father's arms. "Whenever we think about how we spent those months, we get goosebumps. Every time the phone rang, we feared it would bring bad news," Ayesha told The Express Tribune.
Yasir Khan, who suffered a bullet wound to his leg, is among those coming back alive. His wife, Mahwish, said ten families had endured the ordeal together, holding on to the hope that all their loved ones would eventually return alive. "We never imagined that seven families would be reunited with their loved ones alive, while three families would receive their bodies," she said.
For her two sons, the ordeal had a visible cost. Mahwish said smiles disappeared from their faces after their father was taken hostage. "Bashar, in particular, remained withdrawn and quiet most of the time. Now, the smiles have returned to the children's faces."
Five people were killed during the security forces' operation aboard the Honour 25. Four were Pakistanis, including Second Officer Kashif Umar, boiler operator Rafiullah and Third Officer Mahmood Ansari.
Mahmood Ansari's son, Izhar, was making arrangements for his father's grave when contacted by The Express Tribune. He said the family had yet to receive definitive information about when his father's body would be brought back to Pakistan. A family member of one of the injured sailors told The Express Tribune that the four were expected to land in Karachi on Sunday after departing Addis Ababa aboard Ethiopian Airlines flight ET694.
However, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said in a post on X on Friday that the four sailors were scheduled to arrive in Karachi on Saturday.
Meanwhile, the bodies of the three deceased Pakistani crew members remain in Addis Ababa amid documentation-related hurdles. Efforts are underway to bring them back alongside the four injured sailors. For the families, however, the long-awaited homecoming will not be one single moment of relief. For some, it will mean fathers finally returning to their children. For others, it will mean preparing a grave for someone who never made it home alive.

title: FinMin  British envoy  explore reforms
description: FinMin  British envoy  explore reforms
content:
UK reaffirms technical assistance for strengthening investment policy framework
British High Commissioner Jane Marriott met Federal Minister for Finance Muhammad Aurangzeb to discuss Pakistan's economic reform priorities and opportunities to deepen trade and investment cooperation between Pakistan and the United Kingdom.
The high commissioner highlighted the UK's continued interest in supporting Pakistan's economic transformation through technical assistance aimed at strengthening the institutional and policy framework for investment, trade and private-sector development. She appreciated the successful issuance of Pakistan's $3 billion dual-tranche sovereign Eurobond, noting its significance for investor confidence and international market access.
Muhammad Aurangzeb outlined the government's six key priorities: bringing permanence to macroeconomic stability; moving from stabilisation to sustainable, inclusive and responsible growth; staying the course on structural reforms; moving from aid to trade and investment; expanding access to finance; and positioning Pakistan for the "New Economy".
The two sides discussed reform priorities, with particular emphasis on fiscal management, tax administration, digitalisation, expenditure efficiency, trade and investment promotion, public investment and public-private partnerships.
Regarding opportunities to strengthen bilateral trade and investment, the high commissioner highlighted the potential for UK companies and diaspora networks to contribute to private-sector development, including by supporting the growth and internationalisation of small and medium-sized enterprises.
Separately, Muhammad Aurangzeb held a meeting with a World Bank delegation, led by Country Director Bolormaa Amgaabazar, to review progress under the ongoing economic reform partnership and discuss implementation priorities across growth, jobs, fiscal management, revenue mobilisation, capital-market development, trade and investment, and institutional reforms.

Pakistan could secure a "B+" sovereign credit rating by the first quarter (July-September) of fiscal year 2027-28, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb said on Thursday. title: Thousands of cyberattacks blocked every month
description: Thousands of cyberattacks blocked every month
content:
With surge in digital payments, hackers become more active to exploit trend for illicit gains
1Link's system is actively combating the growing threat of hacker attacks amid the rising trend of digital payments in the country and blocks thousands of cyberattacks every month.
1Link Chief Digital and Technology Solutions Officer Azimullah Khan, whose organisation provides backend support for digital transactions to financial institutions, told The Express Tribune in an interview that the rise of artificial intelligence and the emergence of chatbots had further increased the importance of cybersecurity.
He said digital transactions and fund transfers were increasing in Pakistan, as elsewhere in the world, but hackers had also become more active in an attempt to exploit the trend for illicit gains.
Azimullah Khan said the rapid expansion of digital transactions could be gauged from the fact that 1Link's system would process 12 billion transactions in 2026, meaning more than 300 transactions every second. The value of these transactions could exceed Rs90 trillion. These transactions were processed through 42 banks, 22 affiliates, 1,306 government institutions, more than 22,000 ATMs and other channels, he said.
Given the scale and widespread nature of these operations, cybersecurity had assumed even greater importance. He said this did not mean that hackers were not attempting to breach 1Link's systems. "We face cyberattacks all the time and hackers are continuously trying to penetrate such systems," he said. However, 1Link had deployed advanced and effective cyber defences that continuously thwarted these attempts. He said 1Link had been operating for 22 years and, despite handling such a large system, not a single hacker had succeeded in breaching it.
Asked where most hacker attacks originated, Azimullah Khan said hackers made every effort to conceal their identity and location. However, tools were now available that could help identify them. Most hackers attempted to penetrate the system from abroad, while the number of Pakistani hackers was relatively small.
He said that besides human hackers, AI-powered agents were now also attempting to carry out hacking activities. "This is a new kind of challenge." The number of AI agents connected with banks, financial institutions and other organisations linked to the system was increasing. Protocols had been developed to identify rogue or hacker AI agents, he added.
1Link was also continuously upgrading its systems to prevent scams, fraud and social-engineering attacks. Through device fingerprinting, 1Link can determine whether a user's mobile phone or other device has been changed. In such cases, additional security measures are adopted to prevent criminals from using stolen information to defraud the user. 3D Secure technologies are also being used to secure e-commerce transactions.
Azimullah Khan said 1Link was established 22 years ago at the initiative of the State Bank as an organisation providing ATM switching services to banks. However, over more than two decades, 1Link had evolved into a comprehensive digital banking platform.

title: Gold rises despite weekly global losses
description: Gold rises despite weekly global losses
content:
Gains Rs2,000 to Rs440,636/tola; rupee up 3 paisa to 277.07/$
Gold prices in Pakistan rose on Friday, though international bullion markets reversed earlier gains amid pressure from a stronger dollar and elevated US Treasury yields. The price of gold increased by Rs2,000 per tola to Rs440,636, according to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association.
Similarly, the price of 10-gram gold rose Rs1,715 to Rs377,774. On Thursday, gold had declined by Rs3,000 per tola to Rs438,636. In the international market, spot gold fell 0.8% to $4,145.68 per ounce by 11:38 am EDT (1538 GMT), after gaining earlier in the session, as per Reuters. The precious metal was down around 3.3% for the week, putting it on course for a weekly decline. US gold futures were down 0.7% at $4,173.50 per ounce.
The international market remained under pressure as the US dollar, despite edging lower on Friday, remained on track for a weekly gain. Higher Treasury yields also weighed on gold, which does not generate any yield and therefore tends to face pressure when yields rise.
Yields on the benchmark 10-year and 30-year US Treasury bonds reached their highest levels since 2002 on Thursday, adding to the pressure on precious metals. Market sentiment was also influenced by fresh US labour-market data showing that job growth slowed sharply in September. The weaker employment data prompted traders to adjust expectations for the Federal Reserve's rate path, with markets trimming bets on further rate hikes.
Lower expectations for rate increases can generally support bullion by reducing the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets. However, the impact was offset by the dollar and elevated bond yields in Friday's trading. The decline in international gold prices came despite the softer US jobs data, with investors continuing to assess the outlook for rates and the broader US economy.
Other precious metals also remained under pressure internationally, with gold, silver and other metals heading for weekly losses. Meanwhile, local silver prices increased by Rs50 per tola to Rs6,578.
The latest movement comes after considerable volatility in domestic bullion prices in recent sessions, with gold alternating between gains and losses as international prices and currency-market developments influenced local rates.
Meanwhile, the Pakistani rupee closed at 277.07 against the US dollar, gaining Rs0.03 from Thursday's close at 277.10.

title: Provinces  feedback on IEP sought
description: Provinces  feedback on IEP sought
content:
CCOE gives directive to Power Division; response from provinces still awaited
The Cabinet Committee on Energy (CCOE) has directed the Power Division to take provinces on board in the operationalisation and implementation of the national Integrated Energy Plan (IEP).
During discussions in a recent meeting of the CCOE, it was noted that the IEP would be a 10-year plan with a 33-year perspective for the time horizon of 2027-2060. The forum was informed that the proposed governance framework would ensure coordination among federal and provincial stakeholders through the IEP steering committee, IEP Secretariat and sub-working groups, with policy oversight from the CCOE and the Council of Common Interests (CCI).
It was highlighted that responses from provinces were awaited despite a number of reminders and considerable lapse of time. It was also mentioned that representatives of all provincial governments and other stakeholders were present during the steering committee meeting.
The Ministry of Energy (Power Division) explained that the CCOE had approved the proposed Integrated Energy Planning Ecosystem, Secretariat Structure and High-Level Roadmap 2025 on December 24, 2025, with directives that the High-Level Design Report be developed and approved after comprehensive consultations with all relevant stakeholders. Accordingly, the Power Division completed the exercise and developed the IEP High-level Design after engaging in extensive nationwide consultations.
In the process, more than 50 stakeholders including international development partners, leading academic institutions, key ministries, provincial governments, regulatory authorities including Nepra and Ogra, and major energy-sector entities such as Wapda, Private Power and Infrastructure Board, Inter-State Gas Systems, PSO and K-Electric were consulted.
The CCOE appreciated the Ministry of Energy (Power Division) as well as all other stakeholders for having accomplished the task of preparing a national Integrated Energy Plan and expressed confidence that focused efforts of the minister of power and his team would lead to the transformation of Pakistan's power sector.
The Power Division apprised the CCOE that the High-Level Design was developed through extensive consultation, led by the IEP Secretariat, under the Ministry of Energy, and nationwide technical consultations were held with more than 50 federal and provincial stakeholders.
The division added that subsequently the draft High-Level Design, after incorporating the feedback received during consultations, was presented to the IEP steering committee for review and strategic guidance. The steering committee's feedback and recommendations were incorporated into the finalised High-Level Design Report.
The Ministry of Energy (Power Division) emphasised that the IEP High-Level Design "establishes the strategic, analytical and governance framework for developing a comprehensive national Integrated Energy Plan". Key elements of the plan are explicated as follows:
Analytical framework: It is structured around four interdependent pillars: energy (adequate, reliable and resilient supply); economics (competitive and financially sustainable); equity (inclusive and accessible energy transition); and environment (sustainable, low-carbon and climate-resilient future).
The plan covers both demand and supply sides of Pakistan's energy system, integrating infrastructure planning across the energy value chain. IEP is spread over the period 2027-2060, comprising a 10-year action plan.
Governance framework: It ensures coordination among federal and provincial stakeholders through the IEP steering committee, IEP Secretariat and sub-working groups, with policy oversight from the CCOE and the CCI.
The IEP steering committee, chaired by ministers of power and petroleum, is responsible for the development of IEP strategic oversight and reviews progress before submission to the CCOE and the CCI.
The IEP Secretariat, led by the Ministry of Energy (Power and Petroleum Divisions) and the Ministry of Planning, Development and Special Incentives, serves as the central coordinating body responsible for stakeholder engagement, analytical work and development of the IEP and Energy Information System (EIS), supported by sub-working groups comprising federal and provincial stakeholders providing technical input on different IEP activities.
The Power Division sought authorisation for the IEP Secretariat to proceed with the development of the EIS and directives to all relevant ministries/departments and organisations to support and integrate data systems to develop the EIS.

title: Trade deficit widens to  10 8b in first quarter
description: Trade deficit widens to  10 8b in first quarter
content:
Import growth outpaces encouraging momentum in exports
Pakistan's trade deficit remained elevated at $10.8 billion during the first quarter of the current fiscal year, reflecting an increase of $1.4 billion, as import growth outpaced a good momentum in exports.
According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS), the gap between imports and exports was 15% higher during the July-September period of fiscal year 2026-27. In absolute terms, the gap was $1.4 billion more than the last fiscal year, which was higher than the $1.2 billion tranche Pakistan will receive from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in November.
PBS said that cumulative exports during the first quarter increased to $8.4 billion, a surge of $824 million, or 10.8%, over the same period of the last year. The pace of increase in exports was better than the previous months. Data showed that imports jumped to $19.2 billion during the first quarter of FY27, higher by $2.2 billion, or 13.2%.
Early this week, the federal government apprised the IMF that the continuation of tariff rationalisation under the National Tariff Policy would lower production costs and enhance industrial competitiveness. It added that the allocation of Rs88 billion for concessional lending to exporters at 4.5% would improve liquidity, reduce financing costs and support export expansion.
However, it is not for the first time the government has doled out fiscal benefits to the exporters. They have availed themselves of these benefits without bringing any tangible improvement in non-debt creating receipts. Exports have traditionally stuck in the range of $2.5 billion to $3 billion a month. Even rupee devaluation of Rs100 per dollar could not give a major boost to exports.
The government has now projected that during the current fiscal year exports of goods will be $34 billion compared with $30.8 billion in the last fiscal year.
But given the first-quarter trend, the government's trade liberalisation policy has not helped increase exports, contrary to projections made by the Ministry of Commerce, the World Bank and the IMF. Under the liberalisation policy, the commerce ministry and the World Bank had anticipated a 14% increase in exports and only a 7% surge in imports. In the last fiscal year, exports plunged 6% to less than $31 billion.
PBS data showed that on a month-on-month basis, exports increased 16% to $2.9 billion. In absolute terms, they jumped $407 million in September compared to August this year. Imports increased 11.5% on a monthly basis, reaching close to $6.5 billion. The monthly trade deficit was up by 8%, or $263 million, which was better than earlier trends due to higher monthly exports, showed the official statistics.
On an annual basis, imports increased 11%, or $646 million. Compared to that, exports increased 17.6%, or $440 million. The annual trade deficit widened 6% to $3.6 billion, which was $206 million more than the previous year.
During the first two months, the import bill of petroleum crude soared by 40.5%, while the arrival of petroleum products declined by 26%. Similarly, LPG imports rose by 47%, while LNG inflows dropped by 28.6%. PBS data indicated that crude oil imports increased by 13.7% in quantity but surged nearly 40% in value during the July-August period, highlighting the dominant role of rising international oil prices.
However, the authorities believe that the government's austerity and energy-conservation measures are expected to moderate domestic consumption and, consequently, reduce the import demand for petroleum products in the coming months.
Last week, Secretary Finance Imdad Ullah Bosal told the National Assembly Standing Committee on Finance that the government's fuel conservation policy would only save Rs700 million during the three-month austerity period. At the average price of Rs400 per litre, this translates into only 1.8 million litres over a period of three months.
For the current fiscal year, the government has set a modest export target of $32.5 billion but expects imports to grow to $70 billion. The gap is filled by foreign remittances as new loans are taken to pay back the maturing loans.

title: 895m social projects okayed for Sindh
description: 895m social projects okayed for Sindh
content:
CDWP clears seven foreign-funded water, educational schemes
The Central Development Working Party (CDWP) has approved seven foreign-funded development projects for Sindh covering water supply and sanitation, education, irrigation, property revenue enhancement, environmental sustainability and urban infrastructure.
The projects, approved on October 2, carry combined foreign financing of $895 million, besides a major irrigation project estimated at Rs50.99 billion. The largest initiative is the Sindh Transformational Accelerated Rural Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (STAR WASH) Services Phase-I Project, with a total financing of $450 million. The project comprises a $300 million World Bank financing and a $150 million Asian Development Bank (ADB) component and seeks to improve water supply, sanitation and hygiene services in rural areas of Sindh.
The CDWP also approved $15 million in Project Readiness Financing (PRF) for preparing urban and water-sector projects in Sindh. The initiative falls under the Local Government, Housing & Town Planning Department and is aimed at developing projects for future financing and implementation.
Another major project is the Sindh Property Revenue Enhancement Programme (Sindh PREP), supported by a $150 million World Bank financing. The programme, also under the Local Government, Housing & Town Planning Department, is designed to strengthen property revenue systems in the province.
In the education sector, the CDWP approved the $150 million Sindh Early Learning Enhancement Project through Classroom Transformation (SELECT-II), financed by the World Bank. The project will focus on improving early learning outcomes through classroom transformation under the School Education & Literacy Department.
The Sindh Secondary Education Improvement Project – Second Additional Financing was also approved. The project includes a $100 million ADB loan and a $10 million grant to support improvements in secondary education across the province.
Meanwhile, the Pakistan Finance for Lowering Emissions in the Water Sector (PAK-FLOW) project received approval for $20 million in World Bank financing. The initiative aims to reduce emissions in the water sector while supporting environmental sustainability.
The seventh project involves the Water Requirement for K-IV Project, specifically improvement of the Kalari Baghar Feeder and Keenjhar Lake. It includes cement-concrete lining of the Kalari Baghar Feeder Upper Phase-I at an estimated cost of Rs50,989 million and falls under the Sindh Irrigation Department.

title: SPI at 11 5  as war keeps fuel dear
description: SPI at 11 5  as war keeps fuel dear
content:
Week-on-week, index jumps 0.21%; chicken, LPG lift weekly prices
Short-term inflation stayed in double digits for the week ended October 1, with the Sensitive Price Indicator (SPI) up 11.53% from a year earlier, as the energy shock from the US-Israel war with Iran continued to pass into household costs.
The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) said the SPI rose 0.21% week-on-week to 370.46 points, from 369.69 a week earlier. The yearly pace eased from 11.92% in the previous reading, but remained well above single digits.
The conflict, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz since early 2026, is still visible in the annual fuel bill. Diesel is 44.50% dearer than a year ago at Rs402.53 a litre and petrol is up 44.05% at Rs389.51.
Liquefied petroleum gas, widely used for cooking, rose 1.17% in the week to Rs5,103 for an 11.67kg cylinder, and was 66.59% higher than last October. Electricity charges for Q1 were up 58.59% on the year.
There was some relief at the pump. Diesel fell 3.43% and petrol 0.65% over the week, in line with a partial recovery in crude flows, even as supply of refined products remained tight.
Food showed a split picture. Chicken jumped 7.25% in the week to Rs365.31 a kilogramme and was 13.60% higher than a year ago. Garlic rose 1.85%, gram pulse 1.30% and eggs 0.72%.
Onions, up only 0.39% in the week, were 114.20% costlier than a year earlier at Rs189.42 a kilogramme. Wheat flour was up 32.65%, with a 20kg bag at Rs2,697. Mutton was 15.07% higher, beef 12.90% and fresh milk 8.10%.
Offsets came from perishables and sweeteners. Tomatoes were 45.52% cheaper than last year, potatoes 39.54% and sugar 21.95%. Eggs, despite the weekly rise, remained 17.47% below last October.
Of the 51 items tracked in 50 markets across 17 cities, prices of 20 rose, 10 fell and 21 were unchanged. The burden was uneven. The lowest spending group saw a 0.19% weekly rise and a 9% annual increase. The highest quintile recorded an 11.99% year-on-year hike, against 11.53% for the combined index.
It is pertinent to mention that the monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 10.3% year-on-year in September 2026, which was lower than the increase of 11.1% year-on-year in August.

title: Govt may deduct Rs110b from NFC
description: Govt may deduct Rs110b from NFC
content:
Power-sector dues to be recovered from provincial shares
The federal government has informed the International Monetary Fund (IMF) about its plan to recover over Rs110 billion power-sector arrears from provincial shares in the National Finance Commission (NFC) award amid the lender's concerns over fiscal implications of the move.
During the ongoing talks, the IMF has also inquired whether the federal government will abolish uniform electricity tariffs after the privatisation of companies. But the government did not give a straight reply, according to sources privy to the discussions. Under the uniform tariffs, consumers of inefficient and efficient power distribution companies are charged the same price.
These matters came under discussion with the IMF during a recently held meeting, sources told The Express Tribune. They said that the IMF got a detailed briefing from the Power Division on the circular debt trend, particularly an increase of Rs61 billion in the debt in the last fiscal year. The circular debt had jumped to Rs1.675 trillion, which the Power Division blamed on the reduction in budgeted subsidies and payment dispute with K-Electric – the integrated power distribution and generation company.
The IMF was of the view that it was getting difficult to defend the position before the IMF board and the debt stock could have been reduced by using savings, said the sources. The IMF was informed that to recover over Rs110 billion in provincial electricity arrears, a mechanism had been agreed between the Power and Finance Divisions to deduct the amount out of NFC shares, the sources added.
The IMF was further apprised that at least Rs110 billion had been reconciled and there was a plan to recover nearly Rs50 billion soon. The federal government has in the past attempted to adjust these dues out of the NFC shares but the provincial governments opposed it.
The spokesman for the Power Division did not address the question about whether the provincial governments had given their consent to the move and provided debit authority to the central bank. Without the written provincial consent, it will be impossible for the central bank to make these deductions.
"The federal adjuster is in the Finance Division and the Power Division only issues bills and conveys reconciliation to the Finance Division; therefore, they are in the best position to comment," replied the Power Division spokesman. The finance ministry spokesman did not reply.
Sources said that the federal finance ministry had also attempted to cut over Rs6 billion per month from the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa share on account of a reverse cash grant under the National Economic Initiative of Rs1.036 trillion. However, due to the provincial government's refusal to give the debit authority to the central bank, the money could not be deducted from the provincial share.
Sources said that the IMF had concerns that the move could further strain the provincial revenue receipts, which were already under stress due to the requirements of generating Rs1.7 trillion in cash surplus and giving Rs1.036 trillion in cash grants. The provincial governments have rationalised their development plans to make space for giving grants to the federal government. The IMF was told that the Power Division was also in the process of installing smart meters to resolve billing disputes with the provincial governments.
In response to the IMF's view on deducting money from provincial shares, the spokesman said that the Power Division was constrained from commenting on anything related to the IMF review proceedings and it would be appropriate that comments be taken through the Finance Division. However, the finance ministry spokesman did not reply.
Sources said that discussions were also held regarding the timeframe for privatisation of power distribution companies and post-privatisation policies. They said that the Pakistani authorities appeared reluctant to give a clear response on whether the current uniform tariff policy would come to an end.
Without ending the uniform tariff policy, the subsidies' burden on the budget cannot be reduced, as has happened in the case of privatisation of K-Electric. Sources said that detailed discussions were also held over the dispute between K-E and the federal government and its implications for the overall power-sector financial viability.
K-Electric is not making timely payments for the electricity purchased from the federal government due to a dispute over tariffs and subsidy claims. Sources said that the federal government was willing to clear over Rs100 billion claims of K-Electric, subject to the settlement of tariff-related issues.
The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority and the Nepra tribunal have dismissed K-Electric's plea for a tariff of Rs40 per unit and approved a tariff of Rs32.37. The government expects that K-Electric will challenge the decision in courts.
Sources said that the IMF also inquired about the delay in reviewing the industrial incremental support package. After the IMF's concerns, a hearing has been scheduled for October 5. There was a possibility that the incremental tariff prices would go up as a result of the review, the sources added.
The incremental package, envisaging Rs22.96 per unit as a special tariff rate for select industries, was promised to be reviewed after six months of its introduction in December 2025 but it remained unchanged for the ninth month. Power costs for the industry have gone up by 10% due to tariff rebasing.

content:
China's approach in its Muslim-majority Xinjiang region illustrates a different
Pakistan's "well-planned and calibrated" airstrikes against terrorist hideouts inside Afghanistan, described as a continuation of Operation Ghazab Lil Haq, reflect an escalating pattern of unilateral military action in response to TTP- and BLA-linked violence inside the country. Pakistani officials claim these strikes have eliminated dozens, if not hundreds, of militants operating from cross-border sanctuaries.
Officials describe this approach as "unavoidable", with the implied objective of compelling the Kabul regime to take demonstrable action against terrorist groups targeting Pakistan. The closure of border crossings for almost a year is also rooted in the same rationale. Official messaging increasingly suggests that relations with Afghanistan have reached a "point of no return" because of Kabul's alleged failure to rein in violent groups operating from its territory.
However justified Pakistan's counterterrorism responses may be, they carry a costly consequence: deepening hostility with the rulers in Kabul, an endless cycle of mutual accusations and little prospect of an end to daily violence. This exposes a structural flaw in the current policy: every military or militant action triggers reciprocal accusations, further erodes trust and narrows the space for cooperative solutions.
Historical evidence from Vietnam, Afghanistan (both for the US and the former Soviet Union), and Iraq (for the US and UK) suggests that military action can temporarily suppress violence and create space for other measures. Yet, durable outcomes depend heavily on political legitimacy, local ownership, economic opportunity and addressing underlying grievances.
Counterinsurgency doctrine emphasises "clear, hold and build", yet the "build" phase - governance, public services and a sustainable political settlement - has often proved the most difficult.
China's approach in its Muslim-majority Xinjiang region illustrates a different, highly integrated model combining strict security and law-enforcement measures, large-scale deradicalisation and vocational training programmes, as well as substantial economic investment, infrastructure development, poverty alleviation and improved public services. Chinese official data and statements report an absence of major violent terrorist incidents for several years, often dating this trend to around 2017. They also cite a substantial increase in the public's sense of security, from the high 80 per cent range a decade earlier to over 99 per cent in some surveys, alongside the elimination of extreme poverty, significant GDP growth and expanded access to education, healthcare and connectivity.
China, as the sovereign authority with a monopoly over the use of force, extensive control over the public narrative and considerable resources, implemented an integrated strategy involving coercion, ideological re-education and development. Unlike external interventions, this approach operated within a different political and institutional framework, without comparable democratic or legal constraints. It enabled the rapid suppression of violence and produced measurable economic and security gains according to official indicators, although concerns over human rights, coercive practices and restrictions on civil liberties remain central to international assessments of the policy.
Pakistan's own kinetic operations in Swat, Waziristan and Khyber, including Operation Zarb-e-Azb in 2014 and subsequent nationwide efforts such as Radd-ul-Fasaad, also achieved significant tactical successes. Militants were dislodged from key strongholds, large numbers were killed, violence declined sharply for a period in the mid-to-late 2010s, and state authority was re-established in areas previously lost to militant groups.
However, the "hold and build" approach has remained largely confined to the "hold" phase. Reconstruction has been slow, improvements in public service delivery limited, and governance gaps persistent, particularly in the former tribal districts. Socioeconomic grievances, weak institutions and limited economic opportunities continue to provide fertile ground for militant recruitment, the survival of ideological networks and the regeneration of sanctuaries. The Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in August 2021 has further complicated this landscape.
It is, therefore, hardly surprising that violence in Pakistan has resurged and that Islamabad has been unable to persuade the Afghan Taliban to meet its demands for decisive action against the TTP.
The lesson from Pakistan's kinetic campaigns, both at home and across the border, is that force can create temporary security, disrupt militant networks and buy time. But without sustained efforts to establish legitimate governance, deliver responsive public services, expand economic opportunities and ensure political inclusion, the underlying problems persist, recur or mutate into new forms.
Force is often necessary, but it is rarely sufficient. Sustainable solutions require addressing the material and political conditions that allow militancy to take root, while recognising that identity, ideology and external support networks complicate any purely technical fix based on governance and development. Outcomes depend heavily on local context, institutional capacity, political legitimacy and the willingness to move beyond narrowly defined kinetic measures of success.
Pakistan now faces a double whammy: an indigenous militancy rooted in local grievances, including human rights and governance concerns, alongside cross-border and proxy-linked terrorism. This complex challenge requires minimising the factors that fuel non-state agendas while countering external drivers of violence. Counterterrorism demands a coordinated, indiscriminate and sustained whole-of-government approach that targets militant sanctuaries, strengthens local institutions and combines security operations with political engagement and development.
A policy centred predominantly on military pressure and border restrictions risks adding further layers of animosity and discontent on both sides of the divide. The real challenge for Islamabad and Kabul is to break this cycle through a combination of credible security guarantees, sustained dialogue, effective governance and a shared commitment to preventing their territories from being used for violence against each other.

title: India s totalitarian panopticon
description: India s totalitarian panopticon
content:
Her name is not unknown to those who covered the union government's response to the Covid crisis
Last week, when the story of the centralisation of electoral rolls in India and the arbitrary deletion of voters broke, the name of Dr Seema Khanna was propelled into the limelight. Today, as Director General of Information Technology at the Election Commission of India, she oversees ECINet, which journalist Ritika Chopra revealed centralises voter rolls and bypasses decentralised statutory officers.
Her name is not unknown to those who covered the union government's response to the Covid crisis. She oversaw the rapid development and deployment of Aarogya Setu. Deployed by executive decree without statutory safeguards, the tool harvested sensitive health records and mapped citizens' private social networks. Critics warned that vacuuming up medical history and social interactions without privacy laws normalised permanent state surveillance under the cover of a public health crisis.
Of course, you can argue that this speaks to her competence. But as I keep reminding you, competence only compounds the severity of an offence. She cannot plead ignorance to rationalise locking out on-ground Electoral Registration Officers, preventing them from executing statutory duties.
I know, I know, the harvesting of health records and social context is an even graver issue. Consider the warning of UK judge Sir Nicolas Browne-Wilkinson in the 1992 Marcel case: "If the information obtained by the police, the Inland Revenue, the social security offices, the health service and other agencies were to be gathered together in one file, the freedom of the individual would be gravely at risk. The dossier of private information is the badge of the totalitarian state."
The dossier of private information should worry any citizen in any given country. But weigh it against two compounding factors: In which country is this happening? And in which technological age is it happening?
Country first. Last week, when I showed you how Shudra identity is being systematically dissolved, it did not mean their names are already being purged from electoral rolls, nor that prejudice against them has vanished. Their overt targeting is simply deferred until after a Hindu Rashtra is consolidated. Like slow-boiling frogs, right now, they are led to believe that the rising temperature is meant exclusively for Muslims, minorities, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, an intoxicating illusion of "Hindu consolidation" that masks their own gradual erasure.
Yet, while the word "Shudra" has practically been scrubbed from polite public discourse, the ironclad mandate of endogamy has not. Open any newspaper matrimonial page and the obsession with wedding within one's varna stares back at you. When social prejudice cannot be sanctioned by law, it retreats into an unspoken shadow ledger of social rating. India is the textbook case. Consider how many instances of Pratiloma violence, inter-caste honour killings, are sanitised in police registers as random murders or suicides. Even though the constitutional state claims to view its citizens as equals, society does not. Use your imagination: what happens when such a dossier of private information is handed to a centralised state apparatus captured by an entrenched upper-caste elite?
Now consider the age. Only a decade ago, the Cambridge Analytica scandal revealed how mere social media breadcrumbs could be weaponised: first to build psychographic profiles of individual citizens, and then to push their psychological buttons to manipulate democratic outcomes. Technology has not stood still. It has accelerated exponentially since then.
Rukmini S's Whole Numbers and Half Truths reveals a terrifying reality: the ground-level data feeding this surveillance machine is inherently prejudiced. When police manipulate FIRs to classify inter-caste marriages as kidnappings, or municipal clerks miss rural deaths, they hardcode bias and incompetence into the system. Sucked into national registries, this flawed data is laundered into objective truth, weaponised by algorithms to deny welfare and profile citizens under an illusion of infallibility.
The rollout of the surveillance state started ostensibly with great innocence in 2009 when the Unique Identification Authority of India, led by Nandan Nilekani, introduced Aadhaar. Stated as a benevolent tool to plug welfare leakages, it instead created the master architectural key. Tethering biological markers (facial photograph, scans of both irises and ten fingerprints) to a twelve-digit number stripped citizens of anonymity, anchoring all future dossiers.
By 2013, the intellectual engine room moved to Bengaluru with the formation of the Indian Software Product Industry Round Table, or iSPIRT, co-founded by Sharad Sharma. This think tank engineered the India Stack. Where Silicon Valley pioneered surveillance capitalism for advertising, Bengaluru adapted these tools into surveillance statecraft, building the plumbing to monitor, categorise and manage a population.
Between 2014 and 2015, the vision accelerated through the Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and Mobile trinity. Sold for direct benefit transfers, JAM served as a digital enclosure, soldering biological identity, communication trails and banking ledgers. The sledgehammer of 2016 followed. Demonetisation corralled the cash economy onto digital rails, paving the way for the Unified Payments Interface. UPI eliminated the privacy of the informal bazaar, logging transactions to map financial behaviour in real time.
Between 2017 and 2019, the architecture leapt to algorithmic governance. Using Telangana's Samagra Vedika as a testing ground, algorithms fused isolated departmental databases into a single predictive profile without citizen consent. This laid the foundation for the National Social Registry, a 360-degree database tracking every life event, resulting in algorithms silently cancelling pensions.
The 2020 Covid crisis justified completing the biological ledger through Aarogya Setu, developed by the National Informatics Centre with Dr Seema Khanna overseeing operations. Evolving into the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, it converted a temporary epidemic response into permanent biological surveillance.
Now consider this. Nandan Nilekani and Sharad Sharma are Brahmin. Seema Khanna a Khatri. All movers and shakers of iSPIRT belong to the upper castes. The totalitarian state's panopticon is ready and actively being deployed. How it is used after safeguards of a secular state and constitution are removed does not require much imagination.
This raises a final question about Western media, international wire services, search engines and news aggregators. They never tire of spotlighting Chinese security measures, yet this story rarely reaches your screens. We will need another piece to explore exactly why. Stay tuned.

title: Leverage has limits
description: Leverage has limits
content:
Oil mattered to the rise of the dollar system, but it never explained the whole system
A theory popular since 2012 said that Washington's hostility towards Iran was really about defending the "petrodollar". Iraq sold oil in euros, Libya flirted with monetary alternatives, Iran sought non-dollar settlements - and punishment followed. Neat. Too neat.
Oil mattered to the rise of the dollar system, but it never explained the whole system. The dollar still accounted for 57.13% of disclosed global forex reserves in the first quarter of 2026, according to IMF.
The Federal Reserve points to deeper reasons: large and liquid financial markets, safe assets, convertibility, institutional credibility and network effects. Thus, the dollar is not about to disappear because some oil is paid for in yuan, rupees or roubles. The real issue is how monetary power is used.
When so much global finance touches American institutions, sanctions become exceptionally potent. That can be useful. It can also be overused. The more the US turns access to the dollar system into a geopolitical weapon, the more incentive others have to create alternatives.
That is why local-currency settlement, alternative payment channels and reserve diversification matter. They are not yet a replacement for the dollar. They are insurance against dependence on one centre of power.
The latest Middle Eastern development makes the point better than another BRICS declaration.
Saudi Arabia has asked China to help restrain Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis after their advance put greater pressure on shipping around Bab el-Mandeb. Beijing then pressed Tehran privately. China buys most of Iran's seaborne oil, but it also has huge commercial and energy interests in Saudi Arabia and the wider Gulf. That is political economy at work.
China does not need to replace the US militarily to become relevant diplomatically. Economic interdependence is giving it leverage across relationships that cut through old alignments. There is irony on every side.
Iran gains tactical leverage when its allies can threaten strategic sea lanes. However, disruption of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb also hurts China, the very power on which Tehran increasingly depends for oil sales and diplomatic space. Saudi Arabia remains deeply tied to the US for security, but it has turned to Beijing where Chinese economic influence may reach Tehran more effectively.
US retains overwhelming military and financial power. The war with Iran nevertheless remains unresolved more than six months after it began. That should provoke a harder question than whether the dollar is still number one. Iran is not an innocent party. Its regional proxies, missile capability and nuclear activities have created legitimate security concerns. Threatening commercial navigation imposes costs on countries with no part in the conflict. Nevertheless, policy must be judged by outcomes. Decades of sanctions, covert confrontation and now open war have not produced a durable political settlement.
The same test applies to American financial policy. Sanctions may hurt an adversary today while strengthening tomorrow's incentive to trade outside channels Washington controls. Military force may destroy installations while creating new forms of asymmetric resistance. Power works. The question is what it produces.
The US built post-war influence through not only aircraft carriers and sanctions. It also offered markets, institutions and assets that others wanted to. That was leadership because participation was substantially voluntary. Leverage is different. It rests on the cost of saying no.
A global order cannot be sustained indefinitely by making exit painful. Nor can Middle Eastern peace be built by ensuring that every adversary is permanently weaker, sanctioned or bombed.
The petrodollar theory got the mechanism wrong. Its deeper warning survives.
The danger to American primacy is not that the world suddenly abandons the dollar. It is that more states begin treating dependence on an American-centred system as a risk to be hedged.
China's role between Saudi Arabia and Iran is a small but telling sign. The future may not be post-American. It is already less exclusively American. Leverage can compel. Leadership persuades. The Middle East is showing why the distinction matters.

title: Police stations on the move
description: Police stations on the move
content:
Law enforcers are notorious for corruption within the ranks
Punjab's launch of 33 mobile police stations, including six dedicated "Pink" units for women, seems like a good attempt to make it easier for citizens to approach law enforcement authorities. The initiative offers 14 services, from FIR registration to driving licences, and will visit different neighbourhoods, along with universities and colleges, on fixed schedules. This will be of great benefit for anyone who has to get some work done at a police station, but especially for women, who have long hesitated to enter male-dominated police stations to report harassment or domestic violence and may find women's police stations too hard to reach. By saving time and travel costs for citizens in remote areas, the scheme could genuinely bridge the public-police divide.
But the biggest problem for the Punjab Police is not accessibility. It is the Punjab Police. The law enforcers are notorious for corruption within the ranks. Almost 85,000 complaints were lodged against the force in the first seven months of this year, with nearly 15,000 centred on corruption and bribery. Surveys consistently rank Punjab Police as Pakistan's most corrupt provincial department. Mobile stations may make it easier to file a report, but if the underlying culture of impunity - where cases are refused registration and investigations are botched for a price - remains untouched, the vans will merely become new venues for old abuses.
Critics will also question the cost. The 33 units require vehicles, technology and specialised staff, all funded by taxpayers. While the benefits could potentially be huge, that is still an assumption. The expenditure is already a fact. To ensure the taxpayer gets value for money, the exercise needs genuine accountability, with merit-based hiring and staffing and independent oversight.
The mobile police stations could be of great value, but that value can only be realised if provincial leaders in parliament and at the Central Police Office recognise that no fleet of vans can substitute for the difficult work of reforming the institution.

title: Unsafe online
description: Unsafe online
content:
Such spaces offer entertainment and companionship
The internet has become an ordinary part of childhood, but the protections surrounding young users remain anything but ordinary. A new Kaspersky analysis offers a revealing picture of where Pakistani children are spending their time online. During the first eight months of 2026, YouTube accounted for 31.2% of their mobile app activity, followed by Instagram at 18.8% and WhatsApp at 17.4%. Multiplayer games and platforms such as Roblox and Discord also featured prominently in their digital lives.
Such spaces offer entertainment and companionship. The concern is that the same features that make them attractive to young users also make them accessible to people seeking to deceive or exploit them. Multiplayer games allow strangers to communicate directly with children. Phishing links can arrive disguised as offers of free game currency or rewards, while friendships formed online can gradually become vehicles for grooming or blackmail. The scale of the problem in Pakistan is already difficult to dismiss. Research released by UNICEF, ECPAT International and Interpol last month found that nearly one in 16 internet-using Pakistanis between the ages of 12 and 17 had experienced some form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse within a year. That translates into roughly 1.5 million children. The research also found that fear, stigma and possible repercussions within the family often discourage victims from seeking help. AI is making an already difficult problem more complicated. Across an 11-country study, at least 1.2 million children reported having their images manipulated into sexually explicit deepfakes during the preceding years.
Children will not retreat from the digital world, nor should they be expected to. The task is to make that world safer for them. As technology becomes better at creating convincing falsehoods and predators become more adept at exploiting trust, Pakistan's safeguards must evolve just as quickly. Connectivity without protection leaves children carrying risks they are too young to manage alone.

title: Surging Houthis
description: Surging Houthis
content:
Escalation on the part of the Houthis is uncalled for
Despite hopes for a thaw amid the widening Middle East conflict, the Houthis' surge is acting as a spanner in the works. Reports that the pro-Iran Yemeni militia launched drone attacks on an electricity facility in the holy city of Medina have taken the Muslim world by surprise, pushing the regional security paradigm to the edge. Likewise, unconfirmed reports indicate that American authorities are investigating potential Iranian links to a thwarted midair insider attack on a Flydubai airliner en route to Tel Aviv. This, too, has upped the ante, with US warning of a severe backlash against Iran. Finally, an unannounced, lethal conflict between Yemeni state security forces and the Houthis is hampering navigation across the strategic Bab-el-Mandeb waterway, escalating Saudi Arabia's security risks to unprecedented heights.
This escalation on the part of the Houthis is uncalled for. The non-state actor is unnecessarily expanding the orbit of war, inviting retribution with dire consequences for the entire region. Loud explosions were also heard in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which is controlled by Houthi forces. This indicates that the Iranians, too, are engaged in a power struggle, using proxies as leverage for realpolitik. Furthermore, the prospective withdrawal of US troops from Iraq and Syria, paired with Washington's positioning as an ally of Saudi Arabia, represents a new twist in regional dynamics. Moreover, the US deployment of additional Patriot missile batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar and the Pentagon signing a massive contract for the production of SM-6 missiles are clear signs of broadening warfare.
The million-dollar question is: where are statecraft and diplomacy? Why do they take a backseat every second day? Why are the Pentagon and the IRGC so obsessed with warmongering while their respective diplomatic echelons strive for a thaw in all sincerity? It is a fact that non-state actors are a reality in the Middle East power dynamics, but the Houthis are going over the brink as spoilers. Tehran has a responsibility to prevail over the Houthis and ensure that Saudi Arabia's territorial integrity is not breached.

title: Why humanity s quest for order still matters
description: Why humanity s quest for order still matters
content:
Our normal habits focus on creating local order
Human society is caught in a permanent contradiction: while we constantly build rules, routines and industrial systems to keep things organised, the fundamental laws of physics show that every action we take pushes the universe closer to total disorder.
On a daily basis, our normal habits focus on creating local order. Think about a simple morning routine: making coffee, following a strict sleep schedule or organising an office desk. Each action requires energy, whether from personal metabolism or electricity. According to the Second Law of Thermodynamics, energy use is never completely efficient; it always releases waste heat into the surrounding environment. When you clean a room or live a disciplined life, you reduce disorder inside that small space, but you do so by releasing heat and energy that increase the total disorder of the wider world. In short, we create order locally by adding to disorder globally.
This small-scale accumulation of energy use grows into major global problems, such as climate change, severe flooding and melting glaciers. Industrial production, modern cities and large-scale farming consume massive amounts of fossil fuels, turning concentrated resources into waste heat and carbon emissions. From a physics perspective, global warming and extreme weather represent the spread of excess thermal energy through the Earth's climate system. As greenhouse gases trap heat, the atmosphere and oceans absorb that energy, moving the planet toward a more chaotic and unstable thermal state. The physical decline of our environment is the large-scale result of rising entropy.
Given that human actions inevitably produce entropy and disorder, a logical question arises: Why should we care about sustainability, ethics and disciplined living if decay is guaranteed?
Researchers and thinkers across science and philosophy have explored this dilemma. In his book, Entropy: A New World View, economist Jeremy Rifkin argues that while total entropy always increases, human societies can choose how fast we use up natural resources, making a strong case for conservation. Similarly, Nobel laureate Ilya Prigogine showed that living things are open systems that survive by continuously taking in energy and releasing waste into their surroundings.
This scientific reality also connects with spiritual and philosophical views. For instance, the Islamic worldview teaches that the physical universe is finite and moving toward a destined cosmic conclusion. Rather than making human life meaningless, this shared understanding actually increases our moral responsibility. As seen in concepts of environmental stewardship, humans are meant to manage the Earth carefully. Literature and research suggest that we do not seek order to cheat the laws of physics, but to act with responsibility during our temporary time on Earth.
Ultimately, the clash between human discipline and universal entropy reveals the true meaning of our choices. The order we create through daily habits, green technology and environmental protection cannot reverse the laws of physics or stop the ultimate end of the universe. However, the inevitability of decay does not make our actions pointless. We organise our lives and protect nature not because we expect to live forever, but because choosing to create order and care for our world remains the most meaningful way to live.

content:
Khloe Kardashian reveals whether she would join 'The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills' after years on reality TV
Khloe Kardashian has addressed whether she would ever leave The Kardashians for Bravo’s The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills , saying she does not currently see herself joining the franchise.
During the September 30 episode of her Khloe in Wonder Land podcast, Kardashian discussed the possibility with Paige DeSorbo. The reality star said she has primarily worked on television alongside her family since Keeping Up With the Kardashians premiered in 2007.
“I love them, but I have really only worked with my family and I can’t imagine,” Kardashian said, explaining that she believes working on a show such as The Real Housewives could involve competition for screen time.
Kardashian added that she was not fully familiar with the behind-the-scenes dynamics of the Bravo franchise but said she was “probably not” interested in joining.
She also suggested that appearing on a reality competition show would be more appealing to her. Kardashian said she would enjoy participating in a programme such as The Great British Bake Off and expressed interest in hosting a competition show for children.
“I love watching kids baking shows and competition shows like American Ninja Warrior but I like the kids,” she said. “I feel like I could do that.”
Kardashian currently stars on The Kardashians with sisters Kourtney Kardashian, Kim Kardashian, Kendall Jenner and Kylie Jenner, as well as their mother, Kris Jenner.
The reality star is also a mother to True Thompson, 8, and Tatum Thompson, 4, whom she shares with former partner Tristan Thompson.
Kardashian’s comments come as her family continues its long-running presence in reality television. While she remains part of The Kardashians , her remarks indicate that a move to The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills is not something she currently plans to pursue.

title: Tobey Maguire and Jennifer Meyer are finally divorced after years apart
description: Tobey Maguire and Jennifer Meyer are officially divorced nearly 10 years after announcing their separation in 2016
content:
Tobey Maguire and Jennifer Meyer are officially divorced nearly 10 years after announcing their separation in 2016
Tobey Maguire and Jennifer Meyer are officially divorced nearly 10 years after announcing their separation, according to court documents.
The former couple’s marital status was terminated on September 21, with both restored to single status, the documents filed with the Los Angeles Superior Court show. However, the divorce is not fully settled, as Maguire and Meyer still have outstanding issues to resolve.
The pair bifurcated their marital status, meaning the court has legally ended their marriage while retaining jurisdiction over other matters in their divorce proceedings. The documents do not specify which issues remain unresolved.
Maguire and Meyer separated in 2016 after nine years of marriage. The Spider-Man actor and the jewelry designer announced their decision in a joint statement, saying their priority was raising their children together with love, respect and friendship.
Meyer filed for divorce in October 2020, four years after the couple separated. The former spouses later agreed to use a private judge to mediate their remaining disputes as they work towards a broader settlement.
Maguire, 51, and Meyer, 49, share two children: daughter Ruby, 19, and son Otis, 17.
Their divorce proceedings have continued for several years, with the latest court filing formally changing their marital status to single.
Meyer has since moved on with music executive Geoffrey Ogunlesi. The couple became engaged in August 2024 and welcomed their first child, a daughter, earlier this year.
Maguire, meanwhile, has largely kept his personal life out of the spotlight while continuing his career in film. His divorce from Meyer marks the legal conclusion of their marriage, although financial and other matters connected to their separation remain subject to further proceedings.

title: Police reveal what happened before Gypsy Rose   s ex fianc   Ken Urker died
description: Gypsy Rose Blanchard   s ex fianc   Ken Urker was found dead after authorities were warned he had threatened suicide
content:
Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s ex-fiancé Ken Urker was found dead after authorities were warned he had threatened suicide
Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s former fiancé, Ken Urker, was found dead at his Louisiana home after authorities were told he had threatened suicide and had access to a gun.
According to law enforcement records obtained by TMZ , deputies went to Urker’s Raceland residence on Thursday evening for a welfare check after family members said he was not answering his phone or reporting to work.
A caller told dispatchers that Urker had threatened to take his own life, owned a gun and was in a “dark place”. Another caller later told authorities that Urker had killed himself and asked police to check on him.
Gypsy Rose’s brother, Dylan, eventually entered the home through a bedroom window and found Urker unconscious and cold to the touch on his bed. Deputies reportedly found a holstered handgun on a nightstand next to a syringe and two shot glasses.
Authorities also reported finding drug paraphernalia and a brown powdery substance in the bathroom. However, the report did not state that the gun had been fired or that it was used in Urker’s death.
Urker was found dead on his birthday, according to previous reports. Gypsy Rose had reportedly texted him a birthday message but did not receive a response before her brother discovered him.
Urker and Gypsy Rose Blanchard first connected through a prison pen pal programme and became engaged in 2018. They later separated before reconnecting years later. The pair welcomed their daughter, Aurora, together.
An investigation into Ken Urker’s death remains ongoing, and authorities have not publicly confirmed the official cause of death.

title: Amy Robach and T J  Holmes take next step after 2025 engagement
description: Former GMA anchors Amy Robach and T J  Holmes have applied for a marriage license in Arkansas ahead of their wedding
content:
Former GMA anchors Amy Robach and T.J. Holmes have applied for a marriage license in Arkansas ahead of their wedding
Former Good Morning America anchors Amy Robach and T.J. Holmes have taken another step toward marriage by applying for a marriage license in Arkansas.
According to TMZ, the couple applied for the license in Washington County on Sept. 18. The filing comes nearly a year after Robach and Holmes announced their engagement in October 2025.
Arkansas has a personal connection for Holmes, who was born in West Memphis, Arkansas. The couple began their relationship while working together at GMA in New York City before their romance became public in 2022.
Robach and Holmes were both married when photographs of them together surfaced in November 2022. Robach was married to actor Andrew Shue at the time, while Holmes was married to attorney Marilee Fiebig.
Their relationship prompted an internal review at ABC, and both television personalities were eventually taken off the air. Robach and Holmes left ABC in January 2023 following negotiations with the network.
Despite the public attention surrounding their relationship, the pair continued dating and later launched the podcast Amy & T.J. The podcast has featured discussions about their relationship, the scrutiny they faced and the impact of their departures from television.
Their former spouses have also since moved on. Shue and Fiebig later began dating and have appeared publicly together.

title: Michael B  Jordan   s  Battlefield  movie finds a potential home at Sony
description: Sony Pictures is in talks to land the  Battlefield  movie  with Michael B  Jordan and Christopher McQuarrie attached
content:
Sony Pictures is in talks to land the 'Battlefield' movie, with Michael B. Jordan and Christopher McQuarrie attached
Sony Pictures has emerged as the leading bidder for the upcoming Battlefield movie based on Electronic Arts’ popular video game franchise, according to TheWrap .
The studio is in talks to acquire the film package, which has attracted bids from Warner Bros. Discovery, Amazon MGM Studios, Universal and Netflix. Christopher McQuarrie is attached to write, direct and produce the Battlefield adaptation, while Michael B. Jordan is set to produce and could potentially star in the film.
The project is being produced by Jesse Stern of Electronic Arts, Carter Swan of Emerald Neon, Roy Lee and Miri Yoon of Vertigo and Elizabeth Raposo of Outlier Society.
The Battlefield video game franchise began with Battlefield 1942 , which was released for PC and Mac in 2002. The series has since expanded across consoles and explored military conflicts and settings ranging from the Vietnam War to futuristic battlefields.
The latest instalment, Battlefield 6 , was released in 2025 and reportedly became the bestselling game in the franchise. Its commercial performance helped fuel plans to develop a major Hollywood adaptation of the EA franchise.
The Battlefield movie is part of a growing wave of video game adaptations being developed for theatrical and streaming audiences. The project also arrives as Paramount prepares a feature adaptation of rival franchise Call of Duty , with Taylor Sheridan and Peter Berg attached to write and Berg set to direct.
Michael B. Jordan is coming off his work on Sinners , which earned him an Oscar win, while McQuarrie is known for his work on the Mission: Impossible franchise.
Sony Pictures declined TheWrap’s request for comment. Further details about the Battlefield movie, including its cast and release date, have not yet been announced.

title: Mir Raza commission seeks answers from senior police officers
description: AIG Karachi Azad Khan and two DIGs receive sealed questionnaires submitted by Mir Raza   s family
content:
AIG Karachi Azad Khan and two DIGs receive sealed questionnaires submitted by Mir Raza’s family
The Judicial Commission probing the Mir Raza Ali case has sent questionnaires to senior police officers, including AIG Karachi Azad Khan, involved in the investigation, seeking answers to questions raised by the victim’s family.
The sealed questionnaires were delivered through the commission’s designated Nazir, Tajammal Lodhi, to AIG Azad Khan, DIG Amir Farooqi, head of the investigation team, and DIG Farukh Lanjhar.
The questions were submitted to the commission by Mir Raza’s mother, sister and father through their counsel, Advocate Jibran Nasir.
Read : Mir Raza judicial commission’s term extended until October 15
Separately, Sindh government focal person Javed Abro met commission chairman Justice Umar Sial in his chamber and informed him that the commission’s term had been extended until October 15.
The commission has also issued notices to CPLC official Kashif Iftikhar and DSP Siraj Lashari. Their statements will be recorded on October 5.
The commission is examining the circumstances surrounding Mir Raza’s death and has been recording statements and seeking responses from officials and other relevant witnesses.
The Sindh cabinet on Thursday extended the tenure of the Judicial Commission probing the death of Mir Raza Ali until October 15, giving the panel additional time to complete its proceedings and finalise its findings.
The cabinet was told that the commission, headed by Justice Umar Sial, had recorded statements from several witnesses but needed more time to complete its inquiry. It was also authorised to continue proceedings beyond October 15 if required.
Mir Raza Ali, the 25-year-old owner of dessert brand Wafflix, went missing from Karachi’s PECHS area on July 28, 2026. His body was found the following day in bushes near a wedding hall in Gulistan-e-Johar. Police initially treated the death as a possible suicide, but a second post-mortem conducted after his exhumation found a firearm entry wound, multiple ante-mortem injuries and signs of internal bleeding, leading investigators to treat the case as murder.
The initial post-mortem had faced several objections, with the Karachi police surgeon identifying 14 deficiencies, including the absence of an X-ray, failure to collect hand swabs for gunshot-residue analysis and the lack of chemical examination of gunpowder marks around the bullet wound.
The investigation subsequently came under scrutiny from Raza’s family, who alleged serious lapses in the handling of evidence and CCTV footage and sought the formation of a joint investigation team. The Sindh High Court later rejected the family’s plea for a JIT but directed the relevant authorities to conduct the investigation impartially, fairly and expeditiously.
Read More: Mir Raza commission rejects family's plea to summon top cops
Police told a Senate committee in September that they had recorded statements from 78 people but had not found evidence linking anyone to Raza’s alleged murder. Investigators nevertheless continued to treat the case as murder, while reviewing medical, chemical, forensic and digital evidence.
The Sindh government had meanwhile established a judicial commission headed by Sindh High Court Justice Umar Sial to examine the circumstances surrounding Raza’s death, the conduct of the investigation and any possible negligence or concealment of evidence by police or other officials.
The judicial commission had so far examined police records, witness statements and the circumstances surrounding Mir Raza Ali’s death, with its proceedings raising discrepancies in witness accounts, the handling of evidence and the initial post-mortem. The commission also questioned senior police and health officials over the investigation, including the handling of CCTV footage, Raza’s phone and smartwatch, and the initial focus on a possible suicide.
