title: PM for export led economic growth
description: PM for export led economic growth
content:
FinMin emphasises growth will reach 4% in 2027 vs 3.7% last year
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has said that an export-led growth-based economy is the country's goal and the private sector must lead the economy. He made these remarks on Thursday while addressing the gong-striking ceremony for the listing of Naya Nazimabad Apartments REIT at the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX).
The prime minister said the incentives provided to the construction industry in the budget were producing results, with growth particularly visible in Karachi's construction sector. He said various industrial sectors had been provided subsidies since the 1960s, but despite receiving substantial support, they failed to make a significant contribution to exports. Instead, commodity prices increased, while quality and productivity were affected and import substitution could not be achieved. "This is a bitter reality that must be corrected before we can move forward," he said.
He urged exporters to play an effective role in promoting export-led, sustainable economic growth. PM Sharif said that during his recent visits to the US and the UK, he held special meetings with prominent bankers, who appreciated the government's reform efforts. He said the IMF chief had remarked that it was a "new Pakistan", to which he replied that it was not a new Pakistan but a "new team". "We have to demonstrate export-based growth in our economy," he said, adding that the budget provided Rs2.3 trillion in tax breaks. He mentioned that Pakistan had achieved major success with the issuance of Eurobonds. Foreign exchange reserves held by the State Bank of Pakistan had reached $21.4 billion, while remittances were showing significant growth. The government had also provided tax incentives to promote industrial development. The prime minister said the PSX had made substantial progress, but further reforms were needed while keeping other markets in the region in view.
Speaking on the occasion, Federal Minister for Finance Muhammad Aurangzeb said economic growth would reach 4% in 2027, compared with 3.7% last year. He said the government could quickly raise growth to 6% through a consumption-led growth model, but such a short-term increase would create balance-of-payments pressures and push the economy back into a boom-and-bust cycle.
Instead, he said, the government was pursuing an export-led, sustainable economic growth model, under which the economy was expected to achieve 4% growth during the current year. Aurangzeb said the number of tax filers had increased by 45% to more than 5.7 million this year, compared with 3.9 million last year. The government was working on reforms and tax-related issues to increase activity in the capital market.
He said Rs60 billion had been disbursed under the Prime Minister's Apna Ghar Programme, while the banking industry had approved Rs340 billion under the initiative. "The real issue is no longer the issuance of loans," he said. "The banking industry has taken the first step; now the supply side has to take the next step."

title: Petrol subsidy puts govt  IMF at odds
description: Petrol subsidy puts govt  IMF at odds
content:
Deadlock persists over writing off Rs1.4tr receivables of gas firms
Talks between Pakistani authorities and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) hit a deadlock over fuel prices and writing off Rs1.4 trillion receivables of gas companies as the global lender reiterated to waive payments and give any subsidy through a targeted mechanism.
However, despite reservations there were no chances that the government would prematurely end the fuel compensation scheme for motorcyclists and small-car owners but its extension beyond three months may not be possible, the authorities said on condition of anonymity.
They said that the IMF was of the view that the actual fuel compensation cost may be higher than Rs75 billion for the three-month period. Likewise, the Pakistani authorities have not yet accepted the IMF's stance to write off the recoverable receivables of Sui gas distribution companies due to its implications for the gas distribution and exploration firms.
A detailed meeting on the gas-sector circular debt management plan is expected to take place next week after the earlier scheduled meeting was postponed. The IMF mission is holding discussions with various ministries as part of the fourth review of the $7 billion loan package and Article-IV consultations.
Sources said that during this week's meeting there was no clear consensus between the Pakistani authorities and the IMF team over a couple of issues related to the petroleum sector. The IMF was appreciative of the reforms introduced in the gas sector, particularly the reduction in the unaccounted for gas and stemming the flow of debt but it had divergent views on the two critical issues, they said.
Sources added that the Petroleum Division was of the view that the current fuel prices were unfair for the consumers. Its argument was that the imported cost of petrol before any tax and margin was roughly Rs250 but the consumer was paying Rs390 per litre after adding taxes.
Cost breakdown was shared with the IMF. In addition to the imported petrol price of Rs250, the government was charging taxes of nearly Rs110 per litre and added Rs27 per litre on account of various margins. Sources said that the IMF's mission was of the view that setting the priorities was the responsibility of the government. Under the commitment, Pakistan has assured the IMF that it will "refrain from introducing any fuel subsidy or cross-subsidy scheme". But the commitment was breached last month and the IMF wanted to rectify it.
During the staff-level meeting, the IMF again pressed to give only targeted subsidies. Sources said that the IMF reiterated that the government should write off receivables of the gas-sector companies due to the delay in making payments. But the Petroleum Division did not agree, saying the federal government could not go back from its commitments to the gas distribution and exploration companies.
Sources said that the Petroleum Division through the Finance Division had requested another meeting with the IMF team before the start of review talks on the circular-debt management plan. But the finance ministry could not ensure the meeting. In the last meeting, the IMF had asked Pakistan to write off the inter-corporate debt and waive late-payment surcharges estimated at Rs1.7 trillion.
To resolve the issue, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had constituted a committee on implementing structural reforms in the petroleum sector. The government had held various meetings with the IMF from March to July but no solution could be found. The IMF has expressed reservations about using Rs850 billion worth of dividends of the gas companies to settle the debt and said that it was not fiscal neutral.
Pakistan had asked the IMF to suggest an alternative but a meeting with the fiscal affairs department of the IMF could not take place due to the finance ministry, said sources. One of the options was to increase prices but the government did not support such a proposal as it would directly affect all consumers, irrespective of income levels.
The Petroleum Division has proposed that the circular debt, estimated at Rs3.6 trillion, should be settled through tariff differential claims of Sui gas companies, which will pay off OGDC, PPL and GHPL.
The plan seeks a net cash injection in the companies while incorporating cash-flow projections and contractual obligations of the firms. It has been proposed that incremental dividends should be utilised only for OGDC, PPL and GHPL owing to major shareholdings of the government.
One of the concerns of the IMF was that how the proposal covered the leakage to non-controlling interest and minority shareholders and whether the stated coverage through additional inflows, including PDL and LNG-related savings, was realistic given previous discussions where LNG and the gas sector were framed as under severe stress.
The Petroleum Division reiterated that the underlying circularity originated from the tariff differential claims that represented a policy-driven public-service obligation, which stopped Sui companies from full-cost recovery and caused unpaid invoices. The proposal was presented as a mechanism to liquidate legacy receivables and restore credibility in the system, noting that many receivables were significantly aged and would otherwise remain impaired.

title: Ashley Tisdale opens up about postpartum depression and marriage struggles
description: Ashley Tisdale opens up about postpartum depression  anxiety and marriage struggles after welcoming daughter Jupiter
content:
Ashley Tisdale opens up about postpartum depression, anxiety and marriage struggles after welcoming daughter Jupiter
Ashley Tisdale has opened up about her experience with postpartum depression and anxiety, revealing that the period placed significant strain on her marriage to Christopher French.
The actress, 41, discussed her experience during the first episode of French’s new podcast, Recovering . Tisdale said she struggled with postpartum depression after welcoming her first daughter, Jupiter, now 5, and recalled trying to divorce French “so many times” during that period.
Tisdale said she had previously worked on managing her anxiety and believed she was emotionally prepared to become a mother. However, she said postpartum depression made it difficult to rely on the coping strategies she had learned.
The High School Musical star recalled experiencing intense anxiety, including nearly having a panic attack while sitting in traffic. She also said she did not receive a diagnosis of postpartum depression until Jupiter was 2.
“I was like, ‘What? How did you not know to tell me this?’” Tisdale said during the podcast, according to PEOPLE.
Tisdale later welcomed her second daughter, Emerson, now 2, and said her postpartum experience was less severe the second time. She described it as different to go through motherhood again without experiencing the same symptoms.
French, a composer, also discussed how he supported his wife during her postpartum depression. He said he took over household responsibilities, including washing dishes and cleaning bottles, and handled nighttime duties for a period.
French said being present, patient and supportive was important while Tisdale worked through the experience. He also encouraged partners supporting someone with postpartum depression to seek their own support so they can remain patient and understanding.
Tisdale and French have been married since 2014 and share two daughters.

title: K P emergency proposal not linked to PTI long march  Tariq Fazal
description: Says proposed emergency or governor   s rule stems from K P   s worsening security situation
content:
Says proposed emergency or governor’s rule stems from K-P’s worsening security situation
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry on Thursday linked the proposed emergency or governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to the province’s worsening security situation, saying it had nothing to do with the PTI’s planned long march.
Speaking to a private television programme, the minister attributed the worsening security situation to what he described as the provincial government’s lack of cooperation with the federal government in the fight against terrorism.
Talking about the government-PTI talks scheduled for Friday, Chaudhry said political issues would also be discussed during the talks, adding that if the party sought any favour or concession from the federal government, it would be considered within the constitutional and legal framework.
Read : President, PM form committee to initiate talks with PTI leadership
However, he said the issue of the provincial government’s non-cooperation in the fight against terrorism was equally important.
Chaudhry said it should be made clear that postponing the long march would not end the issue of a possible emergency in K-P.
“If it is being thought that if the talks result only in postponing the long march, the issue of emergency will be over, then this should be made clear: the long march has nothing to do with the imposition of emergency,” he said.
He said discussions on the imposition of an emergency had begun despite repeated efforts to explain to the provincial government that terrorism was increasing in the province.
According to the minister, the provincial government was not cooperating with the federal government and law enforcement agencies, resulting in an increase in casualties and making it difficult to establish full control over the situation.
Talking about the comparisons being drawn between terrorism in Balochistan and K-P, he expressed regret over the incident in Balochistan but said the provincial government there stood with the federal government in measures to stop terrorism and was on the front line in the fight against it.
“In K-P, the provincial government is standing like a wall in front of the law enforcement agencies, intelligence agencies and the federal government’s measures to crush terrorism. It does not cooperate, which is why terrorism cannot be brought under control there,” he said.
Also Read : Govt 'seriously' considering imposing emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa: Tariq Fazal
He also criticised the PTI’s governance in the province, saying poor governance had contributed to the growing nexus between terrorism, crime and smuggling, which was indirectly facilitating terrorists.
Chaudhry said the issue would also be discussed during talks with the PTI and that the party would have to provide the federal government with the cooperation required to bring terrorism under control in the province.
He said it was the PTI’s responsibility, politically and otherwise, to stand with the federal government in dealing with terrorism.
On the possibility of an emergency, Chaudhry said all ministers and government spokespersons had maintained that the matter was being seriously considered and that a final decision would be taken after consultations.
He said work had already been carried out on the issue, including an assessment of its pros and cons and the possible consequences of its implementation in K-P.
However, he said the PML-N and its main ally, the PPP, had maintained from the outset that if the grievances of both sides could be resolved through dialogue and mutual understanding, it had always been the position of the prime minister and every member of the cabinet to pursue that course.
The minister’s comments came after the government formed a committee to hold talks with Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) leadership on the current political situation in the country.
The decision was taken during a meeting between President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif at Aiwan-e-Sadr, according to a statement issued by the President House.
The meeting also expressed concern over the security situation in K-P and reviewed the country’s overall security situation.

title: Guillermo Rodriguez takes his salsa nationwide after 1 million tubs sold

content:
Guillermo Rodriguez’s salsa brand tops 1 million tubs as it expands to Kroger, H-E-B and more retailers nationwide
Guillermo Rodriguez’s salsa brand is expanding nationwide after selling more than 1 million tubs since its launch earlier this year, according to PEOPLE .
The comedian and television personality, 55, co-founded Guillermo’s Salsa with Chris Kirby, founder of Ithaca Hummus, in January 2026. The refrigerated salsa brand initially launched in stores across the Northeast and Southeast before expanding to additional retailers.
Guillermo’s Salsa will become available at Kroger locations nationwide beginning October 4. The brand is also set to launch at H-E-B stores on November 4, followed by Stop & Shop later this year and additional retailers in early 2027.
The salsa is available in three varieties: mild, medium and hot. Rodriguez has said the hot version is his favourite, although he enjoys all three flavours. The recipes feature ingredients including tomatoes, lime juice, cilantro and jalapeño.
According to Rodriguez, the idea for Guillermo’s Salsa dates back to a dream he had in 2003. He based the product on his grandmother’s recipe and has credited her approach to cooking with inspiring the brand.
Rodriguez said his grandmother believed that putting “heart,” patience and love into food helped make it taste better. He has carried that philosophy into the development of the salsa.
The Jimmy Kimmel Live! personality also said he regularly eats the salsa with eggs for breakfast and has experimented with pairing it with pizza. He added that chips remain his preferred accompaniment.
Guillermo’s Salsa has also received support from Rodriguez’s friend Jimmy Kimmel and his Dancing with the Stars costars.
As the brand continues its retail expansion, Rodriguez said he hopes to launch his own tequila brand in the future.

title: Ensuing conflicts  emerging economic and security milieu
description: The abdication of responsibility by US to oversee a  rules based world order  engenders chaos  anarchy
content:
The abdication of responsibility by US to oversee a "rules-based world order" engenders chaos, anarchy
The world is currently mired in at least 65 active conflicts, the highest number recorded post-WWII. Of these, 9 are interstate while the remaining 57 are intra-state. However, the US-Iran confrontation remains the most significant given its widespread economic impact. The Houthis capturing the southern coast of Yemen along the Red Sea has introduced a new dimension to this geopolitical imbroglio. To top it all off, President Trump's refusal of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's requests to conduct direct airstrikes - coupled with Houthi assurances that they would not target US and Israeli vessels - has caught the global community by surprise, most notably Washington's long-standing ally, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA).
Connecting these developments to Somaliland and its recognition by Israel in December 2025 and UAE's reported intent to establish a military base there make it a complex maze of geostrategy. Is it a complementary effort by Iran to counter alternative oil supply route of KSA? Or is it a US-Israel tit-for-tat endeavour to pressurise KSA to join Abraham Accords? Nonetheless, it implies that Bab el Mandeb and Red Sea maritime route can be controlled any time by Houthis and Somaliland, albeit with external support.
One must acknowledge that President Trump is actively implementing a distinct strategic vision for the United States. Geopolitical analysts widely deduced at the outset of the confrontation with Iran that Washington's efforts center around critical geopolitical levers: controlling oil and vital mineral reserves, dominating oceanic chokepoints, safeguarding the petrodollar and carving out a new regional security architecture anchored by the Abraham Accords and the MAGA doctrine. Securing a hold on Venezuelan oil, advancing influence over Latin American and African energy reserves and finalising the US-Denmark-Greenland security agreement are all interconnected tactics. In Greenland - where melting ice is carving out new maritime pathways - securing territory is vital for establishing the space-based "Golden Dome" missile defence network and blocking access to its vast natural wealth from Russia and China. Ultimately, these maneuvers serve as the operational means to achieve the ultimate ends of his global strategy.
Let there be no mistake that all these conflicts have the least to do with religion or ideology; rather, they are part of an economic contestation including trade, control of resources, sea and land access, and the war economy. Interestingly, as of now, the largest oil- and gas-producing and exporting country is the US. Despite the war, Iran earns billions of dollars from oil sales, and Russian gas passes through Ukraine, for which Ukraine receives royalties. The other element of the war economy is who benefits the most from the prolongation of the conflict(s) and restricted oil flows? The chief beneficiaries are oil-producing countries, insurance & shipping companies, the black market and military-industrial complexes. Israel has been intentionally kept out of this phase of the war, affording it the opportunity to regroup, reequip and rebuild in order to continue with its expansionist policy and establish itself as a dominant regional power. The systemic genocide of Palestinians persists in this moral and legal vacuum.
In this overarching scenario, the abdication of responsibility by the US to oversee a "rules-based world order" engenders chaos, anarchy and a heightened sense of insecurity. Consequently, smaller and middle powers are building interest-based alliances to secure their respective interests while hedging their positions between rival blocs.
China's speedy rise through win-win economic cooperation remains the primary focus of President Trump's MAGA doctrine, which revolves around imperialist expansion to enhance the US sphere of influence, slow down American decline and scuttle China's rise. The recent meeting between President Xi and President Trump at the White House may not end their contestation, but it could help keep it non-kinetic for now.
The Iran-USA war is likely to continue until both sides lower their negotiating demands. Iran is not likely to settle for less than royalties for the Strait of Hormuz, similar to the Suez Canal, an assured cessation of hostilities, the lifting of sanctions, and integration into the world economic system. The Houthis may follow this lead to come to terms with Yemen and KSA in a somewhat similar manner. The long-term solution to the US-Iran, Houthis-Yemen-KSA, and Israel's access challenges resides in diplomacy and politics, not in the use of the military instrument.
Pakistan's brokering of the ceasefire, the strengthening of Pak-KSA bilateral relations, and the subsequent trilateral joint defence agreement including Türkiye - along with the continued improvement in our relations with all major and middle powers - are manifestations of this fact. Pakistan must continue with its efforts for longer-lasting regional peace by bringing the US and Iran back to the table, helping effect a ceasefire and forging a long-term solution to the Yemen-Houthi-KSA issue. At the same time, this newfound relevance and these friendships must be translated into B2B and P2P long-term partnerships to construct a complex interdependence built on an edifice of intertwined destinies for sustained good relations with all, especially immediate neighbours. The time-tested and trusted Pak-China bond must be cemented further.

title: The pyramid that was never a pyramid
description: The pyramid that was never a pyramid
content:
If the classroom won't question it, art and literature already have
One of the most taught pyramids in Pakistani higher education was never drawn by the man it's credited to. Yet walk into any psychology or business studies classroom, and there it is: the same triangle, five layers ascended firmly in order, with physiological needs at the base, self-actualisation - meaning, fulfillment, even a kind of spirituality - at the peak. Credited to Abraham Maslow, who never drew a pyramid, rather warned against the rigidity of his theory. The shape we now treat as a scripture, was built years after him, not by any psychologist, but by a management consultant selling a formula for motivating employees as economically as possible.
In 1943, Maslow laid out his categories of needs in a paper, A Theory of Human Motivation, published in Psychological Review. In 1954, his book, Motivation and Personality, cautioned against it directly: "We have spoken so far as if this hierarchy was a fixed order but actually it is not nearly as rigid as we may have implied... there have been a number of exceptions" (p. 51). He documented seven exceptions, last and the most striking exception: people driven by high ideals or values, "give up everything for the sake of a particular value" (p. 53) his own word for this was martyrdom. If survival itself can be sacrificed for an ideal, ideals can't only matter once survival is secured.
His method for categorising 'self-actualised' relied on biographical analysis rather than controlled study. Eighteen individuals were the core group he studied and drew 15 characteristics of self-actualised people. Historical figures assessed through biography, from Lincoln to Einstein, alongside personal acquaintances he chose himself. The sample tilted heavily toward educated, high-achieving white men, with only two women, and no one from outside Western prominence. From it, he estimated only two per cent of people ever reach self-actualisation - a figure with no population basis at all.
If Maslow didn't draw the triangle, who did? In 2019, management historians Todd Bridgman, Stephen Cummings, and John Ballard traced its origin in their paper, Who Built Maslow's Pyramid? A 1957 textbook by Keith Davis first illustrated the theory as a staircase leading to the top, where a besuited executive plants a flag, echoing the Iwo Jima photograph. In1960, Charles McDermid, a consulting psychologist in his article, How Money Motivates Men, took the same idea and redesigned it into a triangle we know today by arguing that the shape helps managers achieve "maximum motivation at the lowest cost". It was never a psychological finding rather a sales aid to help managers get more out of employees.
The pyramid arrived in Pakistan the way most of our postcolonial curricula did, through inherited Western textbooks, taught as fact, tested by exam, never questioned. If the classroom won't question it, art and literature already have. Vincent van Gogh produced over 900 paintings and sold only one. Throughout his life he remained destitute and entirely unrecognised, yet his art drew its meaning from inside the deprivation, not after it was resolved. Siddhartha Gautama, the prince of Kapilavastu, known as Buddha, whose story is usually told as a clean epiphany - a prince renounces luxury and becomes the enlightened one. The sharper reading comes from Ashvaghosha's Life of the Buddha (Canto 3, Canto 5): the awakening began with his repeated encounters with old age, sickness and death, not once comfort was secured. Allama Iqbal's philosophy of Khudi is built on the same inversion: selfhood forged through struggle, not preserved by comfort. Albert Camus closed The Myth of Sisyphus by imagining a man condemned to push a boulder uphill for eternity, with no rest or resolution ever coming, insisting us to picture him satisfied and happy anyway. None of these are stories about needs met before self-actualisation arrives; they are stories about self-actualisation despite needs never being met.
If Maslow puts self-actualisation at the summit, reached only once survival is secured, one older tradition put it at the very base. Centuries before Maslow, Muslim legal theorists developed their own framework of three levels of ma?la?ah (public interest): essentials (religion, life itself, the mind, family lineage and wealth), needs (things like trade or marriage, whose absence causes real hardship) and enhancements (refinements of custom and conduct that go beyond necessity), with each tier resting on the one beneath it, so that disruption at the essentials level collapses the other two, while disorder in needs or enhancements leaves the essentials intact. The 11th century jurist al-Juwayni first presented these three layers and named five essentials: religion, life itself, the mind, family lineage and wealth. Later his student, Imam al-Ghazali, kept this same five-part list, placed religion above the other four, not treated as one item among equals. Faith, in his framework, isn't something to attend to once survival is secured. The theory was later schematised by al-Shatibi, who grounded it directly in scripture and stated the consensus plainly: "The Muslim community...[agrees] that the Law was established to preserve the five essentials, namely, religion, human life, progeny, material wealth and the human faculty of reason" (Al-Raysuni, Imam al-Shatibi's Theory of the Higher Objectives, IIIT Books-in-Brief, 2013). In this framework of human essentials, faith is not a luxury attained after survival, but foundational to survival itself.
Al-Ghazali's framework stood for nine hundred years. Maslow's pyramid is barely sixty - and yet no one in the room is allowed to question it. The ask isn't to tear Maslow down - it's more urgent than that: stop teaching a 1960 consultant's sales diagram as settled science. Teach Maslow's own caveats. Teach al-Juwayni, al-Ghazali and al-Shatibi alongside him. Not because one tradition should win, but because a classroom that hands down conclusions instead of teaching students to question them has already failed at its only job.

title: Performance  persona and Asian heritages at the AAS
description: Innovative scholarship can offer  not intellectual simplification  but another route into complexity
content:
Innovative scholarship can offer: not intellectual simplification, but another route into complexity
The Association for Asian Studies (AAS) conference 2026 brought together scholars, artists and thinkers around the theme of Asia's future and its global connectivity. The organisers invited proposals for innovative formats, encouraging participants to move beyond the conventional academic panel keeping in mind the developing culture of academic discourse. What happens when five experts speak, one after another, on an intellectually demanding subject? We expect an audience to listen, absorb, connect and synthesise multiple arguments within a single session. In reality, this may require almost as much intellectual labour from the audience as from the scholars themselves. Could there be another way of engaging with complex ideas - one that is intellectually rigorous but also more immediate, participatory and memorable?
This became the starting point for "Mapping Asian Heritages: Globalization, Indigenous Storytelling and Gender in Historical Novels". Rather than asking scholars simply to speak about selected novels and books, I proposed that they personify their characters - stepping out of the books and into the twenty-first century.
The premise was playful, but the proposition was serious. What might happen if a character from Bahao, The Gardens of Light, Siddhartha, Kafka on the Shore or Aag ka Daryia suddenly found themselves in contemporary Lahore? How might they respond to Bano's world? What would they question, resist or embrace? And what might we discover by encountering history through the consciousness of a fictional character rather than through another scholarly exposition?
The panel therefore became an experiment in Performance as research. The participants were not merely interpreting characters; they were asked to inhabit them - to bring their histories, desires, contradictions and cultural worlds into the present. The boundaries between scholar and character, past and present, text and performance became deliberately porous.
The approach also emerged from what I understand as socially engaged art history: an art history that moves beyond objects, archives and established narratives to engage with people, lived experience, performance and contemporary questions. If cultural histories are carried through stories, memories and acts of remembering, then art history too can become participatory - a space where knowledge is not simply delivered but collectively explored, questioned and performed.
I was fortunate to have an extraordinary group of participants: Sumair Tarar, son of Mustansar Hussain Tarar (the author of Bahao), architect and a serving Customs officer; Dr Khaleeq ur Rehman, a practising urologist and sculptor; Sania Samad, a textile artist and collector; Qurat-ul-Ain Dar, a lecturer and practitioner of art; and Adeel Khalid, an academic. They became not simply performers but interpreters, questioners and, if I may say so, probers of the faith and human histories - each bringing a distinct professional and personal perspective to the characters and worlds they inhabited. Their diversity itself embodied the premise that cultural heritage can be explored through multiple forms of knowledge.
Perhaps this is what innovative scholarship can offer: not intellectual simplification, but another route into complexity. Sometimes we may understand cultural history differently when we encounter it through a voice, personality, gesture or disagreement rather than another lecture.
The experiment also opened another possibility. If characters can step out of books and enter our present, could they eventually inhabit digital or metaverse-like environments, where readers might encounter characters, landscapes, histories and memories interactively?
For me, Mapping Asian Heritages that I conceived and moderated became more than an innovative panel. It became an experiment in how we might read, remember, question and experience Asia differently.
Stay tuned for more insight from the AAS in Asia hosted first time in Pakistan at the LUMS.

title: Ozone depletion
description: Ozone depletion
content:
Lahore's poisoned air is usually discussed as a winter smog problem; not anymore
Lahore's poisoned air is usually discussed as a winter smog problem. But now, Lahore has been identified by EU's Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service among Asian cities experiencing "extremely poor" levels of ground-level ozone, an invisible pollutant whose formation is accelerated by heat and sunlight. In other words, the city's dirty air is increasingly colliding with a warming climate.
Ground-level ozone is not emitted directly. It forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, released largely by vehicles, industry and other combustion sources, react in sunlight. Higher temperatures and stagnant conditions can accelerate these reactions and allow ozone to accumulate. The city has spent years lurching from one smog emergency to another, often responding when visibility collapses and particulate pollution reaches dangerous levels. Ozone poses a different challenge. It cannot necessarily be seen or smelled, yet excessive exposure can cause breathing difficulties, aggravate asthma and reduce lung function. The WHO recommends that the maximum daily eight-hour mean should not exceed 100 micrograms per cubic metre. Pakistan should regard the warning as part of a broader climate threat rather than another entry in Lahore's long pollution record. Extreme heat is already a serious health risk across the country. Lahore needs reliable monitoring of ozone alongside particulate matter, and stricter vehicle and industrial emission standards.
There is also no escaping the regional dimension. Ozone and its precursor pollutants can travel great distances, while CAMS data show elevated concentrations extending far beyond individual cities. Pakistan and its neighbours therefore have an interest in treating the Indo-Gangetic airshed as a shared environmental system. Cross-border cooperation on emissions data and pollution control should be pursued even when political relations are difficult. Air currents recognise no frontier.

title: Elusive hockey gold
description: Elusive hockey gold
content:
Pakistan has not won a hockey gold medal at the Asian Games since 2010
Pakistan has not won a hockey gold medal at the Asian Games since 2010, and their 4 / 3 semifinal loss to arch-rivals India yesterday ensures that the drought will persist through the ongoing Nagoya Games. The Green Shirts put up a spirited fight after conceding three goals in the first 23 minutes. They leveled the score by the 49th minute, raising hopes of a comeback or at least pushing the game into a penalty shootout. While the match remained finely balanced for the next 10 minutes, it ultimately tilted in India's favour with just seconds left before the final hooter.
To add to the embarrassment, the result extended India's unbeaten run against Pakistan to 21 matches. With a spot in the final gone, the Green Shirts are now left fighting South Korea (who were defeated by Malaysia in the other semifinal) for the bronze medal - a podium position they have miserably failed to secure at the Asian Games since the 2006 Doha Games. This current slump stands in stark contrast to the country's glorious past. A total of 14 Asiad medals – 8 gold, 3 silver, and 3 bronze – still makes Pakistan the most successful men's field hockey nation in the tournament's history.
Pakistan's decades-long slump remains a frustrating enigma. A nation that ruled the sport globally through the 1960s, 70s and mid-80s now routinely struggles to beat lower-ranked teams. Remarkably, this decline has persisted despite the team being guided by some of the greatest legends and elite tactical coaches in hockey history. This proves that the root issue is systemic. To reverse this slide, the PHF must abandon short-term fixes and focus entirely on reviving structural infrastructure. Re-establishing robust grassroots hockey, introducing a commercially sustainable franchise league to provide financial security for players, and building modern sporting facilities at the local level are the ways to pull the national game back from total obscurity.

title: Talks in the shadows

content:
Days ahead of the PTI's march on the federal capital, reports of behind-the-scenes talks offer a welcome reprieve
Days ahead of the PTI's march on the federal capital, reports of behind-the-scenes talks offer a welcome reprieve. PM's Adviser Rana Sanaullah's confirmation that "off-the-record" parleys are underway with the opposition has brought a collective sigh of relief. For those prioritising political stability and economic recovery, an immediate breakthrough is vital. The stakes could not be higher: the country is currently battling resurgent terrorism, while disrupted global supply lines have triggered skyrocketing fuel prices and persistent double-digit inflation. At this critical juncture, the last thing Pakistan can afford is institutional infighting and a perpetual standoff between the federation and the provinces. Ultimately, an amicable resolution of this essentially political dispute is entirely possible, provided that wisdom, pragmatism and fair play are allowed to prevail.
The political process, however, remains paralysed by personal egos. The six-party opposition alliance, TTAP, refuses to hold talks at either the Prime Minister's Office or the Speaker's Chamber. Moreover, the opposition leadership insists on meeting with Imran Khan in jail before engaging in any meaningful dialogue. Simultaneously, the federal government, wary of the K-P administration's plans to take to the streets on October 4, is reportedly mulling the imposition of Governor's rule in the province. Such a drastic step would only push the country deeper into an abyss of political decay and confrontation. Ultimately, sober minds on both sides bear the responsibility to intervene; the only viable way forward is an initial thaw to bridge the divide, paving the way for a structured and sustained dialogue.
An immediate and lawful breakthrough could be achieved by implementing the August 18 Supreme Court order. Granting the opposition its legitimate political space and engaging them in long-term dialogue on constitutional reforms - including restructuring an autonomous Election Commission, repealing recent legislation that is ultra vires to the Constitution and releasing political prisoners - presents a genuine win-win scenario for both sides.

title: The privatisation of resilience
description: For poorer citizens  resilience often means trying to navigate weak and apathetic public systems
content:
For poorer citizens, resilience often means trying to navigate weak and apathetic public systems
What happens when powerful people stop believing that the future can be salvaged, and they instead start preparing to survive its destruction?
That is the unsettling question at the heart of End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, the new book by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. The book argues that a new political formation is emerging from the convergence of religious fundamentalists, ethno-nationalists, Silicon Valley billionaires and other reactionaries. What connects them is not necessarily a common political programme, but an increasingly apocalyptic imagination: the conviction that some catastrophic rupture is coming and that they will somehow be the ones to survive it.
Klein calls this "end-times fascism". Unlike twentieth-century fascism, which sought national rebirth through authoritarianism and exclusion, today's far right increasingly wants to prepare for a world shaped by climate change, resource scarcity, mass migration and other crises.
Klein's ongoing work for more than the last two decades has explored the growing power of corporations, how elites exploit crises for their own benefit, and now how the wealthy seek to insulate themselves from catastrophe.
In a recent interview about the book, she offers a jolting observation about wealth itself: "Wealth has its own deranging effects." Humans, she observes, need stories to make sense of the world around them. The ultra-rich are no different: they, too, need stories to explain why they possess so much while others have so little. The answer can become a story of superiority: that there is something about the wealthy person that justifies their extraordinary share of resources, with the implicit conclusion that inequality is deserved.
This is where Klein's argument becomes particularly relevant to the Global South.
In wealthy countries, apocalyptic politics may take the form of the eccentric fantasy of billionaires to build bunkers or imagine escaping to Mars. In countries such as Pakistan, however, catastrophe is already part of everyday political and economic life. Floods, heatwaves, water insecurity and toxic air are no longer distant possibilities. Yet, the consequences of these emergent threats are not distributed equally. Those who can afford it can protect themselves from the harshest forms of the climate apocalypse.
People with money can purchase safer land, gated housing, private security, generators, solar power, air conditioning, private healthcare and reliable water supplies. They can move away from areas threatened by flooding or extreme heat. They can send their children abroad and, if they have the means, can even build new lives elsewhere.
For poorer citizens, resilience often means trying to navigate weak and apathetic public systems. They remain dependent on increasingly resource constrained public hospitals, schools, water supplies and infrastructure.
Even something as mundane as an air purifier has become a marker of class. In Lahore, where toxic air is a recurring crisis, the air purifier has acquired something of the status once occupied by the UPS during the worst of load-shedding: a private technological solution to a public failure.
The idea of "end-times fascism" can thus be extended beyond the politics of the American far right. In the Global South, it can take the form of a politics of elite insulation: the acceptance that public systems will fail, accompanied by the assumption that those with wealth will somehow be protected.
In Pakistan, where the impacts of the global climate crisis are being acutely felt and the country has limited capacity to contend with these threats, the question becomes: who gets to adapt? If resilience must be purchased, it becomes a privilege.
Climate change is not only making Pakistan more unequal; it is also illustrating how affluence determines who can secure some protection from its effects, making those who can afford it increasingly indifferent to the need to address these public problems.
That is not disaster mitigation. It is the privatisation of resilience.

Bradley Cooper will star as Duke in Paramount’s 'G.I. Joe' movie, directed by Danny McBride and based on Hasbro toys
Bradley Cooper is set to lead Paramount Pictures’ new G.I. Joe movie, taking on the role of Duke, the military team’s central leader.
Danny McBride will direct the untitled live-action film and co-wrote the screenplay with Jeff Fradley and John Carcieri. The project is based on Hasbro’s G.I. Joe property, which became widely known through its 1980s cartoon series and Marvel Comics adaptation.
Cooper’s Duke was previously played by Channing Tatum in Paramount’s G.I. Joe: The Rise of Cobra in 2009 and G.I. Joe: Retaliation in 2013. Details about the new film’s story and wider cast have not yet been revealed.
The G.I. Joe movie is among Paramount’s major intellectual property projects as the studio develops new films based on established franchises. The project is being produced by Lorenzo di Bonaventura, Mark Vahradian and Zev Foreman for Hasbro Entertainment.
The casting marks a notable franchise role for Cooper, whose recent work has largely focused on projects outside major action properties. He starred as Leonard Bernstein in Maestro , which he also co-wrote and directed and which received four Oscar nominations.
Cooper also recently co-wrote, directed and starred in Is This Thing On? He is known for voicing Rocket in Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy films and appeared in James Gunn’s Superman .
Cooper previously worked with McBride through an appearance in HBO’s The Righteous Gemstones , which McBride co-created and starred in.

title: 59 women lured to farmhouse for    jobs     stripped of phones
description: Police arrest two suspects  including female coordinator  alleged organiser on the run
content:
Police arrest two suspects, including female coordinator; alleged organiser on the run
A job interview that promised Rs2,000 a day ended with an unexpected exit — 59 women who had arrived at a farmhouse in Gadap hoping to land work were left without their mobile phones after the alleged event organiser disappeared with them.
The women had been lured from different parts of Karachi with promises of a 25-day assignment at a private housing society, complete with daily wages, food and transport. Instead, they found themselves at a farmhouse where the “boss” they had been told would interview them never showed up.
After lunch, the women were asked to hand over their phones on the pretext that ringing devices could disturb the expected meeting with the boss. The phones were collected in a bag — and the man who collected them allegedly walked out with the haul.
Gadap City police registered a case and arrested two suspects, including a female coordinator, while raids were being conducted for the alleged organiser and recovery of the phones.
According to a spokesperson for SSP Malir District, the women had been promised work at an event titled “Activities” at a private housing society along the Superhighway. They were allegedly told that builders and housing society officials would interview them at the farmhouse before the assignment began.
The spokesperson said the farmhouse had been booked by a man identified as Waqas, while a woman named Nargis was allegedly coordinating the participants. Sahil Salman was identified as the event organiser.
The women were picked up from different parts of the metropolis in two buses and brought to the farmhouse at around 1pm on Wednesday. After lunch, Salman allegedly collected their phones before leaving the premises. Nargis also reportedly left around the same time.
The women alerted police, who reached the farmhouse and recorded their statements. An FIR was registered at Gadap City police station on the complaint of Khushnuma Zaib under Sections 379, 420 and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code.
Police arrested Waqas, who had booked the farmhouse, and Nargis, the alleged coordinator. Raids were under way to arrest Salman and recover the phones.
Khushnuma, a resident of Gulistan-e-Jauhar Block 18, told police that a friend had approached her around two months earlier and asked her to submit her CV and video profile for a 25-day event at a private housing society.
She said she was told participants would be paid Rs2,000 a day and would work from 10am to 7pm. Salman later informed her that she had been selected and added her to a WhatsApp group, where Nargis was introduced as the coordinator.
According to Khushnuma, separate WhatsApp groups and coordinators had been assigned to women from different parts of Karachi. The participants were instructed to reach designated bus stops at 9am on September 30 before being taken to the farmhouse.
Farmhouse manager Ashar Ansari said in a video statement that the premises had been booked for an event involving around 50 to 55 women. He said Waqas had made the booking but did not come to the farmhouse, while a man identified as “Asif or Salman” arrived with a woman.
Ansari said that when he later contacted the organiser about payment at checkout, he was told that he was on his way. Shortly afterwards, the caretaker informed him that the man had collected the women’s phones and fled.
The manager said the women had been told to surrender their phones because the “boss” was expected and ringing devices could cause a disturbance. He added that the booking had been made through the required procedure and that the booker’s CNIC details were available with him.
Another affected woman, speaking in a video statement, said the participants had been promised Rs2,000 a day, food and transport for the 25-day assignment involving stalls of different brands at a private housing society.
She said their phones were collected and receipts attached to them before the women were asked to line up for the expected arrival of the owner. They later realised that Salman had allegedly fled with the phones.
Police said statements of the affected women were being recorded and further investigation was under way. Officers were also gathering information about the people who organised the event and booked the farmhouse.

title: John Davidson to watch BAFTA Scotland ceremony from separate venue space | The Express Tribune
description: John Davidson will watch the BAFTA Scotland ceremony from a separate venue space after the 2026 N-word controversy
content:
John Davidson will watch the BAFTA Scotland ceremony from a separate venue space after the 2026 N-word controversy
Tourette syndrome campaigner John Davidson will attend the BAFTA Scotland Awards in Glasgow in November, but will watch the ceremony from a separate space within the venue following an earlier controversy at the BAFTA Film Awards.
Davidson, whose life inspired the film I Swear , involuntarily shouted a racial slur during the 2026 BAFTA Film Awards ceremony in February. The incident occurred while Michael B. Jordan and Delroy Lindo were presenting the first award and subsequently became a major focus of discussion around the event.
I Swear has since received seven BAFTA Scotland nominations, marking the highest number of nominations for a film in the awards' history. The ceremony is scheduled to take place on November 15 in Glasgow.
According to Variety, BAFTA chair Sara Putt and CEO Jane Millichip informed members that the organisation had consulted Davidson, Tourettes Action and Tourette Scotland before deciding on arrangements for his attendance.
Davidson will watch the ceremony through a video link from a relaxed area inside the venue alongside family and friends. BAFTA said the arrangement followed discussions with Davidson and a wider risk assessment.
The British Academy also outlined changes made since the February incident, including strengthened safeguarding and risk assessment procedures, clearer communication and escalation processes, and additional briefings for people involved in live awards events.
An independent review commissioned after the controversy identified “structural weaknesses” in BAFTA's planning and crisis coordination but found no evidence of malicious intent or institutional racism.
BAFTA said it recognises that Davidson experiences coprolalia, a type of vocal tic associated with Tourette syndrome that can involve involuntary words or phrases. The organisation added that such vocalisations are neurological and do not reflect an individual's views or intentions.

title: Pakistani national indicted in US over alleged  126m postage fraud
description: Faheem Akram allegedly operated website that sold over 5 1m counterfeit postage labels  Department of Justice says
content:
Faheem Akram allegedly operated website that sold over 5.1m counterfeit postage labels, Department of Justice says
A federal grand jury in Florida has indicted a Pakistani national for allegedly operating a website that sold more than 5.1 million counterfeit United States postage labels, causing over $126m in losses to the US Postal Service (USPS).
The US Department of Justice said on Monday that Faheem Akram, 33, of Punjab's Khanewal district, operated LabelsBank.com, an online website that allegedly sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate — typically $2 per label — regardless of a package’s weight, size or destination.
LabelsBank.com was not authorised to sell USPS products and services, the department said.
Read : US charges 2 Pakistanis for alleged involvement in $10m health care scheme fraud
It added that the counterfeit labels allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate USPS prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.
“The alleged scheme was simple but massive: sell counterfeit postage online at fixed, cut-rate prices, as little as $2 per label, regardless of a package’s weight, size, or destination, enabling customers to avoid legitimate postal service charges,” US Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida said.
“The indictment alleges more than 5.1m counterfeit labels and more than $126m in losses,” he said, adding that the website had been shut down, its domain seized and federal charges brought against its alleged operator.
The department said the investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals used LabelsBank.com to purchase more than 5.1m counterfeit shipping labels, resulting in over $126m in alleged losses to USPS.
In conjunction with the indictment, USPS obtained a court order authorising the seizure and shutdown of the website, according to the department.
“Our reach goes beyond our borders,” Inspector in Charge Bladismir Rojo of the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) Miami Division said.
“Transnational criminal organisations defrauding the postal service and targeting US consumers by pushing phoney postage will be found and brought to justice,” he added.
Also Read : US launches online portal to report suspected visa fraud
Akram was charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the US and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels and four counts of wire fraud, the department said.
If convicted, Akram faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, according to the department.
The USPIS Miami Division is investigating the case.

content:
Jesse McCartney and wife Katie Peterson are expecting their second baby, with their son Archer becoming a big brother
Jesse McCartney and his wife Katie Peterson are expecting their second child, with the couple announcing the pregnancy on October 1.
The singer, 39, and Peterson, 38, shared the news on Instagram alongside photos of their family, including their 16-month-old son, Archer. The couple revealed that their second baby is due in March 2027.
“Archer is getting promoted to big brother 🤍 March 2027,” they wrote in the announcement.
The photos showed McCartney and Peterson posing with their son in their backyard while wearing coordinated white outfits. Archer also wore a small bowtie as he posed with his parents and a sonogram strip.
McCartney and Peterson welcomed their first child in May 2025 and have since shared occasional glimpses of their family life on social media.
In January, McCartney posted a video of himself working on new music at the piano while Archer was strapped to his chest. The singer jokingly referred to his son as his “new co-writer” in the caption.
Peterson has also documented moments with Archer, including attending one of McCartney’s concerts in New York City. During the outing, Archer was photographed with a custom blanket featuring the words “Beautiful Soul”, a reference to McCartney’s 2004 hit song of the same name.
McCartney later called his son his “favorite roadie” in the comments, while Peterson joked about Archer joining his father at the concert.
The couple also celebrated Archer’s first Halloween last year, dressing him as a puffin while their family dog wore a fish costume.
McCartney and Peterson have been married since 2021. Their second child is expected to arrive in March 2027.

title: Education Expo  brings 60 universities under one roof in Karachi
description: Varsity representatives discuss evolving degree programmes  AI driven concerns and the skills needed for future jobs
content:
Students, representatives discuss evolving degree programmes, AI-driven concerns and the skills needed for future jobs
Scholarships emerged as a key consideration for students exploring higher education options as Education Expo 2026 brought together 60 local and international universities in Karachi on Thursday.
The expo, organised by The City School, drew a large number of high school students from various local schools seeking information about admission to local and international universities. It allowed students to interact directly with university representatives and learn about programmes and career pathways.
Speaking with The Express Tribune , Head of Counselling, Alumni and Placement at The City School, Rabiya Sohail noted that the event featured leading Pakistani universities as well as institutions from the UK, Canada, Malaysia and Turkey.
The local institutions represented included Institute of Business Administration, Indus Valley School of Art and Architecture, Lahore University of Management Sciences, as well as institutions offering accountancy and other programmes. “The response to the expo has been positive, with both students and university representatives showing strong interest,” she said.
Rabiya stated that scholarships were a key factor in determining where students ultimately chose to study. “If students get good scholarships, they will go anywhere,” she said.
“Pakistan is a very big market. South Asia is generally a big market,” Rabiya said, adding that international universities were also keen to attract Pakistani students. “We have one of the biggest youth populations, and they all want to go to universities. We have to give them those opportunities.”
She added that Pakistani students continued to show strong interest in studying in English-speaking countries, although destinations such as Germany, China, Malaysia and Turkey were also now attracting students.
Read: Our higher education participation rate is only 13%: Ahsan Iqbal
Also speaking with The Express Tribune , Canadian Higher Education Advisor Helen Khan said that the number one thing that Pakistani students looked for while making higher education choices was scholarships. She further underscored that students from Pakistan also targeted securing permanent residency after their graduation.
“The thing that they want to know about is available scholarships and what kind of outcome do they get when they graduate? Are they going to be able to get a job? And not only when they graduate, but can they get a job while they are abroad, and can they work while they study?" she said.
When asked if students were giving more preference to programmes like AI, machine learning and cybersecurity, Helen stated that Pakistani students showed great interest in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) courses, as a “general computing science degree might not get you the job that you might want in the future”.
Asked whether universities were adapting artificial intelligence (AI) in their programmes, Rabiya also noted that many international universities were incorporating AI into their courses and offering programmes such as data analytics.
Manager of International Recruitment at the University of Lethbridge, Taseera Lwanga, stated that preparing the students for study abroad was very important and that it came down to the schools, further noting that while some schools in Pakistan were “really good”, others had a bit of catching up to do.
“Generally, for us, students from Pakistan are good students and their success rate is high. Those who end up coming abroad, they do really well and are high performers,” Lwanga remarked.
He further noted that universities in Canada, Australia and the UK were “very expensive”, adding that Pakistani students therefore tend to inevitably inquire about available scholarships. “Higher education abroad is an expensive venture, which is why we offer some partial merit scholarships. Students can, however, work while they study, and that is an incentive,” he added.
Read More: Pakistan's universities are solving yesterday's problem
The impact of AI on the “jobs of the future” and future career pathways has been of considerable interest in both Pakistan and at the global level.
Institute of Chartered Accountants of Pakistan (ICAP) Outreach and Communication Deputy manager Saad Aalam Angaria noted that there were fears among prospective CA students that AI was going to take over their jobs in the future. “This is not true. On the contrary, AI is going to assist chartered accountants and bring more efficiency. The role of the human in decision-making on financial matters can never be replaced by AI,” he said.
He further explained how ICAP had incorporated AI and data analytics as an integrated module in the final level of its programme. “It will be a chartered accountant who is going to determine what expert assistance is required and whether AI has responded to the required prompt. The role of AI in the field of accounting and finance will only be that of a facilitator,” he stated.
Students from The City School, who were interested in pursuing medicine, also said that AI represented a threat because of advances in robotics and biotechnology that could “replace humans” and perform surgeries in the near future.
The expo also featured a panel discussion titled "Building Global Citizens: Inclusivity and Access" on the state of the education system in Pakistan, the challenges faced by schools and teachers in “building global citizens” and how learning outcomes could be improved in the classroom through the use of modern technology.
The panel speakers included Zindagi Trust and Durbeen Head of Communications Tooba Saleem, Aga Khan University Faculty of Arts and Sciences Dean Dr Kulsoom Ghias, Humanex CEO Hassan Tariq, and City School Operations Assistant Director Rehana Afzal.

title: Indian claims of killing Pakistani SSG officer in operation debunked as he appears alongside DG ISPR
description: Chaudhry says false flag operation began with tweet  falsely claiming that Indian military has neutralised a terrorist
content:
Chaudhry says false flag operation began with tweet, falsely claiming that Indian military has neutralised a terrorist
Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry on Thursday rejected Indian claims that a former Pakistan Army soldier had been killed as a Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terrorist in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir (IIOJK), presenting the individual alive before the media and describing the episode as another Indian “false flag operation”.
“So-called terrorist incident, another false flag that has been staged by the Indian military. I will take you step by step through the details," Chaudhry said during a press briefing. He stated that he was there to talk about a claim made by the Indian military of an anti-terror operation conducted on September 29 inside IIOJK.
The military spokesperson said that the false flag started on the night of Sept 29, when the corps of the Indian military in IIOJK made a social media post saying that “based on specific intelligence input, a joint search operation was launched by the Indian army, Jammu Kashmir police and CRPF Srinagar in the general area Korag, Yousmarg. Vigilant troops observed suspicious activity, and upon being challenged, terrorists opened fire, prompting a fierce exchange of gunfire during which one terrorist was neutralised”.
Chaudhry said that after seven hours, the Indian military gave an update yesterday morning, saying that a “body of a Pakistan-based LeT terrorist was recovered in a search operation”, further claiming that he had been identified as Mohammad Asif alias Hashim Moosa.
The press conference came after Indian media claimed that Asif, also known as Hashim Moosa, was killed in an operation in IIOJK and had previously served in the Pakistan Army. According to the reports that emerged in Indian media, Asif was born on March 7, 1980, joined the Pakistan Army in 2000 under service number PA-3106947 and retired with the rank of Havildar. Indian media further claimed that he was inducted into the Special Services Group (SSG) in 2005 and served with the 4 Commando “Yalgar” Battalion.
The reports alleged that Asif was deployed in Balochistan from 2006, where he took part in around 10 operations against Baloch insurgents and was credited with 13 “personal kills”. They also claimed that he served on former president Pervez Musharraf’s VVIP security team between 2006 and 2009.
The DG ISPR stated that the Indian newspaper ANI reported further details about “Asif”, including his joining date, his service number, details of his retirement, his photo, and further claimed that he was a former Hawaldar of the SSG branch of the Pakistan military. “A very interesting story is getting cooked, and you have a face as well. You might recall the false flags of Uri, Pahalgam and Pulwama."
He further stated that the Indian government then claimed through the Home Affairs and Press Information Bureau that the Indian Army had neutralised a LeT “commander”, who was later identified as “Musa aka Asif Fauji”, through an intelligence-led operation.
"According to the Indian government, this was a serious blow to the LeT ecosystem, and Asif had been operating in Jammu and Kashmir since 2022 and was involved in sensational attacks. Asif was neutralised after six months of a sustained operation,” he added.
False Flag Operations by India. Pictorial representation
The military spokesperson said that the “so-called credible Indian media” jumped onto the bandwagon, repeating the claims of the Indian government of killing a Pakistani SSG officer during an Indian military operation.
“Now that the Indian military has claimed that Musa is an ex-Hawaldar of the SSG, the question becomes: where is Musa?” he remarked before presenting Asif to the audience.
“Here is that superman gentleman; you can see this superman. Please tell us about your activities. I would request my dear friend Hawaldar Asif to tell something about himself”.
Asif stated that he had been receiving calls since yesterday from Indian numbers inquiring about him, further adding that he had seen social media commentary about his "killing" in an Indian military operation. “I was sitting at home when I heard these false reports from the Indian media. This is a heinous allegation from the Indian media, and my presence here shows that I am alive”.
“I was inducted in 2000 in the Pakistan Army and joined the SSG in 2005 and served for 18 years and retired from service in 2023,” Asif stated.
“What was the need for this drama from India? There are six reasons for this, and it is important to understand why Indians keep on repeating this drama. It is a very shameful and embarrassing thing that no self-respecting nation does,” DG ISPR stated.
DG Chaudhry said that the first reason for these repeated Indian accusations was to “cover its own track of terrorism”, adding that India was the biggest terrorist state in the world and its involvement in terrorism in the region went back decades through funding and sponsorship of terror outfits.
“They think that every problem can be rectified and addressed through terrorism. They are terrorising Muslims, Sikhs, Kashmiris, Dalits, tribals and Christians inside India. Such a country that lives and breathes in terrorism is afraid that its dark face will be exposed. What better way to cover your tracks than to call everyone else a terrorist? That is why you see these false, concocted stories coming out of India. This list of false flag events goes back decades, and they have been feeding these lies to their own people and to the world at large,” he remarked.
The DG ISPR further stated: “We need to understand that this habit of false flag operations has further encouraged India to even go for transnational killings; you must have seen how they are doing targeted killings far beyond their borders, and the world has seen that. You then need to cover your tracks because they see their own face in the mirror. They are proud of their terrorism."
DG Chaudhry noted that those guilty of perpetrating terrorism internationally could easily concoct stories to accuse Pakistan.
“A normal human cannot comprehend the basis for this drama,” he said, assailing the new false flag operation by India. He said such concocted stories appealed to the Indians to create relevance for Indian oppression in IIOJK.
“IIOJK is the biggest garrison in the world, for every 10th Kashmiri, there is a soldier or security official deployed by the Indian Army,” he highlighted, adding that nearly a million guard IIOJK.
“Hawaldar Asif does not have to go across the border to instigate Kashmiris,” he said, explaining that Indian oppression of Kashmiris and refuting their right to self-determination caused the reaction of Kashmiris that India tries to pin on Pakistan.
“If you wish for a fight, engage with us like you did in Marka-e-Haq and let us teach you a lesson,” DG Chaudhry warned.
He lamented that India was obsessed with Pakistan, built lies surrounding it and came up with theatrics matching Bollywood.
The DG ISPR said if the Indians wished to pursue a fresh conflict, “they are most welcome, but this time we will not leave them so easily.
“This time the cost that Pakistan will inflict on their strategic folly will be very, very severe.”
Talking about the Makkah agreement, he said the matter of troop deployment to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was a “confidential matter”.
He noted that the operationalisation of the defensive actions under the Makkah alliance was a matter of “operational necessity and confidentiality”, adding that it was not a matter for media discourse. “There should be complete clarity that Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia security and sanctity is absolute”.
While answering a question on cross-border terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, the DG ISPR noted that as per the Constitution, the army worked under the federal government and therefore it was the task of the federal government to coordinate with the provincial government, further adding that there would be no compromise on “Pakistan’s territorial integrity and sovereignty” and everything necessary would be done to secure it.
Responding to another question on India’s standing in the world, he stated that “the Indian façade is very well exposed to the whole world. You are hearing from the Canadian prime minister and the US secretary of state talking about Indian terrorism. The façade of Shining India has been exposed."
Answering a question on operations against the Afghan Taliban, DG Chaudhry noted that the Afghan Taliban had made their choice of “abetting and sponsoring terrorism”.
He further asked representatives of international media outlets to probe the Afghan government on why there were Afghans involved in acts of terrorism inside Pakistan and what Afghanistan was doing about it, further adding that Pakistan has nothing against the people of Afghanistan.
“The problem is with the Afghan Taliban regime that has forced itself on the country; it is non-inclusive, non-representative, unelected, and because it’s a forced regime, such regimes need insecurity and oppression to thrive. For that, they have gathered the whole alphabetic soup of terrorist organisations from ISKP to ETIM. Pakistan, as the frontline state, is fighting these groups."
When asked a question on the PTI’s planned long march, he stated that the “army has nothing to do with politics and we will not answer anything related to politics. Politics is for the political parties and the government”.
He suggested adhering to the devised National Action Plan for the elimination of terrorism.
"State supersedes politics; the state supersedes democracy too," the DG ISPR emphasised.
Reverting to the issue of terrorism faced by the country, he said, “Pakistan faces an existential threat from Indian sponsored terrorism.”
He added that the fight against terrorism cannot be sacrificed at the altar of someone’s politics.
On a question regarding litigation in the international court against the blame placed on Hawaldar Asif, the soldier in question placed the discretion on the military to pursue whatever was plausible under the circumstances.
In response, the DG ISPR said the first step was to expose India, which he said he had already done through the press conference, while the rest of the options would be used by the government and Foreign Office.
On a question regarding Afghanistan, he said the military was already doing what it knew best and the rest could be resolved only when those in the upper echelons of Afghanistan realised their error, which had no justification in religion, society or otherwise.
“They are bonded by dollars given to them by international agencies,” he concluded.
This is not the first time India has staged a “false flag operation” against Pakistan. Last year on April 22, 2025, escalation between Pakistan and India began when an attack in Pahalgam killed 26 people. India immediately blamed Pakistan for the incident. However, Pakistan categorically rejected the Indian blame.
In response, India undertook a series of hostile actions the next day, on April 23, 2025, including suspending the 65-year-old Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), cancelling visas for Pakistani citizens, closing the Wagah-Attari border crossing, ordering the shutdown of the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi, and reducing diplomatic staff at each other's embassies.
Tensions further escalated in the early hours of May 7, 2025, when missile strikes hit six cities in Punjab and Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), destroying a mosque and killing dozens of civilians, including women, children, and the elderly.
In a swift military response, Pakistan’s armed forces shot down Indian warplanes, including three Rafale jets. The confrontation intensified again in the early hours of May 10, 2025, when India targeted several Pakistani airbases with missile strikes. In retaliation, Pakistan launched Operation Bunyanum Marsoos , damaging Indian military installations, including missile storage sites, airbases, and other strategic targets.
On May 10, 2025, US President Donald Trump announced that a ceasefire had been reached following intense overnight diplomatic efforts. Minutes later, the agreement was confirmed separately by Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and the Indian foreign secretary.
Pakistan has for decades maintained that India supports and sponsors terrorist activity inside the country. The issue has featured prominently in diplomatic exchanges between the two nuclear-armed neighbours, including at the United Nations.
In October 2015, Pakistan formally presented dossiers to then-UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon alleging Indian involvement in terrorism and instability in Balochistan, Karachi and the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA). The Express Tribune reported that Pakistan's Foreign Office said the dossiers contained details of alleged Indian interference and links between Indian security and intelligence agencies and the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
In January 2017, Pakistan submitted another dossier to the UN concerning what it described as Indian intelligence agency RAW's involvement in terrorism and destabilisation efforts, particularly in Balochistan, FATA and Karachi. The submission followed Pakistan's arrest of Kulbhushan Jadhav, whom Islamabad identified as an Indian intelligence operative.
Pakistan again raised the issue internationally in November 2020, when its UN ambassador handed Secretary-General António Guterres a dossier that Islamabad described as documenting Indian state-sponsored terrorism in Pakistan. Pakistan said the dossier included documents as well as audio and video evidence that showed communications between Indian handlers and militants operating in Pakistan.
The issue also surfaced repeatedly at the UN General Assembly. In September 2022, Pakistani diplomat Saima Saleem said India was supporting terrorist groups including the TTP and Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA).
More recently, Pakistan's accusations have focused heavily on Balochistan. In April 2025, the DG ISPR, Chaudhry, presented evidence of an Indian-sponsored network operating inside Pakistan. He said that Indian personnel were providing militants with explosives, improvised explosive devices and funding.

content:
Trump claims 'annihilation of Iran' possible, will create 'peace'
US President Donald Trump on Thursday vowed to hit Iran "very hard" if Tehran was related to the Dubai-Tel Aviv Flydubai incident.
Asked by reporters if the US would consider retaliation against Iran if it was connected to the incident, he said. "They’ll be hit very hard, don’t worry."
Trump's comments followed an incident involving Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, which was diverted and made an emergency landing in the Saudi city of Tabuk.
