title: Gold up despite global market loss
description: Gold up despite global market loss
content:
Climbs Rs4,300/tola with lagged impact; rupee inches up to 277.11/$
Gold prices in Pakistan increased on Wednesday despite a decline in international markets, with local rates reflecting a lagged impact of previous global price movements.
Gold price per tola rose Rs4,300 to reach Rs441,636, according to rates shared by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association. Similarly, the price of 10-gram gold increased by Rs3,686 to Rs378,631. On Tuesday, gold had declined Rs800 per tola. The increase in local prices came despite weakness in the international market, where gold surrendered earlier gains after briefly rising following the release of softer-than-expected US inflation data.
Spot gold was down 0.7% at $4,152.86 per ounce as of 1:40 pm ET (1740 GMT). The precious metal was down around 6.6% in September, putting it on track for a monthly decline. Higher energy prices have weighed on the metal, offsetting some support from inflation data that reduced expectations for an immediate Federal Reserve rate hike.
Market attention has now shifted towards upcoming US economic data, particularly employment figures due on Friday, which could provide fresh clues about the Federal Reserve's rate outlook.
Adnan Agar, Director at Interactive Commodities, said gold was currently trading within a range of around $4,100 to $4,200 per ounce, with the market awaiting the US employment data for a clearer direction. He noted that gold had recently traded as high as around $4,210, while the market was hovering near $4,154. According to Agar, the employment data will be important for determining whether the precious metal breaks out of its current range.
The US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index rose 0.3% last month, while markets were pricing in a 39% chance of an October rate hike, according to the information cited in the market update.
Meanwhile, other precious metals also remained under pressure internationally, with gold, silver and platinum on track for monthly losses in September, although all three remained positioned for quarterly gains. In Pakistan, silver prices moved in the opposite direction of the international weakness in gold, increasing by Rs20 to Rs6,578 per tola. The divergence between domestic and international prices reflects the timing of local market adjustments, with Pakistani bullion rates not always moving simultaneously with global spot prices.
The Pakistani rupee closed at 277.11 against the US dollar on Wednesday, gaining Rs0.01 from Tuesday's close at 277.12. Globally, the US dollar remained near its 2026 high against the euro and was on track for its strongest monthly gain against the single currency in 14 months, supported by US economic growth and higher rates.

title: Response to fixed tax unsatisfactory
description: Response to fixed tax unsatisfactory
content:
Four new traders file returns; FBR collects Rs3.08tr in Q1, extends deadline
As only four new shopkeepers opted for the fixed tax scheme until the statutory deadline, Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) Chairman Rashid Mahmood Langrial admitted on Wednesday that the response remained below expectations and traders defeated the good faith.
The government also gave a 15-day extension in filing all tax returns after receiving 5.7 million returns by the deadline of September 30 as against the registered 19 million taxpayers. However, the chairman said the filers were 1.7 million more than September last year.
The poor response to the traders' scheme coincided with the close of the first quarter of the current fiscal year and the FBR managed to meet the quarterly target of Rs3.03 trillion, strengthening its bargaining position with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). However, the overall return filers were 5.7 million until the statutory deadline compared to the 19 million registered taxpayers.
Headed by Senator Saleem Mandviwalla of the PPP, the Senate Standing Committee on Finance got a detailed briefing from Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani and the FBR chairman on the new fixed tax scheme.
"We are worried that the response to the tax scheme remained below our expectations," said Langrial while responding to a question. FBR's Member Operations Zubair Bilal said so far 787 tax returns had been filed under the new scheme, of which only four were new filers. But Kayani, the main architect of the scheme, was hopeful that the scheme would pick up momentum once the FBR started chasing the traders. He revealed that there were technical glitches in the application launched to facilitate the first-time filers.
"If the traders do not opt for the scheme and even the fines prove insufficient to convince them, then strong enforcement measures would have to be taken," said Kayani, hoping that the FBR would now go to the field to create awareness of the new scheme.
When the committee decided to review the implementation status after one month, Langrial responded that there was a possibility that the situation might remain the same. "Good faith has been defeated" by the traders, he said, adding that glitches in filing applications were merely an excuse for not filing the returns.
The government had launched the 1% fixed tax scheme, offering retailers to pay a nominal tax in return for complete exemption from audit and installation of Point of Sales.
It was the best-ever scheme offered to any segment in the country, remarked Kayani. "The traders' issue dates back to before my birth and the new scheme is still at the initial stage," he said, hoping that the response would grow once the government started imposing fines.
To a question from PML-N Senator Anusha Rahman about whether the FBR had prepared a list of non-compliant traders, FBR's Member Strategic Transformation Dr Hamid Ateeq Sarwar only said all those who would not file returns would be chased.
To another question, Sarwar said the government was targeting to bring 500,000 to 1 million traders into the tax net out of the 3.7 million who were outside the system. Responding to a query about collecting Rs50 billion from traders in the current year, the FBR chairman said if the scheme remained successful, the collection should be over Rs100 billion but if it failed, there would be negligible payments.
Kayani stated that the government had consulted the traders and introduced the scheme accordingly. He added that within two months, 10,338 retailers registered through the application, covering traders with annual sales of up to Rs200 million. Of these, 2,337 were new but only a very few filed returns.
The committee was informed that penalties would initially be imposed in stages, with fines of Rs10,000 at the first stage, Rs25,000 at the second stage and Rs50,000 at the third stage. The FBR chairman stressed that extensive awareness campaigns had already been launched and noted that there was still a perception among some traders that those who did not register through the application would not face penalties.
Meanwhile, the government on Wednesday extended the statutory date for filing income tax returns for tax year 2026 by 15 days to October 15 because of requests from various trade bodies and tax bar associations. Taxpayers faced a lot of problems in filing returns due to glitches in the system developed by the Pakistan Revenue Automation Limited (PRAL).
The FBR received 5.7 million tax returns compared to the total of 8.5 million returns filed last year, representing a decrease of 32%. But Zubair Bilal said the filers were 1.7 million higher when compared with September 30, 2025.
The FBR bagged Rs3.078 trillion in taxes during the July-September quarter of the current fiscal year, surpassing the target by Rs25 billion. However, the key reason for achieving the target was a very low benchmark as the increase was hardly 6.5% over the same period of last year.
For the current fiscal year, the government and the IMF have given a Rs15.263 trillion annual tax target to the FBR. This requires a 17.4% growth over last year's collection. Unlike in the past, the IMF has made it binding to meet the tax targets and its approval of the sixth loan tranche will be contingent upon achieving the first-half target.
According to the provisional figures, the tax machinery received over Rs1.432 trillion inn income tax, falling short of the three-month target by Rs52 billion. For the third consecutive month, sales tax collection remained higher than the target. The FBR got Rs1.14 trillion worth of sales tax, exceeding the target by Rs85 billion.
Federal excise duty collection stood at Rs197 billion, which was almost equal to the target. Customs duty collection reached Rs312 billion, lower by Rs8 billion than the target.

Daniel Zolghadri has joined Elijah Bynum’s crime thriller My Darling California , replacing Charles Melton, who has exited the upcoming film.

Zolghadri previously appeared in Bo Burnham’s Eighth Grade and HBO’s Fahrenheit 451 before landing a leading role in Prime Video’s science fiction series Tales From the Loop . His recent film credits include Y2K , If I Had Legs I’d Kick You and Lurker .

Bynum wrote and directed My Darling California after making his feature debut with A24’s Hot Summer Nights , starring Timothée Chalamet. He later directed Magazine Dreams , which starred Jonathan Majors.
The film is produced by David Hinojosa, Alex Coco and Sébastien Raybaud, with Anton handling production, financing and international sales.

title: Self rhetorical lies     Pakistan rejects Kabul   s claims over Nuristan clashes
description: Information ministry says Taliban statements seeking to blame Pakistan for fighting reflect    despair and frustration
content:
Information ministry says Taliban statements seeking to blame Pakistan for fighting reflect ‘despair and frustration’
The Ministry of Information on Wednesday rejected the Afghan Taliban minister’s allegations against Pakistan as “self-rhetorical lies”, saying the statements aimed at externalising the regime’s internal problems reflected its “despair and frustration” in dealing with its own issues.
Fighting between the Afghanistan Freedom Front and the Taliban resumed on Tuesday morning, Sept 29, in Nuristan’s Kamdesh district, Afghanistan International reported citing informed sources, adding that the clashes began with a Taliban attack.
Meanwhile, the Taliban Defence Ministry said its operation against armed opponents in Kamdesh had ended, claiming that 41 people were killed and 62 others detained.
In a statement posted on X, the ministry’s fact-checking account described the latest allegations by the Taliban’s “so-called Minister for Borders” and other “mouthpieces” as “self-rhetorical lies” aimed at diverting attention from what it called serious internal oppression, dissent and instability.
Calling the Afghan Taliban a “non-inclusive and non-representative regime”, the ministry said it had imposed itself on the Afghan people through “force and oppression”.
𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐂𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤 | 𝐌𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 & 𝐁𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐝𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 ◼️ The latest allegations by so called Minister for Borders and other mouthpieces of the Taliban regime seeking to attribute the fighting in Nuristan to Pakistan are self rhetorical… pic.twitter.com/S4z5EYre5K
“These comical statements to externalise their internal issues and follow-up rhetoric directed towards Pakistan actually reflect the despair and frustration in handling their own issues,” it said.
The ministry further said the Taliban remained “willingly oblivious” to what it described as their “un-Islamic abetment of terror”, adding that the group was acting as a proxy for a “Hindutva design” for the sake of the interests of some of its leaders.
“This rentier approach of destabilising the region for money as a proxy of agencies is leading the Taliban only towards a self-destructive path, devoid of dignity and honour,” the statement said.
Read : Pakistan rubbishes Afghan Taliban claim of captured post as 'false and fabricated'
The statement came after Taliban Borders, Tribes and Tribal Affairs Minister Noorullah Noori warned Pakistan, saying Islamabad should learn from Afghanistan’s history and that Taliban opponents would be “defeated” if they chose war.
Speaking on Wednesday at a meeting with Kuchi elders from six provinces, Noori said those seeking to destabilise Afghanistan would face “serious consequences”.
Referring to the tensions, Noori said: “Pakistan’s army and intelligence services should understand the people of Afghanistan from a historical, ideological, political and practical perspective.”
Taliban opponents, including the Afghanistan Freedom Front, National Resistance Front and United Front of Afghanistan, have stepped up attacks against the Taliban in recent months.
Criticising the group’s political and military opponents, including the National Resistance Front, the minister said Taliban opponents had stood alongside what he called “occupiers” during the presence of US and Nato forces in Afghanistan but now spoke of fighting for freedom.
This is not the first time the Afghan Taliban regime has levelled allegations against Pakistan. In the past, it has accused Pakistan of facilitating infiltration, carrying out airstrikes and smuggling weapons into Afghanistan, allegations that Islamabad has repeatedly rejected.
According to security officials, the Afghan Taliban regime has been providing sanctuary, support and patronage to terrorist groups. They said documented evidence contradicted Kabul’s repeated denials and pointed to an entrenched terrorist network operating from Afghan soil .
Also Read : 'Frivolous and baseless': Pakistan rejects Taliban claims of involvement in Nuristan violence
Pakistan maintains that the terrorist nexus extended beyond the movement of terrorists across the border to their training, arming and operational support.
Security officials estimate that up to 70 per cent of the Fitna al-Khawarij terrorists infiltrating Pakistan were of Afghan origin. They further claim that the Taliban regime had allowed leftover US and NATO weapons to reach terrorist groups, including Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan .
In 2026 alone, terrorism emanating from Afghan soil claimed the lives of 1,327 Pakistanis and injured another 2,484, according to figures cited by Pakistani authorities.
The United Nations estimated the strength of TTP in Afghanistan at around 6,000 to 6,500 terrorists. UN reporting had also documented more than 600 terrorist attacks against Pakistan during 2025, including attacks launched from Afghan territory.
According to Pakistani security officials, the TTP had established training facilities in Afghanistan’s Kunar, Nangarhar, Khost and Paktika provinces.
The government has maintained that the issue was fundamentally one of Pakistan's national security and that continued attacks from Afghan soil cannot be addressed through denials alone.
Pakistan says it expected the Taliban regime to fulfil its commitments by taking verifiable action against terrorist groups operating from its territory rather than defending or denying their presence.

title: FBR extends income tax returns filing deadline to Oct 15
description: Notification says date has been extended to Oct 15 in view of requests from various trade bodies  tax bar associations
content:
Notification says date has been extended to Oct 15 in view of requests from various trade bodies, tax bar associations
The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) on Wednesday extended the deadline for filing income tax returns for 2026 to October 15, in consideration of "requests from various trade bodies and tax bar associations".
In a notification posted on X, FBR said that "the Federal Board of Revenue is pleased to communicate that the date of filing of income tax return for Tax Year 2026, for the persons who are required to file their returns by September 30, 2026, is hereby extended up to October 15, 2026 in view of the requests from various trade bodies and tax bar associations.”
Read : FBR extends tax return deadline till Oct 31
The FBR has been under pressure to broaden Pakistan's narrow tax base and meet ambitious revenue targets set under an agreement with the International Monetary Fund, making digitisation and taxpayer facilitation central to its stated reform agenda in recent years.
Read More : FBR achieves Rs1.71tr tax target
For the current fiscal year, the government and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have agreed on the annual tax target of Rs15.263 trillion. This requires a 17.4% increase over last year's receipts. Unlike in the past, the IMF has made it binding to meet tax targets and the approval of its sixth loan tranche hinges on achieving the H1 target.
Provinces have promised to give a little over Rs1 trillion in grants to the federal government for defence and water projects, subject to the condition that the FBR collects Rs15.263 trillion in revenues. The government has also taken revenue and enforcement measures of over Rs1 trillion in the budget to enable the FBR reach the target.
According to provisional statistics , the tax authority got over Rs685 billion in income tax, falling short of the two-month target by a wide margin of Rs74 billion. The income tax collection was also Rs29 billion less than the last fiscal year, marking negative growth of 4%.
For the second consecutive month, the sales tax collection remained higher than the target. The FBR received Rs719 billion worth of sales tax, exceeding the target by Rs85 billion. The sales tax collection was also 14%, or Rs86 billion, higher than last year.
Of the total, Rs496 billion, or 69%, of sales tax was generated at the import stage. In the budget, the government has changed the law in order to collect sales tax at market prices of goods, instead of factory-gate prices, for numerous items. This has reduced chances of tax evasion but has broken the value-added chain.
The collection of federal excise duty stood at Rs118 billion, which was almost equal to the target and Rs3 billion higher than the last year. Customs duty collection hit Rs198 billion, which was slightly lower than the target and equal to the previous year's receipts.

title: The geography we cannot change
description: Afghanistan opposed Pakistan s entry into the United Nations in 1947 and has contested the Durand Line ever since
content:
Afghanistan opposed Pakistan's entry into the United Nations in 1947 and has contested the Durand Line ever since
Long after today's governments have gone, Pakistan and Afghanistan will still share the same mountains, passes, tribes, markets and frontier. That simple geographical truth should matter more than the anger of the present moment.
Relations between Islamabad and Kabul have rarely appeared as dangerous as they do today. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban authorities of allowing the TTP and other militants to use Afghan territory for attacks inside Pakistan. Kabul rejects the allegation and accuses Pakistan of violating Afghan sovereignty. Air strikes, border clashes and competing accusations have gradually turned a security dispute into something close to direct confrontation between two states that have neither the geographical space nor the economic luxury for permanent hostility.
The difficulties are old. Afghanistan opposed Pakistan's entry into the United Nations in 1947 and has contested the Durand Line ever since. The Soviet invasion, the arrival of millions of refugees in Pakistan and the years of the Afghan jihad tied the two societies together. After 2001, each side blamed the other for the instability that followed. When the Taliban returned to power in 2021, many in Pakistan expected a more manageable western border. Instead, the TTP became the central dispute.
The record since then shows a gradual shift. Pakistan's early strikes in Afghanistan in 2022 and 2024 were limited and followed by quick de-escalation. In 2025 Islamabad also pursued diplomacy: visits to Kabul, a trilateral meeting with China in Beijing, an agreement to raise diplomatic ties to ambassador level, and a framework for a joint feasibility study of the Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan railway. When attacks continued regardless, the approach hardened.
The Taliban's failure to rein in the TTP cannot be justified on any ground. It repeats an earlier mistake. Sheltering armed groups that other country regards as a mortal threat has once again put Afghanistan on a collision course. Pakistan's response was a strike in Kabul in October 2025 and a sustained air campaign from February 2026, making force a main tool of interaction.
Yet force has not brought security, and confrontation is a course neither country can sustain for long. The strongest argument for peace is not sentimental. It is arithmetic.
Afghanistan is landlocked, and Pakistan offers it some of the shortest routes to the Arabian Sea. Bilateral trade reached nearly $2 billion in FY2024-25 despite political friction. Pakistan, for its part, needs a land route to Central Asia, and Afghanistan is the natural one. Projects such as the Trans-Afghan Railway, CASA-1000 and TAPI are meant to link Central Asia's energy and markets with South Asia. All of them pass through this one border.
Conflict already carries a cost that does not show up on the battlefield. Afghan traders have moved towards Iran and Central Asia after repeated closures of routes through Pakistan, and Afghanistan's total trade actually grew in 2025 as they did so. Pakistan is exploring alternative access to Central Asia through China and Iran. This should worry both governments. Once traders build new supply chains, they rarely return simply because the politics improve. Every prolonged closure moves a share of commerce away, possibly for good.
There is a deeper change required in Kabul. Afghanistan's celebrated resistance to foreign domination has been central to its national memory. But resistance is an instrument of survival, not a model of governance. A society cannot permanently organise itself around the virtues needed to defeat invaders. The qualities that win a war, such as secrecy, hierarchy, ideological rigidity and suspicion, are not necessarily those needed to build universities, run cities, attract investment, educate women and men, negotiate trade agreements and take part confidently in the modern economy. The move from insurgency to government demands an intellectual transition as profound as the military victory that preceded it.
Restraining the TTP is therefore a matter of sovereignty and self-interest, not a favour to Pakistan. A government that hosts groups attacking its largest neighbour will find it hard to attract the capital its economy needs.
Pakistan has its own homework. Geography does not translate into permanent influence and on the expectation that past support buys present.
That is where a new relationship could begin. The two states do not need to agree about everything. France and Germany did not erase their wars before building Europe. Southeast Asian states did not settle every territorial disagreement before building economic cooperation. Successful regions are not composed of countries without historical grievances. They are often composed of countries that eventually decide that prosperity is a more productive use of geography than revenge.
Pakistan and Afghanistan face precisely that choice. One road leads towards an increasingly militarised frontier, alternative trade routes, proxy accusations, radicalisation and generations taught to regard the people across the border as adversaries. The other turns the same geography into corridors: Karachi and Gwadar connected northward, Kabul connected southward, Central Asian energy flowing towards South Asia, and families, traders and students crossing a border regulated by states rather than militants.
The mountain passes will remain whichever road is chosen. So will the Durand Line, Pakistan and Afghanistan. That is the lesson both countries have taken too long to learn: you can choose your policies, allies and governments, but not your neighbour.
Sometimes the most useful act available to societies accustomed to conflict is not to win another battle. It is to turn the page.

title: Transforming global order   the wider debate
description: Saudi and Turkish academics addressed the conference online
content:
Saudi and Turkish academics addressed the conference online
For two weeks we summed up the debate conducted by the Institute for Strategic Studies, Research and Analysis (ISSRA) at the National Defence University (NDU) Islamabad under the annual 'International Programme for Development and Stability' regarding the 'Emerging Global Order (EGO)', strategic autonomy and stability, AI and technology, warfare and conflict prevention, and global competition.
In the last plenary, Saudi and Turkish academics addressed the conference online. The Saudi scholar emphasised that security in the ME will be regionally decided only, when regional states acquire greater [hard power] capability. His formulation of Middle Power (MP) was a state able to generate influence beyond its borders, with bargaining leverage. He endorsed Pakistan's MP status through strategic flexibility, diplomatic balancing, techno-military proficiency and independence, regional partnerships, Islamabad's reach and position, etc – aspects he considered MP prerequisites. That Makkah Agreement combines unique MP capabilities of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye for greater regional influence.
Prof Hussain of Türkiye described Ankara a changed MP, having lost an empire. That Türkiye, enjoying the luxury of its strategic location, uniquely belonged to Middle East, Europe, Central Asia and South Asia simultaneously, through geographic proximity and relationships, like with Pakistan, and alliances like Makkah Agreement, NATO membership and EU aspirations. He underscored the importance of Makkah Agreement in promoting collective security and strategic stability under an environment where the old order was dying, and EGO was yet to be fully operational. Prof Hussian pointed out that in any future regional security architecture, Ankara would emerge as a security provider; Türkiye believed in 'peace at home and peace abroad'; and Iran cannot be ignored.
The three days of deliberations under the IPDS-26 covered a lot of ground and laid correct emphasis, where it belonged, i.e EGO and its implications for the world, the region and especially for Pakistan. It was hard to encapsulate all aspects of this expansive debate in the limited time. Before discussing EGO in the light of the raging academic debate, one would like to evaluate and suggest a sequel to the IPDS-26, to dilate upon EGO in the light of emerging global youth and a youth culture; the implications of lawless unilateralism by the US-Israel nexus in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria; the role of ethics, religion and nationalism in shaping the EGO; the General-Politician debate (Generals misleading the politicians or other way round); the effects of AI proliferation on human intelligence and cognitive capacity; the worrying trend about acceptance of greater civilian losses in warfare, with non-contact warfare no more subservient to the logic of conscience (Israeli barbarism in Gaza and the US/Europe's complicit silence and numb acquiescence); long-term Pakistan-Iran ties, friend or foe; the ultimate American response to Iran under Trump presidency; and the emerging strategy of 'choke points' to include trade, financial and psychological choke points beyond the physical ones.
Let's turn to academics of EGO. In one's reckoning, the outcome of the debate will largely hinge upon the outlook of the only hegemon, the US. The academic divide is among scholars on one side, who think the US displacement by China or an emerging multipolarity is a done deal and only a matter of time. For them China is not a 'rising power' but an already 'risen' and established one, buoyed by its vast human, financial, technological (including AI), military and emerging diplomatic capital and credentials. In this competition, under 'IR's Offensive Realism Theory' parlance, the US is on the decline, waiting to be displaced by China alone or through a multipolar world, that PRC would lead. These scholars cite the red carpet laid for President Xi during his recent US visit, with President Trump receiving him on the tarmac, in break with the US protocol; President Xi's demonstrated confidence, his talking points, and the nuances of negotiations with Trump and his Administration.
The other group of academics do not consider the US in freefall. The current issue of Foreign Affairs magazine debates the 'end of alliances' under the US. In an essay by Kurt Campbell and Rush Doshi, the contemporary US perception is cited as a 'landlord seeking rent', a departure from its partnership credential with the Europe/World. Authors mention the prevalent sentiment in the US that 'alliance system' America's biggest advantage over China – is unlikely to recover. However, in the writers' opinion, the US alliance system would survive and endure the Trump moment and Trump effect, which they consider transient. Because the alliance system has 'weathered now forgotten shocks'; that the main driver of the system, the West Plus threat perception remains unchanged (rather magnifies); and that there is due official diligence in the system to work 'for' and not 'against' the alliance system. They posit that Trump's perceived withdrawal, by default, makes the allies do more, so that the US can do less, and keep its reserves intact. Reducing reliance on Washington strengthens alliance's hard power, de-risks the US, and despite hedging by some Western powers, brings them together.
People in 13 European countries polled that relationship with the US will get better after Trump steps down. Many hold the view that Russian defeat in Ukraine is essential for restraining Chinese ambition. And for that US support is critical, given the enormity of US 'fiscal scale' in AI, chip-making, cloud computing, etc, created by only three American 'hyperscalers', Amazon, Google and Microsoft, accounting for two-thirds of the global cloud market. The allies are undertaking the most significant defence buildup in a generation, funded by American capital. Europe has no alternative to threats it faces, other than America's space-based defence systems for surveillance, reconnaissance, intelligence, early warning and response. The Trump effect unites Europe and augments its defence.
From the ongoing great power competition, the writers come up with five alternatives on 'multipolarity': a) Global multipolarity with no rules, no fixed alliances, and every state on its own; b) World divided into US and Chinese spheres of influence; c) a 'Great power concert' producing 'managed peace' among major powers; d) Partial Chinese preeminence given Beijing's sheer scale; the world deferring to Chinese mass, and: e) An Allied scale, balancing the Chinses scale.
They reckon the last alternative, as plausible. The jury is out!

title: The case of a global concert
description: Charles Kupchan s new proposal would restore that practice
content:
Charles Kupchan's new proposal would restore that practice
In May last year, I wrote in these pages that the ghost of the Concert of Europe should be neither romanticised nor dismissed. It's harder to ignore sixteen months later.
Take a look at the world this week. A war which began in late February with the US-Israel strikes on Iran has expanded to Lebanon and the Strait of Hormuz and drawn in Gulf states. The Houthis and Saudi Arabia have clashed in Yemen, triggering a US security warning over the region recently. In Europe, Russia's war in Ukraine is ongoing, with drones, sabotage and violations of airspace, and senior European officials warning of deliberately ambiguous attacks on NATO territory that are big enough to cause some fear but not enough to trigger the defence clause.
Each fire is handled through ad hoc measures: emergency calls, borrowed mediators, statements after the fact. And they all are connected. British intelligence reportedly believes that the Kremlin may see Washington's focus on Iran as distracting. When things get tough in the Gulf, risks increase in the Baltic, and no one can observe both simultaneously.
It is an old problem. Following the Napoleonic wars, the great powers of Europe convened at the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and resolved disputes without war. The consequence was a Concert of Europe without a constitution, no court, only an informal tradition of consensus diplomacy that for about four decades helped manage disputes among its members.
Charles Kupchan's new proposal would restore that practice. Writing in Foreign Policy Magazine, the Global Concert he pitched would meet not occasionally, like the original, but continuously, every day, in a strategically positioned city, with subconcerts on flashpoints such as Ukraine and Iran. He questioned the impact of fly-in fly-out summits like the recent G-20 and BRICS one. His concert would also run on goodwill mostly, with no charter and no binding commitments.
But can a voluntary body work? Asia offers clues. ASEAN cannot force anyone to do anything but decades of regular meetings have created habits of consultation and crisis management. SAARC was entirely voluntary in its design, but the summits were not regular and, when the relationship turned sour, they ceased. Maybe it's continuity, rather than enforcement that lends goodwill its heft. The stakes are not abstract for the Global South whose economies depend on energy passing through Hormuz and on Gulf labour markets. And when the Gulf is on fire, they burn first.
Trine Flockhart's addition is important here. In her latest essay she argues that there is no multipolar world but rather a multi-order one. She suggests that there are several orders that exist simultaneously and each have its own rule and legitimacy. The relations between orders are as important as the relations within. Today's crises appear to fit here. The Gulf war is not a fight between poles, it's a fight between overlapping orders. Whereas the conflict in Europe is between the liberal and the Russian order. She warns that the liberal order itself could split and Moscow's calculation about Washington's distraction shows how a fracture inside one order becomes an opening for another.
Looking into history, the great powers of then decided on the fate of others without consulting them. Consider Berlin in 1884-85 when Europe partitioned Africa with no Africans at the table. Any modern version of this that spoke only for the strongest ones would inherit that flaw.
I am not claiming to know whether a concert is the answer as it is still an ongoing debate. But the questions it's raising are now hard to ignore. Who communicates with whom on a daily basis when there is a crisis? Who sits in the room and who merely lives with its decisions? The lesson from Vienna is that peace needs a standing habit of talking before acting. And in a world of many orders and many fires, the idea of it may be worth hearing out. Even if only to learn what it lacked then: a seat for everyone else.

title: Sindh s rabies crisis
description: Government s response has focused on expanding treatment infrastructure
content:
Government's response has focused on expanding treatment infrastructure
World Rabies Day passed earlier this week, and Sindh's official figures tell the story of a province being chewed up by a completely preventable disease. At least 35 people have died of rabies in the first nine months of 2026, while dog-bite cases across Sindh have surged past 200,000, including more than 40,000 in Karachi alone. These numbers are objectively terrible and reflect the failure of provincial- and city-level policies to address rabies or stray dog populations.
The government's response has focused on expanding treatment infrastructure. Authorities point to 278 upgraded anti-rabies units, 138,000 vaccine doses administered, and a 30% increase in treatment capacity compared to last year. To their credit, officials have also gone out of their way to urge people to get treated after even a minor interaction with a stray animal, but that is the problem - these worthwhile efforts are reactive, not preemptive or preventive. The lack of effective prevention has let the problem balloon to its current level. Last year, Sindh recorded over 285,000 dog-bite cases, and 85,891 were documented in the first four months of 2026 alone. With more than 700 attacks occurring daily, hospitals cannot treat their way out of this epidemic.
Despite some efforts, including a drive by Sindh's Rabies Control Programme to sterilise over 25,500 dogs and vaccinate more than 36,900 across 20 districts, stray dog populations continue to grow. The WHO recommends vaccinating at least 70% of a dog population to break transmission cycles, and at the current pace, Sindh will likely never come close to that number. If the government wants to make prevention efforts more meaningful, it must greatly increase mass dog vaccination and sterilisation efforts, and realign public awareness campaigns to reach the worst-affected communities, including children and daily-wage workers. The government must also be honest with the people, as covering up the extent of the dog-bite epidemic has done more harm than good.

title: Failed rescue mission
description: Pirates carry responsibility for the killings
content:
Pirates carry responsibility for the killings
The recovery of the MT Honour 25 from Somali pirates should have brought relief after more than five months of captivity. Instead, it has ended in bereavement for the families of three Pakistani sailors. Of the total 17 hostages, including 10 Pakistanis, five were killed and four wounded before Puntland forces secured the tanker. For those who had waited since April for their loved ones to return home, the vessel's recovery is no substitute for the lives that were lost.
The pirates carry responsibility for the killings. What remains unclear, however, is precisely how an operation intended to free the hostages culminated in their deaths. Survivors have said the captors opened fire on the crew when security forces closed in and the pirates began retreating. Puntland authorities have offered a different sequence, saying the five sailors were killed before the operation began. This discrepancy cannot be left unresolved. An authoritative account is now needed of the intelligence available beforehand and the circumstances in which force was authorised. Pakistan, too, has questions to answer since whatever diplomatic activity took place, it did not produce the outcome that mattered most. Islamabad must seek a detailed account from the Somali and Puntland authorities and establish whether Pakistan was informed of the planned operation and what safeguards were contemplated for the hostages. The families of the dead and injured are entitled to know why, after months of waiting, the final attempt to end their ordeal turned fatal.
The surviving sailors have finally been freed. That is welcome. But three Pakistani families will receive coffins. The recovery of the ship cannot be allowed to close the matter. The circumstances of the deaths must be established and responsibility fixed where warranted.

title: The seven day gesture
description: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
content:
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
Behind-the-scenes diplomacy has made some headway. The reported willingness of the US to consider a "seven-day proposal" for tranquility presented by Iran is a welcome development. Washington had earlier rejected the proposal and imposed its own conditions. The fact that Qatar has reached out to Tehran with a nod from the White House - and that this is now being discussed to broker a formal understanding - must graduate into a thaw. There is no room for returning to the theater of war; the region is on edge, and disrupted supply lines are pushing the global economy toward a plausible recession.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, enabling the smooth passage of maritime traffic in exchange for the US lifting its naval blockade and unfreezing Iranian assets. In other words, this means returning to the Islamabad MoU, which had seen life return to normalcy and oil prices slump to $80 a barrel for more than two weeks following the agreement in June. The additional benefit offered by Iran this time around is the inclusion of the nuclear issue in the talks to sort out a permanent modus operandi for peace in the region and beyond. This would not have been possible without the proactive, selfless mediatory roles played by Pakistan, Qatar, Türkiye and Egypt, as all stakeholders sought a thaw, especially during the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
Now is the time to restart parleys and bring the war to a permanent end. High-stakes rhetoric from President Trump and Iran's military brass, meant largely for public consumption, has taken a heavy toll and no longer serves any purpose. Fortunately, China acted as a stabilising force by persuading both the warring sides, as well as the Arab states, to step back from the brink. The silencing of guns by Tehran and Washington would have a resounding impact, compelling the Houthis and Israelis to halt their regional jingoism. This rare consensus, achieved through painstaking diplomatic maneuvers, stands as a crucial reality check of their true sincerity.

title: Is American democracy unresponsive

content:
American president can wage wars after promising to end wars
There have been many debates about American democracy being indirect. The electoral college mechanism was inserted into the system in order to what was then called "excess of democracy".
There is another thing, which I always found quite baffling. An American president is elected after making certain promises to the citizens. He then proceeds to do, in many cases, exactly the opposite of what he promised on campaign trail or does exactly similar to what his opponent stood for, opposition to which got the man elected in the first place. Bush's "read my lips no new taxes", Obama's troop surge in Afghanistan and his sickening surveillance regime, Trump's promise to release the Epstein Files and then him being the only reason they weren't are some of such examples. There is practically nothing the American citizenry can do to stop an American president from doing what they never wanted or asked for.
For four years, an American president can wage wars after promising to end wars, can spy on Americans after promising to end the warrantless surveillance of Americans, send US soldiers in defence of foreign nations after promising to end foreign deployments, and so forth. American citizens can only watch and make noise but the system does not give them the opportunity to cause any change for four years.
However, there is something even deeper and worse that I simply cannot unsee. Let me highlight some big events here. Israel asked President Kennedy for a nuclear weapon. Kennedy said absolutely not. He even asked Israel to stop the enrichment at the Dimona reactor in Israel. Next thing we know is that Kennedy died. Many suspect, and I am one of them, that Israel was behind it. title: Marlene King brings Elle Kennedy   s  Thornbird  to Hulu as new thriller series
description: Marlene King is developing Hulu   s TV adaptation of Elle Kennedy   s bestselling coming of age thriller  Thornbird
content:
Marlene King is developing Hulu’s TV adaptation of Elle Kennedy’s bestselling coming-of-age thriller 'Thornbird'
Hulu is developing a television adaptation of Elle Kennedy’s novel Thornbird , with Pretty Little Liars creator Marlene King attached as writer and executive producer.
The upcoming Hulu series is being developed by 20th Television and will be based on Kennedy’s coming-of-age thriller, which centres on a teenager attempting to escape the shadow of her family’s dark past.
The story follows 17-year-old Ryan Shipley, whose father, Gabriel Thorn, is an infamous serial killer. Ten years after his arrest, Ryan returns to her childhood hometown of Starling, Tennessee, hoping to build a normal life without revealing her identity or connection to her father.
As Ryan tries to fit in, she also hopes to experience a typical teenage life and potentially fall in love. However, her family history continues to follow her as she becomes caught up in a mystery involving the crimes of her past.
Kennedy will executive produce the Hulu adaptation alongside King and Lauren Wagner. Thornbird is the first novel Kennedy has published under the pseudonym E. Kennedy and debuted on the New York Times bestseller list following its June 30 release.
Kennedy is also the author of the Off Campus book series, which has been adapted into a television series for Prime Video. The first season premiered in May and reportedly reached 36 million viewers worldwide within its first 12 days. A second season is currently in production.
Another Kennedy novel, Girl Abroad , is also in development for television at Amazon, with A24 Television and Sorry for Your Loss creator Kit Steinkellner attached.
King is best known for creating and showrunning Pretty Little Liars , which ran for seven seasons on Freeform. Her other credits include Now & Then , Just My Luck and Famous in Love .

Josh Hartnett has opened up about working with an intimacy coordinator while filming intimate scenes with Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson for Verity , amid continued attention surrounding the It Ends With Us drama.

The comments come as intimacy coordinators remain a topic of discussion following the controversy surrounding It Ends With Us . Blake Lively alleged in her legal complaint that intimacy protocols were not followed during filming and raised concerns about the handling of intimate scenes. Baldoni denied Lively’s allegations. The legal dispute between the two actors was settled in May 2026 without the case proceeding to trial.
In Verity , Dakota Johnson plays Lowen Ashleigh, a struggling writer hired to ghostwrite for bestselling author Verity Crawford, portrayed by Hathaway. After arriving at the Crawford estate, Lowen discovers disturbing autobiographical writings involving Verity’s husband Jeremy, played by Hartnett.
Hartnett described Hathaway and Johnson as “professional and intentional” actors and said their chemistry developed through the film’s complicated relationships. Recent coverage has also highlighted a steamy scene between Hathaway and Johnson that director Showalter said was improvised during filming.
Verity , directed by Showalter, is based on Hoover’s bestselling psychological thriller and stars Hartnett, Hathaway and Johnson.

title: Cardiologists warn of rising heart disease among younger Pakistanis
description: Smoking inactivity and obesity linked to growing heart risks among younger Pakistanis says NICVD expert
content:
Smoking inactivity and obesity linked to growing heart risks among younger Pakistanis says NICVD expert
Heart disease is increasingly appearing among younger Pakistanis, with smoking, physical inactivity, obesity and other modifiable risk factors pushing cardiovascular problems into age groups once considered relatively low-risk, a senior cardiologist has warned.
Speaking during a World Heart Day webinar hosted by The Express Tribune, Dr Fawad Farooq, Professor of Interventional Cardiology at the National Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases (NICVD), Karachi, said prevention must begin well before symptoms appear because treatment alone cannot undo the damage caused by cardiovascular disease.
The discussion came ahead of World Heart Day, observed annually on September 29 to draw attention to cardiovascular disease and prevention. During the session, the host noted estimates that cardiovascular disease accounts for around 30% of deaths in Pakistan and that tobacco use causes a substantial number of deaths each year, underscoring the public-health burden behind the discussion.
"Treatment alone is not enough,” Farooq said, stressing that people need to understand their risk factors while they are still healthy. Diabetes, hypertension, obesity, physical inactivity and smoking, he said, do not simply add to cardiovascular risk but can combine to increase it substantially.
Farooq said Pakistan appears to be seeing heart disease at increasingly younger ages. While cardiovascular disease is more commonly encountered after the age of 50 or 60 in many Western populations, he said doctors in Pakistan are now seeing serious cardiac problems among people in their 20s, 30s and 40s.
He acknowledged that precise local data remain limited, but said the trend is evident in clinical practice and emergency rooms.
The shift, he said, reflects lifestyle patterns that often begin in childhood. Reduced physical activity, increased screen time, poor dietary habits and early weight gain can create the conditions for cardiovascular disease years later. He recommended building healthier routines from childhood, including daily physical activity, a balanced diet and a consistent sleep-wake cycle.
He also expressed concern about smoking beginning in the teenage years. Farooq said some people now start as early as 12 to 14, meaning that by their 20s or 30s they may already have accumulated a decade or more of exposure. That, combined with inactivity and excess calorie intake, is helping move cardiovascular risk into progressively younger age groups.
Smoking, however, requires particular attention among younger people. Unlike conditions such as diabetes, hypertension and abnormal cholesterol, which may develop progressively over time, smoking can contribute to sudden events by increasing the tendency of blood to clot.
Dr Farooq warned that a first heart attack in a young person can be especially dangerous because there may have been no previous warning or adaptation to underlying disease.
Explaining why cigarettes are so harmful, Farooq drew a distinction between tobacco, nicotine and combustion. When a cigarette is lit, he said, the burning process produces smoke containing thousands of chemicals, including carcinogens and other toxic compounds. These substances enter the body through the lungs and can damage blood vessels and other organs. Nicotine, meanwhile, is what drives dependence and makes quitting difficult. This dependence is often what brings smokers back to cigarettes even when they understand the health risks. The greater concern with smoking, he explained, is that cigarettes deliver nicotine through the burning of tobacco, a process that produces smoke and exposes the body to more than 6000 harmful chemicals.
His first recommendation to smokers remained complete cessation. “Smoking in any form, or tobacco use in any form, should not be consumed at all,” he said. At the same time, quitting can be extremely difficult for people who have smoked for many years because nicotine dependence can produce both physical and behavioural withdrawal symptoms.
Farooq stated that he regularly sees patients who stop smoking after an acute heart attack but resume once they return to their normal routine.
After years of smoking, he explained, dependence can make quitting difficult, with some patients describing discomfort or a sense that something is missing when they stop. That is why, simply telling a long-term smoker to quit may not always be enough, and cessation often requires a more structured approach.
For long-term smokers who are unable to quit immediately, harm-reduction approaches can form part of a structured quitting strategy under medical guidance.
He referred to nicotine gums, patches, heated tobacco and other non-combustible methods as options intended to reduce exposure to smoke and combustion while dependence is gradually managed. He stressed that such approaches are not for non-smokers and should ultimately support the goal of quitting.
The discussion also focused on the role of healthcare professionals. Smoking should be addressed seriously during medical visits and called for stronger counselling and cessation services.
Doctors and other health professionals, he added, also need to act as role models and reinforce the risks that second-hand smoke creates for families, children and patients in healthcare settings. Smoking should increasingly be treated as socially unacceptable, particularly where it exposes others to smoke.
Beyond smoking, Farooq urged people to monitor basic cardiovascular risk factors such as blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol before they cross into dangerous ranges. Regular physical activity and maintaining a healthy weight, he said, remain central to prevention.
He also highlighted symptoms that should never be ignored. New or severe chest pain, particularly pain brought on by walking, climbing stairs, physical exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest, should prompt immediate medical assessment.
A noticeable decline in exercise tolerance or new shortness of breath during activities that were previously manageable can also signal a problem. Sudden loss of consciousness, an episode of rapid heartbeat followed by fainting, or other abrupt cardiac symptoms should similarly be treated as warning signs.
People with a family history of premature heart disease need to be especially cautious, Farooq asserted. He defined premature family history as a heart attack occurring before the age of 55 in a close male relative or before 65 in a close female relative. Such a history does not make disease inevitable, he said, but it increases risk and makes prevention and early screening more important.
As World Heart Day draws attention to cardiovascular health, Farooq’s central message was that action should start before disease develops. Keeping diet and physical activity in balance, avoiding obesity, checking blood pressure, sugar and cholesterol, and staying away from tobacco are all measures that can reduce risk before treatment becomes necessary.
“Try to keep your heart healthy while you are in health before developing disease,” he advised. Once heart disease has occurred, treatment can be difficult and may never fully return a patient to their earlier baseline.
