title: Can an honest taxpayer sell property in Pakistan
description: Can an honest taxpayer sell property in Pakistan
content:
Difference creates a peculiar problem for the honest taxpayer
The short answer, in practical terms, is a big NO. Here is why!
In Canada and the United States, a property sale is generally handled through a documented legal process involving lawyers, title professionals, licensed real estate agents and banking channels. The buyer and seller need not personally deal with every stage of the transaction. Title, identity, contractual documents and the movement of funds are handled within a regulated framework, and the transaction is recorded at the agreed consideration, subject to applicable tax and anti-money-laundering requirements.
Now consider selling a property in Pakistan, particularly in an affluent locality such as the Defence Housing Authority in Karachi. What should be a straightforward legal transaction can become a long and exhausting exercise. Pakistan's property system remains fragmented, with provincial valuation rates (DC rates), FBR valuation tables and the actual market price often existing side by side. These official values may be used to calculate taxes, duties, fees or other charges, but they do not necessarily represent the property's actual market value or the price agreed between buyer and seller.
This difference creates a peculiar problem for the honest taxpayer. A seller who insists that the genuine market value be recorded and that the entire consideration be received through declared banking channels may find a much smaller pool of willing buyers. He may also face pressure to accept an undervalued sale deed accompanied by an undeclared cash component which finds its way into bank lockers, further fuelling the unproductive black economy thriving in the country. In practical terms, if the seller wants the entire sale proceeds in documented "white money", he may have to accept a significantly lower price, sometimes by a substantial percentage of the market value. The honest taxpayer can therefore end up bearing the financial cost of complying with the law.
The legal difference is important. In a well-integrated system, the buyer's title and the seller's authority to transfer are established through the formal record, while the professionals involved coordinate the documentation and closing. In Pakistan, these functions remain divided among several bodies. The seller may therefore have to satisfy the requirements of the housing authority, revenue or cantonment authorities, the tax authorities and the registration system separately.
The transfer procedure itself can be cumbersome. In Karachi, a seller may have to deal with the DHA, the relevant cantonment or revenue authorities, the tax authorities and the Sub-Registrar, in addition to lawyers and estate agents. Documents may have to be produced repeatedly; identities, signatures and thumb impressions verified; and original papers carried from one office to another. What should be a professional, integrated transaction can become a personal journey through several institutions, each with its own requirements. A separate piece can be written on the dubious process and the allegations of corrupt practices associated with the offices of Sub-Registrars serving Karachi.
For an elderly property owner looking for a clean and peaceful deal, this is particularly burdensome. The continued dependence on physical documents and personal appearances adds inconvenience and risk. A system that should allow professionals to handle most of the transaction still requires the owner to remain closely involved in a process that can be difficult to understand and time-consuming to complete.
There is also a larger contradiction here. Successive governments have spoken of documenting the economy and broadening the tax base, yet real estate remains an area where official values can be substantially detached from market realities. Multiple valuation mechanisms create room for undervaluation, tax avoidance and the concealment of wealth. More importantly, they can disadvantage the very citizens who are willing to declare the full value of their transactions and receive their money through legitimate banking channels.
The answer is not simply to impose more taxes or more paperwork. Pakistan needs a transparent, market-based valuation system, a genuinely unified and accessible digital record of title, traceable banking payments and a transfer process in which the genuine sale consideration is recorded. The various official valuation mechanisms should progressively converge with actual market values. A seller should not have to choose between complying with the law and obtaining the fair market value of his property.
A properly documented property transaction should be simple enough that the citizen can rely on lawyers, agents and the state machinery to complete it, rather than becoming his own investigator, accountant and administrator. If Pakistan genuinely wants to document its economy, it must make honest transactions easier, safer and financially neutral.
The question is therefore a simple one: why should compliance with the law become a financial disadvantage? An honest taxpayer should be able to sell his property honestly, receive the full declared consideration through banking channels and complete the transfer without having to steer his way through disconnected procedures.

title: Pakistan s moment
description: Pakistan s efforts are important not because Islamabad can single handedly resolve a conflict of such complexity
content:
Pakistan's efforts are important not because Islamabad can single-handedly resolve a conflict of such complexity
The conflict in the Middle East has entered a deeply worrying phase. What began as another confrontation in a region accustomed to instability now carries consequences far beyond the borders of the countries directly involved. Energy security, food security, climate security and the frightening possibility of a wider nuclear confrontation have all become part of the conversation. At a time when the international community is searching for avenues to prevent further escalation, attention is naturally focused on Washington and Tehran. Yet Islamabad has constantly been trying to create space for diplomacy.
Pakistan's efforts are important not because Islamabad can single-handedly resolve a conflict of such complexity, but because it possesses something increasingly valuable in international diplomacy: access to different sides.
The first meeting between American and Iranian representatives in Islamabad in April 2026 after years of limited direct engagement was therefore significant. Although, it did not produce an agreement, it did start the dialogue. Diplomacy is often measured not only by the agreements it produces, but also by the conversations it keeps alive. Islamabad was able to provide a useful diplomatic channel when direct communication became difficult.
Pakistan is unusually positioned for this role due to five factors.
The first is geography combined with history. Pakistan shares a long border with Iran and has decades of experience managing a complicated relationship with its western neighbour. At the same time, Islamabad has maintained a longstanding relationship with Washington, including periods of close strategic cooperation and of serious disagreement. The recent warming in the US-Pakistan ties has added another dimension. President Donald Trump's public appreciation of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir has generated considerable attention in Pakistan and abroad. Whatever the personal element in these interactions, their larger significance lies in the opening they create for institutional engagement. If Washington and Islamabad can build on this renewed contact, Pakistan could potentially offer itself as a bridge between countries that do not always have functioning channels of communication.
The second factor is Pakistan's relationship with the Gulf. For decades, millions of Pakistanis have lived and worked across the Gulf states. The Pakistani diaspora has contributed not only through remittances but also through professional expertise, businesses and participation in the economic development of their host countries. These people have become part of the social and economic fabric of the Gulf. Pakistan's ties with Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman and other regional states therefore go beyond formal diplomacy. They are reinforced by economic, cultural, religious and people-to-people connections. Islamabad cannot dictate the policies of Gulf capitals, nor should it attempt to do so. But its longstanding relationships provide diplomatic access at a moment when communication among regional powers is particularly important.
The third factor is Pakistan's diplomatic will and its emerging capacity to act beyond its traditional role. For years, Pakistan's geographical importance was discussed largely as a matter of theory. Its location between South Asia, Central Asia, China, Iran and the Middle East was repeatedly described as an opportunity, but that potential was not always translated into diplomatic influence. That may now be changing. Pakistan's connectivity potential, military capabilities, nuclear deterrence, counterterrorism experience and gradually improving economic prospects have created the ingredients of a different foreign-policy role. A middle power does not have to dominate its neighbourhood. Its influence comes from its ability to communicate with different actors, offer practical alternatives and contribute to the management of regional crises, and Islamabad is playing this role efficiently.
The fourth in the line is the growing international interest in Pakistan's critical minerals. The global economy is undergoing a major transformation, and access to minerals needed for advanced manufacturing, energy technologies and defence industries has become a strategic concern for major powers. Pakistan possesses substantial mineral potential, particularly in Balochistan. If developed transparently and responsibly, these resources could attract foreign investment and create new economic opportunities. They could also increase Pakistan's strategic relevance at a time when countries are looking to diversify their supply chains. Minerals alone, however, will not transform Pakistan. Without political stability, transparent regulation, infrastructure and meaningful participation of local communities, mineral wealth can become a source of controversy rather than prosperity. The real opportunity lies in turning geological potential into sustainable economic value.
Fifth comes China's position and Beijing's longstanding strategic partnership with Islamabad, which gives Pakistan another important diplomatic dimension. China has consistently supported Pakistan on major international issues, while projects under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) have strengthened the economic and connectivity dimensions of the relationship. China's support does not automatically translate into influence over every diplomatic question. But it does give Pakistan strategic depth at a time when great-power competition is reshaping international politics.
The emerging picture is therefore larger than the immediate Middle Eastern crisis. Pakistan is finding itself at the intersection of several major global concerns: energy security, regional conflict, strategic competition, critical minerals and connectivity. The challenge for Islamabad is to convert this moment into lasting diplomatic relevance. That requires patience rather than triumphalism, economic reform rather than slogans, and diplomacy rather than confrontation.
Pakistan may not be able to end the conflicts around it. But it can offer something the world urgently needs: a place where difficult conversations remain possible. If Islamabad can build that reputation carefully, the country's geography, relationships and strategic capabilities could finally translate into the influence that its location has promised for decades.

title: TTP  a threat until it is not
description: TTP  a threat until it is not
content:
Obvious question is no longer whether Pakistan possesses the capacity to confront terrorism
The bloodshed in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa is becoming horrifyingly familiar. In September alone, we witnessed with shock two devastating blasts in K-P which killed police personnel and civilians and left scores injured. The attackers used an explosives-laden vehicle before armed militants stormed the compound. It was not an isolated incident but another entry in a growing catalogue of violence stretching across North Waziristan, Bannu, Lakki Marwat, Tank, Hangu, and beyond.
The obvious question is no longer whether Pakistan possesses the capacity to confront terrorism. It does. Pakistan has sophisticated weapons systems, one of the world's largest professional armies, extensive intelligence organisations, and decades of counterterrorism experience. Yet relatively small militant organisations continue to kill policemen, soldiers and civilians almost at will where and when they choose! This is the paradox Pakistan must confront.
The TTP and associated militant networks do not need to defeat the Pakistani military. They merely need to survive it. An insurgent chooses when to attack, where to disappear and when not to fight. Motivation, mobility, local networks and sanctuary can compensate for extraordinary disparities in conventional military power. And the threat is evolving. The Express Tribune recently reported that militants in K-P are increasingly employing drones, thermal imaging and night-vision technology. Some 156 police personnel were killed in militant attacks during the first seven months of 2026 alone.
So, describing these organisations simply as ragtag bands risks misunderstanding the problem. Their material resources may be tiny compared with those of the state but their ability to adapt should not be underestimated. Pakistan's real difficulty appears elsewhere: consistency of purpose. The country has repeatedly demonstrated that it possesses the military will to confront militants. But military success and strategic success are not synonymous. Terrorists can be removed from a valley today and return tomorrow if intelligence, policing, prosecution, border management, governance and economic opportunity do not fill the space they leave behind. Military operations can suppress an insurgency; they cannot, by themselves, eliminate the ecosystem that reproduces it. That was precisely the insight behind the National Action Plan formulated after the horrific APS massacre. NAP recognised that terrorism required far more than battlefield operations.
The tragedy is not that Pakistan lacked a strategy. It is that implementation repeatedly lagged behind declaration. An equally damaging ambiguity arose from differentiating between militants considered immediately hostile to Pakistan and those whose activities were directed elsewhere. Whatever tactical logic once supported distinctions between so-called "good" and "bad" militants, the experience of subsequent years illustrates their danger. Militant ecosystems are porous. Fighters move, alliances shift, ideologies overlap and yesterday's good can turn bad tomorrow.
There must therefore be one uncomplicated principle: no armed non-state organisation should be permitted to operate outside the law. The Afghan dimension makes the challenge still more serious. A UN monitoring report released in 2026 described the TTP as one of the largest terrorist groups operating in Afghanistan and reported that it had been afforded greater liberty and support there.
Pakistan consequently faces both a domestic counterterrorism challenge and a difficult diplomatic-security problem across its western border. Yet strategic clarity should not mean indiscriminate force. A sophisticated state must distinguish between terrorist leadership, operational fighters, facilitators, sympathisers and people who can genuinely abandon militancy. IBOs, prosecution and reintegration can operate simultaneously.
The fundamental question is not whether Pakistan is powerful enough to defeat terrorism. It is whether that power can be translated into sustained political will, institutional coordination and strategic consistency. Militants do not have to become stronger than the state to threaten it. They only have to survive in the spaces where the state is inconsistent.

title: School van safety
description: Pakistan needs to move towards a much stricter school transport regime
content:
Pakistan needs to move towards a much stricter school-transport regime
The sight of a school van reduced to a burnt-out shell in Murree should be enough to dispel any illusion that Pakistan's existing approach to school transport is working. Children travelling to a school on Tuesday suffered burns after their van left the road and caught fire. Preliminary reports indicate that the vehicle was carrying more passengers than its designated capacity and did not have a fire extinguisher.
The incident raises a basic question. Why are vehicles carrying children still allowed onto the road without the safeguards that could mean the difference between an accident and a catastrophe? This is hardly an unidentified danger. In Lahore only last month, traffic police announced a crackdown on overloaded school vans and prohibited LPG cylinders in vehicles transporting children. In Rawalpindi, previous directives have required school vans to be roadworthy, properly registered and equipped with fire extinguishers and first-aid kits. Drivers are supposed to possess valid licences and vehicles should have fitness certificates. The instructions exist. What is missing is the assurance that a child entering a school van every morning is entering a vehicle that actually complies with them. Notifications issued from government offices cannot provide that assurance.
Pakistan needs to move towards a much stricter school-transport regime in which vehicles carrying children are treated differently from ordinary passenger vans. A Suzuki Bolan or similar vehicles pressed into school duty should not qualify merely because it can accommodate several passengers. School transport should meet a prescribed safety specification before it is permitted to operate. Passenger limits must correspond to the vehicle's actual capacity rather than the number of children who can be squeezed inside. Where modifications have been made, particularly to fuel systems, they must be inspected rather than accepted as an informal feature of commercial transport.

title: Eight years for injustice
description: Eight years for injustice
content:
Case was also the catalyst for the Pashtun Tahafuz Movement (PTM)
Naqeebullah Mehsud, the 27-year-old aspiring model from Waziristan whose murder in Karachi led to nationwide protests, will not receive justice. An anti-terrorism court in Karachi has acquitted the last seven suspects in the case, which has been running since a few weeks after his murder in January 2018. The latest round of acquittals brings the number of suspects walking free to 25, with the court citing "insufficient evidence" because not a single suspect came forward to say the encounter was staged. The only one that did - a head constable - later recanted, claiming he was pressured to identify the men and actually did not know who any of them were.
This was despite the fact that most of Pakistan already knew who at least some of the men were, including Rao Anwar, the disgraced and disgraceful "encounter specialist" alleged to maintain deep underworld connections. We also question how nobody was able to dig up any evidence against police officer Sheikh Muhammad Shoaib, whose nickname was "Shooter", allegedly due to his notoriety as an encounter specialist.
Anwar, the principal accused, was among 18 officers acquitted in January 2023, despite a joint investigation team holding him responsible. All of the acquittals have also again raised questions about whether law enforcement is incompetent, laws are poorly written, or the judiciary's expectations are too unrealistic, because when seemingly straightforward cases linger for years and the final decision still defies expectations, it is clear that something, somewhere, went very wrong.
The case was also the catalyst for the Pashtun Tahafuz Movement (PTM), which reached national stature due to its protests against extrajudicial killings after starting as a localised rights movement following military operations in Waziristan. Despite its wayward and controversial history, PTM pressure may have been the only reason the case was ever taken up. Now, it appears there is no one left to demand a reexamination of the case.

title: US withdrawal from Iraq
description: Voluntary withdrawal comes as an opportunity for the US to reflect on its obsessive overseas deployments
content:
Voluntary withdrawal comes as an opportunity for the US to reflect on its obsessive overseas deployments
The security landscape of the Middle East is in a state of flux. The footprints of the lone superpower, the United States, are shrinking, and new characters are about to fill the vacuum. The scheduled withdrawal of American forces from Iraq could be a game-changer, and the prime beneficiary, of course, will be Iran, which has established its military superiority over its Arab neighbours as a result of its ongoing war with the US and Israel. Though the retreat of the Blue Stripes was ordained under the Biden administration, President Trump is keeping his word, as he believes in lessening America's overseas presence across the globe.
This is going to be the second major US withdrawal from the region following its 2021 departure from Afghanistan. Since Washington was unable to prevail over the Taliban regime in Kabul or enforce the 2020 Doha Accord, Afghanistan is sliding into anarchy and has become a terror hub. Iraq is unlikely to be any different; the resulting void is feared to be filled by pro-Iran Shia militias, as well as remnants of the Islamic State and Al Qaeda.
The fact that Syria has broken away and is no longer under Tehran's influence could be an added factor of instability. Multiple militant organisations operating freely in the Levant could turn Iraq into a bastion for their nefarious activities. Last but not least, with the Houthis on the rampage, the regional security dynamic is bound to become more complex as Iran attempts to make up for the loss of Hezbollah by funding and galvanising the Islamic resistance in Iraq.
The voluntary withdrawal comes as an opportunity for the US to reflect on its obsessive overseas deployments. Having lost around 4,500 troops in Iraq over the last two decades, the heavy price Washington paid - particularly as its military bases were repeatedly targeted by Iran - serves as a moment for strategic recalculation. The US can be a great partner in institution-building and furthering peace, rather than balkanising the region into military alliances.

title: Everyone is happy online  I m suspicious
description: I cannot find these people online
content:
I have started to suspect that I am the only unhappy person on the internet.
Not clinically unhappy. Relax. I am talking about the ordinary, everyday kind of unhappy. The kind where you wake up late, discover there is no tea, your phone is at 8 per cent, someone has sent you a "quick reminder" at 8:03 in the morning, and you immediately wonder whether abandoning society to raise goats in the countryside is still a realistic career option.
Everyone is happy. Well, I have nothing against happiness. Eat your cake, fall in love, get your promotion, go on holiday, buy yourself flowers. I fully support it. But this much happiness? Something is wrong.
I open Instagram, and apparently the entire population has collectively achieved inner peace. Where did I go wrong? Somebody's bio literally says "healed, hydrated, and unbothered." Unbothered by what? You post four times a day. You are extremely bothered. You are the founding father/mother of bothered.
I scroll for eleven seconds more and see three engagement announcements, two pregnancy reveals, one "we bought a house" post, and someone's gender reveal party. Meanwhile, I am celebrating the fact that I changed my bedsheets after only three weeks. Where is my standing ovation? Where is my statue? Where is the street named after me?
And then I follow people who seem to wake up every morning in a state of spiritual achievement. There is always sunlight coming through enormous windows, a cup of coffee placed at exactly the right angle, a perfectly clean table, and somebody sitting there looking peacefully into the distance.
I don't even look peacefully into the distance when I am being photographed. I look confused, like a man being asked, mid-robbery, to describe the suspect.
And also why is everyone's house so clean? Online, everyone lives inside a furniture catalogue. There is not one sock to be found on the ground.
Not one dirty dish in the sink. Not one crumb on the counter.
Then there are the people who have "found themselves." Every few weeks, somebody announces a new era. "My healing era." "My soft era." "My peaceful era." "My self-love era." "My new chapter era."
Next month it'll be "my villain era," the month after "my delulu era," and eventually, inevitably, "my going back to therapy because none of the other eras worked era."
Then there are the morning people. I don't trust people who wake up at 5 am and are happy about it. At 5 am, they are exercising. At 5:15, they are meditating. At 5:30, they are journaling. At 6, they are reading. At 6:30, they have apparently forgiven everyone who ever hurt them. At 7, they are making a protein smoothie. At 7:15, they have already changed their lives.
I wake up at 7:15 and need several minutes to remember what day it is. Correction: I need several minutes to remember WHO I am, WHERE I am, and whether I actually have legs or if that's just a rumour.
7:15. Alarm goes off. I don't move. I can't move. I'm not a person yet. I'm a rock. I'm a fossil. I'm something they'd dig up and put in a museum with a little sign that says "early 2000s, species unknown, probably tired." Eventually I sit up. And everything cracks. My back. My neck. Something in my knee does a sound I don't have a word for. I'm in my twenties making noises my grandfather made.
I don't want a smoothie. I want silence. And preferably nobody. But social media has made everybody suspiciously productive too.
I would like to see one person write: "Today I lost my temper over something extremely stupid, and I regret nothing."

title: Pete Davidson suffered two concussions after doing his own movie stunts
description: Pete Davidson reveals he suffered two concussions in three weeks while filming an indie movie and doing his own stunts
content:
Pete Davidson reveals he suffered two concussions in three weeks while filming an indie movie and doing his own stunts
Pete Davidson revealed that he suffered two concussions within three weeks while filming an independent movie, saying he chose to perform his own stunts before the injuries.
The former Saturday Night Live comedian discussed the injuries during an appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live! on September 28. Davidson wore sunglasses during the interview and explained that he currently has to avoid bright lights as part of his recovery.
Davidson said he sustained the two concussions while working on the unnamed indie film. He explained that he had the option of using a stunt double but decided to perform the scenes himself because he felt the difference in their appearances would be noticeable on screen.
“It was an indie movie,” Davidson said, explaining that his stunt double was significantly taller and larger than him. He said the size difference made it difficult for the double to convincingly stand in for him during the scenes.
Following the injuries, Davidson visited a doctor to assess the severity of his concussions. He also described undergoing a concussion test during the medical evaluation, recalling that he struggled to repeat a series of words given to him by the doctor.
Davidson said he has been advised to avoid bright lights until mid-November. He has continued wearing sunglasses to help with the sensitivity to light.
During the interview, Davidson also joked about the situation, maintaining his usual comedic tone while discussing the injuries.
The comedian has previously spoken publicly about various aspects of his life and career, but the concussion disclosure provides an update on his condition following the movie shoot. Further details about the independent film, including its title and release date, have not been announced.

title: Myanmar airstrike death toll hits 50 as families gather bodies
description: UN chief Guterres  strongly condemns  Myanmar airstrike and ongoing attacks on civilians  spokesman says
content:
UN chief Guterres "strongly condemns" Myanmar airstrike and ongoing attacks on civilians, spokesman says
Families searched for bodies on Tuesday around a charred market in western Myanmar after a military airstrike killed 50 people, one of the deadliest recent bombardments in the country's civil war.
Witnesses said the military's air force raided the riverside commercial hub in Kyauktaw town in western Rakhine state around midday (0530 GMT) on Monday.
"It breaks my heart to see our people dying," said Aung Chay, who was still searching for the remains of his brother-in-law, whom he believed was killed in the attack.
"Civilians are being unjustly murdered, and I can't bear to watch it," the 49-year-old said. "I feel deeply pained and incredibly angry."
It was not possible to contact the Myanmar military for comment on the attack, which initially had a reported death toll of around 30.
"The death toll has reached 50, and 58 people were injured," said aid worker Wai Hun Aung on Tuesday, warning the final fatality figure could be higher because some bodies were lost in fires after the bombing.
A second local volunteer gave the same death toll, requesting anonymity for security reasons.
The Arakan Army, an ethnic rebel force controlling the area, said in a statement that those killed were "innocent passersby, market vendors, shoppers and cargo loaders". It also reported that 50 people died.
Families gathered in the area to claim bodies covered by thin plastic sheeting or placed in plywood coffins under an outdoor pavilion.
"I don't know where to find his body and whom we should ask for help," said Aung Chay.
UN rights chief Volker Turk said the strike underlined the "grave plight faced by civilians across the country -- but none more so than in Rakhine state".
"For years now, Myanmar has been wracked by extreme violence, and the country's population has been subjected to pervasive human rights violations and abuses," Turk said in a statement.
The market and adjacent bridge hit in Monday's bombardment had become a hive of trading activity since civil war broke out in Myanmar following a 2021 military coup.
Rakhine has suffered some of the direst conditions in the war, largely cut off from the rest of Myanmar. The market thrived on a river trade route to India that had become a lifeline.
Su Mon, a senior analyst at conflict monitor ACLED, said there had been only 10 air raids targeting civilians with more than 30 reported deaths since 2022, the war's first full year.
"Rakhine experienced the military's mass killings the most," she said.
The Arakan Army controls almost all of Rakhine, save for a few urban centres still defended by the military, which has a fleet of fighter jets manufactured by Russia and China.
The military's air wing is also accused of committing atrocities targeting civilians at schools, monasteries and religious festivals -- attacks rights groups say may constitute war crimes.
"The military is eager to regain control of Rakhine," Su Mon said, adding that an offensive launched this month "has not yielded battlefield success".
Nearly half a million people are living displaced in Rakhine as a result of the conflict, UN data says.
More than 100,000 people have been killed in Myanmar in the conflict since the 2021 putsch that unseated Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government, ACLED estimates.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was alarmed by reports of the airstrike and "strongly condemns" ongoing attacks against civilians, his spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said Tuesday.
"The secretary general strongly condemns these attacks and calls on all parties to end violence immediately to protect civilians and comply with their obligations under international law," Dujarric told reporters, demanding that those responsible be held to account.
Dujarric said the Sept. 28 bombardment near a market in the town of Kyauktaw reportedly killed 50 people and injured nearly 60, with many survivors sustaining critical wounds.
The attack, he said, brings into "sharp focus" that conditions do not exist for the safe, voluntary, dignified and sustainable return of displaced people, including Rohingya communities.
Guterres urged the warring parties to facilitate "safe, sustained, and unimpeded" passage for the UN and humanitarian partners to deliver vital assistance wherever required.
The UN chief also echoed concerns voiced by the UN Refugee Agency and the UN Human Rights Office about the reported return of roughly 1,500 people to Myanmar by Malaysian authorities, urging Kuala Lumpur to halt the process and cease further deportations immediately.
Malaysia began repatriating 1,476 Myanmar nationals on Tuesday aboard three Myanmar naval vessels. The group comprises 1,370 men, 79 women, 20 boys and seven girls between the ages of 8 and 60, Malaysian state news agency Bernama reported, citing Home Ministry Deputy Secretary-General Makhzan Mahyuddin.
Dujarric stressed that customary international law imposes a binding obligation on all nations prohibiting the return of individuals to countries where they face persecution, torture or severe threats to life and liberty.
Myanmar has been embroiled in a protracted civil war that intensified after Min Aung Hlaing ousted an elected government in February 2021.
Several ethnic opposition groups are fighting Min's government in several parts of the country.
Rakhine is home largely to the Rohingya community, a predominantly Muslim group that has faced persecution by Myanmar's military as well as other opposition groups. Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya have been forced out of the Buddhist-majority Southeast Asian nation over the years.

title: Prime Video developing  Spider Man  Clone Saga series after  Spider Noir  exit

content:
Prime Video is developing a new 'Spider-Man' series based on Marvel’s Clone Saga following Spider-Noir’s cancellation
Prime Video is reportedly developing a new Spider-Man series based on the popular Clone Saga storyline from Marvel Comics, following the cancellation of Spider-Noir after one season.
According to reports, the Amazon streaming service is nearing a green light for the untitled series, which would be set within Sony Pictures' Marvel universe. The project is expected to focus on two Spider-Man clones, drawing inspiration from the long-running Clone Saga storyline in the comics.
The potential series comes after Spider-Noir , starring Nicolas Cage, was canceled following its first season. Cage played Ben Reilly, also known as The Spider, in the Prime Video series. The character has a major connection to the Clone Saga in Marvel Comics.
Details about the new Spider-Man show remain limited, including its cast, release date and specific storyline. However, reports suggest the project could feature its own version of Ben Reilly, a character closely associated with the Clone Saga.
The reported development gives Prime Video another opportunity to expand its collection of Marvel-related projects. The streaming service previously launched Spider-Noir as part of Sony's broader Spider-Man universe, separate from the Marvel Cinematic Universe's main Spider-Man storyline.
Meanwhile, Tom Holland continues to portray Peter Parker in the MCU. His upcoming film Spider-Man: Brand New Day is part of Marvel Studios' continuing plans for the character.
Sony has been expanding the Spider-Man universe across film and television, with projects featuring characters connected to the web-slinger's comic book mythology.
If approved, the new Prime Video Spider-Man series would add another adaptation of Marvel's Clone Saga to the screen, although further details have yet to be announced.

title: Trump unveils AI chatbot for US government services
description: AI powered website  America gov  is aimed at becoming the first stop for Americans to access federal services
content:
AI-powered website 'America.gov' is aimed at becoming the first stop for Americans to access federal services
US President Donald Trump unveiled an AI-powered website on Tuesday aimed at becoming the first stop for Americans to access federal services, hailing the initiative as a "reinvention" of government.
The "America.gov" platform was developed under Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, who joined the Trump administration last year in the newly formed role of chief design officer.
Like other websites using AI-powered chatbots, users type in queries and converse with the system online. While its functions are currently limited, Trump said that America.gov would eventually be able to process all sorts of complicated tasks involving the government, such as applying for a new passport or accessing health and retirement benefits.
Read : US requiring new AI safeguards for government use, transparency
"We're making it dramatically easier, faster, and more convenient to get what you need exactly when you need it," Trump said at a launch event for the platform in Washington, attended by top government officials.
. @POTUS : For our entire lives, we've become used to a government so big, it makes the citizen feel very, very small — but with https://t.co/tMEB6EUUmO , the entire U.S. government will fit in the palm of your hand. https://t.co/7gW15MiV9J pic.twitter.com/gXQDOMXxb6
"It's a restoration of America's founding promise, and it's a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond," he said.
. @POTUS on https://t.co/tMEB6EUUmO : "We are launching today something that is not just simply a website, it's a restoration of America's founding promise and it's a reinvention of your government for the 21st Century and beyond." https://t.co/7gW15MiV9J pic.twitter.com/gFWQRdFcgb
The president also signed an executive order directing all government agencies to integrate their websites with America.gov.
The launch of the new US government platform came the same day that Trump was to meet with an array of top tech executives to discuss the AI sector's rapid development.

A growing list of cyber incidents revealed in recent weeks had raised concerns around the world about risks posed by uncontrollable AI, with some executives urging a slowdown for safety. Trump had dismissed those concerns as a conspiracy to undermine US economic growth and hamper competition with China.
AI and the rapid buildout of data centres have become a significant issue in the November midterm elections. A recent poll published by CNN showed 82 per cent of Americans expressed concern about the pace of AI development.

description: Petrol price decreases to Rs387 54 per litre  while HSD will cost Rs402 24
content:
Petrol price decreases to Rs387.54 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs402.24
The federal government on Tuesday decreased the price of petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs1.49 and Rs2.73 per litre, respectively, for September 30.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs387.54 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs402.24 per litre for Wednesday.
The latest revision comes after the government decreased the price of petrol and HSD by Rs2.27 and Rs3.56 per litre, respectively, for September 29.
Read : Govt decreases petrol by Rs2.27, diesel by Rs3.56 for Sept 29
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
Earlier this month, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.
Oil prices declined ​on Tuesday as investors focused on signs of recovering crude exports from the Middle East and ‌lingering concerns over potential supply disruptions in the region stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran .
Brent crude futures were down $1.38, or 1.3%, to $103.88 a barrel at 1:03 pm ET (1703 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate crude was down $2.04, or 2.16%, to $90.58.
Crude futures were "under pressure this morning ​on news that the Saudi’s East/West pipeline flows have moved up. ... US/Iran negotiations are ⁠also continuing and while seemingly far apart, both are looking for an off-ramp, and as more oil flows ​through the Middle East, the less bargaining power Iran will have," said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of ​trading at BOK Financial.
Saudi Arabia resumed oil tanker loadings from its Red Sea port of Yanbu after restarting operations on the East-West Pipeline, according to trade sources and shipping data, improving the outlook for oil exports from the Middle East.

title: Hudson Williams speaks out over Cornell sexual assault case  calls for arrests
description: Williams    post comes as the case continues to attract attention from public figures
content:
Williams’ post comes as the case continues to attract attention from public figures
Heated Rivalry star Hudson Williams has spoken out over the sexual assault case involving seven former and current Cornell University students, sharing a post calling for their arrest after prosecutors reopened the investigation.
Williams shared an Instagram Story on September 29 featuring photographs of the seven men named as defendants in a civil lawsuit filed by a former Cornell student. The actor wrote, “arrest them. f*ck them and f*ck cornell too,” alongside the images.
Photo: Instagram @hudsonwilliamsofficial
The lawsuit concerns an alleged sexual assault at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. The plaintiff, identified as Jane Doe in court documents, alleges that she was coerced into consuming drugs and alcohol before being sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members while incapacitated.
The seven men named in the lawsuit are Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar. The allegations remain unproven, and none of the seven had been criminally charged as of September 29. Attorneys for some of the defendants have denied the allegations.
The case returned to the spotlight after the civil lawsuit was filed earlier this month. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten announced on September 28 that prosecutors would reopen the criminal investigation and present evidence to a grand jury. The decision followed renewed scrutiny over the handling of the original investigation in 2024.
According to prosecutors, the account provided by the woman to Cornell police in 2024 differed from the allegations contained in the recent lawsuit. Her attorney has disputed that characterisation and criticised the original investigation. The renewed investigation will determine whether additional evidence supports potential criminal charges.
Cornell has said it supports the decision to reopen the case. The university also confirmed that it conducted its own Title IX investigation and that sanctions included expulsions and suspensions, while the Chi Phi chapter involved was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.
Williams’ post comes as the case continues to attract attention from public figures. The Heated Rivalry actor has not publicly elaborated on his Instagram Story beyond the message accompanying the images. His response follows renewed public discussion surrounding the allegations and the decision to bring the case before a grand jury.

title: Somali pirates kill three Pakistanis during rescue operation
description: Two other crew members of Honour 25 ship also killed by pirates in operation by Somali forces
content:
Two other Honour 25 crew members killed; 16 suspected pirates apprehended as Puntland forces conclude operation
Three Pakistani sailors were among five crew members killed after Somali pirates opened indiscriminate fire on the abducted crew of the Honour 25 while fleeing the vessel, while four sailors were injured, according to survivors and the Ansar Burney Welfare Trust.
Three of the injured sailors are also reportedly Pakistani nationals.
Somalia’s Puntland Maritime Police Force said in a post on X that it had "carried out a maritime operation off the coast of Dharin-baar, Bandar Beyla District", rescuing the MT Honour 25 oil tanker, which was hijacked by pirates near Somali waters on April 21.
Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF) has concluded an operation to secure the MT Honer 25. The vessel is now safe and under Puntland Government control. During the operation, 21 suspected pirates were apprehended, while operations to locate the remaining members continue. pic.twitter.com/GYUvHvFvcy
It further said that the vessel was under the control of the Puntland government. The statement initially reported that 21 suspected pirates had been apprehended, but later revised the figure to 16.
Pakistani sailors Hussain Yousuf and Imran Ali, who survived the attack, contacted the Ansar Burney Welfare Trust office in Karachi using the ship captain’s mobile phone and provided details of the incident.
According to the surviving crew members, the governments of Somalia and the semi-autonomous region of Puntland in northeastern Somalia launched a joint operation on Tuesday to free the hostages from the pirates. An exchange of fire took place between Somali security forces and the pirates during the operation.
The Pakistani crew members said that when the pirates came under pressure and began retreating, they opened indiscriminate fire on the abducted crew members before fleeing the vessel.
Speaking to The Express Tribune , Ansar Burney Trust Director Advocate Qurat-ul-Ain said the location where the crew members were killed and injured was a considerable distance from the shore.
She said the pirates also damaged the steering system of the Honour 25 while fleeing, rendering the vessel inoperable. The ship is now being towed to the shore by a Somali naval vessel, a process that is expected to take at least two days.
According to Qurat-ul-Ain, the naval vessel towing the Honour 25 is the same vessel that was used to launch the attack against the pirates.
Also Read : Govt 'actively working' to secure release of Pakistani sailors in Somali pirate captivity: maritime minister
She added that the government of Pakistan and the Ministry of Human Rights had been informed about the entire incident.
Qurat-ul-Ain identified the Pakistani crew members killed in the attack as Second Officer Kashif Umar, Third Engineer Mahmood Ansari and Boiler Rafiullah. An Indian crew member, Tanveer, and the chief engineer from Myanmar were also among those killed.
The injured crew members were identified as Usman, Aqeel, Ameen and Vicky from Indonesia.
Yasir Khan, Hussain Yousuf, Imran Ali and Yaseen remained safe.
All the Pakistani crew members who were killed or injured are from different areas of Karachi. Their families had spent months seeking the safe release of their loved ones, staging peaceful protests and repeatedly approaching government authorities.
The oil tanker Honour 25, sailing under the Somali flag from Oman to Somalia, was hijacked by pirates on April 21. There were 17 crew members aboard, 10 of whom were Pakistani nationals. The families of the Pakistani hostages have continuously appealed to the government for the safe release of their loved ones.
During their captivity, the pirates initially demanded a ransom of $3 million for their release. The demand was later reduced to $1.9 million and subsequently to $1 million.
Puntland police said they had rescued another oil tanker, days after a rescue operation ended with pirates escaping in suspicious circumstances. They added that the Honour 25 had 18,500 barrels of oil on board when it was hijacked.
The police have been chasing three hijacked vessels off the Somali coast in recent days and rescued one of the other oil tankers, Sibu 1, on Friday. However, 28 of the 41 pirates arrested in the operation later escaped while being transferred to jail, with several Puntland security officials accusing local police of complicity.
The Gulf of Aden and Somalia coasts have seen a resurgence in piracy since April, according to figures from the International Maritime Organisation, with at least 15 attacks this year, the highest since 2013.

title: UAE vice president meets Saudi crown prince in Riyadh
description: Visit comes in the backdrop of escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia  continued US Iran regional confrontation
content:
Visit comes in the backdrop of escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, continued US-Iran regional confrontation
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) met United Arab Emirates (UAE) Vice ‌President and Deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Riyadh on Tuesday, the Saudi Press Agency reported.
According to Arab News , MBS and Al Nahyan discussed "bilateral relations and developments in the region", adding that the two leaders also reviewed relations between Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
#PICTURES : Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman meets UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed in Riyadh pic.twitter.com/IiqSCW4yqb
Earlier in the day, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid ​bin Salman received Al Nahyan, Saudi state media ​reported, as Saudi Arabia faces increasing pressure ​from the Houthis, who have ​fired salvos of missiles and drones at the kingdom.
سعدت اليوم بلقاء أخي سمو الشيخ منصور بن زايد آل نهيان نائب رئيس دولة الإمارات العربية المتحدة الشقيقة نائب رئيس مجلس الوزراء رئيس ديوان الرئاسة @MansourBinZayed ، الذي يزور بلده الثاني المملكة؛ لمواصلة التشاور الأخوي، وتبادل الرؤى، في ظل حرص قيادتي بلدينا الشقيقين على استمرار… pic.twitter.com/Gvfxjr4NkY
The UAE withdrew from Yemen earlier this ​year after Saudi Arabia accused it of backing ​a military operation by Yemeni separatists that it ‌said ⁠posed a national security threat to the kingdom.
وزير الدفاع السعودي الأمير خالد بن سلمان يستقبل نائب الرئيس الإماراتي الشيخ منصور بن زايد الذي يجري زيارة للرياض pic.twitter.com/3HP32SM5cM
UAE state news agency WAM said Sheikh Mansour would travel to the ​kingdom in ​a "fraternal visit" ⁠upon the extended invitation, without providing further details.
Saudi Arabia has ​been trying to rally international ​support ⁠to confront the Houthis, but it was not immediately clear if that request ⁠extended ​to the UAE.
The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen's capital since 2014, seized the country's Red Sea coast this month in a lightning advance that routed forces of an internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and based in the south.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters' positions in the highlands, according to the Houthis. But the air power advantage has so far done little to slow the advance of the fighters as Saudi-backed government forces have melted away.
Read : Saudi Arabia reports fresh Houthi attacks, issues warning for Makkah
The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab al-Mandab Strait leading into the Red Sea by taking control of the heights, which would allow them to open new fronts, according to the sources. That would help protect exposed positions the Houthis captured during their advance around Dhubab on the Red Sea and on Perim Island in the strait.
The Houthis' newfound control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait risks cutting off the main alternative route that Saudi Arabia has used for oil exports that bypass disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
On September 24, Saudi Arabia intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles after issuing warnings for several regions, including Makkah.
The missiles were the latest in a series of escalating Houthi attacks since July, when renewed hostilities shattered a years-long truce and embroiled Yemen in the wider Middle East war.
Since then, the Houthis have imposed a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, hitting its tankers and territory and seizing swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast, which is vital for Saudi oil exports.
The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's government since 2015 against the Houthis said six ballistic missiles had been intercepted, thwarting attacks on Taif and Yanbu.
On Monday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu asked UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed during a secret meeting on Sunday to deny a report that he had warned Netanyahu of an imminent Hamas attack before October 7, 2023, Israeli newspaper Haaretz said on Monday, Anadolu Agency reported.
Read More : Netanyahu made a secret visit to UAE
Netanyahu asked bin Zayed to deny reports about their phone conversation and details surrounding the events before October 7 that "could embarrass him," Haaretz said, citing unspecified sources.
Netanyahu asked UAE leader to deny Haaretz Oct. 7 warning report in secret visit https://t.co/5n7BavDi6l
The Israeli premier also asked the Emirati president for what one source described as "moral support," the newspaper reported.
Netanyahu held an hour-long meeting with bin Zayed, according to two people briefed on the trip.
Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported that Netanyahu travelled on a private plane owned by an unnamed Israeli businessman and used by senior Israeli figures for international trips.
It departed Ben Gurion Airport in the afternoon and landed in Abu Dhabi at 3:10 pm (1110GMT), the broadcaster said. It took off for Israel at 7:10 pm (1510GMT), four hours later, and landed shortly after 10pm (1900GMT).
KAN said Netanyahu had also used the aircraft for a trip to Abu Dhabi during the war with Iran.
The visit comes after Haaretz this month reported that bin Zayed had warned Netanyahu a week and a half before October 7, 2023, ​that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel. Haaretz had reported that the warning was not passed to Israeli intelligence agencies or the military.
Netanyahu, ​who denied the report and threatened legal action against the newspaper, is facing a tough reelection campaign. Opposition leaders have accused the prime minister of bearing responsibility for security failures that preceded Hamas' October 7 attack .
Also Read : Netanyahu warned by UAE president before October 7 events, failed to brief security chiefs: Haaretz
The UAE declined to comment on the ​ Haaretz report but said it and Israel maintained "open and direct ​lines of communication" since establishing diplomatic relations in 2020. A UAE source previously told Reuters ‌that ⁠the UAE discusses security matters with countries through the "relevant entities," but not "at the level of national leaders".

title: Celebrating the local partners behind the golden arches | The Express Tribune
description: McDonald’s marks 28 years in Pakistan with a focus on local partnerships, procurement and industrial value creation
content:
McDonald’s marks 28 years in Pakistan with a focus on local partnerships, procurement and industrial value creation
Marking 28 years of commercial presence in Pakistan, McDonald’s hosted a corporate partner recognition ceremony in Lahore, reaffirming its strategic commitment to domestic procurement and industrial value creation.
The gathering at McDonald’s Etihad Town restaurant in Lahore brought together senior executives from key domestic industrial allies, including Packages Limited, Big Bird, Nurpur, Fresh & Freeze, Saima Packaging Pronto Spaces, and the Zaman Foundation, to review nearly three decades of collaborative supply-chain development.
The milestone underscored how multinational food franchises can strengthen domestic economies through structured localisation.
Over 28 years, McDonald’s has partnered with Pakistani manufacturers to transfer technical knowledge, implement international standards, and build resilient cold-chain infrastructure across the country.
This long-term capability-building has enabled local suppliers to modernise their processing lines, expand production capacity, and generate high-skilled employment across the agricultural and manufacturing sectors.
McDonald’s leadership noted that developing a robust, domestic supplier ecosystem has provided essential operational resilience while insulating the business against global supply volatility.
As the company looks toward its next phase of growth, its alliances with Pakistani industry remain the cornerstone of its corporate and operational strategy.
