title: Manchester City s Premier League charges  What comes next
description: A verdict could trigger appeals  financial claims and a wider dispute over past titles
content:
A verdict could trigger appeals, financial claims and a wider dispute over past titles
Manchester City's fate in a legal battle with the Premier League is yet to be sealed, but reports they have been found guilty on widespread financial misconduct has sparked speculation of what comes next.
The dominant Premier League force for more than a decade, swingeing sanctions against City would send shockwaves through English football.
Rival clubs are set to launch their own legal action seeking hundreds of millions of pounds in compensation, while there is debate over whether some of City's many titles and trophies over the past 15 years could be stripped.
AFP Sports looks at the next steps and potential fall out from the case:
The Athletic first reported on Friday that City had been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges they faced.
However, no sanction has yet been approved.
Even once a decision is made on how City will be punished, should they be found guilty, the club are almost certain to appeal.
In a letter to City fans on Saturday, the club's chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said: "Our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began."
A case that began after German outlet Der Spiegel published leaked documents from City executives in 2018, could still take a lengthy time to fully resolve.
According to Premier League rules, the sanction can vary from a points deduction, a fine or even expulsion from the division.
Everton and Nottingham Forest were handed points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of financial sustainability rules. On that basis, City would face almost certain relegation if found guilty of over 100 charges.
Whether the sanction is applied before an appeal is heard will be another bone of contention.
If it is, City could face relegation before overturning any guilty verdict.
On the other hand, if City, who currently sit top of the table, are not punished until after an appeal, it could cost other clubs their place in the top-flight or lucrative European qualification.
Even after the Premier League process if over, there is also the chance that City's Abu-Dhabi backed owners seek redress in England's High Court if they challenge a legal issue regarding how the arbitration process was conducted.
City's rivals were quick to revel in the news of their potential demise.
"Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet," posted former Manchester United defender Rio Ferdinand, who was part of the United team to finish second to City in the 2011/12 season.
The reality is that stripping and retroactively awarding titles is a messy process.
City's charges relate to the period between 2009 and 2018. In that time they won four league titles, with United and Liverpool twice finishing second in those seasons.
Yet City have won another four since, arguably built on foundations that were fraudulently gained.
They also won four League Cups and one FA Cup, the club's first trophy for 35 years, in the period between 2009 and 2018.
"I don't seriously believe any other trophies and titles will be handed back over either," Tony Pulis, whose Stoke side lost the 2011 FA Cup final to City, told the BBC.
"A points deduction and a massive fine feels far more likely. But I still feel cheated."
A more likely source of recompense for clubs that missed out is through financial compensation.
In June, Everton were told they must pay Burnley £35 million ($46 million) after they edged out the Clarets to Premier League survival in the same season they broke financial sustainability rules.
Less than a month ago, City completed the biggest ever transfer spend in one window, splashing out around £460 million on the likes of Enzo Fernandez, Elliott Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi.
The impending verdict on the charges has to this point made little impact on City's ability to attract and retain their star names.
Talismanic striker Erling Haaland signed a nine-year contract in 2025 that could keep him tied down till his 34th birthday.
How many, if any, of the players managed to negotiate exit clauses in the case City were heavily sanctioned remains to be seen.

title: Italy rebound in Turkey as France win late in Belgium
description: Esposito scores as Mancini   s side beat Turkey 4 1
content:
Esposito scores as Mancini’s side beat Turkey 4-1
Italy crushed Turkey 4-1 in the Bursa rain to drag themselves into contention in Nations League Group A1, as leaders France struck late to win 1-0 in Belgium on Monday.
In Brussels, both teams had wasted chances before Michael Olise scampered through the home defence after 88 minutes and drilled a shot inside the post.
"He is a pure talent and he loves to just play. You can see it. He feels the game. I am pleased to be at his side," France coach Zinedine Zidane told broadcaster TF1.
Olise's goal gave Zidane a second victory to start his long-awaited debut as France coach.
Roberto Mancini's return to run Italy had ended in Roman jeers on Friday as Italy lost their opener at home to Belgium.
His team dazzled in the downpour in the first half in Turkey.
"The players all put in an excellent performance today. It was a tough match and we approached it in the right way, staying high up the pitch and playing aggressively throughout the game," Mancini told Italian television at the final whistle.
The hosts quickly slid three goals behind with errors in their muddy goalmouth.
Twice Altay Bayindir struggled to reach low cross-shots from the right.
After nine minutes, the Celta Vigo goalkeeper scooped a drive from Pio Esposito round the post.
From the corner, Bursa-born fullback Zeki Celik, who plays for Juventus in Italy, swung wildly at a low near-post cross deflecting the ball to Alessandro Bastoni. The Inter Milan centre back lunged to fire into the roof of the net.
After 23 minutes, Bayindir flapped an identical cross-shot from Michael Kayode into the path of Lazio's Davide Frattesi, who tucked the ball home.
Intricate Italian passing around the penalty area repeatedly found a player free on the right of box.
When Brentford's Kayode again ran into that space, his shot for the near post eluded the plunging Bayindir.
Turkey gave the restless crowd hope in the 47th minute when Gianluigi Donnarumma was drawn to Oguz Aydin beyond the far post. He found Baris Yilmaz who gleefully drilled into an empty net.
The comeback lasted five minutes. Tottenham's Sandro Tonali, in space, hit the post but Pio Esposito dived to nod home the rebound.
After the game the Inter Milan striker's thoughts turned to family.
"I dedicate today's goal to my grandmother, who is going through a difficult time," said Pio Esposito who was playing alongside older brother Sebastiano of Sassuolo who was making his Italy debut.
"Sharing the pitch with him was incredibly moving; I tried to support him before the match without putting too much pressure on him. Let's hope we get to wear these colours together many more times."
Galatasaray attacker Yilmaz then curled a shot home but Aydin of Besiktas, bouncing up and down in front of Man City's Donnarumma, was offside.
Monday's slick display may ease the pressure on Mancini, while piling it on his former Sampdoria club-mate and fellow ex-Italian international Vincenzo Montella.
Montella led Turkey to the quarter finals at Euro 2024 but his side finished bottom of their group at the summer's World Cup.
For their next match Italy visit the Stade de France on Friday.
"We'll try to recover our strength and be ready for the match in Paris," Mancini told Italian media. "I'm confident. We've got plenty of young players who are fresh and ready."
Zidane, who was without injured captain Kylian Mbappe, made nine changes from his opening win over Turkey, was thinking along the same lines.
"We need a rest now. We have done a lot of travelling and not much training or resting," said Zidane, adding he was happy with his team.
"We were really good in every department. Against a really good Belgium side who made us suffer we held out, we played really well, and we were brave."

title: Afridi demands policy shift to restore peace
description: Afridi demands policy shift to restore peace
content:
Says closed-door strategy has squandered sacrifices; claims provincial plan can restore security
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Muhammad Sohail Afridi on Monday reiterated his strong reservations against the closed-door policy on counter-terrorism, declaring that the hard-won peace secured through the sacrifices of the province's people, police and army has been squandered after the regime-change operation.
Chairing a high-level meeting on law and order at Chief Minister's House, Afridi said more than 80,000 people of K-P had laid down their lives for Pakistan over two decades. Yet the relative calm that followed those sacrifices was lost when militants returned to the mountains and later resettled in settled areas. "At every stage, from the terrorists' arrival in the hills to their resettlement, we repeatedly warned the state and the federation," he said. "We held rallies, processions and protests across districts, but federal ministers dismissed our warnings as propaganda and lies."
The chief minister stressed that the provincial government is already acting beyond its capacity and resources. Billions of rupees have been spent to strengthen the police force and the Counter-Terrorism Department. "All our efforts, however, are being wasted because of an ineffective closed-door policy and a failed strategy," he said. "No measure for peace can succeed until the current policy is changed. If the policy we propose is implemented, peace can be restored within 100 days."
The meeting was attended by the provincial information minister, the special assistant to the chief minister on home and tribal affairs, the chief secretary, the inspector general of police, the additional chief secretary (home), senior CTD officers and other officials. Participants reviewed the prevailing security situation, measures already taken and the way forward. Progress on the CTD uplift programme was also examined.
Afridi specifically sought an update on the establishment of the K-P Forensic Science Laboratory, calling it an urgent necessity. He directed the police to procure essential equipment and utilise existing laboratory facilities until a fully functional facility is ready.

title: K P rejects federal white paper allegations
description: K P rejects federal white paper allegations
content:
Information minister threatens Governor House siege if governor's rule imposed
The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government has categorically rejected the allegations levelled against it in a white paper issued by federal ministers.
Provincial Information Minister Shafi Jan said the province is itself a victim of terrorism, with its people sacrificing lives, yet it continues to face taunts and accusations.
Addressing a press conference in the company of Special Assistant for Home Tariq Saeed, Shafi Jan said the federal government is engaged in a misadventure and that the real issue is not terrorism but Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. "If an attempt is made to impose Governor's Rule, the people of the province will lay siege to the Governor's House," he warned.
He alleged that federal ministers have been continuously spreading propaganda against the provincial government, with ministers assigned duties to hold press conferences against K-P and being given the same script. "We reject the white paper issued against the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government. There is no truth in what has been stated in it," he said.
Shafi Jan questioned why Governor's Rule or an emergency was not first imposed in Balochistan, where the Nawaz League is in power, if terrorism is the concern. "Did terrorism begin during the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's tenure? When the PTI government was formed in 2013, peace was established in this province. PTI also staged a sit-in against drone attacks," he said, adding that imposing Governor's Rule is no joke. "If Governor's Rule is imposed, the Governor House will first be besieged. If the people's mandate is snatched, the people of the province will come out on the streets and then they will not be able to raise their heads again."
He stressed that anti-terrorism policy is formulated by the federation, not the provincial government. "If there is terrorism, then your policy has failed. We keep saying do not take decisions behind closed doors. The people sitting in Islamabad who take these decisions have never even visited Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. What do they know about this province? There is still time to sit and talk. Formulate policy in consultation with those affected by terrorism. But their problem is not terrorism, it is Sohail Afridi. The federal government's intentions as well as its temperament are not right."
Referring to threats received after the announcement of a long march on 27 September, Shafi Jan said they would not come out in the streets with sticks. "This country and the army belong to us. It is the policy of the Nawaz League to pit institutions against the PTI, but we will foil their conspiracy. We have already made payments to federal institutions for the purchase of arms, yet we are not being provided the equipment. We are Pakistanis and will remain with Pakistan."
He also criticised a statement by Maryam Nawaz that Punjab faces a threat not from India but from neighbouring provinces. "They have no idea what fire they are playing with. They are afraid that on 4 October the people will come out on the streets. Do not call us terrorists, that is an abuse for us. Our body is wounded because of terrorism. We have given lives and still have to listen to taunts."

title: Flash floods damage bridge  crops in Mianwali
description: Flash floods damage bridge  crops in Mianwali
content:
Floodwater from hill torrents cuts road links between Chapri, several nearby towns
Heavy early-morning rain and flash floods in hill torrents damaged a section of the Chapri Bridge on the Kot Chandana Road, cutting off road links between Chapri and several towns in the Khatak Belt.
The flash floods also caused breaches in the embankments of Nullah Adwala near Kamar Mashani, inundating hundreds of kanals of standing crops in surrounding areas.
Following heavy rainfall in the northern hilly areas of Mianwali, floodwater from the Chachali hill torrent washed away part of the bridge near Chapri on the Kot Chandana Road.
As a result, road connectivity between Chapri and Kot Chandana, Tola Mangli, Mohabbat Khel, Alf Khel and Janjuani has been severely affected.
The damage is not limited to the Chapri-Kot Chandana Road.
A bridge on the Chapri-Kamar Mashani Road, constructed in 2017, has also remained non-functional due to incomplete work, including the construction of shoulders and other necessary works.
Meanwhile, an embankment of Nullah Adwala near Kamar Mashani Thal was breached, causing floodwater to enter the fields of Wandha Kamalzai and Wandha Nanzian Wala.
Hundreds of kanals of standing crops were damaged, while the floodwater reached areas near the deras on the outskirts of Kamar Mashani.
Another breach occurred in the eastern embankment of Nullah Adwala at Kacha Barzi, allowing floodwater to enter agricultural fields. Farmers fear severe damage to millet, maize and other crops.
Local residents and farmers said they had repeatedly raised concerns over the weak shoulders of the bridge and the condition of embankments and flood channels since last year, urging the authorities to strengthen them. However, they alleged that the local administration and relevant departments failed to take timely action.
They said the latest damage to a bridge built at a cost of millions of rupees, along with losses to agricultural land, had once again highlighted the area's vulnerability to flash floods from hill torrents.
Residents called for immediate measures to strengthen embankments, bridge shoulders and flood channels, as well as clearing silt and debris from the beds of hill torrents and underneath bridges to reduce the risk of future flooding.

title: Lahore Zoo names new hippo  Gubbo
description: Lahore Zoo names new hippo  Gubbo
content:
Male hippopotamus brought from South Africa in March named following children's suggestion
Lahore Zoo has named its newly arrived male hippopotamus "Gubbo" following a suggestion from children.
The naming ceremony featured performances by students of a private school dressed as animals, while a magic show was also arranged for children.
The event aimed to promote interest in wildlife among children and raise awareness about animal conservation.
Lahore Zoo Director Dr Ghulam Rasool, Deputy Director Shahzaib Khurshid, Senior Veterinary Officer Dr Muhammad Mujahid, the CEO and principal of the private school, teachers and students attended the ceremony.
Gubbo was also served his favourite food, including fruits and vegetables, during the ceremony.
Dr Ghulam Rasool said the male hippopotamus had been brought to Lahore Zoo from South Africa in March this year.
The zoo already has a female hippopotamus named Rani.
He said the name Gubbo, suggested by children, was selected to strengthen their interest in and connection with the animal.
Senior Veterinary Officer Dr Muhammad Mujahid said animals could become familiar with names when they were called consistently and repeatedly.
He said an animal could gradually recognise a particular sound as a cue for attention when the same name was used during its daily routine.
He said an animal might become accustomed to a name after it was used consistently for one to two months and could respond through attention, movement or other behaviour when called.
Dr Mujahid clarified that an animal's response to a name did not mean it understood the word in the same way as humans.
Rather, it associated a particular sound with its routine, caregiver or positive experiences such as receiving food. Consistent use of the same name therefore helped the animal become familiar with the sound.
Dr Ghulam Rasool said naming animals was not a new practice, adding that humans had used specific names for centuries to identify and care for domestic animals, particularly cattle, horses and mules.
He said naming captive wild animals was also common at zoos and wildlife centres.
Lahore Zoo has given specific names to dozens of animals, including its female hippopotamus Rani.
According to Dr Rasool, naming animals helped zoo staff identify them and could also foster an emotional connection between visitors, particularly children, and wildlife, encouraging greater interest in animal conservation.

title: Water war brews over 56km pipeline to Pithoro
description: Protesters feared that diverting water to Pithoro would worsen shortages in at least nine other towns
content:
Protesters feared that diverting water to Pithoro would worsen shortages in at least nine other towns
Thousands of farmers took to the streets in Naukot on Sunday against a proposed 56-kilometre pipeline from Mithrao Canal to Pithoro, fearing the scheme could further squeeze water supplies to tail-end areas already struggling with chronic shortages.
Led by Nadir Ali Laghari, Arbab Zafarullah and others, the protesters marched for around five kilometres through Naukot before gathering outside the local press club, where they chanted slogans against irrigation authorities and the provincial government.
The farmers alleged that the project would effectively create a new distributary from a canal that itself receives water from the Nara Canal and remains short of supplies for much of the year. "In the name of the pipeline, a new distributary is practically being carved out from a waterway which faces water shortfall for most parts of a year," Laghari said. The protesters feared that diverting water to Pithoro would worsen shortages in at least nine other towns, including Samaro, Kunri, Jhudo, Kaloi, Diplo, Mithi, Islamkot and Nangarparkar.

title: Mansura ruins to get new lease of archaeological life
description: Mansura ruins to get new lease of archaeological life
content:
Ancient site set to undergo excavation in 2027
The archaeological site of Mansura-Brahmanabad in Sanghar is set to undergo excavation in early 2027 under a joint initiative of the Sindh Archaeology and Antiquities Department and an Italian archaeological mission.
Zahida Qadri, who heads the department's excavation team, and Italian archaeologist Dr Alessandro Tilia told the media in Sanghar on Monday that efforts were also under way to secure World Heritage status for the site.
Dr Tilia said the project was being undertaken under the supervision of Prof Dr Luca Maria Olivieri of the Italian Institute for Middle and Far East (IsMEO). Mansura, he said, was a significant archaeological site in the region, and the project aimed to scientifically examine the different periods of the ancient city, its urban development and cultural continuity, as well as recover artefacts and preserve its remains.
"Road construction, agricultural activities, encroachment and livestock movement around the archaeological site may damage the remains and potentially make long-term research difficult," Dr Tilia cautioned. He appealed to the local administration and residents to consider the protection of Mansura a collective responsibility and refrain from activities that could harm the site.
Qadri recalled that the Italian archaeological mission had been working at the Bhambore site in Thatta district for nearly 15 years. The team, she said, was now expanding its research programme to Mansura. Initial surveys and mapping had identified agricultural activity, roads and other forms of human intervention in different parts of the site, she added.
She said detailed mapping and analysis of the archaeological layers would be key components of the project, helping researchers determine the nature of settlements established at the site during different periods and identify cultural remains beneath the ancient city.
Highlighting the importance of local cooperation, Qadri said support from local authorities and residents at Bhambore had helped prevent damage to the site and facilitated further research. She expressed hope that similar cooperation would be extended at Mansura.
The archaeological site covers around 500 acres and contains the remains of an ancient fortification believed to have stretched for about seven kilometres. Mansura emerged as an important regional centre during the Umayyad and Abbasid periods and developed into a significant settlement and trading centre along the Indus River.
Earlier excavations by the federal archaeology department, particularly those led by F.A. Khan during the 1960s, uncovered significant remains of the ancient city. Large bronze door fittings recovered during those excavations are preserved at the National Museum in Karachi, the Islamabad Museum and the site museum administered by the Sindh Archaeology Department. Qadri said recognition of Mansura as a World Heritage site could help attract domestic and international visitors while creating opportunities for local economic and commercial activity.

title: 35 die of rabies as dog bite cases cross 200 000
description: 35 die of rabies as dog bite cases cross 200 000
content:
Karachi hospitals report over 40,000 cases in nine months amid calls for effective dog-control measures
Sindh's struggle with rabies is turning deadlier, with at least 35 people losing their lives to the disease in the first nine months of the year as dog-bite cases across the province surged past the 200,000 mark.
The scale of the crisis is particularly stark in Karachi, where more than 40,000 dog-bite cases were reported at four major public and welfare hospitals between January and September, highlighting the growing challenge posed by stray dogs and gaps in preventive measures.
Indus Hospital Karachi alone recorded around 14,000 dog-bite cases during the period, while Jinnah Hospital and Civil Hospital Karachi each reported approximately 10,000 cases. More than 7,000 additional cases were reported at other hospitals across the city.
Officials said 26 people died of rabies at Indus Hospital Karachi during the nine-month period. One death was reported at Indus Hospital Badin, while eight rabies-related deaths were recorded at Jinnah Hospital Karachi.
Experts cautioned that the actual number of dog-bite cases in Sindh could be significantly higher than the available figures because reporting and record-keeping systems are not uniform across hospitals and institutions.
They called for an effective dog-sterilisation programme to control the stray-dog population and urged authorities to improve vaccination programmes.
Experts said ensuring the availability of anti-rabies vaccines at hospitals alone was not sufficient, stressing the need for comprehensive measures to prevent dog bites and ensure timely treatment.
Meanwhile Chief Secretary Asif Hyder Shah has urged citizens not to dismiss dog bites or scratches as minor injuries, stressing that immediate treatment is essential to prevent rabies, which becomes fatal once symptoms appear.
In a message issued on World Rabies Day, CS Shah advised people to wash a dog-bite wound immediately with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and then visit the nearest health facility for medical treatment and vaccination. He urged citizens to avoid self-treatment and seek medical assistance without delay following a dog bite or scratch.
Sindh's treatment capacity for dog-bite victims has increased by around 30% compared with the first eight months of last year. Health facilities across the province have treated around 45,000 victims, administering approximately 138,000 doses of anti-rabies vaccine. Around 5,000 doses of rabies immunoglobulin were also administered to patients where required.
CS Shah said 278 anti-rabies units had been upgraded across Sindh, with vaccines, wound-washing facilities and trained medical staff made available to ensure timely treatment. He said public awareness, prompt treatment following dog bites and vaccination of dogs were essential to preventing rabies.

content:
New direct-payment policy leaves 3,800 doctors awaiting three months' salaries and stipends
Thousands of house officers working at government-run hospitals across Sindh have been without salaries and stipends for more than 100 days following the introduction of a new payment mechanism, causing severe financial difficulties for junior doctors.
The delay began after the provincial government changed the procedure for paying house officers in May, replacing the previous system under which hospitals received funds and distributed salaries through bank cheques with direct transfers into doctors' bank accounts.
Officials said the new system required additional documentation and data collection, resulting in delays in processing payments.
Speaking on the condition of anonymity, a finance officer at a public hospital said all house officers had been asked to complete the required forms on the instructions of the Accountant General Sindh (AG). Copies of their CNICs and previous cheques were also collected, while the required data was subsequently submitted to the AG.
"Despite completion of the required process, payments have yet to be released," the officer said.
According to the official, dozens of house officers approach hospital administrations every day to complain about the non-payment of their salaries. He said house officers often worked shifts lasting up to 36 hours but had not received their stipends for three months.
The finance officer said the hospital administration had completed its part of the process and no longer had a role in the direct-payment mechanism. However, the administration had repeatedly contacted the AG and requested the release of the outstanding dues.
Around 280 house officers are working at Karachi's Civil Hospital, while more than 700 house officers and over 450 postgraduate trainee doctors are serving at Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre (JPMC). The total number of house officers working at government hospitals across the province is estimated at more than 3,800. Dr Shahid Awan, president of the Young Doctors Association (YDA) at JPMC, demanded immediate payment of three months' outstanding stipends to house officers and postgraduate doctors.
He warned that if the dues were not cleared within the next few days, doctors would launch protests at the hospital and could subsequently move towards a complete boycott of outpatient departments (OPDs).

title: Mir Raza commission awaits extension
description: Mir Raza commission awaits extension
content:
Proceedings adjourned till Oct 2; cabinet to decide fate of judicial panel
The Judicial Commission probing the murder of Wafflix dessert brand owner Mir Raza Ali has put its proceedings on hold until October 2 after its term expired, as the Sindh cabinet is expected to decide on October 1 whether to extend its mandate.
The commission, headed by Justice Umar Sial, said in a written order that its tenure had expired a day earlier. It had sought an extension until October 15, with the provincial government's focal person informing the commission that chief minister had approved the summary and forwarded it to the cabinet for a decision.
The commission said it was appropriate to defer proceedings until October 2. If the cabinet does not approve the extension, no further witnesses will be summoned and the commission will prepare and submit its report on the basis of statements already recorded.
If the tenure is extended, fresh notices will be issued to witnesses and questionnaires will be sent to three senior police officers.
Meanwhile, counsel for Mir Raza's family, Advocate Jibran Nasir, said the family had not levelled allegations against the police during the commission's proceedings so far, but questioned the progress of the investigation and the failure to establish the circumstances surrounding the killing.
Speaking to the media outside the Sindh High Court, Nasir said the commission was scheduled to record statements of investigating officer Siraj Lashari and CPL officer Kashif. He said senior police officers were also supposed to receive questionnaires.
He said the commission had informed the relevant authorities on September 2 about the need for an extension and that statements of several people whose names had not previously appeared in the investigation had subsequently been recorded.
Nasir questioned the delay in securing the extension, saying the commission had been constituted within a day and a similar process could have been followed for extending its tenure. He said he would submit the family's questions to the commission by 4pm and make them public afterward.
The lawyer also questioned the proposed constitution of a super medical board, arguing that the commission should determine the cause of death under its terms of reference. He said it remained unclear whether the process would involve another exhumation or further medical examination.
Nasir raised questions about CCTV footage from the area where Mir Raza's body was recovered and whether footage from relevant locations had been preserved and examined. He also questioned whether certain individuals and locations linked to the case had been properly investigated.
He said senior police officers should appear before the commission instead of merely responding through questionnaires.
Nasir also referred to statements by doctors and questioned aspects of the medical investigation, saying any facts that had been concealed should be brought before the commission.
He said the commission had itself expressed concern over transparency and maintained that all relevant officials and witnesses should appear before the panel to answer questions about the investigation.

content:
Five Thari students make top 20, while 12 secure places among top 50 in Sindh-wide medical entrance test
From the parched sands of Tharparkar to the country's medical classrooms, students from Sindh's most deprived district have delivered a result that has turned the MDCAT merit list on its head - with five Tharparkar candidates breaking into the top 20, while Karachi drew a blank.
The results of the Medical and Dental College Admission Test MDCAT 2026, conducted by IBA Sukkur for admissions to medical colleges and universities across the province, produced another surprise: the province's biggest metropolis failed to place a single candidate among the 20 highest scorers, despite thousands of its students sitting the test.
Tharparkar's remarkable showing did not stop at the top 20. Twelve students from the desert district made it into the top 50, accounting for nearly a quarter of the highest scorers. The top 20 candidates secured between 176 and 179 marks out of 180, underscoring the intensity of competition.
The results show that Karachi's candidates begin to feature more prominently further down the merit list. Of the top 100 candidates, 18 are from Karachi, rising to 37 among the top 200, 111 among the top 500 and 210 among the top 1,000. Among the top 10,000 successful candidates, 3,327 are from Karachi.
A total of 33,336 candidates appeared for the MDCAT in Sindh, of whom 16,507 passed, putting the overall success rate at 49.5%. Karachi had 9,505 candidates appear, with 5,492 qualifying - a success rate of 57.8%.
The district-wise results also placed Karachi East at the top, with 62% of its candidates qualifying, followed by Karachi Central at 59.9% and Tharparkar at 59.7%.
The passing threshold for MBBS admissions was 99 out of 180 marks.
In Tharparkar, 613 of 1,027 candidates passed. Larkana recorded 623 successful candidates out of 1,410, while Mirpurkhas had 571 qualifiers out of 1,262. Sukkur recorded 503 passes among 984 candidates.
In other districts, 265 of 672 candidates from Jamshoro passed, compared with 652 of 1,611 from Hyderabad, 970 of 2,189 from Khairpur, 669 of 1,441 from Dadu, 630 of 1,485 from Shaheed Benazirabad and 181 of 398 candidates from Thatta.

title: Storm  rain wreak havoc across twin cities
description: Storm  rain wreak havoc across twin cities
content:
Heavy showers flood roads; strong winds topple rooftop tanks, collapse house walls
The first heavy rain of the winter season accompanied by a strong storm lashed the twin cities of Rawalpindi and Islamabad on Monday, causing heavy water tanks installed on rooftops to fall into streets and walls of two houses to collapse.
Torrential rain turned streets and roads in all low-lying areas into ponds, with water standing up to one foot along roads and streets.
Due to disruption in movement, attendance of students in schools and colleges remained considerably low on Monday, while accused persons could also not reach courts on time.
The drainage system, which had been completely paralysed and damaged during the monsoon, has resulted in heavy rain now causing damage not only in low-lying areas but also in posh localities.
Water accumulated along all roads in Rawalpindi Saddar, while up to one foot of water also collected along Saidpur Road, Rawal Road, Iqbal Road, Raja Bazaar, Saddar Road, Girja Road, Dhok Syedan Road and Pindora Road.
In all low-lying areas, floodwater begins receding on its own after four to five hours.
A strong storm began around Sehri time in the morning, blowing away a heavy water tank installed on the roof of a house in Dhok Khabba. The tank fell from the roof and remained hanging over the street from water pipes for five hours, obstructing vehicles and pedestrians.
Another water tank fell from a rooftop into a street in Millat Colony, Mukha Singh Estate. Walls of two houses along the rainwater drain in Fazalabad and Javed Colony collapsed into the drain.
Rain continued for several hours, while water accumulating at different places also accelerated soil erosion along the banks of Nullah Leh.
Although the construction of concrete embankments to prevent soil erosion along Nullah Leh had been announced, work has yet to begin, causing erosion to increase and potentially leading to serious damage at any time.
As rain continued until 9am, a large number of children could not go to school. The first winter rain also brought a chill to the weather and completely broke the heat, with air conditioners switched off and fans running at slower speeds.
The pre-monsoon heavy rain and the first winter rainfall caused widespread waterlogging, while the three dams supplying water to the twin cities - Rawal, Simly and Khanpur - were again filled to capacity, prompting a decision to open their spillways.
PML-N city central leader Sheikh Asad Zahoor demanded an inquiry into flooding in the city despite the government spending billions of rupees on drainage.
Citizen Action Committee Chairman Malik Zaheer Awan called for financial assistance to compensate citizens for losses suffered during flooding in the monsoon season.
RAWALPINDI. Heavy monsoon downpours measuring 20 to 33 millimetres hit the twin cities on Monday morning, prompting WASA Rawalpindi to deploy dewatering machinery across low-lying areas. The autumn temperature decline has also created ideal transmission conditions for dengue and seasonal viral infections.
Warning against heightened dengue threats, Rawalpindi District Health Officer (DHO), Dr Jawad Zahid, said standing rainwater, combined with daytime temperatures dropping into the favourable 22°C30°C range, significantly accelerates mosquito larvae development.
Dr Jawad confirmed that dengue cases in Rawalpindi have reached 27, with over 191,468 larval breeding sites detected and destroyed across the district this season. Further, the authorities have initiated stern legal actions, including registering over 2,717 FIRs and sealing 678 premises against anti-dengue SOP violations.
The DHO urged residents to eliminate stagnant water immediately from rooftops, flowerpots, and water storage containers.
According to a National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) flood bulletin, major rivers remain at normal flow levels, with Nullah Leh recording safe water levels of 5 feet at Katarian and 2 feet at Gawalmandi. However, the NDMA issued an urban flooding alert valid through September 30 for Rawalpindi, Islamabad, and Murree, warning of flash floods in seasonal Potohar streams as the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) forecasts continued isolated heavy rainfall, which in turn maintains a favourable environment for dengue breeding and other diseases.
Addressing the concurrent rise in seasonal illnesses as northern winds signal the gradual transition from summer heat to cooler autumn weather, public health expert Dr Adnan Khan cautioned that sudden temperature fluctuations weaken immunity, triggering influenza, typhoid and acute viral fevers.
He advised consuming boiled or filtered drinking water, avoiding uncovered street food, wearing long-sleeved clothing during peak mosquito activity at dawn and dusk, and seeking immediate medical evaluation at designated hospital fever clinics upon experiencing persistent high fever, body aches, or flu symptoms. title: SpaceX s Starship makes orbital debut
description: SpaceX s Starship makes orbital debut
content:
Reaches orbit for first time on 14th flight
SpaceX's next-generation Starship rocket reached orbit for the first time on Monday despite having one of its engines shut down unexpectedly, overcoming a hitch mid-flight to deploy its first batch of new Starlink satellites in a truncated mission ending hours earlier than originally planned.
The uncrewed 40-story-tall vehicle, consisting of a Super Heavy booster rocket topped by the main upper-stage Starship vessel, thundered off its launch pad from SpaceX's Starbase complex along the Gulf of Mexico near Brownsville.
The mission was scheduled to last 10 hours, but was reduced to three hours because of the engine problem. It was Starship's 14th flight since 2023, as Elon Musk's company plans to put the vehicle into routine use starting later this year.
SpaceX shares, which were up nearly 9% from the IPO price, were down about 1% on Monday.
The Super Heavy booster lofted the Starship upper stage into space before returning itself to Gulf waters for an engine-controlled splashdown, following hard landings for the booster on two previous missions. Some engines on that booster stopped working during its descent, SpaceX said.
Upon reaching space, one of Starship's three main engines shut down prematurely, a development that led SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot to announce on the company's live stream of the mission that the craft would be unable to reach orbit. "The team has made the call not to commit to orbit," Huot said.
But Huot reversed course minutes later after an update from engineers confirmed that the craft could still attempt an engine firing that would boost it into orbit, which Starship successfully did minutes later.

title: UK examines foreign state involvement in airbase plot
description: UK examines foreign state involvement in airbase plot
content:
British police said on Monday they were investigating whether individuals acting for a foreign state were involved in an apparent plot to attack an airbase used by the United States but said five suspects they had arrested would be released on bail.
The five men, all British nationals from London in their early 20s, were detained early on Sunday after police were alerted by a local farmer about three white vans driving towards RAF Fairford, a British base that houses US bombers that fly missions against Iran.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said in July the base was a legitimate target.
Laurence Taylor, who heads Britain's counter-terrorism police, said the men, who had been arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and planning a terrorist act, would be released under stringent bail conditions later on Monday.
"To be very clear, this does not mean that the investigation is over," Taylor said in a statement outside London police headquarters. "They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry."
A source familiar with the investigation had previously told Reuters that an Iranian-linked motive was considered the most likely, although a Russian sabotage operation or an Islamist plot were also being looked at as possibilities.
Iran's embassy in London had earlier said in a statement it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" that it was involved, which it said would fuel "Iranophobia propaganda" in Britain.
Taylor, who did not specifically refer to Iran, said he knew there was significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context had a bearing on this incident.

title: Indonesia ferry death toll hits 71
description: Indonesia ferry death toll hits 71
content:
The death toll from an Indonesian ship that capsized more than two weeks ago rose to 71on Monday, as divers braved leaking fuel and dangerously unsound structures to try to find passengers still listed as missing.
The Virgo Transport 8 ferry was carrying 243 people when it capsized in bad weather in the Java Sea on September 13 during a voyage from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan. Authorities said 108 people survived.
Divers were navigating through unstable debris on the 16th day of the search, Hardiansyah Putra, a senior official from the search and rescue agency, said.
Searchers recovered five bodies from inside the 4,277-ton ship on Monday, senior agency official I Putu Sudayana said.
The vessel kept tilting from side to side, sharp objects were scattered throughout the wreckage, and dense gas concentrations and leaking fuel were adding to the hazards, Putu added.
"Because of these reasons, the divers weren't able to get into the compartments," he said. The ship's operator needed to right the ship and bring it to the surface, he added.

title: KSA  US discuss Yemen escalation
description: KSA  US discuss Yemen escalation
content:
Saudi Arabia has resumed exporting oil via its East-West pipeline after repairing the damage caused by drone strikes earlier this month, people familiar with the matter said Monday, restoring partial flows on a major route that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz.
The development came as Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his Saudi counterpart, Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, in Washington, as Saudi Arabia seeks US backing for its military campaign against the Houthis.
The Trump administration has avoided direct military involvement in Yemen, where the Iran-backed militants launched a sweeping offensive this month to seize the country's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed government forces. The Houthi gains give the group leverage to disrupt shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The Houthis have also attacked Saudi shipping and energy infrastructure, including in Aramco facilities in the port city of Yanbu. On Saturday, Saudi Arabia's military spokesperson, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said Saudi air defenses intercepted two drones and two ballistic missiles fired from Yemen.
The renewed fighting has reignited the civil war in Yemen, which began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and much of the country's north from the internationally recognized government.
Saudi Aramco, the kingdom's flagship oil company, started loading vessels at the Red Sea port of Yanbu via the pipeline on Sunday, the people said. The development comes after the company began testing the pipeline last week for structural integrity and pressure, the people said. The pipeline was shut after drone attacks from Iraq on Sept. 10.
Aramco is currently operating the pipeline at a throughput rate of around 3.5 million barrels a day, the people noted. Part of the current flows will be directed to domestic refineries, they said.
Aramco didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
The East-West pipeline can carry up to 7 million barrels a day--about 2 million for domestic Saudi refiners and the rest for export--but had never operated at full capacity for an extended period before the Iran war began on Feb. 28. Roughly 4 million barrels a day--around 4% of global supply--were flowing through it before the pipeline outage earlier this month, analysts estimate.

title: Thousands huddle in Bangkok shelters
description: Thousands huddle in Bangkok shelters
content:
Residents of the Thai capital waded through waist-deep waters in some areas on Monday, while thousands sheltered in evacuation centres following flooding brought by weekend rains, as swelling reservoirs in an eastern province prompted evacuations.
Entire neighbourhoods in Bangkok were inundated and the drainage network swamped after 320 mm (12.6 inches) of rain fell during two or three days last week, or nearly as much as the sprawling low-lying city usually gets in all of September.
"We have no more food to eat, because we didn't prepare in time," said Bangorn Dednuam, 60, as she braved intermittent showers in a hunt for food, after supplies ran out at home.
"We didn't manage to pack our things in time, so there's nothing stocked in the fridge."
Bangkok is among 41 provinces across Thailand hit by floods since September 16 that killed at least eight people and disrupted more than 580,000 homes, the interior ministry said.
"Over 80,000 residents living in flooded areas are unable to leave their homes," Unsit Sampuntharat, the ministry's permanent secretary, said in a statement, adding that mobile kitchens and boats were being pressed into the relief effort.
"The goal is to provide three meals a day to all residents throughout the ... flooding period and for at least another seven after waters recede," he added.
The floods could cause economic damage of at least 11 billion baht ($327 million) nationwide, with losses likely to rise unless the situation improves, said Aat Pisanwanich of Rangsit University's economics department.
"The flooding is expected to shave 0.3 percentage points off this year's GDP growth, reducing growth to 2.1%, and cut third-quarter growth by about 0.5 percentage points to 1.7%," he told Reuters.
Southeast Asia's second-largest economy, which has lagged regional peers since the COVID-19 pandemic, expanded 1.9% year-on-year in the year's second quarter, but that was still down sharply from the previous quarter's growth of 2.8%.
Bangkok and the eastern region are likely to take the brunt of the impact, particularly wholesale and retail businesses, while industry and agriculture will suffer elsewhere, Aat added.
Economic damage to the capital itself could reach about 7 billion baht, the University of the Thai Chamber of Commerce said in a statement that put the nationwide impact at about 12.3 billion baht. In Bangkok's hard-hit neighbourhood of Bang Kapi, people trudged through floodwaters to buy essentials from vendors, some of whom set up stalls with floating plastic boxes and drums, three days after the incessant rains.
Marisa Singprakhon brought her wares out of a shop and moved to the market's edge to make it easier for customers to buy, but she herself had to stand in waters knee-deep.
"Customers don't want to go in, they don't want to stand in the water for a long time," she said. "So we have to stand in the water outside to sell."
At least 5,901 people in Bangkok have moved to 234 evacuation centres, a city administration official said.
Sitting on a river delta of soft clay just 1.5 m (5 ft)above sea level, heavily-built up Bangkok is sinking by several millimetres a year, while its population of more than 8.4 million often battles floods in its six-month-long rainy season.
Further east, in the coastal province of Rayong abutting a major industrial belt, authorities ordered evacuations on Monday after flood waters swelled two reservoirs beyond their capacity.

title: Netanyahu made a secret visit to UAE
description: Netanyahu made a secret visit to UAE
content:
Israeli PM asked UAE president to deny report on Oct 7 warning
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu asked United Arab Emirates (UAE) President Mohamed bin Zayed during a secret meeting on Sunday to deny a report that he had warned Netanyahu of an imminent Hamas attack before October 7, 2023, Israeli newspaper Haaretz said on Monday, Anadolu Agency reported.
Netanyahu asked bin Zayed to deny reports about their phone conversation and details surrounding the events before October 7 that "could embarrass him," Haaretz said, citing unspecified sources.
The Israeli premier also asked the Emirati president for what one source described as "moral support," the newspaper reported.
Netanyahu held an hour-long meeting with bin Zayed, according to two people briefed on the trip.
Israeli and Emirati authorities had not officially confirmed the reported visit, though a senior Israeli official told Reuters about the meeting.
Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported that Netanyahu travelled on a private plane owned by an unnamed Israeli businessman and used by senior Israeli figures for international trips.
It departed Ben Gurion Airport in the afternoon and landed in Abu Dhabi at 3:10 pm (1110GMT), the broadcaster said. It took off for Israel at 7:10 pm (1510GMT), four hours later, and landed shortly after 10pm (1900GMT).
KAN said Netanyahu had also used the aircraft for a trip to Abu Dhabi during the war with Iran.
The visit comes after Haaretz this month reported that Sheikh Mohamed had warned Netanyahu a week and a half before October 7, 2023, that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel. Haaretz had reported that the warning was not passed to Israeli intelligence agencies or the military.
Netanyahu, who denied the report and threatened legal action against the newspaper, is facing a tough reelection campaign. Opposition leaders have accused the prime minister of bearing responsibility for security failures that preceded Hamas' October 7 attack.

title: Iran leader vows  enemy exit from Arabian Sea
description: Iran leader vows  enemy exit from Arabian Sea
content:
Iran leader vows 'enemy exit from Arabian Sea'
Iranian forces have driven enemy forces back from waters off southern Iran to the Arabian Sea, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said on Monday according to his Telegram channel, warning that Iranian forces would soon push them out of the Arabian Sea as well.
"Today, there are various declarations of readiness throughout Islamic Iran, particularly for armed participation, creating an arena in which our people will gain honour and their enemy disgrace," he wrote on his X account.
He then said that the "bygone days" which Iran's enemies "longed to return to" have passed and "will never be repeated."
Meanwhile, Iran denied involvement in a suspected plot to attack a British airbase used by the United States to strike Iranian sites, and police said five men arrested over explosives and terrorism offences were British nationals.
British police arrested the five early on Sunday after being alerted to three white vans driving towards RAF Fairford, a British base that houses US bombers that fly missions against Iran.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said in July the base was a legitimate target. Police said on Monday the five detained men were British nationals from London in their early 20s, and that they were trying to understand a motive.
A source familiar with the investigation said an Iranian-linked motive was considered ?the most likely although a Russian sabotage operation or an Islamist plot were also being looked at as possibilities.
Iran's embassy in London said in a statement it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations", which it said would fuel "Iranophobia propaganda" in Britain.
Police said they had multiple new lines of inquiry after examining the scene overnight.
Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator Vicki Evans said she was aware of speculation about the motive and geopolitical questions that were being raised, but asked that police be given "the space to work carefully and clearly".
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday the suspects had been looking to do "big damage" and had been under investigation by British and US authorities, but doubts were voiced in British media about the degree to which they had been under surveillance, given how close they had come to the base.
The source familiar with the investigation said the arrests were not "intelligence-led" although security had been heightened at the base, suggesting authorities were aware of an increased threat.
The farmer, who alerted police after seeing a group of "hooded and masked men" running into fields, told reporters she believed it was her phone call to the 999 emergency hotline that foiled any plot.
Defence minister Wes Streeting told the BBC the farmer, who has not been identified, had only a "partial picture" of the investigation, without providing further clarification.
He said he would not speculate about motives during a live investigation, but that Britain faced a general threat from Iran.
"We know that Iran and their proxies wish to do us harm. We know that they hate our democracy, and we know that we regularly have to thwart Iranian attempts to threaten either our interests or indeed our allies," he said.
Britain raised its national terrorism threat level to "severe" from "substantial" in April after a series of antisemitic incidents in north London.
This level indicates a terrorist attack within six months is considered highly likely. Police said they were investigating links with Iran to many of the incidents in which properties connected to the Jewish community or Iranian dissidents were targeted.
Britain imposed sanctions on 12 individuals and entities linked to Iran in May, accusing them of involvement in hostile activity including plotting attacks and providing financial services to groups seeking to destabilise Britain and other countries.
Iran has denied involvement in attacks or plots in Britain and elsewhere. After the Fairford arrests, the US Embassy issued a security alert saying US citizens should "exercise caution" and be "mindful of personal security".
Security was stepped up at other US airbases in Britain. The British government had given authorisation to the US to use bombers based at Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
The government has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is being regularly updated on the incident. He dropped out of several events at his Labour Party's annual conference on Sunday.
In Fairford, police have imposed a 400-metre cordon around the base and evacuated residents from 85 homes.
A bomb disposal robot was on Sunday operating around the three white vans, and security was stepped up around the base.
Armed police stood guard at the main entrance and large machinery blocked other access points. An image on social media purported to show some of the suspects, seated shirtless with hands behind their backs, aftertheir arrest.
Reuters was unable to independently locate and verify the source of the photograph.

title: US war commission turns to Pakistan for Afghan war review
description: US war commission turns to Pakistan for Afghan war review
content:
Co-chairs Shamila N Chaudhary and Dr Colin F Jackson call on Field Marshal Asim Munir
The United States Afghanistan War Commission has sought Pakistan's perspective on the two-decade-long Afghan conflict as it undertakes a comprehensive review of Washington's military, diplomatic and strategic engagement in Afghanistan.
A delegation of the commission, led by its co-chairs Shamila N Chaudhary and Dr Colin F Jackson, called on Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir chief of army staff and chief of defence forces at General Headquarters (GHQ) on Monday, according to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).
"The delegation is undertaking a review of the United States' 20-year engagement in Afghanistan," the military's media wing said.
Discussions covered matters of mutual interest, including Pakistan's support, the regional security environment and developments in Afghanistan, with a particular focus on perspectives relevant to the commission's work.
The army chief shared Pakistan's perspective on the security dynamics that shaped the conflict and highlighted the challenges Pakistan faced during the prolonged war in Afghanistan.
He underscored the importance of incorporating the regional perspective and Pakistan's experience in assessing the strategic, diplomatic and operational dimensions of the conflict, according to ISPR.
The delegation acknowledged Pakistan's longstanding role and sacrifices during the conflict and appreciated its continued contribution to regional peace and stability.
The meeting is significant because Pakistan is one of the countries whose policies and actions will come under close scrutiny in the commission's assessment of the 20-year war.
Established by the US Congress in December 2021, the Afghanistan War Commission is an independent bipartisan body tasked with examining key strategic, diplomatic and operational decisions relating to the war in Afghanistan from September 2001 to August 2021.
Its mandate covers military operations, diplomacy, intelligence assessments, counterterrorism, reconstruction and development assistance, political initiatives and the highest-level policy deliberations of the US government.
It has also been asked to develop lessons and recommendations to inform future decisions by Congress and the US government. The commission consists of 16 members appointed on a bipartisan basis by congressional leaders. Chaudhary and Jackson serve as its co-chairs.
Pakistan has emerged as a specific area of interest in the commission's research. Its second interim report identified "Pakistan's pivotal role: leverage and constraints" as one of 12 major themes emerging from its work.
The commission's assessment recognises that Pakistan played an important role in supporting early US counterterrorism operations and providing supply routes for coalition forces, while also examining the longstanding dispute between Washington and Islamabad over Pakistan's policy towards the Taliban.
That debate goes to the heart of the history of the Afghan war.
Following the September 11, 2001 attacks, Pakistan became a major US partner in the campaign against Al-Qaeda and the Taliban. Islamabad provided logistical access, intelligence cooperation and other forms of support to US-led operations.
At the same time, Pakistan itself became a major victim of the conflict, suffering extensive human and economic losses as terrorism spread across the country.
Relations with Washington, however, increasingly became strained over allegations concerning Taliban sanctuaries, counterterrorism cooperation and the divergent interests of the two countries in Afghanistan.
The relationship reached several major crisis points, including the 2011 US raid in Abbottabad that killed Al-Qaeda chief Osama bin Laden, the NATO airstrikes at Salala that martyred Pakistani soldiers later that year and repeated disputes over the US strategy for ending the war.
For Islamabad, the commission's review therefore offers an opportunity to put its version of the conflict on the official US record.
Pakistan has consistently argued that its role cannot be assessed solely through the prism of US objectives in Afghanistan and that its own security concerns, particularly along the Afghan border, must be taken into account.
The commission has itself stressed that understanding the war requires examining the decisions made over two decades rather than focusing only on the chaotic US withdrawal in August 2021.
Five years after the withdrawal, the commission said recently that the events of August 2021 "cannot be understood through the final days, weeks, or months of the war alone" because they were shaped by two decades of policies, achievements, setbacks and unresolved challenges. On August 15, 2021, the US finally withdrew from Afghanistan amid a speedy return of the Afghan Taliban to power.
The timing of the commission's engagement with Pakistan is also noteworthy because the security environment in Afghanistan has changed considerably since the US withdrawal.
The Taliban remain in power, while Pakistan is once again confronting serious security challenges linked to terrorist groups operating from Afghanistan. Islamabad has repeatedly demanded that the Taliban authorities prevent Afghan territory from being used against Pakistan.
This makes the commission's historical review relevant to current regional security dynamics.
The eventual report could influence how US policymakers understand the causes of the war's prolongation, the failure to achieve a durable political settlement and the circumstances surrounding the Taliban's return to power.
The commission has so far conducted hundreds of interviews, gathered thousands of government records and undertaken fact-finding missions as part of its investigation.
It has organised its research around policy and diplomacy, counterterrorism, conventional military operations, building Afghan security forces, reconstruction and intelligence assessments.
The commission was initially expected to complete its work in 2026. However, in August this year, its co-chairs announced that Congress had approved a one-year extension, with the final report now due in August 2027. The extension was sought to allow the commission to complete additional research and integrate further interviews and government records into its assessment.
For Pakistan, the Rawalpindi meeting represents more than an exchange of views on the past.
It provides Islamabad with a direct channel to place its experience of the Afghan war before the US body responsible for producing what could become one of the most comprehensive official assessments of Washington's longest war.
The commission's eventual findings will help determine how that history including Pakistan's role, its sacrifices and its often-contentious relationship with Washingtonis recorded in the American policy narrative of the Afghanistan war.

title: Afridi rejects threats  vows to stand firm
description: Afridi rejects threats  vows to stand firm
content:
PTI defends K-P govt against Centre's terrorism allegations
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi said on Monday that he was not afraid of threats of governor's rule or an emergency and would not retreat from his position, as the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) hit back at criticism of the provincial government by the federal information minister.
Addressing a meeting in Peshawar, Afridi said the Centre's current policy was wrong and had resulted in the bloodshed of Pashtuns once again. "The policy of once again pushing Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa into the fire of terrorism is unacceptable," he said.
The remarks by Afridi followed statements from several federal ministers, including Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, who spoke of the possibility of governor's rule in K-P, while accusing the provincial government of failing to address the worsening terrorism and governance problems.
Later, in a statement issued by the party's Central Media Department on X, the PTI rejected Atta Tarar's criticism of the K-P government and urged him to focus on the performance of the federal and Punjab governments instead of "levelling allegations" against the province.
"Tarar should remember that the people of K-P stand on the front lines against terrorism, and the PTI will never forget the sacrifices of its martyrs," it said. "The minister should first take a hard look at his own performance at the federal level and in Punjab, and then lecture the people of K-P," it added.
The party also rebuked Tarar for labelling the entire provincial government as facilitators of terrorists and asked him to explain the basis for the allegation. The statement said the people of K-P, police, security personnel and political workers had made the greatest sacrifices in the war against terrorism.
The party cited the killing of its provincial law and parliamentary affairs minister Israrullah Gandapur in a suicide attack in Dera Ismail Khan on October 16, 2013, as evidence of the sacrifices made by its representatives. Gandapur was among at least eight people killed in the attack at his residence.

title: Centre lays ground for governor s rule in K P
description: Centre lays ground for governor s rule in K P
content:
Several federal ministers cite constitutional option Say conditions ripe in province for drastic measure Attack
The possibility of governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) came into sharper focus on Monday as several federal ministers said the Constitution provided for such measures if required, while accusing the provincial government of failing to address worsening terrorism and governance problems.
Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan Affairs Minister Amir Muqam, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry and K-P Governor Faisal Karim Kundi indicated that the situation in the K-P had reached a point where drastic measures could be taken.
"If such circumstances arise, or if they already exist, in which the Constitution allows governor's rule or an emergency to be imposed, then it can be done," Law Minister Tarar said during an informal conversation with journalists in Islamabad.
"The Constitution contains a procedure for such measures and, when the need arose, all this will not only happen but will also be visible," he added. "Governor's rule or an emergency could be imposed in K-P if the constitutional requirements were met."
Speaking at a press conference at the Peshawar Press Club, Kashmir and G-B Affairs Minister Amir Muqam went further, saying consultations on the constitutional and legal option were under way and "anything can happen at any time".
"All legal requirements for imposing governor's rule had been fulfilled in view of the law-and-order situation in the province and the actions of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's [PTI] government led by Chief Minister Sohail Afridi," he added.
According to Muqam, if governor's rule was imposed, K-P Governor Faisal Karim Kundi would lead the new provincial setup. He described Kundi as a "refined person" and said there had been no discussion about removing the governor. "He is doing good work," Muqam said.
Kundi himself, however, urged the provincial government not to push the situation to a point where governor's rule became inevitable. "K-P is facing serious governance and corruption problems," Kundi said, while talking to the media during a visit to a hospital in Peshawar.
"The province's law and order situation could not afford a long march and staging a march on Islamabad was inappropriate under the circumstances," he added, referring to the PTI's planned long march in the federal capital, which was previously scheduled for Sept 27 but has now been postponed to Oct 4.
Kundi described governor's rule as a "measure of necessity". If the situation worsened, the president could impose governor's rule on the prime minister's advice, he said and urged the provincial government not to push matters to the point where the federal government was forced to impose an emergency.
Meanwhile, the federal government stepped up its criticism of the K-P government. At a joint press conference in Islamabad, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar and Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry accused the provincial government of facilitating terrorists for political and financial interests.
"The PTI leadership in K-P is the B team of the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)," Attaullah Tarar charged. "You facilitate terrorists because of your political and financial interests. The K-P government is more concerned about politics and money generated through illegal mining and contracts than the people."
The information minister also accused Chief Minister Afridi of administrative and political failures, alleging that "devastation and ruin" had spread across the province and that the provincial government itself had contributed to the spread of terrorism rather than countering it.
Chaudhry accused the PTI leadership of maintaining a "soft attitude" towards Afghanistan and questioned why the provincial government did not condemn attacks originating from the neighbouring country or publicly identify its alleged proxies.
The minister also criticised the K-P government for not providing sufficient resources to its Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD). He criticised recent changes to the K-P Police Act as well, arguing that they weakened the force's institutional authority.
Amid these accusations, a government white paper presented figures on terrorism, police resources, drugs, smuggling and the provincial government's security measures, showing a sharp rise in casualties among police personnel in K-P during the first half of 2026.
According to the document, 122 police personnel were martyred in K-P during the first half of 2026, compared with 63 in the same period last year, an increase of 93.7%. Injuries rose from 84 to 175, an increase of 108.3%. The document said terrorist attacks from January to September 2026 had risen to 680.
The document said 3,113 personnel were serving against 3,844 sanctioned CTD posts in December 2025, leaving around 19% vacant. It said the K-P CTD had only nine M4 rifles against a requirement of 200 and 11 night-vision devices against a requirement of 35.
The white paper also said the chief minister chaired the first provincial Apex Committee meeting 112 days after assuming office and questioned the implementation of its decisions after subsequent attacks in Bannu, Tank, Hangu and Kohat.

title: FCC narrows scope of workplace harassment
description: FCC narrows scope of workplace harassment
content:
Disagrees with SC; says misconduct not harassment unless it has sexual dimensions
The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) has narrowed the scope of actionable workplace harassment under the Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010, holding that misconduct or other objectionable behaviour does not fall within the ombudsperson's jurisdiction unless the conduct has a sexual dimension.
A three-member FCC bench headed by Chief Justice Amin-ud-Din Khan, in a judgment authored by Justice Ali Baqar Najafi, held that workplace behaviour could generally be described as harassment, but it would not constitute an actionable offence under the Act unless it was inherently sexual in nature.
The ruling marks a departure from the Supreme Court's recent interpretation of the law. In a 2025 judgment, the Supreme Court held that workplace harassment could include gender-based discrimination and the creation of a hostile work environment, emphasising that such conduct could stem from power and domination rather than sexual desire.
The FCC disagreed with that interpretation, holding that the statutory definition in Section 2(h) required the element of sexual harassment for conduct to become actionable before the ombudsperson.
The court observed that any misconduct or behaviour unbecoming of an employee towards another employee or an employer could generically be classified as harassment, but would not, by itself, be actionable under the 2010 Act unless the conduct was demonstrated to be sexual in nature.
It held that grave or otherwise actionable misconduct could have serious consequences but did not fall within the statutory definition of harassment unless it had a sexual origin.
The bench noted that the Act was enacted to protect both working women and men, but specifically against harassment having a sexual dimension at the workplace.
"Undoubtedly, the Harassment Act, 2010 was legislated to protect not only working women but also working men but only against harassment having a sexual dimension at the workplace," it said.
The court further held that conduct amounting to harassment could have a distasteful effect or injurious consequences but would not become cognizable before the ombudsperson unless it was characterised as sexual.
The judgment noted that although the preamble of the 2010 Act uses the word "harassment", Section 2(h), which defines harassment for the purposes of the law, provides sexual harassment as the basis for actionable conduct.
The FCC also distinguished between gender-based sexual discrimination and ordinary misconduct.
It observed that gender-based sexual discrimination resulting from a prejudicial mindset and leading to discriminatory behaviour could be actionable under the Act. In the absence of the key element of sexual conduct, however, departmental disciplinary proceedings could be attracted instead.

title: Pakistan nears historic first astronaut mission
description: Pakistan nears historic first astronaut mission
content:
Two pilots train in China as selection decision expected next month
Two Pakistani pilots are memorising Mandarin, spinning in centrifuge drills and learning to eat, sleep and repair equipment while weightless as a decision nears on which one will become the first foreign astronaut aboard China's Tiangong space station.
The voyage into space would be a first for the South Asian nation. It is part of broader cooperation with Beijing that straddles the Belt and Road Initiative and has produced Chinese-launched Pakistani satellites, a joint satellite-navigation system and a Pakistani-built rover due to fly on China's Chang'e 8 lunar mission around 2028.
Pilots Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud have spent months training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Center in Beijing for a mission that was conceived by the two countries in 2019, said Amer Gilani, who oversees human spaceflight cooperation at Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO.
China has not said which of the two will fly or when, but Gilani said a final astronaut selection decision is expected in mid-to-late October.
Whoever is chosen will not return to Pakistan before launch, setting off into space directly from training in China and returning home after a recovery period following the return to Earth, Gilani told Reuters in an interview.
Training includes intensive Chinese-language instruction, learning spacecraft systems, and adapting to both the microgravity of orbit and the g-forces of liftoff, he added.
The two men beat out roughly 20 finalists culled from an initial Pakistani pool of pilots and scientists, screened for medical fitness, psychological resilience and, according to SUPARCO's director of artificial intelligence Uzair Ansari, a tolerance for g-forces that few scientists possess.
"You cannot easily find scientists who are familiar with travelling and facing high-level g-forces," he said, explaining this is why the two men with backgrounds in high-speed flying were chosen.
The details shared by Gilani and Ansari are the first insight provided by SUPARCO to foreign media since the pilots were selected and deployed to China. China's space agency did not respond to a request for comment about the selection process.
Once in space, the chosen pilot will carry the title of "payload specialist", which is astronaut-speak for someone whose job in orbit is running Pakistan's science experiments rather than flying the ship, Ansari said.
Of more than 300 proposals SUPARCO fielded from universities in Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad after a year-long campaign, Gilani said Chinese institutes picked four for this flight: biotechnology experiments that will help combat food insecurity and climate change.
Every experiment is built and pre-tested in SUPARCO's own labs before Chinese engineers sign off - a rare case, Ansari said, where Pakistani technology gets validated on an international platform.
The scientific payload is modest next to a station that has already hosted more than 180 experiments and produced over 500 research papers and 150 patents, Ansari added.
Tiangong's three modules - Tianhe, Wentian and Mengtian - weigh about 77 metric tons combined and house roughly 14 experiment racks spanning life sciences, materials, fluid physics, combustion and radiation exposure, Gilani said, including some mounted outside the station and exposed directly to space for materials and biotechnology payloads.
The astronaut will fly aboard a Chinese-built spacecraft, launched from a Chinese site, trained by Chinese instructors and communicating in Mandarin in orbit. Pakistan has no independent launch vehicle or crewed spacecraft of its own, and the stay itself will be about a week, a fraction of the roughly six-month rotations of career Chinese crew members.
The Pakistani astronaut is due to return with two members of a Chinese crew that arrived at the space station in May because the third member is expected to stay for a year to enable the study of long-duration human physiology in space.
Since Yuri Gagarin's 1961 first flight, citizens of about 50 countries have flown in space, but only three nations - Russia, the US, and China - have launched their own crewed spacecraft.
China's invitation to Pakistan is the first time it will transport a foreign astronaut. Asked whether Islamabad had secured any promise to send an astronaut to the moon under the same partnership, Gilani said "there is no official commitment or discussion on this matter," adding that what comes next will depend on how "our maiden mission" turns out.
The Pakistani-built lunar rover that is due to fly on China's Chang'e 8 lunar mission around 2028 is a separate strand of that cooperation.
