title: JI demands release of all political prisoners
description: JI demands release of all political prisoners
content:
Warns govt against mistaking JI's peace for weakness
Jamaat-e-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Monday warned the government not to mistake his party's peaceful approach for weakness, saying its street power had already been demonstrated and that it would not retreat from the rights of the people.
He said the relief secured through JI's campaign remained inadequate and demanded the complete abolition of the petroleum levy, deploring it as a "bhatta tax" (extortion) imposed on the public.
Addressing a press conference, Hafiz Naeem said the government was presenting monthly relief of Rs25 billion to Rs30 billion as a major achievement, whereas JI considered it insufficient.
"Our peaceful approach should not be considered our weakness," he said, adding that the government would ultimately have to abolish the petroleum levy.
He also challenged PPP Chairman Bilawal Zardari, saying that if he was genuinely opposed to "establishment's electoral system", he should relinquish the "fake" mayoralty in Karachi and the national and provincial assembly seats obtained on the basis of Form 47.
The JI emir said the country's prevailing political turmoil was causing the genuine issues facing the public to be overlooked.
He said JI fully supported any political party's protest conducted within the Constitution and law and urged the government to hold serious negotiations to resolve the issue involving Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).
He demanded the release of all political prisoners, including women, and specifically referred to Dr Yasmin Rashid, Ejaz Chaudhary, Shah Mahmood Qureshi and Mahmoodur Rashid, saying that some of them were in poor health while remaining incarcerated.
He said merely announcing a committee would not resolve the issue and denounced threatening statements and tones adopted by government ministers.
Referring to reports of alleged plans to impose governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the JI chief warned that such an "unconstitutional" step could backfire on the government.
He said PTI's demands were clear and included access to Imran Khan, medical facilities for him and meetings with him, adding that none of these demands was unjustified when considered in accordance with the law and its rules.
Regarding the law-and-order situation in Karachi, Hafiz Naeem said people were losing their lives to street crime every day. He cited the case of a family in Manghopir that, according to him, buried its child 20 days after the death, and said another young man was killed in a street-crime incident the previous night.
He said JI's campaign had created awareness among the public that the petroleum levy was a form of "bhatta" or extortion-like tax and had no connection with the actual price of petrol.
Hafiz Naeem said the party had given its long march a temporary pause following Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's assurance but had not withdrawn from the protest. He said demonstrations were still continuing across the country.

Couple slammed for making security demands during UK stay
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have faced a "blackmail" accusation from royal biographer Angela Levin as their security arrangements remain under review following their return to the UK.
Speaking to TalkTV, Levin criticised the couple's continued efforts to secure state-funded protection and suggested they could use their children and a potential departure from Britain as leverage.
"It's blackmail, isn't it? That's what I think. It's the two of them now, if you don't give them exactly what they want, when they want," Levin said.
She added, "They're going here, 'you can't see the children' And I think that it's a blackmail thing."
Harry and Meghan returned to the UK late last month, six years after stepping back from royal duties and losing taxpayer-funded security.
Their current arrangements are being reviewed by the Royal and VIP Executive Committee (RAVEC), while Meghan is also having her security assessed by her own Risk Management Board.
According to reports cited in the supplied material, the couple could return to their Montecito, California home if the security review does not produce the outcome they want.
A friend of Harry's reportedly said, "If he doesn't get [security], then I believe he will go back to Montecito for good, and that could be as soon as half-term."
Security concerns have also reportedly affected the couple's children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. Their spokesperson said their move to another school followed discussions with the family's security team about "the practicalities of their current arrangements".
The couple have also reportedly questioned their decision to return to the UK amid tensions with other members of the royal family.
An unnamed source claimed Harry and Meghan now feel "unwelcomed" and have wondered whether returning was a "huge mistake".

title: Paris Women s Fashion Week kicks off amid economic gloom
description: Paris Women s Fashion Week kicks off amid economic gloom
content:
Event to feature 67 catwalk shows; dozens of brands set to show their designs in French capital
Paris Women's Fashion Week opens Monday with a debut show from South African brand MaXhosa Africa and a fresh collection from new-ish Canadian trendsetters Matieres Fecales, look to lift the gloom surrounding the sector.
A total of 67 catwalk shows for 2027 Spring-Summer have been planned for this Fashion Week, with dozens of other brands set to show their designs in private viewings and events around the French capital.
Industry big beasts Christian Dior and Saint Laurent will send their models out on Tuesday.
It could be a last show for Saint Laurent's Belgian designer Anthony Vaccarello, who has been the driving force behind the brand's success for the past decade but is reportedly heading for the exit.
If his departure is confirmed, he is unlikely to be the only creative director heading for the chop as label owners and chief executives look to revive their fortunes in a tough commercial environment for luxury brands.
At Balenciaga, Italian designer Pierpaolo Piccioli is reportedly in the sights of parent company Kering, having failed in the difficult task of maintaining sales levels achieved by his predecessor Demna, according to specialist blog Miss Tweed.
At Chloe, artistic director Chemena Kamali, in the job since 2023, is also being pushed towards the door over a lack of profitability, according to investigative outlet Glitz.
"There were the 'golden years' (for the sector) after Covid, a peak in 2023 and then a luxury market that stabilised," Pascal Morand, executive president of the French Haute Couture and Fashion Federation, told AFP.
"The major groups, mid-sized brands and young designers are not affected in the same way. Markets, outlets and business models are evolving," he said.
Although sales are falling for many brands, there are bright spots.
Since his arrival a year ago at the helm of Chanel, Matthieu Blazy has created a buzz and sales frenzy at the classic French label, with customers queueing outside some boutiques for his latest collections.
His Spring-Summer show takes place next Monday.
Another brand with reason for cheer is MaXhosa Africa, a luxury knitwear group founded in 2010 by textile designer Laduma Ngxokolo, who has already shown collections privately in Paris but has now been invited to join the official programme.
On a mission to promote South African culture and the traditions of the Xhosa people, Ngxokolo counts Michelle Obama and Beyonce as fans.
With his first show on Monday, he will be hoping to emulate the success of Matieres Fecales, the Canadian brand which first appeared in March last year but has gone on to dress a host of celebrities and A-listers.
Its unusual name -- which means faecal matter in French -- was chosen to ensure that people who bought the brand's clothing only wanted it for the design, rather than the name on the label.
After more than seven weeksfashion "month" technically began at Pitti Uomo on January 13the fall 2026 season has finally washed up in Paris. Which, to the die-hards, is the only fashion week that really counts. Not only because it plays host to the world's most powerful brandsChanel, McQueen, Miu Miu, Saint Laurent, Louis Vuitton, Balenciaga, Alaïa, Tom Ford, Christian Dior, Balmainbut because it attracts the world's most famous people, too.
Last season alone, Margot Robbie, Nicole Kidman, both Jenners, Kim Kardashian, three-quarters of the Beckham siblings, Jennifer Lawrence, Rosalía, Zendaya, Anne Hathaway, Emma Stone, Emma Watson, and even Meghan Markle took their seats on the front row.
After events by Julie Kegels, Weinsanto, and Hodakova, the Matieres Fecales show at 7:00pm (1700 GMT) will bring the first day of Paris Fashion Week to a close.

title: Art exhibition explores identity  contradictions
description: Art exhibition explores identity  contradictions
content:
'Morbid Curiosities' presents work by Scheherazade Junejo
An ongoing art exhibition at Sanat Initiative brings together a deeply personal exploration of identity, memory, inherited experiences and the questions that emerge as one moves through different stages of life.
Titled Morbid Curiosities, the exhibition presents three interconnected bodies of work by Karachi-based artist Scheherazade Junejo, examining the artist's relationship with her own material and genetic inheritance, memories and evolving sense of self.
The works are divided into A Wrinkle, The Infinite Loop and Glass Animals, each approaching self-investigation from a different perspective.
Speaking to The Express Tribune, Junejo said she had been working on the exhibition for around nine to 10 months, developing three distinct bodies of work that include still life, figurative pieces, drawing and embossing.
"The narrative of the three bodies of work is a little different, but in a way, it is the same. It is a self-investigation," she said.
According to the artist, the exhibition revolves around fundamental questions of identity and existence "Who am I? Where am I going? And what am I going to become?"
In A Wrinkle, repetitive mark-making becomes a visual record of recurring thoughts and unresolved questions. The work reflects the nature of an overthinking mind, where ideas are repeatedly revisited, questioned and undone rather than conclusively resolved.
Together, the three sections create a visual journey inward, connecting physical forms with psychological and emotional experiences.
Junejo said the exhibition also represents a significant transition in her artistic practice. After nearly 16 to 17 years of developing a recognisable visual identity, she felt the need to question and examine herself more deeply.
"My signature, which has become my work and my identity through my work, has changed a lot with this work," she said.
She explained that growing older naturally brings changes in one's thought process, experiences and questions.
"This is a kind of transition from young adulthood to adulthood, middle-aged life. So, the questions of that go into more depth," she said.
For Junejo, the darker and more uncomfortable aspects of the work are also connected to growing confidence and the courage to confront questions that may once have been avoided.
For Junejo, the exhibition ultimately reflects a willingness to confront the self rather than simply present aesthetically pleasing images. Its three parts move between the exposed surface of thought, the contradictions of the body and the fragile world of memory.

title: China  US to cut tariffs on  60b of goods
description: China  US to cut tariffs on  60b of goods
content:
Beijing says trade truce extension provides room for both sides to resolve economic issues
China and the United States have agreed to cut tariffs imposed on $60 billion worth of goods imported from each other, ranging from US corn to cosmetics and from Chinese household appliances to toys.
Under the US-China Board of Trade, each of the two countries have recommended $30 billion of trade in non-sensitive goods for more favourable tariff treatment, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement on Sunday.
For the United States, that was "unlocking improved market access" for about 30% of US exports to China, he said. The reciprocal tariff reduction as well as an extension in a trade truce were among the key takeaways from the second summit this year between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, hosted in Washington last week.
One of the two lists from the White House showed that China planned to trim duties on a variety of US agricultural goods including corn, wheat, sorghum, meat, dairy, vegetable oils and meals. It did not include soybeans. Beijing will also look to reduce levies on US fish and seafood, logs and wood products, cosmetics and medical devices.
In another list were Washington's reciprocal tariff cuts – for Chinese small appliances such as coffee makers and toasters, tableware, blankets and bed linens. The list also included toys, fireworks, artificial flowers, Christmas tree lamps and other holiday decorations, and children's car seats.
China's commerce ministry said on Monday a two-month extension of a trade truce with the US through January 10 would provide room for both sides to evaluate their ongoing arrangement to resolve economic and trade issues, while considering how to advance on those fronts.

title: PSX wobbles as Hormuz uncertainty persists
description: PSX wobbles as Hormuz uncertainty persists
content:
KSE-100 index sheds 340 points, settles at 170,425.62
Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) struggled to hold its ground on Monday as uncertainty about a diplomatic breakthrough between the US and Iran kept investors on edge, with the unresolved fate of the Strait of Hormuz adding to oil supply fears.
The KSE-100 index initially climbed more than 270 points but quickly reversed course as profit-taking set in, leaving the market swinging between gains and losses amid heightened geopolitical tensions. The index moved between the intra-day high of 171,126.52 and low of 170,120.50.
Brent crude prices rebounded more than 3% in Asian trading after US President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian proposal aimed at resolving the conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which kept tensions in the Middle East elevated. Consequently, the benchmark index lost 339.60 points, or 0.20%, and settled at 170,425.62.
According to Arif Habib Limited (AHL) Deputy Head of Trading Ali Najib, the PSX experienced another range-bound trading session, when the KSE-100 index slid 340 points (-0.20%).
Investor sentiment remained fragile throughout the session as persistent geopolitical uncertainty kept market participants on the sidelines, particularly following media reports that the US president had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal regarding the Strait of Hormuz, while declining to comment on potential military actions post-mid-term elections.
In terms of index contribution, the positive momentum from TRG Pakistan, Fauji Fertiliser, Oil & Gas Development Company, Attock Refinery and Hub Power collectively added 264 points. However, the gains were offset by selling pressure in UBL, HBL, Lucky Cement, Engro Holdings and Mari Energies, which pulled the index down by 321 points.
"Going forward, the market is expected to remain volatile, with selective buying if geopolitical tensions ease and oil prices move down. High energy prices, external-sector risks and the IMF review will be the key factors influencing market direction," Najib wrote.
KTrade Securities mentioned that it was a cautious session marked by selective buying and broad-based selling. KSE-100 volumes stood at 139 million shares. Technology and select refinery stocks showed strength, while commercial banks and cement firms remained under pressure.
TRG, FFC, OGDC and Attock Refinery provided support to the index, whereas UBL, HBL, Lucky Cement and Engro Holdings were among the key drags. The divergence between technology and refinery names and index-heavy sectors reflected a selective approach from investors amid macro and geopolitical uncertainty.
Oil prices continued to move higher over escalating tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea. "Going forward, the sentiment is likely to remain sensitive to oil movements and geopolitical developments, while selective interest may continue in refineries and other stocks benefiting from the elevated oil prices," KTrade added.
Overall trading volumes decreased to 421 million shares compared with Friday's total of 483 million. The value of traded shares stood at Rs17.7 billion.
In the ready market, shares of 496 companies were traded. Of these, 181 stocks rise, 267 fell and 48 remained unchanged.
Cnergyico Pk was the volume leader with trading in 61.6 million shares, rising Rs0.14 to close at Rs13.32. Foreign investors sold shares worth Rs99.2 million, the National Clearing Company reported.

title: New PPRA rules retain direct SOE contracting
description: New PPRA rules retain direct SOE contracting
content:
Govt notifies procurement laws, ignores 40% sub-contracting limit
Pakistan on Monday notified new procurement rules to bring transparency, meeting a condition of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) but without eliminating preference for government-owned entities in the award of contracts without competitive bidding despite the lender's insistence.
After the approval of the federal cabinet last week, the government on Monday notified the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority (PPRA) Rules 2026 by annulling the 2004 rules. The rules were notified just two days before the expiry of the IMF deadline. It coincided with the fourth IMF programme review.
The Public Procurement Rules 2026 have been formally notified through the Gazette of Pakistan and have come into force with immediate effect, according to an announcement by PPRA. It added that the federal cabinet ratified the new rules on the recommendation of the Cabinet Committee for Disposal of Legislative Cases (CCLC), which repealed the Public Procurement Rules.
The government has not accepted one of the IMF's core demands of ending the unrestricted provision of awards of public contracts to the government-owned entities without competitive bidding.
The last IMF report on Pakistan read "the adoption of recently drafted legal amendments of the relevant provisions of the PPRA rules will eliminate preferences for SOEs in awarding public procurement contracts without competition, subject to limited and reasonable exceptions". The language of the new rules showed that Rule 32-F, which deals with direct contract, was different from what the IMF had proposed.
The new rule says that the procuring agency may engage in direct contracting in case the procurement concerns the acquisition of spare parts or supplementary services from original manufacturer or supplier; for reasons connected with protection of exclusive rights or intellectual property, the supplies may be manufactured or delivered only by a particular supplier; where a change of supplier would oblige the procuring agency to acquire material having different technical specifications or characteristics and would result in incompatibility or disproportionate technical difficulties in operation and maintenance; repeat orders not exceeding fifteen per cent of the original contract amount after expiry of the original procurement contract on the same price, terms and conditions and when the price of goods, services or works is fixed by the government or any other Authority, agency or body duly authorised by the government, on its behalf.
Sources said that the IMF had a different position on the issue of direct contracting. They added that the IMF had suggested that a procuring agency shall not engage in direct contracting with state-owned entities such as professional, autonomous or semi-autonomous organisations or bodies of the federal or provincial governments for the procurement of goods, works and services, including consultancy services, except for the procurement of works and services, including consultancy services, which are time-sensitive, scattered, remotely located and in the public interest.
The IMF had proposed some conditions for direct contracting. Sources said that according to the Fund's recommendations, the direct contracting shall only be carried out through e-PADS; the organisation or the body to be engaged in direct contracting shall be eligible to perform the works or render the services; the organisation or the body shall accomplish the work or the services including consultancy services, exclusively through its own resources without involving private sector as a partner or in the form of a joint venture or as a subcontractor; Provided that where specialised project components are required to be outsourced, the state-owned entity may assign the respective work to subcontractors, which shall in no case exceed 40% of the total quantum of the work assigned to the said entity.
According to the other unmet recommendations, in case there is more than one organisation or body eligible to perform the work or render services, the procuring agency shall hold competition amongst them through limited tendering (notifications) without any advertisements; however, giving reasonable time for submission of their applications or proposals. The IMF had also suggested that the procuring agency shall devise a mechanism for determining price reasonableness to ensure that the prices offered by the state-owned entities are reasonable for award of the contract. Provided that, in case the entity engages in subcontracting beyond the permissible limit, it shall fall within the ambit of material deviation.
PPRA Managing Director Hasnat Ahmed Qureshi said that the new rules provide a modern regulatory framework designed to strengthen transparency, competition, accountability, efficiency and value for money in public procurement. Qureshi said the new rules introduce a range of measures to strengthen oversight throughout the procurement cycle, from procurement planning and bidding to contract management, performance evaluation and closure.

title: Food imports raise supply shock risk
description: Food imports raise supply shock risk
content:
FAO says climate change, geopolitical tensions, high prices threaten access to food
Pakistan's food security challenge is rapidly shifting from the question of producing enough crops to whether the country can afford to continue importing the food it fails to produce competitively, with rising import dependence exposing both consumers and foreign exchange reserves to global price and supply shocks.
The problem is not unique to Pakistan. Latest UN estimates show that about 645 million people, or 7.8% of the world's population, faced hunger in 2025, while around 2.1 billion people experienced moderate or severe food insecurity. Although both figures improved from 2024, the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) has warned that progress remains fragile, with climate shocks, geopolitical tensions, trade disruptions and high food prices continuing to threaten food access.
Global food markets have already shown how quickly these pressures can reach importing countries. The FAO Food Price Index averaged 133.3 points in August 2026, up 1.9% from July and 2.5% from a year earlier. FAO attributed the latest increase to supply concerns linked to adverse weather, the Middle East conflict and disruptions affecting trade logistics.
For Pakistan, the vulnerability is particularly significant because agriculture remains a major part of the economy while the country continues to spend substantial amounts of foreign exchange on food that could potentially be produced or processed domestically.
According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, the country's food bill rose 11.66% to $9.150 billion in FY26. Currently, the government is once again looking to import wheat to stabilise markets, despite claims of a bumper crop this year. At the same time, Pakistan's food export performance has weakened. Food exports fell 29.49% to $5.02 billion, creating a deficit of $4.17 billion.
This widening gap between food imports and exports has raised concerns among agricultural and business-sector stakeholders about the structure of Pakistan's farm economy. Shahid Imran, Convener of the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry's Regional Committee on Food, called for greater private investment in seeds and agricultural supply chains, arguing that better inputs and supply-chain efficiency could raise yields, exports and rural incomes.
He said Pakistan needed to diversify its agricultural priorities towards crops such as oilseeds and pulses, where import dependence remained high, while improving productivity, quality and value addition to meet both domestic requirements and international standards.
People associated with agriculture business call such new initiatives long-term investment, which could help the country compete in global markets.
Najam Mazari, head of an organisation working on organic agriculture and products, said Pakistan's inability to develop modern agricultural research, technology and value-addition capacity had limited its ability to compete in international markets. He called for specialised agricultural research and educational institutions focused on technology, food processing, international marketing and agricultural policymaking.
The case for such a shift is strengthened by the performance of Pakistan's agriculture itself. The Economic Survey shows that agriculture grew 2.89% in FY2026, while wheat production increased 4.3% to 29.6 million tons, rice production rose 2.8% to almost 10 million tons and sugarcane output increased 6.2% to 89.45 million tons. However, stronger production of major crops has not eliminated the need for large food imports.
Climate change adds another layer of risk. Pakistan is highly exposed to floods, droughts and heat waves, all of which can disrupt crops, livestock, transport and food supply chains. The World Food Programme estimates that 20.7% of Pakistan's population is undernourished and 40% of children under five are stunted, while recurrent climate shocks continue to affect food and nutrition security.
The challenge, stakeholders say, therefore, is no longer simply to increase the acreage under cultivation. Pakistan needs higher yields, better seeds, efficient water use, storage and cold-chain infrastructure, stronger agricultural research and greater investment in processing and marketing. A more diversified farm economy could also reduce the country's exposure to international commodity prices while creating exportable value beyond traditional crops.

title: Relaxation from ban on new vehicles sought
description: Relaxation from ban on new vehicles sought
content:
PM approves purchase of 45 bulletproof vehicles out of 65 requested
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has turned down a proposal for the procurement of a large number of bulletproof vehicles for the heads of state who will arrive for a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) next September.
The Cabinet Division requested for the procurement of 65 bulletproof vehicles but the PM gave approval for 45 vehicles. The government decided to relax the ban on the purchase of new vehicles imposed by the cabinet under austerity measures to procure bulletproof vehicles.
In a recent meeting, the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) allowed procurement of 15 additional bulletproof vehicles costing Rs3 billion for the SCO Council of Heads of State Summit scheduled for September 2027. It directed the Cabinet Division to submit a case to the cabinet for relaxation in the ban on buying new vehicles.
It also gave directives to prepare a case for exemption from duties and taxes under relevant provisions of the Customs Act 1969, Sales Tax Act 1990 and Federal Excise Act 2005.
During discussions, the Cabinet Division said that the proposal was placed before the ECC in continuation of an earlier summary submitted on September 7, 2026 for provision of Rs12.61 billion through a technical supplementary grant for the purchase of bulletproof and soft-skin vehicles for the SCO Council of Heads of State Summit. In response, the ECC had approved a grant of Rs6.60 billion for 30 Mercedes Benz-Maybach S680 Guard (VR10) for VVIP security.
The Cabinet Division explained that, in line with the ECC directive to resubmit the case for the remaining vehicles, after further review and following the PM's directive and consultation with the deputy PM, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Interior, their approval was taken for the procurement of additional vehicles.
ECC members emphasised that highest-standard bulletproof vehicles were needed on account of high-level security arrangements, especially keeping in view the internal and external threats.
The Cabinet Division shared that in a high-level meeting, chaired by the PM, to review the arrangements being made for the SCO Heads of State Summit, there was a unanimous agreement that 30 bulletproof vehicles would not suffice against the requirement of 65, particularly since the summit needed high-level security protocols.
It was observed that the SCO summit was a historic opportunity for Pakistan to further highlight its international stature and influence for the promotion of national interests. It was also noted that the bulletproof vehicles would take a considerably long time in manufacturing, especially in the case of right-hand drive, and the matter had already been delayed.
The Cabinet Division said that following the meeting, it was directed by the PM Office to place the case before the ECC, in consultation with the deputy PM and the ministries of foreign affairs and interior, at the earliest for an expeditious decision. Accordingly, the case was resubmitted for the PM's consideration prior to placement before the ECC.
Following consideration of the case and endorsements by the deputy PM and the ministries of foreign affairs and interior, the PM gave directives that the number of vehicles to be purchased would be reduced from 65 and only 45 vehicles would be bought. The PM told the Cabinet Division to amend the cost estimates accordingly for submission of the case to the ECC.
The Cabinet Division told the meeting that in compliance with the directive, 15 BMW 760i xDrive (VR9) bulletproof sedans, costing Rs3 billion, may be procured in addition to the 30 bulletproof Mercedes Benz Maybach S680 Guard (VR10) sedans, for which the ECC had already approved a supplementary grant of Rs6.60 billion.

title: Govt seeks funds for ML 1 upgrade
description: Govt seeks funds for ML 1 upgrade
content:
Iqbal informs development partners about advancement of $2.5b Karachi-Rohri rail project
Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal, currently on a three-day visit to Mongolia to attend the Carec International Conference, highlighted the strategic importance of modernising Pakistan Railways' Mainline-1 (ML-1), describing it as critical for expanding trade, freight capacity and regional connectivity.
Addressing the Development Partners Dialogue on Advancing Trade, Tourism and Regional Competitiveness, the minister presented Pakistan's ML-1 modernisation plan and briefed the development partners on the progress made towards upgrading the Karachi-Rohri section. He also held meetings with the Carec Institute and a delegation from Uzbekistan. Ahsan Iqbal said ML-1 was the backbone of Pakistan's railway network, stretching 1,726 kilometres from Karachi to Peshawar and carrying 76% of passenger traffic and 98% of freight traffic, despite significant infrastructure constraints. He stressed that modernising the corridor was not merely a railway development project but a national economic priority directly linked to Pakistan's trade and growth potential.
The minister said the proposed up-gradation would substantially increase line capacity from 34 to 120 train pairs, raise passenger train speeds up to 160 km per hour and freight train speeds from 30 to 80 km/h, while reducing Karachi-Rohri travel time from eight hours to approximately four and a half hours. The upgraded corridor will also support rising freight demand, projected to reach around 21 million tonnes annually by 2035.
Highlighting progress on the Karachi-Rohri section, Ahsan Iqbal said the $2.5 billion project was the most advanced component of ML-1 modernisation, with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) leading the financing effort and AIIB, World Bank, IsDB and EIB engaged as co-financing partners. He said the project had moved beyond the conceptual stage, with project readiness financing secured, engineering work undertaken and procurement and financing processes advancing.
The minister emphasised that Pakistan's objective was not to treat Karachi-Rohri as an isolated project but as the first step towards complete modernisation of the Karachi-Peshawar corridor. He said Pakistan was simultaneously working to develop a financing pathway for the remaining sections from Rohri to Peshawar.
"The key issue is no longer whether ML-1 needs modernisation; the requirement is clear. The priority now is to convert the progress already made on Karachi-Rohri into implementation while securing financing for the remaining corridor in parallel," Iqbal said.

title: Gold falls sharply on rising US Treasury yields
description: Gold falls sharply on rising US Treasury yields
content:
Loses Rs12,800 per tola; rupee inches up to 277.15/$
Gold prices in Pakistan fell sharply on Monday, tracking a steep decline in the international market, as rising US Treasury yields weighed on demand for the non-yielding precious metal.
The price of gold declined by Rs12,800 per tola to Rs438,136, according to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association (APGJSA). The price of 10-gram gold decreased by Rs10,973 to Rs375,631.
Gold had closed at Rs450,936 per tola on Saturday after declining Rs2,100 during the session. The latest decline came as international gold prices fell sharply amid a rise in US Treasury yields and renewed uncertainty surrounding the outlook for US rates. Spot gold dropped as much as 4% on Monday to $4,111 an ounce, its lowest level since August 5, before recovering some of its losses, as per Reuters. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since June 2007.
Higher bond yields can weigh on gold because the precious metal does not offer regular income, making it relatively less attractive when yields on assets rise. Adnan Agar, Director at Interactive Commodities, said gold had fallen to a low of $4,111, while the market was trading around $4,130 after opening near $4,250. The day's high was around $4,285. He attributed the immediate pressure on gold to rising yields on 10-year US Treasury bonds.
Agar said the latest decline could represent another downward leg in the market, but suggested that gold could find some support around $4,000 to $4,050 in the coming days and potentially stage a rebound from those levels.
He also said developments surrounding US-Iran tensions could have a significant impact on gold prices. According to Agar, even a short-term ceasefire between Iran and the United States could prove positive for gold by supporting demand for the precious metal.
Meanwhile, silver prices also declined in the domestic market. The price of silver fell Rs325 per tola to Rs6,578. The sharp movement in international gold prices is expected to remain an important factor for the domestic market, along with movements in the rupee-dollar exchange rate and global geopolitical developments. Local gold prices generally track international bullion rates, with changes also affected by currency movements and domestic market conditions. Meanwhile, the Pakistani rupee extended its marginal gains against the US dollar in the inter-bank market on Monday, closing at 277.15, up Rs0.01. The rupee had closed at 277.16 on Friday, gaining Rs0.09 during the previous week.

title: Govt to address Rs853b discrepancy
description: Govt to address Rs853b discrepancy
content:
Provinces' investment in treasury papers, late expenses behind data mismatch
Pakistan has assured the International Monetary Fund (IMF) that it will provide more information about the statistical discrepancy of Rs853 billion to address concerns as the country also could not boost agriculture income tax collection that stood around Rs5 billion last year.
The visiting IMF mission has held meetings on statistical discrepancies in the budget books of federal and provincial governments, huge federal block allocations, agriculture tax collection and federal revenue prospects. The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has linked the achievement of the annual Rs15.263 trillion target with the Middle East situation and its impact on Pakistan's economy, according to government officials.
Sources said that the IMF asked the finance ministry about the Rs853 billion statistical discrepancies in the accounts of five governments in fiscal year 2025-26. Out of the Rs853 billion, the discrepancies of Rs448 billion were in the federal government accounts.
However, the IMF was told that the discrepancy was more because of investments by the provincial governments in treasury papers, mismatch of cash withdrawals before the end of June and actual expenses in July and onwards.
A Rs266 billion discrepancy has been reported by the government of Punjab. An official of the Punjab Finance Department said that the provincial discrepancy was mainly because of operations of commercial accounts and the difference between outflows and inflows over the year in the commercial accounts. The provincial government said that another reason for the discrepancy was the difference between accounting procedures of the provincial and federal governments. A key factor was the delay in release of development funds till June, which resulted in huge savings.
To utilise the money, cheques are issued before June but the actual cash outflow from account-1 takes place after June 30, according to the provincial government. This is a routine in the last two weeks of June as accounts are closed and cheques are passed by the office of the accountant general but actual outflow takes place after June 30.
Sources said that the absence of a full rollout of the treasury single account was also contributing to large fiscal discrepancies as many government entities and authorities were still not depositing their funds in the single account. They said that the finance ministry had now assured the IMF that it would share more details to satisfy the mission. They added that the discrepancy would not have any adverse impact on the government's primary budget surplus of 2.9% of GDP.
The primary surplus is the core condition of the IMF programme, which the government says it has met and it is hopeful that the review talks will successfully conclude on October 7.
Sources said that the IMF also asked about updates from provincial governments regarding the agriculture income tax collection after increasing the rates from 15% to 45%. The 45% rate is equal to the business income tax rate.
The IMF was told that the agriculture income tax collection remained poor in the last fiscal year and there were chances that Punjab and Sindh would again miss their targets for the current fiscal year. According to details shared with the IMF, in the last fiscal year, the agriculture income tax target was Rs2 billion but the Sindh government collected only Rs1.1 billion. The target for this fiscal year is Rs6 billion, which will be missed again by at least Rs3 billion, said the sources.
The Punjab government's budget books showed that against the last fiscal year's target of Rs10.5 billion, the collection was only Rs4 billion. For this fiscal year, the agriculture income tax target of the Punjab government is Rs12.5 billion.
The IMF was told that a memorandum of understanding between the FBR and the Sindh government required data-sharing by the FBR of the agriculture income in FBR's returns. The FBR provided data of 44,350 people declaring agriculture income in returns for tax year 2025.
However, the provincial government was of the view that there was a need for real-time connectivity between the FBR and the Sindh Revenue Board. The provincial government has already transferred agricultural income tax administration from the Board of Revenue to the Sindh Revenue Board. It has also introduced digital registration and filing mechanisms for taxpayers to successfully achieve 3,650 registrations and 1,912 returns.
The IMF asked the FBR about missing last fiscal year's tax target and the prospects for the current fiscal year. The FBR missed last year's downward-revised target by Rs929 billion.
The IMF was told that the FBR would achieve its all key performance indicator targets, including digital invoicing and monitoring of production lines. The first-quarter target of Rs3 trillion would also be achieved, the IMF was assured.
However, the FBR remained non-committal about meeting the annual target of Rs15.263 trillion and told the IMF that it would depend upon how the regional security situation unfolds, the sources added.
The IMF also inquired about the poor response to the government's second fixed tax scheme for traders. It was told that the purpose was to provide a last chance to traders before the government begins crackdown by imposing penalties, the sources added.

title: Reacher  renewed for season 6 ahead of season 5 premiere

content:
Prime Video renews 'Reacher' for season 6 as Alan Ritchson’s action series continues its global success
Prime Video has renewed Reacher for season 6, extending the action series starring Alan Ritchson before season 5 has premiered.
The renewal comes as the Amazon series continues to attract a large global audience. According to Amazon, Reacher season 4 reached 66 million viewers worldwide within its first 28 days after launching on August 12. The eight-episode season concluded on September 16.
The series has now reached 200 million viewers globally across all seasons, while season 4 ranks among the five most-viewed seasons of an Amazon original series on Prime Video, according to the company.
Ritchson stars as Jack Reacher, the former military investigator at the centre of the series based on Lee Child’s bestselling novels. Season 4 was adapted from Child’s Gone Tomorrow , which follows Reacher after a chance encounter on a subway draws him into a dangerous situation.
Production on Reacher season 5 is currently underway in Toronto. The upcoming season is based on Child’s novel Make Me and will continue Ritchson’s run as the title character.
Nick Santora serves as writer, showrunner and executive producer on the series. Child and Ritchson also executive produce, alongside Don Granger, Scott Sullivan, Mick Betancourt, Lisa Kussner, Sam Hill, Amy Pocha and Seth Cohen.
The renewal follows the recent launch of Neagley , a Reacher spinoff starring Maria Sten as Frances Neagley. The series is produced by Amazon MGM Studios and Paramount Television Studios.
Amazon has not yet announced additional details about the Reacher season 6 storyline or its release date.

title: What a week at Oxford taught me about character formation
description: What a week at Oxford taught me about character formation
content:
'Character' reaches us from the Greek charakter, meaning the mark stamped on a coin
Teaching has gone on in Oxford for nine centuries, and it has never confined itself to what a person knows; it has always cared what a person becomes. In the first week of September I went back to my old university and became a student there again, for five days of Leadership and Character Training, the programme the Oxford Character Project has built on a decade of research.
I did not go there to be persuaded. I had already argued in these pages that education without character cannot build a nation, and that taleem and tarbiyat must be held together rather than one of them left to chance. I went for something narrower: to find out whether character can be formed on purpose in the young men and women who pass through our universities, and if so, how.
I came back with more than I went for. Pakistan has spent decades repairing its institutions by changing rules, structures and faces, and almost never by changing what they form in those who pass through them. Our universities gather a whole generation at the ripe young age when it can still be shaped: if character can be formed on purpose, our campuses offer the most powerful instrument of human development.
"Character" reaches us from the Greek charakter, meaning the mark stamped on a coin. The worth of a coin lies not in the metal but in the imprint; an imprint is not made in one stroke: it is pressed in by the same pressure in the same place, again and again. That is how character is formed: by habit, by reflection on yesterday, by small daily efforts nobody applauds. Aristotle said it plainly: we become just by doing just acts, and brave by doing brave acts. Character is not announced. It is pressed in.
We confuse it with two other things. The first is personality: what we naturally are, the introvert and the extrovert, the cautious and the quick. It is largely given, and it earns us no credit.
The second is values: the beliefs and principles we say matter most. Every organisation in Pakistan has them framed in the reception area, and every university a vision and mission statement to match. They are shallow unless something inside the institution firms up the character they describe. A value statement is an announcement; character is the set of settled habits, formed by repeated practice, that shape how a person thinks, feels and acts.
A value is tested only when holding to it costs you something: money, a promotion, a friendship, or simply your comfort. A value that has never been paid for is only an opinion. Take merit, which every university in Pakistan claims: it means nothing until the day a powerful man's son is turned down. That day the value is either paid for, or exposed; nobody was ever made honest by a powerful poster of values.
Pay that price once and you have done a good thing. Pay it often enough and it stops being a struggle: what began as a decision becomes second nature. Believing that truthfulness matters is a value. Telling the truth when it costs you, and then telling it again the following week, is character.
Then comes the idea that changed how I see my colleagues and myself. We think of virtue and vice as a pair: honesty against dishonesty, courage against cowardice, one good against one bad. Aristotle taught otherwise: every virtue is a middle point between two faults, deficiency and excess. He is careful to add that the middle is not a fixed midpoint; it is the right amount for the situation, and finding it takes judgement. The Oxford Character Project has made that old idea usable, naming for each strength the fault of too little and of too much.
Courage is the middle point between timidity and recklessness. Too little is the colleague who will not say the uncomfortable fact in a meeting, and who blocks a good idea because it is not his own. Too much is the leader who gambles his institution's reputation, because caution looks weak.
Humility sits between putting yourself first and putting yourself down. Too little is the professor whose name appears on papers he never read, and the student who asks a question in every class to be noticed; too much is the student who knows the answer and never raises her hand.
None of this is foreign to us; our own sources say it with greater force. The Quran calls the believers ummatan wasatan, a community of the middle way (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:143). It tells the believer neither to keep his hand chained to his neck nor to open it as wide as it will go (Surah Bani Israil, 17:29): miserliness and extravagance are both faults; the virtue is the measured middle.
And we have the exemplar. Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said he was sent for one purpose: to perfect good character. Long before the first revelation, the people of Makkah called him al-Sadiq and al-Ameen, the truthful and the trustworthy. Those names were earned in ordinary dealings repeated over many years. Character was established first; authority followed.
That leaves the harder question: can such habits be formed on purpose, in a crowded university, among young people already shaped by family and social media? The Oxford Character Project's answer is not sermons but a method: seven ways in which character is built, among them habituation, reflection, exemplars, the words we use, and friendships that hold us to account. That method, and what it would ask of a Pakistani university, is for a second article.
Nations are not built by people who hold the right values. They are built by people whose character holds when it costs them something.

title: Inland waterways of Pakistan  the untapped potential
description: Punjab government established the Inland Water Transport Development Company  IWTDC  as a pilot project
content:
Punjab government established the Inland Water Transport Development Company (IWTDC) as a pilot project
Inland waterways (IWs) are globally recognised as one of the most cost-effective and environmentally sustainable modes of transportation. Pakistan has a vast network of rivers and canals; however, the modal split is imbalanced, and the waterways remain untapped despite their cost-efficiency. This insight argues that Pakistan's untapped inland waterways could serve as a complementary third corridor for cost-effective transportation in the long term, beside roads and rails. Pakistan's modal split is heavily imbalanced, with roads carrying over 96 per cent of inland freight, rail carrying only 4 per cent, and waterways carrying 0 per cent. It increases logistics costs and puts pressure on road infrastructure. Pakistan consumes 58.8 million liters of petroleum products daily, with imports accounting for 67 per cent of the trade deficit. Volatile energy prices and environmental commitments make efficient, cleaner freight essential, underscoring the need to explore inland waterways.
Despite the Indus River system's navigation potential, having a vast network of rivers and canals, inland water transport (IWT) in Pakistan remains untapped due to an unresolved jurisdictional debate between federal and provincial stakeholders. However, colonial laws like the Canal and Drainage Act of 1873 and the Inland Steam-vessels Act of 1917 could be amended for use.
In 2014, the Punjab government established the Inland Water Transport Development Company (IWTDC) as a pilot project. Although it proved the feasibility of a 220 km stretch between Daud Khel and Attock, the pilot project was shelved in 2018 due to the absence of a legal and regulatory framework and a lack of clear financial viability for the provincial budget. The national freight and logistics policy of Pakistan 2020 proposed a three-phase development of IWT. Phase 1 included further work on the pilot project under IWTDC, including the development of an integrated terminal at Daud Khel. Phase 2 included its extension from Daud Khel to Tunsa, and Phase 3 would extend it from Tunsa to Sukkur.
Four primary economic efficiencies could drive the adoption of IWs as a third corridor. Firstly, IWs are the most fuel-efficient mode of bulk transport compared to roads and rail. To move 1,500 tons over 200 km, a single waterborne barge consumes only 1,600 litres of fuel, compared to 4,200 litres for three trains and 15,000 liters for 60 trucks. More precisely, barges use 8 to 10 times less fuel than cargo trucks and 3 to 4 times less than railways. Secondly, a 2022 World Bank report suggests that the operational costs of the Punjab IWT pilot project with roads and rails show that IWT's operating costs are also lower than those of the other models.
In addition, the cost of establishing waterways is also less than that of roads and rails. For instance, the IWT project in Punjab costs Rs 270 million/km, and maintenance costs are estimated at 2.5 per cent of the investment cost. In comparison, the cost of the 1726km ML1 Railway project is Rs1.89 trillion ($6.68 bn), i.e., Rs1075 million/km, while the cost of highway roads ranges from Rs175 to 600 million. Environmental performance provides another advantage. Inland water vessels emit less carbon dioxide per tonne-kilometre. A heavy goods vehicle (HGV) emits 164 grams of CO2 per tonne-kilometre and a train 48.1 grams, while Barges emit 33.4 grams.
Overall, the cost-benefit analysis indicates that the IWs as a third corridor are an economically viable option. The primary benefit arises from reduced transport and logistics costs. Economic viability improves when additional benefits, such as environmental externalities, the development of logistics zones, irrigation efficiency, and flood control measures, are included.
Several challenges to implementing integrated IWT at the national level make it non-viable in the short term. Some barrages (Jinnah, Chashma, Guddu, and Kotri) were already built with navigational locks, but upgrading them may cost Rs6.9 billion each. Some barrages, like the Sukkur barrage, lack navigational locks because they were built primarily for irrigation and flood control. There is also a lack of purpose-built terminals, and building one would cost Rs180 million. Dams, on the other hand, also block waterways. There is also a lack of standardised vessels and accessibility to Karachi Port and Port Qasim. Climate change is another major challenge. During winter, reduced river and canal flows hinder navigation. Climate modelling using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks projects a 17 per cent to 25.6 per cent increase in summer streamflow, potentially increasing the risk of catastrophic flooding and infrastructure damage.
Standard navigability for medium-sized craft requires a channel depth of 6 to 10 feet, which is available in many perennial stretches. However, in some waterways, physical obstructions, such as outcropping rocks and sandbars, narrow the channel. Sediment buildup has reduced flood-handling capacity by 17.75 per cent over 24 years. These challenges require proper dredging to make waterways viable and sustainable during flood seasons.
IWs are viable and cost-effective in the long term if pursued gradually through phased pilot projects on commercially viable stretches, drawing a lesson from Indian policy. However, it would have limited utility due to the existing modal split, infrastructure and geographical factors. Pakistan needs a unified national transport framework that integrates waterways with roads, railways, aviation and maritime transport under a unified Ministry of Transport and Communication.
IWs are not merely a transport alternative but a macroeconomic necessity. The national freight and logistics policy is a step in the right direction. The increasing energy costs, economic potential and environmental needs necessitate its continuation.

title: Which room am I standing in
description: Everyone will remember patriarchy in November
content:
Everyone will remember patriarchy in November
I am dedicating this piece to Ishmal - nine years old, from Madyan, Upper Swat. She went to school, came home, and was raped and killed by a neighbour before she could live to see the protests that followed - led by us, the women in burqas.
Her story leaves me with a question about myself: which room am I standing in? I am not writing this as a confident, blunt, intersectional feminist today. I am writing it as an ordinary Pakistani woman. Powerless - not helpless. There is a difference, and most days I am the only one who seems to know it.
Everyone will remember patriarchy in November - the international 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, running from November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, to December 10, Human Rights Day. Sixteen days, a hashtag, a candle, a panel. This is not that piece. This is about the other three hundred and forty-nine days, when nobody is counting.
A woman was hurt for looking at the sky. A woman was eliminated for dancing. A girl was punished for a TikTok. A woman was silenced for asking for a career.
Go and read about them yourself. I will not do that homework for you. The newspapers exist. The NGO reports exist. Some government data exists too, if you know where to dig, and if you are honest, you already know some of it without digging.
I only have questions today. No numbers. Numbers let you close the tab feeling informed. Questions do not let you close anything. How free am I, really? How liberal am I allowed to be, and by whose permission? How moral do I have to prove myself, every single day, just to walk out of my own front door?
Which place is safe? Home - is home safe? Bus stop. Road. The bus itself, packed, someone's hand where it has no business being. Park, in daylight, with children playing twenty feet away. Workplace, where "networking" and "mentorship" wear a hundred different faces. Grave - is even the grave safe? And what about the space that does not exist in any of those places - the inbox, the DM, the comment section, the group chat I am added to without being asked?
Which age is safe? Tell me. The diapers of a baby have not made her safe in this country. The diapers of an old woman, decades later, do not make her safe either. So where, exactly, in between infancy and old age, is the safe part supposed to be? I have been looking for it since I was a girl. I am still looking.
Whom do I trust? The aaya who raised me. The naukar who has been in the house longer than I have. The driver who knows my school run better than my own mother did. The cook. The father. Dada ji. Nana ji. Bhai jan. The uncle - mamu jan, chachoo, taaya jee - trusted like a holy figure simply because he was family, and family was not a category anyone taught me to question. The teacher. Sir. Molvi sahib, who is supposed to be closest to God. And the mother sometimes - who knows what is happening under her own roof and looks away, because looking away is easier than the alternative, or because she has nowhere else to take her children if she looks straight at it. I am not accusing any one person on this list. I am saying I no longer know, walking into a room, which one of these people is a guarantee and which one is a warning, and neither does any other woman I have ever asked.
Recently I had to ask The Express Tribune to remove my email address from my own introduction. I even changed my byline. A woman author with a listed email, whatever her age or social standing, apparently reads as an invitation for unasked messages. Call me a coward, call it bizarre, call me unable to handle a simple inbox - I am only admitting a vulnerability. And if I am this frightened, at my age, with my name, imagine the young, pretty girls and women with no social support, no wallet of their own.
Imagine what happens to them - in the courtyard, in the courtroom, in some heavily funded NGO running a helpline for survivors of domestic abuse. Imagine. Is geography our destiny? Are we simply in the wrong country, or carrying the wrong labels?
So this month, before anyone lights a candle for November, I am only asking. Not accusing, not quoting, not citing. Asking.
Which room am I standing in, right now, today, in this country I love enough to still be asking?

title: BRT deadline fatigue
description: Government must now ensure that the latest two month commitment is the last one
content:
Government must now ensure that the latest two-month commitment is the last one
For Karachi's commuters, University Road has become less a development project than an endurance test. The latest assurance from Sindh's Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon is that the road will now be completed within two months. That promise comes barely weeks after his earlier deadline to make the entire artery "100% motorable" by September 15 passed without the promised result.
Yet, these two are merely the latest among countless deadlines to have slipped. In January, Mr Memon said the main Red Line corridor along University Road would be completed by March. In June, commuters were told the road would reopen by the end of July. In August came the September commitment. Now, towards the end of September, Karachiites have been handed yet another two-month wait. At some point, repeated deadlines cease to inspire confidence. University Road is one of the city's busiest arteries. Work that drags on here affects a vast section of Karachi and turns an ordinary commute into a daily ordeal and a civic punishment. The government may point to progress on the Red Line and the opening of the Mosamiyat Flyover. That progress is welcome. It does not, however, answer the more important question of why the road itself has remained unfinished for so long despite repeated commitments. The problem is made worse by the enormous public investment involved. The Red Line project has already suffered construction stoppages, contractual difficulties and cost pressures. They point towards weaknesses in execution that deserve scrutiny when citizens have been forced to bear the consequences for years.
The government must now ensure that the latest two-month commitment is the last one. The remaining work should be pursued on a clearly defined schedule, with progress made public and responsibility fixed wherever targets are missed.

title: Taking away taxman s bias
description: Under new model  cases will be selected through computerised  risk based algorithm rather than by individual officers
content:
Under new model, cases will be selected through computerised, risk-based algorithm rather than by individual officers
The establishment of the National Faceless Centre (NFC) in Islamabad by the Federal Board of Revenue marks a significant shift in Pakistan's tax administration. By eliminating direct contact between taxpayers and tax officials, the initiative aims to curb corruption, reduce discretionary powers and enhance transparency in audit and assessment processes. The reform is also not as radical as opponents would claim - similar models have been employed for many years in countries such as the UK, Australia, and even India.
Under the new model, cases will be selected through a computerised, risk-based algorithm rather than by individual officers, and each case will pass through three separate hands - audit, assessment, and quality control. The initial focus will be on third-party data that shows visible wealth discrepancies, including air travel, luxury vehicles and lavish properties. This would help ensure that anyone facing a full audit already has some explaining to do, rather than being randomly called in. Also, given that almost all of Pakistan's ultra-rich underreport their incomes, third-party data alone will provide enough data to keep the FBR busy for several months.
However, legitimate concerns remain. The Finance Bill 2026 provides that NFC orders cannot be challenged on jurisdictional grounds alone. In effect, this means that the faceless adjudicators may well be shielded from procedural accountability. Smaller taxpayers with limited legal capacity may also face pressure to accept algorithmic settlement offers without meaningful paths to appeal. In a positive development, the National Assembly Standing Committee has flagged the need for safeguards against algorithmic manipulation, data tampering and privacy breaches. Hopefully, legislation and competent leadership will ensure that the tax authority does not fall victim to the impunity of its own officers, and citizens can begin to see tax season as a minor inconvenience, rather than a horror story.

title: Failing foreign guests
description: Recurring pattern severely damages Pakistan s international reputation
content:
Recurring pattern severely damages Pakistan's international reputation
The horrific allegations of a gang-rape involving a 20-year-old Azerbaijani business traveler in Lahore highlight a deeply concerning issue, reinforcing why our justice system must maintain a zero-tolerance policy toward such violence. The survivor's courage in recording a formal statement before a magistrate is commendable, challenging the societal stigmas that often silence victims. This legal step provides a pathway for authorities to implement robust damage-control and preventative strategies against such severe crimes. To foster a safer environment, all segments of society must support survivors and advocate for the strict punishment of offenders.
This is the second horrific assault on a foreign national in the last four months, exposing a deeply unsettling trend. In June, two women from the Netherlands and Venezuela were abducted from Islamabad and later sexually assaulted in Lahore, reportedly after they refused to pay extortion money. This recurring pattern severely damages Pakistan's international reputation, entirely undermining ambitious assertions of the country becoming a preferred destination for global tourism and foreign investment. Such heinous acts bring shame to a proud and resilient nation. The absolute minimum required now is a stringent, unyielding national policy where culprits are never spared and cases are prosecuted on an expedited, high-priority basis. Luring foreigners into fraudulent business deals to harm them is entirely unacceptable and must be crushed firmly.
It is high time to overhaul our surveillance and intelligence-gathering systems to ensure that criminal activity is intercepted before it can occur. Likewise, police and magistrates must be fully empowered to go above and beyond in prosecuting and sentencing culprits within an exemplary timeframe. Fast-track courts, statutory time limits and sweeping technological reforms must be legally mandated to ensure swift, undeniable justice. Reviving the largely dormant Safe City initiatives and boosting community involvement are indispensable steps to maintaining a strict vigil on unscrupulous elements.

title: Heroes and public safety
description: Let us keep this thought of risk and service to others in our minds for a second
content:
Let us keep this thought of risk and service to others in our minds for a second
A legacy of the Covid-19 years, I hope, is a broader recognition of the work of frontline workers. During some of the darkest days of the pandemic, there were communities, across the world, that would celebrate the extraordinary work of those at the forefront – physicians, nurses, technicians, first responders and those who took a personal risk to keep the disease at bay. This idea of heroism is the same across many facets of life in a society – of personal risk, high likelihood of a terrible outcome, and service to others.
Let us keep this thought of risk and service to others in our minds for a second. And now bring in another idea – the idea that some of the places among our midst are dangerous, likely to breed infection and are contaminated by nasty bugs. It is places that bring wastewater, sewage and other organic and inorganic waste together. From a public health point of view, making sure that these places follow health and sanitation guidelines is essential for the wellbeing of society. A lapse there can risk the lives of millions.
Now let us combine the two thoughts. Of places of highest risk, and people who work in those places. We all know who works in those places in our society, and yet, we cannot imagine considering these people ever as heroes, or people who we owe a great debt of gratitude. In fact, we are far on the other extreme. We consider those who work in these awfully difficult and toxic places, full of pathogens, as the lowest amongst us. We have all kinds of terrible names for them. So much so that official advertisements for jobs to do this work specifically list that these are only open to non-Muslim members of our community – suggesting that these jobs are beneath the dignity of much of society. I cannot imagine large sections of society would ever consider sanitation workers as people who keep us safe. This notion of recognition of their work as an integral pillar of public safety, worthy of deep respect, would be considered laughable by many and even offensive by a certain sizeable section.
The reason to bring this up this week is three-fold. First, I read an editorial in a leading English daily last week describing the plight of the sanitation workers in Pakistan, and the fact that this year alone, twenty-six sanitation workers have died while doing their jobs. I cannot say that I was shocked, but I am glad that newspapers are bringing up the issue. Second, in the world of infectious diseases, wastewater and sewage has become a major topic of research and discussion, and there is rigorous data showing how these conditions create an enabling environment for nasty pathogens. At conferences on infection, the issue of wastewater is front and centre. To imagine someone working there for a poor salary, and no dignity, would be unacceptable to anyone who cares about human dignity or public health. Third is perhaps a personal reason. I live in a town slightly outside the city that was settled two centuries ago. Our home has its own septic tank (as opposed to town sewage in some of the newer areas). Over the weekend, we got our septic tank serviced. I am indebted to the person who came and serviced it – and if it was not for him (or another person like him), we would risk fines, damage to our property and exposure to disease. Since I had already read the editorial by then, as I spoke to him, I wondered about our interaction. Indeed, this was a professional business transaction, but also one where I was benefitting from his experience, wisdom and his ability to keep my home safe. The idea that somehow he is different from me, or somehow, I am better in any shape or form would be preposterous.
Much is said about our 'values' of respect for those who help us. That may be true, but only after a long list of qualifiers has been applied. For some who keep us safe, we use the most extraordinary language of gratitude, for others, we expect them to be grateful to us for being allowed to exist.

title: Hayden Panettiere   s ex seeks guardianship of daughter Kaya after actress    death
description: Wladimir Klitschko seeks temporary guardianship of Hayden Panettiere   s daughter Kaya following the actress    death
content:
Wladimir Klitschko seeks temporary guardianship of Hayden Panettiere’s daughter Kaya following the actress’ death
Wladimir Klitschko has filed a petition seeking temporary guardianship of his and Hayden Panettiere’s daughter, Kaya, following the actress’ death at age 36.
According to court documents obtained by TMZ, Klitschko is asking to be appointed temporary guardian to protect Kaya’s interests as the sole beneficiary of Panettiere’s estate. The petition states that Kaya is not a California resident but is entitled to assets being handled through probate proceedings in the state.
Klitschko also raised concerns about property belonging to Panettiere’s estate. He claimed that federal agents accessed the actress’ home as part of an ongoing investigation and removed some of her belongings. He is seeking authority to represent the estate and recover any property that may be returned after the investigation concludes.
The petition also states that Panettiere had previously hired a security service to protect her home and belongings following concerns about unauthorised access to her property. According to the filing, the locks were changed after her death, while storage units containing designer clothing and accessories were moved as a precaution.
Klitschko further expressed concern that someone could attempt to take property belonging to Panettiere’s estate. He argued that a personal representative should be appointed to safeguard the actress’ home and belongings.
Panettiere and Klitschko welcomed Kaya in 2014. According to the court filing, Panettiere died without a will, meaning Kaya is expected to inherit her property, including her West Hollywood condominium, subject to the probate process.
Panettiere died on August 16 at the age of 36. The guardianship petition concerns the management and protection of her estate and Kaya’s inheritance.

title: Hugh Laurie joins HBO   s true crime series  The Trial of Louise Woodward
description: Hugh Laurie joins HBO   s true crime series  The Trial of Louise Woodward  as Judge Hiller B  Zobel in key role
content:
Hugh Laurie joins HBO’s true-crime series 'The Trial of Louise Woodward' as Judge Hiller B. Zobel in key role
Hugh Laurie has joined HBO’s upcoming true-crime limited series The Trial of Louise Woodward , adding to the cast of the drama from creator Matthew Barry.
Laurie will play Judge Hiller B. Zobel, the Massachusetts Superior Court judge who presided over the murder trial at the centre of the series. He joins Catriona Chandler, who stars as Louise Woodward, alongside Joanne Froggatt, Meghann Fahy, Sagar Radia and Chloë Sevigny.
The Trial of Louise Woodward is based on the real-life case involving an 18-year-old British au pair who was accused in 1997 of shaking to death Matthew Eappen, a baby in the care of her American host family. The case attracted widespread attention in both the United States and the United Kingdom as Woodward’s trial unfolded.
Froggatt plays Woodward’s mother, Susan, while Fahy and Radia portray Deborah and Sunil Eappen, the parents of the victim. Sevigny plays Woodward’s defence attorney, Elaine Whitfield Sharp.
Barry wrote the limited series and serves as showrunner and executive producer. Susanne Bier is directing all episodes and executive producing alongside Barry, Frank Spotnitz, Emily Feller, Tobi de Graaff and Antoine Douaihy. Big Light Productions and Anton TV are producing the series.
The HBO project marks Laurie’s third collaboration with the network after his roles in Veep and Avenue 5 . He is also known for starring as Dr Gregory House in the medical drama House and has appeared in The Night Manager .
