title: Rs770m  flood fighting  bill despite no flood in Sindh
description: Rs770m  flood fighting  bill despite no flood in Sindh
content:
Provincial irrigation department seeks funds for 2025 emergency works; experts question spending
A Rs770 million "flood-fighting" bill has landed on the Sindh government's table despite the absence of any major flood emergency last year, raising questions over a demand for public funds that the irrigation authorities say was incurred on emergency protection works, The Express Tribune has learnt.
The Sindh Irrigation Department has sought approval from the chief minister for the release of more than Rs770 million in alleged liabilities for works carried out during "Flood Fighting 2025", according to a departmental summary. Sources, however, allege that several of the works listed in the documents were either not carried out or were overstated.
The controversy centres on a summary prepared on the basis of a report by a committee headed by Chief Engineer Junaid Talpur. The central technical committee subsequently cleared the claimed expenditures, while chief engineers reportedly certified the bills as verified.
The department has defended the additional funding demand by pointing to sharp increases in the prices of cement, steel and diesel following the introduction of the Composite Schedule of Rates 2024. But irrigation experts have questioned whether such a substantial expenditure was justified in a year when the province did not face a major flood emergency.
Mir Abdul Karim Talpur, Secretary Information of the Sindh Chamber of Agriculture, called for an independent third-party audit of the works and suggested that satellite imagery be used to establish whether the projects were actually executed.
According to sources, works described in official documents as emergency measures for the protection of embankments were not carried out at several sites. They alleged that construction material, diesel, machinery, and labour costs were cited to justify the claimed expenditure.
The department, however, maintains that the additional funds are justified by the sharp rise in input costs. Officials have argued that prices of cement, steel and diesel have increased substantially since CSR 2024, making additional funding necessary.
The technical committee has also maintained that the expenditures were subjected to scrutiny before the summary was forwarded to the chief minister for approval.
The issue comes against the backdrop of a broader funding dispute within the Irrigation Department. Along with the Rs770 million in alleged flood-fighting liabilities, the department has sought substantial additional allocations for region-wise maintenance for fiscal year 2025-26.
According to the summary, the department requires Rs100 billion, while the Finance Department has released Rs32.543 billion - around 32% of the amount sought. Over the past five years, the department has received a total of Rs30.444 billion, according to the figures cited in the summary, which also include expenditure relating to the devastating floods of 2022.
The conflicting funding claims have raised questions about the department's financial priorities. While officials have cited a shortage of funds for maintenance and improvement of the irrigation network, questions are being raised over the proposed release of more than Rs770 million for works allegedly undertaken during a year without a major flood emergency.
The issue is also linked to longstanding complaints by contractors over unpaid liabilities. According to sources, contractors have billions of rupees outstanding with the department and have repeatedly been told that payments cannot be made because of a lack of funds and existing liabilities.
Multiple attempts were made to obtain the views of Irrigation Secretary Zareef Khero and Technical Committee Chairman Riaz Shah, but neither responded to requests for comment.
Mir Abdul Karim Talpur expressed concern over the scale of the proposed flood-fighting expenditure, saying such a large amount during generally normal weather conditions warranted scrutiny. He called for a third-party audit of all the works listed in the summary and proposed using satellite imagery to independently verify whether the projects had actually been executed.
Talpur said the department could not use an increase in the CSR as a blanket justification for every increase in expenditure. "Flood fighting is essentially an emergency activity and generally involves stone and earthwork," he said, adding that claims involving substantial expenditure on cement and steel should therefore be examined carefully.
He urged the provincial chief minister to order an independent and transparent investigation into the summary before approving the requested funds.
Speaking to The Express Tribune, Talpur said there were also concerns at the local level about the repair of protective embankments and the use of stone and machinery at several sites.
He stressed the need to ensure transparent utilisation of public funds and said accountability institutions, including the National Accountability Bureau and Anti-Corruption Establishment, should examine the matter where warranted.
Several farmers and residents in Hyderabad and Dadu have also expressed concern over the reported expenditure and the condition of flood-protection infrastructure in their areas.
Sindh Agriculture Board Chairman Mahmood Nawaz Shah, speaking to The Express Tribune, criticised what he described as the deteriorating state of the province's irrigation network, inequitable water distribution and alleged irregularities in development projects.
He said Pakistan was already facing a serious water shortage, while problems within the irrigation system were compounding the difficulties faced by farmers and growers.
According to Shah, the biggest challenges confronting Sindh's irrigation network are inequitable water distribution and poor governance. He said the system had deteriorated to such an extent that farmers at the tail-end of canals often failed to receive adequate water even when sufficient quantities were available in the rivers.
Shah said the problem was not limited to years of low rainfall. Even when water was available, he alleged, poor management resulted in crops in tail-end areas drying up. He cited complaints from farmers in Dadu, Wara and adjoining areas, who, according to him, were facing declining agricultural productivity because they were not receiving their due share of irrigation water.
Rainfall, he said, could provide only temporary relief, while the underlying problem remained the equitable and transparent distribution of water.
Speaking about irrigation infrastructure, Shah said much of the provincial network had become old and dilapidated despite substantial funds being allocated for maintenance and repairs. He alleged that funds released for maintenance were being misused while little corresponding improvement was visible on the ground.
Shah referred to the failure of a gate at Sukkur Barrage two years ago and the earlier collapse of part of the Rohri Canal structure, attributing both incidents to what he described as negligence and inadequate maintenance.
He called on the government and relevant authorities to undertake urgent rehabilitation of the province's irrigation infrastructure, introduce modern monitoring technologies, curb corruption and ensure equitable distribution of irrigation water.

title: Pakistan to host SCO coordinators meeting
description: Pakistan to host SCO coordinators meeting
content:
Pakistan is set to hold the first meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation's (SCO) Council of National Coordinators (CNC) under its chairmanship in Islamabad from Monday (today), with the three-day session set to contribute to preparations for the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting that Pakistan will host in August 2027, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Sunday.
According to a statement on X, the meeting will be held from September 28 to 30 and will be chaired by Pakistan's National Coordinator for the SCO, with national coordinators from SCO member states and representatives of the SCO Secretariat in attendance.
The national coordinators will discuss a "wide range of issues relating to SCO cooperation and coordination", including the "programme of activities under Pakistan's Chairmanship", preparations for upcoming SCO meetings and events, and other matters on the organisation's agenda, the FO said.
The meeting would mark an "important initial engagement" under Pakistan's chairmanship and would contribute to preparations for "various high-level engagements and activities" to be undertaken during the chairmanship, including the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting to be hosted by Pakistan in August 2027.
Pakistan, which holds the chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026-27, would seek to advance the organisation's objectives under the theme "Turning Vision into Action: Connectivity, Innovation and Shared Prosperity", according to the FO.
"In this regard, Pakistan's Chairmanship would focus on promoting greater connectivity, fostering innovation, enhancing economic cooperation, and strengthening people-to-people contacts," it said.
The FO said the aim would be to "translate the shared vision of Member States into practical and mutually beneficial initiatives".
"Pakistan would work closely with all Member States and the SCO Secretariat to advance these priorities and further strengthen cooperation within the SCO," it said.
The CNC meeting will therefore provide an early forum for coordination among member states as Pakistan begins its programme of activities as chair of the SCO Council of Heads of State, the FO said.
According to the statement, the meeting would contribute to preparations for various high-level engagements and activities during Pakistan's chairmanship, including the August 2027 meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of State.
Earlier this month, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif travelled to Bishkek for a three-day official visit to attend the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting and the SCO Plus Summit, where Pakistan assumed the organisation's chairmanship for 2026-27.
Under the chairmanship, Pakistan will lead the SCO's top-level deliberations and host the organisation's summit in Pakistan in 2027.
During the visit, Shehbaz proposed an "excellent plan" focused on key sectors including information technology and artificial intelligence, energy development, poverty reduction, disaster management, health, culture and sports.

title: Five arrested near UK airbase used by US
description: Five arrested near UK airbase used by US
content:
British police arrested five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences near a US airbase on Sunday after receiving a tip-off about three suspicious vans heading towards the military airfield, which has been used by the United States to strike Iran.
Counter Terrorism Policing said police received a call about three vehicles apparently travelling towards RAF Fairford in western England in the early hours. Armed officers arrested five men, who were later held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.
Police said the incident was contained and that a 400-metre cordon had been placed around the base while bomb disposal officers examined the vans. Residents of 85 homes in a nearby village were evacuated, while armed officers patrolled the area.
"We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody," Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator Vicki Evans said. "As you would expect we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident."
US President Donald Trump said the suspects had been looking to do "big damage" and had been under investigation by British and US authorities. "The arrest in the UK was fantastic," Trump told reporters, describing it as "an amazing job".
He said the suspects had been under observation for a long time and that cooperation between British and US authorities had led to their arrests. The British police have not publicly identified who they believe was involved.
A source familiar with the investigation said an Iranian-linked motive was considered the most likely, while a Russian sabotage operation or an Islamist plot were also being examined. Security was also increased at other US-used bases, with armoured vehicles and soldiers seen at the gates of RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in eastern England.
The British government has authorised the US to use bombers based at Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. It said Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being updated on the incident.
Britain said in July that its armed forces were ready to protect the country from any attack after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned it against allowing US bombers to fly from Fairford, saying any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.
A local farmer told the Daily Telegraph she had alerted police after seeing vans and men acting suspiciously while returning from a party. Local councillor Tristan Wilkinson said there had been a recent security alert at Fairford and surveillance had been stepped up.
A US Air Force spokesperson declined to discuss specific force protection measures but said the 501st Combat Support Wing and other UK-based wings remained vigilant and would take appropriate measures to ensure the safety and security of US personnel, civilians, contractors and their families.

title: Protest postponement  govt reopens GT Road
description: Protest postponement  govt reopens GT Road
content:
Imran Khan's PTI announced its decision to postpone its much-touted long march to Islamabad two days ago. However, government authorities failed to reopen all routes leading to the federal capital even on Sunday, providing only partial relief to commuters.
On Friday, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, following a meeting of the PTI political committee, announced that the opposition party was postponing the planned protest march originally scheduled for September 27 till October 4.
Following this announcement, government authorities started an operation to clear hurdlesshipping containers and spiked metal sheetsplaced on the GT Road and M-1 and M-14 motorways.
The operation to remove the hurdles at Attock Khurd on National Highway N-5 concluded late Saturday night, allowing traffic on the GT Road to resume. Other points along the GT Road were also reopened, and traffic continued flowing on N-5 on Sunday morning.
The M-1 motorwayclosed in both directions with walls of containers and mud bags erected between Swabi and Islamabadwas also reopened for traffic in the wee hours of Monday.
Traffic, however, remained suspended on the M-14 motorwayalso known as the Hakla-Dera Ismail Khan section of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridoruntil 10pm on Sunday.
Officials said reopening the motorways was taking time because of the manner in which the roads had been sealed. An officer, speaking to The Express Tribune, said the barriers were installed so firmly that the containers first had to be emptied of sand or mud bags before removal.
The officer said work to remove the barriers from M-14 was continuing and the routes would open for traffic as soon as all points were cleared.
Meanwhile, the prolonged closure of roads in Rawalpindi and Islamabad amid security measures ahead of the PTI long march has brought commercial activity in the twin cities to a virtual standstill, leaving transport terminals deserted and thousands of daily-wage workers without employment.
Transporters said goods terminals remained largely empty, while hotels, motels, inns, marriage halls and private hostels were either closed or operating with little business.
Transport Federation Patron-in-Chief Haji Zahoor Arain said transporters had been badly affected by the closure of terminals and demanded that transport stands inside the cities be reopened.
He said the temporary reopening of the Attock Bridge demonstrated that roads could be restored when the security situation permitted, urging the authorities to take similar steps for transport terminals and commercial routes in Rawalpindi and Islamabad.

title: K P abuzz with talk of political change
description: K P abuzz with talk of political change
content:
PTI-led set-up in flux as Centre-province rift widens, Governor's rule, emergency under consideration
Political uncertainty deepened in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) on Sunday amid growing tensions between the federal and provincial governments, with the Centre considering governor's rule and emergency as possible options, while Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) is also weighing its options in response.
According to sources, the federal government is considering imposing governor's rule or emergency in the province amid a deteriorating security and political situation. The PTI, which is governing the province, is also considering an in-house change or dissolution of the provincial assembly.
The developments come amid continued tensions following PTI's announcement of an Islamabad march. Although the protest was postponed from September 27 to October 4, the standoff between the federal and provincial governments remains unresolved, the sources said.
Reports have also emerged about the possible disqualification of the chief minister, his replacement, an in-house change, dissolution of the assembly and a no-confidence motion against him under Article 136 of the Constitution.
The no-confidence motion can be submitted to the assembly secretariat with signatures of 20% of the total membership, following which an assembly session is to be convened within three to seven days on a single-point agenda.
The assembly rules lay down the procedure for a no-confidence motion. After the motion is moved in the house, voting is held through a secret ballot, with members expressing their choice in two separate lobbies. If the motion succeeds, the speaker will issue a schedule for the election of a new chief minister.
The Constitution also provides for the governor to require the chief minister to seek a vote of confidence under Article 130(7). If the governor believes the chief minister has lost the confidence of the majority in the house, the chief minister is required to demonstrate his numerical strength in the assembly.
Amid these speculations, Chief Minister Sohail Afridi said the provincial government did not want confrontation with the federation but wanted terrorism eliminated, peace established and the lives of soldiers, police personnel and civilians protected.
Addressing a press conference during a visit to Dera Ismail Khan, he said the objective was not merely to criticise the federal government but to establish peace and ensure that the voice of K-P, which continued to bear the greatest burden of terrorism, was part of the policy response.
Afridi said the fight against terrorism could be won if the federal government took the K-P government and its people into confidence, accepted the province's proposals and adopted an effective policy to eliminate terrorism.
At the outset of his press conference, he described the terrorist incident in Dera Ismail Khan as deeply tragic and strongly condemnable. He said terrorism was not only affecting the youth of K-P but soldiers serving from across Pakistan were also losing their lives, alongside police personnel and civilians.
"They are all our own people, part of the same society, irrespective of their province, sect or uniform," the chief minister said. "The people and youth of K-P understand how the present situation had emerged and who are paying the price."
Afridi said his government had consistently criticised every policy that harmed the people and Pakistan and voiced its opposition to policies being formulated behind closed doors. He said statements by representatives of the federal government and "those imposed in Punjab" were sufficient to demonstrate their lack of seriousness.
He referred to the Punjab chief minister's statement that there was no threat from India but from the other three provinces, as well as a statement by a Punjab minister describing the people of K-P as terrorists. He said other pro-government representatives were also making similar statements on television.
In contrast, Afridi said the seriousness of the K-P government was evident from its actions. Immediately after assuming office, the government allocated Rs35 billion for peace and security to provide resources to the police and other law-enforcement agencies and strengthen their infrastructure and capacity.
He also questioned the seriousness of the federal government and its institutions, citing the case of Heavy Industries Taxila (HIT), a federal institution that had received payment from the K-P government last year for the procurement of armoured personnel carriers (APCs), but had yet to provide the required equipment.
Similarly, he said, the National Radio and Telecommunication Corporation (NRTC), another federal institution, had been provided the necessary funds but had still not provided the deliverables. "I have raised the matter during recent meetings with federal institutions," he said.
He said modern APCs were available in Islamabad and were being used in operations against PTI, while K-P had repeatedly requested APCs for the fight against terrorism and had already made the payments. He said federal authorities had been asked to provide those APCs to K-P so they could be used against terrorism.
He said false narratives could no longer mislead the people of K-P or Pakistan, who were fully aware of the reality. He warned that language promoting hatred was deepening divisions and could have extremely harmful consequences.
"Pakistan is already facing difficult circumstances," he said, adding that any agenda or narrative creating hatred among provinces and people should be avoided because further escalation would harm everyone. He said policies formulated behind closed doors had not proved effective.
Over the past 22 years, around 22 major operations and 14,000 intelligence-based operations had been conducted, yet terrorism had not been eliminated and was instead increasing. "This demonstrated the need for a policy shift based on ground realities," he said.
He urged the federal government to exercise wisdom, recognise the gravity of the situation and consult those who understood the issue.
During his visit to Dera Ismail Khan, Afridi also visited a hospital and inquired after the health of people injured in the terrorist attack on Aman Mela Check Post. He was briefed on the treatment being provided to the injured. Former chief minister Ali Amin Khan Gandapur also accompanied Afridi during the visit.

title: Sindh offers unique blend of history  culture and natural beauty  CM
description: Sindh offers unique blend of history  culture and natural beauty  CM
content:
Shah says province has vast potential for domestic and international tourism
Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah on Sunday said Sindh offered a unique blend of ancient civilisation, history, culture and natural beauty, with vast potential to become an attractive and safe destination for domestic and international tourists.
In a message on World Tourism Day, CM Shah said Sindh was home to one of the world's oldest civilisations and a custodian of the heritage of the Indus Valley civilisation.
He described Mohen Jo Daro as a testament to thousands of years of Sindh's civilisation and Ranikot Fort, also known as the "Great Wall of Sindh", as an important part of the province's historical heritage.
The chief minister said Sindh's tourism potential extended from its archaeological sites and historic buildings to mountains, deserts, lakes, the Indus River and the coastline.
He highlighted Gorakh Hill for its scenic mountain landscape and Faiz Mahal in Khairpur as an example of the province's architectural and cultural heritage.
He also mentioned Sadhu Belo, Shah Jahan Minar and Sukkur Barrage among Sindh's important historical and cultural attractions.
According to the chief minister, the Kirthar mountain range, Karoonjhar Hills, Thar Desert and Achhro Thar represented the province's distinctive natural beauty and desert culture, while Manchar, Keenjhar and Haleji lakes offered opportunities for tourism and recreational activities.
He said Bhanbhore and Keti Bandar were important symbols of Sindh's ancient civilisation, history and trading heritage, while the province's coastline and marine islands had significant potential for tourism.
The chief minister said islands, including Manora, Bundal, Badu, Shamspir, Baba Bhit and Oyster Rocks could offer opportunities for marine tourism. He added that the coastal belt from Karachi to Keti Bandar, including Sea View, had considerable potential for marine and recreational tourism.
Highlighting Sindh's architectural heritage, CM Shah said the historic Makli necropolis and Chaukhandi tombs reflected the province's rich history, architecture and culture.
He said tourism was not merely about visiting scenic locations but also about connecting with thousands of years of civilisation, history, traditions and culture.
The chief minister said Sindh's Sufi traditions, folk culture, handicrafts, music and hospitality gave the province a distinctive tourism identity. He added that tourism could help strengthen the local economy and create employment and business opportunities, particularly for young people and local communities.
CM Shah said modern technology, digital platforms and artificial intelligence could be used to promote Sindh's tourist attractions globally and attract international visitors. He added that World Tourism Day was a reminder of the need to preserve historical heritage, protect natural beauty and promote sustainable tourism.
The chief minister said his government was continuing efforts to preserve historical sites and improve facilities for tourists. He invited tourists from Pakistan and abroad to explore Sindh, saying the province offered diverse experiences - from Mohen Jo Daro, Ranikot and Gorakh Hill to Karoonjhar, Thar, Keenjhar, Keti Bandar and Karachi's beaches.
The chief minister reiterated the government's commitment to developing Sindh as an attractive, safe and world-class tourism destination while preserving its historical and cultural heritage.

content:
The Sindh Health Department has relieved Drug Inspector Ghulam Ali Lakho of his current responsibilities following a complaint by the pharmaceutical industry alleging misuse of authority, harassment of pharma companies and unlawful demands.
Lakho, who also held the additional charge of Chief Inspector of Drugs, Sindh, has been directed to report to the Health Department. Health Secretary Tahir Hussain Sangi issued a notification formally relieving him of his existing responsibilities.
The Pakistan Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association (PPMA) had taken up the matter with the authorities, submitting a written complaint to the provincial chief secretary, Health Department and other senior officials on September 10, 2026.
In its complaint, the PPMA accused Lakho of allegedly misusing his authority, making unlawful demands and obstructing the lawful business activities of pharmaceutical companies, their authorised distributors and sellers.
The association alleged that some companies had faced threats of stock seizure, sealing of premises, bans on sales and legal action without a report from a government analyst or evidence of any offence.
The PPMA described the alleged actions as violations of the drug inspector's powers and established legal procedures and urged the authorities to intervene and take action.
The association also said the pharmaceutical industry played an important role in the country's economy and healthcare sector, warning that unlawful disruptions to the sale and distribution of medicines could lead to shortages of essential drugs and harm the public.
According to officials, the Health Department reviewed the PPMA's complaint along with other complaints received against Lakho. Following approval from the health minister, the department decided to relieve him of his current responsibilities.
The PPMA had also sent copies of its complaint to the chief minister, health and population welfare minister, health secretary, director general of the Anti-Corruption Establishment Sindh, director general of the FIA Sindh, additional director of DRAP Karachi, chairman of the Sindh PQCB and secretary of the Sindh PQCB, among other relevant authorities.

title: Unfrozen glacial lakes in Pakistan rise to 105
description: Unfrozen glacial lakes in Pakistan rise to 105
content:
Suparco warns of rising GLOF risks amid rising heat
The number of unfrozen glacial lakes in Pakistan has increased from 40 to 105 in less than two months, according to the latest satellite assessment by the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (Suparco), which warned authorities to maintain heightened preparedness amid rising temperatures.
In a press release, Suparco said the latest assessment was based on temporal satellite imagery, with the most recent image acquired on August 5. All identified lakes were mapped using optical satellite imagery to estimate their surface areas and determine whether they were frozen or unfrozen.
The space agency said the increase was expected with rising summer temperatures and the resulting seasonal melting of glaciers.
"At present, 105 lakes are observed to be unfrozen, compared with 40 lakes reported earlier," Suparco said, adding that the latest assessment also showed temporal variation in the extent of some lakes, with a few exceeding their previously recorded maximum extents.
Temporal variation refers to changes in the size or boundaries of a lake over time. Suparco noted that some water bodies had been found to be larger than their maximum recorded extents.
However, persistent cloud cover following the previous assessment in July limited the availability of cloud-free satellite imagery, making it difficult to accurately determine changes in lake areas, the agency said.
On July 2, Suparco had reported 40 unfrozen lakes, indicating accelerated seasonal melting. At the time, most of the unfrozen lakes remained within their previously recorded maximum extents.
According to Suparco, a glacial lake becomes a greater concern when its water extent expands beyond its historical maximum. Such expansion may indicate increased water storage and a greater possibility of moraine dam instability or failure, potentially increasing the risk of a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF).
Given the continuing rise in temperatures and the growing number of unfrozen lakes, Suparco advised all relevant authorities to maintain a high level of preparedness, particularly in downstream valleys located near potentially dangerous glacial lakes.
"Regular satellite monitoring will continue throughout the melt season to detect any rapid lake expansion or other signs of increased GLOF risk," the agency said, adding that the monitoring would enable timely dissemination of alerts and support proactive disaster-risk management.

title: LHC  money laundering separate from taxation
description: LHC  money laundering separate from taxation
content:
Says FBR can probe suspected money laundering without awaiting tax ruling
The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has welcomed a Lahore High Court (LHC) judgment ruling that money laundering is a separate offence and that the tax collector does not have to wait for the final determination of an income tax case before initiating such an investigation.
In a press release, the FBR said the ruling by a two-member LHC bench, comprising Justice Khalid Ishaq and Justice Hassan Nawaz Makhdoom, provided legal clarity and strengthened efforts to combat money laundering and financial crime.
The LHC dismissed a writ petition and related cases challenging the powers and actions of the FBR's Directorate General of Intelligence & Investigation, Inland Revenue (I&I-IR), holding that proceedings relating to money laundering and taxation were distinct and that one did not have to await the conclusion of the other.
The judgment held that the FBR's I&I-IR wing had full legal authority to register cases, investigate and prosecute offences under the Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010, the press release said.
The court held that money laundering involved dealing with proceeds obtained through illegal means and moving or disguising them in a manner intended to make them appear to be legitimate income. It ruled that a person could be prosecuted for money laundering even where there had been no prior conviction for the underlying offence that had generated the money.
The judgment observed that the Anti-Money Laundering Act was a special law and therefore took precedence over general laws in matters falling within its scope. Ongoing tax disputes, it said, could not be used to stop or delay money laundering proceedings.
The judgment also addressed suspicious transaction reports made by banks to the Financial Monitoring Unit (FMU), holding that subsequent action based on such reports fell within the legal framework and was subject to safeguards provided by law.
It further held that a writ petition before the High Court could not ordinarily be used to halt a criminal investigation at its preliminary stage. Questions concerning the source of funds and the manner in which they were moved would be examined by the competent Special Courts.

title: NADRA expands iris scan facility
description: NADRA expands iris scan facility
content:
Scan now available for children at 5,000-plus counters to counter identity theft
In a key safeguard against identity theft, the National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) has expanded biometric identification to minors using iris scans, making the facility available at more than 5,000 counters nationwide.
The ongoing drive is particularly focused on children under the age of 18, whose identification is being strengthened through photographs and biometric features.
According to the database authority, the iris-based identification will help protect children from identity theft and misuse, while also providing an alternative for elderly people, manual workers and others whose fingerprints cannot be captured because of illness or skin conditions.
Speaking to Express News on Sunday, NADRA Director of Media Shabahat Ali said the rules governing Pakistan's national identity card system were codified in 2002, when the country's political, geographical and economic circumstances were markedly different.
The situation surrounding Pakistan, particularly the Afghan war, regional developments and the security challenges facing the country, had also evolved considerably since then.
For nearly 23 years, registration continued under those rules, but several shortcomings emerged over time.
NADRA brought those issues to the Ministry of Interior and sought its guidance, following which the ministry referred the matter to the prime minister and significant reforms were introduced to the country's identity system.
A major component of the reforms was the protection of the identities of citizens below the age of 18, who account for around 46% of Pakistan's population.
Shabahat Ali said identification without a photograph could leave children vulnerable to identity theft or misuse, including situations in which one person could use another child's identity for his or her own child.
The reforms have also broadened the definition of biometric identification. Previously, biometric verification was largely understood in terms of fingerprints, but facial features and the iris of the eye are now also recognised as important identification markers.
NADRA has informed financial institutions that where fingerprints cannot be obtained because of age, illness or any other reason, an individual can be verified through facial recognition. The iris is considered a unique biometric marker and can provide a highly effective means of identifying an individual.

title: President  PM stress access to information
description: President  PM stress access to information
content:
Zardari, Shehbaz call for transparency, fact-checking
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif have reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to ensuring citizens' right to access accurate, timely and reliable information, while highlighting growing challenges posed by misinformation and emerging technologies.
In separate messages on the International Day for Universal Access to Information, being observed on September 28 (today), President Zardari said citizens could participate meaningfully in public life only when they had access to credible and reliable information.
He said the Constitution provided a clear foundation for this right, with the 18th Constitutional Amendment strengthening the framework for freedom of expression and inserting Article 19-A, which gave every citizen the right to access information on matters of public importance, subject to reasonable restrictions.
Zardari said the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017 further provided a legal framework for access to information at the federal level. He noted that the rapid growth of digital platforms, artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies had changed how information was produced, distributed and consumed.
"The challenge is no longer only whether information is available. It is also whether citizens can distinguish reliable information from content that is false, manipulated or deliberately designed to mislead," the president emphasised.
He said information could be distorted or weaponised by state and non-state actors, terrorist and criminal networks, as well as powerful technology companies, making access to accurate and credible information increasingly important for an informed democracy.
He called for greater attention to the role of journalists, media organisations, communication professionals, researchers and other experts in helping citizens navigate the changing information environment.
Prime Minister Shehbaz said the government was committed to providing accurate and authentic information, promoting transparency and safeguarding citizens' right to access information. He said the government was taking measures to strengthen communication between public institutions and citizens by harnessing modern technologies and digital platforms.
Shehbaz said the rapid spread of unverified, misleading and false information had emerged as a serious challenge, with information disorder capable of creating uncertainty and eroding public trust in institutions and information sources.
He stressed that timely dissemination of authentic information, greater transparency, rigorous fact-checking and responsible communication could help counter information disorder. He said that the process of digitising records of government offices and institutions was under way to preserve them and facilitate public access.
Shehbaz expressed confidence that the government, media, civil society, educational institutions, technology experts and citizens would work together to safeguard information integrity and build an informed, responsible and transparent society.

Pakistan Navy's newly inducted submarine PNS/M HANGOR conducted its maiden live weapon firing in the North Arabian Sea, accurately engaging a designated long-range target with an anti-ship cruise missile, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said on Sunday.

According to the ISPR, the ships were conducting a routine patrol when they intercepted a suspicious boat. A boarding operation was subsequently carried out, during which narcotics were recovered from "concealed compartments," it said.
Admiral Ashraf commended the officers and crew for their "professionalism and vigilance", ISPR added.
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif appreciated the Pakistan Navy on the first successful live-weapon firing of Hangor.
The president lauded Pakistan Navy's operational readiness and enhanced maritime defence capabilities.

title: Naqvi orders crackdown against cybercrime
description: Naqvi orders crackdown against cybercrime
content:
Interior minister directs NCCIA to intensify operation
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Sunday directed the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) to further intensify operations against online financial fraud, harassment, digital blackmail and organised cybercrime networks.
During his visit to the NCCIA Central Zone Headquarters in Lahore, the interior minister reviewed ongoing cybercrime operations and investigations in detail. He inspected the complaints cell, forensic laboratory and investigation wing and reviewed the entire process from registration of citizens' complaints to investigation and action against accused persons.
Chairing a special meeting, Naqvi directed that indiscriminate action be taken against organised groups involved in online financial fraud, fake accounts, digital blackmail and online harassment.
"Wherever a cybercriminal may be operating from, he must be brought within the ambit of law," he said.
The interior minister directed authorities to strengthen the immediate response mechanism for financial fraud complaints so that timely coordination with relevant institutions could help secure victims' funds and improve the chances of tracing the suspects.
"A citizen should not have to wait for months after filing a complaint. Timely progress should be visible on every complaint," Naqvi said.
He ordered a case-by-case review of pending cases and complaints and directed officials to eliminate unnecessary delays. He also called for enhanced digital forensic capabilities, the use of modern forensic tools and specialised training for investigation officers.
"New methods of cybercrime cannot be countered through traditional investigations; modern technology and trained human resources are required," Naqvi stated.
The interior minister said the NCCIA was to be developed into a modern cyber police force capable of protecting citizens in the digital world through advanced technology. He directed that complaints involving online harassment, blackmail and digital exploitation of women and children be accorded special priority.
Naqvi further underlined that protecting citizens' data, privacy, and financial interests was a fundamental responsibility of the NCCIA, adding that the agency was being provided with modern technology, necessary resources, and training to fulfil this responsibility.
He also directed the NCCIA to make its public awareness campaign against cybercrime more effective and ensure that citizens were promptly informed about new methods of online fraud.
The Director General (DG) NCCIA briefed the interior minister on the performance of the central zone, cases under investigation, emerging cyber fraud trends and ongoing operations.
DG FIA, inspector general Islamabad Police, director FIA Lahore Zone and other relevant officials were also present.

content:
Ceremony to feature Madonna's return to stage after 23 years; Taylor Swift to receive new career honour
The 2026 MTV Video Music Awards take place on Sunday, September 27, with Madonna returning to the VMAs stage for the first time in 23 years and Taylor Swift receiving a new career honour.
The ceremony will begin at 7:30pm ET/4:30pm PT and will air live on CBS and MTV. Viewers can also stream the ceremony live through Paramount+ Premium, which includes access to a local CBS station.
In a press release, the rapper said, "MTV and the VMAs have been part of my story since the beginning. Some of the biggest moments of my career happened on that stage and on MTV – they gave hip hop a place to be loud, fearless, and seen by the whole world. So to come back now and host the VMAs, all these years later, that's a full-circle moment for me."
Madonna will open the show, while Lisa, Raye, Shaboozey, Gunna, Sienna Spiro, Gener8ion and Yung Lean are among the other performers.
Raye, Sombr and Teddy Swims will honour George Michael, while Kacey Musgraves will perform a Dolly Parton tribute.
Nirvana will receive the Video Vanguard Award, while Swift will become the first recipient of the MTV VMA Artist Director Honors.
She is also set to premiere her new music video for "Patient Zero", starring Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell.
Madonna leads the nominations with 11, followed by Swift with 9. Ariana Grande and Sabrina Carpenter each have 7 nominations, while the ceremony will feature categories including Video of the Year, Artist of the Year, Song of the Year, Best Pop, Best Hip-Hop, Best R&B and Best Country.
The ceremony will recognize outstanding music videos and songs released between June 20, 2025, to June 18, 2026. Madonna was the most nominated artist, with thirteen. Nirvana will be honored with the Michael Jackson Video Vanguard Award, and Taylor Swift with the inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honors. The music video for Swift's song "Patient Zero" is set to premiere during the broadcast.
On September 16, 2026, Madonna was announced as opening performer, her first performance at VMAs in 23 years. The first round of performers were announced on September 17. The performers for the George Michael tribute were announced on September 22. A tribute to Dolly Parton by Kacey Musgraves was announced on September 23.
The nominees were announced on August 18, 2026. The nominees in the social categoriesBest Group, Best Long Form Video, Best Album and Song of Summerwere announced on September 18, with additional nominees for Best Album announced on the next day. Madonna led with thirteen nominations, tying Lady Gaga's 2010 record for the most nominations for an artist in a single year. She is followed by Taylor Swift with eleven; Sabrina Carpenter with nine; Ariana Grande with eight; Bruno Mars with seven; Ella Langley, PinkPantheress and Zara Larsson with five; and Charli XCX, Gener8ion, Katseye, Lisa, Olivia Rodrigo and Yung Lean with four.
The recipient of the Video Vanguard was announced on September 9, 2026. The recipient of the inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honors was announced on September 21.
The host of the ceremony is Snoop Dogg, an American rapper, singer, record producer, record executive, songwriter, and actor. A key figure in West Coast hip-hop, he helped define G-funk and gangsta rap, and is often regarded as one of the greatest rappers of all time. Known for his signature drawled delivery and melodic flow, his lyrics frequently address social issues such as recreational drug use and gun violence.
He rose to prominence in 1992 through his collaborations with Dr. Dre, first on the single "Deep Cover" and later on The Chronic, including "Nuthin' but a 'G' Thang".
Snoop Dogg has sold over 35 million records worldwide. In 2022, he co-headlined the Super Bowl LVI halftime show, earning a Primetime Emmy Award. He has received several accolades including seventeen Grammy Award nominations, two Sports Emmy Awards and a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

title: Mike Leigh shines at San Sebastian Film Festival
description: Mike Leigh shines at San Sebastian Film Festival
content:
British filmmaker wins top prize for 'Tender Loving Care'
British filmmaker Mike Leigh won the top prize Saturday at the San Sebastian film festival for his latest social drama "Tender Loving Care", expected to be the last by the 83-year-old who is suffering from an illness. The film, about social workers supporting vulnerable people, won the Golden Shell for best film at the festival in the northern Spanish city.
"I'm so sorry I can't be with you. What a great honour it is," Leigh said in a video acceptance speech. "Thank you and love to everybody."
Leigh had previously said he was suffering from a medical condition affecting his muscles and that it would probably be his "last film".
He won top prize at the Cannes film festival in 1996 for "Secrets and Lies" and at Venice in 2004 for "Vera Drake".
"Tender Loving Care" also jointly won the best screenplay prize at the Spanish festival, while its actress Kate O'Flynn shared the Silver Shell for best performance.
Swedish filmmaker Amanda Kernell won the best director award for "Brace Your Heart".
The 74th edition marked the introduction of a new official award for the Best Original Music among main competition entries, presented in tandem with SGAE. The opening gala on 18 September was hosted by Fariba Sheikhan and Mariona Terés, and Orlando Bloom gifted Werner Herzog the Donostia Award. On 19 September, Ernest Urtasun presented the National Film Prize to Carmen Machi at Tabakalera. Likewise, J.A. Bayona presented Naomi Watts another Donostia Award. The ceremony was rounded up with the screening of Watts-led The Housewife. On 24 September, the festival unveiled Ink as the surprise film, with screenings programmed for 25 and 26 September.

title: East  West come together at  Kaleidoscopic Karachi
description: East  West come together at  Kaleidoscopic Karachi
content:
Leading fashion houses elaborately display both fashion styles at LAAM Fashion Week 2026 event
The colours, cultural identity and changing character of Karachi were brought to the runway at 'Kaleidoscopic Karachi', a showcase held as part of LAAM Fashion Week 2026.
The one-day event, held at the Indus Valley School of Art and Architecture, brought together several leading fashion houses on a single runway, while also paying tribute to the history of fashion photography in Pakistan.
Collections by Deepak Perwani, Wardha Saleem, Khaadi, The Pink Tree Company and Sana Safinaz were presented during the show. The collections featured a mix of eastern and western silhouettes, with designers offering their own interpretations of Karachi's colours, contrasts and evolving fashion trends.
The event also brought together personalities from the fashion and entertainment industries, including Sharmila Farooqi, Aly Khan , Sarwat Gillani, Fahad Mirza, Maheen Khan, Preshay Adnan and Zainab Qayyum.
The appearance of two of Pakistan's well-known 1990s models, Fariha Altaf and Simi Pasha, was among the highlights of the evening. Their runway appearance brought back memories of an era that played an important role in shaping Pakistan's fashion industry.
Fashion designer Hassan Sheheryar Yasin, widely known as HSY, told Express Tribune that he was pleased to see designers from across Pakistan coming together and appreciating each other's work.
"We just finished watching a show, where I felt so good that all the designers from Pakistan came together and saw the collections. We cheered each other up," he said.
HSY also highlighted Karachi's creative potential, saying the event offered a glimpse of a side of the city that he felt had not been seen for a long time.
"Along with that, we saw the potential of Karachi, which I felt we haven't seen in a long time," he said.
Starting as a fashion choreographer in 1994, Yasin worked both as a choreographer and designer to various shows within Pakistan and international shows including Dubai, London, New York City and Toronto. 2000 marked the introduction of Yasin's own fashion label, HSY. Starting as a bridal and formal wear couture house, it became one of Pakistan's most recognized fashion labels. In 2007, Yasin introduced a jewellery line under the HSY brand.
Speaking about LAAM Fashion Week, HSY described it as an important platform for the growth of the country's fashion industry.
"It's a great platform. It's a platform where fashion will continue to grow, and that's the most important," he said.
Co-created by LAAM and Design 651, LFW is a long-term platform built to activate the entire fashion ecosystem. Anchored by LAAM's e-commerce prowess and driven by Design 651's strategic and creative leadership, LFW serves as a business development engine for the wider fashion community, a cultural and creative showcase for the region, and a retail channel for growth and visibility.
A major part of the event was a retrospective celebrating renowned fashion photographer Tapu Javeri's four decades of work.
The exhibition featured a selection of Javeri's memorable photographs, offering a visual journey through different periods of Pakistani fashion and documenting how the industry and its aesthetics have changed over the years.
Reflecting on the transformation of photography, Javeri recalled a time when taking photographs required considerable care and patience.
"There was a time when photography was done with a lot of effort. There were only a few photographs on one roll, so you had to be very careful while taking a picture that it did not go wrong," he said.
According to Javeri, the arrival of Photoshop changed photography by making image editing much easier and more accessible.
He said the industry had now entered another major phase with the arrival of artificial intelligence, which allows people to create millions of images and alter almost anything in a photograph.
Javeri said he felt traditional photography was now facing a significant transformation, with the nature of the photograph itself changing in the age of AI.
The event ultimately presented Karachi through its many visual identities, its colours, cultural influences, fashion trends and changing relationship with photography bringing its past and present together on a single runway.

Johnson has previously spoken about her relationships with musicians, including Coldplay frontman Chris Martin and singer Role Model. During a recent Vogue interview, she joked about her attraction to musicians while describing them as “tricky”.
The actress also said she values privacy and prefers people not knowing where she is or what she is doing. Johnson explained that she finds the constant documentation of people’s lives uncomfortable and largely avoids social media outside of work.
Her latest comments make clear that she intends to keep speculation about her love life largely private.

title: Can China help Pakistan  myth and reality
description: Can China help Pakistan  myth and reality
content:
Islamabad needs Shenzhen-style reforms to unlock broad benefits of CPEC
Pakistan is struggling to revive its economy. Despite all efforts and claims, the economy continues to deteriorate. Economic growth is not returning to track. Debt is increasing, rising day by day. Social and development indicators are deteriorating. As a result, the country is searching who can help and how. In this situation, it turns to international financial institutions and friendly countries, and is even considering cryptocurrency as a source of economic revival. However, cryptocurrency is a financial instrument that still has to establish its credibility and can never be a source of economic revival.
History shows that China can help Pakistan and is willing to do so. This is not an assumption as China has always shown the intent to provide critical support. It is reflected in the agreements both countries have signed for economic cooperation. The list of such pacts is long, but the most important was the 1989 agreement to protect and enhance bilateral investment.
After that accord, many major Chinese companies invested in Pakistan, including Huawei, China Mobile and Haier. These companies are now leaders in their respective fields. They brought billions of dollars and created thousands of jobs. The Beijing Declaration (2003), the FTA (2006) and the energy framework agreement (2006) further strengthened economic cooperation.
However, the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) reshaped the dynamics of economic cooperation. CPEC has all the ingredients to not only revive the economy but also put Pakistan on the path of sustainable development. The successful implementation of the first phase clearly indicates CPEC's potential. The programme has now entered its second phase, which focuses on industrial, agricultural, technological and scientific cooperation. These are the critical areas that can transform Pakistan's economy.
To fully benefit from this cooperation, Pakistan must take a few steps. It needs to fast-track the establishment of Special Economic Zones, as agreed under CPEC, to accelerate industrialisation. It will generate financial resources to tackle the rising public debt. It will also create hundreds of thousands of jobs by addressing the challenges of youth unemployment and poverty.
In 2025, Pakistan and China also signed an action plan to foster a closer China-Pakistan community with a shared future in the new era. The plan equally focuses on Pakistan's economic and development needs, along with other areas. Thus, its implementation will address economic challenges, revive economy and put it on a sustainable path.
The real question should be: how can Pakistan benefit from CPEC or economic opportunities emerging from China? This is a tricky question and Mohsin Naqvi's statement holds the answer. The most unfortunate reality isn't that the system has collapsed, but that the ruling elite intend to stick to it. They don't want to change it. Why? Because the system protects them and their interests. This is posing a threat to the smooth implementation of economic initiatives. Let's look at an example.
In 2019, the government established the CPEC Authority to break the shackles of the existing system and facilitate CPEC-related projects and interventions. This was a major intervention because CPEC schemes were facing issues. However, the existing system turned it into a weak facilitation centre with no powers to make or implement decisions.
Thus, under the current governance system, it would be difficult to fully realise the potential of CPEC and other opportunities. Against this backdrop, what should the country do? An analysis of ground realities suggests that Pakistan needs to take innovative steps or learn from best practices to advance cooperation and exploit these opportunities. In the present context, the best example to learn from is the Shenzhen case. Pakistan can learn from Shenzhen's transformation from a $40 million economy to a more than $500 billion economy.
The transformation process began when Shenzhen was designated the provincial capital of Guangdong province, prompting the province to upgrade its infrastructure. By 1988, the central government elevated Shenzhen to the provincial status, and in 1992, it got legislative authority, strengthening its decision-making and implementation powers. Additionally, the central government granted greater autonomy in financing, investment and trade decisions.
Building on the trust and authority, Shenzhen introduced many innovative practices. It brought the concept and model of government approval within 24 hours. The process was expedited by unveiling and strengthening the one-roof model, which means all services under one roof. Shenzhen also pioneered contractual job experiments, marking a significant change. Despite China's socialist nature, which prioritises job security, these reforms enhanced Shenzhen's appeal to foreign investors.
Zone authorities provided investors with utility services such as electricity and water as well as facilitated them in dealing with tax matters. The zone established state-of-the-art trade (import and export) facilitation mechanism and infrastructure.
Moreover, the local governments played a leading role by providing quality infrastructure, such as roads, water, electricity, gas, sewerage system and telephone lines. In addition, the investors received basic services at their doorsteps. Local governments also ventured into new areas, providing services such as accounting, legal matters, business planning, marketing, import-export assistance, skills training and management consulting. This helped the investors better understand local laws and the business environment and refine their approaches.
Three inferences can be drawn from the above discussion. First, opportunities do exist and China is ready to help Pakistan. If Pakistan wants to benefit, it needs to restructure its system and introduce Shenzhen-style transformational reforms. Second, failing to exploit CPEC's full potential and other economic opportunities will allow opponents to malign China-Pakistan relations.
Third, to counter propaganda, a comprehensive policy and action plan is needed. It is good that Pakistan, in collaboration with the Chinese embassy, has launched the Information Corridor. Islamabad needs to develop it professionally. It should be professionally sound and equipped to counter propaganda with facts and figures.
THE WRITER IS A POLITICAL ECONOMIST AND A VISITING RESEARCH FELLOW AT HEBEI UNIVERSITY, CHINA

title: Revenuecracy  tax policy and targets
description: Revenuecracy  tax policy and targets
content:
Taxation must move from extraction to equity; parliament must determine tax policy rather than merely endorse revenue
Pakistan has a tax bureaucracy. What it increasingly needs is a rational tax policy. The distinction matters. A good tax policy decides who should pay, according to ability, and how revenue can finance development without destroying productive capacity. A revenue bureaucracy asks a simpler question: where can money be collected quickly enough to meet the target?
Pakistan has gradually converted the second into a system of government for which the late Dr Pervez Tahir coined the term 'Revenuecracy' ['Giving FBR a decent burial', The Express Tribune, November 8, 2019]. Its historical ancestry is uncomfortable. The East India Company could not rule Bengal through military victories alone. After acquiring the Diwani in 1765, it needed records, assessments, collectors and local intermediaries to turn political power into revenue. The conquered economy increasingly financed the machinery governing it.
Pakistan is not a colony. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is not a New East India Company. It possesses no territory, army or revenue jurisdiction. Pakistan negotiates IMF programmes through its government and parliament formally retains constitutional authority over federal taxation. The troubling similarity lies elsewhere.
The company required an indigenous administrative machinery to translate revenue demands into collection. Modern external conditionality also operates through Pakistan's own Ministry of Finance, Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), provincial administrations and regulators. The chain today is not Diwani-collector-company treasury. It is external financing requirement-negotiated conditionality – involving the Ministry of Finance, FBR and taxpayer. That difference is enormous. The institutional mechanism nevertheless deserves scrutiny. The IMF's May 2026 review of Pakistan's Extended Fund Facility (EFF) contains a floor for net tax revenues collected by FBR. It separately monitors revenues from retailers and provincial revenue authorities. From December 2026, the FBR revenue floor is scheduled to become a quantitative performance criterion.
Tax refunds are also monitored. The structural agenda includes audits, digital invoicing, production monitoring and implementation of FBR's transformation programme. Many objectives are perfectly defensible. Pakistan needs documentation.
Agriculture, real estate and other undertaxed sectors cannot indefinitely enjoy privileged treatment. Tax expenditures require scrutiny. Digitalisation can curb evasion. State-owned enterprises cannot endlessly consume public resources. The problem begins when revenue target replaces tax policy. FBR then looks not necessarily for the person who ought to pay, but for the person from whom tax can most conveniently be collected. The salaried employee is visible. The registered company is visible. The importer is stopped at customs. The exporter needs refunds. Electricity and gas consumers can be reached through bills. Banks can deduct taxes. Mobile companies can collect them. Petroleum consumption provides another convenient collection point. The result is a withholding system, advance taxation, minimum taxation and indirect taxation on an extraordinary scale. The politically connected, meanwhile, are much harder to tax. This is revenuecracy: taxing accessibility instead of capacity.
The phenomenon is not new. More than two decades ago, an article was published about IMF involvement in erstwhile Central Board of Revenue (CBR) collection targets. Officials were required to prepare lists of major arrears, pursue specified recovery cases and undertake predetermined numbers of audits. Later came the World Bank-funded Tax Administration Reform Project (TARP). Pakistan borrowed money to reform its own revenue authority and employed expensive foreign consultants in the process. Parliament remained peripheral.
Billions have subsequently been spent on reform, automation, restructuring, consultants and technology. The essential political economy remains remarkably resistant to change. FBR still chases annual targets. Governments still announce exemptions, concessions and preferential regimes. Existing taxpayers still carry much of the additional burden. Refunds can still become involuntary financing for the state. The collector has changed. The mindset survives.
This does not absolve Pakistan by blaming the IMF. Quite the opposite. Pakistan repeatedly approaches the IMF because successive governments have failed to build an equitable fiscal state. External leverage becomes possible because domestic institutions first create the dependency.
The IMF also operates through a governance structure in which voting power is unequal. The United States currently possesses 16.49% of total IMF voting power, followed by Japan with 6.14% and China with 6.08%. Pakistan is a sovereign member, but membership does not mean equality of institutional influence. Former Senate chairman Raza Rabbani called the IMF a "new East India Company" in 2019. The description works as political metaphor, not historical equivalence. The company conquered territory. The IMF conditions financing. The more revealing question is why Pakistan needs the financing repeatedly.
India approached the IMF during its severe 1991 balance-of-payments crisis. It undertook major reforms and eventually moved away from recurrent programme dependence. Whatever disagreements exist over India's economic model, emergency financing did not become a permanent framework for running its fiscal affairs.
Pakistan's experience has been different. Every crisis produces another reform programme. Every programme promises documentation, broadening of the tax base, restructuring and fiscal discipline. Stabilisation arrives. Structural privileges largely survive. The cycle eventually begins again. This makes the argument about sovereignty more complex than slogans about foreign masters. External conditionality can even become convenient for domestic governments. Measures they are unwilling to defend politically can be presented as IMF requirements. The creditor acquires leverage. Government acquires an alibi. Those easiest to tax bear adjustment. Breaking this cycle requires neither anti-IMF rhetoric nor another foreign-funded reform project. It requires making the IMF unnecessary.
Taxation must move from extraction to equity. Parliament must determine tax policy rather than merely endorse revenue measures prepared by the executive. Specialists must run specialised institutions. Tax adjudication must be genuinely independent. Refunds must be paid rather than treated as revenue. Privileges must be dismantled before rates are raised on those already documented.
The test of sovereignty is not how loudly a state invokes independence. It is whether it can finance legitimate public purposes fairly from an economy strong enough to sustain them. Pakistan nationalised the collector after independence. It must now ask whether it also internationalised the revenue target.

title: Debt tsunami threatens Global South
description: Debt tsunami threatens Global South
content:
High borrowing costs squeeze economies; debt service crowds out uplift spending
The next global debt crisis may not arrive with the drama of Lehman Brothers. No spectacular market collapse. No single bank failure. Instead, warning signs could appear quietly. A sovereign bond rolled over at a punishing rate. A development project postponed. A health budget squeezed. Or a cash-strapped government forced to spend more on debt servicing than on health and education.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva has sounded a similar alarm. As advanced-economy bond yields rise, they lift yield curves worldwide, she said after the G20 finance ministers' meeting earlier this month. For some emerging economies, financing costs can more than erase hard-won reductions in risk premiums. Countries that have improved their fiscal credibility can, therefore, find themselves paying more simply because the global price of capital has changed.
The story begins with the post-pandemic monetary tightening. Between March 2022 and July 2023, the US Federal Reserve hiked its rate from near-zero to 5.25%-5.50% in one of the fastest tightening cycles in decades. However, easing that followed hasn't produced a corresponding decline in long-term borrowing costs.
Short-term rates are heavily influenced by central banks, while long-term yields also reflect inflation projections, government borrowing, fiscal sustainability, geopolitical risks, and bond supply and demand.
The IMF's April 2026 Fiscal Monitor paints the broader picture. Global public debt ballooned to nearly 94% of GDP in 2025. And it is projected to soar past 100% by 2029. Much of the increase is driven by major economies facing rising demands for social spending, defence and strategic investment, while interest burdens are also increasing.
This doesn't matter to Washington, London, Tokyo or Paris alone. Government bonds issued by advanced economies provide the benchmark against which much of the developing world borrows. When those yields rise, financing costs elsewhere follow suit.
The World Bank's International Debt Report shows how sharply borrowing costs have increased. Low- and middle-income countries paid a record $415.4 billion in interest on external debt in 2024, up 2.2% from 2023 and more than double the amount a decade earlier. In low-income countries, interest payments made up more than half of total external debt service.
Between 2022 and 2024, low- and middle-income countries paid about $741 billion more in principal and interest on external debt than they received in new financing, according to the World Bank. This constitutes the largest such net outflow in at least five decades.
The consequences show up gradually in government budgets. A road is not built. A power project is postponed. A vaccination programme is trimmed. Or a hospital delays procurement. Lower investment means weaker productivity and slower growth, making debt harder to service and potentially pushing borrowing costs higher.
Much sovereign and corporate borrowing is denominated in dollars. Exchange rates, therefore, compound the problem for developing economies. When the dollar appreciates or local currencies depreciate, the domestic-currency cost of servicing debt rises even if the principal amount borrowed stays unchanged.
Higher global rates can encourage capital to move towards advanced-economy assets. And this adds further strain on the currencies and forex reserves of developing economies. Their central banks may have to maintain tighter monetary conditions, resulting in higher external debt costs, weaker currencies, and slower growth.
Emerging markets, according to the IMF, are particularly vulnerable to such spillovers. The global lender's latest fiscal assessment points to structural changes in sovereign debt markets, including the growing role of leveraged non-bank financial institutions and a reduced safety premium on US Treasuries. If and when central banks will cut rates no longer the question. What matters is whether long-term borrowing costs will fall enough for heavily indebted economies to regain fiscal space.
Launched in 2020, the G20's Common Framework was designed to coordinate debt treatment among official bilateral and private creditors. But restructuring cases have often taken years, exposing the complexity of today's creditor landscape. Governments may simultaneously be indebted to multilateral institutions, traditional Paris Club creditors, China and other bilateral lenders, including commercial banks and bondholders. The longer restructuring takes, the greater the economic damage can become. The IMF MD has urged decisive action by countries with unsustainable debt and improvements to the restructuring process.
Lower policy rates may not resolve the problem because several structural forces are driving up long-term yields. Governments are borrowing heavily. Defence spending is rising. The energy transition requires huge capital investment. Supply chains are being reorganised. And AI is propelling a new wave of infrastructure and data-centre investment.
These activities compete for long-term capital. Investors are also demanding greater compensation for fiscal and inflation risks that were easier to ignore during the era of ultra-low interest rates. A central bank can control its overnight policy rate, but it cannot dictate the yield investors demand to lend to governments for 10, 20 or 30 years.
The most dangerous feature of the current debt environment is its gradual nature. A country may not default when interest rates rise. It may refinance debt, scale down reserves, cut spending, seek multilateral assistance or postpone investment. The system continues functioning for a while.
According to the World Bank, in 2024 the average interest rate paid by developing economies on newly acquired public debt reached a 24-year high, while the average rate paid to private creditors reached a 17-year high. Therefore, the adjustment takes place through cuts in budgetary allocations for health, education, infrastructure and other social spending.
So, what should the Global South economies do? They can strengthen domestic revenue mobilisation, lengthen debt maturities, deepen local-currency bond markets, improve debt management and pursue credible fiscal policies. Domestic reform, however, cannot offset changes in the global price of capital. That is the crux of the IMF MD's warning.
