title: Remittances  Pakistan s lifeline
description: Remittances  Pakistan s lifeline
content:
Inflows do not automatically eliminate poverty; they work best when combined with education, investment, stable econom
Pakistan's remittance story is no longer a marginal economic footnote. It is one of the country's central macroeconomic pillars. Workers' remittances rose to $41.58 billion in FY2026 from $38.30 billion in FY2025, registering an 8.6% year-on-year increase.
Monthly inflows remained above $3 billion throughout the year and touched $4.25 billion in May 2026. In an economy repeatedly constrained by weak exports, low foreign direct investment, narrow fiscal space and recurring balance-of-payments pressures, this inflow has become an indispensable source of stability.
Yet the very strength of remittances also raises a more difficult question: are we using this lifeline merely to survive or can we convert it into a long-term development instrument? The state must ask how these inflows can be channeled from household relief into savings, investment, employment and productivity.
In the household income, the share of remittance is not significant. According to HIES 2024-25, remittances account for 7.77% of monthly household income nationally. However, their weight varies sharply across provinces. In Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, they make up 18.22% of monthly household income, compared with 8.01% in Punjab, 1.34% in Sindh and only 0.90% in Balochistan. These differences reflect migration networks, labour-market access and the uneven spread of financial infrastructure.
But averages can hide ground realities. For thousands of families, money received from abroad pays for food, school fees, healthcare, housing, transport, weddings, debt repayment and small business needs. It also helps smooth consumption when local income is uncertain, especially in households exposed to seasonal employment, agriculture-related shocks or weak local labour markets.
Pakistan-specific evidence suggests that households receiving foreign remittances have 19% to 21% higher consumption than comparable non-recipient households. Other findings associate remittances with improvements in education, healthcare, living standards and purchasing power.
The poverty link is more nuanced but still significant. A study covering data from 1990 to 2022 finds that remittances have historically contributed to poverty reduction and improved living standards in South Asian countries. The lesson is not that remittances automatically eliminate poverty; rather, they work best when combined with education, financial access, local investment opportunities and stable macroeconomic conditions.
Remittances are commonly discussed as money for consumption, but research indicates that they can also increase household savings and investment. Whether they do so depend heavily on the availability of financial and institutional infrastructure. Where formal financial services, reliable information and investment channels are more developed, as in Punjab and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, remittance-receiving households are more likely to save and invest instead of using the entire inflow for immediate consumption. In that sense, remittances can serve as household-level capital, capable of supporting investment and employment.
The inflation debate also requires balance. Higher remittance inflows raise household purchasing power and can increase domestic demand, particularly when a large share is spent on consumption. In a supply-constrained economy, this may create short-term pressure in some markets. However, Pakistan-specific empirical evidence suggests that remittances do not have a persistent inflationary effect.
The impact of a remittance shock on the Consumer Price Index is described as mild and temporary, with the effect fading over time. This means the policy response should not be to fear remittances, but to ensure that rising purchasing power is matched by better domestic supply, investment and productivity.
Pakistan, therefore, needs a remittance policy that goes beyond encouraging overseas Pakistanis to send money through formal channels. Lower transaction costs and digital payment systems are necessary, but not sufficient. The launch of diaspora bonds in 2019 was lacklustre, however Roshan Digital Accounts are a success story. Banks and fintech firms should be encouraged to design products for small savers, women recipients and rural households. Provincial governments can also help by connecting remittance-rich districts with local enterprise development, vocational training and export-oriented clusters. Diversifying destinations, upgrading worker skills and improving formal remittance channels should be treated as part of economic planning, not simply labour-export administration.
There is a largely held view that the flipside of increasing remittances is brain drain. This is a mistake to view outflow of our labour as a loss – it's not a zero-sum game. The talent is distributed according to market demands, whereas emigration serves as the instrument. Without undermining its importance, Pakistan must avoid confusing labour export with economic transformation. Overseas workers have helped stabilise the country's external account and protected millions of households from deeper hardship. But a nation cannot build prosperity on export of its labour alone.
Remittances are a lifeline and Pakistan should be grateful for them. But the real test is whether policymakers can turn this lifeline into a ladder – from consumption to savings, from savings to investment, and from investment to broad-based growth.

title: Digital exports  path to high value knowledge economy
description: Digital exports  path to high value knowledge economy
content:
Export base expanding from conventional software services towards broader range of tech-enabled professional services
Pakistan's digital economy is rapidly becoming an important source of foreign exchange, employment and investment, creating opportunities beyond traditional exports. At a time when the country is seeking to diversify its export base and strengthen its external position, digital services offer an important avenue because they can reach international markets with relatively limited physical infrastructure.
Recent official data shows that information technology, freelancing and related digital services are developing into an increasingly important part of Pakistan's export economy. Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26 reports that ICT export remittances increased by 19.7% to $3.38 billion during July-March FY2026, compared with $2.83 billion in the corresponding period of the previous year. Tech freelancer exports were particularly dynamic, rising by 51% to $856.3 million. The Pakistan Software Export Board also expanded its international outreach, participating in 20 technology events that generated 4,228 qualified business-to-business leads and reported business worth $73.9 million.
The longer-term trend is equally significant. According to the State Bank of Pakistan's Annual Report 2024-25, the ICT services exports increased by 18.3% to $3.8 billion in FY2025. The central bank identified software consultancy and freelancing in computer and information services as major contributors. This follows a strong growth in FY2024, when ICT exports increased 24.1% to $3.2 billion. The figures indicate that Pakistan's digital export base is expanding from conventional software services towards a broader range of technology-enabled professional services.
Freelancing deserves particular attention because it connects Pakistan's young workforce with international markets without requiring workers to migrate. Thousands of individuals can provide software development, graphic design, digital marketing, accounting, engineering and other professional services directly to overseas clients. This model can generate foreign exchange while creating employment opportunities outside traditional corporate structures. The rapid increase in freelancer exports shows that digital work is becoming a meaningful component of Pakistan's services economy.
The domestic digital ecosystem is also expanding. Pakistan Economic Survey reports that broadband subscriptions reached 161 million and total telecom subscriptions hit 207.2 million by the end of March 2026. Telecom revenues stood at Rs837 billion during July-March FY2026. Such connectivity provides the foundation for remote employment, e-commerce, cloud services, online education and digital entrepreneurship. Yet connectivity alone cannot guarantee export growth. Pakistan must continue improving internet reliability, data infrastructure, cybersecurity, digital payments and access to international financial channels. Artificial intelligence is likely to reshape this opportunity further. Pakistan has approved the National Artificial Intelligence Policy, creating a framework for AI innovation, skills development and adoption. For the country, AI should not be viewed only as a technology capable of replacing routine digital jobs. It can also increase the productivity of software developers, engineers, designers, consultants and other knowledge workers by enabling them to provide more sophisticated services to international clients. Developing AI skills could therefore help Pakistan move towards higher-value digital exports.
The next frontier is Web 3.0, including blockchain applications, tokenisation and decentralised technologies. These fields remain relatively new and are rapidly evolving globally. Pakistan will need a regulatory framework that balances innovation with financial stability, consumer protection, cybersecurity and safeguards against illicit financial activity. The objective should be to encourage technology companies to develop commercially useful blockchain applications and services for global markets rather than allowing the Web 3.0 debate to focus primarily on speculative digital assets. Financial facilitation is another important requirement. In April 2026, the State Bank introduced measures to facilitate IT companies and freelancers in the processing of export receipts and outward remittances from exporters' special foreign-currency accounts. It also directed authorised dealers to establish mechanisms for resolving complaints of IT companies and freelancers in a timely manner. Under the revised procedure, the IT companies and freelancers no longer need to submit Form "R" to authorised dealers for their export receipts. Such measures can reduce administrative friction and make it easier for small digital exporters to participate in international markets.
Pakistan must also invest heavily in advanced skills. Basic freelancing has opened the door to international digital markets, but the next stage requires expertise in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, cloud computing, data analytics, enterprise software, semiconductor design and blockchain development. The greater the skill intensity, the greater the potential to move from low-cost outsourcing towards higher-value technology exports. Universities, technical institutions, private training providers and industry should, therefore, align their programmes with international demand.
The opportunity, however, should not be treated as automatic. Policy uncertainty, unreliable electricity and internet services, difficulties in receiving international payments, limited venture capital and shortages of advanced technical skills can restrict the sector's expansion. Pakistan also needs stronger intellectual-property protection, cybersecurity capacity and data-governance systems. A competitive digital economy requires an environment in which a developer or technology company can establish a business, receive international payments, hire local talent and serve global customers efficiently.
Pakistan's digital exports have already crossed an important threshold. ICT export remittances reached $3.38 billion during the first nine months of FY2026, while freelancer exports increased sharply. The challenge now is to convert this momentum into a sustainable, high-value digital economy. IT and freelancing can provide the foundation, while artificial intelligence, cloud computing and Web 3.0 can open new markets. With consistent policies, stronger skills, reliable infrastructure and easier financial channels, Pakistan can transform its large digital workforce into a more competitive and diversified source of export earnings.

title: EV boom reshaping local market
description: EV boom reshaping local market
content:
Pakistan's EV future hinges on localisation, not just imported sales
China's automotive industry has set a record this year as vehicle exports have already surpassed last year's total by August. As Chinese automakers expand into emerging markets to offset Western trade barriers and domestic overcapacity, Pakistan has become one of the clearest beneficiaries.
This global push is disrupting a decades-old Japanese auto oligopoly in Pakistan, aided by Islamabad's New Energy Vehicle Policy (NEVP 2025-2030). As Chinese manufacturers expand into high-tech crossovers and electric vehicles, Pakistan stands at a pivotal crossroads: how to leverage Beijing's manufacturing scale to slash its crippling fossil fuel import bill, while avoiding the substitution of one form of import dependence, ie foreign oil, with another: imported batteries, electronics and high-value automotive components.
The central question is, therefore, larger than whether Chinese EVs will displace Japanese cars. It is whether Pakistan can use Chinese technology and capital to move beyond low-value vehicle assembly towards genuine manufacturing, technology transfer, supplier development and eventually exports.
China's total annualised vehicle exports have soared to 12 million units, anchored by 10 million passenger cars. Its new energy vehicle exports, battery electrics and plug-in hybrids combined, have reached an annualised 5.6 million units, eclipsing Japan's historical peak export figures.
This has upended legacy automakers. In just 24 months, Germany's multibillion-dollar trade surplus with China flipped into a deficit. As Western markets impose defensive tariffs, Chinese manufacturers are redirecting capacity towards the Global South. For Pakistan, this creates an unusual opportunity. Chinese firms possess battery, motor, power electronics and software technologies that would take Pakistan decades to develop alone. The challenge is ensuring access that creates domestic productive capacity, not just a bigger market for imported Chinese parts.
For over 30 years, Pakistan's car market was dominated by Toyota, Honda and Suzuki, shielded by high tariffs with little pressure to modernise. Macroeconomic headwinds, forex constraints and fuel prices crippled traditional assembly lines, opening the door for new entrants.
Chinese brands, Sazgar Haval, Changan, Chery, BAIC, Jetour, have now captured a share in the SUV and crossover segments, with Haval challenging the Toyota Fortuner. On the electric side, BYD (via Hubco subsidiary Mega Motor Company), Changan's Deepal and budget models like Dewan Honri have pushed EVs from a luxury niche into the mainstream.
This isn't simply China replacing Japan as the market is fragmenting, with Chinese, Japanese and Korean makers competing on price, hybrids, software and financing. Japanese firms retain strong dealer networks and supplier relationships, while Chinese entrants bring faster product cycles and EV capability. The NEVP backs this shift with structure: a target of 30% new energy vehicle sales by 2030, rising to 50% by 2040; 3,000 public fast-charging stations by 2030; a 1-3% carbon levy on combustion vehicles funding EV subsidies; concessional duties on CKD/SKD kits; and a capped charging tariff of roughly Rs40/kWh to absorb surplus power generation.
This matters because Pakistan's electrification push is also an energy-security play. Petroleum imports drain foreign exchange, while the power sector has excess capacity and weak demand. But the net forex benefit depends entirely on how much of the EV value chain Pakistan localises, since a fully imported EV kit assembled locally still increases component imports even as it cuts oil use. Success should be measured in forex savings, domestic value addition, supplier development and exports, not just EV sales volume.
The risk is that Pakistan reproduces its old assembly-dependent model with a new technology stack: Chinese tech, imported components and Pakistani final assembly, which is analogous to changing the propulsion system without changing the country's position in the global value chain.
Three factors will determine success. First, manufacturers must be pushed from CKD kit assembly towards local battery manufacturing, parts casting and software integration. This doesn't mean building everything domestically as battery cells and advanced semiconductors need scale that Pakistan can't match. Instead, the policy should target realistic wins: battery-pack assembly, wiring harnesses, castings, plastics, interiors, charging equipment and thermal management.
Secondly, the 3,000-charging-station target needs sustained private investment, grid upgrades and standardised protocols; none of which happen automatically. Low EV penetration makes chargers commercially unattractive, while poor charging infrastructure suppresses adoption – a chicken-and-egg problem. Existing petrol stations could become charging nodes, while battery swapping and fleet charging may matter more for motorcycles, rickshaws and taxis.
Thirdly, Japanese assemblers are introducing their own hybrids to defend their market share, which means more competition that should improve pricing and after-sales service industry-wide.
The bigger opportunity may lie beyond passenger cars. Pakistan's motorcycle, three-wheeler, taxi and commercial-vehicle markets are used intensively and consume heavy fuel, meaning electrification there could deliver faster payback and greater fuel-import savings per rupee of support than premium passenger EVs.
The new Automotive Industry Development Policy 2026-31 raises the stakes further, emphasising localisation, investment and exports. The opportunity is to use Chinese manufacturers' search for new markets to strike a deeper bargain: market access in exchange for supplier development, technology transfer, training and export-oriented production.
Pakistan's domestic market alone won't provide the scale for a globally competitive EV industry. The more ambitious goal is integrating Pakistani suppliers into Chinese global value chains and eventually positioning the country as a regional production base. In the end, an exported Pakistan-made component may ultimately matter more than another locally assembled car.
In a nutshell, China has already solved the technological problem of mass EV production. However, Pakistan's challenge is different: capturing a meaningful share of the economic value that EV technology creates. The real story isn't China replacing Japan but whether Pakistan can turn China's automotive rise into a shift from assembling cars for itself to manufacturing products the world wants to buy.

title: Cameron Rorrison breaks her silence after Presley Gerber   s death at 27
description: Presley Gerber   s ex Cameron Rorrison remembers his  wide open heart  in an emotional tribute after his death at 27
content:
Presley Gerber’s ex Cameron Rorrison remembers his 'wide open heart' in an emotional tribute after his death at 27
Presley Gerber’s ex-girlfriend Cameron Rorrison has paid tribute to the late model, remembering him for his compassion and “wide open heart” days after his death at 27.
Rorrison, who dated Gerber from 2018 to 2020, shared an emotional message on Instagram Stories on September 26. She said she had struggled to find words that could properly describe Gerber and the person he was.
Rorrison highlighted Gerber’s “inspiring compassion” and “incredible understanding”, saying his humanity allowed him to make people feel valued and important. She also described those qualities as rare and said she had not encountered the same “honest and pure” qualities in another person since their relationship.
“He was an angel in this life and will be in the next,” Rorrison wrote in her tribute.
Gerber, the son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber and brother of model Kaia Gerber, died on September 20 at the age of 27. He was found at a rehabilitation facility in Los Angeles, with authorities describing the death as a suspected overdose.
The Santa Monica Police Department said there was no indication of foul play. Gerber’s official cause of death has not yet been determined, with the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner stating that additional testing and studies were required.
Gerber’s death certificate confirmed that his body was cremated five days after his death, while his ashes are reportedly being kept at his parents’ home in Malibu.
Gerber had previously spoken publicly about addiction and his mental health journey. In a 2023 podcast appearance, he discussed his desire to help people experiencing similar struggles and emphasised the importance of offering support without judgment.

title: Neil Patrick Harris to play the devil in  Damn Yankees  Broadway revival
description: Neil Patrick Harris will star as Applegate in the Broadway revival of  Damn Yankees   opening April 20
content:
Neil Patrick Harris will star as Applegate in the Broadway revival of 'Damn Yankees', opening April 20
Neil Patrick Harris is set to star in the upcoming Broadway revival of Damn Yankees , which will open next spring with Julianne Hough and Austin Scott also leading the cast.
The production will begin previews at the Marquis Theatre on March 24 before its official Broadway opening on April 20. It marks the first Broadway revival of Damn Yankees in more than 30 years, following a production at Washington, D.C.’s Arena Stage last fall.
Directed and choreographed by Sergio Trujillo, the new production features a revised book by Will Power and Dough Wright, with additional lyrics by Lynn Ahrens. The story moves the original 1950s setting into the early 2000s.
Harris will play Applegate, a devilish figure who offers baseball fan Joe Boyd a deal that could help his struggling Baltimore Orioles. Hough will make her Broadway debut as Joe’s wife, Lola, while Scott will portray Young Joe.
First staged on Broadway in 1955, Damn Yankees follows a middle-aged baseball fan who makes a Faustian bargain in hopes of helping his team defeat the dominant New York Yankees. The original musical won seven Tony Awards, including Best Musical. It was last revived on Broadway in 1993.
Harris, who won a Tony Award for the 2014 revival of Hedwig and the Angry Inch , said the large-scale musical has been a long-standing goal for him. He also described playing Applegate as an opportunity to embrace a more mischievous role.
The revival will also mark a collaboration between Broadway and Major League Baseball, with MLB and MLB Studios serving as production partners.

title: Angela Stribling  pioneering BET personality and radio host  dies at 58
description: Angela Stribling  pioneering BET personality and radio host  has died at 58  with her cause of death undisclosed
content:
Angela Stribling, pioneering BET personality and radio host, has died at 58, with her cause of death undisclosed
Angela Stribling, a pioneering Black Entertainment Television personality and longtime radio host, has died at 58.
Ed Gordon, the journalist who worked with BET for more than four decades, announced Stribling’s death in a Facebook post on Sunday, September 27. Gordon said the two worked together at the network and remained friends after pursuing other opportunities.
“So very sad to hear Angela Stribling has passed away,” Gordon wrote in his tribute. He remembered her as a “sweet soul” and offered his condolences to her husband and other loved ones.
Further details about Angela Stribling’s death, including her exact date and cause of death, have not been publicly disclosed.
Stribling became known through her work at BET and later built a career in television and radio. According to her LinkedIn profile, she also worked with WJZ-TV and WJLA-TV.
In recent years, Stribling hosted her own radio programme, Pillow Talk with Angela . She also participated in several national awareness campaigns and worked as a voice for television and radio advertising campaigns.
Throughout her career, Stribling interviewed a number of prominent figures from entertainment, music and politics. Her interview subjects included former President Bill Clinton, Stevie Wonder, Quincy Jones, Janet Jackson, 50 Cent, Brandy and Sterling K. Brown.
Gordon also highlighted Stribling’s contribution to radio, describing her voice as a staple across the Washington, D.C., area and Sirius. He recalled regularly crossing paths with her at conferences and events and staying in touch over the years.
Stribling’s death marks the loss of a familiar voice and television personality whose career spanned BET, local television, radio and national media campaigns.

title: Tackling terror  need to shift from reactive to proactive gear
description: Tackling terror  need to shift from reactive to proactive gear
content:
Kohat attack demonstrates the intensity of the terrorist threat confronting Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
The daredevil suicide attack using an explosives-laden vehicle, followed by armed militants storming the police lines and the adjacent Special Branch building, demonstrates the intensity of the terrorist threat confronting Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Thirty-one people, including 17 police personnel, were martyred and around 100 were injured. The police and army personnel put up a brave fight, ultimately killing the attackers. The incident, however, brings to the fore a larger question: why do militant organisations continue to retain the capacity to plan, recruit, equip and execute complex attacks?
This cannot be treated as an isolated incident. On July 15, militants attempted to storm the Miryan Police Station in Bannu with an explosives-laden vehicle, followed by an armed assault that resulted in the martyrdom of a police official and injuries to several security personnel and civilians. On July 24, a joint security checkpost came under attack in Tank, where militants rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into its perimeter, martyring 15 people - including 12 soldiers, two policemen and a former Forest Department official.
On July 29, a group of militants carried out an attack against the Khazina Banda police checkpost in Hangu, resulting in the martyrdom of nine policemen, including a deputy superintendent of police, and injuries to 28 others. On August 2, a suicide bomber detonated near the Kabal Police Station in Swat while a public protest against lawlessness was under way, claiming the lives of 17 people, including seven policemen.
Security forces, including the police and military, continue to discharge their duties with unflinching commitment, with many making the ultimate sacrifice. But security policy cannot be measured merely by heroism at the point of attack. The most pressing question is whether killing terrorists after they strike is enough to break the cycle of militancy.
Tactical history shows that while terrorists are killed, hideouts dismantled and key commanders eliminated, these successes are often short-lived. After a brief lull, subsequent attacks emerge - frequently proving more organised, sophisticated and destructive. While responding to and neutralising an active assault is an essential pillar of counterterrorism, a purely reactive strategy is not a permanent solution.
The government must be mindful of how this organizational machinery operates. How do they recruit? How do they influence young people with extremist narratives? Who radicalises them? How do they maintain their command-and-control systems? Where do their recruits receive training? Who provides weapons, explosives, transport, safe houses and reconnaissance? How are they financed? Who acts as a facilitator, courier, informer or propagandist? Without answering these questions and getting to the bottom of the problem, the counterterrorism apparatus will continue to spin in a vicious cycle.
Counterterrorism in essence is an intelligence-led enterprise. The overall aim should not be merely to kill the attacker after he reaches the gate of a police station or some checkpost, but to identify and intercept him before he departs from his hideout.
That however is not possible without a well-knit intelligence network involving the police, Counter Terrorism Department, Special Branch, Intelligence Bureau and other relevant agencies. Information about militant movement, recruitment, financing, communication, weapons procurement, facilitation and operational planning must be collected, collated, analysed and implemented into preventive action. Advance knowledge is the key to success.
A terrorist does not appear out of the blue and function in a vacuum. Such groups draw strength from an ecosystem of recruits, financiers, facilitators, couriers, safe houses, weapons suppliers, intelligence collectors, ideological sympathisers and propaganda networks. Destruction of one cell does not suffice.
The gaps require attention. The listed gaps include inadequate human intelligence in affected localities; weak investigation and forensic follow-up; insufficient penetration of militant support networks; failure to disrupt weapons, explosives and logistical supply chains; limited expertise in terrorist financing; and weaknesses in converting raw intelligence into preventive action.
Reports from both international and national agencies consistently highlight cross-border facilitation as a critical dimension of Pakistan's security challenges. Islamabad is on record stating that Afghan authorities allow TTP elements to operate from their soil, though Kabul denies the charge. Yet, attributing domestic militancy entirely to external factors oversimplifies a highly complex problem. The fundamental question remains: what internal vulnerabilities enable these militants to operate inside Pakistan?
Basing the entire strategy on the assumption of external support may not be a comprehensive approach unless those external sources are linked to local networks - including local enablers, recruiters, financiers, facilitators, informants, and propaganda machinery. Counterterrorism measures, therefore, must be based on an unsentimental examination of the internal social and logistical space available to militancy.
Many of the troubled localities also suffer from structural flaws caused by applying the exact same policing model to regions facing radically different levels of threat. Bannu is not Abbottabad. Lakki Marwat is not Haripur. Tank is not Chitral. Consequently, North Waziristan cannot be policed on the same threat assumptions as a relatively peaceful district.
Police strength, CTD presence, intelligence resources, armoured protection, surveillance capability, investigation units, specialised weapons and rapid-response capacity should be measured in accordance with the threat, terrain, population, militant capability and vulnerability of installations. A region facing suicide bombers, IEDs, automatic weapons and drones requires a very different security framework than others.
The current situation demands a shift from a reactive mode to a proactive one. While protecting vital installations remains essential, the initiative must not be left to the adversary. The writ of the state is not measured by how forcefully it responds after citizens and policemen have been killed. It is measured by whether the state possesses the intelligence, institutional capacity and legitimacy to prevent those deaths in the first place. K-P has paid too heavy a price in blood - for how much longer must it continue to pay? It is high time the state fought with its full might, seizing the initiative to uproot terrorism in all its forms.

title: Understanding and controlling the adoption of AI
description: Understanding and controlling the adoption of AI
content:
United States is the most advanced developer of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems
The United States is the most advanced developer of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems. Those who are deeply involved in developing the AI systems now seriously worry that the mathematical models that constitute it can – perhaps would – go rogue and hurt humanity to the point of destroying it. This was the assessment by Steven Adler, offered by him in the article published by The New York Times on September 12, 2026. "For months news that artificial intelligence agents from OpenAI had gone rogue and attacked another company's systems (as well as OpenAI's own system) has dripped out and brought harrowing details into focus. The public is struggling to catch up: What are these secret A.I. systems? What are these 'swarms' capable of, today and the near future? Is it possible to stop them from breaking rules and commit cybercrimes?"
In a much longer assessment of the situation published by the same newspaper, Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, captioned his contribution with scary words: "The A.I. safety experts can't sleep, and neither should you." In his essay, he wrote: "One of the disaster scenarios A.I. specialists entertain is that a swarm of rogue A.I.s hack out of their container, gain access to a biological research facility and design a super virus that spreads uncontrollably." Such a development may have already occurred. AI firm Anthropic announced on Stember 10 that it had blocked scientists from attempting to use its model Claude to conduct gain-of-function research. This research aims to produce more lethal viruses so that we can learn to deal with them. As has been speculated, this may have happened in a Chinese laboratory in the city of Wuhan from where the Covid-19 virus escaped and spread around the globe.
These questions are being asked but are not easily answered as work on developing AI models continues. In early September 2026, allegations leaked that OpenAI had broken an industry taboo with one of its powerful new models, GPT-6 Astra. The company is reported to have trained the model with techniques that could understand researchers' ability to find evidence of the model deceiving them. After the details of the work being done by OpenAI came to light, the company's chief scientist wrote that he hoped for "voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace," because he thought that no company has solved the necessary safety challenges. At the time the official gave his statement, it revealed the exitance of yet another model that was "significantly more capable than Astra". In the above quoted assessment by Adler, the author drew the following conclusion: "The current pace of A.I. development is blistering, yet there is much more the A.I. companies could do to relieve imminent danger and to lay bare the gambles they are taking with all our futures. The window for ensuing we are heading to a bright future, and away from catastrophe is closing fast."
"So what do we do now?" asked Witt in the article quoted above. His answer: "Silicon Valley is right in asking for the government to act We need a global monitoring body similar to what we have for uranium enrichment. Getting the large A.I. corporations to comply may actually be the easy part, given that they are the ones asking for it. The harder part will be getting governments and militaries to agree. China has indicated at least some willingness to an international agreement."
That the governments need to act and do so quicky was recognised by the Committee that picks the winner of the Nobel Prize for the year. One of the 2025 winners was the economic historian, Joel Mokyr, who attributes the birth of modernity to "the emergence of a belief in the usefulness of progress". When people fight against change that they do not think that they will gain from, that resistance gets treated as a political rather than an economic problem. "But the political battles over technology," Mokyr has argued "has profound implications for economic history." One of these is "that technological progress in a given society is by and large a temporary and vulnerable process. He warns against taking for granted the social political and economic conditions that produced such incredible improvements in the American way of life during the 20th century. On the contrary, they were hard-won, extraordinary and difficult to maintain. No law of economics or nature guarantees that these conditions will persist. "Once bitten, twice shy," Professor Mokyr warns. "When technology causes a great deal of social harm, it is not surprising that many intrusive techniques of our time, from genetically modified organisms to nuclear power, are regarded with great suspicion."
Witt concluded his long essay with a suggestion and a warning: "The United States needs to lead the world not only in the development of A.I. models but also in the capacity to run them in the broadest possible set of contexts. If this is done right, the economic opportunity is enormous." But he had a caution: "Forgive ordinary citizens their skepticism. They have heard such promises often over the past generation, and the people making changes always seem to be the ones reaping rewards. We are at the start of the reckoning for an era in which innovation was less often done for ordinary Americans and more often done to them. People are rightly asking: What, and who, is technological progress for? The A.I. labs need an answer, fast."
People are right to worry. The voices they have heard are not reassuring. The trillionaire Elon Musk has said "there will come a point where no job is needed. Altman, the founder of OpenAI, talks about a future "where A.I. produces most of the world's basic goods and services" and taxes on the AI companies provide "opportunities to directly distribute ownership and wealth to citizens". In his telling, "people will be freed to spend more time with people they care about, care for people, appreciate art and nature or work towards social good." Properly managed, AI could do more good than harm to mankind. In the article next week, I will discuss how the more advanced nations are treating AI developments.

title: The paradox of our age
description: The paradox of our age
content:
Progressive approach to technology underpins acknowledgement of new advancement for betterment of human civilisation
The progressive approach to technology underpins the acknowledgement of every new advancement for the betterment of human civilisation, but we must be extra cautious when the very advancement threatens the existence of what it feeds on. The context is World News Day, which falls on September 28th and is being observed this year at a time when journalism is existentially threatened by generative AI. The first casualty wrought by the onslaught of generative AI bots is the loss of trust. "This is the paradox of our age. The most connected societies in history are also among the most vulnerable to confusion, manipulation and distrust," says the op-ed 'The Integrity Dividend' by David Whimsley, President, World Editors Forum.
Phil Chetwynd, Global News Director, AFP, labels the utopian future of AI as another so-called 'news agency killer' in his op-ed 'Dystopia, Inc', available on the World News Day organisation's website, and reproduces an ironical question: "Why pay for your professional journalism when information is being delivered free in real time? Why waste money employing journalists to gather information that can be aggregated by our new chatbot friends?" He himself demystifies the fad of AI: "Part of the answer lies in the little chatbot disclaimer which says the information in your AI overview may actually be wrong."
He narrates how global news agencies deployed their journalists to gather the first-hand information of the flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border this August. All the authentic information and visuals came from news agencies like AFP, Reuters and AP. But then what followed was the digital deluge of deepfake images emotionally manipulating the viewers with 'artificially generated destroyed villages and bodies lined up for burial'.
The World News Day organisation asserts 11 world renowned economists gave the clarion call that every sector of society, from the economy to health, education and the military, relies upon the production of factual and robust information. Conversely, governments are funding generative AI tools, spawning untruth. Its fallout includes the comedown of economies. UNESCO estimates that disinformation costs our global economy between 350 and 510 billion US dollars per annum.
The misplaced investment starves the news media with newsrooms closing their doors and cutting staff; no one will be left on the ground to report on the wildfire as it happens or to uncover the next corruption scandal. Experts assert that the investment of only 0.1% of global GDP, equivalent to 15 days of global military spending, will ensure healthy public media. "Getting to the facts costs money, time, expertise and effort," writes Phil Chetwynd.
If tech companies feed upon journalism, should the journalism ecosystem receive a sustainable share of the value created by that very economy? Australia passed this August a legislation, the News Bargaining Incentive, that binds the tech giants to pay millions of dollars in levies if they don't strike commercial deals with local media outlets, whose content helps drive user engagement and advertising revenue on the tech firms' platforms.
The world governments have their own axe to grind in defanging public interest journalism i.e. to evade accountability. Public interest journalism exposes fraud and financial crime. A study of 97 countries found that declining press freedom is associated with a 1-2 per cent reduction in real GDP growth, whereas $1 invested in journalism can generate over $100 in public savings through reduced corruption and better public services. Michael Miller, Executive Chairman, News Corp Australasia, in his op-ed 'Truth in an AI World', cites a 2024 study: 'when local news coverage disappears, corruption in that community rises by roughly seven per cent.'
"A recent academic study out of Europe put a name to the phenomenon – 'the illusion of knowledge': the more people consume AI-generated summaries, the more informed they feel, even as their actual understanding of the reality gets weaker," writes Michael Miller. David Whimsley warns, "Disinformation is therefore not just a communications problem. It's a governance risk, an economic liability and a direct threat to people's ability to make informed decisions."

title: Asiad  dismal Pakistan
description: Asiad  dismal Pakistan
content:
Authorities must resist the familiar temptation to treat isolated achievements as evidence of wider progress
Pakistan's campaign at the Asian Games is exposing the widening gulf between the country's sporting ambitions and its ability to compete consistently at the continental level. Two bronze medals in squash offer some consolation, but the reversals suffered across several disciplines on Saturday have raised familiar questions about the state of national sport. Individual determination remains evident. What is less apparent is the institutional support needed to translate that determination into sustained success.
At the close of Saturday's competitions, China had amassed 176 medals, including 107 golds, while Japan had secured 129 and South Korea 73. India had collected 30 medals, including four golds. Countries like Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have already secured eight gold medals apiece. Pakistan, meanwhile, had secured bronze in women's cricket and was assured of another medal in men's singles squash, with Noor Zaman and Mohammad Ashab Irfan due to contest the third-place play-off. The defeat against Malaysia in hockey was particularly disappointing. Pakistan surrendered a 4-3 advantage to lose 5-4 despite Sufyan Khan scoring all four goals. With the tournament still underway, the national team has an opportunity to recover. It is clear that the successes of individual competitors are too often celebrated without sufficient attention to the circumstances in which they have been achieved.
The Asian Games are not yet over, and Pakistan's remaining athletes deserve every opportunity to improve the country's medal tally. But whatever the final standings, the authorities must resist the familiar temptation to treat isolated achievements as evidence of wider progress. A country with Pakistan's sporting history should be capable of producing competitive athletes across a broader range of disciplines. The task is to build institutions that make such performances possible with greater regularity.

title: Cockroaches on a roll
description: India s CJP has transformed into a formidable pressure group capable of altering the regional governance landscape
content:
India's CJP has transformed into a formidable pressure group capable of altering the regional governance landscape
The Cockroach Janata Party of India has rapidly transitioned into a formidable pressure group capable of altering the regional governance landscape. Fresh from their victory in securing the resignation of the education minister, the group has successfully flexed its political muscle once more by forcing the Election Commission of India onto the backfoot. Following a sharp warning of imminent protests from the party's leadership, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar hastily directed a comprehensive review of the electoral rolls which, according to Indian media reports, were manipulated to benefit the ruling BJP. This surrender by a high-ranking official not only underscores the growing leverage of the Cockroach Party but also signals a profound shift in how grassroots agitation dictates institutional accountability. However, the Chief Election Commissioner still faces the looming threat of dismissal, as he has stopped short of the full resignation demanded by the Cockroach Party.
Ultimately, this standoff serves as a stark reminder about the necessity of an objective, neutral election commission led by an unbiased leader in a functioning democracy. Without absolute neutrality at the helm, the promise of free and fair elections remains entirely hollow. However, achieving this ideal has proven remarkably difficult across the region, including Pakistan. Allegations against the chief of the election watchdog have historically been a common feature of the political landscape in Pakistan. This persistent skepticism stems largely from the reality that the position has almost always functioned as a political appointment. Despite a constitutional safeguard designed to ensure bipartisan agreement, the reality has fallen short. No wonder hardly ever has any election in the country escaped the allegations of rigging. If we want future elections to command public trust, implement rigorous governance standards that guarantee complete independence and transparency in our public institutions.

title: And now DI Khan
description: The Dera attack came just days after the bleeding at Kohat that led to at least 31 precious lives lost
content:
The Dera attack came just days after the bleeding at Kohat that led to at least 31 precious lives lost
Another suicide attack on the border of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan is a grim reminder of a thriving terror nexus in the two terrorism-stricken province, in particular. More than 14 civilians were killed and 36 injured as an explosives-laden vehicle was rammed into Aman Mela police checkpost in Dera Ismail Khan's Darazinda tehsil. The modus operandi of terrorism this time was full of vengeance as rescue personnel were also targeted subsequently. Two volunteers of 1122 lost their lives on duty as their ambulance was ambushed. The incident was supplemented with heavy aerial firing in an attempt to terrorise the locals.
The Dera attack came just days after the bleeding at Kohat that led to at least 31 precious lives lost, indicating our loosening grip on the security of these insurgency-infected provinces. Immediate measures require heightening vigilance and beefing up intelligence gathering. Moving forward, achieving better coordination among law enforcement agencies - particularly by empowering the police - is vital to demonstrate our resolve against this callous enemy. Furthermore, aligning kinetic military operations with cohesive political responses is indispensable if we are to remain on the same page against this existential threat.
Analysing the changing pattern of these attacks is equally critical. The terror nexus is currently focusing on three distinct targets: security personnel, police and civilians. By attacking these groups, disgruntled elements intend to bleed Pakistan while trying to project a narrative of state failure. This systematic pattern proves the violence is not driven by local grievances, but is rather a foreign plot to weaken the country. It's no secret that there are troublesome districts that harbour active sleeper cells linked with local abettors and opportunists. This warrants a foolproof domestic counter-terrorism strategy combined with tactful diplomacy to expose their international patrons.

title: Has US accepted China as superpower
description: Has US accepted China as superpower
content:
Sometimes the symbolism surrounding a summit says as much as the substance of the talks
Sometimes the symbolism surrounding a summit says as much as the substance of the talks. The arrival of Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington last week was one such moment. When Xi's aircraft landed at Joint Base Andrews, a red carpet was rolled out. President Donald Trump himself went to the tarmac to receive his Chinese counterpart. The ceremony included a guard of honour, military bands, national anthems, a 21-gun salute and a flypast by US bombers and fighter jets. American presidents do not normally receive foreign leaders at the airport. The White House is traditionally where such honours are performed. That made Trump's decision to personally welcome Xi particularly significant.
The images from Andrews offered perhaps the clearest indication yet that an old question in international politics is becoming increasingly irrelevant: can China catch up with the United States? China is no longer simply a country trying to catch up with America. It has emerged as a superpower in its own right. Xi's visit was his first trip to Washington in more than a decade. The last Chinese leader to make a state visit was Xi himself in 2015, when Barack Obama was president. A great deal has changed since then. The China that Xi represented in Washington in 2015 was already a rising power. The China arriving in Washington in 2026 is something different: a country with enormous economic weight, advanced technological capabilities, a rapidly modernising military and a global diplomatic footprint. This is why the optics of the Andrews reception deserve attention.
For years, much of Washington's China policy was built around the idea of containing, constraining or slowing Beijing's rise. Trade restrictions, technology controls, military alliances and strategic partnerships in the Indo-Pacific were all part of an effort to preserve America's lead. But there is a fundamental difference between containing a rising power and managing a relationship with an established superpower. The latter appears to be increasingly unavoidable. That does not mean the strategic competition between Washington and Beijing has disappeared. Far from it. Trade, AI, advanced technology, Taiwan and security remain deeply contentious. The two countries are still competing for influence and technological advantage.
The Xi-Trump summit was as much about managing rivalry as producing breakthroughs. But competition between two powers of comparable global weight requires a different approach from an attempt to prevent one power from rising. Xi himself appeared conscious of this new reality. At the White House, he invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the danger of conflict when a rising power challenges an established one. Xi argued that China and the United States should strengthen communication and avoid confrontation, saying both countries stand to gain from cooperation and lose from conflict. That may be the central question of the new era: not whether China can become a superpower, but whether two superpowers can live side by side.
The answer will have consequences far beyond Washington and Beijing. For South Asia, the evolution of US-China relations is particularly important. A recalibration of American policy towards China will inevitably affect Washington's relationships with other countries in the region, including India and Pakistan. For Islamabad, any further deepening of the US-India strategic relationship will require close attention, given Pakistan's own security concerns and its longstanding strategic partnership with China.
China's rise has therefore changed the strategic equation for everyone. Perhaps the most striking message from Xi's Washington visit was not contained in a communique or a trade agreement. It was visible on the red carpet at Andrews. For the first time in decades, America appears to be dealing with China not simply as a rising power knocking at the door, but as a power already inside the room. The challenge now is whether Washington and Beijing can learn to share that room without turning their rivalry into confrontation.

title: Man dies in private security custody
description: Police say post mortem has been conducted  final findings will emerge after forensic report
content:
Police say post-mortem has been conducted, final findings will emerge after forensic report
A 34-year-old man, who was allegedly subjected to violence after picking up two old bottles from garbage in a private housing society within the limits of Rawat police station, died mysteriously on Sunday while in the custody of the housing society’s security staff.
Police registered a case of murder by causation and launched an investigation.
According to sources, Rawat police registered a case under the charge of murder by causation on the complaint of the deceased’s brother, Shehzad Yousaf.
In his complaint, he stated that his 34-year-old brother Adnan Yousaf worked at the private housing society and was the father of three children. His wife and children lived in their village.
He said they were at their home in Abbottabad when they received a phone call informing them that the body of their younger brother Yousaf was at the hospital of the private society.
Upon reaching the hospital, they met Abdul Aleem, who said he was a friend of Yousaf and had a close relationship with him.
He said the two had gone to Phase 8 of the society to deliver gas cylinders. He went to Ata’s flat to deliver the cylinder while Yousaf remained standing near the motorcycle. When he returned after delivering the cylinder, he saw Yousaf picking up two bottles from a garbage bin.
Meanwhile, a man identified as Aqeel Ahmed stopped Yousaf from picking up the bottles and called the private housing society’s security.
When the security team arrived, Ahmed allegedly continued punching Yousaf in the face in the presence of the security team, causing him to fall to the ground. Blood started coming from Yousaf’s mouth and nose.
He said he stopped Ahmed, who allegedly threatened him, saying he should remain silent or he would also be dealt with.
The private housing society’s security staff intervened, put Yousaf in their vehicle and told Ahmed and him to reach the police post.
He said that when he reached the shop 20 to 25 minutes later, he was informed that Yousaf’s body was lying at the society’s hospital.
Yousaf's family was located and informed, as was the police emergency service.
The private housing society’s security staff further told police that Yousaf had jumped from the moving vehicle while being taken to the police post in the presence of supervisor Sajawal Niazi.
He allegedly fell on the road, sustained injuries and died. The body was shifted to the District Headquarters Hospital.
The case further stated that Ahmed and the private housing society’s security staff were involved in Yousaf’s death.
According to police, an initial examination showed blood coming from Yousaf’s nose and mouth, while marks of violence and abrasions were found on his body.
Yousaf's post-mortem had been conducted, and the final situation would become clear after the forensic report. Police officials said a case under Section 322 for murder by causation had been registered and an investigation launched.

title: Parents decry rising private school fees
description: Monthly fees increased 20 to 40   some parents report paying over Rs35k monthly
content:
Monthly fees increased 20 to 40%; some parents report paying over Rs35k monthly
Parents have voiced serious concerns over exorbitant fees charged by private schools, saying the rising cost of education has made quality schooling increasingly unaffordable for middle-class families in the twin cities.
According to parents, several leading private schools and school systems have increased monthly fees by 20 to 40% without providing any clear justification for the hikes.
They said schools issued revised fee vouchers every few months, carrying substantial increases, but failed to provide audited accounts or explain how the additional amounts were being spent. They said the practice had further increased the financial burden on families already struggling with inflation.
In addition to tuition fees, schools charge separately for annual charges, security, laboratory facilities, activities and examinations, further increasing the overall cost of education.
Asma Bano, a parent of a student at a private school in Islamabad, said, “We are paying more than Rs35,000 per month for one child, excluding van charges. With three children, it has become impossible to manage.”
She said schools threatened to strike off students’ names if fees were not paid on time, while there was seemingly no corresponding check on their own fee structures.
Bano said another major concern was the lack of transparency, as many schools did not share audited accounts or details of the formula used for fee increases with parents.
She said annual increases were supposed to be capped and linked to inflation, but schools were implementing what parents described as arbitrary hikes.
Ahmed Raza, another middle-class parent, said, “We received a fee voucher of Rs84,000 for two children for next month, compared with Rs62,000 during the same month last year. There is no new teacher, no new facility, but only a new fee.”
He said that when he went to pay the fee a week late due to a delay in receiving his salary, the school imposed a late-payment surcharge of Rs2,500 and did not allow his son to attend classes for two days.
He called for a uniform fee-regulation policy across the twin cities to provide relief to parents already facing financial pressure due to inflation.
Officials of the Private Educational Institutions Regulatory Authority (PEIRA) said the authority regulated the fee structures of private educational institutions operating in the Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT).
They said permissible fees were determined in accordance with the academic quality of an institution and the educational facilities available to students.
The officials added that private schools were required to comply with fee-related rules and directions issued by PEIRA, while any increase had to remain within the applicable regulatory framework.
They said the authority assessed the academic standards and facilities of private educational institutions and determined fees accordingly to ensure that charges remained commensurate with the quality of education and services provided to students.

title: Frivolous and baseless   Pakistan rejects Taliban claims of involvement in Nuristan violence
description: Calls accusations ironic  says presence of terrorist groups inside Afghanistan  well documented
content:
Calls accusations ironic, says presence of terrorist groups inside Afghanistan 'well documented'
The Ministry of Information on Sunday rejected allegations by the Afghan Taliban regime linking its security forces and intelligence agencies to violence in Afghanistan’s Nuristan province, calling the claims “frivolous, baseless and devoid of any truth”.
"Pakistan categorically rejects the fabricated claims of involvement by its security forces or intelligence agencies in any internal clashes in Nuristan or elsewhere in Afghanistan, including allegations of recruiting or training former Afghan security personnel or facilitating Daesh or any other terrorist group operating in Afghanistan," said the ministry in a statement.
The statement came in response to allegations levelled by the Afghan Taliban’s Ministry of Defence, which claimed that groups affiliated with Daesh, along with what it described as “elements of subversion”, had crossed the Durand Line into Nuristan’s Kamdesh district with the support of Pakistan. The ministry claimed that its security forces had killed 28 of the alleged infiltrators and captured 32 others, while the remaining fighters fled back across the Durand Line.
The ministry further responded to the allegations, stating that not a shred of evidence had been produced to substantiate Pakistan’s involvement
"There were no identities, documents, communications, forensic evidence or independent verification to support the allegations," it said.
The statement also rejected a video being circulated on social media to support the false claim, saying that it "only shows a few unarmed individuals who are not even properly dressed or equipped.'
𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐂𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤 | 𝐌𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 & 𝐁𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐝𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 ◼️ The allegations by the Afghan Taliban regime linking Pakistan with the alleged violence in Nuristan are frivolous, baseless and devoid of any truth. Pakistan categorically rejects… pic.twitter.com/skowInbs0L
The ministry described the footage as appearing to be “a pre-planned video shoot by the Afghan Taliban regime well known for lies and fabricated claims”.
The fact-check graphic attached to the post carried the text, “Afghan Defence Ministry claims arrest of Pakistani military personnel and fighters in Nuristan.” It marked the claim as “false and fabricated” and displayed a document by the Afghan Ministry of Defence dated September 27.
The ministry said the presence and activities of terrorist groups inside Afghanistan were “well documented”, including in successive reports by the United Nations and other international organisations.
Read: ‘Irrefutable evidence’ links Afghan soil to terror attacks in Pakistan
“Attempts to manufacture a Pakistani connection cannot obscure the reality that these terrorist groups continue to find sanctuary and a permissive environment for growth in Afghan territory,” it said.
“It is particularly ironic for the Afghan Taliban regime to accuse Pakistan of supporting terrorism while terrorist organisations operating from Afghanistan continue to pose a direct threat to Pakistan and regional security,” the ministry added.
“Instead of externalising responsibility for its internal security challenges through fanciful allegations, the Afghan Taliban regime should take credible and verifiable action against terrorist organisations operating from its territory,” the ministry said.
It also called on the Afghan authorities to fulfil their commitments that Afghan soil would not be used for terrorism against Pakistan or any other country, “rather than attempting to deflect responsibility through fabricated accusations”.
The statement further added that the allegations were “reflective of lies to externalise internal dissent and oppression of women, children and minorities”.
This is not the first time the Afghan Taliban regime has levelled allegations against Pakistan. In the past, it has accused Pakistan of facilitating infiltration, carrying out airstrikes and smuggling weapons into Afghanistan, allegations that Islamabad has repeatedly rejected.
According to security officials, the Afghan Taliban regime has been providing sanctuary, support and patronage to terrorist groups. They said documented evidence contradicted Kabul’s repeated denials and pointed to an entrenched terrorist network operating from Afghan soil .
Pakistan maintains that the terrorist nexus extended beyond the movement of terrorists across the border to their training, arming and operational support.
Read more: Afghan soil must not be used for terrorism, Pakistan tells UN
Security officials estimate that up to 70 per cent of the Fitna al-Khawarij terrorists infiltrating Pakistan were of Afghan origin. They further claim that the Taliban regime had allowed leftover US and NATO weapons to reach terrorist groups, including Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan .
In 2026 alone, terrorism emanating from Afghan soil claimed the lives of 1,327 Pakistanis and injured another 2,484, according to figures cited by Pakistani authorities.
The United Nations estimated the strength of TTP in Afghanistan at around 6,000 to 6,500 terrorists. UN reporting had also documented more than 600 terrorist attacks against Pakistan during 2025, including attacks launched from Afghan territory.
According to Pakistani security officials, the TTP had established training facilities in Afghanistan’s Kunar, Nangarhar, Khost and Paktika provinces.
The government has maintained that the issue was fundamentally one of Pakistan's national security and that continued attacks from Afghan soil cannot be addressed through denials alone.
Pakistan says it expected the Taliban regime to fulfil its commitments by taking verifiable action against terrorist groups operating from its territory rather than defending or denying their presence.
