title: When the powerful stop pretending the rules apply
description: At the UN  President Trump challenged several of the principles the global body was created to uphold with much of his rhetoric met by silence
content:
At the UN, President Trump challenged principles the global body was founded on, his rhetoric largely met by silence
When Donald Trump stood before the United Nations General Assembly and spoke about annihilating another country, the room listened and for some observers, the more disturbing question was not what the American president said but what that silence revealed about the international system itself.
Standing before the UN General Assembly, Trump spoke about the war against Iran, celebrated American military power, and warned that Tehran faced “annihilation” if it did not make a deal with the US. This was not said at a usual political rally of supporters or a television interview, it was the UN, the institution created after the Second World War around a simple idea that countries should have a place to settle their disputes without turning to conflict.
There were walkouts, Iran’s delegation, as expected, left, as did Cuba’s, and governments have criticised Washington elsewhere, so the speech did not go unanswered in every corner of the building. But there was no collective protest from the General Assembly floor, no institutional interruption, and no immediate challenge to the language coming from the podium. For Jostein Hauge, a scholar of international political economy, that moment was more than just another provocative speech by Trump. “I say this with the utmost seriousness as a scholar of international political economy: the rules-based international order is dead,” Hauge wrote afterwards on X. It is an extraordinary claim, and also a useful place from which to examine what happened at the UN this week, because the question is not simply what Trump said but what the rest of the world can do when the country saying it is the United States.
Ashok Swain, professor of Peace and Conflict at Uppsala University, says the muted response was troubling precisely because of where it happened. “The United Nations is supposed to be the principal forum where threats to peace, attacks on human dignity and rejection of collective global responsibilities are challenged,” he says. Trump’s speech, in Swain’s reading, exposed the gap between that expectation and the reality of international politics. Trump used his address to defend the US war against Iran and present American military power as an instrument for dealing with international problems. He spoke proudly about the damage inflicted on Iran’s military infrastructure and described the United States as possessing unmatched military strength. He also attacked the International Criminal Court, criticised international institutions, and rejected international approaches to issues including climate change and artificial intelligence. On immigration, he repeated his familiar attacks on what he sees as an international system that constrains American sovereignty. But it was Iran that brought the question of war and international law most directly into the room, with Trump saying the choice facing Tehran was a deal or “annihilation.”
The legal question surrounding the US and Israeli attacks on Iran is contested. International law places significant restrictions on the use of force between states, with limited exceptions including self-defence and action authorised by the Security Council. Legal scholars have argued that the attacks violated the UN Charter, while the US and Israel have presented their own legal justifications. What is less ambiguous is the political message Trump was delivering, military power, rather than international institutions, was being presented as the mechanism through which Washington would secure its interests. And that message landed in an institution whose leaders had spent the opening of the General Assembly arguing for almost the opposite. The president of the General Assembly cautioned that international law and humanitarian law could not be applied selectively, and outgoing Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that geopolitical fault lines were widening and called for international law and cooperation to prevail over force. It was at that point that Trump took the podium, delivering a message that ran counter to everything the UN leadership had just said.
For Swain, the gap between what the UN says and what it can enforce goes to the heart of the problem. “When governments remain restrained in confronting a powerful state while speaking much more forcefully against weaker ones, silence itself can reinforce a hierarchy of power,” the Sweden-based academic notes. The hierarchy has always been there, even if the UN Charter speaks in the language of sovereign equality, because countries do not enter the international system with equal political, military or economic power. The United States is a permanent member of the Security Council and has a veto, it has one of the world’s largest economies, an enormous military, and a network of alliances that gives Washington influence far beyond what the formal structure of the General Assembly suggests. The General Assembly, by contrast, gives countries a voice without giving them equal power to enforce what they say. That itself has long frustrated countries in the Global South.
Swain says the issue is not simply that Washington gets away with everything, the deeper problem is that the consequences of violating international norms are themselves shaped by power. “A small or economically vulnerable country in the Global South that threatened another state can face diplomatic isolation, sanctions and potentially international intervention,” he says. The US has far greater capacity to resist those pressures because of its military strength, economic influence, alliances and veto power. “This asymmetry has long contributed to criticism from the Global South that international rules are enforced selectively,” he says. That selective application does something more damaging than create resentment: it weakens the legitimacy of the rules themselves.
The post-1945 international order was never the egalitarian system its rhetoric sometimes suggested. The US was one of its principal architects and, at the same time, one of the states with the greatest ability to shape the system in its own interests. But the system did establish something that created institutions in which smaller states could challenge powerful ones, build coalitions, negotiate, and make their grievances part of an international record. If those institutions cannot constrain the most powerful states, their value becomes harder to defend. That does not mean the UN becomes irrelevant, and Swain is careful about this. “The United Nations still has considerable value,” he adds. “But episodes like this expose the gap between its principles and its capacity to enforce them.” The organisation remains indispensable for diplomacy, humanitarian action, norm-building, and giving smaller countries a political platform. The problem is that the General Assembly does not possess the coercive authority to enforce most of its resolutions, and the Security Council, where enforcement power is greater, is dominated by five permanent members with vetoes, including the US. This has created a contradiction at the centre of the international system: countries are formally equal, but their ability to act on the rules is not.
Swain argues that the UN’s problem is therefore not simply that it has failed to stop Trump, the larger problem is the perception that the international system applies rules differently depending on who is involved. That perception is particularly dangerous in the Global South, where memories of colonialism and intervention already shape attitudes towards international institutions. A country that believes international law will protect it has an incentive to use diplomacy, while a country that believes international law will be ignored when a stronger state wants something else has a different set of incentives. It may seek stronger military alliances, build up its own weapons, or pursue nuclear deterrence. That is where the consequences of Trump’s rhetoric begin to extend beyond Iran. “The greatest danger is the gradual normalisation of the idea that military threats and force are legitimate tools of ordinary foreign policy,” Swain cautions.
He shares an important observation here: offensive rhetoric, Islamophobic statements or climate denial are not, by themselves, automatically violations of international law, whereas the use or threat of force raises a different legal question. But when a US president repeatedly presents overwhelming military power as an acceptable way of dealing with sovereign states, the message does not stop at Washington. Other governments hear it too. If the United States can claim that its military power gives it the right to determine the terms of international disputes, why should other powerful countries accept restraints that Washington itself appears willing to treat selectively? “Russia, China, India or regional powers are all asking why they should accept restraints that Washington itself treats selectively,” Swain says. The result could be a more openly transactional international system in which military strength becomes more important, alliances become more important, arms control becomes harder, disarmament becomes harder, and smaller states become more vulnerable to the calculations of larger ones. The danger is not that every country suddenly decides to ignore international law, it is that the incentive to follow it begins to weaken. And once that happens, the system can deteriorate without ever formally collapsing.
That is why Swain is reluctant to reduce the problem to Trump himself. “The post-1945 system was never as rules-based or equal as its supporters sometimes claimed,” he says. But there was at least a widely accepted principle that military force should be constrained and that international institutions mattered, and that principle is now under pressure. At the opening of the General Assembly, the UN leadership repeatedly warned about a world in which power was replacing law. Trump’s speech showed what that replacement might sound like. There was no need for him to announce that the international system was being dismantled, he simply spoke as though its limits did not apply to him. That is more consequential than one speech, because international orders do not survive only because treaties exist on paper, they survive because governments believe that following the rules is preferable to breaking them, and because powerful states believe there will be consequences if they do. When either belief begins to disappear, the architecture remains standing but its authority starts to drain away.
This is where Hauge’s declaration that the rules-based order is dead becomes difficult to dismiss entirely, even if the word “dead” is too definitive. The order has not disappeared, of course, the UN remains, international law remains, states still invoke it daily, courts still hear cases, governments still negotiate treaties, and UN agencies still provide services on which millions depend. But an international system can survive institutionally while losing political credibility, and that may be the more important story coming out of this year’s General Assembly. Swain puts it more bluntly in terms of consequences. “The most damaging legacy of such rhetoric may therefore be not any single statement, but the precedent it helps establish that international law constrains the weak more effectively than the powerful.” Once that perception becomes deeply embedded, he warns, rebuilding trust in the international system will be extraordinarily difficult.

title: The baby soap child
description: His ugliness has always protected him   until a beautiful child looks at him without fear
content:
His ugliness has always protected him—until a beautiful child looks at him without fear
Believe me: Every criminal is cursed with a birth defect. Most of them are short—really short and thin and diminutive, with somewhat twisted limbs and features. During my long years of incarceration, I have hardly seen a handsome fraudster, drug dealer, rapist, child molester, or murderer.
Even those who are tall or sturdy usually have something seriously wrong with their body proportions. They have either a bit too big or too small a head on a bit too big or too small a torso, with arms and legs that are a bit too long or too short.
This defect sometimes manifests itself in an erasure of the personality with the criminal becoming shapeless, formless and featureless, like figurines made of dough by a five-year-old child.
These are the kind of people you tend not to notice even when they are walking all alone along a deserted road, simply because they merge into the general ugliness of our urban life—with its broken roads, piles of garbage, overflowing gutters, chaotic traffic and horrific buildings.
Illegitimate children—also suffer from these anomalies.
When I see my face in the broken mirror of my prison cell—a dark hole where I am going to spend the rest of my days—I often feel that I am looking at the portrait that Dorian Gray kept hidden behind dark veils—a portrait that reflected the sheer ugliness of his soul.
Earlier, I regarded my abominable deformity as the bane of my accursed existence, which seemed to have no place in the whole wide world—not even in the hearts of my unknown, sinful parents.
However, like Dorian, I later came to value and even love my ugliness as my face struck terror into the hearts of those around me. It was a visage that called to mind the head of a badger poised to attack its prey, its pointed but irregular teeth bared in anticipation of the kill.
My immense ugliness, while shutting me out from any possibility of finding a friend or lover and building a social life at the orphanage and, later, in the world beyond, also protected me from people at large who could feel nothing for me but revulsion and hatred.
This realisation gave me the power to finally connect with my surroundings. Yet the only kind of life that was possible for me in this world was a double life.
During the day, I worked as a delivery man, running around this grotesque, huge and almost interminable city on a motorcycle, with my face covered by a clinical mask. But at night, I did what I then regarded as a social service—a truly charitable act of kindness.
I killed the newborns that sinful mothers left in the dirty cots outside the ugly buildings of Edhi's orphanages so that they might be spared a life of misery and depravity.
I waited patiently in some dark corner with a view of one of these little beds every night, sometimes for days or even months, just for the moment when a car, a rickshaw, or a motorcycle pulled up in front of it.
I started walking towards the cot after the vehicle had sped away, leaving a faint trail of dust behind. When I laid my hands on the small, warm bundle, I heard a weak, muffled cry.
I gently uncovered the little face and looked at it closely. I confess that I was always touched by the vulnerability and innocence of those babies.
But what I looked for was the birth defect—the anomaly of the bastard. And believe me, I came across a glaring abnormality in every case—except the last one.
That night, I was caught off guard, as the child was not brought to the cot in a vehicle.
It was a shadow that had put the little bundle in the cradle much earlier than usual. She was already bending over the cot when I first realized what was happening.
The woman was looking at the baby for the last time. Finally, she started plodding along, and by the time she reached the street corner, I was already at the cradle.
When I removed the cloth from his face, I was startled by his beauty. The newborn was perfectly calm and wide-awake, his pink, round face adorned with golden-brown hair.
I had only seen such a pretty child on the posters for baby soap.
This wasn't possible. The child must have some deformity. There must be something gross about him, I said to myself, as I ran my hand over his little body, removing his clothes.
The child was the epitome of perfection. He looked even more beautiful in his pure nakedness.
As I stared at him in utter confusion, something dawned on me.
This child was also an aberration. He was free from defects, but his very beauty and perfection were a deviation—a departure from the norm that all illegitimate children must follow. He was an anomaly among them and deserved the same treatment as the rest of them.
However, as I was about to cover his beautiful mouth, the child—calm and wide-awake—smiled.
Despite my ugliness, the child was not afraid of me.
For the first time, I had decided to return home without finishing my job.

title: The women who became lionesses
description: Marjan Kamali s gripping tale of friendship  betrayal and resilience amid decades of political upheaval in Iran
content:
Marjan Kamali's gripping tale of friendship, betrayal and resilience amid decades of political upheaval in Iran
‘Friends are forever’ is an old saying but still very applicable. Though there are exceptions. However, here we are not talking about exceptions. We are talking about the bond that bears years of separation and miles of distance, yet withstands the test of friendship.
We see this type of friendship in Marjan Kamali’s book The Lion Women of Tehran. Kamali, is an award winning Iranian-American novelist and author, whose books have international acclaim and have been translated in more than 25 languages. Born in Turkey to Iranian parents, she spent her childhood in Turkey, Iran, Germany, and Kenya, before settling in the US. Her debut novel, Together Tea, was published in 2013 and the second, The Stationery Shop of Tehran was published in 2019. Her latest and hopefully not the last, The Lion Women of Tehran, published in 2024, follows the deep, complex bond between two girls, Ellie and Homa, growing up against the backdrop of political turmoil in Iran during the 1950s and 60s.
Our protagonists, Homa (named after a legendary bird from Iranian mythology that is said to never rest on the ground and lives its entire life invisibly flying above the earth) and Elaheh (meaning goddess) shortened to Ellie, meet each other when they were seven years old in the Tehran of 1950s. Their friendship is tested from time to time as life, social status, wealth, and their families come between them. Both come from different backgrounds—one is born to low-income parents and the other is born to wealthy parents. However, due to the death of her father, Ellie (the wealthy one) and her mother are forced to move to a tiny home in an impoverished area of Tehran, where they (especially the mother) find themselves out of place.
Ellie is admitted to a school in a locality perceived as a slum neighbourhood. Lonely and bearing the brunt of her mother’s endless grievances, she is excited at the prospect of attending a school, dreaming of making some friends. Luckily, on the first day, she meets Homa, a kind, intelligent, and passionate, yet high-spirited, and often reckless girl. Homa, intrigued by the new girl in class, enthusiastically pursues a friendship with her. Despite initial reluctance, Ellie accepts her friendship and the two become best friends.
With time the two girls become inseparable. Though Ellie’s mother, conscious of her elite background (she claimed to be the descendant of a Qajar king), does not approve of their friendship, insists that Homa and her family are far beneath Ellie’s social standing, and forbids Homa to visit her house, the two girls together play games, wander through the colourful stalls of the Grand Bazaar, and share their ambitions for becoming “lion women”. Homa also introduces Ellie to the joy of home-cooked foods crafted in a modest stone cave-like kitchen by her mother, Maman Joon, who also teaches the two girls the secrets of her food preparation, how she selects the ingredients and specific flavours she seeks to achieve in both her savoury and sweet dishes.
Although a rebellious risk-taker, Homa fuels Ellie’s interest in higher education, and urges her to take schoolwork more seriously. Homa’s desire is to attend Tehran University, achieve her dream of becoming a lawyer and ultimately a Judge and fight for people who can’t fight for themselves. She is determined to do all of that with Ellie by her side.
She tells Ellie: “Shir zan. Lionesses. Us. Can’t you just see it, Ellie? Someday, you and me—we’ll do great things. We’ll live life for ourselves. And we will help others. We are cubs now, maybe. But we will grow to be lionesses. Strong women who make things happen.”
But their happiness does not live long and they have to part ways as Ellie and her mother get the opportunity to return to their previous bourgeois life. Over time, Ellie’s memories of Homa begin to fade; she is a popular student at the best girls’ high school in Iran. However, Homa’s sudden reappearance in Ellie’s world forces her to learn to make space for Homa again.
Graduating from high school together, they both join Tehran University, though in different departments yet continue to meet and spend time together along with a couple of other school friends. While Ellie is looking forward to finishing her studies and marrying the love of her life, Homa’s activism continues. As the political conflict, as well as Homa’s activism, increases one well-intentioned praise by Ellie leads to unintentional betrayal and Homa’s life is turned upside down, and the realisation pinches Ellie severely.
Written in the backdrop of political turmoil and struggle for women’s rights in Iran, the story spans several decades and through the years Homa, who is passionately devoted to “fighting” for women’s rights, finds one cause after another to continue her struggle. While she is vehemently against the supreme rule of the Shah, later, when the Shah is deposed in the revolution, Homa finds herself against the religious regime that have replaced the Shah. The change, in terms of rights, that women expected in the wake of the revolution is nowhere to be seen. The new rule fiercely restricts women’s rights, imposes dress code and mandatory hijab laws, and limits any personal prosperity for women in general. Homa sees the new regime as even worse with respect to women’s rights and their freedoms and continues to raise her voice.
A point comes when she is worried about her teenage daughter as she fears she might be arrested again, and has to seek help from her childhood friend who is well settled in America with her husband. Whether Ellie responds positively to her friend in need and what becomes of Homa, I will leave for the readers to find out and not be a spoiler.
But Kamali’s book is not just about friendship. The author addresses several themes, that are important, realistic, relatable, and timely and relevant, such as political turmoil, oppressive regimes, dreams, betrayal, class/socio-economic status, feminism, women’s rights and political activism, choices women make and choices that are available to them, education, careers, and friendship.
Interestingly, while tackling serious themes of socio-political nature, as in her previous book, Kamali also gives us a glimpse into Iranian life and culture, especially Iranian cuisine. To explain the flavours of Iranian cuisine she uses sensory words and phrases like, “The caramelised scent that infused the house as the onions sizzled…” or the “Tangy explosion of sweet and sour”. In Homa’s family kitchen, Maman Joon invites Ellie to taste her home-made pomegranate-filled pastries, known as ghotab, which Homa describes as, “The best thing you can eat.” Even later, Homa’s lunch often has Ghormeh sabzi with, Ellie notices, generous use of fenugreek.
This story of friendship, courage, and resilience follows the girls till 2022, the year when a young Iranian woman Mahsa Amini was killed in Iran by security forces for wearing improper hijab, as a result of which women and girls took to the streets to show that they had had enough. Homa writes in the Epilogue, they “bravely defy the mandatory hijab laws. They throw their headscarves into a bonfire and twirl, dancing for freedom and human rights.” They are arrested, beaten, and even killed, but the protests go on. “But people have had enough. They are tired of being told how to behave, what to say, what to wear, whom to worship. Tired of their rights diminished. Their slogan is … Women, Life, Freedom. … In Persian: ‘Zan, Zendegi, Azadi’.”
Kamali writes in the author’s note: “As I finished this book, Iran’s long quest for freedom and tragic cycles of protests and crackdown happened in real time.”
Though the story is predominantly narrated through Ellie giving her perspective, there are a few segments in Homa’s voice which give her perspective as well. Epilogue in Homa’s words as a letter to her granddaughter connects the missing time and where she had been all this while. One thing that would inspire many readers is that even when she has grown old she continues to not only believe in what the two friends taught each other since their early years but is, in fact, still taking active part in the fight for freedom to do what she believes in and staying true to herself.
The lives of Iranian women are close to Kamali’s heart and it is reflected in her books. In the author’s note, she writes: “Writing about Iranian women has been the central theme of my life. I come from a line of strong, very vocal, and opinionated Iranian women who in some instances broke new grounds, in other instances saw their lives stymied and constrained by political culture and in all cases experienced a hard line government eradicate almost overnight rights for which women had fought for decades.”
The author’s portrayal of the changing socio-political landscape of Iran during the Islamic Revolution and its aftermath with emphasis on women’s rights, shows how freedom and rights that most people take for granted are not extended to all women across the world and women all over the world (including in Pakistan) have fought for in their own time and continue to do so today.
The book aptly shows that women in Iran have always been educated and aware of their rights, and have always fought for them, though due to the present war there are no news of protests, as they probably have taken a back seat in national interest (as Iranians are very patriotic and would not like outside powers to take advantage).
The writer is a freelance journalist and tweets @naqviriz; she can be reached at naqvi59rizwana@gmail.com

title: Not for the faint hearted
description: A throwback to the David Dhawan Govinda classics of the 1990s  featuring satirical moments that subtly highlight issues faced by the average Pakistani
content:
Throwback to David Dhawan-Govinda classics of the 90s, with satire on issues faced by the average Pakistani
If you didn't believe there’s still a Govinda in all of us, you'd better believe it now, because Yasir Hussain's latest theatre play, So-Suite, brings out that very Govinda in everyone. The effect might not last long, but during the 70-minute play, it will make you feel the same way you did when watching the original Coolie No 1, Hero No 1, Saajan Chalay Sasural, Baday Miyan Chote Miyan, Kyo Kii... Main Jhuth Nahin Bolta, or even Partner.
Got the drift? If not, let me elaborate. This play captures the feeling of being caught in one lie and having to invent ten more to cover it up; of running from room to room, desperately trying to keep two worlds from colliding; or of making a complete mess of things while trying too hard.
Directed and written by Yasir Hussain, So-Suite is an old-school comedy set in modern-day Pakistan. It relies on misunderstandings, mistaken identities, frantic cover-ups, sharp dialogue, and physical comedy—all ingredients that have powered some of the subcontinent’s most memorable comedies.
It may not reach the level of Monkey Business, Yasir Hussain’s best work, but its humour belongs to both an earlier era and the present, which is why it appeals to across generations. The best part is that the play doesn’t take itself seriously and gives the audience exactly what they came to see: chaos.
After his bachelor party, Honey (Yasir Hussain) ends up in the honeymoon suite he booked for his soon-to-be wife, Anum (Hifza Tahir). There’s just one problem—Anum isn't there.
Instead, Honey finds himself with a mysterious woman (Afifa Sheikh). Before he can even think of a convincing explanation, his best friend Moon (Umer Aalam) arrives with more bad news: both his girlfriend, Sania, and Honey's fiancée, Anum, are expected to be at the hotel sooner than expected.
What follows is a classic comedy of errors. Honey and Moon devise increasingly elaborate plans to keep the two women from discovering what is going on. But the more they try to control the situation, the more chaotic it grows.
Soon, the suspicious hotel manager (Khizr Ansari), housekeeper Rania (Fahad Hashmi), clueless gangster Gullu (Bilal Yousufzai), and designer Amjad C (Osama Bin Atiq) are dragged into the madness, each with their own idiosyncrasies.
The central joke is simple: everyone is trying to hide something, and everyone is doing a terrible job. That simplicity works because the play keeps escalating. Each attempt to solve one problem creates another, inviting the audience to enjoy the increasingly ridiculous consequences.
So-Suite's biggest strength is Yasir Hussain at his best, who not only wrote and directed the play but also plays the lead role. Usually, when an actor becomes a producer or director, their stage performance varies, but Yasir Hussain is part of a rare breed. He gets better when the stakes are high, which is why, on stage, he is Honey and Yasir Hussain is nowhere to be seen.
Honey is the kind of character that requires an actor who is completely comfortable looking ridiculous. Hussain doesn't hesitate to go all the way, fully embracing the physicality, expressions, and frantic energy that bring the character to life.
This is where the Govinda comparison comes in. Govinda's classic films have a distinct style of Indian comedy: fast-paced misunderstandings, exaggerated reactions, physical humour, and characters perpetually one step away from disaster. Govinda excelled at it; Yasir Hussain builds on it.
Umer Aalam’s Moon comes second for the most hilarious lines, dialogues, and antics; you can compare his situation to Shreyas Talpade in Golmaan Returns, where he does everything to put his boss at ease, only to find out the reality was nothing short of a nightmare.
The two share an excellent camaraderie, evident in their many projects together; others, like the multi-talented Osama Bin Atiq, also join in with his Amjad C (because if Maria can be B, why can’t Amjad be C), a designer with flair. It was good to see Bilal Yousufzai make an appearance, as well as Gullu Badmaash, who finds true love and who, along with other characters, seems to have walked into the wrong comedy—which, of course, is precisely why he works.
Khizr Ansari makes the suspicious hotel manager memorable, though it would have been better if he'd done something significantly different from what he did in Monkey Business. He is one of the talented actors we have who can play Modi Bakht one day and a TikToker another, so he needs to keep that flair going with different characters.
Of all the female characters, Hifza Tahir's Anum provides the perfect counterbalance as the woman who isn't as clueless as everyone assumes. Afifa Sheikh brings both beauty and energy to Sania, and even though her character takes steps one wouldn’t normally take, the audience cheers for her because of her performance.
Fahad Hashmi's Rania (yes, that’s a surprise!) is another example of the play's willingness to embrace absurdity, because that angle makes the audience laugh uncontrollably. If performed poorly, the character could have destroyed the play, but thankfully, it didn’t.
The writing was packed with pop-culture references and topical jokes. The script mentions Fizza Ali when the characters talk about singing in the morning, then KMC comes up when it comes to cleaning or not cleaning; Honey and Moon even bring in the many one-hit-wonder TikTokers in their discussion, and their rapid-fire dialogue delivery earns full marks for being brilliant.
The political satire is particularly enjoyable because it doesn't take itself too seriously. Some jokes are subtle enough to make a reserved audience member smile. Others are delivered with such confidence that anyone willing to laugh will probably laugh loudly.
Then there are the situations. The play repeatedly places its characters in increasingly ridiculous circumstances and lets the performers squeeze as much comedy as possible from them. The result is a show in which even a relatively simple exchange can turn into a full-blown comic sequence. For an audience starved for good live comedy, that matters.
So-Suite isn't without its problems. Some of its humour belongs to an older school of comedy, particularly the repeated use of body-shaming jokes. These jokes may still get laughs from some audience members, but younger viewers may find this kind of humour dated or a tad uncomfortable.
The constant slapping, once an icebreaker in David Dhawan films, also becomes repetitive, though I must admit I loved it. The cross-dressing element also feels dated, particularly for audiences who have seen similar comic devices used in television and films, including Kapil Sharma's comedy.
None of these elements completely derails the play. Still, they reveal the tension at its core: So-Suite deliberately draws on an older comedy tradition while performing for a contemporary audience. At times, that works brilliantly. At other times, it feels like a joke that has already had its moment.
Yasir Hussain is steadily building something Pakistani comedy has been missing for some time: his own comedy universe. Like Umer Sharif before him, he has built a stable of performers who move from one production to another, play different characters, and create familiarity for returning audiences.
They were at Hotel Jaan-e-Jaan. They followed him into Monkey Business. Now they have gathered at So-Suite, which feels like a blend of both. It has the situational chaos of Hotel Jaan-e-Jaan and the comic timing of Monkey Business, while adding its own flavour with topical references, political satire, and an increasingly absurd chain of misunderstandings.
That may ultimately be why So-Suite works. It doesn't pretend to be anything other than a comedy meant to make people laugh. At a time when quality films are scarce in theatres, and comedy shows are increasingly rare on television, a theater production that lets its audience forget everything for a couple of hours is almost exactly what the doctor ordered.
So, if you value your life and don't want to die laughing, perhaps stay away from So-Suite. But if you don't mind losing your composure for a few hours, this suite is definitely worth checking into.

title: The things families don t do anymore
description: Smartphones and busy lives have replaced many of the small rituals that once made families feel connected
content:
Smartphones and busy lives have replaced many of the small rituals that once made families feel connected
There was a time when families did not have to schedule time together. People simply came home. Talked, worked, studied, ate, laughed and cried around each other. They might have cribbed, complained and quarrelled, yet they hung together much more than they do now. It was a family thing.
Fathers came home from work. Mothers were already in the kitchen, often having spent a good part of the day there. Grandparents sat in their usual places. Someone's cousin or relative was invariably visiting. An aunt could arrive without warning, complain that nobody ever visited her and then stay for the next upcoming meal, and she wasn’t unwelcome.
Nobody had sent a calendar invitation. Nobody had checked everybody's availability. Nobody had said, “Let's find a slot that works for all of us.” Family simply happened. Today, of course, families still love one another. They may even be in touch more often than ever before, courtesy of WhatsApp groups, video calls and photographs sent within seconds. Yet something has changed.
We have become constantly connected — and, in many ways, less together. Somewhere between smartphones, streaming platforms, traffic, tuition classes, work deadlines, social commitments and the increasing need for privacy, many of the small rituals that once filled family life have quietly disappeared. Not with a bang, but just gradually.
One day, everyone stopped eating together. Nobody has the time for it anymore, nor schedules, and sometimes neither patience, for a shared meal or people. Another day, children stopped playing outside. Then relatives began calling before visiting. In the same way, the television stopped being communal. And before anyone quite noticed, cousins who once spent entire summers together became people who occasionally liked each other's Instagram posts.
Children returned from school, threw their bags somewhere inconvenient and disappeared until they were summoned for tea or dinner. Kids walked unaccompanied to the nearby store to get candy. They would step out of their homes to gather around the ice-cream vendor and fuss over popsicles. There was a deadline that generations of Pakistani children understood perfectly. You could play outside until Maghrib. The street belonged to children.
Apart from cricket, there was pithhoo, hide-and-seek and endless variations of games whose rules were passed down orally and altered according to the number of children available. Children returned home dirty, sweaty and hungry, but at the appointed home time. Today, many streets are no longer safe enough for that freedom. Traffic has increased. Cities have expanded. Parents have understandable fears. Gated communities and apartment living have changed neighbourhood life. Screens have also provided a more convenient alternative and the child is indoors, relatively safe and occupied. Hence, childhood is now mostly spent behind closed doors.
Weddings by the way were much smaller affairs attended by the whole family because conveniently enough, most weddings were held in shamiyanas or gorgeously coloured marquis pegged up in the nearest open space. Few weddings were held at hotels and clubs, wedding halls and lawns did not exist.
Perhaps nothing illustrates the change better than the family meal. There was a time when dinner meant dinner. People sat down together. Or at least, as many members of the household as possible did. There was conversation, interrogation and occasional argument. Someone complained about the food. Someone else complained that nobody appreciated the effort that had gone into preparing it.
Children were asked about school. “Why did you get these marks?” “What happened to that boy/girl who was always calling you?” “Why do eat so much baigan (aubergines) all the time?” “Why aren't you eating?” “Don't sit like that.” “Finish your sabzi (vegetables).” It may not always have been sophisticated conversation, but it was conversation. People spoke, others listened. There were no phones at the table.
Today, the dining table increasingly competes with the screen. One person is watching something on a phone, a parent or grandparent watching something on TV. Another is replying to messages. Someone has already eaten or will eat later. Teenagers may be in their rooms. Parents are catching up on work, phone calls, messages or are out.
Perhaps what is being lost is not simply the meal but the daily exchange of information that families once took for granted. You knew what was happening in everybody's life because, every evening, everybody was more or less forced into the same room. Family dinner was not quality time carefully created by a parenting expert. It was simply dinner.
Then there was the television. For those who grew up before every bedroom acquired a screen, watching television was a collective experience. There was one television and that meant negotiation. Dad wanted cricket, mom wanted the drama, children wanted cartoons, but the adults had already decided. There were arguments over the remote long before anyone used the expression “screen time.” When a popular drama was on, an entire household watched it together.
Sometimes, an entire neighbourhood did. The next day, people discussed the previous night's episode at school, in offices and over tea. Television created shared references. Everyone knew what everyone else had seen. There were no Netflix or Hulu snobs. Today, a family can sit in the same drawing room while watching four completely different programmes on four different devices, because streaming has given us choice.
It has also taken away the power or perhaps the tyranny of parents and, perhaps, the pleasure of compromise. Nobody has to watch something they don't like anymore, and they don’t. Nobody has to sit through someone else's favourite programme, or get to share a favourite programme either.
In the old Pakistani and subcontinental family universe, relatives did not necessarily require appointments. You thought of visiting, and you went. An aunt's house was not a destination that required a carefully planned visit. It was simply somewhere you could turn up. “Chalo, phuppo ke ghar chalte hain [Let’s go to phuppo’s house]”.
And off went everyone. No messages or checking whether she was busy. No asking whether Sunday afternoon between four and six would be convenient. The doorbell rang, the children were dispatched to open the door and suddenly the house was full. Tea and samosas appeared. Then someone decided tea was insufficient and that everyone was staying over for the next meal. Perhaps lunch was served. Why not dinner too. The inconvenience was built into the system. No one really resented it, nor was anybody schedule deeply destroyed. Today, our homes have become more private. We call before visiting. We message before calling. We apologise for dropping in. “Sorry, I hope I'm not disturbing you.” The spontaneous visit has become almost an act of aggression, but there was something deeply comforting about knowing that some doors did not require an invitation.
For many children, summer holidays were not a carefully curated programme of camps, classes and activities. They simply meant nani's house. Or dadi's. Children arrived with suitcases and often stayed for weeks. Cousins slept in the same rooms, fought over beds, shared secrets and ghost stories, fought again, played games, and ate too many mangoes. Stayed awake far later, than they were permitted to at home. There was always somebody crying after being told off for something by an elder. There was almost always an adult saying, “Bas, enough now!”
Today, families are smaller, schedules are tighter and distances are often greater. Cousins may live in different cities — or different countries. Holidays themselves have become shorter and more structured. The modern child may have more activities, but perhaps there are fewer opportunities simply to get bored together.
Ahh, the luxury of getting bored. And boredom, it turns out, was underrated. A lot of the time, it was out of boredom came games, arguments, inventions, secrets and memories.
Summer evenings had their own rituals. In homes with ac cessible rooftops, families dragged charpais upstairs when the heat became unbearable. Mattresses were laid out under the open sky. Mosquitoes were swatted. Conversations continued long after dinner. Children stared at the stars, while grown-ups discussed relatives, politics, neighbours and household problems.
Someone invariably told a story, an incident from thirty years ago. Everyone including children listened, without appearing to listen. And in this unstructured way, family history travelled from one generation to another. Today, air-conditioning has made life more comfortable, but it has also moved us indoors. The rooftop has become another abandoned room in the house.
What families have lost most of all is the ability to do nothing together. Now, we meet now for a reason, for instance a lunch, dinner, a birthday, a festive occasion, a wedding, a meticulously planned holiday. But older family life was full of purposeless proximity, where people sat together because there was nowhere else to go, and no one cared that it was so. Nobody was fretting about mental health or needing therapy. Children lingered around adults and adults lingered around other adults. Grandparents were not visited as an activity. They were simply there. Stories emerged accidentally, just like advice. No one had to build a premise for a “talk”!
Family history mattered. Children knew who migrated during Partition, who had lost a fortune, who had eloped, who had been a terrible student, and who the family’s greatest scandal was secretly! These family stories were not documented, they were absorbed. Today, many of us know the entire online lives of people we have never met while knowing surprisingly little about our own grandparents' lives.
Before phones became the default answer to boredom, families played. Carrom and Ludo boards appeared after dinner and the games lasted hours. Cards were played. Children cheated and grown-ups accused them of cheating. Several generations could occupy the same space for an entire evening.
Today, gaming is still immensely popular. But increasingly, everyone plays separately. The game may connect you with thousands of people around the world. The person sitting beside you remains silent.
Then there were handwritten letters. Birthday and Eid cards carefully selected from a shop and sent weeks in advance. Waiting for the postman was part of life. Presently, a message reaches someone instantly. A photograph travels across continents in seconds. Technology has made it easier to remain in touch with family, but is speed the same thing as intimacy?
A handwritten letter required time and thought. An Eid card had to be chosen. A message was not dashed off while simultaneously watching television, scrolling through social media and munching crisps. The effort was visible. And perhaps effort itself has become one of the things we miss.
Of course, nostalgia is selective and emotional, and must not be confused with a desire to return to a time when everything was supposedly perfect but perhaps we can admit that something valuable has disappeared without wanting to recreate everything that came with it. Not everything about old family life deserves to be resurrected. The joint family could be suffocating and privacy in those days was often non-existent. While women carried an enormous burden of cooking, cleaning and entertaining, relatives could be intrusive, judgmental and controlling. People tolerated behaviour that should never have been tolerated simply because “family is family”.
Ofcourse, children had fewer choices. Modern life has brought freedom and women have much more independence. Young people have more privacy, and people are more aware about children’s needs and protection.
We don’t need to throw away our smartphones, cancel streaming subscriptions and move back into joint-family homes. Perhaps we could use one dinner a week with phones away, a Sunday lunch where nobody has another commitment, spending a few days together without every hour being planned. Throw in a game of Ludo now and again, look through old photograph albums, asking grandparents questions while they are still here to answer them, or going to visit someone without needing a special occasion isn’t such a bad thing, is it!
Putting down the phone long enough to hear what the person sitting next to us is saying, can make families be more like a family, instead of people living in the same house. We still love and worry about our families and gather for important things or events, but perhaps we have stopped doing many of the ordinary things that once made us feel like a family on ordinary days.
Years from now, our children may not remember every holiday, every expensive gift or every photograph uploaded online, but they may remember the evenings when everybody sat together, the debates and arguments, the stolen nap after lunch at nani’s and the sound of family elders talking late into the night. The ordinary moments that, without anyone noticing, become the things we remember most.

title: After the final whistle
description: When competition ends  Pakistani athletes must rebuild the routines  identities and careers that sport shaped for years
content:
When competition ends, Pakistani athletes must rebuild routines, identities, and careers that sport shaped for years.
Pakistani swimmer and Olympian Kiran Khan's childhood was organised around a swimming pool. There was school, but there was also training before and after it. Weekends meant competitions. Travel had to fit around swimming, as did food, sleep and recovery. When other children had free time to play or socialise, Khan remembers spending much of hers at the pool.
For two years, she even left regular school and was home-schooled so she could train and compete. It was not an easy decision for the family. There were disagreements, she recalls, but her father believed she could make something out of swimming and was determined to give her that chance.
Together, father and daughter would sit down with a calendar whenever another competition approached. They would mark the date and work backwards: how many weeks remained, what training needed to be done and when she needed to be ready.
“There was no room for any other activity,” Khan says.
She knew what each day required of her. Wake up. Train. Study. Recover. Eat properly. Sleep on time. Then do it again. There was always something ahead — a national championship, an international competition, a faster time or some part of her technique that needed improving.
For years, that was normal life. What was less clear was what happened when there was no competition to count backwards from.
“When I'm done with the competition, then you have heaps of time in your hand,” she says. “You don't know what to do.”
Khan did not suddenly stop swimming. Even today, she is reluctant to describe herself as someone who has left the sport. The competition gradually became less important, coaching became more important, and the relationship she had with the pool began to change.
For an athlete, perhaps that is one of the stranger parts of reaching the end of a competitive career. The sport does not necessarily disappear. The routine around it does.
And after spending years preparing for what comes next, there is suddenly no next competition to prepare for.
For Pakistani jiu-jitsu athlete Muhammad Ammar, the end first appeared before he was ready for it.
An accident around 2021 left the jiu-jitsu athlete with a broken leg and kept him away from competition for about a year. During the long recovery, Ammar began to wonder whether his competitive career had already ended. He eventually returned, won a bronze medal at an Asian competition and competed at world level again, but retirement had become something he was willing to think about.
What he did not want was for his final appearance to come after a defeat. “I decided that if I have to retire, I should retire with a good achievement,” says Ammar. “I thought that if Allah gives me a position, I will retire. I got gold and I thought there could not be a better opportunity to retire from my international career.”
He had made the decision before entering what would become his final World Championship. Once it was over, however, achieving the ending he wanted did not make leaving easier.
“When it was over, I had a feeling that I would not participate in the playing squad again,” he said. “It was a very sad moment for me. When a player goes to play, there is a different charm to it. I was very sad, but sometimes you have to make a decision.”
Ammar wanted to leave on his own terms. He had seen athletes continue until defeat made the decision for them and did not want his career remembered that way. For him, winning offered a cleaner point at which to stop.
Former Pakistan hockey goalkeeper Imran Butt reached the same decision under different circumstances.
By the time Pakistan went to the 2018 Hockey World Cup, Butt was 35. He had already begun looking at what was happening around the national game, particularly the financial problems and issues surrounding players' daily allowances. He also felt younger goalkeepers needed their opportunity.
“At that time, I started realising that you can't play mentally relaxed because of financial issues, daily allowance issues, all those things were increasing,” says Butt. “I started realising that I should say goodbye to hockey and give a chance to young players.”
The World Cup became the point at which he intended to leave. Unlike Ammar, Butt was not waiting for one last medal. His decision came from age, circumstances around the sport and an acceptance that another generation needed its chance.
For Kiran, there was no such final tournament.
Her departure from competitive swimming was harder to place on a calendar. Years of competition had also brought injuries, including problems with her foot, shoulder and back. Over time, she began to recognise that her relationship with training was changing.
“I don't think there was one single dramatic moment. It happened gradually,” says Khan. “I remember reaching a point where I realised, I was not getting into the pool with the same pressure of thinking, ‘I have to get faster. I have to make it this time. I have to prepare for the next competition’.”
For Ammar, there was a gold medal and a decision already made. For Butt, there was a final World Cup. Kiran had no comparable last day. She simply reached a point where getting into the pool no longer always meant preparing for the next race.
For Imran Butt, playing hockey had meant moving from one commitment to another. There were national camps, foreign tours and domestic tournaments, and once one ended, another was usually waiting. Even Eid and other occasions were sometimes spent away from home.
“It feels like you are walking in a circle,” says Butt. “You get free from the training camp, go on tours, come back and then there are domestic events. At that time, there was a lot of domestic hockey in Pakistan.”
The routine demanded sacrifices. Butt spent long periods away from his family, but after years of living that way, the schedule had also become normal. Retirement removed it much faster than he expected.
“It disturbed me a lot,” he says. “After getting out of that routine, to keep myself busy, I did some Asian Hockey Federation (AHF) goalkeeper courses. After that, I trained kids and shared my experience.”
What Butt missed was not only playing. It was a life built around playing. Travelling with teammates, sharing rooms, sitting in the dressing room and preparing together for matches had occupied a large part of his adult life. Representing Pakistan had taken him to the level he had spent years trying to reach, and stepping away also meant losing the everyday experiences that came with it.
“There was the Pakistan shirt, travelling, playing and having fun with your colleagues in the dressing room,” he says. “Taking a medal and celebrating after that, sharing with teammates, roommates, making fun. These are things you can never forget.”
For Ammar, the change has been less about stopping training altogether and more about changing its purpose. He still wants to maintain his fitness, but there is no longer a competition demanding the same intensity. The hours that once belonged to his own preparation can now be spent on the athletes he hopes to coach and on developing himself as a referee.
What he expects to miss most is something more specific. “The training that we did under the coach, that training cannot happen again,” says Ammar. “Everything else is connected to sports.”
For years, the relationship between athlete and coach had shaped how he trained. Retirement meant accepting that even if he remained fit and stayed involved in jiu-jitsu, he would probably not train in quite the same way again.
Khan has found it difficult to separate exercise from everyday life at all. More than two decades of competitive sport left behind habits that did not disappear simply because there was no race ahead.
“There has never been a day when I did not train myself,” she says. “You just cannot go from training morning and evening and doing multiple gym sessions to nothing at all.”
She still runs and does weight training. After three children, she says she continues to approach exercise with the mentality she developed as a competitive swimmer. An ordinary workout does not always feel enough.
“Once you're an athlete, you train like an athlete,” says Khan. “When you go and do regular gym, it just doesn't feel right to you. To me, it doesn't feel right.”
The change in routine, however, can also return some of what competition had taken away.
Butt married in 2015 and became a father while he was still playing. Hockey often kept him away, and he says he could not give his family the time he wanted to. Once the playing schedule disappeared, some of that time came back.
The empty space left by competition, then, was not necessarily empty for long. Butt filled part of it with family and goalkeeper training. Khan kept exercising and moved further into coaching. Ammar began redirecting his training hours towards students and refereeing.
The routine that had organised their lives had changed. None of them, however, simply stopped being involved in sport.
For Butt, retirement changed more than his daily schedule. It also changed how people saw him.
During his playing years, recognition came with representing Pakistan. His performances were followed by the media, people associated him with the national team and his name remained visible through hockey. Once he stopped playing, he felt some of that recognition disappear much faster than he had expected.
“When you are representing your country, you are highlighted by sponsors, colleagues, your club and the media,” says Butt. “But after retirement, your identity is lost very quickly.”
The change was particularly noticeable to him because hockey itself no longer receives the attention it once did. Butt says younger players may not even recognise some of those who represented Pakistan before them. It is one reason he has continued talking about hockey and supporting the game through his social media presence.
Ammar looks at the same transition differently. He accepts that the identity he had as an international competitor will change, but does not see retirement as the end of being known within jiu-jitsu.
“Yes, there is a change in identity,” he says. “We will make a new identity.”
That could be as a coach, referee or administrator. For Ammar, the next stage is not about trying to hold on to his old role. It is about finding another one within the sport that occupied much of his life.
Khan is less willing to separate the two in the first place.
“I don't really see it as leaving Kiran Khan the swimmer behind,” she says. “She's still a very important part of who I am. I just learned that I'm more than the medals, records and competition.”
Swimming was how people came to know her, but she does not see the end of regular competition as requiring another identity. Coaching has instead added to the one she already had.
“If I was Kiran Khan as a swimmer, I'll be known as Kiran Khan as a coach as well,” she says.
All three have remained close to their sports, but they have responded differently to no longer being the person competing. Butt has tried to hold on to the recognition that came with playing for Pakistan. Ammar is prepared to build another identity. Khan does not believe she needs to leave the old one behind.
The competition may stop, but deciding what happens to the athlete who existed around it can take longer.
For Butt, one of the biggest uncertainties that can follow retirement was partly taken care of years before he played his final international match.
He joined Pakistan International Airlines through hockey in 2007. The job gave him financial security during his playing career and, eventually, somewhere to go when hockey was no longer his full-time occupation. After retirement, Butt moved into PIA's regular workforce and now works in cargo sales.
“I got financial benefits from PIA because of hockey,” he says. “There was not much money in hockey, but I was lucky that in 2007 there were inductions and I became part of PIA.”
For decades, employment with departments such as PIA, Wapda and Pakistan Railways has provided Pakistani athletes with salaries while they competed. That structure went through a period of disruption when the federal government directed public departments and corporations to stop funding sports teams in 2021. The decision was reversed in 2022, although the restoration of teams and athlete employment has remained a work in progress.
Butt knows that the route available to him is not necessarily available to every athlete coming through the system now.
Ammar also sees employment as one of the advantages departmental sport can offer, but believes athletes need to think beyond it. Prize money or other earnings during a successful period, he says, can be used to establish something that continues to generate income after competition ends.
“You should not keep your career only in sports,” says Ammar. “If you have a small business, then you do not need anyone. And you sponsor yourself.”
The advice comes from someone who admits he did not have his own post-retirement career mapped out while he was competing. At the time, most of his attention was on training and the next competition.
For Khan, preparing for life beyond competition meant making sure swimming was never the only qualification she had.
She continued her education alongside sport, even if that sometimes meant taking breaks and returning to her studies later. She also used whatever time she could find during her competitive years to develop other skills, including online courses.
For women athletes, Khan believes the calculation can be more complicated. Financial independence is important, but decisions about work can also involve mobility, family expectations and whether a workplace feels suitable and safe. When she was competing, she remembers few clearly defined career routes for women once their playing years ended.
Her advice to younger swimmers now is not to abandon sport in anticipation of what may come later, but to make sure there is something alongside it.
“Never let swimming become the only thing you have,” she says. “Your athletic career is important, but it is temporary. Education is something you can continue, even if you have to take a break and come back to it.”
For athletes whose working lives can begin while they are still teenagers, the question is not only when competition will end. It is whether, when it does, they have something else from which to begin.
Khan had been swimming for most of her life when coaching first presented itself as a possible career. But knowing how to swim at an elite level, she realised, did not necessarily mean knowing how to teach someone else.
She first began coaching about 10 years ago after her father told her that some girls were looking for a female coach. What started casually became more serious when he encouraged her to get formal training. Khan went on to pursue coaching courses and certifications outside Pakistan.
“I just did not become a coach overnight because I was a swimmer,” she says. “You have to take the proper route.”
It is a distinction she now feels strongly about. An athlete may understand the physical demands of a sport and know what competition feels like, but coaching requires another set of skills. For Khan, the experience she had accumulated in the pool became useful only when she learnt how to pass it on.
“I just did it out of fun,” she says. “And that fun actually gave me a career.”
Butt came to a similar realisation when he moved towards coaching after retirement. He wanted to pass on what he had learnt as a goalkeeper and completed coaching courses before working with younger players. Once he entered the role, however, he found that playing and coaching were very different jobs.
“I realised that coaching is totally different from playing,” says Butt.
His frustration was not only with the work itself. Butt says he wanted greater authority to change how goalkeepers were developed and selected. Without it, he eventually stepped away from coaching the national side, although he still hopes to establish his own goalkeeper project in the future.
Ammar is only beginning that transition. Coaching, refereeing and administration are now among the paths he sees for himself, even though none formed part of a detailed retirement plan while he was competing.
“There was no plan at all,” he says. “When I thought about retirement, these paths started opening up. When a person thinks of closing a door, his vision becomes clear. He knows which doors he can open.”
The time he once spent preparing himself for competition, Ammar says, can now be directed towards younger athletes.
“The time that we used to spend on our training, we will spend it with the students,” he says. “We will focus on our refereeship and pursue it at the administrative level.”
For all three, staying in sport has therefore not meant continuing the same career under a different title. Khan had to learn how to coach. Butt discovered the limitations and responsibilities that came with the other side of the field. Ammar is still working out which of the available paths will become his own.
Years of competition gave them experience. What came afterwards required them to learn how to use it differently.
Khan can still remember when getting into the pool meant there was always something to chase.
A training session was never simply a swim. There was a time to beat, a competition approaching or another part of her performance that needed work. Even when one event ended, the next one gave the training that followed a reason. “For many years, every lap had a purpose,” she says. “Every training session was connected to my race goal.”
That changed gradually. There was no announcement that her competitive career was over and, even now, Khan does not describe herself as retired from swimming. She simply reached a stage where she could enter the water without preparing for another race.
“I was just swimming without needing to prove anything to the clock,” she says. “But eventually, I started enjoying the water in a different way.”
Perhaps that is why Khan still finds it difficult to say she ever left swimming.
The pool is still there. So is the swimmer.

title: Saudi Arabia warns escalating Middle East threats risk global trade  energy security
description: Urges stronger international cooperation to protect Gulf states and shipping routes at UNGA
content:
Urges stronger international cooperation to protect Gulf states and shipping routes at UNGA
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan on Saturday warned that escalating threats across the Middle East risked international peace, energy security and global trade, calling for stronger international cooperation to protect Gulf states and vital shipping routes.
Addressing the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Prince Faisal said Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region had been subjected to “flagrant Iranian attacks” targeting security resources as well as civilian and economic facilities.
He reaffirmed the Kingdom’s right to protect its security and sovereignty, citizens, residents and national resources, while urging the international community to confront threats to international peace and security.
Read : Trump rejects Iranian proposal to open Hormuz and end fighting
“The security of the Gulf region is part and parcel of the security of the region and the world at large,” he said.
The foreign minister stressed that stability in the Gulf was directly connected to global energy security, international trade and supply chains.
He called for freedom of navigation in international waterways, highlighting the Strait of Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, and rejected their use by any party as an instrument of pressure or threat.
He also called for the situation in the Strait of Hormuz to return to its status before Feb 28, “without the imposition of any fees or restrictions”.
Despite the tensions, he backed efforts to de-escalate, including initiatives by Qatar, Pakistan and other countries, and advocated comprehensive and sustainable regional security arrangements addressing the underlying causes of instability.
20260926 UN Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan a-Saud of Saudi Arabia Addresses the United Nations General Assembly pic.twitter.com/GBdrZVhxdG
He also called for the entire region to be free of weapons of mass destruction and for peaceful nuclear programmes to be subject to international oversight and safeguards.
Turning to the Occupied Palestinian Territory, the foreign minister condemned the targeting of civilians, obstruction of humanitarian assistance, attempted forced displacement and expansion of settlements.
He said a just and lasting peace could only be achieved through a two-state solution and establishment of an independent Palestinian state on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
On Yemen, he called for a comprehensive political solution to restore stability and alleviate suffering, noting that Saudi Arabia had provided more than $29 billion in humanitarian and development assistance.
He also condemned missile and drone attacks by the Houthis against Saudi Arabia and commercial vessels, calling on the international community to reject acts threatening navigation in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb.
Turning to other challenges, Prince Faisal highlighted the achievements of Saudi Vision 2030 and argued that energy security and climate action should be mutually reinforcing rather than competing goals.
He called for realistic energy transitions that did not exclude any source, while pointing to Saudi investments in renewable energy, clean hydrogen, carbon capture technologies and more resilient infrastructure.
On artificial intelligence, the foreign minister urged international cooperation to ensure the technology was used responsibly and in the service of development, highlighting Saudi initiatives on AI capacity-building and ethics.
Concluding, he said the challenges facing the world could not be confronted by individual countries acting alone.
Security, he added, could only be sustained through adherence to the UN Charter, respect for international law and cooperation aimed at peaceful solutions, stability and sustainable development.

title: From power to purpose
description: From power to purpose
content:
Zulfikar Ali Bhutto pursued nationalisation and a highly centralised model of political and state authority
Were half the power that fills the world with terror
Were half the wealth bestowed on camps and courts
Given to redeem the human mind from error
Politics in Pakistan appears to be heading towards another round of confrontation. The country's political history is filled with leaders who promised to bring stability, peace and change, and many believed that their plans failed because others were unwilling to accept them or listen to them. But the deeper problem was not always the plan; it was the method chosen to pursue the plan. Pakistan's political history can, in many ways, be read as a history of methods. President Ayub Khan's method was to centralise executive authority and concentrate political power. President Yahya Khan approached a vital political crisis through a military solution, with consequences that culminated in the shocking breakup of Pakistan in 1971.
Zulfikar Ali Bhutto pursued nationalisation and a highly centralised model of political and state authority, while General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq made Islamisation a central instrument for reshaping the country's political and social order. The democratic decade of the 1990s produced yet another method. Both the PPP and PML-N preferred to engage the military establishment and seek its support to strengthen their respective positions against one another. General Pervez Musharraf's rule, however, eventually pushed the two parties towards cooperation. Their new political method was reconciliation, symbolised by the Charter of Democracy signed in 2006 and the subsequent Murree Declaration in 2008. This wasn't political reconciliation; it was a political understanding and an arrangement not to interfere with each other's political interests.
Imran Khan's emergence transformed this political arrangement once again. His politics was built around confronting this reconciled established political order with a strong tendency to frame political choices in sharply contrasting terms. Khan's method was to treat politics either as black or white, with no room for grey. Yet the inability to seek and sustain political accommodation eventually became a weakness of his method and resulted in his downfall. Pakistan now finds itself in a familiar predicament – a political system in which competing sides continue to see politics largely in terms of black and white, with little room left for grey.
A plan is a roadmap, and that is perhaps what Pakistan has never had. Our politics has rarely been concerned with the difficult question of how the country should be governed, developed, and institutionally strengthened. Instead, the political priority has almost always been what needs to be done to acquire, consolidate or retain power. History is a succession of events, but those events cannot be divorced from the individuals who shape them. Pakistan's leaders have often had political methods, but rarely a comprehensive framework for governing the country, building institutions, generating sustainable economic development and administering the state in the public interest.
Consequently, all methods designed primarily for political survival have repeatedly been mistaken for solutions and have only deepened the structural problems. A prescription based on a faulty diagnosis can rarely produce the desired outcome. Winning or losing a political race is not determined simply by the method of running - whether one runs fast or slow. A runner may lose because of inadequate training, poor preparation, insufficient rest, inappropriate equipment or a badly judged pace. The method of running matters, but understanding why the race is being won or lost matters far more. Pakistan's political problem, therefore, cannot be understood merely by examining the methods adopted by its many political actors in the past and even now. It requires a deep examination and analysis of the underlying conditions that have repeatedly produced political failure.
History has already provided us with numerous analyses of why Pakistan's political races have been lost, yet we have learned few lessons from them. Analysis is not merely an exercise in looking backwards; it is a test of whether a chosen political method or prescription is capable of producing the intended outcome. An examination of Pakistan's political history reveals recurring attempts to maintain political control through coercive power - force, threats and punishment - alongside ideological manipulation, institutional interference, patronage, favouritism and material incentives.
What has remained largely absent is the deliberate attempt to construct consensual or structural power. The ability to secure the willing compliance of citizens by building institutions and a political order in which people see their aspirations reflected. Political success has too often been measured by the ability to maintain, increase or demonstrate power over rivals rather than by the ability to win and sustain legitimate public consent. Had political competition consistently been settled through credible institutions, free and fair elections, and the peaceful transfer of power, Pakistan's political trajectory might have been very different.
Political power in Pakistan has frequently been used as an end in itself rather than as a legitimate instrument for delivering security, justice, prosperity and public relief. Unfortunately, the ordinary Pakistanis, for all these years, seem to have largely been preoccupied with what St Augustine described as humanity's most fundamental motivations: self-preservation i.e. the desire to live rather than perish in misfortune.
What, then, should change in Pakistan? Most political commentators believe that the answer to the country's problems lies simply in changing governments. History suggests that changing governments without changing the political mindset has repeatedly produced the same political instability. The real transformation that Pakistan needs is not merely a change of rulers, but a change in how rulers understand power itself.
Pakistan does not suffer from a shortage of political methods. It suffers from a shortage of political purpose. Governments may change, alliances may shift, and new leaders may emerge, but instability will persist if power continues to be treated as the destination rather than the instrument. The real challenge is to move from politics designed to control people to politics designed to serve them. We need to move from coercive power to consensual power – the power of consent. From political survival to public purpose, and from winning the next political race to building a country that does not have to run the same race again and again.
Longfellow's question therefore remains relevant. What might Pakistan achieve if the resources devoted to the struggle for power were redirected towards redeeming the human condition?
