title: The long   short of PTI s march
description: Time and space separating September 27 with October 4 are vaster than a mere seven days
content:
Time and space separating September 27 with October 4 are vaster than a mere seven days
The time and space separating September 27 with October 4 are vaster than a mere seven days. Therein lies the deviously delicious story of how and why the long march is getting longer in execution and shorter in expectations. Here's how the situation looks presently.
1. Chief Minister K-P Sohail Afridi jumped the gun. The date, when given, was weeks away. It was meant to allow enough time for a workable solution that would not require the march to be, well, marched. His assumption turned out to be misplaced. One reason for this mistake, among others, was the lack of consensus within the PTI leadership on the long march being the best possible option at this time. And that too with a definitive date. Afridi got swept in the emotional momentum and pressure generated by the PTI support base and its social media, and also, probably, his desire to ride the wave of populist sentiment. This, when combined with the exuberance of youth and the power of the office he holds, produced an outcome that may not turn out as intended.
2. The problem however is not just Sohail Afridi. It's the fractured nature of PTI's leadership, and therefore its inability – or at least diminished ability – to firstly build a working relationship, and then forge a consensus on key decisions. In this case, the leadership remains divided till date between those who want the long march to take place regardless of its outcome, and those who still maintain that dialogue can produce better results. The declaration of the date of the march and its postponement at the last minute is a manifestation of this gnawing divide.
3. Then, PTI is alone. The Jamaat-e-Islami has called off its march to Islamabad instead of aligning it with PTI. The Kissan Ittehad is nowhere to be seen. Maulana Fazlur Rehman and his JUI cadres have shown no interest in making it a combined affair. The Tehreek-e-Tahaffuz Ain-e-Pakistan (TTAP) is tagging along but its leaders outnumber its followers. Even within TTAP there is little coherence. Leader of the Opposition Mehmood Khan Achakzai talks about a long march that has wide and dispersed goals like bringing down the government and forcing new elections; Leader of the Opposition in the Senate Allama Nasir Abbas insists that dialogue, even at this stage, is preferrable to a street collision; and to add to these woes, the PTI informed the TTAP about the postponement of the march only after its leadership had already taken a decision.
4. The government's excessive crackdown and blockading of Islamabad was meant to convey a message: there will be zero flexibility in its response. This was conveyed to some of the PTI leadership with elaborate details. The carefully orchestrated leaks about Governor's Rule and ouster of the K-P CM were part of this communication aimed at creating psychological pressure on the PTI. The detention of Imran Khan's family members was also meant as a signal of the government's resolve.
5. PTI's explanation that its decision to push the date of the march ahead by a week is meant to 'tire out' the government is plain silly. This isn't a football match. The state always has a huge advantage when it comes to displaying administrative and law enforcement stamina. The PTI knows well that it has been forced to blink first because of its own internal weaknesses and faulty decision-making process. So what now?
6. Here's where things get interesting. By blinking first, PTI has also allowed the government enough political space to take some initiative and create a 'win-win' situation for both sides. It's tricky, but it's doable. Underneath the bluster of bringing down the government or getting Imran Khan freed from jail, the realistic and acceptable demands of the PTI are basically two: (i) Give family members or leaders access to Khan in jail, (ii) Transfer Khan to the hospital as per the Supreme Court order. These can be met without too much trouble. In fact, they were already under consideration and there was some progress in the talks between Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar. Those advocating dialogue within PTI were saying exactly this: don't use the option of the long march now when the same things can be obtained through talks. The timing was key.
7. Speaking of timing, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has timed his latest initiative well. He has written a letter to Mehmood Achakzai in his position as the leader of the opposition. It is quite probable that a meeting between the two may take place before October 4. The PM is already on his way back from New York after attending the UN General Assembly session. Earlier too he had written a letter to Achakzai to fulfil the constitutional requirement of consultation on key appointments in the Election Commission of Pakistan. Achakzai told me this week he had appreciated the language of the PM's letter. He also acknowledged to me that he was in touch with Nawaz Sharif. Achakzai is now the man to watch.
8. This week would therefore see two parallel trends: continued bluster by the likes of Sohail Afridi competing with the sombre engagement of Achakzai, Allama Nasir Abbas and Barrister Gohar. It is hard to say at this stage which side will prevail, but the government now has the opportunity to help the latter succeed. The most effective initiative it can take is to give Achakzai and Allama Nasir Abbas access to Khan. This could change the dynamics of the situation and pave the way for sustained engagement and relief.
9. Transferring Khan to a hospital (likely PIMS) is not a big deal for the government. But it won't happen if the government feels it is being pressured to do so. Such a step has to be framed as a "win-win" and not a forced concession from the government. The space now available can be made use of for this very possibility to be negotiated keeping in mind sensitivities of both sides. That is, as we are finding out, easier said than done when tempers are this high.
10. The PTI may have blinked first, but it may yet get what it wants if it plays its cards well. For that to happen, the CM K-P may have to take a back seat.

title: The real test of governance
description: Governments have changed  political alliances have shifted and new slogans have repeatedly promised reform
author_name: Dr Umair Baig, Dr Intikhab Ulfat
content:
Governments have changed, political alliances have shifted and new slogans have repeatedly promised reform
Governance is not an abstract idea confined to constitutions, cabinet meetings or policy documents. We experience it in ordinary moments: when a child enters a classroom, when a family member needs medical treatment, or when a citizen seeks justice. Nearly eight decades after independence, Pakistan's democratic journey therefore raises a question that goes beyond elections: how effectively are we governing the country?
Governments have changed, political alliances have shifted and new slogans have repeatedly promised reform. Yet many of the problems confronting ordinary Pakistanis remain familiar. Public trust is fragile, service delivery is uneven and institutions often struggle to perform consistently. This leads to an uncomfortable but necessary question: is democracy merely about deciding who governs, or should it also be judged by how well people are governed?
Elections are indispensable to democracy, but democracy cannot end with the transfer of political power. Citizens expect more from the state. They expect security, justice, education, healthcare, economic opportunity and equal treatment before the law. Democracy determines who receives political authority; governance determines what is done with that authority.
The distinction matters because good governance cannot depend on the personality, popularity or intentions of one individual. Governments come and go. Institutions must endure.
We create policies, rules, commissions and administrative structures, but implementation frequently remains inconsistent. Merit is celebrated in principle, yet appointments can be influenced by considerations unrelated to competence. Policies are announced with enthusiasm, but continuity, monitoring and accountability often receive less attention.
Strong institutions require more than formal existence. They must operate within the Constitution, follow transparent rules, define responsibilities clearly and remain accountable for their performance. They also require sufficient autonomy to discharge their functions without improper interference. Autonomy, however, cannot mean absence of accountability.
A functioning state therefore needs institutions where appointments are based on competence, decisions are informed by evidence and performance is measured honestly. Policies serving the national interest should not disappear merely because political leadership changes. Institutional memory, continuity and professionalism are essential if reform is to survive electoral cycles.
Institutions do not improve simply because a new policy is announced or another committee is constituted. They improve when systems actually work, responsibilities are understood, performance is evaluated and rules are applied consistently. Institutional reform is the cumulative result of competent people doing ordinary things properly, repeatedly and transparently.
This is also why reform is difficult. Pakistan does not suffer from a complete absence of ideas. We broadly know what better governance requires: merit-based appointments, transparent procurement, financial discipline, stronger local institutions, effective public services and credible accountability. The more difficult problem is implementation. Meaningful reform inevitably challenges people and networks that benefit from weak systems, discretionary power and institutional ambiguity.
Reform therefore requires more than policy documents. It requires political will, administrative courage and consistency over time.
The real test of governance is visible not in speeches but in everyday life. Can a child receive quality education regardless of family income? Can a patient obtain healthcare without influence? Can a citizen expect timely justice? Can an ordinary person approach a public office without fear, favour or unnecessary delay? These are not theoretical questions. They define the relationship between citizens and the state.
Nations progress through strong institutions, merit, equal application of rules and responsible public service. Democracy may choose leaders, but good governance determines whether citizens actually benefit from that choice. Lasting progress depends on institutions that remain credible, effective and accountable even when governments change. That is what turns electoral democracy into meaningful and sustainable governance.

title: SC s dower ruling
description: SC s dower ruling
content:
Supreme Court's landmark verdict last week brings much-needed clarity to these deeply entrenched issues
For decades, the contractual and financial rights of women in Pakistan have been systematically taken for granted, reduced to mere ceremonial formalities rather than legally binding safeguards. Despite explicit Islamic tenets declaring haq-mahr i.e. dower a mandatory legal right incumbent upon the husband at the very inception of marriage, societal customs have distorted this obligation. In most cases, dower is treated as a delayed liability, only grudgingly conceded, even weaponised in some cases, at the time of a painful divorce.
Similarly, bridal gifts and jewelry - meant to provide lifelong financial security and independence to the wife - are routinely withheld by the husband or his family during a separation, leaving women economically vulnerable. This exploitation is further aggravated by the widespread practice of leaving columns in the nikahnama blank or poorly filled. By treating this official contract with negligence, society has effectively stripped women of their documented protections before their marital life even begins.
However, the Supreme Court's landmark verdict last week brings much-needed clarity to these deeply entrenched issues. In a decisive ruling, the apex court affirmed that haq-mahr is an unconditional legal right, not a "price" for the wife or leverage for marital disputes. Concurrently, the top court clarified that wedding gifts remain the exclusive, absolute property of the bride, protecting them from predatory reclamation by in-laws. Furthermore, the court issued strict directives for nikah registrars to ensure every column of the marriage contract is meticulously completed.
This judicial clarity deserves immense appreciation. By legally anchoring the true essence of Islamic jurisprudence and enforcing accountability on registrars, the Supreme Court has taken a monumental step toward truly empowering women. It ensures that a woman's dignity, financial security and contractual rights are no longer treated as an afterthought.

title: PM at UNGA
description: PM at UNGA
content:
UN General Assembly offers leaders an opportunity to place their country's position before the world
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's address to the UN General Assembly on Friday was wide-ranging, touching upon nearly every major challenge confronting Pakistan's foreign policy, from the troubled relationship with India and the Kashmir dispute to the Indus Waters Treaty and instability in the wider region. Yet the recurring theme was peace, and Pakistan's argument that even the most intractable disputes must eventually find their way back to the negotiating table. It was a message worth delivering.
The UN General Assembly offers leaders an opportunity to place their country's position before the world. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif did so without ambiguity. The international environment has hardly been hospitable to diplomacy. Conflicts have multiplied, international law has frequently appeared subordinate to power, and institutions established to prevent confrontation have struggled to exercise meaningful influence. Against this backdrop, the PM's insistence that dialogue must retain primacy is both prudent and consistent with Pakistan's own interests. Nowhere is this more relevant than in South Asia. The PM's warning over the IWT was understandably firm: Pakistan cannot be expected to treat lightly any move that threatens a river system on which its agriculture and food security heavily depend. But the more important point was that these concerns were presented alongside an appeal for dialogue rather than as an argument for perpetual confrontation.
There is no weakness in defending national interests while seeking peaceful means to secure them. Pakistan must continue to speak firmly where its vital interests are threatened, but it should also remain prepared to engage whenever meaningful diplomacy becomes possible. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's message at the UN was therefore a sound one. The challenge now is to ensure that the preference for dialogue expressed in New York remains the basis of Pakistan's regional diplomacy long after the speeches have ended.

title: Time to pursue a thaw
description: Time to pursue a thaw
content:
PTI's demands primarily centre on legal and procedural rights
The PTI's decision to delay its long march is a welcome development that could help defuse the prevailing political instability. It hands the government a prime opportunity to initiate talks with the broader opposition alliance, TTAP, and resolve lingering friction points. Even though the PTI aims to launch the protest from Peshawar on October 4, sincerity from both sides can still yield a compromise. A meaningful political thaw is urgently needed to restore daily life in Rawalpindi and Islamabad, where heavy security blockades have severely disrupted the twin cities.
The PTI's demands primarily centre on legal and procedural rights. These include implementing the August 18 Supreme Court directive to transfer Imran Khan to a private hospital and restoring his access to family, counsel and doctors. Since these rights are already guaranteed by the jail manual, it would be politically and legally ill-advised for the government to defy them. Similarly, the party's push to expedite Khan's court hearings and its advocacy for judicial independence and constitutional supremacy ought to strike a chord with the ruling parties in the larger national interest of democracy and the rule of law.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's invitation to Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai for direct talks is a welcome step toward easing Pakistan's political deadlock. However, these discussions must yield concrete outcomes to rescue the nation from economic woes, systemic parochialism and deep-seated political division. A successful national reconciliation hinges on granting the opposition its rightful political space and legal recourse. To establish long-term stability, both sides must collaborate on a new social contract that addresses key public demands, including administrative devolution and the creation of new provinces.
Decades of confrontation have severely damaged the state; today, surging terrorism, financial instability and public unrest present immediate national security threats that require collective attention. The PTI's tactical retreat in delaying its protest offers a crucial window for dialogue that the government should acknowledge and reciprocate.

title: Where we fail in education
description: Where we fail in education
content:
ASER estimates that about 26.2 million school-age children are out of formal schooling
In my classroom, I encounter students who are more concerned with securing marks than acquiring knowledge. Some have learned to memorise answers, while others believe grades could be secured through influence or money. Parents, too, often measure educational success by examination scores and admission to prestigious university programmes. The result is an education culture in which certificates matter more than competence and grades matter more than genuine learning.
While conducting research into why Pakistan has failed to provide the education its children need, I found that the country's education sector is facing a severe learning crisis. Some schools exist only in government records, with little or no student enrolment in reality. Even where schools function, the curriculum and teaching methods often focus more on cramming and examination performance than on practical education.
The 2025 Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) estimates that about 26.2 million school-age children are out of formal schooling. Among those who are enrolled, many still struggle to read and write with a proper understanding of the language used in education. Others lack digital literacy, which is now an important part of education.
Enrolment is not education, and examination success is not learning. This is where the problem of learning poverty begins. A child may attend school for years and still fail to acquire basic literacy and skills. Similarly, a student may achieve high marks through memorisation without developing the ability to think positively, solve problems or apply knowledge to real-life situations.
A grave area of concern is that we have schools, but they face different challenges. Government schools often have resources but lack accountability, suffer from low enrolment and continue to rely on traditional teaching methods. Private schools, meanwhile, may perform better academically but face their own problems, including limited resources, high fees and poorly paid teachers, some of whom have only a graduation-level qualification.
The decline in educational standards is closely linked to whom we entrust with the responsibility of teaching. Hiring teachers who are poorly paid, inadequately trained and reliant on outdated methods means prioritising examination content over developing students' ability to understand and apply the knowledge.
The consequences extend far beyond schools. A society that trains people primarily to memorise may struggle to produce citizens capable of questioning, analysing and solving problems. This has direct implications for the quality of government and public institutions. Public institutions need professionals who can think independently, act ethically and understand that public office is a responsibility rather than a privilege. A weak education system cannot consistently produce a strong culture of public service.
The challenge, therefore, is not simply a shortage of schools or teachers; it is a crisis of educational purpose. The World Bank has estimated Pakistan's learning poverty at 75 per cent, meaning that most children were unable to read and understand a simple age-appropriate text by the age of 10.
In the 21st century, literacy is not confined to the ability to read and write. Education must also develop digital literacy, creative thinking and problem-solving skills. Unfortunately, many children still lack opportunities to access and learn through modern educational technologies.
The answer begins with changing what happens inside the classroom. Teacher training should prioritise classroom psychology and practical pedagogy rather than simply syllabus completion. Examinations should test understanding rather than reward memorisation. Schools should connect learning with real-world problems through projects, experiments, debates and research. Students should be encouraged not only to ask what the answer is, but also why it is the answer and how that knowledge can be applied.
When students are afraid of making mistakes, obsessed with marks and disconnected from what they are learning, education loses its purpose.

title: Relationships  rewritten
description: How technology  migration and a new vocabulary of feelings are quietly changing the way we love and think about the people closest to us
content:
How tech, migration and a new vocabulary of feelings are quietly changing how we love and think of those closest to us
There is a photograph in almost every South Asian home: a wedding portrait from the 1970s or 80s, the couple stiff and unsmiling, surrounded by thirty relatives whose names the grandchildren can no longer recall. Compare it with a wedding photograph taken last month. The couple could be in a passionate embrace, fulfilling an equally passionate request by the photographer, or laughing; mid-air, confetti frozen around them. Behind the photographer stand four people with phones raised, filming for Instagram. Propped up on a chair near the stage, two cousins are streaming it live on a video call, for another two cousins who couldn’t fly in for the wedding.
Nothing about the institution has changed on paper. Everything about how it is felt, performed and understood has.
We do not usually notice changes in our inner life while they are happening. We notice them later, when an older relative says something that sounds strange to us, or when we say something that sounds strange to them. That gap, the small, awkward silence between generations — is the clearest evidence we have that the way we think about relationships is being rewired.
Ask a man of 70, why he stayed married for 45 years and he is likely to answer with a shrug and a phrase like "nibhana parta hai" or one has to make it work. Ask a woman of 28, the same question about her marriage of three years and you will get a longer, more careful answer about respect, communication, shared goals, and whether she still feels like herself.
Both answers are honest. They come from two different perspectives or moral universes.
The older universe treated relationships as roles. You were a son, a daughter-in-law, a brother, a neighbour, and the role told you what to do. There was comfort in that. Nobody had to invent the script. If a marriage was unhappy, the unhappiness was usually regarded as a private weather condition, something to be endured, not solved. The family, the biraderi, the village, the mohalla held the structure in place from the outside.
The newer universe treats relationships as agreements. Two people, or a parent and a grown child, or two old friends, are understood to be continuously choosing each other. If the agreement stops working, it is expected to be renegotiated or ended. This is why a phrase like "we've grown apart" makes complete sense to a thirty-year-old and sounds almost like an insult to a 70-year-old, who might reasonably ask: grown apart from what? You are family.
Consider a real and very ordinary situation. A young couple in Islamabad, both working, decide after two years of marriage to move into a rented flat twenty minutes from the husband's parents' house. Their reason is simple: they want a quieter place, and both work night shifts on international projects. The husband's mother does not hear "we want quiet." She hears "we are leaving you." The son does not hear "your mother is frightened of being alone in old age." He hears "you are trying to control us." Two decent people, one house, and completely different definitions of what love is supposed to look like in practice. That is the fault line running through millions of homes right now.
The phone changed the geometry of intimacy
For most of human history, the people you were close to were the people you were physically near. Distance killed relationships slowly and reliably. Letters took weeks. A trunk call was booked in advance and spoken loudly, briefly, expensively.
Presently, a daughter in Toronto sees her mother's kitchen in Lahore every morning. A father working in Dubai reads his son's exam results before the boy has told his class fellows. Grief, gossip, illness and small triumphs travel instantly.
This is a genuine gain, and it should be said plainly: technology has kept families emotionally alive across borders in a way that would have astonished our grandparents. Migration used to mean a kind of social death. It no longer does.
But the geometry has changed in a subtler way too. Closeness used to require presence. Now it requires attention and attention is the one resource that has not increased.
A family WhatsApp group with 42 members produces an odd feeling: you know everything and you feel nothing. You learn that an uncle has had a stent placed, you send a folded-hands emoji, and you scroll on. Information arrives without the weight that used to accompany it. In an earlier era, that news would have arrived through a person, in a room, and it would have cost you an evening.
Meanwhile, presence has become strangely thin. Anyone who has sat at a dinner table where five people are physically together and mentally elsewhere knows the sensation. A friend visits after two years; within twenty minutes both of you are showing each other things on your screens rather than talking. Nobody is being rude. The pull is simply stronger than the manners.
The result is a peculiar modern condition: we are more contactable than any generation in history and, by many accounts, lonelier. Contact is not the same nutrient as company.
Fifty years ago, most people married someone from a pool of perhaps a dozen realistic options assembled by relatives. Today, a young person in Karachi or anywhere may scroll through a thousand faces in a week on matrimonial sites, on apps, on Instagram and still feel that the right person has not appeared. More options should mean better outcomes. Often they mean the opposite.
When choice is unlimited, every choice feels provisional. Psychologists call this the paradox of choice; ordinary people call it "what if there's someone better." A twenty-six-year-old woman turns down a perfectly decent proposal because something about the man's sense of humour felt slightly flat and she is not being shallow. She has been told, correctly, that she should not settle. But nobody has told her where the line between settling and expecting perfection actually lies, because that line was never something individuals had to draw for themselves before.
Meanwhile, the older system of arranged marriage has not disappeared. It has quietly mutated into something new, what might be called the arranged introduction. Parents find the family; the two young people then talk for three months on WhatsApp, meet twice at a coffee shop, and make their own decision. Two systems, once opposed, have merged into a hybrid that neither the grandparents nor the dating apps quite predicted.
The same shift shows up in friendship. Friendships used to be inherited; the boys on your street, the girls in your class, your cousins. You did not choose them and you could not easily escape them, so you learned to tolerate people who irritated you. That was a skill. Today friendships are increasingly curated: chosen by interest, by profession, by online community. They are more satisfying and more fragile. A curated friendship can be quietly dropped by ceasing to reply. An inherited one turns up at your door.
Today, when a friendship becomes uncomfortable, it can be easier to distance ourselves. When a conversation becomes difficult, we can leave it unanswered. When a relationship does not match our expectations, we may begin looking for something else.
A new vocabulary — powerful, and easy to misuse
Perhaps the biggest change is in language. Words that lived inside therapists' offices thirty years ago are now used at family dinners: boundaries, toxic, trauma, love bombing, gaslighting, closure, emotional labour, and red flag.
This vocabulary has done real good. A woman who once had no word for what was happening to her can now say "this is emotional abuse" and be understood. Young men who were raised to treat every feeling as weakness are learning that anxiety has a name and a treatment. Naming a thing is the first step to changing it.
But borrowed language cuts both ways. A word designed to describe serious harm can be used to describe ordinary friction, and once it is, it ends the conversation instead of opening it.
Furthermore, a few seconds of someone’s “happy” life on social media can make us question our own relationships. We see perfect couples, surprise gifts, family dinners and endless smiles, forgetting that we are watching only a carefully chosen moment, not the whole story. Slowly, comparison replaces contentment, and expectations replace understanding. We start wanting relationships to look perfect instead of simply being real.
A twenty-four-year-old tells his mother, "I need to set a boundary. Please don't comment on my weight." That is clear, specific and fair. It names a behaviour, not a person.
His cousin tells her mother, "You're toxic, I'm going no contact," because the mother pushed too hard about her career choice. That may be justified. It may also be a heavy word doing the work of a lighter one and it may cost her a relationship that a difficult conversation could have repaired.
The honest position is that both over-tolerance and over-diagnosis cause damage. Our grandparents' generation stayed too long in situations that were harming them. Ours sometimes leaves too early, mistaking discomfort for danger. Neither error is more virtuous than the other.
Time poverty and the shrinking of the circle
There is an unglamorous economic reason relationships feel different: people are simply busier and more scattered.
A generation ago, a government clerk finished at two in the afternoon, came home, ate, slept, and sat outside in the evening while children played in the street. Relationships were maintained in that dead time, the unplanned hours when people were merely available to one another.
That dead time has been sold off. It now belongs to a second job, a commute, a side hustle, a phone. Friendship has become an appointment: let's plan something next month. Anyone who has tried to arrange dinner with four working friends knows that the plan will be postponed twice and eventually cancelled by someone's work emergency.
When relationships require scheduling, the circle shrinks. People keep the two or three connections that survive logistics and let the rest thin out into occasional birthday messages. This is not coldness. It is arithmetic.
The Covid years accelerated all of it. Millions discovered that they could work, shop, study and be entertained without leaving a room and also discovered, painfully, what a funeral attended over video call actually feels like. Some people rebuilt their social lives afterwards. Many quietly never did.
It would be a mistake to read all this as decline. Some of the changes are straightforwardly good, and it is worth naming.
A father who hugs his son and says he loves him would have been unusual in 1980 and is now unremarkable. A woman who leaves a violent marriage is now more likely to be supported by her siblings than shamed by them not universally, but far more than before. Grandparents in villages video-call grandchildren in Melbourne and know their faces. Young men talk to each other about mental health in ways their fathers could not.
And beneath every shift of form, the substance has not moved an inch. People still want to be known. They still want someone who notices when they are quiet. They still want to be forgiven for something they are ashamed of. No app, no vocabulary and no generational theory have altered that, and nothing is likely to.
What has changed is only the machinery: who chooses, how we speak, where we live, how fast news travels, how easily we can leave.
If there is a useful conclusion, it is not "technology is ruining us" and not "the old ways were better." Both are lazy.
The more useful conclusion is that relationships used to be held together by external structure; proximity, obligation, community pressure, and lack of alternatives. That structure has largely dissolved. What holds relationships together now is deliberate effort, and deliberate effort is a skill that nobody explicitly teaches.
This means small, unfashionable habits carry more weight than they used to. Calling instead of texting, because a voice carries information a message cannot. Visiting the relative who is difficult rather than the one who is easy.

title: The high cost of Balochistan   s solar transition
description: Solar power promised reliable energy for farmers  But high costs and groundwater depletion threaten the solution
content:
Solar power promised reliable energy for farmers. But high costs and groundwater depletion threaten the solution
The trouble began when the electricity supply to agricultural tube wells in Manjhoshori, Naseerabad, was changed from three-phase to two-phase.
For Mohammad Anwar Manjhoo, a local farmer, the timing could not have been worse.
His Rabi crops, including wheat, corn and pulses, were approaching maturity. His tube well, run on subsidised electricity, was the source of irrigation for his fields. Then, suddenly, the power supply was disrupted, and so was, consequently, the water supply to the crops.
“Just when the crops were approaching maturity, we ran out of water,” Manjhoo said.
Come harvest time and the effect could be seen, even quantified. A 16-acre block that normally produced between 600 and 700 maunds of wheat yielded around 500 maunds after the water shortage, he said. Between 250 and 300 acres of his land was affected.
“This became the story of almost every household,” said Manjhoo.
The interruption came as Balochistan was undertaking a major change in the way its farmers power agricultural tube wells. The government had decided to move thousands of subsidised agricultural connections from the electricity grid to solar power to solve a problem that had been building for years. Agricultural tube wells had depended heavily on subsidised electricity. The subsidy was expensive for the government, while the Quetta Electric Supply Company (Qesco) faced mounting financial pressure and farmers complained that the electricity they were supposed to receive was often unavailable or insufficient.
Solarisation offered the government a different arrangement. Instead of continuing to pay a recurring electricity subsidy, it would provide financial support for solar systems, disconnect the agricultural tube wells from the grid and shift farmers to solar-powered irrigation.
The Balochistan solarisation programme was launched with a promise of completion within three months, with uninterrupted water supply for farmers. The Rs 55 billion project included shifting around 28,000 agricultural tube wells from grid electricity to solar, with the federal government contributing 70 percent of the funding and the remaining 30 percent covered by the Balochistan government. However, implementation was slow and unwieldy.
For Manjhoo, however, the transition was measured in immediate terms. With his crop still standing in the field, the power was interrupted.
Farmers and their representatives say the problem was the sequence in which the transition took place. Khalid Hussain Bathh, chairman of Kissan Ittehad Pakistan, said farmers in Naseerabad were promised compensation for solarisation but faced electricity cuts before receiving the money. “Before payments were made, electricity connections were cut, and the supply was shifted from three-phase to two-phase,” Bathh said.
The result was that tube wells remained shut and crops suffered from the shortage of irrigation water.
“Crops were destroyed due to the unavailability of irrigation water,” he said, adding that farmers had sown crops on the assurance of the provincial irrigation minister but that their seeds went to waste because of the water shortage. Kissan Ittehad took note that farmers were suffering financial losses after electricity connections were disconnected while solarisation funds had not yet been released.
Qesco claims compensation preceded disconnections, but official federal briefings from March 2025 confirm thousands of premature disconnections while energy departments were still negotiating payments in May. Its records show that compensation was paid in phases, followed by disconnection of the corresponding agricultural connections.
If the payments and disconnections happened in the sequence described by Qesco, the problem was one of implementation and timing of individual cases. If farmers' accounts are correct, some were left without adequate irrigation while waiting for the promised transition.
The old system that subsidised power for agricultural irrigation had its own problems. According to energy economist and policy expert Zubair Khan of the Indus Consortium, the agricultural tube well subsidy dates back to July 2001. It was introduced because farmers in Balochistan depended heavily on groundwater for irrigation, particularly in areas with limited canal irrigation.
The arrangement gave farmers access to subsidised electricity, but the subsidy was ultimately paying for the energy used to pump groundwater.
Under the 2015 arrangement, a tube-well owner paid Rs10,000 a month while the government subsidised the remaining electricity bill up to a ceiling of Rs75,000. The federal government contributed 40 percent and Balochistan 60 percent. The arrangement was based on a specified motor size and an assumption of eight hours of electricity supply a day.
Farmers increasingly complained that they were not receiving those eight hours.
By 2023-24, some farmers were reporting that they received only around three hours of electricity a day.That left the government paying a large subsidy while farmers still struggled to irrigate their land.
Khan also pointed to another problem. Because the benefit was tied to subsidised tube-well electricity rather than directly targeted according to need, larger farmers or those with greater groundwater dependence could receive a larger public benefit. The state was subsidising the cost of pumping water. Solarisation changes that arrangement. The government makes a substantial investment at the beginning, and the farmer takes over the cost of operating the system. That makes sense for the government; as for the farmers, it gives them something they had not reliably received from the grid: control over when they irrigate.
The question is who can afford to get there.
While the government capped its contribution at Rs2 million per connection, real conversion costs ran significantly higher. Tariq Bangulzai, who farms 50 acres in Mastung, spent over Rs4 million to install his system which uses between 112 and 115 panels of 615 watts each.
With no dedicated bank financing available, growers were forced to sell livestock or rely on private high-interest loans to cover the shortfall, turning an energy relief programme into an immediate financial burden.
Mohammad Munawwar, an eight- to nine-acre apple grower from Khanozai, faced a similar problem. His solar system, including the panels, wiring, frame and other equipment, cost approximately Rs2.45 million.
The examples show why the solarisation programme cannot be judged only by how much money the government saves on electricity subsidies. For the government, the change converts a recurring expense into a capital investment. But for the farmer, it could mean taking on a large financial obligation immediately.
Zubair Khan argues that farmers who cannot meet the capital cost need affordable financing mechanisms, including concessional agricultural loans, long-term instalments, partial grants for smaller farmers and, where appropriate, cooperative or shared solar systems linked to efficient irrigation.
There is also a question about who is eligible in the first place. The programme is designed around registered subsidised agricultural tube-well consumers. Farmers who never had such a connection, including some who depend on diesel, do not automatically enter the same compensation arrangement. The transition therefore does not affect every farmer in the same way.
While some farmers suffered during the transition, others are pleased with what happened after the solar system was installed. Munawwar says his orchard has not suffered from the change and that his main benefit is no longer having to depend on Qesco for irrigation power.
“I am very happy after shifting to solar,” he said. “At least now I do not have to protest against Qesco over electricity supply.”
This is a gripe that consumers in Pakistan have long held against the grid. For many, including the farmers in Balochistan, solar power is not just access to clean and cheap energy. It is also reliable daytime power, and in that sense an end to dependence on an expensive and unreliable grid. The problem is whether the state can move farmers from one irrigation system to another without leaving them exposed during the transition, without assuming that every farmer can finance the same capital cost and without ignoring what greater pumping capacity means for groundwater.
The experience of Naseerabad shows the first problem. Other parts of Balochistan point towards the third.
The falling groundwater is not primarily a Naseerabad issue. The province's most serious groundwater concerns are found in areas where agriculture depends heavily on aquifers, including parts of Pishin, Quetta, Mastung and Killa Abdullah.
In Dasht Kumbela, Bangulzai operates nine tube wells. Before solarisation, he said, the feeder serving his village supplied around 400 agricultural tube wells. There was not enough electricity for all of them to operate at the same time. Some farmers received electricity one day and others the next.
Solar changed that. It gave farmers greater pumping capacity during daylight hours. Bangulzai believes the change has added pressure to groundwater.
After heavy rains last year, he said, groundwater in his area was around 900 feet deep. During the following seven months, he estimated that 70 to 80 tube wells went dry as farmers drilled deeper.
He said drilling now costs around Rs4,500 per foot as farmers go deeper.
His concern extends beyond agriculture. He fears continued depletion could eventually threaten drinking water in his area.
His account does not prove that solarisation caused those wells to dry. Groundwater depletion in Mastung predates the solar programme and has several causes. But the economic mechanism, however, is simple to follow: When electricity is scarce or expensive, pumping is constrained. When solar makes daytime pumping cheaper and more readily available, that constraint weakens.
Dr Najeeb Ullah, a lecturer in the Department of Geology at the University of Balochistan, describes groundwater depletion as one of northern Balochistan's most serious environmental threats. His research indicates that groundwater levels in parts of the Pishin Basin are declining by around two to five metres annually. Kuchlak and Quetta sub-basins have also experienced excessive extraction accompanied by significant land subsidence.
He estimates that the Quetta Valley is subsiding at around 16 centimetres a year. “Solarisation is a factor, but it becomes dangerous when groundwater extraction remains unchecked,” he said. That is where the policy question moves beyond solar. A tube well does not care whether its pump is powered by electricity, diesel or sunlight. The question is how much water it is allowed to extract.
Irrigation Secretary Sohail-ur-Rehman Baloch says there is currently no province-wide statutory limit on the number of hours a solar agricultural tube well can operate, and no uniform volumetric extraction limit for every solar tube well.
He says any restrictions should take account of crop requirements, aquifer safe yield, groundwater availability, pump capacity and local groundwater stress.
That approach makes more sense for Balochistan than a single province-wide quota on extraction, if only because the groundwater conditions of Naseerabad are not the same as those of Pishin, Quetta or Mastung.
The province already has a groundwater-management framework and a system for monitoring groundwater resources. But monitoring a falling water table is different from controlling the pumping that is causing it.
The 2025 Agricultural Solarisation and Electricity Theft Prevention Act regulates the solarisation process, including the use of government-supported solar facilities and restrictions on unauthorised reconnection to the grid. It does not establish a province-wide limit on pumping hours or a uniform groundwater extraction quota.
Solarisation is, therefore, changing the energy economics of irrigation faster than the province has established a comprehensive system for managing the water being pumped.
Governments elsewhere have encountered the same problem. India's experience with solar irrigation has increasingly focused on creating incentives for farmers to use less electricity and water rather than simply making pumping cheaper. In Gujarat, for example, grid-connected solar pumps have been linked to arrangements under which farmers can sell surplus electricity. National programmes have also incorporated groundwater-stress considerations and promoted efficient irrigation.
The policy lesson is useful for Balochistan. The answer is not to restrict solar because the need for cheap and clean energy transition is an immediate universal need, more so in Pakistan where energy poverty is widespread.
For experts the answer lies in regulating what happens after the solar panels are installed. That could mean monitoring groundwater levels, registering abstraction points, measuring water use, encouraging efficient irrigation and imposing restrictions in aquifers where extraction exceeds safe yield.
Sohail-ur-Rehman Baloch says High-Efficiency Irrigation Systems have been proposed as part of the response, but they are not currently a statutory requirement for every solarised tube well.
The Balochistan Water Policy 2024 also envisages further institutional and legal reforms.
The issue, then, is not whether solar power should be used for irrigation. It is whether the government will build the water rules around the new energy system.
In Naseerabad, Manjhoo's tube well now operates on solar power, and the immediate crisis of transition has passed. "Grid electricity was often unavailable or switched off by the authorities," he said. "From that perspective, solarisation has been very good for farmers."
The state had legitimate reason to end an expensive, failing electricity subsidy, just as farmers had reason to demand reliable power. Solar delivers that power while easing financial strain on Qesco. But an energy transition cannot come at the expense of basic agricultural survival. Crops need water when they need water; solar systems must be operational before grid connections are cut.
Moving forward, the success of Balochistan’s solarisation plan will not be measured by installed panels or removed subsidies. It will depend on whether the state can provide accessible financing for smallholders and enforce groundwater rules to keep cheap energy from draining depleted aquifers.
For the government, the calculation was about offloading an expensive electricity subsidy. For farmers, it has always been about water.

title: How BRICS is filling the void
description: Members are not abandoning the existing global order  they are creating parallel paths and more choices
content:
Members are not abandoning the existing global order, they are creating parallel paths and more choices
In New Delhi, at the BRICS summit, there was something different about the way the leaders discussed many of our current issues, including the war against Iran. They condemned the attacks, called for restraint, and spoke about sovereignty, international law and the need for diplomacy. And they did not all sound the same. In a different world, all this was expected from the United Nations. That is probably the most simple way to understand what BRICS is today.
The group has grown considerably since it began as BRIC—an acronym for Brazil, Russia, India and China, before South Africa joined and the S was added. It now brings together countries with very different political systems, economic interests and relationships with the US. Some are close to Washington, others are under collective Western sanctions. India and China can oppose each other but they still sit around the same BRICS table.
Experts believe that these nations are not bonding on common ideology so much as a shared dissatisfaction with the way global power is organised and the way global governance is so heavily influenced by the West. That dissatisfaction was not only seen but also felt, both in the summit’s language on Iran and in its discussion of trade, tariffs, currencies and the chaos created by Washington’s policies toward the international financial system.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa was among the more straightforward speakers. During his speech, he argued that the world could not claim to support international law while applying its principles selectively. The South African leader was referring to what he called the “illegal war against Iran” and cautioned that the credibility of the international system was being damaged by the selective application of its own rules.
That said, the language in the final declaration was more careful and that is hardly surprising. A document negotiated by 11 full member countries was never going to sound like the speech of one leader. The declaration, as expected, expressed concern over the conflict, called for maximum restraint and reaffirmed the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity. It also pushed diplomacy as the way out of the crisis. India, the host, for obvious reasons, had good reason to keep the language measured. New Delhi has spent decades cultivating relationships on several sides of the geopolitical divide. It buys Russian oil and maintains a strategic relationship with Moscow, and it would like to maintain its partnership with Washington. Iran, meanwhile, is an old partner and an important part of India’s connectivity plans.
According to observers, the summit was never going to produce the kind of blunt, unified condemnation that might come from a much smaller group of countries. Still, something important happened and the argument over Iran did not just end at Iran. For countries such as Russia and Iran, the question of who gets to enforce international rules is inseparable from the question of who controls the levers through which those rules are enforced. After all, sanctions do not stop at government offices, they for every layer of the system, disrupt payments and investment, and make it harder for countries to access foreign currencies. A government or its leader can condemn sanctions in a speech, but the real consequences are felt by companies trying to move money or cargo across borders. In many ways, this explains why the economic discussion at the BRICS summit was almost as interesting as the political one.
There has been plenty of talk over the years about BRICS replacing the dollar. That makes for an easy headline, but it is not quite what is happening or what these countries want collectively. At the moment, there is no BRICS currency waiting to replace the dollar. There is no new financial system that has suddenly made the SWIFT banking system irrelevant or easy to bypass. What these countries appear to be doing is trying to make it easier to trade with one another without having to pass through the same financial channels every time channels that can be influenced by the US. And the New Delhi Declaration backed greater use of national currencies and work on cross-border payment systems, including efforts to make it easier for banks in different countries to connect and move money between them.
That may sound ambitious, but it is not, and to a great extent it has been happening for some time. If Brazil can trade more easily with India in their own currencies, if South African businesses can settle transactions without routing everything through dollars, or if Russian companies have more ways of moving money internationally, then the leverage attached to the existing financial system is reduced significantly, if not made to disappear completely. All that said, the dollar remains deeply embedded in global trade and finance, and replacing that infrastructure is enormously difficult. In fact, the dollar’s share of allocated global reserves rose to about 57.1% in the first quarter of 2026, up from 56.4% in late 2025. For now, the BRICS countries have not solved those problems, but they do appear to be trying to create more choices. This is also why protectionism features so prominently, though cautiously, in the summit’s language.
The New Delhi Declaration criticised unilateral tariffs and other trade restrictions, arguing that they distort trade and weaken the multilateral trading system. It backed support for the World Trade Organization and warned against the use of unilateral economic measures. It did not name the United States directly. The criticism, experts say, comes at an awkward time for the global economy. Tariffs have once again become a central instrument of US economic policy, turning access to the world’s largest consumer market into a bargaining tool that has been used by President Donald Trump. Countries that spent decades building export industries now have to deal with the possibility that a tariff can change the economics of a product almost overnight. At BRICS the answer was not to abandon global trade, it was the opposite. The body’s members want more of it, but they want more room to decide the terms on which they participate. And that is what makes Ramaphosa’s speech particularly important.
For South Africa, the argument is not primarily about replacing the dollar with their local currency or building an anti-American trading bloc. It is about a common problem in the developing world: countries export raw materials and import finished goods, while much of the wealth generated along the way is captured somewhere else. Ramaphosa, at the BRICS summit, also argued for a more inclusive global economy and greater financial cooperation, including stronger use of local currencies and cross-border payment systems. That is not the same argument coming from Russia. For Moscow, alternative payment systems have an immediate strategic value because Western sanctions have made access to conventional financial channels much more difficult. Russia has every reason to want a world in which its ability to trade is less dependent on institutions it does not control. For South Africa, the attraction is more developmental. For India, it is mostly about strategic autonomy. For China, it fits into a much longer effort to increase the international use of its currency and build financial infrastructure that is less dependent on Western institutions. And last but not least, for Iran, the attraction is very obvious under current circumstances. According to experts, these interests overlap, but at the moment, they do not amount to a single BRICS strategy. And this is the part of the BRICS story that often gets lost in the language about a “multipolar world”.
Perhaps that is precisely why the financial agenda is more significant than some of the summit’s political rhetoric. At this point, a common currency would require an extraordinary degree of political and economic integration. BRICS is nowhere close to that. However, countries can cooperate on payments without agreeing on foreign policy; they can settle more trade in local currencies without abandoning the dollar. And according to most independent experts, that is a much more realistic aim for now.
A new currency would send shockwaves, but a payment arrangement between banks in two countries would barely make the news. But if enough of those arrangements develop over time, they can change the way trade is conducted. This is why Russia’s position at the summit is also worth paying attention to. For years, Putin has been among the most vocal advocates of reducing dependence on Western financial infrastructure, but even Russia’s rhetoric needs to be read carefully. The Kremlin has said it is not seeking outright “de-dollarisation” and remains open to different payment methods. The same logic runs through the BRICS discussion on sanctions. The members do not all agree on sanctions, and they certainly do not all agree on the countries that should be sanctioned. But many of them object to a system in which one group of countries can impose financial restrictions with consequences far beyond its own borders.
For many countries in the Global South, there is another concern. Their trade, access to finance and even access to technology can be affected by decisions made in Washington, Brussels or other powerful capitals. That can be uncomfortable even when they have good relations with the West. The push for alternatives, then, is not necessarily about turning away from the West. It is about having more room to make their own choices without needing permission. And that, experts say, may be the most consequential idea to come out of the New Delhi summit.
That said, let’s not over value what is emerging just right now. The dollar still calls the shots in global finance, SWIFT still holds the strings to the world’s banking system, and western financial markets are still vital for companies and governments everywhere. Even the BRICS countries themselves keep using those systems heavily. And then there is no shortage of contradictions inside the bloc.
But perhaps a new international order, if one is emerging, will not arrive with a single announcement at a summit in one of these capitals. It may come through a series of smaller changes such as a payment system here, a local-currency trade agreement there, a new development bank, a supply chain redirected, a country finding another source of financing or another market for its exports. That is a slower process, and in many ways, it is also much harder to reverse. So, in New Delhi, the summit did not produce a new world order, but it did produce something more modest, a group of nations trying to make the existing one less restrictive and perhaps even challenge the way it operates. Whether they can do that together in the long run is another question.

title: China pushes back against US on Iran and Cuba in UN speech
description: China   s Vice President Han Zheng said Beijing has consistently and firmly supported the United Nations
content:
China’s Vice President Han Zheng said Beijing has consistently and firmly supported the United Nations
China ​pushed back against the United States in its speech at the UN General Assembly on Saturday, ‌saying sovereignty of countries in the Gulf should be respected and urging the "relevant country" to stop threatening Cuba and lift its blockade on it.
Vice President Han Zheng did not mention the US by name in his remarks. The US has launched a pressure campaign on ​Cuba that has largely blocked oil from reaching the island. The US war on Iran started with ​US-Israeli strikes in February.
The comments stood in sharp contrast to the bonhomie on display earlier ⁠this week at the White House, where President Donald Trump feted Chinese leader Xi Jinping with military flyovers and ​at a lavish state dinner.
"Major countries should have special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security, and they should take ​the lead in complying with the rules, upholding rule of law, and doing what's right," Han said.
"China holds that the sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected."
Trump warned Xi against providing support to Iran during the ​Washington talks and received assurances that China would not do so, the US ambassador to China said on Friday.
Read More: Xi visit brings fresh progress in China-US strategic stability: Chinese FM
The ​warning followed reports that Beijing had supplied Iran with shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers and that Tehran had found ways to evade ‌sanctions on ⁠its oil sales with Chinese help.
On Cuba, Han said: "China urges the relevant country to immediately stop using threat of force against Cuba and immediately and completely lift the blockade and sanctions against Cuba."
Cuba's electrical grid suffered a total collapse earlier this month, plunging the nation into darkness and leaving millions without power ​as the US presses its ​blockade.
Speaking hours later at ⁠the UN hall, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov echoed the Chinese remarks, calling on Washington to lift the 'siege' of Cuba and restrictions on trade with the largest island ​in the Caribbean.
Lavrov also said the US should strike Cuba off the list ​of state sponsors ⁠of terrorism.
Cuba's aging power generation system has been under severe strain from fuel shortages and decrepit infrastructure for years, but a US-imposed oil blockade that began in January has worsened blackouts and led to frequent grid collapses.t
Han also used the ⁠speech to ​portray China as a reliable partner on the global stage and ​a steadfast defender of developing nations.
"China holds that all countries, big or small, are equal members of the international community, and that world affairs ​should be handled by all through consultation," said Han.
Zheng also said that China has consistently and firmly supported the United Nations (UN).
At a meeting with UN General Assembly (UNGA) President Khalilur Rahman in New York on the sidelines of the 81st UNGA session, Han congratulated Rahman on assuming the presidency.
Also Read: Six big takeaways from a turbulent week of UN diplomacy
In September 2025, Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed the Global Governance Initiative , sending a clear signal of China's firm commitment to safeguarding the authority and central role of the UN, Han said, adding that the initiative has been welcomed and supported by nearly 160 countries and international organizations.
The UNGA is the most representative deliberative and policymaking organ of the UN, as well as a key platform for upholding multilateralism and promoting global governance, Han said, adding that China will continue to support the work of the UNGA and its president.
Chinese Vice President Han Zheng meets with UN General Assembly (UNGA) President Khalilur Rahman on the sidelines of the 81st UNGA session in New York, Sept. 25, 2026. PHOTO: XINHUA
Noting that this year marks the 55th anniversary of the restoration of the lawful seat of the People's Republic of China at the UN, Han said that China-UN cooperation will embrace broader prospects from this new starting point.
China advocates for advancing UN reform and increasing its efficiency to better adapt to the changing times, Han said. China also supports making sustainable development a priority of the 81st UNGA session and delivering more inclusive development outcomes in response to the aspirations of people around the world, he said.
The one-China principle is the political foundation of China-UN cooperation, Han said, expressing his belief that the UNGA president and the assembly will continue to uphold the principle.
Rahman said that China is an important partner of the UN, thanking China for its support for the work of the UNGA.
At a time when unilateralism is prevalent, China has remained committed to multilateralism and put forward positive proposals for addressing challenges facing world peace, security and development, he said.
The four global initiatives proposed by Xi are closely aligned with the six priorities of the 81st UNGA session, Rahman said.
The UNGA president said he looks forward to maintaining close communication and coordination with China, deepening cooperation, and jointly promoting the cause of world peace and development.
He stressed that the UNGA will firmly adhere to the one-China principle.

title: PTI postpones long march to October 4
description: PTI postpones long march to October 4
author_name: Ahtesham Bashir, Usama Iqbal, Rameez Khan
content:
Afridi accuses Centre of trying to repeat May 9-style action
Acknowledging the difficulties and potential consequences of holding a long march amid extensive security and traffic restrictions imposed by the PML-N-led federal and Punjab governments, the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) on Friday announced postponing its much-touted long march on Islamabad, originally scheduled for September 27, until October 4.
The decision appeared to render the federal government in a bind as it with the coordination of the Punjab government made an extensive security operation, which included blocking access points to Islamabad for traffic from Punjab with nail-studded metal barriers, erecting walls of shipping containers across the city, and deploying Rangers and large contingents of police.
Addressing a news conference in Peshawar, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, after securing formal approval from the party's political committee, announced that a "sea of people" would leave Peshawar on the new date as part of the party's political strategy.
He said the decision had been taken purely as a political strategy and that the march would now depart from Peshawar on October 4.
The decision had not, however, been endorsed by PTI's allies in TTAP as of the filing of this report, according to sources, who attributed the disagreement to a lack of coordination. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi said TTAP leaders would join him on stage during the march, while acknowledging differences between PTI and the alliance.
Speculation over a possible postponement had circulated for about 40 hours, with the proposal first discussed at the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa level during a Zoom meeting, according to party sources. A political committee meeting was subsequently convened to formally approve the decision, which sources said was endorsed without significant debate.
One party leader suggested not announcing a new date for the march, arguing that this would keep the government uncertain about PTI's plans. Asad Qaiser disagreed, saying that postponing the march without announcing a new date could be interpreted as a withdrawal, according to the sources.
The party also informed opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai about the decision. The postponement to October 4 was also reported by multiple outlets following the political committee's decision.
Interestingly, Afridi held two news conferences on Friday. At the first, during the day, he vowed to proceed with the march at all costs but remained vague about its date. At a second news conference after the party meeting, he announced that the march had been postponed to Oct 4.
Based on Afridi's remarks, the move appeared aimed at allowing the party to mark PTI founder Imran Khan's birthday, which falls on Oct 5, in Islamabad.
Afridi said October 5, the birthday of PTI founder Imran Khan, would be observed by party workers, who would cut cakes and celebrate a "Victory Day".
The decision to postpone the September 27 march was taken by the PTI political committee. Afridi said a proposal had been placed before the committee two days earlier to defer the march until the first week of October. Following lengthy consultations, the committee agreed to postpone it until October 4.
He said the decision was unanimous and reiterated that the postponement was part of a political strategy.
Afridi claimed that the federal government had become unnerved by the planned march and alleged that all routes leading into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been blocked.
He likened the government's actions to the "same conspiracy" that had preceded the events surrounding East Pakistan and alleged that the measures were aimed at breaking up Pakistan. He questioned what the government hoped to prove by closing the routes.
"We are political people and will pursue a political struggle," Afridi said, adding that those expecting a repeat of the May 9-style operation against PTI were mistaken and that his party would foil "a conspiracy" against it.
He said that if the authorities wanted to arrest people or stop the march, they should come in uniform.
Afridi said PTI respected uniformed personnel, but those arriving in plain clothes would be dealt with differently.
He claimed that Imran Khan could be released within a minute if the courts began functioning properly, adding that the Supreme Court had ordered the PTI founder's transfer to hospital but the order had not been implemented.
Afridi said all relevant issues had been discussed by the political committee and that the committee had agreed that the march would depart from Peshawar on October 4.
He also referred to a statement made some time ago by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz that she feared other provinces rather than India, and questioned the message such remarks sent to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Afridi criticised Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah for calling PTI members terrorists and asked what message the federal government was giving to the province.
He alleged that PTI members of the provincial assembly were being picked up and that roads had been blocked along the K-P border.
Afridi insisted that PTI was a political and peaceful movement and alleged that the government wanted to build cases against the party again in a manner similar to those following May 9.
"Our fight is for the supremacy of the Constitution and the law," he said.
The K-P chief minister alleged that efforts were being made to keep PTI and the establishment locked in confrontation, while planes and vehicles were being purchased.
He further accused the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) of effectively becoming the Punjab police and alleged that PML-N leaders were creating a "terrorist" narrative against PTI.
Afridi alleged that some people were being brought into PTI ranks and said he was warning in advance that anyone planning any action against the party should come in uniform.
He said PTI would not raise sticks against uniformed personnel.
Afridi appealed to the chief justice of the Supreme Court to take action over "efforts to cut Khyber Pakhtunkhwa off from Pakistan".
He said the political struggle was a "Test match" and added that PTI had already won the toss.
Afridi said negotiations would continue after the long march and criticised the extensive use of containers in Islamabad, saying the federal capital had effectively been turned into a "container city".
He warned that those who came out on October 4 would not be under anyone's control.
The decision to postpone the march and the new date were also conveyed to Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas by PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, Afridi said.
He reiterated that postponing the long march was part of PTI's political strategy.
The postponement followed days of uncertainty over the September 27 schedule. PTI had previously been preparing for a nationwide protest and long march towards Islamabad, while opposition leaders had been consulting over the timing and political strategy surrounding the mobilisation.
It is pertinent to note that the decision came amid an internal debate over the feasibility and timing of the march, as party sources said there had been a proposal to "exhaust" the federal government and law-enforcement agencies because the federal capital and several routes had already been closed or restricted.
The sources claimed that the PTI had already achieved what it wanted through the march, with roads shut and hundreds of millions of rupees being spent on law enforcement.
The announcement was welcomed by PTI and some members of TTAP, who said the decision recognized the cost to the government of either maintaining the security arrangements until Oct. 4 or redeploying them closer to the new date.
A TTAP leader described the move as a significant setback for the government, saying the chief minister had gained an advantage simply by postponing the march. The leader said measures introduced to restrict PTI's planned mobilisation could ultimately impose a greater burden on the government if they had to be maintained or reinstated.
According to PTI leaders, the march will now leave Peshawar on October 4. Earlier discussions within the party had also considered October 5 to 10 as a possible new window.
The party sources said the decision had nothing to do with the Jamaat-i-Islami (JI), whose own protest march against the petroleum levy had been postponed at the request of the prime minister.
A senior PTI leader said the postponement offered the party two main advantages: it would increase pressure on a government that had taken extensive measures to prevent the march, while also creating an opportunity for negotiations to resume. PTI leaders have, however, said no meaningful negotiations were currently under way.
The decision was rejected by TTAP, whose leader said Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Nasir Abbas had been repeatedly sidelined by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister during consultations on major decisions. The leader said TTAP had also not been consulted before the Sept. 27 date was announced and was again left out of consultations over the latest postponement, describing it as adding "insult to injury."
Asked about the criticism, Afridi said PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan had communicated the party's decision to both leaders.
According to sources, PTI leadership had contacted Achakzai and requested that he announce a new date for the long march. At the time, however, Achakzai had refused to announce its postponement and maintained that the countrywide movement would begin on September 27.
Sources said Achakzai's position was that the movement would begin in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and other provinces on September 27 and would gradually move towards Islamabad.
The disagreement over postponing the long march between PTI leadership and Achakzai remained unresolved for a time, while efforts to persuade the opposition leader continued.
PTI leadership also continued consultations with opposition leaders over the date of the long march.
Against this backdrop, PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan arrived in Islamabad from Mianwali to meet Achakzai and other opposition leaders.
Gohar subsequently met Achakzai and briefed him on the PTI's position regarding the long march, according to sources.
The sources said PTI leadership wanted the long march postponed and wanted Achakzai, as opposition leader, to announce the decision.
