title: Saudi coalition says it intercepts Houthi missiles  drones
description: Saudi civil defence had sent alerts overnight for Khamis Mushait and    Abha but not for Riyadh
content:
Saudi civil defence had sent alerts overnight for Khamis Mushait and ​Abha but not for Riyadh
Yemen's Saudi-led coalition said early on ​Saturday it had intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones ‌launched by Houthis towards the kingdom.
The coalition said in posts on X that the missiles were headed towards Khamis Mushait and the drones towards the ​capital, Riyadh, adding that it was monitoring the missile threat ​and drones launched at the kingdom, without providing further details.
🔴 BREAKING: Saudi Arabia’s air defenses intercepted two drones launched by the Iran-backed Houthi militia toward Riyadh, the spokesperson for the Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, Major General Turki al-Maliki, says. pic.twitter.com/mXszHAmF65
The ⁠Saudi civil defence had sent alerts overnight for Khamis Mushait and ​Abha but not for Riyadh.
The Houthis, who control the most populous parts ​of Yemen and much of the north, have been launching attacks against Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, with strikes targeting Saudi vessels in ​the Red Sea.
Read: Pakistan, KSA, Turkiye military chiefs slam attack on Makkah
The attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and ​shipping, adding to pressures on global oil supplies caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran ‌and ⁠putting at risk the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains largely blocked.
Hours earlier, the military chiefs of Saudi Arabia and defence allies Pakistan and Turkey ​reviewed threats facing ​Saudi Arabia at ⁠a meeting in the Saudi capital.
The three signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement last month, saying they would regard ​an armed attack on any of them as ​an ⁠attack on all. They said the pact aimed to strengthen collective deterrence and military cooperation.
The Saudi defence minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, said early on ⁠Saturday ​that he had affirmed with the Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff, Asim Munir, in Riyadh continued joint efforts to confront attacks against the kingdom in ​accordance with the pact.

title: OpenAI agents accessed information from US govt sites  company says
description: AI research nonprofit says bots also tried hacking civil rights portal  leaked 53 ChatGPT user images
content:
AI research nonprofit says bots also tried hacking civil rights portal, leaked 53 ChatGPT user images
OpenAI said late on Friday its models accessed information from the websites of the United States Securities and Exchange Commission and the US Census Bureau during research and training activity, but found no evidence of unauthorised access, compromised accounts or security breaches.
Separately, AI research nonprofit Transluce said agents appearing to originate from OpenAI made an unsuccessful attempt to hack a US Department of Education civil rights website.
Transluce said the incident was part of broader AI agent activity probing government websites using tactics including exposed credentials, anti-bot bypasses and fake accounts.
Two months after OpenAI disclosed the accidental hacking of Hugging Face , the ChatGPT maker is still working to understand the full scope of its rogue agent activity , two people briefed on the matter told Reuters .
The latest example came on Friday when OpenAI said its agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users. OpenAI declined to say if the images were AI-generated or identified real people. It also declined to say when the images were posted.
The disclosure and researcher reports on Friday of other previously unknown activity involving several US agencies reveal a new area of privacy risk for the company, and illustrate how difficult it is even for an AI firm at the cutting edge of the technology to inventory all the unauthorised activity tied to its agents.
Read: AI leaders warn UN of security risks as systems grow more powerful
OpenAI’s ongoing battle also reflects a yawning gap between the strength of the models the company is testing and its capacity to oversee or even track their actions.
As of mid-September, one person briefed on the matter estimated that OpenAI had found roughly two dozen incidents of its agents acting in undesirable ways. But the number has continued rising as OpenAI teams sift through internal logs of the agents’ activities and find previously unknown cases, the two people close to the company said.
OpenAI said its review would take months to complete given the scale of the work. The company also said it had notified dozens of third parties about improper activity.
Most of the leaked images have been taken down and OpenAI said it was lobbying hosting providers to remove the rest.
OpenAI's agents had access to these images because the company relies on anonymised user data for part of its model-training process, according to the company, former employees and outside researchers. Enterprise data is not eligible for training, while ChatGPT consumers need to opt out of allowing the company to use their data for training.
Before user posts are used for training, they go through an anonymisation process that strips out metadata, names and other contact information and should make it difficult to trace back to any individual user, the company said.
But the practice carries risks because there is a chance that the data may not be fully stripped of personally identifiable information and that it might leak in the course of the model’s work, three people familiar with OpenAI’s practices said.
In the two months since OpenAI first announced that its agents broke containment, there have been more than 15 different OpenAI-related incidents of varying levels of severity disclosed by the company, by outside researchers, or — just on Wednesday — by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the United Nations, who said OpenAI agents broke into a government health data portal in June.
Past incidents have varied in nature, ranging from spam-like messages left on internet sites all the way to the break-in at Hugging Face, which involved a swarm of agents abusing previously unknown software vulnerabilities to escape their networks and penetrate the AI repository as they hunted for answers to a test. OpenAI also said its agents took aim at its own infrastructure.
Read More: As AI agents act in unexpected ways, is ‘rogue AI’ really here?
Albanese told reporters in New York that OpenAI uncovered the activity in August, and disclosed it on September 10 via an email to a general government inbox. He said he directly told OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that this disclosure process was unacceptable.
OpenAI said some of the sites involved are operated by government, universities and public agencies because the models that are conducting research seek out reputable sources of public information.
The July 21 announcement that OpenAI's agent's had slipped out of control and hacked Hugging Face sparked widespread worries within the AI industry over its ability to control the more powerful AI models under development now. Since then, Anthropic, Alphabet's Google and Meta have said they've found similar behaviour by their agents after the Hugging Face incident prompted them to search.
OpenAI has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behaviour. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain.”
Even so, two people familiar with OpenAI’s investigation into its agents’ activity described it as locked down and shaped by company lawyers. The process has been unusually compartmentalised for a company that some former employees say was more open about these issues in the past, the people said.
Roughly 100 people were in some way involved in the process to understand the Hugging Face hack, three people briefed on the matter said. During that process, evidence of other incidents surfaced.
Reuters has previously reported that OpenAI investigators looking into the Hugging Face breach were discouraged by the company’s lawyers from expanding the scope of the investigation to include other incidents. OpenAI said its lawyers did not discourage deeper investigation.
Many incidents have been uncovered by outside researchers rather than OpenAI directly. In several episodes, the agents took problematic actions that went unnoticed by the company for months.
Also Read: OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are working to create an AI standards body
Earlier this month, a small group of investigators discovered that the company’s agents had hijacked a mostly defunct German wiki site to share tactics to cheat on some tasks, bypass OpenAI’s restrictions and mask their behaviour.
This week, the AI research firm Transluce said it discovered that OpenAI agents had bypassed the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare’s anti-bot controls. The firm also found two other cases that it linked to OpenAI agents. Those incidents were separate from the activity disclosed by Albanese.
In a statement, OpenAI said “much of the activity described in Transluce’s report overlaps with cases at varying stages of investigation in our ongoing review of misaligned model activity.” The company said it is prioritising the most severe cases in its review.
Since the Hugging Face hack, researchers across the AI industry have grown worried that companies will not be able to predict or control their technology. Some have taken the path of former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who publicly resigned this month in a viral social-media thread that said the AI labs are “gambling with our lives.”
In response to those concerns, Altman and his counterpart at Anthropic, CEO Dario Amodei, called for the industry to “pace” the development of AI and move cautiously in its pursuit of “recursive self improvement.” Altman doubled down on that message this week while addressing the United Nations.
Even so, both companies rolled out new models on Tuesday.

title: Saudi defence minister reaffirms joint efforts to confront attacks under Makkah pact in meeting with CDF Munir
description: Saudi  Pakistani leaderships reaffirm their commitment to continuing cooperation
content:
Both discuss 'sinful attacks' that targeted Makkah, civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman reaffirmed continued joint efforts to confront attacks targeting Makkah and civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom during a meeting with the Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff, Field Marshal Asim Munir.
The meeting came after top military commanders from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye held an urgent meeting in Riyadh under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA), marking the first exclusive high-level military coordination between the three countries since the trilateral defence pact was signed last month.
According to the statement issued by the Saudi defence minister, he held a meeting with CDF Munir in Riyadh, where they discussed matters of mutual interest, including the Makkah pact.
“I met with His Excellency the Commander of the Defence Forces and Chief of the Pakistan Army, Field Marshal Asim Munir. We praised the outcomes of the meeting of the chiefs of staff of the countries party to the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, and discussed the sinful attacks that targeted Makkah and civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom,” Khalid said in a post on X.
He further added that “We affirmed continuing joint efforts to confront these attacks in accordance with the MJDA.”
Met with Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defense Forces, Field Marshal Asim Munir. We welcomed the outcomes of the Chiefs of Staff meeting under the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, and discussed the heinous attacks targeting the holy city of Makkah and the Kingdom’s… pic.twitter.com/fKviJMjcP8
Saudi Minister of State, Cabinet Member and National Security Adviser Dr Musaad bin Mohammed Al-Aiban, Chief of General Staff General Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili, and the Minister of Defence's adviser for intelligence affairs, Hisham bin Abdulaziz bin Saif, among other senior officials, also attended the meeting, according to the post.
Read: PM condemns 'dastardly and heinous' attempted drone attack on Makkah, reaffirms support for Saudi Arabia
In August, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed a landmark "Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement" , declaring that "any aggression against either country shall be considered an aggression against both".
On August 7, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye formalised their longstanding strategic relationship through the newly signed Makkah pact, a trilateral security framework that its proponents describe as a defensive arrangement aimed at strengthening collective deterrence, enhancing military cooperation and promoting regional stability.
The conflict in the Middle East has deepened following attacks by Yemen's Houthi group targeting Saudi Arabia, prompting Pakistan to condemn the attacks and warn that the escalation could further threaten regional peace and stability.
In mid-September, Saudi Arabia's air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Makkah before ​it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, while the Saudi-led coalition said the security of the Two Holy Mosques and pilgrims was a “red line,” vowing that the coalition would take measures to deter further attacks.
Earlier, Houthis also attacked the southern Saudi cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, injuring 73 people. Women and children were among those injured.
Read more: Pakistan reiterates support for Saudi Arabia, backs kingdom's right to defend territory after Houthi attacks
The attacks also triggered fires at some energy facilities, where operations were subsequently halted as firefighting and emergency teams worked to contain the blazes and assess the damage.
The latest attacks were not the first time the Houthis had targeted Saudi Arabia’s energy interests. On 23 July, the group said it had struck two Saudi oil tankers in what it described as part of a naval blockade against the kingdom.

title: Pakistan Navy seizes narcotics worth  750m in major Arabian Sea operation
description: Naval chief also reaffirms Navy s commitment to maritime security  combating illicit trafficking at sea
content:
Naval chief also reaffirms Navy's commitment to maritime security, combating illicit trafficking at sea
Pakistan Navy ships HUNAIN and YARMOOK have seized more than 2,800 kilogrammes of narcotics, valued at approximately $750 million, during a joint counter-narcotics operation in the Arabian Sea, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said on Saturday.
According to the military's media wing, the ships were conducting a routine patrol when they intercepted a suspicious boat. A boarding operation was subsequently carried out, during which narcotics were recovered from "concealed compartments," it said.
Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf commended the officers and crew for their "professionalism and vigilance", ISPR said.
The naval chief also reaffirmed Pakistan Navy's commitment to maritime security and combating illicit trafficking at sea, according to the statement.
Pakistan Navy Ships HUNAIN and YARMOOK conducted a joint counter narcotics operation in the Arabian Sea. During routine patrolling, a suspicious boat was intercepted and over 2,800 kg of narcotics, valued at approximately USD 750 million, were seized. 1/2 pic.twitter.com/QSpTwWViRL
President Asif Ali Zardari has praised Pakistan Navy personnel for their successful counter-narcotics operation in the Arabian Sea, according to a statement.
The president commended the professionalism and vigilance of the officers and crew of Pakistan Navy ships HUNAIN and YARMOOK after they seized more than 2,800 kilogrammes of narcotics during a joint operation in the Arabian Sea.

He also praised the Navy's commitment to preventing illegal activities in maritime areas and safeguarding maritime security.
"Pakistan Navy is playing a valuable role in protecting the country's maritime boundaries and sea routes," he said. The president added that "Pakistan is committed to promoting peace and security and curbing illegal activities."
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif praised the Pakistan Navy for recovering more than 2,800 kilogrammes of narcotics during an operation in the Arabian Sea, according to a statement issued by the Prime Minister's Office on Saturday.
The prime minister congratulated the Navy's officers and personnel on the successful operation and praised their "professionalism, vigilance and surveillance".
"Pakistan Navy's operations against drug trafficking are commendable," he said, adding that the Navy plays an important role in protecting Pakistan's maritime boundaries and preventing illegal trafficking through the sea.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi praised the Pakistan Navy for its successful counter-narcotics operation in the Arabian Sea. He appreciated the professionalism and vigilance of Pakistan Navy officers and personnel.
“I pay tribute to the entire team that took part in the operation,” Naqvi said. “Pakistan Navy's operations against drug smuggling are commendable,” he added.
Earlier on Wednesday , the Pakistan Navy and Coast Guard, in coordination with the Joint Maritime Information Coordination Centre (JMICC), confiscated "a sizeable quantity" of liquor and illegal medicines in the Pishukan area of Balochistan, ISPR said.
According to the ISPR, the joint intelligence-based operation "thwarted an attempt to smuggle a large cache of contraband items" in the area. The operation was carried out on "actionable intelligence," the ISPR said, adding that the "seized contraband items have been handed over to the Pakistan Coast Guard for further legal proceedings."
The military's media wing noted that the "successful joint operation underscores the effectiveness of inter-agency coordination in countering smuggling while highlighting the resolve of the Pakistan Navy and Pakistan Coast Guard to prevent the use of Pakistani waters and land for illicit activities."

title: Man City found guilty of Premier League charges
description: The club is set to appeal against the charges
content:
The club is set to appeal against the charges
Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of 115 Premier League charges for breaching financial regulations, according to reports on Friday, in a ruling that will send shockwaves through English football.
No sanctions have yet been decided and it is understood the club are set to appeal.
The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by AFP over the latest developments in the case, reported first by the Athletic.
City have dominated English football for more than a decade but their reputation is on the line and they face potentially swingeing sanctions after a process that has taken two years.
The Abu Dhabi-backed club were charged by the Premier League in 2023 following an investigation into alleged breaches of rules between 2009 and 2018.
A hearing by an independent commission started in September 2024.
City were accused of failing to provide accurate financial information and details of payments to players and coaches, as well as breaches of financial sustainability rules.
They were also charged with failing to cooperate with an investigation.
The club strongly denied all charges at the time and said their case was supported by a "comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence".
A club spokesperson said Friday that their position had not changed.
"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC's position remains consistent with the club's statement of February 2023.
"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."
German outlet Der Spiegel published leaked documents including emails purportedly sent between top City executives in 2018.
It alleged the documents showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from Abu Dhabi state-controlled airline Etihad and telecoms firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from Sheikh Mansour's Abu Dhabi United Group as income.
Other documents purportedly showed off-the-books payments to former manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi.
In 2020, UEFA imposed a two-year European ban on City as well as a fine for breaking financial fair-play rules, though that ban was later overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
If the club are found guilty, sanctions could include a severe points deduction and possibly even expulsion from the Premier League.
Everton and Nottingham Forest were both hit by points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of profit and sustainability rules.
A severe punishment would also raise doubts over the future of City's cast of star players, including prolific striker Erling Haaland.
Other clubs could make a claim for titles to be stripped and for compensation.
"Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet," posted former Manchester United defender Rio Ferdinand, who was part of the United team to finish second to City in the 2011/12 season.
But British Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned people should not "jump to conclusions" on City, when asked whether they should be stripped of their Premier League titles.
"I think we would all need to study the independent commission's report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions," he told ITV Granada Reports.
Spain's World Cup-winning captain Rodri, who left City for Barcelona last month, said: "I believe in the justice system and I believe in the innocence of the club."
Under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour, whose Abu Dhabi United Group acquired the club in 2008, City have become the dominant force in English football.
They have won eight Premier League titles, a Champions League crown and multiple other trophies over the past 15 years.
The latest developments in the case come just months after Pep Guardiola left the club after a golden decade.
Guardiola always backed the club's stance on the charges but threatened to walk away if he felt he had been lied to and they were proven to be true.
Despite Guardiola's departure, City are top of the Premier League after a perfect start under new boss Enzo Maresca.
The Italian has been backed by an outlay of about £460 million ($608 million) on new players including Enzo Fernandez, Elliot Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi.

title: Zidane wins on France debut
description: Italy lose on Mancini return
content:
Zinedine Zidane's debut as France coach was overshadowed by an injury to captain Kylian Mbappe in a 1-0 win away to Turkey on Friday, while Roberto Mancini's first game back in charge of Italy ended in a 2-0 defeat to Belgium.
Zidane, the France legend and member of the team that won the World Cup in 1998, was taking charge of Les Bleus for the first time since being appointed in late July as the successor to Didier Deschamps.
Mbappe gave his side the lead nine minutes into the second half in the UEFA Nations League Group A1 clash at the Kocaeli Stadium in Izmit, just over 100 kilometres outside Istanbul.
But the Real Madrid superstar injured himself in the process of shooting, and looked to be in clear pain when he came off a few minutes later after initially attempting to carry on.
"It's not great. Unfortunately I think he's going to have to go home. We don't want to take any risks," Zidane told broadcaster TF1, suggesting that France's all-time record goal-scorer will play no part in the three Nations League matches still to come over the next 10 days.
"He overextended his knee while shooting. It's not very encouraging."
France held on for the win without their captain, while Turkey finished the game with 10 men after goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir was sent off late on for handling the ball outside his box as he raced out to deny Bradley Barcola.
So it looks set to be without Mbappe that France will head to Brussels for their next game against Belgium on Monday.
Belgium, playing their first match since losing to eventual winners Spain in the World Cup quarter-finals, spoiled Mancini's return to the Italian national team by beating their hosts at the Stadio Olimpico in Rome.
Mika Godts of Paris Saint-Germain ran through to give Belgium a 20th-minute lead, and substitute Dodi Lukebakio fired in from outside the box to double their advantage after the break.
"We need to think positively and not keep banging on all the time about what has happened in the past," Mancini said later when asked if Italy's failure to qualify for the World Cup was still hanging over the nation.
"In any case we can't change what happened now," added Mancini, who also said that boos by the home fans in the crowd of almost 50,000 were "normal" and "part of the game".
Mancini was previously Italy coach between 2018 and 2023 and led them to victory at Euro 2020.
Elsewhere on Friday, Shea Charles of Fulham scored the winner deep in stoppage time as Northern Ireland won 1-0 away to Georgia in Group B2.
That was after PSG star Khvicha Kvaratskhelia had a penalty saved for the home side.
Danylo Sikan's goal gave Ukraine a 1-0 victory in Hungary in the same group, with the visitors holding on after having Oleksandr Nazarenko sent off late on.
Robert Lewandowski captained Poland in their 0-0 draw with Bosnia and Herzegovina in Group B4, while Alexander Isak and Viktor Gyokeres both scored as Sweden beat Romania 2-1 in Stockholm in the same section.
There were also wins for Armenia and Montenegro in League C.
The Nations League action continues on Saturday with England hosting Spain, who are playing their first game since winning the World Cup in July.

title: Trump seeks to withhold  800m in Congress approved funds
description: White House invokes rarely used  pocket rescission  tactic as Senator Susan Collins brands move illegal
content:
White House invokes rarely used 'pocket rescission' tactic as Senator Susan Collins brands move illegal
United States President Donald Trump sought on Friday to unilaterally withhold more than $800 million in spending on immigration, race and education that Congress has approved.
The move was the latest salvo in a fight between the Trump administration and Congress over control of the nation's spending.
"President Trump is committed to utilising all possible tools to cut wasteful and harmful government spending that does not benefit American citizens," the White House said in a statement announcing the steps.
The statement outlined several programs, including some focused on refugee assistance, racial-minority business development and overseas conservation.
Read: Pakistan, China, India among nations flagged by Trump in 23-country drug list
The Constitution gives Congress the power of the purse, but the White House said the programs supported illegal immigration, stoked racial tensions and promoted alarmist approaches to the environment.
The White House is deploying a rarely used technique known as a "pocket rescission" that bypasses Congress.
Senator Susan Collins, who chairs the chamber's Appropriations Committee, described the step as "illegal."
Read More: Trump administration proposes waiving grace period for H-1B holders after job loss
"This is the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget to undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse," said Collins, a member of Trump's Republican Party fighting a tight race for reelection in Maine.
"Any effort to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law."
The Supreme Court last year declined to block Trump from using the same tactic to withhold $4.9 billion in foreign aid Congress had approved, while litigation continued.

title: Japan eSports whizz kid  11  wins Games gold
description: He thrashes series of opponents up to three times his age
content:
He thrashes series of opponents up to three times his age
Japan's 11-year-old eSports prodigy Yuki Kurihara said he was "embarrassed" after winning Asian Games gold on Saturday by thrashing a series of opponents up to three times his age.
The bespectacled primary school student, believed to be the youngest competitor at the Games in Aichi-Nagoya, won the Puyo Puyo Champions final 10-2.
He is the youngest athlete in host country Japan's Asian Games history.
Puyo Puyo Champions is a puzzle game where players try to clear their screen of coloured blobs by lining them up and popping them.
Looking unruffled throughout, Kurihara waltzed into the gold-medal match with a string of dazzling displays.
He crushed Thailand's Tanarak Wongkitkun -- a relative veteran at 28 -- 10-1 in the semi-finals to ensure at least a silver medal.
He did not even smile after beating South Korea's 24-year-old Kang Dongshin in the final, having gone down 1-0 early on.
"To be completely honest, I felt a bit embarrassed, so I couldn't really show my expressions or change my face much," he explained.
Standing on the podium, he bowed slightly as he received his gold medal and gave a small wave to the arena.
"I'm really happy. The gold medal is really beautiful, shiny and heavy," he said.
"Also, the plush toy is super cute, and it's cool that it is gold-coloured too."
Kurihara started playing Puyo Puyo in his first year of primary school and soon started competing and winning in tournaments.
He obtained his pro licence in April this year and regularly beats adults.
"It's hard having to balance it with school and cram school, but it's really fun," he said ahead of the Games.
There are no publicly available records of youngest medallists in the history of the Asian Games, which were first contested in 1951.
But Indonesia's Bunga Nyimas won bronze in women's skateboarding aged 12 in Jakarta in 2018.
Cui Chenxi, 13, won Games gold when she triumphed in the women's street skateboarding event three years ago in Hangzhou.

title: Shajar Abbas advances to 200m semi finals
description: Pakistan sprinter clocks 21 23 seconds in heats to book his place in the next round
content:
Pakistan sprinter clocks 21.23 seconds in heats to book his place in the next round
Shajar Abbas qualified for the men's 200 metres semi-finals at the Asian Games in Nagoya on Saturday after clocking 21.23 seconds in the heats.
Abbas finished 17th overall but secured his place in the semi-finals, completing heat 2 at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium in third position.
Japan's Soshi Mizukubo won the heat in 20.72 seconds, followed by Chinese Taipei's Wu-yen-ming Ke in 20.84 and China's Huang Youwen in 20.90. Saudi Arabia's Abdullah Mohammed and Thailand's Puripol Boonson both ran 20.97.
Abbas crossed the line in 21.23, just 0.13 seconds behind Iran's Benyamin Yousefi, who finished 16th overall in 21.21. The Pakistani sprinter's time was also only 0.10 seconds behind Bahrain's Abbas Ali, who placed 10th.
The result ensured Abbas remained in contention for a place in the 200m final.
The opening round produced a tightly packed field, with several athletes separated by only fractions of a second. Abbas finished ahead of competitors from Oman, South Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Lebanon, Uzbekistan and other nations.
At the sharp end of the heat, Mizukubo's 20.72 seconds was the fastest time recorded in the race. The Games record remains 20.14 seconds, set by Qatar's Femi Ogunode at the 2014 Games in Incheon. China's Xie Zhenye holds the Asian record of 19.88 seconds, while Jamaica's Usain Bolt remains the world-record holder at 19.19.

title: Trump rejects Iranian proposal to open Hormuz and end fighting
description: US Iran war
content:
Iran awaits US move after WSJ report says Trump rejects peace plan
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end ‌fighting in the Middle East.
Iran raised the initiative at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators and that it could reopen the strategic waterway and put an end to hostilities in the region within seven days.
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," he said before leaving for Tennessee. "We're ​winning tremendously.
"They want to make a deal and I think that's fine, I like making a deal too. What they ⁠want to do is immediately open the Hormuz Strait ... because they have no money coming in, because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait," Trump said.
​The US has imposed an economic blockade on Iran to put pressure on Tehran to lift its blockade of Hormuz, which has drastically reduced shipping through the strait, ​even though Trump again asserted that the US had control of the waterway.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected the Iranian proposal, citing unnamed US officials.
It said Trump was privately sceptical that Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November US midterm elections to Congress.
A ​US official had said earlier that discussions with Iran through mediators were "positive and constructive".
Iran’s Pezeshkian calls for Houthi-Saudi dialogue
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera that Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia "must resolve their differences through dialogue" and that Iran "can help resolve the dispute."
"What is happening in Yemen is not linked to Iran", he said, adding that Iran stood "in solidarity with everyone who is subjected to injustice."
He emphasised that Iran "will not be warmongers" and that "a brother should not fight a brother."
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian tells Al Jazeera that Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia "must resolve their differences through dialogue" and that Iran "can help resolve the dispute." 🔴 LIVE updates: https://t.co/QM3FrbEw8v pic.twitter.com/65bPnnRE8Q
His statements came in an interview with Al Jazeera, where he also blamed the US for the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
"It was America that blocked our paths."
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian blames the US for the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, saying "it was America that blocked our paths." 🔴 LIVE updates: https://t.co/M1k1TlfnoS pic.twitter.com/q2f7EM4zdH
"Closing the Strait of Hormuz is a natural response when paths are blocked for Iran."
He added that those who “thought they could target the Iranian people with sanctions miscalculated”.
Pezeshkian said the US and Israel were seeking to “prevent Iran from relying on itself”, but Iran would invest in its people, adding that the US and Israel “dragged” regional countries into war, thinking that the Iranian regime “would fall within days”.
Supreme leader backs new plan to reopen Hormuz: Pezeshkian
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran’s new plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz was coordinated with Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, state media reported, quoting an interview with US media.
Pezeshkian also told broadcaster CBS that the Islamic Republic would fulfil its obligations if the United States agreed to the proposal, according to excerpts released by state news agency IRNA .
Iran awaits US move after WSJ report says Trump rejects peace plan
Iran on Saturday awaited an official US response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting in the wider Middle East war after the Wall Street Journal ​reported that US President Donald Trump had rejected the deal.
Iran raised the diplomatic initiative at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, saying it had been ‌transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators and could reopen the strategic waterway and put an end to hostilities in the region within seven days.
The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the strait, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through one of the world's most critical shipping lanes and taken a toll on the global economy.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday the deal ​would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.
Read: UN Security Council condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
"If there is seriousness on the US side to come to a deal and reopen ​the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," Araghchi said.
If the US were to agree, the warring parties could start wider talks "on mutually agreed subjects," ⁠Araghchi said.
That could potentially include discussions of Iran's nuclear program. Trump has vowed that Tehran will never acquire a nuclear bomb, while a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran will show no ​flexibility over its nuclear program even if the United States accepts its peace deal.
Iran would grant no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the ​country, the official said.
Even so, Iran had put forward a plan that would halt hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon. The plan in turn would require the United States to lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds, and waive its oil sanctions, Araghchi said.
A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, had previously called discussions through mediators "positive and constructive."
But Trump was privately sceptical that Iran would meet his demands, the Journal report said, ​and he told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely.
Reuters could not immediately confirm the Journal report.
Iran will continue punishing US until its seven demands are met: IRGC
Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said Iran will continue punishing the United States until its seven conditions are met, Press TV reported.
IRGC: Iran will continue punishing US until Tehran’s conditions are met https://t.co/azvuGRhFHB
The IRGC spokesman described Iran as the victor of the war, saying the country was converting that victory into “permanent strategic deterrence,” apparently pointing to Iran’s closing the strategic Strait of Hormuz in retaliation and refusing to reopen the chokepoint.
Mohebbi identified freedom of navigation through the strait as one of the US’s stated objectives, arguing that Washington had failed to achieve that objective during the aggression.
“Despite having the world’s largest navy, the United States was unable to keep the Strait of Hormuz open even for a few hours,” he said.
Bahrain rejects permit, fee system for Strait of Hormuz passage
Bahrain rejected any permit or fee system for passage through the Strait of Hormuz, saying transit through the international waterway cannot be suspended or subjected to unilateral conditions, Anadolu reports.
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed to end the war, ​which began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks.
Since then, the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran's conventional forces and damaging Iran's already ailing economy.
Iran and its allies ‌have retaliated by ⁠extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran, which controls the strait along with Oman, has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market. All the while, Iranian-backed Hezbollah has been engaged with Israeli forces in Lebanon.
Araghchi briefed his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan on the understanding between Iran and Oman regarding safe shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's foreign ministry said early Saturday.
Read more: Tehran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
The war's widening toll ​has also united Saudi Arabia's allies to shore up ​the kingdom's defences.
The Saudi-backed, internationally recognised Yemeni ⁠government has come under assault from Houthi fighters, with Houthi missiles striking inside the kingdom.
Yemen's Saudi-led coalition said early Saturday it intercepted two drones launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital Riyadh in addition to intercepting a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Khamis Mushait.
The Houthis, ​who control the most populous parts of Yemen and much of the north, have launched attacks against Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade ​against Riyadh in July, ⁠with strikes targeting Saudi vessels in the Red Sea.
The attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, adding to pressures on global oil supplies caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran and putting at risk the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains largely blocked.
Defence officials of Turkey and Pakistan, both partners in a joint defence pact with Saudi Arabia, met ⁠in Riyadh ​on Friday to review the security situation and discuss intelligence cooperation, military coordination, and integrating forces, the Saudi defence ministry ​said in a statement.
The statement came a day after Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers met within the framework of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement .
Also read: FM Dar reviews Makkah pact implementation with Saudi, Turkish counterparts
The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the United Nations children's agency said on ​Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children.
Pezeshkian says Iran wants peace, 'distrust' of US remains
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Friday that Tehran remains open to resolving the dispute with Washington, but stressed that trust must first be rebuilt, as he arrived in New York for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
In an interview with CBS News , Pezeshkian said the two sides need to "abide by what we have written down," and that the US "needs to show that it does not intend to overthrow our government or our administration."
Also read: Iran seeks deal with US, not war: Pezeshkian
Asking Americans to consider Iran's perspective, he said: "Put yourself in our position. Imagine someone came and martyred your supreme leader. And then, not abide by everything you had agreed upon. What would be your reaction? It's not something that can be resolved that simply."
He questioned whether Washington was genuinely seeking a settlement. "America's intention is to overthrow our administration," he said, noting that "Israel says it in their own speech; what they're doing is neutralising the government, not negotiating."
Pezeshkian asked: "Do you think the United States of America is genuinely interested in solving problems with us? Why, then, does it bomb us in the middle of negotiations? Why does it come and kill our scientists, officials and people?"
"As long as they don't cease doing what they're imposing on us every day, it's difficult to trust them," he said, citing daily sanctions, threats and strikes. He argued that Washington does "not honour what they have put in writing," asking: "So if they engage in talks, will they actually follow through?"
The Iranian president still voiced hope for peace to be "established in the region," calling on the US to halt support for Israel, which he indicated "is carrying out what we consider genocide," and to "act on the basis of justice and fairness" rather than displacing "people from their homes," killing "innocent people," or targeting "children, hospitals, and scientists."
Pezeshkian also said that if the US accepts Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear negotiations, Iran would adhere to its commitments and allow UN nuclear inspectors to enter the country, according to ISNA .

Yemeni forces strike Houthi positions, supply lines in Taiz
Yemeni government forces said on Friday they struck Houthi positions and supply lines in the southwestern province of Taiz.
Military spokesman Majid Abdullah al-Nazili published footage on US social media platform X that he said showed strikes on Houthi fighters and supply routes in Dhubab and other parts of Taiz.
Dhubab is a coastal town in the Bab el-Mandeb district overlooking the Red Sea near the northern entrance to the strategic strait.
Al-Nazili did not provide details on casualties or damage.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree separately claimed Saudi warplanes carried out 14 airstrikes and a missile attack in the previous 24 hours in the Taiz, Amran, Marib and Saada provinces.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthi group seized the national capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014. That prompted a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
Renewed fighting began in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh.
Houthis recently claimed advances along the Red Sea Coast and Bab el-Mandab Strait, and have also targeted the oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia.
Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
Iran will show no ​flexibility over its nuclear program even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen ‌the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until “all of Iran’s conditions ​are met” by the United States.
Under Iran’s proposal, Tehran has offered to reopen the strategically vital Strait of ​Hormuz. Within seven days, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon; the United ⁠States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, Iran's ​Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Thursday.
The proposal follows a sharp escalation in Middle East tensions after seven months ​of war between Iran and the United States, with Iran-backed Houthi militias in Yemen launching missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade ​that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route ​now blocked by Tehran.
In a meeting with journalists on Thursday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Pezeshkian said ⁠he hoped to reach a deal with Washington to end hostilities before the US midterm elections on November 3.
Tehran said it would be prepared to engage in detailed negotiations over its nuclear program only after its conditions are met by the US.
But the official said Iran would give no concessions over its rights, including ​enriching uranium or shipping its ​highly enriched uranium out ⁠of the country, one of the main US demands.
Israel, the United States and other Western states have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, including pointing to its ​move to enrich uranium to 60%, far higher than needed for civilian uses and ​closer to ⁠the 90% needed for a weapon. Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons.
The International Atomic Energy Agency estimates that Iran had 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% when Israel and the US attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. How much ⁠of ​that has survived is unclear.
Iranian authorities have said that Iran could agree ​to dilute its most highly enriched uranium.
In May, Reuters reported that Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a directive that the country's ​HEU should not be sent abroad, according to two senior Iranian sources.

title: 33 terrorists killed in Balochistan since Sept 21
description: 33 terrorists killed in Balochistan since Sept 21
content:
Operation took place based on information regarding the movement of terrorists
Security forces on Friday eliminated 12 terrorists during two separate intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in restive Balochistan.
According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), security forces conducted an operation in Nushki district based on an intelligence report about the presence of terrorists.
"During the operation, own troops effectively engaged the terrorist hideout and after an intense exchange of fire, sent 11 terrorists to hell," the ISPR stated.
According to sources, forces also conducted an operation at the Mazan Band Range of Kech district on Friday, killing a terrorist as he attempted to cross into Iran.
The operation took place based on information regarding the movement of terrorists. Due to the successful operation, terrorists belonging to Fitna al-Hindustan failed to flee to Iran, security sources said. Fitna al-Hindustan is a term used to refer to separatist groups.
On Thursday, security forces busted some terrorist hideouts and, after an intense fire exchange, killed five terrorists of Indian-sponsored Fitna al-Khwarij, a term used to refer to outlawed Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and its affiliates.
The forces also recovered weapons, ammunition and explosives from the hideouts. "Clearance operations will continue until complete neutralisation of the threat from the area," it added.
According to the ISPR, during a "comprehensive counter terrorism operation" against "Indian backed Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan that started on September 21, the security forces have so far killed 33 terrorists.
"Relentless counter terrorism campaign under vision "Azm-e-Istehkam" will continue at full pace to wipe out menace of foreign sponsored and supported terrorism from the country," the ISPR added.
Both the president and the prime minister paid tribute to the security force on successful operations.
In his message, President Asif Ali Zardari commended the bravery and professional competence of the security forces for eliminating more Indian-backed Khawarij during Operation Shaban.
"Elimination of 33 Indian-backed Khawarij and terrorists in Balochistan is a commendable achievement by the security forces," he said adding, "Recovery of weapons, ammunition, and explosives from terrorists' hideouts is proof of the security forces' effective operations."
In a statement issued by the PM Office, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also lauded the professional capabilities of the security forces. "The operations of the security forces and law enforcement agencies will continue with full force until the complete elimination of terrorism," he said.
He said the complete eradication of foreign-sponsored terrorism, including Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan, was the government's top priority.

title: Pakistan  KSA  Turkiye military chiefs slam attack on Makkah
description: Pakistan  KSA  Turkiye military chiefs slam attack on Makkah
content:
High-level meeting reviews threats being faced by Saudi Arabia
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on Friday held an urgent meeting of their top military commanders in Riyadh under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA), marking the first exclusive high-level military coordination between the three countries since the trilateral defence pact was signed last month.
Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, Turkish Chief of General Staff Gen Selcuk Bayraktaroglu and Saudi Chief of General Staff Gen Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili attended the meeting in the Saudi capital, according to a statement issued by the military's media wing.
The chiefs of defense forces and chiefs of general staff reviewed the security situation and the threats facing the kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
They strongly resented the attacks targeting the holy city of Makkah and civilian and economic infrastructure, the Inter-Services Public Relations said.
They appreciated the vigilance and professionalism of the Saudi armed forces for ensuring safety of the people and security of the kingdom, it added.
The participants also discussed ways to further advance cooperation among the armed forces of the three countries and to enhance intelligence sharing, military coordination, and capability integration, thereby strengthening deterrence and collective defense.
The participants commended the longstanding relations and mutual trust that bind the people and the armed forces of the three countries. They noted that their meeting in Riyadh reflects the strength of their defense partnership and their shared determination to immediately translate the commitments of the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement into effective military cooperation.
The participants strongly affirmed their commitment to collective defense thereby demonstrating the resolve of the three countries in defending the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
The meeting came hours after the foreign ministers of the three countries agreed in New York to convene their military chiefs amid intensified attacks targeting Saudi Arabia. The development effectively takes the Makkah agreement from the political and institutionalisation phase into military-level consultations.
The military commanders' meeting assumes particular significance because the MJDA contains a collective-defence provision under which an attack against any one of the three parties would be considered an attack against all.
The immediate backdrop is the escalation of attacks from Houthis targeting Saudi territory and critical infrastructure. Türkiye had already publicly expressed readiness to help meet Saudi Arabia's military requirements under the defence agreement, while Pakistan has reiterated its commitment to Saudi Arabia's defence.
The exact outcome of Friday's meeting, including whether the three sides agreed on any specific military assistance, deployments or operational arrangements, was not immediately disclosed.
The meeting follows a decision by the foreign ministers in New York to prepare for urgent military consultations. Pakistan's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan had reviewed progress on institutionalising the agreement and condemned attacks targeting Makkah as well as Saudi civilian and economic facilities.
The ministers also reaffirmed Saudi Arabia's right to take measures it considers necessary for its defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence in the event of an armed attack.
The Riyadh meeting therefore provides the first opportunity for the military leadership of the three countries to discuss how the collective-defence commitment could be translated into practical cooperation.
The three countries have been steadily building the institutional architecture of the alliance since the agreement was signed in Makkah on August 7 by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman.
At the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee in Istanbul on August 31, the three sides agreed to establish a permanent secretariat in Riyadh and discussed military interoperability, defence capabilities, defence-industry cooperation, joint production and research, as well as counterterrorism coordination.
Pakistan subsequently appointed retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood as the first secretary general of the Makkah Defence Alliance, formally setting the process of establishing the Riyadh-based secretariat in motion.
The three countries have also stressed that the alliance is defensive in nature and is not directed against any particular state. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the alliance was founded on respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity and non-interference and remained open to other countries that shared those principles.
For Pakistan and Turkiye, however, the current crisis presents a more immediate test of the agreement's collective-defence clause. Both countries have simultaneously sought to support Saudi Arabia's security while advocating de-escalation and diplomatic efforts to resolve the wider regional conflicts.
The Riyadh meeting is consequently the first concrete military-level test of how the Makkah pact will operate when one of its members faces sustained attacks.

title: UNSC condemns Houthi attacks
description: UNSC condemns Houthi attacks
content:
The UN Security Council on Friday condemned escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, in a rare show of unity from the world body's top security forum as the Iran-aligned Yemeni group stepped up attacks amid the wider Middle East war.
"The members of the Security Council condemned, in the strongest terms, continued Houthi attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including attacks impacting civilian and energy infrastructure, which have resulted in the injury of civilians, including women and children," said the council's rotating president, French UN envoy Jerome Bonnafont, delivering a joint statement.
The Houthis have intensified attacks on the Saudi-backed government in Yemen and launched strikes into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world's largest crude exporter as the wider regional war enters its eighth month.
Saudi Arabia intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles on Thursday after issuing warnings for several regions, including Makkah. The Houthis said they had fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets, while Saudi authorities said they had intercepted six ballistic missiles.
The escalation comes as fighting in Yemen between government forces and Iran-backed militia fighters intensifies and ceasefire efforts remain stalled. However, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian rejected claims that the Houthis take orders from Tehran, saying the group was responsible for its own actions.
"The Houthis are responsible for their own actions. They don't take directions from us," Pezeshkian said, according to a broadcaster's translation. "We have contacts with them. There is no systematic relationship."
The Houthis have also imposed a naval blockade affecting Saudi tankers and territory and seized parts of Yemen's Red Sea coast, a vital route for Saudi oil exports. Their actions have disrupted shipping through the Red Sea, while Iran has restricted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The war, triggered by US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, has killed thousands and significantly squeezed Saudi oil exports. Rashid al-Alimi, Yemen's President, called on Yemenis to mobilise and join the armed forces while offering amnesty to Houthi fighters who abandon the group.

title: US Republicans seek voter relief before midterm elections
description: US Republicans seek voter relief before midterm elections
content:
Senate plans data centre vote amid concerns over Trump's falling support
US Senate Republicans are seeking to improve their election prospects by voting on legislation aimed at protecting consumers from rising electricity bills linked to data centres, hoping to win over voters struggling with inflation and higher energy costs.
Republicans had the option of leaving Washington on Thursday and staying away until after the November 3 midterm elections. Instead, they chose to return next week to take up the Ratepayer Protection Act at the urging of
Senator Jon Husted, who is trailing Democratic candidate and former Senator Sherrod Brown in Ohio, a state President Donald Trump won by more than 11 points in 2024.
Republicans believe supporting the bill will demonstrate their commitment to voters focused on the cost-of-living crisis. Polls have shown broad opposition to data centres, despite Trump's support for their development.
The planned vote is the latest sign of Republican anxiety over Trump's record-low approval rating less than six weeks before Election Day. The concerns have prompted some Republican candidates to distance themselves from Trump on issues affecting their states.
Senate candidates Mike Rogers of Michigan and Ashley Hinson of Iowa have called for a quick end to the Iran war. Other Republicans, including Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, have expressed concern over immigration enforcement operations in their states, one of Trump's signature initiatives.
Trump's approval ratings have also fallen among Republicans. A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed support for the president among Republicans falling
nine points to 73% in one week. Although Trump is not on the November ballot, he remains central to the campaign.
The Ratepayer Protection Act would require state utility regulators to consider whether large electricity users, including data centres, should bear the additional costs of power infrastructure built to serve them.

title: Turkiye says Makkah pact can be expanded
description: Turkiye says Makkah pact can be expanded
content:
Parliament speaker says Iran could join; FM Fidan rejects Yemen crisis as immediate test
The defence pact between Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan could develop into a broader agreement "for the Muslim world" that includes Iran, Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus said on Friday, adding that it is expected to be submitted for ratification from next month.
The regional powers signed the "Makkah Joint Defence Agreement" in August, weeks before Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis launched attacks against Saudi Arabia in reaction to the wider Iran war. Similar to NATO's Article 5, the pact stipulates that an attack on one ally constitutes an attack on all.
As the three sides holding meetings to lay out the parameters of the accord and assess Riyadh's needs, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has hit back at critics of the pact, saying it was unfair to judge the agreement over the escalation in the decade-long crisis between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
Kurtulmus told reporters in Ankara that the meetings held as part of the agreement were preparatory meetings. "For international agreements to come into effect, parliamentary approval is needed," he said. "I expect this issue to come on the parliament's agenda in the coming period [next month]," he added.
Asked whether the pact was directed against Iran, Kurtulmus repeated Turkiye's position that the agreement did not target any specific country but was primarily aimed at ensuring the security of states in the region amid conflicts and Israel's "hostile policies".
He added that Tehran could potentially join the pact. "We never see the Makkah Agreement as a pact against Iran, it must not be that way. In fact, we hope the Makkah Agreement can turn into a broader agreement for the Muslim world. Iran can join this agreement too; we hope it will become much stronger with the participation of other regional countries," he said.
Meanwhile, speaking at a seminar in New York, Foreign Minister Fidan compared criticism of the defence pact with NATO's record of collective defence, saying NATO's Article 5 – which provides for collective defence – had been invoked only once in its history.
Addressing former US ambassador James Jeffrey, who was also present at the seminar, Fidan asked him when he had joined the army. Jeffrey replied that it was almost 50 years ago. Fidan then asked how many times Jeffrey had witnessed the activation of Article 5 of the NATO Charter. "Only once," Jeffrey replied.
Fidan then said that despite Article 5 being invoked only once during NATO's history, no one described the alliance as a "paper tiger". He questioned why the newly-established defence alliance should immediately be expected to prove its effectiveness by resolving the crisis in Yemen, which continues for nearly 10 years.
"When it comes to a new defence alliance, they point to a 10-year-old crisis and say: Look, it's not working. We've only just started," Fidan said. He emphasised that the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia was aimed at contributing to peace and stability in the region.
The discussion on Makkah agreement focused on its ability to respond to regional challenges. Fidan rejected "premature expectations from the new alliance", arguing that "an alliance that had only just been established should not be judged against a crisis that had persisted for years".

content:
Russia announced on Friday final results of its tightly controlled
saying President Vladimir Putin's party reinforced its supermajority and around a 10th of new MPs would be Ukraine war veterans.
Russia's first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its Ukraine war in 2022 was held between September 18 and 20, with the Kremlin also organising voting in occupied Ukraine. It was conducted without meaningful opposition.
Russia's electoral head, Ella Pamfilova, said that with all the votes counted, the president's United Russia party had won 349 of the 450 seats in the Dumathe lower house of parliament. This beats its previous record of 343 seats and hands it an even larger supermajority.

title: Trump  Xi wrap up summit with tea and archives tour

content:
Leaders tout 'strategic stability' but summit yields few major breakthroughs
US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping wrapped up a three-day summit on Friday with tea at the White House and a tour of the National Archives, showcasing personal diplomacy while producing few major breakthroughs in their strained economic relationship.
The two leaders praised their talks, with Trump saying the summit between the world's two largest economies had produced "great strides" and expressing confidence that US farmers would benefit. Xi described the bilateral relationship as a constructive one based on "strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity".
Trump said he and Xi would meet twice more this year, at the APEC summit in China in November and the G20 summit in Miami in December. Xi also invited Trump and First Lady Melania Trump to visit China.
The summit was marked by elaborate ceremony, including a state dinner, flyovers and tours, but concrete agreements remained limited. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said details of the trade understandings reached by the two sides would be released on Monday.
Greer said the countries had agreed to exempt some key goods from trade disputes, including US agricultural products and medical devices exported to China, as well as consumer and non-sensitive goods imported from China.

title: Two washed away in Bisham floods
description: Two washed away in Bisham floods
content:
Two children were swept away by the flash flood, while a woman was injured
Torrential rain and lightning triggered a sudden flash flood in Shangla's Bisham tehsil on Friday, sweeping away two children and injuring a woman, while residential houses, the Bisham police station, several other buildings and property suffered extensive damage, according to local sources.
The flash flood also affected dozens of vehicles. It damaged electricity poles and power lines, while the Karakoram Highway was hit by floodwaters at several points in Bisham and remained completely closed to traffic until late at night. The Bisham-Alpuri Road was also affected by landslides at several locations.
The sudden deluge occurred after heavy rain caused a local stream in Bisham to swell rapidly, sending a powerful torrent of water, mud and stones through the area.
Two children were swept away by the flash flood, while a woman was injured and shifted to hospital for medical treatment.
The torrent caused severe damage to several properties along its path, including the Bisham police station, residential houses and other buildings. Several vehicles were also caught in the floodwater and debris and were damaged.
Floodwater and debris inundated roads, severely disrupting traffic and causing considerable difficulties for residents. The heavy rain and flash flood also badly affected Bisham's electricity system. Several electricity poles collapsed, and power lines were damaged, disrupting electricity supply in various areas.
Meanwhile, the Karakoram Highway was also affected at several points in Bisham by flash floods, mud and rocks. The highway remained completely closed to traffic until late at night, with long queues of vehicles forming on both sides.

title: LHC seeks reports on Aleema s detention
description: LHC seeks reports on Aleema s detention
content:
The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Friday sought reports from relevant authorities on a petition challenging the detention of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder Imran Khan's sister Aleema Khan and her driver after provincial law officers told the court that the home secretary had fixed September 28 for a review hearing on the detention.
Aleema Khan was detained for 30 days under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) law through an order issued by the Lahore administration. The petition sought judicial intervention against the detention order, while the government placed on record that the home secretary would hear the matter on September 28.
LHC Justice Abher Gul Khan heard the petition filed by Aleema's son Shahraiz, challenging the detention of his mother and her driver.
At the outset of the hearing, Punjab law officers placed before the court a letter stating that the home secretary had fixed Monday, September 28, for a review hearing on Aleema's detention order. The law officer asked the court to dispose of the petition, saying the competent authority would review the matter on that date.
The petitioner's counsel, Rana Mudassar Umar, opposed the request, arguing that the government was causing a procedural delay and that the detention order should be examined independently by the court.
He argued that the order appeared to have been issued on the basis of vague reports and after the alleged arrest, describing it as an "ante-dated" order. The counsel therefore asked the court to immediately suspend the detention order instead of waiting for the administrative review scheduled for September 28.
The court declined to suspend the order at this stage and instead sought reports from the Punjab home secretary, Lahore deputy commissioner (DC) and Superintendent of Jail.
Shortly afterwards, Umar filed the application and asked the court to take it up for hearing on the same day.

title: Defence pact binds Pakistan  Saudi Arabia

content:
Khawaja Asif says Houthi issue raised with Iran
AAMIR ILYAS RANA Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif has said that aggression against either Pakistan or Saudi Arabia would be treated as aggression against both under their defence agreement, while revealing that Islamabad has also discussed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia with Iran.
In an exclusive interview with The Express Tribune in New York, Asif said that responding to attacks by the Houthi militia on Saudi Arabia was the responsibility of all three countries covered by the Makkah Defence Alliance.
"The Makkah defence agreement binds Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in such a way that in the event of any aggression against Saudi Arabia, standing by it becomes an important responsibility for Pakistan," the minister said.
He added that the defence agreement would further strengthen the longstanding relationship between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, which extended beyond defence cooperation to encompass religious, historical and fraternal ties.
Asif revealed that Pakistan had raised the issue of non-state actors operating in the region during a meeting with the Iranian president, stressing that such groups needed to be rendered ineffective because their activities were undermining regional peace efforts. "The Iranian leadership has been told that non-state actors should not carry out operations in any country," he added.
He said the Iranian president had responded positively and agreed that tensions and instability in the region would ultimately harm the people of all sides. He added that Iranian leaders had indicated that they would engage with the Houthis, although practical progress would depend on subsequent steps.
Asked about the need to activate the Makkah agreement in practical terms, Asif said the pact represented a strong bond between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. "Besides the religious ties, the two countries now have a defence agreement under which Pakistan will stand by Saudi Arabia in the event of aggression," he said.
On the country's domestic political situation, Khawaja Asif said the government had tried to pursue negotiations with the PTI and had also offered talks, but the opposition party had chosen the path of protest and confrontation.
"Even a PTI leader spoke about turning Islamabad into 'Somnath'," he said. "The government does not want political tensions at a time when the country is going through a phase of economic recovery," the minister stated, warning that political tensions and protest activities could affect the recovery process.
Speaking about the law and order situation in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), the minister criticised the provincial government, saying federal institutions were playing their role in the fight against terrorism, but the basic responsibility for maintaining law and order rested with the provincial government.
"If the provincial government effectively fulfilled its constitutional responsibilities, it could help control terrorism in the province," Asif said.
However, he alleged that the K-P government wanted to take powers away from the police. Asif said that through amendments to laws, the provincial government wanted the police force to remain under its control, which would make the maintenance of law and order difficult.

title: UK team reviews PIA safety systems
description: UK team reviews PIA safety systems
content:
Examines airline and CAA measures for Pakistan-UK flights
A team from the UK Civil Aviation Authority (UK CAA) visited Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) headquarters and various Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) departments to review safety arrangements for direct flights from Pakistan to the United Kingdom.
According to sources, the UK CAA team examined PIA's Safety Management System (SMS) and other relevant departments. PIA officials, led by Chief Executive Officer Amir Hayat, briefed the British delegation on the airline's safety arrangements and related matters.
The UK CAA officials also questioned PIA authorities on various aspects of the safety of flights and aircraft operating between Pakistan and the UK.
Sources said the UK CAA team expressed satisfaction with PIA's Safety Management System and measures taken in accordance with international standards, and appreciated the airline's safety management arrangements.
According to sources, PIA's measures to comply with international safety standards had contributed to the restoration of permission for direct flights from Pakistan to the UK.
CAA officials accompanied the UK delegation during the visit. After visiting the PIA headquarters, the team also reviewed relevant CAA departments, including licensing, airworthiness and flight standards.
Sources said the UK team also examined the CAA's Safety Management System.
The British team arrived in Karachi a few days earlier and conducted a detailed review of safety arrangements concerning flights operating from Pakistan to the UK.
On July 16, 2025, Britain lifted a five-year ban on Pakistani airlines, allowing them to apply to resume flights to and from the UK. PIA was barred from flying to the UK in June 2020, a month after one of its aircraft plunged into a Karachi neighbourhood, killing 97 people.
The disaster was attributed to human error by the pilots and air traffic control, followed by allegations that nearly a third of its pilots' licences were fake or dubious. Pakistan launched an investigation to examine these claims.
Last year, the UK Air Safety Committee decided to lift the ban following aviation safety improvements in Pakistan. Subsequently, the airline resumed flights to the UK, with flight operations to Manchester resuming in the first phase.
PIA resumed its London flight operations on March 29 after a six-year gap, restoring a long-standing route between Pakistan and the UK.

title: Pakistan selected for COP31 initiative
description: Pakistan selected for COP31 initiative
content:
Pilot countries to develop pathways for climate finance
Pakistan has been selected among the first five pilot countries for a new COP31 initiative aimed at helping developing countries translate their climate commitments into finance-ready projects, a move that could support Islamabad's efforts to mobilize international financing for its climate and development priorities.
The COP31 presidency announced Ethiopia, Fiji, Indonesia, Pakistan and Uzbekistan as the initial pilot countries for its Climate Implementation Bridge (BRIDGE) initiative at New York Climate Week, as part of an implementation-focused agenda ahead of the UN climate summit to be held in Antalya, Türkiye, in November.
The initiative, being delivered in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), seeks to bridge the gap between countries' climate ambitions and the financing required to implement them by developing bankable project pipelines and strengthening national capacity.
For Pakistan, which faces significant climate-related risks including floods, droughts, heatwaves and water stress, the initiative provides a platform to better connect its climate and development priorities with international financing opportunities.
The COP31 Presidency said the pilot countries would develop country-led pathways linking climate finance with investment-ready projects and national development targets. Experience from the initial group would subsequently inform the expansion of the initiative to other participating countries, particularly developing countries, Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries.
The BRIDGE initiative will also seek to identify implementation bottlenecks, strengthen countries' investment readiness and improve access to the existing international climate support system.
In a related development, the COP31 Presidency launched the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility in partnership with ILBANK, UN-Habitat and the World Bank.
