title: Solar system manufacturing urged
description: Solar system manufacturing urged
content:
Governor says development of industry will create millions of jobs, earn forex
Punjab Governor Sardar Saleem Haider Khan has called for establishing a policy framework to promote the domestic manufacturing of solar systems, saying Pakistan can create millions of jobs, generate clean and affordable energy and earn foreign exchange by developing a local solar industry.
"It is unfortunate that solar system manufacturing is not being done due to the lack of a government policy," the governor said while addressing the 3rd International Solar Power Conclave & Solar Technology Excellence Awards 2026, organised by the Energy Update in collaboration with the Pakistan Solar Association (PSA), the Renewable Energy Association of Pakistan and the Pakistan Alternative Energy Association on Friday.
He said the high cost of electricity had made solar energy increasingly important for ordinary Pakistanis, describing sunlight as "Allah's gift" that should be utilised to reduce the burden of electricity bills while also protecting the environment.
"If we are able to set up a solar manufacturing industry, it will create millions of jobs and also produce clean, green energy, which is cheaper for consumers' pockets and better for the environment," he said.
The governor urged the solar business community to take the initiative and begin manufacturing solar systems locally instead of waiting indefinitely for a government policy. He pointed out that the industry had already brought solar technology to Pakistan without substantial state support and said a similar initiative could now help establish a domestic manufacturing base.
With local production, he said, Pakistan would not only meet its own growing demand but could also export solar systems and earn much-needed foreign exchange. He stressed that it was encouraging to see the rapid spread of solar panels across the country, observing that "almost 90% of roofs" in cities appeared to be covered with solar panels.
Highlighting the government's efforts to expand access to solar energy, the governor said the Sindh government had distributed hundreds of thousands of solar panels free of cost among livestock farmers and flood-stricken communities. "We have been bestowed with abundance of sunlight, which must be used to serve the interests of the masses," he remarked.
Referring to recent disruptions to the energy supply chain caused by the war in the region, the governor said electricity load-shedding had increased when LNG containers could not arrive. However, the growing availability of solar energy could eventually make expensive grid electricity less relevant for domestic consumers.
Speaking on the occasion, Punjab Minister for Energy Faisal Ayub said Pakistan had experienced its worst electricity load-shedding crisis beginning in 2009-10, which was overcome during the PML-N government's 2013-18 tenure. He recalled that in Punjab, the then chief minister Shehbaz Sharif had installed power plants to address electricity shortage, but said the country was now facing a different challenge - the high cost of electricity.
"Although it is a federal subject, we will provide support to the solar energy sector to overcome this challenge of expensive electricity," Ayub said. He observed that whether or not governments promoted solar energy, consumers and the industry would eventually move towards it because of the economics of solar power. "The government, therefore, needs to align its policies with this transition."
The minister assured the solar sector of the Punjab government's full support, saying the provincial government would engage the federal energy minister and bring PSA representatives on board to devise a policy to facilitate the expansion of solar energy in Pakistan.
"We will welcome suggestions from energy experts to promote this sector," he said, warning that failure to support the solar sector at this stage could damage Pakistan's interests. He noted that a friendly policy for the solar industry could generate prosperity not only for businesses associated with renewable energy but for the country as a whole.
PSA President Adil Mahmood said solar energy was already contributing up to 40,000 megawatts to Pakistan's energy supply and argued that without this contribution the country would otherwise be experiencing five to seven hours of load-shedding every day.
He said the government was charging four paisa per unit, adding that it translated into a cost of around Rs1.5 million per MW per month, which he said needed to be removed.
Mahmood pointed out that the solar market had expanded rapidly when there was no tax on solar panels, but subsequent measures created hurdles in the way of the industry. He also mentioned that net metering had now been abolished, describing such developments as impediments to further promotion of solar energy.
He urged the government to abolish duties and sales tax on batteries and proposed the establishment of local lithium battery manufacturing plants, which could eventually produce batteries for export as well.

The price of 10-gram gold increased by Rs4,029 to Rs388,404. On Thursday, gold had fallen by Rs5,600 per tola to Rs448,336 after declining for five consecutive sessions. Silver prices also moved higher on Friday, gaining Rs126 to reach Rs6,963 per tola.
The increase in domestic gold prices came despite continued pressure on international bullion markets. Spot gold was trading around $4,275 per ounce on Friday and remained on track for a weekly decline as investors assessed persistent inflationary concerns, rising US Treasury yields and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve monetary policy.
Reuters reported that gold was down about 2% to 2.4% for the week, while the stronger dollar also weighed on demand for the dollar-priced metal. Higher interest rates and bond yields generally reduce the appeal of non-yielding assets such as gold, while making interest-bearing investments more attractive.
Recent comments from Federal Reserve policymakers have strengthened expectations that US rates could remain elevated for longer as policymakers seek to contain persistent inflation.
Adnan Agar, Director at Interactive Commodities, said gold remained under pressure and was trading around the $4,270-$4,275 level, after touching the low of about $4,240.
He identified the $4,200-$4,250 area as a strong support zone, saying gold had bounced from these levels but remained in a vulnerable position. According to him, the recent recovery was not strong enough to remove downside risks, with the metal having recently reached a high of around $4,330.
Agar said rising US Treasury yields remained a major concern for gold prices. He expected gold could decline towards $4,000-$4,100 if selling pressure intensified, although strong physical demand could provide support around those levels.
Looking further ahead, Agar expected gold to regain momentum after any correction, potentially moving towards $5,000-$5,500 over the next three to six months. This outlook represents his market assessment and is subject to changes in interest rates, yields, currency movements, geopolitical developments and physical demand.
Internationally, silver, platinum and palladium were also headed for weekly declines, reflecting a broader weakness across precious metals.
Meanwhile, the Pakistani rupee extended its marginal gains against the US dollar in the inter-bank market, closing at 277.16, up Rs0.01 from Thursday's settlement at 277.17.
Internationally, the US dollar was headed for its first back-to-back weekly gains in more than three months, supported by rising US Treasury yields and expectations of further Federal Reserve rate hikes.

title: SBP launches remittance reward scheme
description: SBP launches remittance reward scheme
content:
Market-based drive offers Rs16b annual prizes to remitters
State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) Governor Jameel Ahmad on Friday inaugurated the Pasban Remittance Reward Scheme, offering Rs16 billion in annual cash prizes to encourage overseas Pakistanis to send remittances through formal banking channels.
Launched under the auspices of the Pakistan Banks Association (PBA), the scheme is fully funded by the banking industry and will not impose any burden on the national exchequer.
Speaking at the launch ceremony, Ahmad said the initiative had been developed with the government and banking industry as a sustainable, market-oriented mechanism to attract workers' remittances through formal channels. He said remittances were vital for millions of Pakistani families, supporting household spending, education, healthcare, investment and economic opportunities.
The governor highlighted the improvement in Pakistan's external position, noting that the SBP's foreign exchange reserves had risen from below $3 billion in February 2023 to $21.4 billion. He said the recent buildup in reserves had primarily been supported by foreign exchange purchases from the market rather than external borrowing.
Workers' remittances reached a record $41.6 billion in FY26, compared with $21.7 billion in FY19, nearly doubling over the period, he added.
Under the Pasban scheme, a beneficiary receiving remittances equivalent to at least $100 each month for three consecutive months in a quarter will qualify for digital entries. Higher remittance amounts will generate additional entries proportionate to the amount received.

title: PSX flat as oil keeps investors cautious
description: PSX flat as oil keeps investors cautious
content:
KSE-100 index rallies late, closes 266 points higher
Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) staged a late-session recovery on Friday, where the benchmark KSE-100 index gained around 265 points, although the market remained broadly range bound amid elevated crude oil prices and uncertainty about US-Iran negotiations.
At the close of trading, the KSE-100 index posted a modest gain of 266.28 points, or 0.16%, and settled at 170,765.22.
Arif Habib Limited (AHL) stated that the PSX saw a late rally on Friday that lifted the KSE-100 into positive territory, allowing it to close the week essentially flat. A total of 68 shares advanced while 32 declined, with HBL gaining 1.13%, UBL rising 0.28% and Bank Alfalah advancing 1.22%, which were the largest positive contributors to the index. On the downside, Meezan Bank fell 0.64%, Fauji Fertiliser dropped 0.25% and Hubco declined 0.31%, acting as the biggest drags.
PSO rose 0.94% after reporting FY26 earnings per share of Rs32.10, a 28% year-on-year decline attributed to lower sales volume stemming from higher inventory losses, elevated petroleum prices and reduced contribution from the LNG segment amid geopolitical tensions. The company declared a final dividend of Rs10 per share for the fourth quarter, bringing its full-year payout to 31%, as per AHL.
Political developments added to market caution as the PTI postponed its planned long march to Islamabad. Authorities had already deployed thousands of security personnel, blocked roads with shipping containers and banned public gatherings to prevent supporters of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan from approaching parliament to demand his release.
"Looking ahead, the KSE-100 remains in a state of flux for the coming week, with the bias still tilted to the downside until the index can demonstrate a clear move away from its July lows," said AHL.
The index closed at 170,765.2, up 266.3 points, or 0.16% on the day. Week-to-date, it was down 119.4 points, or 0.07%, month-to-date it had dived 6,210.5 points, or 3.51%, and calendar-year-to-date it was lower by 3,289.1 points, or 1.89%. Among individual stocks, notable gainers were PGLC, SNGP, NPL, HUMNL and LOTCHEM, while TGL, CNERGY, RMPL, PTC and BNWM featured among the leading decliners.
Topline Securities, in its review, noted that the market remained range bound during the session, with the index trading between the intra-day high of 0.39% and low of 0.36%, before settling at 170,765 points, up 0.16%. The lacklustre activity was attributed to investors' preference to remain on the sidelines amid elevated crude oil prices and a lack of meaningful progress in negotiations between the US and Iran, it said.
Overall trading volumes were recorded at 483 million shares compared with the previous session's tally of 760 million. The value of shares traded during the day was Rs19.3 billion.
Shares of 493 companies were traded. Of these, 219 stocks closed higher, 217 fell and 57 remained unchanged.
Cnergyico Pk was the volume leader with trading in 108 million shares, losing Rs0.29 to close at Rs13.18. It was followed by WorldCall Telecom with 29 million shares, gaining Rs0.02 to close at Rs1.02 and Pakistan Refinery with 28 million shares, gaining Rs0.97 to close at Rs93.11.
Foreign investors sold shares worth Rs32.4 million, the National Clearing Company reported.

title: Govt plans more gas tariff slabs
description: Govt plans more gas tariff slabs
content:
Examines proposal to widen protected net for consumers
The government is likely to introduce additional gas tariff slabs to provide cheaper gas to consumers by bringing more people under the protected category net.
The Cabinet Committee on Energy (CCOE) has directed the Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division) to examine the proposal of introducing a more rational categorisation of protected consumers in the gas sector.
During discussions in a recent meeting of the CCOE, chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, the Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division) revealed that the evaluation carried out by the World Bank as well as advisory firm KPMG for the accumulation of circular debt in the oil and gas sectors over the last five years highlighted a substantial addition to the debt between 2019 and 2023 primarily on account of no increase in consumer gas prices and diversion of RLNG to domestic consumers.
On a query, the meeting was informed that according to an agreed definition with the IMF and World Bank, the circular debt meant "net financial burdens on Sui gas companies due to policy and regulatory decisions". Also, Sui gas companies use a circular debt reporting tool developed by the World Bank to report the debt stock digitally while the components of the circular debt include tariff differentials and power companies' receivables.
It was highlighted that due to lower bill collections by SSGC and SNGPL in proportion to their supplies, coupled with power-sector issues, the gas-sector circular debt had consistently increased, which adversely impacted the financial capacity of state-owned exploration & production companies to invest in their core business, which may turn those profitable entities into loss-making concerns and ultimately put a burden on the national exchequer.
A list of the key factors contributing to the circular debt was shared with the CCOE, which included delayed revision in consumer gas prices (2013-22), the gap between Ogra-determined revenue requirements of Sui gas companies, low recoveries owing to the power sector, diversion of RLNG to the domestic sector in winters (2018-23), inadequate budgetary allocation for subsidies under tariff commitments, pending GST refunds with the FBR, litigation on consumer gas price notifications, demand reduction from high-yielding captive power plants and CNG stations, and the RLNG tariff actualisation effective from February 2025.
The Petroleum Division shared a trajectory curve of the circular debt, showing a very sharp rise from June 2019 to June 2023 and a flatter trend from June 2023 to June 2026. The forum was also briefed on the urgent need to resolve gas bill recovery issues of SSGC in Balochistan, requiring high-level engagements.
The division requested for the settlement of power-sector receivables against supplies of domestic gas, RLNG and oil; settlement of RLNG actualisation tariff of the power sector amounting to Rs42 billion; payment of Rs83 billion by the FBR in GST refunds; and budgetary allocation of Rs160 billion for the elimination of cross-subsidies in the domestic sector to provide relief to the industry for economic growth.
The Petroleum Division also requested that the Finance Division may reach the closure of the ongoing discussions on the gas-sector Circular Debt Management Plan (CDMP) with the IMF, in response to which the Finance Division informed the meeting that the CDMP would be taken up with the fund during the loan programme review in September.
The CCOE considered a summary titled "Circular Debt in the Gas Sector" and gave directives that issues related to the power-sector receivables, tax refunds and the budgeting of subsidy be taken up for ultimate resolution in consultation with all stakeholders.

International Finance Corporation (IFC) Division Director Simon Andrews, accompanied by World Bank Country Director Bolormaa Amgaabazar, called on Federal Minister for Economic Affairs Ahad Cheema to discuss private-sector investment and development cooperation in Pakistan.

Cheema underscored the government's commitment to advancing PPP projects in collaboration with international development partners. He outlined the steps taken to strengthen the Public-Private Partnership Authority (P3A), including placing it under the Privatisation Division and drawing up new legislation to expand its role.
Under the proposed framework, the P3A will help ministries develop and promote projects, mobilise financing and regulate projects implemented through the authority. IFC and World Bank representatives appreciated the initiative to strengthen the PPP framework.
On housing finance, Ahad Cheema said the government was working to help people build their own homes and improve access to housing facilities. The government is also considering ways to strengthen the institutional framework for housing finance. The minister invited the IFC to support efforts to expand housing finance, so that more people could get access to financing to build their homes.

title: Oil shock keeps SPI in double digits
description: Oil shock keeps SPI in double digits
content:
YoY inflation rises 11.92% amid US-Iran tensions; WoW index up 0.99%
Pakistan's short-term inflationary pressure remained elevated, with the Sensitive Price Indicator (SPI) rising 11.92% year-on-year (YoY) in the week ended September 24, as the prolonged US-Iran conflict kept global oil prices at higher levels and added pressure to energy costs.
Brent crude briefly climbed above $106 a barrel before coming back to $103.64 this week amid uncertainty about the conflict and shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
According to data released by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS), the combined SPI increased 0.99% week-on-week during the week under review, marking a further acceleration from the 10.64% YoY spike recorded in the preceding week.
The latest reading shows that the weekly inflation remained in double digits for the second consecutive week, after rising from 8.35% on September 3 to 8.62% on September 10, 10.64% on September 17 and 11.92% on September 24.
Energy prices remained among the major sources of inflationary pressure. LPG prices surged 63.97%, electricity charges for Q1 increased 58.59%, diesel prices rose 51.80% and petrol prices went up 47.49% than a year earlier.
Food prices also contributed significantly to the annual increase. Onion prices jumped 115.98%, wheat flour became 32.41% more expensive, powdered chilli rose 16.37%, mutton 15.75% and beef 13.22%. Fresh milk rates rose 8.10%, while plain bread was up 8.96% year-on-year.
On a weekly basis, however, the movement was mixed. Electricity charges for Q1 surged 18.76%, while egg prices rose 2.02%, garlic 1.57% and LPG 1.55%. These increases were partly offset by the decline in tomato prices by 13.45%, potatoes by 8.33%, diesel by 1.57% and petrol by 0.34%.
PBS data showed that prices of 20 out of 51 items increased, while 10 declined and 21 remained unchanged during the week.
The inflation burden was uneven across income groups. The highest expenditure quintile recorded a 12.31% YoY increase, compared with 9.69% for the lowest-income group, while the combined SPI rose 11.92%.
In August 2026, the monthly Consumer Price Index rose 11.1% YoY, compared with 9.2% in July and 3.1% in August 2025. On a month-on-month basis, inflation remained unchanged at 1.2%, compared with a 0.6% decline in August last year.
In urban areas, the CPI inflation increased 10.4% YoY in August, up from 8.7% in July and 3.5% in August 2025. On a month-on-month basis, the urban inflation rose 0.9%, compared with a 1.2% increase in the previous month and a 0.7% decline in August 2025.
In rural areas, inflation was higher, rising to 12.2% YoY in August from 9.9% in July and 2.5% in August 2025.

title: Rs32 5m collected under fixed tax
description: Rs32 5m collected under fixed tax
content:
Kayani hopes more traders will file returns; FBR launches faceless audit system
The government on Friday asked trade leaders to play their part in creating awareness of the fixed tax scheme, as so far only three new shopkeepers had submitted returns amid high hopes that over 9,800 newly registered persons would soon become filers.
Against the annual tax collection target of Rs50 billion under the new scheme, the government received Rs32.5 million by Friday.
The poor response to the 1% fixed tax scheme could be gauged from the fact that one of the two leading trade leaders, Ajmal Baloch, who negotiated and finalised the scheme with the government, did not submit his tax return. "I have to do it now. I haven't got time," he said.
Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani on Friday reviewed the implementation of the scheme. In a meeting, he was informed that so far 428 shopkeepers had filed returns, according to a press statement. However, out of the 428, the new traders who joined the scheme were only three.
The finance ministry said that so far 1,929 new traders had registered themselves for joining the tax system. However, out of these, only 57 have drafted returns but have not yet submitted, according to government officials. They said so far 9,806 shopkeepers had drafted their return statements but did not file with the FBR. But only 57 of them were new.
Kayani urged the trade leaders to play their role in getting the scheme successful. However, the representatives of traders put the responsibility on the FBR and also complained about hurdles to the online filing of returns. Kayani directed the FBR to immediately address the technical objections raised by shopkeepers and lawyers. He also directed the authorities to provide FBR plates at the earliest to the shopkeepers who had filed returns.
Kayani remarked that the fixed tax scheme "is a unique facility designed specifically for shopkeepers and is not available to any other business". Traders have been given exemption from audit, installation of digital devices for transactions and are required to pay only 1% tax on turnover, compared to 35% for a salaried person.
The salaried class has raised concerns over the preferential treatment meted out to the traders, who contributed very little to the exchequer compared to Rs630 billion in taxes paid by the salaried class in the last fiscal year. To a question, Kayani said it was irrelevant at this stage to say how many new traders had filed returns, hoping that 9,800, including the 1,929 newly registered, would submit their statements by September 30.
He expected that more shopkeepers would join the scheme, saying there was no reason to remain non-filers after the launch of the Asaan Tax scheme. The meeting decided to make daily contacts between the traders and FBR officials to facilitate implementation of the scheme. It was also agreed to further enhance engagement with the tax bars.
The meeting was informed that an Urdu language information booklet had been issued to explain the new scheme, the previous procedure for filing returns and details of penalties applicable after the deadline. A penalty of Rs10,000 would be imposed in the first month after the deadline, Rs25,000 in the second month and Rs50,000 in the third month, the finance ministry said.
Traders' representatives assured the meeting of their full cooperation, stating that the scheme was a good initiative and it might take some time to create awareness among shopkeepers. It is the second such initiative by the government aimed at bringing traders into the tax net after the earlier Tajir Dost scheme failed to deliver desired results. Kayani was hopeful about the success of the scheme due to the involvement of traders in its design and execution.
Although the state minister did not officially give any target for the first year, he voiced hope that a majority of 3.5 million traders would opt for the scheme.
Meanwhile, the FBR has established the National Faceless Centre (NFC) in Islamabad. The decision was taken by the Board in Council in its meeting held on Friday. The centre is a major reform that changes how tax audits and assessments are carried out in Pakistan.
Until now, a taxpayer whose return was picked for audit had to deal with a particular officer in a particular office, often in person. Under the new system, contacts between the taxpayer and the taxman come to an end. Cases will be selected by a computerised, risk-based system rather than by any officer.
Each case will then be assigned automatically to an officer, who may be sitting anywhere in the country. The taxpayer will not know who the officer is and the officer will have no say which case comes to him. Every case will pass through three separate hands. One officer will conduct the audit, the second will make assessment and the third will review the work for quality before any order is issued. No officer will control a taxpayer's case from start to finish.
All notices, replies and hearings will take place electronically through the FBR's IRIS system. Where the law requires a physical verification or recovery, this will be carried out by a separate field team.
The faceless centre draws its legal authority from the Finance Act 2026. It will be headed by a chief commissioner Inland Revenue, with dedicated wings for faceless audit, faceless assessment, quality control and field operations. A Programme Management Unit has already been set up to oversee its rollout.

title: Residents seek protection from eviction
description: Residents seek protection from eviction
content:
Say families have lived in the historic village for more than a century
Residents of Islamabad's oldest densely populated model village, Saidpur, have jointly demanded that families who have lived there for more than a century should not be deprived of their homes or evicted.
They demanded protection of the residential rights of affected residents, transparent verification of records regarding acquisition of land and payment of compensation, and an opportunity for local families to present their position before any action is taken.
The affected residents of Saidpur said their lands were forcibly acquired under the interim laws imposed during martial law when the federal capital was established in 1960.
However, they said compensation for the fertile land, gardens and land irrigated by natural springs was fixed at extremely low rates.
They said the awards issued between 1962 and 1967 were based on old prices, payments were made several years later and compensation was also paid in instalments, while permits for alternative land often proved practically useless.
According to the affected residents, citizens acquired fundamental rights after the 1973 Constitution, but by then the owners of Saidpur had been deprived of effective opportunities for legal recourse.
They said later affected people received better compensation and land-shifting facilities, while the land acquired from them was allegedly used by CDA officials to generate substantial financial benefits later.
Highly expensive sectors have now been established in those areas, they added.
The affected residents of Saidpur Village referred to a 2008 decision by former CDA chairman Kamran Lashari to protect the residential rights of the ancient village and its old residents.
They said that if the decision remains in force, the homes and residential rights of families living there for decades should also be protected.
According to local residents, they possess documents relating to their land and properties, while the relevant records are also available with the CDA.
The affected residents also raised the issue of alleged allotment of plots at low rates and demanded that the record regarding its legal authority, relevant laws and cabinet decisions be made public.
They demanded that before any eviction or demolition operation is carried out in Saidpur Village, the complete record should be transparently examined; awards, compensation, alternative land and the 2008 CDA Board decision from 1960 onwards should be reviewed; and the residential rights of families living there for decades should be protected instead of depriving them of their homes.

Islamabad has formally been divided into three municipal corporations, or towns, under the new local government law, with one municipal town council established under each of the capital's three National Assembly constituencies.

Senior Civil Judge FIA Muhammad Nasrullah Wattoo discharged 68 male and female young employees arrested by the NCCIA Rawalpindi and dismissed the case against them.

Asad Abbasi, Advocate Supreme Court, appeared before the court on behalf of the call-centre owners and employees and termed the case baseless.

The judge agreed with the arguments and not only discharged the accused but also directed the FIA not to harass people unlawfully or arrest them in future.

content:
Affidavits sought from landlords confirming their premises have been vacated
Security has been tightened at Faizabad, a key entry and exit point between the twin cities, ahead of a possible Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) long march and protest, with hotels, restaurants, hostels, guest houses and transport terminals being ordered to close.
Police sources said hotels located in the Faizabad area were being closed, while restaurants and other businesses had been directed to cease operations by evening. Guest houses and transport terminals have reportedly been ordered to close from tonight, while hostels in Faizabad and adjoining areas have been directed to vacate by night.
According to sources, police have also sought affidavits from owners of hotels, restaurants, hostels and other commercial buildings, requiring them to submit the documents to the relevant police stations and undertake that their premises have been completely vacated. Police sources said action had also been ordered against owners who failed to submit the affidavits by the stipulated deadline.
The measures are being taken as part of security arrangements in view of the possible PTI protest and long march.
Faizabad is a major junction connecting Rawalpindi and Islamabad and is also a significant commercial and transport hub. Thousands of people travel between the two cities through the area every day, while inter-district and inter-provincial public transport is an important part of its economy.
The area has bus and wagon terminals as well as hotels, restaurants, hostels, guest houses, general stores, tea stalls, workshops, tyre shops and numerous other businesses. Economic activity continues around the clock, with the livelihoods of thousands of people directly or indirectly linked to transport and passenger movement.
In the past, closures of the Faizabad Interchange and transport activities have caused difficulties for residents of Rawalpindi and Islamabad, passengers, traders and particularly daily-wage workers. As Faizabad is one of the main links between the two cities, a prolonged closure could affect adjoining roads and commercial areas beyond the immediate locality.
Transporters, drivers, conductors, hotel and restaurant workers, rickshaw and taxi drivers, vendors, labourers and other daily-wage earners are among those likely to be affected by the suspension of business activities.
Business representatives said even a one-day complete shutdown could deprive daily-wage workers of their income, while losses could increase if the restrictions continued for several days.
Shakil Abbasi, a transporter who operates a bus service between Faizabad and Faisalabad, said the impact of a vehicle remaining idle was not limited to the transport company, as drivers, conductors, booking staff and their families were also affected.
He said passengers often had advance bookings and the sudden closure of a terminal created difficulties in refunding fares and rearranging vehicle schedules.

title: Livestock fall ill  die after vaccination
description: Livestock fall ill  die after vaccination
content:
Farmers call for examination of all relevant aspects, including vaccine's quality
Several livestock reportedly fell ill and some suckling animals died in Hanjrai Kalan after animals were vaccinated against haemorrhagic septicaemia (HS), commonly known as gal ghoto, by the Livestock Department.
The livestock owners said animals were vaccinated by a livestock department vaccinator in their absence.
They claimed that following the vaccination, some suckling animals died while several other cattle and buffaloes developed health problems.
The owners said the affected animals had stopped or reduced their feed intake, were becoming increasingly weak and showed a deterioration in their general condition.
Some animals also reportedly developed swelling at the sites where injections were administered.
The livestock owners said their animals were a major source of income and livelihood and that the deaths and illness had caused them substantial financial losses, with the affected livestock collectively worth millions of rupees.
They expressed concern that without timely medical treatment, more animals could fall ill, increasing their losses.
They called for veterinary experts to examine the affected animals and determine the actual cause of the deaths and illness before any conclusions were drawn.
Livestock Department vaccinator Dr Gohar Abbas, however, said the animals had been administered a vaccine supplied by the government to the Livestock Department.
He said the vaccine was being used under the department's preventive programme to protect animals against haemorrhagic septicaemia.
The affected livestock owners said the reported deaths and illnesses following vaccination warranted a medical and scientific investigation.
According to livestock farmer Muhammad Rafiq, he rears animals alongside his livestock farming. Four of his animals were affected, while a young, milk-feeding calf died.
Muhammad Sajid works in the fields and also looks after livestock. He said four of his animals were affected.
Meanwhile, Muhammad Iqbal rears livestock for sale and said four of his animals were affected after vaccination.
The affected farmers said they had suffered heavy financial losses as livestock worth millions of rupees were affected and a calf died.
They called for examination of all relevant aspects, including the vaccine's quality, batch number, manufacturing and expiry details, storage conditions, cold-chain arrangements, vaccination procedure and the current medical condition of the affected animals.
They demanded that a team of veterinary experts be immediately dispatched to Hanjrai Kalan to examine and treat the affected livestock.
They also called for appropriate medical and investigative procedures to determine the causes of the deaths of the animals that had died.
The livestock owners stressed that vaccination was an important measure for protecting animals from disease but said any unusual health problems reported after vaccination should be properly investigated.
They called for an impartial inquiry to establish whether the illness and deaths were linked to vaccination or resulted from another medical cause. They said identifying the actual cause would help prevent misinformation and ensure that any negligence, if established, was addressed.
The livestock owners further urged the chief minister and senior Livestock Department officials to ensure immediate treatment of the affected animals, determine the causes of the deaths and conduct a transparent review of the vaccination process to provide relief to affected families and prevent similar incidents in future.

title: Two acquitted in AC murder case
description: Bench observed that prosecution had failed to reliably establish presence of alleged eyewitnesses at crime scene
content:
Bench observed that prosecution had failed to reliably establish presence of alleged eyewitnesses at crime scene
The Lahore High Court (LHC) has acquitted a man and his son who were sentenced to life imprisonment and death, respectively, for the murder of Assistant Commissioner Jhang Imran Jaffar.
A two-member bench comprising Justice Shehram Sarwar Chaudhry and Justice Sardar Akbar Ali Dogar allowed appeals filed by Asghar Ali and his son Sohail Asghar and set aside the judgment of the Sessions Court, Chiniot.
In its detailed judgment issued on Friday, the bench observed that the prosecution had failed to reliably establish the presence of alleged eyewitnesses at the crime scene. It also noted contradictions between witness statements and medical evidence.
The court held that the prosecution was required to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt but had failed to establish an unbroken chain of evidence meeting the required legal standard.
According to the prosecution, Asghar Ali and Sohail Asghar had allegedly shot dead Imran Jaffar on December 5, 2021. At the time, Jaffar was serving as Assistant Commissioner Jhang and was home on leave.
The deceased and accused were close relatives, while their families were also involved in a dispute over drainage and wastewater disposal. The Sessions Court, Chiniot, had sentenced Sohail Asghar to death and Asghar Ali to life imprisonment.

The Punjab government has extended restrictions under Section 144 across the province until October 5, banning gatherings of five or more people at public places, processions and incitement to participate in unlawful assemblies, the Home Department said on Friday.

Provincial Minister and committee chairman Khawaja Salman Rafique chaired the meeting, which was attended by Provincial Minister and co-chairman Bilal Yasin, Provincial Minister Syed Ashiq Hussain Kirmani and Special Assistant to the Chief Minister Rana Bilal Ahmad.
Home Secretary Dr Ahmed Javed Qazi briefed the committee on the law-and-order situation and security arrangements across the province.
Under the extended restrictions, gatherings of five or more people at public places and processions will remain prohibited.
The incitement of people to participate in unlawful assemblies has also been banned.
The restrictions further prohibit the carrying and display of all types of weapons at public places.
The committee approved four JITs and jail trials in 21 cases. However, the Home Department handout did not provide details of the cases, including the offences involved, districts concerned or reasons for conducting the trials in jails.

title: Lahore Zoo aquarium welcomes 100 fish from 15 species
description: Lahore Zoo aquarium welcomes 100 fish from 15 species
content:
New collection includes Green Bird Wrasse, Angelfish, Damselfish
Lahore Zoo's fish aquarium has been enriched with around 100 fish belonging to 15 species, including rare and colourful marine and freshwater varieties, attracting visitors, particularly children.
The newly introduced aquatic collection includes Green Bird Wrasse, Mono Angelfish, various species of Damselfish, Squirrelfish, Red-toothed Triggerfish and Lyretail Wrasse.
Starfish, sand-sifting starfish and different types of corals have also been added to the aquarium.
The fish can be seen swimming in glass tanks of different sizes, with some species moving swiftly through the water while others remain among corals and artificial reef structures, offering visitors a closer look at aquatic life.
A visitor, Fatima, said she was visiting Lahore Zoo for the first time and was surprised by the variety of fish on display. She said she had previously seen some of the species only in documentaries.
Another visitor, Ammara, said she had brought her children to the zoo, adding that they were particularly excited to see the colourful fish and starfish and were also learning about aquatic life. Lahore Zoo Veterinary Officer Dr Muhammad Azhar said the zoo was expanding its aquatic collection alongside its existing collection of wild animals and birds.
"Both marine and freshwater fish have been introduced in the aquarium, and more species will be added in phases," he said, adding that the health of the fish and water quality were regularly monitored to maintain suitable conditions.
Fish aquarium caretaker Adnan Shah said marine and freshwater fish required different methods of care. He said maintaining appropriate salinity, water quality and cleanliness was essential for marine species, while temperature and water quality were particularly important for freshwater fish.
Shah said ornamental fish owners sometimes overfed their fish, resulting in increased organic waste and ammonia levels in the water.

content:
Mobile clinics across Punjab to have digital medical boxes
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif has announced a Hospital of the Month award for healthcare facilities demonstrating outstanding performance across the province.
Presiding over a video-link meeting, the chief minister decided to transform 300 Maryam Nawaz Hospitals (Rural Health Centres) into fully-fledged hospitals. She said 911 Clinics on Wheels had provided medical care to 30 million patients.
It was decided in the meeting to introduce digital medical boxes for the mobile clinics to perform ultrasound, blood sugar, CBC and ECG tests through a single system. A camera can be connected to the digital box for teleconferencing, while a mobile phone-linked smart ultrasound device will also be introduced.
CM Maryam Nawaz ordered that 40,000 doctors and allied health professionals be recruited for hospitals across Punjab.
She was informed that 2,524 doctors, 2,482 women medical officers, 408 consultants and 32 cardiologists had been recruited. In addition, 7,572 lady health visitors (LHVs) and 5,048 support staff have been posted in hospitals across the province.
The chief minister ordered the provision of a new CT scan machine in every district and establishment of telemedicine centres for seasonal and common diseases.
Patients will be able to consult doctors through video calls at the centres and, where necessary, be referred to the relevant hospital and ward. The telemedicine centres will facilitate appointments with the relevant ward, laboratory or other facility.
Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz ordered immediate replacement of the medical superintendents of four hospitals over poor performance and negligence of duties.
She also ordered the formation of a pool of doctors and medical superintendents to deal with emergency situations.
She ordered that cleanliness and parking facilities at district and tehsil headquarters hospitals be improved.
For the first time in the province, Clinic Quality Control Officers will be appointed to assess the treatment provided to patients. A Directorate of Monitoring and Surveillance has been established in the primary healthcare department to ensure 24-hour digital monitoring of every hospital.
The system will cover the DHQ, THQ and Maryam Nawaz Hospitals, Maryam Nawaz Health Clinics, Field Hospitals and Clinics on Wheels.
The participants were informed that Community Health Monitoring Inspectors had completed the registration and data collection of more than 119.8 million people across Punjab.
Medicines were delivered to the homes of 3,444 Type-1 diabetes, 14,286 hepatitis and 13,864 TB patients.
The participants agreed on legislation to link private clinics with the Health Information Management System (HIMS).
Provincial Secretary for Primary and Secondary Healthcare and Population, Nadia Saqib, gave a briefing during the meeting.

title: Threat alert triggers K P secretariat evacuation
description: Threat alert triggers K P secretariat evacuation
content:
Staff evacuated as security forces sealed the complex over possible attack threat
Panic and chaos gripped the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Civil Secretariat on Friday after security alerts of a possible drone or suicide attack targeting government offices or the mosque inside the complex during Friday prayers.
Officials and staff were first ordered to remain confined to their rooms and offices, only to be instructed moments later to evacuate the premises immediately.
Most employees abandoned their cars and motorcycles and fled on foot to safer locations as security forces sealed off the entire secretariat and surrounding areas. While the scramble was still underway, similar evacuation orders were issued for staff at the FATA Secretariat and adjoining offices on Warsak Road as a precaution against any potential terrorist attack. The sudden alerts triggered a full security lockdown across key government installations in Peshawar, with police and other law-enforcement agencies deploying additional personnel to secure the perimeters and screen the area.
To restore calm and normalise the situation, Chief Minister Muhammad Sohail Khan Afridi arrived at the Civil Secretariat without delay. Accompanied by the Chief Secretary, the Chief Minister offered Friday prayers at the Civil Secretariat mosque. His presence at the site during a period of heightened alert was widely seen as a deliberate show of resolve.
After the prayers, the Chief Minister received a detailed briefing on the overall security situation in the province at the Chief Secretary's office. He issued necessary directions to the relevant authorities to maintain heightened vigilance and ensure the safety of government buildings, mosques and public spaces.
Security sources said today's threat specifically targeted government installations, particularly congregational mosques where large numbers of people gather for Friday prayers. The Chief Minister's decision to offer prayers at the Civil Secretariat mosque sent a clear message of the government's determination to confront terrorism and its refusal to bow to efforts aimed at spreading fear among officials and the public.
Chief Minister Afridi stated: "Terrorists cannot intimidate us. The people and the government of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa will never surrender to terrorism. We will confront terrorism with full force on every front, and there will be no compromise on the protection of the lives and property of the people."
Officials later confirmed that the immediate threat had been contained and normal operations at the secretariats were gradually restored.
However, security arrangements around key government buildings in Peshawar remained tightened for the rest of the day as a precautionary measure. The episode underscored the persistent challenges posed by militant threats in the province and the administration's stated commitment to maintain public confidence through visible leadership in the face of such alerts.

title: SHC cracks the whip on hospital committee
description: SHC cracks the whip on hospital committee
content:
Doctor shortages, non-functional theatres and dialysis gaps persist
The Sindh High Court has tightened the screws on a committee tasked with improving services at Civil Hospital Mirpurkhas, directing its members to identify and actually resolve deficiencies instead of merely repeating recommendations in inspection reports.
The SHC's Mirpurkhas bench, comprising Justice Zulfikar Ali Sangi and Justice Amjad Ali Bohio, expressed dissatisfaction with the committee's performance two years after it was constituted to oversee improvements in service delivery at the hospital. "it could not function as required and the prescribed visits were not carried out," the court observed in its order, laying down a fresh roadmap for the committee to discharge its responsibilities more proactively.
The committee comprises the Mirpurkhas Commissioner, District Health Officer and Medical Superintendent. The bench directed its members not only to identify problems at the district headquarters hospital (DHQ) but also to take steps to resolve them.
It ordered that progress made on problems identified in one fortnightly report must be reflected in the subsequent report, making it clear that inspection reports could no longer simply reproduce earlier recommendations.
"The next inspection report should not merely repeat recommendations for improvement," the court observed. The bench also directed officials to stop using vague terms such as "satisfactory", "functional" and "complied with" and instead support their reports with concrete facts and figures. At the previous hearing on August 19, the court had sought separate reports on the state of health services in every department of the hospital. However, the committee submitted a general account instead.
"The report is silent about trauma centre, neurology, psychiatry, gastroenterology, nephrology, thalassemia and scanning department," the order noted, adding that the court had expected a thorough inspection. "The inspection as placed on record does not meet that standard," the bench observed.
The court also questioned whether Civil Hospital Mirpurkhas currently has the facilities and services required to qualify as a tertiary care hospital. The report noted that patients requiring complex surgical procedures were being referred to hospitals outside Mirpurkhas.
The bench also expressed concern over the hospital's human-resource situation, noting that against 160 sanctioned vacancies for doctors, only 102 doctors were working at the DHQ hospital. Similarly, only 17 specialists were available against 47 vacant specialist posts.

title: Govt rejects special funds for KU
description: Govt rejects special funds for KU
content:

The Sindh government has returned a summary seeking special funds for payment of house ceiling to teaching and non-teaching employees of the University of Karachi (KU), saying the provincial government has not adopted the federal policy on the allowance, The Express Tribune has learnt.
According to sources, the Finance Department has raised objections to the summary forwarded by the Universities and Boards Department, stating that universities providing house ceiling to their employees were making the payments from their own resources.
The provincial government has conveyed that it would have no objection if KU also paid the allowance from its available financial resources. However, sources said the release of any special funds for the purpose had been deemed unfeasible in view of the prevailing economic situation.
Following the objections, the KU administration is considering releasing one month's house ceiling along with employees' salaries for the current month, sources said.
The proposed payment could amount to more than Rs40 million. In the absence of a dedicated fund, the administration is considering using one of its existing sources, including the annual non-development grant received through the Sindh Higher Education Commission (HEC), the non-development grant provided by the federal HEC or an endowment fund established through a Sindh HEC grant.
It is not yet clear, however, for how long the university would be able to continue the payments if the Sindh government does not approve a special grant.
Sources said Acting Vice Chancellor Dr Tufail Ahmed was preparing a response to the objections raised by the Finance Department.
The issue has remained a major source of friction between the KU administration and employees. The Teachers' Association of the University of Karachi staged a strike for around 40 days from the first week of May over the non-payment of the house ceiling. Non-teaching employees later joined the protest.
The administration of then VC Dr Khalid Iraqi had maintained that the university did not have sufficient financial resources to pay the allowance. title: HIV crisis at Valika snowballs  toll hits 169
description: HIV crisis at Valika snowballs  toll hits 169
content:
Nine deaths reported but hospital records put fatalities at just two
The HIV crisis at Valika Hospital is snowballing, with the number of affected children reaching 169 and nine deaths confirmed by hospital sources, while a stark discrepancy in the hospital's records shows only two fatalities.
According to hospital sources, the latest figures show that 142 of the affected children have been registered with five medical boards constituted at the hospital to oversee their cases, financial assistance and other related matters.
Of the affected families, 109 have so far had bank accounts opened to facilitate financial assistance, while 76 families have started receiving support through the hospital's endowment fund. These families have already received payments covering two months.
However, 34 other affected families are still waiting for financial assistance. Hospital sources attributed the delay to incomplete documentation and problems involving Benazir Cards, which have hindered the transfer of funds.
The number of affected children has steadily increased since the HIV issue first emerged at Valika Hospital several months ago. The government had initially reported 78 affected children, but subsequent screening and testing led to the identification of additional cases, taking the figure to 169.
The discrepancy over deaths has emerged as another major concern. While nine deaths among HIV-affected children have been confirmed, the hospital's own records contain entries for only two deaths. The gap has left the exact toll a matter requiring reconciliation through a verified record.
Families of the children who died have also not received financial assistance from the endowment fund so far. Sources said the issue is likely to be discussed at an upcoming meeting, where officials may decide the amount of assistance and the mechanism for its disbursement.
Multiple inquiries have been initiated at different levels to investigate the HIV cases. The endowment fund was established to support affected children with treatment, medicines, diagnostic tests, education and other essential needs.
Administrative action has also been taken, with show-cause notices issued to several employees and measures, including suspensions, taken against doctors, dispensers and nursing staff.
Authorities have repeatedly maintained that affected children are being provided treatment, medicines and other facilities. However, the latest figures indicate that major issues surrounding case registration, financial assistance, death records and the rehabilitation of affected families remain unresolved.
Experts have called for all affected children to be brought under a single, comprehensive registration system, discrepancies in death records to be reconciled, and financial assistance to be delivered without further delay to families entitled to support.

title: Reflections from Beijing  China s perspective on Pakistan
description: Reflections from Beijing  China s perspective on Pakistan
content:
President Xi once likened the 56 ethnic groups of China to '56 flowers in a bouquet'
During my recent four-week China assignment, I have been seeking insights into the evolving perception of Pakistan by the Chinese leadership. The traditional "time-tested, all-weather friendship" remains a cornerstone, yet Chinese companies appear to have lost the impetus to invest in the country.
My explorations in Shanghai and Beijing led me to an illuminating quote from Jiang Zaidong, the Chinese ambassador to Islamabad, shared on a local news network:
"Xinjiang's exemplary practice of social stability, economic prosperity, and harmonious coexistence underscores the profound significance of unity. Only through unity can we achieve victory. Regardless of the diverse ethnic groups and regions a country encompasses, collective efforts and shared aspirations can catalyse development momentum and foster a better life. We firmly believe that all political parties and sectors of Pakistani society will unite to promote national development and enhance the well-being of its people."
This quote, delivered by Jiang Zaidong, resonates deeply with the current political climate in Pakistan. While rooted in China's context, it carries a broader message to Pakistani ruling elites.
The Chinese ambassador elucidated the extensive efforts undertaken to foster unity among all ethnic groups across China since the 18th CPC National Congress, when President Xi Jinping embarked on a national mission of embracing all ethnicities.
In fact, the week commencing September 27th marks the inaugural Ethnic Unity and Progress Publicity Week, themed "Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, Forging Ahead on the Journey of Great Rejuvenation". The ambassador recalled that President Xi Jinping consciously pursued the policy of maintaining a balanced approach in addressing the diverse ethnic groups residing in China.
President Xi once likened the 56 ethnic groups of China to "56 flowers in a bouquet", emphasising the importance of party officials' focus on the well-being of all.
This poignant yet veiled message, I believe, was perhaps directed at Pakistani decision-makers and political elites. Without national unity, inclusivity and consensus, enduring progress is elusive.
Until recently, most Chinese officials, former ambassadors and academics refrained from raising critical questions regarding the trajectory of China-Pakistan relations over the past decade. However, the current situation has shifted.
The context is the lackluster progress of CPEC. Many Chinese believe that Pakistan treated CPEC as a blank cheque rather than an industrial catalyst. By prioritising short-term political gains over long-term economic strategy, Pakistan – according to former diplomats and officials – squandered an opportunity to embark on a path to industrialisation. They consistently highlight Islamabad's sovereign guarantees for Chinese Independent Power Producers (IPPs) and the nearly $1.6 billion in circular debt owed to them. Additionally, officials cite the chronic dollar shortages that have prevented Chinese companies from repatriating their profits, with approximately $2.3 billion in unpaid dues and blocked profits currently outstanding.
The prospects for rapid industrialisation are dimmed due to bureaucratic hurdles, the absence of clarity regarding the governing structure, the volatile security landscape, China's withdrawal from the flagship $8 billion Main Line 1 (ML-1) railway project, and the drastic reduction in CPEC-related investments for over a year. These factors are frequently cited by business executives and some officials.
Those familiar with Pakistan's internal dynamics candidly acknowledge that CPEC is facing challenges not only from non-traditional security threats (geopolitical factors) but also from internal governance bottlenecks.
"Pakistan's progress in aligning its actions with the primary objectives of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), which is to foster industrialization and self-reliance, remains inadequate," remarked a prominent think tanker. The expert emphasised the critical need for national unity and consensus to effectively implement policies and achieve equitable development.
Chinese area experts believe that Pakistan's economic growth, coupled with its industrialisation efforts and the establishment of production chains with potential value for China, can transform the nation into a formidable force. They assert that economic development driven by CPEC, coupled with Pakistan's military and diplomatic capabilities, can significantly enhance its regional standing.
Fortunately, Pakistan remains a valued political ally for China. While China seeks Pakistan to assume a more active leadership role in reshaping the Asian landscape, this is closely tied to Pakistan's economic situation and internal political challenges, another South Asia expert observed.
Pakistan is widely regarded as a formidable partner in addressing regional issues. Stronger and more friendly relations between Pakistan and the United States can help mitigate India's influence in Asia.
However, even the most effective diplomacy and advanced defence capabilities cannot fully compensate for economic resilience.
The challenge therefore lies in setting the house in order i.e. prioritising the well-being of Pakistan's citizens first rather than pursuing the quest for relevance abroad. Credibility will likely remain evasive as long as the intent on correcting the political economy is missing.
This Chinese message was even more visible when President Xi landed in Washington; the aircraft that flew him to the US was marked "Air China" – no special sign like US Air Force One!

title: Off the reservation
description: Off the reservation
content:
Vedas divide Hindu society into four varnas
Two controversies are rocking India today. Both about software. One is about the Indian government's decision to allow payment processing companies and banks to charge a 0.4 percent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions over INR 2000. And the second is about the centralisation of electoral rolls by the Election Commission of India through a software called ECInet.
The trigger of the second controversy was provided by The Indian Express journalist Ritika Chopra's brilliant expose. The Reporters' Collective has also done ace work on the matter. The gist of it is that the ECI is using software to lock out decentralised, local staff from the grid and making arbitrary changes to the electoral rolls. Goes without saying that the Muslim population has been disproportionately affected by the changes, which was also the crux of my September 12 piece, "Aap chronology samajhiye!" What interests me is what it all means. What if I told you that while minorities and Dalits are the ruling party's favourite whipping boys meant for amusement and votebank consolidation, they are not the targets? This emerging digital panopticon is meant to disenfranchise the real mark.
Ask yourself, how do you erase a majority? I will show you a half-century-long project to do just that, larger than the incumbent BJP government or the RSS.
A caveat for Pakistani readers: do not congratulate yourselves on being free from casteism. Prejudice changes nomenclature and hides in plain sight. When a member of the Indian elite says he does not believe in caste, he is not advocating for a casteless society or exogamy, but demanding you make peace with the status quo and not challenge their privilege. Caste prejudice is a daily reality in India. According to various human rights sources, Pratiloma (inter-caste) honour killings routinely exceed one thousand per annum.
The Vedas divide Hindu society into four varnas: Brahmins (priestly class), Kshatriyas (warriors and kings), Vaishyas (mercantile class) and Shudras (working class and artisans). The Vedas do not go out of their way to stigmatise the last category. That honour rests with another text called Manusmriti.
A fortnight ago I showed you how the ghost of RSS architect MS Golwalkar drives the ongoing SIR exercise and prejudiced citizenship laws today. The very same man hailed the author of Manusmriti as the "first and greatest lawgiver of the world," writing in his manifesto that the caste hierarchy is not a social flaw but a divine mandate: "Brahmin is the head, Kshatriya the hands, Vaishya the thighs and Shudra the feet... the Hindu People, is our God."
In his book Jyotipunj (2008), PM Modi canonises Golwalkar as his supreme ideological mentor, describing his life as "an unbroken yajna [ritual sacrifice]" for the nation. In Karmayog (2007), Modi rationalises the manual scavenging forced upon Dalit Valmikis as a divine duty rather than exploitation, writing it should continue as an "internal spiritual activity for centuries". A full-throated, fatalist endorsement of the varna system.
To grasp the scale of this hierarchy, consider the math established by Kanshi Ram, pioneer of India's lower-caste political awakening in the 1980s. He popularised the term Bahujan to define the oppressed castes as a collective 85 per cent of the country, identifying Shudras specifically as the single largest demographic majority at 52 per cent. Today, the Shudra population may exceed 60 per cent. Yet you hardly ever encounter the word Shudra in daily discourse. The reason is societal stigma and a deliberate state project of divide and rule. Power and resources remain controlled by the Brahmin-Bania alliance. Bania is a subset of the Vaishya varna. How do these upper castes control the overwhelming majority? By weaponising stigma, imposing sanitised secular labels, and endlessly splintering them.
The British referred to Shudras as the backward castes. Independent India rebranded them Other Backward Classes (OBCs). Then it linked the term to resources: certain Shudra communities were expelled for being affluent, while disadvantaged upper castes were slipped in. Modi's caste, Modh Ghanchi, belongs traditionally to the Vaishya varna, yet was included in the OBC category in 1994.
In 1990 the state finally implemented the Mandal Commission report, granting OBCs a 27 per cent reservation in public jobs and education. However, to prevent this demographic giant from ever consolidating, the Modi government weaponised the Rohini Commission in 2017 to sub-categorise the quota, fracturing collective Shudra identity by pitting thousands of sub-castes against one another for scraps.
That is not all. Through corrupt practices like paper leaks and the bureaucratic sleight of hand known as lateral entry, the Modi government leaves most OBC reserved seats unoccupied. Those already in the system are blocked by endless extensions granted to the upper-caste old guard.
To a marked community, visibility is a curse. To escape the Brahmin-Bania elite, the Shudra economy was historically cash-based and operated outside the formal banking system. Then came the Modi government with demonetisation and the siren song of the free JAM trinity: Jan Dhan bank accounts, Aadhaar biometric IDs, and Mobile connectivity.
Now that the informal bazaar is corralled inside the digital pen, the squeeze begins. The upcoming 0.4 per cent MDR on UPI transactions above INR 2000 is not a technical fee. It is a toll on the informal Shudra economy to be scaled up later. You trap them on a platform, extract their data, and charge them to access their own capital.
Amit Shah has the cunning of a municipal ward boss, but the strategic depth belongs to a technocratic vanguard in Bangalore. Collectives like iSPIRT engineered a digital panopticon disguised as public infrastructure.
The SIR exercise and ECInet may target Muslims and Dalits today to polarise the electorate, but the software is compiling a shadow ledger of the entire Shudra majority. By centralising voter rolls and gutting local oversight, the state ensures the 85 per cent can be partitioned, deleted, or managed at will.
After this come the supermajorities of 2029, engineered by cannibalising electoral rolls, delimitation boundaries and opposition parties. Then the secular constitution, along with all reservations, goes out the window and a Hindu Rashtra is proclaimed. Shudras should open the Manusmriti to see what this means for them. Under Manu, a Shudra raising a limb against a superior faced amputation, and coupling with a higher caste woman meant castration and execution.
If you are a Shudra reading this, you should know Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, Dalits and Adivasis are merely in the way. You are the real target.

title: Trapped in illiteracy
description: Trapped in illiteracy
content:
Pakistan's rural-urban female literacy gap typically spans 17 to 19 percentage points across the provinces
Where does the fault lie? Will heads roll to hold them accountable? These are the questions that first come to mind when one looks at the findings of the recently launched Sindh Government's first Gender Parity Report. The document highlights gender disparities across key sectors such as health, education, justice, governance, economic participation and demographics, but here we will only focus on education.
For decades, this sector has been trapped in a persistent stalemate. As a result, the report offers a grim sense of déjà vu, recycling the same chronic failures in education. Most alarming is the profound rural-urban divide in female literacy. The national average stands at a low 47%, but in rural areas, it collapses to a shocking 27.52%. Behind these percentages lies a harsher reality: over 4.08 million young girls are completely locked out of the school system.
Assuming that the countless ongoing and past education reforms, plethora of the laws making education free and compulsory for every child, launch of non-formal education programmes, recruitment of 100,000 teachers, free distribution of textbooks, waiver on exam fees and substantial input from expensive education experts at the Reform Support Unit were all effective, then why is the outcome so disappointing?
This is a serious indictment of education governance model in Sindh where more than 70% females residing in rural areas cannot read and write. Rural women are the backbone of the PPP's support base, due to which the party has enjoyed uninterrupted rule in the province for nearly two decades. This challenges the narrative of a leadership that frequently asserts its deep devotion to Sindh as the motherland.
A similar trend prevails across the country, with only a few exceptions. Pakistan's overall rural literacy rate stands at 55%, but among rural women, that figure drops to a stark 44%. Province-wise breakdown reveals that Punjab is ahead of other provinces where 54% rural women are able to read and write, followed by Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa with 41%. Meanwhile, Sindh and Balochistan appear to be roughly at the same level with 24% and 25% respectively.
Pakistan's rural-urban female literacy gap typically spans 17 to 19 percentage points across the provinces - except in Sindh, where it reaches a massive 41 percentage points (65% vs. 24%). This striking anomaly demands an explanation. The Sindh government owes the public a clear accounting of why the divide between its urban and rural women is so exceptionally wide.
This data is drawn from the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) Population and Housing Census. A bit discrepancy, however, exists between the PBS and Sindh Gender Parity (SGP) reports, with the national census placing rural female literacy 3.5 percentage points lower than provincial estimates. Although these conflicting figures may confuse audiences, the PBS dataset was chosen because it allows for a nationwide comparative analysis, whereas the SGP report focuses exclusively on Sindh.
Education and democracy are intrinsically linked. When half the country is illiterate, democratic governance exists in name only. It takes little imagination to realise the kind of fragile society that grows out of such conditions.
Being at the helm of affairs in Sindh for two decades at a stretch, the PPP could have laid solid foundations for educating women, which would have, in turn, help uplift their social status and improve their standards of living in an exemplary model for other provinces. Moreover, it would have been a fitting tribute to the memory of Benazir Bhutto.
Unfortunately, this did not happen. This disparity extends far beyond education; data released by the World Bank and other international organisations on the prevalence of multi-dimensional, chronic poverty in rural areas is nothing short of shocking. Had democratic governance been responsive and accountable, the situation would have been far better today.
A business-as-usual approach cannot achieve quick results. To break the cycle of the past decades, the entire edifice of planning and execution must be restructured around ground realities and enforced with real accountability. The era of cosmetic fixes must end.

title: Rising seas threat
description: Rising seas threat
content:
Global sea level rose by almost six millimetres in 2024
Sea levels are rising, and their consequences will be anything but gradual. A unanimous UN General Assembly declaration calling for stronger global action has brought renewed urgency to a threat that has long been treated as a distant consequence of climate change. For small island states, it raises the extraordinary prospect of territories disappearing beneath the ocean. For countries such as Pakistan, the danger may be less dramatic in appearance, but it is already creeping onto the coastline.
There is little room for complacency. Global sea level rose by almost six millimetres in 2024, the largest annual increase on record, while the pace of the rise has accelerated considerably over recent decades. What is measured globally in millimetres eventually translates into flooded settlements and eroding coastlines. Pakistan has particular reason to pay attention. Its coastline stretches more than 1,000 kilometres along Sindh and Balochistan and includes the densely populated metropolis of Karachi as well as the ecologically fragile Indus Delta. Low-lying areas along the Sindh coast are especially vulnerable to the combined effects of sea-level rise, coastal erosion, storm surges and saltwater intrusion. What is often discussed as a future climate threat is, for communities in the delta, already an unfolding reality.
Sea-level projections must become part of decisions being made today. Authorities must identify areas most vulnerable to inundation and erosion, and prevent further development from creating populations and assets that will become increasingly expensive, or impossible, to protect. Natural defences also deserve far greater attention. Mangrove forests along the Sindh coast and Indus Delta provide an important buffer against waves. Pakistan has made considerable efforts to expand mangrove cover, but plantation drives in isolation aren't enough.

title: PSM   dead but bleeding
description: PSM   dead but bleeding
content:
Closed mill haemorrhaged Rs79.3 billion over the past three fiscal years alone
Pakistan Steel Mills (PSM) has been dead since June 2015, when the furnaces closed after gas was shut off due to non-payment of dues. Yet, 11 years later, the state remains in denial and refuses to give the mill a dignified funeral. In its life, the mill was the epitome of a white elephant - apart from a few years in the mid-2000s, the mill lost money every year of its five-decade operational history. But even in death, it continues to burn taxpayer money.
According to the Ministry of Industries, the closed mill haemorrhaged Rs79.3 billion over the past three fiscal years alone, with Rs24 billion lost in FY26. About 72% of the losses since FY24 were interest payments on legacy debt, which will continue to accumulate since the government is unwilling to pay to clear it, and buyers are not particularly interested in operating the mill. The finance ministry has also not helped the situation, as it has failed to follow its own internal advice to restructure PSM's debt through swaps and write-downs. Meanwhile, 'running' costs also painfully hit the exchequer, including salaries, utilities and pensions.
Part of the problem is that the governments in Islamabad and Karachi continue to live in a fool's paradise, believing that PSM can be revived into a profitable entity. The fact is that the cost of modernising and reactivating the mill while covering running and historical expenses makes this proposal a non-starter for most reputable investors. Even the current proposals, including one from Russia, are problematic due to Western sanctions. Public-private partnerships also risk sticking the government with the bill when they invariably fail. And even at its peak, PSM never produced a superior product - it relied on tariffs to make imported steel expensive and keep its own uncompetitive products profitable.
The best-case scenario at this point is thus not revival, but liquidation. Part-selling the real estate and scrapping the mill could probably cover most liabilities and still leave the government with a small profit. Maintaining the status quo, however, is just an insult to everyone.

title: Returning to MoU
description: Need of the hour is to ensure that de escalation takes place instantly
content:
Need of the hour is to ensure that de-escalation takes place instantly
Mediatory efforts received a shot in the arm as the warring sides in the ongoing Middle East conflict surprisingly toned down their confrontational rhetoric. Much transpired on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly session, where officials from the US, Iran, Qatar and Pakistan collaborated to break the stalemate in talks. Their primary focus was on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, normalising the global supply chain and bringing down oil prices.
The nod from Tehran, which is devising a plan with Oman to reopen the strategic water channel in the Persian Gulf within the next seven days, is a promising development. Likewise, Qatar reaching out to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and the consensus on brokering another ceasefire are momentous achievements. Pakistan pushed the envelope further by making both the US and Iran realise that going back to the Islamabad MoU is the way forward. This aspect has been squarely endorsed and appreciated by the UN secretary-general, too.
The need of the hour is to ensure that de-escalation takes place instantly. Reports that a format is being worked out for resuming parleys are encouraging; incidentally, these reports emerged after a huddle in the Oval Office between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. Pezeshkian demonstrated leadership when he told Fox News that his country is not interested in continuing the war and that the ball is in Washington's court. This needs to be read closely with reports that Tehran has hinted at reopening the Strait in exchange for the lifting of the US naval blockade and the unfreezing of its assets.
This impasse is already taking a toll on global economics. The suspension of shipping through the Red Sea's Bab El-Mandeb - as the Houthis have triggered another conflagration - is unnerving. Any broadening of the conflict across Yemen and its spillover into the wider region would be catastrophic. A one-point move can help address all eventualities: Iran and the US must return to the understanding reached in Islamabad. Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian Foreign Minister, has convincingly floated that idea as the way forward.
