title: Dozens of delegates walk out of UN hall at start of Netanyahu speech
description: Netanyahu called delegates who walked out of the UN hall  cowards   saying   Please do so now
content:
Most of the UNGA hall's seats were empty
Dozens of delegates streamed out as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday mounted a forceful defence of Israel's actions in the region at the United Nations, seeking to counter growing international isolation ahead of elections he could lose.
As Netanyahu took to the rostrum, officials walked out of the General Assembly meeting of world leaders in protest, prompting him to describe them as "moral cowards".
Dozens of delegates walked out of the assembly hall as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began his UN General Assembly address on Thursday. Netanyahu’s speech came as Israel faced growing criticism from world leaders at this year’s assembly over its genocidal war in Gaza. pic.twitter.com/QA5nUnI8cM
Before Netanyahu's speech, large crowds demonstrated near UN headquarters and elsewhere in New York, against his appearance and accusing him of committing "genocide" in Gaza.
The protests included anti-Zionist Orthodox Jews carrying signs describing Netanyahu as a "war criminal", as well as American and Israeli Jewish opposition groups and Western and Palestinian organisations opposing the genocidal war.
Delegates walk out as Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US, September 24, 2026. REUTERS
The Yedioth Ahronoth Israeli newspaper said that "large crowds" left the hall immediately after Netanyahu took the podium, before he began speaking.
Israel's Channel 12 also published an image showing most of the hall's seats empty.
Read More: Netanyahu's fleeting visit to New York mirrors strained US ties
Netanyahu has been wanted by the ICC since 2024.
He used his UN address to berate New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani for calling him a war criminal, Western European leaders for what he called succumbing to the "antisemitic mobs", and Qatar and Turkiye for allegedly spreading lies about his country.
"You tried to stop me from coming here. You tried. You tried to silence me. Well, you can't silence me. You can't silence the truth," Netanyahu said of Mamdani.
Mamdani campaigned for office on a promise to have Netanyahu arrested for alleged war crimes should he visit the largest US city, but later said he had determined he lacked the legal authority to do so.
This week, Mamdani described Netanyahu as "the architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians".
Addressing the mayor directly after a feud in the run-up to his arrival in New York, Netanyahu falsely accused Mamdani of supporting Hamas.
"To all those spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the antisemitic mayor of New York, I say this: Shame on you!"
Netanyahu, who rejected the war crimes allegations, was making his first visit to New York since Mamdani took office in January.
In a statement, Mamdani said: "As he has done time and again, Prime Minister Netanyahu used his speech to repeat baseless lies ​meant to sanitise his genocide of Palestinians. Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity.”
Demonstrators protest ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's address to the United Nations 81st General Assembly in New York City, US, September 24, 2026. REUTERS
With general elections less than five weeks away, Netanyahu spoke for about 40 minutes in what amounted to a campaign-style speech, broadcast live in evening prime time on all four of Israel's main television channels.
Ahead of his speech, Netanyahu's government paid to place 500 pro-Israel and anti-Iran billboards and dozens of trucks carrying messages in support of Israel across Manhattan, his office said in a statement.
Netanyahu, who is seen losing power in opinion polls, showcased what he said was Israel's fight on seven fronts.
Israel's longest-serving prime minister has in the past made a visual spectacle of his UN appearances, using charts, diagrams and props to warn of Iran's nuclear programme, which Tehran says is for civilian purposes.
Read More: How would Jewish supremacists act?
On Thursday, he held up a pager in reference to an attack that crippled Iran-backed Hezbollah members in Lebanon and showed a Starlink satellite internet receiver, which he said he would leave for the Iranian delegation.
"So when they inevitably defect, they too will be able to freely tell their story on social media," he said, adding that it was only a matter of time before the Iranian authorities would be toppled by the people.
Anti-Israel protesters took to New York City streets. Several hundred protesters gathered near the United Nations, with dozens blocking traffic and chanting, "Stop arming Israel, let Gaza live" and "Stop arming Israel, let Iran live."
The election campaign in Israel is unfolding amid mounting criticism of the country's Gaza war.
Netanyahu was making a short visit to the United States for his UN address and, unusually, without a planned meeting with US President Donald Trump, whom he praised during his speech.
"We will continue to defend our state. We will continue to win because we have no other choice. In this battle against the barbarians, we've had no greater partner than President Trump. I thank him. I thank him for his bold leadership," he said.
Israel has faced deepening diplomatic isolation since launching its war in Gaza ​in response to the Hamas-led ⁠attacks on Israel nearly three years ago.
Netanyahu is unable to travel to many countries because of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant, issued against him and his then-defence minister as well as the then-military commander of Hamas in 2024.
Earlier this month, once-steadfast allies Britain, France and Canada announced sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which drew a muted response from Washington.
"The leaders of these countries have chosen to succumb to the antisemitic ⁠mobs. They've chosen ​weakness. They've chosen appeasement," Netanyahu said.
He played down worsening violence in the occupied West Bank by Israeli settlers, describing it as "a ​handful of young juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who throw stones, who chop down olive trees".
"Occasionally ... they lit some fires. I can't stand that. I won't stand for vigilantism. We're a country of law."

title: Two wars and the World Order
description: Current geopolitical reality projects a starkly different outcome
content:
Current geopolitical reality projects a starkly different outcome
In the early months of World War-I, HG Wells dubbed it "the war to end all wars" in the hope that such unprecedented devastation would force humanity to abolish conflict forever. Wells was proven wrong. World War-II quickly followed, then the Cold War, and now an endless list of global conflicts. It seems humanity and war simply go hand in hand.
War is, however, the most extreme reaction. It is waged when all other peaceful options have been exhausted, and when at least one side is confident that the war will end the conflict permanently in its favour. But as history shows, that is seldom the case. War only suppresses an enemy's hostility for a limited time; it can never destroy their will to restock, regroup, reassess and reengage. That is human nature. Because human will and agency cannot be chained, they will always find and forge novel paths.
The odd thing about war is that it pulls adversaries into a field fraught with depleting stocks, dwindling manpower, improvisation, urgent action, and the on-the-spot evolution of strategy, technology, and battlefield structure. While a nation may enter a conflict with confident calculations, the mathematics of war change rapidly. In an era where technological advancement constantly hits new peaks, conventional battlegrounds are now fundamentally altered by cyber, AI, space and psychological operations. Crucially, history proves that even the most impoverished populations quickly adapt to counter top-tier militaries, driven by the existential need to survive and protect their freedom.
This brings us to this critical question: can the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East truly pave the way for a lasting peace, whether among rival Middle Eastern factions or between the Global North and Global South? Those who initiated these wars likely believed they could subdue their adversaries for decades, forcibly integrating them into a manufactured world order. However, the current geopolitical reality projects a starkly different outcome.
It may seem that the US and Israel have successfully pitted Middle Eastern states against one another. For instance, Iran has launched ballistic missiles and attack drones against US facilities in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq/Kurdistan, and the UAE. With the Strait of Hormuz already stranded, the Yemenis are threatening to close the Bab al-Mandab. This has practically ignited a second war between Yemen and Saudi Arabia, as the Houthis launch drone and missile salvos targeting Red Sea infrastructure, including Yanbu, and seize coastal areas like Mokha, Dhubab, Mayyum and the Hanish Islands from Yemen's southern government. Simultaneously, Saudi Arabia's critical East-West oil pipeline was struck by Iraqi militias, while the Houthis targeted the Saudi cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran. All the while, Israel continues pounding targets in southern Lebanon and southern Syria.
On the other hand, repeated drone strikes by Ukraine have damaged Russian refineries, reduced fuel production and forced Moscow to restrict exports. By September, half of Russia's six largest diesel-producing refineries had reduced output substantially or were shut altogether. In August, Russian product exports plummeted to around half of the levels recorded a year earlier. In return Russia has started a major operation targeting Ukrainian cities and military infrastructures.
This is surely a daunting scenario. Oil shortages and prices can potentially bring the global economy to a standstill. Prolonged war can bring unprecedented devastation to the regions and can easily spill over into the Middle East neighborhood and Europe. But while the wars are on, a lot of restocking, regrouping, reassessing has gone on. In spite of the US pressure, Saudi Arabia and Turkey have entered the Makkah Defence Pact with Pakistan, and Egypt wants to be a part of it too. Pakistan has also made a defence partnership with Somalia for joint counterterrorism and security assistance. Pakistan Air Force and Pakistan Navy will help build and train the Somali armies, which will perhaps help stop the ongoing balkanisation of Somalia, and my bring us into a direct confrontation with Israel, as Israel supports the separation of Somaliland.
Europe, which envisioned a weakened Russia and the entry of Ukraine into the EU at the conclusion of the conflict, now finds itself on the verge of war. For months, top European generals and leaders have been warning their citizens to prepare for conflict - a clear sign that events have unfolded contrary to their expectations. At the end of the war, the US will likely be irrelevant in the Middle East, its bases torn down and deserted, leaving Israel isolated and vulnerable. Instead, the Middle East will integrate into the Global South, establishing its own security architecture complemented by China and Russia.
This week, just as the Iranian president arrived to deliver his speech at the UN General Assembly in New York, the US Treasury threatened restrictions on 27 Iranian airlines. Washington warned that any entity providing services to these carriers would be frozen out of the dollar system. It is for precisely this type of reason that China, along with its BRICS partners, is moving toward a new gold-backed currency basket to eliminate the risk of unilateral US sanctions. China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System already processes an estimated $26 trillion in cross-border trade using yuan, spanning at least 192 countries and regions including Russia and Iran. Concurrently, large gold vaults have been established in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Singapore, Dubai and Moscow, laying the groundwork for an alternative financial infrastructure where Global South nations can trade without fear of financial blockades.
By the end of these two wars, there may be more wars, but the world will certainly have a new order of things. Nations that successfully navigate these tectonic shifts in the strategic and economic landscape can lead their citizens into an era of strength, peace and progress. Conversely, the naive will be marginalised once more. Ultimately, no historical shift can change the inherent human nature of the dominant actors who crave power. The public must therefore advocate for themselves, driving the hard push toward the lasting peace and prosperity they deserve.

title: Time to divest the hybrid
description: Hybrid is neither here nor there  It is time to make the change
content:
Hybrid is neither here nor there. It is time to make the change
We have been in it for a long time now. It all began on April 10, 2022, when an order was put in place to keep functioning normally. It will soon be five years to that day – the normal tenure of any government. Beyond claims of avoiding an impending default, we can count little else as progress in the domains the governing concoction oversees. Perhaps, legally and constitutionally, we may barely be in the green, but that would not have been possible without large-scale legislative manipulation and court-packing. That in its wake is a certain stink goes without saying. At the hands of some legal luminaries, this surely must count as the lowest point in our national journey of the last five years.
Through it all, we coined, and then popularised, and then normalised the term hybrid, which was as repugnant as the derogatory and symbolic pointing of the fingers at the shoulders when referring to the Establishment whenever a politician was put on the spot. In the meantime, the military forces distinguished themselves in 2025, and then added value to it by employing their global standing for significant diplomatic gains. The function, though, primarily lay in the government's corner. The government has used the opportunity to reinforce the notion of hybridity that this government relishes. It touts PTI as the common threat, but the impunity it employs in this commonness is all too apparent. The government thus continues to enjoy a free ride. And it has flown plenty to all corners of the world without alleviating an iota of difficulty for the common man in whose name they don the ruler's robes.
The war in the Middle East has been a huge impediment, undoubtedly, as most global economies point South, but without it too there was no sign of easing of the frills and the extravagance that has accompanied the style of governance when a default has always loomed. Conscience slowly goes to sleep. In this class, conscience anyway is rare. Some do cry to at least wear a pretence, but when malignance can be easily redirected, why even bother? The rip-off is thus blatant and rampant. Keeping the hybrid as a moniker is injurious to the health of the institution, which is the only one serving the nation with lives and blood. This blood and these lives don't come cheap. Perhaps it is time to ring this by those who do not care much.
Economy, terrorism, poverty, inability to sustain life, taxes, and then more taxes in levies and the like in every activity that needs government involvement, along with now the normalised function of corruption, have the common man on the floor with the government all over it. Nothing has eased for the common man. Suicides at the hands of helplessness, and empty slogans of this and another project and plan continue to consume what is left of this land. Nothing ever gets done. Pilot projects may start, but then cease to go beyond. The frustration is boiling over. Forget the PTI; it is now the common man who is crushed under. PTI is a political beast; it may still live, but not the common souls for whom mere survival is a challenge. The political class has practically washed its hands off the people. They rule in the name of hybridity and are making every moment count in their personal aggrandisement and pleasure.
It is time to call farce by its name, and do what is right for the moment and what will set the nation back on track. Two hundred and fifty million are just too many to be left to the whims of those who only serve their cause. The last five years of ever-increasing debt and financial hamstringing, beginning with the dreaded default, suggest that whatever this nation has produced has only filled the coffers of the few. Debt accumulates because this government borrows between fifteen and twenty billion daily to keep itself functional. What is produced, whether in commodities or in products and energy, remains patently limited to the mercantilists. This has given rise to cartels. The order has conveniently turned rapacious even when it claims to be populist in blatant obfuscation of the truth.
There are two ways to take the word 'hybrid' off the nomenclature. If this were a developed and a genuine democracy, the default recourse would be fresh elections, but then we have strangled ourselves to the point of paralysis, bound in fear of the unknown and the not-so-unexpected. If genuine democracy is not what we can afford, considering multiple apprehensions which limit our choices, it is better to declare a clean break from the façade of anything hybrid and establish a parallel order of an appointed government of specialists and experts for a period of five years to cleanse the system of the malfeasance that has corrupted it. The system is not merely corroded over time; it has been deliberately corrupted to the point of submission. This can only be cleaned from within by expunging what is odious and distorted.
The 1973 Constitution should still be the core framework of the desired system minus its manipulative and exploitative disfigurations. As societies and economies evolve, statutes need updating; where needed, those updates should be incorporated. The appointed government must institute economic and governance reforms with built-in constitutional cover. Local bodies must be fully protected in continuity and tenure. And so much more, including the NFC and its method of allocation. The 18th Amendment needs a wholesome review and a clear separation made of provincial and federal responsibilities. A reversion to full democratic order must accompany a wholesome retention of these commitments as basic structures which should remain unaltered.
We need to bring governance back from non-issues such as 'Long Marches' to matters of utmost importance to people, like governance and resource allocation. The politicos have a way of creating distractions and diversions to obfuscate the essential with the meaninglessly sensational. A more empathetic government with a given role and task will be able to focus on the essentials rather than carve out favours for itself and its cronies in the name of the people. A task-oriented government can deliver better in challenging times. If indeed blame is to be shared without direct involvement in governance, as is the case in the present hybrid arrangement, a more capable set of people should be put in place for a given period across the entire spectrum under Establishment's sole supervision. Just as was done for the PDM. Hybrid is neither here nor there. It is time to make the change.

title: Green energy revolution needs a cleaner supply chain
description: China s success in the green transformation is no accident
content:
China's success in the green transformation is no accident
For years, Western politicians talked about turning the fight against climate change into an economic opportunity. China didn't just talk about it, it built an economic powerhouse around it.
Today, much of the world's clean-energy supply chain runs through China. The country produces roughly 86% of global solar panels and dominates the manufacturing of batteries, electric vehicles, and many of the materials that make them possible. It helped drive down the cost of solar power to levels that once seemed unimaginable, making clean energy more affordable and accessible for countries around the world. China did not merely join the green transition, it has become its leading force.
China's success in the green transformation is no accident. While many governments treated climate policy primarily as an environmental issue, Beijing saw it as an opportunity to invest in industries of the future. The results are difficult to ignore. China now dominates much of the clean-energy supply chain, from solar manufacturing to battery production.
Western governments, meanwhile, are trying to rebuild their own industrial capacity. The US has used the Inflation Reduction Act to incentivise domestic clean-energy investment. The EU has pursued a similar objective through its Net-Zero Industry Act, seeking to expand European manufacturing and reduce strategic dependencies. These efforts indicate that the green transition is no longer just about reducing carbon emissions, it is increasingly being viewed by major powers as a race for technological leadership and more secure control of the supply chains that will power the twenty-first century.
Thus far, China's lead in vital areas of the green economy is undisputed. But now comes the trickier part.
The world should be wary of replacing one form of dependency with another. Dependence on fossil fuels created decades of geopolitical tussles, in addition to their enormous environmental toll. Building a clean-energy future that relies heavily on concentrated and contested supply chains could create a new set of risks.
Consider cobalt, a critical ingredient in many batteries. The Democratic Republic of Congo produces roughly two-thirds of the world's mined cobalt, while China accounts for around three-quarters of global cobalt refining. Yet the cobalt supply chain is plagued by violations related to labour rights and environmental standards.
Indonesia's nickel industry offers a similar warning. Nickel is increasingly important to battery production, yet much of its processing remains heavily dependent on coal-fired power. The green transition risks losing credibility if consumers celebrate cleaner technologies while pollution and environmental damage are shifted elsewhere.
For much of the world, which is not competing with China for clean-technology dominance, the problem is not that China has become a clean-energy powerhouse. The real issue is that the clean-energy revolution cannot be considered a success if its environmental and social costs are simply displaced farther up the supply chain. A solar panel, electric vehicle or battery may produce fewer emissions in use, but that does not make the technology inherently clean if the minerals needed to produce it are extracted through exploitative practices. A sustainable green transition must account for the full life cycle of clean technologies, from mining and refining to manufacturing and, ultimately, the disposal of the products which use renewable energy.
This is what the next phase of the global energy transition must address. Countries and companies that can build not only more diversified and resilient supply chains but also uphold higher standards of transparency, environmental responsibility and labour protection will help define the next phase of the green energy transition.

title: AI and the arms race
description: AI assisted surveillance and automated threat detection could alter how future crises unfold
content:
AI-assisted surveillance and automated threat detection could alter how future crises unfold
Pakistan's warning at a recent UNSC briefing against artificial intelligence becoming another dimension of the global arms race deserves serious attention. The technology is advancing at a pace that threatens to outstrip the institutions responsible for controlling its use, particularly in matters of international security.
AI-assisted surveillance and automated threat detection could alter how future crises unfold. An erroneous assessment of hostile intent or a false warning could trigger a response before the information has been independently verified. The danger lies in human operators becoming increasingly dependent on systems whose conclusions they may have insufficient time to question. Moreover, AI can facilitate sophisticated cyberattacks and expose critical infrastructure to new vulnerabilities. Its ability to generate convincing false information could also complicate diplomatic efforts during periods of heightened tension. There is, however, a fundamental contradiction at the heart of the global debate. The countries and corporations developing the most advanced AI systems are also competing for economic and strategic advantage. Their willingness to accept restrictions is consequently constrained by the fear of falling behind their rivals.
Pakistan's insistence on inclusive governance raises an equally important concern. Measures introduced in the name of safety must not become a means of consolidating technological power in a handful of countries or denying developing nations access to its benefits. Pakistan, for its part, must ensure that its international position is reflected in its domestic preparedness. Its national security institutions need clearly defined protocols governing the deployment of AI in sensitive operations, while civilian authorities must strengthen their capacity to identify and respond to emerging cyber threats. The country must also invest in the expertise required to participate meaningfully in international rule-making rather than remaining a passive recipient of standards developed elsewhere.

title: A fragile recovery
description: Navigating this treacherous path without a misstep is Pakistan s greatest challenge
content:
Navigating this treacherous path without a misstep is Pakistan's greatest challenge
Though economic indicators are moving in the right direction, Pakistan's economy is still in a very fragile shape, according to the latest Asian Development Bank report. The Asian Development Outlook warns that even though the economy has stabilised, it is still perilously vulnerable to shocks beyond its control. According to the report, GDP growth accelerated to 3.7% in FY26, up from 3.2% the previous year. Gains were largely due to a rebound in manufacturing, which grew 6.6%. Resilient services grew 4.1%, and agricultural recovery grew steadily at 2.9%. Private investment rose 8.6% in real terms, and sovereign credit rating upgrades from S&P and Moody's signaled renewed investor confidence.
But these indicators are not enough to offset the fact that inflation is still concerning - it was 7.1% in FY26 and is projected to climb to 8.3% in FY27, well above the SBP's 5% to 7% target range. While external shocks - such as the conflict involving Iran and its impact on global trade and energy prices - have played an outsized role in raising prices, our economy could have absorbed these shocks more easily if it were not already on shaky ground. The government has also not done itself any favours by choosing to increase spending in several non-revenue areas - meaning that these spending increases will not increase government revenue at all. With interest payments eating up the majority of the budget and defence spending rising 16%, it will be impossible to raise revenue growth to the target of 17.6%. And with household consumption growing by less than 1% and a projected sharp drop in remittances from the Middle East, even more problems could be around the corner.
Navigating this treacherous path without a misstep is Pakistan's greatest challenge. Ironically, the IMF programme conditions that successfully stabilised the economy are now the primary obstacle to reallocating funds for long-term resilience.

title: Xi at White House
description: Xi s landmark welcome says it all
content:
A mother of summits in the White House could act as a precursor for a thaw on global affairs. President Xi Jinping and his host Doanld Trump have an immense responsibility to chart out a roadmap for congeniality not only in the military context, but also in the realms of trade and technology. Xi's first visit to Washington in a decade is taking place at a time when the Middle East is on the edge, and the ensuing controversy over AI supremacy has pitched the two great powers in nexus of controversy. Likewise, the trade and tariffs duel are literally keeping them in a nervous zone, implying a deeper impact on international economics.
The three-day visit, however, is an opportunity to make a new start and do away with their perplexed positions. China has already called for a thaw in the Strait of Hormuz by trying to persuade Iran to get back from the brink. That influence is of immense value to Washington as its military might is on a retreat in the region, and the sole superpower has not been able to cow down a state under sanctions for the last four decades. Likewise, Xi is expected to do some plain-talking on Taiwan, exaggerated US tariffs on its products, and the AI row. To what extent a deal is brokered is hard to guess. It is a given that Xi will be talking to Trump from a position of strength as its trade and diplomatic muscles are well-established over 120 nation-states.
Xi's landmark welcome says it all. A military flyover as the guest is received at the Oval Office, combined with a rare tarmac greeting at Joint Base Andrews, marks a new high in their once-checkered bilateral relationship. Having weathered Trump's trade tariffs, China is well-placed to negotiate from a position of strength - securing a new deal regarding technological supremacy while extending the trade truce on favorable terms. At the very least, the desired breakthrough is to agree on a new modus operandi for cooperation and help bring the volatile conflict in the Middle East to an end.

title: Contraception Day  let us put mothers at the centre
description: Around 37  of births in Pakistan occur within less than two years of the preceding birth
content:
Around 37% of births in Pakistan occur within less than two years of the preceding birth
The Holy Quran holds mothers in the highest esteem and reminds Muslims of the immense sacrifices they make. It calls upon believers to be grateful to Allah and to their mothers, who carry a child through hardship, give birth with difficulty, and nurture and care for that child. Yet, in Pakistan, this hardship is too often compounded by unintended pregnancies, closely spaced births, inadequate nutrition and limited access to quality reproductive health services.
The burden falls most heavily on women from poorer households and those living in rural, remote and underserved communities. Around 37% of births in Pakistan occur within less than two years of the preceding birth, exposing mothers and children to avoidable risks. For women already affected by anaemia, repeated and closely spaced pregnancies can further undermine health and, in severe cases, threaten their lives.
The consequences extend to the child. Babies born following short birth intervals are more likely to be born prematurely or with low birth weight, increasing their vulnerability during the critical first months of life. These are not merely demographic statistics; they represent preventable human suffering. They contribute to Pakistan's continuing maternal and infant mortality challenges and to population growth that is increasingly difficult to reconcile with available resources and development aspirations.
Other regional countries, including several Muslim-majority countries, have demonstrated that these outcomes can change when reproductive health and family planning are treated as essential components of human development.
World Contraception Day, observed on 26 September, should therefore be more than another date on the calendar. It should prompt parliament, policymakers, media, professionals and civil society to ask a fundamental question: what are we doing to enable couples to exercise their reproductive intentions safely, voluntarily and with dignity?
Access, affordability and acceptability of services remain deeply unequal. A fragile health system, shortages of commodities, limited counselling and persistent gender norms and other social barriers continue to constrain informed choice. The resulting inequity is a social injustice that should concern us all. Protecting mothers' health and enabling families to plan the timing and number of their children must become central to Pakistan's human development agenda.
This requires coordinated action. The federal government must provide strategic direction and coordination; provinces must ensure effective implementation; adequate financing must follow commitments; the private sector must be meaningfully engaged; and communities must have a voice. Healthcare professionals and programme managers must work together to expand access to high-quality, rights-based family planning, including through private providers and the country's large network of male general practitioners.
But contraception alone cannot carry the burden of development. We must also ask whether development itself is a powerful determinant of fertility. Universal education improved maternal and child health, skills development, decent employment and higher household incomes can expand women's and couples' autonomy choices and aspirations.
The Sustainable Development Goals deadline is approaching rapidly, and progress on health, gender equality, poverty, education and other goals is inseparable from reproductive health and demographic realities. The path forward begins with a healthy, educated and empowered mother and healthy, thriving children.
On World Contraception Day, in Pakistan - where use of contraceptives has stagnated for two decades and lags behind much of the region - let us move beyond rhetoric and symbolism to remove barriers to access, expand choice and reduce the unmet need for family planning. Let us build a people-centred development agenda in which every mother can survive pregnancy, every couple can make informed reproductive choices, and every child can begin life with a fair opportunity to thrive.

title: Pakistan among 12 countries opposing new permanent UN Security Council seats
description: Uniting for Consensus group rejects permanent UN Security Council seats  seeks elected members and longer terms
content:
Uniting for Consensus group rejects permanent UN Security Council seats, seeks elected members and longer terms
Pakistan and 11 other countries, as part of the Uniting for Consensus group, opposed the creation of new permanent seats on the UN Security Council (UNSC) on Thursday, calling instead for an expansion of elected membership, including longer-term rotational seats.
The group, comprising Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Italy, Malta, Mexico, Pakistan, South Korea, San Marino, Spain and Türkiye, issued a joint statement during the high-level week of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
“Our shared goal is to work for a more representative, democratic, transparent, accountable, and effective Council, capable of responding to today’s global challenges,” the statement said.
The group said expanding elected membership would “contribute to the maintenance of international peace and security while preserving the principle of sovereign equality”.
“Such expansion would be the fairest and most democratic way to address Africa’s historical underrepresentation,” as well as that of other underrepresented regions, including Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, it said.
Read More: US and Iran discuss phased deal to reopen Hormuz and end US blockade, sources say
The group “reiterates its opposition to the creation of new permanent seats”, according to the statement.
It also reaffirmed its support for the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) process, calling it “the only legitimate and inclusive platform led by Member States to discuss Security Council reform”.
“The path forward must be based on dialogue, flexibility, and compromise,” the statement said, calling for the reform process to address the “five sets of interconnected issues” and seek “the broadest possible political consensus”.
On the veto, the group said it supported its abolition but called for immediate steps to limit its use in specific circumstances.
“While supporting the abolition of the veto … we should act jointly immediately to move toward its limitation in specific circumstances, including but not limited to mass atrocities and war crimes,” it said.
The statement cited the Franco-Mexican Initiative and the ACT Code of Conduct as existing initiatives aimed at limiting the use of the veto.
The group said it was ready to work with the UN General Assembly president, future IGN co-presidents and all member states during the 81st session to advance comprehensive Security Council reform.

title: Islamabad MoU remains acceptable to Iran  Pezeshkian tells PM Shehbaz in UNGA meet
description: Iranian President hails Pakistan s peace efforts  discusses regional tensions and ways to deepen cooperation
content:
Iranian President hails Pakistan's peace efforts, discusses regional tensions and ways to deepen cooperation
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday said Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had hailed Pakistan’s efforts for peace in the region and conveyed that the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) remained fully acceptable to Iran.
The prime minister was speaking to media representatives alongside his Lebanese counterpart Nawaf Salam after he met with the Iranian president on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Asked about the Islamabad MoU, under which Pakistan had mediated between Iran and the United States, the prime minister said Pakistan’s entire leadership was united in its resolve to further accelerate efforts for peace under the memorandum.
Read More : US and Iran discuss phased deal to reopen Hormuz and end US blockade, sources say
The premier also expressed particular concern over the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, saying brotherly and friendly countries were making efforts to reduce the tensions there.
He said he had also discussed the issue with the Iranian president during their meeting and told him that establishing peace in the region was an urgent need of the hour and that Pakistan would, as before, play its role in this regard.
PM Shehbaz Sharif talks to media https://t.co/olJQsOpRCs
PM Shehbaz said President Pezeshkian had appreciated Pakistan’s efforts and said the Islamabad MoU was still fully acceptable to Iran and that Tehran was ready to take it forward.
Shehbaz condemned the continued atrocities against Lebanon, calling them unacceptable. “Pakistan and Lebanon would work together to promote peace in the region jointly,” he said.
PM Shehbaz reaffirms readiness to play ‘constructive role’ for regional peace
Earlier, PM Shehbaz reaffirmed Pakistan’s readiness to continue playing a “sincere and constructive role” in support of regional peace during a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
The meeting took place a day before the premier is scheduled to address the UN General Assembly on Friday.
According to a statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office, the two leaders reaffirmed the close and longstanding ties between Pakistan and Iran and underscored the need to further strengthen bilateral cooperation across all areas of mutual interest.
Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif met with the President of Islamic Republic of Iran, H.E. Dr. Masoud Pezeshkian today, on the sidelines of the 81st Session of United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York. Deputy Prime Minister/Foreign Minister Senator Mohammad Ishaq… pic.twitter.com/BHkCwC2QNI
“Both leaders also exchanged views on the evolving regional situation,” the statement said.
The prime minister expressed deep concern over the prolonged conflict and emphasised the need for restraint, de-escalation and sustained diplomatic engagement to achieve lasting peace and stability in the region.
PM Shehbaz reaffirmed Pakistan’s readiness to continue playing a sincere and constructive role in support of regional peace and stability, while underscoring the importance of building on and implementing the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.
“President Pezeshkian appreciated Pakistan’s principled diplomacy and concerted efforts for regional peace and security,” the statement said.
The Iranian president also underscored the enduring strength of Pakistan-Iran relations, rooted in shared history, culture and faith, and reaffirmed Tehran’s strong desire to further deepen multifaceted cooperation.
The two sides agreed to work for regional peace, security and prosperity, while underlining the importance of maintaining regular consultations and close coordination to address prevailing challenges and seize opportunities, the statement added.
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Senator Mohammad Ishaq Dar, Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif, SAPM Tariq Fatemi and senior officials from both sides were also present.
The prime minister later, in a post on X, said he had an "important exchange" on the evolving regional situation.
"I reiterated Pakistan’s deep concern over the prolonged conflict and stressed the urgent need for restraint, de-escalation and sustained diplomacy. We remain committed to building on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and will continue to play a sincere and constructive role in the pursuit of lasting peace and stability in the region."
It was a pleasure to meet my dear brother, President Dr. Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York today on the sidelines of UNGA. We reaffirmed the deep and longstanding bonds between Pakistan and Iran and our shared desire to further strengthen bilateral cooperation across all areas of… pic.twitter.com/MB0DkERKVj
Pakistan has already made several mediation attempts during the seven-month-old conflict. Islamabad hosted indirect contacts between the United States and Iran and has continued to argue that the dispute cannot be resolved through military means.
Those efforts have gained urgency as the conflict has begun affecting both major maritime energy routes in the region. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely reduced, while the security situation around Bab el-Mandeb has also deteriorated.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict , with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now ‌blocked by Tehran.
The latest escalation has also pushed up global energy prices and increased pressure on Gulf states to find a diplomatic way out.
Meanwhile, Washington and Tehran remain far from resolving their differences. US President Donald Trump has said he hopes the war with Iran is nearing an end, but negotiations remain stalled.
The talks face a big obstacle as neither side wants to be the first to surrender its leverage, according to comments to Reuters by two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources, but behind Iran's stance is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation.
A deal before the midterms could benefit Trump, as reopening Hormuz could ease tensions in the Gulf, contain oil prices and help bring down politically sensitive US gasoline prices.
Iran's chances of gaining much-needed economic relief may be greater while Trump still has a greater political incentive to strike a bargain.
However, former US negotiator Dennis Ross said he saw only ​a 30% chance of an agreement being reached before the vote, but that both sides may have stronger reasons to make a deal before than after the midterms.
After the midterms, Ross said, Trump may face fewer constraints and be more willing to intensify pressure or consider military options.

title: Talal hopes    better sense    will prevail before PTI march  warns against attempt to turn Islamabad into    Somnath
description: Says no one can dictate terms to state  adds route opened through talks cannot be opened through march
content:
Says no one can dictate terms to state, adds route opened through talks cannot be opened through march
Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry on Thursday said the government’s priority was to resolve the issue with Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) through dialogue and hoped that better sense would prevail before the party’s planned march on Sep 27.
The PTI last month announced a September 27 march in Islamabad to demand the release of Imran Khan, with caravans from across the country expected to converge on the federal capital. The party also planned protests, shutdowns and demonstrations along major highways in cities, including Lahore, Karachi, Hyderabad and Quetta.
Talking to a private television programme, Capital Talk , while recalling the previous PTI protest, the minister admitted that it had not been managed properly last time but said things would be different this time.
Read : PTI Sept 27 protest: IHC rules no political party, public office holder can block roads in Islamabad
“The government believes in minimum use of power, but one thing is very clear this time ... Islamabad is very far away in this manner,” Talal said.
He said the protesters would be treated respectfully, escorted and sent back in the same manner, but warned that if they wanted to come to turn Islamabad into “Somnath”, they would neither be allowed to come nor be able to take anything back.
“The route that can be opened through talks cannot be opened through a march,” he said.
Responding to a question, Talal said there was a difference between the PTI and PML-N long marches, saying the PTI believed that the state would be forced to move on the back foot and did not want to move through political dialogue or the political process.
“If they wanted to move forward, they would never have resigned from the assemblies; neither would May 9 or any such incident have happened. Even now, how are they talking about Somnath?” he said.
He argued that this was the reason why the government was taking all these preventive measures.
The minister said the government’s priority was to resolve the issue without any long march, as this would serve neither the country, their party nor even their leadership.
Also Read : Shafi Jan rejects Naqvi's PTI protest warnings
Asked whether the issue could be resolved through negotiations and dialogue, the minister replied in the affirmative and said that ask the PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar what constitutional right was being denied to the party, describing him as “a very fair man”.
“Ask the K-P chief minister why you are coming and what you want,” he said, adding that the PTI’s demands had nothing to do with the issues of ordinary people but concerned an issue involving a leader.
He warned that no one could dictate terms to the state.
“One thing has to be ended in this country, whether it is TLP or PTI: you cannot dictate terms to the state,” he said, adding that this would not happen and that they would not meet the PTI founder through such means.
Talal also alleged that the PTI was influenced by the Joint Action Committee in Azad Jammu and Kashmir and believed in creating the same environment and adopting the same strategy.
He said the closure of roads would eventually affect ordinary people in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
“All stakeholders of the state are very clear that no nonsense, whether it is from TLP or anyone else, can be allowed. It cannot happen that someone brings 25,000 to 50,000 people to the state, to Islamabad, and says that because I want this, I will get it done before I leave. This will not happen,” he said.
The minister categorically denied that roads had been closed , saying the containers had only been brought to the capital to prevent any situation that could endanger people’s lives and property.
“There is no doubt that hundreds of containers are currently present in Islamabad, but no road has so far been closed,” he said.
He said some routes were currently closed, including the motorway, GT Road and some roads on the northern side, and expressed hope that the issue would be resolved without any confrontation.

“If even a single member of the security forces or a protester is killed, it is Pakistanis who will suffer. We do not want a situation where we are face to face, tear gas is being used,” Talal said, adding that “the other side is always very heavily armed” and referring to them as “non-political people”.
Asked when the containers would be removed, the minister said he was hopeful that they would not have to be used.
“We should remain positive. We hope that before the 27th, within the first 24 to 48 hours, common sense will prevail,” he concluded.

title: Supreme Court puts brakes on Dr Shahnawaz Kumbhar custodial killing trial days before hearing
description: Complainant challenges transfer to sessions court  questions Sindh prosecution s role in police plea
content:
Complainant challenges transfer to sessions court, questions Sindh prosecution's role in police plea
The Supreme Court has stayed the trial of Dr Shahnawaz Kumbhar’s alleged custodial killing and desecration of his body, days before proceedings were due to begin at the Mirpurkhas district and sessions court, throwing into question the Sindh High Court’s order shifting the case from the Anti-Terrorism Court.
The apex court issued the stay on a petition by Dr Ibrahim Kumbhar, complainant in the FIRs concerning Dr Shahnawaz’s alleged custodial killing and desecration . The petitioner has sought restoration of the ATC’s jurisdiction, challenging the SHC’s April 7 order directing the transfer of the case to the sessions court.
The sessions court was scheduled to commence the trial on September 29. Advocate Sajjad Ahmed Chandio, representing the complainant, argued before the Supreme Court that the case should continue before the ATC and objected to the circumstances in which it was transferred.
In a further twist, Chandio told the apex court that Sindh’s deputy prosecutor general, who was expected to prosecute the case against the accused police officers, had instead filed an application on behalf of a DIG and two SSPs accused in the FIR , seeking transfer of the case from the ATC.
The counsel argued that since one of the FIRs under trial had been registered with the FIA , the Sindh deputy prosecutor general had no jurisdiction to represent the accused in seeking transfer of the case. According to him, the matter was supposed to be handled by the federal law officer. The Supreme Court has issued notices to the Prosecutor General Sindh, Advocate General Sindh and Attorney General for Pakistan for October 13, fixing the matter before a three-member bench.
Dr Shahnawaz Kumbhar was shot dead in what the complainant describes as a staged police encounter on September 19, 2024 , after he surrendered to Mirpurkhas police in Karachi in connection with a blasphemy FIR. After his death, his body was allegedly set on fire by a mob while it was being transported to a graveyard in Umerkot district for burial.
The first FIR was registered at Sindhri Police Station, Mirpurkhas, on September 27, 2024, under sections 201, 364, 302, 34, 147, 148, 149 and 120-B of the Pakistan Penal Code, Sections 6 and 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997, and Sections 8 and 9 of the Torture and Custodial Death Prevention and Punishment Act 2022.
A second FIR was registered at the FIA’s Composite Circle Mirpurkhas on October 29, 2024, in connection with the allegation of custodial killing.
Former DIG Mirpurkhas Javed Sonharo Jiskani, former SSP Mirpurkhas Muhammad Asad Chaudhry and former SSP Umerkot Asif Raza Baloch are among 23 accused in the case. The three police officers had approached the ATC Mirpurkhas seeking transfer of the case to the district court, arguing in effect that the terrorism provisions incorporated into the FIR should not apply. The ATC rejected their plea on October 23, 2025. They subsequently approached the SHC, but their two separate criminal revision applications were dismissed on December 12, 2025.
However, a division bench of the SHC comprising Justice Miran Muhammad Shah and Justice Muhammad Hassan subsequently ordered the ATC on April 7, 2026, to transfer the case to the district and sessions court along with the complete record.
The complainant has now challenged that transfer before the Supreme Court, seeking permission for the ATC to proceed with the trial. The apex court’s stay means the sessions court proceedings scheduled for September 29 can not proceed pending further orders in the matter.

title: You botched the case  you   re also suspicious     Judge grills SSP over Mir Raza probe
description: Justice Sial questions police handling of CCTV  evidence  crime scene  and suicide narrative during case proceedings
content:
Justice Sial questions police handling of CCTV, evidence, crime scene, and suicide narrative during case proceedings
The judicial commission probing the death of Mir Raza came down hard on the police investigation on Thursday, with Justice Omar Sial telling SSP Samiullah Soomro that the case had been “botched” in its crucial early days and questioning whether the police officer himself had become a subject of suspicion.
Mir Raza, 25, was allegedly found dead near a wedding hall in Gulistan-e-Johar on July 29. The case had initially been surrounded by uncertainty over whether he had been murdered or died by suicide. The court ordered a second post-mortem exam of the victim after the first report failed to determine the circumstances surrounding his death. The findings of the second post-mortem consolidated his family’s longstanding claim that he had been murdered. The police probe is under serious scrutiny because of lapses that were admitted by the Sindh Police chief.
The commission also grilled senior health officials over the abrupt replacement of a medical board, including the decision to replace Karachi-based specialists with doctors from Hyderabad, and questioned the legal authority behind the changes. The proceedings, headed by Justice Sial, produced a series of pointed exchanges over the handling of CCTV footage, Mir Raza’s mobile phone and smartwatch, the crime scene, witness statements and the police’s apparent focus on a possible suicide and financial-pressure narrative.
Read : Mir Raza case: Commission says Dr Usama targeted Dr Summaiya with smear campaign
During questioning, Justice Sial told SSP Soomro that the first six days of the investigation were crucial and appeared to have seriously compromised the case. “You botched the case. You are also suspicious,” the judge remarked, according to the proceedings.
Soomro told the commission that he had been assigned the investigation on August 2 and headed a team that included SSP East Zubair Nazir, SSP East Investigation Usman Saduzai and, later, officers from the Citizens-Police Liaison Committee.
The commission repeatedly questioned why the family’s statements had not been formally recorded. Soomro said he had directed SSP Zubair Nazir to meet the family, but was told that they had initially declined. Family members disputed that account during the proceedings, saying they had met police officers on August 3.
Justice Sial questioned Soomro over the failure to personally ensure that the family’s statements were recorded, saying that he was the head of the investigation team regardless of the administrative control exercised by other officers.
The commission also challenged the police’s handling of CCTV footage. Soomro acknowledged that only footage from one street had been examined showing Mir Raza travelling in the area, despite the presence of multiple streets and dozens of cameras around the location.
Soomro said more than 30 CCTV clips had been collected, but Justice Sial demanded the relevant memos and questioned why investigators had not systematically secured footage from all surrounding streets before it became unavailable. The judge also questioned a video circulated in the media in which Mir Raza appeared to throw something away. Police had suggested that he was throwing his mobile phone, but Soomro conceded that the footage did not establish this conclusively.
Also Read : Mir Raza commission warns businessman over media interviews
The handling of the mobile phone came under further scrutiny. Soomro said he had neither seen the phone nor the officer who recovered it, while the commission questioned why the recovery and subsequent transfer of such a crucial piece of evidence had not been properly documented.
The smartwatch was another major point of contention. Soomro said it had been seized before he took charge and that he had not personally seen it. Justice Sial pointed out that another police officer had said the smartwatch was handed to Soomro, highlighting conflicting accounts within the investigation. The commission also questioned why no action had apparently been taken against subordinate officers despite contradictions in their statements and evidence-handling procedures.
The treatment of the crime scene drew some of the strongest criticism. Soomro told the commission that investigators had initially failed to find a shell casing and that bushes near the scene were later burned during a search. He said an SIU inspector, Ghaus, had taken the decision to burn the bushes, while a 40-member team subsequently found the shell casing on August 6.
Justice Sial questioned whether burning vegetation at a crime scene was standard investigative practice and demanded the name of the person who had authorised the action.
The judge also questioned why a holster allegedly recovered on July 31 had not been found when Mir Raza’s body was discovered on July 29. Soomro said the holster should have been recovered on the day the body was found if the scene had been properly searched. Justice Sial criticised the overall handling of the crime scene, saying the recovery of evidence had effectively been compromised.
Suicide, financial-pressure narrative questioned
The commission also examined how the narrative of suicide and financial pressure entered the investigation. Soomro said statements from Raza’s friends and business associates referred to financial pressure and that investigators had also received information about his cryptocurrency trading. He denied having deliberately promoted a suicide narrative in the media, saying he had told a journalist that the available evidence raised concerns about suicide. The commission questioned how police could publicly discuss such a theory when the family’s formal statements had not yet been recorded.
Jibran Nasir, counsel for Mir Raza’s family, argued that the police had failed to properly investigate alternative lines of inquiry and had focused disproportionately on financial pressure.
Read More : Cyber probe ordered into online campaign against police surgeon
The commission also questioned the role of ASP Nida, asking why she appeared repeatedly in different stages of the investigation. Soomro said she had initially been involved in speaking to Mir Raza’s fiancée and had accompanied officers during interviews and meetings. Justice Sial questioned whether she had been assigned any specific investigative responsibility and why she was involved in interactions with several officials and agencies.
The proceedings also touched on claims involving Raza’s alleged financial dealings, including screenshots and a voice note attributed to Ali Shahz. The commission questioned how such material reached the media and why some witnesses were not formally examined until weeks after the incident.
Earlier, the commission questioned Health Secretary Tahir Hussain Sangi over the decision to alter the medical board dealing with the case. Justice Sial asked why the board had been changed late at night and why Karachi specialists were replaced by doctors from Hyderabad. Sangi said he had been informed that the existing board did not include sufficiently senior forensic specialists and that adding independent experts was considered more transparent.
The judge questioned the legal basis for changing the board and asked whether the police surgeon had the authority to constitute a medical board for an exhumation. When Sangi referred to previous court orders involving medical boards, Justice Sial challenged him to produce a specific legal precedent, saying the secretary appeared to be shifting responsibility to the courts.
Also Read : NCCIA obtains Binance, crypto transaction data in Mir Raza murder case
The commission also questioned whether Sangi had authorised Special Secretary Health Shaharyar Memon to seek a fresh review of the board. Sangi said he had directed the special secretary to ensure that the board was changed in accordance with the court’s directions, while maintaining that individual members could be added without his personal approval.
Justice Sial questioned why Hyderabad doctors had been brought into a case based in Karachi, asking whether Karachi or Hyderabad was geographically closer under the relevant law. The judge also questioned whether the change had actually improved transparency, noting that the earlier board already contained experienced specialists.
Shaharyar Memon, now director general health services and formerly special secretary, was subsequently summoned by the commission. Memon denied having the authority to replace the medical board, saying he had merely asked the DG Health to review the existing arrangement after learning that the police surgeon had constituted a board. The commission repeatedly pressed him on the legal basis for ordering a review and asked whether he had acted beyond his authority. Memon said the decision was taken in good faith and in light of the court order.
Justice Sial, however, questioned the contradictory accounts between Memon, Sangi and the former DG Health over who had initiated the changes and who had proposed the new members.
The judge also questioned Memon over his connection to Liaquat University, where he had studied, and raised the fact that other individuals connected to the case had also studied there. The commission was told that the police had now requested the formation of a new “super medical board”. Memon confirmed that an application had been received from DIG Amir Farooqi under the Sindh Medico-Legal Act 2023 and was being reviewed.
The commission also questioned the police over witness statements, with the proceedings indicating that several statements had allegedly been recorded by people other than the designated investigating officer and subsequently signed by him. Soomro acknowledged that such a practice would be contrary to procedure and that investigating officers should record statements themselves. Justice Sial questioned whether investigators had deliberately relied on weak investigative procedures and criticised the repeated shifting of responsibility among officers.
The commission also examined geofencing, vehicles and people appearing in CCTV footage, the role of guesthouse employees and the possible movements of a motorcyclist seen in the area.
Read : Police surgeon alleges pressure, threats to hide evidence suggesting murder before Mir Raza judicial commission
Soomro said investigators had interviewed guesthouse employees and found nothing suspicious among four people examined, while one person had reportedly left for Umerkot and another motorcyclist could not be traced. The commission questioned why investigators had not pursued every person appearing in the available footage.
Advocate Nasir also alleged that the family had identified suspicious activity at a guesthouse and that some people fled after being shown Mir Raza’s photograph. These claims were put before the commission during the proceedings.
Advocate Nasir alleges police trying to portray murder as suicide
Later, speaking to reporters after proceedings before the Judicial Commission, Nasir alleged that police had failed to properly investigate the case and were instead attempting to establish the death as a suicide.
He said the police had remained focused from the outset on the premise that there was no killer involved. “The killer’s identity will emerge from CDR and CCTV footage. How can a killer be identified through a bullet mark or acid?” he asked, alleging that police were trying to turn the case into one of suicide.
Nasir said the statements of the Sindh health secretary and SSP Samiullah Soomro were recorded before the commission during Thursday’s proceedings.
He said it had also been confirmed that a request had been made by Amir Farooqui for permission to constitute a super medical board to review the findings of the previous medical boards. “How will a super medical board identify the killer?” Nasir questioned, alleging that the move was aimed at protecting officials from scrutiny.
The Mir Raza family lawyer said the proceedings had exposed shortcomings in the initial police investigation, claiming that there were nine streets in the area but CCTV footage from only one street had been examined.
The police, he alleged, conducted “interviews” of witnesses instead of recording their statements through the prescribed legal procedure and subsequently promoted their own narrative.
Nasir also questioned why investigators had repeatedly recorded the statement of Dr Usama while no member of the medical board had so far had their statement recorded. “Dr Usama was called on August 9, which the SSP has confirmed. But why was Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed not asked to give a presentation in the same manner?” he asked.
According to Nasir, investigators had yet to establish the identities of the person travelling in a white Alto and a motorcyclist seen in connection with the case.
He also said the family had not been informed about the telephone numbers identified through geofencing. “CCTV footage may have been lost, but geofencing and CDR records still exist,” he added.
Read More : Discrepancies emerge in Mir Raza autopsy as ‘missing’ details surface in judicial commission hearing
Nasir alleged that crucial evidence had been lost during the first 10 days of the investigation and questioned whether any action had been taken against police officers responsible for the initial probe. He said the investigation team had also refused to provide access to certain records before the commission.
“The police have given their account on oath and have effectively shown that they did not conduct the investigation properly. The JIT has to do the work that the police investigation failed to do,” he said.
Nasir said there was no legal bar on constituting a Joint Investigation Team and reiterated that the family had demanded a JIT from the first day.
He also alleged that the investigation had failed to establish the movements of Shahzaib Mushtaq in Karachi between August 4 and 6, adding that SSP Soomro had expressed ignorance about the matter.
The commission, according to Nasir, observed that police had examined CCTV footage from only one street and had failed to check other available cameras. He said the family had requested that additional IGs and DIGs concerned be summoned before the commission in their personal capacity.
Nasir further said the request for a super medical board had raised questions about the intentions of the new investigation team. “If the Sindh government takes any administrative decision to constitute a super medical board on the police’s request, we will challenge it,” he added.

title: Punjab approves new curriculum  promises lighter schoolbags and AI education from Class I
description: Attempt to shift classroom teaching away from rote memorisation towards concept based  technology assisted learning
content:
Attempt to shift classroom teaching away from rote memorisation towards concept-based, technology-assisted learning
The Punjab government on Thursday approved a major overhaul of the school curriculum while promising to reduce the volume of textbooks by 25%, introduce artificial intelligence (AI) education from Class I to XII and attach QR codes to textbooks to give students access to video lessons.
The Punjab government also proposed new measures to address corporal punishment and student mental health.
According to details, the decisions were taken at a special meeting on education reforms chaired by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif amid a wider attempt by the provincial government to shift classroom teaching away from rote memorisation towards concept-based and technology-assisted learning.
پنجاب کے بچوں کے لیے پڑھائی کا انداز بدلنے جا رہا ہے! وزیراعلیٰ مریم نوازشریف نے نئے نصاب کی منظوری دے دی جس سے کتابوں کا بوجھ 25 فیصد کم ہوگا، ہر کتاب میں QR کوڈ کے ذریعے ویڈیو سبق ملے گا اور کلاس ون سے بارہویں تک AI کی تعلیم شامل ہوگی۔ اساتذہ کی مینٹل ہیلتھ ٹریننگ، بچوں کے لیے… pic.twitter.com/9FqlVtFwFy
According to details presented at the meeting, the new curriculum would cover subjects including English, mathematics, Urdu, social studies and early childhood education. The Punjab Education Curriculum, Training and Assessment Authority (PECTAA), the provincial body responsible for curriculum, teacher training and assessment, briefed the meeting on the proposed changes. PECTAA described its curriculum mandate as promoting deeper learning, higher-order thinking and innovation rather than merely revising textbook content.
Read : Punjab approves new primary curriculum
One of the most visible changes would be an attempt to reduce the amount of material students had to carry and study. The government said textbook volume would be cut by 25% with the stated objective of discouraging rote learning and allowing greater emphasis on understanding concepts.
However, the implementation of the reduction would be crucial. A smaller textbook did not automatically mean a lighter academic workload if examination requirements, homework and classroom assessments continued to demand the same volume of preparation. The government would therefore face the challenge of ensuring that curriculum reduction was reflected in teaching and assessment practices rather than remaining limited to the physical size of books.
Al Education from Grade 1, QR codes on every textbook for instant access to video lessons CM Maryam Nawaz has approved a new curriculum for Punjab's children. pic.twitter.com/bsIP6Mr5Xe
According to an official of the Punjab education ministry, the new textbooks are also planned to contain QR codes that students could scan to access video lessons related to the relevant topic. The move could provide children with an additional learning resource outside conventional classroom teaching, particularly where teachers had limited time to explain difficult concepts. The effectiveness of the system, however, would depend on access to smartphones or other devices, internet connectivity and the availability of quality digital material in schools and homes.
"پنجاب میں تاریخی جامع تعلیمی اصلاحات" ♦: نصابی کتب کے مصنفین خود اساتذہ کی تربیت کریں گے ♦: ہر نصابی کتاب میں کیو آر کوڈ سکین کر کے متعلقہ موضوع کا ویڈیو سبق دیکھا جا سکے گا pic.twitter.com/QJBZj58BG5
Another major component was the proposed introduction of AI education from Class I through Class XII. The chief minister directed officials to prepare an AI curriculum and also stressed the need for laboratories alongside the new subject.
The proposal represents a substantial expansion of technology education because it envisages exposing children to AI concepts from the earliest years of schooling rather than restricting advanced digital learning to secondary or higher education. Officials would nevertheless have to determine how AI content was differentiated according to age, how teachers would be trained, and what infrastructure would be required before the programme could operate effectively across Punjab's government schools.
Punjab Chief Minister @MaryamNSharif has approved the new curriculum for schools and directed inclusion of artificial intelligence in the curriculum from Classes One to Twelve @GovtofPunjabPK #News #RadioPakistan https://t.co/IysJi08LRL
The government has set a deadline to complete printing of the new textbooks before March in the coming year and has been putting pressure on the education authorities to complete curriculum development, review, production and distribution within a relatively tight schedule.
The reform package also moves beyond academic content, as for the first time in Punjab the government has decided to initiate mental health training for teachers. A proposal to place visiting faculty psychologists in every district was also considered, while the chief minister directed authorities to develop online counselling facilities for students.
The measures indicate an attempt to address behavioural and emotional issues within schools through counselling and trained personnel rather than relying primarily on punishment. Yet the proposed psychologist model would require sufficient professional staff, clear referral mechanisms and confidentiality safeguards if counselling was to become a meaningful service rather than another formal school initiative.
The meeting also agreed in principle on legislation aimed at eliminating corporal punishment in schools. A proposal was discussed to establish “discipline corners” in classrooms as an alternative to physical punishment. The chief minister said physical violence against children could leave lasting effects on their lives.
The government also agreed to dedicate one day every week to teacher training. Under the proposed model, authors of the new textbooks would themselves train teachers in their use, potentially creating a direct link between curriculum design and classroom delivery.
The decision came as PECTAA was already handling curriculum, training, assessment and oversight functions under the provincial education system. Its official material lists existing textbooks and revised curricula across multiple grades and subjects, showing that the new programme would have to operate alongside a sizeable existing academic and administrative framework.
The government said progress had already been made in English language training, with 35,000 teachers in 31 tehsils across 12 districts completing the programme.
Maryam said that she wanted government schools to develop into a strong educational model and stressed that primary education should receive particular attention because weaknesses at the foundation level could affect learning in later grades.
The government also framed increased digital literacy as a priority, but the scale of Punjab's public school system means that the success of the reforms would ultimately depend on execution, such as timely textbook printing, teacher preparation, functioning laboratories, digital access, quality control of QR-linked lessons, counselling capacity and consistent enforcement of the proposed ban on corporal punishment.
The new curriculum therefore represents more than a change in textbooks. Its real test would be whether the promised shift from memorisation to understanding, punishment to counselling and conventional teaching to technology-supported learning could be translated into everyday classroom practice across Punjab.
