title: US  Iran should return to dialogue to end war  Xi tells Trump at White House
description: President Xi expresses China   s support for the US  Iran returning to the framework deal they agreed to in June
content:
President Xi expresses China’s support for the US, Iran returning to the framework deal they agreed to in June
During a closed-door meeting at the White House on Thursday, Chinese President Xi Jinping urged the United States and Iran to return to dialogue to end their war.
US President Donald Trump and President Xi began closed-door bilateral talks at the White House, with security, trade and technology among the issues on the agenda.
China has “always believed that the sovereignty and security of all countries should be respected” and has played a constructive role in easing tensions, Xi told Trump, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency.
It had "encouraged relevant parties to stay committed to peaceful solutions and maintain the momentum of talks," he said.
He expressed China’s support for the US and Iran returning to the framework deal they agreed to in June and voiced hope that both sides ultimately reach a comprehensive agreement covering the nuclear issue and other matters and achieve peace as soon as possible.
🔴 Xi urges the US and Iran to return to the track of resolving issues through negotiations as soon as possible 🔴 China supports the US and Iran in returning to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, President Xi Jinping says pic.twitter.com/CfNwIuwmYb
After the US and Israel launched the war against Iran on February 28, Pakistan helped secure a ceasefire on April 8 and later hosted more than 20 hours of talks between American and Iranian officials in Islamabad.
Following weeks of mediation, Pakistan and Qatar helped secure the June 18 deal, which provided the two sides with a framework and 60 days to negotiate a longer-term agreement aimed at ending the war.
However, the two sides soon resumed retaliatory strikes, with tensions continuing.
Xi also urged the US to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’” and handle the Taiwan question prudently to lay a solid foundation for bilateral strategic cooperation and relations.
Beijing’s position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity was “crystal clear,” he said.
China considers Taiwan a breakaway province, while Taipei has maintained its self-rule since 1949.
Xi also said that building a constructive China-US relationship based on strategic stability was not an expedient measure nor something that could be achieved overnight, additionally calling for translating the new vision of a constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability into action.
Trump hailed his closed-door bilateral talks with President Xi at the White House. “We had a great meeting,” Trump told reporters while giving an exclusive tour of his new helipad and Marine One.
Trump also said Xi “has great interest in granite. He likes granite.”
“He’s an expert on stone aside from many other things. And he loves good granite,” he added.
Trump on Xi: Xi is an expert on stone, and he loves good granite. pic.twitter.com/embCuoDpOH
The Chinese president left the White House after the bilateral talks but was expected to return later with his wife, Peng Liyuan, for a state dinner.
Earlier in the day, Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi to the White House for a lavish state summit expected to be heavy on symbolism but light on substance, with both leaders keen to showcase stable ties despite thorny issues such as AI, trade, Taiwan, and the war with Iran.
Highlights of the welcome ceremony for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House, hosted by U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday morning. pic.twitter.com/hgQoOrgBay
In remarks from the grand foyer of the White House, Trump touted his "truly ‌great friendship" with Xi and said the two powers had made strides on trade since his trip to China in May.
"During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and 'super intelligence,'" Trump said, using his alternative name for artificial intelligence. "The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come."
Speaking after Trump, Xi said the competition between the US and China should be a "healthy one." US companies were welcome in China, he said, adding that he hopes "Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States."
Xi ​also said both militaries should maintain regular dialogue to improve crisis prevention.
Read: Xi starts high-stakes US visit with call to be ‘partners, not rivals’
"The Thucydides trap can be overcome," he said, referring to the academic theory that sees a risk of rivalry between a rising and an established power ​spiralling into open conflict.
The summit, Xi's first visit to Washington in more than a decade, is the second meeting this year between the leaders of the world's two biggest economies.
"President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship actually, built on the mutual respect and the vital interests of our people." President Trump welcomes President Xi Jinping, Madame Peng Liyuan, and the Chinese delegation to the White House to begin their… pic.twitter.com/48bcpMGRGC
For Trump, who relishes ceremony and prizes his ties with powerful leaders, the visit was as much a matter of national prestige as an opportunity for high-stakes diplomacy. The US president aimed to reciprocate the grand welcome he received in China in ​May.
But Trump and Xi's remarks were not carried live by any US television networks, which have collectively declined to provide footage in protest of the White House's ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico .
President Trump and the President of China Deliver Remarks https://t.co/9xOtSXOgNa
Trump greeted Xi on arrival on Wednesday evening with a red carpet ​on the tarmac, the first time a US president has welcomed a foreign leader at Joint Base Andrews since President Barack Obama met Pope Francis in 2015, according to C-SPAN , which tracks presidential events.
Following their remarks on Thursday, the two leaders observed a military ceremony including a flyover at the Rose Garden, with Chinese flags waving from the Oval Office roof alongside US flags, before a scheduled bilateral meeting.
Xi Jinping: We should coexist in peace. As I have said many times, China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy… pic.twitter.com/oXxtu8z1GK
Trump's embrace of Xi could complicate his campaign message at home ahead of November's midterm elections, when Republicans' narrow congressional majorities are at stake.
The president, for months, has labelled Democrats "communists" in an effort to paint them as too extreme, but he welcomed Xi, the head of the Chinese Communist Party, on Thursday as a dear personal friend.
. @POTUS and @FLOTUS join President Xi and Madame Peng for a Military Review in the Rose Garden pic.twitter.com/RwBkD116ph
Despite the fanfare, analysts say "major" breakthroughs are unlikely, with tangible outcomes ​potentially limited to an extension of a trade truce expiring in November and an agreement to examine threats posed by artificial intelligence.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng that they had agreed to extend until ‌January 10 an ⁠agreement that paused a trade war that saw mutual tariffs top 100%.
Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Thursday morning that the two leaders would discuss "super intelligence" but again indicated he has little interest in imposing new regulations, despite concerns from industry leaders that AI could eventually pose a threat to humans.
"Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is," Trump wrote. "That is China's position also."
During his comments on Thursday, Xi said both countries have "the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control."
Analysts say intense competition between the two powers in AI is likely to limit the scope for anything beyond symbolic agreements.
People familiar with the plans say the talks could ​also yield deals to lower some tariffs, combat drug trafficking ⁠and expand military-to-military dialogue, while Trump is expected to seek the release of Americans and others detained in China.
Xi appears to be in a stronger position, having overseen a surge in China's trade and firmly in control of supplies of rare earth minerals that give him powerful leverage.
Both leaders see advantages in keeping relations stable, with Trump mired in the unpopular Iran war ​and Xi grappling with domestic economic challenges. But beneath the surface are challenges that could reignite tensions, including disputes over Taiwan, export controls and AI. Taiwan, a democratically governed island claimed by ​China, is the most contentious issue.
US ⁠allies in Asia are concerned Trump may be tempted to soften Washington's support for Taipei to lock in economic wins with China.
. @POTUS shows off Marine One and the new White House helipad to President Xi pic.twitter.com/mUTvisgqfg
Xi is expected to press Trump to halt Taiwan arms sales and could do this during a planned visit by the two to the US National Archives on Friday, sources who were briefed on the issue told Reuters . In return, China is offering help to put pressure on Iran, the sources added.
After the May summit, Trump said he was holding in abeyance an arms package to Taiwan worth some $14 billion ⁠and called it ​a "very good negotiating chip."
The leaders will likely discuss the Iran war, but there has been little sign Beijing is willing to exert pressure on its ​ally to yield to US demands.
The guest list for Thursday's state dinner includes CEOs like Apple's Tim Cook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, Alphabet's Sundar Pichai, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Tesla's Elon Musk and Nvidia's Jensen Huang, but despite such an array, people familiar with US plans say Trump is likely to maintain firm export ​controls on US tech Xi wants loosened.
Earlier in the day, Trump gave President Xi a rare personal welcome at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, where Xi kicked off a three-day state visit aimed at easing tensions between the world’s two largest economies.
Trump and First Lady Melania Trump greeted Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, beside their aircraft after the Chinese president arrived at the US military base outside Washington.
American children presenting bouquets to Xi and his wife on arrival to the US. Photo: Xinhua
The welcome marked the first time in 11 years that a US president had greeted a foreign leader at the military facility. According to C-SPAN , the previous US president to welcome a foreign leader there was Barack Obama, who received Pope Francis at the base in 2015.
President Trump welcomes Chinese President Xi to US https://t.co/IcNv3G1IEa
Trump, wearing a long coat and gloves, and Xi stood side by side on the tarmac as a military band played national anthems. A noisy flyover by two B-1 bombers clearly jolted Trump, who grimaced at the roar of jets, while his Chinese guest stood by impassively, according to French newspaper Le Monde .
The ceremony included a red carpet measuring about 100 feet, while six F-22 fighter jets and six F-16s were lined up on the tarmac in a display of military hardware. The elaborate reception differed from the usual protocol for visiting foreign leaders.
Xi’s arrival launched a closely watched visit that is expected to feature extensive pageantry, including military ceremonies, an aircraft flyover and a state dinner at the White House on Thursday.
The Chinese president is due to hold talks with Trump at the White House, with trade, tariffs, artificial intelligence, drug trafficking and military-to-military communication expected to figure prominently on the agenda.
The airport welcome was particularly notable because Trump did not receive a similar personal greeting from Xi when the US president visited Beijing in May.
US President Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan review an honour guard as they arrive ahead of a state visit at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, US, Sep 23, 2026. Photo: Reuters
President Donald J. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump greet President Xi Jinping of China and Madame Peng Liyuan upon their arrival in Washington, D.C., ahead of the state visit at the White House. pic.twitter.com/nm2vGonChM
Xi was accompanied by senior Chinese officials, including Cai Qi, a close aide to the president, and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, Chinese state media reported.
Later in the day, President Trump and the First Lady hosted President Xi and Madame Peng in the Rose Garden for a Military Review.
WATCH IN FULL: @POTUS and @FLOTUS host President Xi and Madame Peng in the Rose Garden for a Military Review 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/7kfXbnNEY6
The First Lady also hosted Madame Peng for a cultural visit at the Smithsonian Museum of Asian Art
. @FLOTUS hosts Madame Peng for a cultural visit at the Smithsonian Museum of Asian Art pic.twitter.com/anHkakwSIk
. @FLOTUS and Madame Peng listen to a children's choir during the cultural visit https://t.co/xZpS69faxu pic.twitter.com/XcIjCHDmfG
Two sources told AFP that no Chinese chief executives were part of Xi’s delegation, despite the planned attendance of senior US technology executives, including leaders of major artificial intelligence companies, at Thursday’s White House dinner.
The visit comes as Washington and Beijing seek to manage a range of thorny issues while exploring areas for cooperation. Possible tariff reductions in some sectors, efforts to combat drug trafficking, expanded military-to-military dialogue and cooperation or competition over artificial intelligence are expected to feature in the discussions.
Xi is also scheduled to visit the US National Archives during his stay.

title: Security forces foil Afghan Taliban incursion  kill several terrorists at Balochistan border  state media
description: Strikes were conducted against 10 locations in Afghanistan used for launching and storing drones
content:
Intermittent firing continues as Pakistan strikes 10 Afghan locations following drone attacks
Security forces on Thursday thwarted an attempt by the Afghan Taliban to infiltrate Pakistani territory and carry out an attack in Balochistan's Gulistan sector on the Pak-Afghan border, killing several terrorists in an effective retaliatory action, state media reported , citing security sources.
Security sources said that the Afghan Taliban attempted to enter Pakistani territory and carry out an act of aggression. However, security personnel responded effectively and killed several Afghan Taliban members.
"Intermittent exchange of fire between security forces and Afghan Taliban is still continuing, while troops remain fully alert and vigilant in the border area," the sources said.
They added that security forces remained fully prepared to respond promptly and effectively to any infiltration or aggression from Afghan territory into Pakistan.
#BREAKING Pakistani security forces have foiled an Afghan Taliban aggression attempt in the Gulistan sector, killing several Taliban fighters, security sources say. Intermittent firing continues in the area while Pakistani forces remain fully alert along the border. #Pakistan … pic.twitter.com/vRYYFwi3QC
Pakistan strikes 10 Afghan locations after drone attacks: Tarar
Earlier today, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said Pakistan carried out “precision” aerial and drone strikes against 10 locations in Afghanistan after drones launched from Afghan territory entered Pakistani airspace, describing the strikes as a response to a “deliberate and unlawful incursion”.
"In exercise of its sovereign right to self-defence, Pakistan conducted precision aerial and drone strikes against 10 locations in Afghanistan used for launching and storing these drones. The strikes were deliberate, precise, calibrated and proportionate and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan," said Tarar in a post on X.
The strikes were in response to drone attacks from Afghanistan. A day earlier, Pakistan’s air defence systems had shot down eight drones after they entered the country’s airspace from Afghanistan. Security sources said four of the drones were brought down in areas adjoining the Torkham border, while another four were shot down in mountainous areas near the border with Kohat.
Tarar said the drone incursion on September 23 was a “blatant violation” of Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and a “grave and unacceptable act of aggression”.
“Pakistan condemns in the strongest possible terms the deliberate and unlawful incursion into Pakistan by drones on September 23, launched from Afghan territory,” he said.
The minister said that Pakistan’s Air Defence systems detected, tracked and neutralised all intruding platforms before they could reach any of their intended targets, comprehensively thwarting the attempted attack.
The minister said Pakistan for years had repeatedly conveyed its concerns to the Afghan Taliban regime and its interlocutors over the continued presence of terrorist sanctuaries and support networks on Afghan soil.
“Instead of dismantling these networks and taking credible and verifiable action against those using Afghan territory to perpetrate terrorism against Pakistan, the Afghan Taliban regime has chosen to escalate the situation through hostile drone operations against Pakistan,” he said.
Update-Ghazab lil Haq Islamabad, 24 September 2026; Pakistan condemns in the strongest possible terms the deliberate and unlawful incursion into Pakistan by drones on 23 September 2026, launched from Afghan territory. This constitutes a blatant violation of Pakistan’s…
Tarar warned that Pakistan would not tolerate attacks launched from Afghan territory, "whether by terrorist groups or by the Afghan Taliban regime itself."
“Any violation of Pakistan’s sovereignty will be met with an immediate and decisive response,” he added.
Read: Eight drones shot down after entering Pakistan from Afghanistan: security sources
He called on the Afghan Taliban regime to immediately cease all hostile activity against Pakistan and take effective, concrete, verifiable and sustained action against terrorist entities operating from Afghan soil.
“Afghan territory must not be used to launch attacks or conduct hostile operations against Pakistan,” Tarar said. He added that Pakistan did not seek escalation and remained committed to “regional peace, dialogue and constructive engagement”.
“This commitment must not be mistaken for weakness or an unlimited tolerance of hostile actions,” he said. “Pakistan will defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity and the lives of its citizens with full resolve and will take all necessary measures to protect them,” Tarar added.
In a separate post, Tarar said, “Through precise aerial and drone strikes, as seen in the attached clip, terrorist hideouts and support infrastructure, including drone launching and storage sites across 10 locations in areas under the control of the Afghan Taliban regime, were comprehensively destroyed,” Tarar said.
“Pakistan will continue to defend its territorial integrity and protect the lives and property of its citizens against any externally sponsored, sheltered and abetted threat by terrorist proxies,” he added.
Update-Ghazab lil Haq Islamabad, 24 September 2026; Through precise aerial and drone strikes as seen in attached clip, terrorist hideouts and support infrastructure including drone launching and storage sites across 10 locations in areas under the control of Afghan Taliban… pic.twitter.com/6CrgV4SzSw
The recent tension started between the neighbouring countries after a blast at a mosque in Kohat’s Police Lines during Friday prayers, in which 23 people, including 15 police personnel , were martyred. Eight terrorists were also killed during a subsequent search and clearance operation. Later, Ittihadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), led by Afghanistan-based Hafiz Gul Bahadur, claimed responsibility for the deadly bombing and rampage involving multiple attackers.
A day later, a captain and a lieutenant were among six martyred during an exchange of fire in Hangu district. Following a series of deadly attacks in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), on September 21, Pakistan carried out “calibrated” air strikes against terrorist hideouts near the Afghan border and conducted intelligence-based ground operations that killed a total of 37 terrorists.
Read More: Pakistan carries out 'calibrated' air strikes against terrorist hideouts
Security forces conducted an intelligence-based ground operation against a group of terrorists in Kohat and Hangu districts. "As a result of precise and skilful engagement, nine khwarij belonging to the Indian proxy Fitna al-Khawarij were sent to hell, while several were injured."
The statement said three targets were destroyed in precision strikes, including a training centre for suicide bombers. It said 28 terrorists, along with several suicide bombers, were killed, while large quantities of weapons and ammunition stored at the centres and hideouts were also destroyed.
Pakistan had reported previous incidents involving drones crossing from Afghanistan into its airspace.
On July 1, security forces had shot down four “rudimentary drones ” launched from Afghanistan into Balochistan on June 30. The military accused the Afghan Taliban regime of supporting terrorist groups operating from territory under its control and warned that further cross-border provocations would draw a strong response.
In March, armed forces intercepted a few rudimentary drones launched by the Afghan Taliban in what officials described as a failed attempt to harass civilian populations, according to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations.
The military’s media wing said the drones were detected and neutralised through a combination of defensive measures before they could reach their intended targets. However, falling debris from the intercepted drones caused injuries to civilians in multiple cities.
Two children were injured in Quetta, while one civilian each sustained injuries in Kohat and Rawalpindi. All injured individuals received medical attention and were reported to be in stable condition.
Pakistan has repeatedly raised concerns on international forums over terrorist attacks being launched from Afghan soil.
On September 23, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for “concrete and verifiable” action to prevent Afghan soil from being used for terrorism against neighbouring countries, particularly Pakistan, while addressing the OIC Contact Group on Afghanistan on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.
In a separate warning following the terrorist attack in Kohat, Pakistan said it had the “will and capability” to eliminate terror threats “wherever they are” and urged the international community to press the Afghan Taliban regime to take decisive action against terrorism.
Attributing the attack to “the vilest of Khwarij with roots in Afghanistan” the Information Ministry noted that the attack was a reminder that “terrorism has no religion and no justification”. It added that Islamabad had repeatedly raised “grave concerns” over the alleged use of Afghan territory by the banned TTP and other terrorist groups to plan and launch attacks inside the country.
“The presence of terrorist sanctuaries, alongside their recruitment and support infrastructure in Afghanistan, poses a direct threat to Pakistan’s security,” the ministry had said. It added that these concerns had repeatedly been conveyed to the Afghan Taliban regime and its interlocutors. “They must dismantle these networks rather than deflect responsibility,” Pakistan said.
United Nations Security Council report formally implicated the banned Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and terrorist entities operating from Afghanistan , highlighting tactical collaboration and shared operational logistics between the groups.
Member-state reporting confirmed that BLA terrorists were trained alongside TTP members at facilities in Afghanistan, according to the report, which also described growing operational links among various terrorist groups operating across the border.
This was not the first time a UN report pointed to the threat posed by terrorist groups operating from Afghanistan. In 2023, a UN report also revealed that the TTP had established a new base in K-P in mid-2023, shedding light on close ties between the TTP and the Afghan Taliban, as well as between the TTP and anti-Pakistani groups and Al Qaeda.
K-P had witnessed a significant rise in militant violence last year, with more than 500 attacks reported, marking a 50% increase compared to the previous year.
The fighting ​between Pakistan and Afghanistan that started in October ​has ⁠killed scores of people on both sides, with Afghans taking the brunt. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring ⁠militants ​who launch attacks in Pakistan, ​although Kabul denies this, calling the militancy its neighbour's domestic problem.
Operation Ghazab Lil Haq was launched around the end of February following renewed clashes along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border, after Afghan Taliban forces fired on multiple locations, prompting swift military retaliation by Pakistan.
The clashes intensified after Afghanistan launched a border offensive in response to Pakistani air strikes targeting terrorist positions. The two sides had agreed to a week-long ceasefire on the eve of Eidul Fitr on March 18, following requests from Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
Also Read: Info ministry rejects Afghan Taliban-linked claims of cross-border drone strikes
Pakistan in April put forth three core demands to the Afghan Taliban during peace talks in Urumqi, China, including Kabul formally declaring the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan a terrorist organisation, dismantling its infrastructure, and providing verifiable proof of the action. These demands form the basis of Pakistan's negotiating position, which sources say has hardened amid persistent security concerns.

title: US and Iran discuss phased deal to reopen Hormuz and end US blockade  sources say
description: Saudi Aramco chief says disrupted oil operations can be restored  within days
author_name: Web Desk, Reuters, Anadolu Agency, AFP
content:
Challenge facing negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but to ensure concessions durable for both to trust
US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the ​talks said.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict , with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now ‌blocked by Tehran.
The talks face a big obstacle as neither side wants to be the first to surrender its leverage, according to comments to Reuters by two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources, but behind Iran's stance is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation.
A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.
"One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz," he said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly .
That would involve US ​President Donald Trump accepting another temporary fix, after an earlier understanding collapsed in July. So a central challenge facing the negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but also to ensure any concessions are durable enough for both sides to trust, the sources said.
Trump has said ​he thinks the US and Iran could reach a deal after midterm elections to Congress on November 3. A senior European official said the Iranians "have a very long list of demands".
A White House official said that while "Iran is desperate ⁠for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States."
Trump, he said, remained "open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances" but had no need to negotiate, and the US was in a "very strong position" with control of the Strait of ​Hormuz and an Iranian economy that was "collapsing".
The official said "crushing sanctions" and "one of the most successful blockades in history" have crippled Iran’s economy and left Iran completely broke. Trump was content to let the "inevitable Iranian collapse" play out rather than be "played" by Tehran, the official said.
Former US negotiator Dennis Ross said he saw only ​a 30% chance of an agreement being reached before the vote, but that both sides may have stronger reasons to make a deal before than after the midterms.
"The blockade is what's really squeezing the Iranians. It's strangling them," Ross said.
A deal before the midterms could benefit Trump, as reopening Hormuz could ease tensions in the Gulf, contain oil prices and help bring down politically sensitive US gasoline prices.
Iran's chances of gaining much-needed economic relief may be greater while Trump still has a greater political incentive to strike a bargain.
After the midterms, Ross said, Trump may face fewer constraints and be more willing to intensify pressure or consider military options.
The leverage that brought Washington and Tehran back to negotiations ​could also make compromise harder.
Washington controls the pressure that is hurting Tehran most, while Tehran controls access to a critical energy chokepoint. Neither side wants to surrender that leverage without extracting something tangible in return.
This means the midterms may be less a deadline for diplomacy than for preserving the conditions that make ​the diplomatic efforts possible. If Washington and Tehran cannot turn leverage into a deal before the midterms, the diplomatic window could narrow as the risk of escalation grows.
Even as it seeks a diplomatic off-ramp, Tehran is preparing for the possibility of renewed war with Washington, the Iranian official said, accusing the US of using the economic ‌blockade and threat of ⁠force as tools of coercion.
"Our fingers are on the trigger,” said the senior Iranian official. “The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low.”
Regional sources said Tehran was willing to drop a demand for payment of transit fees to use the Strait of Hormuz from the main agreement and put the demand in a side attachment instead, as ending the blockade had become the more urgent priority.
Gulf states have rejected the proposal for payment of transit fees. Any arrangement would be temporary, not a formal abandonment of Iran’s position, the regional sources said.
The US has tightened the economic vice on Iran, layering new sanctions on top of a blockade that has choked off Iran's oil exports, an important source of hard currency.
This month, it targeted Iran's remaining commercial airlines and support networks as part of a campaign to sever the economic lifelines sustaining the government and the powerful Revolutionary ​Guards. Trump warned that Iran's economy could "rot" unless it reached a deal.
"Iran is ​not primarily focused on imposing tolls in Hormuz but on preserving ⁠its administrative control of the waterway,” he said. "Iran may be willing to defer the toll issue, but they are not going to give up administrative control of the strait.”
At the heart of the diplomacy in New York is a fundamental tension. Washington wants pressure to produce concessions, Tehran wants pressure removed before making them, and the Gulf states want the conflict resolved without allowing the region's strategic waterways to become enduring bargaining chips.
During a separate meeting ​with Trump in New York, Gulf leaders sought clarity on Washington's endgame beyond the midterms, including on whether the US would resume military action if Iran refused to return to negotiations.
They conveyed their collective rejection of any ​Iranian control of Hormuz, saying freedom of ⁠navigation must be restored and that the strategic waterway should not become a tool of coercion against Gulf states, regional sources said.
Yet alongside their warnings over Hormuz, Gulf leaders have pressed hard for de-escalation and a political process, reflecting the region's determination to stay out of any further conflict between the US and Iran.
"It's still not clear what Trump’s endgame is, or what the alternative to the pressure campaign would be," said Ebtessam al-Ketbi, president of the Emirates Policy Centre think tank based in Abu Dhabi.
"The Iranians, by contrast, know what they want. They're reshaping the regional landscape through Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb with a clear objective while Washington has yet to ⁠define its roadmap," she ​said, referring to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
That uncertainty is also shaping Tehran’s calculations. Danny Citrinowicz, a regional analyst and former Israeli ​military intelligence officer, said the New York talks had not altered the basic positions of either side and that Iran was unlikely to retreat as long as it believed Trump wanted to avoid a wider escalation before the midterms.
“The blockade is hurting them, but rather than softening their position, it is likely to drive them to escalate because they believe that if they soften ​their position, they are dead," said Alan Eyre, a former US negotiator on Iran.
A Western official familiar with the talks added: "It is all about opening the Strait of Hormuz. We're all under pressure domestically and the Iranians know that."
Saudi Aramco chief says disrupted oil operations can be restored 'within days'
The chief executive of Saudi oil giant Aramco, Amin Nasser, told Nikkei Asia on Thursday that the company could restore disrupted oil operations within days and was seeking to build alternative export routes, as it faces increasing attacks from Yemen's Houthi group.
According to Nikkei Asia, Aramco was studying "a fourth and a fifth route" for crude oil exports in addition to its three primary ones.
Saudi Aramco chief says any interruption can be fixed 'within days' https://t.co/Evp4PKdtvB pic.twitter.com/Y0wHBI6MWA
Six Houthi ballistic missiles launched at Taif, Yanbu intercepted: Saudi coalition
The Saudi-led coalition in conflict with Yemen’s Houthis said on Thursday that its forces intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the group, thwarting attacks on the Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu.
“Escalations and violations by the terrorist Houthi militia will be dealt with firmly,” said coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki in a series of posts on X.
المتحدث الرسمي باسم قوات التحالف السعودي اللواء الركن تركي المالكي: اعتراض وتدمير 6 صواريخ باليستية أطلقتها الميليشيا الحوثية الإرهابية • اعتراضات الدفاعات الجوية أحبطت محاولة استهداف الطائف وينبع • تصعيد وانتهاكات الميليشيا الحوثية الإرهابية سيتم التعامل معها بحزم pic.twitter.com/tptmZZL1gJ
Greek security sources told ​ Reuters that an air defence system operated by Greek military personnel in Saudi Arabia ​intercepted a ballistic missile and a drone in the wider Yanbu region.
"Both were shot down," one of the sources said, adding ​that the Greek Patriot system launched two ​missiles but not giving details on the origin of the ‌drone ⁠and the ballistic missile.
A second source confirmed the information.
It was the fifth time the Greek-operated system had been used in combat since ​the US ​and Israel ⁠launched their war with Iran at the end of February, underscoring ​the widening military role of European ​allies ⁠in defending Gulf energy infrastructure.
Since 2021, Greece has deployed a US-made Patriot air defence battery operated ⁠by ​Greek personnel in Saudi ​Arabia, under an agreement to help protect the kingdom's energy ​facilities.
Earlier, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence said the danger had passed in Makkah, Taif, and the northwestern region of Tabuk, following earlier emergency warnings for those areas, as well as Jeddah and Yanbu.
In separate all-clear notices, the agency urged residents to continue following its instructions and to avoid gathering or filming.
Makkah, Taif and Jeddah are in western Saudi Arabia. Yanbu is a Red Sea port city farther north, while Tabuk is in the kingdom’s northwest.
The Civil Defence had issued warnings through the national early warning platform about a “potential danger.” The notices did not specify the threat or report casualties or damage.
Saudi Arabia has faced a series of missile and drone attacks attributed to the Houthis in recent days.
Iran may expand war to Indian Ocean if US attacks again: supreme leader's adviser
Iran may expand the Middle East war to the Indian Ocean if the US or Israel attacks again, said an adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
“We do not know what is going on in the minds of (US President) Trump and (Israeli Premier) Netanyahu,” Safavi said.
He said Iranian forces had prepared for the worst-case scenarios in the event of further US or Israeli attacks on the country’s facilities or national interests. In that event, he warned, the scope of the conflict would widen.
“Now that the war has spread from the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea, it is possible that, in the next stage of a potential war with the US, this front could expand further, to the Indian Ocean or elsewhere,” he said.
Iran misreading US political system by waiting for midterms: Rubio
Iran is misreading the US political system if it believes the November midterm elections could restrict President Donald Trump’s ability to act against Tehran, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday.
“I think the Iranians are under this illusion that Democrats are going to win in November, and the president will no longer be able to do things against them,” Rubio told reporters in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Rubio said Tehran appeared not to understand the division of powers in the US, arguing that while Congress plays an important role, the president retains extensive authority over national security matters.
“When it comes to the national security of our country, when it comes to the imposition of both sanctions and the use of military force, the president has extraordinary powers,” he said, pointing to Trump’s constitutional role as commander-in-chief.
His remarks came one day after Trump said he believed Washington would reach an agreement with Iran following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump told the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, claiming Iranian leaders were waiting to see how his Republican Party performed in the vote.
Rubio said the outcome of the elections would not change Trump’s approach, describing Iran’s nuclear program as a national security issue rather than a matter of domestic politics.
“For him, the Iranian issue is not a political issue,” he said.
Rubio argued that US presidents and most countries had agreed for nearly five decades that Iran must not acquire a nuclear weapon but had repeatedly failed to take sufficient action.
Trump, he said, was prepared to act despite the associated costs because the consequences of failing to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran would be “substantially higher,” particularly for future generations.
Iran cancels all flights to United Arab Emirates
All flights operated by Iranian airlines to the United Arab Emirates have been cancelled since midnight, the Iranian Students News Agency ( ISNA ) reported Thursday, citing a spokesman for Iran’s Civil Aviation Organisation.
It also reported that a Tehran-Dushanbe flight was forced to return to Imam Khomeini International Airport in Tehran after Turkmenistan did not grant permission for Iranian airlines to fly through its airspace.
The spokesman said the flight was unable to land at its destination because Turkmenistan had not issued permission for Iranian airlines to cross its airspace, forcing it to return to Tehran.
Iran has seen inaction, not neutrality from some countries during war: Pezeshkian
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told European Council President Antonio Costa on Wednesday that inaction, rather than neutrality, was seen from some countries during the recent war, calling on European states to reconsider their approach and maintain greater independence, according to IRNA .
Meeting on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, Pezeshkian said European countries deprived themselves of a role in international developments by aligning with hostile US actions.
Iran saw inaction, not neutrality, during recent war: @drpezeshkian https://t.co/ZeqQS6PY9a pic.twitter.com/KmgkE6VcVu
He criticised Europe’s approach to the snapback mechanism and the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, saying European governments’ positions reduced their ability to influence international developments. He also referred to comments by the NATO secretary general about European countries’ assistance to the United States during the war and called for a reassessment of European policies.
Pezeshkian said regional security should be the responsibility of countries in the region, stressing that Western intervention has adversely affected security beyond the region.
Costa called for a European role in addressing regional issues, while Pezeshkian said Europe’s alignment with Washington had limited its ability to play such a role.
In a separate message carried by ISNA and Al Mayadeen , Pezeshkian said that Tehran used its appearance at the UN General Assembly to defend Iran’s position and respond to US policies, revealing that he moved away from his prepared remarks after hearing US President Donald Trump’s speech.
“We had prepared a text in advance for the UN General Assembly, but after listening to Trump’s speech, we departed from the prepared text to express the realities being imposed by the United States,” Pezeshkian said.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Thursday that Tehran used its appearance at the UN General Assembly to defend Iran’s position and respond to US policies, revealing that he departed from his prepared remarks after hearing US President Donald Trump’s speech. “We had… pic.twitter.com/JfpJWI4jPn
He accused Washington of acting “in violation of laws and humanitarian frameworks,” adding that it does “nothing but use force and commit acts against humanity.”
پزشکیان: در مجمع عمومی سازمان ملل از حقانیت ملت ایران دفاع کردم -ملت ریشه‌دار و متمدن ایران نابود شدنی نیست ۱/۲ pic.twitter.com/axmvyjzLqJ
He also rejected attempts to pressure Iran, saying, “They cannot eliminate Iran. Iran is a country deeply rooted in history, and despite all the pressure they exert, our people remain steadfast.”
"We tried to express the realities that America imposes on our nation and the world."
Iranian FM spokesperson rebukes Canadian PM for calling ‘annihilation’ threat ‘language of war’
Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Thursday criticised Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney for “reframing a threat to 'annihilate' Iran as merely 'speaking the language of war'”.
Baghaei on X said that “Mark Carney must understand that time is too ruthless to let the shelter of illusion and hypocrisy endure forever.” He has added that “those who sought refuge in the long shadow of American bullying” would eventually learn that “averting their eyes from reality and bartering away their dignity and self-respect buys no salvation.”
To the Canadian Prime Minister who, instead of condemning U.S. blatant aggression and warmongering, chose to appease Washington by reframing a threat to "annihilate" Iran as merely "speaking the language of war": Mark Carney must understand that time is too ruthless to let the… pic.twitter.com/87XRoT8cjc
He also stated that “they will see that the nation they once conspired with empires to crush was the solitary guardian of a sacred flame” which "kept a torch burning" against coercion, "a torch that, if allowed to die, would leave humanity with nothing but the cold embrace of naked force, burying the civilised and humane altars of reason beneath the brutal logic of might."
US Treasury Secretary questions how Iran’s UN delegation will get home as sanctions disrupt flights
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday that he wondered how the Iranian delegation to the UN General Assembly in New York would return home as American sanctions continued to squeeze the country’s international airline operations.
“In terms of Operation Economic Outcast, we are squeezing the Iranians like they've never seen today,” he said.
He said the campaign was affecting Iran's international air links, claiming that more than 80% to 90% of external flights from Iran had been shut down.
Bessent also warned financial institutions, companies and other businesses supporting Iran that Washington would target their operations and bank accounts.
"We have made it very clear around the world, whether it's the financiers, the people who are doing business, the people who are supplying the Iranians, we know who you are, you know who you are," he said.
He described the US strategy as a combination of military action, a naval blockade and financial pressure.
"So we had six weeks of kinetic activity. We have the blockade. And now we have an effort never seen before in terms of constricting and cutting off the financial oxygen to them," he said.
He said Washington's pressure campaign could continue for weeks or months, adding that the US was seeking one of three possible outcomes: divisions within the Iranian leadership, an uprising by the Iranian population, or an agreement under which Tehran would comply with its commitments.
Bessent also said the US had attempted to reach an agreement with Iran earlier in the year but accused Tehran of subsequently escalating attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.
"If there is a deal, I guarantee you they're going to stick with it," he said.
Yemeni government forces stop Houthi attack near key southern provinces
The Yemeni government’s armed forces thwarted an attack and infiltration attempts by the Houthis aiming to reach positions near the road linking the southern and southwestern provinces of Aden, Taiz and Lahj, the Ministry of Defence has said in a statement, Al Jazeera reported.
BREAKING: Yemeni government forces thwart Houthi attack near key southern provinces 🔴 LIVE updates: https://t.co/yIoLRqH3fa pic.twitter.com/GP4Oefje3j
According to the official spokesperson of the Yemeni armed forces, “clashes ensued”, which forced “the attackers to retreat” and inflicted heavy losses in lives and equipment.
Read: Iran says it conveyed conditions for reviving diplomacy with US through Qatar
“We affirm that our armed forces stationed on those fronts have regained the initiative, are highly prepared, and continue to repel attacks and infiltration attempts,” the spokesperson has said.
Shipping traffic via Strait of Hormuz stays lower than 10-day average, data shows
Ten commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, up from seven a day earlier and below the 10-day moving average of about 17, preliminary shipping data showed on Thursday.
Nine vessels entered the strait, including Supramax ships carrying metals, grain and other dry bulk cargoes, as well as an empty very large gas carrier. One Supramax carrying fertiliser exited, according to the data, as of 0923 PKT on Thursday.
The figures exclude any vessels that might have crossed the strait with their transponders turned off to avoid detection.
Before the US-Israeli war on Iran started on February 28, the strait typically handled about 125 large, commercial vessels a day, including tankers, gas carriers, bulkers and container vessels, accounting for some 20% of the world’s daily crude oil and liquefied natural gas supply.
Read more: US president open to making a deal with Iran: Rubio
Iran and the US remain far apart on how to end the war, but diplomacy must continue, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday, after Iran's president told the United Nations General Assembly that Tehran would never surrender to US pressure.
The senior Iranian official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Tehran was reviewing Washington's response to its peace proposals, which prioritise lifting a US naval blockade on Iranian ports and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
In the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, 27 commodity vessels transited the waterway on Wednesday, up from 24 the day before and compared with an average of 26 ships using the strait over the past 10 days.
EU's Costa urges Iran to resume cooperation with IAEA
European Council President Antonio Costa said on Wednesday he spoke with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian and urged Iran to resume its cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency.
Costa also called for an end to Iran's strikes against its neighbours and the full restoration of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump should press Xi to stop support for Iran, Democratic senator says
US Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen said on Wednesday President Donald Trump should press Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit this week over China's support for Iran, saying that Chinese firms were helping Tehran economically and militarily.
In a Senate speech, Shaheen cited reports that Iran obtained high-resolution satellite imagery of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before launching a missile attack that killed three American soldiers and wounded four others.
She noted that about 90% of Iran's oil exports go to China and provided it with "billions of dollars of revenue" and a "critical economic lifeline."
Shaheen said Chinese and Hong Kong companies had also supplied components used in Iranian ballistic missiles and drones
She urged Trump to "use his leverage" with Xi to stop Chinese firms from providing satellite imagery, missile and drone parts and access to markets for sanctioned Iranian oil.
"If we want to bring this war to an end, we need to cut off the outside support that allows Iran to keep fighting, and that starts with China," she said.
Shaheen said the administration should enforce sanctions against Chinese entities helping Iran, "and if China doesn't stop, Congress should impose additional consequences."
She said Trump should also consider using authorities in recently enacted Russian sanctions legislation against Chinese purchasers of Russian energy, arguing that China was "the top funder of the war in Ukraine, as well as being one of the top funders of the war in Iran."

title: The Afghan enigma
description: The Afghan enigma
content:
Afghan transgression across the western frontier is becoming the order of the day. It is an open-and-shut case of interference and a violation of Pakistan's sovereignty. The plot thickens with the patronage that the terror nexus, including the outlawed TTP, enjoys from the Taliban rulers. In a daredevil attack, eight drones were flown from Kabul. However, they were successfully shot down by Pakistan's security forces. The incursion was from across the Torkham border into Kohat city.
It is worth recalling that Kohat was a theatre of a massacre a few days ago when insurgents from Afghanistan targeted the Police Lines area, killing and maiming more than 36 policemen and civilians. Kabul had the audacity to strike deep inside Pakistan with drones, even at a time when the country was at war with India. Back then, the drones targeted Peshawar and Rawalpindi, confirming an inevitable criminal collusion with India to bleed Pakistan.
The recent spike needs to be viewed within the context of evolving geopolitical dynamics. Pakistan is being pushed into a security dilemma on both its eastern and western fronts. Harbouring sleeper cells and terror abettors is part of the game plan. Thus, Islamabad was well within its rights to fly sorties over terror hideouts last week, reportedly killing over two-dozen terrorists. Pakistan had categorically informed the UNSC that it has the right to self-defence and that no violation of its territorial integrity will be tolerated. This brinkmanship from Kabul, apparently at the behest of Delhi, demands the attention of the global community, and its urgency cannot be set aside.
The least Afghanistan should do is learn the ethics of interstate relations. It has no choice but to act against terror hideouts and stop taking on Pakistan for the sake of point-scoring. The UN, regional states, and even the SCO have indicted Kabul for inaction in turning its landmass into a hub for terrorists. It cannot absolve itself by resorting to the gimmick of flying drones.

title: Robert Pattinson says  The Batman  Part II  has different take on Batman
description: Robert Pattinson says  The Batman  Part II  is  a real left turn  from first film while retaining its established feel
content:
Robert Pattinson says 'The Batman: Part II' is 'a real left turn' from first film while retaining its established feel
Robert Pattinson has teased what audiences can expect from The Batman: Part II, describing the upcoming sequel as a different take on the superhero film.
Pattinson, who returns as Bruce Wayne in the 2027 movie, told Collider that the sequel is “a real left turn from the first” film while retaining elements of its established tone.
"It's so ambitious," he said. "I mean, I sort of said the other day on something that the first one was a different take on a Batman movie, and this one is another… It's a real left turn from the first one, but somehow it keeps elements of the kind of feel of it. But it just feels really ambitious, and I'm excited to see how it turns out."

Despite his demanding schedule, Pattinson said during the Venice Film Festival that he would have been “devastated to have dropped any of” his projects this year.

title: Dolly Parton   s estate gets temporary restraining order against nephew
description: Dolly Parton   s estate has secured temporary restraining order against nephew Bryan Seaver and his security company
content:
Dolly Parton’s estate has secured temporary restraining order against nephew Bryan Seaver and his security company
A Tennessee judge has granted Dolly Parton’s estate a temporary restraining order against her nephew Bryan Seaver and his private security company.
The order was granted Wednesday after She's Alive, the entity managing Parton’s estate, filed a complaint against Seaver and Squadron Augmented Protection Services.
The estate accused Seaver of making threats of violence and attempting to interfere with its business operations.
Under the order, Seaver and SAPS must stay at least 1,000 feet (305 metres) away from She's Alive employees, attorneys and business partners.
They are also prohibited from communicating with those individuals and interfering with the estate’s business relationships.
A hearing has been scheduled for October 7.
Seaver owns the security company that provided Parton’s security detail and was previously chosen by the singer to announce her death from cancer last month. He did not immediately respond to an requests for comment.
According to court documents, She's Alive said Seaver sent increasingly threatening messages in the weeks surrounding Parton’s death. The estate said it terminated Seaver and SAPS last week, citing his “terrorizing conduct”.
The documents include text messages and emails that She's Alive says were sent by Seaver. In one message dated September 1, he wrote: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or f——— pay me."
The estate also claimed Seaver referred to his experience working for private military contractors overseas during the Iraq War while making threats.
The court filings say the dispute has affected Parton’s estate operations, with the trusts and estates attorney leaving and some employees resigning. She's Alive also said it hired private security for employees, including at their homes.
Parton died aged 80 last month. Her estate oversees her professional property and business interests, with longtime manager Danny Nozell running She's Alive.

title: Govt decreases petrol by 84 paisas  HSD by Rs2 63 for Sept 25
description: Petrol price decreases to Rs389 28 per litre  while HSD will cost Rs412 12
content:
Petrol price decreases to Rs389.28 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs412.12
The federal government on Thursday decreased the price of petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) by 84 paisas and Rs2.63 per litre, respectively, for September 25.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs389.28 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs412.12 per litre for Friday.
The latest revision comes a day after the government decreased the price of petrol and HSD by Rs1.93 and Rs4.21 per litre, respectively, for September 24.
Read : Govt cuts petrol price by Rs1.93, HSD by Rs4.21 for Sep 24
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
Earlier this month, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.
Oil prices rose about ​2% on Thursday after a Houthi missile attack on Saudi Arabia revived supply disruption fears, but pared earlier gains on reports ‌the US and Iran discussed reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent futures rose $2.04, or 2.0%, to $105.12 a barrel at 12:29 pm EDT (1629 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude rose $1.99, or 2.2%, to $94.15.
US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran ​reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said.
The ⁠strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that ​is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.

title: Financing of historic AI buildout raises systemic risks in US  researcher says
description: AI data centre construction faces US scrutiny over local resource strains  inflation and safety concerns
content:
AI data centre construction faces US scrutiny over local resource strains, inflation and safety concerns
The artificial intelligence buildout is on track to require a larger share of ​US output than the rollout of electricity, railroads, interstate highways or the internet, with an increasingly complicated financial structure that poses ‌potentially systemic risks, according to a new study.
What had been paid for out of the cash stockpiled by companies like Amazon.com, Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google has morphed into an expansion that will consume around 3.6% of gross domestic product annually through 2032, or more than $10 trillion, and is using ever more intricate financing arrangements, Stijn ​Van Nieuwerburgh, a finance and real estate professor at Columbia Business School, wrote in a paper prepared for a Brookings Institution conference ​this week.
That estimate is higher than the 2.2% of annual GDP absorbed by railroads in the late 1800s, which was the ⁠next most costly rollout of a general technology, and a bit more than 1% annually each for construction of the US interstate highway ​system beginning in the 1950s or the telecommunications expansion that started in the mid-1990s.
Just as the rail and telecoms expansions led to notable bubbles ​and busts, Van Nieuwerburgh wrote that the extent of the buildout, the still-untested revenue streams, and the intricate financing structure emerging around AI mean it could be primed for a fall.
Read More: ‘Extreme concern’ as OpenAI’s ‘rogue agent’ breached Australian govt health database
"This is freaking complicated," he said in a briefing with reporters of the arrangements emerging between AI firms, major tech hyperscalers, banks, private credit lenders, real estate firms, ​and a host of other players involved in building what he conservatively estimated at 183 gigawatts worth of new data-center capacity over the ​next seven years, compared with about 57 gigawatts currently installed.
Data center construction and the risks around AI have become a central issue in US ‌political and ⁠economic debates, with some localities increasingly reluctant to host the facilities and worried about strains on local resources, and Federal Reserve officials considering whether the construction boom is adding to inflation. Some AI executives have suggested a slower pace of development might be safer.
The investment underway already has outstripped what the major players can fund from their own cash flows. The shift to outside financing has increased leverage, redistributed risks across the ​economy, and made the venture dependent on revenue ​streams that have yet to ⁠be proven, Van Nieuwerburgh noted in the paper, which will be presented on Friday.
"This opacity of all these special purpose vehicles is somewhat reminiscent of what happened in the subprime mortgage crisis," he said in the conversation ​with journalists, when complex home mortgage financing arrangements went bad at rates that rocked global financial ​systems and triggered the 2007-2009 ⁠recession in the US.
"These developments do not imply that financial distress is imminent. Strong growth in AI applications, high utilization, and continued improvements in model capability could support the projected infrastructure and generate stable cash flows," he wrote. "But the combination of uncertain demand, rapid technological change, execution bottlenecks, and ⁠high leverage ​creates meaningful downside risk if expectations are revised."
As an example, he wrote that the ​AI industry will need to be earning about $3.7 trillion in annual revenue by 2032 to achieve the expected return on the investment, and "given current estimates of annual combined revenues ​of OpenAI and Anthropic of around $100 billion, revenues would need to grow at roughly 80% per year."

title: Presley Gerber death investigation reveals new details
description: New details have emerged about where Presley Gerber was found as authorities investigate suspected overdose
content:
New details have emerged about where Presley Gerber was found as authorities investigate suspected overdose
New details have emerged in the investigation into Presley Gerber’s death, including reports about where the 27-year-old was discovered at a Santa Monica recovery residence.
Sources close to the investigation told TMZ that Gerber was found inside a bedroom at the sober-living residence on Sunday, September 20.
The sources said his body was near the bed rather than on it, although they could not provide further details about his position.
Gerber had reportedly arrived at the residence the previous evening. Separate reports claimed people who encountered him around check-in believed he did not appear sober, although those observations do not establish what caused his death.
Emergency responders were called to the Berkeley Street property at approximately 9:35 a.m. According to dispatch information obtained by the Daily Mail , the initial call referenced “cardiac arrest” before being updated to an “overdose” around three minutes later.
Santa Monica police confirmed that officers responded to a reported possible overdose and found Gerber deceased.
Paramedics pronounced him dead at 9:45 a.m. Police are investigating the death as a suspected overdose and said there was no indication of foul play.
The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner has completed Gerber’s examination, but his cause and manner of death remain deferred while additional testing is conducted.
Sources told TMZ that fentanyl had not emerged as a focus of the investigation, although the drug has not been definitively ruled out. Toxicology testing is expected to establish what substances, if any, were present in Gerber’s system.
Reports have also focused on ketamine. TMZ reported that people in regular contact with Gerber claimed a doctor had prescribed him the drug despite allegedly knowing about previous struggles with it. Authorities have not said ketamine caused or contributed to his death.
Gerber was also reportedly receiving support from a 24/7 sober coach and had explored treatment options, including an ibogaine programme in Mexico earlier this year.
His family, including Cindy Crawford, Rande Gerber and Kaia Gerber, have asked for privacy.

Kahan revealed that the song will be released on October 2 and that he was "so honoured" to have the opportunity
Noah Kahan has announced Draw You Out, the lead single from The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping album, ahead of the upcoming film's cinema release.
The 29-year-old singer-songwriter revealed that the song will be released on October 2. Kahan said he was "so honoured" to have the opportunity to write music specifically for the new film, which is based on Suzanne Collins' dystopian novel.
"This is something I've always wanted to do and I am so grateful for the opportunity to write for this moving film," Kahan said in a social media post, adding that he has long admired Collins' work.
Draw You Out was written specifically for the film and sees Kahan reunite with Grammy-winning producer Aaron Dessner. The pair co-wrote and co-produced the track at Long Pond Studio in New York and studios in Nashville.
Kahan said he was particularly connected to the story of Haymitch Abernathy and his girlfriend Lenore Dove, whose relationship plays a significant role in the prequel.
"I was already totally connected and inspired by the tragic yet hopeful story of Haymitch and Lenore Dove," he said, describing the process of writing about the characters' purpose, grief and perseverance through pain as an experience he would remain grateful for.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the events of the original The Hunger Games story and follows a young Haymitch as he is selected to compete in the 50th Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell.
Joseph Zada plays the younger Haymitch in the film, with Mckenna Grace starring as fellow tribute Maysilee Donner. The cast also includes Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Kieran Culkin as Caesar Flickerman, Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket and Jesse Plemons as Plutarch Heavensbee.
Kahan is not the first major artist to contribute an original song to the Hunger Games franchise. Taylor Swift previously recorded Safe & Sound with The Civil Wars for the first film, while Olivia Rodrigo contributed Can't Catch Me Now to The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.
The full The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping album will arrive on November 13 and features 29 artists across multiple genres. Kahan's Draw You Out will be the first single released from the project.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is scheduled to arrive in cinemas on November 20, 2026.

title: India   s voter roll revision sparks fresh debate over electoral credibility
description: Mass deletions under Special Intensive Revision draw opposition fire  UN concerns and Supreme Court scrutiny
content:
Mass deletions under Special Intensive Revision draw opposition fire, UN concerns and Supreme Court scrutiny
India’s sweeping Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has triggered an intensifying political and legal controversy, with opposition parties and civil society groups alleging mass disenfranchisement while the Election Commission of India (ECI) maintains that the exercise is aimed at cleaning up voter lists and removing ineligible entries.
The controversy has also drawn international attention. In May, three United Nations (UN) special rapporteurs sent a joint communication to the Indian government raising concerns over the reported large-scale removal of names from electoral rolls through the SIR process, particularly in West Bengal and among minority communities. The UN communication said it had received information concerning the removal of millions of names and expressed concern about the potential impact on minority groups.
The SIR was launched in Bihar on June 24, 2025, and has subsequently been extended to other parts of India. The ECI says the exercise is intended to ensure that electoral rolls contain eligible voters while removing entries relating to deceased persons, people who have permanently moved away, duplicate registrations and other ineligible entries.
India’s Supreme Court, in a May 27, 2026 judgment concerning the Bihar SIR, upheld the ECI’s authority to conduct the revision. It also held that the commission could undertake a limited administrative inquiry into citizenship for electoral purposes, while making clear that a final determination of citizenship remains with the competent authority under the Citizenship Act. The court further said that deletion from an electoral roll on citizenship grounds could not itself constitute a final determination of a person's citizenship.
Read: Shutdown in India's Ladakh marks anniversary of deadly autonomy protests
The scale of the exercise has nevertheless fuelled questions about its impact on eligible voters.
Figures cited by political opponents and campaigners point to millions of deletions or voters requiring verification across different states. In Bihar, the draft exercise resulted in around 65 lakh names being excluded, with the net reduction reportedly falling to about 47 lakh after claims and objections. Other figures cited in the controversy include approximately 2.04 crore names in Uttar Pradesh, 74 lakh in Tamil Nadu, 68 lakh in Gujarat, 45 lakh in Andhra Pradesh, 34 lakh in Madhya Pradesh, 31 lakh in Rajasthan and 34 lakh in Haryana.
These figures relate to different stages of the revision process and should not automatically be interpreted as permanent disenfranchisement. The ECI has provided mechanisms for voters to check their names, submit documents and file claims and appeals.
West Bengal has emerged as one of the most contentious cases. The UN communication specifically highlighted concerns over the removal of millions of names in the state, where assembly elections were held in April 2026. The state election authorities have published draft and final rolls, deletion lists and mechanisms for claims and appeals.
Critics argue that the documentation and verification requirements could disproportionately affect poorer voters and minorities, particularly those who lack older records or whose names do not easily match previous electoral rolls.
The political debate has acquired an additional communal dimension because of the BJP government's broader emphasis on identifying alleged illegal migrants from Bangladesh. Critics argue that references to “Bangladeshi infiltrators” have acquired a particular political resonance in Muslim-majority areas. The ECI, however, has not published religion-wise deletion figures that would establish whether Muslims have been disproportionately removed from electoral rolls.
The issue has also reached Delhi, where the Supreme Court on September 22 questioned the manner in which notices were being issued to voters flagged for “logical discrepancies”.
Read more: India's 'cockroach' movement says will launch protest if poll panel chief doesn't quit in 48 hours
According to figures presented in court, the draft Delhi electoral roll excluded around 47 lakh names, while more than 33 lakh voters were identified for notices over “logical discrepancies” or lack of mapping with earlier rolls. The bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant questioned whether some notices appeared to have been issued mechanically and asked the ECI to consider additional safeguards and clearer explanations for affected voters.
The court also suggested that Booth Level Officers should provide greater assistance to voters and that the ECI should prepare standardised guidance explaining the documents and information required to address different categories of discrepancies.
Opposition parties including the Congress, Aam Aadmi Party, Trinamool Congress and Communist Party of India (Marxist) have accused the ECI of facilitating what they describe as “vote theft” and targeted exclusion. Supporters of the revision reject those allegations and argue that an accurate electoral roll is essential to the integrity of elections.
At the heart of the dispute is a basic democratic question: how can electoral authorities simultaneously protect the integrity of voter rolls and ensure that eligible citizens are not excluded through administrative errors, inadequate documentation or flawed verification?
That question has become particularly sensitive in a country of more than a billion people, where even a relatively small error rate can affect millions of voters.
The ECI has made electoral-roll search, document submission and appeals available through its voter services system, while state election authorities have also published deletion lists and supplementary rolls.
For critics of the SIR, however, the central issue is not whether electoral rolls should be cleaned up but whether the process is sufficiently transparent and inclusive to ensure that every eligible voter retains the opportunity to vote.
With the Supreme Court now examining aspects of the exercise and UN experts having raised concerns over its impact on minorities, the SIR controversy has evolved from an administrative exercise into a wider debate over electoral inclusion, institutional safeguards and the credibility of India’s democratic process.
