title: Hindutva and the limits of Indian diplomacy
description: Hindutva and the limits of Indian diplomacy
content:
India likes to present itself as a voice of peace, dialogue and the Global South, but do actions match its rhetoric
India likes to present itself as a voice of peace, dialogue and the Global South. Prime Minister Narendra Modi speaks of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam - the world as one family - and promotes Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas. India has also repeatedly spoken of an era of dialogue and diplomacy rather than war.
But South Asia has a right to ask a simple question: do India's actions towards its neighbours match its rhetoric?
The recent unrest in Nepal provides a disturbing starting point. Violence following a Hindu religious procession in Sunsari exposed growing communal tensions in a country with a long tradition of religious coexistence. Hindu nationalist organisations with links to India have expanded their presence in Nepal, while Hindu identity is increasingly being used for political mobilisation. During Nepal's constitutional transition, Hindu nationalist groups in India openly lobbied for the restoration of Nepal's Hindu-state status.
This is not the first time India has intervened deeply in Nepal's political affairs. During Nepal's 2015 constitutional crisis, the Indian government itself acknowledged maintaining close contact with Nepal's political leadership and monitoring the situation closely. India denied imposing a blockade, while Nepal and others blamed the disruption of supplies on the border crisis. The larger point is that India has long regarded developments in Nepal as a matter of vital strategic interest. The question is whether that interest has now acquired an ideological dimension.
This brings us to Hindutva. The problem is not Hinduism, but the political idea that Hindu identity should occupy a dominant position in the definition of the Indian nation. When that idea becomes the basis of politics, Muslims and other religious minorities inevitably face the question of whether they are being treated as equal citizens or as communities expected to live within a Hindu-majoritarian national framework.
This concern is not merely theoretical. Human Rights Watch has documented increasing vilification of Muslims, discriminatory policies and unlawful demolitions of Muslim homes and properties under the BJP-led government. Its 2026 report also records attacks against Christians and other minorities.
The continuing demolition of Muslim religious and historic sites makes the question even more uncomfortable. Indian authorities have generally cited encroachment, unauthorised construction or development requirements in individual cases. But when mosques, shrines and other Muslim sites are repeatedly removed or challenged, it inevitably raises a larger question: is India merely dealing with illegal structures, or is a new political narrative also attempting to reduce the visible presence of its Muslim history? Recent demolitions of mosques in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh have intensified that debate.
India's Muslim history cannot simply be removed from the national story. It is part of India's history, just as its Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh, Jain and other traditions are. If Hindutva seeks to redefine India primarily through Hindu civilisation, its influence beyond India deserves scrutiny as well.
The contradiction becomes sharper over water.
India placed the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance in April 2025. The treaty governs rivers vital to Pakistan's agriculture and economy and had survived wars and decades of hostility. On August 31, 2026, the Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled unanimously that the treaty remained fully in force and that the grounds cited by India did not justify its suspension. India rejected the ruling.
Water is not an ordinary instrument of geopolitical pressure. For Pakistan, the Indus system is a matter of agriculture, food security and human survival. How does the language of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam sit with using control over a vital resource as leverage against a neighbour?
The same question arises from regional economic cooperation.
SAARC has effectively been paralysed since the 2016 summit was cancelled after India withdrew from the Islamabad meeting following the Uri attack. Bangladesh, Afghanistan, Bhutan and Sri Lanka subsequently also stayed away. India participates actively in the G20, BRICS, SCO, Quad and BIMSTEC, so it is clearly not opposed to multilateralism. The question is whether it prefers regional arrangements in which its enormous weight gives it greater influence, rather than an institution where India and Pakistan sit as equal members.
Afghanistan presents another contradiction.
India has chosen to engage the Taliban. In January 2025, Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri met Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi, with both sides discussing expanding relations, trade and development cooperation.
There is nothing inherently wrong with diplomatic engagement. But if India has access to Kabul, why has it not used that access to help reduce tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan?
China has actively attempted to mediate between Kabul and Islamabad, while Turkey has also worked with both sides to promote dialogue. India has the diplomatic channels to do the same if it chooses to. This is particularly relevant because a UNSC-mandated monitoring report found that the Taliban continued supporting the TTP and that this contributed to increased frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan. The report also identified growing operational links among the TTP, Al Qaeda, ISIL-K and the BLA.
India's engagement with Kabul may serve legitimate strategic interests. But strategic engagement and peace-building are not necessarily the same thing.
India is unquestionably the largest power in the region. But there is a fundamental difference between regional leadership and regional dominance.
Leadership means allowing neighbours to prosper, respecting their constitutional choices, keeping vital resources outside political confrontation, supporting regional institutions and using influence to reduce conflict.
That is why India's slogans deserve to be tested against its conduct. Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam sounds noble. Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas sounds inclusive. But the region will ultimately judge these principles not by speeches in Delhi, but by what happens to its water, trade, security, connectivity, minorities and sovereignty.

title: Debating transformation in the Global Order
description: Debating transformation in the Global Order
content:
Economy, India, Afghanistan are challenges; Iran war, connectivity, balancing ties with US, China are opportunities
Last week, we discussed the salients of annual International Programme for Development and Stability (IPDS-26) conducted recently by Institute for Strategic Studies, Research and Analysis (ISSRA) at the National Defence University (NDU) Islamabad. We discussed the contours of 'Emerging Global Order (EGO)', the role and rise of China and the US/European dimension of the EGO. We continue.
Pakistan's former permanent representative at the UN, Munir Akram, identified three challenges and three opportunities for Islamabad under the EGO. Economy, Indian hostility and Afghanistan were challenges; whereas war in the ME, connectivity and balancing of ties with the US and China were exploitable opportunities. He emphasised 'developing' relations with the US and 'preserving' ties with China, and opined that the war in the ME will create regional security architectures with Pakistan as a security provider, as indicated through Makkah Agreement.
The second plenary of the Conference dealt with technology redefining power. Brig Gen Wharton of the US remained focused on the human dimension of technological development, emphasising technology's subservience to humanity. This, he posited, remains under stress due to 'potential' loss of human control over AI. He was appreciative of China's 'industrial capacity at scale' in the service of humanity at low cost, and as a critical element of national power.
On AI, South Korean speaker, Dr Park, emphasised expert control, while discussing AI development and AI risks. Unlike many countries ambivalent about AI regulation, Pakistan, she said, should have its own AI regulation. Russian panelist, Ms Oksana, also called for country-specific AI regulation and pressed for investing in people, emphasising humanity to be at the core of AI in its genesis, development and proliferation.
Panelists equated data security with national security, pointing out challenges of data centres – including hacking, uninterrupted electricity supply and water needed for cooling – warning about the perils of putting too much data online. On AI regulation, the dominant view gravitated towards the mechanics of doing so, defending 'human cognitive security' without controlling thought, and the dos and don'ts for governments.
The third plenary dealt with EGO-driven changing character of warfare and impacts on strategic stability. An eminent American scholar Dr Robert Pape, while enumerating the lessons of the US war with Iran, declared that the US was in an 'Escalation Trap'. The US dilemma was acute: conceding Iran's control of Hormuz emboldens states like China and encourages countries like India to undertake military unilateralism (against Pakistan). Recent Indian Navy incursion in Pakistan's EEZ is a case in point. While contesting Hormuz control risks escalation and is militarily untenable indefinitely for the US, as of now.
In his opinion, the Iran War is in many ways the 'inverse' of the 1991 War with Iraq. Since the Iraq War, there has been global diffusion of technology and 'democratisation' (inexpensive availability) of precision weapons, challenging the global powers. Prof Pape identified continued smuggling of Iranian oil through Pakistan as an ongoing challenge, and refugee influx and instability as the likely consequences of US ground invasion of Iran through Chahbahar beachhead, etc.
Brig Gen Kimmitt of the US Army theorised whether warfare was undergoing a 'Revolution in Military Affairs' (RMA) or an 'Evolution' (EMA). In his opinion (correctly), the conduct of warfare had changed with new tools at hand, while its nature (principles) remains unchanged. He, however, considered the 'principle of Mass' irrelevant without 'concentration'. He was reminded that 'technological mass' was the likely contemporary manifestation of 'Mass' as a cardinal principle of war; and that AI was the new RMA.
Gen Kimmitt suggested guardrails for AI regulation, postulating that 'unmanned platforms' were the new horizon in warfare, rendering pilots redundant, as machines could handle greater G Forces compared to humans. Swarming the battlefield with inexpensive weapons was the new normal, saturating adversary's response and raising his interception costs. Effective counter-drone capability was still away. And 'Internet of Things (IOT) was being replaced by 'AI of Things' (AIOT). Russian speaker, Dr Alexey, spoke about the 'Drone Revolution' contextual to the war in Ukraine.
Pakistan's Admiral Faisal discussed Iran's 'sea control' vis-à-vis America's 'sea denial'. Iran was employing 'compellence and deterrence' and the US was reacting to it. Iran, by default, decides shipping safety, insurance, freight costs, etc. He considered Hormuz control, Iran's Centre of Gravity and Tehran's political, diplomatic, economic and military leverage. He considered Hormuz critical, whether under Iranian control or under the world, and theorised the Iran war introducing 'strategies of choke points', making security more expansive and global trade more expensive.
The fourth plenary debated global competition and conflict prevention. Brazilian view was 'pro-hedging', as hedging provided more flexibility and strategic autonomy. Hedging by BRICS was beneficial, as BRICS participants shared the table simultaneously with myriad players, without dispensing with the UN/other forums. Platforms like BRICS provide low risk space for Middle Powers (MPs) to operate at universal, multilateral and bilateral levels. South African panelist described reform at the UN, and supported effective mediation, arbitration and facilitation under the UN's good offices. She identified 'middle power diplomacy' as multilateral tool for conflict prevention.
Pakistan's Dr Moeed Yusaf considered EGO another historic continuum. But this time around, the hegemon (US under Trump) had announced voluntary retirement without being displaced through historic decline, like in the past; leaving a fragmented Global Order, and vacuum/uncertainty. This allows MPs to formulate issue-based partnership as opposed to ideological camping; Brazil being a case in point. He suggested that MPs, sidelining NAM, will challenge Western hegemony. He defined MP as a country that cannot be ignored by either the US or China. He concluded that the future is likely to have a 'rule-based order', albeit with different set of rules, bringing together MPs under a resurgent UN.
As per Dr Moeed, Pakistan has a major opportunity under the EGO and it must become part of regional mechanisms. It should optimise its crucial geography like its location, mineral wealth, connectivity and transit potential. Islamabad needs to pursue internal cohesion, cheap energy and cooperative geoeconomics, shunning camp politics. He underscored good relations with both America and China and considered stable Pakistan critical for regional and global peace and stability. He suggested that Islamabad cannot and should not be a 'net security provider' regionally.

title: Please press 9 to lose your mind
description: Please press 9 to lose your mind
content:
For English, press 1. For Urdu, press 2.
For complaints, press 3. For payments, press 4. For technical support, press 5.
For absolutely no reason whatsoever, please press 7.
To spend the next forty-five minutes questioning every decision that brought you to this phone call, please press 8.
And if you would like to completely lose your mind, please press 9.
What else was I supposed to do? Calling customer service has become less like asking for help and more like entering a government examination you did not study for.
And then comes the greatest lie in modern customer service: "Your call is important to us."
If my call was actually important, why am I listening to the same thirty-second piece of elevator music for the seventeenth time? At this point, I know the music better than I know myself. I have developed a relationship with it. I know exactly when the little piano comes in. I know when the mysterious flute starts. I know when it loops. I know when it loops again. I am no longer waiting for the person I am being transferred to. I am waiting for the next verse.
Then, suddenly, someone answers. "Hello, how may I assist you?" I immediately become hopeful. "This is my problem."
Excuse me? You just arrived. You have been here for six seconds. Where are you going? And there it is again.
The music. The beautiful, haunting soundtrack of my suffering.
Twenty minutes later, someone returns. "Thank you for holding."
I want to ask, "Did you enjoy your holiday?" But I remain polite. "Yes."
Because apparently the previous person did not explain it to this person. I explain it carefully. I explain it slowly. I explain it like I am teaching a five-year-old how electricity works.
The representative says, "I understand."
Then comes the sentence that destroys all hope. "Please hold while I transfer you to the relevant department." I have been transferred so many times that I am beginning to wonder whether I am still a customer or whether I have died and this is my afterlife.
And also...why do they make us repeat everything? "Please provide your name." I provide it. "Account number?" I provide it. "Phone number?" I provide it. "Please explain your issue." I explain it. "Can you confirm your name?"
We have already discussed this. You asked me my name before my account number. My name has not changed during this phone call unless the hold music has somehow caused a spiritual transformation.
Then there are the automated systems that ask you to speak. "Please say your account number." I say it. "Sorry, I didn't understand that." I say it again. "Sorry, I didn't understand that." Now I am speaking louder. "123456789." "Sorry, I didn't understand that."
What exactly do you want from me? Should I sing it? Should I perform it? Should I stand on one leg and try a different accent? At this point, I understand why robots are going to take over the world.
And then, miraculously, you finally reach a human being. You think you have won. You have not. They tell you: "Unfortunately, we cannot resolve this from our end."
Of course. Why would we resolve anything today?
Maybe one day customer service will finally become so advanced that you will not need to call anyone. You will simply stare at the screen.
Please press 1 to scream. Press 2 to cry. Press 3 to speak to an agent. Press 4 to repeat the entire process.

title: El Ni  o s health threat
description: El Ni  o s health threat
content:
El Niño is a reminder that the world remains woefully unprepared for the public health consequences of extreme weather
The impending El Niño is a reminder that the world remains woefully unprepared for the public health consequences of extreme weather. The World Health Organisation has warned that the climate phenomenon poses a significant threat to global health, with its effects likely to be felt well into 2027. As global temperatures continue to rise, extreme weather events are becoming an increasingly serious challenge to public health systems that are already struggling to meet routine healthcare needs.
For millions living in poverty, the distinction between a climate emergency and a health emergency is becoming increasingly meaningless. There is a disturbing inequity at the heart of this crisis. Countries with limited healthcare resources and inadequate sanitation are often the least capable of protecting their populations from climate-related diseases. WHO has cautioned that the effects of El Niño will be particularly severe where climate shocks intersect with food insecurity, displacement and weak health systems. Yet international climate responses continue to place insufficient emphasis on the protection of public health. The international community must recognise that climate adaptation is as much about protecting human health as it is about safeguarding infrastructure and economic activity.
Pakistan is particularly exposed to this predicament. The catastrophic floods of 2022 demonstrated how a natural disaster can develop into a prolonged public health emergency when healthcare facilities and access to safe drinking water are compromised. The country's vulnerability is further compounded by the limited reach of preventive healthcare and the persistent neglect of basic sanitation. The government must recognise that the country's vulnerability is not simply a consequence of its geography. It is also a reflection of the persistent failure to invest adequately in preventive healthcare and climate-resilient infrastructure. International assistance will remain important, but it cannot compensate for the absence of sustained domestic planning.

title: Scam centres
description: Scam centres
content:
Call centres in Karachi alone had facilitated international fraud worth approximately $60 million
The arrest of 212 individuals in Islamabad this week on suspicion of running international fraud operations is the latest example of why Pakistan is now widely associated with phone- and internet-based financial scams in wealthy countries. Apart from the arrests, raids by the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) on three call centres also yielded hundreds of computers and mobile phones, which helped underscore how the largely unregulated call centre industry has evolved into a sprawling infrastructure for committing financial fraud abroad.
The Sindh home minister recently revealed that call centres in Karachi alone had facilitated international fraud worth approximately $60 million, with proceeds laundered through Bitcoin and US dollars. Investigators describe networks impersonating Google representatives, running "love-dating" schemes and using private material to extort victims abroad. And while most Pakistani businesses are struggling to attract foreign investment, fraud centres have brought in both investment and expertise.
Foreign experts have noted that Pakistan stands out as a fraud call centre hub because its internet and telephone infrastructure is far behind other notorious countries, but laws regulating the sector are weak and criminal penalties are nominal. Regulatory gaps are most obvious. The PTA has explicitly stated it does not regulate call centres or software houses, while the PSEB has registered over 7,400 call centres but doesn't actually monitor them for illegal conduct. Meanwhile, NCCIA is one of the few agencies with the mandate and capability to act against call centres, but its own staffers are on the take - several months back, NCCIA officers were busted running an extortion racket that collected nearly Rs300 million from illegal call centres in exchange for monthly "protection fees".
The government's recent licensing requirement for call centres is a good step, and only 25 years too late. Still, if we ensure that monitoring and prosecution of call centres will now be up to the mark, we may shed yet another ignominious international title.

title: Dead Poets Society    star Robert Sean Leonard shares why he moved back home
description: Robert Sean Leonard reveals why he left New York and returned to New Jersey to raise his three daughters
content:
Robert Sean Leonard reveals why he left New York and returned to New Jersey to raise his three daughters
Dead Poets Society and House star Robert Sean Leonard has opened up about his decision to move his family back to his hometown in New Jersey to raise his three daughters.
Leonard, 57, returned to Ridgewood, New Jersey, after deciding that he did not want to raise his children in New York City. In an interview with PEOPLE published Tuesday, the actor explained that he wanted his daughters to experience the suburban childhood he remembered fondly.
“I knew I couldn’t do it in New York,” Leonard said, adding that his wife, Gabriella Salick, believed he needed the nostalgia of returning home.
Leonard left New Jersey at 16 to pursue a career in theatre in New York City. Despite building a successful acting career, he said he is happy to have returned to the community where he grew up.
The actor recalled taking part in activities at the same schools he once attended, including handing out pizza at his former grammar school and watching his daughter cheerlead on the high school field where he once spent time.
Leonard said he wanted his daughters to have more space and the opportunity to experience life in a suburban neighbourhood. “I need a screen door and to see kids running around in the backyard,” he said.
Leonard is best known for playing Dr James Wilson on House , appearing in the medical drama for eight seasons alongside Hugh Laurie. He also earned recognition for his role as Neil Perry in Dead Poets Society .
The actor has previously spoken about his preference for theatre and a quieter lifestyle, saying he enjoys reading, walking and cooking more than the demands of television production.

title: Section 144 imposed in Islamabad as PTI gears up for Sept 27 protest
description: Islamabad administration urges citizens to refrain from unlawful gatherings  cooperate with security institutions
author_name: Iftikhar Chaudhary, Saleh Mughal, Naeem Asghar
content:
Islamabad administration urges citizens to refrain from unlawful gatherings, cooperate with security institutions
As Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) gears up for its planned Sept 27 protest in the federal capital, the Islamabad administration on Wednesday reminded citizens that Section 144 was in force for two months, barring gatherings, rallies and demonstrations, and urged them to stay away from illegal activities and cooperate with security institutions.
The order, a copy of which is available with The Express Tribune , was issued by Islamabad Additional District Magistrate Dr Anam Fatima on Sept 18.
It said that the restrictions were imposed in view of reports that certain segments of society were planning to organise unlawful assemblies, including majalis and processions, within the jurisdiction of Islamabad Capital Territory.
Read : PTI's Gohar calls for dialogue as party decries arrests, raids in K-P
The order said such activities could disrupt public peace and tranquillity and cited the prevailing law and order and security situation as grounds for imposing the restrictions.
“Certain segments of the public are planning to take out processions, including religious/sectarian processions, and to stage demonstrations in Islamabad Capital Territory,” the order said.
According to the order, such activities were likely to threaten public peace and tranquillity, cause public annoyance or injury, endanger human life and safety, pose a threat to public property and potentially lead to a riot or an affray, including a sectarian riot, within Islamabad’s territorial limits.
The additional district magistrate said sufficient grounds existed to proceed under Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, and that immediate prevention and speedy remedy were required to protect public life and property.
The order prohibits “all kinds of gatherings of 5 (five) or more persons, processions/rallies and demonstrations” at any public place within the revenue limits of Islamabad.
The restrictions also cover the Red Zone, whose boundaries have been specified in the order.
The order took effect immediately and will remain in force for two months.
In a separate statement, the district administration reminded citizens that Section 144 was in force in the federal capital and that no kind of gathering or assembly was permitted in the city.
It said gatherings were also prohibited under the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act, 2024, and warned that strict action would be taken in accordance with the law in case of any violation.
“The punishment for violating the Act is three years in prison,” the administration said.
It urged citizens not to become part of any illegal activity and asked them to cooperate with security institutions as responsible citizens.
The order came as the Kissan Ittehad and Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) announced plans for separate long marches on Islamabad in the coming week, with the former seeking relief for farmers and the latter demanding the release of party founder Imran Khan from jail.
Twin cities ramp up anti-protest measures
Preparations to deal with the PTI long march have entered the final phase in Rawalpindi Division, with more than 43,000 personnel to be deployed in Attock, Rawalpindi, Murree, Jhelum and Chakwal to prevent protesters from entering the twin cities.
Police authorities have decided to keep Rawalpindi and Islamabad open with all preparations in place until the march enters Punjab territory.
Officials will assess the situation under a “wait and see” policy and take a response according to the situation if marchers cross barriers in Punjab and move closer to the twin cities.
High-level meetings on preparations for the PTI long march are continuing.
Also Read : Govt, PTI on warpath after 'once & for all' threat
A meeting of senior police and administrative officials, including the inspectors general of Punjab, Islamabad and Railways, was also held on Wednesday, where officials were briefed on preparations and the strategy was discussed.
In Rawalpindi Division, more than 43,000 police personnel will perform march-related duties in Attock, Rawalpindi, Murree, Jhelum and Chakwal. Of these, 30,000 personnel will be deployed in Attock.
Around 14,250 personnel will be deployed at sealing points on the M-1 motorway, including Haroon Bridge, Ghazi-Barotha Motorway Bridge, Tower Hill, Hazara Motorway and Pathar Garh.
Another 11,450 personnel will be deployed at sealing points on the N-5 and N-80 routes, including Attock Khurd, Tarbela Road Jhansa, Haro Bridge, Jablat Bridge, Chaska Point and Khushal Garh.
Around 5,000 personnel will be deployed at sealing points on the M-14 CPEC route, including Dhok Syedan Interchange and other M-14 points.
All personnel have been directed to perform duty equipped with riot-control equipment and kits.
In Rawalpindi district, more than 10,000 police personnel will be deployed. Around 3,100 personnel will be stationed at 26 entry points, 1,800 at 73 blocking points in the city area, 3,738 at 152 police pickets, and 300 personnel on 50 roads and streets connecting the twin cities. Another 1,674 personnel will be deployed in responding teams across six sectors.
Read More : Long marches, strikes, sit-ins may cost Pakistan’s economy Rs120b a day: Aurangzeb
In Murree, 224 personnel will be deployed at 16 blocking points, while 1,400 personnel will be deployed at nine blocking points in Jhelum. Chakwal will have 352 police personnel at 10 blocking points.
A survey of petrol pumps and hotels along the GT Road and motorway has also been conducted. Within Rawalpindi, two petrol pumps and 23 petrol pumps were identified on the motorway and GT Road respectively, while there are two hotels on the motorway and 37 on the GT Road.
In Attock, five petrol pumps are located on the motorway and 63 on the GT Road, while there are nine hotels on the motorway and 64 on the GT Road.
Across the five districts of Rawalpindi Region, including Attock, Rawalpindi, Chakwal, Jhelum and Murree, 666 tear-gas guns, 52,118 long-range shells, 7,243 short-range shells, 1,529 splints, 1,531 gas masks and 1,693 gas-mask filters are available.
Additional equipment has been demanded, including 500 repeater guns, 57,000 rubber bullets, 710 tear-gas guns, 61,000 long-range and 10,000 short-range tear-gas shells, 1,200 tear-gas grenades, 7,150 gas-mask filters, 5,600 gas masks and 6,500 splints.
Authorities have also sought 4,050 Robocop anti-riot kits, 4,000 long transparent shields, 3,050 new-pattern helmets, 1,500 bulletproof helmets, 1,500 bulletproof jackets, 200 binoculars, 100 night-vision devices and barbed wire.
For transport and logistics, six armoured personnel carrier (APC) vans, two water cannons, 20 prison vans, 50 megaphones and 12 quadcopters along with operators have also been demanded. Additional surveillance equipment includes 12 quadcopters and their operators.
Police personnel have already reached Attock. Supervisory officers have been directed to ensure security of the areas where the force has been deployed, with police personnel also assigned security duties in shifts.
Meanwhile, the Rawalpindi police and administration have sought Rangers’ assistance for Rawalpindi Region and Mianwali.
In Islamabad, preparations to deal with the PTI march are also at their peak. The city will be monitored from the Safe City headquarters, while more than 200,000 bags of soil have been arranged along with 110,000 tear-gas shells and 1,300 rifles capable of firing tear gas.
According to sources, containers have been delivered to almost every major intersection in the capital. Around 210 containers are required to close the city’s entry points, while soil-filled trolleys have also been brought in to make the containers heavier.
Read : PTI to finalise capital march strategy
Islamabad Police have arranged 110,000 tear-gas shells and currently have 1,300 guns for firing them, while an additional 500 guns have been ordered.
The capital has 22 cranes available for installing and removing containers. Three routes leading to the Red Zone have already been sealed, with containers placed and welded together.
Police personnel from other provinces have already reached Islamabad. The city will be monitored through Safe City cameras and smart vehicles, while the operations room at the Inspector General’s Office will also keep a round-the-clock watch on the situation.

title: Meta testing a  human concierge  for its new personal AI agent  Muse
description: Muse test shows how tech companies sometimes rely on human labour to deliver on promises of autonomous AI
content:
Muse test shows how tech companies sometimes rely on human labour to deliver on promises of autonomous AI
Meta has been testing a “human concierge” for its new personal AI assistant, Muse , which entails having human contractors quietly handle some of the ​phone calls placed via the digital agent, according to internal company posts seen by Reuters .
The Facebook and Instagram owner told employees about the test last week, shortly ‌after the company publicly launched a phone-calling feature for Muse.
The Muse agent, which has topped US app download charts in the two weeks since its debut, is designed to autonomously perform tasks like sending emails, shopping and booking travel on a person's behalf.
With the phone-calling feature, a Muse user can tell the agent to dial phone numbers for US businesses and talk with people on the other end to handle errands like booking haircuts, checking whether a store has ​an item in stock or getting quotes from different contractors.
EXCLUSIVE: Meta testing a 'human concierge' for its new personal AI agent, Muse https://t.co/tDwVczSM0q https://t.co/tDwVczSM0q
Some employees have raised privacy concerns about humans handling those calls, warning that the approach could result in sensitive information being ​shared unintentionally with contractors in call centres, according to internal posts.
"It's baffling to me why we think this feature is worth the risk," one employee ⁠wrote in an internal post. "We are one bug away from unnecessary information being leaked to human callers."
Another employee, who had asked Muse to call an internet and cable provider to negotiate his bill, ​said a transcript showed the human contractor had made a racist reference during the call.
In response, a vice president in Meta's Superintelligence Labs unit acknowledged that "it was a miss" to start testing contractor-placed calls without ​proper disclosures and said the company had "rolled back this feature" for now.
Meta was still "hillclimbing AI calling," she added in her post, noting that some tests indicated that having humans make the calls could get their success rate up to the 95% to 98% range, instead of the "lower percentage of AI calling."
Read : Meta's Zuckerberg says AI agent tech progressing slower than expected
She also apologised to the employee who reported the mention of race during a Muse call and promised that the "human agent" involved would not work on any Meta ​projects going forward.
The Muse test offers a window into how tech companies sometimes rely on human labour behind the scenes to deliver on the promises of autonomous AI, as ​they bump up against reluctance to engage from those on the receiving end of robocalls.
It harks back to an earlier experiment Meta conducted a decade ago, when the company, then known as Facebook, trialled a digital assistant ‌called "M" in its ⁠Messenger service. Media reports later estimated that around 70% of the agent's tasks were actually carried out by humans.
Asked about the Muse "human concierge" plan, a Meta spokesperson said the response from employees had been "overwhelmingly positive" and that the purpose of the test was to "get feedback so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve features before we release them publicly."
"We're working with merchants to continue improving this potential calling feature, and will only roll it out when it's ready and with the proper disclosures," said the spokesperson, Daniel Roberts.
Meta's Muse agent has had more than 2.5 million downloads since its release, according ​to data provided by market intelligence firm Sensor ​Tower.
The company's stock has soared more than 20% since ⁠the launch, adding more than $200 billion in market capitalisation to touch its highest level in more than seven months as of last close.
Shares edged down 0.6% on Tuesday, however.
Meta heavily emphasised the AI assistant's safety protections during its launch, telling would-be users that each agent would have ​its own secure “virtual machine,” or a dedicated computer in the cloud designed to keep people’s sessions isolated, and would keep sensitive information like ​passwords in separate secure storage.
Employees ⁠critiquing the human concierge plan inside Meta cited those security measures in their feedback, warning that it risked undercutting a key selling point for the agent.
Meta began having employees test out the phone-calling capability in August and gradually started rolling it out to Muse users in the days after the app’s debut, the internal posts showed.
Some users have reported problems with those calls, however, including one employee who said he tried calling ⁠his insurance company ​and "they keep hanging up on Muse when they hear it is AI."
Meta enabled the human concierge feature, also referred to ​as “human agent calls,” for half of its employees last week to overcome those issues, according to the internal posts.
“Muse is now able to hand requests to a trained agent, who places the call and works it through,” the post announcing the feature ​to employees said.
Employees who did not want to be included could join an opt-out group, according to the post.

title: Hayden Panettiere reportedly entered rehab weeks before her death
description: Hayden Panettiere reportedly entered rehab weeks before her death  as a coroner   s report reveals new details
content:
Hayden Panettiere reportedly entered rehab weeks before her death, as a coroner’s report reveals new details
Hayden Panettiere had reportedly spent several weeks in a Malibu rehabilitation facility shortly before her death, according to a newly released coroner’s report obtained by Page Six .
The Heroes and Nashville actress died on August 16 at age 36 in Greenville, South Carolina. The Greenville County Coroner’s Office has ruled her death accidental and determined that it resulted from the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine. The autopsy found no trauma that contributed to her death.
According to the report, one of Panettiere’s former partner Brian Hickerson or his brother, Zach, told authorities that the actress had been in a drug rehabilitation facility in Malibu until several weeks before her death. Panettiere’s father, Alan “Skip” Panettiere, also reportedly confirmed that she had recently completed a two- or three-week stay in rehab.
The report also included information about Panettiere’s previous struggles with substance use. Her father reportedly told investigators that she had dealt with addiction since her early 20s and had attended multiple rehabilitation facilities.
Panettiere’s death remains connected to an ongoing investigation. Authorities have been examining circumstances surrounding the drugs involved, while her representative previously urged the public to wait for verified information as the investigation progressed.
The official findings confirm fentanyl and several other substances as contributing to Panettiere’s death, which the coroner classified as accidental.
Panettiere was best known for her roles in Heroes and Nashville , as well as appearances in the Scream franchise.

title: Aangan  returns to television nearly eight years after original run
description: The period drama  starring Sajal Aly  Ahad Raza Mir and Mawra Hocane  is set to return with its sprawling family saga
content:
The period drama, starring Sajal Aly, Ahad Raza Mir and Mawra Hocane, is set to return with its sprawling family saga
Nearly eight years after its original television run, Aangan is making its way back to television, reviving a period drama remembered for its sprawling cast, complicated relationships and Partition-era setting.
The channel announced the return on Instagram with a short teaser, hinting at the drama’s emotional legacy without revealing further details about the production.
The announcement has brought the drama back into the conversation, particularly because of the familiar faces associated with the series.
Sajal Aly, Ahad Raza Mir and Mawra Hocane were among its leading performers, while Ahsan Khan appeared in two roles.
Originally broadcast from December 2018 until June 2019, Aangan was adapted from Khadija Mastoor’s celebrated novel of the same name. Mustafa Afridi adapted the literary work for television, with Mohammed Ehteshamuddin directing the series.
Rather than focusing solely on a single romance, the drama explored the lives of a family as personal relationships collided with the wider social and political changes of the period. The story was set against the turbulent years surrounding the Partition of the subcontinent.
Mawra played Aaliya, a character whose experiences formed one of the central threads of the narrative. Her story unfolded within a complicated household where questions of love, family and changing social circumstances frequently intersected.
The drama also brought together Mir and Sajal as Jameel and Chammi, respectively. Their characters became closely connected to the series’ romantic storyline, adding another emotional dimension to the wider family drama.
Khan’s involvement was particularly notable, as he appeared as both Subhan and Safdar, giving the actor two distinct characters within the same production.
The supporting ensemble was equally extensive. Hira Mani appeared as Tehmina, while Sonya Hussaiyn played Salma. Veteran actor Abid Ali took on the role of Muzaffar, with Zaib Rehman appearing as Khameera Illahi.
Omair Rana was cast as Mazhar, while Madiha Rizvi played Aaliya’s mother. Shehroz Sabzwari, Rabia Butt, Uzma Baig and Hassan Noman were also part of the drama.
One of the series’ defining features was its recreation of an earlier period, from its visual design and costumes to the social environment surrounding its characters. Its large cast allowed the story to move between personal relationships and the broader circumstances shaping the family.
The production has not yet announced an exact date for the drama’s return. For now, the teaser has served as a reminder of a series that brought together some of Pakistan’s most recognisable television actors at an early stage of their careers.

title: We have not lost hope   PM Shehbaz says Pakistan remains focused on US Iran mediation

content:
Rubio says Trump remains open to Iran deal but will not allow Tehran to have nuclear weapons
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said on Wednesday that Pakistan remained fully committed to facilitating dialogue between Iran and the United States, describing Islamabad as a “sincere and honest mediator” in efforts to de-escalate the Middle East conflict.
Speaking to reporters at the United Nations headquarters, the prime minister said Pakistan was “completely focused” on helping bring an end to the hostilities and remained determined to advance diplomatic efforts despite an unpredictable turn in events following the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.
“Pakistan is playing the role of a sincere and honest mediator between Iran, our neighbourly country, and the United States,” PM Shehbaz said, referring to the MoU he signed alongside Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and US President Donald Trump.
“Unfortunately, events after that got a bit unpredictable, but Pakistan is completely focused. We have not lost hope; we [are] absolutely determined that we will further make efforts and make progress to de-escalate the situation,” he added.
Pakistan has continued to advocate dialogue and diplomacy as the means of resolving the Iran-US standoff, with Islamabad describing the MoU as a framework for regional de-escalation.
Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said at UN headquarters on Wednesday, September 23, that Islamabad is playing the role of a “sincere and honest mediator” between Iran and the United States. Referring to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding signed by Sharif, US… pic.twitter.com/lhCv7QHare
US president open to making a deal with Iran: Rubio
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that President Donald Trump was still open to making a deal with Iran to end the war while emphasising that the US would not allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.
“The core issue here is that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. The president is open, still to this moment, to making a deal with Iran that allows Iran to be what it should be, which is a great and prosperous country,” he said, speaking to reporters in New York on sidelines of the UN General Assembly meeting.
SECRETARY RUBIO: Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. pic.twitter.com/COHoSPBivz
A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran was reviewing the US response to its proposal to end hostilities, but significant differences remained between the positions of the two sides as diplomatic efforts continued.
The official said the indirect talks with the United States on Tuesday had also discussed reopening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting the US naval blockade on Iran.
Pezeshkian says Iran will not surrender in war with US, but believes in diplomacy
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian earlier told the annual gathering of ​world leaders at the United Nations that Iran would not ​surrender in the war with the United ‌States, but believed in diplomacy to try to end the conflict.
Pezeshkian said that the Iranian people had been the “victims of terrorism”, rejecting US President Donald Trump’s description of Iran as “terrorists”.
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Pezeshkian displayed images of victims of an American strike on a school in Minab at the start of the war, along with images of a sports hall in Lamerd destroyed by US bombardment.
“The United States, by using weapons with multiple warheads, targeted that sports hall. They martyred and assassinated our scientists, our men, women and children. Innocent children who in truth had committed no crimes, no sins,” he said.
Pezeshkian stressed that while Iran had responded to strikes by the United States and Israel, it had not targeted civilian areas.
The ​United States delegation walked out at the ⁠start of Pezeshkian's speech. The US mission to the ​United Nations did not immediately respond to a request ​for comment.
🔴 LIVE: Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian delivers a speech at the UNGA on the second day of the annual general debate in New York. https://t.co/wo8MrOIloL
“Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee. We did not bow our head,” he said. “We responded, but we did not hit civilian populations.
“They came into surrounding territories and targeted our universities, our healthcare centres, our schools, our hospitals, our infrastructure; all of it against international law,” Pezeshkian added.
He also said that Hamas chief Ismail Haniyeh had been assassinated in Tehran by Israel on the day of his inauguration as president.
“Israel targets any neighbourhood in any city in any province, commits assassinations like a true terrorist,” he emphasised.
“Those who are terrorists, and train and protect terrorists, describe us as such,” he added. “We have only defended ourselves; we are not terrorists.”
In the first part of his speech, the Iranian leader held up an image of the Islamic Republic's late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, who was killed in an airstrike on his compound in Tehran on the first day of the US-Israeli assault on Iran.
He also held up images of children killed in a strike on a school.
A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said earlier this month that it had reasonable grounds to believe that the US was behind two military strikes on a school and a sports facility in Iran, and that these constituted war crimes.
Pezeshkian ⁠addressed the 193-member General Assembly a day after US President Donald Trump spoke. ​Trump used his speech on Tuesday to ​make ⁠the case for his war on Iran, arguing he has prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and ⁠warning ​that he could "annihilate the Islamic ​Republic" if no deal is reached to end the conflict.
Hormuz cannot be used for passage of weapons used against Iran: Pezeshkian
Pezeshkian said Iran wants to have "strong neighbours" near the Strait of Hormuz, but cannot allow those who seek to impose "insecurity" on Iranians to have access to it.
"We cannot let some have free access and gain their interest from a waterway, while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggressions upon us, to impose insecurity upon us, to forbid us access to our own waterways," he stated.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian: Iran does not see her neighbors as security rivals — we want to have strong neighbors. In the waters of the Strait of Hormuz, we do not want to impose insecurity. We cannot let some have free access and gain their interest from a waterway,… pic.twitter.com/q9YcnRREJw
Iran has had its grip on the Strait of Hormuz, which was a conduit for ​a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas before the war.
The strait lies between Oman and Iran, linking the Gulf north of it with the Gulf of Oman to the south and the Arabian Sea beyond.
Iran has said it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the US eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.
"It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access to shipping through this waterway. The permanent deployment of hostile fleets and the expansion of the war will not lead to peace," Pezeshkian said
Iran needs nuclear energy, not a nuclear bomb, Pezeshkian says
Pezeshkian said Iran needs peaceful nuclear energy, not a nuclear bomb.
"For our country, peaceful nuclear technology is part of our inherent progress," he said, adding, "Iran does not accept nuclear technology to be at the exclusive disposal of some, of a handful."
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian: We will not bow our head and give up the right that is inherently ours. We say it clearly: no nuclear weapons, and no limitations to peaceful nuclear technology. pic.twitter.com/YsMSrKNuw0
"We say it clearly, no nuclear weapons and no limitations to peaceful nuclear technology," he said.
Iran threatens to paralyse airports in neighbouring countries if they stop Iranian flights
Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, said in an interview with state TV on Wednesday that if neighbouring countries cooperated with ​the United States ‌by stopping Iranian flights, Iran would ensure ​their airports could not function.
Major General Rezaei: Neighboring states should avoid being drawn into US games and reckless moves when it comes to Iranian aircraft flights. Should that happen, we will likewise halt the flights of aircraft belonging to neighboring countries that side with US.
Hope for progress after US, Iran hold first shuttle talks in months
The first shuttle talks between the United States and Iran in months raised hopes on Wednesday that the adversaries could make some progress towards ending the Middle East war, although neither side spelt out any change in their positions.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, the first such contacts since an interim ceasefire agreement collapsed in July.
"Steve and Jared had a very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran, merely mediators. Let's see what happens with that," US President Donald Trump said. "They've been mediated for a while, but I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal. It's what we're hearing from everybody."
Earlier, Trump had told the UN General Assembly in a speech that he had to decide whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate" the country. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian was due to address the gathering on Wednesday.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaiel Baghaei said Tehran had engaged with the United States through a Qatari mediator in New York and conveyed conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and a halt to US "acts of aggression".
Some Iranian state media had earlier reported that Araghchi and Witkoff had met, but Iranian officials clarified to Reuters that this was not face-to-face. Araghchi met the prime minister of Qatar, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who has been one of the main mediators at previous talks.
The diplomatic opening helped keep oil prices near two-week lows, with Brent crude now holding just below the $100-a-barrel threshold it had shot through this month, after Houthi fighters in Yemen launched a major offensive and fired into Saudi Arabia.
The war, launched by Trump in February alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury", has lasted nearly seven months, killing thousands of people, disrupting global energy supplies and spreading to other countries in the region — first to Lebanon and more recently to Yemen.
Trump repeated previous assertions that the war could end around the time of November's US midterm elections, though he has not explained why.
Since diplomacy broke off in July, the sides have repeatedly exchanged fire, although Trump has held back from a full-blown resumption of strikes after receiving advice from his military commanders that munitions were running low.
An interim agreement reached in June and signed by Trump and Pezeshkian would have given Iran its main demands: lifting financial sanctions and unfreezing assets in return for talks on limiting its nuclear programme.
But that deal unravelled within weeks over shipping rules in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas before the war. Iran wants to exert greater control of the strait and collect fees from ships that use it, which Washington rejects.
Despite near-daily attacks on tankers, traffic through the strait has gradually increased in recent weeks. Oil producers have paid shipping companies fees worth as much as a quarter of a cargo's value to switch off transponders, navigate the route and transfer crude to other vessels beyond the strait.
Exports from the United Arab Emirates have already recovered to pre-war levels, and Saudi Arabia has sold 60 million barrels of Gulf oil for both this month and next, to be delivered beyond the strait off the coast of Oman, a big increase from August.
Even so, disruption continues to squeeze global energy markets. About a third of Gulf oil is estimated to be missing from global supplies. Shortages have particularly hit refined products such as diesel, causing inflation, pushing up interest rates and hurting Trump's Republicans ahead of the elections.
The risk of further disruption has increased since the Iran-backed Houthis advanced in Yemen this month, threatening traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, an alternative export route used by Saudi Arabia.
Washington, for its part, has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, deepening Iran's economic crisis. Iranian officials say they are willing to endure the blockade to achieve their goals, and will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until it is lifted.
Iran airlines cancel flights as US sanctions hit
Iranian airlines were forced to cancel some international flights after the US tightened sanctions on Iran’s aviation industry in a new effort to cripple its economy.
Flights to Baghdad, Muscat, Qatar, Georgia and Azerbaijan were suspended, but routes to multiple other destinations remained available, including China, AFP reported, citing a travel agent in Tehran.
Some flights to Istanbul were also scheduled, though others had been cancelled, the travel agent said, adding: “The situation is unstable and we are no longer selling tickets for the time being for fear of cancellation.”
Yemen's Houthis to target US interests if it supports Saudi-led strikes: report
A Houthi military adviser told AFP that the group would attack US interests in the Middle East if Washington intervenes in Yemen’s conflict in support of Saudi Arabia or tries to unblock the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
“If America dares to intervene militarily with its fleets or tries to take control of Bab al-Mandeb, it is a red line for them and anyone else… we will fight over it,” military adviser Abed Mohammed al-Thawr said.
Europe cannot claim support for rule of law while supporting US-Israeli aggression against Iran: Araghchi
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said European countries cannot claim to support the rule of law and human rights while remaining indifferent to, or supporting, the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran, according to Iranian media outlet IRNA .
Araghchi made the remarks during a meeting with Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen on Tuesday on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York.
The two foreign ministers discussed bilateral relations as well as regional and international developments.
Araghchi criticised European countries’ double standards toward regional developments, particularly their silence regarding hostile US and Israeli actions against Iran.
Europe cannot claim support for law while backing US-Israeli aggression: @araghchi https://t.co/4P2jwZZ8ku pic.twitter.com/smjMk4EWWK
He also said repeated US treaty violations and its pursuit of war were the main causes of insecurity in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.
Araghchi said that restoring peace and stability in the region requires an end to US illegal and aggressive actions and respect for Iran’s national rights and interests.
Berendsen, for his part, stressed the importance of diplomacy and outlined the Netherlands’ views on current regional developments and interactions between Iran and Europe.
Iran calls Trump ‘annihilation’ threat a sign of ‘strategic desperation’
Iran’s military dismissed Trump’s threats against the country that he made in his address to the UN General Assembly, warning that it is ready to respond to further attacks, Al Jazeera reported on Wednesday.
BREAKING: Iran calls Trump 'annihilation' threat a sign of ‘strategic desperation’ 🔴 LIVE updates: https://t.co/P3eetlPDMu pic.twitter.com/J6IRLEMWOj
In a statement carried by the Mehr News Agency , Iran’s General Staff has accused the US president of using the UN podium to justify “aggression”.
“Such words demonstrate America’s strategic dead end in its aggression against the Iranian nation,” it says. It has described Trump’s repeated threats as “not a sign of power but a sign of their strategic desperation”.
The military’s statement, according to Mehr, also warns that Iran’s armed forces are ready to deliver strikes against the US and Israel that would be more severe, more crushing and less predictable than earlier in their war.
US senator rebukes Trump's threat to 'annihilate' Iran at UN
US Senator Bernie Sanders, responding to a clip of President Donald Trump’s speech at the United Nations regarding Iran, urged Congress to end “Trump’s war in Iran”.
Sanders said Trump’s threat to “annihilate” Iran is a “war crime”.
“That is barbarism. And it is something the United States must never be associated with.”
Sanders said in his post that "Trump’s war in Iran is illegal and unconstitutional. Congress must end it NOW.”
Macron says France ready to be more engaged to make Strait of Hormuz transit possible
French President Emmanuel Macron told US media that he does not “want to engage in a confrontation with any country, but we are ready to be more engaged to protect some capacities to make this transit possible”, regarding the Strait of Hormuz, Al Jazeera reported on Wednesday.
In an interview with ABC News , Macron has said that the “main objective” of his meeting with US President Donald Trump was “to find the right deal to open” the vital waterway and address the escalating global energy crisis.
He has criticised the US decision to go to war in the first place, saying that “regime change by bombing a country is not something I think feasible”. He has added that “it doesn’t work. And we did this mistake several times in the past decades”.
Regarding the decision not to assist the US earlier, Macron notes that “when you want to engage people, you strategise with them, and you ask them before launching a war, and we decided not to join this war because we considered, and I still consider, it was not the right option”.
FM Araghchi criticises France’s ‘interventionist’ stance toward Iran
Araghchi has criticised France’s interventionist positions toward Iran in a meeting with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot on Tuesday afternoon on the sidelines of the 81st UNGA session, stressing the need for the French embassy to respect the Islamic Republic’s laws and regulations, according to IRNA .
The two officials discussed Iran-France diplomatic relations as well as regional and international developments.
Araghchi emphasised that the French embassy must comply with Iranian laws and regulations.
He called France’s stance on regional developments, particularly its position regarding the US and Israeli military aggression against Iran, unacceptable.
Referring to France’s double standards on human rights, Araghchi said Paris could not claim concern for human rights while remaining silent over crimes against humanity by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, including the killing of Iranian women and children.
He also criticised France for cooperating in the implementation of illegal US sanctions against the Iranian people.
Araghchi stressed that Iran seeks relations based on mutual respect and interests with all countries, including France, but will act firmly and decisively to defend its interests and national interests.
Iran says it conveyed conditions for end to war to US through Qatari mediator, IRNA reports
Baghaei said the communication took place through a Qatari mediator, adding that “the aim of this interaction was to convey Iran’s conditions, including ending the war in all areas, stopping US aggressive actions and the naval blockade and economic war, and releasing Iranian assets.”
Baghaei said Iran's conditions also included an end to the naval blockade and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets, IRNA reported.
US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff said on X that the US side “engaged in lengthy talks with the Iranian delegation through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day,” on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
Today, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, we engaged in lengthy talks with the Iranian delegation through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day. They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove…
“They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising. The mediators will continue their work,” Witkoff added in his post.
Iran says 50% of damaged South Pars gas field production capacity restored, Fars news reports
Iran has restored about 50% of damaged production capacity at the South Pars gas field, Deputy Oil Minister Ahmad Zeraatkar was reported as saying on Wednesday by the semi-official Fars news agency, adding that all planned restoration work would be completed before winter.
Zeraatkar said in late August that about 40% of the damaged capacity had been returned to production.
Shipping traffic via Strait of Hormuz stays below 10-day average, data shows
Three commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, down from four a day earlier and below the 10-day moving average of about 15, preliminary shipping data showed on Wednesday.
Read: Trump says US, Iran held ‘very good’ meeting, another scheduled soon
The figures may change as some ships typically switch off their transponders during the voyage.
All three vessels, including one Panamax tanker, were exiting the strait, the data from ship tracker Kpler showed at 0700 PKT.
One ballast liquefied natural gas tanker, Al Mafyar, however, reappeared inside the strait on Tuesday, after being last seen outside of the waterway on September 19, according to both Kpler and LSEG data.
The Strait of Hormuz carried a fifth of the world's oil and gas before the US-Iran conflict.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he could annihilate Iran if there is no deal to end the war, but also suggested an agreement could come soon amid a diplomatic push at the United Nations.
Meanwhile, 22 commodity vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Tuesday, another maritime chokepoint on the southwest tip of Yemen and a vital trade route for oil between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
The data showed 14 vessels heading towards the Red Sea and 8 towards the Gulf of Aden. They included five Panamax tankers, six Supramax vessels, four Aframax tankers, a Suezmax tanker and a very large crude carrier.
Read more: Trump says there will be a deal with Iran after the midterms
The number is compared with an average of around 26 ships using the strait in the past 10 days.
Yemeni government forces seize strategic mountain in southern Taiz
Yemeni government forces established full control on Tuesday over strategic Mount Qarfan in southern Taiz province following clashes with Houthi rebels, said a defence official.
Government forces backed by popular resistance from the sons of Bani Omar tightened their control over Mount Qarfan, said Major General Abdulaziz Al-Majidi, chief of staff of the Taiz military axis, in a statement issued by the Armed Forces Media Centre.
Majidi said the confrontations resulted in more than five Houthi fighters being killed and the injury of around 20 others, adding that the group continued launching mortar rounds against military positions.
The Houthis did not immediately comment on the territorial loss.
Mount Qarfan occupies a key position along the rugged mountain chain on the Jardad-Bani Omar front between Ash Shamaytayn and Al-Wazi'iyah districts, giving holding forces command of fire control and surveillance across the surrounding valleys.
The advance unfolded amid escalating hostilities that have shifted front lines since July following recent Houthi advances along the western coastline toward the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Separately, Yemen's armed forces downed a Saudi surveillance drone over Al-Mokha in the Taiz province.
Yemeni armed forces downed an armed Saudi surveillance drone over Al-Mokha in Taiz province, on Yemen's western coastline. pic.twitter.com/LonEgIYJVM
Iran’s president arrives in New York for 81st UN General Assembly
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arrived in New York to attend and address the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, his office announced on Tuesday.
Iranian diplomatic officials, including Iran's ambassador and deputy permanent representative to the UN, welcomed the delegation upon their arrival following their morning departure from Tehran.
Pezeshkian is expected to hold separate meetings with several participating heads of state alongside engagements with various political and cultural figures during the diplomatic summit. His formal address before the General Assembly Hall will take place on Wednesday.
The trip comes amid the ongoing war between the US and Iran and follows an announcement by the Trump administration confirming that Washington would permit a core Iranian delegation to attend the high-level week in line with host country obligations under the UN Headquarters Agreement.
The approved delegation includes Pezeshkian, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and essential diplomatic personnel, though US authorities denied entry visas to several supplementary members, including segments of the president's media staff.
Explosion heard near Iran's Qeshm Island in Strait of Hormuz
An explosion was heard near Qeshm Island in southern Iran's Hormozgan province, state media reported.
The official news agency IRNA said the noise originated from the direction of the sea rather than land.
The agency said that no rockets or missiles struck the island, while local authorities have not issued a formal statement explaining the exact source or nature of the blast.
Qeshm Island, situated within the strategic Strait of Hormuz, is the largest island in the Gulf.
The incident coincides with persistent maritime and military friction in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy transit chokepoint that has served as a central theatre throughout the Iran war.
Kaja Kallas discusses Hormuz reopening, Iran diplomacy with Araghchi
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas discussed diplomatic prospects and maritime security with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, emphasising the need to ensure free navigation.
"We addressed diplomatic prospects for ending the US-Iran war and fully re-opening the Strait of Hormuz. There were no tolls or fees for passage before the war, and there should be none after the war," she said in a post on X.
Kallas said that “navigation must be free and unimpeded, both in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.”
I met with Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. We addressed diplomatic prospects for ending the US-Iran war and fully re-opening the Strait of Hormuz. There were no tolls or fees for passage before the war, and there should be none… pic.twitter.com/u5ZqUMWCDz
“I also raised domestic repression inside Iran, including the sharp rise in executions and death sentences,” she said.

title: Taking cricket to the next generation  PCB expands school programme to unearth Pakistan   s emerging talent
description: The pathway takes young cricketers from district contests via divisional and provincial stages to the national level
content:
The pathway takes young cricketers from district contests via divisional and provincial stages to the national level
There is no doubt about the abundance of cricketing talent in Pakistan.
This is a country where players have consistently emerged from streets, neighbourhoods and school grounds to go on to represent Pakistan at some of the biggest cricketing venues around the world. The challenge is not a lack of talent, but reaching that talent at the right time, identifying it and providing it with the right direction to progress.
The Pakistan Cricket Board believes that its responsibility goes beyond organising matches and tournaments. A strong cricketing system is built when talented children are identified at an early age, given opportunities to play, provided with the right training to develop their abilities, and offered a clear pathway to progress.
This is what makes school cricket so important to the future of Pakistan cricket.
PCB Chairman Mohsin Naqvi has placed special emphasis on the promotion of school cricket and the identification of new talent in Pakistan. With this objective, a number of new tournaments and programmes have been introduced at the school level.
The School Cricket Programme launched last year was an important step in the same direction. During 2025–26, 450 schools from 39 districts participated in the programme, representing the largest participation in school cricket in Pakistan at that time.
Building on that experience, the Pakistan Cricket Board has significantly expanded the programme this year, taking it to a much larger scale across the country. Around 21,000 students from 1,400 schools across 100 districts will participate this year, with a total of 2,895 matches scheduled to be played.
The real significance of these numbers lies not simply in their scale, but in the opportunities they will create for thousands of young players to showcase their abilities, compete and come under the system’s radar. Both government and private schools are participating in the programme, further broadening the reach of school cricket.
PCB has also made a conscious effort to ensure that the search for talent is not limited to traditional cricketing centres, but reaches remote and less-exposed areas of the country. Schools from different regions, from Gilgit to Gwadar, are taking part.
The participation of 124 schools from FATA, more than 80 schools from Dera Ismail Khan, as well as young players from Kashmir, Larkana and other areas, demonstrates that Pakistan’s cricketing talent is not confined to any one city or region.
This year, the programme will not be limited to matches alone. Skills development camps are being conducted across the 1,400 schools, focusing on batting, bowling, fielding and fitness. Experienced regional and district coaches, including former and international cricketers, are playing their part in training and developing the young players.
An important aspect of PCB’s school cricket initiative is to ensure that talented players identified through these competitions have a clear pathway to progress. The journey will move from the district level to the divisional, provincial and ultimately national stages.
District league pool matches will be held from September to October, followed by a knockout phase involving 100 teams in November, while the national stage will take place from late November through December. The national final will be played on 5 December.
For a young cricketer, the significance of this journey goes beyond winning a trophy. Players who demonstrate outstanding performances will have opportunities to progress into U15, U17 and U19 cricket, as well as gain access to 16 regional academies and regional cricket.
A schoolboy from a remote district of Pakistan may today be playing only for his school team. But if he possesses the ability, this programme can provide him with the opportunity to be seen, assessed and given a pathway to progress.
That is the real strength of school cricket. This is not simply a tournament. It is a structured effort to reach young Pakistanis who want to play, want to progress and dream of one day wearing the green shirt of Pakistan.
The initiatives under the leadership of Mohsin Naqvi to introduce new tournaments at the school level and continuously expand the reach of school cricket are part of a broader effort to identify Pakistan’s emerging talent at an early stage, provide young players with opportunities for training and competitive cricket, and create a clear pathway towards national cricket.
The Pakistan Cricket Board’s objective is to ensure that this opportunity is not limited to the major cities, but reaches every child and young player across the country who has the potential to become part of Pakistan’s cricketing future.

title: PM Shehbaz reaffirms support for Syria   s sovereignty in meeting with President Sharaa
description: Meets Syrian president on UNGA sidelines  stresses dialogue  diplomacy and respect for UN Charter to promote peace
content:
Meets Syrian president on UNGA sidelines, stresses dialogue, diplomacy and respect for UN Charter to promote peace
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday reiterated Pakistan’s principled support for Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and expressed readiness to contribute to the country’s reconstruction and economic recovery.
The prime minister made the remarks during a meeting with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, according to a statement issued by the Prime Minister's Office.
PM Shehbaz reaffirmed Pakistan’s strong commitment to its historic and fraternal relations with Syria and reiterated its support for Syria’s sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity and political independence.
The two leaders discussed ways to further strengthen bilateral relations, including through enhanced high-level exchanges, activation of institutional mechanisms and cooperation in trade and investment, education, information technology and other areas of mutual interest.
Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif met today with President of the Syrian Arab Republic, H.E. Mr. Ahmed al-Sharaa, on sidelines of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The Prime Minister reaffirmed Pakistan’s strong commitment to its historic… pic.twitter.com/pTaqhXCbcW
The prime minister reaffirmed Pakistan’s readiness to contribute to Syria’s reconstruction and economic recovery, while reiterating its principled support for the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The two leaders also exchanged views on the regional situation, with the prime minister underscoring the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and respect for the principles of the UN Charter in promoting peace and stability in the region.
The prime minister reaffirmed Pakistan’s steadfast support for the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and for a just and lasting resolution of the Palestine issue in accordance with relevant UN resolutions and international law.
He also expressed good wishes for the Syrian people in their efforts towards national stabilisation, cohesion, peace and economic recovery.
The meeting provided an opportunity to reaffirm the longstanding bonds of friendship between Pakistan and Syria and to further strengthen bilateral cooperation in the years ahead.
