title: Finance ministry dismisses fiscal numbers only claim
description: Finance ministry dismisses fiscal numbers only claim
content:
Says IMF loan is whole-of-govt programme, not a single division's project
A day after Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal sought a role for the Planning Commission in the International Monetary Fund (IMF) talks and described it as "fiscal numbers" focused, the Ministry of Finance on Tuesday turned down the assertion.
The "IMF programme is demonstrably not confined to numbers or fiscal targets", said the ministry in a detailed response. The finance ministry also sought to make a distinction between its role "for overall programme coordination" and agreement on benchmarks that were the responsibility of other divisions and provincial governments. The ministry's reaction came the day the IMF mission landed in Karachi for the fourth review of the $7 billion loan programme, which is expected to continue till October 7.
"Concerned ministries and institutions participate and lead technical discussions, including benchmark setting relating to their respective mandate," said the finance ministry. A day earlier, Ahsan Iqbal had said that he recommended to the prime minister that a representative of the Planning Commission should also be included in the team that would negotiate with the IMF. The planning minister said that the IMF programme was not just about numbers, but it would have implications for economic growth, development and people.
The statement added that the Finance Division "fully recognises that macroeconomic stabilisation is a means towards sustainable and inclusive economic growth". The finance ministry further said that certain assertions and interpretations regarding the Ministry of Finance, Pakistan's engagement with the IMF, and the government's economic stabilisation programme did not accurately reflect the facts or institutional process.
It said that this could create an incorrect impression among the public and market participants. "The IMF programme is a whole-of-government programme, not a Finance Division programme," it added. The characterisation that the Ministry of Finance has maintained tight control over programme design and negotiations did not accurately reflect the institutional arrangements underlying Pakistan's IMF programme, said the ministry.
It added that a clear distinction needed to be maintained between the Finance Division's responsibility for overall programme coordination, and the agreement on benchmarks with the IMF leading to policymaking, legislative and implementation responsibilities of respective federal ministries and provincial governments.
However, the finance ministry did not comment whether it was ready to accept a representative of the Planning Commission as part of the IMF parleys. But the ministry said that the appropriate policy debate was therefore not stabilisation versus growth but how to transition from stabilisation towards sustainable growth without any fiscal and external imbalances that necessitated reverting to the IMF stabilisation programmes, as witnessed in the past.
It added that the IMF's Extended Fund Facility and the Resilience and Sustainability Facility encompassed reforms and commitments falling within the mandates of multiple federal and provincial institutions, including the Finance Division, Planning Commission, Ministry of Planning, Ministry of Energy, provincial governments, FBR, SBP and other relevant stakeholders.
The ministry stressed that the published IMF programme explicitly encompassed growth-enhancing structural reforms, social protection, governance, energy-sector efficiency, climate resilience and reduction of distortions in the economy. The latest IMF staff report specifically states that policy discussions focused on accelerating reforms to support stronger growth, while protecting vulnerable households. While reacting to the talk of petroleum levy being the central point of the IMF programme, the finance ministry said that the levy was not the central point of the loan programme.
The assertion that the Finance Division has made PDL the "central point" of the IMF programme is misleading. The programme's fiscal strategy was substantially broader and revolved around FBR revenue mobilisation, expansion of the tax base, provincial taxation and expenditure rationalisation, it added. The finance ministry said that for the current fiscal year, the IMF programme specifically emphasised the need for additional revenue mobilisation and strengthening FBR performance rather than relying solely on petroleum taxation.
The petroleum levy is one of the revenue instruments, and describing it as the centrepiece of the programme materially overstates its role, according to the ministry. The finance ministry admitted that while the programme did not prescribe a single permanent headline PDL rate in the manner suggested, the published programme documents contained explicit details concerning petroleum pricing and levies. These include the alignment of domestic fuel prices with international prices through regular adjustments.

title: EU envoy sees scope to expand trade
description: EU envoy sees scope to expand trade
content:
Says 12.2b Pak-EU economic ties can grow with more investment, B2B relations
The European Union ambassador has said that there is significant scope for expanding economic and commercial relations between Pakistan and the European Union through higher exports, greater investment, technology transfer and stronger business-to-business (B2B) cooperation.
EU Ambassador Raimundas Karoblis was talking to an All Pakistan Business Forum (APBF) delegation, where the two sides discussed bilateral trade and investment, joint ventures, GSP+ market access, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), technical and vocational education and training (TVET), and emerging regulatory requirements in the European market.
The meeting was attended by APBF President Syed Maaz Mahmood, Secretary-General Amir Munir Malik, Mian Faheem Qamar, Patron-in-Chief of Sundar Trade and Industry Association, Haroon Ali Khan, Chairman Pakistan Chemical Manufacturing Association, Shahzad Azam, Chairman PIEDMC, Brigadier (Retd) M Sajid Khokhar, Chairperson Tevta Punjab, Nasir Ali Zia, Director Masood Textile, Aziz Ullah Goheer, Secretary-General Pakistan Textile Exporters Association and other business leaders.
The ambassador said Pakistan had benefited considerably from the GSP+ scheme and stressed that the country could further benefit by fully implementing ILO conventions, diversifying its export base, increasing value addition and developing a skilled workforce.
According to the latest European Commission assessment, Pakistan's exports to the EU reached about 8.3 billion, with the EU accounting for around 28% of Pakistan's total exports. The EU remained Pakistan's largest export market, while textiles and clothing constituted roughly 75% of Pakistan's exports to the bloc. In 2025, bilateral trade in goods between the EU and Pakistan stood at 12.2 billion.
Karoblis emphasised closer interaction between Pakistani and European businesses to identify new areas of commercial cooperation. He also highlighted the importance of skills development and workforce preparation.
APBF appreciated EU support for technical and vocational education and training, saying a better-skilled workforce could serve both Pakistan's domestic economy and overseas labour markets. EU-supported TVET programmes have focused on demand-driven skills and employment opportunities, while an evaluation of the TVET-III programme recorded 118,946 competency-based training graduates and 19,530 workplace-based trainees.
Pakistan's overseas workforce is also an important source of foreign exchange. Workers' remittances reached a record $41.6 billion in FY2025-26, with remittances from EU countries contributing about $5.23 billion during the year.
APBF President Syed Maaz Mahmood said Pakistan's business community wanted stronger and more practical economic engagement with the EU, particularly through B2B contacts, investment and joint ventures.
He also called for greater support for SMEs to meet European certification, documentation and compliance requirements and make fuller use of GSP+ market access.
Maaz Mahmood said SMEs constituted a major part of Pakistan's economic base, but many smaller businesses faced difficulties in meeting the cost of international certifications and increasingly stringent European standards. Technical assistance and easier access to information, he said, could help Pakistani SMEs enter European supply chains and expand exports.
The APBF president also briefed the EU envoy on the forum's initiatives to develop business linkages between Pakistani enterprises and international markets, saying the organisation was ready to facilitate direct interaction between Pakistani and European businesses through B2B meetings, sector-specific linkages and joint ventures.
APBF Secretary-General Amir Munir Malik welcomed Ambassador Karoblis and his team while APBF members shared sector-specific views and highlighted the challenges faced by SMEs in meeting international standards, obtaining certifications and completing documentation for foreign markets.
During the interaction, the participants of the meeting said stronger technical cooperation with European institutions could help Pakistani companies improve production standards, meet environmental and social requirements and become more competitive in international supply chains.

Despite Trump remarks, flows through Hormuz increase
Oil prices rose on Tuesday as traders worried about global supplies after US President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly in a speech that a peace deal with Iran could come after the US mid-term elections, which are not until early November.
Trump also said that without a peace deal he could "annihilate" Iran. He was expected to meet with world leaders at the UN in New York this week, feeding hopes for stability in the Middle East and perhaps even progress in ending Russia's 4-1/2-year-old war in Ukraine.
The Brent crude futures November contract was at $99.94 a barrel at 1507 GMT. The WTI October contract, which was expiring on Tuesday, stood at $95.43 a barrel.
Trump's comments burst mounting hopes that a deal could come during this week's UN General Assembly meeting in New York. Feeding the optimism, flows through the Strait of Hormuz were seen increasing in recent days.
"Saudi Arabia is acting, not waiting," said Phil Flynn, Senior Analyst at Price Futures Group. "After Houthi hits on the East-West pipeline forced a shutdown of Yanbu loadings, Aramco loaded about 14 million barrels of crude onto seven VLCCs inside the Gulf. Satellite and tracker data showed Saudi oil moving through Hormuz averaging about 2.9 million barrels a day over the last six days, up from roughly 700,000 barrels a day in August."

title: China s gold buying tops 1 000 tons
description: China s gold buying tops 1 000 tons
content:
Bullion price falls Rs1,800 to Rs455,736/tola as global market slips
China imported more than 1,000 tons of gold through August 2026, according to the latest customs data. That volume already exceeds the country's total gold imports for the entire 2025.
"Strong investment demand keeps onshore gold prices at a slight premium to world benchmarks. That premium attracts more imports into China," said Adnan Agar, Director at Interactive Commodities.
Customs records that go back to 2017 show January-to-August 2026 imports as the highest for that period. The 2026 bar on the chart stands well above the previous years and crosses the 1,000-ton mark.
Zijie Wu, an analyst at Jinrui Futures Company, cited by Bloomberg, noted that the premium and robust investment demand continued to pull gold into the country.
A firmer yuan and lower international prices also support buying, said Agar. Meanwhile, gold prices in Pakistan declined on Tuesday in line with losses in the international market, as investors priced in a more restrictive monetary policy path from the US Federal Reserve this year and kept a close watch on the conflict in the Middle East.
According to rates issued by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association (APGJSA), the 24-karat gold fell Rs1,800 per tola to Rs455,736. Ten grams of 24-karat gold were quoted at Rs390,720 after a drop of Rs1,543, while 10 grams of 22-karat gold declined Rs1,414 to Rs358,173.
The slide extended Monday's sharper correction, when the per-tola rate dropped Rs2,700 and closed at Rs457,536. Silver also weakened, falling Rs62 to Rs7,038 per tola. Ten grams of silver dropped Rs54 to Rs6,033. The association put the international silver price at $65.60 an ounce after a decline of $0.62.
In global trade, spot gold was down 0.4% at $4,325.03 per ounce by 12:10 pm ET (1610 GMT). US gold futures fell 0.5% to $4,362, according to Reuters. APGJSA reported the international rate at $4,332 an ounce after a decline of $18. Bullion is now more than 22% below the all-time high recorded in January.
Markets have shifted towards a tighter Federal Reserve stance. Traders see a 90% chance of a rate increase in December, according to the CME FedWatch tool, up from about 80% a week earlier.
St Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee both said further hikes may be needed to contain inflation driven by strong demand and elevated energy prices. That follows last week's increase in the US policy rate and comments from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh flagging additional tightening in the months ahead.
Higher interest rates typically reduce gold's appeal because the metal pays no yield, while a firmer dollar makes bullion more expensive for holders of other currencies.
"The problem remains that despite oil trending down somewhat, the market is continuing to robustly price Fed hikes over the last few days, we've had a bit of strength on the US dollar side, and that's typically a negative for gold," said Bart Melek, Global Head of Commodity Strategy at TD Securities.
Furthermore, the Pakistani rupee extended its marginal gains against the US dollar in the inter-bank market on Tuesday, closing at 277.21, up Rs0.01 from Monday's settlement at 277.22.
Globally, a firm dollar kept the Japanese yen under pressure as traders wagered that policymakers in Japan would struggle to match a hawkish turn by other major central banks, leaving Japanese rates far below those of peers. After slipping on Monday, the yen traded at 157.33 versus the dollar early Tuesday.
Moves were contained by a holiday in Japan and the risk of intervention after the Nikkei reported authorities checked dollar/yen rates on Friday, often a precursor to stepping into the market. Broader financial markets were buoyed by falling oil prices.

title: 100 acre mariculture estate planned at Korangi harbour
description: 100 acre mariculture estate planned at Korangi harbour
content:
Zone will comprise hatcheries, research activities, value addition and cold chain
Federal Minister for Maritime Affairs Muhammad Junaid Anwar Chaudhry has outlined a plan to establish a 100-acre Mariculture Investment and Development Estate (MIDE) at the Korangi Fisheries Harbour Authority (KoFHA).
Speaking at a briefing on the proposed project, the minister said the estate would integrate mariculture and aquaculture operations with hatcheries, research and innovation, processing, value addition, cold-chain facilities and commercial services under a single development framework.
Mariculture ecosystem operations are the management and functioning of marine farming systems within coastal and ocean environment. They involve cultivating marine organisms such as fish, shrimp, oysters, mussels and seaweed while managing their interaction with the surrounding ecosystem.
According to the concept master plan, the estate would have four principal zones including a 30-acre mariculture zone, a 20-acre hatchery zone, a 20-acre aqua research park and a 20-acre commercial district.
"The development of a modern mariculture ecosystem can help Pakistan move towards higher-value fisheries production, strengthen aquatic seed production and promote value addition and export-oriented activities," Chaudhry said. He said the hatchery zone would support advanced aquatic seed production, while the research park would provide facilities for research, innovation and training.
The estate will also include processing and cold-chain infrastructure, commercial and hospitality facilities, sustainable infrastructure and green spaces.
The proposed infrastructure will comprise an internal road network, power and renewable-energy facilities, water supply and treatment systems, wastewater treatment, information and communication technology, smart-estate management, security and surveillance, and green belts and landscaping.
Chaudhry said the initiative was aimed at attracting investment, increasing exports, generating employment and promoting technology and innovation as part of the country's blue economy.
"Investing in modern marine infrastructure and technology is essential for building a sustainable blue economy and creating new economic opportunities for coastal communities," he said.
The concept plan identifies the national deep-sea fishing harbour, KoFHA, as the institutional setting for the proposed development.

title: Oil  gas reserves hit 3 72b BOE
description: Oil  gas reserves hit 3 72b BOE
content:
Life extends to 19 years; crude volumes climb 15% to 276m barrels
Pakistan's recoverable oil and gas reserves climbed to an estimated 3.72 billion barrels of oil equivalent (BOE) by June 2026, as new discoveries and reserve upgrades offset depletion at several mature fields, according to an Arif Habib Limited (AHL) research report based on Pakistan Petroleum Information Service (PPIS) data.
The country's oil reserves increased 15% year-on-year to 276 million barrels from 240 million barrels in June 2025. Natural gas reserves rose 9% to 20,664 billion cubic feet (bcf), compared with 18,981 bcf a year earlier.
The improvement lifted Pakistan's estimated overall hydrocarbon reserve life to around 19 years, up from 15 years in June 2024 and June 2023.
The strongest contribution to oil reserves came from the Baragzai field, whose reserves reached 49.09 million barrels, compared with 21.01 million barrels reported in December 2025. Gains at Mardankhel, Mamikhel South, Maramzai and Spinwam also supported the increase.
These additions outweighed declines at mature fields including Nashpa, Adhi, Pasakhi/Pasakhi North East, Makori East, Kunar and Sono. Gas reserve growth was led by Mari Ghazij, where reserves jumped 74% year-on-year to 1,723 bcf, and Spinwam, where reserves increased more than fivefold to 489 bcf.
Contributions from Baragzai and Soho also helped offset depletion at Sui, Kandhkot, Nashpa, Uch and Qadirpur.
Newly discovered fields – Spinwam, Baragzai, Bitrism East, Chakar and Faakir – collectively added 53.52 million barrels of oil and 772.97 bcf of gas to the national reserve base.
Among major listed exploration and production companies, Oil and Gas Development Company's oil reserves rose 16% to 152 million barrels, while Pakistan Petroleum Limited recorded a 58% increase to 33 million barrels. Mari Energies' oil reserves grew 5% to 10 million barrels, whereas Pakistan Oilfields Limited's reserves declined 5% to 14 million barrels.
Gas trends were mixed. Mari's gas reserves increased 15% to 6,353 bcf, supported by Mari Ghazij, Spinwam and Soho. In contrast, OGDC's gas reserves fell 4% to 5,750 bcf, PPL's reserves declined 3% to 2,178 bcf, and POL's deposits eased 2% to 211 bcf.
AHL estimated the remaining reserve life at 21 years for Mari, 19 years for OGDC and 10 years each for PPL and POL.

title: Fixed tax draws only 2 new traders
description: Fixed tax draws only 2 new traders
content:
Rs26m can be collected from traders so far vs annual target of Rs50b
Only two new traders have so far opted for the 1% fixed tax scheme while another 315 shopkeepers who have filed returns are already part of the tax regime – an outcome that suggests that the government's scheme may fail.
With only a week left in the deadline to file returns, a mere Rs26 million, with an average of Rs81,944 per trader, could be generated so far against the annual target of collecting Rs50 billion from traders under the new scheme. Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani on Tuesday reviewed the status of the fixed tax scheme.
According to details, so far two new shopkeepers have availed of the scheme, one from Quetta and another from Rawalpindi. A further 44 new shopkeepers had drafted their returns but did not submit them till Tuesday.
Total beneficiaries of the new scheme have remained a mere 317 traders, of which 315 were already income tax filers. The government had launched the scheme under which small retailers could pay a fixed 1% tax on sales in return for exemption from tax audits and the requirements related to digital transaction systems.
It is the second such initiative by the government aimed at bringing traders into the tax net after the earlier "Tajir Dost" scheme failed to deliver the desired results. Kayani was hopeful about the success of the scheme due to the involvement of representatives of traders in its design and execution.
Although the state minister never officially gave any target of traders to be brought in the tax net in the first year, he did hope that a majority of 3.5 million traders would opt for the scheme.
A statement issued by the finance ministry on Tuesday said that the meeting decided to intensify the awareness campaign for shopkeepers. Kayani directed tax commissioners across the country to coordinate with local tax bars so that shopkeepers could get forms filled from lawyers of their choice. Progress on the Easy Tax Scheme was reviewed in the meeting.
As per the points agreed with trader representatives, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has the authority to impose a penalty on shopkeepers who neither file tax returns under the new scheme nor opt to submit returns under the regular income option.
"Under the tax scheme, the shopkeeper who does not use either option will face a penalty of Rs10,000 in the first month, Rs25,000 in the second month and Rs50,000 in the third month," said the official statement. Shopkeepers would either pay the fixed tax on the basis of turnover or file regular returns, it added.
The state minister stressed that information about the scheme should reach every shopkeeper with the help of trader representatives. By acting on the demands of traders, the government has fulfilled its promise; now shopkeepers must make the scheme a success, he said.
However, the new scheme could not encourage many unregistered traders. Details showed that there were another 44 new traders who had prepared the draft of income tax return but did not file it.
The statutory deadline for filing tax returns by the traders and all taxpayers is September 30, which is expected to be extended due to poor results.
A total of 6,631 traders have so far prepared draft returns under the new scheme but about 6,587 were already the return filers, who may accept the new scheme because of exemption from audit and the installation of digital mode of payments.
Out of the total 317 filers so far, the maximum number of 87 shopkeepers were from Rawalpindi, including one new trader. There were hardly 61 filers from Lahore but none of them were new filers. From Karachi, a mere 24 traders have so far opted for the new scheme but none of them is a new filer.
From Sahiwal, 33 traders have so far come under the scheme; all of them already part of the tax regime. From Sialkot, just 25 shopkeepers embraced the new scheme and from Islamabad, there were only 23. Last week, Bilal Azhar Kayani affixed a green plate on the outlet of a shopkeeper registered under the new scheme.
FBR staff cannot enter the premises of a shopkeeper who joins the scheme and generally no audit of such a shopkeeper will be conducted. But even this benefit could not encourage the traders.
The new scheme also exempts participants from installing the Point-of-Sale system and from acting as withholding tax agents. Shopkeepers owning a single outlet with annual sales below Rs200 million over the past three consecutive years can join the scheme. Eligible participants will pay a 1% tax on the total value of goods sold.
Where the government goes soft on traders and real estate agents, it has not done enough for the marginalised salaried class. Income tax collection from the salaried class amounted to Rs91 billion during July and August of the current fiscal year. It was higher by Rs6.3 billion, or 7.5%, compared to the same period of last year.
FBR data showed that income tax collection from the real estate sector decreased by 28% to Rs28 billion in the current fiscal year. In just two months, the real estate sector paid Rs11.2 billion less than last year despite an expected increase in property transactions.

title: Robert Eggers sets his sights on Shakespeare   s  Romeo and Juliet
description: Robert Eggers will direct a new  Romeo and Juliet  adaptation for Focus Features after a competitive bidding war
content:
Robert Eggers will direct a new 'Romeo and Juliet' adaptation for Focus Features after a competitive bidding war
Robert Eggers is set to direct a new film adaptation of William Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet for Focus Features, according to reports.
The filmmaker is expected to direct and produce the project, which emerged from a bidding war involving Focus Features, A24, Sony and Warner Bros. The film is planned as Eggers’ next production after his upcoming werewolf movie Werwulf .
The new Romeo and Juliet adaptation will reportedly feature actors speaking in Olde English, reflecting Eggers’ focus on historical detail and period authenticity. Further details about the cast and other producers have not yet been announced.
Shakespeare’s tragedy follows Romeo Montague and Juliet Capulet, two young lovers whose families are locked in a bitter feud in Verona, Italy. First written in the 1590s, the play has inspired numerous film adaptations, including Franco Zeffirelli’s 1968 version and Baz Luhrmann’s 1996 film Romeo + Juliet , starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes.
The deal for Eggers’ adaptation is reportedly valued in the high tens of millions of dollars, covering filmmaker and talent fees as well as production costs.
The project will reunite Eggers with Focus Features, which has worked with the filmmaker on several of his previous movies. The studio released The Northman and Nosferatu , while also handling international distribution for The Lighthouse .
Eggers’ next film, Werwulf , stars Aaron Taylor-Johnson and Lily-Rose Depp, who previously appeared in Nosferatu . The horror film is scheduled for a Christmas Day theatrical release.
The new Romeo and Juliet film will add another period-focused project to Eggers’ filmography while offering a fresh interpretation of one of Shakespeare’s best-known tragedies.

content:
Mary Beth Barone will write and star opposite Joe Alwyn in 'Still We Met', with Lena Dunham among the EPs
Comedian and writer Mary Beth Barone is set to make her feature screenwriting and acting debut with Still We Met , an original romantic comedy that will see her star opposite Joe Alwyn.
Barone wrote the film, which is loosely inspired by her own experiences. The story follows a young woman at a crossroads who meets a charming British stranger and spends an unforgettable night exploring New York City. As they spend time together, the pair reveal more about themselves than either initially intended.
Zackary Drucker, known for the Emmy-nominated short-form docuseries This Is Me , will make her narrative feature directorial debut with the project. Production is scheduled to begin this fall in New York.
Jack Heller and Caitlin de Lisser-Ellen will produce the film for Assemble Media, while Alex Bach and Daniel Powell will produce for Irony Point. Lena Dunham and Michael Cohen are executive producing through their Good Thing Going banner, with Madison Wolk serving as co-producer alongside Blake Mars.
Barone recently wrote and starred opposite Benito Skinner in the Amazon/A24 comedy Overcompensating . She also recently released her Netflix stand-up special Galaxy Brain , which reached the platform’s Top 10.
Alwyn, meanwhile, has recently appeared in Chloé Zhao’s Hamnet and Brady Corbet’s The Brutalist . He is also set to appear in Sam Esmail’s upcoming film Panic Carefully alongside Julia Roberts, Eddie Redmayne and Elizabeth Olsen, as well as Apple TV+ series The Husbands .

title: Trump TV coverage halted in extraordinary press revolt | The Express Tribune
description:
Trump TV coverage halted 
in extraordinary press revolt
content:
Television networks boycott coverage of US president in protest against his ban on three media outlets
US television networks staged an extraordinary revolt Monday when they effectively boycotted coverage of President Donald Trump in protest at his decision to ban three leading outlets from the White House.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico also went to court after Trump on Friday ordered them to be barred, as the 80-year-old Republican stepped up his years-long assault on the US media.
As a result of the row, Trump's opening of his cherished new White House helipad and his trip to the United Nations General Assembly were proceeding without live television coverage.
In a rare move, the top five US broadcasters said on Monday that they were halting "pool" coverage of the White House -- where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day -- in solidarity with CNN.
CNN had been scheduled to serve Monday as the White House TV pool.
"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said in a statement.
The result is an almost unprecedented test of wills between the Trump administration and the press, in a critical week during which Chinese President Xi Jinping is visiting the White House.
There will be no live TV of Trump's meetings with foreign leaders at the UN in New York, an annual forum that is closely watched around the world.
Meanwhile the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the giant granite helipad on the South Lawn was only streamed on the White House's website -- and Trump's comments were completely inaudible.
Several photo news organizations working at the White House, including AFP, decided to delay the release of photographs of Trump at the helipad in solidarity with the three banned media organizations.
Trump was unrepentant, branding the media a "cancer" and a threat to national security.
"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
"It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America."
Vice President JD Vance -- a former CNN commentator before his move into politics -- accused the outlets of disseminating "left-wing propaganda."
"They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They're just not going to get an office in the White House anymore," he told reporters.
Trump's ban however went further than simply revoking office space from the outlets.
Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied any access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated.
In their lawsuit, the three organizations asked for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.
"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the organizations said in a court filing.
A US district judge set a hearing on the complaint for Wednesday.
Trump's sudden announcement of the ban on Friday stunned the media -- and reportedly many in his own administration.
The president has not detailed what prompted the ban, but said in response to a question from an AFP reporter in the Oval Office on Friday that it was "really just cumulative stories over the last two years."
Trump warned Friday that other outlets could face a similar fate, without saying which.
The billionaire former reality TV star has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people."
But the ban comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows, his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections, and the Iran war drags on with no end in sight.

title: LHC declines to suspend Ali Zafar defamation ruling
description: LHC declines to suspend Ali Zafar defamation ruling
content:
Singer had prevailed in his suit against fellow singer Meesha Shafi
The Lahore High Court has declined to suspend a defamation judgment in favour of Pakistani singer and actor Ali Zafar in his case against fellow singer Meesha Shafi.
A division bench, in an order issued on 4 May 2026, granted only limited interim relief to Shafi concerning the damages awarded by the trial court.
The court said 50% of the decretal amount would have to be deposited with the Deputy Registrar (Judicial), while a surety bond would have to be furnished for the remaining 50% within two months for the limited suspension of the decree to take effect.
The appeal against the trial court's judgment remains pending.
The dispute began in 2018, when Shafi publicly accused Zafar of sexual harassment. He denied the allegation and subsequently filed a defamation case against her.
In March 2026, a trial court partially allowed Zafar's defamation suit. It found that the allegations against him were false and defamatory and that they had not been made for the public good.
The court also issued an injunction restraining Shafi from repeating the allegations.
Shafi challenged the judgment before the Lahore High Court and sought a suspension of the decree while her appeal was being heard.
The High Court did not grant the blanket suspension sought by her. Instead, its interim order dealt specifically with the damages component and attached conditions to any suspension.
The order does not amount to a final decision on Shafi's appeal. The High Court is yet to examine the appeal on its merits.
The trial court's findings and injunction therefore remain part of the existing judgment while the appeal is pending.
A further issue concerns whether the conditions attached to the interim relief were fulfilled.
Zafar's side has maintained that the two-month period expired without Shafi depositing the required amount or furnishing the surety bond.
If that position is upheld, the conditional suspension of the damages component would not have taken effect.
The High Court's eventual decision on the appeal will determine whether the trial court's judgment is upheld, modified or overturned.
Neither the admission of the appeal nor the limited interim relief granted by the High Court should be treated as a final determination of the underlying dispute.
Alongside his acting and singing career, Ali Zafar participates in tours, concerts, and stage shows, is active in humanitarian work, and has a number of endorsement deals. On 23 March 2021, he was awarded the highest literary award, Pride of Performance, for his contribution in the field of arts and music.

title: Presley Gerber was reportedly prescribed ketamine before his death | The Express Tribune
description: Presley Gerber reportedly prescribed ketamine despite substance issues as official cause of death remains pending
content:
Presley Gerber reportedly prescribed ketamine despite substance issues as official cause of death remains pending
Presley Gerber’s doctor allegedly prescribed him ketamine despite being aware of his reported issues with the substance, according to people who were regularly in contact with the model before his death.
Sources with direct knowledge told TMZ that ketamine had been a recurring concern for Gerber. However, it remains unclear whether ketamine or any other drug was present in his system when he died.
Gerber died at a rehabilitation facility on Sunday, September 20, at the age of 27. His official cause of death has not yet been released. An autopsy has been completed, but authorities are still awaiting toxicology results and other findings.
People who had contact with Gerber during his final hours reportedly told TMZ that he appeared to be under the influence while at the rehab facility. The source of any drugs involved remains under investigation, with police reportedly speaking to other patients at the facility.
Gerber had previously discussed his struggles with ketamine with close friends, according to the sources. Some people close to him have questioned why he was prescribed the drug and have called for further investigation into the circumstances.
Ketamine has medical uses, including anaesthesia and certain mental health treatments, although its use and regulation vary depending on the treatment and jurisdiction. It is not FDA-approved specifically to treat drug addiction.
Gerber had reportedly explored alternative approaches to addiction treatment in the months before his death, including ibogaine, a psychoactive substance that has been studied in connection with substance use disorders.
His death has drawn comparisons to the 2023 death of actor Matthew Perry, who had received ketamine treatment. However, the circumstances surrounding the two cases are different, and there is currently no confirmed evidence linking Gerber’s death to ketamine.
Authorities have yet to determine Gerber’s official cause of death.

title: From justice at the doorstep to the palm of your hand
description: If technology can shrink distance elsewhere  it can shorten the journey to justice
content:
If technology can shrink distance elsewhere, it can shorten the journey to justice
At the heart of every justice system lies a promise: justice should be within every citizen's reach, unhindered by distance, cost or unnecessary difficulty. For years, judicial reform has pursued the aspiration of "justice at the doorstep". Technology has widened that possibility. The world has become a global village: from a mobile phone, we transfer money, communicate across continents and access services once requiring a physical journey. If technology can shrink distance elsewhere, it can shorten the journey to justice.
Consider an ordinary litigant who repeatedly travels to court to file a document, obtain a copy or check a hearing date. Each journey costs money and time. If the case moves to a higher court, documents already within the judicial system may again have to be collected, copied and submitted. Technology can change that experience by allowing information to travel instead of repeatedly requiring the citizen to do so.
This speaks directly to Article 37(d) of the Constitution, which calls for inexpensive and expeditious justice. Technology cannot replace due process, but it can remove avoidable difficulties surrounding litigation.
Against this backdrop, the proposed National Unified E-Filing and Electronic Judicial Record System assumes significance. It goes beyond filing cases online. A case would be filed once, given a permanent identity, and remain connected with its authenticated electronic record throughout its judicial journey.
At its heart is the Universal Case Identification Number, or UCIN: one permanent national identity for a case. Once assigned to the originating case, it would remain linked through appeal, revision, review or other connected proceedings, connecting the electronic record from the trial court to the Supreme Court. Court-level numbers may continue for administrative purposes, but the case would retain one permanent identity: one case, one identity, one continuously connected judicial record.
For litigants, the benefit is practical. Instead of rebuilding the record at every stage, an authorised higher court could retrieve the authenticated record of the preceding court through the UCIN. Documents already forming part of that record would ordinarily not need to be filed again, subject to law and access requirements. That could mean fewer papers, visits and costs.
The same identity could make a case easier to track. A litigant could see the current stage, latest order, next hearing date and case status without searching through the entire record. For someone waiting for a dispute to be resolved, such information brings greater certainty to an otherwise stressful journey.
The benefits extend to courts. A connected record could show how a case is progressing and where delays are developing. Technology cannot guarantee disposal within a fixed period, nor should fairness be sacrificed for speed. But it can make delay visible. Cases requiring attention could be identified through reliable data and timelines. Over time, this can support better case management, improved services, greater predictability and measurable institutional improvement. What can be traced and measured can be better managed.
The proposed family cases pilot provides a practical starting point, testing the electronic lifecycle from the Family Court through the appellate hierarchy to the Supreme Court. The UCIN and connected record would continue throughout, reducing duplication.
Technology can also reduce visits made to obtain information. Courts will remain physical institutions where hearings, evidence or personal appearance require them, but every interaction need not require a physical journey. The aspiration can therefore move from justice at the doorstep to justice in the palm of the hand.
Greater convenience requires greater trust. As pleadings, evidence, orders and judgments become electronic, they must be protected against unauthorised access, alteration or loss. Strong cybersecurity, controlled access and reliable audit trails, supported by the proposed Judicial Cyber Emergency Response Team, will therefore be essential.
Looking ahead, blockchain technology could be explored as an additional layer of security and trust. For critical documents such as judgments and final orders, a unique cryptographic code could be generated after authentication and linked with the UCIN, issuing court, date and version. The document would remain securely stored in the judicial repository. Any later alteration would change the code, making the alteration detectable and the authenticity of the record verifiable.
This could make critical judicial records more tamper-resistant and traceable without depending on any individual official. Blockchain should complement rather than replace cybersecurity, digital signatures and secure judicial repositories, and should be considered only where testing demonstrates added security, reliability and value.
Ultimately, digital justice will not be judged by portals launched or files scanned. Its real measure will be the difficulties a litigant no longer faces: the journey no longer required, the document no longer reproduced, the case that can be tracked, the delay that can be seen and the judicial record that can be trusted.
Technology is only a means. The true measure of a justice system lies in the trust it commands, the fairness it upholds, and the assurance it gives every citizen that they will be heard, treated with dignity, and receive justice. From justice at the doorstep to justice in the palm of the hand, technology can help turn the constitutional aspiration of inexpensive and expeditious justice into an everyday reality.

title: The squandered legacy of statecraft
description: Mohajirs must reclaim their affinity for the civil service by raising their educational standards
content:
Mohajirs must reclaim their affinity for the civil service by raising their educational standards
Ethno-lingual identity has never been my concern. However, as the descendant of an Urdu-speaking migrant from India, my cultural background remains a frequent point of reflection. Growing up in Karachi, I often experienced the subtle social frictions and distinct dynamics that exist between native communities and migrant families. Over time, these differences highlight a unique historical contrast: while the local Sindhi community served as generous hosts, many migrants arrived with formal educational backgrounds that allowed them to actively shape Pakistan's early administrative and civil services.
The migrants, mocked as mohajirs (refugees), prided themselves in their culture of Oudh, Osmania's Hyderabad, Lucknow, the State of Madras, Bihar and Kavi Narmad's Gujarat. For them Bahadur Shah Zafar, Rani of Jhansi, Nawab Osman Ali Khan, Mir Anees, Mirza Ghalib and Rabindranath Tagore were proprietary legends. It is a fact that 'men of pen' came from India to form the backbone of Pakistan's infant bureaucracy. Many were from the prestigious ICS and IAS cadres, and moved to the new-born state in pursuit of political pluralism, hoping for a career and identity that is professional to the core.
These officers were lucky enough to be buckled up with a great number of junior associates who were well-versed in writing English prose, and understood the ethics of office management. They started from scratch, and the tale has it that they bought pens and stationery, at times, on their own. Some of the migrated stalwarts who rubbed shoulders in the highest echelons with Muhammad Ali Jinnah included Chaudhry Muhammad Ali; Mian Kifait Ali; Ghulam Muhammad, an ICS officer from Aligarh who became Pakistan's third Governor-General; Akhter Hussain; and Iskander Mirza, a Sandhurst-cum-IPS officer from Hyderabad Deccan who served as the first President of Pakistan.
The pool of immeasurable talent comprised Abbas Khalili of Shirazi dynasty who was reckoned as a pioneer in industrial and administrative development of early Pakistan. He was the first civilian to aid Field Marshal Ayub's Khan's cabinet, and is recognised as the founder of SITE and KDA. It is said that Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru came to Palam Airport to request Khalili to stay back. The billionaire from Tamil Nadu abandoned everything to choose Pakistan. The Mirza Ispahanis, who gave Orient Airways to the nascent state; Raja Amir Ahmed Khan of Mahmudabad, who opened his treasure troves to fund the nascent state; MA Habib of the Habib Group; and Agha Hasan Abedi of BCCI fame are unforgettable contributors. Valika, Adamjee, Dawood, Bawany too were cardinals in development.
I will surely fall short of knowledge if I attempt to name all of these luminaries. Yet, I seek to recall as many of them as possible to eulogise a forgotten community. Agha Shahi from Mysore served as the Foreign Minister under General Zia-ul-Haq; his brother, Agha Hilaly, an ICS officer from Bangalore, was an equally distinguished diplomat. Nagpur's M Ikramullah, Pakistan's first Foreign Secretary, was the sibling of the renowned jurist Sir Mohammad Hidayatullah, who became the Vice-President of India in 1979. Bihar's SK Dehlavi, an ICS officer, is credited with transitioning Pakistan's civil services, while Bengal's JA Rahim, also an ICS officer, is remembered as the architect behind Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's rise to power and the PPP's first Secretary-General. From Ambala came the illustrious Qudratullah Shahab, who held the unique distinction of serving as the Principal Secretary to three heads of state and authored the seminal Shahab Nama. Finally, Abu Talib Naqvi, an ICS officer and Magistrate of Aligarh from 1942 to 1947, became the Chief Commissioner of Karachi during the 1950s and is remembered for convincing the legendary Urdu poet Josh Malihabadi to migrate to Pakistan in 1955.
Among other learned, Urdu-speaking jewels was Lucknow's Syed Hashim Raza, an ICS officer who served as the first Administrator of Karachi and later as the Governor of East Pakistan. His brother, Syed Kazim Raza of the Indian Police, migrated to Pakistan as an SP and went on to become an IG and the second Director of the Intelligence Bureau from 1949 to 1953. The group also included Hadi Hussain and Usman Ali from Madras, who were both civil servants and the scions of the revered Shia scholar Shamsul Ulema Syed Hasan Raza. Furthermore, ZA Bokhari - brother of the legendary writer Patras Bokhari - became the first Director-General of Radio Pakistan. Amritsar's Aziz Ahmed, an ICS officer, later served as the Foreign Secretary under ZA Bhutto, while East Punjab's Qazi Nawaz Khan served as a Revenue Collector. Finally, Karnataka's Qamar-ul Islam distinguished himself as an ambassador and as the Deputy Chairman of Pakistan's Planning Commission from 1971 to 1973.
These officers instilled professionalism and the core values of meritocracy. The mohajir community, however - despite being the descendants of this educated tribe - could not sustain that momentum in later decades. Their prospects of rising to the higher cadres of the bureaucracy steadily diminished. Since the 1970s, ethnic radicalism has pitted the Urdu-speaking community against local Sindhis, culminating in the 1972 Sindhi Language Bill riots. These events tragically shifted the entire paradigm, permanently altering the political identity and destiny of the migrants.
The quota disparity for Sindh, embedded in the 1973 Constitution for a period of 10 years, cemented the ethnic divide. The SPSC became a tool to further ethnic nepotism, and Urdu-speakers were discriminated against in jobs. Likewise, the Sindh quota had a unique formula, which was further subdivided into 40% urban and 60% rural in federal jobs. Mohajirs felt the bite, as for them the Bhutto era and the subsequent martial law blocked the path of social mobility in federal services.
The intellectual decline of the mohajir community had begun. Their inclination toward the CSS exams slumped by 10% between the 1970s and 1980s. The once-learned community began resigning itself to its fate. Meanwhile, the MQM, as the sole political voice of the mohajirs, did nothing to bridge this widening gap, remaining preoccupied with its own political maneuvers. As government jobs took a back seat, Mohajir graduates pivoted toward medicine, engineering, law and entrepreneurship. Tragically, this shift took a more lethal turn as many youth succumbed to street crime and the politics of violence, plunging the community deep into parochialism.
This impasse must end. Mohajirs must reclaim their affinity for the civil service by raising their educational standards. Their forefathers left an indelible mark on Pakistan's once-enterprising bureaucracy. Returning to officialdom with those same ethics and standards will go a long way in ushering in a renewed sense of belonging with the republic, allowing the community to become a valuable participant in national decision-making. It is high time for Urdu-speaking intellectuals, peers and political circles to kickstart a renaissance in thought.

title: AI is already in the office
description: The problem is that  in many organisations  the technology arrived before the rules governing its use
content:
The problem is that, in many organisations, the technology arrived before the rules governing its use
Artificial intelligence is no longer something organisations are preparing for. It is already inside the workplace. Employees are using generative AI platforms to summarise lengthy documents, draft correspondence, review contracts, analyse data, prepare presentations and carry out research. Work that once consumed several hours can now be completed in minutes. The attraction is obvious. The problem is that, in many organisations, the technology has arrived before the rules governing its use.
Consider a fairly ordinary situation. An employee receives a hundred-page confidential document and needs to prepare a summary before the next morning. Uploading it to an AI platform may appear to be the most efficient solution. Within seconds, the system produces a neat summary. But a more important question is often never asked: was that employee authorised to place the organisation's information on an external platform in the first place?
This is where Pakistan's conversation about AI needs to become more practical. The Federal Cabinet approved the National AI Policy 2025, providing a much-needed national direction for innovation, data protection, cybersecurity, responsible AI and domestic capacity. The policy is an important beginning. But national policy alone cannot determine how a bank, regulator, hospital, law firm, university or company should manage AI inside its own workplace.
Every organisation now needs its own rules. Employees should know which AI systems they are permitted to use; what information may be entered into them and what material must remain completely outside public AI platforms. Confidential contracts, personal data, internal investigations, legal advice, financial information and sensitive government records cannot be treated in the same way as a publicly available newspaper article. AI governance must begin with this basic distinction.
The answer, however, is not to prohibit AI, as it would ignore both technological reality and human behaviour. If a tool can reduce a three-hour task to 20 minutes, employees will want to use it. Organisations should therefore focus on providing safer alternatives: approved enterprise systems, controlled AI applications or privately hosted models where the sensitivity of information justifies greater control.
There is also a larger opportunity here. Government organisations possess years, sometimes decades, of valuable institutional knowledge buried in files, circulars, decisions, manuals, contracts and correspondence. Instead of employees repeatedly uploading individual documents to external systems, organisations can develop internal AI tools capable of searching their own authorised records. An employee could ask whether a similar issue had arisen before and receive relevant internal precedents within seconds rather than spending hours searching old files.
Such systems could significantly improve productivity while reducing dependence on public AI platforms. Pakistan should not limit its AI ambition to becoming a large market for foreign technology. Our institutions should develop the capacity to use existing models within controlled environments, train or adapt suitable systems for local requirements and build solutions around Pakistani laws, languages, administrative practices and specialised institutional knowledge.
But control over data is only half the issue. AI-generated answers must also be treated with caution. These systems can produce excellent work, but they can also misunderstand documents, invent references and present incorrect information with remarkable confidence. Human review therefore remains essential, particularly in law, medicine, finance, engineering, regulation and public administration. AI may assist judgement, but responsibility for a decision must remain with the human being making it.
Pakistan's real AI challenge is therefore not simply how quickly we adopt new technology. It is whether our institutions can adopt it intelligently. The organisations that benefit most from AI will not necessarily be those that use it the most, but those that know where it should be used, what information it may access and where human judgement must remain decisive. AI is already reshaping the workplace; our rules and safeguards must now keep pace.

title: Saving our sharks
description: According to a 2021 assessment by WWF Pakistan  shark landings in the country fell by more than 85  over five decades
content:
According to a 2021 assessment by WWF-Pakistan, shark landings in the country fell by more than 85% over five decades
Pakistan has announced its first national action plan for shark conservation, marking a long-overdue effort to protect its declining marine biodiversity. The 10-year initiative, unveiled by Maritime Affairs Minister Muhammad Junaid Anwar Chaudhry, seeks to restore the declining shark populations. With an estimated funding requirement of $3.8 million to $5 million during its first five years, the plan offers a framework for addressing a problem that has received insufficient attention despite its ecological and economic consequences.
According to a 2021 assessment by WWF-Pakistan, shark landings in the country fell by more than 85% over five decades. Although falling catches do not necessarily reflect the precise extent of population loss, they point to a deeply troubling deterioration in Pakistan's marine resources. Sharks play an important role in maintaining the balance of marine ecosystems, and their disappearance can disrupt food webs and threaten the health of other marine species. Their conservation is essential to safeguarding the long-term productivity of fisheries that support thousands of coastal households. Yet destructive fishing practices and the commercial demand for shark fins continue to place vulnerable species under pressure. Equally important is the involvement of coastal fishing communities, whose livelihoods cannot be ignored in the pursuit of conservation.
The government's proposed measures are necessary steps towards addressing these threats. However, enforcement must extend beyond regulatory announcements to fishing harbours and commercial operations, where illegal catches and the trade in protected species must be effectively monitored. Federal and provincial authorities will need to coordinate their efforts, while scientific research must inform fishing restrictions and habitat protection. The proposed National Advisory Committee must be empowered to oversee implementation, while annual performance assessments should be made public to ensure accountability.

title: Learning on the ruins
description: 98  of schools in Gaza damaged or destroyed  Unicef reports 660 000 students  education affected by Israeli onslaught
content:
98% of schools in Gaza damaged or destroyed; Unicef reports 660,000 students' education affected by Israeli onslaught
Hundreds of thousands of Gaza's children are returning to in-person schooling after nearly three years. But while the milestone is significant, it is hardly cause for celebration. Every school in the territory will be missing students who were killed by Israel's bloodthirsty security forces. About 98% of schools in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed, and Unicef reports that some 660,000 students' education has been affected by the Israeli onslaught. Those students are still thankful that their lives have turned out better than the 22,000 students and 770 education workers murdered by Israel.
Then there is the physical reality of the new academic year. With almost all school buildings unusable, students are crammed into tents, tarpaulins and sheet metal structures, with some classrooms furnished with only mattresses and a blackboard. Abject poverty means many parents can't afford basics such as books, pens or uniforms. Some students who were able to take classes online or on the phone said it is the first time they have met their teachers.
Meanwhile, Unesco said 95% of university campuses in Gaza have been affected, with 22 of the 38 campuses completely destroyed. Over 1,100 university staff and faculty members have been reported killed. Gaza used to have an education rate of 97% before Israel's bloodlust struck. Now, the Palestinian Ministry of Education has described the dismantling of the schools and universities as "educide", which is catchy, but takes away from the actual genocide around the schools.
Experts have noted that the assault on education is not just causing pain today or even tomorrow. The damage done by Israel will reverberate for several decades, as Gaza struggles to cope with the loss of hundreds of doctors, nurses, engineers and teachers who could have helped the impoverished territory rise. The poverty rate in Gaza is over 90%. Even if hostilities stopped today, the area lacks the base to sustain its student population through high school, let alone university. The international community could change this, but for that they would have to care.

title: A thought for de escalation
description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio hints at a possible meeting between Trump and his Iranian counterpart
content:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio hints at a possible meeting between Trump and his Iranian counterpart
There is a breath of fresh air as de-escalation moves onto the agenda of the warring sides. The contention from Tehran that it is willing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, provided Washington eases military pressure and lifts the blockade of Iranian ports, is a welcome development. For many, it is déjà vu. Both the US and Iran had reached a similar understanding following their agreement in Islamabad, and global supply chains was heaving a sigh of relief as oil prices had slumped back to $80 a barrel.
This development has luckily coincided with Secretary of State Marco Rubio hinting at a possible meeting between President Trump and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly. That, however, is a utopian thought as far as the Islamic Republic is concerned. Iran's military brass has recently upped the ante by saying it is ready for a long war, and this time around, all American interests in the region would be its targets.
Iran's demand - that the US should agree on a timeline for how the process will move forward - can be worked out. This demand, incidentally, has come a day after Pakistan's Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi met with high-ranking Iranian officials in his earnest efforts to iron out a deal to end the stalemate. This makes a perfect case for reverting to diplomacy and picking up where the Islamabad MoU left off. A cooling-off phase is desired during which a ceasefire comes into force and Tehran convinces the Houthis to step back. The warfare deep inside Saudi Arabia, which is under attack from the Yemeni militia, is proving lethal to oil supplies on both sides of the Red Sea.
There is an opportunity amid the disaster for the UN, too, to revive its image. It must play a role in forging a consensus between Iran and the US. This will not only help further prospects for peace in the Middle East and beyond, but also strengthen the weakened muscles of international law. The UNGA needs to return to its Uniting for Peace resolution and broker a thaw without delay.

title: Gender equality  the distance between progress and power
description: The country s gender parity score has risen to 59 5 per cent
content:
The country's gender-parity score has risen to 59.5 per cent
Pakistan ranks 143rd out of 145 economies in the World Economic Forum's Global Gender Gap Report 2026. The country has moved up five places from last year, when it ranked 148th out of 148 countries. Our gender-parity score has risen to 59.5 per cent.
Progress matters. But can we afford to be satisfied?
For a country with millions of talented and ambitious women and girls, these figures should prompt us to ask whether women are not only educated, but economically empowered; not only encouraged, but given genuine opportunities; and represented in decision-making. After more than 25 years of working in women's and girls' empowerment, I ask: Are we moving fast enough? What will it take to ensure that no woman or girl is left behind?
Let's keep in mind that education is the beginning, not the destination. Throughout my career, I have seen the transformative power of education. A girl who gains confidence, skills and knowledge of her rights is better equipped to navigate the world. Education opens doors and builds resilience.
But education alone cannot dismantle the barriers that prevent women from participating fully in society. Can girls translate education into meaningful employment? Can women access decent work, financial independence and leadership? Do they have a voice in decisions that shape their lives? Education must lead to opportunity. Opportunity must lead to agency.
The gender gap is also an economic challenge.
Female labour-force participation in Pakistan is approximately 24%, compared with around 80% for men. Behind these figures are millions of women whose talent and productive potential remain underused in the formal economy.
Many women also contribute through unpaid family work, agriculture, home-based employment and caregiving - essential contributions that often remain invisible in economic measurements. Barriers include unsafe transport, limited childcare, workplace discrimination, restricted mobility, lack of digital access and inadequate employment opportunities.
The issue is not whether women can contribute. It is whether our systems are designed to recognise, support and benefit from that contribution. Women's empowerment is not simply a social responsibility. It is an economic imperative, a development priority and a matter of justice.
Critically, there is need to move from empowerment to economic agency. Empowerment must mean more than programmes, workshops and inspiring speeches. It must mean agency: the ability to make decisions, earn, own, lead and pursue education and employment without discrimination.
We need to invest in skills, digital inclusion, entrepreneurship, accessible education and decent employment, creating pathways into work and leadership. Women should not have to prove their worth repeatedly before being given an opportunity.
There is no single experience of being a woman. A girl in a rural community may face different barriers from a woman in an urban professional environment. A woman with a disability may encounter additional obstacles in education, employment, accessibility and digital participation.
This is why inclusion cannot be an afterthought. Women and girls with disabilities must be part of the gender-equality conversation - not only as beneficiaries, but as active participants, leaders and decision-makers. We cannot speak about equality while leaving women with disabilities behind.
However, the Report should not leave us discouraged. It should make us more determined. Every girl who enters school, every woman who gains employment and every institution that becomes more inclusive represents progress.
But we cannot confuse movement with transformation. Equality is not achieved when a few women succeed. It is achieved when every woman and girl has a fair opportunity to succeed. That is a future worth working for not leaving equality to another generation, but achieving meaningful progress in our lifetime.

content:
Rejects international oversight of AI, calling efforts to regulate the technology a 'globalist scheme'
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that US government documents would use "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence going forward, and repeated his previous claims that warnings about AI were a hoax.
"From this point forward, all of United States documents, and hopefully the world's will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'super' as opposed to artificial. So it's super intelligence," Trump said in a speech to the UN General Assembly.

"Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity. To establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation," Guterres said.
"At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognise the need to manage shared existential risks."

description: Taylor Swift announces new single  Patient Zero   set for September 25  with three limited collector   s CDs available
content:
Taylor Swift announces new single 'Patient Zero', set for September 25, with three limited collector’s CDs available
Taylor Swift has announced a new single, "Patient Zero", with the track set to arrive on September 25 following weeks of speculation from fans.
The 14-time Grammy winner revealed the news on Instagram on September 22, saying she had been waiting to share the announcement with her fans. The new Taylor Swift single will be available to pre-order through her website for 24 hours.
Swift also announced three collector’s edition CDs for "Patient Zero". The editions include the standard, acoustic and piano versions of the song, with each CD featuring two different images of the singer. The limited editions will be available for 24 hours or while supplies last.
The announcement followed several cryptic updates from Swift earlier on Tuesday. Her Instagram bio was changed to read, "And, baby, that’s sh0w business f0r y0u. ❤️‍🔥", featuring three zeroes. A countdown also appeared on her official website, prompting further speculation among fans.
Swift also appeared to have a presence across Spotify, where album-specific animations were added to the play/pause button. Different albums feature different visual effects, including sparkles for The Life of a Showgirl and hearts for Lover .
The new single comes shortly before Swift is scheduled to receive the Artist Director Honors at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards on September 27. The award recognises artists whose work behind the camera has contributed to music video and visual storytelling.
Swift has directed several of her own music videos and made her solo directorial debut with "The Man" in 2020. She later directed All Too Well: The Short Film , which earned multiple MTV VMAs and a Grammy Award.
Swift’s latest album, The Life of a Showgirl , was released in 2025.

title: PPP pushes through mayor administrator amendment
description: MQM  JI and PTI oppose allowing outgoing mayors and chairmen to stay in office until fresh local elections
content:
MQM, JI and PTI oppose allowing outgoing mayors and chairmen to stay in office until fresh local elections
A proposed amendment to Sindh’s local government law has emerged as the sole point of disagreement between the government and opposition parties, with the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) insisting on retaining existing mayors and chairmen as administrators after their terms expire until fresh local government elections.
The provision was among several amendments proposed by the PPP to the Sindh Local Government Act. However, all opposition parties represented in the Sindh Assembly, including the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM), Jamaat-e-Islami (JI) and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), opposed it.
Members of all parties were part of a special committee constituted to examine the proposed amendments. The committee reviewed the changes clause by clause, with the government and opposition showing flexibility on most provisions. As a result, several additional proposals were also incorporated into the bill.
However, neither side was willing to compromise on the provision allowing existing mayors and chairmen to continue as administrators until new elections. The PPP subsequently used its numerical majority in the Sindh Assembly to get the amendments passed, including the contentious provision.
Opposition representatives said they opposed the amendment on principle, arguing that neutral administrators should be appointed between the expiry of local governments’ terms and fresh elections.
Speaking to The Express Tribune , MQM Deputy Parliamentary Leader in the Sindh Assembly Taha Ahmed said the amendment would allow existing mayors and chairmen to serve as administrators until the new elections.
“These are political people. How can they be neutral?” he said, adding that the MQM would challenge the amendment in court.
Read More: Mustafa Kamal says 18th Amendment created 'four countries' instead of empowering provinces
JI Sindh Assembly member Muhammad Farooq also said the provision was the only point on which his party had disagreed with the government.
Farooq pointed out that JI-affiliated chairmen currently head nine towns and 87 union councils in Karachi. Despite this, he said, his party opposed the amendment because political figures should not be appointed as administrators during an interim period.
He said government officials had traditionally been appointed as administrators after local governments’ terms expired.
PPP Sindh Assembly member and Sindh government spokesperson Sukhdev Asardas Hemnani, however, defended the amendment, saying government officials had traditionally been appointed during interim periods, but political parties had repeatedly criticised the practice.
According to Hemnani, opposition parties had argued that government officials could not be neutral because they worked under the provincial government.
“To avoid this criticism, the PPP introduced this amendment,” he said.
Hemnani said that during the interim period, mayors and chairmen serving as administrators would only carry out essential day-to-day functions. He added that election-related powers would remain with the Election Commission of Pakistan.
He also claimed that opposition representatives had not offered an alternative and were instead seeking to delay the amendment bill.
However, he maintained that the government remained open to further changes in the law. “Laws change with time. If the opposition comes forward with good proposals, the government can introduce further amendments to the local government law,” he said.
Hemnani added that the government was willing to discuss with opposition parties granting further powers to local government institutions.
The terms of the existing local government bodies are due to expire in mid-2027. Under the amended law, the Sindh government will have to inform the Election Commission of Pakistan three months before their terms expire, after which the commission will begin preparations for new elections.
The Election Commission will also have to carry out fresh delimitation of local government constituencies at least six months before the elections. The exercise could increase the number of union councils, towns and other local government units across Sindh, including Karachi.

title: Trump praises PM Shehbaz as    terrific man     recalls India Pakistan mediation at UNGA
description: Says Shehbaz called him responsible for saving millions of lives after the India Pakistan conflict
content:
Says Shehbaz called him responsible for saving millions of lives after the India-Pakistan conflict
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday again claimed credit for helping avert a full-fledged war between nuclear-armed India and Pakistan, while calling Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif a “terrific man” during his address to the United Nations General Assembly.
Addressing the opening session of the 81st UN General Assembly, Trump highlighted what he described as his diplomatic achievements over the past year, saying he had helped settle eight wars, including the conflict between India and Pakistan.
“Since I took office, it has been my great honour to settle eight wars and in so doing, become friendly with the leaders of many of those countries,” he said.
Trump says Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif is 'a terrific man' pic.twitter.com/73iihZ4IDY
“It was a great honour to do it,” Trump told the gathering of world leaders, including PM Shehbaz, who arrived in New York on Monday to attend the UNGA session, adding that he had used his “very relationships” to help reach the settlements.
“Very special relationships to this day, very, very special trade, the use of tariffs and the threat of tariffs and various other reasons depending on the country,” he said.
Trump specifically highlighted his role in the India-Pakistan conflict while also referring to other settlements involving Cambodia and Thailand, Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as the war in Gaza.
PM Sharif arrives at UN headquarters to attend the UNGA session pic.twitter.com/dUqSGvtygv
He said “almost every one” of the countries involved had written him a letter of thanks, singling out PM Shehbaz, whom he described as a “terrific man”.
“The prime minister of Pakistan, terrific man, said that Donald Trump was responsible for saving 30 million lives, and probably many more than that,” Trump said.
This is not the first time President Trump has publicly praised the premier; he previously commended PM Shehbaz and Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, calling them “two fantastic people”.
At the inaugural meeting of the Board of Peace, he also praised PM Shehbaz’s leadership while recalling Pakistan’s role in halting regional escalation with India.
Trump has on other occasions praised Field Marshal Munir, describing him as a “highly respected general”, a “great fighter” and “my favourite”.
Shehbaz, meanwhile, has previously described Trump as a “man of peace” and praised his efforts to end conflicts around the world.
Thanking Trump for his role in mediating the ceasefire between India and Pakistan following their four-day military conflict in May, the prime minister had said the US president helped “avert a major catastrophe in South Asia”.
Read More : 'Two fantastic people': Trump all praise again for PM Shehbaz, CDF Munir after Hormuz breakthrough
The Pakistan-US relationship experienced a significant thaw in 2025–2026, transitioning from a cold period to warm, strategic, and pragmatic engagement during Trump's second term. This shift was largely driven by a major reset in relations following President Trump's intervention in regional conflicts, particularly his role in brokering a ceasefire between Pakistan and India in May 2025.
The first thaw in Pakistan-US relations came via secret counterterrorism exchanges, signalling substantive cooperation. In March last year, Trump unexpectedly praised Pakistan’s counterterrorism efforts during a national address, prompting a policy shift.
The short but intense May skirmish with India in May 2025 became a decisive turning point, showcasing Pakistan’s military discipline, strategic focus, and asymmetric capabilities — qualities that reportedly surprised Trump.
Despite India’s repeated denials, PM Shehbaz continued to praise President Trump for his role in brokering a ceasefire between the two nuclear-armed neighbours, and nominated him for the Nobel Peace Prize, saying his intervention had helped save millions of lives.
The praise was reciprocated, with Trump commending the premier and also lauding CDF Munir, as he reiterated claims that he had helped avert a war between Pakistan and India in May 2025.
Ties between the countries took a further turn when Trump invited CDF Munir to a luncheon — the first such meeting for a Pakistani military chief — followed by a red-carpet visit to US Central Command headquarters for high-level talks.
Following a ceasefire after the prolonged war in Gaza, Trump announced the formation of a “Board of Peace” that included Pakistan, again singling out PM Shehbaz for praise during its inaugural summit.
Read : Trump lavishes praise on CDF Munir
Addressing the event, Trump said, “I like this guy,” referring to the premier, as he recounted efforts that led to last year’s ceasefire between Pakistan and India. He also praised CDF Munir during his remarks.
In June this year, President Trump credited Pakistan with “really helping” the United States secure a peace deal with Iran while especially praising Field Marshal Munir and PM Shehbaz.
“In Pakistan, you have Field Marshal Asim Munir, who is great, and you have the Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and they just get along great,” he said during an interview with Axios .
