title: Arsenic threat lurks in Multan water
description: Arsenic threat lurks in Multan water
content:
Experts call for comprehensive scientific assessment
Arsenic contamination has emerged as a serious water-quality concern in Multan, but its extent across the city remains unclear.
Water-testing experts have stressed the need for a comprehensive and representative survey to determine the current level of contamination and identify areas requiring intervention.
A water testing research officer, Saima Gul, said arsenic levels could not be generalised for the entire city on the basis of limited samples because contamination might vary according to location, source, groundwater depth and the period during which samples were collected and tested.
She said drinking water in the city was obtained from different sources, including WASA supplies, tube wells and hand pumps, household sources and commercial filtration plants. Therefore, proper assessment required systematic sampling from all major areas and different types of water sources rather than relying on results from limited locations.
Groundwater is widely used in parts of Multan and surrounding areas. Arsenic contamination may remain unnoticed because affected water does not necessarily show any obvious change in colour, taste or smell. Regular laboratory testing is, therefore, essential to determine whether a source is safe for consumption.
A published study examining drinking water in high schools in four tehsils of Multan found arsenic concentrations ranging from 3.25 to 184 micrograms per litre. It reported that 99 per cent of the tested samples exceeded the World Health Organisation (WHO) guideline of 10 micrograms.
Another study covering groundwater in five areas of Punjab, including Multan, found that 75% of 123 tested wells exceeded the WHO guideline, while 41% were above Pakistan's permissible limit of 50 micrograms per litre.
Samples were collected from hand pumps, electric pumps and tube wells at varying depths, showing differences in contamination.
The Pakistan Council of Research in Water Resources (PCRWR) has also reported arsenic contamination in groundwater in several areas, including Multan.
A national assessment covering 45,920 water sources found 13% above the WHO guideline and 3% above Pakistan's permissible limit of 50 micrograms.
The difference between the two standards is important.
The WHO considers inorganic arsenic a confirmed human carcinogen and says long-term exposure through drinking water and food can cause serious health effects, including skin lesions and cancers. It identifies contaminated groundwater as a major source of human exposure and recommends testing water sources and providing safe supplies or appropriate treatment where contamination is found.
In Muzaffargarh, around 20% of water samples examined during the past three years were reported to contain arsenic. A water testing management research officer for Layyah for Layyah and Muzaffargarh said the findings covered parts of the Muzaffargarh, Alipur and Jatoi tehsils.
In Layyah, arsenic was detected in up to 30% of drinking-water samples from different areas, with the maximum concentration reaching around 120 parts per billion. The affected sources included hand pumps and tube wells.
The experts called for regular testing, monitoring and purification of drinking-water sources, particularly in areas heavily dependent on groundwater.
The variation in findings from different locations and sources underlines the need for a systematic assessment.
A comprehensive city-wide survey covering WASA supplies, groundwater, tube wells, hand pumps, household sources and commercial filtration plants could provide a clearer picture of the situation.
This would help identify high-risk areas and determine where treatment or alternative safe water supplies are urgently required, they said.

CM orders province-wide enrolment drive as newly built, upgraded schools near completion
Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah on Sunday ordered a province-wide enrolment campaign to bring around 250,000 children into schools as 838 newly constructed, upgraded and rehabilitated schools near completion.
Chairing a review meeting on Education Management Organisations (EMOs) at his office, CM Shah directed the School Education Department, district administrations and EMOs to launch a large-scale public outreach campaign so that every new or rehabilitated school becomes fully operational from the first day of its opening.
The chief minister said the government had made substantial investments in expanding educational infrastructure across Sindh, but the real measure of success would be the number of children enrolled and retained in the education system.
Education Minister Syed Sardar Ali Shah told the meeting that 838 schools were being constructed, upgraded or rehabilitated under the Asian Development Bank-supported Sindh Secondary Education Improvement Project (SSEIP). The programme includes 116 new secondary schools and 722 climate-resilient schools being reconstructed under the flood rehabilitation component.
The projects are expected to create educational opportunities for around 250,000 children, including more than 221,000 students in flood-affected districts and over 28,000 students in newly upgraded secondary schools.
CM Shah directed the education department to prepare district-level enrolment plans well before completion of the schools and involve elected representatives, local leaders, school management committees, parents, community organisations and EMOs in the campaign.
"We need to identify out-of-school children, reach out to families and ensure that every child living in the catchment areas of these schools is enrolled," the chief minister said.
He said investment in educational infrastructure should translate into higher literacy, particularly among girls and children living in areas where access to quality education remained limited.
"Our objective is not simply to construct school buildings. We must ensure that every classroom is filled with enthusiastic children ready to learn," CM Shah said, adding that the new schools had the potential to bring nearly a quarter of a million children into the education system.
The education minister told the meeting that 257 schools were scheduled for completion by December 2026, while the number would rise to 611 by June 2027. The remaining schools were targeted for completion by the end of 2027.
Of the 116 schools under the original SSEIP project, 64 secondary schools are expected to be completed by December 2026 and the remaining 52 by June 2027.
The chief minister also directed the School Education Department to set measurable targets for enrolment, student retention and educational outcomes and submit a comprehensive operational plan for each school before its completion.
The government is prioritising educationally deprived districts and girls' education, with the new schools featuring science and computer laboratories, digital libraries, solar power systems, common rooms for girls and other student facilities.

title: Sparks fly inside NICH nursery packed with newborns
description: Sparks fly inside NICH nursery packed with newborns
content:
Welding carried out near oxygen-dependent infants as fresh footage exposes fire-safety concerns at health facility
Sparks from a welding torch flew inside a nursery packed with newborns, some of them dependent on oxygen, at the National Institute of Child Health (NICH), raising fresh and serious questions about fire safety at the city hospital.
Video footage obtained by The Express Tribune shows a man carrying out welding work inside the nursery while newborn babies lie on beds just metres away - a scene unfolding in one of the hospital's most vulnerable wards.
Sources said between 80 and 120 children were under treatment in the nursery when the welding and repair work was carried out, most of them newborns receiving oxygen. The work was reportedly aimed at creating an emergency exit in the emergency nursery and installing an iron grille to provide a new access route to the semi-critical unit.
However, the decision to carry out welding work inside an occupied nursery has raised questions about whether adequate safety arrangements were made to protect the newborns and medical staff. It was also unclear whether the infants were moved to a safe location or whether a separate area was designated for the welding work.
Experts said welding near oxygen cylinders and newborns receiving oxygen was highly hazardous. Sparks generated during welding can ignite flammable material in an oxygen-rich environment, potentially causing a fire within seconds.
They said repair work in such a sensitive area should be carried out only after making alternative arrangements to ensure the safety of patients and staff.
The incident comes against the backdrop of previously identified fire-safety deficiencies at NICH. A fire-safety audit had declared the hospital's fourth, fifth and sixth floors extremely hazardous and highlighted several shortcomings in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).
According to the audit report, electrical and oxygen points in the NICU were installed in close proximity. The report also identified leakage in the oxygen line and pipe joints that had reportedly been sealed with tape. Exposed and unsafe electrical wiring was also identified as a fire risk.
The audit found the hospital's fire alarm system non-functional, while most smoke detectors were either faulty or inactive. It also noted an inadequate number of fire extinguishers, insufficient fire-emergency training for staff and the absence of regular fire drills.
Emergency exits were reportedly found blocked by equipment and waste, while the power room was easily accessible to the public. The report also pointed out that the power room lacked smoke detectors and adequate firefighting arrangements.
The NICU's mechanical ventilation system was also found to be non-functional, while exposed and temporary wiring connected to old air-conditioning units was declared a fire-safety hazard.
NICH has witnessed fire incidents in the past. A fire broke out in the hospital's ICU on June 30, while in January 2020, a newborn died after an incubator caught fire.
The fire-safety audit had recommended immediate corrective measures, including securing the electrical, oxygen and ventilation systems, activating fire alarms and smoke-detection systems, clearing emergency exits and conducting regular fire drills.
It had also called for comprehensive fire-safety arrangements throughout the hospital.
The footage showing welding being carried out in an occupied nursery has now raised fresh questions over compliance with basic fire-safety protocols during repair work in one of the hospital's most sensitive areas.
Meanwhile, attempts were made to obtain the NICH administration's version of the incident. NICH Director Professor Nasir Saleem was contacted several times, but he did not respond.

He said the people of Tando Allahyar, Hyderabad and Mirpurkhas had already expressed their support, adding that Karachi had also spoken in favour of the party's demands. He maintained that the units should be created on administrative rather than linguistic grounds so that the benefits of democracy could reach people at their doorsteps. He said MQM-P had raised its voice for citizens' rights, approached the courts and presented what it described as the people's case.
"We have endured every kind of oppression, but our culture is not power; our culture is our strength," he said, calling for an end to what he described as further coercion and demanding that citizens be given their rights.
Dr Siddiqui said MQM-P was a party of workers and had enabled young people from the poor and middle classes to reach the assemblies. He added that the party would continue to use the power of the vote to pursue its demands.
Senior MQM-P leader Dr Farooq Sattar said the large turnout reflected the determination of Karachi's people to secure greater administrative powers and their rights. He said "18 years of patience" had ended and claimed that people across Sindh had now taken to the streets for their rights.

title: Foul smell leads to grisly discovery
description: Foul smell leads to grisly discovery
content:
Days-old bodies of doctor, wife, three daughters found in locked flat
A foul smell from a locked seventh-floor apartment led police to a grim discovery in Ahsanabad on Sunday, where the decomposed bodies of a doctor, his wife and their three young daughters were found lying in a single room. The five-member family is believed to have been dead for several days, as police began piecing together the circumstances surrounding the deaths.
The five bodies were shifted to hospital for post-mortem examination after police broke open the locked doors. Authorities said the definitive cause of death would be established only after forensic and post-mortem reports. The bodies were recovered from an apartment in Sector 1, Ahsanabad, within the jurisdiction of Site Superhighway Industrial Area police station. Police said the deceased were identified as 45-year-old Dr Omar, his wife Mehwish, aged around 30 to 35, and their three daughters. One daughter was identified as 10-to-12-year-old Zainab, while the identities of the other two girls had yet to be established.
According to SHO Site Super Highway Muhammad Nawaz, Dr Omar had been working at the nearby East City Hospital but resigned on September 13, reportedly after being diagnosed with kidney cancer last month. The officer said the diagnosis had left the doctor deeply distressed and may have been linked to his decision to quit his job. Police have not, however, drawn any final conclusion about the deaths.
Investigators found no mobile phones believed to have been used by Dr Omar or his wife inside the flat. The keys to the main entrance were reportedly recovered near Dr Omar's head.
The investigation has also brought to light signs of financial distress in the family's final days. According to police, Dr Omar's wife had attempted to sell their oven to a neighbour for Rs10,000 the previous week. The neighbour declined to buy it but gave her Rs2,000 to help the family.
Residents told police that Dr Omar and his family had lived in the apartment for around three years and described him as a decent and peaceful man who had no known enmity with anyone. He had also opened a clinic near the apartment some time ago, but closed it after it failed to attract enough business.
Neighbours further said Dr Omar had recently fallen victim to a street robbery after collecting his salary. According to them, the incident occurred around September 9 or 10 near the apartment, when armed snatchers took his salary money and mobile phone. They said the doctor subsequently asked them about selling household belongings to raise money, but they discouraged him and instead helped him financially.
Dr Omar was last seen in the apartment around two to three days before the bodies were discovered, according to residents.
SSP East Zubair Nazir Sheikh said Dr Omar's brother, who lives in a city in Punjab, had reportedly distanced himself from the doctor, while police were attempting to establish contact with other members of the family.
Meanwhile, Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar sought a detailed report on the incident and directed the SSP East to brief him immediately on the initial police action. He ordered investigators to establish the factors and circumstances behind the deaths by examining eyewitness accounts and physical evidence from the scene, and directed the SSP to personally supervise the investigation and keep the provincial authorities informed of its progress.

title: Container seizures cripple supply of goods
description: Container seizures cripple supply of goods
content:
Wholesale markets hit by record slump as vegetables, fruits, dry fruits begin to spoil
Goods Transport Federation and wholesale dealers have protested the seizure of around 1,000 containers, heavy vehicles, trailers and trucks loaded with food items, medicines and dry fruits in the twin cities of Rawalpindi and Islamabad to deal with four long marches this week.
The closure of these containers and trucks has caused dry fruits, fruits, medicines and other essential items loaded in them to start spoiling, raising fears among wholesale dealers that goods worth millions of rupees could be wasted.
Container rents have also started increasing.
As the continued seizure of containers and heavy vehicles persists, dealers have stopped the supply of goods and parked and hidden containers and heavy vehicles in far-flung areas.
Fearing the seizure of containers and heavy vehicles, the arrival of heavy goods transport in wholesale markets of Rawalpindi and Islamabad has stopped, creating a shortage of vegetables, fruits and grocery items.
If the situation continues for the next 72 hours, vegetables, fruits, pulses, sugar and flour brought from other districts will start becoming scarce and more expensive.
Supplies of all kinds of food and essential items from Karachi, Faisalabad and Sargodha to Rawalpindi and Islamabad have been suspended.
The heavy presence of containers at Faizabad, Rawat and within the city has also begun affecting supplies of sugar, flour, vegetables and fruits to other districts.
The seizure of containers has also left thousands of workers involved in loading and unloading goods without work.
Wholesale Dealers Association Vice President Sajid Khan said that after the seizure of containers, their owners had stopped supplies of vegetables, fruits, meat and milk from Quetta, Karachi and Faisalabad to Rawalpindi and Islamabad.
He demanded that the government immediately stop the seizure of the nearly 1,000 containers, vehicles and trucks and allow the vegetables, fruits and dry fruits loaded in the seized vehicles to be unloaded so that they do not spoil.
He said the goods would start rotting and become unfit for consumption if they remained inside sealed containers for 72 hours.
He also demanded that more containers carrying food items be allowed to enter the twin cities, even if they were checked at sale points, warning that otherwise prices could increase by another 100 per cent by the end of the week and a shortage of essential items could develop.
Meanwhile, the Goods Transport Association has sent letters to the prime minister and Punjab chief minister protesting the seizure of containers and vehicles and demanding their immediate release.
Goods Transport Federation Vice President Haji Iqbal said, "On the one hand, we are being ruined by petrol and diesel prices, and now our containers and vehicles have also been seized. Where should we go? Our businesses have been ruined for the past three years and now we have no option except to bring the goods transport system to a halt."

The people of Punjab may "face" flour shortages after Pakistan Flour Mills Association (PFMA) on Sunday announced that flour mills across Punjab would go on strike and suspend operations in protest against, what they called, anti-industry policies.
The Association strongly condemned the suspension of wheat and flour quota permits, alleged heavy bribery by the District Food Controller (DFC), and the sealing of flour mills and imposition of fines of up to Rs5 million over minor issues,
It also announced plans to file a reference with the Anti-Corruption Establishment (ACE)) against the DFC over the alleged forced collection of Rs150,000 for issuing each permit. It criticised the appointment of a Grade-15 employee as DFC and demanded his removal and the appointment of a senior DFC on merit.
PFMA Chairman Riazullah Khan said at an association meeting that the millers were not political people and did not want to benefit from political instability.
"We consider the PML-N government a government of traders, but under this very government, earning a lawful livelihood has been made difficult, if not impossible, for us," he said.
He alleged that the junior-most DFC, Azhar Baloch, had opened a "gateway to corruption and bribery". He said Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz had introduced an online portal to facilitate flour mills, allowing mills across Punjab to generate permits according to their requirements for the transportation of wheat and flour.
However, he said, this authority had been handed over to the DFC in Rawalpindi Division, who allegedly charged Rs100,000 to Rs150,000 for each permit.
Khan said bran was used as animal feed and that an agreement had been reached with the Director General Food under which flour mills would only provide lists of trucks for its transportation. However, he alleged that the DFC had also discontinued this arrangement and was allegedly demanding Rs100,000 to Rs150,000 for the lists.
He said the transportation of wheat and flour to other districts and provinces had also been stopped and quotas abolished, making wheat and flour more expensive and transportation increasingly difficult and costly.

AEOs, Dy DEOs given mandatory daily school visit targets
The Punjab School Education Department has issued detailed instructions to field education officers and heads of schools, requiring Assistant Education Officers (AEOs) to inspect four schools and one high school daily, while Deputy District Education Officers (Dy DEOs) will visit four schools each day.
Heads of schools will personally inspect their institutions three times a day.
The directives have been issued to strengthen monitoring and accountability in educational institutions. During a Zoom meeting chaired by the Secretary of the Punjab School Education Department, field officers and heads of schools across the province were given instructions regarding cleanliness, the educational environment, school monitoring and field visits.
Under the directives, every AEO will visit four schools in their respective centre and one high school daily. They will inspect cleanliness, the educational environment and available facilities on the spot, and record all observations in the school visit logbook.
Deputy DEOs will visit at least four schools daily, including one secondary school and three other schools in their assigned areas. All observations and corrective measures must also be recorded in the visit register.
Every head of school will personally inspect the school three times a day and ensure cleanliness and overall arrangements before leaving the premises. Particular attention will be paid to the cleanliness of classrooms, washrooms, computer and science laboratories, grounds, corridors and other areas.
All field officers have been directed to be present in the field before 7am and ensure cleanliness before schools open. Where necessary, whitewashing and minor improvement works may be carried out using available funds in accordance with financial rules.
Photographic evidence of field visits will be mandatory, with the date, time and location services activated. Effective coordination will also be maintained with Suthra Punjab teams to improve cleanliness in schools, while school councils will be actively involved in monitoring sanitation.

title: Leh erosion puts homes  shops at risk
description: Leh erosion puts homes  shops at risk
content:
Aftermath of Sep 1 floods continues to threaten communities along Nullah Leh
Although the flood surge in Nullah Leh following nearly 200mm of rain on September 1 has receded, its destructive aftermath continues, with widespread soil erosion and landslides threatening homes, shops, roads, bridges and passageways along a roughly 15-kilometre stretch from New Katarian to Gulistan Colony.
The situation is particularly alarming near Ganj Mandi, where severe landsliding has put 10 shops and three houses at risk of collapse. The district administration has declared the affected area dangerous and sealed it to prevent movement. A bridge connecting Ratta with Dhoke Ratta has also been closed as a precaution.
The torrential rain on September 1 caused a powerful flood surge in Nullah Leh, severely eroding its banks at several points. Even after the water receded, soil erosion and landsliding have continued.
Along the stretch from New Katarian to Gulistan Colony, the ground is giving way at several locations, while roads and pathways have been washed away. In some areas, residential and commercial buildings have been left dangerously close to the nullah.
The situation near Ganj Mandi is especially serious, where a large section of land along the nullah has collapsed. Continued erosion has placed 10 shops and three houses in danger, prompting the administration to restrict movement in the affected area.
In Sagri Mohalla, erosion has washed away a passage in front of residential houses, causing severe difficulties for residents. An unpaved route leading from Ratta Road towards Ganj Mandi has also been swept away by floodwaters.
Local residents have blamed illegal dumping of construction waste along Nullah Leh for aggravating the destruction. They said bricks, gravel, construction debris and household solid waste had been dumped along the nullah and its banks throughout the year using tractor-trolleys.
The accumulation of waste obstructed the natural flow of water at several points, residents said, while changes in the direction of floodwaters during the deluge intensified erosion along the banks.
According to residents, some settlements were around 50 yards from Nullah Leh before September 1, but severe erosion has reduced the distance to roughly 10 metres at several locations.
Residents fear that further rainfall or another flood surge could put homes and commercial buildings directly in danger. They have demanded immediate construction of concrete retaining walls and reinforced embankments at vulnerable points, as well as strict legal action against those dumping construction waste and the tractor-trolley owners involved.
Meanwhile, the embankments of the Gowalmandi Bridge were also damaged by the September 1 flood. The powerful flow of water battered the bridge and its approaches, weakening parts of the structure. The administration has since begun repair work on the damaged embankments.
The bridge connecting Ratta with Dhoke Ratta has also been closed as a safety measure to prevent any major accident caused by weakened sections.
Rawalpindi Deputy Commissioner Captain (retd) Nadeem Nasir said the issue of modernising and improving Rawalpindi's drainage system had been included in the Punjab Development Project.

title: Gawalmandi park remains closed for five years
description: Gawalmandi park remains closed for five years
content:
Rusting swings, overgrown weeds, dengue larvae turn neglected park into a hazard
The 50-year-old Ladies and Children Park in Gawalmandi, the city's 200-year-old residential area, has remained completely closed for the past five years, leaving the swings installed for children of poor families rusted and unusable.
The iron from these swings has also started being stolen. As night falls, the park becomes a safe haven for drug addicts and people using narcotics. Grass, weeds and wild plants up to five feet high have grown throughout the park, resulting in an abundance of rats, cats, snakes and mongooses.
These dangerous creatures frequently move out of the park onto roads and into residential areas.
With the only recreational park serving a densely populated area of around 100,000 people completely closed, residents, families and children have been deprived of recreation.
Five years ago, the park was active, with elderly men and women and female students from nearby areas coming there every morning for jogging, morning walks and exercise.
In the evening, families, women and children would visit the park for walks and recreation.
After the park was completely closed, motor mechanic workshops were established around all four sides of it. The facility was a major central ladies and children park for women and children in Rawalpindi but has now turned into a wreck.
Garbage heaps have accumulated near the entrance gates, while stagnant rainwater at various places in the park has led to a large amount of dengue larvae, which are developing into dengue mosquitoes and spreading into nearby areas.
As a result, the recreational park, which had remained a centre of positive activities for 50 years, has now become a source of trouble for local residents.
Area residents Fayyaz Hashmi, Shehbaz Ali, Imran Khan and Makhdum Ali Raza have appealed to the commissioner, deputy commissioner and chief executive officer of the board to open the Gawalmandi park, install new swings and restore its old status as a recreational facility by cutting the five- to six-foot-high grass and wild weeds.

title: Residents decry unequal taxes
description: Residents decry unequal taxes
content:
RCB, CCB taxpayers face water, sewerage & streetlight issues despite revised taxes
Residents of Rawalpindi and Chaklala cantonment boards have questioned different sanitation tax rates for residents in one city. The sanitation tax is higher in Rawalpindi Cantonment Board than in Chaklala Cantonment Board.
The Rawalpindi Cantonment Board has revised the heavy rates of water charges and property tax with minor relief. Residents continue to face problems related to drinking water, sanitation, streetlights, sewerage systems and damaged streets and roads.
According to residents, sanitation tax (conservancy charges) has surprisingly been imposed at different rates by the two cantonment boards. Chaklala Cantonment Board charges Rs1,200 annually from houses measuring one to three marlas, while the rate in Rawalpindi Cantonment Board was Rs2,500, which has now been reduced to Rs2,100 annually.
For houses measuring three to five marlas, the Chaklala Cantonment rate is Rs2,000, while the Rawalpindi rate was fixed at Rs3,600 and has now been reduced to Rs3,200. In Chaklala, the annual rate for five to seven marla houses is Rs2,592, compared with Rs4,800 in Rawalpindi, which has now been reduced to Rs4,400.
The annual rate for seven to 10 marla houses in Chaklala is Rs3,600, while Rawalpindi had imposed Rs5,400, reducing it to Rs5,200. Chaklala charges Rs4,800 annually for houses measuring 10 to 15 marlas, while Rawalpindi charges Rs7,000.
For houses measuring 15 to 20 marlas, Chaklala collects Rs6,000 annually compared with Rs10,000 in Rawalpindi. For 20 to 40 marla houses, the annual rate is Rs12,000 in Chaklala and Rs15,000 in Rawalpindi.
For houses measuring 40 marlas or more, Chaklala charges Rs14,000 annually, compared with Rs18,000 in Rawalpindi.
Meanwhile, residential water charges imposed by the Rawalpindi Cantonment Board are also a matter of concern.
For water supplied for 15 days a month, or every alternate day, annual water charges for one-to-five marla houses have been reduced from Rs14,400 to Rs12,200.
The charges for five-to-seven marla houses are Rs23,000, Rs33,500 for seven-to-10 marla houses, Rs44,000 for 10-to-15 marla houses, Rs45,000 for 15-to-20 marla houses, Rs62,000 for 20-to-40 marla houses and Rs72,000 annually for houses larger than 40 marlas.
The Rawalpindi Cantonment Board has also reduced residential property tax rates for Category-B houses.
The annual tax for one-to-five marla houses has been reduced from Rs14,400 to Rs10,800, while the rate for five-to-seven marla houses has been reduced from Rs20,400 to Rs18,800. For seven-to-10 marla houses, the new annual rate is Rs28,000 against Rs30,600 previously, while the rate for 10-to-15 marla houses has been reduced from Rs40,800 to Rs37,000.
The new rate for 15-to-20 marla houses is Rs40,000 against Rs43,200 previously, while the rate for 20-to-40 marla houses has been reduced from Rs56,100 to Rs52,000.
For houses larger than 40 marlas, the annual property tax has been reduced from Rs66,300 to Rs60,000.
The Rawalpindi Cantonment Board has also reduced the annual rental value increase for Category-C houses from 30 per cent to 20pc for 2026 to 2029.
Residents will have to pay sanitation tax, water charges and property tax according to the new rates. However, residents say they do not receive drinking water according to their needs and ground realities. Water is supplied every alternate day, meaning residents have to pay a full month's water charges for water supplied for only 15 days.
Except for posh cantonment areas, sanitation conditions in densely populated backyards are extremely poor.
Despite property tax, the condition of paved streets, functional sewerage systems and streetlights remains similar in densely populated backyard areas as well as posh localities. Potholes in roads and streets, dysfunctional sewerage systems and absence of streetlights have created severe difficulties for residents.
The tenure of the elections held in 2021 in Rawalpindi, Chaklala and other cantonment boards across the country ended in 2025. Residents are waiting to know when new elections will be held and when elected representatives will highlight public issues before the relevant authorities.
Several attempts were made to contact Rawalpindi Cantonment Board spokesman and Assistant Secretary Imran Habib for the board's opinion on the imposition of sanitation tax, water charges and property tax and the problems faced by residents, but he could not be reached.

title: Iran  US trade threats as Houthi attacks escalate
description: Iran  US trade threats as Houthi attacks escalate
content:
Iran and the United States exchanged new threats on Sunday, with President Donald Trump warning Iran would fail economically or face its leadership being wiped out if it didn't make a deal, and the Iranian military saying it would retaliate harshly to any fresh attack.
The conflict has looked stalemated for months, with no sign either side was ready for concessions even as it has deepened a global energy crisis, cratered swathes of Iran's economy and spilled ?over into new regional escalations.
In a phone call with a Fox News reporter, Trump said Iran's leaders should make a deal, rot economically or be wiped out, the reporter said. However, with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly, Trump said he would be open to meeting him, the Fox reporter added.
Trump has repeatedly made vague threats of major military escalations during the conflict that began with US and Israeli strikes on February 28, without carrying them out.
Earlier, Iran's military central command said any new attack would trigger sustained retaliation against US bases and interests and that Washington's regional allies would be considered parties to the conflict.
The Iranian military added that it had information that an attack was being prepared, without elaborating on what that information might be.
Gulf allies have already been badly scarred by a war that the US and Israel launched with no warning, bringing their cities under Iranian fire and hammering their economies with the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway blockaded.
On Saturday their predicament worsened further, with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi group launching missile and drone strikes at the Saudi capital after having made sudden military gains in Yemen's reignited civil war earlier this month.
Reuters video showed a massive plume of black smoke billowing from the area of Riyadh's main international airport following booms overnight.
The US State Department issued a security alert citing the Houthi hostilities. It said there was potential for unforeseen escalation in the Middle East, and Americans should exercise more vigilance and be aware of possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.

title: 2 officers among 6 servicemen martyred in Hangu ambush
description: 2 officers among 6 servicemen martyred in Hangu ambush
content:
During an exchange of fire, security forces also eliminate eight terrorists
Six personnel of the Pakistan Armyincluding two officersembraced martyrdom when their convoy came under attack in district Hangu of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P).
According to a statement issued by the military's media wing on Sunday, the forces also eliminated eight terrorists of the Fitna al-Khawarija term used to refer to outlawed Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)during the exchange of fire.
The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) stated that two officers, Captain Abuzar Farooq, aged 23 and Lieutenant Sheraz Babar, aged 22, laid down their lives while leading their troops from the front.
Captain Farooq hailed from District Gujranwala and Lieutenant Babar was a resident of District Chakwal.
"[They] fought gallantly and paid the ultimate sacrifice and embraced shahadat along with their four men," the statement said, adding that a sanitization operation was under way in the area to eliminate any other Indian sponsored Kharji found in the area.
"A relentless counter terrorism campaign under vision Azm-e-Istehkam will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign sponsored and supported terrorism from the country. These sacrifices of our brave soldiers reinforce our unwavering commitment to safeguarding our nation at all costs," it added.
In separate statements, both the president and the prime minister expressed grief over the martyrdom of the officers and troops in the Hangu attack.
President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to those who lost their lives in the line of duty and commended the security forces for eliminating terrorists.
He also extended his heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families and prayed to Allah Almighty to elevate the ranks of the martyrs and grant patience to their families.
Prime Minister Shehbaz also paid tribute to Captain Abuzar Farooq, Lieutenant Sheraz Babar and the four soldiers, adding that the martyred officers and soldiers demonstrated unparalleled bravery in the defence of the beloved homeland and in the war against terrorism.
The martyrs sacrificed their lives for the nation's future and the country's security, he said, adding that the entire nation salutes its brave men. He said the operations of security forces and law enforcement agencies against Fitna Al-Khawarij will continue till the complete elimination of terrorism.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi paid tribute to the six security personnel, adding that the martyrs had bravely confronted the terrorists of Fitna-al-Khawarij.
"The martyrs are the pride of the nation and their eternal sacrifices will always be remembered," Naqvi said, adding that the nation can never repay the debt owed to the great sacrifices of the martyrs.

title: No respite for fuel consumers in Pakistan
description: No respite for fuel consumers in Pakistan
content:
Supply routes disrupted as global prices, freight and insurance costs surge
Pakistani consumers have experienced oil shocks in recent months and are expected to face further difficulties in the near future, as fears of oil shortages in the country grow amid escalating tensions in the Middle East.
A major portion of Pakistan's oil imports comes from Saudi Arabia. The Strait of Hormuz is already closed, while Pakistan's alternate route through the Red Sea has also been disrupted by Houthi attacks, effectively affecting Saudi Arabia's oil exports.
In August, the Pakistan government had arranged three oil cargoes, but they were stopped by the Yemeni Houthis. However, the Pakistani establishment approached Iran for intervention, and the Houthis later released the cargoes.
The government is currently rerouting oil supplies. With global oil prices rising, pressure is building on the economy and inflation is increasing. Pakistan will be required to spend more dollars on oil in the future. The government is therefore considering diversifying its crude sources away from the Gulf.
Despite the challenges, Pakistan has kept its petroleum supply chain running despite a sharp escalation in the Middle East that has knocked out the main alternative routes the country relied on two months ago. However, officials and industry sources warn that securing cargoes for November will be far harder and costlier.
When the US-Iran truce collapsed on July 8 and Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz again, Pakistan still had a fallback. Crude was moving from Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Yanbu, supplied through the kingdom's East-West pipeline, and the cargoes reached Karachi without major disruption.
That buffer has now been badly damaged. This month, drone strikes shut down the East-West pipeline, which carries about 5 million barrels per day. Houthi forces seized a strategic island at the mouth of the Red Sea, while a vessel was struck inside Hormuz.
Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik has said Saudi supplies are currently out of reach because of Houthi attacks on the kingdom's oil facilities, and that a Pakistani vessel is being kept on standby. The Petroleum Division, however, stresses that the country is holding stocks for more than 20 days.
The 20-day buffer is above the minimum level required by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) for Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs). According to officials, September supplies have been secured and October has been derisked even under adverse scenarios, while planning for November is under way.
Inside the country, prices have risen at the pumps. On July 22, shortly after the government switched from weekly to daily price revisions, petrol was priced at Rs320.73 per litre and high-speed diesel at Rs367.21. By September 20, petrol stood at Rs389.14 and diesel at Rs424.04.
This means petrol and diesel prices rose by Rs68 and Rs57 per litre, respectively, in just two months. The increase in domestic fuel prices comes against the backdrop of an overall rise in global oil prices during the past few months.
Benchmark Brent futures, which had gone up after the US-Israel attack on Iran on February 28, had fallen to around $70 per barrel on July 1, but prices rebounded above $100 by late July and peaked at about $109 in early September. However, they have since eased to around $100.
The physical market, from which Pakistan actually buys its cargoes, is far tighter. According to S&P Global Platts assessments, Dated Brent, the physical benchmark, stood at $125.42 per barrel on September 18. Dubai, the benchmark for most of Pakistan's Gulf-sourced crude, was at $118.40. Industry officials said physical Dubai crossed $126 earlier this month.
Refined products, which Pakistan prices on an import-parity basis against Arab Gulf benchmarks, have moved in the same direction. Gasoline 92 RON was assessed at $132.73 per barrel FOB Arab Gulf on September 18, against about $104 in July, an increase of roughly 28%.
Gasoil 10ppm, the benchmark for Pakistan's diesel, touched a high of around $177 this month, up from about $149 in July, before easing to $169.74 on September 18. Jet fuel was assessed at $161.30, while marine fuel at Fujairah stood at $985 per tonne, about $175 above Singapore, reflecting the premium now attached to Gulf-loaded barrels.
The cost of delivering those barrels to Karachi has risen even faster. Industry officials said freight and war-risk insurance premiums had increased three to four times. Tankers are avoiding Hormuz, taking longer routes and paying higher insurance cover to operate in contested waters. These costs feed directly into the import-parity price that OGRA uses to set domestic fuel prices.
Even so, Pakistani consumers are paying less for diesel than motorists in the United States. The average US retail diesel price reached a record $6.285 per gallon in the week of September 14, according to the US Energy Information Administration. That is equivalent to about Rs461 per litre at the current exchange rate, roughly Rs37 above Pakistan's diesel price.
The diplomatic outlook has also deteriorated. A meeting between Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states and Iran, scheduled for September 13, was called off with no new date. It had been expected to discuss temporary Omani and Iranian oversight of Hormuz traffic. Analysts say Pakistan-mediated backchannel talks are now the only active diplomatic track.
Officials said three steps have kept fuel flowing, with the first being the maximisation of local refining. Pakistan has largely stopped importing refined diesel since June, apart from a single cargo in early August. Instead, the government pushed more crude to local refineries to produce diesel domestically.
With Gulf diesel trading about $51 per barrel above crude, refining locally has been far cheaper than importing the finished product. The country's five refineries have a combined capacity of around 450,000 barrels per day and meet roughly 70% of diesel demand and 30% of petrol demand. Domestic crude production stands at about 63,000 to 64,000 barrels per day.
The second step was diversifying crude sources away from the Gulf. The government is considering supplies from Oman and Fujairah and exploring Libya, the United States, West Africa and Kazakhstan. Because Pakistani ports lack the draft to berth very large crude carriers, officials plan to park a US-origin VLCC near Sohar in Oman or off Hub and move its cargo through ship-to-ship transfers.
Cnergyico is the only refinery that can berth a vessel twice the size of those accommodated at other Pakistani ports at its SPM. Refined petrol is being brought in from Singapore and Oman.
Refinery officials said crude cargoes for September and October had already been booked, with more supplies now coming from the US and West Africa and less from the Gulf. They said the longer voyages were not expected to significantly affect refining operational viability.
The officials also said local refineries were holding ample diesel stocks and there was so far no need for refined diesel imports. They added that imports could be avoided through the peak season if OGRA managed the supply side effectively, including product allocation among OMCs and upliftment from refineries.
The third step was direct state intervention. The federal government has cut fuel allocations for official vehicles by 50% for three months and restricted official travel. This came days after it approved Rs75 billion in targeted subsidies to shield low-income motorists.
The Pakistan Navy has escorted energy tankers under Operation Muhafiz-ul-Bahr since March. On Saturday, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar urged Tehran to ensure uninterrupted energy supplies and safe passage for shipping.
Other import-dependent countries in the region have struggled more. Bangladesh, which imports more than 90% of its petroleum, has had to ration power and temporarily close garment factories. In Sri Lanka, fuel distributors have begun restricting supplies ahead of expected price increases.
Industry, however, warns that the coming months will be tougher and that the pressure point for oil marketing companies is not diesel. OMC officials said their main concern was liquidity. In its latest letter to OGRA, the Oil Companies Advisory Council (OCAC) said about Rs66.7 billion in price differential claims remained outstanding, roughly equal to five petrol cargoes, with much of the amount pending since March.
OCAC also flagged an approved Rs1.22 per litre increase in OMC margins that has yet to be notified. It warned that if liquidity continued to be drained, any resulting supply disruption should not be blamed on the oil industry.
Their second concern is petrol. With local refineries meeting only about 30% of demand, roughly 70% of the country's petrol must still be imported, and the main nearby source, Fujairah, is effectively out of reach. Cargoes from Singapore carry significantly higher freight costs, while Oman's exportable surplus is limited by its own domestic demand. Pakistan consumes about 21,000 tonnes of petrol a day.
OCAC has also cautioned that diesel availability during the October-December harvesting season will depend on how many crude cargoes reach Pakistan in October, and that any shortfall would force expensive imports from the open market.
Industry sources said prices being quoted for November cargoes were significantly higher, while Red Sea detours were adding around 10 days to each voyage.
The minister has himself described the central risk. With all of the country's diesel now coming from refineries running at maximum throughput, a single break in the crude supply chain could cause a diesel shortage. However, he remains optimistic that the alternate arrangements will keep the supply chain uninterrupted.

title: Govt draws line ahead of PTI march
description: Govt draws line ahead of PTI march
content:
Thousands of personnel deployed to fortify capital entry points
Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry warned the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) on Sunday against engaging in violence or illegal activity during its planned long march on September 27, saying those arriving as "terrorists would not be allowed" to return.
The warning came as the authorities concerned take their preparations for the PTIs protest to the final stages, which included trenches, soil filled containers and deployment of thousands of policemen and other law-enforcement personnel to stop the marchers.
"If you are peaceful citizens, come to Islamabad by any route, but if you come as terrorists, we will not let you leave," Talal said, according to Express News. He added the Islamabad High Court's orders would be implemented in full and that the government would not tolerate any illegal activity during the PTI protest.
The minister of state also criticised the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government, saying that it had failed to control terrorism in the province and had been unable to provide basic facilities, including health and education, to its people.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar also reacted strongly to the PTI protest, describing it as a plan to create "chaos and destruction". Responding to remarks by PTI's K-P President Junaid Akbar about the long march, Tarar said the statement showed that the party's objective was to spread disorder and destruction. "These people do not believe in peaceful protest; rather, they want violence and bloodshed," Tarar said.
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said that recent statements by PTI leaders regarding their planned march towards Islamabad had raised concerns about the possibility of violence, and stressed that the government would take measures to maintain law and order in the federal capital.
Speaking to a private TV channel, Chaudhry referred to a reported statement by a senior PTI leader, who said that they were coming towards the capital to "make it Somnath". Chaudhry described the remark as a threat and said the government had a responsibility to ensure that normal life was not disrupted. "Islamabad is the city of all Pakistanis, and no one will be allowed to deteriorate its law-and-order situation," he said.
The minister's remarks come amid preparations for a PTI protest march scheduled for September 27.
Meanwhile, security preparations in Islamabad and Rawalpindi have entered their final stages ahead of the possible long march by the PTI and other opposition parties, with thousands of personnel being deployed and roads fortified.
More than 22,000 personnel will be deployed in Islamabad under eight DIGs, 10 SSPs, 40 SPs and 58 DSPs, while 30,000 personnel are being deployed in Attock and more than 13,000 police personnel will perform duties in Rawalpindi.
Additional police personnel and Frontier Constabulary units have been sanctioned for Islamabad and districts across the Rawalpindi Division. Personnel from Punjab districts including Sheikhupura, Dera Ghazi Khan, Multan and Faisalabad are also being deployed in Attock.
The provincial law-enforcement authorities will also provide additional personnel in Attock, the key district connecting Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa with Punjab, as the government prepares to deal with the possible movement of protesters towards Islamabad.
In Rawalpindi, a senior police officer told The Express Tribune on condition of anonymity that approximately 6,500 to 7,000 operational personnel were already available, while an equal number of additional personnel had been requisitioned, taking the total deployment to around 13,000.
Police staff from training colleges and schools, personnel attending courses and staff undergoing training are also being assigned duties. Holidays for police officers and personnel in Rawalpindi had already been cancelled several days earlier.
Meanwhile, authorities are taking strict measures at Islamabad's entry points, including digging trenches, constructing barricades and placing soil-filled sacks inside containers positioned on major roads and around the Red Zone.
Dozens of labourers have been deployed to fill sacks with soil from morning until evening, while tractor-trolleys carrying soil are being brought into the Red Zone. Soil-filled sacks will also be placed on major roads to block vehicular movement.
Sources said barricades made from soil-filled sacks would be constructed at Red Zone entry checkpoints, while roads at entry points would also be dug up to prevent protesters from entering the capital.
A plan has been prepared to dig trenches across access roads and make movement through them impossible, while Rawalpindi and Islamabad police officers have been directed to arrange machinery and labourers for the work.
A large number of containers have already been taken into custody in the twin cities and kept on standby along roadsides and at open spaces to block possible movement during the protest.
Authorities have also completed a survey of the Sports Complex, Pak-China Friendship Centre, schools and colleges to accommodate additional police personnel, with a report covering more than 100 buildings submitted to officials.

title: Imran s sister detained ahead of PTI protest
description: Aleema sent to Kot Lakhpat Jail for 30 days  PTI founder s sister accused of inciting people
content:
Aleema sent to Kot Lakhpat Jail for 30 days, PTI founder's sister accused of inciting people
Authorities in Punjab's provincial capital on Sunday detained former prime minister Imran Khan's septuagenarian sister Aleema Khan for 30 days and transferred her to Lahore Kot Lakhpat Jail amid a protest by the PTI and other parties in an opposition alliance, the TTAP.
The move occurred just a week before the PTI's planned protest march, scheduled to start on September 27, aimed at forcing the PML-N-led federal government to release Imran, the PTI founder, who has been detained in a Rawalpindi jail for over three years.
On Sunday, Lahore Deputy Commissioner (DC) Muhammad Ali Ijaz issued an order stating that Aleema Khan and a PTI leader, Muhammad Ameer, had been ordered to be arrested and detained for 30 days under Section 3 of the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960.
The order stated that police and intelligence officials reported the two were involved in the May 9, 2023 protests and road blockades and allegedly motivated workers to damage public and government property.
It also said they were mobilising workers through social media and public meetings, raising slogans that could provoke or incite people. The DC said the District Intelligence Committee endorsed the material provided by the police and unanimously recommended their detention.
He said their presence at public places would pose a "grave threat to the public safety" and could lead to a breach of public peace and order. The detention order also stated that Aleema might make a representation against the detention to the provincial government.
Aleema's son Shahrez Khan wrote on X that his mother was abducted after leaving home on Sunday morning, adding that the family had had no contact with her or information about her whereabouts.
"She is on bail in all cases against her in Lahore. We demand the government immediately disclose her whereabouts and ensure her safe return," he added.
Police also detained Hajra Niazi, Imran's niece, and her husband. According to sources, police officials stopped the couple at a checkpoint near Aleema's residence before taking them into custody.
The sources said the couple were subsequently taken to different police stations and remained in police custody for some time before being released. Hajra Niazi is the daughter of Imran's sister Noreen Niazi and sister of incarcerated PTI worker and Imran's nephew Hassan Niazi
Authorities in Islamabad also detained three PTI leaders from the federal capital's Red Zone near the Parliament Lodges on Sunday and later transferred them to an undisclosed location.
These detentions came ahead of the PTI protest which Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Friday the government would do everything to stop.
Opposition leaders strongly condemned the detention.
PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan decried Aleema's arrest, saying it was the first step toward worsening the situation. "Our march will be peaceful and political. We do not want any confrontation or violence," he said.
Gohar called on the government to immediately stop such measures and release her. He added that the party would soon announce its course of action against such measures.
The TTAP also strongly condemned Aleema's detention, terming it an escalation of the ongoing crackdown on political workers and their families. In a statement, the TTAP said the detention created an atmosphere of fear among political workers and their families.
The statement further alleged that the Punjab government's actions against political workers aimed at disrupting political activity ahead of the September 27 protest.
"The relentless crackdown on political workers in Punjab has now reached families. Aleema's detention under 3-MPO, with no charge and days before September 27, is repression at its peak. It will not break our resolve. Resisting it is our duty," said TTAP provincial leader Shayyan Bashir.
Senate Leader of Opposition Raja Nasir Abbas also condemned the move, calling the detention of Imran Khan's sister "extremely regrettable and condemnable". He said peaceful political struggle and the right to expression could not be suppressed through arrests.
PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi also criticised the detention, with Raja alleging that political workers were being arrested across Punjab ahead of the September 27 protest.
Afridi described the detention as political victimisation and questioned the use of arrests against women in political disputes. PTI leader and a close aide to Imran, Zulfi Bukhari, described the arrest as "absolutely despicable" in a post on X, adding that "the fear of the 27th protest is clearly taking its toll".
Meanwhile, the Human Rights Council of Pakistan also expressed concern over Aleema's detention.

title: Islamabad s PIMS placed on high alert until 30th Sept
description: Islamabad s PIMS placed on high alert until Sept 30
content:
The Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), the capital's main public hospital, has been placed on high alert until September 30 in view of the prevailing situation.
The administration has ordered round-the-clock emergency preparedness, uninterrupted ambulance services and the availability of essential medical staff and supplies.
According to a high-alert circular issued by the PIMS administration on Sunday, heads of all clinical and non-clinical departments have been directed to remain at their stations, while duty rosters are to be kept updated and essential staff made available around the clock.
Medical leave is the only exception to restrictions placed on staff leave during the high-alert period. The circular ordered that ambulance services remain available 24 hours a day throughout the period.
Director Emergency PIMS Dr Sharjeel Zaheer has been designated as the focal person for any emergency situation.
The emergency department, intensive care units, operating theatres, trauma services, nursing and diagnostic departments have been directed to remain fully operational.
The hospital's blood bank and pharmacy services have also been ordered to remain fully functional.
The administration has directed that additional beds be kept available in case of a large influx of patients. Additional stretchers and wheelchairs are also to be made available for such a situation.

title: PM to lead Pakistan delegation at UNGA
description: PM to lead Pakistan delegation at UNGA
content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will lead Pakistan's delegation to the high-level session of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York from September 21 to 25, where he will present Pakistan's position on regional and global security and highlight the country's priorities on major international issues.
The high-level segment of the 81st UN General Assembly will be held from September 22 to 26 and on September 28, with this year's general debate theme set by the newly elected president as 'Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all'.
Pakistan's Permanent Representative to the United Nations Asim Iftikhar Ahmad gave journalists a background briefing in New York on Pakistan's participation in the General Assembly session.
He said PM Shehbaz would address the General Assembly on September 25 and present Islamabad's position on the regional and global security situation. He would emphasise the need for peaceful resolution of conflicts, dialogue, diplomacy and restraint, he added.
According to the permanent representative, the prime minister's address would also highlight Pakistan's priorities on sustainable development, climate change, counterterrorism, Islamophobia, global economic challenges, reform of the United Nations and the Sustainable Development Goals, among other key international issues.
Asim Iftikhar Ahmad said Pakistan would also draw the international community's attention to issues involving prolonged occupation and the right to self-determination, including Palestine and occupied Jammu and Kashmir, and would call for their resolution in accordance with relevant UN resolutions.
During the General Assembly session, PM Shehbaz will hold bilateral meetings with world leaders and the UN secretary-general.

title: JI s  super train march  chugs towards capital
description: JI s  super train march  chugs towards capital
content:
Warns campaign could turn into movement to oust govt
Jamaat-e-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Sunday launched the party's Karachi-to-Islamabad "super train march" against the petroleum levy, "cruel" agreements with independent power producers (IPPs), warning that the ongoing campaign could intensify into a movement to oust the government if its demands were not accepted.
Thousands of JI workers and participants gathered at Karachi Cantonment Railway Station for the departure, while women office-bearers of the party bade farewell to the marchers with prayers.
Hafiz Naeem said the caravan would reach Islamabad as the voice of the people's demands, while other caravans from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan were also due to set off for the capital.
Addressing the participants, the JI emir said the government should "read the writing on the wall", adding that the issue was not about anyone's ego. He urged the government to take credit for providing relief to the public and abolish the petroleum levy.
He said a path to relief was available to the government and that the additional burden on the people should be reduced by ending the levy. He stressed that the Islamabad march was not being held for any political party or individual but for the rights of the people.
According to Hafiz Naeem, government policies had pushed the public into severe hardship, with the lower and middle-income sections struggling to survive while the government continued to shift the burden of its mismanagement and poor policies onto citizens.
He said the government was using the international market as an excuse to impose an additional burden on consumers through higher petroleum prices.
Instead of restraining the ruling elite, reducing official and elite expenditure, cutting the number of vehicles and reviewing "cruel IPP agreements", he said, the government was imposing further taxes on the people.
The JI emir said the government and its representatives were present in IPPs and that questions had also repeatedly been raised about the presence and interests of government figures in the oil marketing, refinery, flour and sugar sectors.
He said the public was constantly being told to bear every difficulty, but warned that if people continued to sit at home and tolerate everything, further burdens would continue to be imposed on them.
Hafiz Naeem said JI had chosen to take to the streets for the rights of the people. The party had staged a 35-day sit-in in Karachi, while sit-ins were continuing in Sukkur, Larkana and Hyderabad, with marches and protest sit-ins also under way in different parts of Punjab.

title: Protests may cost economy Rs120b daily  claims Aurangzeb
description: Protests may cost economy Rs120b daily  claims Aurangzeb
content:
Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Sunday warned that long marches, sit-ins and strikes could cost Pakistan's economy around Rs120 billion a day, describing disruptions to economic activity as "self-inflicted pain" at a time when the country was trying to shift from economic stabilisation to sustained growth.
The statement came after three groups, Jamaat-e-Islami (JI), Kissan Ittehad and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), announced plans for long marches in Islamabad in the coming week. The groups were protesting separate issues, with JI demanding the removal of the petroleum development levy, Kissan Ittehad seeking relief for farmers, and PTI calling for the release of party founder Imran Khan from jail.
In a televised recorded message, Aurangzeb said the government had worked with the Planning Commission's economic wing to assess the potential impact of protests, road blockages and business closures, drawing on both previous experience and the country's current economic conditions.
"If this economic stabilisation that we have achieved with great effort, difficult decisions and continuous efforts is disrupted by protests, sit-ins, road blockages and the closure of business and economic activities, what would the results be?" he said.
Based on the assessment, he said such disruption could result in an estimated Rs120 billion loss per day, with the services sector expected to bear the largest share of the impact.
"We estimate that there could be a loss of around Rs86 billion per day in the services sector", Aurangzeb said. The estimate covered financial services, communications, transport, retail, wholesale and hospitality.
The industrial sector could suffer another Rs25 billion in daily losses, he said, with the estimate covering construction, finished goods, raw materials and supply chain-related activity. Agriculture could account for a further Rs9 billion a day in losses, including the impact on transportation, perishable goods, dairy, supply chains and agricultural trade.

A total of 9,923 candidates registered in Balochistan, while 2,761 candidates registered from AJK and 1,721 from Gilgit-Baltistan. Islamabad had 1,245 registered candidates. Punjab had the highest number of registered candidates at 49,199.

title: Kohat attackers had planned long siege
description: Kohat attackers had planned long siege
content:
Initial investigations into the Friday terrorist attack on the Kohat Police Lines have revealed that the attackers were not merely planning a suicide bombing but had entered the compound with a plan to maintain a prolonged siege for several hours.
Sources said the terrorists were carrying hand grenades, sniper rifles, other weapons and explosives. After entering different parts of the Police Lines, they opened fire and used hand grenades during the attack. The FIR registered by police also mentions the use of firearms and hand grenades.
According to investigators, the attack began when an explosives-laden vehicle resembling a rickshaw was rammed near the Police Lines, causing a powerful blast. Immediately after the explosion, armed terrorists entered the compound and moved towards several key buildings.
Police said seven armed terrorists, including a sniper, initially entered the compound. Investigators said the attackers intended to use the explosion and gunfire to disperse police personnel and remain inside the compound for as long as possible.
However, police personnel continued to resist despite coming under heavy fire and suffering injuries, preventing the attackers from advancing as planned.
A senior police officer told The Express Tribune that the use of drone technology during the attack, along with the timely response by police and other security forces, played an important role in monitoring the terrorists' movement and conducting the operation.
According to the officer, the forces promptly brought the situation under control and prevented the attackers from spreading further inside the compound.
Officials said a prolonged exchange of fire continued after the terrorists entered the buildings. Later, operation continued for around 20 to 21 hours.

title: Pakistan opens power market to competition
description: Pakistan opens power market to competition
content:
400MW wheeling auction targets large consumers
Energy Minister Awais Leghari on Sunday announced the launch of a competitive electricity market in Pakistan, saying the new system would initially allow industrial and other large consumers using more than one megawatt to purchase electricity directly from producers before being extended to ordinary consumers in the coming years.
"The government is practically withdrawing from electricity procurement," he said in a video message, explaining that electricity producers and consumers would instead be able to buy and sell power directly through a transparent mechanism.
The announcement came as the Independent System and Market Operator of Pakistan (ISMO) issued a request for proposals (RFP) for Pakistan's first 400-megawatt wheeling auction under the Competitive Trading Bilateral Contract Market (CTBCM) framework.
Leghari also shared the ISMO public notice on X, saying he was "proud to announce" that the RFP had been issued and that a "decades-old commitment" of successive governments had now been practically implemented. "Suppliers and consumers of power can now transact with each other," he said in his post.
Under the existing electricity market structure, the government purchases the power generated by producers and supplies it to consumers. The terms and rates under which electricity is procured have long been a subject of scrutiny, particularly in relation to independent power producers (IPPs).
He said the new system would fundamentally alter that arrangement, with producers and consumers able to enter into transactions directly rather than relying on the government as the central buyer and seller. "Electricity producers and users will buy and sell directly through a transparent mechanism," he added.
The first phase of the competitive market will cover industrial and other large consumers using more than one megawatt of electricity. Ordinary consumers will be brought into the system at a later stage, with Leghari saying the expansion was expected to take place over the next few years.
The minister said the eventual expansion would give consumers greater choice over their electricity suppliers and allow them to seek cheaper power. "For an ordinary consumer, this will mean that they will have the choice of buying cheaper electricity," he said.
Leghari further stated that lower electricity costs would also help Pakistani industry compete in international markets and support exports. "If electricity becomes cheaper, our industry will be able to compete internationally, and our exports will increase," he added.

title: Pakistan wants an AI future  but is it ready for one
description: Pakistan wants an AI future  but is it ready for one
content:
Walk into a university library in Lahore or a corporate office in Karachi and you will see the same quiet routine. A student polishes an assignment with a chatbot. An executive drafts a report in minutes rather than hours. A small trader writes marketing captions in Urdu and English using an AI app. On family WhatsApp groups, a strangely convincing video or cloned voice note does the rounds before anyone works out whether it is real. Artificial intelligence has already made itself at home in the Pakistani life. The harder question is whether the country is genuinely ready for what comes next.
There is a meaningful difference between adopting AI and being ready for it. Millions of Pakistanis now open a chatbot the way earlier generations opened a search engine. Interest is easy to demonstrate; readiness is harder, since it depends on implementation capacity, functioning governance and accountable institutions. The federal cabinet's approval of the National AI Policy 2025 in July 2025 was a genuinely useful step, setting out funding for innovation and targets for training AI professionals. But a policy document, however well written, is not the same as a prepared country. Policies succeed or fail in their implementation.
Readiness begins with ordinary people, not only programmers. Students, teachers, civil servants, journalists, managers, healthcare workers and parents need a working sense of what AI can help with, and where it goes wrong. That means knowing a confident-sounding answer can still be inaccurate, that outputs need checking rather than blind trust, that confidential client or patient information should never go into a public AI tool and that a convincing voice note is not proof a conversation happened. The most serious AI divide in Pakistan may not be between those with access to these tools and those without, but between those who question AI and those who trust it blindly.
This runs through education and work alike. Students already use generative AI for essays and exams, whether institutions permit it or not, and blanket bans have proved unworkable elsewhere. Schools and universities can realistically set clear guidelines, redesign assessments so thinking rather than typing gets graded and train teachers to work with AI rather than only police it. The same applies at work: Pakistan needs not only AI developers but accountants, managers and shopkeepers who know when to trust these tools and when not to. The question is no longer whether students and employees will use AI, but whether institutions will teach them to use it responsibly.
None of this matters if the basic foundations are missing. Meaningful AI adoption needs reliable electricity, affordable internet and cybersecurity capacity that keeps pace with new risks. Pakistan has made real gains: government data released this year shows individual internet use climbing from 17 per cent in 2019 to 57 per cent in 2025. Yet urban-rural and income gaps remain wide, and national literacy, recently reported at 63 per cent with a sharp urban-rural split, shapes who can use these tools at all. AI that works well in English but struggles with Urdu, Sindhi, Pashto or Punjabi will leave many behind, and unless inclusion is deliberate, AI risks widening the gaps it should close.
The risks deserve honest treatment, without treating AI as inherently dangerous. Deepfakes and cloned voices are already used for impersonation and financial fraud and misinformation spreads faster when it looks authentic. Data privacy, cybersecurity and quietly biased automated decisions carry real consequences, particularly when nobody is accountable for the harm an AI-assisted decision causes. Sensible regulation does not treat every use of AI alike. Grammar correction carries little risk; AI in recruitment, healthcare, lending, law enforcement or identity verification deserves stronger safeguards and human review, a risk-based approach that protects people without smothering innovation.
Government has a practical role here, and it need not be complicated. A public AI-literacy campaign in English, Urdu and regional languages would reach citizens faster than any policy document. Age-appropriate AI education in schools, and proper training for teachers, civil servants and regulators, would build the human capacity the National AI Policy already promises on paper. Clear standards for high-risk uses, mandatory human oversight for consequential decisions and simple channels for reporting deepfakes or AI fraud would turn ambition into trust. In workforce technology, I have often seen organisations acquire new tools faster than they prepare people to use them, and in teaching, I have watched students experiment with generative AI while institutional guidance lags behind. Pakistan's AI story risks the same pattern unless people, not just policy, receive equal attention.
None of this need be a reason for pessimism. Pakistan does not have to choose between innovation and safety. Sensible safeguards build the public trust that wider AI adoption depends on, and a young, entrepreneurial population gives the country a genuine headstart if it invests in people alongside platforms. The country should act now, before AI-related harm becomes widespread, but fear should never smother invention. Pakistan's AI readiness will not be measured by how quickly it adopts new tools, but by how wisely, safely and inclusively it uses them.

Carrot Top’s Monday night performance at the Luxor in Las Vegas has been cancelled as the comedian remains hospitalized and continues receiving medical care.
The 61-year-old comedian’s scheduled Monday show was called off following his hospitalization, according to reports. His Saturday night performance at the Las Vegas casino had also been cancelled as he continued to receive care.
Carrot Top was taken to a local Las Vegas hospital on Friday following a reported suicide attempt. Details about his condition have not been publicly disclosed, and his representatives have not provided further information about his recovery.

The cancellations affect Carrot Top’s Las Vegas residency, where the comedian has regularly performed his prop comedy show at the Luxor. Further updates regarding his upcoming performances are expected as more information becomes available.
Carrot Top, whose real name is Scott Thompson, has been performing professionally for decades and is known for his distinctive prop-based comedy. His Las Vegas shows have been a major part of his career in recent years.
Anyone experiencing suicidal thoughts or emotional distress can seek immediate support through local emergency services or a crisis hotline. In the US, people can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
