title: China  US find new trade ties in services
description: China  US find new trade ties in services
content:
AI, finance, IP and professional services deepen economic interdependence
China built its economic power by manufacturing things – consumer electronics, machinery, just about everything – and shipping them abroad in huge quantities. For decades, that is what China did, and in doing so it became the factory of the world. Few imagined that within a few decades, it would be the world's second-biggest economy, behind only the United States.
That model has changed. What Chinese companies send across borders today is far less visible: software, artificial intelligence (AI), engineering knowhow, logistics, fintech and other professional skills. The next chapter of China's globalisation may rest less on what it produces than on the services wrapped around its products and supply chains. The shift was no accident. Merchandise trade faces tariffs, geopolitical friction and protectionism everywhere. Services slip past most of that, moving through software, data, intellectual property and digital platforms, with no container and no customs inspection. That does not mean services will replace manufacturing. China is instead beginning to export the capabilities that surround what it makes.
In 2024, China was the world's fifth largest exporter of commercial services and its second largest importer, according to the World Trade Organisation (WTO). Services make up roughly 27-28% of global trade, and they are outpacing goods. Global trade expanded around 6% in 2025, while services went up by over 8%. About half of China's services exports are now digitally deliverable or knowledge-intensive. And the momentum is building – in the first seven months of 2026, China's services exports jumped 17.1% year-on-year to RMB 1.77 trillion. Knowledge-intensive exports climbed 12.2% to RMB 948 billion, more than half the total.
This shift is about capabilities rather than software as such. Chinese firms now use AI and digital tools to read markets in over 100 countries, spot consumer demand, design products, write marketing material, run supply chains and keep track of regulatory rules. Software, engineering, financing and compliance all travel with the physical goods. The old line between goods and services is blurring fast. A smartphone is worth as much for its apps, streaming and payment features as for the hardware, and even manufacturing now leans heavily on engineering, finance, logistics and data. In effect, China's globalisation is moving from selling products to selling whole systems.
This produces something of a paradox in its rivalry with the world's No 1 economy. Even as China and the United States work to need each other less in goods and technology, their economies may need each other more in services. America is still the world's biggest services trader, and 2025 brought a record surplus of $339.5 billion. Its surplus with China stood at $34.4 billion and in the first quarter of 2026 alone it hit $9.366 billion, up 8.26% from 2025, powered by travel, intellectual-property royalties and financial services.
Interestingly, this side of the China-US trade relationship rarely makes the news, lost as it is in the cacophony over tariffs and trade deficits. Despite all the politically motivated noise, complementarity of the two economies is strong. US firms bring global brands, deep financial and professional networks and unmatched expertise in intellectual property, foundational software and frontier AI. China, on the other hand, brings scale – something few markets can copy; a massive consumer base, vast digital infrastructure, sophisticated e-commerce ecosystem and real-world environments to test and refine new technologies. American companies need markets and customers for their technology; Chinese firms going overseas need market intelligence, risk assessment, compliance help, financial expertise and professional advice. Every factory, research centre and supply chain a Chinese company builds abroad creates demand for exactly the services Western companies do best.
All of this matter even more in the current AI era. The United States still leads in foundational models, chip design, electronic design automation and the software everything runs on. China has become formidable at applying AI at scale – its market, engineering base, manufacturing ecosystem and sheer volume of use cases see to that. The two sit at different points of the same technology chain: American innovation supplies the foundations, Chinese companies build the applications across enterprise AI, smart devices, e-commerce, digital healthcare, logistics, fintech and industrial automation.
Nevertheless strategic competition won't go away. Technology controls, data-security worries and national-security concerns will keep limiting what the two tech powerhouses can do together, even as AI makes economic decoupling harder to imagine. Services run on interconnected layers of software, data, infrastructure and intellectual property; pull them apart and costs rise on both sides. The real danger is that governments spin out incompatible rules faster than businesses can keep up. Data, AI and digital platforms are already tangled in what trade lawyers call a "spaghetti bowl" of national and regional regulation – a new generation of trade barriers in the making.
What China does at home would determine whether it becomes a services leader abroad. Services already generate 57.7% of China's economic output, up from around 40% two decades ago, yet Beijing remains less services-oriented than most advanced open economies. According to OECD research, more domestic competition and market opening would sharpen international competitiveness. Beijing has taken some steps such as a negative-list approach to services, openings in tourism, healthcare and telecommunications, and encouragement of imports in R&D, design, IP and digital-technology services. Those doors matter to American firms, and foreign competition, in turn, forces Chinese providers to raise their game.
This new services economy will globalise in a different way from the manufacturing era. Goods trade is easy to see as a product crosses a border and gets counted. Services slip invisibly into everything – a factory, a financial transaction, an algorithm, an online marketplace. For developing economies, Chinese expansion could mean local partnerships, technology transfer and investment, but none of it happens automatically. Whether the gains are widely shared depends on local participation, transparent regulation, market access and a genuine say in writing the rules.
For China and the US, the stakes are highest of all. Beijing needs foreign expertise, IP, finance and professional capability as its companies proliferate globally; American firms need China's market, its industrial ecosystem and its appetite for sophisticated services. The rivalry is real, yet competition and interdependence have coexisted before. China and the US may spend years shoring up their vulnerabilities in goods and critical technologies, only to find themselves more deeply intertwined than ever – through networks of services nobody can see.
So the next frontier of China's global trade may not announce itself with another wave of container ships steaming out of its ports. It will look more like an AI agent running in a foreign country, an engineer in Shenzhen designing a project an ocean away, a Chinese firm hiring American financial expertise, or a piece of software quietly managing a supply chain thousands of kilometres from wherever it was written. In the services economy, borders still count. Capabilities count more. And that makes decoupling the two economies all but impossible.
THE WRITER IS AN INDEPENDENT JOURNALIST WITH A SPECIAL INTEREST IN GEO-ECONOMICS

title: Rising remittances  falling exports
description: Rising remittances  falling exports
content:
Pakistan needs to turn inflows into productive investment and jobs
Pakistan is receiving more dollars from overseas Pakistanis while earning less at home, slowing momentum from its own productive economy. This is the paradox confronting policymakers: remittances are rising strongly, but exports are struggling to maintain their pace, trade deficit is widening, foreign direct investment remains weak and domestic investment is insufficient to create jobs for a rapidly growing young population.
The latest remittance figures are certainly encouraging. Workers' remittances reached $3.66 billion in August 2026, up 16.5% year-on-year and 0.7% from July. During the first two months of FY2027, remittance inflows stood at $7.29 billion, an increase of 14.7% over the corresponding period, compared with exports in the same period at $5.46 billion.
Trade deficit surged in the current fiscal year's first two months (July-August) by 18% year-on-year to $7.12 billion from $6.01 billion in the same period of last fiscal year. Pakistan received a record $41.6 billion in remittances in the last fiscal year 2026, which cushioned the current account deficit to remain within the comfort zone of $139 million despite a huge trade deficit of $39.5 billion.
The State Bank's latest data shows total liquid foreign exchange reserves of around $21.72 billion as of September 4, providing a significantly better cushion than Pakistan had in recent years. But there is a question we must ask: how long can Pakistan continue relying on its brothers, sisters, cousins' remittances and friendly countries to finance its consumption? Remittances are the generosity and hard-earned income of Pakistan's diaspora. They are a valuable external-sector asset, but they cannot become a permanent substitute for exports, investment and productivity.
Saudi Arabia remains the largest source of remittances, while inflows from the UAE, UK, EU and US are also growing. The stronger performance of the UK and Europe is particularly encouraging because it provides some diversification beyond the traditional Gulf countries. Yet the fundamental weakness remains: Pakistan is earning too few dollars through producing and selling competitively to the world.
The warning is visible in the trade numbers. During the first two months of FY2027, Pakistan's trade deficit widened by 18% to $7.12 billion, from $6.01 billion in the same period of last year. Exports amounted to about $2.96 billion in July but fell to approximately $2.51 billion in August, a monthly decline of around 15%. Although exports during July-August reached $5.46 billion, up 7% year-on-year, the monthly loss of momentum is concerning at a time when imports are rising faster.
The issue is not simply that exporters need another subsidy. Pakistan's production structure itself has become increasingly uncompetitive. High energy prices, taxation, financing costs, logistics charges, port inefficiencies and expensive domestic inputs are squeezing exporters' margins. Our economy has become increasingly consumption-oriented without generating sufficient productive surplus. A country cannot permanently consume more than it produces and expect remittances to fill the gap.
We do not fundamentally have a revenue problem. The Federal Board of Revenue collects significantly more each year. We have a spending problem. The government's expenditure continues to rise, while the tax burden on the existing formal economy becomes heavier. Even an ordinary Pakistani household with electricity and gas connections can face substantial withholding taxes, regardless of whether the individual is actually liable to pay income tax. This broad-based extraction increases the cost of survival and, for companies, the cost of doing business, reducing disposable income without necessarily expanding the productive tax base.
The prolonged US-Iran conflict and disruptions in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz have added another layer of risk. Brent crude has crossed $100 a barrel amid escalating attacks and supply concerns. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea has also fallen dramatically. Recent vessel traffic was reported at only a fraction of pre-war levels, threatening energy and commodity supply chains.
For Pakistan, the greatest danger is not necessarily an immediate balance-of-payments crisis. It is that an external energy shock could derail the fragile economic recovery just as it is beginning. At sustained crude oil prices of $90-100 or above, the arithmetic changes. The import bill rises, inflationary pressures intensify, interest-rate cuts may be delayed or reversed and economic growth could weaken further.
Pakistan's reserves and a relatively stable exchange rate can absorb a temporary shock. They cannot indefinitely absorb a prolonged combination of expensive oil, costly LNG, higher freight, shipping insurance and weak exports. The reported increase in container freight to Gulf destinations – from a few hundred dollars to several thousand dollars for a 20-foot container – is especially damaging for low-margin commodity exporters.
The traditional response would be to demand export rebates, freight subsidies or another DLTL scheme. This would be the wrong response; it would subsidise foreign consumers and inflate domestic prices. Pakistan has little fiscal space for rent-seeking incentives that reward exporters regardless of underlying competitiveness. Cash incentives ultimately subsidise foreign consumers while encouraging domestic price distortions and hoarding.
The answer must instead be to lower the cost of production and logistics for everyone. Federal and provincial governments should undertake an aggressive reduction in non-development expenditures and reconsider the sequencing of lower-priority long-term development projects. The fiscal space created should be redirected towards reducing the cost of energy, taxation and logistics for export-oriented industries.
At the farm level, provinces should directly support growers through targeted inputs assistance for fertiliser, seed, diesel and pesticides rather than allowing high production costs to destroy the competitiveness of agricultural exports. A bumper crop should never become a liability because farmers cannot produce at internationally competitive prices.
Build the infrastructure of competitiveness
Leading exporting countries provide three basic logistics advantages that Pakistan still lacks. First, efficient ports: competitive handling and port charges, and swift customs clearance. Second, modern storage: adequate warehousing, cold chains, silos and temperature-controlled logistics to reduce post-harvest losses and prevent forced selling or hoarding. Third, multimodal transport: efficient railway cargo, waterways where feasible and competitive road freight with rational toll structures.
These are not subsidies. They are investments in national competitiveness. Pakistan also needs predictable taxation, cheaper and reliable energy, lower financing costs, trade facilitation and consistent long-term policies. Exporters should compete because Pakistan is efficient – not because the government writes them a cheque.
The ultimate objective should be to transform remittances from a consumption cushion into a bridge towards investment. The government and financial sector should create credible, transparent instruments through which overseas Pakistanis can invest in export-oriented manufacturing, logistics, agribusiness, technology, housing and infrastructure without bureaucratic uncertainty.
Remittances should continue to flow through formal channels, but Pakistan must gradually convert a portion of diaspora wealth into productive capital that creates jobs and earns future dollars. The real measure of economic success is not how much money Pakistanis abroad send home. It is whether Pakistan can increasingly earn enough itself.
Remittances can protect us from a crisis. Exports, investment and productivity are what can build a prosperous economy. Pakistan must therefore stop celebrating rising remittances as though they were a substitute for economic reform. They are a blessing – but exports are a necessity.
THE WRITER IS A FORMER VICE PRESIDENT OF KCCI, FORMER BOARD MEMBER OF REAP AND AN INTERNATIONAL TRADE EXPERT

title: G B budget and overall economy
description: G B budget and overall economy
content:
Region has limited fiscal space to build infrastructure, productive capacity to expand its economic, revenue base
The Gilgit-Baltistan (G-B) government presented a delayed full-year budget of Rs218.845 billion for fiscal year 2026-27 on Tuesday. The budget carries a deficit of more than Rs52 billion and the government is seeking additional funds from the federal government to meet various liabilities.
In July, the G-B government had presented an interim budget of Rs20.478 billion for the first quarter of FY27 and said the full-year budget would be presented after three months. Senior Minister Mohammad Ali Akhtar, who also holds the finance portfolio, presented the budget in the G-B Assembly.
Akhtar said the elected government had assumed office at the end of June 2026. Since only limited time was available between the end of the previous financial year and the start of the new one, the government had to ensure continuity and timely essential spending. He said the government preferred to take time with the full-year budget so it could reflect the genuine needs, priorities and aspirations of the people.
The total budget is estimated at Rs218.845 billion, with Rs43.97 billion for development and Rs149.87 billion for non-development expenditure. Tax revenues are targeted at Rs16.98 billion, while efforts are underway to secure federal funds to meet the budget deficit of Rs52.65 billion. The size of the Annual Development Plan was increased from Rs22 billion to Rs23 billion, while the amount allocated under the federal Public Sector Development Programme was increased from Rs15 billion to Rs20.973 billion. Wheat subsidy fund, which had been reduced to Rs15 billion, was raised to Rs22 billion. Estimated revenue from wheat sales was Rs3 billion.
G-B has requested a special stabilisation package of around Rs153.30 billion from the federal government for economic and administrative stability. The package covers local government stability, law and order, education, health, tourism, flood compensation, municipal services, food supply, e-governance, agriculture, climate change, institutional capacity building and various liabilities. Akhtar said 1% of development funds would now be diverted to a consolidated climate account and non-development budgets of all departments would be reduced by 30%.
Substantial allocations were made for health, education and agriculture. These included an additional Rs170 million for medicines and a health endowment fund, Rs50 million for water management and Rs50 million for agriculture-sector reforms. Another Rs50 million each was allocated for youth loans, local bodies' elections and renovation of local bodies' offices. About Rs78 million was allocated for the water and power department and Rs18 million for tourism. Development projects in 10 districts received Rs5.034 billion. The numbers, however, raise a broader question: where does a Rs218.845 billion budget fit into Pakistan's wider economic structure? The answer lies less in its headline size than in its composition. Development expenditure of Rs43.97 billion is substantially smaller than non-development spending of Rs149.87 billion. This leaves limited fiscal space for building infrastructure and productive capacity capable of expanding G-B's own economic and revenue base.
The revenue side highlights the structural problem. Against expenditure of more than Rs200 billion, the tax revenue target is only Rs16.98 billion. The resulting gap has to be covered largely through federal assistance. The requested Rs52.65 billion for the budget deficit and the much larger stabilisation package underline the region's dependence on Islamabad. This reflects a broader feature of Pakistan's public finances. Regions with a narrow taxable economic base have limited capacity to finance public services from their own revenues, while the federal government itself faces substantial fiscal pressures.
For G-B, the longer-term challenge is therefore to convert public expenditure into productive economic activity. Tourism, hydropower, agriculture, mining and information technology offer potential avenues for expanding the economic base. But natural advantages alone do not automatically translate into employment or fiscal revenue. Infrastructure, energy, skills, connectivity and institutional capacity are equally important. Tourism is perhaps the most visible opportunity. G-B's mountains, valleys and cultural heritage give it a distinctive advantage, but inadequate infrastructure, seasonality and environmental pressures can limit its contribution. Sustained investment and better planning are needed if tourism is to generate a larger and more stable economic return.
Hydropower presents another opportunity. The region possesses substantial water resources, but converting that potential into economic value requires investment in generation, transmission and supporting infrastructure, along with clear arrangements for financing and revenue sharing. Agriculture and small-scale enterprise can also contribute. Allocations for water management, agricultural reforms and youth loans are modest relative to the overall budget, but their economic impact could be greater if linked to productivity, market access and employment.
The decision to cut non-development budgets by 30% is significant as a fiscal objective. If implemented effectively, savings from administrative expenditure could create additional room for development. But expenditure reduction needs to be accompanied by better management so that essential services are not weakened. The climate allocation is also relevant. G-B's geography leaves its infrastructure and communities exposed to climate-related risks. Setting aside 1% of development funds for climate-related purposes could provide a more systematic source of financing for adaptation, provided the funds are directed towards clearly defined projects.
The wheat subsidy presents another policy challenge. Raising the allocation to Rs22 billion provides support to consumers, but subsidies also carry an opportunity cost. The longer-term issue is whether such support can be made more targeted and efficient while protecting the vulnerable households. For Islamabad, the G-B budget represents both a fiscal obligation and an economic opportunity. Federal transfers are necessary to maintain public services and development in a geographically remote region with a limited revenue base. But recurring assistance without a corresponding expansion of economic activity can leave the region dependent on the federal exchequer.

title: Cheaper student loans led economic growth
description: Cheaper student loans led economic growth
content:
PM Apni Taleem programme with eligibility for educational finance from Rs50,000 to Rs5 million proposed
If Pakistan can subsidise a house with successful PM Apna Ghar scheme, an exporter's working capital and potentially an electric vehicle, can it not finance a child's (read Pakistan's) future?
The government has raised subsidised housing finance to Rs10 million at 5% customer pricing, with Islamic financing options. Export refinance reportedly costs 4.5%. Proposals also envisage a Rs10 million EV financing ceiling to support cleaner transport and fuel savings. The EV proposal awaits final rules; export working capital and expansion finance are distinct facilities. These priorities deserve support. But where is education? Consider a parent earning Rs30,000-100,000 monthly, supporting three or four children. Food, rent, electricity, gas, fuel, healthcare, school fees and phone bills consume the salary. What remains for a housing deposit or an EV down payment? A subsidised export facility means little to someone struggling to keep the kitchen running.
Imagine this parent paying for an affordable private school until a child reaches 12, 15 or 18. Then comes the calculation nobody should have to make: another year studying, or another income from a shop, workshop or construction site? Plumbing, electrical work and mechanics are valuable options for father but better to have engineers, doctors, lawyers, financial analysts, accountants and AI developers. Low earnings force interrupted schooling; interrupted schooling restricts future earnings. Poverty renews its own contract. Pakistan's 2023 census recorded literacy among people aged 10 and above at approximately 60.7%: 68% for males and 52.8% for females. Unicef estimates 25.1 million children aged 5-16 are outside school – 35% of that age group. These are tomorrow's workers, taxpayers and parents.
Attendance alone is insufficient. A World Bank evaluation, using Unesco data available in September 2023, reported minimum primary mathematics proficiency of 8% in Pakistan against 91% in Vietnam, although underlying assessments differ. South Korea, once poor and now advanced, ranks among the strongest PISA performers. Our challenge is both access and learning. Pakistan already has an NBP-administered interest-free student-loan scheme. What it lacks is universal, dependable access comparable to mainstream asset finance. England's outstanding student loans reached £295 billion in March 2026 – roughly 10% of the UK GDP. Nor should we mistake growing student debt for proof of faster GDP growth: useful learning and productive employment must justify borrowing. Student debt is highly correlated to stronger GDP growth for middle and developed countries.
A PM Apni Taleem programme with nationwide eligibility for educational finance from Rs50,000 to Rs5 million, covering accredited schools, colleges, universities and vocational institutions, is needed. Guarantee a 5% annual borrower rate on a reducing balance for 30 years. Offer independently approved Shariah-compliant alternatives. Universal eligibility should coexist with larger grants for poorer families. For schoolchildren, grants and attendance stipends must lead; loans cannot replace free compulsory education or compensate fully for lost household earnings.
There are practical models. India's PM-Vidyalaxmi offers eligible families three percentage points of interest subsidy, while qualifying poorer technical students receive full moratorium-period interest support through its companion scheme. PNB provides repayment over 15 years after the course-plus-one-year moratorium. Britain generally collects undergraduate repayments at 9% of earnings above a threshold. Pakistan should borrow income protection, while avoiding excessive balances and poor-value degrees. Split budgeted subsidies and guarantee costs equally between federal and participating provincial governments, with development agencies and philanthropy contributing. Banks could receive Kibor plus 2%, government paying the difference and guaranteeing 50% of verified net credit losses. Banks must retain meaningful risk. At an illustrative 11% Kibor, the subsidy gap is eight percentage points: Rs8 billion annually per Rs100 billion outstanding, before defaults and administration.
Disburse fees directly to accredited institutions with FBR registration, audited accounts, digital receipts and published learning and employment outcomes with globally verifiable educational standards. Mandate all private schools to offer student loan to minimum 25% pupils to receive tax breaks. This would improve transparency and collection of legally due taxes without treating every private educator as an evader. Build one application portal with assisted access through banks, microfinance institutions, telcos and fintechs. Use consent-based FBR, EOBI and provincial social-security records, including SESSI, to identify earnings when students enter job pool. Job-portal registration should trigger support, not repayment. Collections should begin above a protected income threshold through payroll or authorised weekly or monthly debits, with hardship pauses and eventual write-off.
Mobilise pension and impact capital through 30-year education funding instruments. Annual diaspora "Pakistan Education Bonds" could supplement rupee funding, with foreign-exchange exposure explicitly budgeted. The prime minister should commission a 90-day design, co-led by federal and provincial ministries of finance, education, educational chains, SBP, banks, microfinance institutions, fintech, edtech, employers, philanthropists, donors and established players such as Akhuwat, etc. Done well, this could expand skilled employment, women's participation, wages, entrepreneurship and service exports; strengthen public-service delivery; and reduce vulnerability to crime and dependence on assistance. These gains require jobs and quality, not loans alone. A fuel concession wins attention today. Keeping a child learning can earn a family's trust for decades. In 2047, Pakistan turns 100. We have 21 years. What better centenary investment than an educated Pakistani.
The writer is an independent economic analyst

title: Talk climate in rupees  not rainfall
description: Talk climate in rupees  not rainfall
content:
Pakistan knows its floods risk but yet to build financial tools to price it
Every monsoon season, Pakistan produces the same headlines: submerged villages, displaced families, ruined crops. The story is always told as tragedy. It is rarely told that it is a balance sheet problem, hiding in plain sight that Pakistan's economic system has simply chosen not to price. That omission is starting to look less like an oversight and more like a structural flaw in how the economy runs.
Let us start with what has already been measured. The floods in 2022 caused an estimated $14.9 billion in damages and $15.2 billion in broader economic losses – roughly 4.8% of GDP wiped out in a single season. Housing absorbed the largest hit, at $5.6 billion, with agriculture, livestock and fisheries close behind at $3.7 billion. GDP growth for that fiscal year was cut nearly half from initial projections and independent estimates suggest 9 to 12 million people were pushed into poverty almost overnight.
None of this was a one-off. A UN report modelling worst-case climate scenarios estimated Pakistan could face average annual losses equal to more than 9% of GDP going forward. And the pattern has already repeated. Flooding in subsequent monsoon seasons has again battered the country's agricultural core, pushing up food prices and straining supply chains once more.
This is not a series of disasters. It is a recurring, semi-predictable cost that shows up in accounts every few years, the way a bad loan eventually shows up on a bank's books. The only difference is that nobody is required to reserve against it. In any functioning risk market, a cost this large, this recurring, and this geographically concentrated would be priced through insurance premiums, lending terms, land valuations or crop financing. In Pakistan, it mostly is not.
Consider agriculture, which accounts for roughly a quarter of GDP and employs half the labour force, yet operates with almost no meaningful crop insurance penetration. Farmers in flood-prone districts of Sindh, which absorbed nearly 70% of total damages and losses in 2022, plant and hope, year after year, with no financial instrument to smooth the blow when the water comes. When it does come, the loss is not absorbed by a diversified pool of capital; it's absorbed by whichever household happened to be standing in its path.
The same is true of housing and small enterprise. Banks lend against flood-exposed property with financing terms that look identical to those for property nowhere near a floodplain. Insurers, where they exist at all for ordinary households, treat monsoon as background weather rather than a modelled risk variable. The result is that climate risk is real, recurring and enormous, and almost entirely unpriced, unpooled and unhedged.
As the risk is not priced in advance, it gets paid for after the fact and disproportionately by people with the least capacity to absorb it. More than 70% of Pakistan's labour force works in the informal sector, largely outside any formal social protection net. When floods hit, these households don't file insurance claims; they sell livestock, pull children from school, or take on informal debt at punishing rates. The floods of yesteryears alone are estimated to have cost roughly 2 million jobs.
This is the quiet subsidy structure of Pakistan's climate exposure; the state and international donors step in after each disaster with relief and reconstruction financing. The reconstruction needs from 2022 alone were estimated above $16 billion, while the underlying risk that caused the damage remains unpriced and therefore uncorrected. Every flood season, the country effectively refinances the same exposure rather than reducing it.
This does not require a political argument about who caused climate change or who should pay reparations for it, the debate that usually swallows this topic. It requires something narrower and more technical, ie, building the market infrastructure to price a known, recurring risk.
That means parametric insurance products for smallholder farmers, where payouts are triggered automatically by rainfall or flood-level data rather than slow claims assessments. Such models are already piloted in Bangladesh and parts of East Africa. It includes differentiated lending terms for property and agriculture in high-exposure zones, so capital naturally migrates away from the riskiest ground over time instead of being incentivised to double down on it.
It means the State Bank and the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan building the regulatory scaffolding for a domestic catastrophe-risk insurance market, rather than leaving climate financing entirely to post-disaster international assistance. None of this, however, eliminates the floods. But it changes who absorbs the cost, and when. Right now, the cost lands entirely on the household, entirely post facto, with no mechanism to spread it across time or across a risk pool. Pricing the risk in advance, however imperfectly, converts a repeated, uninsured shock into a manageable, budgeted cost. That is a more resilient economy, even if the weather doesn't change at all.
Pakistan is not short on climate data. Meteorological modelling, flood-mapping and rainfall attribution studies exist in reasonable depth. What is missing is the translation of that data into financial instruments that ordinary households and small businesses can actually use.
Every year this gap persists, the bill compounds. Reconstruction becomes more expensive than prevention would have been. Displaced agricultural labour shows up later as urban unemployment. Informal debt taken on after one flood makes households more vulnerable to the next.
The climate conversation in Pakistan tends to default to blame on who emitted what, who owes whom. That conversation matters, but it has also become a way of deferring the more immediate question: why hasn't Pakistan's own financial system built the tools to price in a risk it already knows?
THE WRITER IS AN INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIST

title: Ed Sheeran speaks out after Macklemore   s removal from his US tour
description: Ed Sheeran says he felt abandoned by friends and family during the backlash over Macklemore   s tour removal
content:
Ed Sheeran says he felt abandoned by friends and family during the backlash over Macklemore’s tour removal
Ed Sheeran became emotional during his Philadelphia concert as he addressed the controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from his Loop Tour and said he felt abandoned by people close to him.
During his September 19 performance at Lincoln Financial Field, Sheeran told the audience that friends, family members and people he had known for years had distanced themselves amid the fallout. He also thanked the 50,000 fans who attended the show despite calls for him to cancel the concert.
The controversy began after Macklemore made pro-Palestinian remarks during a September 4 performance at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Macklemore was subsequently removed from the remaining US dates of Sheeran’s Loop Tour. Sheeran said the decision was made by the tour promoter after stadium owners indicated they would not host shows with Macklemore on the lineup.
The fallout led several supporting acts, including Finneas, Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe, as well as Sheeran’s backing band, to leave the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.
Sheeran also took additional security precautions during the Philadelphia concert, removing a stage that would have placed him closer to the centre of the crowd because he was concerned about possible objects being thrown at him.
Macklemore has since said he will donate $1 million from his tour earnings to Palestinian relief efforts. Robert Kraft later announced a $2 million donation after Sheeran asked him to contribute.
Sheeran is scheduled to perform at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts on September 25 and 26, venues connected to the controversy over Macklemore’s removal.

title: 'The Savant' finally gets a release window after Apple TV delay | The Express Tribune
description: Apple TV confirms Jessica Chastain thriller 'The Savant' will finally premiere in spring 2027 after a lengthy delay
content:
Apple TV confirms Jessica Chastain thriller 'The Savant' will finally premiere in spring 2027 after a lengthy delay
Apple TV has announced a new release window for The Savant , the Jessica Chastain-led thriller that was postponed shortly before its planned 2025 premiere.
The series is now scheduled to debut in spring 2027, marking roughly a year and a half since Apple TV removed it from its release calendar. The platform initially postponed The Savant in September 2025 without providing a specific reason, saying it had decided to delay the series and would release it at a later date.
Chastain, who stars in and executive produces the series, subsequently said she disagreed with the decision. In a statement shared on Instagram, she noted that the show deals with violence in the United States and follows people working to prevent potential attacks.
The Savant centres on Jodi Goodwin, played by Chastain, a veteran, wife and mother who works undercover in online communities where white supremacists gather and, in some cases, discuss domestic terrorist attacks.
Creator Melissa James Gibson developed the series from journalist Andrea Stanley’s 2019 Cosmopolitan article, “Is It Possible to Stop a Mass Shooting Before It Happens?”
The show’s release has remained uncertain since its postponement. Although The Savant continued to appear on Apple TV’s press website, the streamer repeatedly delayed announcing a premiere date.
Chastain said earlier this year that the series would eventually reach audiences, while reports subsequently suggested several possible release windows that passed without a premiere.
The latest scheduling places The Savant after the November 2026 US midterm elections. Apple TV has not yet announced an exact premiere date.
The series is among several upcoming Apple TV productions led by prominent female actors and will now return to the platform’s release calendar for spring 2027.

title: New Found Glory founding member Chad Gilbert dead at 45 | The Express Tribune
description: New Found Glory guitarist Chad Gilbert dies at 45 as band confirms he passed away peacefully on September 20 at home
content:
New Found Glory guitarist Chad Gilbert dies at 45 as band confirms he passed away peacefully on September 20 at home
Chad Gilbert, guitarist and founding member of pop-punk band New Found Glory, has died at the age of 45.
The band announced Gilbert’s death on Instagram on Sunday, September 20, saying they were “devastated and shocked” by his passing. According to the statement, Gilbert died peacefully in his sleep surrounded by family and friends, with his wife and mother by his side.
“On the morning of September 20th, Chad Everett Gilbert passed away peacefully in his sleep,” the band said.
Gilbert had faced several serious health challenges in recent years. In March, he underwent brain surgery to remove three tumours. He had also previously received treatment for metastatic pheochromocytoma, a rare form of adrenal gland cancer that had spread to his spine and lungs.
Following the announcement, New Found Glory paid tribute to Gilbert and highlighted his contributions to the band. The group credited his guitar playing, songwriting, humour and determination with helping shape its music and career over more than three decades.
Gilbert co-founded New Found Glory in 1997, alongside Jordan Pundik, Ian Grushka and Steve Klein. The band became a prominent name in the pop-punk scene and went on to release 14 studio albums.
One of the group’s best-known songs is “My Friends Over You”, which became a defining track of their career and remains closely associated with the band.
Gilbert was also known for his work beyond New Found Glory, including performances and songwriting projects throughout his career.
The band did not provide further details about his death beyond confirming that he passed away peacefully. Gilbert was 45.

title: Sparks fly inside NICH nursery packed with newborns
description: Audit finds the hospital   s fire alarm system non functional  while most smoke detectors are either faulty or inactive
content:
Audit finds the hospital’s fire alarm system non-functional, while most smoke detectors are either faulty or inactive
Sparks from a welding torch flew inside a nursery packed with newborns, some of them dependent on oxygen, at the National Institute of Child Health (NICH), raising fresh and serious questions about fire safety at the city hospital.
Video footage obtained by The Express Tribune showed a man carrying out welding work inside the nursery while newborn babies lay on beds just metres away — a scene unfolding in one of the hospital’s most vulnerable wards.
Sources said between 80 and 120 children were being treated in the nursery when the welding and repair work took place, most of them newborns receiving oxygen. The work was reportedly aimed at creating an emergency exit in the emergency nursery and installing an iron grille to provide a new access route to the semi-critical unit.
However, the decision to carry out welding work inside an occupied nursery raises questions about whether adequate safety arrangements were made to protect the newborns and medical staff. It was also unclear whether the infants were moved to a safe location or whether a separate area was designated for the welding work.
Experts said welding near oxygen cylinders and newborns receiving oxygen was highly hazardous. Sparks generated during welding could ignite flammable material in an oxygen-rich environment, potentially causing a fire within seconds.
They said repair work in such a sensitive area should be carried out only after making alternative arrangements to ensure the safety of patients and staff.
The incident comes against the backdrop of previously identified fire-safety deficiencies at NICH. A fire-safety audit had declared the hospital’s fourth, fifth and sixth floors extremely hazardous and highlighted several shortcomings in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).
Read : Fire safety gaps expose children hospitals to tragedy
According to the audit report, electrical and oxygen points in the NICU were installed in proximity. The report also identified leakage in the oxygen line and pipe joints that had reportedly been sealed with tape. Exposed and unsafe electrical wiring was also identified as a fire risk.
The audit found the hospital’s fire alarm system non-functional, while most smoke detectors were either faulty or inactive. It also noted an inadequate number of fire extinguishers, insufficient fire-emergency training for staff and the absence of regular fire drills.
Emergency exits were reportedly found blocked by equipment and waste, while the power room was easily accessible to the public. The report also pointed out that the power room lacked smoke detectors and adequate firefighting arrangements.
The NICU’s mechanical ventilation system was also found to be non-functional, while exposed and temporary wiring connected to old air-conditioning units was declared a fire-safety hazard.
NICH has witnessed fire incidents in the past. A fire broke out in the hospital’s ICU on June 30, while in January 2020, a newborn died after an incubator caught fire.
Read More : Infant deaths expose deadly gaps in hospital fire safety
The fire-safety audit had recommended immediate corrective measures, including securing the electrical, oxygen and ventilation systems, activating fire alarms and smoke-detection systems, clearing emergency exits and conducting regular fire drills.
It had also called for comprehensive fire-safety arrangements throughout the hospital.
The footage showing welding being carried out in an occupied nursery has now raised fresh questions over compliance with basic fire-safety protocols during repair work in one of the hospital’s most sensitive areas.
Meanwhile, attempts were made to obtain the NICH administration’s version of the incident. NICH Director Professor Nasir Saleem was contacted several times, but he did not respond.

title: Pakistan wants an AI future  but is it ready for one
description: Pakistan wants an AI future  but is it ready for one
content:
There is a meaningful difference between adopting AI and being ready for it
Walk into a university library in Lahore or a corporate office in Karachi and you will see the same quiet routine. A student polishes an assignment with a chatbot. An executive drafts a report in minutes rather than hours. A small trader writes marketing captions in Urdu and English using an AI app. On family WhatsApp groups, a strangely convincing video or cloned voice note does the rounds before anyone works out whether it is real. Artificial intelligence has already made itself at home in the Pakistani life. The harder question is whether the country is genuinely ready for what comes next.
There is a meaningful difference between adopting AI and being ready for it. Millions of Pakistanis now open a chatbot the way earlier generations opened a search engine. Interest is easy to demonstrate; readiness is harder, since it depends on implementation capacity, functioning governance and accountable institutions. The federal cabinet's approval of the National AI Policy 2025 in July 2025 was a genuinely useful step, setting out funding for innovation and targets for training AI professionals. But a policy document, however well written, is not the same as a prepared country. Policies succeed or fail in their implementation.
Readiness begins with ordinary people, not only programmers. Students, teachers, civil servants, journalists, managers, healthcare workers and parents need a working sense of what AI can help with, and where it goes wrong. That means knowing a confident-sounding answer can still be inaccurate, that outputs need checking rather than blind trust, that confidential client or patient information should never go into a public AI tool and that a convincing voice note is not proof a conversation happened. The most serious AI divide in Pakistan may not be between those with access to these tools and those without, but between those who question AI and those who trust it blindly.
This runs through education and work alike. Students already use generative AI for essays and exams, whether institutions permit it or not, and blanket bans have proved unworkable elsewhere. Schools and universities can realistically set clear guidelines, redesign assessments so thinking rather than typing gets graded and train teachers to work with AI rather than only police it. The same applies at work: Pakistan needs not only AI developers but accountants, managers and shopkeepers who know when to trust these tools and when not to. The question is no longer whether students and employees will use AI, but whether institutions will teach them to use it responsibly.
None of this matters if the basic foundations are missing. Meaningful AI adoption needs reliable electricity, affordable internet and cybersecurity capacity that keeps pace with new risks. Pakistan has made real gains: government data released this year shows individual internet use climbing from 17 per cent in 2019 to 57 per cent in 2025. Yet urban-rural and income gaps remain wide, and national literacy, recently reported at 63 per cent with a sharp urban-rural split, shapes who can use these tools at all. AI that works well in English but struggles with Urdu, Sindhi, Pashto or Punjabi will leave many behind, and unless inclusion is deliberate, AI risks widening the gaps it should close.
The risks deserve honest treatment, without treating AI as inherently dangerous. Deepfakes and cloned voices are already used for impersonation and financial fraud and misinformation spreads faster when it looks authentic. Data privacy, cybersecurity and quietly biased automated decisions carry real consequences, particularly when nobody is accountable for the harm an AI-assisted decision causes. Sensible regulation does not treat every use of AI alike. Grammar correction carries little risk; AI in recruitment, healthcare, lending, law enforcement or identity verification deserves stronger safeguards and human review, a risk-based approach that protects people without smothering innovation.
Government has a practical role here, and it need not be complicated. A public AI-literacy campaign in English, Urdu and regional languages would reach citizens faster than any policy document. Age-appropriate AI education in schools, and proper training for teachers, civil servants and regulators, would build the human capacity the National AI Policy already promises on paper. Clear standards for high-risk uses, mandatory human oversight for consequential decisions and simple channels for reporting deepfakes or AI fraud would turn ambition into trust. In workforce technology, I have often seen organisations acquire new tools faster than they prepare people to use them, and in teaching, I have watched students experiment with generative AI while institutional guidance lags behind. Pakistan's AI story risks the same pattern unless people, not just policy, receive equal attention.
None of this need be a reason for pessimism. Pakistan does not have to choose between innovation and safety. Sensible safeguards build the public trust that wider AI adoption depends on, and a young, entrepreneurial population gives the country a genuine headstart if it invests in people alongside platforms. The country should act now, before AI-related harm becomes widespread, but fear should never smother invention. Pakistan's AI readiness will not be measured by how quickly it adopts new tools, but by how wisely, safely and inclusively it uses them.

title: Is India building its own SOSUS
description: Is India building its own SOSUS
content:
The ability to operate undetected has traditionally been a submarine's greatest defence
The ability to operate undetected has traditionally been a submarine's greatest defence. For nuclear-armed states, concealment is particularly important: an undetected submarine can preserve the ability to retaliate even after other nuclear forces may have been destroyed. India's underwater surveillance project raises the prospect that parts of the Indian Ocean could become progressively less opaque.
India's Defence Research and Development Organization (DRDO) has initiated development of an Underwater Fibre Optic Sensing System (UFOSS). Led by its Naval Physical and Oceanographic Laboratory, the proposed system would place sensor nodes on the seabed, connect them through undersea fibre-optic cables and transmit data to a shore station for monitoring and analysis. India in the short to medium term may not achieve a geographical reach or technological maturity of United States Cold War Sound Surveillance System, better known as SOSUS. But UFOSS follows a similar operational logic: persistent seabed sensing can narrow the enormous search area supporting anti-submarine forces.
That distinction matters. SOSUS did not make the oceans transparent. Its strategic value lay in detecting acoustic contacts, accumulating information on Soviet submarine signatures and cueing aircraft, warships and attack submarines towards smaller search areas. It became progressively more useful as fixed sensors were integrated with mobile anti-submarine warfare assets. Cold War operations reveal how consequential such tracking could become. For instance, in 1969, the US attack submarine USS Lapon covertly followed a Soviet Yankee-class ballistic-missile submarine throughout a 47-day deterrent patrol. Similarly, in 1978, USS Batfish tracked another Soviet Yankee-class submarine for approximately 50 days and for nearly 9,000 nautical miles. The Soviet Union reportedly remained unaware of the latter operation until it was declassified years later. These missions allowed the US to study Soviet operating patterns and acoustic characteristics without revealing that the submarines had been compromised.
India increasingly possesses the components needed to develop a comparable, although geographically smaller, architecture. Alongside UFOSS, the Indian Navy operates P-8I maritime patrol aircraft, MH-60R helicopters, submarines and ASW-capable surface vessels. The result could eventually be a network where a fixed sensor provides an initial detection and mobile forces perform the much harder tasks of localisation, classification and potential tracking. According to Indian media reports, persistent monitoring and the cueing of anti-submarine warfare assets are among UFOSS's central functions.
India does not need to monitor the entire Indian Ocean. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands overlook approaches connecting the Pacific and Indian Oceans. Chinese submarines entering the Indian Ocean would have to navigate a limited number of passages through Southeast Asia. Selectively positioned sensors could therefore function as barriers around strategically valuable approaches rather than attempting continuous surveillance across millions of square kilometres.
The Interpreter noted in 2017 that growing Chinese submarine presence had encouraged Indian interest in a line of undersea sensors in the eastern Indian Ocean. Chinese submarines were already using deployments to acquire experience with the Indian Ocean's distinctive hydrology, bathymetry and thermoclines. UFOSS potentially gives this older strategic requirement a more concrete indigenous technological foundation.
The longer-term advantage would be cumulative. A sensor contact that cannot be continuously tracked can still reveal when a submarine entered an area, its probable direction and elements of its acoustic behaviour. Repeated observations could contribute to signature libraries and patterns of deployment. Integrated with satellite surveillance, maritime patrol aircraft and increasingly sophisticated data analysis, individual detections may result in a much larger intelligence picture. Public reporting on UFOSS specifically identifies both Chinese submarines and Pakistan's Hangor programme among the developments driving India's requirement.
Persistent surveillance could therefore acquire nuclear significance. A submarine suspected of carrying nuclear weapons may interpret Indian ASW activity very differently from a conventionally armed vessel. During a crisis, attempts to locate such submarines could be viewed not simply as maritime surveillance but as an effort to hold a retaliatory capability at risk.
However there is another consequence that deserves greater attention. An Indian underwater surveillance system would not hear only Chinese and Pakistani submarines. The Indian Ocean is visited by several nuclear navies. In October 2022, for example, the US took the unusual step of publicly revealing that the Ohio-class ballistic-missile submarine USS West Virginia had visited Diego Garcia during an extended deterrence patrol. The deployment placed one of US most sensitive strategic assets in the same wider oceanic space in which India seeks greater undersea awareness.
This creates a paradox for India's Indo-Pacific partners. The US, Australia and Japan may have strong reasons to welcome greater Indian capacity to monitor Chinese naval activity. Indian and partner surveillance capabilities can contribute to a more favourable maritime balance as the PLA Navy becomes increasingly active in the Indian Ocean.
But acoustic sensors are politically indifferent. A network capable of collecting information on Chinese submarine movements could also encounter American, British and eventually Australian nuclear-powered submarines operating in the wider region. For Australia, for instance, this question will become increasingly relevant as it moves towards operating nuclear-powered submarines under AUKUS. Undersea cooperation with India could offer considerable strategic value, but greater Indian acoustic awareness also raises questions about data ownership, information sharing and protection of sensitive submarine signatures. This also demonstrates why undersea information is unusually sensitive. Repeated detections can reveal more than the presence of a submarine; over time, they can contribute to understanding operating patterns and acoustic characteristics.
Nor will India's competitors remain passive. China can respond through quieter submarines, alternative transit patterns, deception, unmanned underwater systems and efforts to map or circumvent fixed sensors. Pakistan's AIP-equipped submarines are designed for prolonged stealth operations. UFOSS would therefore initiate another round in the longstanding competition between detection and concealment rather than end it.
SOSUS became strategically important not because it could see everything, but because persistent sensing progressively reduced uncertainty and allowed US forces to exploit data collected on Soviet submarines. UFOSS suggests India may be moving towards the same logic.

title: Where s the wit  Why English Op Eds are so serious
description: Where s the wit  Why English Op Eds are so serious
content:
The absence of humour writing in English newspapers has been an intriguing question for me
The absence of humour writing in English newspapers has been an intriguing question for me. In Urdu newspapers these d X ays, Ata-ul-Haq Qasmi and Gul-e-Nokheiz Akhtar constitute an irresistible attraction for readers – and that too when print media is past its heydays.
The absence is more a matter of linguistics than anything else. The elitist approach of the users of English lends an air of seriousness to their creative outpourings. Laughter is attached, in our context, with Punjabi. We often see celebrities and intellectuals code-switching between English and Urdu on one side and Punjabi on the other whenever they want to add pizzazz to their discourse. There is a folk maxim that corroborates this linguistic racialism: Jokes and indecencies can achieve their impact when they are worded in Punjabi. Such an approach by contrast attributes all seriousness to English, being considered the mark of one's being civilised and cultured. This ideation dates back to our colonial past.
Our English columnists write as an authority or expert, taking readers as an audience or laypersons. Such a relationship between a writer and his readers eschews all intimacy -- a prerequisite for the humour to be communicated. The social status attached to English and its speakers burden them with heavy social freight, which suffocates humour. To keep up appearances of suited and booted high gentry all the time in public demeanour straitjackets one's mind, which then forgets to take long and high flights -- the threshold where mind becomes imagination.
The virtuosos of the art of writing assert that writing humour is much more a difficult skill than writing serious, both emotionally and technically. Humour writing requires a touch of exaggeration. As English op-ed writers have to be down to earth, they feel stymied in developing a knack for exaggeration in themselves. Similarly, the students of English struggling with its grammar all the time confine themselves to regurgitating what is in the cellar of their mind as they don't grope for novelty in their mental attic. To read, write and understand humour, one has to be well versed with the figurative meanings of words and sentences.
The English columnists argue that they have to cater to the interests of a specific readership: the urban upper and middle classes, the bureaucracy, and students of competitive exams. It leaves no room for using humour as a medium. Here, Urdu newspapers score a point over English newspapers by highlighting serious issues in a lighter vein.
The elitist background of English columnists deprives them of sharing any cultural commonalities as they suffer from penury of local culture. They are incapacitated for playing on puns, innuendos or witticisms, whose major staple is local culture. Their elitism permeates even deeper into the selection of subjects of their columns. A sense of superiority forces them to assert their worldliness, their sophistication or their connection to global discourse. They find it inferior to come down to treating various facets of a common man's daily life. Traffic problems, weddings imbued in local culture or children's schooling issues might sound local to them. Factually, 'no topic is off-limits for comedy'.
An English columnist can write tediously on inflation while an Urdu columnist will talk about the rising prices of tomatoes or potatoes. The latter will amuse the readers while highlighting the issue. The former writes abstract while the latter writes concrete. The concrete writing creates a bonhomie, while the abstract one, otherness. A serious columnist tells us what is wrong, while a humour columnist, without turning us cynical, shows how ridiculous wrongness has become.
On the remedial front, the English newspapers might start with the English translation of Urdu columns of humourists like Ata-ul-Haq Qasmi, Athar Shah Khan (Jaidi) and Qamar Ali Abbasi, who are our common national asset. In the letter to the editor section, humour writing can be invited to find the untapped talent. The cartoonists can also be employed to write op-eds, as they already have the flair to say light what's heavy. We will have to discover our own PG Woodhouse.

title: Closing the gender gap
description: Closing the gender gap
content:
Female literacy stands at 47% against 68% for men
Sindh's first Gender Parity Report is useful precisely because it makes the province's gender divide difficult to obscure. Female literacy stands at 47% against 68% for men, falling to just 27% among rural women. More than 4.08 million girls between five and 16 are out of school. Women constitute only 4.34% of the police force, 18.3% of prosecutors and 13.7% of judges. The report also records 3,085 cases of gender-based violence in 2024.
There has been progress, particularly in maternal health and political participation. Maternal mortality has fallen from 314 to 224 deaths per 100,000 live births, while the number of women contesting general elections increased from 23 in 2018 to 53 in 2024. These improvements deserve recognition. But they also demonstrate why the government must resist the temptation to regard isolated gains as evidence that the broader problem is being solved. A girl who never enters school is less likely to acquire skills, enter formal employment, control an income or participate in public life. The World Bank has similarly identified rural girls as particularly vulnerable to dropping out and argues that improving their enrolment and retention requires interventions addressing several barriers at once. This is why simply announcing more schemes will not be enough. The government needs to make the gender report an accountability instrument. Every department should be given measurable targets. Education should receive the immediate focus. The millions of girls outside school cannot be reached through conventional enrolment drives alone.
The government must also stop treating women's economic participation simply as a matter of employment numbers. Access to skills and essential services determines whether women can enter better-paid and more secure work. Sindh already knows where the gaps are. What is required now is the political and administrative discipline.

title: Fight against polio
description: Fight against polio
content:
The K-P government's anti-polio campaign, involving 35,000 personnel, needs strong support
The K-P government's anti-polio campaign, involving 35,000 personnel, needs strong support. The week-long drive, set to begin today, aims to reach 7.3 million children to administer polio drops. The focus, however, remains on merged districts and areas deeply impacted by lawlessness. Paramedics and volunteers must be respected and supported in their work, as their goal is to free society and newborns from the permanent disability caused by the virus. Peers, religious scholars - especially those in mosques - and teachers have a vital role to play by extending their support to immunisation campaigns and not being swayed by illogical assumptions.
Pakistan has been deeply engaged in the fight against poliovirus since the 1970s. The Pakistan Polio Eradication Programme, launched in 1994 with the WHO on board, boasts a sizeable team of 339,521 trained and dedicated frontline workers, making it the largest network of its kind in the world. This new drive comes on the heels of three special campaigns conducted over the past three months in Upper South Waziristan, Lower South Waziristan, North Waziristan and Bannu. It is highly commendable that the provincial government, despite its limited resources, has successfully recruited and deployed 2,400 doctors across 72 remote hospitals to provide free medical coverage, which includes routine immunisation.
Yet, it remains a matter of grave concern that despite these utmost efforts and extensive international assistance, Pakistan is one of only two countries, alongside Afghanistan, where the virus remains endemic. In 2026, four polio cases have been reported so far, primarily from the vulnerable districts of K-P. It is deeply worrisome that a section of society still views the vaccine as a conspiracy against their children, remaining trapped in unfounded misconceptions and keeping their wards away from compulsory vaccination. This alarming situation necessitates a complete policy overhaul to ensure healthcare workers can safely reach every child and that immunisation campaigns are free from societal resistance.

title: Asiad opens
description: Asiad opens
content:
Pakistan has entered 23 disciplines as athletes from 45 countries and regions gather for competition across 43 sports
For Pakistan, the 20th Asian Games have begun with expectations that are considerably more modest than the size of the contingent might suggest. As athletes from 45 countries and regions gather in Nagoya, Japan, for competition across 43 sports, Pakistan has entered 23 disciplines. Yet after years of declining results, we must ask where the country can realistically challenge for medals.
All eyes, inevitably, will be on Arshad Nadeem. The Olympic champion remains Pakistan's biggest individual sporting name, and the javelin remains the clearest opportunity for a gold medal. But expectations must be tempered by his recent form. Arshad finished fifth at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship last week with 81.49 metres, while Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage won with a remarkable 91.09m. The two are expected to renew their contest in Nagoya, with the javelin final scheduled for September 28. Squash may offer another meaningful opportunity. Noor Zaman, one of Pakistan's flag-bearers, enters the men's singles as the third seed and has already won the Under-23 World Championship. He and Ashab Irfan represent a younger generation trying to restore a sporting glory. Hockey remains another traditional medal prospect, although Pakistan's 11th-place finish at the recent World Cup is disappointing. The team has nevertheless targeted a place in the Asian Games final. Cricket has already delivered one disappointment. Pakistan's women defeated Thailand in the quarter-final but were eliminated by Sri Lanka in Sunday's semi-final. The green caps will now play the bronze-medal match on September 22.
At Hangzhou in 2023, Pakistan won only three medals, compared with four in 2018 and a far richer haul in earlier editions. Funding, preparation, coaching, facilities and international exposure remain recurring weaknesses. Even for these Games, reports have highlighted concerns over delayed preparations and questions about financial support for athletes. That is perhaps the most useful way to view these Games.

title: The Pak Afghan deadlock
description: The Pak Afghan deadlock
content:
Fresh diplomatic effort to ease tensions between Islamabad and Kabul facing an immediate test after Kohat attack
A fresh diplomatic effort by Turkey and Qatar to ease tensions between Islamabad and Kabul is facing an immediate test after the deadly terrorist attack on a police mosque in Kohat, with Pakistani authorities linking one of the suicide bombers to Afghanistan. Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin travelled to Kabul last week, where he held talks with senior Taliban officials. A senior Qatari security official also visited the Afghan capital. Kalin subsequently travelled to Islamabad, where he met Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Field Marshal Asim Munir and ISI chief Lt Gen Asim Malik.
Turkey and Qatar have previously played a role in facilitating contacts between Islamabad and Kabul, while China has also brought the two sides together through the Urumqi process. But Pakistan's position has remained unchanged: it is willing to talk, but wants Kabul to take verifiable action against the banned TTP, which Islamabad accuses of using Afghan territory to launch attacks inside Pakistan. The Taliban regime denies the allegations.
For Islamabad, however, assurances are no longer sufficient. The latest Kohat terrorist attack has further complicated the diplomatic effort. Pakistani authorities say one of the suicide bombers has been identified as an Afghan national, providing fresh ammunition to Islamabad's longstanding argument that terrorist networks continue to find space across the border. Pakistan has also reported repeated attempts by terrorists to cross the border and carry out attacks.
The concerns highlighted by Islamabad are also reflected in international assessments of the security situation in Afghanistan. A recent South Asia Times study, "Taliban 2.0: The Five-Year Ledger", estimates that more than 20 terrorist organisations are operating in Afghanistan alongside thousands of foreign fighters. It also highlights the continuing presence of the TTP and the scale of attacks attributed to the group inside Pakistan. Its broader assessment raises questions about how much the security environment in Afghanistan has changed since the Taliban returned to power in 2021. The study also revisits the prisoner releases associated with the Doha peace process. Research published in 2020 on released Taliban prisoners found that a large majority subsequently returned to the insurgency or took up military and political roles within the Taliban movement. That finding is relevant to the debate over whether the assumptions underpinning the Doha process produced the desired outcome.
That the Taliban now run the state, control the security apparatus and exercise authority over the country has made Pakistan's argument more pointed. If Kabul is now a government, Islamabad argues, it carries responsibility for preventing terrorist groups from operating from territory under its control. That is also the central challenge facing the latest Turkish and Qatari mediation effort.
The issue is not a lack of communication. Islamabad and Kabul continue to maintain channels of contact. Nor is there a shortage of mediators. Turkey, Qatar and China have all been involved in efforts to facilitate dialogue. The difficulty is that the two sides remain fundamentally divided over the question of terrorism. Pakistan wants action against the TTP. Kabul has so far failed to provide the assurances that Islamabad considers credible and verifiable. The latest diplomatic initiative could help reopen political channels and reduce tensions. But the Kohat attack demonstrates how quickly security developments can undermine such efforts.
For Pakistan, the choice is not between diplomacy and confrontation. It continues to keep the door open to dialogue while insisting that its security concerns must be addressed. The problem is that unless there is a visible change in Kabul's approach towards the TTP and other terrorist groups, there is little basis for expecting a major breakthrough. Turkey and Qatar may succeed in bringing the two sides back to the table. But whether that produces anything beyond another round of talks will ultimately depend on what happens on the ground.

title: Flour prices surge to Rs3 000 per 20kg bag in Shangla
description: Traders blame rising transport costs  alleged inter provincial supply restrictions as inflation squeezes households
content:
Traders blame rising transport costs, alleged inter-provincial supply restrictions as inflation squeezes households
Flour prices have risen sharply in Shangla, with a 20-kilogram bag now selling for between Rs2,950 and Rs3,000, while prices in several remote areas have crossed the Rs3,000 mark, traders said.
The increase has added to the difficulties of people already struggling with rising inflation, as repeated increases in fuel prices have pushed up the cost of food and other essential commodities. Low-income households and employees working in the private sector are facing particular financial pressure, with many finding it increasingly difficult to meet household expenses, support their children and afford basic food.
Traders from different parts of Shangla said they were purchasing a 20kg flour bag for around Rs2,900 and selling it for Rs2,950 to Rs3,000. In remote areas, transportation and other additional costs had pushed the price above Rs3,000, they added.
The traders expressed concern over the increase, claiming that alleged restrictions or obstacles imposed by the Punjab government on inter-provincial transportation and trade were affecting markets in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P). They said the situation could further affect the availability and prices of flour in the province.
Read : Flour prices soar as Punjab blocks supply to K-P
They said that while fuel prices continued to rise, flour, cooking oil, sugar, pulses and other essential commodities were also becoming increasingly unaffordable for ordinary consumers. Rising daily expenses had disrupted household budgets, particularly for middle- and low-income families, while limited business activity and unemployment prevented any significant increase in incomes.
According to the traders, employees working in private institutions, shops, markets and other sectors on low salaries were among the worst affected. Many low-paid workers earn around Rs30,000 a month or even less, making it extremely difficult to meet the basic expenses of a household under the prevailing inflationary conditions.
Rising fuel prices had also increased the difficulties faced by employees who commute to work on motorcycles, traders and residents said. For low-paid workers, even purchasing petrol for daily travel has become a burden, while they must continue paying transportation costs to reach their workplaces.
They said higher prices of flour and other food items, combined with electricity, gas and water bills, school fees, medical expenses and other essential costs, had placed poor and salaried families under severe economic pressure. Limited incomes were making it increasingly difficult for households to meet these competing expenses.
The traders also expressed concern over measures attributed to the Punjab government, saying that obstacles to inter-provincial trade and the movement of essential commodities could affect ordinary consumers. They referred to Article 151 of the Constitution, which deals with freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse throughout Pakistan.
Read More : Punjab flour halt drives prices higher
They said K-P was home to millions of Pakistanis belonging to different political parties and schools of thought and that the uninterrupted supply of essential food items should be ensured irrespective of political affiliations.
The traders said any political or administrative tensions between Punjab and K-P should not burden ordinary citizens, workers, salaried employees and businesspeople. Difficulties in the movement of essential commodities between provinces, they added, could drive prices higher and further affect people already struggling with inflation.
