title: The truths we tell about ourselves
description: In this post truth age of fake news and eroding trust  how much truth do writers tell to transform memory and experience into stories
content:
In this post-truth age of fake news and eroding trust, how much truth do writers tell to turn memory into stories?
In an age where trends on social media are transient, I spent many years harbouring an enduring, even unhealthy, obsession with a term that was widely discussed after the Brexit referendum and Trump’s first stint as president. Billed as Oxford Dictionaries’ word of the year in 2016, ‘post-truth’ wasn’t just an adjective, but an indictment of the human condition. The term marked the death of objective facts and the dawn of an era where emotional appeals hold sway.
For almost a decade, this term became part of my everyday vocabulary, prompting me to inhabit the skin of a sceptic. Using ‘post-truth’ before any noun had morphed into a bad habit and, perhaps even, a tool of convenience. It didn’t serve as just another compound adjective in phrases such as ‘post-truth realities’ or ‘post-truth politics’. Instead, it was a critical device through which I viewed the world and gauged its commitment to honesty.
As an avid reader, I’ve always found solace in the printed word, viewing it as a window into reality. Burdened by a post-truth lens, I’d become increasingly cynical about facts and insisted on subjecting them to scrutiny until I could find in them some semblance of a verifiable truth. In those years, I was drawn more towards memoirs than autobiographical accounts.
For most readers, the terms ‘autobiography’ and ‘memoir’ are used interchangeably. Life-writing, though, is a complex art, and it is difficult to rely on a single technique to chronicle the many shades and flavours of our lives. Autobiographical texts benefit from the spirit of completeness as they attempt to portray the highs and lows of an individual’s entire life in vivid detail. Rooted in facts, formal autobiographies are believed to possess greater historical significance by critics owing to their objectivity and fearlessness.
However, memoirs tend to be far more selective in their scope, presenting only a snapshot of a person’s life. Even if they are fragmentary, memoirs are strengthened by their perceived subjectivity. Memoirists often rely on literary devices used by fiction writers to reconstruct a forgotten or, perhaps, vaguely remembered moment. This shouldn’t be viewed as an attempt to fabricate information. Memory, as many of us will concur, is unreliable; it can elude us just as easily as it can whisper secrets into our ears. Faced with such a wildly unpredictable beast, most memoir writers prefer to recreate the past based on hindsight, thereby viewing it from observations and reflections made in the present.
As I grew increasingly suspicious of an inherently ‘post-truth’ world, autobiographies became anathema. I was unapologetic about my aversion to them. Why wouldn’t I harbour suspicion about such fact-driven enterprises? In these harrowing times, when fake news haunts us like a spectre, information in all its forms is dangerous, akin to a life-threatening virus. Trust, therefore, is an asset that is constantly losing value. Could I then trust autobiographies to provide me anything other than half-truths, vainglorious accounts of valour and self-congratulatory praise?
Memoirs were safer as they didn’t disguise themselves behind a veneer of objectivity. From the outset, they exposed their leanings, reminding me that I didn’t have a front-row seat to a game of deception. Memoirs weren’t afraid of the murkier space where facts lost ground and some form of fictionalising seemed integral. They were, to me, an ideal map to navigate the doom and gloom of those post-truth realities I dreaded so much.
Yet, as a storyteller, I couldn’t escape the pull of fiction, which opened a doorway into the lives of characters who were possibly based on real people. Fascinated by the porous boundaries between fiction and life-writing, I read novels and short fiction based on the lives of their authors.
In 2020, as the pandemic struck, I devoured Zeeba Sadiq's 38 Bahadurabad, a novel that skilfully welds fictional and autobiographical elements. In this slim debut novel, the author attempts to understand Dr Sadiq, her beloved father, with whom she spent her early childhood years in the eponymous residence in Karachi. In a series of interconnected sketches that alternate between the first- and third-person voices, the author examines memories of her father from various angles. The purpose of this exercise is to confront his paradoxical image as an upstanding family man who once abandoned his first family in England.
While 38 Bahadurabad is often categorised as fiction, the unique treatment of its autobiographical strands renders this book a fascinating exploration of how fact can be presented in life-writing. For instance, Zeeba Sadiq frequently uses humour as a crutch to evade uncomfortable conversations or painful epiphanies about Dr Sadiq’s life.
At the same time, she relies on narrative foils to reveal her father's unique attributes. In this novel, facts aren't overlooked; they are merely scrutinised and presented in a palatable form.
British-Pakistani author Aamer Hussein's short stories were my truest companions as I negotiated the dilemmas of a post-truth world. For decades, his work has navigated the flexible boundaries between fiction and autobiography to advantage. The author often examines events from his own life, such as a cancer diagnosis and his experience with grief, through a fictional lens. For instance, ‘The Garden Spy’ introduces us to a narrator who copes with loss, cancer and the uneasy solitude of Covid-19 lockdown.
In his exclusively memoir pieces, Hussein fashions himself as an onlooker who comes alive on the page through the people, places and eras he evokes. 'Words and Music’ hearkens back to the 1960s when a young Hussein discovers that Pakistani film actor Shamim Ara is his neighbour in Karachi. This memory is a catalyst through which the author evokes a bygone era when he developed a fascination with film songs and poetry. ‘Uncle Rafi’ offers a glimpse of the brief literary career of the author’s maternal granduncle. ‘Teacher’ portrays Hussein as an eager student to purple-robed Shah Sahab, an Urdu teacher he encountered in London at a pivotal stage in his life. ‘Suyin: A Friendship’ pays homage to Chinese-born Eurasian author Han Suyin. As Hussein’s close friend, she urged him to explore the inner rhythm of his mother tongue whenever he put pen to paper.
Even so, as a literary critic, I found myself reading and interpreting conventional autobiographical works, and deriving an unexpected joy from their formalistic spirit. It was through these reviewing assignments that my faith in facts was ultimately restored. However, I didn’t simply rebuild my trust; I simply learnt to accept their claim to objectivity while recognising that they may not paint a complete portrait. As a reader, I swiftly began taming the instinct to blindly trust information. Instead, I chose to embrace facts as a version of reality instead of the unvarnished truth. The techniques adopted by some authors of autobiographical texts helped me analyse the ways in which facts were being handled.
Scholar and former diplomat Masuma Hasan’s Pakistan in an Age of Turbulence didn't strike me as a typical autobiography. Using sound research and objectivity as a weapon, she situated her story against Pakistan's broader political context. What emerges from this account is a captivating story of a woman who remained an insider within the power corridors and rose to a position of prominence in the Civil Service. Hasan neither boasts about her achievements nor sugarcoats realities – qualities that render her memoir all the more neutral.
At first glance, Shahbaz Taseer's Lost to the World: A Memoir of Faith, Family and Five Years in Terrorist Captivity could be viewed as a memoir rather than a strictly autobiographical text. The text stands out for effortlessly straddling objective truth and subjective reality. Taseer's memoir came through as poignant because he didn't shy away from exploring the emotional turmoil he encountered during his confinement. As a consequence, Lost to the World moves beyond reportage and shines a revealing light on the tumultuous years the author spent in captivity.
Similarly, Mukhtar Husain's Foundations and Form: Memoirs of a Pakistani Architect offers a dispassionate, well-modulated account of a life with clinical precision. Relying on subheadings, the narrative reproduces every facet of the author's life, leaving little room for gaps and blind spots.
Above all, the book offers a compelling social history of Karachi from the 1950s to the contemporary moment, which suggests that life-writing doesn’t have to be a self-centred endeavour.
My reservations about autobiographical texts in a post-truth era were somewhat allayed when Annie Ernaux won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2022. Ernaux clinched the coveted award for “the courage and clinical acuity with which she uncovers the roots, estrangements and collective restraints of personal memory”. Curiously enough, she is known to have pioneered “autosociobiography”, a literary genre that views the personal memoir as a portal of sorts into the broader structures of society. Her expansive oeuvre boasts stellar examples of texts that bypass her private emotions and use her experiences as case studies of how women’s bodies and desires are policed by society. In Happening, Ernaux draws an intimate line of connection between her clandestine abortion and class constraints and institutional pressures in France of the 1960s. Simple Passion turns an intimate gaze on an intense love affair and reveals how social pressure dictates women’s romantic interactions.
Since then, I have made a conscious effort to understand the motivations of autobiographical writers in the hope that they will help me erase all my doubts about facts in a post-truth world.
“Autobiographies are interesting to read,” novelist, translator and memoirist Rehana Alam says. “But only those people who have unique lives in some way or who can shed light on world events from exceptional perspectives.”
Memoirs, she believes, allow authors “the latitude to write about only remarkable periods of their lives and not to chronicle the entire span from birth onward.” Her own memoir, My Life as a Corporate Gypsy, spans the nearly three decades when she and her family moved across four continents owing to her husband’s job. This is her third book and first autobiographical work. Captivating, enriching and emotionally resonant, Alam’s memoir traces the contours of her peripatetic life, revealing its many moments of turbulence and tranquility. Yet, this is not a conventional travel memoir peppered with cliched reminiscences. Within its pages emerges a tableau of how one can fashion homes in foreign lands through successive relocations.
“That time [in our lives, which was] one of great adventure and adaptation for us, also delineates a method of doing business by multinational corporations which has now been abandoned,” Alam says. Her words are a comforting reminder of how memoirs embody both individual and collective realities.
At times, memories elude us and authors have to rely on diary entries for guidance. Alam, though, possesses an almost photographic memory of key events.
“The dates of our sojourn in the various countries [are] etched on my mind together with the outstanding experiences and anecdotes of those periods,” she says. “Diaries and notes were not needed to write my memoir.”
Much like Alam, Talat Rahim wrote other books before venturing into life-writing.
"I chose to write my memoir after I had written four books on other people," she says. Rahim wrote about bureaucrats, divorcees, hypocrites and even published a book of 22 interviews with people from India and Pakistan. All of these books were steered by factual accounts.
Her publisher once referred to Rahim as "a very unusual woman" who spends her time talking and writing about other people.
"That really got my goat," she says. "I braced myself to write my own story, published under the title I Did It My Way: My Life Uncensored."
Shifting gears came with its own challenges. "It takes a lot of courage to write with a no-holds-barred attitude," Rahim asserts. "I was afraid people would not be interested in my story, but this was the only story I had withheld and not talked about earlier."
Despite her initial reservations, Rahim wasn't plagued by writer's block, but felt some sections were "tough to write".
"I would stop midway with the question of the intrinsic worth of such a book," Rahim says. "Nonetheless, I decided for my own amusement to write about incidents I could recall as I went down memory lane. I spoke of myself and the very eventful and unusual life I have led, [which was] so different from [those of] my contemporaries who were all married after graduation, had babies and are now grandmothers."
Unlike her peers, Rahim married late, had no children and lost her husband. She worked with, and for, bureaucrats for 25 years, and travelled the world at "government expense".
"After taking a golden handshake from government service, [I] started to write books and published In 2023, I wrote my memoir."
Rahim confesses that she has never maintained a diary in her life.
"The Almighty has bestowed me with an elephant's memory," she proudly declares. "My memoir records interesting details of a well-lived life, all from memory!"
The underlying purpose of Rahim's memoir is to encourage women "to learn and understand how to live life on their own terms".
“I don't want them to be bogged down by that very distasteful remark, 'What will people say?'," Rahim says. Her creative vision reaffirms the fact that memoirs are more than just a document of personal victories; they can also serve the collective good.
As I plumb the depths of the autobiographer’s mind, it gradually dawns on me that my concerns about post-truth realities are a bit extreme, if not entirely trivial. Facts aren’t ghoulish entities we must fear; they are a potent force we must actively confront.

title: Back to the shadows
description: Putting the detective back in Batman  the Caped Crusader   s second season gets it right
content:
Putting the detective back in Batman, the Caped Crusader’s second season gets it right
If you think Sony/Marvel were the first to launch a Prime Video project featuring their prized superhero in a noir world, think again. Batman predates the term "film noir," and the Caped Crusader Season 2 reminds you that it’s the Dark Knight’s territory.
Batman has been reinvented so often that simply announcing another version of the character no longer generates excitement. The question is what a new adaptation can bring to the table. Batman: Caped Crusader offers a fairly convincing answer: go back to the beginning.
The second season continues to explore Bruce Wayne's early years as Batman, as he is still finding his footing as Gotham's masked vigilante. Alfred is younger—and noticeably plumper—than in most versions of the story. Batman has very few friends in the Gotham City Police Department, and Commissioner Gordon's office remains one of the few places where he is tolerated. More importantly, Gotham itself feels like a character.
Inspired by the Batman stories of the 1940s and 1960s and heavily influenced by film noir, Caped Crusader depicts a city consumed by corruption, organised crime, and gang warfare. This Batman has not yet become the all-knowing superhero audiences expect. He is still learning, making mistakes, and, most importantly, investigating. That’s where the series finds its greatest strength.
Is it truly the successor to Batman: The Animated Series?
Nothing featuring Batman in an animated world has surpassed Batman: The Animated Series, which revived the character in the 1990s, so comparisons to the OG series are inevitable. Both series understand that Batman works best when the world around him is as compelling as the man behind the mask.
Yet the Caped Crusader isn’t simply trying to recreate the magic of the animated classic associated with Bruce Timm, who also served as showrunner for this reincarnation. Instead, it takes some of the era’s core ideas and places them in a darker, more serialised world.
The biggest difference is its storytelling approach; rather than treating each episode as an isolated adventure, Caped Crusader gradually builds a larger narrative through individual detective cases. Characters evolve, relationships shift, and Gotham's power structures begin to overlap, just like they did in the previous season. This makes the show feel more like a crime drama than a conventional animated superhero series.
Despite being the central character, Batman isn’t always the most interesting person in the room. Harley Quinn, Crime Smasher, The Riddler, Joker, Barbara Gordon, and other familiar characters get plenty of attention, especially when they’re portrayed differently from their comic book version. That willingness to play with established mythology matters because it keeps Caped Crusader from becoming a predictable retelling of Batman's origin story.
To get Batman right, you first have to get the people who understand the character. Bringing on Bruce Timm as writer, producer, developer, and showrunner was a masterstroke, since he is an authority on the Dark Knight. The series also benefits enormously from director Matt Reeves, whose The Batman embraced the character’s detective and noir elements, and from renowned filmmaker J.J. Abrams, both of whom serve as producers.
There are action sequences, of course, as well as familiar villains, confrontations, and moments of superhero theatrics. The disappearing act is still there, despite Batman being relatively new to the game, and so are the lines that remind you not only of the animated series and films but also of the many films he has been part of.
And yes, thankfully, the show understands that Batman's greatest weapon is not necessarily his technology or physical strength—it's his ability to investigate. That can be lost in modern Batman adaptations, where the character's detective skills are often overshadowed by increasingly elaborate action sequences. The Caped Crusader puts the detective back in Batman.
Usually, a series that isn’t well established has to first earn viewers’ trust and then bank on it; however, with this reiteration of Batman, that wasn’t the case. He was a well-established character, and the scenario was also familiar to the audience because of previous versions and, in this series’ case, the season.
What this season does exceptionally well is take recognisable Batman ingredients and place them in what feels like a parallel universe. You know the names, but you cannot always predict what these characters will do, how they will evolve, or, in some cases, whether they will survive the season. That familiarity creates an interesting balance. Viewers are given enough of the Batman mythology to feel comfortable, while the changes keep them curious.
The film noir setting also contributes to the show's distinctive atmosphere. Characters speak and behave in ways appropriate to the period-inspired setting, while the writing doesn't shy away from the darker aspects of Gotham. The media is present, but it resembles that of the 1940s and 1950s, when black-and-white TV was making inroads and radio was still the main source of news and entertainment.
Then there is the action. The series understands that a noir story cannot remain static. When Batman finally throws a punch, chases a suspect, or confronts one of Gotham's criminals, the action carries greater weight because the show has spent time establishing the circumstances that lead to it. That combination of investigation, setting, and action gives the series its rhythm.
Why should the Caped Crusader be taken seriously?
Calling the Caped Crusader ‘another Batman cartoon’ would be a huge mistake because it is anything but that. The show is attempting something specific: a hard-edged crime narrative within a framework that remains accessible to adult audiences.
It is unafraid to make Gotham ugly. The police can be corrupt, criminals can manipulate the system, and even those supposedly working for the greater good can have questionable motives. At the same time, it doesn’t lose sight of Batman's core appeal. It remains a story about a man who chooses to fight crime because he believes Gotham can be better, no matter how many monsters emerge from its dark alleys.
The narrative can occasionally feel imbalanced, especially when attention to supporting characters comes at the expense of Batman's own journey. Some relationships and developments can also feel forced rather than organically integrated into the larger story. Yet these issues do not undermine the overall achievement. The creators understand that reinvention does not necessarily mean abandoning what made Batman work in the first place. Sometimes it means returning to it.
If you think Spider-Noir was the first major superhero property to adopt the language of film noir, you are mistaken. Batman predates the term "film noir," and the Caped Crusader Season 2 reminds you that it’s the Dark Knight’s territory.
He was created as a detective before becoming the near-mythological superhero modern audiences know. His city is built for shadows, where he operates without any superpowers. His villains often embody psychological and moral problems as much as physical threats.
That makes noir almost a natural playground for the Dark Knight. Batman: Caped Crusader understands this better than most recent adaptations. It does not try to make Batman the biggest superhero in the room. Instead, it repositions him as a detective. And perhaps that is exactly why the second season works.
If the series makes you interested in film noir, you can trace its roots by watching some of the best Hollywood films that helped popularise that genre. Films such as Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, Strangers on a Train, The Big Heat, and Ace in the Hole helped establish noir's visual and thematic vocabulary.
If one had a detective chasing a rare bird statue because he found the client irresistible, the other predicted the evil of the media long before it dominated our lives; murdering a person to cash his insurance policy was also discussed in one of these films, whereas the idea of ‘exchanging murders’ was introduced in another flick in such a way that it looked interesting and complex at the same time.
In a world where superhero adaptations are constantly seeking the next big reinvention, Caped Crusader makes a surprisingly simple choice: it goes back to the source, changes enough to stay fresh, and trusts Batman's oldest strength—solving the mystery in the shadows. That’s why it works.
The writer is a freelance contributor who writes about film, television, and popular culture

title: Trump warns he has entered  deciding mode  on Iran  says  big things  are in store
description: Iran warns regional states will be  considered complicit  if US strikes resume
content:
Iran warns regional states will be 'considered complicit' if US strikes resume
US President Donald Trump warned on Sunday that he had entered a critical decision phase in the ongoing war with Iran, cautioning that major developments would occur if Tehran failed to change its conduct.
"My question is if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They had better behave," Trump told Fox News , detailing his approach to the war.
The US president described his current options as wiping the country out, allowing it to "rot" economically, or negotiating a deal, adding that “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future.”
BREAKING: President Trump told Fox News Chief Foreign Correspondent @TreyYingst that he is in a “deciding mode” and "very big things" are going to happen in the near future regarding the US-Iran war. Trump said, "My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They… pic.twitter.com/JcAXh9QN84
When asked about the UN General Assembly high-level week, which starts on Monday, Trump signalled a willingness to engage diplomatically, saying he would "probably be open" to meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Addressing wider regional hostilities, Trump said Washington remained in constant communication with Yemen's Houthis following their recent ballistic missile attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, asserting that the group agreed to avoid fighting American forces.
Iran warns regional states will be 'considered complicit' if US strikes resume
Iran received information that the United States, with the backing of some regional countries, was preparing to resume actions against Tehran, the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' (IRGC's) joint military command, said in a statement on Sunday, according to state media.
🔴 Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters warns US against any aggression, saying US bases will face painful attacks. Follow: https://t.co/oa9JV4ikYQ pic.twitter.com/ba2yxDSCSr
The military said that any US had been given a "green light" by unnamed regional countries at a joint meeting in Europe to resume action against Tehran.
According to state media, the military added that any US attack would lead to Iranian retaliation "without any limitations or considerations" on US bases and interests. Regional countries involved in any US attack on Iran, the military said, should not expect restraint from Tehran's armed forces and would be considered complicit and parties to the conflict.
Separately, Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, stated that US President Donald Trump had waged a foolish war on Iran and was foolishly continuing it, IRNA reported.
Rezaei added, however, that Iran “stands ready to give a stronger and more painful response should the US resume military aggression.”
Top security official: Trump foolishly continues war, but Iran fully ready for self-defense https://t.co/3LWLeV8Se6 pic.twitter.com/HU0zOnTs8v
“We have fully prepared ourselves for a decisive war, and the US’ military vulnerabilities are completely known to us. And we are far better prepared this time,” he said, according to IRNA .
The secretary further noted, “Netanyahu plunged Trump into a quagmire.” It was and is in the benefit of the US to accept Iran’s conditions and end the war because the more the conflict drags on, the worse the US’ situation will become, IRNA quoted him as having said.
Iran's Army Ground Forces Commander Brigadier General Jahanshahi also noted separately that Tehran's border units remained deployed and on constant alert in various border areas, Press TV reported.
🔴 Iran’s Army Ground Forces Commander Brigadier General Jahanshahi: 🔺Iranian Army border units remain deployed and on constant alert in various border areas, prepared to counter any potential threats and protect the country’s security and territorial integrity. pic.twitter.com/npBqzXU6HU
Jahanshahi added that the units were prepared to counter any potential threats and to protect the country's security and territorial integrity.
Ghalibaf vows to 'deal devastating blows' to enemy at 'critical moment'
Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said "one must both fight and negotiate." He added, “This means at the critical moment we must push the enemy back and deal them devastating blows using our full military might,” Al Jazeera reported.
Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf says “one must both fight and negotiate” as the nearly seven-month war with the United States drags on. 🔴 LIVE updates: https://t.co/qJleYbnwN8 pic.twitter.com/3qwO4fZLHx
“However, once we have achieved significant success on the battlefield and the enemy is in a position of weakness, we must use diplomacy to consolidate these gains,” Ghalibaf said.
The speaker noted that Iran’s position in negotiations was “entirely clear, rational, and non-negotiable.”
Earlier, Ghalibaf said the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the US fulfils its commitments under a now-defunct peace deal signed in June, Al Jazeera reported.
Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf says the Strait of Hormuz will stay closed until the US fulfils its commitments under the now-defunct peace deal that was signed in June. 🔴 LIVE updates: https://t.co/qJleYbmYXA pic.twitter.com/y6TiZv3kZT
Flames, smoke seen near Riyadh airport, Houthis claim attacks on Saudi capital
Yemen's Houthis said they attacked "sensitive" sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh on Saturday with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large ​plume of smoke were seen near the city's main airport.
Saudi Arabia had sent alerts overnight warning of potential danger around Riyadh, amid an escalation in attacks ‌by the Houthis in the kingdom.
Reuters video and photographs showed a huge pillar of black smoke rising in the area, with the airport highway, main terminal building and other facilities in the foreground. At one point in the video, flames were visible rising from behind what appeared to be fuel tanks.
While the Houthis have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia since July, Saturday's claim appeared to be their first reported strike on Riyadh since ​the current escalation began.
The Houthis did not specify what they had targeted in Riyadh, but said they had also attacked an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of ​Yanbu, a key Saudi oil export hub.
They said the operation came as a response to an attack in the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
The Saudi-led military ⁠coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had destroyed a missile fired by the Yemeni group toward Riyadh early on Saturday.
In a statement, the coalition also said it had foiled ​attacks targeting civilians in the Saudi cities of Bish and Farasan in the southwest and Taif in the west, as well as Yanbu on the Red Sea coast. It did not say whether ​there was any damage.
Read: Houthis threaten ‘decisive’ response if Pakistan, Türkiye intervene in Yemen
Saudi civil defence sent the alerts by phone overnight for potential danger of aerial attacks in Riyadh and the city of Al-Kharj east of the capital, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning. A Reuters journalist in Riyadh's Olaya area heard booms before the all-clear was sent.
Although some alerts had been issued in Riyadh this year after the start of the US-Iran war, these were the first since the escalation with the ​Houthis began in July.
The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has developed as a new theatre of conflict in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran ​at the end of February. US President Donald Trump has rebuffed Saudi requests for direct US military intervention against the Houthis.
UN, Gulf Cooperation Council chiefs condemn Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) head Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi on Saturday strongly condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, warning that the group’s targeting of civilian objects poses a severe threat to regional peace and security.
Guterres received Albudaiwi in New York on the sidelines of the GCC chief’s participation in the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, according to a statement from the GCC Secretariat General.
“Both officials strongly condemned the Houthi militia’s attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and their deliberate targeting of civilian objects, underscoring the severe threat these hostile actions pose to regional peace and security,” it said.
Read more: Houthis fire 'ballistic missile' at Riyadh
The two officials also reviewed cooperation between the GCC and the UN, and discussed ways to deepen collaboration in areas of shared interest. They exchanged views on geopolitical developments and discussed regional issues and diplomatic efforts to resolve them.
Guterres commended “the substantial progress and prosperity achieved by GCC member states” and praised their contributions to promoting lasting stability worldwide.
US urges Americans to reconsider travel to Middle East amid rising tensions
The US on Saturday urged Americans outside the Middle East to seriously reconsider travel to and through the region, citing a complex security environment and the potential for rapid escalation.
The State Department's Travel.Gov account on a US social media platform said Americans in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be prepared for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.
“Due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation,” it said.
It warned that Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks involving civilian airports, and said the conflict “has the potential to escalate rapidly.”
Also read: Italian aircraft hit during air base attacks in Saudi Arabia
Americans traveling to or from the region were advised to monitor information on airport and airline operations.
The State Department also warned that US diplomatic facilities, including those outside the Middle East, have been targeted and that Iran and groups supporting it may target other US interests overseas or locations associated with the US and Americans worldwide, including US businesses and other institutions.
Trump cuts short Camp David stay amid rising Middle East tensions
US President Donald Trump cut short his weekend stay at Camp David and was expected to return to the White House late on Saturday, according to a White House pool report.
The White House updated the president’s schedule to show his return to Washington on Marine One, with the presidential helicopter expected to arrive at the Ellipse at about 7 pm local time (2300GMT), USA Today reporter Joey Garrison reported in a pool report.
No reason was given for the change to Trump's schedule.

title: Seminary records sought in Mangi Dam attack probe
description: Seminary records sought in Mangi Dam attack probe
content:
Judicial commission orders district-wise verification of madaris across Balochistan
The judicial commission investigating the Ziarat Mangi Dam terrorist attack has directed Balochistan authorities to submit a fully verified, district-wise record of all registered religious seminaries (madaris) operating across the province.
Presiding over an open court hearing in Quetta, Justice Muhammad Amir Nawaz Rana stressed the need for strict regulatory compliance, verification and financial transparency in the administration of religious institutions.
After examining a preliminary report on seminary governance, the commission summoned the in-charge officer of the Directorate General of Religious Education to appear in person at the next hearing. The official has been directed to submit a comprehensive report covering registration procedures, verification mechanisms, sources of funding and monitoring arrangements for all religious seminaries in Balochistan.
The commission also took up the issue of delayed compensation to families of victims of the attack. Advocate Habibullah Khan Nasir, representing the bereaved families, informed the bench that the relief packages promised by the government had yet to be disbursed to the heirs of the martyrs.
The Additional Chief Secretary (Home) assured the commission that sanction orders for the compensation had already been issued and advised the affected families to approach his office directly.
To ensure that the payments were not further delayed, the commission directed officials, including Naseemullah and Izzatullah, to coordinate immediately with the Home Department and expedite the release of all pending compensation.
Meanwhile, new evidence was also formally placed on the record. Citizen Abdul Baqi submitted an FIR concerning the theft and disappearance of personal belongings and the mobile phone of martyred Anti-Terrorism Force Constable Jan Dad Khan.
Baqi also presented video footage related to the incident. The commission accepted the footage as part of the official record for further investigative examination.

title: K P overhauls school curriculum
description: K P overhauls school curriculum
content:
Elementary and Secondary Education Department is implementing most substantial curriculum reforms in about 20 years
The Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government has decided to introduce major changes to the provincial education curriculum from primary to intermediate level after nearly two decades, with a significant reduction in the number of subjects and teaching content.
Under the new curriculum, the number of subjects taught up to primary level has been reduced. From Class 8 to Class 12, the volume of subjects has also been cut, and the number of lessons within those subjects has been decreased.
On the directions of the provincial government, the Elementary and Secondary Education Department is implementing the most substantial curriculum reforms in about 20 years. A new curriculum has been approved for Classes 9 to 12, under which the national curriculum will be adopted in eight key subjects. These include English, Urdu, Mathematics, Computer Science, Chemistry, Physics and General Science.

title: Afridi calls for review of anti terror policy
description: Afridi calls for review of anti terror policy
content:
CM praises security forces, says Rs35b provided beyond ADP to strengthen police
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Mohammad Sohail Afridi has paid tribute to police, Counter Terrorism Department (CTD), Special Branch, Rescue 1122, doctors, district administration and the people of Kohat for their courage during an almost 20-hour operation against terrorists.
During his visit to Kohat, the chief minister met the families of those martyred in the Police Lines blast and expressed solidarity with them. He prayed for the elevation of the martyrs' ranks and early recovery of those injured.
Afridi said police personnel and civilians had sacrificed their lives while confronting terrorists to protect the country and its people. He said K-P had been fighting terrorism since 2004, during which, according to him, around 80,000 precious lives had been lost.
The chief minister said peace had been restored in the province after years of sacrifices and claimed that K-P had experienced a period of peace during the government of former prime minister Imran Khan. He said the foreign policy at that time had been framed while keeping national and public interests in view.
He maintained that despite differences between Pakistan and the Afghan government, Imran Khan had played the role of a statesman by inviting Afghanistan to Pakistan and seeking improved bilateral relations, which, he claimed, had contributed to a significant decline in terrorism.
Afridi said the situation had now reversed, with relations with Afghanistan strained, the border closed, trade disrupted and economic activity restricted in the tribal districts. He claimed that the border closure had caused losses of more than Rs8 billion to K-P during the last financial year and would continue to affect the provincial economy during the current fiscal year.
He attributed the rising incidents of terrorism partly to what he termed an unsuccessful foreign policy, saying the same policy had been followed for 22 years. If a policy was not producing effective results, he said, it needed to be reviewed.
The chief minister said the provincial government's proposed counterterrorism policy was aimed at protecting the interests of K-P and Pakistan rather than benefiting any political party. He claimed that peace could be restored within 100 days if the policy was implemented.
Afridi also criticised the federal government and state institutions, alleging that greater attention was being given to restricting Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf's political activities than to combating terrorism.
He said the provincial government had allocated an additional Rs35 billion, outside the Annual Development Programme, to enhance police capacity, provide modern weapons and equipment, and improve infrastructure. The police budget, he added, had been increased from around Rs81 billion to Rs190 billion.

title: PHC upholds 14 year sentence in lecturer murder case
description: PHC upholds 14 year sentence in lecturer murder case
content:
AAG maintained that the accused, being a security guard, had no justification for opening fire on the lecturer
The Peshawar High Court (PHC) has dismissed an appeal filed by Sher Mohammad, convicted in the murder case of Islamia College Peshawar lecturer Bashir Ahmad, and upheld the 14-year imprisonment awarded to him by the trial court.
A two-member bench comprising Justice Waqar Ahmad and Justice Farah Jamshed announced the verdict after hearing the appeal against the judgment of the Peshawar Sessions Court.
During the proceedings, Additional Advocate General Alam Khan Adinzai told the court that Sher Mohammad had opened fire on Bashir Ahmad at Islamia College Peshawar on February 19, 2023. The accused was performing duties as a security guard at the college when the incident occurred.
The government lawyer argued that substantial evidence was available against the accused and that the CCTV footage clearly showed that he had not fired in self-defence but had deliberately attacked the lecturer.
The AAG maintained that the accused, being a security guard, had no justification for opening fire on the lecturer. He said the evidence on record could not be ignored and that the accused was not entitled to any concession.

title: 23 abductees rescued  6 terrorists killed in Kalat
description: 23 abductees rescued  6 terrorists killed in Kalat
content:
Security forces foiled an attempt by terrorists to establish a check post for abducting people and snatching vehicles along the Pakistan Highway near Kalat, rescuing 23 abductees and killing six terrorists, the military's media wing said on Sunday.
According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the operation was conducted during the night of Sept 18-19, when terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan attempted to disrupt the movement of people along the Chaman-Karachi N-25 highway near Kalat.
The terrorists were allegedly trying to establish a check post for abductions for ransom, extortion and vehicle snatching, the statement said.
"Security Forces responded immediately, and after intense fire exchange, five terrorists belonging to Indian-sponsored proxy of Fitna al-Hindustan were sent to hell due to effective response by Armed Forces," the ISPR said.
The federal government last year officially designated all terrorist groups operating in Balochistan as Fitna al-Hindustan, accusing India of sponsoring a proxy war through the outfits.
Security forces also recovered 23 abductees from the terrorists' hideout, along with six trucks, three buses and two cars.
A large quantity of weapons, ammunition and explosives was also recovered from the hideout, according to the statement.
The ISPR said the successful operation had thwarted the "nefarious designs" of the Indian-sponsored proxy of Fitna al-Hindustan.
"Sanitisation operations are continuing in the surrounding areas to eliminate any remaining terrorists and ensure the safety and security of the local population and the vital National Highways," it said.
The military's media wing said the counter-terrorism campaign under the vision of "Azm-e-Istehkam", approved by the Federal Apex Committee on the National Action Plan, would continue "with full resolve".

content:
Police claimed to have arrested one of two suspects after a girl was allegedly sexually assaulted and a video of the incident was circulated on social media in the Treda Makhnewala area of Kanganpur police station.

Kanganpur police registered a case and arrested Ali Hamza, described by police as the main suspect. Allah Rakha remains at large, police said.
The police said the girl had been shifted to a government hospital for medical examination and further legal proceedings.

title: Family seeks access to PTI s Hammad
description: Family seeks access to PTI s Hammad
content:
Plea in LHC accuses SHO of refusing to receive application
The mother and wife of PTI leader Hammad Azhar have approached the Lahore High Court (LHC) with a plea seeking permission for them and his counsel to communicate with him during his physical remand.
The applicants challenged an Anti-Terrorism Court (ATC) order directing them to approach the police for the access.
The petition filed by Ishrat Azhar and Mariam Hammad contended that the ATC had misinterpreted Rule 26.28 of the Police Rules, 1934, by directing the petitioners to approach the station house officer (SHO) for a meeting with Azhar.
They argued that the rule provides alternative, rather than cumulative, avenues for obtaining permission to communicate with a prisoner in police custody.
The ATC had granted 21 days' physical remand of Azhar on September 7. The petitioners had submitted an application before the ATC on September 10, seeking permission to meet him and requesting access for his lawyers as well.
The ATC disposed of their application, directing them to approach the SHO, of Sarwar Road.
The petition argued that meaningful access to legal counsel is particularly important in police custody.
It stated that after being directed by the ATC to approach the SHO, the petitioners had submitted an application but he had allegedly refused to receive it.
They requested the LHC to set aside the ATC's September 17 order and direct the authorities to provide Hammad Azhar's immediate family members reasonable and regular access to him during his custody.
A judicial magistrate on Saturday reserved his verdict on a contempt of court petition filed by Punjab Information Minister Azma Zahid Bukhari against the counsel for PTI activist Falak Javed in a case relating to the alleged circulation of a fake video.
Judicial Magistrate Naeem Wattoo also reserved his decision on Bukhari's application seeking exemption from personal appearance in the case.
During the hearing, Bukhari's counsel argued that Falak Javed's lawyer Mian Ali Ashfaq had tried to pressure the court in the previous hearing to issue arrest warrants for the complainant.
He contended that attempting to exert pressure on the court amounted to contempt.
Mian Ashfaq opposed the petition, arguing that Bukhari had failed to appear for cross-examination despite court orders.
He said the law provided for issuance of warrants if a complainant failed to appear despite directions.
He maintained that the contempt petition was an attempt to delay proceedings, claiming that the case had been adjourned 14 times because of the complainant.
Bukhari's counsel said courts never came under pressure.
The counsel also objected to social media commentary on the proceedings. He added that some social media activists were present in the court to support the defence lawyer.
The counsel questioned the absence of Falak Javed, pointing out that although she had been in jail for a long period, she was on bail in the present case.
The defence lawyer objected to what he termed personal attacks against him.
Bukhari's counsel also submitted an application seeking exemption from her appearance, saying another petition filed by her was pending before the LHC and regular proceedings on it were scheduled from Monday. He requested that further proceedings in the trial be taken up after the high court decided the matter.
Mian Ashfaq said he would argue on the exemption after completing his submissions on the contempt petition.
At one point, the defence counsel asked the court to reject Bukhari's exemption plea and issue her arrest warrants.
The magistrate urged both sides to focus on their legal arguments and avoid creating hurdles in the trial.
The court reserved its decisions on both the contempt petition and application for exemption from personal appearance.

title: Punjab to strengthen mental healthcare
description: Punjab to strengthen mental healthcare
content:
He called for collective efforts to address the stigma surrounding mental illness
Punjab Health Minister Khawaja Salman Rafique on Saturday said the provincial government was working to strengthen mental healthcare services under the proposed Mental Health Policy Framework 2026-2035, stressing the importance of counselling in treatment and rehabilitation.
He was speaking as the chief guest at a provincial consultative meeting on the Mental Health Policy Framework 2026-2035 held at King Edward Medical University (KEMU). The minister said people suffering from mental illnesses were being provided medical facilities in Punjab, while greater awareness and counselling were needed to support their rehabilitation and reintegration into society.
He called for collective efforts to address the stigma surrounding mental illness, saying people with mental health conditions should not be treated as "disabled" but as "differently-abled" individuals requiring greater care and support.
Khawaja Salman congratulated Professor Dr Mahmood Ayaz on his reappointment as KEMU vice chancellor and appreciated the university administration for organising the consultation.
He said the government was taking measures to improve healthcare facilities in the province in line with the vision of Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif, adding that new hospitals were also being established across Punjab.

title: CM pledges equitable uplift
description: CM pledges equitable uplift
content:
MPAs praise construction of flood embankments
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif has said the province's development focus is no longer limited to any city but extends to all 41 districts of the province.
Speaking to members of the Punjab Assembly and PML-N election candidates from Multan, she said development projects were being planned for the first time while keeping in view the population ratios.
The chief minister said modern green electric buses had been introduced in remote areas of Punjab before being launched in Lahore.
She also said a cancer ablation machine imported from China had been installed at Nishtar Hospital in Multan after its introduction at Mayo Hospital in Lahore and the treatment had already begun. She said the machine would provide non-surgical cancer treatment not only to patients from Multan but also to those from other provinces.
Development projects and public issues of Multan were discussed in the meeting.
According to a statement, the lawmakers thanked the CM for the construction of the Jalalpur Pirwala and Noraj Bhutta flood protection embankments in record time.
The chief minister agreed to a proposal for the construction of a bridge over the Chenab between Shujaabad and Khan Garh and directed authorities to examine a suggestion for converting a jail site into a park. She also ordered expansion and redesigning of the Khanewal Road.
The chief minister ordered that lawmakers be kept involved in development projects in their constituencies until their completion.
The lawmakers expressed support for the chief minister and praised her government's development and law-and-order measures. They said the benefits of development had started reaching the people and described the government's flood response and measures against land grabbing as significant.
They said Punjab had emerged as an example of development and the chief minister had taken a lead in the province's development.
Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz also issued a statement expressing appreciation for successful security operations against terrorists in Balochistan.
In another development, a team of the Chief Minister's Inspection Team (CMIT) paid a surprise visit to the Suthra Punjab machinery store in Shorkot.

title: Lahore ranks among most polluted cities
description: Lahore ranks among most polluted cities
content:

The metropolis has ranked among the world's most polluted major cities, recording an air quality index (AQI) of 156 to place third behind Kuching in Malaysia and Kolkata in India.
The AQI is classified as "unhealthy for sensitive groups", with particulate matter PM2.5 recorded at 54 micrograms per cubic metre as the main pollutant.
The air quality remained at a level causing concern in several parts of the city, with Model Town recording an AQI of 211, Iqbal Town 190 and DHA Phase V 171. The readings in Chaman Park, Barki Road and Bedian Road stood between 165 and 160.
The city's daily air quality forecast showed an AQI of 155 for Saturday, with the level expected to rise to 163 on Sunday.
The forecast for Monday stood at 158, Tuesday 157, Wednesday 136, Thursday 135 and Friday 148.
Meanwhile, the Pakistan Meteorological Department forecast mainly dry weather across Punjab on Sunday, with hot conditions likely in the plains. Murree, Galiyat and adjoining areas are expected to remain dry, with partly cloudy conditions possible during the afternoon.
The weather is also expected to remain mainly dry across most parts of the country, while the plains are likely to experience hot conditions during the daytime. Partly cloudy weather is expected in northern hilly areas during the afternoon.
The synoptic situation indicates that continental air is prevailing over most parts of the country.
In Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, dry weather is expected in most districts, with hot conditions likely in the plains during the day and partly cloudy conditions in upper districts during the afternoon.
Sindh is expected to experience hot and dry weather, with partly cloudy conditions possible along coastal areas. Balochistan is also likely to remain hot and dry.
Dry weather is also expected over Kashmir, while Gilgit-Baltistan is likely to experience partly cloudy conditions, with isolated light rain possible during the afternoon.
Islamabad and adjoining areas are expected to remain dry, with hot conditions during the daytime.
Mainly dry and hot weather prevailed across most parts of the country during the past 24 hours.

title: Elderly car lifter from Ghotki arrested in Karachi
description: Elderly car lifter from Ghotki arrested in Karachi
content:
Accused posed as a worshipper at mosques before stealing vehicles
A 57-year-old alleged car lifter from Ghotki, who reportedly posed as a worshipper at mosques before stealing vehicles parked outside, has been arrested in Karachi, according to SSP Anti-Vehicle Lifting Cell (AVLC) Khalid Mustafa Korai.
The suspect allegedly travelled from Ghotki to Karachi specifically to steal cars, moving the stolen vehicles out of the city before dawn and selling them in Quetta, police officials said. Investigators have also traced a criminal record comprising 14 cases against him.
According to police, CCTV footage recorded several months ago at a mosque in a posh area of Gulshan-e-Iqbal went viral on social media. The footage showed the suspect offering prayers inside the mosque and then, immediately after coming out, skilfully stealing a Mehran parked outside.
Using the CCTV footage, AVLC investigators identified and subsequently arrested the suspect, identified as Insaf Ali, son of Mir Khan.
Police said the suspect had allegedly been involved in criminal activities since 2000. His first case, registered 26 years ago, involved an alleged vehicle theft, followed by several other cases over the years. Police said he was adept at disguising himself and had been selling stolen vehicles in Balochistan.
SSP AVLC Khalid Mustafa Korai said police had traced 14 cases on the suspect's criminal record.
During interrogation, the suspect allegedly disclosed that he targeted vehicles around Fajr prayers and moved the stolen cars out of Karachi before sunrise, Korai said.
According to the SSP, the suspect also disclosed that he sold the stolen vehicles in Quetta. Police have obtained information about a buyer of the stolen vehicles, and an AVLC team will travel to Quetta to arrest him, he said.
Korai said the suspect did not stay in Karachi for long and would flee directly to Ghotki after stealing a vehicle.
The SSP urged citizens to install two trackers in expensive vehicles, explaining that car-lifting gangs often disable the first tracker, while a second device can help police track the vehicle and trace the suspects.
Police are also tightening the net around other individuals identified during the investigation, officials said.
Meanwhile, Karachi Police Chief Azad Khan has directed police officers to utilise all available resources to curb crime, including car and motorcycle lifting, protect the lives and property of citizens, and maintain law and order in the city.
He ordered that effective action against criminal elements be intensified.
He said the Karachi police's top priority was to protect citizens' lives and property, eliminate crime and maintain peace and order in the city. He also directed all police officers to improve their performance and ensure result-oriented measures to achieve these objectives.

title: Hattar factories put under scrutiny

content:

A special committee was formed on Saturday to ensure minimum wages and legal rights for workers employed at factories and industrial units in Hattar Industrial Estate.
The decision was taken at a meeting chaired by Haripur Deputy Commissioner Islahuddin, which reviewed workers' welfare, payment of the government-mandated minimum wage and compliance with labour laws.

Several industrial units had also failed to register employees, particularly women workers, with the Employees' Old-Age Benefits Institution (EOBI) and Employees' Social Security Institution (ESSI), depriving them of essential medical and financial protection.
The committee, headed by the Khanpur Assistant Commissioner, will include representatives of the Labour Department, Industries and Consumer Protection Council, EOBI, ESSI, KPEZDMC, Hattar Economic Zone and the DC's Office.
The DC directed the committee to conduct a comprehensive daily survey of all factories and submit reports on wages, working hours, social security and EOBI registration, workplace safety measures, CSR funds and salary payment systems.
The industrial estate will also undergo e-mapping through the GIS analyst at the Deputy Commissioner's Office to create a comprehensive geographical record and database of all industrial units.
Factories facing complaints over minimum wages, excessive working hours or failure to register workers will be surveyed on a priority basis, with strict legal action promised against violators.
According to the DC, he would personally review the committee's performance and survey reports every 15 days to ensure workers received their full legal rights and protection.

title: Fear of failure serious concern among GenZ
description: Fear of failure serious concern among GenZ
content:
Experts, youngsters say inflation, unemployment, social pressure contribute to growing anxiety
The fear of failure is becoming a serious issue among young people in Pakistan due to inflation and unemployment. Many young people believe that a wrong decision or failure in an examination could determine their entire future in education, employment and personal life.
Dr Kamal Tarrar, a psychologist practising in Islamabad, said that when young people were taught that their worth was linked only to success, failure became a symbol of fear rather than an opportunity to learn.
"An intense fear of failure can lead to anxiety, depression and emotional problems. Therefore, timely psychological support is necessary," she said while speaking to Express.
She said young people in societies where failure was considered a source of disgrace avoided trying new opportunities, taking positive risks and using their creative abilities. She said considering failure part of the learning process rather than a personal defeat was essential for mental resilience and emotional health.
Maryam, a university student, said the fear of failing examinations often forced her to stay awake throughout the night because delays in education could place an additional financial burden on her family.
However, she said a reasonable level of fear made a person feel responsible and encouraged them to work hard, provided it did not affect their mental health.
She said that even after passing an examination, she could not see any future ahead.
On the other hand, Farah Khan, the human resources manager of a leading Pakistani company, said employers valued people who faced difficulties, learned from them and moved forward rather than those with an entirely flawless record.
According to her, perseverance and the ability to adapt to circumstances were more valuable than a continuous record of success.
People in society are often judged on the basis of their success, profession and financial status, causing young people to fear criticism, disappointment and embarrassment. Social media has also increased this pressure, with posts showcasing daily successes forcing young people to make unnecessary comparisons with others.
The fear of failure is not limited to education but also affects young people in job selection, interviews, businesses, relationships and social interactions. Saima Nozain said young female students should pursue cooking and chef training as there was considerable demand in the field.

title: 136 year old Leh bridge hangs by a thread
description: 136 year old Leh bridge hangs by a thread
content:
Sources say historic bridge in Dhoke Ratta got damaged by recent floods
Recent monsoon rains have brought a 136-year-old wooden-and-iron bridge built during the British era on the verge of collapse, with fears that the historic Dhoke Ratta bridge over Nullah Leh could be swept away by any major flood.
The bridge, made of pure deodar wood and iron, has suffered extensive damage because of recent rains and flooding.
Residents fear that if the Archaeology Department, district administration and Rawalpindi Municipal Corporation fail to repair it immediately, the historic structure could fall into Nullah Leh, taking with it a part of the city's history.
The monsoon rains and severe flooding have damaged its century-old wooden structure, while the iron railings have rusted. Its floor has also broken at several places and parts of it have fallen into the nullah, making it dangerous even for pedestrians.
Dangerous landslides and soil erosion have also occurred around the bridge's foundations.
The plank bridge connecting Dhoke Ratta and Ganj Mandi is not merely a structure of wood and iron but a living witness to Rawalpindi's centuries-old history, culture and changing times.
It was once the only and busiest link between the two important commercial and residential centres of Ratta Amral and Ganj Mandi. Trade and daily necessities were transported through the bridge by horse carts and handcarts. The sounds of horses' hooves, coachmen and vendors were once part of the city's daily life.
The bridge kept commercial and social activity moving between the two areas. When the water of Nullah Leh was clean, people would stand on the bridge to watch it flow below, making it a symbol of Rawalpindi's romantic past.
The Ganj Mandi bridge is one of the oldest historic and cultural bridges over Nullah Leh. It was constructed with iron and strong deodar wood and is still locally known as the "Lakri Wala Pul" or wooden bridge.
British forces built it over Nullah Leh to connect the city with military barracks and railway quarters in Westridge.
During British rule, the area on the other side of the bridge was known as Sarai Beli Ram. A red-light area reportedly existed there before and after Partition until the 1960s, because of which the bridge became popularly known as "Chaklay Wala Pul".
The name has remained widely recognised in Rawalpindi for the past 136 years.

title: UN chief stresses smooth Lebanon pull out
description: UN chief stresses smooth Lebanon pull out
content:
The head of United Nations peacekeepers in Lebanon said on Saturday it was critical to ensure other UN agencies and Lebanese troops could assume the tasks carried out by the ?force before it begins withdrawing at the end of this year.
Major General Diodato Abagnara of Italy spoke to Reuters in southern Lebanon at a position operated by ?the UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL, which has been monitoring hostilities in southern Lebanon for nearly 50 years.
Since a new war erupted between Israel and Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah in March, the force has also provided security escorts for humanitarian aid convoys to residents in a small cluster of predominantly Christian southern Lebanese towns now encircled by Israeli troops. ?
Residents in much of the rest of southern Lebanon have been forcibly displaced by Israeli strikes and evacuation orders.
The UN Security Council has ordered UNIFIL to begin withdrawing at the end of 2026, triggering concerns over whether aid deliveries can continue and how the force can transfer its positions to Lebanese troops.
"There are other United Nations entities here in the south, and ?so what is very important for us (is) to conduct a very smooth transition to different entities, or for the future of a new mission," Abagnara told Reuters.
He said UNIFIL was already working with the UN's country team to ensure humanitarian assistance in Israeli-occupied areas and information sharing with the Lebanese army about "sensitive areas (and) how they can manage this situation."
Abagnara acknowledged that it could be "very difficult" to hand over some of UNIFIL's posts to Lebanese troops given that more than half lie within areas now controlled by Israeli troops.
Diplomats worry UNIFIL's departure will mean an end to the UN's "eyes and ears" in southern Lebanon.
Abagnara spoke to Reuters at a position overlooking Mansouri, a town where Israeli forces have been carrying out demolitions since ordering residents to leave in June, despite a ceasefire.
Reuters reporters could see excavators in the town knocking down trees and multi-storey homes. Abagnara described demolitions as "another violation" of UN Security Council resolutions on Lebanon. Israel's military has said it is destroying Hezbollah infrastructure across southern Lebanon.
As a US-backed plan for Lebanon's army to disarm Hezbollah and take control of southern Lebanon has stalled, a diplomatic scramble is underway to address the vacuum that will be left by UNIFIL's withdrawal. Lebanon wants an extension.

The bill, now called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," to honor the South Carolina Republican who died in July, passed the House of Representatives on Wednesday and the Senate last month. Graham, a longtime Russia hawk, was a staunch backer of the legislation.

title: Trump deal won t compromise  sovereignty
description: Trump deal won t compromise  sovereignty
content:
Denmark, Greenland and US reach agreement on Greenland security; signing expected next week
Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with ?the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington "permanent control" over the Arctic island's security, leaving its precise scope unclear.
The United States, Denmark and Greenland said late ?on Friday they had reached an agreement for the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island.
Key details of the ?agreement have not been made public, including the scale of US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.
Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump's threats to seize control of Greenland.
"Next week could be a good ?week - for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States," Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said in a statement posted on Facebook on Saturday.
"A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe - while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom's red lines," he said.
But some residents in Greenland's capital Nuuk expressed scepticism about closer ties with ?Washington.
"The US should not control Greenland. I think it's better if we have cooperation with NATO," said Jakob Ludvigsen, 65. "Trump should stay far, far, far away from Greenland," Marianne Hansen, a 71-year-old retired chef, told Reuters in Nuuk.
"He should not expect our children and grandchildren to become Americans in the future." Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland is not for sale.

title: France s debt climbs to highest since 1995  ministry
description: France s debt climbs to highest since 1995  ministry
content:
France's debt mountain is growing and will this year be at its highest level since 1995 because of a soaring deficit, the country's finance ministry said Saturday.
A ministry source told reporters the public debt will reach 119.3 percent of GDP in 2026 and 121.7 percent in 2027 -- double the 60-percent-of-GDP reference limit EU member countries are required to aim for.
Those debt figures will set records since the state statistics agency INSEE started recording debt levels under the current methodology in late 1995.
The source said the rise in France's debt was "automatic" as "a consequence of a deficit that remains high".
Under EU rules, the public deficit -- the annual shortfall of revenue to spending -- is meant to be no more than three percent of GDP.
But last year, it came in at 5.1 percent of GDP, and the government forecasts it will hit 5.4 percent this year.
France, which has been under special EU monitoring for the past two years because of those high figures, expects its deficit to drop to five percent next year -- when it holds elections to choose its next president and government.
The government has submitted its draft 2027 budget measures to an independent fiscal watchdog, the High Council of Public Finances, to evaluate their viability in macroeconomic terms.
Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu said on Thursday as he outlined the draft budget that the government planned to make adjustments and cuts worth 54 billion euros ($62 billion) in the 2027 budget.
But with elections on the horizon, he left it to parliament to decide some of the more sensitive measures, such as a government proposal to reduce tax breaks for pensioners.

title: Trump says CNN  Politico  MS NOW banned from White House
description: Trump says CNN  Politico  MS NOW banned from White House
content:
US President Donald Trump said Friday he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news" about his administration.
The 80-year-old Republican -- who has long had a fiery relationship with the media -- warned that other outlets could face a similar fate but did not say which ones.
The move by Trump drew immediate accusations that it was unconstitutional and would be thrown out by the courts, while the impacted news outlets said they would not be cowed.
"I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW...and Politico...from the White House as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
Trump did not say what prompted the move but added that "media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States."
Later in the Oval Office, Trump told reporters: "I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they're going to write false stories all the time."
Asked if any particular stories had sparked the ban, he replied: "It's really just cumulative stories over the last two years."
"You get sick of it," he said. "They purposely write negative news, and they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration."
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has brought in tight restrictions at the Pentagon, backed Trump's new ban and accused the outlets of having "endangered troops" with unspecified stories.
Journalists for broadcasters CNN and MS NOW -- which was until recently known as MSNBC -- and Politico remained on White House premises following Trump's announcement.
Reporters for the two TV news channels could still be seen broadcasting from their stations on the White House driveway.
CNN said Trump's ban was an "illegal assault" on US press freedom, adding that its reporting was "fair and accurate" and was protected under the US Constitution.
Politico vowed Friday to "vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them."
The White House Correspondents Association -- the independent body representing journalists covering the presidency -- said it "stands in defense" of the journalists "who are being singled out for doing their jobs."
Both of Trump's White House terms have seen him lash out repeatedly at media whose coverage displeases him.
He has filed multiple defamation suits against news outlets, attacked the press on Truth Social and verbally assaulted several reporters, notably women, including CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins.

title: Govt opens talks with opposition
description: Naqvi asked Raja Nasir to meet PM Shehbaz  saying that meeting could pave way for relief for Imran Khan  Bushra Bibi
content:
Naqvi asked Raja Nasir to meet PM Shehbaz, saying that meeting could pave way for relief for Imran Khan, Bushra Bibi
Government-opposition contacts intensified on Saturday over the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's (PTI) September 27 protest as Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas confirmed a meeting with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi but said that only PTI founder Imran Khan could decide whether the planned long march would be postponed.
The contact, which took place at Naqvi's request, focused on Imran Khan's situation and the September 27 protest.
Sources said PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan helped arrange the meeting and also attended it, while Raja Nasir publicly maintained that no one could postpone the protest without first meeting Imran.
Nasir said the meeting had taken place at Naqvi's request and that he had not approached anyone for it.
According to sources, the meeting lasted around one hour and 15 minutes and was held at the residence of one of Raja Nasir's relatives. Gohar was also present, the sources said.
Nasir confirmed that matters relating to the PTI founder had been discussed, adding that there had also been detailed talks on the long march and other issues concerning Imran.
According to sources, Naqvi asked Raja Nasir to meet Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, saying that the meeting could pave the way for relief for Imran Khan and Bushra Bibi.
The interior minister also sought the cancellation of the September 27 protest, sources said.
He maintained that negotiations would require the resumption of meetings with Imran and that the PTI leadership should consult him directly before deciding whether to withdraw the protest call.
According to the sources, Naqvi told Raja Nasir that the opposition should arrange a meeting with Imran so that he could be consulted over calling off the protest.
He also conveyed the position that once the call was withdrawn, it should remain withdrawn and the protest should not be revived.
Raja Nasir also arranged a telephone conversation between Naqvi and Tehreek-e-Tahafuz-e-Aain Pakistan (TTAP) chief Mahmood Khan Achakzai, according to the sources.
The sources said the message conveyed during the contact was that a meeting with Imran should be facilitated so that he could be consulted on whether the protest call should be withdrawn.
Gohar subsequently met Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi over the matter, the sources said, while consultations regarding the September 27 protest were also held on Monday and Tuesday.
However, opposition alliance sources said the contacts produced no final progress on the September 27 protest and did not prove particularly meaningful in terms of reaching an agreement.
Similarly, in a post on X on Saturday, Raja Nasir said Naqvi had called on him and that he had told the interior minister that only Imran could postpone the September 27 protest.
TTAP spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Ahmed Yousufzai said the meeting had been held on September 14 on Naqvi's request and that Raja Nasir and Gohar had attended it on behalf of the opposition.
Responding to questions after a press conference at Khyber Pakhtunkhwa House in Islamabad, Raja Nasir said: "He (Naqvi) came to meet [us]. We have stated our stance and they will find out that no individual can postpone the September 27 march without a meeting with Imran Khan sahib."
He asserted, "Imran Khan cannot be minused; we will not let Imran Khan sahib be minused. Therefore, no issue can be resolved without a meeting with Imran Khan sahib."
During the press conference, Raja Nasir said providing basic facilities to the people and protecting their constitutional rights were major issues. He said that even a senior federal minister had acknowledged that the country's system had "collapsed".
TTAP leader and former Sindh governor Mohammad Zubair said there was a wide gap between the lifestyle of the ruling elite and the economic difficulties faced by ordinary citizens.
He claimed that poverty, unemployment and inflation had increased compared with four and a half years ago.
Zubair said electricity prices had risen two to threefold, while people had made sacrifices in the hope that economic conditions would improve.
PTI leader and former K-P finance minister Taimur Saleem Jhagra criticised government spending, questioning the reported purchase of a jet costing Rs10 billion and expenditure on official and private travel.
He said every rupee of public money should be accounted for and questioned why relief was not being provided to people facing rising fuel prices.
Against this backdrop, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi met Raja Nasir and Mahmood Khan Achakzai in Islamabad on Saturday for further consultations on the September 27 protest.
TTAP spokesperson Hussain Ahmed Yousafzai was also present.
According to the opposition alliance, the meeting covered detailed political consultations on the September 27 call, including the future course of action, political strategy and ways of advancing the democratic struggle.
The leaders discussed taking the protest call forward as an "effective and organised political struggle for upholding the supremacy of the Constitution, democratic rights, provincial rights, and the protection of the public mandate".
The meeting was the second between the three leaders this week. They had also met on Thursday, shortly after Afridi returned from his visit to Punjab, with the September 27 protest among the issues discussed.
