title: Makkah pact being  institutionalised
description: Makkah pact being  institutionalised
content:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that the Makkah defence alliance involving Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia is at an advanced stage, with the establishment of its headquarters and deployment of personnel as the remaining steps towards its institutionalisation, describing it as a potentially "game-changing platform".
Signed by Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia on August 7, the pact is based on the principles of shared responsibility and regional ownership amid growing regional and global instability. The agreement aims to promote security, peace, stability and prosperity while strengthening collective deterrence.
Under the agreement, an attack against any one of the signatory states will be considered an attack against all parties.
Speaking in a live interview on Turkish broadcaster NTV, Fidan said there was "very strong will" behind the alliance and expressed confidence that further discussions would take place on expanding it to include other countries in the region.
"The Makkah alliance is at a good stage, and there's a very strong will behind it," Fidan said. "The only stage remaining now is to deploy personnel and establish its headquarters."
He said the alliance could subsequently be expanded. "I believe that once steps toward institutionalisation are taken, further talks will be held on bringing in new allies from the region."
Fidan described the alliance as a potentially significant regional platform. "The Makkah alliance will be a very game-changing platform."
Commenting on Houthi attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, the Turkish foreign minister said Ankara stood in solidarity with Riyadh over what he described as attacks on its territorial integrity.
"We're now seeing very serious attacks targeting Saudi Arabia's territorial integrity. We stand in solidarity on this issue," he said.
The foreign minister said Saudi Arabia's territorial integrity and sovereignty had come under serious attack, adding that Türkiye was bound by its alliance commitments.
"Saudi Arabia may need military-level support. As the Makkah alliance, we will take this up with Pakistan and can provide the necessary technical support," he said.
He said Türkiye's Foreign Ministry had condemned the attacks on oil infrastructure near Makkah, adding that the alliance was closely monitoring the situation. Any military support, he noted, would likely focus on specific technical areas.
Fidan also said Saudi Arabia should not be drawn into the conflict between Iran and the United States.
"We won't allow this to be made part of the ongoing conflict between Iran and the US. Saudi Arabia should be kept out of this," he said.
Responding to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's statements targeting Türkiye, Fidan said the Israeli leader was seeking to preserve his political position at home.
"Netanyahu is declaring himself indispensable and pursuing various means to remain in power and strengthen his political position at home," he said.
He warned that Israel would face growing isolation under Netanyahu's policies. "Israel will not only grow increasingly isolated, but will also pay the price for this together with Netanyahu."
"Under Netanyahu's policies, Israel is a threat to the world," he added.
On efforts to resolve the crisis around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, Fidan said several initiatives were under way but needed to produce concrete outcomes through the parties concerned.
"There are many initiatives, but these initiatives need to produce certain outcomes through the relevant parties," he said.

title: Govt lifts five litre fuel relief ceiling
description: Govt lifts five litre fuel relief ceiling
content:
Registration is continuing nationwide via SMS to 9771
The government on Saturday moved to widen and streamline Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's fuel relief scheme, directing that every operational fuel station be brought onto the system while permanently closed and diesel-only outlets are removed, as the premier further eased the token structure to facilitate beneficiaries.
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar issued the directions while chairing a meeting of the National Steering Committee on Fuel Subsidy, while Information Technology Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja announced that the five-litre petrol limit linked to a single token had been abolished and registration messages would be made completely free.
"Every fuel station which is open and operating" should be brought onto the system, while stations found permanently closed or dealing exclusively in diesel should be identified and removed from the list, the statement quoted Dar as saying.
The committee was informed that an overwhelming majority of fuel stations across the country were now operational on the system and that citizens were redeeming fuel tokens.
Registration is continuing nationwide via SMS to 9771.
The committee also approved the redemption of fuel tokens through SMS at stations in areas without internet connectivity. Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) and the provinces were asked to furnish lists of such stations so that they could be brought onto the scheme without delay.
The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) informed the committee that all payment claims received over the past three days had been settled in full, with claims received each day processed on the same day.
Dar appreciated the efforts of the provincial administrations and the cooperation extended by the SBP, stressing that "the relief must continue to reach the intended beneficiaries without hindrance".
Separately, Shaza Fatima said Prime Minister Shehbaz had announced that registration messages for eligible individuals would be completely free and that the five-litre petrol limit on a single token had been abolished.
She said motorcyclists, as well as owners of Qingqis and rickshaws who purchased less than five litres of petrol, would receive Rs500 in relief within a week.
The Prime Minister's Office Media Wing, in a press release issued on Saturday, said: "Upon the prime minister's instructions, motorcyclists, as well as owners of Qingqis and rickshaws who purchase less than five litres of petrol, will also be entitled to a discount of Rs 500 against a single token within a week."
One token will be issued every week, with a total of four tokens to be issued in a month.
Users of vehicles up to 800cc will continue to receive a discount of Rs100 per litre on 10 litres of petrol every 10 days, according to the earlier decision. Accordingly, three tokens for 10 litres of petrol will be issued each month.
The Prime Minister's Special Relief Scheme has been successfully rolled out across Pakistan, with petrol being provided at a subsidised rate of Rs100 per litre under the scheme.
Prime Minister Shehbaz is personally monitoring every aspect of the relief scheme and has directed that its outreach be further expanded.
He has also instructed the relevant authorities to ensure that the petrol subsidy is provided to beneficiaries with dignity, convenience and without any hurdles.
In light of feedback received from across the country, the prime minister took another decision to further facilitate beneficiaries of the scheme.
Shaza Fatima said 91.6% of registrations under the scheme were for two- and three-wheelers, while vehicles of up to 800cc accounted for 8.4% of registrations.
She said 1,493,848 citizens had so far been issued fuel tokens under the scheme, while 655,067 citizens had already received fuel.
The federal minister appealed to the public not to share their personal information with anyone to protect themselves from fraud.
The prime minister had earlier directed that 20-year-old motorcycles, rickshaws and Qingqi rickshaws be included in the fuel relief scheme, and implementation of the decision had taken place.
All motorcycles, rickshaws and Qingqi rickshaws registered on or after January 1, 2006, are now eligible for registration under the Prime Minister's Fuel Relief Scheme.

title: Twin cities on tenterhooks as JI vows  sea of people
description: Twin cities on tenterhooks as JI vows  sea of people
content:
Party's talks with govt fail to produce breakthrough
The federal capital braces for long marches, putting the government, administration and police in a tight situation, with authorities deciding to close all educational institutions, colleges and universities, hotels, motels, rest houses and inns in Rawalpindi from next week
The first in a series of long marches on the federal capital will be led by JI Emir Hafiz Naeem-ur-Rehman, after the fifth round of talks between the government and Jamaat-e-Islami ended without a final agreement on the party's demands, including the withdrawal of the petroleum levy, as differences over its planned long march remained unresolved.
The government delegation asked the JI to postpone the long march in view of security threats, while the party maintained that the protest would continue until the petroleum levy was withdrawn.
The talks were held at JI headquarters in Mansoorah. The government team comprised Federal Minister Ahsan Iqbal, Senator Rana Sanaullah and Punjab Minister Khawaja Salman Rafique. The JI delegation included Deputy Emir Liaqat Baloch, acting Secretary General Nazir Ahmad Janjua, Special Assistant Umair Idrees, JI Lahore Emir Ziauddin Ansari and Information Secretary Shakeel Ahmed Tarabi.
During the meeting, the government delegation cited security concerns and requested the JI to defer the long march. Government representatives also assured the party that practical measures would be taken soon to provide significant relief to the public.
The government team said Pakistan was facing pressure from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), adding that an IMF delegation was also expected to visit the country soon.
Liaqat Baloch said the long march would remain necessary until the petroleum levy was abolished. He called on the government to take practical steps to address public demands, warning that protests and the long march would proceed otherwise.
According to Baloch, the "Super Long March" would begin from Karachi on Sunday under the leadership of JI Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman, as scheduled.
Lights and mobile internet services will be shut down during the long marches, while all 1,500 cameras installed under the Safe City project in Rawalpindi have been activated to monitor protesters.
Transport and goods transport terminals will also remain completely closed, while Metro Bus and Green Electric Bus services will remain suspended.
Markets and wholesale markets across the city will also be closed. Large spiked containers, fitted with eight-inch spikes, have started being installed at entry points of the twin cities, including Faizabad, Chungi No. 26, Rawat, Chakri, Adiala Road, Pirwadhai, Bharakahu and 17-Mile, with entry routes being sealed. Monitoring will also be carried out through drones.
Emergency has been imposed at all hospitals in the twin cities and leaves of doctors, nurses and paramedical staff have been cancelled.
Fresh contingents of Rangers and Punjab Constabulary have been called in. Thousands of rubber bullets and tear-gas shells have been supplied to Rawalpindi and Islamabad police.
Attock police have been provided heavy Rangers contingents, armoured vehicles, prison vans, heavy weapons and personnel, who will assume duties on Wednesday and Thursday. The central long march coming from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa will be stopped at all costs, officials said.
The Jamaat-i-Islami long march will start from Karachi on Sunday, Sept 20, while caravans from all six districts of Rawalpindi division will also start reaching Liaquat Bagh from Sunday. Jamaat-i-Islami emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman will leave Karachi for Rawalpindi by train on Sunday, with his train march scheduled to reach Rawalpindi on Tuesday, Sept 22.
Daily protest sit-ins will continue in Rawalpindi until his arrival.
Due to road closures and the large number of spiked containers being installed at different places, all business, commercial and social activities in Rawalpindi will remain paralysed from Monday, Sept 21 to Sept 27.

title: Who trains the mind
description: Pakistan trains athletes for the physical demands of sport  but mental preparation remains an uneven part of the system
content:
Pakistan trains athletes for the physical demands of sport but mental preparation remains an uneven part of the system
The night before Pakistan’s horseback archery team was due to compete at the World Nomad Games, Arshaq Naeem was carrying more than the pressure of hitting a target from a moving horse.
There were expectations, doubts and, as he puts it, a “cocktail of emotions”. Wearing Pakistan’s colours on a world stage was a privilege, but for the captain of the horseback archery team, it also brought what he describes as a considerable mental toll.
Training had prepared him for the physical challenge. Horseback archery demands balance and stamina while keeping an eye on the target as the horse strides forward, leaving the rider only seconds to aim and release the arrow. But training could not entirely recreate what awaited him on competition day.
“In training, when there is no external pressure or audience, nerves are relatively calm,” says Naeem. “But the match-day experience is quite different. On match day you have just one chance. Your every move counts towards your final score.”
That difference had troubled him before. Until the World Nomad Games, Naeem had never worked with a sports psychologist. He had relied on his coach and his own understanding to build what he calls his “psychological stamina”. What he found particularly difficult was the sudden strain that could arrive on competition day, something he says he did not know how to manage.
It returned on the first day of the Nomad Games.
As athletes prepared to compete, Naeem felt a sudden surge of self-doubt. This time, however, sports psychologist Mohsin Nawaz was with the Pakistani contingent. He reminded Naeem of the hours he had spent practising. Together, they mentally rehearsed what could go wrong while he was shooting and considered how he might respond to different situations. Naeem also used positive self-talk and box breathing before mounting his horse.
A sports psychologist's presence at the World Nomad Games itself was unusual. The Traditional Sports and Games Pakistan Association had, for the first time, formally appointed a sports psychologist to work with its national contingent. For a support role that has long sat alongside coaches, physiotherapists and conditioning staff in elite sport elsewhere in the world, sports psychology remains far less routinely embedded across Pakistan's sporting structure.
For Nawaz, the difference between practice and competition is not simply the presence of a scoreboard. An athlete can spend months repeating the same movement in training, know the technique and possess the physical ability to execute it, yet find that the body responds differently when the same movement has to be performed with an audience watching and a result depending on it.
“There are a number of psychophysiological changes that take place when suddenly an athlete has to perform under pressure,” says Nawaz. “This pressure cannot be copied in practice. It is exclusive to match day.”
He recalls working with an athlete who possessed considerable physical strength, consistently performed well in practice and knew the techniques required of him. Yet when the final selection came, he failed to make the team.
“It was quite unexpected for me that such an excellent athlete would fail the final selection test,” says Nawaz. When the two sat down for a mental assessment, he says they discovered a deeper fear: the athlete had convinced himself that something would go wrong at the last moment and he would not be selected.
“This belief triggered an uncontrollable amount of anxiety in him, and he could not deliver what he had learnt in practice,” says Nawaz. They worked on reconstructing that belief and, according to Nawaz, when the athlete next appeared for selection, he made the team.
Naeem knew the difference between training and competition. “It happens quite often that while shooting the arrow, all of a sudden the nerves get triggered,” he says. “It happens rarely in training when there is no external pressure or audience and the nerves are relatively calm. But the match-day experience is quite different. Simply saying ‘Do not take pressure’ does not work at all,” he says. Mental toughness, he argues, has to be practised rather than demanded.
For Naeem, part of the training for mental grit involved examining the conversation taking place inside his own head. When Naeem began analysing those thoughts, he recognised a negative internal dialogue that was contributing to sudden bursts of anxiety. Before mounting, at the Nomad Games, he used positive self-talk and box breathing. He and Nawaz also mentally rehearsed possible problems he could encounter while shooting and considered alternative responses.
The objective was not to make the pressure disappear. It was to prepare Naeem for what to do when it arrived.
The World Nomad Games did more than introduce Naeem to a different way of handling competition pressure. They also made him question why that training had come so late.
Before reaching the international stage, he had never had access to a sports psychologist through an academy, club or domestic competition. Until then, he says, he had largely relied on his coach and his own experiences to work out how to handle the mental side of the sport.
“Now that I have met a sports psychologist, I believe I was missing out on a major valuable part of performance,” says Naeem. “I had little idea how to deal with the cocktail of mental challenges that I had previously experienced.”
Looking back, he no longer sees psychological preparation as something an athlete should encounter only when an international competition is approaching.
“Access to a sports psychologist is not an option, but in fact is as important as physical training,” he says. “Mental training starts much before the actual competition, or even before the start of your sports career.”
It is an argument Professor Dr Ejaz Asghar, Dean of the School of Sports, Rehabilitation and Allied Sciences at the Health Services Academy in Islamabad, makes even more strongly. Asghar believes psychological preparation should begin alongside an athlete’s technical and physical development, rather than being introduced once a player has already reached a national camp. “Mental preparation is needed from the beginning of the practice sessions,” he says. “Unless you practise these mental rehearsals, you can’t excel.”
The distinction is important because sports psychology, Asghar says, is still sometimes misunderstood as something an athlete needs only when there is a mental health problem. “It’s a misconception,” he says. Athletes practise physical, technical and tactical skills repeatedly until they become familiar with them; he argues psychological skills should be approached in much the same way. “You should prepare yourself mentally with regard to your mental toughness, and it must be a part of your regular daily training.”
That means the question of access cannot begin and end with Pakistan’s national teams. An athlete may spend years moving through academies, clubs and domestic competitions before reaching a national camp. By then, Asghar argues, much of the athlete’s behaviour under pressure has already been shaped.
Even if a sports psychologist is introduced at national level, he says, there is still work that can be done. During a national camp, Asghar suggests a series of sessions could introduce athletes to techniques such as deep breathing, imagery, visualisation and progressive muscular relaxation. But he sees that as an intervention rather than a substitute for years of preparation.
“Sports psychologists should be part of your team, just like coaches, trainers, fitness trainers and conditioning coaches,” says the sports psychologist who is currently with the Chess team in Uzbekistan. “That’s the way we can enhance regular performance and build teamwork as well.”
Nawaz makes a similar argument about where that support should exist. He wants access to sports psychologists not only in national federations, but in sports academies, clubs and universities.
“It is a mental support system that is necessary before the game, during the game and after the game,” says Nawaz, because the psychological demands on an athlete do not suddenly begin when they walk into an international arena.
Asghar is currently working as a mental trainer with Pakistan’s national rifle shooting team. He says he has been holding regular sessions with the shooters, including during their preparation for the Asian Games.
“They are practising regularly. They are taking advice and guidelines regarding this on a regular basis,” says Asghar, who believes the arrangement should not be unusual. “Sports psychologists should be part of your team, just like coaches, trainers, fitness trainers and conditioning coaches.”
For Olympian shooter Kishmala Talat, the support comes after years in which mental preparation was present, but was not a separate, structured part of her training. As a young shooter, she says, much of her understanding of pressure and nervousness came through competing, making mistakes and learning from experience.
That has changed ahead of the Asian Games. Talat says the National Rifle Association of Pakistan and Army Marksmanship Unit have provided the shooters with access to a qualified sports psychologist and structured mental-performance training.
The need for it is particularly apparent in a sport where even a change in breathing, heartbeat or concentration can affect the execution of a shot. Talat says nervousness can make her heartbeat more noticeable and alter her breathing and concentration. The challenge is not necessarily to eliminate those nerves, but to prevent them from affecting what comes next. “If I carry one bad shot into the next shot, then one mistake can become two, three or more,” she says.
Looking back at her progression from domestic competition to the Olympics, Talat believes this kind of preparation should begin much earlier. “I definitely think mental performance should be developed alongside technical and physical skills from the academy level,” she says.
The contrast within the same Asian Games contingent illustrates how uneven access can be. Shooting has incorporated mental-performance support into its preparation, while no sports psychologist has been identified with the wider Pakistan contingent.
Elsewhere, psychological support is appearing more explicitly in preparations for the same Games. India is travelling with a large sports-science support setup, with mental-health experts included alongside doctors and physiotherapists. Oman’s men’s hockey team, which will face Pakistan in the group stage, has psychologist Abdullah al Noufali listed among its support staff, while Qatar’s shooting team has also been preparing with a specialist sports psychologist as part of its technical and mental preparation for major competitions, including the Asian Games.
Pakistan is not entirely outside this shift. Nawaz’s appointment for the World Nomad Games gave traditional-sports athletes access to structured psychological preparation, while Pakistan cricket has introduced psychological assessment and mental-skills work at youth level. Hockey, too, has moved towards incorporating sports psychology into its high-performance setup.
For Nawaz, though, these individual appointments do not yet amount to consistent access across Pakistani sport. “Pakistani athletes are still struggling with their access to a sports psychologist domestically and internationally,” he says, arguing that representation remains limited.
That perhaps leaves Pakistan somewhere between recognition and routine. Sports psychology is no longer entirely absent from the system: a horseback archer can work with Nawaz, shooters can receive structured mental-performance support and younger cricketers can be introduced to mental-performance work. The question is whether an athlete receives that support because it is considered a normal part of development, or simply because they happen to belong to a team that has decided to provide it.
For Naeem, the value of psychological preparation became clearer only after he had experienced both sides of it. For much of his career, pressure was something he had learnt to deal with largely through experience, his coach and whatever methods he could develop himself. At the World Nomad Games, for the first time, there was someone specifically responsible for helping him understand what was happening when those nerves arrived.
The difference was not that he stopped feeling them.
On the first day of competition, the self-doubt still came. There was still anxiety before mounting the horse, still the knowledge that one mistake could affect his score. What had changed was his response. He could slow his breathing, recognise the negative conversation beginning inside his head and return to the situations he and Nawaz had already rehearsed.
It is a relatively small change in the machinery surrounding an athlete: another specialist alongside the people responsible for technique, fitness, conditioning and recovery. But for Naeem, it changed how he understood preparation itself.
“Access to the sports psychologist is not an option,” he says. “It is as important as physical training, because mental training starts much before the actual competition.”
For Pakistan, perhaps that is where the larger question now sits. There are signs that the mind is beginning to find a place in the country's sporting setup, from shooters receiving structured mental-performance training ahead of the Asian Games to young cricketers being introduced to such work earlier in their development. But Kishmala’s and Naeem’s experiences also show how much athletes can learn through competition before that structured support arrives. The question remains not whether they can learn to handle pressure, but how far they must travel in their careers before someone teaches them how.

title: Mind your digital manners
description: From one word replies to AI written emotions  smartphones have altered etiquette  It s time we rewrote it   with a little more consideration
content:
From one-word replies to AI-written emotions, smartphones altered etiquette. Let's rewrite it with a little more care
Every generation inherits a code of manners that fit perfectly into the society. Ours happens to fit neatly inside a smartphone. As our lives have migrated online, the distinction between acceptable and inconsiderate behaviour has grown hazy, shaped by convenience, constant connectivity and an ever-present screen. Yet technology has not abolished etiquette; it has merely created a new one that many of us are still failing to observe.
Do you keep looking at your screen in one-on-one meetings? Randomly make promises to connect with people, provide information or share numbers but never follow through? Do you have loud conversations on your phone in the doctor’s waiting room or in a queue at the checkout? If you answered yes to two out of the three of the above questions, you need to brush up your manners.
Do you have the remarkable ability of ending a conversation without beginning it? Single word responses like yes, not, sure, done and noted give the impression that you are insanely busy. One kind of response cannot be used for everyone. Depending on who you are replying to, an appropriate one liner would be much appreciated. Promise it won’t keep you away from scrolling for longer than 30 seconds.
Then there is overdependence on texting. There is a colleague who cannot seem to get up from her desk and walk over to mine. Whether it is a work-related query or something as mundane as asking if I have a safety pin, it arrives as a message on my phone. Never mind that I am sitting barely a few metres away and fully visible from where she is. In an age of instant communication, we seem to have forgotten that not every interaction requires a screen. Sometimes, the shortest distance between two people is not Wi-Fi, but simply getting out of one's chair. Not only is it good for her/his blood circulation to get up and take a few steps, the request would also get a better response as one registers the effort made.
Why is there always a dog barking, a child chattering incessantly, or the relentless whirr of a blender coming through someone's unmuted microphone during a Zoom or Google Meet? If five other people can hear the soundtrack to your home, your microphone probably shouldn't be on. Muting yourself isn't just a technical feature; it's basic digital courtesy.
I once received an unexpected lesson in public etiquette from a well-known television actress. I was at a salon when I sent an urgent voice note that lasted no more than 10 seconds. The beautician was working on my face, so typing wasn't exactly an option. "Please stop this now. We don't want to hear your plans," she declared, loudly enough for everyone in the salon to hear. I caught her eye in the mirror, slightly embarrassed. Barely half a minute later, she launched into a booming phone conversation, updating someone on every detail of her recently completed Umrah. Apparently, her conversation had diplomatic immunity. Mine did not.
It reminded me of the countless people who have never mastered one of the simplest phrases in the English language: "I'll call you back." Instead, they happily treat buses, cafés, waiting rooms and airport lounges as extensions of their living rooms, sharing every intimate detail with an unwilling audience. We learn about a daughter-in-law's difficult C-section, the family's holiday itinerary as it's being negotiated with a travel agent, or the mysterious leak in someone's bathroom plumbing.
Walking around with a Bluetooth earpiece permanently lodged in one ear while carrying on a phone conversation as you interact with people serving you is one of modern life's quieter acts of discourtesy. You are asking the supermarket assistant where the cereal is, paying the cashier, ordering a coffee, handing over your boarding pass to an airline agent, checking into a hotel, speaking to a pharmacist, asking a security guard for directions or thanking the courier at your gate—all while continuing a conversation with someone else. It sends an unmistakable message: the person in front of me is less important than the one in my ear.
Yet even these accidental broadcasters are easier to tolerate than the people who insist on playing videos, reels, voice notes or music at full volume in public spaces. Picnic buses, cafés, restaurants, hospital waiting rooms—apparently no place is too sacred for an unsolicited soundtrack. Headphones exist. So does consideration.
Unless the call is a genuine emergency, the polite thing to do is simple. Pause the conversation for 30 seconds. Look up. Make eye contact. Say "please" and "thank you." Give the person helping you your full attention before returning to your call. The world is not your hands-free headset. The people serving you deserve your attention, not just your transaction.
Voice notes, however, are a different ball game altogether. There are times when they make perfect sense. Perhaps you're driving, your hands are occupied, or you're walking on the street and simply can't type or make your mobile available for a quick snatching incident. Maybe your reply is too long to thumb out on a tiny keyboard, so speaking it feels quicker and more natural.
But voice notes come with their own etiquette. The very short ones—"Yep," "Okay," "On my way"—are almost pointless. It would have taken less time to type them than to record, send and make someone else press play. The marathon voice notes are no better. Five minutes of rambling thoughts, side stories and forgotten points are really saying, "I'm too busy to type this, but you can spare the time to listen, remember it all and then reply." You've saved yourself time by spending someone else's.
The polite approach is simple. If it's brief, type it. If it's long, ask first: "Is now a good time for a voice note?" Better still, organise your thoughts before you hit record, keep it concise, and if the conversation is becoming complicated, pick up the phone instead. Some things are meant to be conversations, not podcasts.
Adding a person to your Whatsapp group without their consent is an invasion of privacy. Suddenly you start receiving an avalanche of texts from people you don’t even know. Also people don’t use Whatsapp groups for their specific purpose. They want the entire group of God knows how many people to appreciate what you share, simply because you subscribe to that thought, humour or opinion. The impulse to share must be controlled, to show respect for other people’s time and phone space. Does it occur to you how you are mindlessly cluttering their digital space, their phone data? Apparently not.
For all the time you spend with your phone and on your phone, have the courage to decline when you don’t plan on being part of an activity or a social event. It takes two seconds, but it is better than leaving them hanging and wondering if you have seen the message, thought about it, have the will to join in or not.
It is also polite to let people know why you have decided to leave a certain group.
Likewise, also control the urge to put up and share every mundane experience with your child, BFF or bae, however life altering it might have been for you. People can live without the picture of your perfectly served plate of daal-chawal or grilled chicken and veggies for that matter.
Which brings us to weddings that have now become vulnerable to creating content for the 200 hundred or so guests. Actually, the same extends to conferences and other work, social and professional events. You are a participant, or a guest, so don’t try to volunteer your endeavours as their self-employed production or PR team. You don’t have to film every detail. Recently, at a wedding and a conference, my toes were crushed quite a few times when ardent social media lovers, v-loggers and You-Tubers made a beeline for just about anything they thought can be filmed or recorded, irrespective of whose view they were blocking, whose feet they were stepping on, literally, in order to capture content for their feeds.
Guest etiquette at a wedding means remembering that you are there to witness, support and add warmth to the day, and that is where it ends. A selfie with the newly-married couple is just about fine, as long as you are not including images of random people who may not want to be part of your digital life.
Another highly irritating, invasive and rude behaviour here is that when people are recording, they are also catching and later broadcasting private conversations in the background.
Documenting other people’s children, however cute they might be, is a big no-no. They are children and not poodles in a dog-show. Are you quite sure their parents are happy with what you are posting about their kids online? Kids being innocent and clueless and may not object but it is important to be aware of your responsibility around your and other people’s kids.
Time for a confession. I once used AI to write a condolence message.
It was for my daughter's mother-in-law after the death of her ex-husband—my daughter's father-in-law—a man who had spent years squandering the family's wealth on addiction. I was paralysed by writer's block. It was one of those impossible moments where grief, relief, anger and sadness all occupied the same space. What do you say when someone has died after years of causing pain, and everyone had, in quieter moments, wished for the suffering to end long before it did?
I couldn't find the words, so I borrowed them. AI did what it does best: it produced something eloquent, measured and compassionate. It helped me over a hurdle I simply couldn't clear that day.
But I have never quite shaken the guilt. Some things should never be outsourced. A condolence message is one of them. It doesn't have to be beautifully written or grammatically perfect. It doesn't even have to be profound. It simply has to sound like you. A few heartfelt, imperfect sentences carry far more comfort than a flawlessly crafted paragraph generated by a machine. In the moments that matter most, people deserve your voice, not your algorithm.
Smartphones did not kill good manners. They simply exposed where they were missing. Technology has made communication faster, easier and more convenient, but convenience should never come at the expense of consideration. Behind every text, voice note, Zoom call, WhatsApp group and Instagram story is a real person with limited time, attention and patience.
Good digital etiquette isn't about learning new rules. It's about applying the old ones in new places. Look up from your phone. Wear your headphones. Mute your microphone. Ask before you post someone else's photograph. Decline an invitation if you're not going. Write your own condolence message. And every once in a while, put the phone away and have a conversation with the person sitting right in front of you.
Manners have never gone out of fashion. They've just logged on.

title: PML N  PPP in race for AJK presidency
description: PML N  PPP in race for AJK presidency
content:
Naqi, Latif Akbar file nomination papers as Sept 24 election takes shape
The ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and opposition Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) formally entered the race for the Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) presidency on Saturday, filing nomination papers for their respective candidates and setting the stage for a September 24 contest.
PML-N nominee Dr Najeeb Naqi and PPP candidate Chaudhry Latif Akbar submitted their papers to Chief Election Commissioner Justice (retd) Ghulam Mustafa Mughal, who is also the returning officer for the presidential election. Both nomination papers were declared valid after scrutiny, clearing the way for the vote in the newly elected Legislative Assembly.
The office of the AJK president has remained vacant since January following the death of Barrister Sultan Mahmood.
Then-Legislative Assembly Speaker Chaudhry Latif Akbar had initially served as acting president. The role was subsequently assumed by incumbent Legislative Assembly Speaker Chaudhry Tariq Farooq after he was elected speaker on August 25.
Under the AJK Constitution, the president is elected by members of the Legislative Assembly by a majority of the total membership, in the manner prescribed by law.
The PML-N has fielded 62-year-old former minister Dr Najeeb Naqi. His nomination was proposed by senior PML-N leader and former prime minister Raja Farooq Haider and seconded by AJK Prime Minister Iftikhar Gillani.
The PPP has nominated 78-year-old Chaudhry Latif Akbar for the office. His nomination was proposed by former minister Deevan Ali Khan Chughtai and seconded by fellow legislator Sardar Mukhtar Ahmed Abbasi.
The PML-N candidate arrived at the Election Commission office accompanied by his proposer and seconder, along with several other party legislators, including PML-N's regional president Shah Ghulam Qadir.
Haider and Gillani first posed for photographs with the nomination paper as they appeared to formally hand it over to the chief election commissioner.
Subsequently, several other PML-N legislators, including the party president and ministers, also posed with the same nomination paper, standing alongside the chief election commissioner and appearing to hand it over to him in a similar manner.
Akbar was likewise accompanied by several PPP legislators, who posed for photographs during the submission of his nomination papers.
Candidates may withdraw their nomination papers by 11:30am on September 23, while polling will be held at the AJK Assembly Secretariat from 10am to 1pm on September 24. Counting of votes and announcement of the result will follow on the same day.

title: SC draws limits on trial courts  powers
description: SC draws limits on trial courts  powers
content:
Lays down principles for exercise of Section 540 CrPC
Issuing guidelines to trial courts on the exercise of their powers under Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1898, the Supreme Court has observed that a criminal court is neither a silent spectator nor a substitute for the prosecutor.
"Its duty is to adjudicate impartially upon the charge brought by the state, while using the powers conferred by law where necessary to ensure that the decision is reached upon the material essential for justice." says a 10-page judgement authored by Justice Muhammad Salahuddin Ahmed Panwar.
The case pertains to a matter wherein role of a criminal court in an adversarial process, and the relationship between sections 94 and 540 (CrPC), Article 161 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 and the constitutional guarantee of a fair trial have been arisen.
"The contest belongs to the parties; the burden of proving guilt remains upon the prosecution; but the responsibility for a lawful and just adjudication remains with the Court," it adds,
The three-judge bench led by Justice Muhammad Hashim Kakar has noted that Section 94 (CrPC) enables the court, whenever it considers the production of a document or other thing necessary or desirable for the purposes of an inquiry or trial, to compel its production.
"Section 540 authorises the court, at any stage, to summon any person as a witness, examine a person present, or recall and re-examine a person already examined; and its latter part commands the Court to do so where the evidence appears essential to the just decision of the case.
The court said that first, the ordinary structure of a Pakistani criminal trial is adversarial, but the court possesses limited statutory powers of an inquisitorial character under sections 94 and 540 (CrPC) and Article 161 QSO.
Second, the first part of Section 540 is discretionary, while its second part becomes mandatory only when the evidence appears essential to the just decision of the case.
Third, neither omission from the calendar of witnesses nor absence of a prior statement under Section 161 is, by itself, an absolute bar to examination under Section 540.
Fourth, the order said that section 265-C requires timely supply of existing material which the law makes disclosable; it does not require production of a statement never recorded.
Fifth, the Court must not use Section 540 merely to strengthen a party's case or to cure an inherent evidentiary deficiency.
Sixth, the order said that whenever additional evidence is received, the accused must be protected against unfair surprise through disclosure, preparation and cross-examination.
Seventh, the remedy for any irregularity depends upon actual prejudice; a de novo trial is not the automatic consequence of every mid-trial exercise of Section 540, says the order.

content:
The Medical and Dental College Admission Test (MDCAT) 2026 will be held today (Sunday) in 34 cities across Pakistan and at an international centre in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
According to the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC), a total of 138,160 candidates have registered for the entrance examination this year.
Punjab has the highest number of registered candidates at 49,199, followed by Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa with 38,841 and Sindh with 34,233 candidates.

Separate question papers have been prepared for each province, with at least two different papers for every province. Each question paper contains 180 questions.
The relevant universities may retain the question papers after the examination, according to the test arrangements.
The practical conduct of the MDCAT examination is the responsibility of the respective provincial authorities and designated universities.
The PMDC, meanwhile, has a statutory role in determining the examination framework, methodology and standards for the MDCAT. The test is a key requirement for admission to medical and dental colleges across the country.

title: AJK  G B refuse to lift imported wheat
description: AJK  G B refuse to lift imported wheat
content:
Regional govts raise concerns over quality
Pakistan's agriculture procurement agency imported poor quality wheat, raising serious concerns in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) and Gilgit-Baltistan (G-B). The governments of the regions have decided not to accept that imported wheat stock and have sought 100% locally procured wheat.
The Ministry of National Food Security and Research briefed the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) on the issue during a recent meeting, informing the forum that AJK and G-B had expressed reservations over the quality of imported wheat being supplied to them.
The Pakistan Agricultural Storage and Services Corporation (Passco) is currently holding around 1.088 million metric tons (MMT) of local and imported wheat as of August 5, 2026, with 87% local and 13% imported wheat in its overall stock.
Of this stock, 300,000 metric tons have been allocated to AJK for the 2026-27 food year, covering May 1, 2026 to April 30, 2027, while 160,000 metric tons have been allocated to GB.
According to the ministry, the ECC approved a mechanism on November 1, 2024, under which Passco would provide wheat to recipient agencies in a 50:50 ratio of local and imported wheat, except G-B, for which a 75:25 local-to-imported ratio was approved.
In accordance with that decision, Passco has been supplying AJK wheat in a 50:50 local-to-imported ratio since November 2024. Out of AJK's total allocation of 300,000 metric tons for the current food year, 63,801 metric tons have been lifted so far, leaving 236,199 metric tons still to be lifted.
The ministry told the ECC that the AJK prime minister in a letter addressed to the prime minister of Pakistan, had raised concerns over the quality of imported wheat being supplied to the region.
The AJK prime minister requested that Passco provide 100% local wheat from its stocks to improve the quality of flour supplied to consumers in the region. The Prime Minister's Office subsequently directed the Ministry of National Food Security to consider the matter and take necessary action.
The G-B government in a letter dated May 30, 2026, conveyed its reservations regarding the quality of imported wheat in Passco stocks and requested that the region be provided 100% local wheat.
Under the existing ECC-approved mechanism, Passco has been supplying wheat to G-B in a 75:25 ratio of local and imported wheat since November 2024.
Of the 160,000 metric tons allocated to G-B for the 2026-27 food year, 38,015 metric tons have been lifted, leaving 121,985 metric tons yet to be supplied.
The ministry also informed the ECC about the recommendations of the Passco Board of Directors concerning the corporation's overall wheat stock position.
At its 166th meeting held on June 15, 2026, the Passco board reviewed the available wheat stocks and noted that the current composition was approximately 85% local and 15% imported wheat.
The board recommended that the Ministry of National Food Security approach the ECC for approval of an 85:15 local-to-imported wheat release ratio for all recipient agencies. The rationale was to ensure the timely disposal of Passco's imported wheat stocks along with the locally procured wheat.
The Finance Division subsequently endorsed the proposal through an official memorandum dated August 5, 2026.

title: A devoted father  human stories behind Kohat attack
description: Luqman s family described him as deeply committed to his children s education
content:
Luqman's family described him as deeply committed to his children's education
The family of SP Akbar Muhammad Shinwari, who was among those martyred in the Kohat Old Police Lines suicide attack and rampage, has been receiving a steady stream of mourners at their home in Hathian village, Mardan, BBC Urdu reported on Saturday.
According to his nephew Tufail Akbar, Shinwari spent much of his police career serving in areas including Dir, Bajaur and Swat during periods of intense militancy, taking part in several major and dangerous operations. "He was very brave. He received threats too, but rarely spoke about them," Tufail told BBC Urdu.
The officer had been particularly devastated by the death of his younger brother, Motorway Police Sub-Inspector Javed Akbar, who was killed after being struck by a dumper truck on July 15.
Shinwari had repeatedly lamented his brother's death, saying: "Why did Javed leave me? It would have been better if I had gone instead."
Two months later, Shinwari himself was killed in the Kohat terror attack.
Tufail said Shinwari had two sons and two daughters, with his youngest daughter only six months old. He said the officer had been particularly delighted at her birth and considered her "the apple of his eye".
Despite holding the rank of SP, Shinwari was regarded by people in his native area as a friend and someone they could turn to for help, Tufail said. "Whenever people had a problem involving a hospital, doctor or government department, they would come to him," he said, adding that Shinwari generally returned home only on weekends.
The terror attack also claimed the lives of Muhammad Luqman and two young children, including his four-and-a-half-year-old son Abdullah, according to BBC Urdu.
Luqman's brother-in-law Muhammad Tanveer told BBC Urdu that he had been at work in Kohat when his sister called in distress, asking about her husband and children. Tanveer repeatedly tried calling Luqman but received no response. Soon afterwards, he learned about the blast and rushed to hospital.
When he arrived, he found Luqman's body. The bodies of two children were also brought to the hospital shortly afterwards. The second child, Asad, aged around three-and-a-half, was Luqman's nephew, Tanveer said.
Luqman, 37, worked as a laboratory technician and was also a volunteer with the Alkhidmat Foundation. He was involved in arranging blood for people in need and served as the organisation's district blood-donation president, according to his family.
His friend Muhammad Maskeen, who was also injured in the blast, told BBC Urdu that Luqman had picked up his children from school and stopped to offer Friday prayers.
Maskeen said he had spoken to Luqman before the prayers and suggested that they meet afterwards to buy something for the children to eat and have tea together. "I went to pray, and I was in the middle of the mosque when the explosion suddenly occurred," Maskeen said. He suffered minor injuries and was taken to hospital.
He later saw Luqman's body being brought to the hospital, followed by the bodies of his children.
Luqman's family described him as deeply committed to his children's education.

title: Middle East conflict dents exports
description: Middle East conflict dents exports
content:
Earnings decline by more than $1.2 billion
Pakistan's exports have started showing the adverse impact of the deteriorating situation in the Middle East, with the country's overall export earnings declining by more than $1.2 billion during the last financial year compared with the previous year.
According to available data, Pakistan's total exports fell from around $32 billion in fiscal year 2024-25 to $30.8 billion in FY2025-26, reflecting a decline of more than $1.2 billion.
Rice exports recorded the largest drop, declining by around $1.02 billion during the period. Exports of textile products, sugar and other agricultural commodities also remained under pressure.
The data further showed that exports to Gulf countries declined by around $100 million, while exports to Central Asian countries and Afghanistan recorded a decline of up to 59%.
Officials attributed the deterioration in export performance to the impact of regional tensions on trade routes, transportation and logistics costs. The disruption has affected the movement of goods and increased the cost of transporting export consignments to key regional markets.
Officials said the government is continuing efforts to reduce energy costs and taxes to provide relief to businesses and support economic activity.

title: Govt cuts profit rates on saving certificates
description: Govt cuts profit rates on saving certificates
content:
Rs100,000 investment in Defence Savings to mature at Rs300,000 after 10 years
The federal government has reduced the profit rates on two major National Savings schemes Defence Savings Certificates and Behbood Savings Certificatesand issued the revised rates for September 2026.
Under the new rates, Defence Savings Certificates have a maturity period of 10 years. An investment of Rs100,000 will grow to Rs300,000 at maturity.
According to the revised schedule, an investment of Rs100,000 will amount to Rs110,000 after the first year, Rs121,000 after the second year, Rs133,000 after the third year, Rs147,000 after the fourth year and Rs163,000 after the fifth year.
The amount will rise to Rs182,000 in the sixth year, Rs204,000 in the seventh year, Rs230,000 in the eighth year and Rs262,000 in the ninth year. At the end of the 10-year maturity period, the investment will reach Rs300,000.
The government has also reduced the profit rate on Behbood Savings Certificates.
Under the revised rate, an investment of Rs100,000 in a Behbood Savings Certificate will earn a monthly profit of Rs1,050, equivalent to an annual rate of 12.60%.
Behbood Savings Certificates were introduced specifically to cater to the financial needs of widows and senior citizens, providing them with a regular source of income from their savings. The revised rates will apply from September 2026.

title: PM trims UN delegation under austerity
description: PM trims UN delegation under austerity
content:
Key world leaders to address UNGA on first day
The schedule for speeches by world leaders at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has been released.
The premier is due to arrive on Monday and will address the General Assembly on September 25.
The Pakistani delegation has been significantly streamlined as part of the government's austerity measures. Dar and senior foreign-policy adviser Tariq Fatemi will form the core of the prime minister's delegation, while several federal ministers who had initially been expected to travel have been dropped from the trip, according to sources at the country's UN mission.
Information and Broadcasting Minister Attaullah Tarar, Minister for Climate Change and Environment Dr Musadik Malik and Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal are among those not attending, added the sources.
Dar's preparatory meetings are expected to focus on Pakistan's priorities for the UNGA high-level week and the rapidly changing regional situation.
The Middle East crisis has already figured prominently in discussions at the UN headquarters, with the Security Council holding several meetings on the deteriorating situation in Yemen and the wider region in recent days.
US President Donald Trump, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, French President Emmanuel Macron and Qatar Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani are among the leaders set to address the General Assembly on the opening day.
The General Debate of the 81st UN General Assembly session will begin on September 22 and continue through September 28, with meetings scheduled from September 22 to September 26 and again on September 28.
According to the UN's programme, the opening session will begin at 9am on September 22. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will be the first speaker, followed by US President Donald Trump.
The morning session will also feature addresses by Jordan's King Abdullah II, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, Qatar Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and the leaders of Lithuania, Peru, Chile and France, among others.
A second session will begin at 3pm on September 22, with leaders from Mongolia, South Korea, Suriname, Sierra Leone, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Switzerland and Vietnam among those scheduled to address the assembly.

title: Opp assails govt over failures  apathy
description: Opp assails govt over failures  apathy
content:
Abbas questions official response to public hardships
Opposition leaders on Saturday lashed out at the PML-N-led federal and Punjab governments, accusing them of failing to address mounting public hardships while continuing to spend lavishly and remaining disconnected from the problems faced by ordinary citizens.
Speaking at a media briefing alongside PTI leaders, Senate Leader of the Opposition Allama Raja Nasir Abbas and TTAP leader Muhammad Zubair cited Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi's July statement as evidence of the government's failure to deliver.
Naqvi told the Pakistan Economic Summit in Islamabad on July 30 that "the system we are living under has collapsed", arguing that the existing governance structure could no longer address the country's challenges and calling for structural reforms and new administrative units.
Abbas said "an important federal minister" himself had acknowledged that the country's system had collapsed. He claimed that Pakistan's economic and judicial systems had been severely damaged and cited recent incidents as signs of wider institutional problems.
He said providing facilities to citizens and standing up for their rights were fundamental responsibilities of the state. He criticised the rulers' approach to governance, saying the public could be astonished by their priorities.
Raja Nasir Abbas referred to the incident at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), saying such incidents reflected the problems confronting the country.
He also criticised the detention of lawyers Imaan Mazari and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha despite court orders concerning their release, and praised Mazari for continuing to raise her voice.
"Imaan Mazari deserves recognition for raising her voice," he said. The two lawyers were sentenced to 17 years each in a controversial-tweets case; courts have subsequently taken up matters concerning the suspension of their sentence.
Muhammad Zubair, who was a part of the ruling PML-N till 2023, also referred to Naqvi's system collapse comment, adding that "the admission" by "one of the country's most powerful ministers" showed the present system was incapable of benefiting the people.
He questioned how the government could claim progress when millions of Pakistanis were struggling to meet basic needs while leaders continued to enjoy what he called extravagant lifestyles.
"More than 120 million people have gone below the poverty line," Zubair claimed, criticising expenditure on official travel and other privileges.
He alleged that millions of rupees had recently been spent on a private trip and questioned the justification for such expenditure when the government was asking people to make further sacrifices.
The opposition leader also referred to the marriage of Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz's daughter, contrasting the lavish lifestyle of the ruling elite with the economic difficulties confronting ordinary families.
Zubair said the issue was not simply a family celebration but concerned whether rulers were sufficiently sensitive to the population's economic circumstances.
He also criticised the use of public resources by senior officials.
