title: One year  one footpath
description: They came to Karachi seeking help  A year later  the footpath outside Karachi Press Club is still their home
content:
They came to Karachi seeking help. A year later, the footpath outside Karachi Press Club is still their home
The family living on the footpath outside the Karachi Press Club has now spent a year here. They are the family of Amanullah Buzdar, a former Sindh police officer from Ghotki. Journalists who visit the Press Club every day, as well as employees working in nearby offices, have come to know them well. The family has been living here since September 2, 2025. They sleep, eat, bathe and wash their clothes on the same footpath. For the past year, it has been their temporary home.
The family consists of Amanullah, his disabled wife, Mai Sanam, and their four children. The eldest daughter is around 14 years old, while the youngest of their three sons, Ali Waris, is about seven. During their stay here, a Russian-breed dog has also become part of the family. Some time ago, an acquaintance gave Amanullah the injured dog. He had it treated at the government veterinary hospital on MA Jinnah Road.
Amanullah is from Jarwar in Ghotki district, while he was posted in Kandhkot, in Kashmore district. In 2022, his wife suffered a severe stroke. Because he had to care for her, Amanullah began missing duty and was eventually dismissed from the police force. According to Amanullah, his wife remained bedridden and semi-conscious for three months after the stroke. During this period, he had to care for her as well as look after their children.
Amanullah had two brothers, three sisters and other close relatives in his village. Yet there was no one willing to care for his wife because she did not belong to Amanullah’s community. Amanullah is from the Baloch tribe, while his wife belongs to the Soomro community of Sukkur. Amanullah had married her by choice. His relatives had opposed the marriage for two reasons. First, Amanullah had previously been engaged to a girl from his own family. The second was that Sanam belonged to another community.
The biradari system remains quite strong in Sindh. In rural areas, people often marry within their own community. The distinction between Baloch and Samat tribes also remains significant. Baloch families generally seek matches for their sons and daughters within Baloch communities. Similarly, families belonging to Samat tribes tend to prefer marriages within their own tribal communities.
After Sanam’s illness and Amanullah’s dismissal from the police, difficult times began for the family. They first sold their goats and then had to sell the only property they owned in their village: their house. When they had nothing left there, they came to Karachi. Initially, Amanullah stayed with his family in Bhittaiabad, near the airport, where he worked as a daily-wage labourer to support his children. But with his low income, it became difficult to pay rent and meet other household expenses. Within a year, he had to leave the area. He did not have enough money to rent a house elsewhere. In these circumstances, he began efforts to have his police job reinstated.
In August 2025, he brought his family to the Karachi Police Office on Shahrah-e-Faisal and sat outside the building. He believed that staying there might help get his job restored. However, after spending a month there, the police removed him from the site. He then came and sat outside the Karachi Press Club on September 2, 2025.
In the early days, he would stand there wearing his police uniform in an attempt to attract media attention. Journalists initially raised his issue in the media, but as time passed, this coverage declined. The government also paid no attention to his case. With nowhere else suitable to live, the family eventually made the footpath outside the Press Club their temporary home.
Over the course of the year, the family also had to endure extreme weather. When winter arrived, they did not even have a single blanket for the entire family. A kind-hearted man living nearby brought them two blankets from his home. The whole family spent the winter nights sharing those two blankets. Then came the intense summer heat, followed by torrential rains. During the rain, they would seek shelter under the awnings of nearby buildings. There was no washroom outside the Press Club, so they put up a makeshift screen at one end of the footpath to attend to their basic needs.
Before coming to Karachi, Amanullah’s daughter and his two older sons were enrolled in Grade 3 at a private school in their area. When they came to Karachi, his daughter brought her books with her. She would sit on the footpath and write something or other. But her books were also destroyed in the rains. After that, she began spending her time with the Russian-breed dog. They named him Tommy.
After spending several months hoping that his job would be restored, Amanullah started working as a security guard. His two sons, aged 10 and 12, have also begun doing manual labour. Meanwhile, people have given money to his disabled wife, gradually getting her accustomed to begging. It has now become routine for her to sit near Zainab Market and beg for money every day. Her youngest son, Ali Waris, is also with her almost all the time.
His daughter, however, no longer lives on the footpath. She spent around 10 months living there, but for the past two months, a non-governmental organisation in Lahore has enrolled her in a government boarding school it operates. She now has a safe place to live, a bed to sleep in, regular meals and books again.
But eight-year-old Ali Waris is still living on the same footpath. He has not yet started school. He too is eager to study. His disabled mother has bought him some books and pencils. Her wish is for her youngest son to go to school as well.
For now, the footpath remains home for Amanullah, his wife and their two sons. A year after they first arrived at the Press Club, their circumstances have changed little and the family continues to live with the uncertainty of each passing day.
For Amanullah’s family, the hope is simple: a roof over their heads, a secure future for their children and, above all, the chance for Ali Waris to go to school. For a child who has spent much of his life on a footpath, even that modest wish remains a distant one.

title: Worms in the system
description: Poor sanitation  unsafe water expose kids to preventable stomach infections  threatening nutrition  growth   education
author_name: Muhammad Ilyas, Wisal Yousafzai, Tufail Ahmed
content:
Poor sanitation, unsafe water expose kids to preventable stomach infections, threatening nutrition, growth & education
A school is meant to be a place where children learn, grow and prepare for the future. But for millions of children across Pakistan, some of the most basic conditions for healthy learning — clean drinking water, functional toilets, soap and regular health checks — remain uncertain.
Intestinal worms are often invisible, but their consequences are not. For children, an infection that may begin with contaminated water, unhygienic food, poor sanitation or inadequate handwashing can gradually affect nutrition, physical development, energy levels and concentration in the classroom.
Symptoms of a worm infection may include recurrent abdominal pain, weakness, fatigue, loss of appetite, nutritional deficiencies, iron deficiency anaemia and impaired physical growth. Hookworm infections are particularly associated with anaemia among young girls, although infection patterns can vary according to environmental and lifestyle conditions.
In this case, intestinal worms are more than a medical problem. They deprive children of nutrients, affect growth and make it harder to concentrate in the classroom. While school-based deworming programmes have reached millions of children, health experts caution that a dose of medicine cannot solve a problem that is repeatedly recreated by unsafe water, poor sanitation and inadequate hygiene.
The question, therefore, is not simply how many children receive deworming medicine, but whether schools are providing the conditions needed to keep them healthy after the medicine has been administered. Across Punjab, Sindh and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), accounts from students, parents, doctors and education and health officials point to gaps in facilities, monitoring and continuity that could undermine efforts to protect children from preventable infections.
Therefore, health experts and school administrations continue to confront a problem that extends beyond the simple provision of medicine. Deworming tablets may treat an existing infection, but without clean drinking water, functional toilets, soap, proper handwashing facilities and sustained health education, children remain exposed to the same conditions that can lead to reinfection.
According to figures cited in Pakistan’s national soil-transmitted helminth survey, based on World Health Organisation (WHO) estimates, around 21.7 million school-age children and 9.3 million preschool children in Pakistan are infected with soil-transmitted helminths. WHO says such infections are particularly common in communities where sanitation and hygiene are inadequate. Globally, around 1.5 billion people are affected by these parasitic infections, with children among the groups most vulnerable to their effects.
The problem is particularly significant because school-based health programmes cannot reach every child. In Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, for instance, the 2023 Population Census recorded 4.92 million children aged five to 16 as out of school, representing 37.49 per cent of children in that age group. The figure includes around 2.92 million girls and two million boys. The large number of children outside the formal education system presents an obvious challenge for programmes that rely on schools as the primary point of access.
The Interactive Research and Development (IRD) has been implementing a school-based deworming programme in Pakistan since 2019. According to its Pakistan Deworming Initiative (PDI), the programme has so far reached 25.3 million children. They told The Express Tribune that 26,753 schools in 22 districts of K-P are registered with the programme, covering both public and private educational institutions. It said the initiative was not limited to K-P, adding that the Balochistan government had also formally taken ownership of the programme.
Yet the question remains whether reaching millions of children through periodic campaigns is enough to break the cycle of infection. Public health experts maintain that medicine alone cannot address the environmental conditions that allow intestinal worms to persist. Improved sanitation, safe drinking water, handwashing facilities and hygiene education are equally important components of prevention.
In Punjab, this question assumes particular importance as the School Health and Nutrition Programme already provides a framework for screening children, raising awareness about health and hygiene and referring children to health facilities when necessary. What remains essential is determining how consistently these services translate into functioning facilities and measurable outcomes at school level.
Schools need to be examined not merely for whether they possess toilets or water points on paper, but whether children can actually use clean toilets, access safe drinking water, wash their hands with soap and receive timely health information. Equally important is the availability of district-wise records showing how many children are receiving deworming medicine, how many schools are covered and whether programmes are being repeated according to health requirements.
A toilet sign on a crumbling school wall means nothing when the water tap is bone-dry and the washbasin is covered in grime. Across the country, the illusion of school hygiene is quietly failing children, turning classrooms into breeding grounds for preventable infections both inside the gates and at the snack stalls outside.
In Punjab’s schools, the condition of basic facilities can determine whether a deworming programme addresses the problem or merely treats one stage of it. During reviews of public and private educational institutions, questions have emerged over whether toilets are clean, whether drinking water is continuously available, whether washbasins are functional and supplied with soap, and whether school administrations regularly conduct deworming programmes.
The distinction between having a facility and having a usable facility is significant. A water tap without safe water, a washbasin without soap or a toilet that is rarely cleaned may technically exist but offer limited protection against infection.
Students themselves have highlighted these gaps. Some students said that while their schools had water facilities, soap or adequate handwashing arrangements were not always available. Others reported that washrooms were not cleaned regularly. Some children said they had received deworming medicine but were not given sufficient information about its benefits or why the medicine was necessary.
For students, the connection between facilities and health is often straightforward. Many believe that consistently available clean drinking water, soap and clean washrooms could help prevent illness and make schools healthier places. When it comes to female students, the absence of clean and safe toilets, water and soap can create an additional burden, particularly during menstruation.
The problem is not restricted to Punjab. In Karachi, government schools have long faced complaints regarding sanitation, toilets, handwashing facilities and drinking water. According to Professor Dr Waseem Jamalvi, President of the Pakistan Paediatric Association Sindh, government-school toilets often lack proper cleanliness arrangements as well as soap and sanitiser. He described the absence of clean drinking water and proper toilet facilities at the primary-school level as a serious concern.
Private schools, according to Jamalvi, generally have better-maintained washrooms and handwashing facilities. However, differences between institutions mean that access to basic health and hygiene services cannot be assumed simply on the basis of whether a child attends a public or private school.
The situation becomes more complicated when children leave school premises. In Karachi, unhealthy food and drinks are frequently sold at roadside stalls around government schools. Brightly coloured beverages and other unhygienic food items may expose children to gastrointestinal problems, particularly where clean water and handwashing facilities are already inadequate.
Parents also face an information gap. Symptoms such as abdominal pain, loss of appetite and weakness may be dismissed as ordinary childhood problems, delaying medical examination. Health experts advise that children experiencing persistent symptoms should be medically assessed rather than being treated on assumptions.
Ayesha Tariq, a resident of PIB Colony, said her six-year-old son, Shayan, repeatedly complained of abdominal pain and loss of appetite and appeared restless at night. Initially, she did not associate the symptoms with intestinal worms and consulted a family physician. A stool test and other examinations subsequently confirmed the infection.
She said the experience made her realise that parents often underestimate the relationship between contaminated water, food, hand hygiene and intestinal infections. She advised parents to teach children to wash their hands before eating and after using the toilet, ensure drinking water is clean and safe, and provide hygienic food.
The mother of seven-year-old Rimsha, who was receiving treatment at the National Institute of Child Health (NICH), described a similar experience. Her daughter had suffered severe abdominal pain for around a month and had difficulty eating properly. Medical examinations, including blood and stool tests, detected intestinal worms and intestinal inflammation.
According to Rimsha’s mother, doctors linked her daughter’s illness to unhygienic food and contaminated water. She said the child frequently ate market food, including French fries, before developing health problems. The child was later admitted to the NICH emergency department, where she received treatment.
Treating children for intestinal infections while leaving them to navigate contaminated water, missing soap, and defunct health screenings is like bailing water from a sinking boat. Without clean facilities, routine checkups, and a continuous system of care, one syrup alone will never stop the cycle of reinfection.
Health experts say intestinal worm infections are closely associated with poor hand hygiene, contaminated drinking water, inadequate toilets and poor sanitation. For girls, the condition of school facilities has an additional importance. Clean and private toilets, adequate water and soap are essential for menstrual hygiene and dignity. Poor facilities can cause discomfort and may contribute to absenteeism during menstruation.
The lack of regular school health screening adds to the prob]lem. Karachi’s School Health Services programme, launched in 1987 with WHO and UNICEF cooperation, once provided routine medical examinations to schoolchildren. According to the report, 423 doctors were assigned to examine around 600,000 children. Female doctors were assigned to girls’ schools and male doctors to boys’ schools.
Students received medical examinations, hygiene education, dental checks and monitoring for nutritional deficiencies, weight problems and anaemia. The programme continued for about 25 years before being discontinued by the Health Department in 2012. Its closure left government schools without the same system of routine health screening, making it difficult to establish reliable data on intestinal worms and other illnesses.
Pakistan has conducted several phases of deworming through the Pakistan Deworming Initiative, reaching millions of children. However, more detailed district-level information is needed, particularly in Punjab, to determine how many public and private schools are covered, how many children receive treatment each year, and how many miss or decline the medicine.
Schools should maintain clear records of their deworming activities, including when the last campaign was conducted, how many children received medicine, how parents were informed and what instructions were given to staff.
Experts stress that deworming should not be treated as a one-time campaign. It needs to be linked with school health, nutrition, safe drinking water, sanitation and handwashing programmes. Regular monitoring of toilets, water points and handwashing facilities could help identify the conditions that allow infections to return.
Punjab’s School Health and Nutrition Programme provides a possible framework for this approach through health screening, hygiene awareness and referrals to healthcare facilities. However, reliable district-wise data is needed to measure how consistently these services are being provided.
Research involving schoolchildren in different parts of Punjab has also reported a significant prevalence of intestinal parasitic infections and linked them with sanitation, water quality, personal hygiene and socioeconomic conditions. Experts therefore emphasise that medicine alone cannot prevent reinfection. Deworming may remove worms, but it cannot provide clean water, soap or safe toilets.
The challenge is even greater for children who are out of school, particularly in K-P, because school-based programmes cannot reach children who are not enrolled or regularly attending classes. Karachi faces a different challenge because the discontinuation of school health services removed a system that once provided routine medical examinations to large numbers of children.
Experts also emphasise prevention at home. Parents should teach children to wash their hands with soap after using the toilet and before eating, provide clean drinking water, keep their nails trimmed and discourage children from putting soil or dirty objects into their mouths.
A deworming syrup can clear an infection, but it cannot stop the next one from taking hold. True protection requires clean water, safe toilets, soap, and regular health checks. Until these basics become the everyday reality inside every school, children will remain trapped in a relentless loop of preventable illness.

title: Pak films must give audiences a reason to buy a ticket
description: Pak films must give audiences a reason to buy a ticket
content:
In exclusive interview, actor Zara Noor Abbas says public can't be expected to support domestic cinema simply out of
Pakistani actor Zara Noor Abbas believes filmmakers cannot expect audiences to support local cinema simply out of loyalty. Pakistani films, she said, must first give people a reason to spend their money and time at the cinema.
Speaking to The Express Tribune about her upcoming film Sheroes, Abbas said audiences want to be entertained, and filmmakers must repeatedly prove themselves by creating films that offer both enjoyment and confidence in the local industry.
"Supporting Pakistani cinema is a very old statement. If people want to support Pakistani cinema, they should have a reason to do so. People want entertainment," she said.
"If someone has finished eating out and wants to watch something, only then will they go to the cinema. We, as filmmakers, have to prove ourselves again and again."
Abbas plays Saira, a Bomb Disposal Unit (BDU) officer, in the film's action-oriented segment Gear Up. The anthology brings together three stories centred on women. Saira's story follows her struggle to work in a male-dominated environment where her abilities are repeatedly questioned.
"The Sindh Police has a specialised department called the Bomb Disposal Unit, which exists within police forces across the country. I play Saira, a BDU officer, and the story is about her struggle as a woman in a male-dominated workplace," she said.
"I think Saira is the first woman bomb disposal officer in her office. She faces gender discrimination and is given a task that nobody believes she can accomplish. That is essentially the premise of the story."
Abbas said the character's strength and resilience felt familiar to her.
"I found Saira quite similar to me in terms of her strength and resilience. As actors, we immerse ourselves in different characters. Whenever I talk about a character, I feel as if it is almost like a possession a different entity enters my body and I become that person," she said.
Playing a BDU officer also required Abbas to learn technical police terminology.
"The dialogue delivery was challenging because television usually allows more pauses and emotional dialogue, whereas this character had a lot of technical terminology," she said.
"There were terms about cordoning off an area, setting a perimeter and calculating the radius. The police and military have their own coded language, so understanding it, delivering it naturally and speaking quickly was difficult."
She credited writer Hashim Nadeem's script and dialogues for helping her manage the challenge.
Most scenes were shot on specially created sets, with little time for preparation.
"We created sets and did everything there. We didn't have much time for preparation because we had to shoot the project quite quickly. We actually shot it in January this year."
Sheroes marks Abbas' return to cinema after almost seven years. She made her film debut in 2019 with Wajahat Rauf's Chhalawa and appeared in Asim Raza's Parey Hut Love the same year. Sheroes is her third film.
She said local filmmakers should not ask audiences to watch Pakistani films simply because they are Pakistani. Instead, they must create franchises and characters that make people confident about spending money on local productions.
"When Spider-Man comes out, people rush to watch it. Some even dress up like Spider-Man because the character has already created its own niche. Spider-Man has a huge franchise behind it through Marvel," she said.
"We need to build those franchises and create confidence among audiences that if they are spending Rs1,500 or Rs2,000 on a ticket, they will get something enjoyable in return."
For Pakistani filmmakers, she believes the immediate task is to encourage audiences to give new films a chance.

title: Brigitte Bardot widower slams sale of star s belongings
description: Brigitte Bardot widower slams sale of star s belongings
content:
Late actress's foundation to auction hundreds of her personal items
The widower of French screen icon Brigitte Bardot on Saturday slammed as a "joke" the planned auction of hundreds of the late star's personal belongings organised by her animal welfare foundation.
The sale, featuring more than 300 items ranging from portraits and toiletries to a flamenco guitar and a black tutu, is due to take place Monday at Paris auction house Drouot.
"These are personal items. Why hold this sale? For the animals? It's a joke," Bernard d'Ormale told AFP, adding it amounted to a "disrespect to Brigitte's memory".
"All of this could have been kept for the day when people are able to visit La Madrague," he added, referring to Bardot's famed home in Saint-Tropez.
He said around three-quarters of the items came from Bardot's Paris apartment, with the remainder from La Madrague.
Her belongings should have been preserved as part of her legacy rather than sold to raise funds for the foundation she created, d'Ormale argued, adding that Bardot "would not have agreed to this sale".
The Brigitte Bardot Foundation rejected the criticism, saying the auction was approved by the board in June, including Bardot's widower, who was then its president.
However, d'Ormale said he had not understood the auction would involve such personal items.
The dispute comes days after he was removed as head of the foundation, a role he had held since the star's death in December.
The 85-year-old, who remains on the foundation's board, also complained he no longer has free access to La Madrague.
"I've lived there for 35 years and now they're throwing me out. It's quite something," d'Ormale said.
Founded by the actor in 1986, the Brigitte Bardot Foundation says it has taken in 13,000 animals through four shelters and 150 partner facilities, supports 350 groups in France and operates in 70 countries.
Born and raised in Paris, Bardot was an aspiring ballerina during her childhood. She began her acting career in 1952 and achieved international recognition in 1957 for her role in And God Created Woman (1956), catching the attention of many French intellectuals and earning her the nickname "sex kitten". She was the subject of philosopher Simone de Beauvoir's 1959 essay The Lolita Syndrome, which described her as a "locomotive of women's history" and built upon existentialist themes to declare her the most liberated woman of France. She won a 1961 David di Donatello Best Foreign Actress Award for her work in The Truth (1960). Bardot later starred in Jean-Luc Godard's film Le Mépris (1963). For her role in Louis Malle's film Viva Maria! (1965), she was nominated for the BAFTA Award for Best Foreign Actress. French president Charles de Gaulle called Bardot "the French export as important as Renault cars".
After retiring from acting in 1973, Bardot became an animal rights activist and created the Brigitte Bardot Foundation. She was known for her strong personality, outspokenness, speeches on animal welfare, and for her long-term support of far-right views. She was fined twice for public insults, and five times for inciting racial hatred for her criticism of Muslims in France and calling residents of Réunion "savages". She responded: "I never knowingly wanted to hurt anybody. It is not in my character [...] Among Muslims, I think there are some who are very good and some hoodlums, like everywhere." AFP

title: Ed Sheeran continues to be dogged by Palestine controversy
description: Ed Sheeran continues to be dogged by Palestine controversy
content:
Protests planned at British superstar's Philadelphia concert; Macklemore ticket prices surge
Ed Sheeran has changed the start time of his Philadelphia concert as the fallout from Macklemore's removal from his Loop Tour continues, with pro-Palestinian protesters also planning a demonstration outside the venue.
Sheeran is scheduled to perform at Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday, September 19. The concert was originally scheduled to begin at 5:30pm local time, but the start time has since been moved to 8pm on Ticketmaster. The change follows the withdrawal of the tour's supporting acts, leaving Sheeran without announced opening performers for the Philadelphia show.
Macklemore was removed from the remaining US dates of the tour after making pro-Palestinian comments during his performance at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium earlier this month. Sheeran has said the decision was made by the promoter after upcoming venues communicated that they would pull the shows if Macklemore remained on the line-up.
Following Macklemore's departure, Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Sheeran's backing band Beoga all withdrew from the remaining dates. Beoga said it fully supported Macklemore's message, while the other departures further reshaped the remaining tour schedule.
The Philadelphia concert is also expected to draw protests. Local pro-Palestinian groups have announced plans to rally outside Lincoln Financial Field ahead of the show, with organisers saying the demonstration will focus on Palestinian advocacy and concerns over the treatment of Macklemore's comments.
Ticket resale prices for the Philadelphia show have also fallen as the concert approaches. Tickets that were listed at $91 on Thursday were available for as little as $66.30 on Friday, while other reporting put the cheapest available ticket at around $67. TicketData founder Keith Pagello cautioned that falling resale prices are common immediately before concerts and do not necessarily indicate an effect from the controversy.
Sheeran has said he has personal views about the Israel-Palestine conflict but does not want his concerts to become political forums. He has also denied being responsible for Macklemore's removal from the tour.
Macklemore's ticket prices have surged following his removal from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour after the rapper spoke publicly in support of Palestine.
According to ticket-tracking company TicketData, the cheapest available ticket for Macklemore's October concert at Colorado's Red Rocks Amphitheatre rose 45% over three days, climbing from $108 to $157. TicketData founder Keith Pagello told CNBC the increase would not have happened without the events surrounding Macklemore's departure from Sheeran's tour.
Macklemore was removed from the remaining US dates of Sheeran's tour after making pro-Palestinian comments during a performance at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium on September 4. He later said he had been told stadium owners had threatened to cancel shows if he remained on the line-up.
The fallout has also affected Sheeran's ticket market. Resale prices for nine of the 10 remaining venues on the Loop Tour have declined, according to TicketData, although Pagello cautioned that falling prices are common as concert dates approach and may not necessarily be connected to the controversy.
There has, however, been an increase in resale activity for Sheeran's upcoming shows. TicketData reported that tickets have been changing hands at a higher rate than at previous tour stops at a similar point in their sales cycle.
The dispute has continued to escalate, with all of Sheeran's other supporting acts, including Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga, withdrawing from the remaining dates after Macklemore's removal.
Sheeran has maintained that Macklemore's departure was the promoter's decision rather than his own. Meanwhile, Macklemore announced that he would donate $1 million from his net earnings from the tour to organisations supporting Palestinians.
Macklemore & Ryan Lewis's 2012 single "Thrift Shop" (featuring Wanz) became the first self-released song to top the Billboard Hot 100 in 11 years. Their second single, "Can't Hold Us" (featuring Ray Dalton), also peaked on chart, making Macklemore and Lewis the first duo in the chart's history to have their first two singles both reach the peak position. Their debut studio album The Heist (2012) peaked at number 2 on the U.S. Billboard 200. The duo entered into a slightly unusual three-month, one-album contract with Warner Bros.'s independent distribution arm ADA, which allowed them to retain control over their intellectual property and maintain their "artistic integrity".
The ticket-market changes add a financial dimension to the growing fallout surrounding the tour, although the available data does not establish whether the shifts are directly attributable to the controversy.

title: Anthropic mulls releasing new AI model
description: Anthropic mulls releasing new AI model
content:
Launch to counter OpenAI pressure, follows call for slowdown due to safety concerns
Anthropic is considering rolling out a new AI model to counter OpenAI's momentum since its launch of GPT-6 Astra, according to sources, ahead of an expected IPO and after its CEO called for an industry-wide slowdown.
The timing of a potential launch aimed at addressing competitive pressure from a direct rival follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's call on the global AI community to slow down the pace of releasing new capabilities to address safety concerns, the sources said. "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote in a 3,800-word essay on September 12.
The essay, which painted a bleak picture of swarms of AI agents taking over the internet and outpacing human control, drew support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, released this month, has gained traction among businesses, prompting concerns among some investors who told Reuters they are re-evaluating Anthropic's position as the leading provider of enterprise AI tools.
Anthropic is evaluating the safety of its next model as part of its deliberations over a release, one of the people familiar with the matter said. Some of the discussions involve how to balance investment in releasing new models with efforts to strengthen the company's profitability as rising interest rates make investors more focused on the timing of expected profits, said people familiar with the company's thinking.
The debate over spending highlights the increasing pressure on the firms at the centre of the AI boom to produce sustainable cash flows sooner, thanks both to rising rates and tough competition from open-source AI providers, especially in China.
Anthropic declined to comment for this story. The potential launch would test how Anthropic can defend its enterprise market position against OpenAI while maintaining the safety-first identity that has distinguished it from competitors.
OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on September 3, touting gains in computer use, software engineering, cybersecurity and professional work. The model has received a strong response from enterprise users and developers, prompting potential Anthropic IPO investors to scrutinise whether OpenAI could begin taking share from Anthropic, which has been viewed for months as the leader in enterprise AI.
Astra accounted for about 13% of enterprise AI spending tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with about 8% for Anthropic's Claude Fable, according to the latest data.
Astra has also pulled ahead on OpenRouter, a widely used platform that routes developer traffic across AI models. OpenRouter said its users spent more on OpenAI models than on Anthropic models last week, the first time OpenAI has led on that measure in more than two and a half years.
Some existing investors and those who expect to invest in both Anthropic's and OpenAI's IPOs said they do not believe Astra poses a significant threat to Anthropic, given the size of its lead in the market for enterprise AI tools and the amount of time it takes to unseat incumbent vendors to large companies.
Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate topped $65 billion by the end of July, up from about $9 billion at the end of 2025. It is also projecting a 2028 revenue of roughly $190 billion to $200 billion, Reuters previously reported. OpenAI's annualised revenue run rate passed $40 billion in July.
Investors also expect leadership among Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet's Google and other major AI developers to shift repeatedly as companies release new generations of models, making any advantage potentially short-lived.
A potentially bigger challenge for Anthropic and other leading AI providers is the rise of open-source and open-weight models, which can lower token costs and allow companies to build more of their own AI infrastructure rather than rely on providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI, investors said.
The shift could put pressure on the economics of the AI industry as companies have more options to develop and run models outside the leading commercial providers, broadening the competitive threat beyond the race between Anthropic and OpenAI.
Meta Platforms has been among Anthropic's largest customers, but is looking to reduce its use of Anthropic's models as it develops more AI capabilities internally, people familiar with the matter said.
OpenAI, meanwhile, has taken some pressure off the race to public markets. Its CEO, Altman, confirmed on Saturday that the company would not go public in 2026, saying concerns around AI safety made this an ill-advised time for a listing.

title: Diplomatic support sought to boost B2B connectivity

content:
LCCI urges deeper links between business community & foreign missions
Lahore Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) President Faheem Ur Rehman Saigol has called for stronger cooperation between Pakistan's business community and diplomatic missions to promote trade, attract investment and build business-to-business linkages.
Speaking at the LCCI Ambassadors' Dinner 2026, Saigol said embassies and their commercial sections helped Pakistani businesses find new markets, identify reliable partners and gain confidence to invest abroad. He praised them for arranging business meetings, sharing trade information and connecting local firms with companies in their countries. "This support is especially valuable for businesses entering unfamiliar markets."
Saigol said diplomacy had become even more important for business because companies needed peace, stability and predictable policies to grow. He hoped wisdom would prevail and tensions would ease.
He saw potential for cooperation in agriculture, textile, pharmaceuticals, information technology, renewable energy, logistics, mining, tourism and other sectors, and said that Pakistan's large population offered opportunities for international partnerships.
He also asked for more support for small and medium enterprises, saying they could offer quality products but needed guidance on global market requirements and quality standards. He stressed that the LCCI was ready to work with missions through regular meetings and sector-specific interactions and proposed follow-up mechanisms so that contacts made at such events could lead to practical business. Chief Guest Atadjan Movlamov, Turkmenistan's Ambassador and Dean of the Diplomatic Corps, said economic diplomacy had become an indispensable tool of international relations. He said goodwill should be turned into practical, high-impact economic cooperation, and the event's success should be judged by the business delegations, joint ventures and removal of trade barriers that would follow it.
Movlamov named trade facilitation, investment, renewable energy, agriculture, textile, IT and logistics as key areas. He said Pakistan's location could connect South Asia with Central Asia and the Middle East.
He described the TAPI gas pipeline as an example of regional cooperation and said work on it was progressing. He also referred to cooperation in power transmission and fibre-optic links, and said Turkmenistan saw Pakistan as an important maritime gateway.
German Ambassador Ina Lepel said the strongest themes were business-to-business linkages, trade and investment, private-sector cooperation, vocational and technical education, climate and sustainable development. She said Germany attached great importance to stronger economic cooperation with Pakistan and saw considerable potential to expand trade, investment and business links. Portugal Ambassador Paulo Domingues said his country was keen to strengthen economic and commercial ties with Pakistan through more trade, investment and private-sector linkages. He said there was significant potential in agriculture, IT, education and the blue economy. He stressed the importance of stronger institutional and business-to-business connections.

title: SECP clears adjudication cases backlog
description: SECP clears adjudication cases backlog
content:
Issues decisions in 573 cases, imposes penalties of Rs4.7b for violations
The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) disposed of 98% of its adjudication caseload, issuing decisions in 573 cases and imposing penalties exceeding Rs4.73 billion for violations of the Companies Act and other applicable laws.
Following the appointment of SECP Chairman Dr Kabir Ahmed Sidhu, the commission further strengthened its adjudication functions. Of the 969 Adjudication Recommendation Notes available for assessment, 953 were reviewed, while proceedings in 573 cases were concluded through the issuance of orders, said a news release. The remaining recommendations for initiating legal proceedings were subsequently processed through strengthened oversight and effective case management, resulting in the clearance of the entire adjudication backlog.
The proceedings involved listed, unlisted and private companies, as well as regulated entities including securities' brokers, insurance companies and Non-Banking Finance Companies (NBFCs). The violations related to the Companies Act, the Securities Act and other applicable laws and regulatory requirements.
The commission also placed particular emphasis on compliance by state-owned enterprises and issued 117 adjudication orders concerning violations of applicable corporate and regulatory requirements by the SOEs. Major violations included failure to submit financial statements and statutory information, delays in holding annual general meetings, non-disclosure of mandatory information, breaches of financial-reporting and corporate-governance requirements, and failure to appoint female and independent directors.
The SECP chairman said the commission was ensuring timely, transparent and evidence-based decisions in all adjudication matters. He said the SECP's priorities included expeditious disposal of pending proceedings through effective case management, strengthening the rule of law, promoting a culture of regulatory compliance among companies and protecting the interests of investors, particularly minority shareholders.
Furthermore, the SECP on Friday approved Shaamilkar Tajir, a digital application offering Shariah-compliant financing of up to Rs3 million to eligible small businesses. Developed by the SECP-licensed Shaamilkar Financial Services, the application will enable micro-entrepreneurs to purchase inventory from approved suppliers through a simpler and faster digital process, said a news release. The initiative aims to bring underserved businesses into the formal credit system and help them expand their operations.
"Technology-enabled financing can expand access to formal credit for underserved businesses," SECP Chairman Dr Kabir Ahmed Sidhu said, adding that the commission would facilitate responsible digital financing while ensuring regulatory oversight and consumer protection.
The approval supports the federal government's access to finance agenda for SMEs and other priority sectors. Between July 2025 and June 2026, the licensed lending NBFCs provided Rs253 billion through 2.5 million loans to micro, small and medium enterprises. APP

content:
KSE-100 index gains 0.22% as diplomatic hopes lift sentiment in the end
The KSE-100 index gained 0.22% week-on-week to close at 170,885 points at the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) as geopolitical tensions kept the market under pressure for most of the week before expectations of diplomatic engagements ahead of the UN General Assembly session lifted investor sentiment.
On a day-on-day basis, g, which ed almost the whole week, swayed on Monday, and the PSX witnessed a negative session. The KSE-100 declined 2,541 points (-1.49%) to close at 167,971.
Nevertheless, Tuesday was a positive day. The index gained 1,422 points (+0.85%) to close at 169,392. Wednesday was again a negative day, when the market fell 1,371 points (-0.81%) at 168,022. Last two days of the trading week recorded consolidation near 170k. On Thursday, the KSE-100 gained 1,021 points (+0.61%) to close at 169,043 while it posted a gain of 1,841.39 points, or 1.09%, on Friday and settled at 170,884.59.
Arif Habib Limited (AHL) observed that the KSE-100 index rose 0.22% week-on-week to close at 170,885 points versus 170,512 last week as the market remained under pressure from geopolitical concerns for most of the week before sentiment was lifted by anticipation of diplomatic engagements ahead of the UNGA session commencing September 22.
The monetary policy committee (MPC) kept the policy rate unchanged at 11.5%, with seven out of ten members voting in favour of the decision. The committee noted that the intensifying Middle East conflict pushed the already elevated global commodity prices higher, while supply chain disruptions persisted.
In Aug'26, a current account deficit of $98 million was recorded, compared to a deficit of $324 million in Aug'25 and a deficit of $445 million in Jul'26. Pakistan's trade deficit rose 15.1% year-on-year to $3.3 billion in Aug'26 as exports fell 5.2% YoY (-13.9% MoM) to $2.5 billion while imports rose 10.6% YoY (-15.2% MoM) to $5.8 billion.
During 2MFY27, the net foreign direct investment inflow went up by 24% YoY to $494 million compared to the inflow of $399 million in 2MFY26, noted AHL. During Aug'26, technology exports rose 17% YoY, but fell 6% MoM, to $394 million, contributing 45% to the overall services.
Auto sales (cars, LCVs, vans & jeeps) rose 11% YoY but fell 21% MoM to 15.6k units in Aug'26. Excluding Sazgar Engineering, which did not report Aug'26 numbers, volumes were up 20% YoY and down 19% MoM. Auto financing increased 33.8% YoY to Rs393 billion in Aug'26, up from Rs294 billion in Aug'25. On a MoM basis, it increased 1.8%.
Oil production declined 1.4% WoW to 67.5k barrels per day, mainly due to lower flows from Makori East and Pasakhi, while gas production decreased 2.6% WoW to 3,008 million cubic feet per day, driven by lower production from Mari and Shewa.
State Bank's reserves rose $3,061 million WoW to their highest-ever level of $21.4 billion, post-Eurobond receipts, marking the largest weekly increase since June 2025. The rupee appreciated marginally by 0.03%, closing at Rs277.25/$ versus Rs277.32/$ previously, AHL said.
Wadee Zaman of JS Global noted that the KSE-100 remained volatile during the week, rising by 72 points WoW to 170,885 as geopolitical tensions between Iran and the US persisted, although direct skirmishes between the two sides eased. Meanwhile, continued clashes between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia pushed Brent crude higher, with prices peaking at $109/barrel before retreating to around $103 during the week.
On the domestic front, fuel prices continued their upward march, with petrol rising Rs19.99 WoW to Rs390.79/litre, while high-speed diesel prices increased Rs26.88 to Rs424.92/litre. The State Bank kept its policy rate unchanged at 11.5%, noting that recent domestic macroeconomic data remained broadly in line with MPC's expectations.
Pakistan's current account deficit narrowed 78% YoY in Aug'26 to $98 million as a lower import bill and reduced income outflows more than offset weaker exports. The 2MFY27 deficit stood at $543 million, down 36% YoY. Meanwhile, large-scale manufacturing grew a modest 3% YoY, while rising 9.5% MoM in Jul'26.
On the external front, Pakistan was seeking to expand its China swap line, due to expire in 2027, while awaiting the US response to a proposed $10 billion exchange stabilisation facility, Zaman said.

title: Govt aims to strengthen IT education
description: Govt aims to strengthen IT education
content:
Moves to tighten accreditation framework, bridge industry skills gap
Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Establishment Division Senator Ahad Cheema has called for establishing a comprehensive mechanism to address the issue of unaccredited IT institutions, protect students from enrolling in unrecognised programmes and ensure that IT graduates possess internationally competitive skills.
Chairing a high-level meeting to review the IT Skills Assessment Test and the accreditation framework for computing education, the minister asked the Ministry of Information Technology to ascertain the number of graduates completing their degrees from unaccredited institutions and examine the extent of the problem. He emphasised the need for coordinated measures to prevent admissions to institutions and programmes lacking the required accreditation. The minister directed the authorities concerned to develop a mechanism for identifying unaccredited institutions and ensuring that prospective students had access to reliable information about the accreditation status of universities, affiliated colleges and individual programmes before seeking admission.
Reviewing the IT Skills Assessment Test, in which more than 33,000 students from 188 institutions participated, Ahad Cheema called for aligning the assessment framework with international standards and the evolving requirements of the technology industry.
He emphasised that the credibility of assessment process must be ensured through appropriate scrutiny, quality assurance and institutional checks and balances. He directed that a comprehensive report should be prepared on the performance of participating institutions, including an analysis of competency test results to identify institutions requiring corrective measures.
He underlined the need for examining discrepancies between academic qualifications and practical competencies, particularly in cases where students successfully complete degree requirements but fail the skills assessment, or pass the assessment despite not completing their degrees. Such cases require a thorough examination of academic standards, assessment methodologies and the alignment of university curricula with industry requirements. Senator Cheema stressed the importance of stronger industry-academia collaboration to ensure that IT education translates into employable skills and meaningful job opportunities.
He directed relevant authorities to engage the Pakistan Software Houses Association (P@SHA) and other industry stakeholders to align competency assessments, professional certifications and academic programmes with actual requirements of the IT sector.
The meeting also discussed the proposed introduction of mandatory competency assessments at different stages of academic programmes. The minister gave directives that implications of the proposal, particularly for students and educational institutions, be carefully examined before finalising any decision. Reviewing the existing accreditation framework, the minister underscored enhanced coordination among the Higher Education Commission, the National Computing Education Accreditation Council, the Ministry of Information Technology and relevant federal and provincial authorities.
He advocated that provincial higher education authorities be brought on board and relevant education secretaries be engaged to develop a coordinated approach to institutional accreditation and quality assurance.
Cheema emphasised the need to strengthen public awareness regarding accredited and non-accredited institutions. An assessment should also be conducted of existing awareness initiatives, including their reach and engagement on social media, to determine whether prospective students are receiving the necessary information.
The meeting reviewed the participation and performance of various institutions, including the Virtual University, and discussed the need for closer scrutiny of assessment results and institutional performance.
Senator Cheema gave instructions that institutions be provided with a structured mechanism to identify weaknesses in their academic programmes and undertake necessary improvements. He underlined that the objective of the initiative must be to establish a credible, transparent and industry-responsive skills assessment framework that improves the quality of IT education, safeguards students' interests and enhances the employability of Pakistani graduates.

title: Rs60m penalty slapped on edible oil tanker owners
description: Rs60m penalty slapped on edible oil tanker owners
content:
Competition authority blames association for price fixing, business allocation
The Competition Commission of Pakistan (CCP) has imposed a total penalty of Rs60 million on the All Pakistan Edible Oil Tanker Owners Association (APEOTOA) for fixing transportation charges and allocating business among tanker owners through a restrictive queue system, in violation of Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2010. The commission imposed Rs30 million each for price fixing and market allocation.
The case originated from the CCP's market surveillance, which detected circulars fixing transportation charges for edible oil, ghee and fats from Karachi ports to destinations across Pakistan. A suo motu enquiry was initiated in August 2024, followed by search and inspection in February 2025.
The probe established from the material impounded during the search that APEOTOA revised transportation rates 89 times between 2019 and 2025, comprising 52 increases and 37 decreases. Corresponding circulars issued by the Pakistan Vanaspati Manufacturers Association (PVMA) communicated matching rate changes, while APEOTOA representatives acknowledged that transport rates were set through an agreement between the two associations.
The commission rejected APEOTOA's claim that its rate circulars were merely advisory, holding that even non-binding recommendations by a trade association may restrict competition by influencing members' independent commercial decisions. It also relied on the Supreme Court's judgment in the PVMA case, affirming that competitors must remain free to determine their prices independently. The commission separately found that APEOTOA's queue system allocated consignments among tanker owners instead of allowing independent competition for business. The association issued slips (parchis) for lifting consignments and enforced compliance with the system.

Pakistan-Africa Economic Council Patron-in-Chief Hamid Asghar Khan has said that the upcoming Rwanda-Pakistan Business and Investment Forum will play a pivotal role in strengthening bilateral economic and trade relations and opening new avenues for investment between the two countries.
Speaking at a press conference at the embassy of Rwanda ahead of the departure of a Pakistani business delegation for Rwanda, he said the forum, scheduled to be held from September 23 to 25, would provide an important platform for Pakistani businesses to explore investment, trade and joint-venture opportunities in the East African country.

Referring to Rwanda, he said the country had established itself as a competitive and business-friendly economy, with factors including security and stability, skilled human resources, land availability, energy access and a conducive operating environment creating opportunities for international investors.

The Pakistani delegation will hold meetings with Rwandan government institutions, business leaders, investors and private-sector representatives during its visit. title: Data gaps linked to governance
description: Data gaps linked to governance
content:
Effective regulations, better governance can address budget discrepancy
An executive director of London-based Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA) has said that Pakistan can address the issue of large budget discrepancies by improving the governance framework, effective regulations and bringing information transparency.
In an interview with The Express Tribune, Lucia Real Martin said that the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) are "gold standards" but local adjustments can be made, provided there is no deviation that undermines confidence. ACCA Executive Director Relations Lucia Real Martin spoke about a host of issues related to the association's possible support for improving public finance management in Pakistan, the future of the accounting profession, statistical discrepancies and implementation of the IFRS.
She spoke at length on a question about a Rs853 billion statistical discrepancy reported by the federal and four provincial governments in the accounts of fiscal year 2025-26. "There are a number of things to ensure that those discrepancies are not there. We need to contribute to those institutions in becoming credible and they can become credible, if they understand the importance of reporting transparent information and to do that they need to actually understand what they need to report on," said Martin.
She said that improvement in governance framework, training and knowledge can help address the statistical discrepancy in the budget. The governance framework definitely has to be one of the elements in addition to effective regulations to address large statistical discrepancies, she added.
The executive director said that four elements are to have credible institutions, which have governance frameworks that help bring transparency in information. Having all of that is professional capacity, and this is where the ACCA comes in to provide capacity not only at the technical level but at the ethical level, said Martin.
The Cabinet Committee on SOEs last week relaxed the international reporting standards to avoid booking losses in accounts of energy-sector companies and commercial banks due to the chronic circular debt.
"From ACCA's perspective, global standards are the gold standards, but even the global standards need a journey," said the executive director. She noted that over 140 countries are now applying the IFRS, although many have adapted to these standards according to their local context. Adopting the IFRS according to the pace of the country is not wrong and continuing to strive to embrace the global standards would give confidence to investors and the narrative to the government and institutions and promise to the youth that Pakistan is a country that can be global, she added.
She further explained that if the adjustment in these standards is to deviate from the global standards and to create a separate local environment, then it is a breach and once the dent is created, then the separation between the local environment and the global investment environment becomes challenging. Ongoing commitment to the global standards will continue to build confidence in the international arena, with the IMF and with investors, said Martin.
The Central Monitoring Unit (CMU) of the finance ministry had also warned against relaxing these standards but the Cabinet Committee on SOEs did not comply with the advice. According to Rule 9 of the IFRS, aging receivables previously treated as guaranteed recoverable now generate direct impairment charges, exposing systemic fiscal interconnectedness, warned the CMU. During her visit, the executive director also met with Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb. She said that the ACCA has been discussing with Pakistan the possibility of cooperation in the service economy.
Responding to a question about the ACCA affiliates and members settling in Dubai and London, Martin said there are always people who want to get either international experience or move abroad for a different life and this happens everywhere but obviously in Pakistan it is disproportionate.
She said that the answer to this is to build a service economy where organisations are part of global organisations or serve global clients and therefore young people in Pakistan can be able to work with the UK, the US and other Asian countries right from Pakistan.
Unlike a decline in interest in the accounting profession, Martin said that the trend is encouraging in Pakistan. But she added that there are only 22,000 active professional accountants in Pakistan and for the ambitions that the government has for export of services, this number is not enough. "Pakistan's young population is a goldmine, and these people are willing to become professional accountants." Accounting profession has a bright future, and it hinges on the young talent of Pakistan. ACCA members do not have authority to sign statutory audits of companies. But these members work for large corporate firms and perform all other tasks.
ACCA charges the fee in pound sterling. To a question, she said that in future fee structures can be considered in local currencies but she did not give a timeframe. There is a rate card for Pakistan, which is lower than in the UK, but it is still paid in pounds. The economic hardship cases are also acknowledged.

title: 23 abductees rescued  5 terrorists killed as security forces thwart attempt to set up check post near Kalat
description: Six trucks  three buses and two cars recovered from terrorist hideout near Kalat  says ISPR
content:
Six trucks, three buses and two cars recovered from terrorist hideout near Kalat, says ISPR
Security forces foiled an attempt by terrorists to establish a check post for abducting people and snatching vehicles along the Pakistan Highway near Kalat, rescuing 23 abductees and killing five terrorists, the military’s media wing said on Sunday.
According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the operation was conducted during the night of Sept 18-19, when terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan attempted to disrupt the movement of people along the Chaman-Karachi N-25 highway near Kalat.
The terrorists were allegedly trying to establish a check post for abductions for ransom, extortion and vehicle snatching, the statement said.
“Security Forces responded immediately, and after intense fire exchange, five terrorists belonging to Indian-sponsored proxy of Fitna al-Hindustan were sent to hell due to effective response by Armed Forces,” the ISPR said.
The federal government last year officially designated all terrorist groups operating in Balochistan as Fitna al-Hindustan , accusing India of sponsoring a proxy war through the outfits.
Read : Security forces kill seven terrorists in two Balochistan operations: state media
Security forces also recovered 23 abductees from the terrorists’ hideout, along with six trucks, three buses and two cars.
A large quantity of weapons, ammunition and explosives was also recovered from the hideout, according to the statement.
The ISPR said the successful operation had thwarted the “nefarious designs” of the Indian-sponsored proxy of Fitna al-Hindustan .
“Sanitisation operations are continuing in the surrounding areas to eliminate any remaining terrorists and ensure the safety and security of the local population and the vital National Highways,” it said.
The military’s media wing said the counter-terrorism campaign under the vision of “Azm-e-Istehkam”, approved by the Federal Apex Committee on the National Action Plan, would continue “with full resolve”.
“Security Forces and Law Enforcement Agencies remain committed to eliminating the menace of foreign-sponsored and foreign-supported terrorism from the country,” the statement said.
President Asif Ali Zardari has paid tribute to security forces for thwarting an attempt by terrorists to disrupt civilian movement on the Pakistan Highway in the Kalat area of Balochistan.
The president commended the security forces for their effective action, which resulted in the elimination of terrorists affiliated with Fitna al-Hindustan. He also praised the forces for safely recovering abducted individuals from a terrorist hideout and retrieving trucks, buses and other vehicles.
“The entire nation stands shoulder to shoulder with its security forces in the war against terrorism,” the president said.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has praised security forces for their successful operation against terrorists near Kalat on the Pakistan Highway, Chaman-Karachi, N-25. He also commended the forces for conducting timely and effective action that killed five terrorists and safely recovered 23 abducted people from a terrorist hideout.
PM Shehbaz said the security forces had thwarted an attempt by the terrorists to disrupt peaceful civilian movement on the national highway, as well as their efforts to carry out kidnappings for ransom, extortion and vehicle snatching, and also praised the forces for recovering six trucks, three buses and two vehicles, along with a large quantity of weapons, ammunition and explosives from the terrorists.
He said decisive operations against terrorism would continue under the “ Azm-e-Istehkam ” initiative and that terrorism carried out with foreign backing and assistance would be eliminated.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has paid tribute to security forces for their successful operation against terrorists affiliated with Fitna al-Hindustan on the N-25 highway in Kalat. Naqvi praised the professional capabilities of the security forces for killing five terrorists and safely recovering 23 abducted people.
He said the forces had foiled the “nefarious designs” of the terrorists through timely action. “The security forces acted with courage and bravery and safely recovered 23 citizens,” Naqvi said.
He added that the nation stood shoulder to shoulder with the security forces in the fight against terrorism.
Read More : Security forces kill three terrorists during IBO in Balochistan's Awaran: state media
Terrorism is a growing problem for Pakistan, with the number of attacks rising every year since 2022, according to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a global monitoring organisation. Data from ACLED shows attacks in Pakistan rose nearly fourfold to 2,425 in 2025 from 658 in 2022.
Although Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) has borne the brunt of terrorism, Balochistan has also remained a major target of Indian proxies, which often target civilians and military installations in the province.
In one such attack on the last day of 2025, terrorists targeted innocent civilians in Balochistan’s Gwadar and Kharan districts, where 18 people, including women, children, the elderly and labourers, embraced martyrdom.
On August 21, security forces, in coordination with police, killed 49 terrorists in a series of IBOs across K-P and Balochistan over several days.
Earlier this week, security forces killed seven terrorists in Balochistan; six more were killed near Kalat.
A few days ago, security forces killed three terrorists during an IBO in the Badrang area of Awaran district, according to security sources. The operation was conducted under Operation Radd-ul-Fitna 3 against terrorists affiliated with Fitna al-Hindustan , with weapons and ammunition recovered from those killed.

title: Houthis threaten    decisive    response if Pakistan  Turkiye intervene in Yemen
description: Says group will respond forcefully if Pakistan and T  rkiye intervene militarily alongside Saudi Arabia
content:
Say group will respond forcefully if Pakistan and Turkiye intervene militarily alongside Saudi Arabia
As tensions between Yemen’s Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia mount amid renewed attacks, the group has issued a direct warning to Pakistan and Türkiye, threatening a “decisive and painful response” if either country intervened militarily alongside Saudi Arabia in Yemen.
Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of Ansar Allah’s political bureau and governor of Dhamar, made the remarks during an interview with the Iraqi television programme Another Reading .
“By God, if Türkiye and Pakistan become involved, we will strike them with an iron fist,” al-Bukhaiti said, adding that the Houthis would “teach” both countries a lesson if they joined what he described as Saudi aggression against Yemen.
A senior Houthi political figure has issued an unusually direct warning to Pakistan and Türkiye, threatening a “decisive and painful response” if either country intervenes militarily alongside Saudi Arabia in Yemen. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of Ansar Allah’s political… pic.twitter.com/ZKTW3AjjjS
The warning comes as continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have placed growing attention on the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye.
Al-Bukhaiti nevertheless acknowledged what he described as strong sympathy for Yemen among the Pakistani and Turkish populations, saying his warning was directed at their governments if they became militarily involved.
The Houthi warning has brought renewed focus on Pakistan’s position following the signing of the Pakistan-Saudi Arabia-Türkiye defence agreement earlier this year.
Signed by Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia on August 7, the pact is based on the principles of shared responsibility and regional ownership amid growing regional and global instability. It aims to promote security, peace, stability and prosperity while strengthening collective deterrence.
Under the agreement, an attack against any one of the signatory states will be considered an attack against all parties.
The pact has assumed greater significance amid the renewed attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia and growing concerns over possible military involvement by its signatories.
The Houthi warning came as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty had come under serious attack and that Türkiye, bound by its alliance commitments, stood in solidarity with Riyadh.
“Saudi Arabia may need military-level support. As the Makkah Alliance, we will take this up with Pakistan and can provide the necessary technical support,” Fidan said.
He said Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry had condemned attacks on oil infrastructure near Makkah and that the alliance was closely monitoring the situation.
Fidan added that any military needs would likely centre on specific technical areas.
Yemen has been gripped by war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised Yemeni government.
The group has been engaged in renewed fighting with government forces since July, when it declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh, and has recently claimed advances along the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis have also targeted Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure, further raising concerns over oil prices in the international market.
Pakistan has, from the outset, condemned the Houthi attacks on the Kingdom, describing them as a serious violation of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity while reaffirming its solidarity with Riyadh.
However, following the reported attack near Makkah, Islamabad adopted a more forceful stance, with its concerns also being voiced at the United Nations.
That increasingly forceful position was articulated by Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who told a private television channel that Pakistan would defend Makkah and Madinah, calling their protection an “eternal agreement”.
“Their protection is our religious obligation. So yes, there are worldly agreements, and they have their sanctity, which we also honour, but if an attack takes place on the House of God or the place where the Prophet (PBUH) was born, then no Muslim sitting anywhere would ultimately need to wait for any agreement. This is our religious duty — to protect it,” he added.
Later, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry reinforced the position , reiterating Pakistan’s “unconditional” commitment to Saudi Arabia and saying the country would “go to any extent” required to ensure the security of the Haramain Sharifain and the Kingdom.
“Nothing stops us, nothing bars us, nothing is there which hesitates our commitment from going, so whatever is required, whatever is asked, we will go to any extent to that,” he said.

title: Naqvi to visit Tehran today for bilateral discussions  Iranian foreign ministry
description: Baghaei says Pakistan   s Naqvi will visit Tehran to follow up on previous bilateral understandings
content:
Baghaei says Naqvi will visit Tehran to follow up on previous bilateral understandings
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Saturday confirmed that Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi would visit Tehran on Sunday, stressing that the trip was “entirely” within the framework of bilateral discussions.
Iranian outlet IRIB reported that speaking to state television’s Khabar network, Baghaei said Iran’s relations with Pakistan had particularly improved in recent months and that Tehran’s neighbourhood policy was based on using cultural, historical and other shared links to strengthen ties.
Asked about Naqvi’s visit and speculation that he could carry a US message or proposal, Baghaei said Iran had “very good and growing relations” with its neighbour.
Read : Pakistan plans fresh diplomatic push
“The visit of Pakistan’s interior minister is entirely within the framework of bilateral discussions,” he said, adding that one of Pakistan’s economic ministers might also accompany him.
According to Baghaei, the main purpose of the visit was to follow up on previous understandings between the two countries, particularly decisions reached at the leadership level.
He said Pakistan, having played a mediating role, could naturally use such opportunities to raise regional issues.
“But so far, there has been no discussion of him carrying any specific message or proposal from the United States,” he said.
Asked about a message posted by the Foreign Office regarding a telephone conversation between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, Baghaei said the two foreign ministers remained in close contact and consultation on various regional and bilateral issues.
He said the two sides had agreed to meet and hold talks on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
“Alongside active participation in the General Assembly meetings, extensive plans have been made for bilateral consultations with officials from various countries,” he said.
Read More : Dar underscores need for uninterrupted energy supplies, safe passage of ships in call with Iranian FM
He added that a meeting with Dar was among the planned engagements on the sidelines of the visit, with a wide range of bilateral relations and international developments expected to be discussed.
Earlier, it was reported that Islamabad was preparing to send another high-level delegation to Tehran in a fresh diplomatic push aimed at breaking the stalemate between Iran and the United States and containing rapidly escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis.
The visit comes at a particularly sensitive moment for Pakistan, which has been trying to maintain its role as a bridge between Iran and the United States while simultaneously managing its growing security commitments to Saudi Arabia.
Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts have acquired another dimension as fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthis has intensified.

Saudi Arabia and the Houthis exchanged fresh attacks this week, with Riyadh carrying out airstrikes against Houthi positions while the group launched drone and missile attacks against Saudi territory.
The escalation has raised concerns about the security of Saudi energy infrastructure and shipping routes around the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb.
The latest diplomatic initiative also follows a telephone conversation between Araghchi and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir. Iranian media reported that the two discussed the latest regional developments while Araghchi was in Beijing.
According to the Financial Times , CDF Munir subsequently conveyed Pakistan’s concerns to Iranian officials over the Houthi attacks and urged Tehran to restrain the group. The report said Islamabad had warned that the situation could have implications for Pakistan’s defence commitments to Saudi Arabia.
Pakistan’s position has become more consequential following the signing of the Pakistan-Saudi Arabia-Türkiye defence agreement in August, under which an attack on one of the signatories is to be treated as an attack on all.
