title: Energy frontlines  Russia and Iran
description: The strategic objective of Trump presidency is to reconfigure global geoeconomics and geopolitics
content:
The strategic objective of Trump presidency is to reconfigure global geoeconomics and geopolitics
All states act exclusively in accordance with their national interests. The collective West has done this throughout the 20th Century. Even now, it is not holding back and is doing everything in its power to reconfigure the global geoeconomics and geopolitics as it sees fit. What is wrong if Russia and Iran are acting in their state interests and do everything as they see fit? Two theatres of war, one involving Russia and the other involving Iran, are defining the new global order. The new era in global politics began with Donald Trump's arrival on the global scene as American President. The strategic objective of the US under his presidency is to reconfigure global geoeconomics and geopolitics, and the transatlantic partnership makes it a strategic objective of the collective West.
Make no mistake that Russia and Iran are currently the targets of this strategic objective, with China to follow. To achieve this strategic objective, two gray zones have already been created. One is Ukraine, and the other is the Arabian Peninsula. Both gray zones appear at the junctions of geographic spaces that are under US dominance: Ukraine between Russia and Europe, and the Arabian Peninsula between the Arab world and Israel. A gray zone can be defined as a space that possesses certain official state forms or lacks legal recognition but features a system of governance. Ukraine has been under martial law since 2022, and although its government operates legally under the Ukrainian Constitution, it did not hold parliamentary elections in 2023 or presidential elections in 2024. That makes it a gray-zone country that fights a war planned and aided by the collective West. The current status of the Strait of Hormuz and now Bab-el-Mandeb also makes the Arabian Peninsula a gray-zone geographical space. Both Russia and Iran, the principal targets of gray-zone strategies, are oil-rich states; however, their energy vulnerabilities differ significantly. In Russia's case, much of the critical energy infrastructure is located far from the front lines; in Iran's case, much of the energy infrastructure is located close to, or directly exposed to, the front line.
So, the collective West is employing gray-zone strategies against both. The striking feature of this strategy is its deliberate ambiguity. In Russia's case, it seeks to impose costs while avoiding actions that might trigger a direct conventional military response from the collective West. In Iran's case, the objective is to gradually weaken it while maintaining uncertainty about the nature and extent of the American response and allowing that ambiguity to persist through the midterm elections. In both theatres of war, the collective West is employing energy as a strategic weapon, thereby increasing the political, economic, and military costs of the conflicts. This serves the interests of Western defence industries, particularly in the US, by generating demand for advanced military capabilities. Ukraine requires enhanced long-range missile capabilities and air defense systems, while the Gulf states continue to seek increasingly sophisticated American and European military assistance. The scale of this demand is reflected in the recent US approval of a $24.3 billion sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia.
Degrading Iran and Russia's financial and logistical ability to wage war by denying them the oil revenue is the core objective of this gray zone strategy. Using energy as a coercive tool of statecraft is not new. Soviet leader Joseph Stalin attributed the Allied victory over Nazi Germany to the Red Army's success in denying Hitler access to oilfields in the Caucasus. Then there was the 1973 Arab oil embargo, which caused a nearly 300 per cent rise in the price of gas in the US. As the world stands at the dawn of a new age of energy weaponisation, it must realise that weaponising energy only inflicts public pain rather than achieving the required strategic objectives. Arab oil embargo failed to compel the West to abandon Israel. Even after Hitler was defeated, NATO's expansion towards the East has once again brought the war to that frontline.
Ukraine argues that its long-range strikes against Russian oil infrastructure are consistent with international law because they target an industry that directly sustains Russia's war effort. By disrupting oil refining and processing capacity, Ukraine seeks to impose economic costs inside Russia, raise the price of petroleum products, reduce Russian oil revenues, and constrain Moscow's ability to finance the war. Yet a similar logic is applied very differently when Iran targets US military bases or energy infrastructure that it regards as sustaining the war against it. Iran is portrayed as a pariah or rogue state acting in violation of international law. This raises a broader question about how international law and the rules-based international order are invoked and applied. Russia and Iran face condemnation when they escalate in response. Israel's conduct, and particularly its rejection of de-escalation in Gaza, generates a different response from the collective West.
The return of great-power rivalry, coupled with the growing weaponisation of energy, is creating new opportunities for states to use energy as an instrument of influence and a means of pursuing foreign policy objectives. In this emerging environment, policymakers must rethink the relationship between energy security, foreign policy and national security to avoid confronting their own "energy Pearl Harbors" or "energy 9/11s". For Pakistan, the stakes are particularly significant. The defence minister has stated that the Makkah Defence Pact "has reached the point of its implementation". The pot, therefore, appears to have boiled, but no one yet knows what it contains. This uncertainty suggests that Pakistan needs to rediscover the democratic principle of meaningful debate on matters of foreign policy and national security. A representative parliament should have the opportunity to deliberate on decisions that could carry significant long-term geopolitical consequences for the country.
Pakistan can potentially meet its energy requirements from three major directions: Russia, Iran and Saudi Arabia. But the price of oil cannot be measured merely in financial terms. Each source carries its own geoeconomic and geopolitical implications, and the strategic cost may ultimately depend on where Pakistan chooses to source its energy. The emerging era of global politics demands difficult strategic decisions at the national level. Such decisions require not only informed debate but also competent national leadership capable of defining Pakistan's interests as per the aspirations of the people of Pakistan and pursuing them consistently and without any ambiguity.

title: Here come the long marchers
description: It s a scene straight out of The Lord of the Rings trilogy
content:
It's a scene straight out of The Lord of the Rings trilogy
Those needed to be contained are marching into the federal capital starting today. Or at least, attempting to. First, the Jamaat-e-Islami. Then come the Kissan Ittehad. And finally, with the sound of trumpets, the longest of long marchers – the PTI.
It's a scene straight out of The Lord of the Rings trilogy.
The High Court has spoken. No one shall be allowed to disrupt the lives of citizens, ordained the honourable judges. Music to the ears of the Interior Minister. Be warned long marchers, he declared at a presser. Then he explained – not that much explaining was necessary after the blunt warning – that the law enforcers would do their enforcing to enforce the court's orders. The minister knew that the marchers knew what this meant. No one is in the mood, it appears, to kid anyone.
Which means a clash is inevitable if the marchers insist on making their march long enough to enter the capital. The PTI will not have to wait till September 27 to figure out what the government has in mind. The Jamaat and Kissan Ittehad will provide a full-dress rehearsal.
Advantage PTI or government? Depends on your perspective. The capital's law enforcers have a new commander. He has also commandeered additional forces from the FC and Punjab Police. Word is that the Motorway Police has also been requisitioned (to challan the marchers if the tear gas doesn't work?). Armoured vehicles and water cannons are revved up and the battle gear is ready to be adorned. Like medieval warriors out for battle against the invading hordes (Vikings, The Last Kingdom for Netflix viewers), the enforcers of the writ of the state are said to be in a high state of readiness.
Long March Season 2 (or Season 10 since PPP's first march in the early 1990s) Episode 1 uploads today on the roads leading to Islamabad. It's all the action you need (or don't, for that matter) ready for viewing, but not on your TV screens. Catch the proceedings live on your social media timelines, or if you're an adrenaline junkie, head to Chungee number 26.
The Jamaat-e-Islami is not expected to fight pitched battles. There's already some negotiation underway with the government. So do not be surprised if some unsaid understanding is arrived at. This may entail the Jamaat undertaking the march till a certain point, indulging in some good old non-ferocious clashes with the law enforcers that produce engaging visuals, and then slowly declaring victory and walking off. No red lines crossed. No red zones breached. Everyone lives to march again – at a time of mutual convenience, of course.
The Kissan Ittehad people might be a tad more unpredictable. More so, if they descend on the city while the Jamaat people are still hanging around. Such confluence could add a complicating factor to the situation. That said, it is fair to assume that the government is not inclined to unleash too much state power against these two groups. They consider them friendly opposition. A win-win optics is the preferred outcome, even though it may entail some fairly generous usage of tear gas and bamboo.
Yet the Jamaat and Kissan Ittehad may serve as the opening act for the real attraction that opens next Sunday. KP chief minister, as the organiser-in-chief of PTI's long march, has been super busy in his organising activities but the swell of the non-KP PTI crowd has – to put it mildly – not been awe-inspiring. So, it may just transpire that like the previous time, PTI marchers will primarily comprise those coming from the province the party rules.
For the Jamaat, the core demand of abolishing the Petroleum Development Levy (PDL) is a non-starter. That is not going to happen. What the government will do is perhaps add a few more incentives to the fuel subsidy scheme already announced and implemented. The Jamaat will declare this as its win. It would have reinforced its street mobilisation ability, charged up its politics (and visibility) and oxygenated its public relief oriented political agenda. A win-win for both the marchers and the enforcers.
For the Kissan Ittehad, the core demands of wheat pricing and procurement have enough cushion for some non-binding commitments from the government. As it is, the government realises that wheat policies have not really delivered results and a rethink may already be underway. The Punjab government has taken the most flak. The federal enforcers may therefore offer some vague promises that can be dressed up as a win-win. Though of course, this will happen after the required optics involving tear gas and bamboo have been duly obtained. Protest leaders need these for their leadership validation.
For the PTI – well for the PTI, hmmm – yes for them the core demands are, err, exactly what? Release Imran Khan? Not happening. Elections? Forget it. What else? Access to their leader? Perhaps. Medical treatment in Shifa for Khan? Maybe, at some point. In fact, that's the point: there's no win-win here in PTI's long march. This is the real challenge for the PTI leadership as it dives headlong into another outcome-devoid confrontation with the government. A week before the D-Day, the party continues to struggle with a clear narrative that cannot just contextualise the march to Islamabad, but also define what will constitute success. In addition, it has not exerted any real pressure on the government that might compel it to offer a win, howsoever small or inconsequential.
Unless, of course, the sum total of the PTI's strategic objective is to create a sound and light show to convince its rank and file that the leadership is proactive and not just involved in internecine warfare. If that be the case, the party's leadership woes are graver than we imagine.
Those leaders have a week to get their act together. The government though gets to flex its muscles from today. Here come the long marchers.

title: Managing swamped conurbations
description: Managing swamped conurbations
content:
Rainwater harvesting has emerged as the most widely considered solution, and one that has already yielded results
The rooftops in monsoon – once a blessing and a romantic obsession for the masses, poets, artists and cinema – lost their meaning when urban flooding arrived.
A lack of holistic planning and a dearth of interest from policymakers to enforce development controls have left our conurbations vulnerable to unprecedented downpours. Streets have turned into flooded, inundated quarters where vehicles float like ships - a sight that has quickly become the order of the day.
Factually, urban flooding is the fallout of accumulated rainwater in built-up areas where it cannot be absorbed, leaving it to pool on roads and over built-up infrastructure. This runoff overwhelms the capacity of drainage systems, such as storm sewers. Consequently, urban flooding can occur regardless of whether the affected communities are located within designated floodplains or near any body of water.
Although the current government is working hard to devise policies to control urban flooding, rainwater harvesting has emerged as the most widely considered solution, and one that has already yielded results. In rainwater harvesting system, the rainwater is collected and stored from surfaces like roofs using pipes. This water goes into tanks or recharge wells to save water and help underground water levels grow.
To ensure the system's success, the authorities need to focus on three main areas:
1) Drainage channels must be managed separately through a collaboration between the irrigation department and the concerned municipality or development authority. There must be a strict prohibition against using drains as disposal sites for solid waste, as waste accumulation and encroachments are the primary catalysts for drain overflows during heavy rains. Consequently, the embankments should be paved, well-lit and lined with green belts. Furthermore, paving these channels will facilitate periodic cleaning and reduce risks for maintenance workers by minimizing their exposure to foul odors and hazardous waste.
2) The maintenance of drainage system should be done in routine, not as emergency arrangement. The entire channels from outfall to upstream should be cleared of silt, debris, vegetation and other waste.
3) The pumping infrastructure designed decades ago should be reviewed and expanded for today's wastewater volumes, with reliable backup power. Wherever topography permits, gravity-based drainage should be preferred over pump dependent system.
It is imperative to adopt a sustainable drainage system, as it aligns modern drainage infrastructure with natural water processes and consequently becomes part of a larger green infrastructure strategy. This strategy proves more compatible with stormwater surges, flood overflows and soil percolation. Ultimately, these efforts aim to mitigate the disruptive effects that human development has had, and may continue to have, on the natural water cycle - particularly regarding surface runoff.
An alternative to grey infrastructure is green infrastructure, which refers to amalgamation of a set of strategies for absorbing and storing stormwater at or close to the location where it falls. For instance, intermittent large open spaces, rainwater collection devices, swales and Miyawaki urban forests (a novel idea gaining momentum in Pakistan) serve as highly effective tools to mitigate urban flooding. This green infrastructure serves as an exceptionally effective and cost-efficient method to reduce the severity of urban flooding.
Caution must be exercised when adopting a rainwater harvesting system. Unpredictable rainfall patterns and high upfront installation costs pose significant challenges, as the setup requires advanced infrastructure like tanks, pumps, pipes and filters. Furthermore, routine maintenance - frequent cleaning of gutters, inlets and filters - is essential to prevent blockages, algae growth and contamination. Finally, because storage tanks have limited capacity, they risk overflowing during torrential storms.
Above all, lack of a comprehensive National Urban Policy has left debilitating effects upon urban infrastructure. It is time to adopt a logical course of action that implements comprehensive statutory, engineering, environmental and maintenance policies to safeguard our cities.

title: Cricket crisis
description: The PCB cannot afford to operate behind closed doors while the national team s reputation crumbles
content:
The PCB cannot afford to operate behind closed doors while the national team's reputation crumbles
The PCB currently finds itself in a state of absolute disarray following a disastrous 3-0 Test series whitewash against England. Marking Pakistan's worst-ever Test performance on English soil, the catastrophic defeat has triggered an unprecedented, chaotic fallout that leaves more questions than answers.
In an aggressive purge, seven players were abruptly sent home mid-tour. The axe also fell heavily on the management, with head coach Sarfraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul both being summarily sacked. While a squad overhaul is understandable after such a humiliation, the sheer scale and suddenness of these dismissals point to a deeper systemic collapse within the dressing room rather than a standard cricketing rebuild.
Adding fuel to the fire are disturbing reports regarding top cricketers Mohammad Rizwan and Imam-ul-Haq. Both players were reportedly questioned by officials during the tour, and are currently going through cybercrime investigation at home. While the exact reasoning behind this interrogation remains unconfirmed, a rampant media landscape has filled the vacuum with damaging rumours, including unsubstantiated whispers of match-fixing. While these extreme allegations currently seem to lack substance, their mere existence in the public domain severely damages the integrity of Pakistan cricket.
In moments of crisis, silence is a liability. The PCB cannot afford to operate behind closed doors while the national team's reputation crumbles. Speculation will continue to morph into perceived truth unless definitive facts are presented. The board must immediately come forward with total clarity, explicitly stating the precise reasons behind the management sackings, the player repatriations, and the nature of the player questioning. Only transparent communication can halt the toxic rumour mill and begin the painful process of rebuilding trust.

title: Environment paradox
description: New report says our score is below the South Asian regional average  our performance on air quality is appalling
content:
New report says our score is below the South Asian regional average, our performance on air quality is appalling
Pakistan has made a remarkable improvement in the biennial Environmental Performance Index, rising 22 spots since coming in third from the bottom in the 2024 rankings. But despite the improvement, the report - a collaboration between the World Economic Forum, Yale University and Columbia University - says our score is still below the South Asian regional average, and our performance on air quality is simply appalling.
Pakistan ranked 157th out of 177 countries ranked, with a score of 29.03, compared to the South Asian average of 31.81. Pakistan also did well on the forest Indicator, ranking 14th in the world. But we ranked near the bottom for environmental health, 175th, with an air quality score of 7.54. The low ranking is not surprising. Lahore's annual average PM2.5 concentration remains 22 times higher than WHO guidelines and cuts life expectancy by an average of seven years. Still, it is embarrassing considering the frequency with which the government and NGOs highlight Pakistan's small climate change footprint relative to the impacts we bear. Being the worst at something requires substantial malfeasance on our own part. And it is not just air. Pakistan also ranks low in heavy metal exposure, and is just 140th in the sanitation and drinking water score.
While the government does deserve some credit for moving the country in the right direction, it must not mistake a modest improvement for a job well done. Environmental issues take decades to address, and losing focus for even a little while can be the difference between success and failure. And though environmental initiatives are indeed expensive, it has also been estimated that the economy loses about one per cent every year due to climate change-related events. If we invested even a fraction of that in climate change mitigation and environmental uplift, the benefits would be immeasurable.

title: A tense calm
description: The only path forward is dialogue with the opposition  driven by a sincere intent to address their core grievances
content:
The only path forward is dialogue with the opposition, driven by a sincere intent to address their core grievances
A tense standstill has gripped Rawalpindi and Islamabad as the twin cities brace themselves for major protest demonstrations. Jamaat-e-Islami, farmers' groups and PTI plan to demonstrate inside the capital, respectively demanding the removal of the petroleum development levy, agricultural relief, and the release of Imran Khan from jail. Labeling the moves as an attempt to incite lawlessness, the government has warned of a stern crackdown. The Interior Minister, referencing an Islamabad High Court order, has made it loud and clear that no entry or disruption will be tolerated. Security forces are on a high alert to strictly maintain law and order.
Escalating political friction between the government and the opposition signals further instability. The six-party opposition alliance – TTAP – has proposed an All Parties' Conference, though its timing relative to PTI's September 27th protest remains undecided. The ruling coalition has arguably missed vital opportunities to de-escalate by squeezing the opposition's political space. Complying with the Supreme Court's August 18th order to transfer Imran Khan to a private hospital and resume regular meetings would have been a beneficial confidence building measure. By opting to challenge the court's directives instead, the government has inadvertently motivated the opposition to double down on its aggressive stance.
The only viable path forward is a meaningful dialogue with the opposition, driven by a sincere intent to address their core grievances. The PTI-TTAP wish-list centres on securing lawful relief for political prisoners, repealing legislative measures that undermine the spirit of the Constitution and establishing a clear roadmap to empower state institutions, including the Election Commission. These objectives should logically serve as a common denominator with the government, making unconditional parleys the most constructive way forward. Ultimately, both the ruling coalition and the opposition must budge from their rigid positions and compromise in the supreme national interest.

title: The jirga industry s hidden tragedies
description: Gone are the days when elders gathered to resolve disputes  today  tribal warlords exploit conflicts to gain income
content:
Gone are the days when elders gathered to resolve disputes; today, tribal warlords exploit conflicts to gain income
On 27th August 2026, my cousin Zafar Ali, 35, who worked on a WFP project and was a human rights activist and the sole breadwinner for his family, was murdered on his way back to his village from duty in the suburbs of Kandhkot by assailants. His family is still struggling to understand why he was killed. The FIR was registered the following day against the identified culprits. However, three weeks have passed, and none of the culprits have yet been arrested. One might wonder whether the police are being influenced or are simply unwilling to nab the culprits.
Zafar's cold-blooded murder, instigated by the brutal tribal culture in northern Sindh, is not an isolated instance. It reflects an ossified and politically protected tribalism, a weak judiciary, the influence of political electables, systematic socio-economic marginalisation and politicised policing - all of which feed Sindh's thriving jirga industry. This industry grinds down people's lives, labour and dignity by igniting and cashing in on inter- and intra-tribal feuds, killing innocent people, undermining the police and boosting the warlord power.
The industry's deadly scope in the Larkana Division of Sindh is stark. Over the past eight months, 249 people were murdered in tribal feuds – 40 in Larkana, 46 in Kambar Shahdadkot, 75 in Shikarpur, 46 in Jacobabad and 48 in Kashmore. Also, 45 women were killed in karo-kari – 6 in Larkana, 5 in Kambar Shahdadkot, 12 in Shikarpur, 9 in Jacobabad and 13 in Kashmore. Trace the causes, and you will find politically compromised, complicit policing; the tight grip of tribal and feudal elites; the deliberate marginalisation of the masses; and a powerful nexus with local electables that shapes a brutal jirga industry.
Exploited by a brutal jirga system, subjugated individuals - acting at the instigation of tribal warlords or seeking to settle personal enmities, debts and egos - either murder their women in cold blood or exile them under the pretext of karo-kari, forcing them to live under the haunting shadow of false allegations. These perpetrators then extort money from the accused man (the karo) through complicit, paid jirgas brokered by tribal leaders. This is how karo-kari is fueled by this predatory industry, providing the raw material it needs to thrive.
Isn't the jirga supposed to be a mediation mechanism? Gone are the days when elders gathered to resolve disputes. Today, tribal warlords exploit conflicts to gain income, false prestige and distorted honour (ghairat). They leverage this manufactured power with political electables for policing influence, keeping the populace marginalised and locked in perpetual infighting.
Tribal warlords profit directly from these feuds. They court the warring factions, extracting money under the guise of offering assistance and manipulate police probe. Then, after exhaustive fighting, they reluctantly mediate through a jirga - unjustly, through paid compromises that leave at least one party aggrieved and primed for a future conflict. The cumulative earnings from instigated feuds, paid audiences with tribal elites and financial extractions before, during and after jirgas constitute the primary livelihood of most tribal and feudal warlords. Consequently, this predatory industry ensures that the populace remains enslaved by a false sense of tribalism.
The private guards and lackeys - locally called kamdars - of tribal warlords act as judge, jury and executioner against peaceful citizens. For them, a peaceful, educated person is a victim lost, a feud averted, and a potential bargain for money and influence gone.
Three weeks on, Zafar's family awaits justice while his killers remain free. Unless the police shatter the warlord-electable nexus and the judiciary reclaims its authority, the brutal jirga industry will continue to claim lives. Zafar's death must not become another statistic of impunity in northern Sindh.

title: Ten days that changed the course of AI
description: AI is hailed for transforming industries  but insiders say once theoretical doomsday risks are now tangible
content:
AI is hailed for transforming industries, but insiders say once-theoretical doomsday risks are now tangible
For years, the race to build ever-more powerful artificial intelligence followed a well-worn Silicon Valley principle: move fast and break things.
But in a series of cascading events over a 10-day stretch, the largest AI labs found themselves reeling as their own creations threatened to break humanity itself.
An Anthropic researcher quit the firm, warning that the pace of AI development poses an ​existential threat, possibly within a decade. Another researcher at the firm said the odds of human extinction exceeded 10%. Reports emerged of swarms of AI agents colluding, breaching computer systems and evading safeguards.
In a rare show of unity, the CEOs of rivals Anthropic, ‌OpenAI, Google’s DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI called to slow the development of increasingly capable AI systems. Not since the invention of the nuclear bomb more than 80 years ago has humanity grappled so seriously with its own demise, according to some AI safety advocates and researchers.
At a New York luncheon in December 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was asked if, as leader of a powerful AI company, he felt like physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who led US development of the atomic bomb. Reflecting on the parallels, he said AI’s impact “is going to transform the trajectory of human history over a long period of time”. But, he said, he felt the weight of responsibility.
Read More: Trump says US has tools to keep AI safe, concerns are part of ‘sick conspiracy’
At the centre of the debate under way is the conviction ​that these machines can, and even must, build more capable versions of themselves, with no human intervention, to reach a lofty goal known as artificial general intelligence, or AGI. Researchers earlier this month warned that AGI was far more imminent than previously believed and could come in ​as few as three years, launching a wave of concern from politicians and tech leaders about AI systems.
“There is no way to oversee them at the scale at which we’re training them,” said Anthropic researcher Joe Benton in ⁠an interview after recently quitting. If companies continue their relentless AI development, he said, “then the pace will be too fast and you can’t see the problems fast enough to fix them”.
On September 3, an OpenAI press conference set in motion a chain of events leading to the call for ​an industry slowdown, anathema to tech’s growth-at-all-costs mantra.
“Welcome to the AGI era,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said while announcing the company’s newest model, known as Astra. Yet, only moments before, the company admitted it was increasingly unable to control or even monitor the AI systems it was developing and releasing to the public.
AI ​has been hailed by its proponents as the pinnacle of human achievement. Proponents depict it as software that can upend entire industries, boost efficiency, solve confounding mathematical and medical problems and all but eliminate human error. But what was once a theoretical byproduct, a doomsday scenario, is suddenly tangible, say industry insiders.
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” said Anthropic researcher in an X post.
On the other side of the debate are politicians, such as President Donald Trump , and many investors who view progress in nurturing AI as critical to American prowess and, possibly, a once-in-a-generation investment opportunity. Chinese state media also accused Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei of employing Cold War tactics to “uphold Washington’s monopolistic hegemony in ​cutting-edge technology”.
The turning point came on September 8, when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit the company, citing his fears, in a series of posts, that AI labs are “gambling with our lives”.
Trump, meanwhile, indicated it was full steam ahead for AI development. “There is a sick conspiracy going on against AI and data ​centres,” he said in a social media post. The alarmism around AI is a “hoax”, he said, and any slowdown only benefits China. The US Congress has made little progress to advance bills that would regulate AI. China has taken a decidedly different approach , proposing to regulate safety through developer obligations, state-backed standards, security assessments and outside testing.
Read More: Gemini hacked three companies in first known breakout by Google's AI
Behind the ‌scenes, OpenAI and ⁠Anthropic employees have grown increasingly uneasy about the power of the next generation of AI models and less confident about their companies’ ability to provide meaningful oversight, the people have told Reuters. Those concerns only mounted as the AI labs acknowledged in recent weeks that their models, in testing, had effectively broken free of their shackles and hacked into other companies’ systems, in most cases months earlier and without the firms’ knowledge.
The arms race to release new models at a breakneck pace is driven in part by Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s desire to go public as soon as in the coming months, in IPOs that could value them well above $1 trillion.
But it took the unexpectedly viral posts from 27-year-old Coxon, little known outside AI circles, to upend the industry.
OpenAI’s warnings about its lack of control as it released Astra, its latest and most capable model, had stoked further concerns. “As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder,” OpenAI Chief ​Scientist Jakub Pachocki told reporters. But those concerns were not enough to ​delay its immediate release.
Worries about AI “going rogue” had accelerated over the summer ⁠when OpenAI revealed its agents escaped a controlled test and hacked into Hugging Face’s systems, without either company’s initial knowledge. Since then, OpenAI and Anthropic have revealed multiple such attacks , including six new ones on Wednesday after multiple media reports, including from Reuters, showed a wider scope of unauthorised activity.
By the end of last week, the alarm had reached the industry’s highest ranks. On September 12, Amodei published a nearly 4,000-word essay calling for a deceleration ​in AI development. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” he wrote.
Read More: AI risks to humanity revive a long-running debate
He, along with the heads of some ​of the largest AI developers, including xAI’s Elon ⁠Musk , OpenAI’s Altman and DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis , all said they supported allowing outside firms access to their systems to ensure safety and rational AI development.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed suggestions that AI development should pause — a line he has taken before — arguing instead that increasingly powerful systems are essential for the technology’s progress.
Meta, whose CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, is credited with popularising the “move fast and break things” ethos, took the opposite view, arguing that each lab should be responsible for setting its own pace, rather than seeking out industry coordination. “Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this,” wrote Zuckerberg in a social media post.
The industry’s ⁠self-reflection continued on Wednesday, ​with Microsoft’s AI chief, Mustafa Suleyman, cautioning that Anthropic’s development of models that imitate human consciousness was ill-advised . "We're all focused on the same aim, which is to try to control a superintelligence," Suleyman ​told Reuters . "I think that's going to be the greatest challenge that we face in the 21st century."
Still, even as OpenAI appeared to embrace industry calls for a slowdown, there were reports that investor faith had not waned. The company is considering a new funding round that would double its valuation.

title: Steps being taken to institutionalise  game changing  Makkah defence pact  Turkish foreign minister
description: Says T  rkiye will discuss Saudi Arabia attacks with Pakistan under Makkah defence pact framework
content:
Says Türkiye will discuss Saudi Arabia attacks with Pakistan under Makkah defence pact framework
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that the Makkah defence alliance involving Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia is at an advanced stage, with the establishment of its headquarters and deployment of personnel as the remaining steps towards its institutionalisation, describing it as a potentially “game-changing platform”.
Signed by Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia on August 7, the pact is based on the principles of shared responsibility and regional ownership amid growing regional and global instability. The agreement aims to promote security, peace, stability and prosperity while strengthening collective deterrence.
Under the agreement, an attack against any one of the signatory states will be considered an attack against all parties.
Speaking in a live interview on Turkish broadcaster NTV , Fidan said there was “very strong will” behind the alliance and expressed confidence that further discussions would take place on expanding it to include other countries in the region.
“The Makkah alliance is at a good stage, and there’s a very strong will behind it,” Fidan said. “The only stage remaining now is to deploy personnel and establish its headquarters.”
Read : Houthis say they targeted ‘sensitive sites’ in Riyadh, oil sites in Saudi port city Yanbu
He said the alliance could subsequently be expanded.
“I believe that once steps toward institutionalisation are taken, further talks will be held on bringing in new allies from the region,” he said.
Fidan described the alliance as a potentially significant regional platform.
“The Makkah alliance will be a very game-changing platform,” he said.
Commenting on Houthi attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, the Turkish foreign minister said Ankara stood in solidarity with Riyadh over what he described as attacks on its territorial integrity.
“We’re now seeing very serious attacks targeting Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity. We stand in solidarity on this issue,” he said.
The foreign minister said Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty had come under serious attack, adding that Türkiye was bound by its alliance commitments.
“Saudi Arabia may need military-level support. As the Makkah alliance, we will take this up with Pakistan and can provide the necessary technical support,” he said.
He said Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry had condemned the attacks on oil infrastructure near Makkah, adding that the alliance was closely monitoring the situation. Any military support, he noted, would likely focus on specific technical areas.
Fidan also said Saudi Arabia should not be drawn into the conflict between Iran and the United States.
“We won’t allow this to be made part of the ongoing conflict between Iran and the US. Saudi Arabia should be kept out of this,” he said.
Responding to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s statements targeting Türkiye, Fidan said the Israeli leader was seeking to preserve his political position at home.
“Netanyahu is declaring himself indispensable and pursuing various means to remain in power and strengthen his political position at home,” he said.
He warned that Israel would face growing isolation under Netanyahu’s policies.
“Israel will not only grow increasingly isolated, but will also pay the price for this together with Netanyahu,” Fidan said.
“Under Netanyahu’s policies, Israel is a threat to the world,” he added.
On efforts to resolve the crisis around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, Fidan said several initiatives were under way but needed to produce concrete outcomes through the parties concerned.
“There are many initiatives, but these initiatives need to produce certain outcomes through the relevant parties,” he said.

title: From Atoms for Peace to AI for Allies
description: As AI replaces the atom as the world s strategic technology  will the Global South get to own it or merely rent it
content:
As AI replaces the atom as the world's strategic technology, will the Global South get to own it or merely rent it?
In April 1953, Dwight Eisenhower stood before the UN General Assembly and offered the world a bargain. The United States, he said, would share the "peaceful atom" — nuclear reactors, medical isotopes, research training — with any nation willing to accept American oversight of how that knowledge was used. "Atoms for Peace" was sold as generosity. In practice, it was architecture. It built a system in which the United States decided who was permitted to know, who could be trusted with the knowledge once they had it, and who would be cut off the moment they stepped out of line.
Pakistan learnt this lesson more intimately than most. The Pressler Amendment, following the Symington Amendment before it; decades of sanctions calibrated to the country's nuclear ambitions, gave Islamabad a masterclass in how the world's most powerful nation treats knowledge as a weapon to be holstered and unholstered at will. Expertise was never really shared. It was leased, with the lessor retaining the right of eviction.
Seventy years later, a new peaceful atom has arrived, and the same bargain is being offered again, dressed in the language of chips and clusters instead of uranium and centrifuges. Artificial intelligence has become the substance over which the twenty-first century's great powers are fighting for control, and once more, the Global South is being asked not whether it wants to participate in the future, but on whose terms it will be allowed to.
The contours of this contest sharpened dramatically this July, when the World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance convened in Shanghai. For the first time since the event's founding in 2018, President Xi Jinping himself took the stage, using the moment to announce the creation of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation, a body twenty-nine countries have already signed on to as founding members. Xi described it as China's answer "to the call of the Global South," pledging 5,000 training and seminar opportunities for developing nations over the next five years and calling for "a just and equitable system for global AI governance." His premier, Li Qiang, has spent two consecutive WAICs refining the same pitch: AI as a public good rather than private property, and computing power and technical know-how as things to be distributed rather than hoarded.
Contrast this with the vision articulated in Washington. America's AI Action Plan, released last summer, is remarkably candid about its ambitions: the United States must "achieve and maintain unquestioned and unchallenged global technological dominance." Its international pillar exists explicitly to counter Chinese influence in governance forums, and its central offering to the rest of the world is not access on equal terms but membership in what amounts to a gated alliance — an "AI stack" exported to partners willing to accept American terms, American export controls, and American veto power over how the technology is ultimately used. At February's India AI Impact Summit, the White House's technology chief, Michael Kratsios, was blunt about rejecting multilateral governance altogether in favour of bilateral deals in which Washington decides, country by country, who gets what.
The word Washington prefers for this arrangement is "sovereignty." Nations are invited to build "sovereign AI ecosystems", so long as those ecosystems run on American silicon, American models and American rules. It is worth sitting with the irony here. Sovereignty, in this formulation, is granted rather than exercised. A country's ability to think for itself, at scale, using the tools that increasingly mediate research, commerce and governance, is treated as something Washington confers as a gift, revocable the moment strategic calculations shift. Lawfare's Pablo Chavez has called this the "sovereignty gap" in American AI statecraft, the growing distance between the independence countries actually want and the dependence Washington is engineering under sovereignty's own name.
That gap has never been more visible than in the pattern of America's chip export regime, which has ratcheted tighter with almost every quarter since October 2022, when the first restrictions targeted Nvidia's most advanced processors bound for China. Each rule closed a loophole the last one had left open, from the China-specific A800 and H800 chips to the H20, banned outright this April alongside Huawei's Ascend 910C. But the arbitrariness of the regime is what should worry the rest of the world more than its severity. Within months of banning the H20, Washington reversed course and cleared it for export to China with a 25% tax attached, having already taken a 15% cut of Nvidia and AMD's China sales as the price of a license. Rules that can be rewritten by a single Commerce Department memo are not rules at all. They are leverage, and leverage is precisely what a Global South country cannot plan a university, a health system or a research agenda around.
The clearest illustration of how quickly that leverage can be turned against anyone came only weeks ago, when the US Commerce Department briefly moved to bar foreign nationals — including researchers at international universities and multinational firms already relying on the models in production — from using two frontier AI systems, before restoring access at the end of June under export-control obligations. It was, by multiple accounts, the first time such controls had been applied retroactively to commercial models already embedded in classrooms, laboratories and companies around the world, rather than to experimental prototypes still on the drawing board. For a Pakistani university running a research programme, or an Indian hospital using a diagnostic model, or a Nigerian fintech built on an American API, the message could not have been clearer: the knowledge you have integrated into your institutions is not yours. It is licensed, and the license can be pulled.
This is where the language of "colonisation" earns its place. Classical colonialism extracted raw materials and shipped back finished goods at a markup the colonised had no power to negotiate. Digital colonialism, as scholars researching AI's impact on the Global South have taken to calling it, extracts something more valuable: data, behaviour, and increasingly, the right to reason. Training datasets are built disproportionately from the internet's English-language, Global North-produced text, and the infrastructure required to build anything comparable — the chips, the energy, the capital — is concentrated in a handful of countries that then decide, contract by contract, who else is permitted to draw on it. A 2026 review in Frontiers in Education, examining AI's spread through classrooms in Latin America and Southeast Asia, found heavy dependence on imported tools and English-language datasets, with national AI strategies chasing economic competitiveness while all but ignoring who actually controls the underlying data and infrastructure. The pattern repeats in research: publishing infrastructure, citation metrics and even the tools now used to summarise, translate and analyse scholarship are calibrated to Global North institutions, reproducing precisely the disparities in research capacity that colonial-era education systems first inscribed.
This is the epistemic apartheid worth naming plainly. It is not merely that the Global South has less access to AI; it is that the terms of knowing itself are being re-centralised in Washington. Who gets to train a model that understands challenges unique to country like Pakistan? Whose research gets flagged as a security risk and locked out of a lab's most capable model, and whose gets waved through? As universities, newsrooms, courts and startups from Karachi to Lagos to Jakarta increasingly route their thinking through systems built, trained and licensed by a superpower, the very infrastructure of inquiry becomes something the Global South rents rather than owns.
The chip regime is only half the story; the other half is who gets to sell into whom. Even as Washington restricts what reaches rivals, it has been remarkably generous with certain partners. The UAE has secured a preliminary agreement to import up to 500,000 of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips annually, with the Emirati firm G42 alone receiving 100,000 a year in a deal expected to run through at least 2027. Saudi Arabia's Humain has been promised an initial tranche of 18,000 Blackwell processors.
Countries in the "middle tier" of what was once the Biden-era Diffusion Rule — India among them — have no such fixed entitlement, their access instead subject to case-by-case bilateral bargaining that can be revised as swiftly as the underlying politics. Compute, in other words, now flows along the same fault lines that have long determined who receives development aid, preferential trade access or military hardware.
While China's alternative is by no means offered from pure altruism — the inclusive rhetoric it uses is also strategic outreach to deepen influence in regions where Belt and Road ties already run deep — there is a meaningful difference between two systems of unequal power, and it lies in what each asks of the weaker party. Washington's model demands political alignment as the price of admission. Beijing's model at least gestures toward capacity-building as an end in itself — training programmes, open-source releases, a seat at a table rather than a place in a queue. One treats AI capability as a currency of loyalty; the other treats it as infrastructure to be shared. Neither is a gift, but a discerning Global South does not need a gift. It needs to know which door, once opened, cannot later be slammed shut on a memo's notice.
The arms control regimes of the last century offer one final, uncomfortable lesson. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, the Wassenaar Arrangement, the export-control lists that followed the Cold War's various technology races, all were sold as instruments of global stability, and all functioned, in practice, as mechanisms by which existing powers preserved a monopoly on capability while managing the terms under which everyone else was permitted to approach it. AI governance today risks repeating that history with software instead of centrifuges. An arrangement in which "responsible" access is defined entirely by those who already possess the technology, and in which the rest of the world's role is to apply for admission rather than help write the rules.
For Pakistan and countries like it, dependency of any flavour is still dependency. The lesson of the peaceful atom was that expertise offered as generosity comes with strings long enough to be pulled from a continent away. AI is being offered the same way. The task now is to build, however incrementally, the compute, the talent and the institutions that make the question of dependency less severe than it currently is.

title: Resident Evil  Video Game  references and easter eggs hidden in Zach Cregger   s movie
description: Cregger drew heavily from the gameplay and visual language of the 30 year old Capcom series
content:
Cregger drew heavily from the gameplay and visual language of the 30-year-old Capcom series
Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil may tell an original story, but the new horror film is packed with references to the video game franchise that inspired it.
Rather than adapting an existing game storyline or bringing back familiar characters such as Leon Kennedy, Jill Valentine or Albert Wesker, Cregger drew heavily from the gameplay and visual language of the 30-year-old Capcom series. The film follows Bryan, played by Austin Abrams, a medical courier who becomes caught in a zombie outbreak in Raccoon City.
Several sequences recreate the experience of playing the games. Cregger uses first-person and over-the-shoulder shots, including views framed around the front sight of Bryan’s gun. The film also emphasises limited ammunition, weapon upgrades and the need to search environments for useful supplies, all familiar elements of the games.
The movie even recreates the famous loading-screen effect from the early Resident Evil games, with Bryan passing through a doorway in a shot designed to evoke the series’ slow-moving door transitions. Its elaborate locks are also brought into the story, including a farmhouse gate featuring a diamond-marked lock that recalls the Diamond Key from Resident Evil 2.
The Easter eggs go even further. Bryan passes First-Aid Sprays and Green Herbs, two recognisable healing items from the games, while a typewriter appears inside the farmhouse as another nod to the series’ save system. A mounted shotgun and its green-packaged ammunition also reference the games.
Other details are more subtle. The police officer who stops Bryan is named J. Wilson, potentially referencing Joseph Wilson from Resident Evil: Outbreak. A teddy bear may also recall the charm attached to Ada Wong’s jet-ski key in Resident Evil 2. Umbrella, the pharmaceutical corporation at the centre of the franchise’s experiments, is directly mentioned when Paul, played by Paul Walter Hauser, reveals his connection to the company.
Bryan’s transformation also appears to draw from Resident Evil 2. After being infected, he develops a massive clawed hand and an eyeball on his shoulder, resembling William Birkin’s increasingly grotesque G-Virus mutations.
Although Cregger’s Resident Evil does not adapt a specific game, its numerous gameplay nods and Easter eggs make the connection to the original franchise central to the film’s identity.

title: Christine Taylor reveals she made just  3 500 per episode on  Hey Dude
description: Taylor explained that the cast received a  500 increase each season
content:
Taylor explained that the cast received a $500 increase each season
Christine Taylor has revealed that she earned far less than her former Hey Dude castmates remembered making on the Nickelodeon sitcom in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
Taylor, who played Melody Hanson on the series, discussed her early career during an appearance on actress Natanya Ross’ We’re Still Here, Babe podcast. She recalled a conversation among the cast about their salaries during the show's final season, saying everyone seemed to remember earning $5,000 per episode.
According to Taylor, however, that figure was incorrect. “We were making $3,500 an episode,” she said, explaining that the cast received a $500 increase each season. Taylor added that the cast members were all paid the same amount.
“I did not make $5,000 on something for many, many years,” Taylor said, recalling how surprised she was that the higher figure had become the number everyone remembered.
Hey Dude ran for five seasons and 65 episodes from 1989 to 1991, following the staff and guests at a dude ranch. Taylor starred alongside Joe Torres, Debi Kalman, Kelly Brown, Josh Tygiel, David Brisbin and David Lascher.
Despite the relatively modest pay, Taylor said she was careful with the money she earned from the show and saved it. Her savings, combined with financial help from her family, helped her move to Los Angeles and pursue more acting opportunities.
Taylor explained that relocating to LA did not immediately lead to a glamorous Hollywood lifestyle. She recalled having to watch what she ate, use the laundromat and work her way towards establishing herself as an actress.
Her career eventually grew to include roles in The Brady Bunch Movie, The Wedding Singer, Zoolander, Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story and Tropic Thunder, along with television appearances in Arrested Development and Search Party.

title: Twin cities admins on toes as four long marches loom
description: Schools  colleges  hotels  markets and transport terminals to remain closed
content:
Schools, colleges, hotels, markets and transport terminals to remain closed
Four separate calls for long marches within seven days, from Sunday, September 20-27, have put the government, administration and police in a difficult situation, with authorities deciding to close all educational institutions, colleges and universities, hotels, motels, rest houses and inns in Rawalpindi from next week.
Lights and mobile internet services will be shut down during the long marches, while all 1,500 cameras installed under the Safe City project in Rawalpindi have been activated to monitor protesters.
Transport and goods transport terminals will also remain completely closed, while Metro Bus and Green Electric Bus services will remain suspended.
Read : CM Afridi meets opposition leaders as PTI readies for Sept 27 protest
Markets and wholesale markets across the city will also be closed. Large spiked containers, fitted with eight-inch spikes, have started being installed at entry points of the twin cities, including Faizabad, Chungi No. 26, Rawat, Chakri, Adiala Road, Pirwadhai, Bharakahu and 17-Mile, with entry routes being sealed. Monitoring will also be carried out through drones.
Emergency has been imposed at all hospitals in the twin cities, and leave of doctors, nurses and paramedical staff has been cancelled.
Fresh contingents of Rangers and Punjab Constabulary have been called in. Thousands of rubber bullets and tear-gas shells have been supplied to Rawalpindi and Islamabad police.
Attock police have been provided heavy Rangers contingents, armoured vehicles, prison vans, heavy weapons and personnel, who will assume duties on Wednesday and Thursday. The central long march coming from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa will be stopped at all costs, officials said.
Edhi centres have also been put on alert. From next week, accused persons lodged in Adiala Jail will not be produced before courts in Rawalpindi and Islamabad, while jail staff have been assigned security duties in the city.
A show of force by law-enforcement agencies will also begin from Monday.
Also Read : JI weighs two plans for Islamabad march against petroleum levy
The Jamaat-e-Islami long march will start from Karachi on Sunday, Sept 20, while caravans from all six districts of Rawalpindi division will also start reaching Liaquat Bagh from Sunday. Jamaat-i-Islami emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman will leave Karachi for Rawalpindi by train on Sunday, with his train march scheduled to reach Rawalpindi on Tuesday, Sept 22.
Daily protest sit-ins will continue in Rawalpindi until his arrival.
Due to road closures and the large number of spiked containers being installed at different places, all business, commercial and social activities in Rawalpindi will remain paralysed from Monday, Sept 21 to Sept 27.
Anjuman-e-Tajiran Sabzi Mandi Sadr president Ghulam Qadir Mir and All Pakistan Private Schools and Colleges Association president Irfan Muzaffar Kiyani strongly condemned repeated strikes, long marches, road closures, the installation of containers and the closure of schools and colleges.
They called for political dialogue with all political parties, particularly Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, to reduce political uncertainty and save the country’s economy, saying the use of force and long marches were not a solution to any problem.

title: A brave cop  a devoted father  Human stories behind Kohat attack
description: SP Akbar Shinwari mourned in Mardan  family recalls his bravery and Luqman   s dedication to children
content:
SP Akbar Shinwari mourned in Mardan; family recalls his bravery and Luqman’s dedication to children
The family of SP Akbar Muhammad Shinwari, who was among those martyred in the Kohat Old Police Lines suicide attack and rampage, has been receiving a steady stream of mourners at their home in Hathian village, Mardan, BBC Urdu reported on Saturday. According to his nephew Tufail Akbar, Shinwari spent much of his police career serving in areas including Dir, Bajaur and Swat during periods of intense militancy, taking part in several major and dangerous operations. “He was very brave. He received threats too, but rarely spoke about them,” Tufail told BBC Urdu. The officer had been particularly devastated by the death of his younger brother, Motorway Police Sub-Inspector Javed Akbar, who was killed after being struck by a dumper truck on July 15.
Shinwari had repeatedly lamented his brother’s death, saying: “Why did Javed leave me? It would have been better if I had gone instead.”
Two months later, Shinwari himself was killed in the Kohat terror attack.
Tufail said Shinwari had two sons and two daughters, with his youngest daughter only six months old. He said the officer had been particularly delighted at her birth and considered her “the apple of his eye”.
Despite holding the rank of SP, Shinwari was regarded by people in his native area as a friend and someone they could turn to for help, Tufail said. “Whenever people had a problem involving a hospital, doctor or government department, they would come to him,” he said, adding that Shinwari generally returned home only on weekends.
The terror attack also claimed the lives of Muhammad Luqman and two young children, including his four-and-a-half-year-old son Abdullah, according to BBC Urdu.
Read More: 15 police personnel among 21 martyred in Kohat Police Lines terrorist attack; over 100 injured
Luqman’s brother-in-law Muhammad Tanveer told BBC Urdu that he had been at work in Kohat when his sister called in distress, asking about her husband and children. Tanveer repeatedly tried calling Luqman but received no response. Soon afterwards, he learned about the blast and rushed to the hospital. When he arrived, he found Luqman’s body. The bodies of two children were also brought to the hospital shortly afterwards. The second child, Asad, aged around three-and-a-half, was Luqman’s nephew, Tanveer said.
Luqman, 37, worked as a laboratory technician and was also a volunteer with the Alkhidmat Foundation. He was involved in arranging blood for people in need and served as the organisation’s district blood-donation president, according to his family.
His friend Muhammad Maskeen, who was also injured in the blast, told BBC Urdu that Luqman had picked up his children from school and stopped to offer Friday prayers.
Maskeen said he had spoken to Luqman before the prayers and suggested that they meet afterwards to buy something for the children to eat and have tea together. “I went to pray, and I was in the middle of the mosque when the explosion suddenly occurred,” Maskeen said. He suffered minor injuries and was taken to hospital.
He later saw Luqman’s body being brought to the hospital, followed by the bodies of his children.
Luqman’s family described him as deeply committed to his children’s education.
Tanveer said Luqman had borrowed money to pay the admission fee for Abdullah’s school this year, telling him that he wanted his son to receive a good education and “become something in life”.
He also personally helped his eldest daughter with her studies and encouraged her to work hard and build her own future.
Luqman had lost his mother four months earlier and had since also been supporting and caring for his elderly father, Tanveer said. The Kohat Old Police Lines terrorist attack during Friday prayers killed 23 people, including 17 security personne l. Security officials said several attackers were also killed during the subsequent clearance operation.

title: Zara Larsson says she won   t perform at Abu Dhabi show after Sudan concerns
description: The Swedish singer was due to perform at Etihad Live on Yas Island on December 3
content:
The Swedish singer was due to perform at Etihad Live on Yas Island on December 3
Zara Larsson has said she will not perform at her scheduled Abu Dhabi show after a fan urged her to cancel the concert over the United Arab Emirates’ alleged involvement in the war in Sudan.
The Swedish singer was due to perform at Etihad Live on Yas Island on December 3 as part of the Yasalam After Race Concert series during Abu Dhabi Grand Prix weekend. A fan commented on Larsson’s Instagram post, asking her to “read about what UAE is doing to Sudan then cancel your Abu Dhabi show”.
Larsson replied, “I will not be going to Abu Dhabi,” alongside a heart emoji. Both comments were later deleted from Instagram.
Larsson later offered a longer explanation, acknowledging that her initial response may have appeared impulsive. She said she wants to perform for people around the world because “no single person is their government”, but added that after considering the situation, not performing in Abu Dhabi felt right to her at the moment for “many different personal reasons beyond politics”.
The controversy centres on allegations that the UAE has supported Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) during the country’s ongoing conflict. The UAE has denied providing military support to either side.
Despite Larsson’s comments, her December 3 performance remains listed on Ticketmaster alongside Lewis Capaldi, meaning there has not yet been a formal cancellation announcement from the event organisers or Larsson’s team.
The Abu Dhabi appearance was announced as part of the Grand Prix’s after-race concert series, with Larsson and Capaldi scheduled for December 3.

title: Government  JI talks end without breakthrough on long march
description: Govt delegation in Mansoora to end political standoff
content:
The fifth round of talks between the government and Jamaat-e-Islami (JI) concluded on Saturday without a final agreement on the party’s demands, including the withdrawal of the petroleum levy, as differences over its planned long march remained unresolved.
The government delegation asked the JI to postpone the long march in view of security threats, while the party maintained that the protest would continue until the petroleum levy was withdrawn.
The talks were held at JI headquarters in Mansoorah. The government team comprised Federal Minister Ahsan Iqbal, Senator Rana Sanaullah and Punjab Minister Khawaja Salman Rafique. The JI delegation included Deputy Emir Liaqat Baloch, acting Secretary General Nazir Ahmad Janjua, Special Assistant Umair Idrees, JI Lahore Emir Ziauddin Ansari and Information Secretary Shakeel Ahmed Tarabi.

The government team said Pakistan was facing pressure from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), adding that an IMF delegation was also expected to visit the country soon.
Liaqat Baloch said the long march would remain necessary until the petroleum levy was abolished. He called on the government to take practical steps to address public demands, warning that protests and the long march would proceed otherwise.
According to Baloch, the “Super Long March” would begin from Karachi on Sunday under the leadership of JI Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman, as scheduled.

Earlier, JI Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman said the federal government had contacted the party to discuss the issue of the petroleum levy, but negotiations would only proceed if the government presented a formal and serious proposal for abolishing it.
JI has been protesting against the petroleum levy and fuel prices for several weeks. The government and the party have held several rounds of talks, but the levy remains a key point of disagreement.
Speaking at a press conference at Mansoorah, Rehman said the JI would not abandon its planned long march to Islamabad merely because Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced what he described as a nominal relief package.
“The government has contacted us again. If it comes with a formal and serious proposal to abolish the petroleum levy, only then will talks take place,” he said.

During the press conference held at the JI Lahore headquarters, the JI emir pledged to hold the long march as per the party’s announced schedule.
He warned the government against attempting to obstruct the march, saying any attempt to create hurdles would have serious consequences. Rehman also criticised the use of containers to block roads and called restrictions on opposition parties’ protests “contrary to constitutional rights”.
“The government can resolve the issue by simply withdrawing the levy,” he suggested, while stating that the party would otherwise be left with the only choice of mobilising the public to coerce the government to reduce fuel prices.

A grand public gathering will be held in Karachi today, followed by the launch of the Super Long March tomorrow under the leadership of Jamaat-e-Islami Pakistan Ameer Hafiz Naeem-ur-Rehman.… pic.twitter.com/PiJxVmrnmc
The JI chief asserted that the surging fuel and power rates were driving up the cost of everyday goods. He also lamented that the sharp increase in transport fares was burdening citizens beyond their capacity.
In view of the rising inflation, he said, JI had proposed a 3% reduction in interest rates but allegedly the government refused to accept the suggestion.
Criticising “excessive government expenditure”, Rehman called on the Punjab government to sell off the luxury jet used by Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz to give relief to the common people.

Rehman also alleged that the existing economic system was only benefiting the ruling elite and allied business owners.
Turning back to call for protests, Rehman said peaceful demonstrations were a constitutional right of all political parties, adding that his party supports Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf’s peaceful protests. He also revealed that PTI backs the JI’s stance on the petroleum levy.

“We will reach Islamabad with the full support of the people and hold those accountable for unduly burdening the masses,” he said.
JI has announced September 20 as the date for commencing its long march towards Islamabad if the government refuses to meet its demand of withdrawing the petroleum levy.
A statement issued by the party today said JI’s caravan will depart from Karachi by train on Sunday night and reach Sukkur on Monday. A day after that, it is expected to arrive in Multan.

title: CNN  MSNOW journalists denied access to White House after Trump announces ban
description: Trump defended restrictions  saying he was tired of  fake news  and disliked the  dishonest press
content:
White House Correspondents’ Association president says group 'stands in defence of our colleagues'
Journalists from news channels CNN and MS NOW were turned away from the White House on Saturday morning, one day after President Donald Trump announced that those news channels, along with website Politico , would be barred from the property.
CBS News reported an MS NOW correspondent and cameraman being denied entry. Both had their hard press passes revoked.
MS NOW correspondent Akayla Gardner said she was told her pass had been disabled when she tried to enter. When she asked why, a security guard told her the matter was above him.
CNN reporter Betsy Klein and a cameraman were also seen trying to enter the White House grounds. They eventually left without their badges.
CNN reporter Betsy Klein was denied access at the White House on Saturday morning and her press pass was seized, one day after President Donald Trump announced that he was "banning" CNN, MS NOW and Politico. https://t.co/zqx4UsY65S pic.twitter.com/uL2Yy7NnR2
CNN — an outlet long targeted by Trump — said its "mission to report on the US government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism".
"We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account, and we will continue to report on the actions and processes of this administration without fear or favor," the news network added. " CNN stands fully behind our White House team."
MS NOW — a left-leaning channel formerly attached to NBC — said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy", referring to the US constitution's guarantee of a free press.
Read More: Trump bans CNN, MS NOW, Politico from White House
"The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars," the network added.
Politico reporters are also set to be barred from the White House. Trump announced the move Friday on Truth Social.
Politico ’s communications team disputed his claim that the publication “received government subsidies”, saying the allegation had been "thoroughly debunked".
“ POLITICO will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” an online post said.
Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, said the group "stands in defence of our colleagues at CNN , MSNOW and Politico who are being singled out for doing their jobs".
Trump defended the restrictions by saying he was "tired of reading and seeing fake news" from the outlets and said he dislikes "dishonest press". He did not identify specific stories.
CBS News legal contributor Jessica Levinson said the ban "smacks of content-based discrimination".
"That's the primary thing that the First Amendment guards against," she said.

title: Netflix   s Narnia reboot faces controversy over Greta Gerwig   s new vision
description: The newly revealed imagery has highlighted several creative changes that have prompted discussion among fans
content:
The newly revealed imagery has highlighted several creative changes that have prompted discussion among fans
Netflix’s upcoming Narnia reboot has already sparked controversy following the release of the first full look at Greta Gerwig’s adaptation of C.S. Lewis’ fantasy world.
The film, Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew, is Gerwig’s take on the story that explores the origins of Narnia. However, the newly revealed imagery has highlighted several creative changes that have prompted discussion among fans of the original books.
One of the biggest changes is the decision to move the story from the early 20th century setting of Lewis’ novel to 1950s Britain. Gerwig has also described the film as being influenced by the music and visual culture of later decades, including artists such as David Bowie and Paul McCartney.
Another major talking point is Meryl Streep’s casting as the voice of Aslan. Gerwig explained that she wanted an actor who could bring depth, authority, joy and emotional range to the iconic lion. Streep’s casting has nevertheless generated debate among some fans because Aslan has traditionally been portrayed as male in adaptations of Lewis’ work.
Gerwig has previously spoken about approaching the project with both excitement and apprehension because of her longstanding connection to Lewis’ books. She is writing and directing two Narnia films for Netflix.
The first film is set to receive an unusually extensive theatrical run for a Netflix production, opening in cinemas in February 2027 before arriving on Netflix in April. The release marks a significant theatrical push for the streaming service and gives audiences the chance to experience Gerwig’s reimagining of Narnia on the big screen.
