title: Gold rises Rs6 900 on global bullion strength
description: Gold rises Rs6 900 on global bullion strength
content:
International prices hit one-week high; rupee inches up to 277.25/$
Gold prices in Pakistan rose sharply on Friday, tracking gains in the international bullion market, as softer crude oil prices eased concerns over prolonged inflationary pressures while a stronger US dollar limited the advance.
The price of gold increased by Rs6,900 per tola to reach Rs460,336, according to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association. The price of 10-gram gold increased by Rs5,914 to Rs394,663.
The latest increase came after gold prices had fallen by Rs3,800 per tola on Thursday, closing at Rs453,436. Friday's market move therefore more than reversed the previous day's decline and pushed the local price to a new level for the week.
The increase in domestic gold prices broadly followed the international market, where bullion climbed to a one-week high and remained on course for its first weekly gain in four weeks.
Spot gold rose 0.3% to $4,352.39 per ounce by 11:17 am EDT (1517 GMT), after touching its highest level since September 11 earlier in the session, as per Reuters. The metal was up around 0.2% for the week.
Market conditions were also influenced by movements in crude oil prices. Brent crude fell for a third consecutive session, reducing some concerns that higher energy costs could keep inflation elevated for longer.
Lower oil prices can ease inflation expectations by reducing pressure on transport and production costs. This, in turn, can affect investor expectations about interest rates and the broader demand for safe-haven assets such as gold.
However, gains in bullion remained constrained by a stronger US dollar. A stronger dollar generally makes gold more expensive for holders of other currencies, limiting demand and putting pressure on dollar-denominated bullion prices.
Despite the mixed signals from oil and currency markets, gold remained supported by demand for precious metals as investors assessed inflation, interest-rate expectations and broader global economic risks.
All major precious metals were also heading towards weekly gains, indicating broader strength across the precious metals market. In the domestic market, silver prices followed gold higher. The price of silver increased by Rs300 per tola to Rs7,169.
Pakistani rupee edged up Rs0.01 against the US dollar in the inter-bank market on Friday, closing at 277.25, compared with 277.26 a day earlier. Globally, the Japanese yen started weaker against the dollar and euro ahead of an expected Bank of Japan rate hike.

title: Provinces seek seats in OGRA
description: Provinces seek seats in OGRA
content:
Insist they must have equal say with centre in deciding fate of oil, gas resources
The Punjab government has asked the federal government to give representation to all provinces in the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) along with federal representatives in a bid to deal more effectively with administrative matters in the hydrocarbon sector.
The centre has sent a summary to the Council of Common Interests (CCI), seeking to exclude the role of provinces in day-to-day administrative affairs of the oil and gas sector.
The summary has been circulated to the ministries of finance, planning, development and special initiatives, law & justice, Cabinet Division and Attorney General (Pakistan) along with provinces of Sindh, Punjab, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan for views and comments.
However, the provinces have objected to the proposal of bypassing the CCI while tackling every-day oil and gas-related administrative matters.
The government of Punjab has partially supported the proposal and has stated that regulatory bodies should function independently in accordance with the prevailing laws, rules, regulations and policies.
Furthermore, it said, there should be representation from all provincial governments and the federal administration in those regulatory bodies. If any provincial government has grievances about any regulatory or administrative decision, it may refer it to the CCI.
The government of Sindh has objected to the proposal (iii) of the summary and stated that Article 172(3) envisaged vesting of oil and gas, lying within the province/territorial waters adjacent thereto, jointly and equally between the federal government and provinces. It confers equal title on provinces with the right to dispose of oil and gas with the federal government by becoming a co-licensor.
Therefore, the proposal may be amended that all administrative matters about the management of entities operating in the oil and gas sector are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal government and the respective provincial government and need not to be submitted to the CCI.
The government of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa was of the view that the power of parliament could not be denied but in the present context, the parliament could not legislate contrary to the true letter and spirit of Article 172(3) of the Constitution.
"There can be no cavil that Article 172(3) of the Constitution envisages the vesting of oil and gas resources within provinces or the territorial waters adjacent thereto, jointly and equally in the federation and concerning province(s)," it said. "As such, the provinces have an equal say as the federal government in deciding the fate of these resources. The federal government in the exercise of its executive powers is to act as a fiduciary under Article 172(3) for provincial rights and not as an absolute owner."
The government of Balochistan conveyed that policy matters and amendments needed to be formulated with approval of the CCI and regulatory decisions should be taken by the regulator concerned in accordance with the rules and guidelines imparted at the CCI level.
"Furthermore, excluding the CCI from the administrative matters is not tenable since the cumulative provisions of Article 154, 156 and 172(3), read with Entry 2 of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution, provide for enhanced supervisory role of the CCI in the operational framework for mineral oil and natural gas," it said.
"In terms of Articles 154 and 172(3) by the apex court, it falls within the domain of the CCI to deliberate upon and render appropriate policy guidelines on the scope and modalities of executive authority of the CCI/provinces in the operational and management framework for mineral oil and natural gas."

title: Digital payments target merchant growth
description: Digital payments target merchant growth
content:
Ecosystem moving beyond adoption to become part of everyday financial behaviour
Pakistan's digital payments ecosystem is moving beyond the early adoption phase, with instant payment infrastructure increasingly being integrated into everyday financial transactions, according to banking and payment industry officials.
According to the State Bank of Pakistan's Payment Systems Quarterly Review, 3.7 billion retail transactions were recorded during January-March 2026. Digital channels accounted for 3.4 billion transactions, or approximately 92% of the total, with the digital transaction value reaching Rs68.3 trillion.
"The digital payments ecosystem is entering a phase where the focus needs to shift from access to adoption," said Muhammad Hamayun Sajjad, CEO Mashreq Pakistan, the country's first newly launched digital bank to offer the full suite of Raast services. It has just introduced Raast Person-to-Merchant (P2M) payments, allowing merchants to receive instant payments through QR codes and customers to pay through digital banking channels.
Raast processed approximately 742 million transactions worth Rs23.27 trillion during the quarter. Person-to-person (P2P) payments accounted for 664 million transactions valuing at Rs18.88 trillion compared with 603 million transactions worth Rs15.69 trillion in the preceding quarter.
Total Raast transactions increased from 295.7 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2024-25 to 371.2 million in the third quarter and 412.1 million in the fourth quarter. The volume rose to 543.9 million in the first quarter of FY2025-26, 645.7 million in the second quarter and 742 million in the third quarter.
By March 2026, Pakistan had 95.8 million branchless banking mobile app users, 28.9 million banking mobile app users and 7.3 million electronic money institution wallet app users, highlighting the expanding base of consumers with access to digital financial services.
Raast Payments Pakistan CEO Ahson Bin Saeed said the next phase of the national payment infrastructure would involve strengthening the system, broadening participation and ensuring that institutions could build reliable and accessible payment experiences on top of it.
He said the launch of Raast P2M was another step towards translating the national payment infrastructure into everyday use for merchants and consumers.
However, industry stakeholders have pointed to commercial and behavioural challenges that could affect the pace of adoption.
"The adoption of Raast in Pakistan is progressing at a relatively fast pace; however, a significant part of this momentum appears to be driven by regulatory encouragement and the strong push from the regulator, rather than entirely by organic market demand," said iPath CEO Abdus Samad Khan.
He said the absence of a direct consumer-fee model created commercial challenges for banks, fintechs and payment service providers. Unlike the previous inter-bank funds transfer model, Raast P2P and P2M payments are required to remain free for consumers.
While this benefits users, service providers must recover the costs of technology, infrastructure, compliance, customer support and transaction processing through other revenue streams.
Khan also identified limited consumer awareness and merchant behaviour as challenges. Many consumers remain unfamiliar with how Raast works, where it can be used and how it differs from other digital payment channels.
In some cases, merchants reportedly encourage customers to pay in cash or use established wallets such as easypaisa and JazzCash instead of formal Raast merchant payment channels, limiting the growth and visibility of the P2M ecosystem.
Merchant payments are emerging as the next major frontier for digital payments. According to the State Bank, more than 2.6 million merchants had been onboarded or registered their aliases for Raast P2M by the end of March 2026.
The challenge, however, is to convert merchant registration into regular usage. Smaller businesses face issues related to onboarding, reconciliation, settlement, digital literacy and perceptions regarding taxation and transaction records.
State Bank's Director of Digital Innovation & Settlements Department Muhammad Imad Uddin said the central bank remained focused on developing the regulatory and technological foundations for a more connected and inclusive payments landscape. The real measure of progress, he added, was how effectively the infrastructure was adopted across the ecosystem.
The government allocated Rs3.5 billion to support Raast P2M QR transactions between September 2025 and June 2026.

Discussions focused on Pakistan's future economic direction, investment opportunities and the sustainability of its ongoing economic transformation. Amin Khowaja, CEO and Country Head JP Morgan Pakistan, was also present during the meetings.
Setting out the government's economic direction, the finance minister outlined six key priorities: bringing permanence to macroeconomic stability and strengthening fiscal and external shock-absorbing capacity; moving from stabilisation to sustainable and responsible growth driven by productivity, investment and exports; staying the course on structural reforms; moving from aid to trade and investment; expanding access to finance for people and communities; and positioning Pakistan for the new economy, including digitalisation, blockchain and Web 3.0.
Aurangzeb said that over the last three years, Pakistan's overriding task had been to restore macroeconomic stability and rebuild credibility. He noted that significant progress had been made in fiscal consolidation, external-sector stability, inflation, debt management and international market access.
GDP growth recovered to 3.7% in FY26, while fiscal deficit declined to 2.6% of GDP, a multi-year low.

title: Fuel hikes push SPI into double digits
description: Fuel hikes push SPI into double digits
content:
Inflation jumps 10.64% YoY; weekly index up 0.49% on expensive energy, food
The year-on-year inflation measured by the Sensitive Price Indicator (SPI) surged back into double digits, reaching 10.64% in the week ended September 17, as the fallout from the Middle East situation pushed up fuel prices and added to pressure on household budgets.
The latest increase marked a sharp acceleration from the 8.62% year-on-year rise recorded in the preceding week and the 8.35% increase two weeks earlier, according to data released by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) on Friday. The SPI tracks prices of 51 essential commodities across 50 markets in 17 cities.
The weekly reading rose 0.49%, reflecting fresh increases in petroleum products and other essential items. Diesel prices increased 7.29% over the week, while petrol became 6.40% more expensive and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices rose 3.26%.
The increase in fuel prices comes amid heightened uncertainty in the Middle East, with regional tensions raising concerns over energy supplies and transportation costs. The PBS data, however, reports price movements and does not independently attribute them to the regional situation.
The year-on-year data showed that energy-related items were among the main drivers of the renewed inflationary pressure. LPG prices were 60.42% higher than a year earlier, diesel prices increased 54.21% and petrol prices rose 48%. Electricity charges for the first quarter were 33.54% higher.
Food prices added to the burden, particularly for households reliant on basic staples. Onion prices more than doubled, rising 117.77% year-on-year, while wheat flour became 33.27% more expensive. Prices of powdered chilli, mutton and beef increased 16.37%, 15.86% and 12.88%, respectively.
Several food items, however, recorded annual declines. Potato prices fell 35.31%, sugar 20.95%, eggs 19.31% and chicken 15.26%. Prices of gram, masoor and moong pulses declined 12.42%, 11.26% and 8.49%, respectively.
The impact of inflation varied across income groups. The highest expenditure group recorded the steepest year-on-year increase of 11.13%, compared with 8.79% for the lowest expenditure group. The second, third and fourth groups registered increases of 9.91%, 8.86% and 9.37%, respectively.
During the week, prices of 19 items increased, nine declined and 23 remained unchanged. The latest reading suggests that the recent easing in weekly inflation has been interrupted, with fuel and selected food items contributing to renewed pressure on consumers.
The monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI)-based inflation increased 11.1% year-on-year in August 2026 as compared to an increase of 9.2% in the previous month and 3.1% in August 2025. On a month-on-month basis, it remained unchanged at 1.2% in August 2026 as compared to the previous month and stood higher against a decrease of 0.6% in August 2025.

title: Pak Sweden BIT talks in Nov
description: Pak Sweden BIT talks in Nov
content:
Govt keen to review 45-year-old pact due to international arbitration concerns
Ambassador Alexandra Berg von Linde has said that Sweden is looking forward to renegotiating the Bilateral Investment Treaty and a Pakistani official said that both sides would hold the first round in November to rewrite the 45-year-old pact due to Islamabad's concerns over international arbitration.
The Swedish ambassador emphasised the need for continued efforts to honour Pakistan's international commitments under the duty-free access scheme of Europe, known as the Generalised System of Preferences Plus (GSP+). She was speaking during the launching ceremony of the Sweden-Pakistan Business Guide 2026-28.
"Sweden is very much looking forward to restarting negotiations over updating the Bilateral Investment Treaty," remarked Linde.
Her remarks came after Pakistan sent a notice to terminate the 1981 treaty as part of its strategy to renegotiate all the existing investment treaties. Islamabad was keen to review the investment treaties to avoid huge fiscal exposures due to international arbitration.
The government has appointed an investment ombudsman for dispute resolution and has also approved a template for the treaty, which it wants to apply with all partner countries.
A government official said that the first round of talks between Pakistan and Sweden was scheduled for November 17-18 in Islamabad. The government has also been negotiating its investment treaty with Hungary, hoping for an early agreement with these two nations.
The Swedish ambassador also spoke about the GSP Plus scheme. "Continued efforts need to be made to advance international commitments under the GSP Plus," she said.
She was the second European ambassador in the past less than three weeks having echoed such comments, which were earlier made by the Netherlands ambassador.
EU Ambassador Raimundas Karoblis also said on Friday in Lahore that Pakistan would have to show progress on implementation and formulation of various laws and conventions necessary for availing itself of the next GSP Plus status.
Karoblis urged exporters to take immediate measures for implementation of the requisite conventions and to engage with the government with reference to concerns of the European Commission, especially those relating to human and labour rights, governance and environmental issues, to facilitate the path for future extension of the GSP Plus for the next 10 years.
Federal Commerce Secretary Jawad Paul said that the government had successfully completed its fifth review under the EU's GSP Plus status. He stated this while speaking as chief guest at the launch of the Sweden-Pakistan Business Guide 2026-2028.
He added that preparations were already underway for formal re-application. Paul expressed confidence that compliance with international obligations would enable Pakistan to transition smoothly into the new EU regulatory framework.
According to the GSP+ monitoring report that the EU released recently, the club of 27 nations asked Pakistan that "to ensure further GSP+ eligibility and compliance with international commitments", it had to reverse negative developments that took place from 2023 to 2025.
"Grave concerns remain as significant systemic challenges persisted in the implementation of human rights conventions, with a deterioration of the situation relating in particular to enforced disappearances, minority rights, freedom of media and freedom of expression and peaceful assembly," stated the report.
The monitoring report stated that impunity for human rights violations continued to be a major concern. The EU said that Pakistan needed to take robust steps to reverse negative trends in relation to enforced disappearances and violations of freedom of expression. "In this regard, laws on blasphemy, cybercrime (such as PECA), defamation, counterterrorism and sedition should be amended or repealed."
The European Commission has already approved new GSP regulations, from January 1, 2027 until the end of 2036. This completes the review process and transitions from the 2012 Regulation to the new GSP Regulation.
According to the European Commission, the new GSP will provide reduced or zero tariffs on imports from 65 developing countries for the next decade, supporting poverty reduction and sustainable development. Moreover, the updated GSP strengthens accountability by linking trade benefits more closely to human and labour rights, climate and environment, and good governance. It also introduces improved monitoring, greater transparency, and reinforces and updates the links between trade preferences and compliance with international standards.
It does so by increasing the number of relevant international conventions beneficiaries must adhere to, and by introducing an urgent withdrawal procedure, which allows for the suspension of preferences in case of serious and systemic violations of the principles underpinning such conventions.
Finally, the new GSP includes an automatic safeguard on rice imports, protecting EU producers while preserving the development objectives of the scheme. In practice, this means that if imports from a beneficiary rise sharply above the average of their past imports over 10 years, the EU will suspend preferential rates for the rest of the year and introduce a tariff rate quota (TRQ) for the following year to prevent market disruption.

title: Turbulent world and Confucian strategic patience
description: Turbulent world and Confucian strategic patience
content:
Yi also said that relations between Tehran and Beijing are significant due to their strategic partnership
When foreign ministers Wang Yi and Seyed Abbas Araghchi met in Beijing on September 17, both agreed that safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz required a reinforced, multilateral security architecture in West Asia.
Yi offered China's support for de-escalating tensions in the region, while Araghchi consented that the transformation in the security landscape required security cooperation among regional countries to preclude interference by foreign forces. Both countries agreed that the present tensions are rooted in the US and Israeli military attacks against Iran early this year.
During the meeting, Yi also said that relations between Tehran and Beijing are significant due to their strategic partnership, and that Beijing is keen on strengthening and developing these ties.
Yi's messaging was consistent as ever; peace and tranquility in the Middle East and West Asia, as well as peaceful conflict resolution based on respect for sovereignty of individual nations.
Only a few days earlier, during the recent 18th BRICS summit in India, similar messages resonated across the conference hall. President Xi Jinping anchored his speech in multilateral cooperation, the urgency for upholding the international rule of law, respect for sovereign equality, and perusal of the peaceful settlement of disputes. And China, Xi declared, is ready to act as an anchor, a stabilising force for achieving these ideals. He reiterated the need for expanding the Global South, instituting AI collaboration and joining hands for global-governance reform.
Curiously, however, Xi avoided mention of counter-terrorism and security issues and presumably - as a tactical move - allowed the Indians to slip the explicit condemnation of the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam attack into the New Delhi Declaration. The inclusion of this text represents a notable diplomatic success. It gave the Indians a "feel-good" diplomatic achievement, with no last minute altercation since the Chinese leadership did not want to inject any negativity on the occasion of Xi's visit after seven long years.
From the Indian perspective, inclusion of issues such as cross-border movement of terrorists, terror financing, safe havens, accountability for perpetrators and supporters, rejection of double standards and zero tolerance into BRICS was a diplomatic achievement.
For Beijing, this was a small concession in view of the big challenges that China as a BRICS lead country is trying to deal with – very much reflective of the Confucian spirit of accommodation and peaceful conflict resolution.
Quietly but consistently, the leadership pursues planning for the future while staying clear of international conflicts, securing internal stabilisation through people-centric policies and at the same time pursuing nation's long-term economic interests abroad.
Conversations with scholars and officials as well as the major contours of Beijing's policies are quite enlightening and guide you to an unmistakable conclusion; contemporary Chinese statecraft, security doctrine and social policy continue to draw heavily on Confucian and Mencian ideas of legitimate authority.
Mencius was an ancient Chinese philosopher and one of the most important figures in Confucianism. He is traditionally regarded as the "Second Sage" second only to Confucius himself.
Mencius taught that coercion can compel outward compliance but never wins genuine allegiance; only virtue and moral example secure lasting loyalty.
This distinction underpins the classic contrast between the brittle "hegemonic way" (badao), which relies on coercion, and the sustainable "kingly way" (wangdao), in which others follow voluntarily because they recognise the ruler's benevolence and competence.
"A confident state first puts its own house in order, strengthening domestic stability and social cohesion so that foreign policy need not manufacture external enemies for internal legitimacy."
When this Mencius quote resonated through the Beijing conference hall on September 16, it must have reminded several Asian participants of the situation in their own countries, where rulers tend to rely on 'foreign enemies' to address domestic legitimacy issues.
This was a remarkable speech by Chan Chun Sing, Singapore's Defence Minister, when speaking of the present day "security dilemma" – a combination of wisdom, sagacity and cautious public policy.
"How do we strengthen our own security without weakening the security of others, or without aggravating the insecurity of others," asked Sing in what appeared to be an indirect jibe at the USA's strident policies concerning Veneuzuela and Iran.
Without directly accusing the US of triggering the current security crisis in the Gulf following its attacks on Iran since early this year, the Singapore defence minister implicitly dubbed phrases such as "freedom of navigation" (through Hormuz) or "sanctions" (on Iran) as unnecessary stunts. In other words, it is like sailing warships near the other's coast just to show off, or adding new punishments for no clear reason. It's like taking money out of that account. Building up that trust again is slow and hard. But you can drain the whole account in a single moment - one bad decision and all the trust is gone.
Sing's was a brilliant summation of the current paradox accompanying the Trump administration's Middle East policy – total exceptionalism vis-a-vis Israel, and absolute strident, self-serving attitude towards Iran. This also resonated the present day Chinese approach in international relations: the more responsible major powers are, the less concerned small countries will be.
Equally compelling message in Sing's speech was that "leadership confident at home doesn't need foreign enemies to hold itself together, and can therefore act in its 'enlightened long-term interest' abroad."

title: The challenge of parenting in our age
description: The challenge of parenting in our age
content:
Distinction has become especially important in Pakistan
A child begins life completely dependent on parents, yet the ultimate purpose of upbringing is to produce an adult capable of thinking, deciding and living without constantly requiring parental direction. Much of our difficulty with parenting in Pakistan comes from forgetting this paradox. Parents naturally want the best for their children, but "the best" can mean very different things. Sometimes it means producing a replica of ourselves. Sometimes it means producing an idealised version of the child we wish we had been. Sometimes it means preparing children intelligently for the realities of their own age. And sometimes, unfortunately, parenting amounts to little more than providing food, education and shelter while leaving emotional and intellectual development largely unattended.
The first temptation is self-projection. Many Pakistani parents imagine their children as extensions of themselves. A doctor wants another doctor, a businessman expects someone to continue the business, and parents who struggled for social mobility often decide very early what prestigious career their children must pursue. There is nothing wrong with transmitting experience or values. The problem begins when guidance becomes replication. A child is biologically connected to the parent but psychologically belongs to a different generation. Temperament, interests and circumstances may all be different. When parents insist that children reproduce their choices, inheritance can quietly become imprisonment.
A second tendency is perfectionism. Children must attend the best school, secure the highest grades, enter medicine, engineering, civil service or some fashionable profession, and speak impeccable English. Social comparison strengthens the pressure. Another child's examination results, university admission or professional achievement quickly becomes a benchmark against which one's own child is measured. Children may gradually conclude that their value depends upon performance. Failure becomes frightening not merely because something has gone wrong, but because parental approval itself appears endangered.
At the opposite end lies parental disengagement. Some parents confuse freedom with absence. They provide material necessities but know remarkably little about what their children think, fear, watch, believe or experience. In an era when smartphones, algorithms, influencers and peer networks compete constantly for children's attention, parental withdrawal does not create a neutral space. It simply allows other forces to become the educators. The more sensible alternative is realistic parenting - raising children for the world they are entering rather than the world their parents remember.
This distinction has become especially important in Pakistan. Parents who grew up believing that a university degree automatically produced a secure career are raising children in an economy where qualifications alone increasingly guarantee very little. AI is transforming professions. Employment patterns are changing. Information is abundant while judgement is scarce. Communication, adaptability, emotional intelligence, creativity and the capacity to learn continuously may matter as much as traditional academic credentials.
Realistic parenting therefore requires a change of question. Instead of asking, "How can my child become what I want?", parents might ask, "What capacities will this child need to flourish twenty years from now?"
Yet realism should not mean surrendering children completely to contemporary culture. Children should understand technology without becoming enslaved by it; become ambitious without measuring human worth entirely through money; develop confidence without arrogance; compete without losing empathy; and learn independence without abandoning responsibility toward family and society.
The most constructive model may therefore be developmental parenting. Such parents neither manufacture replicas of themselves nor attempt to engineer perfect children. They provide values without dictating every conclusion, boundaries without suffocation, freedom without abandonment and guidance without permanent control. Their authority changes as the child grows. Parenting that refuses to evolve eventually becomes control.

title: Sudden disappearances
description: Sudden disappearances
content:
Question is why so many people can disappear in a city that has invested heavily in surveillance and policing
A dozen kidnapping cases registered in Islamabad in a single day should alarm the capital's police authorities. The incidents involve a newborn taken from PIMS Hospital, a teenage boy allegedly abducted from his home, several young women who disappeared, and two drivers who went missing along with vehicles. Whether every case ultimately proves to be an abduction is for investigators to establish. What cannot be ignored is the sheer number of families who turned to the police on the same day.
The question is why so many people can disappear in a city that has invested heavily in surveillance and policing. Islamabad has a dense network of cameras and a police force that regularly highlights improvements in its crime-fighting capabilities. Yet technology is of little value if it does not translate into rapid intervention. In cases involving children, every hour matters. There are several possible explanations for the apparent rise in such reports. Some disappearances may involve family disputes, voluntary departures, elopement or other circumstances that are initially reported as kidnapping. Others may involve genuine abductions, criminal exploitation or attempts to obtain ransom. The police must establish these distinctions through proper investigation rather than allowing all missing-person cases to be treated alike. But neither should an abduction be prematurely reduced to a domestic matter simply because the circumstances are unclear.
Islamabad Police needs to tell citizens what is happening. A single day's cases may eventually prove to be unrelated. But when so many families report disappearances at once, the burden is on the authorities to establish whether there is a wider pattern. Residents of the capital should not have to wonder whether their police force is discovering crimes after they happen or preventing them before they do. Security is ultimately measured by how quickly the state responds when someone disappears.

title: Gender gap at crisis level
description: Gender gap at crisis level
content:
One area where Pakistan is objectively doing well in the gender gap ranking
Pakistan continues to be ranked near the bottom of the table in terms of its gender gap, with the WEF's Global Gender Gap Report 2026 ranking only two nations lower than us - Iran and Chad. While spin doctors may try to highlight the ranking this year as an improvement, that is only true because we ranked dead last in 2025. Most of the structural problems that earned us last place are still there, and no government has been able to take substantive measures to address them. In fact, we have been so bad in recent years that this year's improvement - the one that took us from last place to third from the bottom - is also our biggest gain ever in the rankings.
The headline figures are terrible, and even then, they do not tell the whole story, because allocating reserved seats for women in parliament and government offices skews the numbers higher - at least some of these women would not have gotten their jobs in a competitive situation. Parliament is the most egregious example, as familial ties to any relatively prominent male politician are usually the only qualification required. The handful of women who do win direct elections, or who can genuinely be considered technocrats, end up having their reputations hurt by scores of unqualified reserved-seat holders. Despite the reserved jobs, female labour force participation remains astoundingly low, at a mere 28.2% against 81.5% for men, and barely 6% of all senior officials and managers are women.
Meanwhile, the one area where Pakistan is objectively doing well in the gender gap ranking - education - is also an area where Pakistan has consistently been among the worst across gender lines. Although we now have some of the highest tertiary enrolment rates for women, our overall literacy rate is among the worst in the world. Experts also say that having many people with higher education is unhelpful because a lack of economic opportunities will lead them to migrate to developed nations. Developing economies should instead focus on primary and secondary education, develop a productive workforce and let demand for skilled workers grow organically.

title: Another cross border attack
description: Another cross border attack
content:
Security forces are doing a remarkable job to stem the rot
Another attack masterminded in Afghanistan has led to the martyrdom of 21 people in K-P's Kohat division. The Ittehadul Mujahideen Pakistan of Hafiz Gul Bahadur has claimed responsibility for a deadly bombing at Kohat Police Lines and subsequent rampage involving multiple attackers. This brazen operation underscores the extent of terrorists' penetration across the western frontiers and is an indictment of the regime in Kabul. Twenty-one of those martyred in the bombing included fifteen policemen. The terrorists detonated a device at a mosque before perpetrating further violence via a suicide bomber. This well-coordinated attack is a grim reminder that our kinetic and political responses are dangerously inadequate against a threat that is staring us in the face.
The Kohat mayhem is the latest addition to a string of similar attacks in the strategically vulnerable belt of Karak, DI Khan, Bannu, Lakki Marwat and Tank. These areas have been on the receiving end since the Taliban took over Kabul five years back. Similarly, North Waziristan, the newly merged districts and Kurram bordering the reclusive Southwest Asian state have seen unprecedented upheaval, as cross-border infiltration remains the order of the day. The ground situation becomes more complex because these non-state actors have abettors and sleeper cells across the province. Likewise, Balochistan is simmering as the BLA, Majeed Brigade and the TTP have turned the province into what is virtually a no-go area for locals.
This delicate moment once again calls for serious introspection. Security forces are doing a remarkable job to stem the rot. However, a more coordinated socio-political response designed to reinforce the state's narrative is vital for a winning proposition. Also, the ongoing bloodshed must compel international attention toward the ruthless regime in Kabul, which routinely flouts the rules of interstate civility. That the terror nexus remains comfortably entrenched inside Afghanistan is a universal truth requiring a collective counter-terrorism strategy. Pakistan will not be the last to bleed if the Taliban continue to have their way.

title: Wealth  inequality and generosity in Pakistan
description: Wealth  inequality and generosity in Pakistan
content:
Elite private schools prepare students for admission to leading universities at home and abroad
Pakistan is a country of striking contrasts. For some, life offers quality housing, private education, advanced healthcare and opportunities that extend far beyond the country's borders. For others, daily life is a struggle to secure the basics. The divide between these realities is not merely visible in income; it is reflected in the quality of education, healthcare and opportunity available to different sections of society.
Nowhere is this contrast more apparent than in education. Elite private schools prepare students for admission to leading universities at home and abroad, while many government schools continue to operate with limited resources. The result is a system in which a child's prospects can depend heavily on where they are born, the school they attend and the resources available to their family.
This inequality exists alongside something that is both remarkable and deeply Pakistani: an extraordinary culture of generosity. Millions of Pakistanis give to others through cash, food, clothing, zakat, donations and voluntary service. Charity is woven into social and religious life, particularly during Ramazan and Eid. Businesses, too, contribute significant amounts to charitable causes.
Yet there is a paradox here. A society capable of such generosity continues to struggle with poverty and weak public provision in areas such as education and healthcare. The question, therefore, is not whether Pakistanis give enough. They clearly give. The more important question is whether enough of that generosity is being channelled in ways that can address the structural causes of poverty.
A substantial share of charitable giving goes directly from one individual to another. This person-to-person support is valuable and often indispensable. In many communities, it functions as an informal safety net where formal systems do not reach people effectively.
But there is a limit to what this model can achieve on its own. When charitable resources are overwhelmingly directed towards immediate consumption, they provide relief without necessarily creating the conditions for long-term mobility. A donation that feeds a family today is essential; a donation that also enables a child to receive a quality education, acquire skills or access healthcare can change the trajectory of that family for years.
This does not mean that personal charity is misplaced. The willingness of ordinary Pakistanis to help one another is one of the country's greatest social strengths. It is a form of social capital that has repeatedly helped communities withstand economic hardship. The challenge is to complement this generosity with stronger institutions and more strategic philanthropy.
This spirit of giving exists across social classes. People with modest incomes often give beyond what might seem reasonable because helping another person is regarded as a social and moral responsibility. That generosity is an asset that Pakistan can build upon.
The opportunity lies in connecting this extraordinary culture of giving with long-term development. More charitable resources could be directed towards schools, libraries, vocational training, primary healthcare, scholarships and other interventions that expand people's capabilities. Better transparency and stronger charitable institutions could also help donors see how their contributions translate into lasting outcomes.
Pakistan does not suffer from a shortage of compassion. It suffers from a gap between compassion and institutional capacity. The country's generosity already represents a powerful social resource. If even a greater portion of that generosity could be organised around education, health, skills and opportunity, charity could become more than a response to poverty. It could become part of the solution to it.
The generosity of Pakistanis is something to cherish. The greater task is to ensure that this generosity does not merely help people survive difficult circumstances, but helps them build better lives. In a country of fractured realities, that may be one of the most promising bridges between the Pakistan we have and the Pakistan we want.

title: Trump bans CNN  MS NOW  Politico from White House
description: Indicates will ban other media outlets too  moves likely to face constitutional legal challenges
content:
Indicates will ban other media outlets too, moves likely to face constitutional legal challenges
US President Donald Trump said ‌on Friday he is banning three ⁠major ​news outlets - CNN, MSNOW and Politico - from the White House ​in his latest move to crack ‌down on the independent press.
Trump wrote ​that he is banning the outlets for allegedly "reporting FAKE NEWS" in a move that is likely to be challenged as conflicting with the US Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech ⁠and a free press.
"Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES ‌when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," Trump wrote on social media. "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow."
CNN, MSNOW (now MSNBC), Politico and the National Press ⁠Club did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNN's team ⁠remains at the White House ​working as if ‌it were a normal Friday afternoon, CNN reporter Brian Stelter said on air.
Trump has a long history of bickering with members of the press corps and has stepped up his complaints during his second term in office. And he has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programs he dislikes or which have joked about or criticized him or his administration, calling on the Federal Communications Commission to strip disfavored ⁠broadcast stations of their licenses.
Read: Trump Media's quarterly loss widens to $238 million from $20 million a year earlier
In 2019, the White House credential of Brian Karem, a Playboy magazine correspondent, was suspended after ⁠he traded insults with Sebastian Gorka, then an aide to the president, in the White House Rose Garden. A judge later ordered the White House to reinstate Karem's credential.
Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has openly badgered reporters, particularly from US television networks. Last year, he also banned the Associated Press from the usual pool of reporters that cover his movements because the news agency did not adopt Trump's preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico, which Trump ⁠has instructed executive branch employees to refer to as the Gulf ​of America.
US Representative Frank Pallone, the lead Democrat on the House of Representatives Energy and Commerce Committee, called Trump's action censorship.
"If Trump thinks banning media outlets from the White House will make his presidency seem less like a failure, he's delusional," Pallone said.

title: Kashmiris in Europe protest outside Geneva UN office  urge action on IIOJK
description: Protesters called for international accountability and an end to alleged rights violations by Indian forces in IIOJK
content:
Protesters call for international accountability and an end to alleged rights violations by Indian forces in IIOJK
Kashmiris living in Europe staged a protest demonstration outside the United Nations Office in Geneva on Friday, urging the international community to press for an immediate end to alleged human rights violations in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir (IIOJK) and calling on the UN to implement its pending resolutions on the disputed territory to bring peace in South Asia.
The protest was organised by the International Kashmir Peace Forum (IKPF) and led by its Chairman Zahid Hashmi who travelled from Paris to Geneva along with hundreds of other Kashmiris.
Hashmi said India was violating basic human rights in IIOJK.
Describing the Kashmiri people’s right to self-determination as an inalienable and non-negotiable right, Hashmi urged the UN Security Council to take effective steps towards implementing its resolutions recognising the people of Jammu and Kashmir’s right to determine their political future.
Voicing serious concern over what he described as India’s “imperialist designs” in the region, the IKPF chairman said the Indian government’s pursuit of a Hindu nationalist agenda in IIOJK, including land acquisition, interference in religious affairs and demographic engineering, was aimed at altering the demographic composition of the territory.
He also condemned India’s continued use of what he described as repressive laws, including the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA) and the Public Safety Act (PSA).
Hashmi said these laws were frequently used by Indian authorities to silence civil society activists, human rights defenders and political leaders.
He expressed serious concern over what he described as the systematic suppression of political dissent in IIOJK, saying political leaders, activists and human rights defenders continued to face harassment, intimidation and prolonged detention.
“The use of restrictive laws and coercive measures has created an atmosphere of fear, severely constraining political activity, freedom of expression and the legitimate exercise of fundamental rights,” Hashmi said.
The prolonged incarceration of political leaders, he added, reflected what he described as a broader pattern of suppressing dissent and silencing voices calling for political and human rights reforms.
Citing the case of Kashmiri political leader Yasin Malik and other prisoners, Hashmi alleged that judicial and legal mechanisms were being used to silence voices advocating the political rights of the Kashmiri people.
Hashmi called for an end to what he described as the misuse of judicial processes and urged the international community to closely monitor the trials, detention conditions and treatment of Kashmiri political prisoners.
He also criticised India’s portrayal of its development initiatives in the territory, describing them as part of what he termed a broader settler-colonial project.
The protest demonstration concluded with renewed calls for international accountability and an end to what the protesters described as human rights violations by Indian forces in IIOJK.

title: Do not  desire  any confrontation  long march to remain peaceful  CM Afridi
description: Says every citizen of Pakistan has the right to  peacefully  raise their voice  assemble for fundamental rights
content:
Says every citizen of Pakistan has the right to 'peacefully' raise their voice, assemble for fundamental rights
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Friday said he and his party did not "desire" any confrontation and that the long march on September 27 would remain peaceful and would be conducted within the bounds of the Constitution and the law.
The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) had announced that it would march to Islamabad on September 27 to press for the release of founder Imran Khan. The party has been preparing a central convoy from K-P, with caravans from other parts of the country expected to join before proceeding towards the federal capital.
In a post on X, Afridi stated that PTI's planned long march to Islamabad on September 27 was a "peaceful, democratic, and constitutional struggle", adding that every citizen of Pakistan had the right to "peacefully" raise their voice and assemble for their fundamental rights while remaining within the bounds of the Constitution and the law. "We will use this constitutional right to carry our voice to the people and the relevant institutions".
Read : Afridi vows to lead long march to Islamabad
The chief minister said that the "continuous threatening statements" from the federal ministers who were "imposed on the country by crushing the public mandate" were a cause for concern for any democratic society.
"Instead of suppressing dissent or intimidating citizens, the Form 47 government should listen to the people's demands, respect constitutional rights, and seek solutions to political matters through dialogue, law, and democratic processes," Afridi remarked.
ہمارا 27 ستمبر کا لانگ مارچ ایک پُرامن، جمہوری اور آئینی جدوجہد ہے۔ پاکستان کے ہر شہری کو آئین اور قانون کے دائرے میں رہتے ہوئے اپنے بنیادی حقوق کے لیے پُرامن طور پر آواز بلند کرنے اور اجتماع کرنے کا حق حاصل ہے۔ ہم اسی آئینی حق کو استعمال کرتے ہوئے اپنی آواز عوام اور متعلقہ…
He further stated that every conscious citizen of Pakistan was demanding the restoration of the Constitution to its original state and the release of political prisoners who had been unjustly detained, adding that Pakistan's youth were also demanding jobs and a better future, and workers were struggling for their economic rights and a dignified life.
"Farmers want fair compensation for their labour and economic security. And every citizen is demanding justice, equality, constitutional freedoms, and the right to a dignified life. These voices should be answered not with threats but through serious political dialogue and effective governance".
Afridi underlined that he also expected the state institutions and the "Form 47 government" to respect the constitutional rights of citizens and, instead of "obstructing peaceful political activities, ensure the supremacy of the law".
The chief minister said that the country would improve when "attention was given to public issues instead of threats; when public opinion is respected; when Parliament effectively fulfils its constitutional responsibilities; when judicial independence and the rule of law are ensured; when the Constitution is restored, and political prisoners are released; and when journalism is allowed to perform its role freely".
"Our demand is clear: restoration of the Constitution, rule of law, release of political prisoners, protection of fundamental rights, and respect for the voice of the people," he remarked.
Afridi stated that "pressure, threats, or fear cannot stop our peaceful and constitutional struggle", adding that his party would continue to raise their voice for democratic rights while respecting the law.
Earlier today, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi warned that anyone who violated the Islamabad High Court’s (IHC) detailed judgment and attempted to create unrest in the federal capital or any province would face legal action, including contempt of court proceedings.
Read More : Naqvi warns of legal action against violators of IHC protest ruling
Speaking at a press conference at Jinnah Convention Centre in Islamabad, Naqvi said a detailed law-and-order meeting had been held to discuss the call for protests in the coming days. The meeting also reviewed the internal security situation, with officers from other provinces and law enforcement agencies in attendance.
Naqvi said the IHC’s detailed judgment had left no room for any attempt to create unrest in the federal capital or any province.
قانون نافذ کرنے والے اداروں کو وضاحت کی ہے کہ اگر کوئی نکلنے کی کوشش کرے تو ہرممکن طریقے سے روکیں گے، وفاقی وزیرداخلہ مزید پڑھیں : https://t.co/BGlyRH06HJ #ExpressNews #MohsinNaqvi #Islamabad #Protest pic.twitter.com/Dj4xEcQy3Q
He said all law enforcement agencies had been given clear instructions that anyone attempting to come out in violation of the court’s judgment would first face legal action in the form of contempt-of-court proceedings. “Secondly, we will stop them by any means possible,” he said.
He urged political leadership to hold protests within their respective areas and cities but warned against bringing demonstrators to the federal capital with plans to shut it down or entering another province to carry out attacks.
“I want to request all leadership that they can protest, protest in your area, in your city, but coming like this to the federal capital with plans to shut it down or going to a province and attacking it like this; this can be in no way permissible to you,” he said.

title: Archbishop of Canterbury    withdraws    award given to Tahir Ashrafi
description: Ashrafi says some of his statements have been presented  out of context   including on Osama Bin Laden  blasphemy
content:
Ashrafi says some of his statements have been presented 'out of context', including on Osama Bin Laden, blasphemy
Lambeth Palace, the London residence and office of the Archbishop of Canterbury, has withdrawn the Hubert Walter Award for Reconciliation and Interfaith Cooperation 2026, days after presenting it to Pakistan Ulema Council Chairman Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mahmood Ashrafi, citing previous comments over Osama bin Laden.
Ashrafi was presented with the award on the 25 th anniversary of 9/11 at a ceremony held at Lambeth Palace in London in recognition of his services to interfaith reconciliation and cooperation.
Read : Tahir Ashrafi receives Hubert Walter Award for reconciliation, interfaith cooperation in London
The comment that led to the withdrawal dated back to 2007, when Ashrafi said he would confer the title “Saifullah”, meaning “Sword of God”, on then-Al Qaeda chief Osama bin Laden — the orchestrator of the Sept 11 attacks — in protest against Britain awarding a knighthood to writer Salman Rushdie, whose book he described as blasphemous.
In a video statement posted on X regarding the withdrawal, Ashrafi said some of his statements had been presented "out of context" and that the decision to withdraw the award was based on them. He alleged that an “Indian and Ahmadi lobby” had played a role in the decision.
حافظ محمد طاہر محمود اشرفی نے کہا: “ہم ناموسِ رسالت ﷺ، عقیدۂ ختمِ نبوت اور اپنی اسلامی اقدار پر قائم تھے، قائم ہیں اور قائم رہیں گے؛ اور اسی مضبوطی کے ساتھ امن، مکالمے، بین المذاہب ہم آہنگی اور ہر انسان کے جائز حقوق کے لیے اپنی جدوجہد بھی جاری رکھیں گے۔ ایوارڈ ہونا یا نا ہونا… pic.twitter.com/TUfgq4tz8r
He said the Office of the Archbishop of Canterbury had sought clarification from him before withdrawing the award over several matters, including Pakistan’s blasphemy law, Salman Rushdie, Osama bin Laden and his wife’s hijab.
Ashrafi said he had clarified that he supported retaining the blasphemy law but opposed its misuse.
Explaining an earlier statement about Osama bin Laden, he said he was opposed to the use of religion for terrorism and had cited “Saifullah” as an example at the time.
Regarding his previous remarks about Salman Rushdie, Ashrafi said he could not retract the statement and would not withdraw from his views.
Read More : Religious leadership must play active role in ending wars, global peace: Ashrafi
A statement issued by Lambeth Palace on Sept 17 said interfaith dialogue and cooperation required engagement “across deeply-held differences”.
“It is a longstanding principle of interfaith dialogue and co-operation that we must engage with one another across deeply-held differences, and that remains the case,” it said.
“However, previous comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light that have led Lambeth Palace to reconsider this award, and we can now confirm today that the award has been withdrawn.”
In a related development, the Church of Pakistan honoured Ashrafi on Friday with a Global Peace Award for his services to peace, interfaith harmony and religious tolerance.
President of the Church of Pakistan Bishop Azad Marshall presented the award to Ashrafi at a ceremony in Lahore.
According to the Church of Pakistan, the award recognised his services in promoting peace, religious harmony, dialogue among followers of different faiths and protection of the rights of non-Muslim citizens.
Church of Pakistan honours Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi with Global Peace Award https://t.co/1RPXQeHCdT
Bishop Marshall said Ashrafi had continued to play a role in promoting dialogue and harmony among followers of different religions in Pakistan. He also appreciated his efforts for interfaith peace and harmony at national and international levels.
After receiving the award, Ashrafi thanked the Church of Pakistan and Bishop Marshall.
He said that under Bishop Marshall’s leadership, the Church of Pakistan was working with leaders of different religions and Muslim schools of thought for peace, national security and stability in Pakistan.
Ashrafi said joint efforts by Muslim and non-Muslim religious leaders through the National Paigham-e-Peace Committee would further strengthen peace, interfaith and sectarian harmony and national unity in Pakistan.
He also expressed his resolve to continue working for peace, religious harmony and the protection of the legitimate rights of all Pakistanis.

title: Rs50 000 fine and compensation for charging Rs30 for shopping bag
description: Consumer court awards Rs25 000 compensation  imposes Rs25 000 fine  terms practice  unfair trade
content:
Peshawar consumer court penalises popular clothing brand on shopper’s complaint
A consumer protection court has accepted a complaint against a leading clothing brand, directing the company to refund Rs30 charged to a customer for a shopping bag, pay her Rs25,000 in compensation, and deposit a fine of Rs25,000 to the government.
Consumer Case No 84/CC of 2026 was decided by Judge Nasrullah Khan Gandapur of the Consumer Protection Court, who heard arguments from the complainant's counsel, Ahsan Sardar, and the brand's counsel, Muhammad Omea.
The complainant, Shafaq Aamir, had filed the case on February 14 under Section 13 of the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Consumer Protection Act, 1997, alleging that on December 20, 2025, she purchased clothing worth Rs7,000 from the outlet of the clothing brand on Peshawar’s University Road and was additionally charged Rs30 for a carrying bag printed with the brand’s promotional logo.
Read: Judiciary proposes Commercial Court
The respondent did not deny the allegation, but contended that it was not obligated to provide bags free of cost and offered them only on specific customer demand.
In his judgment, Judge Gandapur observed that the receipt annexed with the complaint clearly showed the extra Rs30 charge, and that customers were under the belief that purchased items would be delivered in a carrying bag without charges.
The court observed that the bag, bearing the brand's logo, was "obviously provided for promotion of the brand and that too at the cost of the consumers," noting that the company would otherwise have to provide ordinary bags to customers.
"The respondent not only charged the complainant an extra amount but also used the bag for promotion of its brand," the judgment read, holding the practice to be an unfair trade practice under Section 2(O) (Unfair trade practice (xii) advertising for the sale or supply (xiii) creating the impression that something is being given or offered free of charge) of the act.
The decision was announced on September 16 after the court perused the record and heard both sides under Section 14(2)(b) of the Act. The file has been consigned to the record room after completion.

title: Five month old Afghan baby allowed entry into Pakistan on humanitarian grounds
description: Baby and parents are allowed to enter Pakistan through Torkham without documents on humanitarian grounds
content:
Baby and parents are allowed to enter Pakistan through Torkham without documents on humanitarian grounds
A five-month-old Afghan baby suffering from a heart condition has been allowed to enter Pakistan for treatment without documents on humanitarian grounds, after authorities granted the child and the family special permission to cross the Torkham border.
The baby was shifted to the Hayatabad Medical Complex (HMC) in Peshawar, where the child has been admitted and is receiving treatment.
According to Khyber district social worker Islam Badshah Afridi, the baby and the parents were allowed to enter Pakistan through the Torkham gate with special permission from the relevant authorities on humanitarian and goodwill grounds.
Afridi welcomed the move, saying this was the second child to be allowed entry into Pakistan through the Torkham gate without documents on special humanitarian grounds so that timely medical treatment could be provided.
Since February, the Torkham border — a key trade route between Pakistan and Afghanistan — has been closed due to tensions and intermittent clashes between Pakistani security forces and operatives of the Taliban regime in Afghanistan.
The federal government had introduced a new system to replace the British-era arrangement that allowed people from Afghanistan and Pakistan to travel without visas, in another move aimed at regulating the movement of people and goods amid tensions between the two neighbours following the introduction of a deportation drive in November 2023.
Earlier, Afghans could travel to Pakistan without visas at certain border crossings using “Tazkirah”, a special permit that had been used for decades under the British-era easement rights.
The arrangement was originally aimed at facilitating divided families and tribes living on both sides of the border after Britain demarcated the border known as the Durand Line.
The government implemented a “single-document regime” at all international border crossings with Afghanistan. The earlier facility, however, was allegedly misused as people often travelled beyond the areas permitted under those easement rights.

title: Asian Games begin today | The Express Tribune
description: Pakistan to feature in 23 sports disciplines as organizational concerns shadow Nagoya
content:
Pakistan to feature in 23 sports disciplines as organizational concerns shadow Nagoya
The wait is over. The 20th Asian Games officially get underway in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday (today).
As many as 1700 athletes and officials from 45 countries will feature in these Games in 43 sports disciplines. However organizers are taking an unconventional approach to accommodation by avoiding a formal athletes’ village. Instead, athletes and officials will stay in hotels, converted containers and the Costa Serena, an Italian cruise ship that will serve as a floating village with space for up to 5,000 people.
The decision is aimed at controlling costs after billions of dollars were spent on the Tokyo Olympics, which were postponed from 2020 to 2021 because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Nagoya, Japan’s third-largest metropolitan area after Tokyo and Osaka, is an industrial city on the Pacific coast with a population of about 9.5 million in its wider metropolitan area.
The Games will bring together 45 countries and regions, including North Korea, which is sending about 100 athletes after skipping the Tokyo Olympics. An Olympic Council of Asia refugee team will also compete.
Japan is sending about 900 athletes, the largest delegation, followed by China with 815 and Hong Kong with about 580.
China dominated the 2023 Games, winning 201 gold medals, ahead of Japan with 52 and South Korea with 42.
The Asian Games on Friday were facing more accusations of poor organisation with a world champion gymnast "totally exhausted", the public drafted in to rescue stranded athletes and South Korea lodging a complaint about a Japanese warlord.
The continent's premier sporting spectacle opens in Nagoya and Aichi prefecture on Saturday, but the build-up has been soured by several issues.
That includes a shortage of rooms for the more than 17,000 athletes and officials, a bigger number than the Olympics.
Some teams have also criticised the quality of the accommodation, including beds that are too short.
To save money there is no athletes' village, organisers instead putting competitors in hotels, temporary cabins and on a cruise ship.
Organisers say the accommodation is safe, cost-effective and comfortable.
Chinese gymnast Zhang Boheng, who won two silver medals at the Paris Olympics and has two world championship titles to his name, said he and some of his team-mates were left waiting for six hours after landing on Wednesday.
"I'm totally exhausted," he said in a video published Thursday and shared widely on Chinese social media.
"I didn't expect that after breakfast at 7:00 am the next time I could eat would be close to 7:00 pm," the 26-year-old said.
He said the wait was caused by registration and paperwork, before heading to the cruise ship where 4,000 Games participants will be housed in Nagoya's port area.
But when they arrived at the ship, he said heavy rain prevented them from boarding.
"A whole day was basically wasted like this," added Zhang.
"In the end we really couldn't take it any more so we decided to book rooms at a hotel to rest."
The video has since been taken down but Chinese state media said that other Chinese athletes also faced travel delays upon arrival.
Beijing's consulate in Nagoya contacted Chinese citizens in the area to give the badminton team lifts after issues with a shuttle bus and a shortage of public transport tickets, Xinhua reported.
Chinese social media users applauded athletes, including table tennis star Sun Yingsha, for stretching and exercising at the airport.
The hashtag "Asian Games absurd" has since been viewed more than 94 million times on Weibo.
India's team had similar delays at the airport.
"There was an issue in getting accreditation for athletes at the airport during immigration. There were long queues with a lot of other nations there," India's chef de mission and Indian Olympic Association (IOA) treasurer Sahdev Yadav told AFP.
"But these things happen and we have got everything sorted.
He added: "These are all teething problems and our focus is now on performance."
South Korea's Yonhap news agency reported that some of the country's athletes waited at the airport for more than five hours on Thursday.
"We are aware of the situation including reports that athletes have had to wait for hours and we are doing our best to handle it," a Korean Sport and Olympic Committee (KSOC) official told AFP.
Also on Friday, the KSOC said it had filed a complaint with Games organisers for featuring a Japanese warlord at a welcoming ceremony.
The event on Tuesday included a person dressed as Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who led Japan's invasions of Korea in 1592-1598, and the ceremony prompted a backlash in South Korea.
Historical issues are sensitive between South Korea and Japan, with Hideyoshi's invasion a significant episode in Korean history and Korea under Japanese colonial rule from 1910 to 1945.
Meanwhile Asia's Olympic chief said Friday that he wished the Asian Games in Japan had an athletes' village and hinted that future editions of the multisport event could be even bigger.
"We wish that we have an athlete village, number one, but number two we also have to be flexible," he said.
"We need to listen also to the organiser, to the host, how they would look for the future, after the Games, after the closing ceremony.
"It's very easy, you can insist on the athlete village, and then you build the athlete village, you spend an amount of money but then you need to see what's going to happen after the Games," he added.
South Korean officials said earlier this week that there was "a serious shortage of accommodation" at the Games.
Officials from the Philippines said they had resorted to Airbnb.
Al-Musallam said that "every athlete, every official, every coach has accommodation".
"There is no single accredited person without accommodation," he added.
Local organisers initially expected 15,000 athletes and officials and argued last month that they had "neither the manpower nor the budget" to deal with ballooning numbers.
Women cricket: India and Sri Lanka women powered into the Asian Games cricket semi-finals on Friday with dominant quarter-final wins, while Pakistan men’s team set to begin preparations for their own campaign.
India women on Friday demolished Japan women by eight wickets in their Asian Games event quarter-final, racing to their modest target in just five overs to book their place in the semi-finals in Nisshin.
Chasing 58 for victory after Japan were bowled out for 57 in 19.5 overs, India made light work of the chase as opener Shafali Verma smashed an unbeaten 40 from only 15 balls.
Verma struck six fours and two sixes in a breathtaking assault.
Richa Ghosh added an unbeaten 12 from six balls, including two fours, as India reached 59 for two with 90 balls to spare.
Japan made a cautious start after being sent in to bat and struggled to build momentum against India's disciplined attack.
Ayaka Kato-Stafford top-scored for Japan with 25 from 47 balls, but the innings never gathered pace. Haruna Iwasaki contributed 10 while the remaining batters failed to reach double figures.
India's Shree Charani was the standout bowler, taking four wickets for ten runs from her four overs. Shafali also made an impact with the ball, claiming two wickets for 13 runs, while Deepti Sharma and Shreyanka Patil took one each.
Japan lost wickets regularly after reaching 24 for two, slipping to 46 for four before collapsing to 57 all out in the final over.
Earlier in the third quarter-final at the same venue Sri Lanka demolished Malaysia by 86 runs thanks to a blistering fifty from captain Chamari Athapaththu.
Athapaththu smashed 63 from 37 balls, including seven fours and three sixes, as Sri Lanka posted 160 for four after electing to bat.
Kavisha Dilhari added an unbeaten 44 from 27 balls, while Harshitha Samarawickrama struck 25 from 18 to keep the scoreboard moving.
Malaysia struggled in reply, finishing at 74 for seven from their 20 overs. Winifred Duraisingam top-scored with 28 from 47 balls, while Mahirah Izzati Ismail made 24.
Sri Lanka's bowlers kept Malaysia under constant pressure, with Dilhari taking two wickets for four runs and Mithali Ayodhya claiming two for 15. Athapaththu also chipped in with two wickets for three runs.
Pakistan men cricket: Pakistan’s men’s cricket team will kick-start their training at Karachi on Sunday. The Green-shirts have been directly placed in the quarter-finals along with holders India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
Pakistan will be fielding a heavy 246-memebr contingent in 23 sports disciplines in these Games.
So far squads of soft tennis, women cricket, squash, table tennis, rowing, swimming, kabaddi, boxing, equestrian, wushu, triathlon and hockey have arrived in Japan.
However it is not yet known how many athletes and officials will represent Pakistan during the opening ceremony which will be held on Saturday.
“We will soon get a final list from the organisers,” a senior official of Pakistan contingent told The Express Tribune from Nagoya.
Pakistan’s squads leave via Thai Airways and Qatar Airways and a team normally takes 30 to 34 hours to reach Japan.
Squash star Noor Zaman and Pakistan women cricket team captain Fatima Sana will lead Pakistan’s contingent as flag-bearers.
Soft Tennis: In soft tennis Pakistan had a disappointing start as both their men’s and women’s teams failed to win even a single match on the opening day of the Asian Games on Friday.
Pakistan men’s side lost with identical score 3-0 in their matches against Philippines, Japan and Cambodia.
Meanwhile Pakistan women also went 3-0 down to Korea, Japan and Cambodia. With input from AFP.

title: PM Shehbaz expands petrol subsidy scheme  announces Rs500 weekly relief for motorcycle  rickshaw users
description: PMO says two  three wheelers  registered after January 1  2006  would be eligible for registration
content:
Also orders 20-year-old motorcycles and rickshaws be made eligible for registration
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday expanded the Special Relief Scheme, allowing motorcycle, Chingchi and rickshaw users buying less than five litres of petrol to avail a Rs500 weekly subsidy through a single token, with four tokens to be issued each month.
The decision was taken in light of feedback received from across the country, while the scheme, under which petrol is being provided at a subsidised rate of Rs100 per litre, continues to be implemented nationwide, according to a statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office.
The statement said the prime minister had taken “another important decision” based on feedback received regarding the scheme.
وزیراعظم خصوصی ریلیف سکیم کا پورے پاکستان میں کامیاب اجراء، ریلیف سکیم کے تحت پاکستان بھر میں 100 روپے فی لیٹر رعائتی نرخوں پر پٹرول کی فراہمی کامیابی سے جاری ہے. وزیراعظم محمد شہباز شریف نے ملک بھر سے سکیم سے متعلق موصول ہونے والی آراء کی روشنی میں ایک اور اہم فیصلہ کیا ہے.…
“On the prime minister’s directive, motorcycle, Chingchi, and rickshaw users purchasing less than five liters of petrol will also receive a subsidy of Rs500 per week on one token,” it said.
“One token will be issued weekly, and a total of 4 tokens will be issued per month,” the statement added.
The PMO said vehicle users with engines of up to 800cc will continue to receive a subsidy of Rs100 per litre on 10 litres of petrol every 10 days, as before.
“Thus, the process of issuing 3 tokens for 10 liters each per month will also continue,” the statement said.
In an earlier notification, the prime minister directed the immediate inclusion of 20-year-old motorcycles, rickshaws and Qingqi rickshaws in the Prime Minister Fuel Relief Scheme.
According to the PMO's statement on X, the prime minister had issued “special directives” to provide further relief to the public under the scheme.
وزیراعظم محمد شہباز شریف نے پرائم منسٹر فیول ریلیف سکیم میں عوام کو مزید سہولت فراہم کرنے کی خصوصی ہدایت کر دی. وزیراعظم فیول ریلیف سکیم میں 20 سال پرانی موٹر سائیکلوں، رکشوں اور چنگ چی رکشوں کو فی الفور شامل کرنے کی ہدایت، یکم جنوری 2006ء کے بعد رجسٹرڈ تمام موٹر سائیکلیں،…
The statement further added that all motorcycles, rickshaws and Qingqi rickshaws registered after January 1, 2006, would be eligible for registration in the Prime Minister Fuel Relief Scheme.
“Individuals operating 20-year-old motorcycles, rickshaws and Qingqi will also be able to benefit from the Prime Minister Fuel Relief Scheme,” the PMO said.
The Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme, announced on September 13 and rolled out across the country at midnight on September 16 amid a continuous rise in fuel prices due to a war in the Gulf, provides a Rs100-per-litre petrol subsidy to eligible motorcycles, rickshaws, other two- and three-wheelers, and cars of up to 800cc
مشرق وسطی میں حالیہ کشیدگی اور اسکے باعث عالمی منڈی میں بڑھتی ہوئی تیل کی قیمتوں کا عوام پر بوجھ بڑھنے کا فوری نوٹس لیتے ہوئے وزیرِ اعظم محمد شہباز شریف کی جانب سے ایک خصوصی ریلیف سکیم کا اجراء کر دیا گیا ہے. وزیر اعظم نے سکیم کا اجراء کرتے ہوئے کہا ہے کہ تیل کی قیمتوں میں…
The prime minister directed the establishment of facilitation desks comprising administration officials, volunteers and petrol pump staff to assist citizens in easily obtaining the subsidy.
Read: Fuel relief scheme to go nationwide at midnight tomorrow
He directed that personnel deployed at the facilitation desks should guide eligible citizens and provide them with all possible assistance in registration and other necessary procedures.
PM Shehbaz also asked the relevant authorities to remain proactive in creating public awareness about the scheme.
Targeted fuel relief scheme to benefit low-income motorists
Federal Minister for Climate Change and Environmental Coordination Dr Musadik Malik said the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme had been designed primarily to support low-income citizens, including delivery riders, rickshaw drivers and families dependent on motorcycles and small cars.
the minister said eligible motorcycle users would receive Rs100 per litre in fuel relief on up to 20 litres of petrol per month, providing maximum monthly assistance of Rs2,000.
Meanwhile, owners of small cars would be eligible for relief on up to 30 litres of petrol, translating into Rs3,000 in monthly assistance, he added.
The minister observed the targeted initiative was aimed at cushioning the impact of rising fuel prices on people who rely on motorcycles, rickshaws and small vehicles for their livelihoods and essential daily travel.
Read more: JI announces Sept 20 long march on Islamabad over petroleum levy
He said delivery riders were among those hit hardest by rising fuel prices, as they continued to cover the same distances while their fuel expenses had increased significantly.
“Rs2,000 can make a significant difference to a low-income delivery rider’s household,” the minister said, adding that the amount could help families meet basic expenses such as food, milk and eggs.
He also cited the example of a woman who drives a Qingqi rickshaw to support her family, saying the monthly fuel relief could help her pay her child’s school fee.
According to the Pakistan Economic Survey 2024-25, petroleum products constitute one of the country's largest import categories, making the economy highly vulnerable to changes in global crude oil prices.
Domestic refineries satisfy only part of national demand, while the remainder is met through imports of crude oil and refined petroleum products. Consequently, every increase in international oil prices raises Pakistan's import bill, pressures foreign exchange reserves, and contributes to inflation.
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
